skills.description: Use when you need to report what proportion of chemical features in an untargeted LC-MS/MS dataset receive structural annotations from spectral library matching versus in silico fingerprint prediction, or to benchmark annotation coverage against the Qemistree food-omics reference rates.
skills.name: annotation-rate-benchmarking
skills.search_text: annotation-rate-benchmarking Use when you need to report what proportion of chemical features in an untargeted LC-MS/MS dataset receive structural annotations from spectral library matching versus in silico fingerprint prediction, or to benchmark annotation coverage against the Qemistree food-omics reference rates. The dataset's features are already identified with authentic standards at known purity — spectral/fingerprint prediction rates are irrelevant as a coverage metric. The goal is chemically informed sample comparison (e.g., Weighted UniFrac on a Qemistree hierarchy) rather than quantifying annotation coverage. Features carry only MS1 data with no MS/MS spectra — Qemistree excludes features without MS/MS, so annotation-rate benchmarking cannot be applied. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Quantifies chemical annotation coverage in an untargeted LC-MS/MS metabolomics dataset by computing the fraction of features annotated via GNPS spectral library matches, in silico CSI:FingerID fingerprint predictions (via Qemistree/SIRIUS), and ClassyFire chemical taxonomy, benchmarking against the FoodOmics reference rates (~20% FBMN matches, ~91% fingerprint coverage of 663 quality-filtered features, ~92% ClassyFire assignment). metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41589-020-00677-3
skills.summary: Quantifies chemical annotation coverage in an untargeted LC-MS/MS metabolomics dataset by computing the fraction of features annotated via GNPS spectral library matches, in silico CSI:FingerID fingerprint predictions (via Qemistree/SIRIUS), and ClassyFire chemical taxonomy, benchmarking against the FoodOmics reference rates (~20% FBMN matches, ~91% fingerprint coverage of 663 quality-filtered features, ~92% ClassyFire assignment).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset's features are already identified with authentic standards at known purity — spectral/fingerprint prediction rates are irrelevant as a coverage metric. The goal is chemically informed sample comparison (e.g., Weighted UniFrac on a Qemistree hierarchy) rather than quantifying annotation coverage. Features carry only MS1 data with no MS/MS spectra — Qemistree excludes features without MS/MS, so annotation-rate benchmarking cannot be applied.

skills.description: Use when per-feature GNPS/FBMN annotations contain missing or InChI-less matches that would otherwise be dropped, and MS2DECIDE needs complete c_g, t_g,i, t_g,s indicator values per feature.
skills.name: annotation-score-discounting
skills.search_text: annotation-score-discounting Use when per-feature GNPS/FBMN annotations contain missing or InChI-less matches that would otherwise be dropped, and MS2DECIDE needs complete c_g, t_g,i, t_g,s indicator values per feature. The feature already matched under the strict q(6, 0.02) query with InChI available — no relaxation or discounting is needed The zero annotation itself is informative (as with the strict 0.02 Da ISDB-LOTUS search, where a zero answer reflects the novelty definition and must not be defaulted) You are scoring Sirius failures, which use a different default (0.5 for the Sirius matching score), not the GNPS 0.7 fallback A progressive-relaxation procedure (GNPS iterative weighted analog search, GNPS I) that salvages annotation scores for features failing the strict GNPS library search: the strict query q(6, 0.02) is relaxed stepwise (0.02→0.1→10 Da mass tolerance, relaxed shared-peak minimum) and the first returned cosine score is discounted by the relaxation degree, with 0.7/0 fallback defaults. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/cmtd.202400088
skills.summary: A progressive-relaxation procedure (GNPS iterative weighted analog search, GNPS I) that salvages annotation scores for features failing the strict GNPS library search: the strict query q(6, 0.02) is relaxed stepwise (0.02→0.1→10 Da mass tolerance, relaxed shared-peak minimum) and the first returned cosine score is discounted by the relaxation degree, with 0.7/0 fallback defaults.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The feature already matched under the strict q(6, 0.02) query with InChI available — no relaxation or discounting is needed The zero annotation itself is informative (as with the strict 0.02 Da ISDB-LOTUS search, where a zero answer reflects the novelty definition and must not be defaulted) You are scoring Sirius failures, which use a different default (0.5 for the Sirius matching score), not the GNPS 0.7 fallback

skills.description: Use when a PUG-View bulk annotation request under a 'heading' path returns more entries than needed and you want to restrict results to one provider (e.g. source=DrugBank) rather than all annotation sources.

skills.search_text: annotation-source-filtering Use when a PUG-View bulk annotation request under a 'heading' path returns more entries than needed and you want to restrict results to one provider (e.g. source=DrugBank) rather than all annotation sources. skills.name: annotation-success-rate-benchmark-comparison
skills.search_text: annotation-success-rate-benchmark-comparison Use when you have deconvolved MS2 spectra from SWATH-MS untargeted metabolomics data and need to quantify what fraction can be assigned a metabolite/formula annotation by MetDNA or Sirius, compared against a reported ~90% benchmark. Input spectra are raw multiplexed SWATH-MS MS/MS spectra that still need deconvolution — use DecoMetDIA's deconvolution skill first rather than benchmarking annotation directly Input is already a metabolite feature/annotation table with no MS2 spectra to annotate The goal is accuracy comparison against experimental DDA MS2 spectra rather than downstream annotation success-rate estimation http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Benchmarks the annotation success rate of deconvolved MS2 spectra (e.g. from DecoMetDIA SWATH-MS processing) by submitting them to metabolite annotation tools such as MetDNA and Sirius, then compares the achieved fraction against the paper's reported ~90% success rate across biological samples. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.9b02655
skills.summary: Benchmarks the annotation success rate of deconvolved MS2 spectra (e.g. from DecoMetDIA SWATH-MS processing) by submitting them to metabolite annotation tools such as MetDNA and Sirius, then compares the achieved fraction against the paper's reported ~90% success rate across biological samples.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra are raw multiplexed SWATH-MS MS/MS spectra that still need deconvolution — use DecoMetDIA's deconvolution skill first rather than benchmarking annotation directly Input is already a metabolite feature/annotation table with no MS2 spectra to annotate The goal is accuracy comparison against experimental DDA MS2 spectra rather than downstream annotation success-rate estimation

skills.description: Use when MZmine/GNPS2 FBMN output (annotated feature tables with row ID, m/z, retention time) needs consolidation into a per-strain .csv summary, especially when KEGG pathway assignments must be attached and compared across strains.
skills.name: annotation-table-csv-processing
skills.search_text: annotation-table-csv-processing Use when MZmine/GNPS2 FBMN output (annotated feature tables with row ID, m/z, retention time) needs consolidation into a per-strain .csv summary, especially when KEGG pathway assignments must be attached and compared across strains. Input is raw .mzXML or unprocessed MS/MS spectra that still require MZmine preprocessing and RegFilter feature selection before annotation consolidation. Spectral library matching or in silico annotation itself is the goal — use the GNPS2 FBMN/ChemWalker/SIRIUS annotation workflow first; this skill handles the post-annotation table processing only. A single strain or non-metabolomics dataset is under analysis, where cross-strain KEGG pathway comparison is not meaningful. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Post-annotation processing of feature tables exported from MZmine into annotated .csv files that record strain-level occurrence and metabolite counts, with downstream KEGG-based pathway reporting for the actinomycete strains BRA006, BRA010, and BRA177. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.08.07.607073
skills.summary: Post-annotation processing of feature tables exported from MZmine into annotated .csv files that record strain-level occurrence and metabolite counts, with downstream KEGG-based pathway reporting for the actinomycete strains BRA006, BRA010, and BRA177.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw .mzXML or unprocessed MS/MS spectra that still require MZmine preprocessing and RegFilter feature selection before annotation consolidation. Spectral library matching or in silico annotation itself is the goal — use the GNPS2 FBMN/ChemWalker/SIRIUS annotation workflow first; this skill handles the post-annotation table processing only. A single strain or non-metabolomics dataset is under analysis, where cross-strain KEGG pathway comparison is not meaningful.

skills.description: Use when working with an MSHub deconvolution feature/quantification table of GC-MS compounds and you must attach a balance score to each compound row and filter the annotation set at a threshold before downstream use.
skills.name: annotation-table-format-handling
skills.search_text: annotation-table-format-handling Use when working with an MSHub deconvolution feature/quantification table of GC-MS compounds and you must attach a balance score to each compound row and filter the annotation set at a threshold before downstream use. The input is raw GC-MS vendor or mzML-type spectra that still require spectral deconvolution — use MSHub auto-deconvolution first; this skill operates on the already-deconvoluted compound table. The goal is molecular-network construction or visualization (e.g. Cytoscape/network mapping via GNPS or pyMolNetEnhancer) rather than balance-score-based filtering of the annotation table. The table already carries balance scores and has been threshold-filtered, so re-annotating would duplicate fields. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Handling of GC-MS annotation tables produced by MSHub/GNPS deconvolution: annotating each deconvoluted compound with its balance score (reproducibility of its fragmentation pattern across samples) and filtering the table at a balance-score threshold to retain reliable annotations. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41587-020-0700-3
skills.summary: Handling of GC-MS annotation tables produced by MSHub/GNPS deconvolution: annotating each deconvoluted compound with its balance score (reproducibility of its fragmentation pattern across samples) and filtering the table at a balance-score threshold to retain reliable annotations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw GC-MS vendor or mzML-type spectra that still require spectral deconvolution — use MSHub auto-deconvolution first; this skill operates on the already-deconvoluted compound table. The goal is molecular-network construction or visualization (e.g. Cytoscape/network mapping via GNPS or pyMolNetEnhancer) rather than balance-score-based filtering of the annotation table. The table already carries balance scores and has been threshold-filtered, so re-annotating would duplicate fields.

skills.description: Use when two annotation methods (e.g. SMART 2.0 and atomic sort) have been run on the same compounds and you need a side-by-side concordance table with explicit difference notes per mismatched call.
skills.name: annotation-table-merging-across-methods
skills.search_text: annotation-table-merging-across-methods Use when two annotation methods (e.g. SMART 2.0 and atomic sort) have been run on the same compounds and you need a side-by-side concordance table with explicit difference notes per mismatched call. Only one annotation method was applied and there is no second method's calls to reconcile against The compounds lack a shared identifier key, so SMART 2.0 and atomic sort rows cannot be matched compound-by-compound http://edamontology.org/topic_3366 A tabular reconciliation skill for comparing chemical-class annotation calls from two annotation approaches — here SMART 2.0 (NMR-based CNN) and the 'atomic sort' method — on the same natural product set (swinholide A, samholides A–I, symplocolide A), producing a per-compound agreement/difference table. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jacs.9b13786
skills.summary: A tabular reconciliation skill for comparing chemical-class annotation calls from two annotation approaches — here SMART 2.0 (NMR-based CNN) and the 'atomic sort' method — on the same natural product set (swinholide A, samholides A–I, symplocolide A), producing a per-compound agreement/difference table.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only one annotation method was applied and there is no second method's calls to reconcile against The compounds lack a shared identifier key, so SMART 2.0 and atomic sort rows cannot be matched compound-by-compound

skills.description: Use when you have experimental MS/MS spectra (e.g. human blood metabolomics MGF files) and need to quantify which reference library annotates the most spectra across a range of similarity cutoffs, to choose a library or benchmark coverage gains.
skills.name: annotation-threshold-benchmarking
skills.search_text: annotation-threshold-benchmarking Use when you have experimental MS/MS spectra (e.g. human blood metabolomics MGF files) and need to quantify which reference library annotates the most spectra across a range of similarity cutoffs, to choose a library or benchmark coverage gains. The experimental spectra are not MS/MS fragment spectra (e.g. MS1-only peak lists) — library search relies on precursor m/z and matched fragment ions. You need de novo annotation or machine-learning spectral prediction rather than direct reference-library matching against existing curated spectra. Input libraries lack harmonized metadata (precursor m/z, adduct, structure) so that matchms comparison would be unreliable without prior curation. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0219 Benchmarks reference MS/MS spectral libraries (Spectraverse, MassSpecGym, NPLIB1) by counting how many experimental metabolomics MS/MS spectra each annotates at successive cosine similarity thresholds, revealing which library offers the broadest coverage for a given sample matrix. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c06256
skills.summary: Benchmarks reference MS/MS spectral libraries (Spectraverse, MassSpecGym, NPLIB1) by counting how many experimental metabolomics MS/MS spectra each annotates at successive cosine similarity thresholds, revealing which library offers the broadest coverage for a given sample matrix.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The experimental spectra are not MS/MS fragment spectra (e.g. MS1-only peak lists) — library search relies on precursor m/z and matched fragment ions. You need de novo annotation or machine-learning spectral prediction rather than direct reference-library matching against existing curated spectra. Input libraries lack harmonized metadata (precursor m/z, adduct, structure) so that matchms comparison would be unreliable without prior curation.

skills.description: Use when an FBMN feature table (.csv quantitative export from MZmine >2.53) plus MGF spectra have parallel annotations from GNPS, Sirius 6, and ISDB-LOTUS and you must rank features by knownness/novelty.
skills.name: annotation-tool-output-aggregation
skills.search_text: annotation-tool-output-aggregation Use when an FBMN feature table (.csv quantitative export from MZmine >2.53) plus MGF spectra have parallel annotations from GNPS, Sirius 6, and ISDB-LOTUS and you must rank features by knownness/novelty. Only a single tool's annotations are available (e.g., a GNPS-only FBMN job) — the Tanimoto-based aggregation of GNPS/Sirius/ISDB-LOTUS outputs cannot be computed. The goal is de novo structure elucidation rather than prioritizing/ranking already multiannotated features in a molecular network. Input is a raw LC-MS/MS dataset with no feature-based molecular networking preprocessing (no quantitative .csv and MGF exported from MZmine). http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Aggregates multiannotated tandem MS/MS spectra from GNPS, Sirius 6, and ISDB-LOTUS using MS2DECIDE's decision-theory knownness score K, enabling prioritization of novel natural products against chemodiverse libraries (e.g., the 95-NP benchmark). metabolomics/v3 10.1002/cmtd.202400088
skills.summary: Aggregates multiannotated tandem MS/MS spectra from GNPS, Sirius 6, and ISDB-LOTUS using MS2DECIDE's decision-theory knownness score K, enabling prioritization of novel natural products against chemodiverse libraries (e.g., the 95-NP benchmark).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only a single tool's annotations are available (e.g., a GNPS-only FBMN job) — the Tanimoto-based aggregation of GNPS/Sirius/ISDB-LOTUS outputs cannot be computed. The goal is de novo structure elucidation rather than prioritizing/ranking already multiannotated features in a molecular network. Input is a raw LC-MS/MS dataset with no feature-based molecular networking preprocessing (no quantitative .csv and MGF exported from MZmine).

skills.description: Use when comparing variant annotation tools (ANNOVAR, SnpEff, VEP) and you need to measure how many NM/NR or ENST transcripts each tool exposes on RefSeq/Ensembl and how much their transcript-accession sets overlap, to explain downstream annotation discordance.
skills.name: annotation-tool-transcript-counting
skills.search_text: annotation-tool-transcript-counting Use when comparing variant annotation tools (ANNOVAR, SnpEff, VEP) and you need to measure how many NM/NR or ENST transcripts each tool exposes on RefSeq/Ensembl and how much their transcript-accession sets overlap, to explain downstream annotation discordance. You already have per-variant HGVS or coding-impact outputs and need variant-level concordance rates (58.52%/84.04%/85.58%) — use a variant-annotation comparison skill instead, not transcript-set counting The tools have been configured to use identical, restricted transcript sets (e.g., ClinVar-selected or MANE transcripts), so the transcript-availability gap you intend to measure has been eliminated by design http://edamontology.org/topic_3577 http://edamontology.org/topic_0085 Quantifies the transcript availability (NM/NR and ENST) of ANNOVAR, SnpEff, and VEP on RefSeq and Ensembl reference sets and computes the cross-tool transcript-accession concordance (22.68% RefSeq, 8.53% Ensembl), exposing the low overlap that drives downstream HGVS/impact discrepancies. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.10.11.617756
skills.summary: Quantifies the transcript availability (NM/NR and ENST) of ANNOVAR, SnpEff, and VEP on RefSeq and Ensembl reference sets and computes the cross-tool transcript-accession concordance (22.68% RefSeq, 8.53% Ensembl), exposing the low overlap that drives downstream HGVS/impact discrepancies.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You already have per-variant HGVS or coding-impact outputs and need variant-level concordance rates (58.52%/84.04%/85.58%) — use a variant-annotation comparison skill instead, not transcript-set counting The tools have been configured to use identical, restricted transcript sets (e.g., ClinVar-selected or MANE transcripts), so the transcript-availability gap you intend to measure has been eliminated by design

skills.description: Use when comparing RMSE distributions of multiple imputation methods (e.g. KNN-TN vs KNN-CR vs KNN-EU) across 100 simulated datasets to test whether observed differences are statistically significant.
skills.name: anova-contrast-testing
skills.search_text: anova-contrast-testing Use when comparing RMSE distributions of multiple imputation methods (e.g. KNN-TN vs KNN-CR vs KNN-EU) across 100 simulated datasets to test whether observed differences are statistically significant. RMSE values come from a single replication or non-numeric metric — ANOVA contrast testing on a single observation per cell cannot detect method differences The comparison goal is downstream statistical concordance (metabolite list concordance index, MLCI) rather than error magnitude — use MLCI-based assessment instead http://edamontology.org/topic_0089 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Multi-factor ANOVA modeling of imputation RMSE values with pre-defined contrasts to statistically test whether KNN-TN achieves lower root mean square error than KNN-CR and KNN-EU. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-017-1547-6
skills.summary: Multi-factor ANOVA modeling of imputation RMSE values with pre-defined contrasts to statistically test whether KNN-TN achieves lower root mean square error than KNN-CR and KNN-EU.
skills.when_to_use_negative: RMSE values come from a single replication or non-numeric metric — ANOVA contrast testing on a single observation per cell cannot detect method differences The comparison goal is downstream statistical concordance (metabolite list concordance index, MLCI) rather than error magnitude — use MLCI-based assessment instead

skills.description: Use when a metabolomics dataset has sample metadata (e.g., demographics) and you need to assess which variables drive variation (SOV), or when exploratory PCA/t-SNE views are needed before classification.
skills.name: anova-f-score-confounder-analysis
skills.search_text: anova-f-score-confounder-analysis Use when a metabolomics dataset has sample metadata (e.g., demographics) and you need to assess which variables drive variation (SOV), or when exploratory PCA/t-SNE views are needed before classification. The goal is disease classification or prognosis prediction — those belong to Lilikoi's feature-selection/machine-learning or Cox-PH/Cox-nnet prognosis modules, not exploratory SOV analysis. No sample metadata/demographic variables are available to test as sources of variation. The data are already pathway-transformed (e.g., a PDS matrix from lilikoi.PDSfun) rather than raw metabolite-level measurements. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Exploratory source-of-variation (SOV) analysis from Lilikoi v2.0 that quantifies confounder effects in metabolomics data by computing ANOVA F-scores across metadata variables, optionally alongside PCA and t-SNE dimension-reduction plots rendered via the M3C visualization routines. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/gigascience/giaa162
skills.summary: Exploratory source-of-variation (SOV) analysis from Lilikoi v2.0 that quantifies confounder effects in metabolomics data by computing ANOVA F-scores across metadata variables, optionally alongside PCA and t-SNE dimension-reduction plots rendered via the M3C visualization routines.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is disease classification or prognosis prediction — those belong to Lilikoi's feature-selection/machine-learning or Cox-PH/Cox-nnet prognosis modules, not exploratory SOV analysis. No sample metadata/demographic variables are available to test as sources of variation. The data are already pathway-transformed (e.g., a PDS matrix from lilikoi.PDSfun) rather than raw metabolite-level measurements.

skills.description: Use when a transf_data-normalised targeted or untargeted metabolomics feature table has one or two grouping factors (e.g. study group, time point) and per-feature ANOVA plus post-hoc Tukey HSD pairwise tables are needed.
skills.name: anova-posthoc-tukey-hsd-analysis
skills.search_text: anova-posthoc-tukey-hsd-analysis Use when a transf_data-normalised targeted or untargeted metabolomics feature table has one or two grouping factors (e.g. study group, time point) and per-feature ANOVA plus post-hoc Tukey HSD pairwise tables are needed. The comparison is strictly pairwise between two groups — use gentab_P.t.test with FDR plus gentab_FC and a volcano plot (Volcano_ttest_FC) instead of ANOVA. The response is longitudinal/censored — GetFeatistics routes these to mixed-effects or Tobit regression models, not the gentab_P ANOVA functions. Intensities are still raw (missing values not replaced, not log-transformed, not pareto-scaled); run transf_data first or the p-values will be computed on unnormalised data. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 GetFeatistics-style one- and two-way ANOVA with post-hoc Tukey HSD comparisons and FDR correction for metabolomics feature-intensity tables, implemented as gentab_P.1wayANOVA_posthocTukeyHSD and gentab_P.2wayANOVA_posthocTukeyHSD on transf_data-normalised data. metabolomics/v3 10.1515/jib-2025-0047
skills.summary: GetFeatistics-style one- and two-way ANOVA with post-hoc Tukey HSD comparisons and FDR correction for metabolomics feature-intensity tables, implemented as gentab_P.1wayANOVA_posthocTukeyHSD and gentab_P.2wayANOVA_posthocTukeyHSD on transf_data-normalised data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The comparison is strictly pairwise between two groups — use gentab_P.t.test with FDR plus gentab_FC and a volcano plot (Volcano_ttest_FC) instead of ANOVA. The response is longitudinal/censored — GetFeatistics routes these to mixed-effects or Tobit regression models, not the gentab_P ANOVA functions. Intensities are still raw (missing values not replaced, not log-transformed, not pareto-scaled); run transf_data first or the p-values will be computed on unnormalised data.

skills.description: Use when PCA sample scores derived from a prepared DSO (X data matrix with biological/blank class labels) must be tested for class separation across biological groups, especially when more than two classes require post hoc comparisons.
skills.name: anova-tukey-kramer-posthoc-analysis
skills.search_text: anova-tukey-kramer-posthoc-analysis Use when PCA sample scores derived from a prepared DSO (X data matrix with biological/blank class labels) must be tested for class separation across biological groups, especially when more than two classes require post hoc comparisons. The input is raw mass spectral data that has not yet been processed (peak picking, alignment, replicate/blank/sample filtering, missing value imputation) and combined into a DSO. The goal is visual inspection of PCA score plots or loadings — this tool produces no graphical output. A two-class comparison is needed and a standalone univariate t-test would suffice; note Galaxy-M's current implementation includes no separate univariate statistics tools, so the scores-test route is tied to PCA output. http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 Statistical evaluation of PCA sample scores in the Galaxy-M 'PCA with Scores Test' tool: a per-principal-component univariate test of class separation (t-test for two classes; one-way ANOVA with Tukey-Kramer post hoc comparisons for more than two), replacing visual interpretation of PCA plots with formal significance testing. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13742-016-0115-8
skills.summary: Statistical evaluation of PCA sample scores in the Galaxy-M 'PCA with Scores Test' tool: a per-principal-component univariate test of class separation (t-test for two classes; one-way ANOVA with Tukey-Kramer post hoc comparisons for more than two), replacing visual interpretation of PCA plots with formal significance testing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw mass spectral data that has not yet been processed (peak picking, alignment, replicate/blank/sample filtering, missing value imputation) and combined into a DSO. The goal is visual inspection of PCA score plots or loadings — this tool produces no graphical output. A two-class comparison is needed and a standalone univariate t-test would suffice; note Galaxy-M's current implementation includes no separate univariate statistics tools, so the scores-test route is tied to PCA output.

skills.description: Use when a pathway must be completed by inference from a knowledge base of atom/bond-encoded molecules and reactions (e.g. .lp files), given a source metabolite, goal molecules, and constraints like m/z filtering or absent molecules.
skills.name: answer-set-programming-inference
skills.search_text: answer-set-programming-inference Use when a pathway must be completed by inference from a knowledge base of atom/bond-encoded molecules and reactions (e.g. .lp files), given a source metabolite, goal molecules, and constraints like m/z filtering or absent molecules. The target pathway already has a complete, well-annotated reaction set with no unassigned peaks or missing enzymes — direct database lookup (e.g. MetaCyc) is preferable The task requires fully automated atom numbering or scalable genome-scale reconstruction — the authors state Pathmodel is only 'a working prototype' and atom numbering during reactions 'cannot be fully automated' The knowledge base of molecular structures and reactions has not been manually encoded — the authors note the main limitation is 'the user time necessary to properly encode the starting knowledge base' http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 http://edamontology.org/topic_3391 Skill for driving analogical biochemical inference with Answer Set Programming (ASP) in clingo, as implemented by PathModel: reaction sites are extracted from known reactions, and an incremental solver infers novel reactions and metabolite structures from a source molecule toward goal molecules under metabolomic constraints. metabolomics/v3 10.1016/j.isci.2020.100849
skills.summary: Skill for driving analogical biochemical inference with Answer Set Programming (ASP) in clingo, as implemented by PathModel: reaction sites are extracted from known reactions, and an incremental solver infers novel reactions and metabolite structures from a source molecule toward goal molecules under metabolomic constraints.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The target pathway already has a complete, well-annotated reaction set with no unassigned peaks or missing enzymes — direct database lookup (e.g. MetaCyc) is preferable The task requires fully automated atom numbering or scalable genome-scale reconstruction — the authors state Pathmodel is only 'a working prototype' and atom numbering during reactions 'cannot be fully automated' The knowledge base of molecular structures and reactions has not been manually encoded — the authors note the main limitation is 'the user time necessary to properly encode the starting knowledge base'

skills.description: Use when the task requires benchmarking newly mined BGCs against known-function clusters in MIBiG 2.0, quantifying the fraction of BGCs lacking MIBiG homology, or correlating antibacterial BGC abundance with AMR gene counts across metagenomic soil samples.
skills.name: antibacterial-bgc-amr-correlation-analysis
skills.search_text: antibacterial-bgc-amr-correlation-analysis Use when the task requires benchmarking newly mined BGCs against known-function clusters in MIBiG 2.0, quantifying the fraction of BGCs lacking MIBiG homology, or correlating antibacterial BGC abundance with AMR gene counts across metagenomic soil samples. Input BGCs are already known-function entries stored in MIBiG — the skill benchmarks novel clusters against MIBiG, not MIBiG against itself The reference corpus should be candidate BGCs of unknown function such as IMG-ABC or antiSMASH-DB, which 'store many thousands' of clusters rather than BGCs 'associated with molecules of known chemical structure' The task is curating or depositing new BGC entries into MIBiG (accession request, extended entry form, Annotathon workflow) rather than consuming it as a homology baseline http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 A downstream-analysis skill that uses the MIBiG 2.0 reference set (2021 curated BGCs of known function) as a homology baseline to assess BGC novelty (Crits-Cristoph et al. soil-bacteria analysis) and to correlate antibacterial BGC abundance with antimicrobial resistance genes across soil metagenomes (Bahram et al.). metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkz882
skills.summary: A downstream-analysis skill that uses the MIBiG 2.0 reference set (2021 curated BGCs of known function) as a homology baseline to assess BGC novelty (Crits-Cristoph et al. soil-bacteria analysis) and to correlate antibacterial BGC abundance with antimicrobial resistance genes across soil metagenomes (Bahram et al.).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input BGCs are already known-function entries stored in MIBiG — the skill benchmarks novel clusters against MIBiG, not MIBiG against itself The reference corpus should be candidate BGCs of unknown function such as IMG-ABC or antiSMASH-DB, which 'store many thousands' of clusters rather than BGCs 'associated with molecules of known chemical structure' The task is curating or depositing new BGC entries into MIBiG (accession request, extended entry form, Annotathon workflow) rather than consuming it as a homology baseline

skills.description: Use when antibody amino acid sequences must be turned into a protein search database to generate database-search-derived pseudo-ground truth (high-confidence PSMs) against which de novo sequencing tool predictions on antibody MS/MS data are evaluated.
skills.name: antibody-reference-database-construction
skills.search_text: antibody-reference-database-construction Use when antibody amino acid sequences must be turned into a protein search database to generate database-search-derived pseudo-ground truth (high-confidence PSMs) against which de novo sequencing tool predictions on antibody MS/MS data are evaluated. You already have de novo sequencing predictions and want to assemble them into full-length antibody sequences (use the de Bruijn assembler ALPS workflow instead) The data are non-antibody proteomics samples where a full proteome database, not a small antibody-sequence database, is the appropriate search target You only need spectral pre-processing (e.g. MGF conversion) without any database-search-based reference generation http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Constructs the antibody protein reference database and derives a pseudo-ground-truth PSM set by running combined MS-GF+ and X!Tandem searches (via SearchGUI v.4.1.7) against antibody sequences, post-processing with PeptideShaker v.2.2.2, and filtering at 1% FDR to benchmark de novo sequencing predictions. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bib/bbac542
skills.summary: Constructs the antibody protein reference database and derives a pseudo-ground-truth PSM set by running combined MS-GF+ and X!Tandem searches (via SearchGUI v.4.1.7) against antibody sequences, post-processing with PeptideShaker v.2.2.2, and filtering at 1% FDR to benchmark de novo sequencing predictions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You already have de novo sequencing predictions and want to assemble them into full-length antibody sequences (use the de Bruijn assembler ALPS workflow instead) The data are non-antibody proteomics samples where a full proteome database, not a small antibody-sequence database, is the appropriate search target You only need spectral pre-processing (e.g. MGF conversion) without any database-search-based reference generation

skills.description: Use when you have assembled contigs from de novo peptide predictions for monoclonal antibody chains and need to quantify sequence coverage and accuracy against known light/heavy chain references, including CDR regions.
skills.name: antibody-sequence-coverage-accuracy-calculation
skills.search_text: antibody-sequence-coverage-accuracy-calculation Use when you have assembled contigs from de novo peptide predictions for monoclonal antibody chains and need to quantify sequence coverage and accuracy against known light/heavy chain references, including CDR regions. You only have raw MS/MS spectra without de novo peptide predictions — assembly and coverage calculation presuppose confidence-filtered predictions from tools like Casanovo or Novor Your goal is database-dependent identification of antibody sequences rather than database-independent assembly evaluation (e.g. Supernovo-style workflows with database search and in silico genetic recombination) You need to discriminate isoleucine/leucine or resolve Q vs AG and deamidated N vs D — these cannot be resolved via MS/MS even with higher-resolution spectra and tools http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_2830 Computes per-chain protein sequence coverage and accuracy of de novo antibody sequencing assemblies by aligning assembled contigs (e.g. ALPS output from Casanovo/Novor predictions) to ground-truth antibody sequences with BLAST, benchmarked against reported values for light and heavy chains. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bib/bbac542
skills.summary: Computes per-chain protein sequence coverage and accuracy of de novo antibody sequencing assemblies by aligning assembled contigs (e.g. ALPS output from Casanovo/Novor predictions) to ground-truth antibody sequences with BLAST, benchmarked against reported values for light and heavy chains.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only have raw MS/MS spectra without de novo peptide predictions — assembly and coverage calculation presuppose confidence-filtered predictions from tools like Casanovo or Novor Your goal is database-dependent identification of antibody sequences rather than database-independent assembly evaluation (e.g. Supernovo-style workflows with database search and in silico genetic recombination) You need to discriminate isoleucine/leucine or resolve Q vs AG and deamidated N vs D — these cannot be resolved via MS/MS even with higher-resolution spectra and tools

skills.description: Use when a MADByTE chemical similarity network from an NMR platform (TOCSY/HSQC spin system features) of a prefractionated extract library must be annotated with antimicrobial screening results to identify which network clusters concentrate activity.
skills.name: antimicrobial-screening-data-integration
skills.search_text: antimicrobial-screening-data-integration Use when a MADByTE chemical similarity network from an NMR platform (TOCSY/HSQC spin system features) of a prefractionated extract library must be annotated with antimicrobial screening results to identify which network clusters concentrate activity. skills.description: Use when you need to annotate previously unidentified recurrent MS/MS spectra (e.g. ARUS plasma/urine spectra) by ranking candidate compounds via in silico predicted fragment spectra.
skills.name: arus-spectrum-annotation
skills.search_text: arus-spectrum-annotation Use when you need to annotate previously unidentified recurrent MS/MS spectra (e.g. ARUS plasma/urine spectra) by ranking candidate compounds via in silico predicted fragment spectra. Input is already a feature table with known compound identities or a spectral library match at high confidence — this skill targets unidentified recurrent spectra needing de novo candidate ranking. The experimental spectra were acquired at only one or a few collision energies (e.g. GNPS, MSDial, MassBank-style data) — the article notes such libraries 'often lack sufficient curation' and completeness for this workflow's ranking. Candidate molecules exceed the 1,000 most-frequented m/z positions in the training set or fall outside the m/z coverage of the released ModelVal*.pickle files — predicted spectra will be incomplete and ranking unreliable. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Annotates recurrent unidentified spectra from the ARUS database (NIST Mass Spectrometry Data Center) by predicting MS/MS spectra for BUDDY-assigned candidate molecules with SingleFrag ANN models and ranking candidates by spectral similarity, confirming annotations by expert manual elucidation. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.11.04.621329
skills.summary: Annotates recurrent unidentified spectra from the ARUS database (NIST Mass Spectrometry Data Center) by predicting MS/MS spectra for BUDDY-assigned candidate molecules with SingleFrag ANN models and ranking candidates by spectral similarity, confirming annotations by expert manual elucidation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a feature table with known compound identities or a spectral library match at high confidence — this skill targets unidentified recurrent spectra needing de novo candidate ranking. The experimental spectra were acquired at only one or a few collision energies (e.g. GNPS, MSDial, MassBank-style data) — the article notes such libraries 'often lack sufficient curation' and completeness for this workflow's ranking. Candidate molecules exceed the 1,000 most-frequented m/z positions in the training set or fall outside the m/z coverage of the released ModelVal*.pickle files — predicted spectra will be incomplete and ranking unreliable.

skills.name: asics-linear-mixture-fitting
skills.search_text: asics-linear-mixture-fitting Use when you have one or more 1H NMR plasma spectra (chemical shifts plus one intensity column per sample) and need a baseline automated deconvolution into reference metabolite spectra with fitted concentrations, e.g. for RMSE-based reconstruction benchmarking. The goal is the best possible reconstruction accuracy — the paper shows NMRQNet consistently outperformed ASICS on whole-spectrum RMSE and in the 3-4 ppm region of EDTA plasma, so ASICS is a baseline rather than the method of choice. The input is not 1H NMR spectra of plasma in the csv shift-column-plus-sample-columns layout expected by the NMRQNet-style pipeline. You need quantification methods that tolerate no manual setup but also need strong false-positive control — the paper's broader evaluation covers alternatives (Batman, rDolphin, AQuA, Chenomx) with different trade-offs. Apply ASICS, a linear-regression-based deconvolution method that models an NMR mixture spectrum as a linear combination of library reference spectra, to obtain per-sample reconstructed spectra and fitted metabolite concentrations for 1H plasma NMR data. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2023.03.01.530642
skills.summary: Apply ASICS, a linear-regression-based deconvolution method that models an NMR mixture spectrum as a linear combination of library reference spectra, to obtain per-sample reconstructed spectra and fitted metabolite concentrations for 1H plasma NMR data.

skills.description: Use when you have SIRIUS top-50 molecular formula candidate lists for a batch of compounds (e.g. from a dendroides-style LC-MS/MS run) and need to build the weighted candidate/edge graph that ZODIAC's Bayesian Gibbs-sampling model consumes.
skills.name: assignment-graph-construction
skills.search_text: assignment-graph-construction Use when you have SIRIUS top-50 molecular formula candidate lists for a batch of compounds (e.g. from a dendroides-style LC-MS/MS run) and need to build the weighted candidate/edge graph that ZODIAC's Bayesian Gibbs-sampling model consumes. If you only have a single compound's SIRIUS result with no related-compound network context — the graph construction depends on pairwise fragmentation-tree similarity across related compounds and has no edges to form. If your goal is adduct or structural annotation rather than molecular formula reranking; the graph is specifically the candidate formula node/edge structure consumed by ZODIAC's Gibbs sampler. If the SIRIUS fragmentation trees have not yet been computed for the candidate formulas — the similarity scores (equations 6-7) cannot be calculated. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Constructs ZODIAC's weighted molecular-formula assignment graph, where nodes are SIRIUS top-50 formula candidates (plus a dummy node) weighted by softmax likelihoods, and edges encode fragmentation-tree similarity scores with spectral-library anchor bonuses. This graph is the input that ZODIAC's Gibbs sampler operates on to rerank molecular formulas in LC-MS/MS datasets. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s42256-020-00234-6
skills.summary: Constructs ZODIAC's weighted molecular-formula assignment graph, where nodes are SIRIUS top-50 formula candidates (plus a dummy node) weighted by softmax likelihoods, and edges encode fragmentation-tree similarity scores with spectral-library anchor bonuses. skills.description: Use when 1H-NMR spectra (rows = samples, columns = chemical shifts in ppm) still show baseline distortions after phase correction and internal referencing, and a smooth baseline must be fit and subtracted before downstream analysis.
skills.name: asymmetric-least-squares-baseline-estimation
skills.search_text: asymmetric-least-squares-baseline-estimation Use when 1H-NMR spectra (rows = samples, columns = chemical shifts in ppm) still show baseline distortions after phase correction and internal referencing, and a smooth baseline must be fit and subtracted before downstream analysis. skills.description: Use when you must rank which node attributes of a trained graph neural network (e.g., SigmaCCS atom features in model.h5) drive CCS prediction accuracy, by masking each attribute and measuring the prediction-error increase on a test set.

skills.search_text: attribute-importance-quantification Use when you must rank which node attributes of a trained graph neural network (e.g., SigmaCCS atom features in model.h5) drive CCS prediction accuracy, by masking each attribute and measuring the prediction-error increase on a test set. The model input is not a graph with distinct node attributes (e.g., DeepCCS one-hot encoded SMILES strings fed to a CNN), so masking atom attributes is not applicable. skills.description: Use when precursor-ion peak metrics have been extracted for auto-tracked and user-specified ions and the operator needs packaged CSV reports and JPG/PDF figures to inspect and track ion metrics over a batch of MS runs.

skills.search_text: auto-tracked-ion-metric-tracking Use when precursor-ion peak metrics have been extracted for auto-tracked and user-specified ions and the operator needs packaged CSV reports and JPG/PDF figures to inspect and track ion metrics over a batch of MS runs. Input is raw MS data that has not yet been converted and peak metrics extracted — the reporting step operates on extracted metrics tables, not on raw vendor formats (e.g. Agilent 'd', Thermo '.raw', Bruker 'd', mzML). The goal is identification-based QC (e.g. counting spectral matches in proteomics); PeakQC is explicitly positioned as a precursor-ion-metric-based alternative because identification-based tools 'do little to pinpoint the specific causes of performance deterioration'. No batch of MS runs exists to track across — single-run inspection without batch-level metric tracking is not the target use case described in the article. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 PeakQC's reporting and visualization step that packages extracted precursor-ion peak metrics (mass, retention-time and arrival-time errors) for auto-tracked and user-specified ions into CSV reports and JPG/PDF figures per ion and per metric, so instrument operators can inspect and track MS data quality across a batch. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jasms.4c00146

skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw MS data that has not yet been converted and peak metrics extracted — the reporting step operates on extracted metrics tables, not on raw vendor formats (e.g. Agilent 'd', Thermo '.raw', Bruker 'd', mzML). skills.description: Use when a colocalization significance test requires scrambled randomizations of a two-color image (e.g., CFP/YFP or red/green confocal pairs) and the independent scrambling unit (block size) must match the image texture or PSF rather than individual pixels.
skills.name: autocorrelation-based-psf-block-size-estimation
skills.search_text: autocorrelation-based-psf-block-size-estimation Use when a colocalization significance test requires scrambled randomizations of a two-color image (e.g., CFP/YFP or red/green confocal pairs) and the independent scrambling unit (block size) must match the image texture or PSF rather than individual pixels. The image is too small to contain many independent blocks at the estimated PSF/texture size, so block scrambling cannot generate a meaningful random-overlap distribution The goal is only M1/M2 coefficient computation from already-classified pixels, with no need for a scrambling-based significance threshold Pixels are actually independent (no measurable texture or PSF correlation), where individual-pixel scrambling would be the appropriate randomization unit Estimates the scrambled-block size used in the Costes et al. colocalization significance test by measuring the widths of the autocorrelations of the two color channels, so that randomization mimics image texture/PSF-scale correlation instead of destroying it. metabolomics/v3 10.1529/biophysj.103.038422
skills.summary: Estimates the scrambled-block size used in the Costes et al. colocalization significance test by measuring the widths of the autocorrelations of the two color channels, so that randomization mimics image texture/PSF-scale correlation instead of destroying it.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The image is too small to contain many independent blocks at the estimated PSF/texture size, so block scrambling cannot generate a meaningful random-overlap distribution The goal is only M1/M2 coefficient computation from already-classified pixels, with no need for a scrambling-based significance threshold Pixels are actually independent (no measurable texture or PSF correlation), where individual-pixel scrambling would be the appropriate randomization unit

skills.description: Use when a two-channel fluorescence image shows correlated pixel intensities from texture or the microscope PSF, so that per-pixel scrambling would produce an unrealistically narrow random-overlap distribution and a significance threshold that falsely flags colocalization.

skills.search_text: autocorrelation-width-block-sizing Use when a two-channel fluorescence image shows correlated pixel intensities from texture or the microscope PSF, so that per-pixel scrambling would produce an unrealistically narrow random-overlap distribution and a significance threshold that falsely flags colocalization. Images whose pixel intensities are spatially uncorrelated (no texture or PSF-driven neighborhood correlation) — per-pixel scrambling suffices and block sizing would add unnecessary coarse-graining Single-channel images or comparisons where no two-channel overlap distribution is being built — the block-scrambling scheme is defined for red/green colocalization testing Very small regions where the number of independent blocks is too low for a meaningful 200-randomization null distribution http://edamontology.org/topic_3385 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Sizes randomization blocks for the colocalization significance test to the texture or PSF autocorrelation width, so the null distribution of random overlap accounts for intensity correlations between adjacent pixels rather than treating pixels as independent. metabolomics/v3 10.1529/biophysj.103.038422
skills.summary: Sizes randomization blocks for the colocalization significance test to the texture or PSF autocorrelation width, so the null distribution of random overlap accounts for intensity correlations between adjacent pixels rather than treating pixels as independent.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Images whose pixel intensities are spatially uncorrelated (no texture or PSF-driven neighborhood correlation) — per-pixel scrambling suffices and block sizing would add unnecessary coarse-graining Single-channel images or comparisons where no two-channel overlap distribution is being built — the block-scrambling scheme is defined for red/green colocalization testing Very small regions where the number of independent blocks is too low for a meaningful 200-randomization null distribution

skills.summary: SERDA is a denoising autoencoder normalization workflow that trains on cohort pool QC samples interleaved with biological samples in large-scale GC-MS metabolomics batches, correcting batch and time-varying drift that sum-based or internal-standard normalizations cannot remove.

skills.when_to_use_negative: You are analyzing a single 2D tissue section with no serial-section 3D volume to co-embed (single-pixel UMAP visualization suffices) You need supervised anatomical classification with gradient-boosted trees rather than feature-image generation for registration The MSI data are raw short-transient transients that have not yet undergone deep-learning signal reconstruction and peak binning/normalization

skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a feature table or motif-loading matrix rather than raw MS2 peak lists Spectra are information-poor (few fragments, e.g., single collision energy on simple mixtures) — MS2LDA works best on complex mixtures with information-rich MS2 spectra from ramped or stepped collision energy The goal is classical spectral matching against libraries like Mass Bank or NIST, where neutral losses are not supported and must be omitted

skills.search_text: baseline-conditional-quantification-of-weak-signals Use when processing full-scan AEMS data (e.g. precursor-ion or neutral-loss scans from 384-/1536-well plates) where a persistent high-intensity baseline signal obscures weak analyte peaks, so that frame boundaries must be derived from clear high-mass reference peaks rather than from the weak. skills.search_text: baseline-model-benchmarking-trial-efficiency Use when evaluating whether transfer learning from a pre-trained metabolomics VAE (e.g. 2,736-feature mzLearn matrix) improves downstream prediction and Optuna search efficiency versus random initialization or traditional ML. skills.name: batch-replicate-pair-matching
skills.search_text: batch-replicate-pair-matching Use when you have replicate pairs of identical biological samples run in subsequent batches, log(e)-transformed intensities, and need to rank normalization methods by cross-batch correspondence rather than by QC-sample RSD reduction or differential-abundance counts. When the data set contains no between-batch replicate pairs (identical biological samples split across subsequent batches) — this metric requires true replicate-pair structure and cannot be computed from QC samples alone. When the goal is to select a normalization method by maximizing the number of differentially abundant metabolites or by minimizing QC-sample RSD — the authors explicitly flag these as misleading benchmarking proxies. When only a single batch exists and no cross-batch correspondence assessment is needed. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0219 Quantifies cross-batch intensity correspondence between between-batch replicate run pairs by computing the MAD of mean-rescaled intensity differences for each normalization method (tGAM, rGAM, rLOESS, SERFF, TIGER, QC-RLSC, QC-RSC, unnormalized), a replication-based benchmarking metric the authors explicitly recommend over QC-RSD proxies. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c06841
skills.summary: Quantifies cross-batch intensity correspondence between between-batch replicate run pairs by computing the MAD of mean-rescaled intensity differences for each normalization method (tGAM, rGAM, rLOESS, SERFF, TIGER, QC-RLSC, QC-RSC, unnormalized), a replication-based benchmarking metric the authors explicitly recommend over QC-RSD proxies.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the data set contains no between-batch replicate pairs (identical biological samples split across subsequent batches) — this metric requires true replicate-pair structure and cannot be computed from QC samples alone. When the goal is to select a normalization method by maximizing the number of differentially abundant metabolites or by minimizing QC-sample RSD — the authors explicitly flag these as misleading benchmarking proxies. When only a single batch exists and no cross-batch correspondence assessment is needed.

skills.description: Use when multi-batch DDA LC-MS data (e.g. converted TripleTOF or QE HF vendor files) show retention-time shifts for targeted compounds between batches and quantification peaks must be re-integrated at corrected TargetRT values batch-wide.
skills.name: batch-rt-correction-with-internal-standards
skills.search_text: batch-rt-correction-with-internal-standards Use when multi-batch DDA LC-MS data (e.g. converted TripleTOF or QE HF vendor files) show retention-time shifts for targeted compounds between batches and quantification peaks must be re-integrated at corrected TargetRT values batch-wide. Input is already a processed feature table or peak list with final RTs — no EIC-level re-integration is possible in MetaPro Data were not acquired in DDA mode and not converted to the Aird format, since MetaPro supports MS data acquired with the DDA method Only a single sample needs RT adjustment with no batch context — per-compound manual inspection without batch re-application is more appropriate http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Corrects per-batch retention-time drift in semi-targeted LC-MS quantification by resetting the TargetRT of each compound against analyte and internal-standard libraries and re-applying corrected integration parameters across all samples in a batch, as implemented in MetaPro's batch QC inspection workflow. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-023-02018-6
skills.summary: Corrects per-batch retention-time drift in semi-targeted LC-MS quantification by resetting the TargetRT of each compound against analyte and internal-standard libraries and re-applying corrected integration parameters across all samples in a batch, as implemented in MetaPro's batch QC inspection workflow.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a processed feature table or peak list with final RTs — no EIC-level re-integration is possible in MetaPro Data were not acquired in DDA mode and not converted to the Aird format, since MetaPro supports MS data acquired with the DDA method Only a single sample needs RT adjustment with no batch context — per-compound manual inspection without batch re-application is more appropriate

skills.description: Use when several raw GCxGC NetCDF/CDF chromatograms must be peak-aligned against a single reference chromatogram in one batch operation, and the alignment function requires samples bundled as a named R list.
skills.name: batch-sample-list-construction-for-alignment
skills.search_text: batch-sample-list-construction-for-alignment Use when several raw GCxGC NetCDF/CDF chromatograms must be peak-aligned against a single reference chromatogram in one batch operation, and the alignment function requires samples bundled as a named R list. When only a single sample chromatogram needs alignment — use the single-pair 2D-COW path (twod_cow) rather than assembling a batch list. When the data are already preprocessed peak tables or unfolded matrices rather than raw NetCDF chromatograms; read_chrom expects NetCDF files and batch_2DCOW operates on folded 2D-TIC objects. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Constructs a named list of GCxGC 2D-TIC chromatogram objects so that multiple samples can be simultaneously aligned to a reference chromatogram via batch_2DCOW (2D Correlation Optimized Warping) in the RGCxGC package. metabolomics/v3 10.1016/j.microc.2020.104830
skills.summary: Constructs a named list of GCxGC 2D-TIC chromatogram objects so that multiple samples can be simultaneously aligned to a reference chromatogram via batch_2DCOW (2D Correlation Optimized Warping) in the RGCxGC package.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When only a single sample chromatogram needs alignment — use the single-pair 2D-COW path (twod_cow) rather than assembling a batch list. When the data are already preprocessed peak tables or unfolded matrices rather than raw NetCDF chromatograms; read_chrom expects NetCDF files and batch_2DCOW operates on folded 2D-TIC objects.

skills.description: Use when a large set of MS/MS query spectra (e.g., an MSP file from AD plasma on Orbitrap Astral or Exploris 240) must each be denoised or matched against a reference library, and per-spectrum loops would be too slow.
skills.name: batch-spectra-parallel-processing
skills.search_text: batch-spectra-parallel-processing Use when a large set of MS/MS query spectra (e.g., an MSP file from AD plasma on Orbitrap Astral or Exploris 240) must each be denoised or matched against a reference library, and per-spectrum loops would be too slow. Only one or a few spectra need denoising or searching — use the single-spectrum sd.spectral_denoising or sd.denoising_search calls instead The task requires adapting the method to non-Orbitrap mass analyzers, where parameters must first be retuned and validated Input is already a feature/annotation table rather than raw or query MS/MS spectra in MSP form http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Run Spectral Denoising and Denoising Search over all query spectra from an MSP file in parallel using the spectral_denoising package's *_batch functions, which are implemented with Python multiprocessing. This enables instrument-scale annotation counting (e.g., Orbitrap Astral vs Exploris 240 AD plasma) instead of spectrum-by-spectrum calls. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-025-02646-x
skills.summary: Run Spectral Denoising and Denoising Search over all query spectra from an MSP file in parallel using the spectral_denoising package's *_batch functions, which are implemented with Python multiprocessing. This enables instrument-scale annotation counting (e.g., Orbitrap Astral vs Exploris 240 AD plasma) instead of spectrum-by-spectrum calls.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only one or a few spectra need denoising or searching — use the single-spectrum sd.spectral_denoising or sd.denoising_search calls instead The task requires adapting the method to non-Orbitrap mass analyzers, where parameters must first be retuned and validated Input is already a feature/annotation table rather than raw or query MS/MS spectra in MSP form

skills.description: Use when a cohort metabolomics dataset (e.g. Metabolon OrigScale sheet input) has passed the metaboprep QC pipeline and you must visualise/quantify how available batch variables influence the data in a disclosure-ready HTML report.
skills.name: batch-variable-association-visualization
skills.search_text: batch-variable-association-visualization Use when a cohort metabolomics dataset (e.g. Metabolon OrigScale sheet input) has passed the metaboprep QC pipeline and you must visualise/quantify how available batch variables influence the data in a disclosure-ready HTML report. The Metaboprep object has not yet passed quality_control — summaries, PC plots and the dendrogram will not be populated, so the qc_report sections (including batch-variable panels) cannot render correctly. You need a standalone statistical batch-effect test on raw data rather than the package's standardized disclosure report; metaboprep provides a report of influence of available batch variables, not a custom modelling workflow. The input is not metabolomics/omics feature data loadable into a Metaboprep object (e.g. an already filtered feature table without sample batch annotations). http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Generates the metaboprep qc_report HTML report whose batch-variable section plots associations between available batch variables (e.g. run_day, box_id, lot) and the metabolomics data as boxplots annotated with type-II ANOVA eta-squared estimates, for open disclosure of preanalysis data quality. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btac059
skills.summary: Generates the metaboprep qc_report HTML report whose batch-variable section plots associations between available batch variables (e.g. run_day, box_id, lot) and the metabolomics data as boxplots annotated with type-II ANOVA eta-squared estimates, for open disclosure of preanalysis data quality.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The Metaboprep object has not yet passed quality_control — summaries, PC plots and the dendrogram will not be populated, so the qc_report sections (including batch-variable panels) cannot render correctly. You need a standalone statistical batch-effect test on raw data rather than the package's standardized disclosure report; metaboprep provides a report of influence of available batch variables, not a custom modelling workflow. The input is not metabolomics/omics feature data loadable into a Metaboprep object (e.g. an already filtered feature table without sample batch annotations).

skills.description: Use when unnormalized metabolomics intensity matrices (raw compounds × sample runs) show instrument drift or batch effects across multiple acquisition batches and must be normalized batchwise before differential abundance testing.
skills.name: batchwise-drift-normalization
skills.search_text: batchwise-drift-normalization Use when unnormalized metabolomics intensity matrices (raw compounds × sample runs) show instrument drift or batch effects across multiple acquisition batches and must be normalized batchwise before differential abundance testing. When a downstream workflow needs a fair benchmark across very different normalization philosophies (e.g. multivariate methods such as SERFF or TIGER) — the article explicitly notes these were not benchmarked with Metanorm When the data contain unexpected differences between QC and biological samples — these require analyst scrutiny rather than blind normalization, per the article's recommendation When the goal is statistical inference on DAMs requiring controlled false discovery — multiple testing correction is essential but was out of scope for this work http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Applies Metanorm's drift-correcting metabolomics normalization (robust tGAM/rGAM/rLOESS or QC-sample-based QC-RLSC/QC-RSC) separately per batch, using a QC-type vector and batch labels so that within-batch signal drift is removed before downstream testing. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c06841
skills.summary: Applies Metanorm's drift-correcting metabolomics normalization (robust tGAM/rGAM/rLOESS or QC-sample-based QC-RLSC/QC-RSC) separately per batch, using a QC-type vector and batch labels so that within-batch signal drift is removed before downstream testing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When a downstream workflow needs a fair benchmark across very different normalization philosophies (e.g. multivariate methods such as SERFF or TIGER) — the article explicitly notes these were not benchmarked with Metanorm When the data contain unexpected differences between QC and biological samples — these require analyst scrutiny rather than blind normalization, per the article's recommendation When the goal is statistical inference on DAMs requiring controlled false discovery — multiple testing correction is essential but was out of scope for this work

skills.description: Use when LC-MS metabolomics runs are split into multiple acquisition batches and signal drift plus batch effects must be corrected together, especially when QC samples may not represent biological samples.
skills.name: batchwise-metabolomics-normalization
skills.search_text: batchwise-metabolomics-normalization Use when LC-MS metabolomics runs are split into multiple acquisition batches and signal drift plus batch effects must be corrected together, especially when QC samples may not represent biological samples. When only a single acquisition batch exists and batch subsets would be too small to support a separate additive model per batch When QC samples are demonstrably representative and simple QC-based normalization (e.g. QC-RLSC with QConly = TRUE) suffices without batch subsetting When the goal is generic feature filtering or downstream differential-abundance testing rather than drift/batch correction of raw intensities http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 A batch-aware metabolomics normalization procedure that fits a separate robust additive model (tGAM, rGAM or rLOESS) per batch subset and optionally checks whether QC samples are representative of biological samples before choosing which sample type drives the correction. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.09.30.679445
skills.summary: A batch-aware metabolomics normalization procedure that fits a separate robust additive model (tGAM, rGAM or rLOESS) per batch subset and optionally checks whether QC samples are representative of biological samples before choosing which sample type drives the correction.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When only a single acquisition batch exists and batch subsets would be too small to support a separate additive model per batch When QC samples are demonstrably representative and simple QC-based normalization (e.g. QC-RLSC with QConly = TRUE) suffices without batch subsetting When the goal is generic feature filtering or downstream differential-abundance testing rather than drift/batch correction of raw intensities

skills.search_text: bayesian-hyperparameter-optimization Use when training RT-prediction regressors (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, DKL, DNN) on alvaDesc fingerprints/descriptors and you need tuned hyperparameters with leakage-free nested-CV error estimates. skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is RT projection between chromatographic methods (PredRet meta-learned GP workflow) rather than regressor training — that is a separate skill in this paper The compounds lack SMILES/SDF structures to feed alvaDesc, so no fingerprints or descriptors can be generated You only need the published best model's performance rather than re-tuning — the paper branch already reports MAE 39.2 ± 1.2 s and MEDAE 17.2 ± 0.9 s

skills.description: Use when re-ranking ISDB-DNP (or similar MS annotation) candidate structures with taxonomically informed scores and the family/genus/species weight combination must be fitted rather than hand-set.
skills.name: bayesian-hyperparameter-optimization
skills.search_text: bayesian-hyperparameter-optimization Use when re-ranking ISDB-DNP (or similar MS annotation) candidate structures with taxonomically informed scores and the family/genus/species weight combination must be fitted rather than hand-set. The taxonomic weight combination is already known and validated (0.81 / 1.62 / 2.55) and only needs to be applied by 2_taxo_scorer.Rmd — re-optimization is unnecessary The scoring system is a plain taxonomic filtering process rather than a scoring objective with tunable continuous weights that a Gaussian-process optimizer can explore Benchmarking compounds are not present in the reference database (e.g. non-DNP annotations), making the F1 objective on the benchmarking dataset an unreliable optimization target http://edamontology.org/topic_3391 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Tunes the taxonomically informed scoring parameters (family, genus, species weights) used to re-rank metabolite annotation candidates by optimizing the taxo_scorer objective with the parallelizable ParBayesianOptimization R package, converging on scores of 0.81, 1.62 and 2.55. metabolomics/v3 10.3389/fpls.2019.01329
skills.summary: Tunes the taxonomically informed scoring parameters (family, genus, species weights) used to re-rank metabolite annotation candidates by optimizing the taxo_scorer objective with the parallelizable ParBayesianOptimization R package, converging on scores of 0.81, 1.62 and 2.55.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The taxonomic weight combination is already known and validated (0.81 / 1.62 / 2.55) and only needs to be applied by 2_taxo_scorer.Rmd — re-optimization is unnecessary The scoring system is a plain taxonomic filtering process rather than a scoring objective with tunable continuous weights that a Gaussian-process optimizer can explore Benchmarking compounds are not present in the reference database (e.g. non-DNP annotations), making the F1 objective on the benchmarking dataset an unreliable optimization target

skills.search_text: bayesian-mcmc-metabolite-quantification Use when quantifying metabolites in 1H NMR plasma spectra with a Bayesian approach, or when benchmarking a deep-learning or targeted-profiling quantification method against an MCMC-based baseline. skills.description: Use when you have a compound library with SMILES/InChIKey structures and experimentally measured LC-HRMS retention times, and need a trained regressor to predict RTs for metabolites lacking authentic standards.
skills.name: bayesian-neural-network-regression
skills.search_text: bayesian-neural-network-regression Use when you have a compound library with SMILES/InChIKey structures and experimentally measured LC-HRMS retention times, and need a trained regressor to predict RTs for metabolites lacking authentic standards. No experimentally measured RTs are available for training — the regressor requires a labeled descriptor–RT dataset and cannot validate metabolites from structures alone. The goal is structural annotation or biotransformation discovery of xenobiotic metabolites — that is CMDN's top-down annotation task (DMS/RCS/SSN layers), not RT regression. The compounds fall outside the pesticide-like chemical space used to fit the model, where descriptor-based RT predictions would not be calibrated. http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Trains a Bayesian regularized neural network (BRNN) to regress LC retention time (RT) from molecular descriptors computed on SMILES/InChIKey structures, serving as one of three benchmark models (with XGBoost and Random Forest) for validating chromatographic behavior of CMDN-annotated pesticide metabolites when authentic standards are unavailable. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.est.5c08558
skills.summary: Trains a Bayesian regularized neural network (BRNN) to regress LC retention time (RT) from molecular descriptors computed on SMILES/InChIKey structures, serving as one of three benchmark models (with XGBoost and Random Forest) for validating chromatographic behavior of CMDN-annotated pesticide metabolites when authentic standards are unavailable.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No experimentally measured RTs are available for training — the regressor requires a labeled descriptor–RT dataset and cannot validate metabolites from structures alone. The goal is structural annotation or biotransformation discovery of xenobiotic metabolites — that is CMDN's top-down annotation task (DMS/RCS/SSN layers), not RT regression. The compounds fall outside the pesticide-like chemical space used to fit the model, where descriptor-based RT predictions would not be calibrated.

skills.summary: Bayesian posterior probability annotation of LC-MS untargeted metabolomics features using ipaPy2's IPA method, which integrates mass accuracy, isotope patterns, adduct formation, retention time ranges and prior knowledge to output statistically rigorous posterior probabilities per annotation.

skills.search_text: bayesian-tpe-hyperparameter-search Use when training retention-time (or other regression) models whose hyperparameters (DNN layer sizes, dropout, learning schedules, GBM depths) must be tuned to maximize median absolute error rather than MAE, before nested-CV evaluation. You already have fixed hyperparameters and only need final evaluation — running the TPE search would waste trials; use the test/nested-CV path instead. The task is meta-training the GP for RT projections between chromatographic methods (make train_projections) — that uses a different objective and the PredRet database, not the RT-predictor TPE search. Your targets or evaluation metric differ fundamentally (e.g., classification of non-retained vs retained molecules is a separate step, not what the TPE search optimizes). http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Tunes RT-prediction regressors (hidden-layer sizes, dropout rates, activations, restart/annealing lengths) with a TPE Bayesian search (via Optuna) maximizing the negative median absolute error (MEDAE) on the SMRT dataset, then evaluates tuned models with nested cross-validation. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-022-00613-8
skills.summary: Tunes RT-prediction regressors (hidden-layer sizes, dropout rates, activations, restart/annealing lengths) with a TPE Bayesian search (via Optuna) maximizing the negative median absolute error (MEDAE) on the SMRT dataset, then evaluates tuned models with nested cross-validation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You already have fixed hyperparameters and only need final evaluation — running the TPE search would waste trials; use the test/nested-CV path instead. The task is meta-training the GP for RT projections between chromatographic methods (make train_projections) — that uses a different objective and the PredRet database, not the RT-predictor TPE search. Your targets or evaluation metric differ fundamentally (e.g., classification of non-retained vs retained molecules is a separate step, not what the TPE search optimizes).

skills.description: Use when training a binary NMR spectral-pair classifier (compound-present vs. absent) on imbalanced labeled data in PyTorch, where a sigmoid-constrained probability output and a weighted positive-class loss are required to reach high TPR.
skills.name: bcewithlogitsloss-weighted-classifier-training
skills.search_text: bcewithlogitsloss-weighted-classifier-training Use when training a binary NMR spectral-pair classifier (compound-present vs. absent) on imbalanced labeled data in PyTorch, where a sigmoid-constrained probability output and a weighted positive-class loss are required to reach high TPR. The task is multi-class classification or regression rather than binary presence/absence — BCEWithLogitsLoss with a single positive weight is designed for the paper's two-class formulation. Inputs are not paired spectral data (e.g. no mixture spectrum to compare against), since the bi-encoder/cross-encoder pipeline expects both a compound and a mixture spectrum. The dataset is already balanced and a weighted loss would distort calibration — the weight of 3 is specific to the paper's imbalanced positive-class scenario. http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 A training procedure for the FlavorFormer hybrid CNN–Transformer classifier that uses PyTorch's BCEWithLogitsLoss with a positive-class weight of 3 to counter class imbalance when predicting whether a compound is present in an NMR mixture, combined with fusion pooling of the cross-encoder's [CLS] token and mean-pooled sequence features. metabolomics/v3 10.1016/j.microc.2025.115372
skills.summary: A training procedure for the FlavorFormer hybrid CNN–Transformer classifier that uses PyTorch's BCEWithLogitsLoss with a positive-class weight of 3 to counter class imbalance when predicting whether a compound is present in an NMR mixture, combined with fusion pooling of the cross-encoder's [CLS] token and mean-pooled sequence features.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is multi-class classification or regression rather than binary presence/absence — BCEWithLogitsLoss with a single positive weight is designed for the paper's two-class formulation. skills.search_text: beam-search-over-attention-decoder Use when converting a trained transformer's MS2-spectrum representation into a molecular lipid species prediction requires autoregressive token-by-token decoding over a fixed lipid-name vocabulary, with greedy or beam-search alternatives. skills.summary: Implements the token-level decoding stage of LipiDetective's transformer: the encoder representation is mapped through a linear head onto a 1,032-token lipid-shorthand vocabulary and decoded autoregressively (greedy or beam search) until the end-of-sequence token, yielding lipid species strings with adduct and a confidence score.
