skills.description: Use when you need to enumerate or audit evidence codes and annotations (e.g. 13 NRPS substrate-selectivity evidence codes) directly from the MIBiG JSON schema or its entry JSON files.
skills.name: biosynthetic-gene-cluster-metadata-extraction
skills.search_text: biosynthetic-gene-cluster-metadata-extraction Use when you need to enumerate or audit evidence codes and annotations (e.g. 13 NRPS substrate-selectivity evidence codes) directly from the MIBiG JSON schema or its entry JSON files. The goal is BGC detection from raw DNA sequence — use a detection tool such as antiSMASH, fungiSMASH, GECCO or DeepBGC instead; this skill only extracts annotations already curated in MIBiG. The input is a PKS AT-domain selectivity problem or generic chemical-structure cross-linking (NP Atlas, PubChem, ChemSpider, LOTUS, ChEMBL) rather than NRPS A-domain substrate-selectivity evidence codes from the MIBiG schema. Entries lack curated status in `cluster.status` (e.g. low-quality or duplicate entries removed in MIBiG 3.0) — verify entry quality before treating extracted annotations as validated. http://edamontology.org/topic_0780 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Extracts structured biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) metadata — including NRPS A-domain substrate-selectivity evidence codes and their literature references — from the MIBiG JSON-formatted data standard hosted in the mibig-secmet/mibig-json repository, converting schema enumerations into tabular summaries such as a Table 1 mirror. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkac1049
skills.summary: Extracts structured biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) metadata — including NRPS A-domain substrate-selectivity evidence codes and their literature references — from the MIBiG JSON-formatted data standard hosted in the mibig-secmet/mibig-json repository, converting schema enumerations into tabular summaries such as a Table 1 mirror.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is BGC detection from raw DNA sequence — use a detection tool such as antiSMASH, fungiSMASH, GECCO or DeepBGC instead; this skill only extracts annotations already curated in MIBiG. The input is a PKS AT-domain selectivity problem or generic chemical-structure cross-linking (NP Atlas, PubChem, ChemSpider, LOTUS, ChEMBL) rather than NRPS A-domain substrate-selectivity evidence codes from the MIBiG schema. Entries lack curated status in `cluster.status` (e.g. low-quality or duplicate entries removed in MIBiG 3.0) — verify entry quality before treating extracted annotations as validated.

skills.description: Use when you have antiSMASH-processed GenBank files (or MIBiG reference BGCs) and need pairwise BGC distances to build a similarity network or call GCFs, especially across large, mixed complete/fragmented BGC sets.
skills.name: biosynthetic-gene-cluster-pairwise-distance-computation
skills.search_text: biosynthetic-gene-cluster-pairwise-distance-computation Use when you have antiSMASH-processed GenBank files (or MIBiG reference BGCs) and need pairwise BGC distances to build a similarity network or call GCFs, especially across large, mixed complete/fragmented BGC sets. The input is not domain-annotated BGC GenBank data (e.g., raw genome contigs or a plain sequence FASTA without antiSMASH BGC prediction) — run BGC prediction and domain detection first. You need full-length gene/protein sequence phylogeny rather than domain-content-based BGC comparison (e.g., single-gene phylogenetics — use CORASON-style multi-locus phylogenies or a standard aligner instead). Only one BGC is available, so no pairwise comparison or network can be constructed. http://edamontology.org/topic_0084 Compute pairwise distances between biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) using BiG-SCAPE's three-component metric — Jaccard domain-type index, Domain Sequence Similarity (DSS) index, and Adjacency index — so that BGCs can be placed in sequence similarity networks and grouped into gene cluster families (GCFs). metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41589-019-0400-9
skills.summary: Compute pairwise distances between biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) using BiG-SCAPE's three-component metric — Jaccard domain-type index, Domain Sequence Similarity (DSS) index, and Adjacency index — so that BGCs can be placed in sequence similarity networks and grouped into gene cluster families (GCFs).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is not domain-annotated BGC GenBank data (e.g., raw genome contigs or a plain sequence FASTA without antiSMASH BGC prediction) — run BGC prediction and domain detection first. You need full-length gene/protein sequence phylogeny rather than domain-content-based BGC comparison (e.g., single-gene phylogenetics — use CORASON-style multi-locus phylogenies or a standard aligner instead). Only one BGC is available, so no pairwise comparison or network can be constructed.

skills.description: Use when starting from complete or draft genome assemblies (GenBank/WGS files) and BGC predictions are needed as the entry point for a comparative biosynthesis workflow such as BiG-SCAPE GCF clustering.
skills.name: biosynthetic-gene-cluster-prediction-antismash
skills.search_text: biosynthetic-gene-cluster-prediction-antismash Use when starting from complete or draft genome assemblies (GenBank/WGS files) and BGC predictions are needed as the entry point for a comparative biosynthesis workflow such as BiG-SCAPE GCF clustering. Input is already antiSMASH GenBank output — proceed directly to BiG-SCAPE clustering instead of re-running prediction The goal is GCF phylogenetic ordering rather than de novo BGC detection — use CORASON on existing antiSMASH outputs instead Genomes are highly fragmented metagenomic assemblies where the study itself notes current methods fail to measure similarity between complete and fragmented clusters http://edamontology.org/topic_0780 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Predicts biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) from genome sequences with antiSMASH, producing antiSMASH GenBank outputs that serve directly as inputs for downstream BiG-SCAPE/CORASON sequence similarity networking and gene cluster family (GCF) assembly. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41589-019-0400-9
skills.summary: Predicts biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) from genome sequences with antiSMASH, producing antiSMASH GenBank outputs that serve directly as inputs for downstream BiG-SCAPE/CORASON sequence similarity networking and gene cluster family (GCF) assembly.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already antiSMASH GenBank output — proceed directly to BiG-SCAPE clustering instead of re-running prediction The goal is GCF phylogenetic ordering rather than de novo BGC detection — use CORASON on existing antiSMASH outputs instead Genomes are highly fragmented metagenomic assemblies where the study itself notes current methods fail to measure similarity between complete and fragmented clusters

skills.description: Use when you need synthetic PKS/NRPS/hybrid BGCs of controlled module count (e.g. 1-10 modules, 10 BGCs per type) to benchmark rendering speed, validate drawing correctness/readability, or stress-test biosynthetic pathway visualization pipelines.
skills.name: biosynthetic-gene-cluster-random-generation
skills.search_text: biosynthetic-gene-cluster-random-generation Use when you need synthetic PKS/NRPS/hybrid BGCs of controlled module count (e.g. 1-10 modules, 10 BGCs per type) to benchmark rendering speed, validate drawing correctness/readability, or stress-test biosynthetic pathway visualization pipelines. When you need real, experimentally characterized BGCs — use the MIBiG database instead, as randomly generated clusters are synthetic and unvalidated against known products When you need mature natural product structures from raw antiSMASH output — RAIChU can generate scaffolds but not mature natural products from raw antiSMASH output When regio- and stereochemistry of tailoring enzymes must be predicted automatically — users must specify their reaction targets http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Generates random PKS, NRPS, and PKS/NRPS hybrid biosynthetic gene clusters (1-10 modules) using RAIChU's cluster generation functionality, enabling benchmarking tasks such as the paper's drawing-speed assessment where 10 BGCs per module number (1-10) and module type are produced and timed. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00898-x
skills.summary: Generates random PKS, NRPS, and PKS/NRPS hybrid biosynthetic gene clusters (1-10 modules) using RAIChU's cluster generation functionality, enabling benchmarking tasks such as the paper's drawing-speed assessment where 10 BGCs per module number (1-10) and module type are produced and timed.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When you need real, experimentally characterized BGCs — use the MIBiG database instead, as randomly generated clusters are synthetic and unvalidated against known products When you need mature natural product structures from raw antiSMASH output — RAIChU can generate scaffolds but not mature natural products from raw antiSMASH output When regio- and stereochemistry of tailoring enzymes must be predicted automatically — users must specify their reaction targets

skills.description: Use when antiSMASH-predicted BGC GenBank files (plus optional MIBiG reference BGCs) need to be organized into sequence similarity networks and GCFs/GCCs to map biosynthetic diversity across large genome sets.
skills.name: biosynthetic-gene-cluster-similarity-network-analysis
skills.search_text: biosynthetic-gene-cluster-similarity-network-analysis Use when antiSMASH-predicted BGC GenBank files (plus optional MIBiG reference BGCs) need to be organized into sequence similarity networks and GCFs/GCCs to map biosynthetic diversity across large genome sets. Input BGCs are not antiSMASH-processed GenBank files; BiG-SCAPE relies on antiSMASH annotations (e.g. 'Core Biosynthetic' gene markers) for adjacency and LCS rules Analysis goal is the phylogenetic resolution within one GCF rather than global GCF/GCC assignment across many BGCs; use CORASON instead for multi-locus phylogenies within a GCF A prior normalized or harmonized GCF/GCC clustering already exists and only counts are needed — recomputing the network would duplicate the step http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Constructs and clusters sequence similarity networks of biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) with BiG-SCAPE, computing pairwise distances from domain content, order, copy number and sequence identity, then grouping clusters into gene cluster families (GCFs) and gene cluster clans (GCCs). metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41589-019-0400-9
skills.summary: Constructs and clusters sequence similarity networks of biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) with BiG-SCAPE, computing pairwise distances from domain content, order, copy number and sequence identity, then grouping clusters into gene cluster families (GCFs) and gene cluster clans (GCCs).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input BGCs are not antiSMASH-processed GenBank files; BiG-SCAPE relies on antiSMASH annotations (e.g. 'Core Biosynthetic' gene markers) for adjacency and LCS rules Analysis goal is the phylogenetic resolution within one GCF rather than global GCF/GCC assignment across many BGCs; use CORASON instead for multi-locus phylogenies within a GCF A prior normalized or harmonized GCF/GCC clustering already exists and only counts are needed — recomputing the network would duplicate the step

skills.description: Use when a predicted or MIBiG-derived modular PKS/NRPS BGC needs an automated, readable pathway visualisation at module resolution (spaghetti diagram in SVG), or when manually drawn biosynthetic models are too laborious/error-prone.
skills.name: biosynthetic-gene-cluster-spaghetti-diagram-layout
skills.search_text: biosynthetic-gene-cluster-spaghetti-diagram-layout Use when a predicted or MIBiG-derived modular PKS/NRPS BGC needs an automated, readable pathway visualisation at module resolution (spaghetti diagram in SVG), or when manually drawn biosynthetic models are too laborious/error-prone. The goal is BGC detection/annotation from nucleotide sequence — RAIChU visualises clusters but, unlike antiSMASH, does not predict gene clusters The task requires predicting regio- and stereochemistry of tailoring enzymes — users must specify reaction targets themselves, so untargeted tailoring prediction is out of scope A mature natural product must be generated directly from raw antiSMASH output — RAIChU can generate natural product scaffolds but not mature natural products in that setting http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Renders a modular PKS/NRPS biosynthetic gene cluster as a RAIChU 'spaghetti diagram' — domains as circles, genes as rectangles, and a vertically aligned backbone across modules — exported as an SVG, using RAIChU's bond-angle layout rules to maximise drawing readability. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00898-x
skills.summary: Renders a modular PKS/NRPS biosynthetic gene cluster as a RAIChU 'spaghetti diagram' — domains as circles, genes as rectangles, and a vertically aligned backbone across modules — exported as an SVG, using RAIChU's bond-angle layout rules to maximise drawing readability.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is BGC detection/annotation from nucleotide sequence — RAIChU visualises clusters but, unlike antiSMASH, does not predict gene clusters The task requires predicting regio- and stereochemistry of tailoring enzymes — users must specify reaction targets themselves, so untargeted tailoring prediction is out of scope A mature natural product must be generated directly from raw antiSMASH output — RAIChU can generate natural product scaffolds but not mature natural products in that setting

skills.description: Use when raw antiSMASH BGC annotations must be converted into per-gene protein-family tokens before statistical or topic-model sub-cluster mining, and clade-level subPfam resolution is needed to differentiate related domains.
skills.name: biosynthetic-gene-domain-tokenisation
skills.search_text: biosynthetic-gene-domain-tokenisation Use when raw antiSMASH BGC annotations must be converted into per-gene protein-family tokens before statistical or topic-model sub-cluster mining, and clade-level subPfam resolution is needed to differentiate related domains. The BGCs are already tokenised into (sub)Pfam gene content — re-tokenisation would be redundant The goal is linking MS/MS-derived Mass2Motifs to existing sub-clusters rather than preparing gene content for sub-cluster prediction Input consists of single genes or non-biosynthetic loci rather than antiSMASH-predicted BGCs, since tokenisation is defined per BGC gene http://edamontology.org/topic_0157 Converts antiSMASH-predicted biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) into token sequences of (sub)Pfam protein-family domains — including clade-resolved subPfams built with build_subpfam — after removing non-biosynthetic Pfams, so that sub-cluster prediction methods (PRESTO-STAT, PRESTO-TOP/LDA) can operate on gene content as words. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1010462
skills.summary: Converts antiSMASH-predicted biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) into token sequences of (sub)Pfam protein-family domains — including clade-resolved subPfams built with build_subpfam — after removing non-biosynthetic Pfams, so that sub-cluster prediction methods (PRESTO-STAT, PRESTO-TOP/LDA) can operate on gene content as words.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The BGCs are already tokenised into (sub)Pfam gene content — re-tokenisation would be redundant The goal is linking MS/MS-derived Mass2Motifs to existing sub-clusters rather than preparing gene content for sub-cluster prediction Input consists of single genes or non-biosynthetic loci rather than antiSMASH-predicted BGCs, since tokenisation is defined per BGC gene

skills.description: Use when MEANtools/ClusterONE has produced overlapping feature clusters from a paired transcriptome-metabolome dataset and you need to annotate which FCs contain biosynthetic genes from known pathways to validate clustering or generate hypotheses.

skills.search_text: biosynthetic-gene-to-cluster-mapping Use when MEANtools/ClusterONE has produced overlapping feature clusters from a paired transcriptome-metabolome dataset and you need to annotate which FCs contain biosynthetic genes from known pathways to validate clustering or generate hypotheses. skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is de novo pathway reconstruction via reaction rules (RetroRules/LOTUS) rather than validating clustering against known gene sets — MEANtools' prediction step handles that separately When no prior biosynthetic gene knowledge exists for the pathway of interest, since this skill relies on curated gene lists as mapping targets When the dataset has not been clustered into FCs yet (MAD rescaling, MR correlation, and ClusterONE must run first)

skills.description: Use when a genome assembly must be searched for candidate BGC regions responsible for known or orphan metabolites, and sub-cluster motifs (e.g. methylaminosugar, (amino)deoxysugar, halogenated aromatic ring) are needed to prioritise the region.
skills.name: biosynthetic-region-annotation
skills.search_text: biosynthetic-region-annotation Use when a genome assembly must be searched for candidate BGC regions responsible for known or orphan metabolites, and sub-cluster motifs (e.g. methylaminosugar, (amino)deoxysugar, halogenated aromatic ring) are needed to prioritise the region. The input is MS/MS data needing molecular substructure motifs (Mass2Motifs) rather than genomic regions — correlation of Mass2Motifs to sub-clusters is a separate downstream step, not region annotation itself The BGCs are already fully characterised and present in MIBiG — re-annotating known reference clusters adds little The goal is de novo sub-cluster discovery rather than querying existing regions against an annotated motif set http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Annotate candidate biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) regions in a genome and flag the sub-cluster motifs (e.g. sugar, halogenated-ring modules) they contain, using antiSMASH region detection followed by iPRESTO sub-cluster motif querying. This links orphan metabolites to genomic loci via substructure-level motif signatures. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1010462
skills.summary: Annotate candidate biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) regions in a genome and flag the sub-cluster motifs (e.g. sugar, halogenated-ring modules) they contain, using antiSMASH region detection followed by iPRESTO sub-cluster motif querying. This links orphan metabolites to genomic loci via substructure-level motif signatures.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is MS/MS data needing molecular substructure motifs (Mass2Motifs) rather than genomic regions — correlation of Mass2Motifs to sub-clusters is a separate downstream step, not region annotation itself The BGCs are already fully characterised and present in MIBiG — re-annotating known reference clusters adds little The goal is de novo sub-cluster discovery rather than querying existing regions against an annotated motif set

skills.description: Use when you need to validate that a BGC feature-space embedding (e.g., BiG-SLiCE GCF models at T = 900) preserves biosynthetic signal, by testing whether within-MIBiG-group distances separate from between-group distances.
skills.name: biosynthetic-signal-separation-analysis
skills.search_text: biosynthetic-signal-separation-analysis Use when you need to validate that a BGC feature-space embedding (e.g., BiG-SLiCE GCF models at T = 900) preserves biosynthetic signal, by testing whether within-MIBiG-group distances separate from between-group distances. When the goal is GCF querying or novelty assessment of a new BGC (use BiG-SLiCE --query mode instead of distance-distribution validation) When using BiG-SLiCE v2.0, whose clustering uses cosine-like (l2-normalized) distances rather than the Euclidean metric this validation was built on When input BGCs are not yet clustered into GCF models at a defined threshold (T = 900 here); the validation requires preprocessed feature vectors from a completed run http://edamontology.org/topic_0780 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Validates that BiG-SLiCE's Euclidean feature-space representation of BGCs preserves the biosynthetic signal linking genomic similarity to chemical similarity, by showing that distances within curated MIBiG groups separate from distances between groups (bimodal distribution, Fig. 3C). metabolomics/v3 10.1093/gigascience/giaa154
skills.summary: Validates that BiG-SLiCE's Euclidean feature-space representation of BGCs preserves the biosynthetic signal linking genomic similarity to chemical similarity, by showing that distances within curated MIBiG groups separate from distances between groups (bimodal distribution, Fig. 3C).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is GCF querying or novelty assessment of a new BGC (use BiG-SLiCE --query mode instead of distance-distribution validation) When using BiG-SLiCE v2.0, whose clustering uses cosine-like (l2-normalized) distances rather than the Euclidean metric this validation was built on When input BGCs are not yet clustered into GCF models at a defined threshold (T = 900 here); the validation requires preprocessed feature vectors from a completed run

skills.description: Use when you have predicted sub-cluster motifs (e.g. PRESTO-TOP LDA topics over tokenised BGCs) and a characterised reference set (SubClusterBlast sub-clusters, MIBiG) and need to link motifs to chemical substructures for genome-based structure prediction.
skills.name: biosynthetic-substructure-curated-annotation
skills.search_text: biosynthetic-substructure-curated-annotation Use when you have predicted sub-cluster motifs (e.g. PRESTO-TOP LDA topics over tokenised BGCs) and a characterised reference set (SubClusterBlast sub-clusters, MIBiG) and need to link motifs to chemical substructures for genome-based structure prediction. When no experimentally characterised reference sub-clusters (SubClusterBlast or MIBiG) are available to anchor motif annotations — the method depends on matching to validated sub-clusters When the goal is de novo sub-cluster discovery rather than annotation of existing motifs — use iPRESTO's PRESTO-STAT/PRESTO-TOP prediction first When single-gene (length-1) motif matches must be trusted — these are treated as noise and ignored http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Annotates unsupervised sub-cluster motifs (e.g. the 1,000 PRESTO-TOP motifs from iPRESTO) with the natural product substructures they encode by matching predicted sub-clusters against 90 experimentally validated SubClusterBlast sub-clusters and sub-cluster instances in MIBiG BGCs, yielding a curated motif library usable to predict substructures genome-wide. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1010462
skills.summary: Annotates unsupervised sub-cluster motifs (e.g. the 1,000 PRESTO-TOP motifs from iPRESTO) with the natural product substructures they encode by matching predicted sub-clusters against 90 experimentally validated SubClusterBlast sub-clusters and sub-cluster instances in MIBiG BGCs, yielding a curated motif library usable to predict substructures genome-wide.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When no experimentally characterised reference sub-clusters (SubClusterBlast or MIBiG) are available to anchor motif annotations — the method depends on matching to validated sub-clusters When the goal is de novo sub-cluster discovery rather than annotation of existing motifs — use iPRESTO's PRESTO-STAT/PRESTO-TOP prediction first When single-gene (length-1) motif matches must be trusted — these are treated as noise and ignored

skills.description: Use when building MetaboDirect mass-difference transformation networks from FT-ICR MS peak/formula tables and each candidate edge must be labeled biotic or abiotic per the transformation key scheme.

skills.search_text: biotic-abiotic-transformation-classification Use when building MetaboDirect mass-difference transformation networks from FT-ICR MS peak/formula tables and each candidate edge must be labeled biotic or abiotic per the transformation key scheme. skills.summary: Classifies putative mass-based biochemical transformations in MetaboDirect transformation networks as biotic or abiotic, using mass differences computed between all peaks in each sample and matched (≤1 ppm error) against a predefined biochemical transformation key file.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The peak table has not yet been through MetaboDirect pre-processing filters (m/z filtering, 13C isotopic peak removal, 0.5 ppm formula-assignment error cutoff), since unfiltered masses will inflate spurious matches The goal is de novo metabolite identification rather than mass-difference-based transformation network edge annotation Data are not direct injection high-resolution MS (e.g., FT-ICR MS) peak/formula data with assigned molecular formulas

skills.description: Use when untargeted LC-HRMS feature tables lack library MS2 matches but samples are enzymatic incubations (e.g., human liver S9) of known parent xenobiotics, so candidates can be derived in silico from reaction rules rather than reference spectra.
skills.name: biotransformation-reaction-rule-matching
skills.search_text: biotransformation-reaction-rule-matching Use when untargeted LC-HRMS feature tables lack library MS2 matches but samples are enzymatic incubations (e.g., human liver S9) of known parent xenobiotics, so candidates can be derived in silico from reaction rules rather than reference spectra. Input data are targeted assays of known compounds with authentic standards already available — rule-based mass matching adds no benefit over direct confirmation. No parent structure library exists (e.g., truly unknown exposure mixtures) — without parent identities, reaction-rule enumeration cannot proceed. MS2 spectral libraries already give high-confidence library matches for all features — the RCS layer is redundant when bottom-up annotation succeeds. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Enumerates theoretical biotransformed metabolite candidates by applying curated phase-I reaction rules (e.g., 290 KEGG-sourced rules) to parent compound structures, then preannotates dysregulated LC-HRMS features by accurate-mass matching within a 5 ppm m/z tolerance. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.est.5c08558
skills.summary: Enumerates theoretical biotransformed metabolite candidates by applying curated phase-I reaction rules (e.g., 290 KEGG-sourced rules) to parent compound structures, then preannotates dysregulated LC-HRMS features by accurate-mass matching within a 5 ppm m/z tolerance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data are targeted assays of known compounds with authentic standards already available — rule-based mass matching adds no benefit over direct confirmation. No parent structure library exists (e.g., truly unknown exposure mixtures) — without parent identities, reaction-rule enumeration cannot proceed. MS2 spectral libraries already give high-confidence library matches for all features — the RCS layer is redundant when bottom-up annotation succeeds.

skills.description: Use when an MS/MS query spectrum is unannotated but a spectral-similarity neighbor (anchor) with a known SMILES and a precursor mass difference is available, and candidate molecular structures for the suspect are needed.
skills.name: biotransformation-rule-application
skills.search_text: biotransformation-rule-application Use when an MS/MS query spectrum is unannotated but a spectral-similarity neighbor (anchor) with a known SMILES and a precursor mass difference is available, and candidate molecular structures for the suspect are needed. skills.summary: Apply biotransformation rules to a known 'anchor' molecule to enumerate and rank candidate derivative structures for a spectrally similar unknown 'suspect' molecule, using PROXIMAL2 for rule application and GNN-SOM for site-of-metabolism ranking.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the query spectrum already has a library-annotated molecular structure from standard spectral library searching against the default GNPS spectral libraries When no spectral-similarity anchor molecule with a known structure and similar precursor mass is available for the query When only molecular formula annotation is required (use formula/structure tools like SIRIUS instead of rule-based structure enumeration)

skills.description: Use when a query spectrum has high spectral similarity to a known anchor molecule in a molecular network, and the precursor mass difference between suspect and anchor must be converted into a list of plausible biotransformation-derived candidate structures.
skills.name: biotransformation-rule-mass-difference-matching
skills.search_text: biotransformation-rule-mass-difference-matching Use when a query spectrum has high spectral similarity to a known anchor molecule in a molecular network, and the precursor mass difference between suspect and anchor must be converted into a list of plausible biotransformation-derived candidate structures. No known anchor molecule with high spectral similarity to the query spectrum is available (the mass difference is undefined) The precursor mass difference cannot be matched to any biotransformation rule in the chosen rule set (e.g. only 41% of RetroRules rules are applicable at unit resolution) The suspect is expected to arise from non-biochemical transformations not represented in RetroRules/KEGG/MetaCyc rule databases http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3473 Matches an observed precursor mass difference between an anchor and suspect molecule against biotransformation rules extracted from RetroRules/KEGG (via PROXIMAL2), then applies the matching rules to the anchor structure to enumerate derivative candidate structures for ranking. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c01565
skills.summary: Matches an observed precursor mass difference between an anchor and suspect molecule against biotransformation rules extracted from RetroRules/KEGG (via PROXIMAL2), then applies the matching rules to the anchor structure to enumerate derivative candidate structures for ranking.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No known anchor molecule with high spectral similarity to the query spectrum is available (the mass difference is undefined) The precursor mass difference cannot be matched to any biotransformation rule in the chosen rule set (e.g. only 41% of RetroRules rules are applicable at unit resolution) The suspect is expected to arise from non-biochemical transformations not represented in RetroRules/KEGG/MetaCyc rule databases

skills.description: Use when you need to convert a raw reaction dataset (e.g. RetroRules dump, KEGG reaction list) into a clean set of reaction-center substructure rules that can be applied to query molecules by PROXIMAL2.
skills.name: biotransformation-rule-normalization
skills.search_text: biotransformation-rule-normalization Use when you need to convert a raw reaction dataset (e.g. RetroRules dump, KEGG reaction list) into a clean set of reaction-center substructure rules that can be applied to query molecules by PROXIMAL2. When the metabolites CSV is empty or lacks a metabolite present in the reaction list — the metabolite is excluded rather than retained (unless only the name and any RetroRules information exist). When you need mass-difference-matched rule filtering for BAM (e.g. unit-resolution precursor mass difference matching to 17,254 rules); that filtering is a separate downstream step, not part of rule normalization. When applying already-normalized operators to new queries — skip to the GenerateProducts/GenerateMolFiles steps of runPROX2.py instead of re-generating operators. http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Extract and deduplicate reaction-center biotransformation rules from biochemical reaction databases (e.g. RetroRules, KEGG, MetaCyc) via PROXIMAL2, producing a normalized, redundancy-free operator set that can be applied to anchor molecules for structure discovery. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c01565
skills.summary: Extract and deduplicate reaction-center biotransformation rules from biochemical reaction databases (e.g. RetroRules, KEGG, MetaCyc) via PROXIMAL2, producing a normalized, redundancy-free operator set that can be applied to anchor molecules for structure discovery.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the metabolites CSV is empty or lacks a metabolite present in the reaction list — the metabolite is excluded rather than retained (unless only the name and any RetroRules information exist). When you need mass-difference-matched rule filtering for BAM (e.g. unit-resolution precursor mass difference matching to 17,254 rules); that filtering is a separate downstream step, not part of rule normalization. When applying already-normalized operators to new queries — skip to the GenerateProducts/GenerateMolFiles steps of runPROX2.py instead of re-generating operators.

skills.description: Use when a compiled chemical list (SMILES/structures, e.g. the >20,000-chemical human exposome set) needs in-silico metabolite prediction across EC-based, CYP450, phase II, and gut microbial biotransformation modules.
skills.name: biotransformer-batch-metabolite-prediction
skills.search_text: biotransformer-batch-metabolite-prediction Use when a compiled chemical list (SMILES/structures, e.g. the >20,000-chemical human exposome set) needs in-silico metabolite prediction across EC-based, CYP450, phase II, and gut microbial biotransformation modules. The input chemical has MW >900 Da or belongs to a nonmatched chemical category — such chemicals were excluded from prediction (4,225 of the original list) The goal is experimentally confirmed metabolites rather than machine-learning-predicted biotransformation products The chemical contains structural classes outside BioTransformer's trained domain — BioTransformer cannot predict all metabolites and results may be inaccurate for some chemicals http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Batch prediction of biotransformation products for a large chemical inventory using BioTransformer's four machine-learning modules (EC-based, CYP450, phase II, human gut microbial), producing a deduplicated predicted metabolite database with per-module counts. metabolomics/v3 10.1289/ehp7722
skills.summary: Batch prediction of biotransformation products for a large chemical inventory using BioTransformer's four machine-learning modules (EC-based, CYP450, phase II, human gut microbial), producing a deduplicated predicted metabolite database with per-module counts.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input chemical has MW >900 Da or belongs to a nonmatched chemical category — such chemicals were excluded from prediction (4,225 of the original list) The goal is experimentally confirmed metabolites rather than machine-learning-predicted biotransformation products The chemical contains structural classes outside BioTransformer's trained domain — BioTransformer cannot predict all metabolites and results may be inaccurate for some chemicals

skills.description: Use when you have a set of generated SMILES and a set of known metabolite SMILES and need to verify that the generated structures resemble plausible metabolic transformation products rather than arbitrary synthetic compounds.
skills.name: biotransformer-one-step-transformation-recapitulation
skills.search_text: biotransformer-one-step-transformation-recapitulation Use when you have a set of generated SMILES and a set of known metabolite SMILES and need to verify that the generated structures resemble plausible metabolic transformation products rather than arbitrary synthetic compounds. Input molecules are experimentally observed MS/MS peaks or spectra rather than a pool of generated SMILES — use spectral library matching instead. You need to predict transformations for a specific metabolite, not assess the global biosynthetic plausibility of a generator; run BioTransformer directly on the molecule of interest. The model was trained on a metabolome very distant from human (e.g. plant or bacterial), where the one-step transformation rules calibrated on human metabolism may not transfer. http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Validates whether molecules generated by a chemical language model (e.g. DeepMet/CLM) correspond to known metabolic transformation products by comparing them against one-step BioTransformer-predicted transformation products of known metabolites, reporting the fraction recapitulated (target ≈77.5%). metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.11.13.623458
skills.summary: Validates whether molecules generated by a chemical language model (e.g. DeepMet/CLM) correspond to known metabolic transformation products by comparing them against one-step BioTransformer-predicted transformation products of known metabolites, reporting the fraction recapitulated (target ≈77.5%).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input molecules are experimentally observed MS/MS peaks or spectra rather than a pool of generated SMILES — use spectral library matching instead. You need to predict transformations for a specific metabolite, not assess the global biosynthetic plausibility of a generator; run BioTransformer directly on the molecule of interest. The model was trained on a metabolome very distant from human (e.g. plant or bacterial), where the one-step transformation rules calibrated on human metabolism may not transfer.

skills.description: Use when candidate drug metabolites detected by untargeted LC-HRMS need to be annotated as known/predicted or novel by matching detected precursor masses against a BioTransformer 3.0 prediction database.
skills.name: biotransformer-prediction-curation
skills.search_text: biotransformer-prediction-curation Use when candidate drug metabolites detected by untargeted LC-HRMS need to be annotated as known/predicted or novel by matching detected precursor masses against a BioTransformer 3.0 prediction database. Input is raw LC-HRMS vendor data that has not yet been processed into a feature table (run MZmine 2.53 with ADAP chromatogram builder first) The goal is de novo structural elucidation of novel metabolites — cross-referencing only classifies detected signals as predicted or novel and does not determine structures Metabolites generated extrahepatically (e.g., intestine, kidney) or by enzymes not abundant or active in liver S9 fraction — this workflow cannot detect them http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Curation of experimentally detected drug-metabolite features by cross-referencing observed mass signals (±5 ppm) against in silico predictions from BioTransformer 3.0, enabling classification of metabolites as predicted vs. novel for PharmMet DB. metabolomics/v3 10.1016/j.dmd.2025.100183
skills.summary: Curation of experimentally detected drug-metabolite features by cross-referencing observed mass signals (±5 ppm) against in silico predictions from BioTransformer 3.0, enabling classification of metabolites as predicted vs. novel for PharmMet DB.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw LC-HRMS vendor data that has not yet been processed into a feature table (run MZmine 2.53 with ADAP chromatogram builder first) The goal is de novo structural elucidation of novel metabolites — cross-referencing only classifies detected signals as predicted or novel and does not determine structures Metabolites generated extrahepatically (e.g., intestine, kidney) or by enzymes not abundant or active in liver S9 fraction — this workflow cannot detect them

skills.description: Use when curating LC-HRMS-detected postincubation (24-hour) drug metabolite features from human liver S9 incubations against BioTransformer 3.0 predicted metabolites to label each as predicted or unpredicted (novel).
skills.name: biotransformer-prediction-matching
skills.search_text: biotransformer-prediction-matching Use when curating LC-HRMS-detected postincubation (24-hour) drug metabolite features from human liver S9 incubations against BioTransformer 3.0 predicted metabolites to label each as predicted or unpredicted (novel). Features have already been labeled predicted/unpredicted (e.g. loaded from the deposited PharmMet DB curation output) — rerunning matching would duplicate work Input is raw vendor LC-HRMS data rather than an MZmine 2.53-derived feature table; feature detection (0-hour vs 24-hour MS1/RT comparison) must happen first The analysis targets metabolites from enzymes not abundant in liver S9 or from extrahepatic compartments — the article notes PharmMet DB is expected to lack these http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Matches LC-HRMS-detected drug-metabolite features against BioTransformer 3.0 in silico predictions within a ±5 ppm mass tolerance, labeling each detected postincubation feature as 'predicted' or 'unpredicted' (novel). This curation step underpins PharmMet DB's quantification of novel metabolites across 1114 therapeutic drugs. metabolomics/v3 10.1016/j.dmd.2025.100183
skills.summary: Matches LC-HRMS-detected drug-metabolite features against BioTransformer 3.0 in silico predictions within a ±5 ppm mass tolerance, labeling each detected postincubation feature as 'predicted' or 'unpredicted' (novel). This curation step underpins PharmMet DB's quantification of novel metabolites across 1114 therapeutic drugs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Features have already been labeled predicted/unpredicted (e.g. loaded from the deposited PharmMet DB curation output) — rerunning matching would duplicate work Input is raw vendor LC-HRMS data rather than an MZmine 2.53-derived feature table; feature detection (0-hour vs 24-hour MS1/RT comparison) must happen first The analysis targets metabolites from enzymes not abundant in liver S9 or from extrahepatic compartments — the article notes PharmMet DB is expected to lack these

skills.description: Use when S9-incubation LC-HRMS annotation tables carry BioTransformer 3.0 reaction-type tags and you need per-reaction detected/predicted counts (oxidation, glucuronidation, etc.).
skills.name: biotransformer-reaction-type-curation
skills.search_text: biotransformer-reaction-type-curation Use when S9-incubation LC-HRMS annotation tables carry BioTransformer 3.0 reaction-type tags and you need per-reaction detected/predicted counts (oxidation, glucuronidation, etc.). The metabolism of interest is extrahepatic or driven by enzymes absent or inactive in liver S9 (e.g., intestine, kidney) — S9-based reaction-type counts will not capture those metabolites. The input is unprocessed raw LC-HRMS data with no 0-hour vs 24-hour differential feature table yet — run MZmine 2.53 processing and candidate drug metabolite feature detection first. The goal is isolation and structural elucidation of novel metabolites rather than reaction-type counting of already-annotated detected features. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Aggregates LC-HRMS-detected human liver S9 drug metabolites by BioTransformer 3.0 biotransformation reaction type and tabulates detected-vs-predicted counts and detection fractions per reaction class (oxidation, glucuronidation, etc.). It turns the PharmMet DB curation pipeline into a quantitative reaction-type inventory. metabolomics/v3 10.1016/j.dmd.2025.100183
skills.summary: Aggregates LC-HRMS-detected human liver S9 drug metabolites by BioTransformer 3.0 biotransformation reaction type and tabulates detected-vs-predicted counts and detection fractions per reaction class (oxidation, glucuronidation, etc.). It turns the PharmMet DB curation pipeline into a quantitative reaction-type inventory.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The metabolism of interest is extrahepatic or driven by enzymes absent or inactive in liver S9 (e.g., intestine, kidney) — S9-based reaction-type counts will not capture those metabolites. The input is unprocessed raw LC-HRMS data with no 0-hour vs 24-hour differential feature table yet — run MZmine 2.53 processing and candidate drug metabolite feature detection first. The goal is isolation and structural elucidation of novel metabolites rather than reaction-type counting of already-annotated detected features.

skills.description: Use when confirmed parent suspects (e.g., carbamazepine, benzotriazole) from LC-HRMS suspect screening need candidate transformation product structures before TP suspect screening and componentization.
skills.name: biotransformer-tp-structure-prediction
skills.search_text: biotransformer-tp-structure-prediction Use when confirmed parent suspects (e.g., carbamazepine, benzotriazole) from LC-HRMS suspect screening need candidate transformation product structures before TP suspect screening and componentization. You only need parent suspect screening or classical NTA feature finding/annotation without transformation products A curated experimental TP library exists and in-silico prediction is unnecessary (patRoon also supports library-based TP screening) The data is not mass-spectrometry based or lacks chromatographic feature information to link predicted TPs to http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 In-silico prediction of transformation product (TP) structures for confirmed parent compounds using BioTransformer through patRoon's generateTPs interface, providing the candidate TP suspects that feed patRoon 2.0's automated TP screening workflow. metabolomics/v3 10.21105/joss.04029
skills.summary: In-silico prediction of transformation product (TP) structures for confirmed parent compounds using BioTransformer through patRoon's generateTPs interface, providing the candidate TP suspects that feed patRoon 2.0's automated TP screening workflow.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need parent suspect screening or classical NTA feature finding/annotation without transformation products A curated experimental TP library exists and in-silico prediction is unnecessary (patRoon also supports library-based TP screening) The data is not mass-spectrometry based or lacks chromatographic feature information to link predicted TPs to

skills.description: Use when you have full-scan mzML files with picked peak bounding boxes and a TopN mzML with a known N (MS2 scans per MS1) and want the theoretical optimum of fragmentable ions for that injection.
skills.name: bipartite-graph-construction-from-scan-schedule
skills.search_text: bipartite-graph-construction-from-scan-schedule Use when you have full-scan mzML files with picked peak bounding boxes and a TopN mzML with a known N (MS2 scans per MS1) and want the theoretical optimum of fragmentable ions for that injection. The goal is to measure actual observed DDA coverage from a real acquisition rather than the theoretical upper bound for any possible method No peak bounding boxes can be exported (e.g., only fragmented MS2 spectra without full-scan peak picking with MZmine 2), so RT/mz eligibility edges cannot be defined The acquisition is not TopN-style with a definable MS2-per-MS1 scan schedule (e.g., DIA or scheduled inclusion-list methods) http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Constructs a bipartite graph between MS2 scan slots (from a TopN scan schedule) and picked-peak bounding boxes (RT/mz min-max boxes from MZmine 2) and solves maximum matching (Hopcroft–Karp) to compute the theoretical upper bound on the number of ions any DDA method could fragment in a single injection. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c03895
skills.summary: Constructs a bipartite graph between MS2 scan slots (from a TopN scan schedule) and picked-peak bounding boxes (RT/mz min-max boxes from MZmine 2) and solves maximum matching (Hopcroft–Karp) to compute the theoretical upper bound on the number of ions any DDA method could fragment in a single injection.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to measure actual observed DDA coverage from a real acquisition rather than the theoretical upper bound for any possible method No peak bounding boxes can be exported (e.g., only fragmented MS2 spectra without full-scan peak picking with MZmine 2), so RT/mz eligibility edges cannot be defined The acquisition is not TopN-style with a definable MS2-per-MS1 scan schedule (e.g., DIA or scheduled inclusion-list methods)

skills.description: Use when you have a cross-validated MiMeNet interaction-score matrix (microbes x metabolites) and want to reveal the underlying structure of the microbe-metabolite interaction network as module-level nodes and edges.
skills.name: bipartite-module-network-construction
skills.search_text: bipartite-module-network-construction Use when you have a cross-validated MiMeNet interaction-score matrix (microbes x metabolites) and want to reveal the underlying structure of the microbe-metabolite interaction network as module-level nodes and edges. You only have raw metabolite or microbial abundance tables and no trained MiMeNet model — the input must be an interaction/attribution score matrix, not a feature table. You want metabolite-level (not module-level) edges — mmvec-style conditional probabilities or NED's latent-space interpretation does not reveal shared interaction-pattern modules, so this biclustering network is inappropriate for that goal. The score matrix has fewer features than the number of consensus clusters implied by the delta-area threshold, making the 8x8 module structure degenerate. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Bicluster the MiMeNet microbe-metabolite attribution-score matrix into 8 microbe modules and 8 metabolite modules via consensus clustering (Euclidean distance, complete linkage, delta-area threshold 0.025), then score module-module edges by mean normalized attribution within each block and export a Cytoscape-compatible bipartite network. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009021
skills.summary: Bicluster the MiMeNet microbe-metabolite attribution-score matrix into 8 microbe modules and 8 metabolite modules via consensus clustering (Euclidean distance, complete linkage, delta-area threshold 0.025), then score module-module edges by mean normalized attribution within each block and export a Cytoscape-compatible bipartite network.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only have raw metabolite or microbial abundance tables and no trained MiMeNet model — the input must be an interaction/attribution score matrix, not a feature table. You want metabolite-level (not module-level) edges — mmvec-style conditional probabilities or NED's latent-space interpretation does not reveal shared interaction-pattern modules, so this biclustering network is inappropriate for that goal. The score matrix has fewer features than the number of consensus clusters implied by the delta-area threshold, making the 8x8 module structure degenerate.

skills.description: Use when dereplicating query MS/MS spectra against a reference library (e.g., GNPS community libraries) and you must compute peak-level match scores, or detect putative analogs via precursor mass-difference delta shifts.
skills.name: bipartite-peak-matching-scoring
skills.search_text: bipartite-peak-matching-scoring Use when dereplicating query MS/MS spectra against a reference library (e.g., GNPS community libraries) and you must compute peak-level match scores, or detect putative analogs via precursor mass-difference delta shifts. Constructing molecular networks between consensus spectra from the same dataset — that requires the mutual top-K neighbor edge-retention rule on MSCluster consensus spectra, not library matching Query spectra already have a confident library annotation and no analog detection is intended Identifying novel compounds with no close reference spectrum — GNPS reported only 1.01% of public spectra matched, indicating insufficient chemical space coverage for unmatched chemistry Scores MS/MS library-vs-query spectrum pairs by formulating peak correspondences as a maximum bipartite matching under a fragment mass tolerance and scoring the assignment with a normalized dot product; underpins GNPS exact spectral search and, with delta edges, modification-tolerant variable dereplication. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/nbt.3597
skills.summary: Scores MS/MS library-vs-query spectrum pairs by formulating peak correspondences as a maximum bipartite matching under a fragment mass tolerance and scoring the assignment with a normalized dot product; underpins GNPS exact spectral search and, with delta edges, modification-tolerant variable dereplication.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Constructing molecular networks between consensus spectra from the same dataset — that requires the mutual top-K neighbor edge-retention rule on MSCluster consensus spectra, not library matching Query spectra already have a confident library annotation and no analog detection is intended Identifying novel compounds with no close reference spectrum — GNPS reported only 1.01% of public spectra matched, indicating insufficient chemical space coverage for unmatched chemistry

skills.name: biplot-taxa-overlay-in-ordination-space
skills.search_text: biplot-taxa-overlay-in-ordination-space Use when you have a QIIME principal coordinates file plus a metadata mapping file and need to display taxa (biplot arrows) or compare two ordinations (procrustes) in the same interactive 3D scatter. You need generic 3D plotting without microbiome metadata integration — commercial or generic packages such as SpotFire, MATLAB, Mathematica, R, Excel or Matplotlib are the alternatives the article contrasts with EMPeror The command line interface environment is unsupported: EMPeror's CLI is limited to OS X (10.6 and higher) and Linux only, with Python 2.7, QIIME (python libraries only), NumPy, BIOM 1.1.0 and PyCogent as requirements The visualization must render in a browser other than Chrome — the stated requirement is Chrome specifically, so compatibility elsewhere is untested http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Overlay taxon biplot arrows and auxiliary layers (procrustes comparisons, jackknifed beta diversity plots) onto a 3D principal coordinates visualization using EMPeror, so intrinsic data patterns in the ordination space can be interpreted alongside the sample points. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/2047-217x-2-16

skills.when_to_use_negative: You need generic 3D plotting without microbiome metadata integration — commercial or generic packages such as SpotFire, MATLAB, Mathematica, R, Excel or Matplotlib are the alternatives the article contrasts with EMPeror The command line interface environment is unsupported: EMPeror's CLI is limited to OS X (10.6 and higher) and Linux only, with Python 2.7, QIIME (python libraries only), NumPy, BIOM 1.1.0 and PyCogent as requirements The visualization must render in a browser other than Chrome — the stated requirement is Chrome specifically, so compatibility elsewhere is untested

skills.description: Use when a cluster of peaks with similar m/z signals has S1 and S2 similarity scores below user thresholds and needs its matrix-related ions separated from co-clustered isobaric or overlapping ions by their spatial distributions.
skills.name: bisecting-kmeans-spatial-clustering
skills.search_text: bisecting-kmeans-spatial-clustering Use when a cluster of peaks with similar m/z signals has S1 and S2 similarity scores below user thresholds and needs its matrix-related ions separated from co-clustered isobaric or overlapping ions by their spatial distributions. Clusters whose S1 and S2 scores already exceed the user-specified thresholds — the paper states the overlapping detection algorithm is only executed in those clusters that report scores under a threshold Situations with no spatial ion-image information available, since the bisection is driven entirely by Pearson correlations between spatial distributions of ions When a simple, non-recursive peak-level matrix annotation without overlapping/isobaric disambiguation is sufficient (the recursive splitting is specifically for preventing misclassification of overlapped ions) http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Recursive bisection of an experimental peak cluster into spatially coherent subgroups via k-means on Pearson-correlated ion images, used by rMSIcleanup to separate matrix-related ions from co-clustered isobaric or overlapping endogenous ions. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-020-00449-0
skills.summary: Recursive bisection of an experimental peak cluster into spatially coherent subgroups via k-means on Pearson-correlated ion images, used by rMSIcleanup to separate matrix-related ions from co-clustered isobaric or overlapping endogenous ions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Clusters whose S1 and S2 scores already exceed the user-specified thresholds — the paper states the overlapping detection algorithm is only executed in those clusters that report scores under a threshold Situations with no spatial ion-image information available, since the bisection is driven entirely by Pearson correlations between spatial distributions of ions When a simple, non-recursive peak-level matrix annotation without overlapping/isobaric disambiguation is sufficient (the recursive splitting is specifically for preventing misclassification of overlapped ions)

skills.description: Use when MS/MS spectra (MGF peak files with quantized peak m/z and L2-normalized intensities) must be represented compactly as binary hypervectors for fast distance-based clustering, or when HV memory footprint dominates storage.
skills.name: bit-packed-binary-hypervector-storage
skills.search_text: bit-packed-binary-hypervector-storage Use when MS/MS spectra (MGF peak files with quantized peak m/z and L2-normalized intensities) must be represented compactly as binary hypervectors for fast distance-based clustering, or when HV memory footprint dominates storage. Input spectra have not passed HyperSpec preprocessing (precursor-peak removal, <5 valid peaks or <250 Da mass-range filtering, top-50 peak retention, L2 normalization) — encoding raw spectra will produce noisy HVs The goal is exact peak-level comparison rather than approximate similarity — binary HV encoding trades exactness for the 8-fold compression and GPU speedup No GPU/CUDA environment is available and the dataset scale does not warrant HDC encoding overhead http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Encodes mass spectra as binary hypervectors (default D=2048, quantization Q=16) using HyperSpec's level-ID HDC encoding, then bit-packs each HV into 32-bit integers so each spectrum HV is stored as ⌈D/32⌉ integers — an 8-fold memory reduction versus byte storage. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.2c00612
skills.summary: Encodes mass spectra as binary hypervectors (default D=2048, quantization Q=16) using HyperSpec's level-ID HDC encoding, then bit-packs each HV into 32-bit integers so each spectrum HV is stored as ⌈D/32⌉ integers — an 8-fold memory reduction versus byte storage.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra have not passed HyperSpec preprocessing (precursor-peak removal, <5 valid peaks or <250 Da mass-range filtering, top-50 peak retention, L2 normalization) — encoding raw spectra will produce noisy HVs The goal is exact peak-level comparison rather than approximate similarity — binary HV encoding trades exactness for the 8-fold compression and GPU speedup No GPU/CUDA environment is available and the dataset scale does not warrant HDC encoding overhead

skills.name: bitpacking-sidechain-index-encoding

skills.description: Use when you need bitter/nonbitter labels for small molecules and have either known chemical structures (with descriptors) or experimental EI-MS / ESI-MS/MS positive-mode mass spectra, e.g. for metabolome screening where most spectra lack assigned structures.
skills.name: bitterness-classification-prediction
skills.search_text: bitterness-classification-prediction Use when you need bitter/nonbitter labels for small molecules and have either known chemical structures (with descriptors) or experimental EI-MS / ESI-MS/MS positive-mode mass spectra, e.g. for metabolome screening where most spectra lack assigned structures. skills.description: Use when raw LC-MS/MS files include blank media or QC injections and you want to strip those signals from the feature matrix before marker selection or quantification, as configured through UmetaFlow's blanks.tsv/config.yaml.
skills.name: blank-sample-removal-qc
skills.search_text: blank-sample-removal-qc Use when raw LC-MS/MS files include blank media or QC injections and you want to strip those signals from the feature matrix before marker selection or quantification, as configured through UmetaFlow's blanks.tsv/config.yaml. When the dataset contains no blank or QC injections (blanks.tsv would be empty), skip the removal rule instead of running it on all samples. When starting from an already-generated feature table rather than raw vendor/mzML files — the blank/QC filter operates during UmetaFlow pre-processing, not on downstream annotation tables. When you intentionally want blank/QC signals retained (e.g. for QC-drift visualisation); enabling the rule would remove them from the consensus map. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 An optional UmetaFlow pre-processing sub-step that removes blank and QC samples and their associated consensus features (via a minfrac filter on missing values) so that feature detection, alignment, and downstream statistics operate only on true biological samples. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-023-00724-w
skills.summary: An optional UmetaFlow pre-processing sub-step that removes blank and QC samples and their associated consensus features (via a minfrac filter on missing values) so that feature detection, alignment, and downstream statistics operate only on true biological samples.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the dataset contains no blank or QC injections (blanks.tsv would be empty), skip the removal rule instead of running it on all samples. When starting from an already-generated feature table rather than raw vendor/mzML files — the blank/QC filter operates during UmetaFlow pre-processing, not on downstream annotation tables. When you intentionally want blank/QC signals retained (e.g. for QC-drift visualisation); enabling the rule would remove them from the consensus map.

skills.description: Use when an XCMS feature table from LC-HRMS/MS samples includes blank injections and contains low-quality or carryover-derived features that must be removed before comparative statistical analysis of sample groups.
skills.name: blank-subtraction-quality-filtering
skills.search_text: blank-subtraction-quality-filtering Use when an XCMS feature table from LC-HRMS/MS samples includes blank injections and contains low-quality or carryover-derived features that must be removed before comparative statistical analysis of sample groups. skills.summary: Reduces an XCMS-detected feature table from untargeted HPLC-HRMS/MS data by removing features attributable to carryover/contaminants via blank subtraction and discarding poorly shaped peaks via Peak Quality thresholding, as used in Metaboseek to reduce >700,000 features from C. elegans hacl-1 vs WT metabolomes to ~150,000 retained features.

skills.description: Use when a vendor feature table from a real sample (e.g., AFFF) must be de-noised against matched solvent-blank feature tables before PFAS annotation, to strip features attributable to background.
skills.name: blank-threshold-signal-filtering
skills.search_text: blank-threshold-signal-filtering Use when a vendor feature table from a real sample (e.g., AFFF) must be de-noised against matched solvent-blank feature tables before PFAS annotation, to strip features attributable to background. The input is already a blank-filtered feature table — reapplying the sample-vs-blank threshold would only remove features that legitimately exceed background. The goal is annotation or identification of retained features — blank filtering is only the second step of FluoroMatch Flow 2.0, which continues with exact mass matching, mass defect filtering, and homologous series detection. No matched solvent-blank injections exist for the sample acquisition, since the threshold is computed from blank average and SD across blanks. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Removes background/sample-container features from LC-HRMS feature tables by comparing each sample feature's maximum abundance against the average plus 3× standard deviation of that feature across solvent-blank injections, as implemented in the FluoroMatch 2.0 blank-filtering workflow. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s00216-021-03392-7
skills.summary: Removes background/sample-container features from LC-HRMS feature tables by comparing each sample feature's maximum abundance against the average plus 3× standard deviation of that feature across solvent-blank injections, as implemented in the FluoroMatch 2.0 blank-filtering workflow.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a blank-filtered feature table — reapplying the sample-vs-blank threshold would only remove features that legitimately exceed background. The goal is annotation or identification of retained features — blank filtering is only the second step of FluoroMatch Flow 2.0, which continues with exact mass matching, mass defect filtering, and homologous series detection. No matched solvent-blank injections exist for the sample acquisition, since the threshold is computed from blank average and SD across blanks.

skills.description: Use when a metabolomics/lipidomics sequence includes procedural blank injections alongside real samples and you must separate genuine endogenous signals from carryover or background contaminants before further QC.
skills.name: blank-to-sample-intensity-ratio-analysis
skills.search_text: blank-to-sample-intensity-ratio-analysis Use when a metabolomics/lipidomics sequence includes procedural blank injections alongside real samples and you must separate genuine endogenous signals from carryover or background contaminants before further QC. Features are already known internal standards or labeled surrogates whose blank behavior is irrelevant to the decision. skills.summary: Screens metabolomics features for background contamination by comparing mean intensity in real study samples against mean intensity in procedural blank injections, using the QComics 3x sample-to-blank criterion to flag rather than blindly remove features.

skills.description: Use when raw LC-HRMS non-target data include blank-solvent and spiked-standard triplicates, and features must be filtered by blank absence, replicate abundance and minimum intensity before annotation or suspect screening.
skills.name: blank-vs-standard-sample-processing
skills.search_text: blank-vs-standard-sample-processing Use when raw LC-HRMS non-target data include blank-solvent and spiked-standard triplicates, and features must be filtered by blank absence, replicate abundance and minimum intensity before annotation or suspect screening. The input is already a cleaned feature table with blank subtraction applied — re-filtering would be redundant and may remove genuine standard features. The experiment provides no blank solvent injections, so the blank-presence filter cannot be evaluated. The goal is absolute quantification with calibration curves rather than non-target feature clean-up; patRoon's filter() is a rule-based NTA pre-treatment, not a quantification method. http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Applies patRoon's harmonized rule-based filtering to LC-HRMS feature data using triplicate blank-solvent (solvent-X) and spiked-standard-mixture (standard-X) injections from patRoonData, so that only features with genuine signal in the standard and absence in blanks survive for annotation. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-020-00477-w
skills.summary: Applies patRoon's harmonized rule-based filtering to LC-HRMS feature data using triplicate blank-solvent (solvent-X) and spiked-standard-mixture (standard-X) injections from patRoonData, so that only features with genuine signal in the standard and absence in blanks survive for annotation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a cleaned feature table with blank subtraction applied — re-filtering would be redundant and may remove genuine standard features. The goal is absolute quantification with calibration curves rather than non-target feature clean-up; patRoon's filter() is a rule-based NTA pre-treatment, not a quantification method.

skills.search_text: blast-gene-id-mapping Use when merging or comparing genome-scale metabolic reconstructions generated by different pipelines whose draft models use different gene ID namespaces, and GPR rules must be aligned. skills.name: blast-homology-search
skills.search_text: blast-homology-search Use when mass spectrometry identifications must be linked to biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) in paired genomic data, e.g., validating molDiscovery molecule annotations on microbial strains by BLAST against MIBiG reference clusters. Input lacks paired genomic data — BLAST-based BGC linking requires genome mining annotations for the same strains as the mass spectra The goal is small molecule identification from spectra alone (use molDiscovery database search against PubChem/DNP instead of genome homology) Gene cluster candidates cannot meet the >=90% coverage and >=70% identity thresholds, e.g., highly divergent novel clusters where strict BLAST criteria would wrongly discard true links http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Sequence homology search skill (BLAST-style alignment) used to cross-validate metabolite identifications against genome mining, linking identified small molecules to their biosynthetic gene clusters by comparing gene clusters to MIBiG references with coverage and identity thresholds. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-021-23986-0
skills.summary: Sequence homology search skill (BLAST-style alignment) used to cross-validate metabolite identifications against genome mining, linking identified small molecules to their biosynthetic gene clusters by comparing gene clusters to MIBiG references with coverage and identity thresholds.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input lacks paired genomic data — BLAST-based BGC linking requires genome mining annotations for the same strains as the mass spectra The goal is small molecule identification from spectra alone (use molDiscovery database search against PubChem/DNP instead of genome homology) Gene cluster candidates cannot meet the >=90% coverage and >=70% identity thresholds, e.g., highly divergent novel clusters where strict BLAST criteria would wrongly discard true links

skills.description: Use when GC/MS chromatograms contain co-eluting compounds and extensive EI fragmentation, and pure compound spectra plus integrated areas must be reconstructed from raw chromatographic data rather than via peak-picking.
skills.name: blind-source-separation-compound-extraction
skills.search_text: blind-source-separation-compound-extraction Use when GC/MS chromatograms contain co-eluting compounds and extensive EI fragmentation, and pure compound spectra plus integrated areas must be reconstructed from raw chromatographic data rather than via peak-picking. The chromatograms have not yet been noise-filtered and baseline-corrected — eRah requires the cleaned chromatograms produced by the preceding preprocessing step as input. Data are already in the form of a fragment-ion peak table or feature matrix (e.g. output from XCMS centWave, MetAlign or ChromaTOF) — eRah's quantitative variables are compound-spectrum-based, not m/z, retention-time-window and fragment-area based, so re-deconvolving a peak table is the wrong scope. Only compound identification by spectral library matching is needed and quantification is not required — the deconvolution step is specifically the spectrum/area extraction stage, downstream of which alignComp(), recMissComp() and identifyComp() operate. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Applies eRah's two-step blind source separation — compound match by local covariance (CMLC) followed by orthogonal signal deconvolution (OSD) — to extract pure compound spectra and quantitative compound profiles from co-eluted GC–MS chromatograms. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.6b02927
skills.summary: Applies eRah's two-step blind source separation — compound match by local covariance (CMLC) followed by orthogonal signal deconvolution (OSD) — to extract pure compound spectra and quantitative compound profiles from co-eluted GC–MS chromatograms.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The chromatograms have not yet been noise-filtered and baseline-corrected — eRah requires the cleaned chromatograms produced by the preceding preprocessing step as input. Data are already in the form of a fragment-ion peak table or feature matrix (e.g. output from XCMS centWave, MetAlign or ChromaTOF) — eRah's quantitative variables are compound-spectrum-based, not m/z, retention-time-window and fragment-area based, so re-deconvolving a peak table is the wrong scope. Only compound identification by spectral library matching is needed and quantification is not required — the deconvolution step is specifically the spectrum/area extraction stage, downstream of which alignComp(), recMissComp() and identifyComp() operate.

skills.description: Use when ranking drug combinations for synergy relative to a metabolite-predictor network — e.g. combinations from DrugCombDB whose targets overlap top features, to be scored and compared against random background combinations.
skills.name: bliss-independence-scoring
skills.search_text: bliss-independence-scoring Use when ranking drug combinations for synergy relative to a metabolite-predictor network — e.g. combinations from DrugCombDB whose targets overlap top features, to be scored and compared against random background combinations. The random forest models are not directly transferrable to predicting metabolomics from other sources due to differences between in vitro and in vivo conditions, cell line panels, and limited feature overlap — do not reuse predictor lists from outside CCLE-trained models without revalidation. When a mechanistic (rather than associational) synergy ranking is required — the 'guilt by association' strategy may not identify causative mechanisms, and network associations are descriptive, not necessarily mechanistic. http://edamontology.org/topic_3315 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Scores drug-combination synergy using the Bliss independence interaction score, applied here to drug combinations whose targets overlap top predictors from Metab8D random forest regression models, contrasted against a randomly selected drug-combination background. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.08.17.608400
skills.summary: Scores drug-combination synergy using the Bliss independence interaction score, applied here to drug combinations whose targets overlap top predictors from Metab8D random forest regression models, contrasted against a randomly selected drug-combination background.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The random forest models are not directly transferrable to predicting metabolomics from other sources due to differences between in vitro and in vivo conditions, cell line panels, and limited feature overlap — do not reuse predictor lists from outside CCLE-trained models without revalidation. When a mechanistic (rather than associational) synergy ranking is required — the 'guilt by association' strategy may not identify causative mechanisms, and network associations are descriptive, not necessarily mechanistic.
