skills.summary: Reconstructs the prepareAdjMat step of netgsa: cluster large gene networks with igraph community-detection algorithms, estimate weighted adjacency matrices per cluster, and reassemble them into a block-diagonal adjacency matrix for each condition before NetGSA pathway enrichment.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Every connected component already contains ≤1,000 genes, so no clustering-based decomposition is needed The downstream method does not accept a block-diagonal adjacency structure and requires a single full p x p adjacency matrix Adjacency matrices across tested groups must share an identical block diagonal structure that this skill's per-condition reassembly does not guarantee

skills.description: Use when a background-corrected two-color (red/green) fluorescence image pair needs an automated colocalization significance threshold, and visual inspection is ambiguous.
skills.name: block-scrambled-randomization-threshold-estimation
skills.search_text: block-scrambled-randomization-threshold-estimation Use when a background-corrected two-color (red/green) fluorescence image pair needs an automated colocalization significance threshold, and visual inspection is ambiguous. Measuring protein-protein interaction proximity: colocalization coefficients quantify overlap, not binding — FRET is required to detect interaction when the average distance between binding proteins is <10 nm, and FRET was negative for the Rev-CRM1 complex even where the algorithm applied. Input is a single-channel image or a non-registered two-color pair with no red-green intensity pairing to build the 2D histogram from. Scrambling individual pixels instead of texture/PSF-sized blocks — this violates the randomization design and inflates significance of spatially autocorrelated signals. http://edamontology.org/topic_3382 Estimates a statistically significant colocalization threshold for two-color fluorescence images by scrambling image blocks (sized by the texture/PSF from image autocorrelations) 200 times and selecting a cutoff (e.g., the 95th percentile of the random overlap distribution), as described by Costes et al. 2004. metabolomics/v3 10.1529/biophysj.103.038422
skills.summary: Estimates a statistically significant colocalization threshold for two-color fluorescence images by scrambling image blocks (sized by the texture/PSF from image autocorrelations) 200 times and selecting a cutoff (e.g., the 95th percentile of the random overlap distribution), as described by Costes et al. 2004.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Measuring protein-protein interaction proximity: colocalization coefficients quantify overlap, not binding — FRET is required to detect interaction when the average distance between binding proteins is <10 nm, and FRET was negative for the Rev-CRM1 complex even where the algorithm applied. Input is a single-channel image or a non-registered two-color pair with no red-green intensity pairing to build the 2D histogram from. Scrambling individual pixels instead of texture/PSF-sized blocks — this violates the randomization design and inflates significance of spatially autocorrelated signals.

skills.description: Use when analyzing background-corrected two-color (e.g., CFP/YFP) 2D or 3D confocal images to determine which pixels are truly colocalized versus random overlap, and to compute the proportion of each protein colocalized with the other.
skills.name: block-scrambling-randomization-statistics
skills.search_text: block-scrambling-randomization-statistics Use when analyzing background-corrected two-color (e.g., CFP/YFP) 2D or 3D confocal images to determine which pixels are truly colocalized versus random overlap, and to compute the proportion of each protein colocalized with the other. When the question is physical protein-protein binding distance rather than colocalization — FRET is required (FRET detects interaction only if average distance <10 nm, and FRET was negative for Rev-CRM1 despite colocalization, presumably due to CRM1's 130 kDa size). When the input is a single-channel image or the two channels have not been background-corrected — the 2D histogram selection and random-overlap distribution require paired, corrected two-color data. When the image texture/PSF cannot be estimated (no measurable autocorrelation widths) — block size depends on the smaller autocorrelation width of the two channels. A statistical colocalization-threshold method from Costes et al. (Biophys J 2004) that builds a random-overlap distribution by scrambling image blocks (not pixels) and automatically selects colocalized pixels in a 2D red/green intensity histogram, yielding colocalization coefficients without user-set thresholds. metabolomics/v3 10.1529/biophysj.103.038422
skills.summary: A statistical colocalization-threshold method from Costes et al. (Biophys J 2004) that builds a random-overlap distribution by scrambling image blocks (not pixels) and automatically selects colocalized pixels in a 2D red/green intensity histogram, yielding colocalization coefficients without user-set thresholds.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the question is physical protein-protein binding distance rather than colocalization — FRET is required (FRET detects interaction only if average distance <10 nm, and FRET was negative for Rev-CRM1 despite colocalization, presumably due to CRM1's 130 kDa size). When the input is a single-channel image or the two channels have not been background-corrected — the 2D histogram selection and random-overlap distribution require paired, corrected two-color data. When the image texture/PSF cannot be estimated (no measurable autocorrelation widths) — block size depends on the smaller autocorrelation width of the two channels.

skills.description: Use when a HORDB peptide hormone table (figshare deposit 10.6084/m9.figshare.c.5522241) needs filtering on the 'cross BBB' activity annotation to quantify BBB-crossing peptide hormones.
skills.name: blood-brain-barrier-annotation-extraction
skills.search_text: blood-brain-barrier-annotation-extraction Use when a HORDB peptide hormone table (figshare deposit 10.6084/m9.figshare.c.5522241) needs filtering on the 'cross BBB' activity annotation to quantify BBB-crossing peptide hormones. skills.summary: Extracts and counts peptide hormone entries from the HORDB database that are annotated as crossing the blood-brain barrier, by exact string filtering on the activity field of the deposited peptide information table.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The table is not the HORDB peptide hormone information table (e.g. peptide drugs or marketed pharmaceutical preparations), since the 'cross BBB' field is defined for peptide hormone entries. A quantitative BBB permeability prediction is needed — this skill only extracts the deposited annotation, not a computed permeability value.

skills.description: Use when building or extending a pre-analytical stability database from published EDTA plasma/serum studies that report fold changes due to time delay and temperature during sample processing.

skills.description: Use when simulating blood plasma/serum 1H NMR spectra where metabolite-only peaks look unrealistically clean and a realistic broad macromolecular background is needed to approximate real blood spectra.
skills.name: blood-plasma-protein-background-modeling
skills.search_text: blood-plasma-protein-background-modeling Use when simulating blood plasma/serum 1H NMR spectra where metabolite-only peaks look unrealistically clean and a realistic broad macromolecular background is needed to approximate real blood spectra. The target biofluid is urine or cerebral spinal fluid — the broad protein background enhancement is specific to blood spectrum realism. You need a 2D simulation (J-Res or COSY); the protein-background blood realism result reported here applies to the 1D 1H blood plasma spectrum. You only need metabolite peak lists or concentrations rather than a simulated full spectrum with realistic background. http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Enhances simulated blood 1H 1H NMR spectra by adding a broad protein (albumin) background, which brings the simulated spectrum close to a real blood spectrum (Pearson correlation ~0.82), as implemented in MetAssimulo 2.0. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btaf045
skills.summary: Enhances simulated blood 1H 1H NMR spectra by adding a broad protein (albumin) background, which brings the simulated spectrum close to a real blood spectrum (Pearson correlation ~0.82), as implemented in MetAssimulo 2.0.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The target biofluid is urine or cerebral spinal fluid — the broad protein background enhancement is specific to blood spectrum realism. You need a 2D simulation (J-Res or COSY); the protein-background blood realism result reported here applies to the 1D 1H blood plasma spectrum. You only need metabolite peak lists or concentrations rather than a simulated full spectrum with realistic background.

skills.description: Use when you have de novo peptide assignments (e.g. from Casanovo on clustered unidentified MS/MS spectra) and want to test whether discordant or mismatched assignments are enriched for variants explainable by single-nucleotide substitutions.
skills.name: blosum62-substitution-enrichment-analysis
skills.search_text: blosum62-substitution-enrichment-analysis Use when you have de novo peptide assignments (e.g. from Casanovo on clustered unidentified MS/MS spectra) and want to test whether discordant or mismatched assignments are enriched for variants explainable by single-nucleotide substitutions. Peptides were identified by standard database searching with no de novo predictions, so there are no mismatched assignments to test for substitution consistency The input spectra have not been clustered (e.g. no GLEAMS cluster identifiers), so per-spectrum predictions cannot be aggregated into cluster-level consensus peptides before mismatch testing Predicted and reference peptides differ by multiple amino acids, which cannot be attributed to a single-nucleotide substitution and fall outside this single-mismatch analysis http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Tests whether amino-acid mismatches between de novo peptide predictions (from Casanovo) and database peptide matches are consistent with single-nucleotide substitutions, and quantifies this with a BLOSUM62 enrichment statistic — the analysis that showed 83.4% of Casanovo's predicted substitutions on GLEAMS dark-proteome clusters correspond to potential single-nucleotide substitutions versus 38.6% expected. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-49731-x

skills.description: Use when building a chemical shift prediction training or benchmark set that requires experimentally assigned shifts paired with 3D structures, e.g. harvesting matching BMRB/PDB entries and filtering to non-paramagnetic, standard-residue proteins.
skills.name: bmrb-pdb-dataset-curation
skills.search_text: bmrb-pdb-dataset-curation Use when building a chemical shift prediction training or benchmark set that requires experimentally assigned shifts paired with 3D structures, e.g. harvesting matching BMRB/PDB entries and filtering to non-paramagnetic, standard-residue proteins. The protein of interest is paramagnetic or contains non-standard residues — the curated training corpus explicitly excluded these, so the trained models are not supported by such data. You need a ready-made evaluation set and the ShiftX2 61-protein test dataset suffices — reuse it directly instead of re-curation. Curating RNA chemical shift data — the RNA predictor uses a separate dataset (371 RNA molecules with BMRB assignments and PDB structures) and FM models trained by stochastic gradient descent, a distinct workflow. http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Assembles matched protein training/test datasets for chemical shift prediction by pairing experimental chemical shift assignments from BMRB with 3D structures from PDB, filtering to non-paramagnetic proteins with standard residues. This curation underpins training and benchmarking of NMRFx's protein shift prediction model. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s42004-025-01812-8
skills.summary: Assembles matched protein training/test datasets for chemical shift prediction by pairing experimental chemical shift assignments from BMRB with 3D structures from PDB, filtering to non-paramagnetic proteins with standard residues. This curation underpins training and benchmarking of NMRFx's protein shift prediction model.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The protein of interest is paramagnetic or contains non-standard residues — the curated training corpus explicitly excluded these, so the trained models are not supported by such data. You need a ready-made evaluation set and the ShiftX2 61-protein test dataset suffices — reuse it directly instead of re-curation. Curating RNA chemical shift data — the RNA predictor uses a separate dataset (371 RNA molecules with BMRB assignments and PDB structures) and FM models trained by stochastic gradient descent, a distinct workflow.

skills.description: Use when evaluating the interpretability of a fragmentation-graph predictor (e.g. ICEBERG) by checking whether its predicted bond breakages match chemistry intuition across a test set.
skills.name: bond-breakage-type-frequency-statistics
skills.search_text: bond-breakage-type-frequency-statistics Use when evaluating the interpretability of a fragmentation-graph predictor (e.g. ICEBERG) by checking whether its predicted bond breakages match chemistry intuition across a test set. Input spectra come from a black-box predictor that does not expose per-breakage bond annotations (e.g. NEIMS, MassFormer), since no bond-type statistics can be extracted. The goal is absolute spectrum prediction accuracy rather than interpretability of fragmentation pathways; frequency statistics do not measure cosine similarity or retrieval performance. Only a single molecule or very few molecules are available, making the frequency distribution too sparse to judge chemistry-level trends. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Aggregate the bond types broken across ICEBERG's predicted fragmentations on a held-out test set into a frequency table, revealing whether weaker heteroatom bonds (C-O, C-N) break more reliably than C-C bonds or complex ring breakages, and validating the model's chemical interpretability. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c04654

skills.description: Use when generating candidate fragmentation graphs for small molecules (SMILES/SDF, up to ~2000 Da) to match against tandem mass spectra during in silico database search, especially when rule-based enumeration is too slow for heavy molecules.
skills.name: bond-disconnection-rule-application
skills.search_text: bond-disconnection-rule-application Use when generating candidate fragmentation graphs for small molecules (SMILES/SDF, up to ~2000 Da) to match against tandem mass spectra during in silico database search, especially when rule-based enumeration is too slow for heavy molecules. The query molecule is peptidic and you need a p-value — molDiscovery's MCMC p-value approach is limited to peptidic molecules, and extending it to general molecules 'is challenging as it involves generation of random molecular structures' The molecule is very small (<400 Da): the article notes existing methods 'do not perform well for super small molecules (<400 Da)', and molDiscovery itself reports lower accuracy below 600 Da because 'fewer fragments are generated for molecules in this range' Accurate modeling of resonant structures or rearrangement rules is required — molDiscovery 'naively treats benzene ring or large resonant structures as alternate single bonds and double bonds' and covers only a limited number of bond types and rearrangement rules http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Generates in silico mass spectrometry fragments for small molecules by disconnecting candidate bonds (bridges and 2-cuts) in a molecular graph, as implemented in molDiscovery to improve efficiency and accuracy of small molecule identification from tandem mass spectra. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-021-23986-0
skills.summary: Generates in silico mass spectrometry fragments for small molecules by disconnecting candidate bonds (bridges and 2-cuts) in a molecular graph, as implemented in molDiscovery to improve efficiency and accuracy of small molecule identification from tandem mass spectra.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The query molecule is peptidic and you need a p-value — molDiscovery's MCMC p-value approach is limited to peptidic molecules, and extending it to general molecules 'is challenging as it involves generation of random molecular structures' The molecule is very small (<400 Da): the article notes existing methods 'do not perform well for super small molecules (<400 Da)', and molDiscovery itself reports lower accuracy below 600 Da because 'fewer fragments are generated for molecules in this range' Accurate modeling of resonant structures or rearrangement rules is required — molDiscovery 'naively treats benzene ring or large resonant structures as alternate single bonds and double bonds' and covers only a limited number of bond types and rearrangement rules

skills.description: Use when ranking candidate small-molecule structures against a high-resolution MS/MS peak list requires fragment matching scores weighted by bond dissociation energies of cleaved bonds.
skills.name: bond-dissociation-energy-scoring
skills.search_text: bond-dissociation-energy-scoring Use when ranking candidate small-molecule structures against a high-resolution MS/MS peak list requires fragment matching scores weighted by bond dissociation energies of cleaved bonds. The measured spectrum is dominated by one or only a few fragments (e.g. a water loss) explainable by most candidates — it lacks the information content needed to discriminate candidates The goal is spectral-library matching against reference spectra (e.g. MassBank) rather than in silico fragmentation of database candidates Candidates come as already-scored feature tables without structure-to-fragment assignments, so BDE-weighted rescoring cannot be applied http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Computes the MetFrag2.2 in silico fragmentation score (S_C_Frag) that ranks candidate structures against an HR-MS/MS spectrum by summing matched-peak contributions of relative mass^alpha x relative intensity^beta, each divided by the summed bond dissociation energy (BDE) of the cleaved bonds raised to the power gamma, with optimized exponents alpha=1.84, beta=0.59, gamma=0.47. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-016-0115-9
skills.summary: Computes the MetFrag2.2 in silico fragmentation score (S_C_Frag) that ranks candidate structures against an HR-MS/MS spectrum by summing matched-peak contributions of relative mass^alpha x relative intensity^beta, each divided by the summed bond dissociation energy (BDE) of the cleaved bonds raised to the power gamma, with optimized exponents alpha=1.84, beta=0.59, gamma=0.47.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The measured spectrum is dominated by one or only a few fragments (e.g. a water loss) explainable by most candidates — it lacks the information content needed to discriminate candidates The goal is spectral-library matching against reference spectra (e.g. MassBank) rather than in silico fragmentation of database candidates Candidates come as already-scored feature tables without structure-to-fragment assignments, so BDE-weighted rescoring cannot be applied

skills.search_text: bond-order-atom-type-pair-parsing Use when you have rooted fragment graphs G = (V, E, VL, EL, R) from cleaved bonds and need canonical, index-invariant topological features (bond orders, atom types, BFS ordering) for ML spectral prediction. skills.search_text: bond-order-based-fragment-identification Use when you have raw CIDMD trajectories (from TeraChem NVE B3LYP/6–31G* runs) and need to extract stable, charged fragment ions by analyzing Mayer bond order time series to build an in silico CID-MS/MS spectrum. skills.description: Use when a univariate linear model is fitted on each column of an NMR peak-value feature matrix (e.g., 31 x 677 from speaq 2.0) and raw p-values must be family-wise corrected before declaring significant features.
skills.name: bonferroni-multiple-testing-correction
skills.search_text: bonferroni-multiple-testing-correction Use when a univariate linear model is fitted on each column of an NMR peak-value feature matrix (e.g., 31 x 677 from speaq 2.0) and raw p-values must be family-wise corrected before declaring significant features. The input is raw 1D NMR spectra rather than a completed peak-value feature matrix — peak picking, grouping, and peak filling must be run first (getWaveletPeaks, PeakGrouper, BuildFeatureMatrix). The feature matrix columns are unscaled — apply the metabolomics scaling (e.g., Pareto scaling) before univariate statistics, as done in the wine analysis. Only a handful of hypothesis tests are involved, where a family-wise Bonferroni correction across hundreds of features is not the intended multiplicity scope. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Bonferroni family-wise correction applied to per-feature p-values from speaq 2.0's linear-model differential analysis on an NMR peak-value feature matrix, used to call significant discriminating peaks (e.g., 33 red-vs-white wine features; 9 peaks in the onion intake in mice study). metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1006018
skills.summary: Bonferroni family-wise correction applied to per-feature p-values from speaq 2.0's linear-model differential analysis on an NMR peak-value feature matrix, used to call significant discriminating peaks (e.g., 33 red-vs-white wine features; 9 peaks in the onion intake in mice study).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw 1D NMR spectra rather than a completed peak-value feature matrix — peak picking, grouping, and peak filling must be run first (getWaveletPeaks, PeakGrouper, BuildFeatureMatrix). The feature matrix columns are unscaled — apply the metabolomics scaling (e.g., Pareto scaling) before univariate statistics, as done in the wine analysis. Only a handful of hypothesis tests are involved, where a family-wise Bonferroni correction across hundreds of features is not the intended multiplicity scope.

skills.search_text: bonferroni-multiple-testing-correction Use when many correlated biomarkers (e.g., 226 Nightingale NMR metabolomics measures) are simultaneously tested and an explicit family-wise alpha split (0.05 divided by the number of tests) is needed to declare significance or prune a model. The biomarker panel or hypothesis count differs from 226 — the threshold must be recomputed as 0.05 divided by the actual number of tests, not copied as 2.21 x 10^-4 False discovery rate control (e.g., FDR/q-values) is the desired error metric rather than family-wise error control, since Bonferroni is conservative for correlated biomarkers Testing a small pre-specified set of hypotheses where no multiplicity correction was planned http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Applies Bonferroni family-wise error control across the 226 NMR metabolic biomarkers tested for association with all-cause mortality, yielding a significance threshold of 2.21 x 10^-4 (0.05/226) that governs both initial significance calls and the backward-removal step of the forward-backward biomarker selection. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-019-11311-9
skills.summary: Applies Bonferroni family-wise error control across the 226 NMR metabolic biomarkers tested for association with all-cause mortality, yielding a significance threshold of 2.21 x 10^-4 (0.05/226) that governs both initial significance calls and the backward-removal step of the forward-backward biomarker selection.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The biomarker panel or hypothesis count differs from 226 — the threshold must be recomputed as 0.05 divided by the actual number of tests, not copied as 2.21 x 10^-4 False discovery rate control (e.g., FDR/q-values) is the desired error metric rather than family-wise error control, since Bonferroni is conservative for correlated biomarkers Testing a small pre-specified set of hypotheses where no multiplicity correction was planned

skills.description: Use when a benchmarking workflow produces one P value per metabolite per feature set (e.g. Pearson correlations from 2,025 cross-validated RF models) and a per-metabolite significance call is needed.

skills.search_text: bonferroni-multiple-testing-correction Use when a benchmarking workflow produces one P value per metabolite per feature set (e.g. Pearson correlations from 2,025 cross-validated RF models) and a per-metabolite significance call is needed. When only a handful of metabolites or hypotheses are tested — the 0.05/225 correction is calibrated to this panel size and would be overly conservative elsewhere; recompute the denominator from the actual number of tests When the goal is FDR control at a target q-value rather than family-wise error control — a Benjamini-Hochberg procedure would be the appropriate alternative When P values are not independent or not validly computed (e.g. correlations from overlapping CV folds) — Bonferroni does not repair invalid base tests http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Determines which metabolite prediction models are statistically significant by applying a Bonferroni-corrected P value threshold of 0.05/225 across the 225 metabolite x 9 feature set models, controlling the false discovery rate when thousands of correlation tests are run in parallel. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.08.17.608400
skills.summary: Determines which metabolite prediction models are statistically significant by applying a Bonferroni-corrected P value threshold of 0.05/225 across the 225 metabolite x 9 feature set models, controlling the false discovery rate when thousands of correlation tests are run in parallel.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When only a handful of metabolites or hypotheses are tested — the 0.05/225 correction is calibrated to this panel size and would be overly conservative elsewhere; recompute the denominator from the actual number of tests When the goal is FDR control at a target q-value rather than family-wise error control — a Benjamini-Hochberg procedure would be the appropriate alternative When P values are not independent or not validly computed (e.g. correlations from overlapping CV folds) — Bonferroni does not repair invalid base tests

skills.description: Use when you have METASPACE MS1 annotations (e.g. spatial or single-cell metabolomics, HMDB v4 at FDR <= 0.1) where isomers/isobars cannot be resolved, and you need ORA or MSEA results that account for molecular identification ambiguity.
skills.name: bootstrap-based-enrichment-analysis
skills.search_text: bootstrap-based-enrichment-analysis Use when you have METASPACE MS1 annotations (e.g. spatial or single-cell metabolomics, HMDB v4 at FDR <= 0.1) where isomers/isobars cannot be resolved, and you need ORA or MSEA results that account for molecular identification ambiguity. If your identifications come from MS2 or other data that resolve isomeric/isobaric molecules, ambiguity propagation is unnecessary — conventional ORA applies If your background contains terms mapped only to sum formulas and you cannot tolerate name/sum-formula mapping differences (e.g. LION ontology which lacks the mapping), check S2IsoMEr background support first Input is a rank-based (scored) metabolite list for GSEA-style testing — use the MSEA entry points (Run_bootstrap_MSEA), not Run_bootstrap_ORA http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Bootstrapping-based overrepresentation and metabolite set enrichment analysis (ORA/MSEA) with the S2IsoMEr R package, which propagates isomeric/isobaric annotation ambiguity from MS1 imaging MS data into enrichment results via iterative random sampling. It distinguishes robust terms from false positives that appear significant under standard ORA that ignores ambiguity. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioadv/vbaf100
skills.summary: Bootstrapping-based overrepresentation and metabolite set enrichment analysis (ORA/MSEA) with the S2IsoMEr R package, which propagates isomeric/isobaric annotation ambiguity from MS1 imaging MS data into enrichment results via iterative random sampling. It distinguishes robust terms from false positives that appear significant under standard ORA that ignores ambiguity.
skills.when_to_use_negative: If your identifications come from MS2 or other data that resolve isomeric/isobaric molecules, ambiguity propagation is unnecessary — conventional ORA applies If your background contains terms mapped only to sum formulas and you cannot tolerate name/sum-formula mapping differences (e.g. LION ontology which lacks the mapping), check S2IsoMEr background support first Input is a rank-based (scored) metabolite list for GSEA-style testing — use the MSEA entry points (Run_bootstrap_MSEA), not Run_bootstrap_ORA

skills.description: Use when reporting a cross-validated ROC AUC (or other performance metric) from a supervised metabolomics or chemometric classifier — e.g. OPLS-DA scores from GCxGC-TOFMS data — and you need a defensible interval around it rather than a single point value.
skills.name: bootstrap-confidence-interval-estimation
skills.search_text: bootstrap-confidence-interval-estimation Use when reporting a cross-validated ROC AUC (or other performance metric) from a supervised metabolomics or chemometric classifier — e.g. OPLS-DA scores from GCxGC-TOFMS data — and you need a defensible interval around it rather than a single point value. The input is raw metabolite feature data (195 metabolites × 37 samples) rather than already cross-validated classifier scores — fit the OPLS-DA / PCA model first before bootstrapping the AUC. You need calibration or hypothesis-testing of the model itself (e.g. CV-ANOVA p = 0.0031 or p = 1.4×10−7) rather than uncertainty around a performance metric. Sample labels are continuous or multi-class without a defined positive class — ROC AUC and its bootstrap CI require a two-class comparison. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Estimates 95% confidence intervals around ROC AUC (and related classifier metrics) via bootstrap percentile resampling with 1,000 bootstraps, as used to qualify the OPLS-DA carriage-diagnostic AUCs in the Nepali cholecystectomy metabolomics study. Provides the uncertainty quantification that turns point AUC estimates from cross-validated pattern-recognition models into interpretable ranges. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pntd.0006215
skills.summary: Estimates 95% confidence intervals around ROC AUC (and related classifier metrics) via bootstrap percentile resampling with 1,000 bootstraps, as used to qualify the OPLS-DA carriage-diagnostic AUCs in the Nepali cholecystectomy metabolomics study. Provides the uncertainty quantification that turns point AUC estimates from cross-validated pattern-recognition models into interpretable ranges.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw metabolite feature data (195 metabolites × 37 samples) rather than already cross-validated classifier scores — fit the OPLS-DA / PCA model first before bootstrapping the AUC. You need calibration or hypothesis-testing of the model itself (e.g. CV-ANOVA p = 0.0031 or p = 1.4×10−7) rather than uncertainty around a performance metric. Sample labels are continuous or multi-class without a defined positive class — ROC AUC and its bootstrap CI require a two-class comparison.

skills.search_text: bootstrap-confidence-interval-estimation Use when NPP performance metrics (found peaks, split peaks, alignment loss, isotopologue-ratio degeneration) computed against an mzRAPP benchmark need point estimates with bootstrap CI bounds per pre-processing stage. Analyzing targeted peak-picking quality directly rather than assessing NPP output reliability against a benchmark.

skills.description: Use when reporting top-1/top-10 candidate ranking accuracies from a spectral retrieval benchmark and you need statistically grounded 95% confidence intervals rather than point estimates.

skills.search_text: bootstrap-confidence-interval-estimation Use when reporting top-1/top-10 candidate ranking accuracies from a spectral retrieval benchmark and you need statistically grounded 95% confidence intervals rather than point estimates. skills.summary: Estimate bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for retrieval top-k accuracy metrics (top-1/top-10 hit rates) when benchmarking ICEBERG against baseline spectrum prediction models on NPLIB1, NIST20, and CASMI22 candidate ranking tasks.

skills.search_text: bootstrap-empirical-pvalue-estimation Use when a concordance table of Cohen's kappa and Pearson correlation scores (e.g. RPS vs RAS, RPS vs FFD) is available and per-reaction significance of concordance must be assessed without a parametric null model. skills.description: Use when a fitted PathIntegrate Multi-View MB-PLS model (e.g. COPDgene, tuned to 4 latent variables) needs a resampling check that the per-block y-variance explained by each latent variable is stable, complementing permutation p-values on MB-VIP.
skills.name: bootstrap-variance-estimation
skills.search_text: bootstrap-variance-estimation Use when a fitted PathIntegrate Multi-View MB-PLS model (e.g. COPDgene, tuned to 4 latent variables) needs a resampling check that the per-block y-variance explained by each latent variable is stable, complementing permutation p-values on MB-VIP. The MB-PLS number of latent variables has not yet been tuned — run the 5-times repeated nested 5-fold cross-validation first The question of interest is pathway-level significance rather than stability of block-level explained variance — use MB-VIP permutation testing instead The omics views are not measured on the same individuals, since PathIntegrate cannot handle samples missing entire omics rows http://edamontology.org/topic_3577 Resampling-based stability assessment for PathIntegrate Multi-View MB-PLS models: refit the tuned multi-block PLS on 100 bootstrap resamples and record the y-variance explained per latent variable per omics view to show how stable each block's contribution is. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011814
skills.summary: Resampling-based stability assessment for PathIntegrate Multi-View MB-PLS models: refit the tuned multi-block PLS on 100 bootstrap resamples and record the y-variance explained per latent variable per omics view to show how stable each block's contribution is.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The MB-PLS number of latent variables has not yet been tuned — run the 5-times repeated nested 5-fold cross-validation first The question of interest is pathway-level significance rather than stability of block-level explained variance — use MB-VIP permutation testing instead The omics views are not measured on the same individuals, since PathIntegrate cannot handle samples missing entire omics rows

skills.description: Use when mzRAPP's derive_performance_metrics has produced Peak Picking (or alignment) metrics with bootstrapped confidence intervals on a Benchmark.csv-derived dataset and you must judge whether values such as the split-peaks percentage are within the expected range.
skills.name: bootstrapped-confidence-interval-interpretation
skills.search_text: bootstrapped-confidence-interval-interpretation Use when mzRAPP's derive_performance_metrics has produced Peak Picking (or alignment) metrics with bootstrapped confidence intervals on a Benchmark.csv-derived dataset and you must judge whether values such as the split-peaks percentage are within the expected range. The benchmark has not yet been generated and validated from user-supplied target/SampleGroups_MTBLS267.csv/Target_File_MTBLS267.csv inputs — match and metric derivation require a valid Benchmark.csv. The input is raw centroided mzML data rather than an NPP output table (XCMS, MZmine 2, MS-DIAL, etc.) — this skill interprets post-matching metric intervals, not raw spectra. The NPP tool output has no mzRAPP import function among the five supported pre-processing tools, so matching against the benchmark cannot be performed. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Interprets the NPP performance metrics that mzRAPP reports for benchmark-matched non-targeted pre-processing runs, where metrics such as the split-peaks proportion are accompanied by bootstrapped confidence intervals. For the MTBLS267/XCMS run 2 example, the split-peak percentage from the bootstrapped CI must fall within the 1–3% range stated in the article. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btab231
skills.summary: Interprets the NPP performance metrics that mzRAPP reports for benchmark-matched non-targeted pre-processing runs, where metrics such as the split-peaks proportion are accompanied by bootstrapped confidence intervals. For the MTBLS267/XCMS run 2 example, the split-peak percentage from the bootstrapped CI must fall within the 1–3% range stated in the article.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The benchmark has not yet been generated and validated from user-supplied target/SampleGroups_MTBLS267.csv/Target_File_MTBLS267.csv inputs — match and metric derivation require a valid Benchmark.csv. The input is raw centroided mzML data rather than an NPP output table (XCMS, MZmine 2, MS-DIAL, etc.) — this skill interprets post-matching metric intervals, not raw spectra. The NPP tool output has no mzRAPP import function among the five supported pre-processing tools, so matching against the benchmark cannot be performed.

skills.description: Use when performing overrepresentation analysis of imaging-MS (spatial or single-cell metabolomics) annotations where isomeric/isobaric ambiguities prevent conventional ORA, e.g. METASPACE formula-adduct results against LION or CoreMetabolome.
skills.name: bootstrapped-overrepresentation-analysis
skills.search_text: bootstrapped-overrepresentation-analysis Use when performing overrepresentation analysis of imaging-MS (spatial or single-cell metabolomics) annotations where isomeric/isobaric ambiguities prevent conventional ORA, e.g. METASPACE formula-adduct results against LION or CoreMetabolome. Rank-based analysis of quantitative abundance differences is needed — use Run_bootstrap_MSEA / MSEA instead of ORA Input is a feature table with unambiguous molecule structures (no isomeric/isobaric ambiguity), where conventional ORA suffices The annotation list uses non-lipid sum-formula features against LION, which only supports lipid name features http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Bootstrapping-based overrepresentation analysis (ORA) implemented in the S2IsoMEr R package and the METASPACE web app, which propagates isomeric/isobaric ambiguity of MS1 imaging annotations into enrichment results by running ORA over repeated random resolutions of ambiguous formula-adduct assignments. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioadv/vbaf100
skills.summary: Bootstrapping-based overrepresentation analysis (ORA) implemented in the S2IsoMEr R package and the METASPACE web app, which propagates isomeric/isobaric ambiguity of MS1 imaging annotations into enrichment results by running ORA over repeated random resolutions of ambiguous formula-adduct assignments.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Rank-based analysis of quantitative abundance differences is needed — use Run_bootstrap_MSEA / MSEA instead of ORA Input is a feature table with unambiguous molecule structures (no isomeric/isobaric ambiguity), where conventional ORA suffices The annotation list uses non-lipid sum-formula features against LION, which only supports lipid name features

skills.description: Use when performing ORA on MS1-only spatial or single-cell metabolomics data (METASPACE/HMDB-annotated ions) where isomers/isobars cannot be resolved and conventional ORA would give ambiguous hits.
skills.name: bootstrapping-based-ora-enrichment
skills.search_text: bootstrapping-based-ora-enrichment Use when performing ORA on MS1-only spatial or single-cell metabolomics data (METASPACE/HMDB-annotated ions) where isomers/isobars cannot be resolved and conventional ORA would give ambiguous hits. When metabolites are resolved structurally (e.g., MS/MS-identified) and conventional ORA/MSEA apply without ambiguity When the input is already an enrichment table or feature table rather than an annotated ion-by-cell/ion-by-pixel matrix For lipid-specific ontology queries needing LION terms — use the lipid/MSEA variant with annot_db 'LION' instead of the HMDB metabolite ORA path http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 S2IsoMEr-based overrepresentation analysis for imaging-MS (METASPACE) annotations that propagates isomeric/isobaric molecular ambiguity into enrichment results by running iterative random sampling (bootstrapping) of annotations and summarizing per-term enrichment statistics. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioadv/vbaf100
skills.summary: S2IsoMEr-based overrepresentation analysis for imaging-MS (METASPACE) annotations that propagates isomeric/isobaric molecular ambiguity into enrichment results by running iterative random sampling (bootstrapping) of annotations and summarizing per-term enrichment statistics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When metabolites are resolved structurally (e.g., MS/MS-identified) and conventional ORA/MSEA apply without ambiguity When the input is already an enrichment table or feature table rather than an annotated ion-by-cell/ion-by-pixel matrix For lipid-specific ontology queries needing LION terms — use the lipid/MSEA variant with annot_db 'LION' instead of the HMDB metabolite ORA path

skills.description: Use when pre-processing whole-sample MALDI MSI measurements where matrix/off-tissue pixels must be identified automatically without defining known matrix peaks in advance.
skills.name: border-connectivity-cluster-selection
skills.search_text: border-connectivity-cluster-selection Use when pre-processing whole-sample MALDI MSI measurements where matrix/off-tissue pixels must be identified automatically without defining known matrix peaks in advance. You already have a curated list of known matrix peaks to subtract — direct peak filtering suffices and border-connectivity detection is unnecessary The dataset is not a whole-sample measurement — the article notes the approach's applicability relies on tissue architecture and borders, so cropped/tissue-only regions lack the matrix shell it detects Performing the msi_segmentation_flow tissue segmentation itself — this skill targets matrix detection during pre-processing, not downstream dim. reduction/clustering for tissue segmentation http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 An unsupervised matrix/off-tissue pixel detection method for MALDI MSI in which UMAP-embedded pixel spectra are clustered with HDBSCAN and the cluster connected to the most border pixels of the measured area is designated as the matrix cluster. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-55306-7
skills.summary: An unsupervised matrix/off-tissue pixel detection method for MALDI MSI in which UMAP-embedded pixel spectra are clustered with HDBSCAN and the cluster connected to the most border pixels of the measured area is designated as the matrix cluster.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You already have a curated list of known matrix peaks to subtract — direct peak filtering suffices and border-connectivity detection is unnecessary The dataset is not a whole-sample measurement — the article notes the approach's applicability relies on tissue architecture and borders, so cropped/tissue-only regions lack the matrix shell it detects Performing the msi_segmentation_flow tissue segmentation itself — this skill targets matrix detection during pre-processing, not downstream dim. reduction/clustering for tissue segmentation

skills.description: Use when you have an SBML genome-scale metabolic model (e.g., iHsaEC21 or iAB-AMØ-1410 integrated with SARS-CoV-2) and need to identify flux-dependent chokepoint reactions as candidate drug targets.
skills.name: bottleneck-drug-target-identification
skills.search_text: bottleneck-drug-target-identification Use when you have an SBML genome-scale metabolic model (e.g., iHsaEC21 or iAB-AMØ-1410 integrated with SARS-CoV-2) and need to identify flux-dependent chokepoint reactions as candidate drug targets. The model still contains dead-end metabolites and has not been FVA-refined — unrefined bottleneck counts will not be comparable to the growth-dependent sets (e.g., 1,598 for the airway epithelial model, 1,595 for the macrophage model) The analysis goal is pathway enrichment or gene-expression deconvolution rather than identifying topologically essential reactions in a constraint-based metabolic model The input is not a constraint-based metabolic model in SBML format (findCPcli expects genome-scale SBML models) http://edamontology.org/topic_2259 http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 Computes chokepoint (bottleneck) reactions in genome-scale metabolic models using findCPcli, combining network topology with FVA-derived dynamic flux information to identify reactions required for SARS-CoV-2 maintenance and replication as candidate drug targets. metabolomics/v3 10.26508/lsa.202000954
skills.summary: Computes chokepoint (bottleneck) reactions in genome-scale metabolic models using findCPcli, combining network topology with FVA-derived dynamic flux information to identify reactions required for SARS-CoV-2 maintenance and replication as candidate drug targets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The model still contains dead-end metabolites and has not been FVA-refined — unrefined bottleneck counts will not be comparable to the growth-dependent sets (e.g., 1,598 for the airway epithelial model, 1,595 for the macrophage model) The analysis goal is pathway enrichment or gene-expression deconvolution rather than identifying topologically essential reactions in a constraint-based metabolic model The input is not a constraint-based metabolic model in SBML format (findCPcli expects genome-scale SBML models)

skills.description: Use when you have run ProGeM (or SNiPA) on sentinel mQTL variants and need to parse per-locus candidate gene calls, score sensitivity against a curated causal-gene reference, and benchmark false positives.
skills.name: bottom-up-candidate-gene-output-parsing
skills.search_text: bottom-up-candidate-gene-output-parsing Use when you have run ProGeM (or SNiPA) on sentinel mQTL variants and need to parse per-locus candidate gene calls, score sensitivity against a curated causal-gene reference, and benchmark false positives. You need top-down or cooccurring ('concurrent') candidate genes — parse 'OUTPUT_top_down_scores.txt' or the combined candidate strategy instead Your QTLs are trans-pQTLs, where ProGeM's positional top-down strategy is not directly applicable and a different approach is required No high-confidence reference causal gene set is available for your molecular QTL type, making sensitivity/FP scoring uninterpretable http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 Parse ProGeM's 'OUTPUT_bottom_up_summary.txt' to extract bottom-up candidate mediating genes per sentinel rsID, map them to a reference causal gene set, and compute sensitivity and false-positive counts (e.g. against the 227 curated mQTLs and tools like SNiPA). metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gky837
skills.summary: Parse ProGeM's 'OUTPUT_bottom_up_summary.txt' to extract bottom-up candidate mediating genes per sentinel rsID, map them to a reference causal gene set, and compute sensitivity and false-positive counts (e.g. against the 227 curated mQTLs and tools like SNiPA).
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need top-down or cooccurring ('concurrent') candidate genes — parse 'OUTPUT_top_down_scores.txt' or the combined candidate strategy instead Your QTLs are trans-pQTLs, where ProGeM's positional top-down strategy is not directly applicable and a different approach is required No high-confidence reference causal gene set is available for your molecular QTL type, making sensitivity/FP scoring uninterpretable

skills.description: Use when you have sentinel variants (with GRCh37 coordinates and optional LD proxies) at molecular QTLs and need to nominate candidate causal genes positionally and functionally, then benchmark those nominations against a high-confidence causal gene reference set.
skills.name: bottom-up-causal-gene-prioritization
skills.search_text: bottom-up-causal-gene-prioritization Use when you have sentinel variants (with GRCh37 coordinates and optional LD proxies) at molecular QTLs and need to nominate candidate causal genes positionally and functionally, then benchmark those nominations against a high-confidence causal gene reference set. The QTL is trans (e.g. trans-pQTL): ProGeM's top-down proximity-based strategy does not directly apply and a different approach would be needed No high-confidence reference causal gene assignments are available, so enrichment-based validation of the bottom-up criteria cannot be performed You need literature/text-mining or database-knowledge prioritisation of genes with no positional link to a sentinel variant (use top-down/complementary tools such as Phenolyzer instead) http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 Prioritises candidate causal genes at molecular QTLs using ProGeM's bottom-up criteria — nearest genes, LD-overlapping genes, cis-eQTL target genes, and VEP HIGH/MODERATE IMPACT variants — and validates them by Fisher's exact enrichment against high-confidence causal gene assignments. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gky837
skills.summary: Prioritises candidate causal genes at molecular QTLs using ProGeM's bottom-up criteria — nearest genes, LD-overlapping genes, cis-eQTL target genes, and VEP HIGH/MODERATE IMPACT variants — and validates them by Fisher's exact enrichment against high-confidence causal gene assignments.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The QTL is trans (e.g. trans-pQTL): ProGeM's top-down proximity-based strategy does not directly apply and a different approach would be needed No high-confidence reference causal gene assignments are available, so enrichment-based validation of the bottom-up criteria cannot be performed You need literature/text-mining or database-knowledge prioritisation of genes with no positional link to a sentinel variant (use top-down/complementary tools such as Phenolyzer instead)

skills.description: Use when running ProGeM on sentinel molecular QTL variants and you need the primary causal candidate list: genes that are simultaneously bottom-up (functional impact/proximity/eQTL) and top-down (local metabolic annotation) candidates.
skills.name: bottom-up-top-down-candidate-intersection
skills.search_text: bottom-up-top-down-candidate-intersection Use when running ProGeM on sentinel molecular QTL variants and you need the primary causal candidate list: genes that are simultaneously bottom-up (functional impact/proximity/eQTL) and top-down (local metabolic annotation) candidates. The locus has no credible set / proxy information and no VEP output, so bottom-up candidates cannot be assembled and the intersection would be empty by construction The molecular phenotype is not metabolism-related and no replacement top-down .RData gene list (e.g. lipidomics) has been prepared for the phenotype in question Analysing trans-pQTLs, where the article states the top-down local-window strategy does not directly apply http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 Derives ProGeM 'cooccurring' candidate causal genes by intersecting, per sentinel variant, the bottom-up candidates (nearest genes, LD-overlapping genes, cis-eQTL targets, VEP HIGH/MODERATE IMPACT genes) with top-down candidates (local genes annotated as metabolic by GO, KEGG, Orphanet, Reactome and MGI), so that only genes satisfying both causal assumptions are prioritised. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gky837
skills.summary: Derives ProGeM 'cooccurring' candidate causal genes by intersecting, per sentinel variant, the bottom-up candidates (nearest genes, LD-overlapping genes, cis-eQTL targets, VEP HIGH/MODERATE IMPACT genes) with top-down candidates (local genes annotated as metabolic by GO, KEGG, Orphanet, Reactome and MGI), so that only genes satisfying both causal assumptions are prioritised.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The locus has no credible set / proxy information and no VEP output, so bottom-up candidates cannot be assembled and the intersection would be empty by construction The molecular phenotype is not metabolism-related and no replacement top-down .RData gene list (e.g. lipidomics) has been prepared for the phenotype in question Analysing trans-pQTLs, where the article states the top-down local-window strategy does not directly apply

skills.description: Use when you have time-series extracellular metabolomics (intensities at a start and end time point) and need to infer which reactions are active or missing from a KEGG-based organism network.
skills.name: boundary-flux-calculation
skills.search_text: boundary-flux-calculation Use when you have time-series extracellular metabolomics (intensities at a start and end time point) and need to infer which reactions are active or missing from a KEGG-based organism network. When intracellular flux estimation with isotope tracing or FBA is required for absolute reaction rates - boundary fluxes from intensity profiles are semi-quantitative only When the organism's metabolic network is already complete and validated, leaving no missing reactions to infer When the metabolomics dataset lacks paired time points or a consistent time interval, as the flux is defined by change between two time points http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 Quantifies directional change of extracellular metabolite intensities between paired time points (e.g. 0 h vs 72 h Borrelia cultures) to label boundary metabolites as consumed or produced, enabling inference of missing metabolic reactions such as purine and pyrimidine pathway steps. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c04501
skills.summary: Quantifies directional change of extracellular metabolite intensities between paired time points (e.g. 0 h vs 72 h Borrelia cultures) to label boundary metabolites as consumed or produced, enabling inference of missing metabolic reactions such as purine and pyrimidine pathway steps.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When intracellular flux estimation with isotope tracing or FBA is required for absolute reaction rates - boundary fluxes from intensity profiles are semi-quantitative only When the organism's metabolic network is already complete and validated, leaving no missing reactions to infer When the metabolomics dataset lacks paired time points or a consistent time interval, as the flux is defined by change between two time points

skills.description: Use when you have time-resolved metabolomics intensity data and/or boundary fluxes for an organism and want to identify reactions absent from KEGG (e.g., flagged light-gray nodes/edges) in a species-specific metabolic network.
skills.name: boundary-flux-network-overlay
skills.search_text: boundary-flux-network-overlay Use when you have time-resolved metabolomics intensity data and/or boundary fluxes for an organism and want to identify reactions absent from KEGG (e.g., flagged light-gray nodes/edges) in a species-specific metabolic network. Input lacks empirical metabolomics intensity or boundary-flux data (only genomic annotation is available) — MINNO's refinement loop requires metabolite evidence to flag missing reactions The goal is a genome-scale stoichiometric FBA model rather than visual network refinement — MINNO explicitly avoids complex mathematical modeling and can access BiGG models only for network viewing http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Overlay empirical temporal metabolite intensity profiles and boundary fluxes (e.g., extracellular consumption/secretion, isotope labeling) onto a KEGG/NCBI-RefSeq-derived organism-specific metabolic network in MINNO to visually flag disconnected nodes and missing reactions, without complex mathematical modeling. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c04501
skills.summary: Overlay empirical temporal metabolite intensity profiles and boundary fluxes (e.g., extracellular consumption/secretion, isotope labeling) onto a KEGG/NCBI-RefSeq-derived organism-specific metabolic network in MINNO to visually flag disconnected nodes and missing reactions, without complex mathematical modeling.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input lacks empirical metabolomics intensity or boundary-flux data (only genomic annotation is available) — MINNO's refinement loop requires metabolite evidence to flag missing reactions The goal is a genome-scale stoichiometric FBA model rather than visual network refinement — MINNO explicitly avoids complex mathematical modeling and can access BiGG models only for network viewing

skills.description: Use when you must fit nonlinear (e.g. extended log-normal kernel) models to CE-dependent fragment intensities and need robust global parameter estimates via bounded grid search plus Levenberg-Marquardt refinement.
skills.name: bounded-grid-search-parameter-estimation
skills.search_text: bounded-grid-search-parameter-estimation Use when you must fit nonlinear (e.g. extended log-normal kernel) models to CE-dependent fragment intensities and need robust global parameter estimates via bounded grid search plus Levenberg-Marquardt refinement. No CE-dependent fragmentation measurements exist for the target lipid class — LipidCreator's CE models are currently exclusive to lipid mediators and expansion requires more structurally diverse lipid standards and CE-dependent measurements of their fragmentation behavior The data lack a swept independent variable (e.g. collision energy) — the bounded grid search over kernel parameters presumes CE-dependent relative intensities to fit dissociation profiles against http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Fits fragment-specific nonlinear regression models (an extended log-normal kernel) to collision-energy-dependent relative fragment intensities using minpack.lm's Levenberg-Marquardt least squares, stabilized by nls.multstart's bounded grid search for robust starting values and global fits. Used by LipidCreator/flipR to model dissociation profiles on QExactive HF (NCE 10–60) and QTOF (CE 10–100) instruments. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-020-15960-z
skills.summary: Fits fragment-specific nonlinear regression models (an extended log-normal kernel) to collision-energy-dependent relative fragment intensities using minpack.lm's Levenberg-Marquardt least squares, stabilized by nls.multstart's bounded grid search for robust starting values and global fits. Used by LipidCreator/flipR to model dissociation profiles on QExactive HF (NCE 10–60) and QTOF (CE 10–100) instruments.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No CE-dependent fragmentation measurements exist for the target lipid class — LipidCreator's CE models are currently exclusive to lipid mediators and expansion requires more structurally diverse lipid standards and CE-dependent measurements of their fragmentation behavior The data lack a swept independent variable (e.g. collision energy) — the bounded grid search over kernel parameters presumes CE-dependent relative intensities to fit dissociation profiles against

skills.description: Use when selecting or validating Bowtie2 alignment mode/preset for metagenomic read mapping to gene cluster references, or when reproducibly benchmarking abundance-profiling accuracy against simulated libraries with known abundances.
skills.name: bowtie2-alignment-mode-comparison
skills.search_text: bowtie2-alignment-mode-comparison Use when selecting or validating Bowtie2 alignment mode/preset for metagenomic read mapping to gene cluster references, or when reproducibly benchmarking abundance-profiling accuracy against simulated libraries with known abundances. When only real (non-simulated) metagenomes are available and no ground-truth abundances exist — F1 against truth cannot be computed; use differential-abundance analysis instead When the goal is GCF grouping rather than mapping-parameter selection — use the BiG-SCAPE redundancy-filtering step of bigmap-family, not alignment-mode tuning http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Benchmark Bowtie2 end-to-end vs. local alignment modes (including the 'fast' preset) by mapping reads to non-redundant representative gene clusters and scoring abundance calls against known ground truth with precision/recall/F1. In the BiG-MAP mock-community benchmark, MASH similarity 0.8 plus Bowtie2 'fast' end-to-end mode yielded the best F1 and became the tool defaults. metabolomics/v3 10.1128/msystems.00937-21
skills.summary: Benchmark Bowtie2 end-to-end vs. local alignment modes (including the 'fast' preset) by mapping reads to non-redundant representative gene clusters and scoring abundance calls against known ground truth with precision/recall/F1. In the BiG-MAP mock-community benchmark, MASH similarity 0.8 plus Bowtie2 'fast' end-to-end mode yielded the best F1 and became the tool defaults.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When only real (non-simulated) metagenomes are available and no ground-truth abundances exist — F1 against truth cannot be computed; use differential-abundance analysis instead When the goal is GCF grouping rather than mapping-parameter selection — use the BiG-SCAPE redundancy-filtering step of bigmap-family, not alignment-mode tuning

skills.description: Use when a FASTA of dereplicated representative gene cluster sequences (e.g., BiG-MAP.GCF.fna from bigmap-family) must be indexed with Bowtie2 so FASTQ shotgun reads can be mapped for MGC/GCF abundance and coverage profiling.
skills.name: bowtie2-index-construction
skills.search_text: bowtie2-index-construction Use when a FASTA of dereplicated representative gene cluster sequences (e.g., BiG-MAP.GCF.fna from bigmap-family) must be indexed with Bowtie2 so FASTQ shotgun reads can be mapped for MGC/GCF abundance and coverage profiling. Gene clusters have not been redundancy-filtered first — indexing raw antiSMASH/gutSMASH output without the MASH (0.8 similarity) or BiG-SCAPE step will cause ambiguous mapping of reads across near-identical clusters. The goal is functional pathway quantification against reference databases (e.g., KEGG/MetaCyc) rather than gene cluster abundance — BiG-MAP deliberately does not depend on such pathway databases. Input data are amplicon reads rather than shotgun metagenomic/metatranscriptomic reads, which the mapping-to-reference-clusters design does not address. http://edamontology.org/topic_0114 Constructs Bowtie2 indices from medoid-selected representative metabolic gene cluster (MGC/GCF) nucleotide sequences so metagenomic/metatranscriptomic reads can be mapped to quantify gene cluster abundance (counts, TPM/RPKM) and coverage in BiG-MAP. metabolomics/v3 10.1128/msystems.00937-21
skills.summary: Constructs Bowtie2 indices from medoid-selected representative metabolic gene cluster (MGC/GCF) nucleotide sequences so metagenomic/metatranscriptomic reads can be mapped to quantify gene cluster abundance (counts, TPM/RPKM) and coverage in BiG-MAP.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Gene clusters have not been redundancy-filtered first — indexing raw antiSMASH/gutSMASH output without the MASH (0.8 similarity) or BiG-SCAPE step will cause ambiguous mapping of reads across near-identical clusters. The goal is functional pathway quantification against reference databases (e.g., KEGG/MetaCyc) rather than gene cluster abundance — BiG-MAP deliberately does not depend on such pathway databases. Input data are amplicon reads rather than shotgun metagenomic/metatranscriptomic reads, which the mapping-to-reference-clusters design does not address.

skills.description: Use when a model has been retrained many times (e.g., 20 sessions of 10-fold cross-validation) under several configurations of a numeric factor (e.g., number of data Augmentations), and you must compare central tendency AND variability of AUC distributions rather than single-point scores.
skills.name: boxplot-distribution-analysis-of-model-variability
skills.search_text: boxplot-distribution-analysis-of-model-variability Use when a model has been retrained many times (e.g., 20 sessions of 10-fold cross-validation) under several configurations of a numeric factor (e.g., number of data Augmentations), and you must compare central tendency AND variability of AUC distributions rather than single-point scores. You have only a single train/test split or one cross-validation run, so there is no distribution of AUC values to summarize as a box plot The comparison factor is a single pairwise contrast (e.g., baseline vs CHESHIRE only) rather than an ordered multi-level ablation such as 1/3/5/7 Augmentations The output metric is deterministic (no session-to-session variance), making whisker-range analysis of variability meaningless http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Aggregates micro-average AUC results from repeated cross-validation sessions (e.g., 20 sessions of 10-fold CV) into per-configuration box plots (median, mean, maximum AUC, interquartile range, and whisker range) to quantify both central performance and run-to-run variability of a model, as done for NetAurHPD across 0/1/3/5/7 data Augmentations. metabolomics/v3 10.48550/arxiv.2410.22030
skills.summary: Aggregates micro-average AUC results from repeated cross-validation sessions (e.g., 20 sessions of 10-fold CV) into per-configuration box plots (median, mean, maximum AUC, interquartile range, and whisker range) to quantify both central performance and run-to-run variability of a model, as done for NetAurHPD across 0/1/3/5/7 data Augmentations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have only a single train/test split or one cross-validation run, so there is no distribution of AUC values to summarize as a box plot The comparison factor is a single pairwise contrast (e.g., baseline vs CHESHIRE only) rather than an ordered multi-level ablation such as 1/3/5/7 Augmentations The output metric is deterministic (no session-to-session variance), making whisker-range analysis of variability meaningless

skills.description: Use when a large multi-batch MRM dataset contains batch-pooled QC (BQC) samples and you need to quantify whether batch-effect correction (e.g., QC-RLSC) removed injection-order drift.
skills.name: bqc-regression-slope-r2-evaluation
skills.search_text: bqc-regression-slope-r2-evaluation Use when a large multi-batch MRM dataset contains batch-pooled QC (BQC) samples and you need to quantify whether batch-effect correction (e.g., QC-RLSC) removed injection-order drift. The dataset contains no QC or batch-pooled QC samples, so batch-effect correction and its regression-based evaluation are not applicable The goal is comparing peak-detection/quantitation accuracy across tools (e.g., coeluted or noisy peak handling) rather than assessing batch-effect correction Abundance drift must be assessed against something other than injection order (e.g., RT drift), since this skill specifically fits BQC abundance vs injection order http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Evaluates batch-effect correction quality in targeted MRM metabolomics by regressing batch-pooled QC (BQC) abundances against injection order and comparing regression slope and R2 before vs after QC-RLSC correction; successful correction flattens the BQC regression line. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c02462
skills.summary: Evaluates batch-effect correction quality in targeted MRM metabolomics by regressing batch-pooled QC (BQC) abundances against injection order and comparing regression slope and R2 before vs after QC-RLSC correction; successful correction flattens the BQC regression line.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset contains no QC or batch-pooled QC samples, so batch-effect correction and its regression-based evaluation are not applicable The goal is comparing peak-detection/quantitation accuracy across tools (e.g., coeluted or noisy peak handling) rather than assessing batch-effect correction Abundance drift must be assessed against something other than injection order (e.g., RT drift), since this skill specifically fits BQC abundance vs injection order

skills.description: Use when targeted LC-MS/MS peak areas (e.g. MultiQuant exports) show intensity drift over the injection sequence and calibration standards are interspersed with samples, especially when internal standards are unavailable or unsuitable.
skills.name: bracketing-based-quantification
skills.search_text: bracketing-based-quantification Use when targeted LC-MS/MS peak areas (e.g. MultiQuant exports) show intensity drift over the injection sequence and calibration standards are interspersed with samples, especially when internal standards are unavailable or unsuitable. Input is raw, unintegrated chromatographic data — QuantyFey works as additional software on already-integrated MS data and provides no integration capabilities The dataset shows no intensity drift over the injection sequence, so a single default bracketing baseline (no drift correction) suffices Compound-specific cases where analyte and analogue trends diverge (e.g. 4-hydroxy-proline, methionine sulfoxide) — bracketing strategy choice must be tailored per compound http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Quantify targeted LC-MS/MS analytes against calibration curves positioned around sample blocks (custom bracketing) or weighted by sample position between consecutive calibration curves (weighted bracketing), as implemented in the QuantyFey Shiny app to compensate for signal intensity drift. metabolomics/v3 10.1016/j.aca.2025.344571
skills.summary: Quantify targeted LC-MS/MS analytes against calibration curves positioned around sample blocks (custom bracketing) or weighted by sample position between consecutive calibration curves (weighted bracketing), as implemented in the QuantyFey Shiny app to compensate for signal intensity drift.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw, unintegrated chromatographic data — QuantyFey works as additional software on already-integrated MS data and provides no integration capabilities The dataset shows no intensity drift over the injection sequence, so a single default bracketing baseline (no drift correction) suffices Compound-specific cases where analyte and analogue trends diverge (e.g. 4-hydroxy-proline, methionine sulfoxide) — bracketing strategy choice must be tailored per compound

skills.summary: Annotates DEREPLICATOR+ metabolite fragmentation graphs breadth-first with preprocessed tandem MS peaks and scores metabolite-spectrum matches (MSMs) as the number of unique spectrum masses that annotate a graph node, feeding the Poisson-binomial P-value/FDR evaluation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The target metabolite class or fragmentation graph is not expressible under the C–N/C–O 2-cut and single C–C cut rules (DEREPLICATOR+ is not applicable to all classes of compounds) The spectra are not centroided or not in an open format (MGF, mzXML, mzML, mzData) The goal is identification of peptidic natural products specifically, where the original DEREPLICATOR PNP pipeline (rather than fragmentation-graph dereplication) applies

The input is already a peak-picked or extracted feature table — NPFimg is designed to operate directly on the two-dimensional MS map without conventional peak picking The analysis requires the conventional peak-picking workflow (e.g. XCMS-style peak detection) rather than image-based marker identification http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Applies NPFimg, an image-processing and machine-learning method, to two-dimensional GC–MS maps (m/z vs retention time) of human breath to identify multivariate chemo-/biomarker features without conventional peak picking, even at parts-per-billion analyte levels. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c03163

skills.description: Use when generating in silico MS/MS fragmentation candidates for small molecules from structure databases (e.g., SMILES/SDF, 0-2000 Da), especially when enumerating all possible single- and double-bond disconnections efficiently is needed for spectral matching.
skills.name: bridge-and-cut-detection-in-molecular-graphs
skills.search_text: bridge-and-cut-detection-in-molecular-graphs Use when generating in silico MS/MS fragmentation candidates for small molecules from structure databases (e.g., SMILES/SDF, 0-2000 Da), especially when enumerating all possible single- and double-bond disconnections efficiently is needed for spectral matching. The input is already a peak list or mass spectrum rather than a molecular structure — this skill generates fragments from structures, not from spectra Accurate prediction requires modeling resonance-aware fragmentation: molDiscovery naively treats benzene rings and large resonant structures as alternating single/double bonds The molecule requires fragmentation rules beyond N-C, O-C, and C-C bond disconnections, since only a limited number of bond types and rearrangement rules are covered http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 An efficient graph algorithm used by molDiscovery to generate mass spectrometry fragmentations: it detects bridges and 2-cuts in molecular graphs (atoms as nodes, bonds as edges) to enumerate single- and double-bond-cut fragments for spectral matching in database search of small molecules. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-021-23986-0
skills.summary: An efficient graph algorithm used by molDiscovery to generate mass spectrometry fragmentations: it detects bridges and 2-cuts in molecular graphs (atoms as nodes, bonds as edges) to enumerate single- and double-bond-cut fragments for spectral matching in database search of small molecules.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a peak list or mass spectrum rather than a molecular structure — this skill generates fragments from structures, not from spectra Accurate prediction requires modeling resonance-aware fragmentation: molDiscovery naively treats benzene rings and large resonant structures as alternating single/double bonds The molecule requires fragmentation rules beyond N-C, O-C, and C-C bond disconnections, since only a limited number of bond types and rearrangement rules are covered

skills.description: Use when a SIRIUS/ZODIAC-annotated molecular formula contains Br (or another element with a distinctive isotope signature) and the MS1 isotope pattern of the annotated precursor peak can be extracted to confirm or refute the formula assignment.
skills.name: bromine-isotope-signature-interpretation
skills.search_text: bromine-isotope-signature-interpretation Use when a SIRIUS/ZODIAC-annotated molecular formula contains Br (or another element with a distinctive isotope signature) and the MS1 isotope pattern of the annotated precursor peak can be extracted to confirm or refute the formula assignment. The goal is de novo molecular formula annotation from MS/MS fragmentation trees (SIRIUS/ZODIAC ranking), not validation of an already-annotated formula against its MS1 isotope pattern. The adduct type of the precursor is unknown — the paper notes adduct information cannot be reliably deduced from isotope pattern and MS/MS data, so a [M+H]+ assumption must come from preprocessing. The query compound's M+2 intensity pattern is expected to be weak or ambiguous (no halogen; e.g. a single Cl gives only ~32% M+2, not the near-100% bromine signature), leaving the pattern non-diagnostic. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Validates a bromine-containing molecular formula annotation (e.g. the novel ZODIAC formula C24H47BrNO8P from the diatoms dataset) by comparing the measured high-resolution MS1 isotope pattern against a SIRIUS-simulated pattern, exploiting the diagnostic ~50:50 79Br/81Br signature that places M+2 at ~100% of the monoisotopic peak. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s42256-020-00234-6
skills.summary: Validates a bromine-containing molecular formula annotation (e.g. the novel ZODIAC formula C24H47BrNO8P from the diatoms dataset) by comparing the measured high-resolution MS1 isotope pattern against a SIRIUS-simulated pattern, exploiting the diagnostic ~50:50 79Br/81Br signature that places M+2 at ~100% of the monoisotopic peak.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is de novo molecular formula annotation from MS/MS fragmentation trees (SIRIUS/ZODIAC ranking), not validation of an already-annotated formula against its MS1 isotope pattern. The adduct type of the precursor is unknown — the paper notes adduct information cannot be reliably deduced from isotope pattern and MS/MS data, so a [M+H]+ assumption must come from preprocessing. The query compound's M+2 intensity pattern is expected to be weak or ambiguous (no halogen; e.g. a single Cl gives only ~32% M+2, not the near-100% bromine signature), leaving the pattern non-diagnostic.

skills.summary: An RSelenium-driven browser call-out to the KEGG database used inside metGWAS 1.0's Module 1 to retrieve the metabolite entries belonging to each significant KEGG pathway and return them as HMDB IDs.

skills.description: Use when the goal is to embed or reuse an interactive 3D ordination visualization (e.g. PCoA plots) inside another tool or web page, and you need to confirm it renders correctly in a browser.
skills.name: browser-based-visualization-component-testing
skills.search_text: browser-based-visualization-component-testing Use when the goal is to embed or reuse an interactive 3D ordination visualization (e.g. PCoA plots) inside another tool or web page, and you need to confirm it renders correctly in a browser. Input is raw sequencing reads or a feature table — this skill assumes ordination results already computed upstream (PCoA on a beta diversity distance matrix), not raw data processing. The target environment must render WebGL/HTML5 in a specific browser; per the paper's requirements, the graphical user interface requires Chrome, so this skill is not the right choice when the consumer must use a browser without WebGL support or a non-Chrome engine. The task is a static publication figure rather than an interactive embedded component; EMPeror's value here is interactive manipulation and metadata-driven recoloring, which a static image does not need. http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Validates that EMPeror's interactive 3D principal-coordinates visualization can be generated from QIIME PCoA and mapping files and embedded as a reusable component in a host web page, without extra plugins. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/2047-217x-2-16
skills.summary: Validates that EMPeror's interactive 3D principal-coordinates visualization can be generated from QIIME PCoA and mapping files and embedded as a reusable component in a host web page, without extra plugins.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sequencing reads or a feature table — this skill assumes ordination results already computed upstream (PCoA on a beta diversity distance matrix), not raw data processing.
