It was used to show that cyclopropane-containing N-acyl GPEs (e.g., GPE 13:1, m/z 496.2317) accumulating in hacl-1 mutants are food-derived. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-022-28391-9
skills.summary: An untargeted comparative metabolomics workflow in Metaboseek that tests whether worm-enriched metabolites derive from the bacterial food source by comparing feature intensities between worms fed OP50 and the cyclopropane-deficient E. coli strain JW1653-1. It was used to show that cyclopropane-containing N-acyl GPEs (e.g., GPE 13:1, m/z 496.2317) accumulating in hacl-1 mutants are food-derived.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is formula prediction or structural filtering of already-annotated features (Seven Golden Rules element/valence/H/C filters), not tracing features to the bacterial diet The dataset lacks matched worm groups fed both the wild-type diet (OP50) and the modified bacterial strain (e.g., JW1653-1), so no diet-contrast can be computed Input is raw MS/MS spectra for spectral similarity search rather than comparative feature-intensity data across biological replicates

skills.description: Use when a C. elegans genetics article reports per-genotype quantitative phenotypes (e.g. DAPI-stained body counts at diakinesis in Results figures such as 1E, 6C, S5E) that must be extracted verbatim into a machine-readable table.
skills.name: c-elegans-mutant-genotype-phenotype-curation
skills.search_text: c-elegans-mutant-genotype-phenotype-curation Use when a C. elegans genetics article reports per-genotype quantitative phenotypes (e.g. DAPI-stained body counts at diakinesis in Results figures such as 1E, 6C, S5E) that must be extracted verbatim into a machine-readable table. The phenotype of interest is only shown as a plotted panel with no numeric mean (±SD) stated in the Results text — extraction would require re-measurement, not curation The question concerns molecular interactions or localization (e.g. BTR complex recruitment, GFP::MSH-5 focus dynamics) rather than per-genotype quantitative phenotype values Input is raw imaging data (DAPI-stained nuclei) that must be counted de novo; this skill only curates counts already published in the article Curates quantitative genotype-phenotype data reported in C. elegans meiosis papers — e.g. mean (±SD) DAPI-stained body counts at diakinesis for alleles such as rtel-1, top-3-ZnF, rmh-2(jf94) — into a structured genotype -> (mean, SD, source figure) table, preserving verbatim published values. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkac408
skills.summary: Curates quantitative genotype-phenotype data reported in C. elegans meiosis papers — e.g. mean (±SD) DAPI-stained body counts at diakinesis for alleles such as rtel-1, top-3-ZnF, rmh-2(jf94) — into a structured genotype -> (mean, SD, source figure) table, preserving verbatim published values.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The phenotype of interest is only shown as a plotted panel with no numeric mean (±SD) stated in the Results text — extraction would require re-measurement, not curation The question concerns molecular interactions or localization (e.g. BTR complex recruitment, GFP::MSH-5 focus dynamics) rather than per-genotype quantitative phenotype values Input is raw imaging data (DAPI-stained nuclei) that must be counted de novo; this skill only curates counts already published in the article

skills.description: Use when two weighted mortality/risk scores must be compared for discrimination in a prospective cohort — e.g., C-statistic differences for 5- and 10-year follow-up windows, optionally stratified by age.
skills.name: c-statistic-discrimination-analysis
skills.search_text: c-statistic-discrimination-analysis Use when two weighted mortality/risk scores must be compared for discrimination in a prospective cohort — e.g., C-statistic differences for 5- and 10-year follow-up windows, optionally stratified by age. The goal is biomarker discovery rather than head-to-head comparison of two pre-specified risk scores — use the stepwise forward-backward selection procedure instead. The score is intended for clinical patient classification: the article warns the biomarker score 'is not yet suitable for classification of patients in the clinic, since it is based on scaled biomarker values created separately for each cohort'. The outcome is not right-censored survival data amenable to a Cox model with age as the time scale. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Compares predictive discrimination of competing risk scores (e.g., a metabolic biomarker score vs. a conventional risk factor score) by fitting Cox proportional hazards models with age as the time scale and reporting Harrell's C-statistic differences and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI). metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-019-11311-9
skills.summary: Compares predictive discrimination of competing risk scores (e.g., a metabolic biomarker score vs. a conventional risk factor score) by fitting Cox proportional hazards models with age as the time scale and reporting Harrell's C-statistic differences and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is biomarker discovery rather than head-to-head comparison of two pre-specified risk scores — use the stepwise forward-backward selection procedure instead. The score is intended for clinical patient classification: the article warns the biomarker score 'is not yet suitable for classification of patients in the clinic, since it is based on scaled biomarker values created separately for each cohort'. The outcome is not right-censored survival data amenable to a Cox model with age as the time scale.

skills.description: Use when two nested mortality-prediction models must be compared in an independent validation cohort to decide whether adding predictors (e.g., conventional risk factors to 14 metabolic biomarkers) improves 5- or 10-year risk prediction.
skills.name: c-statistic-model-comparison-survival
skills.search_text: c-statistic-model-comparison-survival Use when two nested mortality-prediction models must be compared in an independent validation cohort to decide whether adding predictors (e.g., conventional risk factors to 14 metabolic biomarkers) improves 5- or 10-year risk prediction. The goal is selecting which biomarkers independently associate with mortality — use the stepwise forward-backward meta-analysis procedure with the Bonferroni threshold of 2.21 × 10^-4 (0.05/226) instead Model weights would be estimated and evaluated on the same cohort, overestimating predictive ability — weights must come from a separate training cohort (here, Estonian Biobank) The outcome is not time-to-event mortality or no validation cohort independent of the weight-estimation cohort is available http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Compares the predictive accuracy of two nested survival models (e.g., a metabolic biomarker score vs. a combined score with conventional risk factors) using Harrell's C-statistics for 5- and 10-year mortality plus integrated discrimination improvement (IDI), evaluated in a held-out validation cohort. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-019-11311-9
skills.summary: Compares the predictive accuracy of two nested survival models (e.g., a metabolic biomarker score vs. a combined score with conventional risk factors) using Harrell's C-statistics for 5- and 10-year mortality plus integrated discrimination improvement (IDI), evaluated in a held-out validation cohort.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is selecting which biomarkers independently associate with mortality — use the stepwise forward-backward meta-analysis procedure with the Bonferroni threshold of 2.21 × 10^-4 (0.05/226) instead Model weights would be estimated and evaluated on the same cohort, overestimating predictive ability — weights must come from a separate training cohort (here, Estonian Biobank) The outcome is not time-to-event mortality or no validation cohort independent of the weight-estimation cohort is available

skills.description: Use when a GC-MS hit-table compound (e.g. from Agilent Unknowns Analysis) has no PubChem CID after webchem get_cid() lookup, and a canonical SMILES plus simulated mass/structure data is needed to keep the compound in the spread database.
skills.name: cactus-canonical-smiles-fallback-lookup
skills.search_text: cactus-canonical-smiles-fallback-lookup Use when a GC-MS hit-table compound (e.g. from Agilent Unknowns Analysis) has no PubChem CID after webchem get_cid() lookup, and a canonical SMILES plus simulated mass/structure data is needed to keep the compound in the spread database. The compound already resolves to a PubChem CID with exact monoisotopic mass — the CACTUS fallback is only for CID-less compounds Data are MS2, MS3, or ion mobility + MS2 — uafR's published-spectrum-dependent algorithms (and hence this annotation step) do not yet apply Input is not a vendor peak table with the strict uafR column schema (e.g. already a processed feature table) http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 A fallback resolution step in the uafR spreadOut() pipeline: compounds from the Agilent Unknowns Analysis hit table that lack a PubChem CID are sent to the NCI CACTUS resolver to obtain a canonical SMILES, which is then used to simulate mass and structure data so every tentative compound can be represented in the spread database. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pone.0306202
skills.summary: A fallback resolution step in the uafR spreadOut() pipeline: compounds from the Agilent Unknowns Analysis hit table that lack a PubChem CID are sent to the NCI CACTUS resolver to obtain a canonical SMILES, which is then used to simulate mass and structure data so every tentative compound can be represented in the spread database.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The compound already resolves to a PubChem CID with exact monoisotopic mass — the CACTUS fallback is only for CID-less compounds Data are MS2, MS3, or ion mobility + MS2 — uafR's published-spectrum-dependent algorithms (and hence this annotation step) do not yet apply Input is not a vendor peak table with the strict uafR column schema (e.g. already a processed feature table)

skills.description: Use when the input is a tabular time series of intensity/signal values per recording trace (e.g. optical recordings of neuron activity) and the goal is to remove baseline offsets or compute AUC over the time axis.
skills.name: calcium-imaging-trace-processing
skills.search_text: calcium-imaging-trace-processing Use when the input is a tabular time series of intensity/signal values per recording trace (e.g. optical recordings of neuron activity) and the goal is to remove baseline offsets or compute AUC over the time axis. Data are high-dimensional omics measurements (gene/protein expression matrices) rather than continuous signal-over-time traces - use clustering/dimensional-reduction workflows instead. Only a single static value per condition is available (e.g. densitometric immunoblot bands or qPCR Ct values) with no time axis, since baseline correction and AUC require a continuous time series. Raw imaging frames rather than extracted intensity-vs-time traces - trace extraction must happen before this correction step. Baseline-correct and quantitate continuous optical activity traces, such as bundled POMC neuron recordings, by subtracting per-trace pre-stimulus mean intensity and optionally extracting area-under-the-curve metrics interactively. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41598-018-31154-6
skills.summary: Baseline-correct and quantitate continuous optical activity traces, such as bundled POMC neuron recordings, by subtracting per-trace pre-stimulus mean intensity and optionally extracting area-under-the-curve metrics interactively.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are high-dimensional omics measurements (gene/protein expression matrices) rather than continuous signal-over-time traces - use clustering/dimensional-reduction workflows instead. Only a single static value per condition is available (e.g. densitometric immunoblot bands or qPCR Ct values) with no time axis, since baseline correction and AUC require a continuous time series. Raw imaging frames rather than extracted intensity-vs-time traces - trace extraction must happen before this correction step.

skills.description: Use when a CCS calibration workflow needs calibrant ion drift/arrival times: raw IMS-MS data is in MZA (HDF5) format and per-calibrant ATDs and IonMobilityTime metadata must be pulled before fitting a calibration.
skills.name: calibrant-arrival-time-extraction
skills.search_text: calibrant-arrival-time-extraction Use when a CCS calibration workflow needs calibrant ion drift/arrival times: raw IMS-MS data is in MZA (HDF5) format and per-calibrant ATDs and IonMobilityTime metadata must be pulled before fitting a calibration. The data is not in MZA format or has no ion mobility dimension — mzapy targets 'complex data containing the ion mobility spectrometry dimension' and MZA files; plain LC-MS-only data needs no ATD extraction. Only mass calibration (no CCS) is needed — mass calibration uses mzapy.calibration.MassCalibration on m/z data and does not require arrival-time distributions. The file only contains pre-computed vendor CCS calibration coefficients (CCScalDT, CCScalSLIM, CCScalTIMS stored as HDF5 datasets during conversion) and no new calibrant ATDs need to be measured. Extracts arrival-time distributions (ATDs) and ion-mobility metadata headers for calibrant ions from raw IMS-MS data stored in the MZA/HDF5 format using mzapy.MZA, providing the drift/arrival-time inputs required for downstream CCS calibration. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c01653
skills.summary: Extracts arrival-time distributions (ATDs) and ion-mobility metadata headers for calibrant ions from raw IMS-MS data stored in the MZA/HDF5 format using mzapy.MZA, providing the drift/arrival-time inputs required for downstream CCS calibration.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data is not in MZA format or has no ion mobility dimension — mzapy targets 'complex data containing the ion mobility spectrometry dimension' and MZA files; plain LC-MS-only data needs no ATD extraction. Only mass calibration (no CCS) is needed — mass calibration uses mzapy.calibration.MassCalibration on m/z data and does not require arrival-time distributions. The file only contains pre-computed vendor CCS calibration coefficients (CCScalDT, CCScalSLIM, CCScalTIMS stored as HDF5 datasets during conversion) and no new calibrant ATDs need to be measured.

skills.description: Use when raw TWIM-MS calibration solution data (.mzML, e.g. Waters Major Mix or Agilent Tune Mix) must be converted into arrival-time inputs paired with reference DTCCSN2 values to build class-specific CCS power-law calibrations.
skills.name: calibrant-arrival-time-extraction
skills.search_text: calibrant-arrival-time-extraction Use when raw TWIM-MS calibration solution data (.mzML, e.g. Waters Major Mix or Agilent Tune Mix) must be converted into arrival-time inputs paired with reference DTCCSN2 values to build class-specific CCS power-law calibrations. When calibration data are already processed — use the UserDT executable path of MOCCal instead, which needs no Python/DEIMoS installation and takes user-supplied drift/arrival-time tables When the analyte class is outside small molecules, lipids, or peptides, or the data are negative ionization mode — MOCCal's calibrations are currently limited to these classes on TWIM-MS platforms When the CCS platform is drift-tube or TIMS rather than traveling-wave IM — the arrival time recorded is the detector time on TWIM platforms, not drift time, so the power-law fit is TWIM-specific Extracts calibrant arrival times from raw TWIM-MS calibration files (.mzML) using DEIMoS Gaussian-apex extraction, then optimizes class-specific power-law regression parameters for CCS calibration of small molecules, lipids, and peptides in the MOCCal workflow. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c04290
skills.summary: Extracts calibrant arrival times from raw TWIM-MS calibration files (.mzML) using DEIMoS Gaussian-apex extraction, then optimizes class-specific power-law regression parameters for CCS calibration of small molecules, lipids, and peptides in the MOCCal workflow.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When calibration data are already processed — use the UserDT executable path of MOCCal instead, which needs no Python/DEIMoS installation and takes user-supplied drift/arrival-time tables When the analyte class is outside small molecules, lipids, or peptides, or the data are negative ionization mode — MOCCal's calibrations are currently limited to these classes on TWIM-MS platforms When the CCS platform is drift-tube or TIMS rather than traveling-wave IM — the arrival time recorded is the detector time on TWIM platforms, not drift time, so the power-law fit is TWIM-specific

skills.description: Use when you have single-field DTIMS-MS feature files plus IMS frame metadata (e.g., RapidFire SPE-IMS-MS runs) and need calibrated CCS values for analytes such as rotenone using Agilent tune-mix calibrant CCS.
skills.name: calibrant-based-ccs-determination
skills.search_text: calibrant-based-ccs-determination Use when you have single-field DTIMS-MS feature files plus IMS frame metadata (e.g., RapidFire SPE-IMS-MS runs) and need calibrated CCS values for analytes such as rotenone using Agilent tune-mix calibrant CCS. Data were acquired in stepped-field DTIMS mode with multiple fields per analyte — use AutoCCS --mode multi instead of calibrant-based single-field Data come from traveling wave-based IMS (TWIMS/SLIM or Bruker timsTOF), which require traveling-wave or linearized power calibration functions rather than the DTIMS single-field method Input is already a table of calibrated CCS values with no raw IMS feature/frame metadata available http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Determines collision cross-section (CCS) values from single-field DTIMS-MS measurements by calibrating against reference calibrant ions (e.g., Agilent tune-mix) using AutoCCS, optionally with per-run pressure and temperature corrections to stabilize CCS across instrument condition fluctuations. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btab429
skills.summary: Determines collision cross-section (CCS) values from single-field DTIMS-MS measurements by calibrating against reference calibrant ions (e.g., Agilent tune-mix) using AutoCCS, optionally with per-run pressure and temperature corrections to stabilize CCS across instrument condition fluctuations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data were acquired in stepped-field DTIMS mode with multiple fields per analyte — use AutoCCS --mode multi instead of calibrant-based single-field Data come from traveling wave-based IMS (TWIMS/SLIM or Bruker timsTOF), which require traveling-wave or linearized power calibration functions rather than the DTIMS single-field method Input is already a table of calibrated CCS values with no raw IMS feature/frame metadata available

skills.description: Use when detected calibrant features (m/z + arrival time) must be assigned known CCS values from a reference table (e.g., Agilent TuneMix-CCS) prior to fitting a TWIMS polynomial or linearized power calibration function.
skills.name: calibrant-ccs-reference-matching
skills.search_text: calibrant-ccs-reference-matching Use when detected calibrant features (m/z + arrival time) must be assigned known CCS values from a reference table (e.g., Agilent TuneMix-CCS) prior to fitting a TWIMS polynomial or linearized power calibration function. When CCS can be computed directly from the fundamental low-field ion mobility equation, e.g., stepped-field DTIMS-MS runs where --mode multi is used without a calibrant file When the input is raw instrument frames (e.g., UIMF) rather than already-extracted feature tables, since matching operates on feature CSVs When calibrant CCS reference values for the tune-mix composition are unavailable or the sample is not a recognized tunemix_sample_type http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Matches calibrant ion features (e.g., Agilent tune-mix compounds) against a reference arrival-time/CCS table within a ppm tolerance so the matched pairs can drive TWIMS/DTIMS calibration function fitting in AutoCCS. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btab429
skills.summary: Matches calibrant ion features (e.g., Agilent tune-mix compounds) against a reference arrival-time/CCS table within a ppm tolerance so the matched pairs can drive TWIMS/DTIMS calibration function fitting in AutoCCS.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When CCS can be computed directly from the fundamental low-field ion mobility equation, e.g., stepped-field DTIMS-MS runs where --mode multi is used without a calibrant file When the input is raw instrument frames (e.g., UIMF) rather than already-extracted feature tables, since matching operates on feature CSVs When calibrant CCS reference values for the tune-mix composition are unavailable or the sample is not a recognized tunemix_sample_type

skills.description: Use when raw m/z values extracted from an MZA file show systematic mass error and a list of known calibrant species must be converted into accurate reference m/z values before fitting mzapy.calibration.MassCalibration.
skills.name: calibrant-reference-mass-selection
skills.search_text: calibrant-reference-mass-selection Use when raw m/z values extracted from an MZA file show systematic mass error and a list of known calibrant species must be converted into accurate reference m/z values before fitting mzapy.calibration.MassCalibration. Measured peaks are unknown analytes with no assigned compound formula — monoiso_mass/ms_adduct_mz require known compositions to generate reference masses The goal is CCS calibration for single-field DTIMS rather than m/z mass calibration — use the mzapy CCS calibration routine instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Builds a reference calibrant list for mass calibration by computing exact monoisotopic neutral masses and adduct m/z values with mzapy.isotopes (monoiso_mass, ms_adduct_mz), using element masses sourced from Unimod, so measured m/z values from MZA files can be paired with accurate reference masses for fitting a MassCalibration model. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c01653
skills.summary: Builds a reference calibrant list for mass calibration by computing exact monoisotopic neutral masses and adduct m/z values with mzapy.isotopes (monoiso_mass, ms_adduct_mz), using element masses sourced from Unimod, so measured m/z values from MZA files can be paired with accurate reference masses for fitting a MassCalibration model.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Measured peaks are unknown analytes with no assigned compound formula — monoiso_mass/ms_adduct_mz require known compositions to generate reference masses The goal is CCS calibration for single-field DTIMS rather than m/z mass calibration — use the mzapy CCS calibration routine instead

skills.description: Use when performing external CCS calibration for single-field DTIMS (e.g., RapidFire) and you need to map calibrant feature-table ions to known reference CCS values from a calibrant file such as TuneMix-CCS.txt.
skills.name: calibrant-reference-value-mapping
skills.search_text: calibrant-reference-value-mapping Use when performing external CCS calibration for single-field DTIMS (e.g., RapidFire) and you need to map calibrant feature-table ions to known reference CCS values from a calibrant file such as TuneMix-CCS.txt. Stepped-field DTIMS experiments, where CCS can be determined directly from multiple fields without external calibrant reference mapping (use --threshold_n_fields 5 stepped-field workflow instead) Data lacking a calibrant run or a reference CCS list (e.g., no Agilent TuneMix or equivalent calibrant file) — external calibration cannot be anchored Traveling-wave platforms (Bruker timsTOF, Waters Synapt, SLIM) needing non-linear or linearized power calibration functions rather than single-field linear calibration http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Associates measured calibrant ion features (charge state, ion mass, drift/arrival time) with their known reference CCS values from a calibrant list (e.g., Agilent TuneMix CCS values) so that AutoCCS can build an external single-field DTIMS calibration curve. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btab429
skills.summary: Associates measured calibrant ion features (charge state, ion mass, drift/arrival time) with their known reference CCS values from a calibrant list (e.g., Agilent TuneMix CCS values) so that AutoCCS can build an external single-field DTIMS calibration curve.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Stepped-field DTIMS experiments, where CCS can be determined directly from multiple fields without external calibrant reference mapping (use --threshold_n_fields 5 stepped-field workflow instead) Data lacking a calibrant run or a reference CCS list (e.g., no Agilent TuneMix or equivalent calibrant file) — external calibration cannot be anchored Traveling-wave platforms (Bruker timsTOF, Waters Synapt, SLIM) needing non-linear or linearized power calibration functions rather than single-field linear calibration

skills.description: Use when lipid RTs were measured under a modified HILIC gradient or a different column length (100, 50, or 30 mm Kinetex HILIC) than the LiPydomics reference database and must be mapped onto the reference RT scale.
skills.name: calibrant-selection-and-rt-interpolation
skills.search_text: calibrant-selection-and-rt-interpolation Use when lipid RTs were measured under a modified HILIC gradient or a different column length (100, 50, or 30 mm Kinetex HILIC) than the LiPydomics reference database and must be mapped onto the reference RT scale. RTs were measured on the exact reference HILIC gradient/column, so measured and database RTs are already on the same scale and no calibration is needed Candidate calibrant lipids belong to lipid classes without reference HILIC retention times in the database (only 23 of 45 classes carry HILIC RTs) The goal is CCS prediction or lipid identification from m/z and CCS alone rather than retention-time scale harmonization Calibrates measured lipid retention times from modified HILIC gradients or columns onto the LiPydomics reference HILIC RT scale via piecewise linear interpolation between two to four calibrant lipids, so identification can proceed against the package's lipid database under non-reference chromatographic conditions. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c02560
skills.summary: Calibrates measured lipid retention times from modified HILIC gradients or columns onto the LiPydomics reference HILIC RT scale via piecewise linear interpolation between two to four calibrant lipids, so identification can proceed against the package's lipid database under non-reference chromatographic conditions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: RTs were measured on the exact reference HILIC gradient/column, so measured and database RTs are already on the same scale and no calibration is needed Candidate calibrant lipids belong to lipid classes without reference HILIC retention times in the database (only 23 of 45 classes carry HILIC RTs) The goal is CCS prediction or lipid identification from m/z and CCS alone rather than retention-time scale harmonization

skills.description: Use when a Waters Synapt (or similar untargeted MS metabolomics) run shows suspicious m/z deviations or poor mass accuracy and you need to check whether the calibrant signal drifted, dropped intermittently, or disappeared entirely.
skills.name: calibrant-signal-loss-detection
skills.search_text: calibrant-signal-loss-detection Use when a Waters Synapt (or similar untargeted MS metabolomics) run shows suspicious m/z deviations or poor mass accuracy and you need to check whether the calibrant signal drifted, dropped intermittently, or disappeared entirely. When the input is already a post-correction feature table with no per-injection calibrant intensity or m/z-deviation traces — the method requires time-resolved QC-pool metrics When the goal is correcting intensity drifts postanalysis rather than diagnosing instrument-level calibration problems (QC-MXP-style drift correction is a different skill) http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Retrospective diagnostic technique from QC4Metabolomics that plots calibrant-compound m/z deviation and intensity over analysis time to detect calibration offsets and calibrant-signal loss (e.g., the May/June 2022 offset and the end-2022/early-2023 intermittent-then-complete calibrant loss caused by a malfunctioning calibrant pump on a Waters Synapt). metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c07078
skills.summary: Retrospective diagnostic technique from QC4Metabolomics that plots calibrant-compound m/z deviation and intensity over analysis time to detect calibration offsets and calibrant-signal loss (e.g., the May/June 2022 offset and the end-2022/early-2023 intermittent-then-complete calibrant loss caused by a malfunctioning calibrant pump on a Waters Synapt).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is already a post-correction feature table with no per-injection calibrant intensity or m/z-deviation traces — the method requires time-resolved QC-pool metrics When the goal is correcting intensity drifts postanalysis rather than diagnosing instrument-level calibration problems (QC-MXP-style drift correction is a different skill)

skills.search_text: calibrated-ccs-error-computation Use when MOCCal has produced calibrated TWCCSN2 values for experimental features (e.g. ADH/enolase digests, polyalanine peptides spiked into NIST SRM 1950) and you need to quantify their accuracy against reference drift tube CCS values. When raw, unprocessed calibration files must first be extracted and Gaussian-fitted before calibration parameters exist (run the RawDT workflow with DEIMoS instead) When features are not singly charged — the three-candidate calibration and ΔCCS selection procedure applies to singly charged features; multiply charged assignments skip the class trendline comparison (default score 0) http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Computes percent differences between MOCCal-calibrated TWCCSN2 values and reference drift tube (DTCCSN2) values to validate calibration accuracy for peptides from protein digests and polyalanine calibrants. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c04290
skills.summary: Computes percent differences between MOCCal-calibrated TWCCSN2 values and reference drift tube (DTCCSN2) values to validate calibration accuracy for peptides from protein digests and polyalanine calibrants.

skills.description: Use when LA-ICP-MS signal data (Agilent MassHunter, Perkin Elmer Elan, Thermo Qtegra exports) must be converted into concentration-based elemental images using standards of known concentration, and the calibration regression coefficients need to be reported or exported for validation and reuse.
skills.name: calibration-coefficient-reporting
skills.search_text: calibration-coefficient-reporting Use when LA-ICP-MS signal data (Agilent MassHunter, Perkin Elmer Elan, Thermo Qtegra exports) must be converted into concentration-based elemental images using standards of known concentration, and the calibration regression coefficients need to be reported or exported for validation and reuse. The data has no ion mobility dimension (no arrival-time distributions) — mzapy's calibration utilities target IMS-MS data; plain LC-MS quantitation or mass-only workflows should use mass calibration (MassCalibration) instead The instrument is a Bruker TimsTOF where the stored quantity is 1/k0 (Vs/cm2) rather than arrival time in ms — vendor CCScalTIMS coefficients apply, not the TWIMS/SLIM power-function calibration The task is only raw data extraction or peak finding (find_peaks_1d_localmax, find_peaks_1d_gauss) with no calibration step required Fits and validates collision cross section (CCS) calibration functions for TWIMS/SLIM ion mobility data using mzapy.calibration, checking the fitted power-function parameters and back-calculated calibrant CCS values against the tolerances asserted in mzapy's unit tests. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c01653
skills.summary: Fits and validates collision cross section (CCS) calibration functions for TWIMS/SLIM ion mobility data using mzapy.calibration, checking the fitted power-function parameters and back-calculated calibrant CCS values against the tolerances asserted in mzapy's unit tests.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data has no ion mobility dimension (no arrival-time distributions) — mzapy's calibration utilities target IMS-MS data; plain LC-MS quantitation or mass-only workflows should use mass calibration (MassCalibration) instead The instrument is a Bruker TimsTOF where the stored quantity is 1/k0 (Vs/cm2) rather than arrival time in ms — vendor CCScalTIMS coefficients apply, not the TWIMS/SLIM power-function calibration The task is only raw data extraction or peak finding (find_peaks_1d_localmax, find_peaks_1d_gauss) with no calibration step required

skills.name: calibration-residual-visualization
skills.search_text: calibration-residual-visualization Use when HILIC retention times were measured under a modified gradient or a different column (e.g. 100, 50, or 30 mm Kinetex HILIC) than the reference database and must be mapped to the reference RT scale, with residuals checked for non-calibrant lipids. The lipid feature belongs to one of the lipid classes without reference HILIC retention times (only 23 of the 45 lipid classes carry HILIC RTs in the database) The chromatographic conditions match the reference database exactly, so no RT calibration transfer is needed The goal is CCS prediction or identification, which uses the package's CCS models and identification module rather than RT calibration http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Maps measured HILIC retention times acquired under modified gradients or shorter columns onto a reference lipid RT scale by piecewise linear interpolation between calibrant lipids, then visualizes interpolated vs reference RTs for non-calibrant lipids to expose residuals. This validates that RT-based lipid identification in LiPydomics remains accurate across changed chromatographic conditions. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c02560

skills.description: Use when scRNA-seq count matrices from tumor microenvironment datasets (e.g. melanoma, head-and-neck cancer) need cell-type-resolved metabolic flux quantification, especially glucose-glutamine flux comparisons across cancer and stromal cells.
skills.name: cancer-metabolic-heterogeneity-analysis
skills.search_text: cancer-metabolic-heterogeneity-analysis Use when scRNA-seq count matrices from tumor microenvironment datasets (e.g. melanoma, head-and-neck cancer) need cell-type-resolved metabolic flux quantification, especially glucose-glutamine flux comparisons across cancer and stromal cells. The goal is reconstruction of context-specific (disease, tissue, or cell type specific) metabolic networks/modules — the tool's authors state this capability does not yet exist. The input is metabolomics or proteomics data rather than transcriptomics — flux estimation for other omics types is not yet available. Strict biochemical constraints (redox balance, pH balance, energy balance) must be enforced in the flux solution — these are not yet implemented in scFEA. http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Estimates cell-wise metabolic flux from tumor microenvironment scRNA-seq using scFEA/FLUXestimator with a Glucose-Glutamine module network (e.g. cName_c70_m168.csv), then compares flux distributions across cancer, myeloid, and T cells to rank glucose metabolic activity (cancer > myeloid > T cells). metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkad444
skills.summary: Estimates cell-wise metabolic flux from tumor microenvironment scRNA-seq using scFEA/FLUXestimator with a Glucose-Glutamine module network (e.g. cName_c70_m168.csv), then compares flux distributions across cancer, myeloid, and T cells to rank glucose metabolic activity (cancer > myeloid > T cells).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is reconstruction of context-specific (disease, tissue, or cell type specific) metabolic networks/modules — the tool's authors state this capability does not yet exist. The input is metabolomics or proteomics data rather than transcriptomics — flux estimation for other omics types is not yet available. Strict biochemical constraints (redox balance, pH balance, energy balance) must be enforced in the flux solution — these are not yet implemented in scFEA.

skills.summary: Decomposes cancer omics data matrices (transcriptome, methylome, proteome, single-cell) into independent components yielding metagene (source, sk) and metasample (mixing, ak) matrices, using the IJMS review's companion Jupyter notebook and stabilized ICA tooling, with PCA/NMF as comparison baselines.

skills.search_text: candidate-derivative-tie-resolved-ranking Use when a molecular-networking anchor–suspect pair is known (anchor SMILES plus observed precursor mass difference) and a ranked list of derivative candidates is needed to assign the suspect's structure. No anchor molecule with high spectral similarity to the query spectrum has been identified — candidate generation and ranking depend on an anchor–suspect mass difference from a molecular network edge. SIRIUS-based molecular formula annotation has not succeeded for the query — the BAM workflow only performs structure annotation if the correct molecular formula was generated first. The task is full reaction-template promiscuity prediction rather than ranking candidate derivatives from one anchor — use PROXIMAL2's standalone pipeline instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Ranks candidate derivative structures generated from a known anchor molecule by applying biotransformation rules and scoring each derivative with GNN-SOM site-of-metabolism likelihoods, resolving rank ties using the average-rank method so that the suspect's true structure surfaces in a ranked top-k table. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c01565

skills.name: candidate-filter-module-implementation
skills.search_text: candidate-filter-module-implementation Use when a MetFrag candidate list from PubChem/ChemSpider retrieval or a user-supplied SDF must be pruned or re-scored by InChIKey skeleton block, element restrictions, or SMARTS substructure inclusion/exclusion before fragmentation and ranking. Candidates are already unique at the first-InChIKey-block level, so stereoisomer redundancy reduction would be a no-op The analysis goal is suspect-list presence filtering (e.g. STOFF-IDENT suspects supplied to MetFrag), which is a separate MetFrag2.2 feature The task is fragment-vs-product-ion scoring after bond dissociation fragmentation rather than pre-fragmentation candidate filtering http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Implements the MetFrag2.2 pre-fragmentation candidate-filtering modules: InChIKey first-block filtering to collapse stereoisomeric redundancy, element restriction in include/require/exclude modes, and SMARTS substructure inclusion/exclusion scoring (Eqs. 3-4, W_include = W_exclude = 0.5). metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-016-0115-9
skills.summary: Implements the MetFrag2.2 pre-fragmentation candidate-filtering modules: InChIKey first-block filtering to collapse stereoisomeric redundancy, element restriction in include/require/exclude modes, and SMARTS substructure inclusion/exclusion scoring (Eqs. 3-4, W_include = W_exclude = 0.5).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Candidates are already unique at the first-InChIKey-block level, so stereoisomer redundancy reduction would be a no-op The analysis goal is suspect-list presence filtering (e.g. STOFF-IDENT suspects supplied to MetFrag), which is a separate MetFrag2.2 feature The task is fragment-vs-product-ion scoring after bond dissociation fragmentation rather than pre-fragmentation candidate filtering

skills.description: Use when evaluating whether a learned scoring/filtering model retains the true chemical formula among its top-ranked candidates (e.g., top-256 recovery) and how large enumerated candidate sets are before filtering.
skills.name: candidate-filter-statistics-evaluation
skills.search_text: candidate-filter-statistics-evaluation Use when evaluating whether a learned scoring/filtering model retains the true chemical formula among its top-ranked candidates (e.g., top-256 recovery) and how large enumerated candidate sets are before filtering. Input spectra are negative-mode: MIST-CF/FastFilter models were trained only for positive-mode data, so filtered rankings would be out of scope. Candidate lists are already database-restricted (e.g., NIST/GNPS/HMDB/PubChem lookup); the skill targets large database-independent RDBE-permissive enumerations from SIRIUS decomp. Goal is final structure annotation rather than formula candidate filtering statistics; use CSI:FingerID or downstream MIST-CF evaluation instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Quantifies how well a neural formula-filtering model (FastFilter, from the MIST-CF pipeline) downselects large RDBE-permissive chemical formula candidate sets by measuring pre-filter candidate-count distributions and the top-k recovery rate of the true formula. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jcim.3c01082
skills.summary: Quantifies how well a neural formula-filtering model (FastFilter, from the MIST-CF pipeline) downselects large RDBE-permissive chemical formula candidate sets by measuring pre-filter candidate-count distributions and the top-k recovery rate of the true formula.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra are negative-mode: MIST-CF/FastFilter models were trained only for positive-mode data, so filtered rankings would be out of scope. Candidate lists are already database-restricted (e.g., NIST/GNPS/HMDB/PubChem lookup); the skill targets large database-independent RDBE-permissive enumerations from SIRIUS decomp. Goal is final structure annotation rather than formula candidate filtering statistics; use CSI:FingerID or downstream MIST-CF evaluation instead.

skills.description: Use when a formula-identification pipeline produces multiple candidate formulas per MS/MS spectrum (e.g. after SENIOR-rule refinement against precursor mass) and you need to order them by predicted correctness using learned MS/MS spectral features.
skills.name: candidate-formula-ranking
skills.search_text: candidate-formula-ranking Use when a formula-identification pipeline produces multiple candidate formulas per MS/MS spectrum (e.g. after SENIOR-rule refinement against precursor mass) and you need to order them by predicted correctness using learned MS/MS spectral features. The input is a single known formula or already a ranked candidate list with calibrated scores — retraining a rescore model is unnecessary The MS/MS spectra fall outside the retained scope (fewer than five peaks, peaks below 50 m/z, m/z above 1500, or molecules with atoms beyond C, H, O, N, F, S, Cl, P, B, I, Br, Na, K or more than 300 atoms) You need a formula-free predictor — the rescore step only ranks candidates already generated within the precursor mass tolerance by the refinement step FIDDLE's secondary deep learning rescore model estimates confidence scores for the candidate formulas produced by breadth-first refinement and ranks them so the top-5 list reflects the most likely molecular formula for a tandem mass spectrum. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-025-66060-9
skills.summary: FIDDLE's secondary deep learning rescore model estimates confidence scores for the candidate formulas produced by breadth-first refinement and ranks them so the top-5 list reflects the most likely molecular formula for a tandem mass spectrum.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a single known formula or already a ranked candidate list with calibrated scores — retraining a rescore model is unnecessary The MS/MS spectra fall outside the retained scope (fewer than five peaks, peaks below 50 m/z, m/z above 1500, or molecules with atoms beyond C, H, O, N, F, S, Cl, P, B, I, Br, Na, K or more than 300 atoms) You need a formula-free predictor — the rescore step only ranks candidates already generated within the precursor mass tolerance by the refinement step

skills.description: Use when a diffusion-based or other generative structure-prediction model outputs many candidate molecular graphs per mass spectrum and you must distill them into a frequency-ranked top-1/top-10 prediction and score it against known ground-truth molecules.
skills.name: candidate-frequency-ranking-for-denovo-annotation
skills.search_text: candidate-frequency-ranking-for-denovo-annotation Use when a diffusion-based or other generative structure-prediction model outputs many candidate molecular graphs per mass spectrum and you must distill them into a frequency-ranked top-1/top-10 prediction and score it against known ground-truth molecules. When evaluating a beam-search baseline such as MSNovelist, which ranks candidates by computed log-likelihoods rather than sample frequency When the task is chemical formula inference (e.g., SIRIUS, BUDDY, MIST-CF) rather than ranking full molecular structures When the model emits a single deterministic structure prediction instead of a pool of sampled candidates http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Converts a generative model's stochastic samples into a ranked de novo molecular annotation by sampling 100 molecules per spectrum with DiffMS's graph diffusion decoder, removing invalid or disconnected molecules, and selecting top-k (k=1, 10) candidates by frequency, then scoring them against ground truth with MassSpecGym de novo generation metrics (top-k accuracy, maximum Tanimoto similarity of RDKit Morgan fingerprints, minimum MCES distance). metabolomics/v3 10.48550/arxiv.2502.09571
skills.summary: Converts a generative model's stochastic samples into a ranked de novo molecular annotation by sampling 100 molecules per spectrum with DiffMS's graph diffusion decoder, removing invalid or disconnected molecules, and selecting top-k (k=1, 10) candidates by frequency, then scoring them against ground truth with MassSpecGym de novo generation metrics (top-k accuracy, maximum Tanimoto similarity of RDKit Morgan fingerprints, minimum MCES distance).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When evaluating a beam-search baseline such as MSNovelist, which ranks candidates by computed log-likelihoods rather than sample frequency When the task is chemical formula inference (e.g., SIRIUS, BUDDY, MIST-CF) rather than ranking full molecular structures When the model emits a single deterministic structure prediction instead of a pool of sampled candidates

skills.description: Use when a Bayesian direction-of-effect model identifies traits with confident positive enrichments or depletions and you need to name the concrete genes (e.g. Fig. 6 candidates) driving those enrichments across time points and tissues.
skills.name: candidate-gene-prioritization
skills.search_text: candidate-gene-prioritization Use when a Bayesian direction-of-effect model identifies traits with confident positive enrichments or depletions and you need to name the concrete genes (e.g. Fig. 6 candidates) driving those enrichments across time points and tissues. When the goal is genome-wide heritability partitioning (LDSC/MESC hSNP2 estimation) rather than naming specific exercise-by-disease candidate genes When no S-PrediXcan output or PrediXcan-DEG intersecting gene sets exist for the trait of interest — direction signs and effect sizes cannot be assigned When qualitative sex-specificity of exercise adaptation is the target; the article explicitly states this 'fell outside the scope considered here' http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Prioritizes trait-specific candidate genes at the intersection of exercise-induced differential expression and PrediXcan disease associations, by tracing direction-of-effect posterior means across training time points and compiling genes with tissue, +/- direction sign (product of DE and PrediXcan association directions), and standardized effect size. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-45966-w
skills.summary: Prioritizes trait-specific candidate genes at the intersection of exercise-induced differential expression and PrediXcan disease associations, by tracing direction-of-effect posterior means across training time points and compiling genes with tissue, +/- direction sign (product of DE and PrediXcan association directions), and standardized effect size.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is genome-wide heritability partitioning (LDSC/MESC hSNP2 estimation) rather than naming specific exercise-by-disease candidate genes When no S-PrediXcan output or PrediXcan-DEG intersecting gene sets exist for the trait of interest — direction signs and effect sizes cannot be assigned When qualitative sex-specificity of exercise adaptation is the target; the article explicitly states this 'fell outside the scope considered here'

skills.description: Use when validating a candidate causal gene prioritization tool or component against curated molecular QTL reference assignments, to quantify how many true positive causal genes are recovered and how many false positives are introduced.
skills.name: candidate-gene-prioritization-benchmarking
skills.search_text: candidate-gene-prioritization-benchmarking Use when validating a candidate causal gene prioritization tool or component against curated molecular QTL reference assignments, to quantify how many true positive causal genes are recovered and how many false positives are introduced. Input QTLs are trans-pQTLs: ProGeM's top-down strategy is not directly applicable and would call for a different top-down strategy. No high-confidence reference causal gene set is available for the QTL dataset, so sensitivity cannot be rigorously assessed. The goal is running ProGeM itself on new sentinel variants rather than evaluating its components against a curated reference. http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 Benchmark the sensitivity and specificity of the bottom-up and top-down components of ProGeM, applied individually, against a reference set of 227 curated metabolite QTL causal gene assignments (Supplementary Table S1), computing per-component recovery rates and precision and comparing them to reported benchmarks. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gky837
skills.summary: Benchmark the sensitivity and specificity of the bottom-up and top-down components of ProGeM, applied individually, against a reference set of 227 curated metabolite QTL causal gene assignments (Supplementary Table S1), computing per-component recovery rates and precision and comparing them to reported benchmarks.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input QTLs are trans-pQTLs: ProGeM's top-down strategy is not directly applicable and would call for a different top-down strategy. No high-confidence reference causal gene set is available for the QTL dataset, so sensitivity cannot be rigorously assessed. The goal is running ProGeM itself on new sentinel variants rather than evaluating its components against a curated reference.

skills.description: Use when you have both metPropagate (LPA) propagated scores and Exomiser-Phenotype scores for the same patient's candidate gene list and want a combined ranking that reduces metabolomic false-positive prioritization in suspected IEM patients.
skills.name: candidate-gene-prioritization-scoring
skills.search_text: candidate-gene-prioritization-scoring Use when you have both metPropagate (LPA) propagated scores and Exomiser-Phenotype scores for the same patient's candidate gene list and want a combined ranking that reduces metabolomic false-positive prioritization in suspected IEM patients. No per-patient untargeted metabolomics are available (no DAM z-scores to propagate), so metPropagate cannot contribute a term to the combination Feature-to-metabolite mapping for the metabolomic system is unavailable and the candidate gene set cannot be linked to HMDB-annotated metabolites (as in the TIDEX system) Trio WES data with parental filters already shortens candidate lists enough that re-ranking by metabolomic scores adds little, per the authors' note that trio WES simplifies prioritization http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 A weighted additive scoring skill that combines metPropagate's network-propagated metabolomic scores with Exomiser's phenotype-based candidate gene scores to re-rank exome candidate lists, penalizing metPropagate's bias toward genes with many HMDB-annotated first-degree neighbors. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41525-020-0132-5
skills.summary: A weighted additive scoring skill that combines metPropagate's network-propagated metabolomic scores with Exomiser's phenotype-based candidate gene scores to re-rank exome candidate lists, penalizing metPropagate's bias toward genes with many HMDB-annotated first-degree neighbors.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No per-patient untargeted metabolomics are available (no DAM z-scores to propagate), so metPropagate cannot contribute a term to the combination Feature-to-metabolite mapping for the metabolomic system is unavailable and the candidate gene set cannot be linked to HMDB-annotated metabolites (as in the TIDEX system) Trio WES data with parental filters already shortens candidate lists enough that re-ranking by metabolomic scores adds little, per the authors' note that trio WES simplifies prioritization

skills.description: Use when you have per-patient prioritized candidate gene lists (281-609 genes from Exomiser filtering) plus each patient's previously diagnosed causative gene, and need head-to-head rank comparison of scoring schemes.
skills.name: candidate-gene-rank-evaluation
skills.search_text: candidate-gene-rank-evaluation Use when you have per-patient prioritized candidate gene lists (281-609 genes from Exomiser filtering) plus each patient's previously diagnosed causative gene, and need head-to-head rank comparison of scoring schemes. Causative gene is unknown for the patient cohort — rank comparison requires a previously diagnosed causative gene per patient. Candidate gene lists were not produced through Exomiser's variant filtering pipeline — the comparison assumes a common candidate universe per patient. Your metabolomic system cannot measure the disease's diagnostic metabolites (e.g., large glycosaminoglycans for the IDS patient), since metPropagate scores will be insensitive for those samples. Per-patient benchmarking of causative-gene ranks across prioritization schemes — specifically comparing the rank of each patient's known causative gene under metPropagate's post-propagation Score.ID ordering against Exomiser's hiPHIVE phenotype-driven ranking. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41525-020-0132-5
skills.summary: Per-patient benchmarking of causative-gene ranks across prioritization schemes — specifically comparing the rank of each patient's known causative gene under metPropagate's post-propagation Score.ID ordering against Exomiser's hiPHIVE phenotype-driven ranking.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Causative gene is unknown for the patient cohort — rank comparison requires a previously diagnosed causative gene per patient. Candidate gene lists were not produced through Exomiser's variant filtering pipeline — the comparison assumes a common candidate universe per patient. Your metabolomic system cannot measure the disease's diagnostic metabolites (e.g., large glycosaminoglycans for the IDS patient), since metPropagate scores will be insensitive for those samples.

skills.description: Use when you have per-gene propagated network scores and a WES-derived candidate gene list (e.g., 281-609 Exomiser genes) and need to assess whether causative genes rank in the top 20th percentile.
skills.name: candidate-gene-rank-percentile-analysis
skills.search_text: candidate-gene-rank-percentile-analysis Use when you have per-gene propagated network scores and a WES-derived candidate gene list (e.g., 281-609 Exomiser genes) and need to assess whether causative genes rank in the top 20th percentile. Input is raw untargeted LC-MS feature intensity data — this skill starts from already-propagated gene scores, not XCMS output No known causative gene exists for the patient, making percentile-hit evaluation undefined (prioritization itself may still be exploratory) Candidate gene lists are far shorter than 281 genes (e.g., trio WES-filtered lists), where the top-20th-percentile metric calibrated on 281-609-gene lists becomes less comparable http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 Ranks a patient's Exomiser candidate gene list by propagated metPropagate score (Score.ID) and evaluates whether at least one known causative gene falls in the top 20th percentile, the success metric used across the 11 TIDEX neurometabolic patients. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41525-020-0132-5
skills.summary: Ranks a patient's Exomiser candidate gene list by propagated metPropagate score (Score.ID) and evaluates whether at least one known causative gene falls in the top 20th percentile, the success metric used across the 11 TIDEX neurometabolic patients.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw untargeted LC-MS feature intensity data — this skill starts from already-propagated gene scores, not XCMS output No known causative gene exists for the patient, making percentile-hit evaluation undefined (prioritization itself may still be exploratory) Candidate gene lists are far shorter than 281 genes (e.g., trio WES-filtered lists), where the top-20th-percentile metric calibrated on 281-609-gene lists becomes less comparable

skills.description: Use when benchmarking gene-prioritization criteria against a reference set of curated causal genes at QTL loci and you need per-criterion odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals from 2x2 contingency tables.
skills.name: candidate-gene-set-contingency-analysis
skills.search_text: candidate-gene-set-contingency-analysis Use when benchmarking gene-prioritization criteria against a reference set of curated causal genes at QTL loci and you need per-criterion odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals from 2x2 contingency tables. Your reference causal gene set is not independent of the prioritization tool (e.g. KEGG guided both ProGeM's top-down component and the expert literature review), so enrichment/sensitivity estimates may be inflated and this contingency benchmark would overstate performance You are evaluating trans-pQTL loci: ProGeM's top-down strategy and its candidate definitions are not directly applicable there and would require a different approach You need candidate scoring/ranking within a locus rather than aggregate enrichment of candidate definitions across loci http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 Quantify how enriched each ProGeM candidate causal gene definition (bottom-up nearest-gene, concurrent, moderate-impact sentinel variant, etc.) is with reference 'true positive' causal genes at the 227 curated mQTLs by building 2x2 contingency tables (candidate vs non-candidate x reference-causal vs non-causal) and running Fisher's exact test in R. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gky837
skills.summary: Quantify how enriched each ProGeM candidate causal gene definition (bottom-up nearest-gene, concurrent, moderate-impact sentinel variant, etc.) is with reference 'true positive' causal genes at the 227 curated mQTLs by building 2x2 contingency tables (candidate vs non-candidate x reference-causal vs non-causal) and running Fisher's exact test in R.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your reference causal gene set is not independent of the prioritization tool (e.g. KEGG guided both ProGeM's top-down component and the expert literature review), so enrichment/sensitivity estimates may be inflated and this contingency benchmark would overstate performance You are evaluating trans-pQTL loci: ProGeM's top-down strategy and its candidate definitions are not directly applicable there and would require a different approach You need candidate scoring/ranking within a locus rather than aggregate enrichment of candidate definitions across loci

skills.description: Use when you have MetFrag fragment scores for multiple candidate structures (from PubChem/ChemSpider/SDF retrieval) plus auxiliary terms (PubChem/ChemSpider reference counts, log P-based RT predictions, suspect/substructure penalties) that must be placed on a common scale before weighted.
skills.name: candidate-list-score-normalization
skills.search_text: candidate-list-score-normalization Use when you have MetFrag fragment scores for multiple candidate structures (from PubChem/ChemSpider/SDF retrieval) plus auxiliary terms (PubChem/ChemSpider reference counts, log P-based RT predictions, suspect/substructure penalties) that must be placed on a common scale before weighted. When the candidate list has been reduced to a single candidate — normalization across candidates is meaningless When comparing raw counts or BDE-derived denominators directly without normalization is the desired output (e.g. for reporting literature statistics rather than ranking candidates) When the goal is to rank candidates without auxiliary information and only one scoring term (e.g. fragment score alone) is used — no cross-term normalization is needed http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 Normalizes MetFrag2.2's per-candidate fragment (S_C_Frag), reference (S_C_Ref/PCR/CCR), retention (S_C_RT) and user-defined scores across the candidate list so weights summing to 1 combine them into one final ranking score. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-016-0115-9
skills.summary: Normalizes MetFrag2.2's per-candidate fragment (S_C_Frag), reference (S_C_Ref/PCR/CCR), retention (S_C_RT) and user-defined scores across the candidate list so weights summing to 1 combine them into one final ranking score.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the candidate list has been reduced to a single candidate — normalization across candidates is meaningless When comparing raw counts or BDE-derived denominators directly without normalization is the desired output (e.g. for reporting literature statistics rather than ranking candidates) When the goal is to rank candidates without auxiliary information and only one scoring term (e.g. fragment score alone) is used — no cross-term normalization is needed

skills.description: Use when a candidate structure list (from PubChem, ChemSpider, KEGG, or a user SDF) contains stereoisomeric duplicates that would crowd out distinct scaffolds in the ranked MetFrag output.
skills.name: candidate-list-stereoisomer-filtering
skills.search_text: candidate-list-stereoisomer-filtering Use when a candidate structure list (from PubChem, ChemSpider, KEGG, or a user SDF) contains stereoisomeric duplicates that would crowd out distinct scaffolds in the ranked MetFrag output. When stereoisomeric identity itself is the question (e.g. chiral LC separations), since the filter intentionally discards all but one stereoisomer per skeleton. When the candidate list comes from a stereochemistry-unaware source that has already collapsed InChIKey blocks, as grouping would be a no-op. When ranking must be preserved for all candidates (e.g. suspect-list confirmation), because removing stereoisomers changes the downstream rank distribution. http://edamontology.org/topic_0219 Reduces redundant candidate structures by grouping compounds sharing the first InChIKey block (identical molecular skeleton, differing only in stereochemistry) and retaining the single best-scored representative per group, as implemented in MetFrag2.2. This shrinks candidate lists before/after scoring so stereoisomers do not occupy multiple high ranks. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-016-0115-9
skills.summary: Reduces redundant candidate structures by grouping compounds sharing the first InChIKey block (identical molecular skeleton, differing only in stereochemistry) and retaining the single best-scored representative per group, as implemented in MetFrag2.2. This shrinks candidate lists before/after scoring so stereoisomers do not occupy multiple high ranks.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When stereoisomeric identity itself is the question (e.g. chiral LC separations), since the filter intentionally discards all but one stereoisomer per skeleton. When the candidate list comes from a stereochemistry-unaware source that has already collapsed InChIKey blocks, as grouping would be a no-op. When ranking must be preserved for all candidates (e.g. suspect-list confirmation), because removing stereoisomers changes the downstream rank distribution.

skills.description: Use when a detected MS1 metabolic feature (precursor m/z) must be matched against a candidate compound database (e.g., CQMD, KEGG, HMDB) before MS/MS-based LFP scoring, and candidates need pruning to a ppm-level mass window prior to similarity ranking.
skills.name: candidate-mass-tolerance-filtering
skills.search_text: candidate-mass-tolerance-filtering Use when a detected MS1 metabolic feature (precursor m/z) must be matched against a candidate compound database (e.g., CQMD, KEGG, HMDB) before MS/MS-based LFP scoring, and candidates need pruning to a ppm-level mass window prior to similarity ranking. The MS/MS data were acquired at a single collision energy only, so no longitudinal fragment profile across multiple CEs can be constructed for Jaccard scoring The goal is de novo structure elucidation with no candidate database entries to filter, rather than ranking known candidates against detected features The feature table already contains similarity scores or a final ranking column — re-running the mass filter would discard the existing ranked output http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 A candidate filtering and ranking step for metabolite identification with longitudinal fragment profiles (LFPs): retain only database candidates whose precursor m/z matches a detected feature within a 10 ppm mass tolerance, then rank the survivors by the criterion factor derived from Jaccard-similarity matches of longitudinal fragment profiles. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c01414
skills.summary: A candidate filtering and ranking step for metabolite identification with longitudinal fragment profiles (LFPs): retain only database candidates whose precursor m/z matches a detected feature within a 10 ppm mass tolerance, then rank the survivors by the criterion factor derived from Jaccard-similarity matches of longitudinal fragment profiles.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The MS/MS data were acquired at a single collision energy only, so no longitudinal fragment profile across multiple CEs can be constructed for Jaccard scoring The goal is de novo structure elucidation with no candidate database entries to filter, rather than ranking known candidates against detected features The feature table already contains similarity scores or a final ranking column — re-running the mass filter would discard the existing ranked output

skills.description: Use when you have MS/MS or MSn peak lists (hierarchical m/z:intensity parenthesis format) for an unknown precursor, a set of candidate structures from PubChem/cheminformatics database, and you need to rank candidates by how well the observed fragment peaks are explained by in silico generated.
skills.name: candidate-molecule-fragmentation-scoring
skills.search_text: candidate-molecule-fragmentation-scoring Use when you have MS/MS or MSn peak lists (hierarchical m/z:intensity parenthesis format) for an unknown precursor, a set of candidate structures from PubChem/cheminformatics database, and you need to rank candidates by how well the observed fragment peaks are explained by in silico generated. When reference spectra of known standards are available and can be matched directly — MAGMa is for the case where spectra must be annotated solely from candidate structures without informative reference spectra When the precursor formula is unknown and no candidate set can be assembled from an accurate-mass database search — scoring cannot proceed without candidates When peaks arise from fragmentation pathways requiring more than 3 bond dissociations plus hydroxyl/primary amine neutral losses (e.g. challenge 16's higher-energy peaks at m/z 122.0408, 178.03072, etc. remained unexplained under default settings) http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 Ranks candidate molecules by matching MS/MS (and MSn) peak m/z values against in silico generated substructures, converting match quality into an intensity-weighted penalty score per candidate. This skill underpins structure annotation in MAGMa when no reference spectra exist. metabolomics/v3 10.5702/massspectrometry.s0033
skills.summary: Ranks candidate molecules by matching MS/MS (and MSn) peak m/z values against in silico generated substructures, converting match quality into an intensity-weighted penalty score per candidate. This skill underpins structure annotation in MAGMa when no reference spectra exist.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When reference spectra of known standards are available and can be matched directly — MAGMa is for the case where spectra must be annotated solely from candidate structures without informative reference spectra When the precursor formula is unknown and no candidate set can be assembled from an accurate-mass database search — scoring cannot proceed without candidates When peaks arise from fragmentation pathways requiring more than 3 bond dissociations plus hydroxyl/primary amine neutral losses (e.g. challenge 16's higher-energy peaks at m/z 122.0408, 178.03072, etc. remained unexplained under default settings)

skills.description: Use when reproducing or validating the FMP-10 candidate-pool reduction over HMDB — i.e., before metabolite identification in MALDI-MSI, to confirm the derivatization-filter subset counts (26,202 all vs 4,951 endogenous) against reported values.
skills.name: candidate-pool-size-verification
skills.search_text: candidate-pool-size-verification Use when reproducing or validating the FMP-10 candidate-pool reduction over HMDB — i.e., before metabolite identification in MALDI-MSI, to confirm the derivatization-filter subset counts (26,202 all vs 4,951 endogenous) against reported values. The goal is metabolite identification/annotation of m/z features from MALDI-MSI data rather than verifying the candidate-pool sizes upstream of identification The data were acquired with a conventional (non-derivatizing) matrix whose expected adducts are [M+H]+ / [M-H]- and no FMP-10 functional-group filter applies The metabolite database is a custom or user-supplied target list rather than the Met-ID-parsed HMDB (or LIPID MAPS) SQLite database, so the 26,202 / 4,951 reference counts are not meaningful Verifies the derivatizable-candidate pool sizes that Met-ID generates when applying the FMP-10 derivatization functional-group filter to the parsed HMDB SQLite database, confirming 26,202 candidates for all HMDB metabolites and 4,951 for the endogenous-only subset. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c00633
skills.summary: Verifies the derivatizable-candidate pool sizes that Met-ID generates when applying the FMP-10 derivatization functional-group filter to the parsed HMDB SQLite database, confirming 26,202 candidates for all HMDB metabolites and 4,951 for the endogenous-only subset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is metabolite identification/annotation of m/z features from MALDI-MSI data rather than verifying the candidate-pool sizes upstream of identification The data were acquired with a conventional (non-derivatizing) matrix whose expected adducts are [M+H]+ / [M-H]- and no FMP-10 functional-group filter applies The metabolite database is a custom or user-supplied target list rather than the Met-ID-parsed HMDB (or LIPID MAPS) SQLite database, so the 26,202 / 4,951 reference counts are not meaningful

skills.description: Use when ranking candidate structures for an LC-HR-MS/MS unknown where spectral library matches are insufficient and extra evidence (reference/patent counts, RT–log P, CFM-ID predictions) should be fused into the MetFrag score.
skills.name: candidate-rank-optimization
skills.search_text: candidate-rank-optimization Use when ranking candidate structures for an LC-HR-MS/MS unknown where spectral library matches are insufficient and extra evidence (reference/patent counts, RT–log P, CFM-ID predictions) should be fused into the MetFrag score. Candidate lists are already provided (e.g. the candidate files shipped in the EA/UF/EQEx/EQExPlus/HILL dataset ZIP archives) — skip retrieval and use them directly The target space is a small, specific database (KEGG, HMDB, STOFF-IDENT, NORMAN suspects) rather than the large general databases — the article notes smaller, specific databases greatly improve top-rank chances The identification goal is a direct spectral library match (e.g. MassBank combined query) rather than de novo candidate ranking http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Retrieves candidate compound structures from the PubChem and ChemSpider databases (or a user-supplied SDF) for a given precursor mass/formula, producing the candidate lists that MetFrag2.2 scores against HR-MS/MS spectra. Database choice and size directly control ranking difficulty, so retrieval must be configured consistently with the scoring step. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-016-0115-9
skills.summary: Retrieves candidate compound structures from the PubChem and ChemSpider databases (or a user-supplied SDF) for a given precursor mass/formula, producing the candidate lists that MetFrag2.2 scores against HR-MS/MS spectra. Database choice and size directly control ranking difficulty, so retrieval must be configured consistently with the scoring step.
