skills.description: Use when a fragment must be converted from a rooted molecular graph (e.g. from RDKit) into a fixed, index-invariant topological feature vector for training or applying CFM-ID 4.0-style fragmentation transition models.
skills.name: canonical-fragment-feature-encoding
skills.search_text: canonical-fragment-feature-encoding Use when a fragment must be converted from a rooted molecular graph (e.g. from RDKit) into a fixed, index-invariant topological feature vector for training or applying CFM-ID 4.0-style fragmentation transition models. Input is already a numeric feature table or spectral vector — this skill operates on rooted fragment graphs, not on precomputed features The fragment cannot be rooted on a cleaved-bond atom, since canonical indexing and topological distance are defined relative to that root A representation needing 3D coordinates or bond-energy descriptors is required — this encoding is purely 2D topological (adjacency and atom/bond types) http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 Encodes a rooted fragment graph as a canonical 1-D feature vector by flattening the un-duplicated (i<j) part of a one-hot bond-type adjacency tensor Tadj together with an atom-type/neighbor-count tensor Tvertex, as used by CFM-ID 4.0 to learn ESI-MS/MS fragmentation transition probabilities. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c01465
skills.summary: Encodes a rooted fragment graph as a canonical 1-D feature vector by flattening the un-duplicated (i<j) part of a one-hot bond-type adjacency tensor Tadj together with an atom-type/neighbor-count tensor Tvertex, as used by CFM-ID 4.0 to learn ESI-MS/MS fragmentation transition probabilities.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a numeric feature table or spectral vector — this skill operates on rooted fragment graphs, not on precomputed features The fragment cannot be rooted on a cleaved-bond atom, since canonical indexing and topological distance are defined relative to that root A representation needing 3D coordinates or bond-energy descriptors is required — this encoding is purely 2D topological (adjacency and atom/bond types)

skills.description: Use when a mass spectrum needs a database-independent, reproducible identifier (SPLASH) and the input is a peak list such as a MassBank record (e.g. caffeine PR100026) rather than an existing SPLASH string.
skills.name: canonical-spectrum-string-normalization
skills.search_text: canonical-spectrum-string-normalization Use when a mass spectrum needs a database-independent, reproducible identifier (SPLASH) and the input is a peak list such as a MassBank record (e.g. caffeine PR100026) rather than an existing SPLASH string. The input is already a SPLASH identifier (e.g. splash10-0002-0900000000-b112e4e059e1ecf98c5f) — only the hash block needs matching, not re-normalization. The spectrum is raw instrument data (e.g. mzML/mzCloud raw files) with noise peaks and no curated peak list; SPLASH requires a defined ion-intensity list. The goal is fuzzy spectral similarity search rather than exact identity matching — the SPLASH hash only flags exact (or near-exact) duplicates, as identical SPLASHes arose only for single-ion spectra of the same mass in the 53.25-million-spectrum test. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Convert a peak list into the SPLASH canonical single-line spectrum string (ion:intensity pairs space-delimited, m/z scaled by 10^6 as 64-bit integers) so that a deterministic SHA256 hash block can be computed and compared across spectral databases. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/nbt.3689
skills.summary: Convert a peak list into the SPLASH canonical single-line spectrum string (ion:intensity pairs space-delimited, m/z scaled by 10^6 as 64-bit integers) so that a deterministic SHA256 hash block can be computed and compared across spectral databases.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a SPLASH identifier (e.g. splash10-0002-0900000000-b112e4e059e1ecf98c5f) — only the hash block needs matching, not re-normalization. The spectrum is raw instrument data (e.g. mzML/mzCloud raw files) with noise peaks and no curated peak list; SPLASH requires a defined ion-intensity list. The goal is fuzzy spectral similarity search rather than exact identity matching — the SPLASH hash only flags exact (or near-exact) duplicates, as identical SPLASHes arose only for single-ion spectra of the same mass in the 53.25-million-spectrum test.

skills.description: Use when you must benchmark a fingerprint-prediction model on tandem MS/MS spectra against MIST on the CANOPUS benchmark, or when reproducing DreaMS's fingerprint retrieval and molecular-property prediction results.
skills.name: canopus-benchmark-protocol
skills.search_text: canopus-benchmark-protocol Use when you must benchmark a fingerprint-prediction model on tandem MS/MS spectra against MIST on the CANOPUS benchmark, or when reproducing DreaMS's fingerprint retrieval and molecular-property prediction results. When the task is spectral similarity or spectral-library retrieval rather than fingerprint-based structure retrieval — the paper fine-tunes a separate DreaMS head for spectral similarity, where it 'substantially outperforms 44 standard spectral similarity measures'. When the input spectra are in negative ionization mode or have multiply charged precursor ions — the paper notes these were not incorporated in training. When a large-scale or fully generalizable fingerprint-prediction method is required — the paper states this fine-tuning 'should be understood as a proof of concept that our approach can achieve competitive performance with MIST' on a benchmark that 'is limited in size, covering 8,000 spectra from 7,000 unique molecules'. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 A protocol for evaluating MS/MS-to-structure models by predicting 4,096-bit Morgan fingerprints from tandem mass spectra and retrieving candidate structures from PubChem, scored by accuracy@k on the MIST CANOPUS benchmark (8,000 spectra, 7,000 unique molecules), with fine-tuned DreaMS compared against the MIST and FFN baselines. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41587-025-02663-3
skills.summary: A protocol for evaluating MS/MS-to-structure models by predicting 4,096-bit Morgan fingerprints from tandem mass spectra and retrieving candidate structures from PubChem, scored by accuracy@k on the MIST CANOPUS benchmark (8,000 spectra, 7,000 unique molecules), with fine-tuned DreaMS compared against the MIST and FFN baselines.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the task is spectral similarity or spectral-library retrieval rather than fingerprint-based structure retrieval — the paper fine-tunes a separate DreaMS head for spectral similarity, where it 'substantially outperforms 44 standard spectral similarity measures'. When the input spectra are in negative ionization mode or have multiply charged precursor ions — the paper notes these were not incorporated in training. When a large-scale or fully generalizable fingerprint-prediction method is required — the paper states this fine-tuning 'should be understood as a proof of concept that our approach can achieve competitive performance with MIST' on a benchmark that 'is limited in size, covering 8,000 spectra from 7,000 unique molecules'.

skills.name: canopus-chemical-class-prediction
skills.search_text: canopus-chemical-class-prediction Reference for annotating per-feature chemical classes from DDA MS2 spectra after MZmine feature detection, when structural annotation (SIRIUS/CSI:FingerID) and class taxonomy (CANOPUS, NPClassifier) are needed in an RDF workflow. Input is already a curated structure-to-class mapping (e.g. a LOTUS/ISDB-LOTUS annotation table) rather than raw MS2 spectra needing class prediction The workflow needs RT-based feature alignment across batches; CANOPUS class prediction is per-sample/feature and does not solve alignment Features were not processed with MZmine or lack an associated MS2 scan; class prediction from spectra alone without the ENPKG export step is not covered http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Predicts NPC chemical classes for LC-MS/MS features by running CANOPUS within the ENPKG in-silico structural annotation stage, then mapping the candidate 2D structures' anisomeric SMILES through the NPClassifier API so both class schemes are stored per feature in the knowledge graph. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acscentsci.3c00800
skills.summary: Predicts NPC chemical classes for LC-MS/MS features by running CANOPUS within the ENPKG in-silico structural annotation stage, then mapping the candidate 2D structures' anisomeric SMILES through the NPClassifier API so both class schemes are stored per feature in the knowledge graph.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a curated structure-to-class mapping (e.g. a LOTUS/ISDB-LOTUS annotation table) rather than raw MS2 spectra needing class prediction The workflow needs RT-based feature alignment across batches; CANOPUS class prediction is per-sample/feature and does not solve alignment Features were not processed with MZmine or lack an associated MS2 scan; class prediction from spectra alone without the ENPKG export step is not covered

skills.description: Use when a canopus_npc_summary table of predicted chemical classes per feature/extract must be reduced to high-confidence, recurring classes prior to novelty scoring (e.g., computing the CC score against LOTUS/NPClassifier reports).
skills.name: canopus-npclassifier-class-confidence-filtering
skills.search_text: canopus-npclassifier-class-confidence-filtering Use when a canopus_npc_summary table of predicted chemical classes per feature/extract must be reduced to high-confidence, recurring classes prior to novelty scoring (e.g., computing the CC score against LOTUS/NPClassifier reports). Input is a raw SIRIUS/CANOPUS project space that has not yet been summarized via canopus_treemap's npcSummary() — generate the summary table first. The analysis does not involve chemical-class novelty assessment against literature reports (e.g., only FC or SC components are needed) — class filtering is specific to the CC component. Class predictions come from a different ontology (e.g., GNPS molecular networking annotations rather than NPClassifier) — the CC score compares NPClassifier classes to LOTUS's NPClassifyre ontology. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Filters the CANOPUS/NPClassifier chemical-class predictions produced from a SIRIUS project space by class-confidence and recurrence thresholds before they are compared against literature-reported classes in Inventa's Class Component (CC) score. metabolomics/v3 10.3389/fmolb.2022.1028334
skills.summary: Filters the CANOPUS/NPClassifier chemical-class predictions produced from a SIRIUS project space by class-confidence and recurrence thresholds before they are compared against literature-reported classes in Inventa's Class Component (CC) score.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a raw SIRIUS/CANOPUS project space that has not yet been summarized via canopus_treemap's npcSummary() — generate the summary table first. The analysis does not involve chemical-class novelty assessment against literature reports (e.g., only FC or SC components are needed) — class filtering is specific to the CC component. Class predictions come from a different ontology (e.g., GNPS molecular networking annotations rather than NPClassifier) — the CC score compares NPClassifier classes to LOTUS's NPClassifyre ontology.

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify how likely two arbitrary carbon chains share no double bond at the same position (mismatch probability) — e.g. to validate that a lipidomics tool's double bond similarity is meaningful rather than trivially satisfied.
skills.name: carbon-chain-pairwise-comparison
skills.search_text: carbon-chain-pairwise-comparison Use when you need to quantify how likely two arbitrary carbon chains share no double bond at the same position (mismatch probability) — e.g. to validate that a lipidomics tool's double bond similarity is meaningful rather than trivially satisfied. Input lipid entries are not at the highest structural resolution level (double bond positions unspecified, e.g. PC 18:1) — the mismatch computation is undefined for chains without explicit positions The goal is lipidome-level sample statistics (PCA, Hausdorff distances, feature analysis) rather than structural-correctness benchmarking of double bond comparison You only need pairwise lipid similarity for exploration — use the full LipidSpace MCS/Jaccard workflow instead of the aggregate mismatch statistics Grounds the correctness evaluation of double bond position comparisons in reference lipid structure databases (LIPID MAPS, SwissLipids) by extracting all lipids at the highest structural resolution level, then performing an all-against-all pairwise comparison of fatty acyl carbon chains under two counting conventions (forward from the carbonyl carbon, backward/omega from the methyl end). metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c02449
skills.summary: Grounds the correctness evaluation of double bond position comparisons in reference lipid structure databases (LIPID MAPS, SwissLipids) by extracting all lipids at the highest structural resolution level, then performing an all-against-all pairwise comparison of fatty acyl carbon chains under two counting conventions (forward from the carbonyl carbon, backward/omega from the methyl end).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input lipid entries are not at the highest structural resolution level (double bond positions unspecified, e.g. PC 18:1) — the mismatch computation is undefined for chains without explicit positions The goal is lipidome-level sample statistics (PCA, Hausdorff distances, feature analysis) rather than structural-correctness benchmarking of double bond comparison You only need pairwise lipid similarity for exploration — use the full LipidSpace MCS/Jaccard workflow instead of the aggregate mismatch statistics

skills.description: Decision support for ranking or weighting compound identifications in INADEQUATE-based NMR metabolomics when a simulated INADEQUATE database derived from BMRB contains metabolites whose carbons have multiple possible chemical shift assignments.
skills.name: carbon-shift-ambiguity-scoring
skills.search_text: carbon-shift-ambiguity-scoring Decision support for ranking or weighting compound identifications in INADEQUATE-based NMR metabolomics when a simulated INADEQUATE database derived from BMRB contains metabolites whose carbons have multiple possible chemical shift assignments. The compound set is not amenable to 13C INADEQUATE simulation, e.g. metabolites without structural/carbon connectivity data or 1D 13C spectra in the reference database The goal is peak picking or spectral filtering of an experimental INADEQUATE spectrum rather than building or scoring the reference database Only unlabeled samples are available — the PyINETA approach relies on 13C labeling, so unlabeled workflows cannot use ambiguity scoring based on labeled carbon networks Computes a per-compound ambiguity score (CA/CT) from a simulated INADEQUATE database built from BMRB 13C chemical shifts and structural information, quantifying how many carbons carry multiple chemical shift assignments relative to the total carbon count so downstream matching can account for assignment uncertainty. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c03966
skills.summary: Computes a per-compound ambiguity score (CA/CT) from a simulated INADEQUATE database built from BMRB 13C chemical shifts and structural information, quantifying how many carbons carry multiple chemical shift assignments relative to the total carbon count so downstream matching can account for assignment uncertainty.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The compound set is not amenable to 13C INADEQUATE simulation, e.g. metabolites without structural/carbon connectivity data or 1D 13C spectra in the reference database The goal is peak picking or spectral filtering of an experimental INADEQUATE spectrum rather than building or scoring the reference database Only unlabeled samples are available — the PyINETA approach relies on 13C labeling, so unlabeled workflows cannot use ambiguity scoring based on labeled carbon networks

skills.summary: Configure and apply the CSMT (carbon shift matching tolerance) and NCMT (connectivity matching tolerance) thresholds in PyINETA's database-matching module, deciding when a picked peak network corresponds to a metabolite in the simulated INADEQUATE database.

skills.name: cartographical-snapshot-reproducibility
skills.search_text: cartographical-snapshot-reproducibility Use when a finalized 'ili molecular map view (spot rendering on an STL 3D model or PNG 2D background) must be saved, shared, or exactly reproduced later, or when validating that a received cartographical_snapshot.json restores the intended view. When the goal is first-pass feature detection/quantification rather than view reproduction — that belongs to the Optimus workflow (mzML feature detection, alignment, filtering), before any snapshot exists. When the underlying 'ili_input.csv or the 2D/3D model has changed since the snapshot was taken — reload fidelity is only guaranteed for the same model and input table. When a different visualization app is used (e.g., OptimusViewer, which renders XIC plots, MS peaks and MS2 spectra from the Optimus *.db output rather than spatial map views). Use 'ili's cartographical snapshots (Ctrl/Cmd+E) to save a molecular map view as a JSON file that records the selected map, colormap, and view position, so the exact visualization can be shared and reproduced by reloading the snapshot with the same 2D/3D model and 'ili_input.csv. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/nprot.2017.122
skills.summary: Use 'ili's cartographical snapshots (Ctrl/Cmd+E) to save a molecular map view as a JSON file that records the selected map, colormap, and view position, so the exact visualization can be shared and reproduced by reloading the snapshot with the same 2D/3D model and 'ili_input.csv.

skills.search_text: cartographical-snapshot-sharing Use when a spatial molecular map visualized in 'ili must be shared or re-displayed reproducibly, e.g. after tuning a logarithmic scale or hotspot quantile to reveal faint keypad traces, so the identical view can be restored. You only need a static publication figure and no reproducible interactive view — a PNG screenshot alone suffices. Data are plain LC-MS feature tables with no spatial coordinates; 'ili snapshots require spatially mapped data. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Saving and sharing 'ili cartographical snapshots: files that record a molecular map together with its visualization settings so the exact 3D/2D view (e.g. the urocanate m/z 139.050 ATM keypad map) can be reloaded and reproduced by others. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/nprot.2017.122
skills.summary: Saving and sharing 'ili cartographical snapshots: files that record a molecular map together with its visualization settings so the exact 3D/2D view (e.g. the urocanate m/z 139.050 ATM keypad map) can be reloaded and reproduced by others.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need a static publication figure and no reproducible interactive view — a PNG screenshot alone suffices. The molecular map and quantification matrix have not yet been produced by Optimus (ili_input.csv does not exist); run the Optimus workflow first. Data are plain LC-MS feature tables with no spatial coordinates; 'ili snapshots require spatially mapped data.

skills.description: Use when searching high-resolution query spectra (e.g. iPRG2012 TripleTOF mzML) against a large target-decoy spectral library and you need to confidently identify both unmodified and modified peptides via open modification searching at 1% FDR.
skills.name: cascade-open-modification-spectral-search
skills.search_text: cascade-open-modification-spectral-search Use when searching high-resolution query spectra (e.g. iPRG2012 TripleTOF mzML) against a large target-decoy spectral library and you need to confidently identify both unmodified and modified peptides via open modification searching at 1% FDR. Query spectra are low-resolution or the goal is a closed/unmodified-only search — a standard narrow-window library search suffices, since the cascade's open level targets modified peptides No suitable target spectral library exists for the sample's organism/instrument — the skill requires library spectra (library-based, not sequence database search like MSFragger) Only exact (unmodified) matches are of interest and the ANN index/shifted dot product overhead is unnecessary http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Two-level cascade spectral library search (ANN-SoLo) that first identifies unmodified peptides in a narrow 20 ppm precursor window with the standard dot product, then runs an open search in a 300 Da window using approximate nearest neighbor indexing and the shifted dot product to identify modified peptides at controlled FDR. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.8b00359
skills.summary: Two-level cascade spectral library search (ANN-SoLo) that first identifies unmodified peptides in a narrow 20 ppm precursor window with the standard dot product, then runs an open search in a 300 Da window using approximate nearest neighbor indexing and the shifted dot product to identify modified peptides at controlled FDR.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Query spectra are low-resolution or the goal is a closed/unmodified-only search — a standard narrow-window library search suffices, since the cascade's open level targets modified peptides No suitable target spectral library exists for the sample's organism/instrument — the skill requires library spectra (library-based, not sequence database search like MSFragger) Only exact (unmodified) matches are of interest and the ANN index/shifted dot product overhead is unnecessary

skills.description: Use when performing open modification spectral library searches where unmodified and modified peptides must be identified separately with strict FDR control, e.g. searching query spectra against a large target-decoy spectral library with ANN-SoLo.
skills.name: cascade-search-configuration
skills.search_text: cascade-search-configuration Use when performing open modification spectral library searches where unmodified and modified peptides must be identified separately with strict FDR control, e.g. searching query spectra against a large target-decoy spectral library with ANN-SoLo. When only unmodified peptide identifications are needed, a standard closed spectral library search without the open-search cascade level suffices When the spectral library is small enough that exhaustive open searching is computationally feasible, the ANN-indexed candidate selection step of the cascade is unnecessary When accurate FDR estimation for very small mass-difference subgroups is critical — the article cautions that FDR may be underestimated when too-small subgroups are used http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Configure and run ANN-SoLo's two-level cascade open search: first identify unmodified peptides within a narrow precursor mass window, then open-search remaining spectra for modified peptides via ANN-indexed candidate selection and the shifted dot product, with two-phase target–decoy FDR control. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.8b00359
skills.summary: Configure and run ANN-SoLo's two-level cascade open search: first identify unmodified peptides within a narrow precursor mass window, then open-search remaining spectra for modified peptides via ANN-indexed candidate selection and the shifted dot product, with two-phase target–decoy FDR control.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When only unmodified peptide identifications are needed, a standard closed spectral library search without the open-search cascade level suffices When the spectral library is small enough that exhaustive open searching is computationally feasible, the ANN-indexed candidate selection step of the cascade is unnecessary When accurate FDR estimation for very small mass-difference subgroups is critical — the article cautions that FDR may be underestimated when too-small subgroups are used

skills.description: Use when you have a peak-intensity matrix with case/control experimental groups (e.g. Stage_1/Control, Stage_2/Control comparisons) plus peak-to-compound annotations (KEGG or ChEBI IDs) and need to rank significantly changing metabolite sets.
skills.name: case-control-pathway-ranking-analysis
skills.search_text: case-control-pathway-ranking-analysis Use when you have a peak-intensity matrix with case/control experimental groups (e.g. Stage_1/Control, Stage_2/Control comparisons) plus peak-to-compound annotations (KEGG or ChEBI IDs) and need to rank significantly changing metabolite sets. When peak features lack compound annotations — peaks without annotations will not be used for pathway analysis When the goal is benchmarking against ORA/GSEA rather than the more robust mPLAGE decomposition — although PALS includes ORA and GSEA, the paper reports mPLAGE is more robust to noise and missing peaks When analysing groups of metabolites that are not database pathways without supplying the user-defined metabolite sets (e.g. GNPS Molecular Families or MS2LDA Mass2Motifs) — these must be provided explicitly http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Rank metabolic pathways by their activity-level changes between case and control groups using PALS (Pathway Activity Level Scoring), which decomposes pathway activity via the mPLAGE method on metabolomics peak-intensity data and is more robust to noise and missing peaks than ORA or GSEA. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo11020103
skills.summary: Rank metabolic pathways by their activity-level changes between case and control groups using PALS (Pathway Activity Level Scoring), which decomposes pathway activity via the mPLAGE method on metabolomics peak-intensity data and is more robust to noise and missing peaks than ORA or GSEA.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When peak features lack compound annotations — peaks without annotations will not be used for pathway analysis When the goal is benchmarking against ORA/GSEA rather than the more robust mPLAGE decomposition — although PALS includes ORA and GSEA, the paper reports mPLAGE is more robust to noise and missing peaks When analysing groups of metabolites that are not database pathways without supplying the user-defined metabolite sets (e.g. GNPS Molecular Families or MS2LDA Mass2Motifs) — these must be provided explicitly

skills.search_text: casmi-2017-benchmark-evaluation Use when a de novo structure-prediction model must be benchmarked on CASMI 2017 challenge spectra and compared with SIRIUS4/MetFrag baselines using correct-structure rate and molecular similarity metrics. Spectra were recorded in negative ion mode or in non-H+ adduct form, since TeFT was trained only on positive ion mode (H+) spectra High-resolution spectra are the evaluation target — the authors note TeFT may not outperform deep models like SIRIUS4, MSNovelist, or MassGenie on high-quality resolution spectra The input is a structure library search task with known reference spectra rather than de novo structure generation from MS2 spectra http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 A benchmarking protocol that evaluates the TeFT de novo structure-generation model on the 93 CASMI 2017 positive-mode MS2 spectra and statistically contrasts its performance against SIRIUS4 and MetFrag using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s42004-024-01189-0
skills.summary: A benchmarking protocol that evaluates the TeFT de novo structure-generation model on the 93 CASMI 2017 positive-mode MS2 spectra and statistically contrasts its performance against SIRIUS4 and MetFrag using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Spectra were recorded in negative ion mode or in non-H+ adduct form, since TeFT was trained only on positive ion mode (H+) spectra High-resolution spectra are the evaluation target — the authors note TeFT may not outperform deep models like SIRIUS4, MSNovelist, or MassGenie on high-quality resolution spectra The input is a structure library search task with known reference spectra rather than de novo structure generation from MS2 spectra

skills.description: Use when evaluating predicted tandem mass spectra against CASMI 2016/2022 challenge data, or when you need to quantify how peak-annotation coverage bounds cosine similarity of in silico fragmentation predictions.
skills.name: casmi-benchmark-evaluation
skills.search_text: casmi-benchmark-evaluation Use when evaluating predicted tandem mass spectra against CASMI 2016/2022 challenge data, or when you need to quantify how peak-annotation coverage bounds cosine similarity of in silico fragmentation predictions. The task is retraining or hyperparameter tuning of FIORA itself rather than benchmarking prediction quality on CASMI challenge data Comparing against CFM-ID, where evaluation must instead use the closest matching collision energy among 10, 20, 40 eV rather than a merged stepped spectrum Input spectra have missing collision energies or unclear formats, which the article explicitly excludes http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Benchmark FIORA's predicted MS/MS spectra against the CASMI 2016 and CASMI 2022 challenge sets by relating annotated peak-intensity coverage to spectral_sqrt_cosine similarity, reproducing Fig. 6. Coverage metrics are validated against reported values (~50%/25% annotation rates; ~80%/32% median coverage) and checked against the sqrt(coverage) >= cosine invariant. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-025-57422-4
skills.summary: Benchmark FIORA's predicted MS/MS spectra against the CASMI 2016 and CASMI 2022 challenge sets by relating annotated peak-intensity coverage to spectral_sqrt_cosine similarity, reproducing Fig. 6. Coverage metrics are validated against reported values (~50%/25% annotation rates; ~80%/32% median coverage) and checked against the sqrt(coverage) >= cosine invariant.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is retraining or hyperparameter tuning of FIORA itself rather than benchmarking prediction quality on CASMI challenge data Comparing against CFM-ID, where evaluation must instead use the closest matching collision energy among 10, 20, 40 eV rather than a merged stepped spectrum Input spectra have missing collision energies or unclear formats, which the article explicitly excludes

skills.description: Use when you have CASMI 2016 positive-mode MS2 spectra with reference structure annotations and de novo candidate SMILES from MSNovelist, and need retrieval/top-1 metrics.
skills.name: casmi-benchmark-structure-retrieval-evaluation
skills.search_text: casmi-benchmark-structure-retrieval-evaluation Use when you have CASMI 2016 positive-mode MS2 spectra with reference structure annotations and de novo candidate SMILES from MSNovelist, and need retrieval/top-1 metrics. The spectra are negative-mode: MSNovelist is only trained for positive-mode data and CSI:FingerID performance is slightly lower on negative-mode MS2 spectra, so results will not be comparable. The spectra have fewer than three fragment ions: MSNovelist processes MS2 spectra with a minimum of three fragment ions, so candidate generation is unreliable. The task is validating an established spectral-library annotation rather than evaluating de novo structure generation on a benchmark set. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Evaluate de novo structure identification candidates from MSNovelist on the CASMI 2016 positive-mode MS2 challenge spectra, scoring retrieval (correct structure among candidates) and top-1 rank (correct structure ranked first) both overall and on the CASMI-OK subset where database search succeeded. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-022-01486-3
skills.summary: Evaluate de novo structure identification candidates from MSNovelist on the CASMI 2016 positive-mode MS2 challenge spectra, scoring retrieval (correct structure among candidates) and top-1 rank (correct structure ranked first) both overall and on the CASMI-OK subset where database search succeeded.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The spectra are negative-mode: MSNovelist is only trained for positive-mode data and CSI:FingerID performance is slightly lower on negative-mode MS2 spectra, so results will not be comparable. The spectra have fewer than three fragment ions: MSNovelist processes MS2 spectra with a minimum of three fragment ions, so candidate generation is unreliable. The task is validating an established spectral-library annotation rather than evaluating de novo structure generation on a benchmark set.

skills.description: Use when you have ready-to-identify candidate lists (e.g. SIRIUS or MS-DIAL outputs for CASMI 2022 challenges) and want to check whether retention-order scores improve correct-structure ranking or prune candidates before MS/MS scoring.
skills.name: casmi-challenge-candidate-ranking
skills.search_text: casmi-challenge-candidate-ranking Use when you have ready-to-identify candidate lists (e.g. SIRIUS or MS-DIAL outputs for CASMI 2022 challenges) and want to check whether retention-order scores improve correct-structure ranking or prune candidates before MS/MS scoring. The chromatography is HILIC rather than reversed-phase LC — ROASMI currently applies only to RPLC systems and the shipped models assume eluent pH around 2.7 Candidate structures fall outside the elemental restrictions of C, H, N, O, P, and S, where ROASMI's chemical-space coverage is unexplored The goal is de novo structure elucidation without a pre-computed candidate list — this skill only re-ranks existing ready-to-identify candidate sets http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 Re-ranks small-molecule candidate lists from MS/MS tools (SIRIUS, MS-DIAL) using ROASMI-predicted retention scores alone and integrated with MS/MS scores via the msms_rt_score_integration probabilistic framework, then evaluates top-k accuracy and candidate reduction on the CASMI 2022 and dataset_38 re-annotation benchmarks. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-025-00968-8
skills.summary: Re-ranks small-molecule candidate lists from MS/MS tools (SIRIUS, MS-DIAL) using ROASMI-predicted retention scores alone and integrated with MS/MS scores via the msms_rt_score_integration probabilistic framework, then evaluates top-k accuracy and candidate reduction on the CASMI 2022 and dataset_38 re-annotation benchmarks.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The chromatography is HILIC rather than reversed-phase LC — ROASMI currently applies only to RPLC systems and the shipped models assume eluent pH around 2.7 Candidate structures fall outside the elemental restrictions of C, H, N, O, P, and S, where ROASMI's chemical-space coverage is unexplored The goal is de novo structure elucidation without a pre-computed candidate list — this skill only re-ranks existing ready-to-identify candidate sets

skills.description: Use when benchmarking an annotation confidence score against published contest scores: you need the CASMI 2016 per-compound hit scores from MetFrag, MAGMa+, CFM-ID, CSI:FingerID and CSI:FingerID IOKR to compute ROC curves, FDR-corrected hit counts, and mean ranks of correct hits.
skills.name: casmi-contest-score-retrieval-and-harmonization
skills.search_text: casmi-contest-score-retrieval-and-harmonization Use when benchmarking an annotation confidence score against published contest scores: you need the CASMI 2016 per-compound hit scores from MetFrag, MAGMa+, CFM-ID, CSI:FingerID and CSI:FingerID IOKR to compute ROC curves, FDR-corrected hit counts, and mean ranks of correct hits. You only want to re-run the annotation tools on raw mzML/mzXML spectra instead of comparing the published contest scores — re-running will not reproduce the exact CASMI 2016 submissions. The annotation confidence score being evaluated was not computed on the same 127 CASMI 2016 compounds or the same candidate databases, so score comparability breaks. The task is spectral library search de-replication on biological data, not contest-score retrieval for method benchmarking on the CASMI 2016 reference compounds. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Retrieve the published per-compound hit scores of the CASMI 2016 contest methods (MetFrag, MAGMa+, CFM-ID, CSI:FingerID original and CSI:FingerID IOKR) from the contest results web page, merge them with COSMIC confidence scores for the same 127 CASMI 2016 compounds, and harmonize the candidate lists so that every score is evaluated on an identical ranking task. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41587-021-01045-9
skills.summary: Retrieve the published per-compound hit scores of the CASMI 2016 contest methods (MetFrag, MAGMa+, CFM-ID, CSI:FingerID original and CSI:FingerID IOKR) from the contest results web page, merge them with COSMIC confidence scores for the same 127 CASMI 2016 compounds, and harmonize the candidate lists so that every score is evaluated on an identical ranking task.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only want to re-run the annotation tools on raw mzML/mzXML spectra instead of comparing the published contest scores — re-running will not reproduce the exact CASMI 2016 submissions. The annotation confidence score being evaluated was not computed on the same 127 CASMI 2016 compounds or the same candidate databases, so score comparability breaks. The task is spectral library search de-replication on biological data, not contest-score retrieval for method benchmarking on the CASMI 2016 reference compounds.

skills.description: Use when a trained MS2-to-structure model needs standardized head-to-head comparison on the CASMI 2016 Challenge set, e.g. to report direct ISMILES accuracy and fingerprint-similarity top-1 ranking accuracy on positive-mode spectra.
skills.name: casmi2016-benchmark-evaluation
skills.search_text: casmi2016-benchmark-evaluation Use when a trained MS2-to-structure model needs standardized head-to-head comparison on the CASMI 2016 Challenge set, e.g. to report direct ISMILES accuracy and fingerprint-similarity top-1 ranking accuracy on positive-mode spectra. Data are real-world environmental samples spiked with the 96-pollutant mixture rather than the CASMI 2016 benchmark — use the sample-level evaluation (77.1% vs SIRIUS/TraceFinder) instead. skills.summary: Evaluates a formula-to-ISMILES transformer model (MSThunder) on the CASMI 2016 Challenge positive-mode benchmark of 127 MS2 spectra, reporting direct-prediction accuracy (52.8%) and top-1 candidate-ranking accuracy (59.1%) against ground-truth structures.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are real-world environmental samples spiked with the 96-pollutant mixture rather than the CASMI 2016 benchmark — use the sample-level evaluation (77.1% vs SIRIUS/TraceFinder) instead. Input spectra are negative-ion mode or lack the high-resolution two-decimal mass accuracy required by MSThunder's dataset rules. Only raw vendor files (ThermoFisher, Agilent) are available and cannot be converted via MSConvert, since the current version does not support offline raw-data processing.

skills.name: catalogue-of-life-taxonomic-resolution-filtering
skills.search_text: catalogue-of-life-taxonomic-resolution-filtering Use when biological-source metadata contains free-text organism names that must be resolved against the Catalogue of Life and filtered to species-level completeness before joining structures to sources. The goal is scoring or re-ranking annotation candidates (taxo_scorer), not building a taxonomically filtered benchmarking set. Entries with genus- or family-level-only taxonomic information are acceptable — this filter would wrongly discard them by design. Input is a feature table or spectra with no biological-source metadata, so no organism names can be resolved. Resolves organism names extracted from biological-source metadata against the Catalogue of Life backbone and retains only entries whose taxonomy is complete down to the species level, producing the structure–source table used to build the 2,107-entry benchmarking dataset. metabolomics/v3 10.3389/fpls.2019.01329
skills.summary: Resolves organism names extracted from biological-source metadata against the Catalogue of Life backbone and retains only entries whose taxonomy is complete down to the species level, producing the structure–source table used to build the 2,107-entry benchmarking dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is scoring or re-ranking annotation candidates (taxo_scorer), not building a taxonomically filtered benchmarking set. Entries with genus- or family-level-only taxonomic information are acceptable — this filter would wrongly discard them by design. Input is a feature table or spectra with no biological-source metadata, so no organism names can be resolved.

skills.description: Use when you have a categorate() result (eight standard tables: reactives, LOTUS, KEGG, FEMA, FDA_SPL, FMCS, FunctionalGroups, ChemMatch) and need to derive a filtered chemical query list by database membership, FMCS properties, or chemical-library group.
skills.name: categorate-result-query-construction
skills.search_text: categorate-result-query-construction Use when you have a categorate() result (eight standard tables: reactives, LOTUS, KEGG, FEMA, FDA_SPL, FMCS, FunctionalGroups, ChemMatch) and need to derive a filtered chemical query list by database membership, FMCS properties, or chemical-library group. Input is a raw GC-MS hit table (Component.RT, Component.Area, Base.Peak.MZ, File.Name, Compound.Name, Match.Factor columns) that has not yet been annotated with categorate() — use spreadOut()/mzExacto() instead. Selection should be driven by library match score rather than chemical annotation — derive the query directly from Match.Factor thresholds (e.g. Match.Factor > 80) on the raw Unknowns Analysis output. Data are MS2, MS3, or ion mobility + MS2 spectra, which uafR does not yet support because published spectra are unavailable in PubChem. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 Constructs user-defined subsetting queries against a categorate() output using uafR's exactoThese(), selecting chemicals that meet database-, structure-, or library-group criteria. This is the bridge step between chemical annotation and re-extraction of targeted compounds from GC-MS peak tables. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pone.0306202
skills.summary: Constructs user-defined subsetting queries against a categorate() output using uafR's exactoThese(), selecting chemicals that meet database-, structure-, or library-group criteria. This is the bridge step between chemical annotation and re-extraction of targeted compounds from GC-MS peak tables.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a raw GC-MS hit table (Component.RT, Component.Area, Base.Peak.MZ, File.Name, Compound.Name, Match.Factor columns) that has not yet been annotated with categorate() — use spreadOut()/mzExacto() instead. Selection should be driven by library match score rather than chemical annotation — derive the query directly from Match.Factor thresholds (e.g. Match.Factor > 80) on the raw Unknowns Analysis output. Data are MS2, MS3, or ion mobility + MS2 spectra, which uafR does not yet support because published spectra are unavailable in PubChem.

skills.description: Use when a table carries categorical annotation columns (e.g. GO terms, cellular localization, signaling pathway) and rows must be retained only if their category term matches a searched category, then annotated.
skills.name: categorical-annotation-filtering
skills.search_text: categorical-annotation-filtering Use when a table carries categorical annotation columns (e.g. GO terms, cellular localization, signaling pathway) and rows must be retained only if their category term matches a searched category, then annotated. The goal is substring search over free-text rather than category membership — use Instant Clue's 'Find String(s) & Annotate' filter instead Filtering criteria are user-defined numerical or custom rules rather than a categorical annotation term — 'Custom Categorical Filter' or numerical filtering is the appropriate mechanism The input lacks any categorical annotation columns to match against (no GO/PFAM/pathway/localization terms) http://edamontology.org/topic_0089 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Implements Instant Clue's 'Find Category & Annotate' categorical filter: subset rows of an annotated table (e.g. GO, PFAM, MitoCarta or GSEA-derived term columns) by matching a searched category term and add an annotation label without altering the source data. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41598-018-31154-6
skills.summary: Implements Instant Clue's 'Find Category & Annotate' categorical filter: subset rows of an annotated table (e.g. GO, PFAM, MitoCarta or GSEA-derived term columns) by matching a searched category term and add an annotation label without altering the source data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is substring search over free-text rather than category membership — use Instant Clue's 'Find String(s) & Annotate' filter instead Filtering criteria are user-defined numerical or custom rules rather than a categorical annotation term — 'Custom Categorical Filter' or numerical filtering is the appropriate mechanism The input lacks any categorical annotation columns to match against (no GO/PFAM/pathway/localization terms)

skills.description: Use when a labeled spreadsheet/CSV has one categorical column (e.g., peptide hormone family annotations) and the goal is a frequency table of all distinct categories plus identification of the most abundant category.
skills.name: categorical-frequency-counting
skills.search_text: categorical-frequency-counting Use when a labeled spreadsheet/CSV has one categorical column (e.g., peptide hormone family annotations) and the goal is a frequency table of all distinct categories plus identification of the most abundant category. The input lacks a harmonized categorical label column — entries must first receive exactly one family label under the UniProt-based criteria before counting. The goal is continuous-variable statistics or correlation analysis rather than discrete category frequencies. The entity set is not the HORDB peptide hormone dataset and no comparable curated classification scheme exists for it. http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Counts and ranks category frequencies over an annotated spreadsheet of entities — here, the HORDB 'Peptide hormones infomation.xlsx' file classified into UniProt-based peptide hormone families — to reproduce distribution tables and bar plots such as HORDB's Fig. 8 (80 families, FMRFamide-related peptides most abundant with 856 entries). metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41597-022-01287-5
skills.summary: Counts and ranks category frequencies over an annotated spreadsheet of entities — here, the HORDB 'Peptide hormones infomation.xlsx' file classified into UniProt-based peptide hormone families — to reproduce distribution tables and bar plots such as HORDB's Fig. 8 (80 families, FMRFamide-related peptides most abundant with 856 entries).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input lacks a harmonized categorical label column — entries must first receive exactly one family label under the UniProt-based criteria before counting. The goal is continuous-variable statistics or correlation analysis rather than discrete category frequencies. The entity set is not the HORDB peptide hormone dataset and no comparable curated classification scheme exists for it.

skills.description: Use when a set of categorical behavioral questionnaire items (e.g., ASEBA CBCL item scores) must be reduced to a small number of continuous dimensions whose explained variance can be reported per dimension.
skills.name: categorical-item-factor-extraction
skills.search_text: categorical-item-factor-extraction Use when a set of categorical behavioral questionnaire items (e.g., ASEBA CBCL item scores) must be reduced to a small number of continuous dimensions whose explained variance can be reported per dimension. The data are continuous molecular measurements (DNA methylation, metabolomics) — the ACTIONdemonstrator uses MOFA2 for those omics layers, not MCA The input is already a reduced factor or dimension table rather than raw categorical item scores The questionnaire items are not categorical or have not been imputed/prepared by the ACTIONdemonstrator_preprocessing workflow http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Runs multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) with the R library FactoMineR (v2.4) on categorical questionnaire items—here parent-rated ASEBA CBCL externalizing behavior items from the ACTION cohorts—to extract dimensions (factors) that capture underlying behavioral patterns. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/gigascience/giad115
skills.summary: Runs multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) with the R library FactoMineR (v2.4) on categorical questionnaire items—here parent-rated ASEBA CBCL externalizing behavior items from the ACTION cohorts—to extract dimensions (factors) that capture underlying behavioral patterns.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are continuous molecular measurements (DNA methylation, metabolomics) — the ACTIONdemonstrator uses MOFA2 for those omics layers, not MCA The input is already a reduced factor or dimension table rather than raw categorical item scores The questionnaire items are not categorical or have not been imputed/prepared by the ACTIONdemonstrator_preprocessing workflow

skills.description: Use when auditing a curated database deposit (e.g., HORDB's /datasets/ folder) to confirm per-category record counts match the manuscript-reported totals, such as 6024 total entries split into 5729/40/255.
skills.name: category-level-record-classification-verification
skills.search_text: category-level-record-classification-verification Use when auditing a curated database deposit (e.g., HORDB's /datasets/ folder) to confirm per-category record counts match the manuscript-reported totals, such as 6024 total entries split into 5729/40/255. The deposit is not a categorically structured database (no per-category entry tables) and count reconciliation against a manuscript total is not the goal You need biological/sequence validation of HORDB records (e.g., IC50/EC50/ED50 activity fields or sequence checks) rather than record-count classification verification http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Verifies that records deposited in the HORDB figshare collection (DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.c.5522241) classify into the three HORDB categories — peptide hormones, peptide drugs, and marketed pharmaceutical preparations — and that category counts reconcile to the published totals of 6024 entries. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41597-022-01287-5
skills.summary: Verifies that records deposited in the HORDB figshare collection (DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.c.5522241) classify into the three HORDB categories — peptide hormones, peptide drugs, and marketed pharmaceutical preparations — and that category counts reconcile to the published totals of 6024 entries.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The deposit is not a categorically structured database (no per-category entry tables) and count reconciliation against a manuscript total is not the goal You need biological/sequence validation of HORDB records (e.g., IC50/EC50/ED50 activity fields or sequence checks) rather than record-count classification verification

skills.description: Use when enumerating cathinone-templated derivative libraries and you must prune functional groups whose repeated substitution (n = 2, 3) makes derivatives too hard to synthesize, per ΔSCScore < α^n.
skills.name: cathinone-analog-screening
skills.search_text: cathinone-analog-screening Use when enumerating cathinone-templated derivative libraries and you must prune functional groups whose repeated substitution (n = 2, 3) makes derivatives too hard to synthesize, per ΔSCScore < α^n. The analyte mass spectrum already matches a reference library (NIST/Wiley/SWGDRUG), so conventional GC/EI-MS screening suffices and no synthetic NPS database needs to be built. Functional-group filtering is already complete and the task is downstream spectrum prediction (NEIMS) or fingerprint-based ranking (DeepEI) of enumerated derivatives. The drug template is not being recursively substituted (no n = 2 or n = 3 enumeration levels), so a per-level synthesis-difficulty differential cannot be computed. http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 Screen enumerated functional groups by synthesis difficulty using SCScore, retaining only groups whose average synthesis-difficulty differential (ΔSCScore) relative to the cathinone template falls below α^n (α = 1.2) at each enumeration recursion level. This prevents highly challenging-to-synthesize derivatives from inflating the synthetic NPS database. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c05019
skills.summary: Screen enumerated functional groups by synthesis difficulty using SCScore, retaining only groups whose average synthesis-difficulty differential (ΔSCScore) relative to the cathinone template falls below α^n (α = 1.2) at each enumeration recursion level. This prevents highly challenging-to-synthesize derivatives from inflating the synthetic NPS database.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analyte mass spectrum already matches a reference library (NIST/Wiley/SWGDRUG), so conventional GC/EI-MS screening suffices and no synthetic NPS database needs to be built. Functional-group filtering is already complete and the task is downstream spectrum prediction (NEIMS) or fingerprint-based ranking (DeepEI) of enumerated derivatives. The drug template is not being recursively substituted (no n = 2 or n = 3 enumeration levels), so a per-level synthesis-difficulty differential cannot be computed.

skills.description: Use when patients have both a metPropagate post-propagation score file and a competing prioritization tool's score list (e.g. Exomiser hiPHIVE), plus a known causative gene, and you need a head-to-head ranking comparison.
skills.name: causative-gene-rank-comparison
skills.search_text: causative-gene-rank-comparison Use when patients have both a metPropagate post-propagation score file and a competing prioritization tool's score list (e.g. Exomiser hiPHIVE), plus a known causative gene, and you need a head-to-head ranking comparison. When the causative gene is unknown or unconfirmed — there is no ground-truth rank to compare against. When only one prioritization score is available per patient — a rank comparison needs at least two scoring schemes. When candidate gene lists use incompatible gene identifiers without a mapping, so a gene's rank cannot be traced across schemes. http://edamontology.org/topic_3577 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Compare per-patient candidate gene rankings of the causative gene produced by two or more prioritization scores (e.g. metPropagate propagated scores vs Exomiser hiPHIVE phenotype scores) by sorting each candidate list descending by each score and recording the causative gene's rank under each scheme. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41525-020-0132-5
skills.summary: Compare per-patient candidate gene rankings of the causative gene produced by two or more prioritization scores (e.g. metPropagate propagated scores vs Exomiser hiPHIVE phenotype scores) by sorting each candidate list descending by each score and recording the causative gene's rank under each scheme.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the causative gene is unknown or unconfirmed — there is no ground-truth rank to compare against. When only one prioritization score is available per patient — a rank comparison needs at least two scoring schemes. When candidate gene lists use incompatible gene identifiers without a mapping, so a gene's rank cannot be traced across schemes.

skills.description: Use when a cohort has cause-of-death coded vital status (e.g., cardiovascular, cancer, infection, other) and you must test whether metabolic biomarkers associated with all-cause mortality also associate with specific causes of death.
skills.name: cause-specific-mortality-endpoint-classification
skills.search_text: cause-specific-mortality-endpoint-classification Use when a cohort has cause-of-death coded vital status (e.g., cardiovascular, cancer, infection, other) and you must test whether metabolic biomarkers associated with all-cause mortality also associate with specific causes of death. The cohort only has all-cause vital status with no cause-of-death coding — there are no cause-specific endpoints to classify against. The goal is de novo biomarker selection/discovery (stepwise forward-backward selection over 226 biomarkers with Bonferroni threshold 2.21 x 10^-4), not testing already-identified biomarkers across endpoints. Cause-specific event counts are too small to support stable Cox estimates for the rarer endpoints (e.g., nonlocalized infections). http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Fits biomarker-specific Cox proportional hazards models against distinct cause-of-death endpoints (cardiovascular, cancer, nonlocalized infections, other) in addition to all-cause mortality, to test whether mortality-associated metabolic biomarkers reflect general health status rather than a single disease pathway. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-019-11311-9
skills.summary: Fits biomarker-specific Cox proportional hazards models against distinct cause-of-death endpoints (cardiovascular, cancer, nonlocalized infections, other) in addition to all-cause mortality, to test whether mortality-associated metabolic biomarkers reflect general health status rather than a single disease pathway.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The cohort only has all-cause vital status with no cause-of-death coding — there are no cause-specific endpoints to classify against. The goal is de novo biomarker selection/discovery (stepwise forward-backward selection over 226 biomarkers with Bonferroni threshold 2.21 x 10^-4), not testing already-identified biomarkers across endpoints. Cause-specific event counts are too small to support stable Cox estimates for the rarer endpoints (e.g., nonlocalized infections).

skills.description: Use when annotating IM-MS features in untargeted metabolomics and a list of molecular-formula/structure candidates exists for an m/z within ~10 ppm, and an experimental CCS value is available to prune false positives.
skills.name: ccs-based-annotation-filtering
skills.search_text: ccs-based-annotation-filtering Use when annotating IM-MS features in untargeted metabolomics and a list of molecular-formula/structure candidates exists for an m/z within ~10 ppm, and an experimental CCS value is available to prune false positives. No experimental CCS value is available for the target feature, so no ΔCCS window can be defined The annotation involves dimers ([2M+H]+, [2M-H]-), less common adducts, or in-source fragments, which the current CCSP 2.0 training sets do not support Candidates are already restricted to a verified standard or structure-confirmed annotation where CCS filtering adds no discriminating power http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Filters false-positive metabolite annotation candidates by predicting collision cross section (CCS) values with CCSP 2.0 linear-kernel SVR models and retaining only candidates whose predicted CCS falls within a ΔCCS threshold of the experimental value. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2022.08.09.503345
skills.summary: Filters false-positive metabolite annotation candidates by predicting collision cross section (CCS) values with CCSP 2.0 linear-kernel SVR models and retaining only candidates whose predicted CCS falls within a ΔCCS threshold of the experimental value.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No experimental CCS value is available for the target feature, so no ΔCCS window can be defined The annotation involves dimers ([2M+H]+, [2M-H]-), less common adducts, or in-source fragments, which the current CCSP 2.0 training sets do not support Candidates are already restricted to a verified standard or structure-confirmed annotation where CCS filtering adds no discriminating power

skills.description: Use when a metabolomics/lipidomics query set has measured precursor m/z (and optionally RT) and you must narrow a large candidate library (e.g. LipidBlast) using CCS from a 3D-conformer GNN before identification.
skills.name: ccs-based-compound-identification
skills.search_text: ccs-based-compound-identification Use when a metabolomics/lipidomics query set has measured precursor m/z (and optionally RT) and you must narrow a large candidate library (e.g. LipidBlast) using CCS from a 3D-conformer GNN before identification. The candidate molecule contains elements outside C, H, O, N, P, S, F, Cl, Br, I, Co, As, Se — SigmaCCS cannot predict those structures The adduct type is not one of [M+H]+, [M+Na]+, [M-H]- — SigmaCCS only encodes these three ion types 3D conformer generation/minimization fails (ETKDG failed for a small number of PubChem/CCSbase molecules and MMFF94 minimization failed for 662 molecules), so no CCS prediction is possible http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Improves LC-MS compound identification by using SigmaCCS-predicted collision cross sections (CCS), together with precursor m/z and GNN-RT-predicted retention time, as orthogonal filtering dimensions to re-rank candidate lipid annotations and raise Recall@1/Recall@30. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s42004-023-00939-w
skills.summary: Improves LC-MS compound identification by using SigmaCCS-predicted collision cross sections (CCS), together with precursor m/z and GNN-RT-predicted retention time, as orthogonal filtering dimensions to re-rank candidate lipid annotations and raise Recall@1/Recall@30.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The candidate molecule contains elements outside C, H, O, N, P, S, F, Cl, Br, I, Co, As, Se — SigmaCCS cannot predict those structures The adduct type is not one of [M+H]+, [M+Na]+, [M-H]- — SigmaCCS only encodes these three ion types 3D conformer generation/minimization fails (ETKDG failed for a small number of PubChem/CCSbase molecules and MMFF94 minimization failed for 662 molecules), so no CCS prediction is possible

skills.description: Use when a candidate list of molecular structures (e.g. PubChem hits within a 10 ppm mass window of a deprotonated/protonated ion) must be filtered using ion-mobility-derived CCS values.
skills.name: ccs-based-false-positive-filtering
skills.search_text: ccs-based-false-positive-filtering Use when a candidate list of molecular structures (e.g. PubChem hits within a 10 ppm mass window of a deprotonated/protonated ion) must be filtered using ion-mobility-derived CCS values. When the analyte forms dimers such as [2M+H]+ or [2M−H]− or other less common adducts or in-source fragments — current training sets only cover [M−H]−, [M+H]+, [M+Na]+, and [M+K]+. When no experimental CCS value is available for the unknown ion, since the ΔCCS filtering step compares predicted CCS against a measured CCS. When small-scale prediction in a non-Python environment is needed and local installation is impractical — the Google Colab version caps runs at 12 hours and disconnects after ~20 minutes idle. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Predict collision cross section (CCS) values with CCSP 2.0's linear support vector regression models and filter false-positive metabolomic annotation candidates using a ΔCCS threshold of 2.8% combined with a 10 ppm mass-error window. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.2c03491
skills.summary: Predict collision cross section (CCS) values with CCSP 2.0's linear support vector regression models and filter false-positive metabolomic annotation candidates using a ΔCCS threshold of 2.8% combined with a 10 ppm mass-error window.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the analyte forms dimers such as [2M+H]+ or [2M−H]− or other less common adducts or in-source fragments — current training sets only cover [M−H]−, [M+H]+, [M+Na]+, and [M+K]+. When no experimental CCS value is available for the unknown ion, since the ΔCCS filtering step compares predicted CCS against a measured CCS. When small-scale prediction in a non-Python environment is needed and local installation is impractical — the Google Colab version caps runs at 12 hours and disconnects after ~20 minutes idle.

skills.description: Use when measured (LC-)IM-MS lipidomics data contain U13C-labeled ('heavy') lipid entries with CCS values and you need to quantify CCSN2 bias against the DTCCSN2 library, per lipid class-adduct combination.
skills.name: ccs-bias-calculation
skills.search_text: ccs-bias-calculation Use when measured (LC-)IM-MS lipidomics data contain U13C-labeled ('heavy') lipid entries with CCS values and you need to quantify CCSN2 bias against the DTCCSN2 library, per lipid class-adduct combination. You only have CCS values without any U13C-labeled ('heavy') lipid entries — the DTCCSN2 library only contains values for uniformly 13C-labeled yeast lipids, so nothing can be matched. Your goal is CCS correction rather than bias quantification alone — use MobiLipid_CCS-bias-calculation_CCS-correction.Rmd, which additionally builds linear correction functions requiring a minimum of 3 lipids per lipid class-adduct combination. Your measured data use adducts outside [M+H], [M+NH4], [M+Na], [M-H], [M+HCOO] or lipid class-adduct combinations absent from the library's permitted table. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Calculates the percent CCS bias between measured IM-MS CCS values and DTCCSN2 library values of U13C-labeled yeast lipids using MobiLipid, enabling internal standardization-based CCS quality control of IM-MS lipidomics without external calibration measurements. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c01253
skills.summary: Calculates the percent CCS bias between measured IM-MS CCS values and DTCCSN2 library values of U13C-labeled yeast lipids using MobiLipid, enabling internal standardization-based CCS quality control of IM-MS lipidomics without external calibration measurements.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only have CCS values without any U13C-labeled ('heavy') lipid entries — the DTCCSN2 library only contains values for uniformly 13C-labeled yeast lipids, so nothing can be matched. Your goal is CCS correction rather than bias quantification alone — use MobiLipid_CCS-bias-calculation_CCS-correction.Rmd, which additionally builds linear correction functions requiring a minimum of 3 lipids per lipid class-adduct combination. Your measured data use adducts outside [M+H], [M+NH4], [M+Na], [M-H], [M+HCOO] or lipid class-adduct combinations absent from the library's permitted table.

skills.description: Use when LC-IM-MS lipidomics samples (e.g., from a Bruker timsTOF Pro TIM-MS or Agilent 6560 DTIM-MS) are spiked with U13C-labeled yeast extract standards and you need to quantify CCSN2 bias per ionization mode against a DT reference library.
skills.name: ccs-bias-calculation-ion-mobility-lipidomics
skills.search_text: ccs-bias-calculation-ion-mobility-lipidomics Use when LC-IM-MS lipidomics samples (e.g., from a Bruker timsTOF Pro TIM-MS or Agilent 6560 DTIM-MS) are spiked with U13C-labeled yeast extract standards and you need to quantify CCSN2 bias per ionization mode against a DT reference library. Data were not spiked with U13C-labeled yeast internal standards, so no 'heavy' entries can be matched to the DTCCSN2 library The lipid class-adduct combination is not in the compatibility table (e.g., TG with [M+H]) or fewer than 3 U13C-labeled lipids per class-adduct combination are available, which restricts the downstream linear-regression CCS correction Measured CCS values were acquired under drift gas or calibration conditions incompatible with the N2-based DTCCSN2 library http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Quantifies collision cross section (CCS) bias in IM-MS lipidomics by comparing measured TIMCCSN2 values of U13C-labeled yeast lipid internal standards against the DTCCSN2 reference library, reporting mean absolute bias per ionization mode using the MobiLipid R Markdown workflow. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c01253
skills.summary: Quantifies collision cross section (CCS) bias in IM-MS lipidomics by comparing measured TIMCCSN2 values of U13C-labeled yeast lipid internal standards against the DTCCSN2 reference library, reporting mean absolute bias per ionization mode using the MobiLipid R Markdown workflow.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data were not spiked with U13C-labeled yeast internal standards, so no 'heavy' entries can be matched to the DTCCSN2 library The lipid class-adduct combination is not in the compatibility table (e.g., TG with [M+H]) or fewer than 3 U13C-labeled lipids per class-adduct combination are available, which restricts the downstream linear-regression CCS correction Measured CCS values were acquired under drift gas or calibration conditions incompatible with the N2-based DTCCSN2 library

skills.description: Use when IMS-MS feature tables contain calibrant ions with reference CCS values and you need a fitted calibration function (linear, polynomial, or linearized power) to convert arrival times into CCS for unknown analytes.
skills.name: ccs-calibration-curve-fitting
skills.search_text: ccs-calibration-curve-fitting Use when IMS-MS feature tables contain calibrant ions with reference CCS values and you need a fitted calibration function (linear, polynomial, or linearized power) to convert arrival times into CCS for unknown analytes. Stepped-field DTIMS experiments, where CCS can be computed directly from the fundamental low-field ion mobility equation rather than by fitting a calibration curve Data without calibrant ions of known reference CCS values — the regression requires reference compounds such as Agilent tune-mix Input data lacking arrival-time measurements (e.g. only m/z-intensity feature tables without drift/arrival times) Fits CCS calibration curves with AutoCCS by regressing known calibrant CCS values (e.g. Agilent tune-mix) against arrival times: linear or polynomial functions for single-field DTIMS and TWIMS, and a linearized power function (Ruotolo et al. 2008) for traveling-wave platforms. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btab429
skills.summary: Fits CCS calibration curves with AutoCCS by regressing known calibrant CCS values (e.g. Agilent tune-mix) against arrival times: linear or polynomial functions for single-field DTIMS and TWIMS, and a linearized power function (Ruotolo et al. 2008) for traveling-wave platforms.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Stepped-field DTIMS experiments, where CCS can be computed directly from the fundamental low-field ion mobility equation rather than by fitting a calibration curve Data without calibrant ions of known reference CCS values — the regression requires reference compounds such as Agilent tune-mix Input data lacking arrival-time measurements (e.g. only m/z-intensity feature tables without drift/arrival times)

skills.description: Use when calibrating traveling-wave ion mobility arrival times or assigning unknown features to biomolecular classes and you need trusted DTCCSN2 reference values for small molecules, lipids, or peptides.
skills.name: ccs-compendium-reference-value-handling
skills.search_text: ccs-compendium-reference-value-handling Use when calibrating traveling-wave ion mobility arrival times or assigning unknown features to biomolecular classes and you need trusted DTCCSN2 reference values for small molecules, lipids, or peptides.
