When only a single calibration method/platform was run and no reference CCS values exist — there is nothing to compare against When the target analyte's arrival time lies outside the calibrant range (e.g. Pterin relative to TAA calibrants), since the comparison is confounded by extrapolation rather than method quality For stepped-field DTIMS analysis, where CCS is determined directly from physics rather than calibrated against reference values http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Compares CCS values computed by AutoCCS (across calibration methods or IMS platforms, e.g. SLIM IMS-MS vs. DTIMS-MS) against reference CCS values to quantify relative deviation and select the best-performing calibration approach. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btab429
skills.summary: Compares CCS values computed by AutoCCS (across calibration methods or IMS platforms, e.g. SLIM IMS-MS vs. DTIMS-MS) against reference CCS values to quantify relative deviation and select the best-performing calibration approach.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When only a single calibration method/platform was run and no reference CCS values exist — there is nothing to compare against When the target analyte's arrival time lies outside the calibrant range (e.g. Pterin relative to TAA calibrants), since the comparison is confounded by extrapolation rather than method quality For stepped-field DTIMS analysis, where CCS is determined directly from physics rather than calibrated against reference values

skills.description: Use when evaluating annotation-candidate filtering by predicted-vs-measured CCS, especially when testing whether ROC AUC holds across candidate-list mass windows (10, 7, 5, 3, 1, 0 ppm) or across SVR training-set compositions (chemically diverse vs class-matched).
skills.name: ccs-threshold-roc-curve-computation
skills.search_text: ccs-threshold-roc-curve-computation Use when evaluating annotation-candidate filtering by predicted-vs-measured CCS, especially when testing whether ROC AUC holds across candidate-list mass windows (10, 7, 5, 3, 1, 0 ppm) or across SVR training-set compositions (chemically diverse vs class-matched). The goal is CCS value prediction itself (CCSP 2.0 model fitting/descriptor calculation) rather than evaluating filtering performance — use the CCSP 2.0 prediction workflow, not ROC AUC evaluation Candidate labels are unknown (no confirmed true standard structure per compound), making true/false positive classification at each ΔCCS threshold impossible The training set involves dimers ([2M+H]+, [2M-H]-), less common adducts, or in-source fragments, which the current CCSP training sets do not support http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 Computes ROC AUC scores for CCS-based filtering of metabolite annotation candidates by sweeping ΔCCS (absolute relative difference between CCSP-predicted and experimentally measured CCS) thresholds and scoring true/false positive discovery rates with scikit-learn across mass-window conditions (10 to 0 ppm). Used to quantify how well CCSP 2.0 predictions filter false positives and whether efficacy is stable under narrower precursor mass windows and different training-set compositions. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2022.08.09.503345
skills.summary: Computes ROC AUC scores for CCS-based filtering of metabolite annotation candidates by sweeping ΔCCS (absolute relative difference between CCSP-predicted and experimentally measured CCS) thresholds and scoring true/false positive discovery rates with scikit-learn across mass-window conditions (10 to 0 ppm). Used to quantify how well CCSP 2.0 predictions filter false positives and whether efficacy is stable under narrower precursor mass windows and different training-set compositions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is CCS value prediction itself (CCSP 2.0 model fitting/descriptor calculation) rather than evaluating filtering performance — use the CCSP 2.0 prediction workflow, not ROC AUC evaluation Candidate labels are unknown (no confirmed true standard structure per compound), making true/false positive classification at each ΔCCS threshold impossible The training set involves dimers ([2M+H]+, [2M-H]-), less common adducts, or in-source fragments, which the current CCSP training sets do not support

skills.description: Use when building or customizing a CCS prediction training set from McLean CCS Compendium-style records (neutral InChI strings, per-adduct CCS values) before fitting linear SVR models.
skills.name: ccs-training-data-preparation
skills.search_text: ccs-training-data-preparation Use when building or customizing a CCS prediction training set from McLean CCS Compendium-style records (neutral InChI strings, per-adduct CCS values) before fitting linear SVR models. The query molecules are dimers such as [2M+H]+ or [2M-H]-, other less common adducts, or in-source fragments — the current CCSP 2.0 training sets do not support them Input is already a cleaned, scaled descriptor table ready for direct SVR/RFECV training — re-preparation would duplicate the InChI-to-descriptor pipeline The intended use is CCS prediction on a pre-trained model rather than creating or customizing a training set http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Prepare molecular training data for CCSP 2.0 collision cross section prediction: convert InChI strings to isomeric SMILES, encode MOL files with RDKit, compute 1613 2D descriptors with Mordred, and split/scale the cleaned per-adduct dataset for SVR training. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2022.08.09.503345
skills.summary: Prepare molecular training data for CCSP 2.0 collision cross section prediction: convert InChI strings to isomeric SMILES, encode MOL files with RDKit, compute 1613 2D descriptors with Mordred, and split/scale the cleaned per-adduct dataset for SVR training.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The query molecules are dimers such as [2M+H]+ or [2M-H]-, other less common adducts, or in-source fragments — the current CCSP 2.0 training sets do not support them Input is already a cleaned, scaled descriptor table ready for direct SVR/RFECV training — re-preparation would duplicate the InChI-to-descriptor pipeline The intended use is CCS prediction on a pre-trained model rather than creating or customizing a training set

skills.description: Use when you need CCS predictions for an adduct or compound class not covered by CCSP 2.0's shipped models (e.g., [2M+H]+, [2M−H]−, [M+K]+ beyond default coverage, or a specific superclass), and you can assemble experimental CCS values into a curated training table to rebuild the SVR model.
skills.name: ccs-training-set-curation
skills.search_text: ccs-training-set-curation Use when you need CCS predictions for an adduct or compound class not covered by CCSP 2.0's shipped models (e.g., [2M+H]+, [2M−H]−, [M+K]+ beyond default coverage, or a specific superclass), and you can assemble experimental CCS values into a curated training table to rebuild the SVR model. The target adduct is already covered by a shipped CCSP 2.0 model ([M − H]−, [M + H]+, [M + Na]+, [M + K]+) with sufficient accuracy — in that case use the published models rather than retraining. You lack a defensible training set of experimentally measured CCS values for the target adduct or class; ML CCS prediction fundamentally requires that 'the specific training set to be used prior to predicting CCS values' be defined first, so retraining cannot proceed without curated measurements. You are predicting CCS for the common adducts under production filtering workflows where a ΔCCS threshold of 2.8% and 10 ppm mass error were validated — a custom retrain on a small set may not reproduce that validated filtering performance. http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 http://edamontology.org/topic_3336 Curates and uses a user-defined training set of experimental CCS values to train/retrain CCSP 2.0's linear SVR models so CCS predictions cover adduct types or molecular classes absent from the published [M − H]−, [M + H]+, and [M + Na]+ models (e.g., dimers such as [2M + H]+ or [2M − H]−). This operationalizes CCSP 2.0's design goal of letting users 'customize their own CCS predictions based on their unique training sets and workflow needs'. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.2c03491
skills.summary: Curates and uses a user-defined training set of experimental CCS values to train/retrain CCSP 2.0's linear SVR models so CCS predictions cover adduct types or molecular classes absent from the published [M − H]−, [M + H]+, and [M + Na]+ models (e.g., dimers such as [2M + H]+ or [2M − H]−). This operationalizes CCSP 2.0's design goal of letting users 'customize their own CCS predictions based on their unique training sets and workflow needs'.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The target adduct is already covered by a shipped CCSP 2.0 model ([M − H]−, [M + H]+, [M + Na]+, [M + K]+) with sufficient accuracy — in that case use the published models rather than retraining. You lack a defensible training set of experimentally measured CCS values for the target adduct or class; ML CCS prediction fundamentally requires that 'the specific training set to be used prior to predicting CCS values' be defined first, so retraining cannot proceed without curated measurements. You are predicting CCS for the common adducts under production filtering workflows where a ΔCCS threshold of 2.8% and 10 ppm mass error were validated — a custom retrain on a small set may not reproduce that validated filtering performance.

skills.description: Use when a CCS training table (e.g. CCSBase parquet/CSV with 'ccs', 'smiles', 'adduct' columns) contains multiple experimental records per SMILES-adduct pair and inconsistent replicate values must be removed before model training.
skills.name: ccs-value-mean-absolute-deviation-filtering
skills.search_text: ccs-value-mean-absolute-deviation-filtering Use when a CCS training table (e.g. CCSBase parquet/CSV with 'ccs', 'smiles', 'adduct' columns) contains multiple experimental records per SMILES-adduct pair and inconsistent replicate values must be removed before model training. Input is already deduplicated or a split training/test file (e.g. metlin_train_3d.parquet, ccsbase_3d.parquet used by train-test.py) — no duplicate collapsing is needed Applying the threshold-5 dedup rule to METLIN-CCS or other non-CCSBase datasets without first re-analyzing the deviation distribution, since the 5 cutoff was derived from CCSBase duplicate histograms The goal is filtering model predictions by confidence rather than cleaning experimental training records — use the confidence-model filtering approach instead http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Data-standardization skill for removing inconsistent duplicate SMILES-adduct CCS records from CCSBase (v1.3): duplicate pairs with a mean absolute CCS deviation greater than 5 are dropped, and remaining duplicates are collapsed to a single record with the mean CCS value before GNN training. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00899-w
skills.summary: Data-standardization skill for removing inconsistent duplicate SMILES-adduct CCS records from CCSBase (v1.3): duplicate pairs with a mean absolute CCS deviation greater than 5 are dropped, and remaining duplicates are collapsed to a single record with the mean CCS value before GNN training.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already deduplicated or a split training/test file (e.g. metlin_train_3d.parquet, ccsbase_3d.parquet used by train-test.py) — no duplicate collapsing is needed Applying the threshold-5 dedup rule to METLIN-CCS or other non-CCSBase datasets without first re-analyzing the deviation distribution, since the 5 cutoff was derived from CCSBase duplicate histograms The goal is filtering model predictions by confidence rather than cleaning experimental training records — use the confidence-model filtering approach instead

skills.description: Use when a metabolite annotation list (e.g., PubChem candidates within 10 ppm of an exact mass) needs CCS values predicted for [M-H]-, [M+H]+ or [M+Na]+ adducts to enable ΔCCS-threshold filtering.
skills.name: ccs-value-regression-prediction
skills.search_text: ccs-value-regression-prediction Use when a metabolite annotation list (e.g., PubChem candidates within 10 ppm of an exact mass) needs CCS values predicted for [M-H]-, [M+H]+ or [M+Na]+ adducts to enable ΔCCS-threshold filtering. The analytes are dimers ([2M+H]+, [2M-H]-), less common adducts, or in-source fragments — the current training sets do not support them CCS predictions are needed across multiple IM-MS instrument types (drift tube vs. travelling wave) — this cross-platform generalization is explicitly left as future work The user cannot define a specific training set prior to prediction, since CCSP requires the training set to be defined beforehand http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Predict gas-phase collision cross section (CCS) values with a linear-kernel support vector regression model (CCSP 2.0) trained on user-curated IM-MS data, using 1613 Mordred 2D molecular descriptors, so predicted CCS can be used to filter false-positive metabolite annotations. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2022.08.09.503345
skills.summary: Predict gas-phase collision cross section (CCS) values with a linear-kernel support vector regression model (CCSP 2.0) trained on user-curated IM-MS data, using 1613 Mordred 2D molecular descriptors, so predicted CCS can be used to filter false-positive metabolite annotations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analytes are dimers ([2M+H]+, [2M-H]-), less common adducts, or in-source fragments — the current training sets do not support them CCS predictions are needed across multiple IM-MS instrument types (drift tube vs. travelling wave) — this cross-platform generalization is explicitly left as future work The user cannot define a specific training set prior to prediction, since CCSP requires the training set to be defined beforehand

skills.description: Use when preparing CCSBase for CCS-prediction model training and the loaded table contains multiple records sharing the same SMILES and adduct, requiring deduplication driven by a deviation-based consistency threshold.
skills.name: ccsbase-duplicate-smiles-adduct-grouping
skills.search_text: ccsbase-duplicate-smiles-adduct-grouping Use when preparing CCSBase for CCS-prediction model training and the loaded table contains multiple records sharing the same SMILES and adduct, requiring deduplication driven by a deviation-based consistency threshold. Input is already a deduplicated dataset or a single-record-per-SMILES-adduct table (e.g. a prepared train/test split such as metlin_train_3d.parquet) — grouping would be a no-op You are deduplicating METLIN-CCS rather than CCSBase — the paper applies similar standardization across datasets, but this specific mean-absolute-deviation > 5 rule was derived from histogram analysis of CCSBase duplicates You need to filter model predictions (e.g. confidence-model-based filtering of predicted CCS) rather than clean experimental training values http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Standardizes CCSBase (v1.3) by grouping entries on SMILES-adduct pairs, flagging duplicate groups whose mean absolute CCS deviation exceeds 5 for removal, and collapsing remaining duplicates to a single mean-CCS record. This removes inconsistent experimental replicate values before GNN (SigmaCCS/GraphCCS/Mol2CCS) training. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00899-w
skills.summary: Standardizes CCSBase (v1.3) by grouping entries on SMILES-adduct pairs, flagging duplicate groups whose mean absolute CCS deviation exceeds 5 for removal, and collapsing remaining duplicates to a single mean-CCS record. This removes inconsistent experimental replicate values before GNN (SigmaCCS/GraphCCS/Mol2CCS) training.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a deduplicated dataset or a single-record-per-SMILES-adduct table (e.g. a prepared train/test split such as metlin_train_3d.parquet) — grouping would be a no-op You are deduplicating METLIN-CCS rather than CCSBase — the paper applies similar standardization across datasets, but this specific mean-absolute-deviation > 5 rule was derived from histogram analysis of CCSBase duplicates You need to filter model predictions (e.g. confidence-model-based filtering of predicted CCS) rather than clean experimental training values

skills.description: Use when a compound library (SMILES + experimental retention times, e.g. HILIC MoNA or RPLC RIKEN PlaSMA sets) must be converted into a numeric molecular-descriptor feature table for training or applying retention time prediction models.
skills.name: cdk-chemical-descriptor-calculation
skills.search_text: cdk-chemical-descriptor-calculation Use when a compound library (SMILES + experimental retention times, e.g. HILIC MoNA or RPLC RIKEN PlaSMA sets) must be converted into a numeric molecular-descriptor feature table for training or applying retention time prediction models. Input is already a computed descriptor table — proceed directly to model fitting (caret split, cesc() centering/scaling, proc.data() cleaning) The task requires 3D conformer-dependent descriptors — Retip's pipeline deliberately uses 2D-based descriptors to avoid 3D computational overhead Compounds contain salts or metals that will fail rCDK — standardize or exclude them first rather than passing raw SMILES to getCD() http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Computes 286 CDK molecular descriptors per compound from standardized SMILES structures using Retip's getCD() function built on the rcdk package, producing the numeric feature matrix that feeds Retip's retention-time prediction models (RF, BRNN, XGBoost, LightGBM, Keras, H2O autoML). metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.9b05765
skills.summary: Computes 286 CDK molecular descriptors per compound from standardized SMILES structures using Retip's getCD() function built on the rcdk package, producing the numeric feature matrix that feeds Retip's retention-time prediction models (RF, BRNN, XGBoost, LightGBM, Keras, H2O autoML).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a computed descriptor table — proceed directly to model fitting (caret split, cesc() centering/scaling, proc.data() cleaning) The task requires 3D conformer-dependent descriptors — Retip's pipeline deliberately uses 2D-based descriptors to avoid 3D computational overhead Compounds contain salts or metals that will fail rCDK — standardize or exclude them first rather than passing raw SMILES to getCD()

skills.description: Use when you need to convert SMILES structures of metabolomics compound sets into a CDK descriptor matrix — e.g., for Retip retention-time models or PCA chemical-space overlap checks before training/test validation.
skills.name: cdk-descriptor-generation
skills.search_text: cdk-descriptor-generation Use when you need to convert SMILES structures of metabolomics compound sets into a CDK descriptor matrix — e.g., for Retip retention-time models or PCA chemical-space overlap checks before training/test validation. The input is already a computed descriptor/feature matrix and the goal is model fitting rather than featurization The task is retention-time prediction itself rather than descriptor generation or chemical-space overlap assessment Compounds are outside the study's chemical classes — e.g., high-molecular-weight lipids such as triacylglycerols or phosphatidylcholines, which were largely excluded from the original training sets http://edamontology.org/topic_3332 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Compute 2D CDK molecular descriptors (286 features) for compound sets using Retip's getCD() built on the rcdk package, then center/scale the descriptor matrix so it can be used for retention-time model building and chemical-space (PCA) overlap analysis between HILIC/RPLC training, test, and validation libraries. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.9b05765
skills.summary: Compute 2D CDK molecular descriptors (286 features) for compound sets using Retip's getCD() built on the rcdk package, then center/scale the descriptor matrix so it can be used for retention-time model building and chemical-space (PCA) overlap analysis between HILIC/RPLC training, test, and validation libraries.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a computed descriptor/feature matrix and the goal is model fitting rather than featurization The task is retention-time prediction itself rather than descriptor generation or chemical-space overlap assessment Compounds are outside the study's chemical classes — e.g., high-molecular-weight lipids such as triacylglycerols or phosphatidylcholines, which were largely excluded from the original training sets

skills.description: Use when training or applying FingerScorer-style SVM fingerprint predictors over a 11416-bit CDK fingerprint space, and you must prune to the 2500 occupied bits before per-bit model training or Jaccard ranking.
skills.name: cdk-fingerprint-bit-occupancy-filtering
skills.search_text: cdk-fingerprint-bit-occupancy-filtering Use when training or applying FingerScorer-style SVM fingerprint predictors over a 11416-bit CDK fingerprint space, and you must prune to the 2500 occupied bits before per-bit model training or Jaccard ranking. Your reference fingerprint scheme is not the CDK 11416-bit union (e.g. a different fingerprint type), so the 2500-bit occupancy mask would be invalid Input spectra are not in ChemDistiller's internal hierarchical format and no conversion is available yet You need to predict fingerprints for bits never observed in the reference database — training models on unoccupied bits is exactly what this filter prevents http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Restricts FingerScorer's fingerprint prediction target space from the full 11416-bit CDK fingerprint union down to the 2500 occupied bits, so one binary libSVM model is trained per occupied bit only. This cuts model count and training cost while keeping every bit that actually occurs in the reference compound database. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/bty080
skills.summary: Restricts FingerScorer's fingerprint prediction target space from the full 11416-bit CDK fingerprint union down to the 2500 occupied bits, so one binary libSVM model is trained per occupied bit only. This cuts model count and training cost while keeping every bit that actually occurs in the reference compound database.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your reference fingerprint scheme is not the CDK 11416-bit union (e.g. a different fingerprint type), so the 2500-bit occupancy mask would be invalid Input spectra are not in ChemDistiller's internal hierarchical format and no conversion is available yet You need to predict fingerprints for bits never observed in the reference database — training models on unoccupied bits is exactly what this filter prevents

skills.description: Use when building a bond-of-metabolism (BoM) or site-of-metabolism classifier from annotated SDF compounds (e.g. EBoMD.sdf) and you need per-bond feature vectors for training/evaluation.
skills.name: cdk-molecular-descriptor-feature-generation
skills.search_text: cdk-molecular-descriptor-feature-generation Use when building a bond-of-metabolism (BoM) or site-of-metabolism classifier from annotated SDF compounds (e.g. EBoMD.sdf) and you need per-bond feature vectors for training/evaluation. Input is not bond-annotated metabolite/substrate data but raw reaction records without BoM labels — no per-bond instances can be formed The task is whole-molecule reactant classification (CypReact's job) rather than locating reactive bonds within a substrate Compounds contain η+η (Cyclization) BoMs only — the paper found these too rare (4 of 828 reactions) to model and excluded them http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 Generates the 473-feature vector per [compound, bond] instance that underlies the CypBoM η−η bond-site predictor, using the Chemistry Development Kit (CDK) to compute molecular descriptors, fingerprints, bond atom types, and neighbor atom features from canonically ordered atom pairs. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jcim.1c00144
skills.summary: Generates the 473-feature vector per [compound, bond] instance that underlies the CypBoM η−η bond-site predictor, using the Chemistry Development Kit (CDK) to compute molecular descriptors, fingerprints, bond atom types, and neighbor atom features from canonically ordered atom pairs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is not bond-annotated metabolite/substrate data but raw reaction records without BoM labels — no per-bond instances can be formed The task is whole-molecule reactant classification (CypReact's job) rather than locating reactive bonds within a substrate Compounds contain η+η (Cyclization) BoMs only — the paper found these too rare (4 of 828 reactions) to model and excluded them

skills.description: Use when a query molecule's subgraph fingerprint has already narrowed candidates (e.g. via $allBitsSet on PubChem fingerprints stored as BinData in MongoDB) and you must confirm true substructure isomorphism with CDK pattern matching.
skills.name: cdk-substructure-pattern-matching
skills.search_text: cdk-substructure-pattern-matching Use when a query molecule's subgraph fingerprint has already narrowed candidates (e.g. via $allBitsSet on PubChem fingerprints stored as BinData in MongoDB) and you must confirm true substructure isomorphism with CDK pattern matching. When the query is a full-structure (identity) match or a similarity/LSH search — COCONUT implements those as separate endpoints (hashed InChI/SMILES indexes or LSH-based similarity per the ChEMBL blog post), not as fingerprint-bit + CDK isomorphism matching. When candidate sets are already exhaustively confirmed or the database is small enough for a direct CDK isomorphism scan on all molecules — the $allBitsSet pre-filter step is redundant in that case. http://edamontology.org/topic_0089 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Pattern-matching step of the COCONUT online substructure search: after candidate filtering via $allBitsSet on PubChem fingerprints, CDK confirmatory subgraph isomorphism is run (Ullmann by default, or Vento-Foggia or depth-first) and confirmed matches are written to substructure_search_results.json. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-020-00478-9
skills.summary: Pattern-matching step of the COCONUT online substructure search: after candidate filtering via $allBitsSet on PubChem fingerprints, CDK confirmatory subgraph isomorphism is run (Ullmann by default, or Vento-Foggia or depth-first) and confirmed matches are written to substructure_search_results.json.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the query is a full-structure (identity) match or a similarity/LSH search — COCONUT implements those as separate endpoints (hashed InChI/SMILES indexes or LSH-based similarity per the ChEMBL blog post), not as fingerprint-bit + CDK isomorphism matching. When candidate sets are already exhaustively confirmed or the database is small enough for a direct CDK isomorphism scan on all molecules — the $allBitsSet pre-filter step is redundant in that case.

skills.description: Use when ranking LC-MS/MS candidate structures where reference standards with measured RTs are available on a reverse-phase column and retention-time plausibility should contribute to MetFrag scoring.
skills.name: cdk-xlogp-descriptor-calculation
skills.search_text: cdk-xlogp-descriptor-calculation Use when ranking LC-MS/MS candidate structures where reference standards with measured RTs are available on a reverse-phase column and retention-time plausibility should contribute to MetFrag scoring. Analysis is not LC-based on a reverse-phase column, so RT and log P are not meaningfully correlated No reference standards with measured retention times are available to fit the RT–log P model Candidates are gas-phase or GC-MS identifications where retention indices, not log P, drive retention behaviour Calculates octanol–water partition coefficients (log P) with the CDK XlogP descriptor (or PubChem XLOGP3 as an alternative) to link retention times to candidate structures in MetFrag2.2. The log P values feed the RT–log P regression used for retention-time scoring of candidate metabolites. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-016-0115-9
skills.summary: Calculates octanol–water partition coefficients (log P) with the CDK XlogP descriptor (or PubChem XLOGP3 as an alternative) to link retention times to candidate structures in MetFrag2.2. The log P values feed the RT–log P regression used for retention-time scoring of candidate metabolites.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Analysis is not LC-based on a reverse-phase column, so RT and log P are not meaningfully correlated No reference standards with measured retention times are available to fit the RT–log P model Candidates are gas-phase or GC-MS identifications where retention indices, not log P, drive retention behaviour

skills.description: Use when de novo peptide predictions have been assembled into antibody contigs (e.g. with ALPS) and you must verify that CDR and variable-region sequences were recovered, not just overall chain coverage.
skills.name: cdr-region-assembly-validation
skills.search_text: cdr-region-assembly-validation Use when de novo peptide predictions have been assembled into antibody contigs (e.g. with ALPS) and you must verify that CDR and variable-region sequences were recovered, not just overall chain coverage. When only whole-chain coverage is needed and CDR-level resolution is not required — plain BLAST-based coverage against the full chain suffices. When the goal is database-search-based sequence confirmation (e.g. Supernovo-style workflows with in silico genetic recombination) rather than database-independent de novo assembly validation. http://edamontology.org/topic_2830 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Validation step for de novo antibody assembly that assesses whether assembled contigs reconstruct the functionally important variable regions and complementarity-determining regions (CDRs), using the Natural Antibody database to retrieve reference CDR sequences for each antibody. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bib/bbac542
skills.summary: Validation step for de novo antibody assembly that assesses whether assembled contigs reconstruct the functionally important variable regions and complementarity-determining regions (CDRs), using the Natural Antibody database to retrieve reference CDR sequences for each antibody.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When only whole-chain coverage is needed and CDR-level resolution is not required — plain BLAST-based coverage against the full chain suffices. When the goal is database-search-based sequence confirmation (e.g. Supernovo-style workflows with in silico genetic recombination) rather than database-independent de novo assembly validation.

skills.description: Use when running the SpaceM workflow on MALDI-imaging mass spectrometry data from cultured cells and you need per-cell segmentation of the stitched pre-MALDI microscopy tiles to assign metabolite intensities to individual cells.
skills.name: cell-image-segmentation-with-cellprofiler
skills.search_text: cell-image-segmentation-with-cellprofiler Use when running the SpaceM workflow on MALDI-imaging mass spectrometry data from cultured cells and you need per-cell segmentation of the stitched pre-MALDI microscopy tiles to assign metabolite intensities to individual cells. Input is a single-cell gene-expression dataset or already-segmented cell masks — CellProfiler segmentation of pre-MALDI tiles is specific to SpaceM's microscopy + MALDI-IMS integration. The microscopy is not a tiled acquisition with black penmarks and out.txt tile coordinates; SpaceM currently requires tile stitching optimized for the Nikon Ti-E microscope output format. Ablation marks are overlapping or not visible in the post-MALDI microscopy, which the README states is critical for correct co-registration. http://edamontology.org/topic_3382 http://edamontology.org/topic_3391 Segments individual cultured cells in the stitched pre-MALDI microscopy image using a CellProfiler pipeline, producing per-cell segmentation masks that SpaceM co-registers with MALDI laser ablation marks to build the per-cell spatio-molecular matrix. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-021-01198-0
skills.summary: Segments individual cultured cells in the stitched pre-MALDI microscopy image using a CellProfiler pipeline, producing per-cell segmentation masks that SpaceM co-registers with MALDI laser ablation marks to build the per-cell spatio-molecular matrix.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a single-cell gene-expression dataset or already-segmented cell masks — CellProfiler segmentation of pre-MALDI tiles is specific to SpaceM's microscopy + MALDI-IMS integration. skills.search_text: centroided-spectrum-preprocessing Use when MS/MS peaks are already centroided and normalized (sum = 1) and a low-entropy, ion-poor spectrum (S < 3) needs intensity re-weighting prior to entropy similarity or library matching. The spectrum is ion-rich with high entropy (S >= 3): w stays at 1, and applying a power transformation with w < 1 there decreases similarity scoring performance. Peaks are not yet centroided or normalized: run ms_entropy.clean_spectrum() first (remove empty peaks, remove peaks above precursor_mz - precursor_ions_removal_da, merge peaks within +/- min_ms2_difference_in_da, noise threshold, top max_peak_num, normalize to sum 1) instead of computing entropy directly. The downstream scoring uses unweighted similarity (e.g. calculate_unweighted_entropy_similarity or classic dot product), where entropy weighting is not part of the method. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Entropy-dependent intensity weighting of already centroided, normalized MS/MS peak lists: spectral entropy S is computed and ion intensities are transformed as I^w with w = 0.25 + 0.25*S for low-entropy (S < 3) spectra, boosting low-abundance ions before entropy similarity scoring. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-021-01331-z
skills.summary: Entropy-dependent intensity weighting of already centroided, normalized MS/MS peak lists: spectral entropy S is computed and ion intensities are transformed as I^w with w = 0.25 + 0.25*S for low-entropy (S < 3) spectra, boosting low-abundance ions before entropy similarity scoring.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The spectrum is ion-rich with high entropy (S >= 3): w stays at 1, and applying a power transformation with w < 1 there decreases similarity scoring performance. Peaks are not yet centroided or normalized: run ms_entropy.clean_spectrum() first (remove empty peaks, remove peaks above precursor_mz - precursor_ions_removal_da, merge peaks within +/- min_ms2_difference_in_da, noise threshold, top max_peak_num, normalize to sum 1) instead of computing entropy directly. The spectra are already centroided and your goal is only to compare similarity scoring functions rather than evaluate whether to add a centroiding filter You need electronic or chemical noise removal rather than peak-shape binning; use the spectral_denoising variant instead The analysis targets instrument-specific peak-picking fidelity rather than the downstream effect on spectral-similarity discrimination measured by AUROC http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Generates centroided variants of raw profile MS/MS spectra using a matchms/SpectralEntropy-derived cosine scoring framework, to test whether centroiding changes the AUROC with which cosine similarity separates same-compound from different-compound spectrum pairs. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c06256
skills.summary: Generates centroided variants of raw profile MS/MS spectra using a matchms/SpectralEntropy-derived cosine scoring framework, to test whether centroiding changes the AUROC with which cosine similarity separates same-compound from different-compound spectrum pairs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The spectra are already centroided and your goal is only to compare similarity scoring functions rather than evaluate whether to add a centroiding filter You need electronic or chemical noise removal rather than peak-shape binning; use the spectral_denoising variant instead The analysis targets instrument-specific peak-picking fidelity rather than the downstream effect on spectral-similarity discrimination measured by AUROC

skills.description: Use when starting from raw LC–MS files (e.g., mzML) from untargeted metabolomics acquisitions and you need feature detection — peak picking, deisotoping, adduct grouping — to build the extracted data matrix that subsequent curation filters will operate on.
skills.name: centwave-feature-detection-lcms
skills.search_text: centwave-feature-detection-lcms Use when starting from raw LC–MS files (e.g., mzML) from untargeted metabolomics acquisitions and you need feature detection — peak picking, deisotoping, adduct grouping — to build the extracted data matrix that subsequent curation filters will operate on. Input is already an extracted feature table or data matrix (e.g., exported from MZmine2, XCMS, or MSDIAL) rather than raw mzML — TidyMS curation pipelines then operate on the DataContainer instead. Feature annotation is the goal: the paper shows TidyMS lacks feature annotation capability, so it is the wrong tool for assigning compound identities to detected features. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Extract chromatographic spectral features from raw LC–MS data using TidyMS's CWT-based peak picking, chromatogram building, and centWave-style feature-detection routines, turning mzML files into a feature table (data matrix plus feature/sample descriptors). metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo10100416
skills.summary: Extract chromatographic spectral features from raw LC–MS data using TidyMS's CWT-based peak picking, chromatogram building, and centWave-style feature-detection routines, turning mzML files into a feature table (data matrix plus feature/sample descriptors).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already an extracted feature table or data matrix (e.g., exported from MZmine2, XCMS, or MSDIAL) rather than raw mzML — TidyMS curation pipelines then operate on the DataContainer instead. Feature annotation is the goal: the paper shows TidyMS lacks feature annotation capability, so it is the wrong tool for assigning compound identities to detected features.

skills.description: Use when AutoTuner peak detection has produced per-peak parameter estimates across raw metabolomics samples (mzML, mzXML, CDF) and they must be reduced to one dataset-wide centWave parameter vector.
skills.name: centwave-parameter-aggregation
skills.search_text: centwave-parameter-aggregation Use when AutoTuner peak detection has produced per-peak parameter estimates across raw metabolomics samples (mzML, mzXML, CDF) and they must be reduced to one dataset-wide centWave parameter vector. Input is already a dataset-wide parameter vector rather than a per-peak estimate table You need the Group difference parameter fully automated — it is estimated through a non-automatable cross-sample comparison during the TIC peak detection step You need mzDiff or retention-time correction tuning — mzDiff is the one continuous centWave parameter AutoTuner does not optimize http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Final integration stage of the AutoTuner R/BioConductor package that collapses the table of per-peak parameter estimates into a single dataset-wide set of eight centWave/XCMS parameters (ppm, S/N Threshold, Scan count, Noise, Prefilter intensity, Minimum/Maximum Peak-width, Group difference) for untargeted metabolomics data processing. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/812370
skills.summary: Final integration stage of the AutoTuner R/BioConductor package that collapses the table of per-peak parameter estimates into a single dataset-wide set of eight centWave/XCMS parameters (ppm, S/N Threshold, Scan count, Noise, Prefilter intensity, Minimum/Maximum Peak-width, Group difference) for untargeted metabolomics data processing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a dataset-wide parameter vector rather than a per-peak estimate table You need the Group difference parameter fully automated — it is estimated through a non-automatable cross-sample comparison during the TIC peak detection step You need mzDiff or retention-time correction tuning — mzDiff is the one continuous centWave parameter AutoTuner does not optimize

skills.description: Use when raw untargeted metabolomics data (mzML, mzXML, or CDF from qTOF, orbitrap, or FT-ICR analyzers) must be processed with XCMS/MZmine2 centWave and dataset-specific peak-picking parameters must be estimated in one pass rather than by iteratively testing parameter combinations.
skills.name: centwave-parameter-estimation-from-raw-scan-data
skills.search_text: centwave-parameter-estimation-from-raw-scan-data Use when raw untargeted metabolomics data (mzML, mzXML, or CDF from qTOF, orbitrap, or FT-ICR analyzers) must be processed with XCMS/MZmine2 centWave and dataset-specific peak-picking parameters must be estimated in one pass rather than by iteratively testing parameter combinations. Input is already a processed feature table — AutoTuner performs statistical inference on raw scan-level data, not on feature tables You need retention-time correction parameterization across samples — AutoTuner's divide-and-conquer approach does not compare EIC peaks across samples to estimate retention time correction You need the Group difference parameter — it requires a non-automatable cross-sample comparison during TIC peak detection and cannot be estimated by this stage AutoTuner's single-step statistical-inference stage that estimates the ppm mass-error parameter and the remaining continuous centWave peak-picking parameters (S/N threshold, scan count, noise, prefilter intensity, peakwidth) directly from scan-level raw data, replacing iterative parameter sweeping. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/812370
skills.summary: AutoTuner's single-step statistical-inference stage that estimates the ppm mass-error parameter and the remaining continuous centWave peak-picking parameters (S/N threshold, scan count, noise, prefilter intensity, peakwidth) directly from scan-level raw data, replacing iterative parameter sweeping.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a processed feature table — AutoTuner performs statistical inference on raw scan-level data, not on feature tables You need retention-time correction parameterization across samples — AutoTuner's divide-and-conquer approach does not compare EIC peaks across samples to estimate retention time correction You need the Group difference parameter — it requires a non-automatable cross-sample comparison during TIC peak detection and cannot be estimated by this stage

skills.description: Use when starting an untargeted metabolomics workflow from raw MS files and the XCMS/MZmine2 centWave parameters (peakwidth, ppm, snthresh, noise, mzdiff, etc.) have not yet been tuned for this dataset.
skills.name: centwave-peak-detection-parameterization
skills.search_text: centwave-peak-detection-parameterization Use when starting an untargeted metabolomics workflow from raw MS files and the XCMS/MZmine2 centWave parameters (peakwidth, ppm, snthresh, noise, mzdiff, etc.) have not yet been tuned for this dataset. Input is already a processed feature table rather than raw mzML/mzXML/CDF data — AutoTuner operates on raw instrument files only. Data are not untargeted metabolomics LC-MS from qTOF, Orbitrap, or FT-ICR instruments — AutoTuner has been validated only on those analyzer types. The goal is retention-time correction algorithm selection — AutoTuner's divide-and-conquer design does not compare EIC peaks across samples for that purpose. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Derives dataset-specific centWave peak-picking and grouping parameters from raw metabolomics data (e.g. mzML from qTOF, Orbitrap or FT-ICR instruments) using AutoTuner, replacing iterative parameter sweeping (IPO-style) with a single-step statistical inference on extracted-ion chromatograms. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/812370
skills.summary: Derives dataset-specific centWave peak-picking and grouping parameters from raw metabolomics data (e.g. mzML from qTOF, Orbitrap or FT-ICR instruments) using AutoTuner, replacing iterative parameter sweeping (IPO-style) with a single-step statistical inference on extracted-ion chromatograms.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a processed feature table rather than raw mzML/mzXML/CDF data — AutoTuner operates on raw instrument files only. Data are not untargeted metabolomics LC-MS from qTOF, Orbitrap, or FT-ICR instruments — AutoTuner has been validated only on those analyzer types. The goal is retention-time correction algorithm selection — AutoTuner's divide-and-conquer design does not compare EIC peaks across samples for that purpose.

skills.description: Use when raw LC-HRMS data (mzXML from e.g. Bruker Impact II UHR-QqTOF runs) must be converted into a feature table, and the analysis relies on XCMS 3.11.4+ centWave feature detection feeding downstream rescue or annotation steps.
skills.name: centwave-peak-picking-parameterization
skills.search_text: centwave-peak-picking-parameterization Use when raw LC-HRMS data (mzXML from e.g. Bruker Impact II UHR-QqTOF runs) must be converted into a feature table, and the analysis relies on XCMS 3.11.4+ centWave feature detection feeding downstream rescue or annotation steps. You need MS2 spectral annotation only, without re-picking features; use the downstream dot-product scoring step of DaDIA.R instead. Your XCMS version is below 3.11.4 — the article states this minimum is required to run DaDIA.R. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Parameterize and run XCMS's centWave peak-picking to extract metabolic features from DaDIA LC-MS mzXML files (DDA pooled-QC and DIA individual samples), as implemented inside the DaDIA.R pipeline. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c05022
skills.summary: Parameterize and run XCMS's centWave peak-picking to extract metabolic features from DaDIA LC-MS mzXML files (DDA pooled-QC and DIA individual samples), as implemented inside the DaDIA.R pipeline.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are already a processed feature table — centWave only operates on raw mzXML LC-MS files. You need MS2 spectral annotation only, without re-picking features; use the downstream dot-product scoring step of DaDIA.R instead. Your XCMS version is below 3.11.4 — the article states this minimum is required to run DaDIA.R.

skills.description: Use when lipid molecule name strings (e.g. from Metabolomics Workbench study ST001111 or Skyline exports) need class/chain-length/double-bond annotations, or when full-chemical-name ceramide entries fail name parsing and must be mapped to shorthand notation.
skills.name: ceramide-nomenclature-mapping
skills.search_text: ceramide-nomenclature-mapping Use when lipid molecule name strings (e.g. from Metabolomics Workbench study ST001111 or Skyline exports) need class/chain-length/double-bond annotations, or when full-chemical-name ceramide entries fail name parsing and must be mapped to shorthand notation. The dataset is already a lipidr LipidomicsExperiment with class/chain annotations inferred at import time — re-parsing names would be redundant The goal is downstream statistics (normalization, univariate analysis, LSEA) on already-annotated lipids rather than name-to-annotation mapping itself Molecule names fall outside lipidr's supported lipid patterns and no RegEx renaming (update_molecule_names) can be supplied — entries will simply be flagged as unparseable http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Parses lipid molecule name strings against lipidr's lipidnames_pattern regex rules to infer lipid class, total chain length, and unsaturation, renaming unparseable full-chemical-name ceramides to shorthand via update_molecule_names so annotations can be correctly inferred. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.0c00082
skills.summary: Parses lipid molecule name strings against lipidr's lipidnames_pattern regex rules to infer lipid class, total chain length, and unsaturation, renaming unparseable full-chemical-name ceramides to shorthand via update_molecule_names so annotations can be correctly inferred.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset is already a lipidr LipidomicsExperiment with class/chain annotations inferred at import time — re-parsing names would be redundant The goal is downstream statistics (normalization, univariate analysis, LSEA) on already-annotated lipids rather than name-to-annotation mapping itself Molecule names fall outside lipidr's supported lipid patterns and no RegEx renaming (update_molecule_names) can be supplied — entries will simply be flagged as unparseable

skills.description: Use when you have a TIC-normalised, lipid-annotated MSI pixel matrix (e.g. massPix image.norm.csv) and need to segment pixels of high spectral similarity into anatomical tissue regions and extract their average spectra.
skills.name: cerebellum-tissue-region-classification
skills.search_text: cerebellum-tissue-region-classification Use when you have a TIC-normalised, lipid-annotated MSI pixel matrix (e.g. massPix image.norm.csv) and need to segment pixels of high spectral similarity into anatomical tissue regions and extract their average spectra. You need non-k-means segmentation — massPix cluster.type currently only supports 'kmeans' clustering; use a spatially-aware clustering tool such as Cardinal instead. The input is raw vendor data not yet pre-processed — deisotoping, annotation and TIC normalisation (process=T in massPix) must be run first to obtain image.norm.csv. Your goal is lipid identification rather than tissue segmentation — accurate-mass annotation against the generated lipid library is a separate massPix step (makelibrary/annotate). http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Classifies mass spectrometry imaging pixels into tissue regions using k-means clustering in the massPix R package, producing clustered 2D tissue maps and cluster-center spectra. In the source paper this differentiated the three major cerebellum regions (white matter, granular and molecular layers) by lipid profile. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-017-1252-5
skills.summary: Classifies mass spectrometry imaging pixels into tissue regions using k-means clustering in the massPix R package, producing clustered 2D tissue maps and cluster-center spectra. In the source paper this differentiated the three major cerebellum regions (white matter, granular and molecular layers) by lipid profile.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need non-k-means segmentation — massPix cluster.type currently only supports 'kmeans' clustering; use a spatially-aware clustering tool such as Cardinal instead. The input is raw vendor data not yet pre-processed — deisotoping, annotation and TIC normalisation (process=T in massPix) must be run first to obtain image.norm.csv. Your goal is lipid identification rather than tissue segmentation — accurate-mass annotation against the generated lipid library is a separate massPix step (makelibrary/annotate).

skills.name: certified-feature-list-matching
skills.search_text: certified-feature-list-matching Use when benchmarking feature detection of LC-MS processing tools on datasets with known ground truth, e.g. HZV029 (402 Thermo-verified features), Yeast2021 (314 certified features), or E. coli (643 certified features). Input is already a feature table that has been annotated or matched to a compound database (e.g. via khipu pre-annotation against HMDB 4) — this skill benchmarks detection recall, not compound annotation The dataset has no manually verified or certified ground-truth feature list, so detection counts cannot be validated against reference features MS/MS-based identification is the goal — asari ignores MS/MS spectra in its default LC-MS workflow, so this matching is on MS1 features only http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Match LC-MS features extracted by a processing tool (asari, XCMS, MZmine) against manually certified/Thermo-verified reference feature lists to quantify feature detection recall and benchmark tools. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-023-39889-1
skills.summary: Match LC-MS features extracted by a processing tool (asari, XCMS, MZmine) against manually certified/Thermo-verified reference feature lists to quantify feature detection recall and benchmark tools.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a feature table that has been annotated or matched to a compound database (e.g. via khipu pre-annotation against HMDB 4) — this skill benchmarks detection recall, not compound annotation The dataset has no manually verified or certified ground-truth feature list, so detection counts cannot be validated against reference features MS/MS-based identification is the goal — asari ignores MS/MS spectra in its default LC-MS workflow, so this matching is on MS1 features only

skills.search_text: ceumass-restful-querying Use when a task needs compound records from CMM 3.0 via its RESTful API, or when verifying that newly added taxonomy and ontology metadata fields are present and populated for a set of queried metabolites. skills.description: Use when diagnosing why FSA rank-1 formula accuracy differs across datasets by comparing spectral-feature distributions (fragment count, peak-distance SD, CF ratio, top-2 score gap) between R1 and R2+ assignments.
skills.name: cf-ratio-distribution-interpretation
skills.search_text: cf-ratio-distribution-interpretation Use when diagnosing why FSA rank-1 formula accuracy differs across datasets by comparing spectral-feature distributions (fragment count, peak-distance SD, CF ratio, top-2 score gap) between R1 and R2+ assignments. Features are normally distributed and a parametric comparison (t-test/ANOVA) would be more appropriate than the non-parametric Wilcoxon rank-sum test Formulas were ranked by tools that use structural information (e.g., Buddy or SIRIUS), where FSA's CF-ratio-based feature interpretation does not apply Spectra contain elements beyond C, H, O, N, S, and P, which FSA has not been validated on Interprets the corrected-fragment (CF) ratio and companion spectral features (fragment count, inter-peak-distance SD, top-two score gap) as discriminators between correctly-ranked (R1) and incorrectly-ranked (R2+) formula assignments produced by FSA, using non-parametric group comparison and boxplot visualization per dataset. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-025-02379-0
skills.summary: Interprets the corrected-fragment (CF) ratio and companion spectral features (fragment count, inter-peak-distance SD, top-two score gap) as discriminators between correctly-ranked (R1) and incorrectly-ranked (R2+) formula assignments produced by FSA, using non-parametric group comparison and boxplot visualization per dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Features are normally distributed and a parametric comparison (t-test/ANOVA) would be more appropriate than the non-parametric Wilcoxon rank-sum test Formulas were ranked by tools that use structural information (e.g., Buddy or SIRIUS), where FSA's CF-ratio-based feature interpretation does not apply Spectra contain elements beyond C, H, O, N, S, and P, which FSA has not been validated on

skills.description: Use when ranking candidate compounds for Orbitrap HR-MS/MS spectra by fragmentation-only scoring (no reference or retention terms), particularly when comparing in silico fragmenters or when MetFrag's bond-dissociation scoring alone underperforms.
skills.name: cfm-id-spectral-prediction-scoring
skills.search_text: cfm-id-spectral-prediction-scoring Use when ranking candidate compounds for Orbitrap HR-MS/MS spectra by fragmentation-only scoring (no reference or retention terms), particularly when comparing in silico fragmenters or when MetFrag's bond-dissociation scoring alone underperforms. When the goal is the best possible identification with reference and retention information available — the article's combined MetFrag2.2 workflow (420 Top 1 with ChemSpider, 336 with PubChem) vastly outperforms fragmentation-only CFM-ID, so use the full MetFrag2.2 scoring instead. When spectra are dominated by one or only a few fragments (e.g. a single water loss) that most candidates can explain — the article notes such spectra 'simply do not contain enough information' to distinguish candidates, so any fragmentation-only scorer including CFM-ID will struggle. When ranking across a much larger or differently instrumented dataset without re-verification — the article's 43 Top 1 figure was established on the 473-spectrum Hill dataset and could shift after retraining CFM-ID on Orbitrap data. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Applies CFM-ID's competitive fragment modelling to predict in silico fragments for candidate structures and rank them against measured HR-MS/MS spectra using fragmentation information only, as benchmarked by MetFrag2.2 on the 473-spectrum Hill dataset (CFM-ID achieved 43 Top 1 ranks vs. MetFrag2.2's 30 with PubChem candidates). metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-016-0115-9
skills.summary: Applies CFM-ID's competitive fragment modelling to predict in silico fragments for candidate structures and rank them against measured HR-MS/MS spectra using fragmentation information only, as benchmarked by MetFrag2.2 on the 473-spectrum Hill dataset (CFM-ID achieved 43 Top 1 ranks vs. MetFrag2.2's 30 with PubChem candidates).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is the best possible identification with reference and retention information available — the article's combined MetFrag2.2 workflow (420 Top 1 with ChemSpider, 336 with PubChem) vastly outperforms fragmentation-only CFM-ID, so use the full MetFrag2.2 scoring instead. When spectra are dominated by one or only a few fragments (e.g. a single water loss) that most candidates can explain — the article notes such spectra 'simply do not contain enough information' to distinguish candidates, so any fragmentation-only scorer including CFM-ID will struggle. When ranking across a much larger or differently instrumented dataset without re-verification — the article's 43 Top 1 figure was established on the 473-spectrum Hill dataset and could shift after retraining CFM-ID on Orbitrap data.

skills.description: Use when an LC-MS peak table (mz/rt/intensity) must be annotated with homologue series by seeding 2-tuples from root peaks and extending chains under an m/z increment, 5 ppm tolerance, and 1–100 s rt constraints (targeted mz_steps like 44.02628 or untargeted 10–20 Da).
skills.name: chain-extension-with-ppm-and-rt-tolerances
skills.search_text: chain-extension-with-ppm-and-rt-tolerances Use when an LC-MS peak table (mz/rt/intensity) must be annotated with homologue series by seeding 2-tuples from root peaks and extending chains under an m/z increment, 5 ppm tolerance, and 1–100 s rt constraints (targeted mz_steps like 44.02628 or untargeted 10–20 Da). Input is raw LC-MS data (e.g. mzML) rather than an already peak-picked table with mz, rt, and intensity columns — chain extension operates on a filtered peak table. You need to evaluate or manage already-detected series (overlap checks, summaries, database push) rather than detect them — sdbCheckContained, sdbPush, and sdbSummarize cover that workflow. Expected m/z increments fall outside the untargeted search window (mz_min = 10 to mz_max = 20) and no targeted mz_steps are supplied. http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Reconstructs homologueDiscoverer's two-phase series detection: initializeTargeted/initializeUntargeted seed 2-tuples from root peaks, then expandChains extends each chain by screening the peak table for peaks matching the tuple's m/z increment within 5 ppm under the 1–100 s retention-time window, returning homologue_id-annotated peak tables. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btac647

skills.search_text: chemical-attribute-serialisation Use when a ViMMS 2.0 workflow has just sampled a synthetic chemical mixture (e.g. via ChemicalMixtureCreator with HMDB-backed or uniform m/z formula samplers) and the sampled chemical attributes need to be persisted for simulation, replay or ground-truth comparison. When chemicals are extracted from existing mzML files (the empirical route) rather than generated synthetically — the article states chemicals are 'produced synthetically or extracted from existing mzML files', and the empirical path has its own feature-extraction tooling. When the downstream step needs raw instrument scans (mzML output from an Environment run) rather than a ground-truth chemical list. When chemical identities are unknown and must remain simulated anonymous m/z features — serialising KnownChemical assumes formula-level ground truth. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Serialises ViMMS 2.0-simulated chemical objects (KnownChemical) to a machine-readable file capturing each chemical's m/z, retention time, intensity and formula after sampling via ChemicalMixtureCreator, so downstream simulation runs have a ground-truth chemical list. metabolomics/v3 10.21105/joss.03990
skills.summary: Serialises ViMMS 2.0-simulated chemical objects (KnownChemical) to a machine-readable file capturing each chemical's m/z, retention time, intensity and formula after sampling via ChemicalMixtureCreator, so downstream simulation runs have a ground-truth chemical list.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When chemicals are extracted from existing mzML files (the empirical route) rather than generated synthetically — the article states chemicals are 'produced synthetically or extracted from existing mzML files', and the empirical path has its own feature-extraction tooling. When the downstream step needs raw instrument scans (mzML output from an Environment run) rather than a ground-truth chemical list. When chemical identities are unknown and must remain simulated anonymous m/z features — serialising KnownChemical assumes formula-level ground truth.

skills.description: Use when you have generated k candidate SMILES from MSNovelist's RNN decoder for a tandem mass spectrum and need to deduplicate, validate, and rank them to pick the top de novo structure.
skills.name: chemical-candidate-dereplication-and-platt-reranking
skills.search_text: chemical-candidate-dereplication-and-platt-reranking Use when you have generated k candidate SMILES from MSNovelist's RNN decoder for a tandem mass spectrum and need to deduplicate, validate, and rank them to pick the top de novo structure. Input is already a validated, deduplicated, ranked structure list from a database search (e.g. CSI:FingerID output) — no de novo dereplication is needed. The MS2 spectrum has fewer than three fragment ions, so SIRIUS/CSI:FingerID cannot produce a reliable fingerprint and formula to rank against. Working with negative-mode spectra: MSNovelist is currently trained only for positive-mode data, so candidate quality and re-ranking reliability will be degraded. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Post-generation step of MSNovelist in which the k SMILES structures produced by the encoder-decoder RNN are validated, deduplicated, and then re-ranked against the query fingerprint using the modified Platt score. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-022-01486-3
skills.summary: Post-generation step of MSNovelist in which the k SMILES structures produced by the encoder-decoder RNN are validated, deduplicated, and then re-ranked against the query fingerprint using the modified Platt score.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a validated, deduplicated, ranked structure list from a database search (e.g. CSI:FingerID output) — no de novo dereplication is needed. The MS2 spectrum has fewer than three fragment ions, so SIRIUS/CSI:FingerID cannot produce a reliable fingerprint and formula to rank against. Working with negative-mode spectra: MSNovelist is currently trained only for positive-mode data, so candidate quality and re-ranking reliability will be degraded.

skills.description: Use when a set of significant metabolites (e.g. fold change ≥1, adjusted p < 0.05) needs to be interpreted structurally as an interaction network, to identify hub metabolites and compare topology against a published network figure.
skills.name: chemical-chemical-interaction-network-construction
skills.search_text: chemical-chemical-interaction-network-construction Use when a set of significant metabolites (e.g. fold change ≥1, adjusted p < 0.05) needs to be interpreted structurally as an interaction network, to identify hub metabolites and compare topology against a published network figure. The goal is pathway over-representation or MetSEA rather than metabolite-metabolite interaction topology — EnrichMet's Fisher's Exact Test and fgsea modules are the appropriate modules instead The metabolite set cannot be mapped to STITCH compound identifiers (e.g. lipid species without chemical-chemical interaction records; for lipidomics EnrichMet instead uses LION lipid-ontology associations) Input is raw metabolomics intensity data that has not yet undergone differential analysis to define the significant metabolite query set http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Builds a metabolite-metabolite interaction network from STITCH chemical-chemical relationships (filtered at combined score ≥100) and applies EnrichMet topology-based network analysis in R to rank hub metabolites by node degree and betweenness centrality, as demonstrated in the control-vs-mutant lung cancer case study where Xanthine emerged as a hub. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.08.28.672951
skills.summary: Builds a metabolite-metabolite interaction network from STITCH chemical-chemical relationships (filtered at combined score ≥100) and applies EnrichMet topology-based network analysis in R to rank hub metabolites by node degree and betweenness centrality, as demonstrated in the control-vs-mutant lung cancer case study where Xanthine emerged as a hub.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is pathway over-representation or MetSEA rather than metabolite-metabolite interaction topology — EnrichMet's Fisher's Exact Test and fgsea modules are the appropriate modules instead The metabolite set cannot be mapped to STITCH compound identifiers (e.g. lipid species without chemical-chemical interaction records; for lipidomics EnrichMet instead uses LION lipid-ontology associations) Input is raw metabolomics intensity data that has not yet undergone differential analysis to define the significant metabolite query set

skills.name: chemical-class-based-metabolite-grouping
skills.search_text: chemical-class-based-metabolite-grouping Use when a metabolomics/lipidomics feature table contains redundant or chemically related features (e.g. correlated isomers, shared chemical class) that should be collapsed into single nodes prior to DNEA network construction. The feature table is already reduced or contains only distinct, chemically unrelated metabolites with no correlated duplicate features You need every individual metabolite as a separate network node for downstream pathway or ID-level interpretation, since aggregation merges features into singular nodes The data are not from two experimental conditions with approximately normal peak-intensity values, which DNEA's joint network estimation requires http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 The aggregateFeatures() step of the DNEA R package (Step 1.2) collapses metabolomic features that are highly correlated and/or belong to the same chemical class into singular features, producing a collapsed_DNEAobj that reduces network dimensionality before joint estimation. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-024-05994-1
skills.summary: The aggregateFeatures() step of the DNEA R package (Step 1.2) collapses metabolomic features that are highly correlated and/or belong to the same chemical class into singular features, producing a collapsed_DNEAobj that reduces network dimensionality before joint estimation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The feature table is already reduced or contains only distinct, chemically unrelated metabolites with no correlated duplicate features You need every individual metabolite as a separate network node for downstream pathway or ID-level interpretation, since aggregation merges features into singular nodes The data are not from two experimental conditions with approximately normal peak-intensity values, which DNEA's joint network estimation requires

skills.search_text: chemical-class-enrichment-analysis Use when an IDSL.CSA-aligned compound matrix annotated with InChIKey/SMILES/molecular formula meta-variables must be clustered into chemical families and statistically tested for class-level abundance differences between two sample groups (e.g. Crohn's vs healthy controls). When the input is a raw mzXML/mzML/netCDF file rather than an already-aligned, CSA-annotated compound matrix — use IDSL.IPA/IDSL.CSA first When the question is peak-level (single compound) rather than class-level enrichment across chemically similar families When MS2-based annotation is required — this skill depends on CSA MS1-derived annotations and is not a replacement for MS/MS library searches via IDSL.FSA http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 A downstream metabolomics analysis skill that performs ChemRICH set enrichment analysis on chemically similar families of compounds derived from IDSL.CSA-annotated aligned peak tables, using a Kolmogorov–Smirnov test on effect-size-ranked compound lists to identify significantly altered chemical classes between disease and control groups. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c00376
