skills.summary: Counts unique referenced structure-organism pairs in a curated LOTUS deposit table at full stereochemical (3D) and flat (2D) levels, cross-checking structure and organism tallies to confirm the reported dissemination total of 750,000+ pairs (~30% of 2.5M+ initial pairs).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is the raw initial table (2.5M+ pre-validation pairs) rather than the curated 3_curated table — deduplication counts on unharmonized data will not reproduce the reported figures The goal is applying curation/filtering rules (manual validation of 420 pairs, filter_dirty.R, sanitization via MolVS) rather than counting the already-curated output Counts are needed from the Wikidata mirror via SPARQL queries rather than from the deposited flat TSV table

skills.description: Decision support for measuring the fraction of a compound collection (e.g. PubChem's >91 million compounds as of June 2016) classified under a manually maintained chemical ontology such as MeSH, when arguing for automated classification.
skills.name: chemical-ontology-coverage-quantification
skills.search_text: chemical-ontology-coverage-quantification Decision support for measuring the fraction of a compound collection (e.g. PubChem's >91 million compounds as of June 2016) classified under a manually maintained chemical ontology such as MeSH, when arguing for automated classification. The input is already a per-compound classification table — use per-entity taxonomy assignment (e.g. ClassyFire's four-step classification process) instead of re-deriving coverage from aggregate baselines. The classification system's coverage is being measured empirically by running the classifier on the database rather than comparing published baseline figures. The goal is to evaluate classification accuracy or rule correctness rather than to quantify how much of a database an ontology covers. http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Quantify how much of a large compound database is covered by a chemical classification system by computing absolute classified counts and percent-coverage ratios from reported baseline figures, to expose the manual-annotation gap that motivates automated taxonomies like ClassyFire's ChemOnt. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-016-0174-y
skills.summary: Quantify how much of a large compound database is covered by a chemical classification system by computing absolute classified counts and percent-coverage ratios from reported baseline figures, to expose the manual-annotation gap that motivates automated taxonomies like ClassyFire's ChemOnt.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a per-compound classification table — use per-entity taxonomy assignment (e.g. ClassyFire's four-step classification process) instead of re-deriving coverage from aggregate baselines. The classification system's coverage is being measured empirically by running the classifier on the database rather than comparing published baseline figures. The goal is to evaluate classification accuracy or rule correctness rather than to quantify how much of a database an ontology covers.

skills.description: Use when two chemical prioritization rankings (e.g., RI vs PrHQ) cover overlapping chemical sets and you need to quantify agreement between their orderings via rank correlation and overlap extraction.
skills.name: chemical-prioritization-overlap-analysis
skills.search_text: chemical-prioritization-overlap-analysis Use when two chemical prioritization rankings (e.g., RI vs PrHQ) cover overlapping chemical sets and you need to quantify agreement between their orderings via rank correlation and overlap extraction. Chemicals lacking a CASRN — the HTS method is based on the U.S. EPA Chemistry Dashboard, so only chemicals with CASRN can retrieve the relevant domain data Chemicals absent from the SEEM database, which was unable to cover all compounds in the study Cases requiring internal-dose-based prioritization — the risk score was calculated using external exposure, and the IVIVE model was deferred to future studies Compares two risk-based chemical prioritization schemes — a Risk Index (RI = rescaled log-normalized SEEM exposure × ToxPi score from ToxCast) and a probabilistic hazard quotient (PrHQ) — by extracting each overlapping chemical's rank in both rankings and computing the Pearson correlation between the rank sets (r = 0.1, p < 0.001 for 7,770 RI-ranked chemicals). metabolomics/v3 10.1289/ehp7722
skills.summary: Compares two risk-based chemical prioritization schemes — a Risk Index (RI = rescaled log-normalized SEEM exposure × ToxPi score from ToxCast) and a probabilistic hazard quotient (PrHQ) — by extracting each overlapping chemical's rank in both rankings and computing the Pearson correlation between the rank sets (r = 0.1, p < 0.001 for 7,770 RI-ranked chemicals).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Chemicals lacking a CASRN — the HTS method is based on the U.S. EPA Chemistry Dashboard, so only chemicals with CASRN can retrieve the relevant domain data Chemicals absent from the SEEM database, which was unable to cover all compounds in the study Cases requiring internal-dose-based prioritization — the risk score was calculated using external exposure, and the IVIVE model was deferred to future studies

skills.description: Use when you have human exposure estimates and predicted toxicity (e.g., oral LD50) for a chemical set and need a ranked risk prioritization spanning many orders of magnitude.
skills.name: chemical-priority-ranking
skills.search_text: chemical-priority-ranking Use when you have human exposure estimates and predicted toxicity (e.g., oral LD50) for a chemical set and need a ranked risk prioritization spanning many orders of magnitude. The goal is a multi-domain toxicity ranking (e.g., ToxPi scoring from ToxCast HTS assays) rather than an exposure/hazard quotient — the paper computed ToxPi scores separately for comprehensive toxicity ranking Chronic or subchronic toxicity risk assessment is required — the LD50-based PrHQ approach may underestimate such risks A chemical lacks SEEM exposure coverage — the SEEM database was unable to cover all compounds in the study Prioritizes chemicals by probabilistic hazard quotient (PrHQ), computed as the ratio of SEEM-based exposure estimates (EHE) to LD50-derived probabilistic reference doses (HDMI), producing a risk-ranked list of exposome chemicals. metabolomics/v3 10.1289/ehp7722
skills.summary: Prioritizes chemicals by probabilistic hazard quotient (PrHQ), computed as the ratio of SEEM-based exposure estimates (EHE) to LD50-derived probabilistic reference doses (HDMI), producing a risk-ranked list of exposome chemicals.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is a multi-domain toxicity ranking (e.g., ToxPi scoring from ToxCast HTS assays) rather than an exposure/hazard quotient — the paper computed ToxPi scores separately for comprehensive toxicity ranking Chronic or subchronic toxicity risk assessment is required — the LD50-based PrHQ approach may underestimate such risks A chemical lacks SEEM exposure coverage — the SEEM database was unable to cover all compounds in the study

skills.description: Use when a task needs the complete annotation/summary content for one specific PubChem record (e.g. Compound Summary for a CID) via programmatic access, and the record can be named by a single CID, SID, or AID.
skills.name: chemical-record-identifier-mapping
skills.search_text: chemical-record-identifier-mapping Use when a task needs the complete annotation/summary content for one specific PubChem record (e.g. Compound Summary for a CID) via programmatic access, and the record can be named by a single CID, SID, or AID. The task requires retrieving annotations for many records in one call — a PUG-View request cannot take multiple input record identifiers. The task needs specific individual computed compound properties — use PUG-REST, which is best suited for that. The task needs specialized (especially tabular) data that come from other backend services and are not accessible through PUG-View. http://edamontology.org/topic_3315 http://edamontology.org/topic_0218 Retrieves full-record annotation content for a single PubChem record (compound CID, substance SID, or assay AID) by constructing a PUG-View REST request URL that embeds the database, the record identifier, and the output format, then saving the returned JSON. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-019-0375-2
skills.summary: Retrieves full-record annotation content for a single PubChem record (compound CID, substance SID, or assay AID) by constructing a PUG-View REST request URL that embeds the database, the record identifier, and the output format, then saving the returned JSON.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task requires retrieving annotations for many records in one call — a PUG-View request cannot take multiple input record identifiers. The task needs specific individual computed compound properties — use PUG-REST, which is best suited for that. The task needs specialized (especially tabular) data that come from other backend services and are not accessible through PUG-View.

skills.description: Use when you need programmatic SVG QR codes linking a compound (CID) to its PubChem safety summary, or to retrieve biologic depiction images and annotation attachments via PUG-View special reports.
skills.name: chemical-safety-qr-linking
skills.search_text: chemical-safety-qr-linking Use when you need programmatic SVG QR codes linking a compound (CID) to its PubChem safety summary, or to retrieve biologic depiction images and annotation attachments via PUG-View special reports. When you need specific individual computed compound properties — PUG-REST, not PUG-View, is the interface best suited for that. When you need all structural neighbors of a compound — the PUG-View neighbors form returns only neighbors with pre-defined annotation types; use PUG-REST instead. When a request must accept multiple record identifiers or retrieve annotations under multiple headings at once — PUG-View cannot take multiple input record identifiers and multiple headings require full-annotation retrieval. http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 Reconstructs and applies the PUG-View special-report request variants — QR codes that encode a compound's link to its PubChem chemical safety summary (LCSS), biologic depiction images, and annotation attachment retrieval — as executable URL templates. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-019-0375-2
skills.summary: Reconstructs and applies the PUG-View special-report request variants — QR codes that encode a compound's link to its PubChem chemical safety summary (LCSS), biologic depiction images, and annotation attachment retrieval — as executable URL templates.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When you need specific individual computed compound properties — PUG-REST, not PUG-View, is the interface best suited for that. When you need all structural neighbors of a compound — the PUG-View neighbors form returns only neighbors with pre-defined annotation types; use PUG-REST instead. When a request must accept multiple record identifiers or retrieve annotations under multiple headings at once — PUG-View cannot take multiple input record identifiers and multiple headings require full-annotation retrieval.

skills.description: Use when preprocessed, window-selected 1H-NMR spectra (spectra_df) still contain residual peak shifts and must be reduced to a lower-dimensional bucketed feature table before multivariate statistical analysis.
skills.name: chemical-shift-axis-partitioning
skills.search_text: chemical-shift-axis-partitioning Use when preprocessed, window-selected 1H-NMR spectra (spectra_df) still contain residual peak shifts and must be reduced to a lower-dimensional bucketed feature table before multivariate statistical analysis. Input is already a binned/feature table rather than a full-resolution spectra_df matrix The spectra have not yet been preprocessed and window-selected (e.g. no phase correction, internal referencing, or baseline correction has been applied) Peak-shift correction is needed without dimensionality reduction — use Icoshift peak alignment instead of binning http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Reduces the high dimensionality of 1H-NMR spectra by partitioning the chemical shift axis into equidistant bins (e.g. 0.1 ppm) and integrating the area under the curve within each bin via Protomix's binning function, yielding a bucketed data matrix for downstream multivariate analysis such as PCA. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioadv/vbae192
skills.summary: Reduces the high dimensionality of 1H-NMR spectra by partitioning the chemical shift axis into equidistant bins (e.g. 0.1 ppm) and integrating the area under the curve within each bin via Protomix's binning function, yielding a bucketed data matrix for downstream multivariate analysis such as PCA.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a binned/feature table rather than a full-resolution spectra_df matrix The spectra have not yet been preprocessed and window-selected (e.g. no phase correction, internal referencing, or baseline correction has been applied) Peak-shift correction is needed without dimensionality reduction — use Icoshift peak alignment instead of binning

skills.description: Use when 1D 1H NMR metabolomics spectra show uncontrolled chemical-shift variations between spectra that must be calibrated and realigned before binning or statistical analysis.
skills.name: chemical-shift-calibration-and-alignment
skills.search_text: chemical-shift-calibration-and-alignment Use when 1D 1H NMR metabolomics spectra show uncontrolled chemical-shift variations between spectra that must be calibrated and realigned before binning or statistical analysis. The region of interest contains intertwined peaks but the spectra do not have the same amount of peaks there — Parametric Time Warping only gives a better result when peak counts match. Input is already a binned/bucketed feature table (Intelligent, variable size or fixed width binning) — realignment operates on calibrated spectra before binning. A fully automatic, black-box batch pipeline for non-expert use is required — the article states automated batch-mode workflows have not reached full maturity and interactive processing with a spectra viewer is still needed. http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 Interactive calibration of the ppm scale and realignment of resonances across sets of 1D 1H NMR spectra in NMRProcFlow, using the Least-Square realignment algorithm per selected ppm area or Parametric Time Warping (Bloemberg et al. 2010) for regions with intertwined peaks, so that uncontrolled chemical-shift variations between spectra do not distort downstream binning. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-017-1178-y
skills.summary: Interactive calibration of the ppm scale and realignment of resonances across sets of 1D 1H NMR spectra in NMRProcFlow, using the Least-Square realignment algorithm per selected ppm area or Parametric Time Warping (Bloemberg et al. 2010) for regions with intertwined peaks, so that uncontrolled chemical-shift variations between spectra do not distort downstream binning.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The region of interest contains intertwined peaks but the spectra do not have the same amount of peaks there — Parametric Time Warping only gives a better result when peak counts match. Input is already a binned/bucketed feature table (Intelligent, variable size or fixed width binning) — realignment operates on calibrated spectra before binning. A fully automatic, black-box batch pipeline for non-expert use is required — the article states automated batch-mode workflows have not reached full maturity and interactive processing with a spectra viewer is still needed.

skills.description: Use when you have paired experimental NMR mixture spectra and pure-component reference spectra and need to quantify how far identical peaks shift (ppm) between mixture and reference before applying shift-tolerant identification.
skills.name: chemical-shift-deviation-computation
skills.search_text: chemical-shift-deviation-computation Use when you have paired experimental NMR mixture spectra and pure-component reference spectra and need to quantify how far identical peaks shift (ppm) between mixture and reference before applying shift-tolerant identification. You need compound identification of mixture spectra itself — use the pSCNN classification model, not this deviation statistics computation Your spectra are simulated/augmented training spectra with no experimental mixture-vs-reference pairing, since the deviation interval is defined only for experimental spectral pairs Peaks cannot be reliably paired between mixture and reference spectra (e.g., severe peak overlapping with no unambiguous correspondence) http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Computes the magnitude and interval of chemical shift deviations (in ppm) between experimental NMR mixture spectra and their pure-component reference spectra, after excluding active-hydrogen and DMSO-d6/HDO solvent signals, to quantify the chemical shift variation problem that motivates pSCNN. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/molecules27123653
skills.summary: Computes the magnitude and interval of chemical shift deviations (in ppm) between experimental NMR mixture spectra and their pure-component reference spectra, after excluding active-hydrogen and DMSO-d6/HDO solvent signals, to quantify the chemical shift variation problem that motivates pSCNN.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need compound identification of mixture spectra itself — use the pSCNN classification model, not this deviation statistics computation Your spectra are simulated/augmented training spectra with no experimental mixture-vs-reference pairing, since the deviation interval is defined only for experimental spectral pairs Peaks cannot be reliably paired between mixture and reference spectra (e.g., severe peak overlapping with no unambiguous correspondence)

skills.description: Use when user-defined 1H NMR ROIs (e.g., 18 ROIs over 0.5-4.5 ppm) must be screened against a reference metabolite library to list every metabolite with at least one chemical shift peak inside each ROI.
skills.name: chemical-shift-roi-matching
skills.search_text: chemical-shift-roi-matching Use when user-defined 1H NMR ROIs (e.g., 18 ROIs over 0.5-4.5 ppm) must be screened against a reference metabolite library to list every metabolite with at least one chemical shift peak inside each ROI. Automated ROI identification or ROI accuracy checking is needed — it is beyond the scope of the current ROIAL-NMR version; ROIs must be user-defined and the program was not built to test their accuracy. Absolute quantification of compounds is the goal — the program's primary aim is identification and categorization of potential metabolites, not quantification. Only chemical shift values are available without metabolite-specific SRRMs — the paper found both are required for accurate metabolite identification. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Screens a reference metabolite NMR library (chemical shift values and SRRMs for 891 HMDB metabolites) against user-defined proton NMR spectral regions-of-interest, marking each SRRM with a peak inside a ROI and scoring a match ratio (matched/total SRRMs, kept if >=0.5) to shortlist candidate metabolites without over-identification. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/nbm.70131
skills.summary: Screens a reference metabolite NMR library (chemical shift values and SRRMs for 891 HMDB metabolites) against user-defined proton NMR spectral regions-of-interest, marking each SRRM with a peak inside a ROI and scoring a match ratio (matched/total SRRMs, kept if >=0.5) to shortlist candidate metabolites without over-identification.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Automated ROI identification or ROI accuracy checking is needed — it is beyond the scope of the current ROIAL-NMR version; ROIs must be user-defined and the program was not built to test their accuracy. Absolute quantification of compounds is the goal — the program's primary aim is identification and categorization of potential metabolites, not quantification. Only chemical shift values are available without metabolite-specific SRRMs — the paper found both are required for accurate metabolite identification.

skills.description: Use when a task requires per-atom assigned chemical shifts (residue, atom name, shift value) from a BMRB macromolecule or metabolomics entry, or when building CSV/NEF tables from NMR-STAR files.
skills.name: chemical-shift-table-extraction
skills.search_text: chemical-shift-table-extraction Use when a task requires per-atom assigned chemical shifts (residue, atom name, shift value) from a BMRB macromolecule or metabolomics entry, or when building CSV/NEF tables from NMR-STAR files. Input is a processed/derived table rather than an archival NMR-STAR entry — route chemical shift tables through the STARch converter instead of re-parsing NMR-STAR. The goal is structure deposition or coordinate validation (e.g. OneDep/ADIT-NMR workflow) rather than shift data extraction. You need time-domain or processed spectra files themselves rather than the assigned shift loop — fetch those from the BMRB FTP metabolomics directory instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_3366 Programmatically retrieve a BMRB entry in NMR-STAR format via the BMRB REST API, parse and validate it with PyNMR-STAR, and extract the assigned chemical shift loop (Atom_chem_shift records) into a comma-delimited shift table. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/978-1-0716-0270-6_14
skills.summary: Programmatically retrieve a BMRB entry in NMR-STAR format via the BMRB REST API, parse and validate it with PyNMR-STAR, and extract the assigned chemical shift loop (Atom_chem_shift records) into a comma-delimited shift table.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a processed/derived table rather than an archival NMR-STAR entry — route chemical shift tables through the STARch converter instead of re-parsing NMR-STAR. The goal is structure deposition or coordinate validation (e.g. OneDep/ADIT-NMR workflow) rather than shift data extraction. You need time-domain or processed spectra files themselves rather than the assigned shift loop — fetch those from the BMRB FTP metabolomics directory instead.

skills.description: Use when you need to verify that a spectral mixture-identification model is robust to chemical shift variation, by generating shifted spectral pairs and mapping the shift interval over which predictions stay above a threshold (here 0.5).
skills.name: chemical-shift-variation-simulation
skills.search_text: chemical-shift-variation-simulation Use when you need to verify that a spectral mixture-identification model is robust to chemical shift variation, by generating shifted spectral pairs and mapping the shift interval over which predictions stay above a threshold (here 0.5). The task is training or fine-tuning a model rather than stress-testing a pretrained model's robustness to chemical shift variation The spectra are not NMR spectra of small-molecule mixtures, so the ppm-scale chemical shift perturbation scheme is not meaningful You only need point-performance metrics (ACC/TPR/FPR) on an unchanged test set rather than a shift-sweep robustness interval http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Systematically perturb NMR spectral pairs with a grid of chemical shift variations and run the pretrained pSCNN model on the varied spectra to quantify how large a shift the model tolerates before its predicted probabilities drop below 0.5. This tests the translational-invariance claim of CNN-based compound identification in NMR mixtures. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/molecules27123653
skills.summary: Systematically perturb NMR spectral pairs with a grid of chemical shift variations and run the pretrained pSCNN model on the varied spectra to quantify how large a shift the model tolerates before its predicted probabilities drop below 0.5. This tests the translational-invariance claim of CNN-based compound identification in NMR mixtures.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is training or fine-tuning a model rather than stress-testing a pretrained model's robustness to chemical shift variation The spectra are not NMR spectra of small-molecule mixtures, so the ppm-scale chemical shift perturbation scheme is not meaningful You only need point-performance metrics (ACC/TPR/FPR) on an unchanged test set rather than a shift-sweep robustness interval

skills.description: Use when running a Pickaxe/MINE-Database reaction-rule expansion that explodes in compound counts and you want to bias the network toward chemical space near defined target structures via a hard Tanimoto cutoff.
skills.name: chemical-similarity-cutoff-filtering
skills.search_text: chemical-similarity-cutoff-filtering Use when running a Pickaxe/MINE-Database reaction-rule expansion that explodes in compound counts and you want to bias the network toward chemical space near defined target structures via a hard Tanimoto cutoff. The goal is to hold network size constant per generation (e.g., exactly 2000 compounds); use the similarity sampling filter instead, which samples from a weighted distribution of similarity scores. The filtering criterion is metabolomics peaks, thermodynamic Gibbs energy, or reaction feasibility rather than structural similarity to targets. No target compounds are defined, so no maximum-similarity score can be computed for pruning. A Pickaxe on-the-fly network-pruning method that computes each candidate compound's maximum Tanimoto similarity to a set of target compounds and removes any compound whose maximum score falls below a specified cutoff before the next expansion generation, preventing exponential network growth. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-023-05149-8
skills.summary: A Pickaxe on-the-fly network-pruning method that computes each candidate compound's maximum Tanimoto similarity to a set of target compounds and removes any compound whose maximum score falls below a specified cutoff before the next expansion generation, preventing exponential network growth.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to hold network size constant per generation (e.g., exactly 2000 compounds); use the similarity sampling filter instead, which samples from a weighted distribution of similarity scores. The filtering criterion is metabolomics peaks, thermodynamic Gibbs energy, or reaction feasibility rather than structural similarity to targets. No target compounds are defined, so no maximum-similarity score can be computed for pruning.

skills.description: Use when you need to connect metabolites lacking known biochemical intermediates via structural similarity: identifiers (names, KEGG, HMDB, InChIKey) must be converted to PubChem CIDs, fingerprints compared by Tanimoto coefficient, and edges filtered at a specified cutoff.
skills.name: chemical-similarity-network-edge-filtering
skills.search_text: chemical-similarity-network-edge-filtering Use when you need to connect metabolites lacking known biochemical intermediates via structural similarity: identifiers (names, KEGG, HMDB, InChIKey) must be converted to PubChem CIDs, fingerprints compared by Tanimoto coefficient, and edges filtered at a specified cutoff. When the goal is biochemical transformation networks based on KEGG RPAIR substrate-product pairs rather than structural similarity When input compounds have no structural annotation and no retrievable PubChem fingerprints (mass spectral similarity may be the only extension for unknowns) When edges should derive from empirical associations (Pearson, biweight, or Spearman correlations) rather than structural similarity http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 Constructs a metabolite structural similarity network by translating identifiers to PubChem CIDs, retrieving PubChem Substructure Fingerprints, computing pairwise Tanimoto coefficients, and retaining only edges whose Tanimoto score exceeds the >0.7 threshold used by MetaMapR. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btv194
skills.summary: Constructs a metabolite structural similarity network by translating identifiers to PubChem CIDs, retrieving PubChem Substructure Fingerprints, computing pairwise Tanimoto coefficients, and retaining only edges whose Tanimoto score exceeds the >0.7 threshold used by MetaMapR.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is biochemical transformation networks based on KEGG RPAIR substrate-product pairs rather than structural similarity When input compounds have no structural annotation and no retrievable PubChem fingerprints (mass spectral similarity may be the only extension for unknowns) When edges should derive from empirical associations (Pearson, biweight, or Spearman correlations) rather than structural similarity

skills.description: Use when you have TOCSY/HSQC spectra for a sample set (e.g., prefractionated extract library) and need to cluster samples by shared structural features to dereplicate known scaffolds or locate bioactivity hotspots.
skills.name: chemical-similarity-network-generation
skills.search_text: chemical-similarity-network-generation Use when you have TOCSY/HSQC spectra for a sample set (e.g., prefractionated extract library) and need to cluster samples by shared structural features to dereplicate known scaffolds or locate bioactivity hotspots. The compounds of interest have exclusively shielded 1H signals (e.g., sterols, low MW isoprenoids, lipids, volatile terpenes) — the <2.5 ppm TOCSY shielded quadrant is excluded, so these classes are precluded unless user-supplied reference spectra are added You have a single spectrum rather than a sample set — the network step matches spin system features BETWEEN samples and requires multiple samples Input is already a molecular fingerprint/MS/MS spectral library similarity table rather than NMR spin system features — MADByTE operates on TOCSY/HSQC-derived spin systems MADByTE's network generation converts pairwise spin-system similarity scores (derived from paired TOCSY/HSQC spectra) into full association, similarity, and hybrid chemical similarity networks exported as graphML for dereplication and bioactivity-guided prioritization of natural product mixtures. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jnatprod.0c01076
skills.summary: MADByTE's network generation converts pairwise spin-system similarity scores (derived from paired TOCSY/HSQC spectra) into full association, similarity, and hybrid chemical similarity networks exported as graphML for dereplication and bioactivity-guided prioritization of natural product mixtures.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The compounds of interest have exclusively shielded 1H signals (e.g., sterols, low MW isoprenoids, lipids, volatile terpenes) — the <2.5 ppm TOCSY shielded quadrant is excluded, so these classes are precluded unless user-supplied reference spectra are added You have a single spectrum rather than a sample set — the network step matches spin system features BETWEEN samples and requires multiple samples Input is already a molecular fingerprint/MS/MS spectral library similarity table rather than NMR spin system features — MADByTE operates on TOCSY/HSQC-derived spin systems

skills.description: Use when sample-level NMR feature tables (spin systems with 1H/13C shifts) from multiple samples must be compared to build a similarity matrix for network generation or dereplication.
skills.name: chemical-similarity-scoring
skills.search_text: chemical-similarity-scoring Use when sample-level NMR feature tables (spin systems with 1H/13C shifts) from multiple samples must be compared to build a similarity matrix for network generation or dereplication. Input is already a network edge list or an already-symmetrized similarity matrix — this skill operates on raw spin system feature tables. Compounds contain exclusively shielded 1H signals (e.g. sterols, low MW isoprenoids, lipids, volatile terpenes) — MADByTE excludes TOCSY cross-peaks where both F1 and F2 are < 2.5 ppm, so features for these classes are missing and scores are unreliable. Comparing 1D-only spectra or non-TOCSY/HSQC feature representations — the scoring depends on paired (1H, 13C) HSQC cross-peaks. http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_3292 Scores pairwise similarity between samples by matching spin system features (overlapping (1H, 13C) pairs) derived from TOCSY/HSQC data, populating an asymmetric correlation matrix whose edges use the higher of the two directional scores. This drives MADByTE chemical similarity network construction for dereplication and metabolite prioritization. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jnatprod.0c01076
skills.summary: Scores pairwise similarity between samples by matching spin system features (overlapping (1H, 13C) pairs) derived from TOCSY/HSQC data, populating an asymmetric correlation matrix whose edges use the higher of the two directional scores. This drives MADByTE chemical similarity network construction for dereplication and metabolite prioritization.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a network edge list or an already-symmetrized similarity matrix — this skill operates on raw spin system feature tables. Compounds contain exclusively shielded 1H signals (e.g. sterols, low MW isoprenoids, lipids, volatile terpenes) — MADByTE excludes TOCSY cross-peaks where both F1 and F2 are < 2.5 ppm, so features for these classes are missing and scores are unreliable. Comparing 1D-only spectra or non-TOCSY/HSQC feature representations — the scoring depends on paired (1H, 13C) HSQC cross-peaks.

skills.description: Use when you need a database-independent molecular formula candidate space for untargeted LC/HRMS annotation (e.g., exposomics compounds absent from metabolite databases) and must constrain which elemental compositions are enumerated before building a theoretical isotopic profile database (IPDB).
skills.name: chemical-space-boundary-definition
skills.search_text: chemical-space-boundary-definition Use when you need a database-independent molecular formula candidate space for untargeted LC/HRMS annotation (e.g., exposomics compounds absent from metabolite databases) and must constrain which elemental compositions are enumerated before building a theoretical isotopic profile database (IPDB). Your formula candidates come from a known biochemical/database-dependent source (e.g., RefMet, reaction-network or MS2-based tools like SIRIUS/ZODIAC) — the enumeration space is for database-independent annotation where such databases would miss exposome compounds The raw enumerated space exceeds ~10^27 compositions and exhaustive enumeration is intractable — IDSL.UFAx applies a heuristic approach instead The goal is peak picking rather than formula-space definition — use IDSL.IPA first to generate mz-RT peaklists from mzXML/mzML/netCDF, then apply this skill to define the annotation space http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Defines and constrains a database-independent enumerated chemical space (ECS) of molecular formulas by applying IDSL.UFA's four enumeration rules — the 16-element set, the C/N chemical-space elemental-boundary rule for organics, the extended SENIOR valence rule, halogen-count caps, and a maximum-number-of-elements cap — so a tractable candidate set can feed isotope-profile database (IPDB) generation for MS1 formula annotation. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.2c00563
skills.summary: Defines and constrains a database-independent enumerated chemical space (ECS) of molecular formulas by applying IDSL.UFA's four enumeration rules — the 16-element set, the C/N chemical-space elemental-boundary rule for organics, the extended SENIOR valence rule, halogen-count caps, and a maximum-number-of-elements cap — so a tractable candidate set can feed isotope-profile database (IPDB) generation for MS1 formula annotation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your formula candidates come from a known biochemical/database-dependent source (e.g., RefMet, reaction-network or MS2-based tools like SIRIUS/ZODIAC) — the enumeration space is for database-independent annotation where such databases would miss exposome compounds The raw enumerated space exceeds ~10^27 compositions and exhaustive enumeration is intractable — IDSL.UFAx applies a heuristic approach instead The goal is peak picking rather than formula-space definition — use IDSL.IPA first to generate mz-RT peaklists from mzXML/mzML/netCDF, then apply this skill to define the annotation space

skills.description: Use when you have multiple MGF-format spectral libraries with SMILES structure annotations and need a visual, structure-based comparison of which library spans more chemical space.
skills.name: chemical-space-coverage-comparison
skills.search_text: chemical-space-coverage-comparison Use when you have multiple MGF-format spectral libraries with SMILES structure annotations and need a visual, structure-based comparison of which library spans more chemical space. You are comparing libraries by spectral similarity (cosine or spectral-entropy scores) rather than by chemical-structure coverage of their SMILES annotations. The spectra lack parseable or standardizable SMILES structure annotations, so no structure-level union table can be built. The goal is de-duplication or near-duplicate removal of spectra, not cross-library coverage visualization. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 Compares the chemical-space coverage of machine-learning-ready MS/MS spectral libraries (Spectraverse, MassSpecGym, NPLIB1) by embedding their unique structure annotations (SMILES) into a shared 2D UMAP space and rendering per-library density overlays, demonstrating Spectraverse's broader coverage. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c06256
skills.summary: Compares the chemical-space coverage of machine-learning-ready MS/MS spectral libraries (Spectraverse, MassSpecGym, NPLIB1) by embedding their unique structure annotations (SMILES) into a shared 2D UMAP space and rendering per-library density overlays, demonstrating Spectraverse's broader coverage.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You are comparing libraries by spectral similarity (cosine or spectral-entropy scores) rather than by chemical-structure coverage of their SMILES annotations. The spectra lack parseable or standardizable SMILES structure annotations, so no structure-level union table can be built. The goal is de-duplication or near-duplicate removal of spectra, not cross-library coverage visualization.

skills.description: Use when you need to visually compare the structural diversity or chemical-space coverage of multiple compound libraries (e.g., OMSLs vs. natural-product catalogues) by embedding a fixed molecular fingerprint representation into 2-D with t-SNE.
skills.name: chemical-space-dimensionality-reduction
skills.search_text: chemical-space-dimensionality-reduction Use when you need to visually compare the structural diversity or chemical-space coverage of multiple compound libraries (e.g., OMSLs vs. natural-product catalogues) by embedding a fixed molecular fingerprint representation into 2-D with t-SNE. Input compounds already have a low-dimensional embedding or PCA/UMAP coordinates available — t-SNE is stochastic and not designed to replace an existing projection. The goal is quantitative similarity search between individual spectra rather than global chemical-space visualization — use spectral similarity scoring (dot product / reverse dot product) instead. Compound identifiers lack normalized InChIKeys or PubChem fingerprint coverage (e.g., purely in-silico spectra without chemical identifiers), so the descriptor vector cannot be built. http://edamontology.org/topic_3339 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Reduces PubChem molecular fingerprints to a 2-D t-SNE projection so that the chemical-space coverage of different open mass spectral libraries (GNPS, MoNA, MassBank, MS-Dial-VS17) can be visually compared, with compounds colored by NPClassifier superclass. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c02219
skills.summary: Reduces PubChem molecular fingerprints to a 2-D t-SNE projection so that the chemical-space coverage of different open mass spectral libraries (GNPS, MoNA, MassBank, MS-Dial-VS17) can be visually compared, with compounds colored by NPClassifier superclass.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input compounds already have a low-dimensional embedding or PCA/UMAP coordinates available — t-SNE is stochastic and not designed to replace an existing projection. The goal is quantitative similarity search between individual spectra rather than global chemical-space visualization — use spectral similarity scoring (dot product / reverse dot product) instead. Compound identifiers lack normalized InChIKeys or PubChem fingerprint coverage (e.g., purely in-silico spectra without chemical identifiers), so the descriptor vector cannot be built.

skills.description: Use when a user-supplied table of compound names (with aggregate p-value/fold-change statistics) contains naming synonyms or ambiguous identifiers that must be harmonized to a single identifier scheme before meta-analysis.
skills.name: chemical-standardization-inchikey-resolution
skills.search_text: chemical-standardization-inchikey-resolution Use when a user-supplied table of compound names (with aggregate p-value/fold-change statistics) contains naming synonyms or ambiguous identifiers that must be harmonized to a single identifier scheme before meta-analysis. Input compounds already carry consistent InChIKeys or other unambiguous identifiers and need no name-based lookup The analysis goal is the meta-analysis itself (p-value/fold-change combination) rather than pre-analysis identifier harmonization — use the amanida meta-analysis step instead Compounds are not indexable by name in PubChem or the conversion services (e.g. unnamed features, isotopologues without CAS/name entries) http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3292 Harmonizes compound names in a metabolomics dataset by resolving each name to unambiguous chemical identifiers — PubChem CID, Molecular Formula, Molecular Weight, Canonical SMILES, InChIKey, and KEGG/ChEBI/HMDB/DrugBank cross-references — using webchem's PubChem retrieval and identifier-conversion functions, a prerequisite for valid compound-name combination in the Easy-Amanida meta-analysis. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/jrsm.1713
skills.summary: Harmonizes compound names in a metabolomics dataset by resolving each name to unambiguous chemical identifiers — PubChem CID, Molecular Formula, Molecular Weight, Canonical SMILES, InChIKey, and KEGG/ChEBI/HMDB/DrugBank cross-references — using webchem's PubChem retrieval and identifier-conversion functions, a prerequisite for valid compound-name combination in the Easy-Amanida meta-analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input compounds already carry consistent InChIKeys or other unambiguous identifiers and need no name-based lookup The analysis goal is the meta-analysis itself (p-value/fold-change combination) rather than pre-analysis identifier harmonization — use the amanida meta-analysis step instead Compounds are not indexable by name in PubChem or the conversion services (e.g. unnamed features, isotopologues without CAS/name entries)

skills.description: Use when you have standardized chemical structures (SMILES/Molfile) and need machine-readable structural features — functional groups, ring counts, heteroatom composition, property constraints — to drive rule-based category assignment.
skills.name: chemical-structural-feature-extraction
skills.search_text: chemical-structural-feature-extraction Use when you have standardized chemical structures (SMILES/Molfile) and need machine-readable structural features — functional groups, ring counts, heteroatom composition, property constraints — to drive rule-based category assignment. Your classification must be based on biological activity, use, or textual metadata rather than purely on chemical structure — ClassyFire assigns categories using only structures and structural features The compound is undergoing/representing a reaction state (e.g. loss of oxygen, substitutions) that may not satisfy category description constraints You only need parent-level labels without structural justification — a pre-computed annotation database (e.g. PubChem's ClassyFire classification) may suffice http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 Extract structural features (substructures, functional groups, ring systems, physico-chemical properties) from a chemical structure so it can be matched against rule-based taxonomy categories such as ChemOnt's >4800 categories. This is the core engine step of ClassyFire's purely structure-based classification. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-016-0174-y
skills.summary: Extract structural features (substructures, functional groups, ring systems, physico-chemical properties) from a chemical structure so it can be matched against rule-based taxonomy categories such as ChemOnt's >4800 categories. This is the core engine step of ClassyFire's purely structure-based classification.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your classification must be based on biological activity, use, or textual metadata rather than purely on chemical structure — ClassyFire assigns categories using only structures and structural features The compound is undergoing/representing a reaction state (e.g. loss of oxygen, substitutions) that may not satisfy category description constraints You only need parent-level labels without structural justification — a pre-computed annotation database (e.g. PubChem's ClassyFire classification) may suffice

skills.description: Use when auditing a curated BGC or compound database (e.g. MIBiG JSON entries) before/after a re-curation release, to quantify entries lacking product chemical structures and entries with incomplete property annotations.
skills.name: chemical-structure-annotation-coverage-analysis
skills.search_text: chemical-structure-annotation-coverage-analysis Use when auditing a curated BGC or compound database (e.g. MIBiG JSON entries) before/after a re-curation release, to quantify entries lacking product chemical structures and entries with incomplete property annotations. The goal is BGC discovery or novelty assessment against MIBiG (e.g. antiSMASH homology searches), not auditing annotation completeness of the repository itself The dataset is a candidate-BGC prediction set from genome mining with no curated chemical structure fields to audit Entries already carry validated structures and the purpose is query/filtering of the repository (e.g. Boolean queries by compound name or biosynthetic class) rather than coverage accounting http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Audits a curated biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) repository to quantify chemical-structure annotation completeness: how many entries lack product structures, how many have missing/incomplete chemical property fields (formula, mass, chirality), and how many gained structure annotations after re-curation. Modeled on the MIBiG 2.0 re-annotation audit, which reported 770 entries lacking product structures and 500 entries with missing or incomplete properties out of 2021 BGCs, with new structure info metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkz882
skills.summary: Audits a curated biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) repository to quantify chemical-structure annotation completeness: how many entries lack product structures, how many have missing/incomplete chemical property fields (formula, mass, chirality), and how many gained structure annotations after re-curation. Modeled on the MIBiG 2.0 re-annotation audit, which reported 770 entries lacking product structures and 500 entries with missing or incomplete properties out of 2021 BGCs, with new structure info
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is BGC discovery or novelty assessment against MIBiG (e.g. antiSMASH homology searches), not auditing annotation completeness of the repository itself The dataset is a candidate-BGC prediction set from genome mining with no curated chemical structure fields to audit Entries already carry validated structures and the purpose is query/filtering of the repository (e.g. Boolean queries by compound name or biosynthetic class) rather than coverage accounting

skills.description: Use when a GNPS molecular network's nodes have structure annotations (GNPS library hits, NAP or DEREPLICATOR outputs with SMILES) and you need per-molecular-family chemical class scores at each ClassyFire ontology level.
skills.name: chemical-structure-classification
skills.search_text: chemical-structure-classification Use when a GNPS molecular network's nodes have structure annotations (GNPS library hits, NAP or DEREPLICATOR outputs with SMILES) and you need per-molecular-family chemical class scores at each ClassyFire ontology level. The task is mapping MS2LDA Mass2Motif substructure information onto the network (prob/overlap/top parameters), not chemical class scoring — use the Mass2Motifs_2_Network workflow instead. The input data has no structure annotations (no SMILES/InChIKeys) — ClassyFire classification cannot proceed without structural representations. Input is raw MS/MS spectra rather than an annotated molecular network; create the molecular network through GNPS and perform in silico annotation (NAP, DEREPLICATOR, or another tool of preference) first. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 Assign ClassyFire chemical classes to molecular-network nodes and compute per-family chemical classification scores at each ClassyFire ontology level (superclass, class, subclass), as implemented in MolNetEnhancer/pyMolNetEnhancer. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo9070144
skills.summary: Assign ClassyFire chemical classes to molecular-network nodes and compute per-family chemical classification scores at each ClassyFire ontology level (superclass, class, subclass), as implemented in MolNetEnhancer/pyMolNetEnhancer.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is mapping MS2LDA Mass2Motif substructure information onto the network (prob/overlap/top parameters), not chemical class scoring — use the Mass2Motifs_2_Network workflow instead. The input data has no structure annotations (no SMILES/InChIKeys) — ClassyFire classification cannot proceed without structural representations. Input is raw MS/MS spectra rather than an annotated molecular network; create the molecular network through GNPS and perform in silico annotation (NAP, DEREPLICATOR, or another tool of preference) first.

skills.description: Use when a curated BGC entry carries compound name and chemical structure metadata and you need to inventory which external chemical resources (PubChem, Natural Products Atlas, GNPS) hold a corresponding cross-link for that entry.
skills.name: chemical-structure-correspondence-curation
skills.search_text: chemical-structure-correspondence-curation Use when a curated BGC entry carries compound name and chemical structure metadata and you need to inventory which external chemical resources (PubChem, Natural Products Atlas, GNPS) hold a corresponding cross-link for that entry. The input consists of candidate BGCs mined from genomes with unknown products (e.g. antiSMASH/IMG-ABC output) rather than BGCs of known function with annotated compound names/structures — no matching keys exist The goal is BGC novelty assessment or homology searching against MIBiG, not chemical cross-reference curation Only a single chemical database is of interest and no per-accession link inventory is needed http://edamontology.org/topic_3332 Curation skill that establishes and tabulates cross-links between annotated MIBiG biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) records and external chemical/analytical resources (Natural Products Atlas, GNPS spectral library, PubChem) by matching compound names and chemical structures, mirroring the MIBiG 2.0 feature of direct link-outs to chemical structure databases. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkz882
skills.summary: Curation skill that establishes and tabulates cross-links between annotated MIBiG biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) records and external chemical/analytical resources (Natural Products Atlas, GNPS spectral library, PubChem) by matching compound names and chemical structures, mirroring the MIBiG 2.0 feature of direct link-outs to chemical structure databases.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input consists of candidate BGCs mined from genomes with unknown products (e.g. antiSMASH/IMG-ABC output) rather than BGCs of known function with annotated compound names/structures — no matching keys exist The goal is BGC novelty assessment or homology searching against MIBiG, not chemical cross-reference curation Only a single chemical database is of interest and no per-accession link inventory is needed

skills.description: Use when a chemical structure dataset (e.g. MIBiG JSON entries with compound SMILES and substrate SMILES fields) needs syntax-level correctness checking before downstream ML training or database release.
skills.name: chemical-structure-curation-flagging
skills.search_text: chemical-structure-curation-flagging Use when a chemical structure dataset (e.g. MIBiG JSON entries with compound SMILES and substrate SMILES fields) needs syntax-level correctness checking before downstream ML training or database release. Input SMILES are already provided by a curated chemical database cross-link (NP Atlas, PubChem, ChemSpider, LOTUS, ChEMBL) with known-valid structures — validation adds little here The goal is validating chemical correctness (stereochemistry, valence) of a drawn structure rather than SMILES string syntax/parsability http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Validates the SMILES syntax of compound structures and protein-domain substrate annotations in MIBiG 3.0 JSON entries by parsing each string with the PIKAChU toolkit, and flags any string that fails syntax validation. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkac1049
skills.summary: Validates the SMILES syntax of compound structures and protein-domain substrate annotations in MIBiG 3.0 JSON entries by parsing each string with the PIKAChU toolkit, and flags any string that fails syntax validation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input SMILES are already provided by a curated chemical database cross-link (NP Atlas, PubChem, ChemSpider, LOTUS, ChEMBL) with known-valid structures — validation adds little here The goal is validating chemical correctness (stereochemistry, valence) of a drawn structure rather than SMILES string syntax/parsability

skills.description: Use when editable ChemDraw .cdxml structure records (e.g., DNA adducts drawn with unspecified modification positions) must be converted to .mol files and standard identifiers (SMILES, InChI, InChIKey) for a chemical database.
skills.name: chemical-structure-format-conversion
skills.search_text: chemical-structure-format-conversion Use when editable ChemDraw .cdxml structure records (e.g., DNA adducts drawn with unspecified modification positions) must be converted to .mol files and standard identifiers (SMILES, InChI, InChIKey) for a chemical database. Input identifiers are already SMILES/InChI and only need merging or harmonization of names and formulas — the conversion step is redundant. The objects are spectra (e.g., mzML HRMS/MS files from the LC-HRMS workflow) rather than chemical structure records — use spectral processing, not structure-format conversion. Convert ChemDraw-drawn chemical structures (.cdxml) into interoperable computational identifiers (.mol files, IUPAC nomenclature, SMILES, InChI, InChIKey) so a small-molecule database — here, 582 DNA adduct entries — can be searched, linked, and merged into .xlsx tables. metabolomics/v3 10.3389/fchem.2022.908572
skills.summary: Convert ChemDraw-drawn chemical structures (.cdxml) into interoperable computational identifiers (.mol files, IUPAC nomenclature, SMILES, InChI, InChIKey) so a small-molecule database — here, 582 DNA adduct entries — can be searched, linked, and merged into .xlsx tables.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input identifiers are already SMILES/InChI and only need merging or harmonization of names and formulas — the conversion step is redundant. The objects are spectra (e.g., mzML HRMS/MS files from the LC-HRMS workflow) rather than chemical structure records — use spectral processing, not structure-format conversion.

skills.description: Use when building or extending a small-molecule/chemical database where each entry needs machine-readable structure identifiers (.mol, .cdxml, SMILES, InChI, InChIKey) before spectral prediction or search.
skills.name: chemical-structure-identifier-extraction
skills.search_text: chemical-structure-identifier-extraction Use when building or extending a small-molecule/chemical database where each entry needs machine-readable structure identifiers (.mol, .cdxml, SMILES, InChI, InChIKey) before spectral prediction or search. The input is already a normalized identifier table (e.g. an SDF or SMILES list) and you only need spectral prediction downstream. You are annotating spectra without any new chemical structure — this skill assumes you have or can generate structure files for each adduct. Your target molecules lack defined chemical structures (e.g. you only have m/z peaks with no candidate formula). http://edamontology.org/topic_3335 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Extracts computer-readable chemical structure identifiers (SMILES, InChI, InChIKey, IUPAC names) plus structure files (.cdxml, .mol) and monoisotopic masses from a curated DNA adduct database, so each entry can be fed to downstream in silico fragmentation tools like CFM-ID. metabolomics/v3 10.3389/fchem.2022.908572
skills.summary: Extracts computer-readable chemical structure identifiers (SMILES, InChI, InChIKey, IUPAC names) plus structure files (.cdxml, .mol) and monoisotopic masses from a curated DNA adduct database, so each entry can be fed to downstream in silico fragmentation tools like CFM-ID.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a normalized identifier table (e.g. an SDF or SMILES list) and you only need spectral prediction downstream. You are annotating spectra without any new chemical structure — this skill assumes you have or can generate structure files for each adduct. Your target molecules lack defined chemical structures (e.g. you only have m/z peaks with no candidate formula).

skills.description: Use when a tool renders many predicted biosynthetic cluster diagrams (PKS, NRPS, or hybrid 'spaghetti diagrams') and you must quantify how many are structurally correct and visually legible.
skills.name: chemical-structure-readability-evaluation
skills.search_text: chemical-structure-readability-evaluation Use when a tool renders many predicted biosynthetic cluster diagrams (PKS, NRPS, or hybrid 'spaghetti diagrams') and you must quantify how many are structurally correct and visually legible. Validating chemical product structures against known compounds (e.g. MIBiG entries) — the article notes fingerprinting-based automatic validation of MIBiG BGCs was considered but not implemented, and predicted scaffolds may not match mature natural products from raw antiSMASH output Assessing prediction accuracy of BGC detection/annotation itself (use antiSMASH/PRISM evaluation rather than diagram readability scoring) http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 A validation protocol for automatically generated biosynthetic 'spaghetti diagrams' in which each rendered cluster is manually scored for drawing correctness (depicted structures match encoded module/domain composition) and readability (legible bond angles, no text/structure overlap), benchmarked against RAIChU's reported 100% correctness and 97.66% readability. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00898-x
skills.summary: A validation protocol for automatically generated biosynthetic 'spaghetti diagrams' in which each rendered cluster is manually scored for drawing correctness (depicted structures match encoded module/domain composition) and readability (legible bond angles, no text/structure overlap), benchmarked against RAIChU's reported 100% correctness and 97.66% readability.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Validating chemical product structures against known compounds (e.g. MIBiG entries) — the article notes fingerprinting-based automatic validation of MIBiG BGCs was considered but not implemented, and predicted scaffolds may not match mature natural products from raw antiSMASH output Assessing prediction accuracy of BGC detection/annotation itself (use antiSMASH/PRISM evaluation rather than diagram readability scoring)

skills.description: Use when building a weighted molecular network for annotation propagation and you need edge weights that blend MetFrag candidate scores, spectral cosine similarity and structural similarity of candidate compounds.
skills.name: chemical-structure-similarity-calculation
skills.search_text: chemical-structure-similarity-calculation Use when building a weighted molecular network for annotation propagation and you need edge weights that blend MetFrag candidate scores, spectral cosine similarity and structural similarity of candidate compounds. When the molecular network already provides reliable edge weights and no MetFrag candidate scores are available, since the weight function requires per-candidate MetFrag annotation scores as input When annotating isolated spectra with no molecular network, since structural-similarity edge weights depend on pairs of connected network nodes http://edamontology.org/topic_0089 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Compute pairwise chemical (structural) similarity among candidate structures produced by MetFrag in silico fragmentation, and combine these similarities with spectral cosine scores and MetFrag annotation scores through a MetFusion-style sigmoid weight function to derive the edge weights w_ij of the ChemWalker weighted graph. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad078
skills.summary: Compute pairwise chemical (structural) similarity among candidate structures produced by MetFrag in silico fragmentation, and combine these similarities with spectral cosine scores and MetFrag annotation scores through a MetFusion-style sigmoid weight function to derive the edge weights w_ij of the ChemWalker weighted graph.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the molecular network already provides reliable edge weights and no MetFrag candidate scores are available, since the weight function requires per-candidate MetFrag annotation scores as input When annotating isolated spectra with no molecular network, since structural-similarity edge weights depend on pairs of connected network nodes

skills.description: Use when tentative GC-MS compound names (e.g. from Unknowns Analysis output with a Match.Factor column) need substructure descriptors or Tanimoto structural matching against a user-defined chemical category library.
skills.name: chemical-structure-substructure-descriptor-extraction
skills.search_text: chemical-structure-substructure-descriptor-extraction Use when tentative GC-MS compound names (e.g. from Unknowns Analysis output with a Match.Factor column) need substructure descriptors or Tanimoto structural matching against a user-defined chemical category library. Input is MS2, MS3, or ion mobility + MS2 data — uafR depends on published spectra and its algorithms do not yet apply to these modes Compounds lack a PubChem entry or cannot have a canonical SMILES generated — the decontaminate step removes these, so no structure is available for descriptor extraction The goal is only GC-MS peak-area aggregation without structural interpretation — use spreadOut()/mzExacto()/standardifyIt() directly instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Extracts ring, subgroup, atom-count, and charge substructure descriptors from resolved compound structures (via ChemmineR) and runs maximum common substructure (fmcsBatch) Tanimoto comparisons against a user-labeled chemical library, splitting matches into strong (>0.95) and moderate (>0.85) tiers. This is the structural-comparison core of uafR's categorate() cheminformatics workflow. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pone.0306202
skills.summary: Extracts ring, subgroup, atom-count, and charge substructure descriptors from resolved compound structures (via ChemmineR) and runs maximum common substructure (fmcsBatch) Tanimoto comparisons against a user-labeled chemical library, splitting matches into strong (>0.95) and moderate (>0.85) tiers. This is the structural-comparison core of uafR's categorate() cheminformatics workflow.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is MS2, MS3, or ion mobility + MS2 data — uafR depends on published spectra and its algorithms do not yet apply to these modes Compounds lack a PubChem entry or cannot have a canonical SMILES generated — the decontaminate step removes these, so no structure is available for descriptor extraction The goal is only GC-MS peak-area aggregation without structural interpretation — use spreadOut()/mzExacto()/standardifyIt() directly instead

skills.description: Use when training or scoring RASSP models that need a candidate set of fragment subformulae and atom subsets for a small molecule (≤48 atoms, HCONFSPCl only), or when reproducing the RASSP featurization pipeline that converts molecules into graph, subformula, and spectra tensors.
skills.name: chemical-subformula-enumeration
skills.search_text: chemical-subformula-enumeration Use when training or scoring RASSP models that need a candidate set of fragment subformulae and atom subsets for a small molecule (≤48 atoms, HCONFSPCl only), or when reproducing the RASSP featurization pipeline that converts molecules into graph, subformula, and spectra tensors. The molecule contains elements outside HCONFSPCl or exceeds 48 total atoms / 4096 unique fragment formulae — the RASSP pipeline filters these out before enumeration. The goal is predicting the mass spectrum of a molecule with resolution above 48 atoms for FormulaNet (or 64 for SubsetNet per the spectroscopy.ai API limits), where the enumeration is not defined. Exotic fragmentation schemes beyond recursive bond-breaking to depth 3 with hydrogen rearrangements are required — the authors explicitly note these were ignored. http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Enumerates all chemically valid subformulae of a molecular formula (e.g. all subsets of C7H8) by recursively taking the setwise Cartesian product of per-element subformula sets, then applies heuristic bond-breaking (to depth d=3) with exhaustive hydrogen rearrangements to generate the physically plausible fragment candidates that FormulaNet and SubsetNet score in RASSP EI–MS prediction. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.2c02093
skills.summary: Enumerates all chemically valid subformulae of a molecular formula (e.g. all subsets of C7H8) by recursively taking the setwise Cartesian product of per-element subformula sets, then applies heuristic bond-breaking (to depth d=3) with exhaustive hydrogen rearrangements to generate the physically plausible fragment candidates that FormulaNet and SubsetNet score in RASSP EI–MS prediction.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The molecule contains elements outside HCONFSPCl or exceeds 48 total atoms / 4096 unique fragment formulae — the RASSP pipeline filters these out before enumeration. The goal is predicting the mass spectrum of a molecule with resolution above 48 atoms for FormulaNet (or 64 for SubsetNet per the spectroscopy.ai API limits), where the enumeration is not defined. Exotic fragmentation schemes beyond recursive bond-breaking to depth 3 with hydrogen rearrangements are required — the authors explicitly note these were ignored.

skills.description: Use when you have MS/MS spectra with InChIKey annotations and 2D embeddings (e.g., t-SNE or UMAP of MS2DeepScore vectors) and need to check whether the projection groups spectra by chemical (super)class.
skills.name: chemical-superclass-annotation
skills.search_text: chemical-superclass-annotation Use when you have MS/MS spectra with InChIKey annotations and 2D embeddings (e.g., t-SNE or UMAP of MS2DeepScore vectors) and need to check whether the projection groups spectra by chemical (super)class. Spectra lack InChIKey (or equivalent structure) annotations, so no ClassyFire superclass can be assigned You need per-compound classification beyond the 14 ClassyFire superclasses (e.g., fine-grained chemical classes) — this skill only validates coarse superclass-level clustering The goal is predicting Tanimoto similarity scores between spectrum pairs rather than validating embedding chemical meaningfulness via class-colored visualization http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Annotates mass spectra (via their compounds' InChIKeys) with one of 14 ClassyFire chemical superclasses and overlays these labels on 2D dimensionality-reduction plots (t-SNE of 200-dim MS2DeepScore embeddings) to verify that embeddings cluster spectra by chemistry. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-021-00558-4
skills.summary: Annotates mass spectra (via their compounds' InChIKeys) with one of 14 ClassyFire chemical superclasses and overlays these labels on 2D dimensionality-reduction plots (t-SNE of 200-dim MS2DeepScore embeddings) to verify that embeddings cluster spectra by chemistry.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Spectra lack InChIKey (or equivalent structure) annotations, so no ClassyFire superclass can be assigned You need per-compound classification beyond the 14 ClassyFire superclasses (e.g., fine-grained chemical classes) — this skill only validates coarse superclass-level clustering The goal is predicting Tanimoto similarity scores between spectrum pairs rather than validating embedding chemical meaningfulness via class-colored visualization

skills.description: Use when evaluating a chemical structure-class classifier (e.g., DeepSAT on HSQC spectra) and you need per-superclass F1-scores to identify the lowest-performing NPClassifier structure classes and their causes.
skills.name: chemical-superclass-classification-evaluation
skills.search_text: chemical-superclass-classification-evaluation Use when evaluating a chemical structure-class classifier (e.g., DeepSAT on HSQC spectra) and you need per-superclass F1-scores to identify the lowest-performing NPClassifier structure classes and their causes. You need whole-model summary metrics (top-1 accuracy, fingerprint cosine score, MW R-squared) rather than per-structure-class breakdowns. The classifier output is a molecular fingerprint for similarity search (cosine > 0.8) rather than discrete NPClassifier superclass labels. http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_3292 Computes per-class precision, recall, and F1-scores for each of the 59 NPClassifier superclass labels predicted by a multi-task CNN (DeepSAT) trained on 143,467 1H-13C HSQC spectra, ranking classes to expose the weakest structural categories and diagnosing why they underperform. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-023-00738-4
skills.summary: Computes per-class precision, recall, and F1-scores for each of the 59 NPClassifier superclass labels predicted by a multi-task CNN (DeepSAT) trained on 143,467 1H-13C HSQC spectra, ranking classes to expose the weakest structural categories and diagnosing why they underperform.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need whole-model summary metrics (top-1 accuracy, fingerprint cosine score, MW R-squared) rather than per-structure-class breakdowns. The classifier output is a molecular fingerprint for similarity search (cosine > 0.8) rather than discrete NPClassifier superclass labels.

skills.description: Use when you need compound-level bioactivity and molecular-target coverage statistics from MIBiG JSON entries, e.g. to reproduce the 1002-compound / 51-bioactivity / 95-target annotation table.
skills.name: chemical-target-annotation-extraction
skills.search_text: chemical-target-annotation-extraction Use when you need compound-level bioactivity and molecular-target coverage statistics from MIBiG JSON entries, e.g. to reproduce the 1002-compound / 51-bioactivity / 95-target annotation table. Input is antiSMASH-style predicted BGC output rather than manually curated, experimentally validated MIBiG entries — MIBiG annotations come from community curation, not automated prediction. You need sequence-structure-function training data (e.g. A-domain substrates) rather than compound-level bioactivity/target coverage counts. The MIBiG version predates 3.0 (e.g. MIBiG 2.0, 2021 entries), so the 1002-compound / 51-bioactivity / 95-target tallies will not validate. http://edamontology.org/topic_0218 http://edamontology.org/topic_3407 Parses MIBiG 3.0 JSON-formatted cluster entries to extract compound bioactivity annotations and the subset carrying chemical (molecular) target data, then normalises bioactivity terms into the 68 standardised functional categories and tallies per-category compound coverage. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkac1049
skills.summary: Parses MIBiG 3.0 JSON-formatted cluster entries to extract compound bioactivity annotations and the subset carrying chemical (molecular) target data, then normalises bioactivity terms into the 68 standardised functional categories and tallies per-category compound coverage.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is antiSMASH-style predicted BGC output rather than manually curated, experimentally validated MIBiG entries — MIBiG annotations come from community curation, not automated prediction. You need sequence-structure-function training data (e.g. A-domain substrates) rather than compound-level bioactivity/target coverage counts. The MIBiG version predates 3.0 (e.g. MIBiG 2.0, 2021 entries), so the 1002-compound / 51-bioactivity / 95-target tallies will not validate.

skills.description: Use when a merged Qemistree feature-data artifact already carries structures (ms2_smiles and/or csi_smiles) and you need ClassyFire chemical ontology labels per molecule to color tree subtrees, check class-level sample patterns, or compute class annotation coverage.
skills.name: chemical-taxonomy-assignment
skills.search_text: chemical-taxonomy-assignment Use when a merged Qemistree feature-data artifact already carries structures (ms2_smiles and/or csi_smiles) and you need ClassyFire chemical ontology labels per molecule to color tree subtrees, check class-level sample patterns, or compute class annotation coverage. The feature data artifact has no resolved structures because make-hierarchy has not yet been run or all features were filtered out as MS1-only without fingerprints — ClassyFire classification requires a SMILES structure. The goal is to assign taxonomy from raw spectra directly, without prior GNPS spectral library matching or CSI:FingerID fingerprint prediction — spectral matches alone typically cover only 1–20% of features and ClassyFire operates on annotated structures. Input is a feature table or MGF of raw MS/MS data rather than the merged feature-data artifact output by qemistree make-hierarchy. http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Assigns each MS1 feature a ClassyFire 5-level chemical taxonomy (kingdom, superclass, class, subclass, direct_parent) using the structures obtained from GNPS MS2 spectral library matches and CSI:FingerID predictions, so that chemical classes (e.g., acyl-carnitines, flavonoids) can be traced as subtrees on the Qemistree chemical hierarchy. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41589-020-00677-3
skills.summary: Assigns each MS1 feature a ClassyFire 5-level chemical taxonomy (kingdom, superclass, class, subclass, direct_parent) using the structures obtained from GNPS MS2 spectral library matches and CSI:FingerID predictions, so that chemical classes (e.g., acyl-carnitines, flavonoids) can be traced as subtrees on the Qemistree chemical hierarchy.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The feature data artifact has no resolved structures because make-hierarchy has not yet been run or all features were filtered out as MS1-only without fingerprints — ClassyFire classification requires a SMILES structure. The goal is to assign taxonomy from raw spectra directly, without prior GNPS spectral library matching or CSI:FingerID fingerprint prediction — spectral matches alone typically cover only 1–20% of features and ClassyFire operates on annotated structures. Input is a feature table or MGF of raw MS/MS data rather than the merged feature-data artifact output by qemistree make-hierarchy.

skills.description: Use when a structure list (e.g. SMILES tagged by organism origin) must be classified with NPClassifier and summarized into per-pathway or per-superclass counts to compare chemical space across organism groups.
skills.name: chemical-taxonomy-hierarchy-aggregation
skills.search_text: chemical-taxonomy-hierarchy-aggregation Use when a structure list (e.g. SMILES tagged by organism origin) must be classified with NPClassifier and summarized into per-pathway or per-superclass counts to compare chemical space across organism groups. When structures are already annotated with taxonomy labels from another source (e.g. ClassyFire or Dictionary of Natural Products classes) and no reclassification is needed When the goal is structural similarity clustering rather than hierarchical category counting — NPClassifier predicts fixed pathway/superclass/class labels, not pairwise similarities http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Aggregates NPClassifier's three-level structural predictions (pathway, superclass, class) for a set of structures into per-taxonomy count tables, enabling organism-level comparisons such as bacterial-vs-fungal terpenoid and PKS superclass distributions in the Natural Products Atlas. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jnatprod.1c00399
skills.summary: Aggregates NPClassifier's three-level structural predictions (pathway, superclass, class) for a set of structures into per-taxonomy count tables, enabling organism-level comparisons such as bacterial-vs-fungal terpenoid and PKS superclass distributions in the Natural Products Atlas.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When structures are already annotated with taxonomy labels from another source (e.g. ClassyFire or Dictionary of Natural Products classes) and no reclassification is needed When the goal is structural similarity clustering rather than hierarchical category counting — NPClassifier predicts fixed pathway/superclass/class labels, not pairwise similarities

skills.description: Use when building or reconstructing a hierarchical chemical ontology from structural classification rules — e.g. assembling the ChemOnt tree from SMARTS/Markush rules into an OBO file with parent 'is_a' links.
skills.name: chemical-taxonomy-hierarchy-construction
skills.search_text: chemical-taxonomy-hierarchy-construction Use when building or reconstructing a hierarchical chemical ontology from structural classification rules — e.g. assembling the ChemOnt tree from SMARTS/Markush rules into an OBO file with parent 'is_a' links.
