You need to classify a query compound against an already-built taxonomy — that is ClassyFire's classification pipeline (feature extraction, rule-based category assignment, direct-parent selection), not taxonomy construction The domain is fully covered by an existing ontology (e.g. organic compounds in established ontologies) — ChemOnt's dedicated construction effort targets the inorganic/organometallic coverage gap You need non-structural, usage-based classification rather than rules computable purely from chemical structure http://edamontology.org/topic_0089 Constructs a large, computable, purely structure-based chemical taxonomy (ChemOnt) as a hierarchy of >4800 categories across up to 11 Linnaean-style levels, encoding each category with machine-executable structural rules (SMARTS, Markush patterns, or logical expressions) in OBO format plus a JSON mirror. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-016-0174-y
skills.summary: Constructs a large, computable, purely structure-based chemical taxonomy (ChemOnt) as a hierarchy of >4800 categories across up to 11 Linnaean-style levels, encoding each category with machine-executable structural rules (SMARTS, Markush patterns, or logical expressions) in OBO format plus a JSON mirror.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need to classify a query compound against an already-built taxonomy — that is ClassyFire's classification pipeline (feature extraction, rule-based category assignment, direct-parent selection), not taxonomy construction The domain is fully covered by an existing ontology (e.g. organic compounds in established ontologies) — ChemOnt's dedicated construction effort targets the inorganic/organometallic coverage gap You need non-structural, usage-based classification rather than rules computable purely from chemical structure

skills.description: Use when untargeted LC-MS/MS features have predicted molecular fingerprints (e.g., from SIRIUS/CSI:FingerID on MZmine2 MGF output) and you need a chemical hierarchy for downstream tree-based analyses like UniFrac or Faith's phylogenetic diversity.
skills.name: chemical-tree-construction
skills.search_text: chemical-tree-construction Use when untargeted LC-MS/MS features have predicted molecular fingerprints (e.g., from SIRIUS/CSI:FingerID on MZmine2 MGF output) and you need a chemical hierarchy for downstream tree-based analyses like UniFrac or Faith's phylogenetic diversity. Features have only MS1 data and no MS/MS fragmentation spectra — Qemistree only includes chemical features with MS/MS data A tree already exists but needs trimming — use the prune-hierarchy method to keep only molecules with annotations instead of rebuilding You only need library-match-based classification (e.g., ClassyFire 5-level taxonomy) rather than a fingerprint-derived hierarchy http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Build a rooted chemical hierarchy (Qemistree) by hierarchically clustering CSI:FingerID fingerprint vectors so that mass-spectrometry features occupy tips of a phylogeny-like tree, enabling tree-based ecological analyses of metabolomics data. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41589-020-00677-3
skills.summary: Build a rooted chemical hierarchy (Qemistree) by hierarchically clustering CSI:FingerID fingerprint vectors so that mass-spectrometry features occupy tips of a phylogeny-like tree, enabling tree-based ecological analyses of metabolomics data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Features have only MS1 data and no MS/MS fragmentation spectra — Qemistree only includes chemical features with MS/MS data A tree already exists but needs trimming — use the prune-hierarchy method to keep only molecules with annotations instead of rebuilding You only need library-match-based classification (e.g., ClassyFire 5-level taxonomy) rather than a fingerprint-derived hierarchy

skills.description: Use when raw MS/MS peak lists contain m/z values of adducted ions (e.g. [M+H]+, [M-H]-) that must be converted to monoisotopic neutral Da before fragment formula matching or precursor mass comparison.
skills.name: cheminformatics-adduct-mass-correction
skills.search_text: cheminformatics-adduct-mass-correction Use when raw MS/MS peak lists contain m/z values of adducted ions (e.g. [M+H]+, [M-H]-) that must be converted to monoisotopic neutral Da before fragment formula matching or precursor mass comparison. Input peaks are already monoisotopic neutral masses in Da, not m/z of adducted ions — a second correction would shift masses. The ionization adduct type is unknown or the spectrum contains mixed/unknown adducts, since Eq. (1) requires a specific adduct assumption. Compounds composed of elements beyond C, H, O, N, S, and P, which FSA has not been validated on. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0153 Converts m/z peak values to monoisotopic neutral masses via the adduct-corrected Eq. (1) from the FSA pipeline, a prerequisite before formula matching in LC-MS/MS metabolomics. Uses the FiehnLab ms-adduct-calculator adduct masses and cleans spectra (centroiding/deisotoping) beforehand. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-025-02379-0
skills.summary: Converts m/z peak values to monoisotopic neutral masses via the adduct-corrected Eq. (1) from the FSA pipeline, a prerequisite before formula matching in LC-MS/MS metabolomics. Uses the FiehnLab ms-adduct-calculator adduct masses and cleans spectra (centroiding/deisotoping) beforehand.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input peaks are already monoisotopic neutral masses in Da, not m/z of adducted ions — a second correction would shift masses. The ionization adduct type is unknown or the spectrum contains mixed/unknown adducts, since Eq. (1) requires a specific adduct assumption. Compounds composed of elements beyond C, H, O, N, S, and P, which FSA has not been validated on.

skills.search_text: chemont-taxonomy-category-reduction Use when a compound's detected structural features have been mapped to ChemOnt categories and you must prune redundant ancestor categories before picking the direct parent in a ClassyFire-style pipeline. Before feature detection — if structural features have not yet been mapped to ChemOnt categories via superstructure search against the ~9000 SMARTS/Markush pattern library or the ~200 IUPAC-name parsing rules, there is nothing to reduce When the goal is selecting the Direct Parent itself — this skill only prunes ancestor nodes; the Direct Parent selection uses the reduced list plus feature weights, structural keys and the exception list http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 Part of the ClassyFire classification engine: after structural features are detected and mapped to ChemOnt categories, this skill reduces the assigned category set by iteratively removing parent categories whenever a child category is present (e.g. retain 1,2-dioxanes over dioxanes), before selecting the direct parent. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-016-0174-y
skills.summary: Part of the ClassyFire classification engine: after structural features are detected and mapped to ChemOnt categories, this skill reduces the assigned category set by iteratively removing parent categories whenever a child category is present (e.g. retain 1,2-dioxanes over dioxanes), before selecting the direct parent.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Before feature detection — if structural features have not yet been mapped to ChemOnt categories via superstructure search against the ~9000 SMARTS/Markush pattern library or the ~200 IUPAC-name parsing rules, there is nothing to reduce When the goal is selecting the Direct Parent itself — this skill only prunes ancestor nodes; the Direct Parent selection uses the reduced list plus feature weights, structural keys and the exception list

skills.description: Use when annotated molecular network nodes (with CF_superclass/class/subclass labels) must be summarized per taxon or clade, e.g. contrasting metabolite classes between plant clades or bacterial groups.
skills.name: chemotaxonomic-distribution-analysis
skills.search_text: chemotaxonomic-distribution-analysis Use when annotated molecular network nodes (with CF_superclass/class/subclass labels) must be summarized per taxon or clade, e.g. contrasting metabolite classes between plant clades or bacterial groups. Network nodes lack ClassyFire chemical class annotations (CF_ columns absent), so there is nothing to aggregate per taxon. No taxonomic grouping metadata exists for the molecular families, preventing clade-level contrast. The goal is per-node annotation rather than group-level class distribution comparison — direct node-level CF columns in Cytoscape suffice. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3292 Aggregates MolNetEnhancer-annotated chemical class assignments (ClassyFire CF_subclass etc.) per taxonomic grouping or network component, normalizing counts to build class-distribution tables that contrast metabolite profiles between taxa. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo9070144
skills.summary: Aggregates MolNetEnhancer-annotated chemical class assignments (ClassyFire CF_subclass etc.) per taxonomic grouping or network component, normalizing counts to build class-distribution tables that contrast metabolite profiles between taxa.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Network nodes lack ClassyFire chemical class annotations (CF_ columns absent), so there is nothing to aggregate per taxon. No taxonomic grouping metadata exists for the molecular families, preventing clade-level contrast. The goal is per-node annotation rather than group-level class distribution comparison — direct node-level CF columns in Cytoscape suffice.

skills.description: Use when a host application or pipeline must store processed spectra per the Chemotion ELN contract: one original byte-preserving artifact plus a server-composed edited version and generated png per upload.
skills.name: chemotion-eln-attachment-storage
skills.search_text: chemotion-eln-attachment-storage Use when a host application or pipeline must store processed spectra per the Chemotion ELN contract: one original byte-preserving artifact plus a server-composed edited version and generated png per upload. The goal is interactive spectrum editing or NMR analysis (peak-picking, integration, coupling constants) rather than per-spectrum attachment storage The input is a proprietary MS RAW file that first requires msConvert-in-docker conversion to mzML and then JCAMP-DX via pymzML before storage The data is 2D NMR or formats outside JCAMP-DX/mzML/Bruker/BagIt scope, which chem-spectra-app does not cover per the paper's stated future work http://edamontology.org/topic_3315 Replicates the file-management contract that the Chemotion ELN implements around a single uploaded spectrum by producing three artifacts per file: the untouched original upload, the last edited JCAMP-DX version, and an automatically generated png image of the spectra. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-020-00481-0
skills.summary: Replicates the file-management contract that the Chemotion ELN implements around a single uploaded spectrum by producing three artifacts per file: the untouched original upload, the last edited JCAMP-DX version, and an automatically generated png image of the spectra.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is interactive spectrum editing or NMR analysis (peak-picking, integration, coupling constants) rather than per-spectrum attachment storage The input is a proprietary MS RAW file that first requires msConvert-in-docker conversion to mzML and then JCAMP-DX via pymzML before storage The data is 2D NMR or formats outside JCAMP-DX/mzML/Bruker/BagIt scope, which chem-spectra-app does not cover per the paper's stated future work

skills.description: Use when ranking MetFrag2.2 candidate structures needs non-spectral evidence: ChemSpider reference/data-source/patent counts per candidate must be fetched via web services and normalized across the candidate list.
skills.name: chemspider-reference-count-retrieval
skills.search_text: chemspider-reference-count-retrieval Use when ranking MetFrag2.2 candidate structures needs non-spectral evidence: ChemSpider reference/data-source/patent counts per candidate must be fetched via web services and normalized across the candidate list. Candidates were retrieved from a database with no ChemSpider mapping (e.g. KEGG-only or local SDF without ChemSpider IDs), so no reference counts can be fetched The analysis relies only on HR-MS/MS fragment scores and no reference/retention information is desired (MetFrag2.2 with PubChem alone ranked only 30 Top 1) Offline/local database mode (LocalPubChemDatabase settings) where web-service retrieval of reference counts is not intended http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Retrieves five per-candidate reference counts from ChemSpider web services and combines them into a normalized ChemSpider combined reference score (S_C_CCR) used as a scoring term in MetFrag2.2 candidate ranking, improving identification when spectral libraries are sparse. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-016-0115-9
skills.summary: Retrieves five per-candidate reference counts from ChemSpider web services and combines them into a normalized ChemSpider combined reference score (S_C_CCR) used as a scoring term in MetFrag2.2 candidate ranking, improving identification when spectral libraries are sparse.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Candidates were retrieved from a database with no ChemSpider mapping (e.g. KEGG-only or local SDF without ChemSpider IDs), so no reference counts can be fetched The analysis relies only on HR-MS/MS fragment scores and no reference/retention information is desired (MetFrag2.2 with PubChem alone ranked only 30 Top 1) Offline/local database mode (LocalPubChemDatabase settings) where web-service retrieval of reference counts is not intended

skills.description: Use when tabulating binary found/missing outcomes (e.g., 134 of 187 experimentally characterized reactions present in RetroRules via MEANtools) and you must test if the presence rate exceeds chance (χ2, DF = 1).
skills.name: chi-square-significance-testing
skills.search_text: chi-square-significance-testing Use when tabulating binary found/missing outcomes (e.g., 134 of 187 experimentally characterized reactions present in RetroRules via MEANtools) and you must test if the presence rate exceeds chance (χ2, DF = 1). Input is not a binary found/missing categorization — e.g., continuous correlation or edge-score data from MEANtools FCs, which require MR/exponential-decay weighting instead Expected cell counts are too small for a valid chi-square approximation; use exact tests (e.g., Fisher's exact) instead http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Applies a chi-square goodness-of-fit test to assess whether an observed coverage count (e.g., biosynthetic reactions recovered from MEANtools using the strict RetroRules dataset) deviates significantly from chance expectation. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pbio.3003307
skills.summary: Applies a chi-square goodness-of-fit test to assess whether an observed coverage count (e.g., biosynthetic reactions recovered from MEANtools using the strict RetroRules dataset) deviates significantly from chance expectation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is not a binary found/missing categorization — e.g., continuous correlation or edge-score data from MEANtools FCs, which require MR/exponential-decay weighting instead Expected cell counts are too small for a valid chi-square approximation; use exact tests (e.g., Fisher's exact) instead

skills.description: Use when a linear mixed-effects model has been fitted per metabolite (e.g. with fixed effects 'Sex','Age','BMI','Stage','Location','Tissue' and random intercept '(1|Id)') and you need chi-square p-values for fixed-effect terms such as a VAT-vs-SAT tissue effect.
skills.name: chi-square-significance-testing
skills.search_text: chi-square-significance-testing Use when a linear mixed-effects model has been fitted per metabolite (e.g. with fixed effects 'Sex','Age','BMI','Stage','Location','Tissue' and random intercept '(1|Id)') and you need chi-square p-values for fixed-effect terms such as a VAT-vs-SAT tissue effect. Raw, non-LMM-fitted data — before LMM fitting, cholesterol signals were randomly mixed and indistinguishable in the M0 dataset, so the tissue-effect test is not meaningful Inputs lacking paired/subject metadata needed for the random intercept '(1|Id)' and the fixed-effect design (Sex, Age, BMI, Stage, Location, Tissue) http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Assess significance of LMM fixed-effect coefficients (e.g. the Tissue/VAT term in the CRC adipose lipid data) via chi-square tests returned by lmm2met's getFixCoeff, enabling metabolite-level hypothesis testing such as the cholesterol VAT-vs-SAT contrast reported in Table S-2. metabolomics/v3 10.1016/j.csbj.2019.04.009
skills.summary: Assess significance of LMM fixed-effect coefficients (e.g. the Tissue/VAT term in the CRC adipose lipid data) via chi-square tests returned by lmm2met's getFixCoeff, enabling metabolite-level hypothesis testing such as the cholesterol VAT-vs-SAT contrast reported in Table S-2.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Raw, non-LMM-fitted data — before LMM fitting, cholesterol signals were randomly mixed and indistinguishable in the M0 dataset, so the tissue-effect test is not meaningful Inputs lacking paired/subject metadata needed for the random intercept '(1|Id)' and the fixed-effect design (Sex, Age, BMI, Stage, Location, Tissue)

skills.description: Use when a kernel machine score statistic's null distribution is approximated by moment matching and the final deliverable is an upper-tail chi-square p-value per pathway.
skills.name: chi-square-tail-probability-evaluation
skills.search_text: chi-square-tail-probability-evaluation Use when a kernel machine score statistic's null distribution is approximated by moment matching and the final deliverable is an upper-tail chi-square p-value per pathway. When the input is an effect-size or coefficient estimate rather than a quadratic-form score statistic under the null hypothesis When the null distribution of the test statistic is known exactly (e.g. from permutation) and moment matching to a scaled chi-square would add unnecessary approximation error When the goal is to compare p-values across methods on a full cohort of over 1,000 observations, where the paper reports that P-values from the compared methods were indistinguishable; the paper only demonstrated differences via random subsets of 100–500 subjects http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Evaluates the upper-tail probability of a scaled chi-square distribution fitted by Satterthwaite moment matching to a quadratic-form score statistic Q, converting pathway-level kernel association statistics into null-hypothesis p-values in PaIRKAT. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2021.04.23.440821
skills.summary: Evaluates the upper-tail probability of a scaled chi-square distribution fitted by Satterthwaite moment matching to a quadratic-form score statistic Q, converting pathway-level kernel association statistics into null-hypothesis p-values in PaIRKAT.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is an effect-size or coefficient estimate rather than a quadratic-form score statistic under the null hypothesis When the null distribution of the test statistic is known exactly (e.g. from permutation) and moment matching to a scaled chi-square would add unnecessary approximation error When the goal is to compare p-values across methods on a full cohort of over 1,000 observations, where the paper reports that P-values from the compared methods were indistinguishable; the paper only demonstrated differences via random subsets of 100–500 subjects

skills.description: Use when you have a SMITER-simulated mzML with known precursor peptides and overlapping retention times and need to predict how many peptides co-fragment into each MS2 spectrum before running a real MS experiment.
skills.name: chimeric-spectrum-cofragmentation-quantification
skills.search_text: chimeric-spectrum-cofragmentation-quantification Use when you have a SMITER-simulated mzML with known precursor peptides and overlapping retention times and need to predict how many peptides co-fragment into each MS2 spectrum before running a real MS experiment. The data are real (non-simulated) LC-MS/MS runs where precursor ground truth is unknown — this skill relies on SMITER's known simulated composition to attribute fragments to peptides The goal is de novo or database-search peptide identification from spectra rather than quantifying co-fragmentation multiplicity The simulated dataset has no overlapping retention times, so chimeric spectra are not expected to arise http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Quantifies co-fragmentation (chimeric MS2 spectra) in a simulated LC-MS/MS run by annotating each MS2 spectrum against theoretical fragment ions generated by the SMITER PeptideFragmentor, then tallying how many distinct peptides contribute fragments per spectrum. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/genes12030396
skills.summary: Quantifies co-fragmentation (chimeric MS2 spectra) in a simulated LC-MS/MS run by annotating each MS2 spectrum against theoretical fragment ions generated by the SMITER PeptideFragmentor, then tallying how many distinct peptides contribute fragments per spectrum.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are real (non-simulated) LC-MS/MS runs where precursor ground truth is unknown — this skill relies on SMITER's known simulated composition to attribute fragments to peptides The goal is de novo or database-search peptide identification from spectra rather than quantifying co-fragmentation multiplicity The simulated dataset has no overlapping retention times, so chimeric spectra are not expected to arise

skills.description: Use when integrating a discretised ChIP-chip regulator-gene matrix with another omic dataset (e.g. yeast time-course expression) and you need a per-dataset kernel for multiple-kernel integrative clustering with KLIC.
skills.name: chip-chip-data-clustering
skills.search_text: chip-chip-data-clustering Use when integrating a discretised ChIP-chip regulator-gene matrix with another omic dataset (e.g. yeast time-course expression) and you need a per-dataset kernel for multiple-kernel integrative clustering with KLIC. The input is already a similarity/kernel matrix or you want a single-dataset clustering rather than integration of multiple omic layers The ChIP-chip data are not discretised and you cannot run BHC-based consensus clustering on them http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_0749 Cluster ChIP-chip regulatory data as one kernel layer of an integrative clustering analysis, by building a consensus kernel from the discretised ChIP-chip matrix (Harbison et al. 2004, 117 regulators) using Consensus Clustering (Monti et al. 2003) with BHC as the base algorithm, then letting Kernel Learning Integrative Clustering (KLIC) weight this layer against other datasets such as gene expression. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btaa593
skills.summary: Cluster ChIP-chip regulatory data as one kernel layer of an integrative clustering analysis, by building a consensus kernel from the discretised ChIP-chip matrix (Harbison et al. 2004, 117 regulators) using Consensus Clustering (Monti et al. 2003) with BHC as the base algorithm, then letting Kernel Learning Integrative Clustering (KLIC) weight this layer against other datasets such as gene expression.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a similarity/kernel matrix or you want a single-dataset clustering rather than integration of multiple omic layers The ChIP-chip data are not discretised and you cannot run BHC-based consensus clustering on them

skills.description: Use when you have a finite set of characterized substrate/product structures and a reference database (e.g., LOTUS), and you must report how many structures are present plus the statistical significance of that overlap.
skills.name: chisquare-significance-testing
skills.search_text: chisquare-significance-testing Use when you have a finite set of characterized substrate/product structures and a reference database (e.g., LOTUS), and you must report how many structures are present plus the statistical significance of that overlap. The goal is de novo pathway reconstruction or mass-feature annotation (e.g., MR-based correlation, ClusterONE clustering, or adduct-based LOTUS matching at 20 ppm tolerance) rather than validating database overlap of known structures. The comparison data are continuous (e.g., Pearson correlations or mutual ranks needing exponential-decay edge weighting) rather than countable matched/unmatched categories suitable for a chi-square contingency. The reference database differs from the fixed LOTUS snapshot (10/10/2023) and you need a version-agnostic or MS/MS-spectral-library-based annotation assessment instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 A statistical validation skill that tests whether the observed overlap between a set of characterized biosynthetic reaction structures and a reference metabolite database (LOTUS) is significantly greater than expected, using a chi-square test on the matched/unmatched presence-absence contingency (DF=1). metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pbio.3003307
skills.summary: A statistical validation skill that tests whether the observed overlap between a set of characterized biosynthetic reaction structures and a reference metabolite database (LOTUS) is significantly greater than expected, using a chi-square test on the matched/unmatched presence-absence contingency (DF=1).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is de novo pathway reconstruction or mass-feature annotation (e.g., MR-based correlation, ClusterONE clustering, or adduct-based LOTUS matching at 20 ppm tolerance) rather than validating database overlap of known structures. The comparison data are continuous (e.g., Pearson correlations or mutual ranks needing exponential-decay edge weighting) rather than countable matched/unmatched categories suitable for a chi-square contingency. The reference database differs from the fixed LOTUS snapshot (10/10/2023) and you need a version-agnostic or MS/MS-spectral-library-based annotation assessment instead.

skills.description: Use when the goal is to identify potential drug targets in an SBML genome-scale metabolic model by computing chokepoint reactions whose flux bounds and dead-end-metabolite status have been refined via FVA.
skills.name: chokepoint-computation-genome-scale-models
skills.search_text: chokepoint-computation-genome-scale-models Use when the goal is to identify potential drug targets in an SBML genome-scale metabolic model by computing chokepoint reactions whose flux bounds and dead-end-metabolite status have been refined via FVA. The model has not been refined with FVA and DEM removal — chokepoint counts on the raw input model differ substantially from the FVA-refined, DEM-free variant and are not comparable to the paper's reported sets The goal is general pathway enrichment or gene essentiality without flux/topology coupling — MEMOTE quality control or plain FBA/FVA alone is the appropriate skill The input is not an SBML genome-scale metabolic model parseable by COBRApy (findCPcli takes SBML as input) http://edamontology.org/topic_2259 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Computes growth-dependent chokepoint (bottleneck) reactions in genome-scale metabolic models using findCPcli, which combines network topology with FVA-derived flux dynamics to flag reactions required for organism/viral growth and survival. Applied here to the integrated human airway epithelial cell/SARS-CoV-2 model (iHsaEC21_SARS-CoV-2) and the macrophage model to predict drug targets. metabolomics/v3 10.26508/lsa.202000954
skills.summary: Computes growth-dependent chokepoint (bottleneck) reactions in genome-scale metabolic models using findCPcli, which combines network topology with FVA-derived flux dynamics to flag reactions required for organism/viral growth and survival. Applied here to the integrated human airway epithelial cell/SARS-CoV-2 model (iHsaEC21_SARS-CoV-2) and the macrophage model to predict drug targets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The model has not been refined with FVA and DEM removal — chokepoint counts on the raw input model differ substantially from the FVA-refined, DEM-free variant and are not comparable to the paper's reported sets The goal is general pathway enrichment or gene essentiality without flux/topology coupling — MEMOTE quality control or plain FBA/FVA alone is the appropriate skill The input is not an SBML genome-scale metabolic model parseable by COBRApy (findCPcli takes SBML as input)

skills.description: Use when you have an integrated host–pathogen genome-scale metabolic model plus experimental PPI data (e.g. Gordon et al 2020 SARS-CoV-2 PPIs) and need to pinpoint which host metabolic reactions hijacked via PPIs are also network bottlenecks or essential for viral growth.
skills.name: chokepoint-essential-reaction-intersection-analysis
skills.search_text: chokepoint-essential-reaction-intersection-analysis Use when you have an integrated host–pathogen genome-scale metabolic model plus experimental PPI data (e.g. Gordon et al 2020 SARS-CoV-2 PPIs) and need to pinpoint which host metabolic reactions hijacked via PPIs are also network bottlenecks or essential for viral growth. The PPI data cannot be mapped onto model enzymes via GPR associations (no gene identifiers shared between the PPI dataset and the model) The metabolic model has not had dead-end metabolites handled or flux bounds refined, so chokepoint/bottleneck sets are unreliable for intersection analysis The goal is de novo drug-target prediction from network topology alone without experimental PPI evidence (use plain chokepoint/bottleneck analysis instead) http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_2259 A three-step labelling procedure that identifies reactions at the intersection nodes between virus–host protein–protein interactions (PPI) and metabolic pathways by crossing PPI-mapped human metabolic enzymes against bottleneck/chokepoint and essential reaction sets computed with findCPcli on the iHsaEC21+SARS-CoV-2 model. metabolomics/v3 10.26508/lsa.202000954
skills.summary: A three-step labelling procedure that identifies reactions at the intersection nodes between virus–host protein–protein interactions (PPI) and metabolic pathways by crossing PPI-mapped human metabolic enzymes against bottleneck/chokepoint and essential reaction sets computed with findCPcli on the iHsaEC21+SARS-CoV-2 model.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The PPI data cannot be mapped onto model enzymes via GPR associations (no gene identifiers shared between the PPI dataset and the model) The metabolic model has not had dead-end metabolites handled or flux bounds refined, so chokepoint/bottleneck sets are unreliable for intersection analysis The goal is de novo drug-target prediction from network topology alone without experimental PPI evidence (use plain chokepoint/bottleneck analysis instead)

skills.description: Use when a steady-state SBML metabolic model (e.g. iHsaEC21_SARS-CoV-2, MODEL2007210001) must be refined before chokepoint or bottleneck analysis: flux bounds need updating from FVA, dead-end metabolites must be excluded, or reaction reversibility must be determined from flux ranges.
skills.name: chokepoint-pipeline-model-preprocessing
skills.search_text: chokepoint-pipeline-model-preprocessing Use when a steady-state SBML metabolic model (e.g. iHsaEC21_SARS-CoV-2, MODEL2007210001) must be refined before chokepoint or bottleneck analysis: flux bounds need updating from FVA, dead-end metabolites must be excluded, or reaction reversibility must be determined from flux ranges. The goal is FBA-only biomass or growth-rate computation (Orth et al 2010) without downstream chokepoint/bottleneck analysis — flux-bound refinement is unnecessary The input is not a constraint-based metabolic model (e.g. it is interaction data, expression data, or a non-steady-state model) A published curated model is already supplied in a refined variant, so re-running FVA refinement would only add computation without changing bounds http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 http://edamontology.org/topic_2259 Preprocesses a genome-scale metabolic model (SBML) before chokepoint/bottleneck analysis by computing FVA-updated flux bounds and/or removing dead-end metabolites with findCPcli, yielding refined model variants (model_fva.xml, model without DEM) on which reaction reversibility and chokepoint computations are more accurate. metabolomics/v3 10.26508/lsa.202000954
skills.summary: Preprocesses a genome-scale metabolic model (SBML) before chokepoint/bottleneck analysis by computing FVA-updated flux bounds and/or removing dead-end metabolites with findCPcli, yielding refined model variants (model_fva.xml, model without DEM) on which reaction reversibility and chokepoint computations are more accurate.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is FBA-only biomass or growth-rate computation (Orth et al 2010) without downstream chokepoint/bottleneck analysis — flux-bound refinement is unnecessary The input is not a constraint-based metabolic model (e.g. it is interaction data, expression data, or a non-steady-state model) A published curated model is already supplied in a refined variant, so re-running FVA refinement would only add computation without changing bounds

skills.description: Use when you have a post-QC NMR biomarker table (output of remove_technical_variation()) filtered to the 107 non-derived biomarkers and need to derive the 76 additional ratios of biological significance, including cholesterol fractions.
skills.name: cholesterol-fraction-computation
skills.search_text: cholesterol-fraction-computation Use when you have a post-QC NMR biomarker table (output of remove_technical_variation()) filtered to the 107 non-derived biomarkers and need to derive the 76 additional ratios of biological significance, including cholesterol fractions. The input is the raw UK Biobank exported field data before technical variation removal — the README states no prefiltering of samples or columns should be performed prior to remove_technical_variation() You only need the 61 composite biomarkers and 81 original Nightingale ratios — use recompute_derived_biomarkers() instead of the extended-ratio functions The biomarker table already contains the extended ratios computed from directly-adjusted concentrations — these would not match ratios re-derived from adjusted component biomarkers http://edamontology.org/topic_3334 Computes extended biomarker ratios — including free/esterified cholesterol fractions and lipoprotein fatty acid fractions — from post-technical-variation UK Biobank NMR metabolomics data using the ukbnmr R package's compute_extended_ratios() and compute_lipoprotein_fatty_acids() functions. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41597-023-01949-y
skills.summary: Computes extended biomarker ratios — including free/esterified cholesterol fractions and lipoprotein fatty acid fractions — from post-technical-variation UK Biobank NMR metabolomics data using the ukbnmr R package's compute_extended_ratios() and compute_lipoprotein_fatty_acids() functions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is the raw UK Biobank exported field data before technical variation removal — the README states no prefiltering of samples or columns should be performed prior to remove_technical_variation() You only need the 61 composite biomarkers and 81 original Nightingale ratios — use recompute_derived_biomarkers() instead of the extended-ratio functions The biomarker table already contains the extended ratios computed from directly-adjusted concentrations — these would not match ratios re-derived from adjusted component biomarkers

skills.description: Use when a workflow needs to shrink large MRM raw datasets (e.g. PXD009543, PXD031038, Skyline test set) for web-based rendering or storage, or when benchmarking file-format compression ratios.
skills.name: chromatogram-aird-compression
skills.search_text: chromatogram-aird-compression Use when a workflow needs to shrink large MRM raw datasets (e.g. PXD009543, PXD031038, Skyline test set) for web-based rendering or storage, or when benchmarking file-format compression ratios. The goal is quantitative MRM analysis or manual peak inspection rather than storage compression — use MRMPro/Skyline analysis instead Data must be shared in an interchange format accepted by third-party tools that do not read Aird (use mzML/mzXML, which AirdPro also exports but which are not the compression target) Files are already in Aird format — recompression offers no further volume benefit http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0219 Convert vendor MRM mass spectrometry raw files to the computation-oriented Aird format using AirdPro, benchmarking on-disk volume against 32-bit mzML (MSConvert) and vendor formats to quantify the >60% (vendor) and >80% (mzML) compression gains reported by the MRMPro paper. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-024-05685-x
skills.summary: Convert vendor MRM mass spectrometry raw files to the computation-oriented Aird format using AirdPro, benchmarking on-disk volume against 32-bit mzML (MSConvert) and vendor formats to quantify the >60% (vendor) and >80% (mzML) compression gains reported by the MRMPro paper.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is quantitative MRM analysis or manual peak inspection rather than storage compression — use MRMPro/Skyline analysis instead Data must be shared in an interchange format accepted by third-party tools that do not read Aird (use mzML/mzXML, which AirdPro also exports but which are not the compression target) Files are already in Aird format — recompression offers no further volume benefit

skills.description: Use when processing centroided high-resolution LC-MS mzML files where you need to convert sparse MS1 spectra into continuous chromatographic mass tracks and quantify baseline noise to gate smoothing and peak-detection thresholds.
skills.name: chromatogram-binning-and-noise-level-estimation
skills.search_text: chromatogram-binning-and-noise-level-estimation Use when processing centroided high-resolution LC-MS mzML files where you need to convert sparse MS1 spectra into continuous chromatographic mass tracks and quantify baseline noise to gate smoothing and peak-detection thresholds. Input data are low resolution — the paper states 'The software does not work with low resolution data.' Data are of very high noise, which the authors say may need customized processing You need MS/MS spectra — 'MS/MS spectra are ignored by asari.' in the default LC-MS workflow http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Asari-style discretization of m/z values into 0.001 amu bins to build full-RT mass tracks, plus flank-based noise estimation that decides whether smoothing is applied before statistical elution peak detection. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-023-39889-1
skills.summary: Asari-style discretization of m/z values into 0.001 amu bins to build full-RT mass tracks, plus flank-based noise estimation that decides whether smoothing is applied before statistical elution peak detection.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data are low resolution — the paper states 'The software does not work with low resolution data.' Data are of very high noise, which the authors say may need customized processing You need MS/MS spectra — 'MS/MS spectra are ignored by asari.' in the default LC-MS workflow

skills.description: Use when raw GCxGC-MS acquisition data are stored as NetCDF/CDF files (e.g. 08GB.cdf, 09GB.cdf from MetaboLights MTBLS579) and must be converted into RGCxGC 2D-TIC chromatogram objects before preprocessing or multivariate analysis.
skills.name: chromatogram-cdf-file-import
skills.search_text: chromatogram-cdf-file-import Use when raw GCxGC-MS acquisition data are stored as NetCDF/CDF files (e.g. 08GB.cdf, 09GB.cdf from MetaboLights MTBLS579) and must be converted into RGCxGC 2D-TIC chromatogram objects before preprocessing or multivariate analysis. Data are already preprocessed chromatograms or extracted feature/peak tables rather than raw NetCDF files Data are 1D GC-MS or LC-MS runs not acquired in comprehensive two-dimensional (GCxGC) mode, since the folding step assumes modulated 2D data http://edamontology.org/topic_3391 Import a raw GCxGC chromatogram from a NetCDF/CDF file with the RGCxGC package's read_chrom, folding the one-dimensional raw signal into a two-dimensional Total Intensity Chromatogram (2D-TIC) object that downstream preprocessing (smoothing, baseline correction, 2D-COW alignment) and MPCA can consume. metabolomics/v3 10.1016/j.microc.2020.104830
skills.summary: Import a raw GCxGC chromatogram from a NetCDF/CDF file with the RGCxGC package's read_chrom, folding the one-dimensional raw signal into a two-dimensional Total Intensity Chromatogram (2D-TIC) object that downstream preprocessing (smoothing, baseline correction, 2D-COW alignment) and MPCA can consume.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are already preprocessed chromatograms or extracted feature/peak tables rather than raw NetCDF files Data are 1D GC-MS or LC-MS runs not acquired in comprehensive two-dimensional (GCxGC) mode, since the folding step assumes modulated 2D data

skills.description: Use when MRM/LC-MS samples show retention time shifts that break peak correspondence across EICs and you need per-sample drift estimates to align peaks or group EICs across runs.
skills.name: chromatogram-cosine-similarity-optimization
skills.search_text: chromatogram-cosine-similarity-optimization Use when MRM/LC-MS samples show retention time shifts that break peak correspondence across EICs and you need per-sample drift estimates to align peaks or group EICs across runs. Input is already an aligned feature/peak table where RT correspondence across samples is established Data is DDA/DIA rather than targeted MRM — MRMPro's drift estimation is designed for MRM EICs; use a proteomics-wide alignment method instead The goal is improving peak extraction accuracy itself — the paper states peak extraction accuracy is not yet improved and defers that to future work http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Estimates retention time (RT) drifts between MRM samples by maximizing cosine similarity between extracted-ion chromatograms (EICs), using a combined coarse grid search and gradient descent refinement against a reference EIC. This powers peak alignment and automatic EIC grouping in MRMPro. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-024-05685-x
skills.summary: Estimates retention time (RT) drifts between MRM samples by maximizing cosine similarity between extracted-ion chromatograms (EICs), using a combined coarse grid search and gradient descent refinement against a reference EIC. This powers peak alignment and automatic EIC grouping in MRMPro.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already an aligned feature/peak table where RT correspondence across samples is established Data is DDA/DIA rather than targeted MRM — MRMPro's drift estimation is designed for MRM EICs; use a proteomics-wide alignment method instead The goal is improving peak extraction accuracy itself — the paper states peak extraction accuracy is not yet improved and defers that to future work

skills.description: Use when preprocessing a batch of mzML MRM chromatograms (quantifier + qualifier traces) whose peak RTs drift between samples and need alignment before peak integration, e.g. HILIC 1a-style demodata batches in automRm.
skills.name: chromatogram-cross-correlation-rt-shift-estimation
skills.search_text: chromatogram-cross-correlation-rt-shift-estimation Use when preprocessing a batch of mzML MRM chromatograms (quantifier + qualifier traces) whose peak RTs drift between samples and need alignment before peak integration, e.g. HILIC 1a-style demodata batches in automRm. Acquisition lacks at least one qualifier in addition to the quantifier, since automRm's cross-correlation requires qualifier traces for optimal performance Data are not MRM-mode LC-MS chromatogram batches (e.g. profile MS1 data or single-sample files with no reference sample to correlate against) Peaks are already aligned/reported and only quality scoring or peak picking is needed — use the ML peak-picking/reporting workflow instead Estimates per-metabolite retention time (RT) shifts in LC-QQQ-MS MRM batches by cross-correlating each sample's quantifier and qualifier chromatograms against a reference sample, then smooths the shifts across the chromatogram by fitting them as a quadratic function of RT. This removes retention-time drift before prototype chromatogram summing and ML-based peak reporting in automRm. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c05224
skills.summary: Estimates per-metabolite retention time (RT) shifts in LC-QQQ-MS MRM batches by cross-correlating each sample's quantifier and qualifier chromatograms against a reference sample, then smooths the shifts across the chromatogram by fitting them as a quadratic function of RT. This removes retention-time drift before prototype chromatogram summing and ML-based peak reporting in automRm.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Acquisition lacks at least one qualifier in addition to the quantifier, since automRm's cross-correlation requires qualifier traces for optimal performance Data are not MRM-mode LC-MS chromatogram batches (e.g. profile MS1 data or single-sample files with no reference sample to correlate against) Peaks are already aligned/reported and only quality scoring or peak picking is needed — use the ML peak-picking/reporting workflow instead

skills.description: Use when raw LC-HRMS2 chromatograms (converted from Thermo RAW via MSConvert) contain co-eluting or partially resolved peaks that the ADAP chromatogram builder grouped into a single chromatogram, and distinct peak boundaries must be recovered before MS2 export.
skills.name: chromatogram-deconvolution
skills.search_text: chromatogram-deconvolution Use when raw LC-HRMS2 chromatograms (converted from Thermo RAW via MSConvert) contain co-eluting or partially resolved peaks that the ADAP chromatogram builder grouped into a single chromatogram, and distinct peak boundaries must be recovered before MS2 export. The input is already a deconvoluted MZmine feature list or feature quantification table — no peak-boundary recovery is needed. The goal is feature alignment across batches/samples rather than per-sample peak resolution; the ENPKG framework deliberately skips RT-based alignment because it hinders cross-batch comparison. The data are acquired on an instrument whose chromatography or scan rate makes the ADAP wavelet defaults inappropriate without re-validation (e.g., very fast separations outside the 0.02–0.5 min peak duration range). http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Deconvolute co-eluting chromatographic peaks in MZmine feature lists using the ADAP wavelets algorithm, as configured in the ENPKG sample-centric LC-HRMS2 workflow, to produce distinct peaks ready for MS2-linked feature filtering and quantification. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acscentsci.3c00800
skills.summary: Deconvolute co-eluting chromatographic peaks in MZmine feature lists using the ADAP wavelets algorithm, as configured in the ENPKG sample-centric LC-HRMS2 workflow, to produce distinct peaks ready for MS2-linked feature filtering and quantification.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a deconvoluted MZmine feature list or feature quantification table — no peak-boundary recovery is needed. The goal is feature alignment across batches/samples rather than per-sample peak resolution; the ENPKG framework deliberately skips RT-based alignment because it hinders cross-batch comparison. The data are acquired on an instrument whose chromatography or scan rate makes the ADAP wavelet defaults inappropriate without re-validation (e.g., very fast separations outside the 0.02–0.5 min peak duration range).

skills.description: Use when you have MS1-only LC/HRMS data (mzXML, mzML, netCDF) from untargeted metabolomics and need to deconvolve co-eluting MS1 ions into composite spectra without DDA MS2 files.
skills.name: chromatogram-deconvolution
skills.search_text: chromatogram-deconvolution Use when you have MS1-only LC/HRMS data (mzXML, mzML, netCDF) from untargeted metabolomics and need to deconvolve co-eluting MS1 ions into composite spectra without DDA MS2 files. You already have DDA MS2 spectra and need true tandem fragmentation spectra rather than MS1 composite spectra Input is already a peak/feature table produced by another peak picker (e.g. MZmine, xcms, MS-DIAL) with no IDSL.IPA peaklists/peak_alignment directories The goal is searching spectra against reference libraries (that is IDSL.FSA's role, downstream of CSA library creation) http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Group co-eluting, correlating MS1 extracted ion chromatograms into composite spectra (CSA clusters) using the IDSL.CSA R package, so that LC/HRMS peaks lacking MS2 fragmentation can still be exported as re-usable .msp spectral libraries for chemical annotation. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c00376
skills.summary: Group co-eluting, correlating MS1 extracted ion chromatograms into composite spectra (CSA clusters) using the IDSL.CSA R package, so that LC/HRMS peaks lacking MS2 fragmentation can still be exported as re-usable .msp spectral libraries for chemical annotation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You already have DDA MS2 spectra and need true tandem fragmentation spectra rather than MS1 composite spectra Input is already a peak/feature table produced by another peak picker (e.g. MZmine, xcms, MS-DIAL) with no IDSL.IPA peaklists/peak_alignment directories The goal is searching spectra against reference libraries (that is IDSL.FSA's role, downstream of CSA library creation)

Input is already a preprocessed/feature table or peak metrics CSV rather than raw mzXML/mzML MS data The goal is untargeted peak picking across all features rather than EIC generation for a defined panel of standard analytes http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Generates extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) for target standard analytes from mzXML/mzML LC-MS files using a specified m/z window, as the first step of the MetaMOPE chromatographic peak evaluation workflow before IRLS baseline correction and Savitzky-Golay smoothing. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioadv/vbad061

skills.search_text: chromatogram-extraction-from-parquet-ms-data Use when a chromatogram (TIC, BPI, or EIC for a specific m/z window) must be computed from an on-disk Parquet HRMS file too large to load fully into memory (e.g. ~1.9 Gb in-RAM, 200-400 MB Parquet profile data). skills.name: chromatogram-import-and-processing-in-ms-dial
skills.search_text: chromatogram-import-and-processing-in-ms-dial Use when raw centroid-mode LC–MS all-ion-fragmentation chromatograms need feature detection and pseudo-MS/MS deconvolution to produce a comparable annotation baseline (e.g. against MetaboAnnotatoR rank-1 or manual expert lists) on datasets like Lipid+, Lipid−, or HILIC+. When the goal is to annotate only a statistically pre-selected subset of significant features rather than all detected features, since MS-DIAL performs annotation in an untargeted manner and such a selection is currently not possible When chromatograms are in profile (non-centroid) mode, as the workflow requires raw LC–MS AIF data acquired/transformed in centroid mode When targeted MS/MS fragmentation experiments have already been acquired and a dedicated DDA spectral matching workflow is preferred http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Imports raw centroid-mode LC–MS AIF chromatograms into MS-DIAL 4.38, runs feature detection, and applies MS2Dec deconvolution to reconstruct pseudo-MS/MS spectra by correlating co-eluting fragment peaks with parent ions, producing annotated feature lists for benchmark comparison against other annotation workflows. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c03032

skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is to annotate only a statistically pre-selected subset of significant features rather than all detected features, since MS-DIAL performs annotation in an untargeted manner and such a selection is currently not possible When chromatograms are in profile (non-centroid) mode, as the workflow requires raw LC–MS AIF data acquired/transformed in centroid mode When targeted MS/MS fragmentation experiments have already been acquired and a dedicated DDA spectral matching workflow is preferred

skills.description: Use when the starting point of a GCxGC-MS analysis is a raw instrument chromatogram stored in NetCDF (e.g. a .cdf file) and it must be converted into a folded 2D-TIC object before preprocessing or multivariate analysis.
skills.name: chromatogram-netcdf-import
skills.search_text: chromatogram-netcdf-import Use when the starting point of a GCxGC-MS analysis is a raw instrument chromatogram stored in NetCDF (e.g. a .cdf file) and it must be converted into a folded 2D-TIC object before preprocessing or multivariate analysis. The chromatogram is already imported and folded (an RGCxGC chromatogram object or an .rda/.rds file of one) — re-importing would discard prior preprocessing such as baseline correction or smoothing. Data are two-dimensional chromatograms already stored in RGCxGC's unfolded matrix form for supervised mixOmics modeling via unfold_chrom, not raw NetCDF instrument files. The file is not a NetCDF chromatogram (e.g. mzML or plain spectra tables) — read_chrom's RNetCDF-based reader is specific to NetCDF GCxGC files. http://edamontology.org/topic_3361 Import a raw comprehensive two-dimensional gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GCxGC-MS) chromatogram from a NetCDF file with the RGCxGC read_chrom function and fold it into the two-dimensional Total Intensity Chromatogram (2D-TIC) representation, producing an S4 chromatogram object that carries first-dimension retention times, file name, and modulation time. metabolomics/v3 10.1016/j.microc.2020.104830
skills.summary: Import a raw comprehensive two-dimensional gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GCxGC-MS) chromatogram from a NetCDF file with the RGCxGC read_chrom function and fold it into the two-dimensional Total Intensity Chromatogram (2D-TIC) representation, producing an S4 chromatogram object that carries first-dimension retention times, file name, and modulation time.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The chromatogram is already imported and folded (an RGCxGC chromatogram object or an .rda/.rds file of one) — re-importing would discard prior preprocessing such as baseline correction or smoothing. Data are two-dimensional chromatograms already stored in RGCxGC's unfolded matrix form for supervised mixOmics modeling via unfold_chrom, not raw NetCDF instrument files. The file is not a NetCDF chromatogram (e.g. mzML or plain spectra tables) — read_chrom's RNetCDF-based reader is specific to NetCDF GCxGC files.

skills.description: Use when a smoothed, baseline-corrected two-dimensional chromatogram (2D-TIC) must be warped pixel-wise onto a reference chromatogram of the same dataset to remove retention-time shifts before multivariate analysis.
skills.name: chromatogram-peak-alignment-2dcow
skills.search_text: chromatogram-peak-alignment-2dcow Use when a smoothed, baseline-corrected two-dimensional chromatogram (2D-TIC) must be warped pixel-wise onto a reference chromatogram of the same dataset to remove retention-time shifts before multivariate analysis. Input chromatograms are raw NetCDF imports that have not yet been baseline-corrected (asymmetric least squares) and smoothed — preprocessing precedes peak alignment in the RGCxGC workflow A whole batch of chromatograms must be aligned together — use the batch_2DCOW interface (reference, sample_chroms, segments, max_warp, add_ref) rather than single-sample twod_cow The data are one-dimensional chromatograms or feature tables rather than folded two-dimensional GC×GC 2D-TIC chromatograms Aligns a single preprocessed GC×GC 2D-TIC chromatogram to a reference chromatogram by pixel-level two-dimensional correlation optimized warping (2D-COW) via the twod_cow function of the RGCxGC package, using per-dimension segment counts and warp limits. metabolomics/v3 10.1016/j.microc.2020.104830
skills.summary: Aligns a single preprocessed GC×GC 2D-TIC chromatogram to a reference chromatogram by pixel-level two-dimensional correlation optimized warping (2D-COW) via the twod_cow function of the RGCxGC package, using per-dimension segment counts and warp limits.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input chromatograms are raw NetCDF imports that have not yet been baseline-corrected (asymmetric least squares) and smoothed — preprocessing precedes peak alignment in the RGCxGC workflow A whole batch of chromatograms must be aligned together — use the batch_2DCOW interface (reference, sample_chroms, segments, max_warp, add_ref) rather than single-sample twod_cow The data are one-dimensional chromatograms or feature tables rather than folded two-dimensional GC×GC 2D-TIC chromatograms

skills.description: Use when MassQL queries have been run over a directory of mzML files (e.g., SST deuterated acylcarnitine standards on a UHPLC-HRMS) and the peak/scan results need to be visualized as EICs, Gaussian fits, and MS2 plots and exported as tables and PDF reports.
skills.name: chromatogram-plotting-from-massql-results
skills.search_text: chromatogram-plotting-from-massql-results Use when MassQL queries have been run over a directory of mzML files (e.g., SST deuterated acylcarnitine standards on a UHPLC-HRMS) and the peak/scan results need to be visualized as EICs, Gaussian fits, and MS2 plots and exported as tables and PDF reports. Input data is not in an open-source MS format (mzML) — vendor .raw files must first be converted via MSConvert/msconvert before MassQL queries and plotting can run The goal is evaluating absolute intensity or peak shape quality — the illustrative SST assessment explicitly notes 'the intensity and peak shape were not evaluated' You need interactive spectral exploration rather than static per-query reports — MassQL itself offers Dash-based visualization and a web /visualize/ms1 and /visualize/ms2 API instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Visualizes and tabulates MassQL query results from MassQLab system suitability testing by plotting extracted ion chromatograms, Gaussian peak fits, peak areas, and MS/MS product ion spectra as PDF/PNG images, and exporting raw and analysis csv tables, all organized by timestamp in a MassQLab_Output directory. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/rcm.10132
skills.summary: Visualizes and tabulates MassQL query results from MassQLab system suitability testing by plotting extracted ion chromatograms, Gaussian peak fits, peak areas, and MS/MS product ion spectra as PDF/PNG images, and exporting raw and analysis csv tables, all organized by timestamp in a MassQLab_Output directory.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data is not in an open-source MS format (mzML) — vendor .raw files must first be converted via MSConvert/msconvert before MassQL queries and plotting can run The goal is evaluating absolute intensity or peak shape quality — the illustrative SST assessment explicitly notes 'the intensity and peak shape were not evaluated' You need interactive spectral exploration rather than static per-query reports — MassQL itself offers Dash-based visualization and a web /visualize/ms1 and /visualize/ms2 API instead

skills.description: Use when you have a feature table plus .mzXML/.mzML raw files, a CNN model (EVA/pyEVA) producing predicted EIC quality classes, and manually annotated good/poor labels against which classification accuracy must be measured.
skills.name: chromatogram-quality-label-comparison
skills.search_text: chromatogram-quality-label-comparison Use when you have a feature table plus .mzXML/.mzML raw files, a CNN model (EVA/pyEVA) producing predicted EIC quality classes, and manually annotated good/poor labels against which classification accuracy must be measured. You have no manually annotated (manually inspected) good/poor EIC labels, so there is no ground truth to compare predicted labels against — use EVA purely for prediction instead. Your chromatograms are not LC-MS-based metabolomics EIC plots (e.g. GC-MS, LC-MS/MS spectra, or non-chromatographic data), which the EVA CNN was not trained to classify. Your goal is peak detection or feature deconvolution rather than evaluating feature fidelity/peak quality labels of already-extracted metabolic features. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3391 Evaluate a CNN-based EIC peak-quality classifier (EVA/pyEVA) by running inference on manually inspected extracted ion chromatogram plots and comparing predicted good/poor labels against ground-truth annotations, yielding an overall classification accuracy metric. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c01309
skills.summary: Evaluate a CNN-based EIC peak-quality classifier (EVA/pyEVA) by running inference on manually inspected extracted ion chromatogram plots and comparing predicted good/poor labels against ground-truth annotations, yielding an overall classification accuracy metric.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have no manually annotated (manually inspected) good/poor EIC labels, so there is no ground truth to compare predicted labels against — use EVA purely for prediction instead. Your chromatograms are not LC-MS-based metabolomics EIC plots (e.g. GC-MS, LC-MS/MS spectra, or non-chromatographic data), which the EVA CNN was not trained to classify. Your goal is peak detection or feature deconvolution rather than evaluating feature fidelity/peak quality labels of already-extracted metabolic features.

skills.description: Use when building an in-house LC-MS RT/m/z library with metScribeR and EIC peaks (from mzML files of authentic standards) show poorly assigned start/end boundaries or noisy baselines, requiring tuning of smoothing and density-filter settings before applying peak-finding thresholds.
skills.name: chromatogram-smoothing-parameter-tuning
skills.search_text: chromatogram-smoothing-parameter-tuning Use when building an in-house LC-MS RT/m/z library with metScribeR and EIC peaks (from mzML files of authentic standards) show poorly assigned start/end boundaries or noisy baselines, requiring tuning of smoothing and density-filter settings before applying peak-finding thresholds. Input is already a filtered peak table or feature table rather than raw mzML chromatograms needing smoothing adjustment The workflow requires MS/MS-based identification — metScribeR library construction uses only MS1 and RT data and does not require or use MS2 spectra A fully unattended peak-finding pipeline is needed; this step is deliberately interactive and requires visual human judgment on a peak subset http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 An interactive parameter-tuning step in metScribeR's Shiny app where the user visually adjusts the density filter and data smoothing on EIC peaks before committing filtering thresholds, ensuring peak boundaries are correctly assigned for LC-MS metabolite standard library construction. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.5c00548
skills.summary: An interactive parameter-tuning step in metScribeR's Shiny app where the user visually adjusts the density filter and data smoothing on EIC peaks before committing filtering thresholds, ensuring peak boundaries are correctly assigned for LC-MS metabolite standard library construction.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a filtered peak table or feature table rather than raw mzML chromatograms needing smoothing adjustment The workflow requires MS/MS-based identification — metScribeR library construction uses only MS1 and RT data and does not require or use MS2 spectra A fully unattended peak-finding pipeline is needed; this step is deliberately interactive and requires visual human judgment on a peak subset

skills.description: Use when an LC/MS EIC must be scored for quality via smoothing- and background-similarity measures, or when benchmarking a comparator EIC metric against a proposed alternative (e.g. the global zigzag index).
skills.name: chromatogram-smoothing-similarity-analysis
skills.search_text: chromatogram-smoothing-similarity-analysis Use when an LC/MS EIC must be scored for quality via smoothing- and background-similarity measures, or when benchmarking a comparator EIC metric against a proposed alternative (e.g. the global zigzag index). EICs with high background signals or containing only a single peak need a fair quality verdict — the paper explicitly states the MCQ index 'cannot fairly evaluate' these cases; use the global zigzag index instead Peak-level (not EIC-level) quality evaluation — the paper's six peak quality metrics (sharpness, Gaussian similarity, SNR, peak significance level, TPASR, local zigzag index) apply to detected chromatographic peaks, not whole EICs http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Implements the MCQ (mass chromatographic quality) index for extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) by quantifying similarity between an EIC and its smoothed version (spike detection) and its mean-subtracted version (background detection), then combining the two similarities into a 0–1.0 quality score. The paper shows this index works for selecting/aligning analyte components but fails to fairly evaluate EICs with high background signals or only a single peak. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/1471-2105-15-s11-s5
skills.summary: Implements the MCQ (mass chromatographic quality) index for extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) by quantifying similarity between an EIC and its smoothed version (spike detection) and its mean-subtracted version (background detection), then combining the two similarities into a 0–1.0 quality score. The paper shows this index works for selecting/aligning analyte components but fails to fairly evaluate EICs with high background signals or only a single peak.
skills.when_to_use_negative: EICs with high background signals or containing only a single peak need a fair quality verdict — the paper explicitly states the MCQ index 'cannot fairly evaluate' these cases; use the global zigzag index instead Peak-level (not EIC-level) quality evaluation — the paper's six peak quality metrics (sharpness, Gaussian similarity, SNR, peak significance level, TPASR, local zigzag index) apply to detected chromatographic peaks, not whole EICs

skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data has already been converted to an exchange format such as mzML — use conventional R readers (e.g., mzR) instead of the vendor-API path Only scan-level spectra or header metadata are needed (use readSpectrum/rawrrSpectrum readers, not readChromatogram) Input files are not Thermo Fisher Scientific .raw files — the RawFileReader API only reads this vendor's proprietary format

skills.search_text: chromatogram-total-ion-current-aggregation Use when you have a columnar Parquet HRMS file with rt, intensity and mslevel columns and need a TIC (intensity summed per retention time for MS1 scans) without loading the whole file into memory. skills.summary: Computes a total ion chromatogram (TIC) from an HRMS Parquet file (e.g. arcMS-converted Waters UNIFI (HD)MS^E data) using an on-disk Apache Arrow/dplyr query, so only the ~64 Kb aggregated result is collected into RAM instead of the ~1.9 Gb full dataset.

skills.when_to_use_negative: You need a spectrum (m/z vs intensity) plot instead of a retention-time trace — use mzapy.view.plot_spectrum on collect_ms1_arrays_by_rt output instead The data is still in a proprietary vendor format (.raw, Agilent .d, Bruker ion mobility .d) and has not been converted to MZA/HDF5 with the mza converter Interactive visualization or downstream numerical analysis of the trace is the goal rather than producing a saved figure file

skills.search_text: chromatogram-xic-extraction-from-raw-files Use when the input is a Thermo Fisher Orbitap .raw file (e.g., 20181113_010_autoQC01.raw) and you need chromatographic traces/XICs for target masses in R, e.g., to derive retention times for iRT peptides. skills.summary: Extracts MS1-level extracted ion chromatograms (XICs) directly from proprietary Thermo Fisher .raw files in R using rawrr::readChromatogram, enabling downstream analyses such as iRT retention-time regression without converting raw data to mzML via ProteoWizard.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data has already been converted to an exchange format like mzML (the rawR workflow exists to avoid ProteoWizard conversion of Thermo .raw files) The raw file is not from a Thermo Fisher Scientific instrument — rawrr wraps only the Thermo RawFileReader .NET API The analysis operates on preprocessed/peptide-level estimates (e.g., MSstats processing MaxQuant or Skyline outputs) rather than raw spectral/chromatographic data

skills.description: Use when longitudinal LC-MS/MS SST data (e.g., deuterated acylcarnitine standards in mzML) must be screened for retention time drift, column-lot shifts, or wrong chromatographic method use prior to experimental acquisition.
skills.name: chromatographic-anomaly-diagnosis
skills.search_text: chromatographic-anomaly-diagnosis Use when longitudinal LC-MS/MS SST data (e.g., deuterated acylcarnitine standards in mzML) must be screened for retention time drift, column-lot shifts, or wrong chromatographic method use prior to experimental acquisition. Intensity and peak shape evaluation is required — the illustrative SST assessment explicitly did not evaluate intensity and peak shape The goal is MS/MS consistency assessment via DDA SST — the stochastic nature of DDA MS/MS triggering is problematic for assessing consistency, and the authors state SST MS/MS evaluation is not warranted in their use case Input data are not LC-MS mzML-queryable (e.g., already-processed feature tables); MassQL operates on raw mzML scan data, so feature-level inputs bypass this skill http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 A system suitability testing (SST) skill that uses MassQLab (built on MassQL) to run named MassQL queries over directories of LC-HRMS mzML files, tabulate retention times and EIC peak areas, and diagnose chromatographic anomalies such as column-lot-linked retention time shifts and columns run with the wrong method before full data collection. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/rcm.10132
skills.summary: A system suitability testing (SST) skill that uses MassQLab (built on MassQL) to run named MassQL queries over directories of LC-HRMS mzML files, tabulate retention times and EIC peak areas, and diagnose chromatographic anomalies such as column-lot-linked retention time shifts and columns run with the wrong method before full data collection.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Intensity and peak shape evaluation is required — the illustrative SST assessment explicitly did not evaluate intensity and peak shape The goal is MS/MS consistency assessment via DDA SST — the stochastic nature of DDA MS/MS triggering is problematic for assessing consistency, and the authors state SST MS/MS evaluation is not warranted in their use case Input data are not LC-MS mzML-queryable (e.g., already-processed feature tables); MassQL operates on raw mzML scan data, so feature-level inputs bypass this skill

skills.description: Use when raw LC/MS data in mzML format must be converted into an MS1 ion-feature table without manually tuned detection thresholds, and noise must be separated from true chromatographic peaks in a data-driven, parameter-free way.
skills.name: chromatographic-auto-correlation-noise-filtering
skills.search_text: chromatographic-auto-correlation-noise-filtering Use when raw LC/MS data in mzML format must be converted into an MS1 ion-feature table without manually tuned detection thresholds, and noise must be separated from true chromatographic peaks in a data-driven, parameter-free way. The input is already a feature/peak table rather than raw mzML LC/MS data — this skill operates on raw MS1 spectra from mzML files De-isotoping, metabolite annotation, or MS/MS identification is required — mzLearn results are at the ion MS1 level and it does not perform de-isotoping or MS/MS identification User-set parameters or expert-tuned thresholds are desired or mandated by an existing validated pipeline (e.g., a tuned XCMS or ASARI workflow that must be reproduced as-is) http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 mzLearn's data-driven MS1 signal-detection core: it partitions rt/m/z space into dynamically resized patches, separates true chromatographic peaks from noise via auto-correlation, and learns its own thresholds from highest-quality 'pin' patches over ~3 iterations, requiring no user-set parameters or QC samples. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.01.26.634927
skills.summary: mzLearn's data-driven MS1 signal-detection core: it partitions rt/m/z space into dynamically resized patches, separates true chromatographic peaks from noise via auto-correlation, and learns its own thresholds from highest-quality 'pin' patches over ~3 iterations, requiring no user-set parameters or QC samples.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a feature/peak table rather than raw mzML LC/MS data — this skill operates on raw MS1 spectra from mzML files De-isotoping, metabolite annotation, or MS/MS identification is required — mzLearn results are at the ion MS1 level and it does not perform de-isotoping or MS/MS identification User-set parameters or expert-tuned thresholds are desired or mandated by an existing validated pipeline (e.g., a tuned XCMS or ASARI workflow that must be reproduced as-is)

skills.search_text: chromatographic-batch-variation-assessment Use when LC-MS/MS samples span two chromatographic batches (a metadata 'batch' column) and you need to test whether chemical-hierarchy-based beta diversity mitigates the batch effect versus an unweighted feature-table distance. No chemical hierarchy is available for the features (weighted UniFrac requires a phylogeny; only the tree-agnostic comparison is possible) Sample metadata lacks a batch/experiment grouping, so no PERMANOVA hypothesis about chromatographic batches can be tested Features are only MS1 peaks without MS/MS spectra — such features cannot receive fingerprints and are excluded from the hierarchy Quantifies whether a tree-informed distance metric (weighted UniFrac on a Qemistree chemical hierarchy) reduces chromatography-driven batch signal relative to a tree-agnostic metric (Bray-Curtis), by comparing one-sided PERMANOVA pseudo-F statistics between batches in QIIME 2. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41589-020-00677-3
skills.summary: Quantifies whether a tree-informed distance metric (weighted UniFrac on a Qemistree chemical hierarchy) reduces chromatography-driven batch signal relative to a tree-agnostic metric (Bray-Curtis), by comparing one-sided PERMANOVA pseudo-F statistics between batches in QIIME 2.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No chemical hierarchy is available for the features (weighted UniFrac requires a phylogeny; only the tree-agnostic comparison is possible) Sample metadata lacks a batch/experiment grouping, so no PERMANOVA hypothesis about chromatographic batches can be tested Features are only MS1 peaks without MS/MS spectra — such features cannot receive fingerprints and are excluded from the hierarchy

skills.summary: Benchmark quantification accuracy of MRM peak-integration tools by fitting least-squares calibration curves (peak area vs. concentration) for each transition and comparing R-square values, as done for MRMPro vs. Skyline on the Drug_light/Drug_heavy transitions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset lacks known concentrations, so no calibration curve (peak area vs. concentration) can be regressed Only one tool's peak areas are available — the skill is a comparative benchmark requiring paired areas from two tools or two integration conditions The acquisition is not targeted MRM (e.g., DDA/DIA discovery data), where transition-level peak-area calibration curves of this form do not apply
