skills.description: Use when filtering candidate peaks detected from GC×GC–MS 4D intensity arrays (CDF-derived GcDuo objects) by signal-to-noise and peak-shape criteria before deconvolution, to discard false positives such as incomplete or sub-threshold signals.
skills.name: chromatographic-peak-snr-filtering
skills.search_text: chromatographic-peak-snr-filtering Use when filtering candidate peaks detected from GC×GC–MS 4D intensity arrays (CDF-derived GcDuo objects) by signal-to-noise and peak-shape criteria before deconvolution, to discard false positives such as incomplete or sub-threshold signals. Input is already a curated peak/feature table rather than raw GC×GC–MS CDF-derived 4D intensity data — SNR and Gaussian-form filtering of blobs assumes Module II ROI detection is being (re)run. Analytes of interest are known to be very low abundance: strict SNR thresholds can miss them entirely (decane required lowering the SNR from 3 to 1), so a targeted or relaxed-threshold approach is preferable. Peaks are strongly non-Gaussian by nature (e.g., saturated or badly resolved chromatographic signals) — the Gaussian-form requisite will discard them even if signal is strong. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 A peak-filtering step from GcDUO's Module II in which candidate blobs (3D peaks with 2D coordinates) detected by the inverse-watershed ROI selection on GC×GC–MS data are retained only if they exhibit adequate signal-to-noise ratios in both chromatographic dimensions and conform to a Gaussian chromatographic form. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bib/bbaf080
skills.summary: A peak-filtering step from GcDUO's Module II in which candidate blobs (3D peaks with 2D coordinates) detected by the inverse-watershed ROI selection on GC×GC–MS data are retained only if they exhibit adequate signal-to-noise ratios in both chromatographic dimensions and conform to a Gaussian chromatographic form.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a curated peak/feature table rather than raw GC×GC–MS CDF-derived 4D intensity data — SNR and Gaussian-form filtering of blobs assumes Module II ROI detection is being (re)run. Analytes of interest are known to be very low abundance: strict SNR thresholds can miss them entirely (decane required lowering the SNR from 3 to 1), so a targeted or relaxed-threshold approach is preferable. Peaks are strongly non-Gaussian by nature (e.g., saturated or badly resolved chromatographic signals) — the Gaussian-form requisite will discard them even if signal is strong.

skills.description: Use when processing high-throughput LC-MS/MS MRM ion chromatograms where peaks may be coeluted, noisy, or unevenly sampled and per-transition peak tips, valleys, and coelution flags must be resolved before quantitation.
skills.name: chromatographic-peak-tip-detection
skills.search_text: chromatographic-peak-tip-detection Use when processing high-throughput LC-MS/MS MRM ion chromatograms where peaks may be coeluted, noisy, or unevenly sampled and per-transition peak tips, valleys, and coelution flags must be resolved before quantitation. Input is not an MRM ion chromatogram from targeted LC-MS/MS data (e.g. it is already a quantified peak table), since this skill operates on raw chromatographic signal during peak detection Only a single, isolated, symmetric peak is expected and no deconvolution or coelution handling is needed — simpler fixed-window peak picking may suffice Locates chromatographic peak tips in MRM ion chromatograms using MATLAB's findpeaks after dynamic signal smoothing, tracing left/right bounds from each tip, reporting HWHM, and flagging/limiting coelution within 2.5× the half-width-at-half-maximum. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c02462
skills.summary: Locates chromatographic peak tips in MRM ion chromatograms using MATLAB's findpeaks after dynamic signal smoothing, tracing left/right bounds from each tip, reporting HWHM, and flagging/limiting coelution within 2.5× the half-width-at-half-maximum.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is not an MRM ion chromatogram from targeted LC-MS/MS data (e.g. it is already a quantified peak table), since this skill operates on raw chromatographic signal during peak detection Only a single, isolated, symmetric peak is expected and no deconvolution or coelution handling is needed — simpler fixed-window peak picking may suffice

skills.description: Use when you have raw untargeted metabolomics files (mzML/mzXML/mzData) plus a user-defined list of m/z and RT pairs for QC or contaminant compounds, and need to track observed m/z, retention time, intensity, and peak shape over time or batches.
skills.name: chromatographic-peak-tracking-for-user-defined-compounds
skills.search_text: chromatographic-peak-tracking-for-user-defined-compounds Use when you have raw untargeted metabolomics files (mzML/mzXML/mzData) plus a user-defined list of m/z and RT pairs for QC or contaminant compounds, and need to track observed m/z, retention time, intensity, and peak shape over time or batches. When the compound list is a set of contaminant ions to monitor generically — module_Contaminants (nearly 800 known contaminant ions) is the dedicated path, not a bespoke m/z-RT tracking list When the goal is intensity-drift correction or normalization of the full feature table (e.g. QC-MXP-style correction) rather than targeted tracking of a few compounds When the input is already a processed peak/feature table with no raw mzML files to extract peaks from http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Detects and time-lines the intensity of user-specified compounds (m/z + RT pairs) across mzML injections using the QC4Metabolomics module_TrackCmp workflow, revealing drifts such as the three-week tryptophan intensity decrease in long-term QC samples. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c07078
skills.summary: Detects and time-lines the intensity of user-specified compounds (m/z + RT pairs) across mzML injections using the QC4Metabolomics module_TrackCmp workflow, revealing drifts such as the three-week tryptophan intensity decrease in long-term QC samples.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the compound list is a set of contaminant ions to monitor generically — module_Contaminants (nearly 800 known contaminant ions) is the dedicated path, not a bespoke m/z-RT tracking list When the goal is intensity-drift correction or normalization of the full feature table (e.g. QC-MXP-style correction) rather than targeted tracking of a few compounds When the input is already a processed peak/feature table with no raw mzML files to extract peaks from

skills.description: Use when replicate LC/MS injections of chemical standard mixtures (mzXML/mzML with blank runs) must be filtered into validated peaks to build a retention-time reference library, e.g. the HILIC LC-MS platform's 571-metabolite library.
skills.name: chromatographic-peak-validation
skills.search_text: chromatographic-peak-validation Use when replicate LC/MS injections of chemical standard mixtures (mzXML/mzML with blank runs) must be filtered into validated peaks to build a retention-time reference library, e.g. the HILIC LC-MS platform's 571-metabolite library. Input is already a validated peak/feature table — re-running the Std/Blk > r, RSD < c, intensity > I filters would double-filter and misassign validation flags. The goal is de novo peak picking on untargeted samples without chemical-standard replicates and accompanying blank runs, since Std/Blk and RT RSD criteria cannot be computed. Assessing mobile-phase peak quality end-to-end rather than validating individual metabolite peaks for a reference library (use the mobile-phase-scoring skill instead). http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Validates metabolite peaks detected from LC-MS standard-mixture replicates using MetaMOPE's eight per-peak metrics (MCQ, maximum intensity, RT RSD, Std/Blk ratio, jaggedness, asymmetry factor, FWHM, modality) against user-specified thresholds (r, c, I), producing validation flags and validated retention times for a reference library. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioadv/vbad061
skills.summary: Validates metabolite peaks detected from LC-MS standard-mixture replicates using MetaMOPE's eight per-peak metrics (MCQ, maximum intensity, RT RSD, Std/Blk ratio, jaggedness, asymmetry factor, FWHM, modality) against user-specified thresholds (r, c, I), producing validation flags and validated retention times for a reference library.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a validated peak/feature table — re-running the Std/Blk > r, RSD < c, intensity > I filters would double-filter and misassign validation flags. The goal is de novo peak picking on untargeted samples without chemical-standard replicates and accompanying blank runs, since Std/Blk and RT RSD criteria cannot be computed. Assessing mobile-phase peak quality end-to-end rather than validating individual metabolite peaks for a reference library (use the mobile-phase-scoring skill instead).

skills.description: Use when you have profile-mode LC-HRMS chromatograms and a user-defined reference-feature list (ground truth) and need to distinguish true chromatographic peaks from background/walls with a custom-trained CNN.
skills.name: chromatographic-peak-vs-background-classification
skills.search_text: chromatographic-peak-vs-background-classification Use when you have profile-mode LC-HRMS chromatograms and a user-defined reference-feature list (ground truth) and need to distinguish true chromatographic peaks from background/walls with a custom-trained CNN. Input is already a peak table or feature matrix rather than profile-mode LC-HRMS chromatogram data — PeakBot operates on raw profile-mode data via local-maxima extraction No user-defined reference-feature list (ground truth) is available and fewer than 100 reference features can be specified Reference chromatograms contain co-eluting compounds (isomers) at the reference-feature locations, which breaks the gradient-descend property estimation http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Train and apply PeakBot, a TensorFlow 2.5.0 CNN that classifies local-maxima extracted from LC-HRMS profile-mode chromatograms as true chromatographic peaks (with left/right isomeric compounds) versus background signals (e.g., walls), reporting peak-type, peak-center, and bounding-box. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btac344
skills.summary: Train and apply PeakBot, a TensorFlow 2.5.0 CNN that classifies local-maxima extracted from LC-HRMS profile-mode chromatograms as true chromatographic peaks (with left/right isomeric compounds) versus background signals (e.g., walls), reporting peak-type, peak-center, and bounding-box.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a peak table or feature matrix rather than profile-mode LC-HRMS chromatogram data — PeakBot operates on raw profile-mode data via local-maxima extraction No user-defined reference-feature list (ground truth) is available and fewer than 100 reference features can be specified Reference chromatograms contain co-eluting compounds (isomers) at the reference-feature locations, which breaks the gradient-descend property estimation

skills.description: Use when you need to set chromatographic peak-width parameters for an LC-MS feature extraction run (e.g. XCMS CentWave peak width, MS-DIAL tolerances) from raw untargeted metabolomics data.
skills.name: chromatographic-peak-width-measurement
skills.search_text: chromatographic-peak-width-measurement Use when you need to set chromatographic peak-width parameters for an LC-MS feature extraction run (e.g. XCMS CentWave peak width, MS-DIAL tolerances) from raw untargeted metabolomics data. Your data are already a processed feature table and peak parameters were previously fixed — the skill measures parameters from raw LC-MS data, not from extracted features. You only need a single non-LC-MS parameter (e.g. alignment or statistics settings) — the skill targets the four universal LC-MS parameters measured by Paramounter. You require dereplication filtering decisions (mzdiff handling) rather than peak-width estimation — that is handled separately in the README notes on mzdiff, not by the peak-width measurement itself. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Paramounter automatically measures the chromatographic peak width from raw LC-MS metabolomics data, prior to feature extraction, as one of four universal parameters used to tune feature-extraction software like XCMS CentWave or MS-DIAL. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c04758
skills.summary: Paramounter automatically measures the chromatographic peak width from raw LC-MS metabolomics data, prior to feature extraction, as one of four universal parameters used to tune feature-extraction software like XCMS CentWave or MS-DIAL.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your data are already a processed feature table and peak parameters were previously fixed — the skill measures parameters from raw LC-MS data, not from extracted features. You only need a single non-LC-MS parameter (e.g. alignment or statistics settings) — the skill targets the four universal LC-MS parameters measured by Paramounter. You require dereplication filtering decisions (mzdiff handling) rather than peak-width estimation — that is handled separately in the README notes on mzdiff, not by the peak-width measurement itself.

skills.description: Use when configuring eRah deconvolveComp() on GC-EI MS chromatograms (netCDF/mzXML) and you must set min.peak.width, min.peak.height, noise.threshold, or avoid.processing.mz before running CMLC/OSD.
skills.name: chromatographic-peak-width-tuning
skills.search_text: chromatographic-peak-width-tuning Use when configuring eRah deconvolveComp() on GC-EI MS chromatograms (netCDF/mzXML) and you must set min.peak.width, min.peak.height, noise.threshold, or avoid.processing.mz before running CMLC/OSD. Input is already a deconvolved MetaboSet and the task is downstream alignment or identification (use setAlPar/alignComp or identifyComp instead) Data are LC-MS or non-EI where ion-redundancy covariance patterns exploited by CMLC/OSD do not apply The goal is generic peak picking of individual fragment ions (e.g. XCMS centWave) rather than resolving co-eluting compounds into pure spectra http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Tunes eRah's deconvolution parameter object (setDecPar) — minimum peak width, minimum peak height, noise threshold, and excluded m/z ranges — so that CMLC/OSD spectral deconvolution resolves co-eluted GC-MS compounds without fragmenting or inflating peaks. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.6b02927
skills.summary: Tunes eRah's deconvolution parameter object (setDecPar) — minimum peak width, minimum peak height, noise threshold, and excluded m/z ranges — so that CMLC/OSD spectral deconvolution resolves co-eluted GC-MS compounds without fragmenting or inflating peaks.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a deconvolved MetaboSet and the task is downstream alignment or identification (use setAlPar/alignComp or identifyComp instead) Data are LC-MS or non-EI where ion-redundancy covariance patterns exploited by CMLC/OSD do not apply The goal is generic peak picking of individual fragment ions (e.g. XCMS centWave) rather than resolving co-eluting compounds into pure spectra

skills.description: Use when targeted LC–MS peak integration (e.g., TARDIS on raw metabolomics/lipidomics runs) has produced per-target peak tables and you need quantitative quality metrics to filter poor-quality peaks or validate QC-run clustering.
skills.name: chromatographic-quality-metric-calculation
skills.search_text: chromatographic-quality-metric-calculation Use when targeted LC–MS peak integration (e.g., TARDIS on raw metabolomics/lipidomics runs) has produced per-target peak tables and you need quantitative quality metrics to filter poor-quality peaks or validate QC-run clustering. Data are untargeted — the article positions TARDIS for targeted peak extraction, noting that 'targeted peak extraction outperformed untargeted peak searching'; use untargeted tools like xcms, MZmine, or OpenMS instead. Input is already a processed feature/peak table — quality metrics must be computed during integration from raw chromatographic data. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Compute TARDIS's peak-quality metrics (area under the curve, maximum intensity, points over the peak, custom signal-to-noise ratio, and bell-curve similarity) for targeted LC–MS chromatographic peaks to assess integration quality before downstream statistics. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c00567
skills.summary: Compute TARDIS's peak-quality metrics (area under the curve, maximum intensity, points over the peak, custom signal-to-noise ratio, and bell-curve similarity) for targeted LC–MS chromatographic peaks to assess integration quality before downstream statistics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are untargeted — the article positions TARDIS for targeted peak extraction, noting that 'targeted peak extraction outperformed untargeted peak searching'; use untargeted tools like xcms, MZmine, or OpenMS instead. Input is already a processed feature/peak table — quality metrics must be computed during integration from raw chromatographic data.

skills.description: Use when you must programmatically score the quality of extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) or detected chromatographic peaks in LC/MS metabolomics data — especially EICs with high background signals or containing only a single peak — before downstream peak detection.
skills.name: chromatographic-quality-metric-implementation
skills.search_text: chromatographic-quality-metric-implementation Use when you must programmatically score the quality of extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) or detected chromatographic peaks in LC/MS metabolomics data — especially EICs with high background signals or containing only a single peak — before downstream peak detection. Evaluating EICs selected for analyte component alignment where the MCQ index is appropriate — the paper notes the MCQ index is suited for selecting and aligning analyte components, but fails on EICs with high background signals or only a single peak, which is exactly where the zigzag index applies Centroided/peak-picked data with no extracted continuous ion chromatogram intensity profile — the first-order derivative computation requires an EIC intensity series Automated machine learning-based peak identification — the paper reports SVM-based identification is not yet implemented because a curated training set of 'good' and 'bad' representative peaks does not yet exist http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Implements and validates chromatographic quality metrics from Zhang & Zhao (2014), most notably the EIC-related global zigzag index computed from an EIC's first-order derivatives, plus six chromatographic peak quality metrics (sharpness, Gaussian similarity, SNR, peak significance level, TPASR, local peak-related zigzag index) used to filter 'bad' EICs and peaks in LC/MS-based metabolomics data. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/1471-2105-15-s11-s5
skills.summary: Implements and validates chromatographic quality metrics from Zhang & Zhao (2014), most notably the EIC-related global zigzag index computed from an EIC's first-order derivatives, plus six chromatographic peak quality metrics (sharpness, Gaussian similarity, SNR, peak significance level, TPASR, local peak-related zigzag index) used to filter 'bad' EICs and peaks in LC/MS-based metabolomics data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Evaluating EICs selected for analyte component alignment where the MCQ index is appropriate — the paper notes the MCQ index is suited for selecting and aligning analyte components, but fails on EICs with high background signals or only a single peak, which is exactly where the zigzag index applies Centroided/peak-picked data with no extracted continuous ion chromatogram intensity profile — the first-order derivative computation requires an EIC intensity series Automated machine learning-based peak identification — the paper reports SVM-based identification is not yet implemented because a curated training set of 'good' and 'bad' representative peaks does not yet exist

skills.description: Use when absolute quantitation of targeted compounds from MRM data is needed and calibration standard samples (e.g. 14 standards spanning 0.025–500 mol/mL) are available to build concentration–abundance curves.
skills.name: chromatographic-quantitation-curve-modeling
skills.search_text: chromatographic-quantitation-curve-modeling Use when absolute quantitation of targeted compounds from MRM data is needed and calibration standard samples (e.g. 14 standards spanning 0.025–500 mol/mL) are available to build concentration–abundance curves. Compounds were run without standards — use constant-abundance mode rather than fitting an SC Only two usable calibration points remain after excluding saturated/unchecked points — a two-point straight line fallback, not a user-selected quadratic model, is the appropriate fit The goal is relative quantitation without calibration (e.g. batch-effect correction on BQC samples), which does not require SC construction http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Fits standard curves (SCs) for absolute quantitation of targeted MRM ion chromatograms by regressing computed peak abundances against known concentrations, with flexible regression models and weighting. Implemented in MRMQuant (MATLAB) with automatic exclusion of unreliable calibration points and fallback modes for sparse data. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c02462
skills.summary: Fits standard curves (SCs) for absolute quantitation of targeted MRM ion chromatograms by regressing computed peak abundances against known concentrations, with flexible regression models and weighting. Implemented in MRMQuant (MATLAB) with automatic exclusion of unreliable calibration points and fallback modes for sparse data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Compounds were run without standards — use constant-abundance mode rather than fitting an SC Only two usable calibration points remain after excluding saturated/unchecked points — a two-point straight line fallback, not a user-selected quadratic model, is the appropriate fit The goal is relative quantitation without calibration (e.g. batch-effect correction on BQC samples), which does not require SC construction

skills.description: Use when a predicted-versus-true retention time table exists and you need to set an RT matching window (e.g., ±2 SD) for metabolite identification and quantify how many true matches that window would exclude.
skills.name: chromatographic-retention-matching-window-analysis
skills.search_text: chromatographic-retention-matching-window-analysis Use when a predicted-versus-true retention time table exists and you need to set an RT matching window (e.g., ±2 SD) for metabolite identification and quantify how many true matches that window would exclude. The dataset contains non-retained molecules and you have not removed them — error statistics will be inflated (33.41 s vs 27.30 s average absolute error when not-retained molecules are excluded) Chromatographic conditions differ from those the model was transferred to — RT-Transformer must first be fine-tuned on a dataset for the specific chromatographic method before error distributions can be trusted You need per-candidate metabolite scoring rather than RT-window statistics — this skill characterizes the error distribution, it does not rank candidate structures Quantifies RT-Transformer retention-time prediction error on a retained-molecule test set (e.g., the SMRT retained set of 7,790 molecules) and derives candidate-matching windows (±2 SD = 52.80 s) with associated false negative rates, so that RT filters can be used to prune metabolite annotation candidates. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae084
skills.summary: Quantifies RT-Transformer retention-time prediction error on a retained-molecule test set (e.g., the SMRT retained set of 7,790 molecules) and derives candidate-matching windows (±2 SD = 52.80 s) with associated false negative rates, so that RT filters can be used to prune metabolite annotation candidates.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset contains non-retained molecules and you have not removed them — error statistics will be inflated (33.41 s vs 27.30 s average absolute error when not-retained molecules are excluded) Chromatographic conditions differ from those the model was transferred to — RT-Transformer must first be fine-tuned on a dataset for the specific chromatographic method before error distributions can be trusted You need per-candidate metabolite scoring rather than RT-window statistics — this skill characterizes the error distribution, it does not rank candidate structures

skills.description: Use when the goal is to predict elution order of metabolites directly from molecular structure (InChI) across LC systems, especially when retention times are not comparable across instruments/configurations.
skills.name: chromatographic-retention-order-prediction
skills.search_text: chromatographic-retention-order-prediction Use when the goal is to predict elution order of metabolites directly from molecular structure (InChI) across LC systems, especially when retention times are not comparable across instruments/configurations. When you need an absolute retention time value rather than an ordering — use the SVR baseline (src/evaluation_scenarios_main.py estimator 'svr') instead, since the paper notes SVR was limited in using data from other chromatographic systems. When the molecules of interest have very small retention times (not interacting with the chromatographic system) — the workflow removes such molecules for each system before training. When a single homogeneous dataset with directly comparable retention times is available and no cross-system transfer is needed — simpler regression may suffice. http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Trains a ranking support vector machine (RankSVM) on pairwise retention-order preferences extracted from heterogeneous LC retention-time datasets (e.g. PredRet), using MACCS counting or binary molecular fingerprints as representations, to predict the order in which molecules elute from an LC column for any target chromatographic system. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/bty590
skills.summary: Trains a ranking support vector machine (RankSVM) on pairwise retention-order preferences extracted from heterogeneous LC retention-time datasets (e.g. PredRet), using MACCS counting or binary molecular fingerprints as representations, to predict the order in which molecules elute from an LC column for any target chromatographic system.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When you need an absolute retention time value rather than an ordering — use the SVR baseline (src/evaluation_scenarios_main.py estimator 'svr') instead, since the paper notes SVR was limited in using data from other chromatographic systems. When the molecules of interest have very small retention times (not interacting with the chromatographic system) — the workflow removes such molecules for each system before training. When a single homogeneous dataset with directly comparable retention times is available and no cross-system transfer is needed — simpler regression may suffice.

skills.description: Use when raw LC-MS or LC-IMS-MS files (Agilent 'd', Thermo '.raw', Bruker 'd', mzML) need per-ion mass, retention-time, and arrival-time error metrics for QC of chromatographic performance.
skills.name: chromatographic-retention-time-error-tracking
skills.search_text: chromatographic-retention-time-error-tracking Use when raw LC-MS or LC-IMS-MS files (Agilent 'd', Thermo '.raw', Bruker 'd', mzML) need per-ion mass, retention-time, and arrival-time error metrics for QC of chromatographic performance. The goal is fragmentation-spectrum QC (expected fragment ions/intensities) — use the separate MS2 diagnostic step instead The goal is MS/MS spectral library matching or targeted peak quantitation — TandemMatch or PeakQuant, not this RT-error tracking step Only infusion (no LC front-end) data where retention time is undefined http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Track retention-time (and, for IMS runs, arrival-time/1/K0) errors of precursor ions across an MS batch — PeakQC computes these peak metrics for both auto-tracked MS1 ions and user-specified reference ions to flag chromatographic drift. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jasms.4c00146
skills.summary: Track retention-time (and, for IMS runs, arrival-time/1/K0) errors of precursor ions across an MS batch — PeakQC computes these peak metrics for both auto-tracked MS1 ions and user-specified reference ions to flag chromatographic drift.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is fragmentation-spectrum QC (expected fragment ions/intensities) — use the separate MS2 diagnostic step instead The goal is MS/MS spectral library matching or targeted peak quantitation — TandemMatch or PeakQuant, not this RT-error tracking step Only infusion (no LC front-end) data where retention time is undefined

skills.description: Use when you need to train or retrain RT-Transformer on a retention time dataset prepared as InChI+RT CSV, or reproduce the SMRT full-data MAE of 33.41 s.
skills.name: chromatographic-rt-dataset-preparation
skills.search_text: chromatographic-rt-dataset-preparation Use when you need to train or retrain RT-Transformer on a retention time dataset prepared as InChI+RT CSV, or reproduce the SMRT full-data MAE of 33.41 s. Your input is already a processed prediction (per-molecule RT values) and you only need to score MAE/MedAE on an existing test set without training — test.py covers validation only. Your data lacks InChI structures or RT annotations, e.g. only SMILES strings without retention time labels — the pipeline requires 'InChI' and 'RT' columns. You need retention time prediction under a single, well-covered chromatographic method where the pretrained model already suffices; then use the Hugging Face web server or QuickStart.ipynb instead of retraining. http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 http://edamontology.org/topic_3391 Prepares a chromatographic retention time dataset (e.g. the SMRT small-molecule dataset with 80 038 molecules or a transfer-learning set from PredRet) as a CSV with InChI and RT columns, and trains the RT-Transformer (graph attention network + 1D-Transformer) on it, evaluating MAE/MedAE on the test split. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae084
skills.summary: Prepares a chromatographic retention time dataset (e.g. the SMRT small-molecule dataset with 80 038 molecules or a transfer-learning set from PredRet) as a CSV with InChI and RT columns, and trains the RT-Transformer (graph attention network + 1D-Transformer) on it, evaluating MAE/MedAE on the test split.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your input is already a processed prediction (per-molecule RT values) and you only need to score MAE/MedAE on an existing test set without training — test.py covers validation only. Your data lacks InChI structures or RT annotations, e.g. only SMILES strings without retention time labels — the pipeline requires 'InChI' and 'RT' columns. You need retention time prediction under a single, well-covered chromatographic method where the pretrained model already suffices; then use the Hugging Face web server or QuickStart.ipynb instead of retraining.

skills.description: Use when constructing metScribeR reference libraries from mzML files of authentic standards and you must choose the m/z and RT tolerances for EIC extraction and adduct distinction.
skills.name: chromatographic-rt-tolerance-configuration
skills.search_text: chromatographic-rt-tolerance-configuration Use when constructing metScribeR reference libraries from mzML files of authentic standards and you must choose the m/z and RT tolerances for EIC extraction and adduct distinction. The task requires MS/MS-based identification: metScribeR focuses library building on MS1 and RT data and does not use or require MS2 spectra for library construction You need untargeted feature detection or RT prediction across instruments: RT is not consistently transferable across different LC-MS conditions, so these tolerances only apply to within-laboratory, method-specific data The data are already processed feature tables or peak lists rather than raw mzML files of authentic standards http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Setting the eic_mz_tolerance and eic_rt_tolerance parameters in metScribeR's user_data_input() so EICs are extracted at expected adduct m/z values and adducts of the same standard are distinguished. Tolerances must be grounded in the LC-MS instrument's ability to confidently separate two signals. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.5c00548
skills.summary: Setting the eic_mz_tolerance and eic_rt_tolerance parameters in metScribeR's user_data_input() so EICs are extracted at expected adduct m/z values and adducts of the same standard are distinguished. Tolerances must be grounded in the LC-MS instrument's ability to confidently separate two signals.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task requires MS/MS-based identification: metScribeR focuses library building on MS1 and RT data and does not use or require MS2 spectra for library construction You need untargeted feature detection or RT prediction across instruments: RT is not consistently transferable across different LC-MS conditions, so these tolerances only apply to within-laboratory, method-specific data The data are already processed feature tables or peak lists rather than raw mzML files of authentic standards

skills.description: Use when processing MRM acquisition data where EIC peak features across samples must be grouped by chromatographic shape (e.g., same target peptide transition across samples), and manual inspection needs pre-grouped EICs to keep low-intensity noise features separated from real signal.
skills.name: chromatographic-shape-similarity-analysis
skills.search_text: chromatographic-shape-similarity-analysis Use when processing MRM acquisition data where EIC peak features across samples must be grouped by chromatographic shape (e.g., same target peptide transition across samples), and manual inspection needs pre-grouped EICs to keep low-intensity noise features separated from real signal. Data are DDA/DIA acquisitions rather than MRM — MRMPro's EIC grouping and collaborative manual inspection are dedicated to MRM data analysis in large volumes The goal is peak detection/picking accuracy itself — the article notes peak extraction accuracy is not yet improved and improvement is deferred to future work; the grouping only organizes already-picked EIC features A feature table with pre-assigned transition groups already exists — regrouping via DBSCAN would duplicate existing group information http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Groups extracted-ion-chromatogram (EIC) peak features from MRM datasets by clustering EICs with similar chromatographic shapes, as implemented in MRMPro using DBSCAN on normalized retention-time drift and intensity-difference features. It automates EIC grouping so that batch manual calibration can proceed on coherent transition groups rather than per-EIC. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-024-05685-x
skills.summary: Groups extracted-ion-chromatogram (EIC) peak features from MRM datasets by clustering EICs with similar chromatographic shapes, as implemented in MRMPro using DBSCAN on normalized retention-time drift and intensity-difference features. It automates EIC grouping so that batch manual calibration can proceed on coherent transition groups rather than per-EIC.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are DDA/DIA acquisitions rather than MRM — MRMPro's EIC grouping and collaborative manual inspection are dedicated to MRM data analysis in large volumes The goal is peak detection/picking accuracy itself — the article notes peak extraction accuracy is not yet improved and improvement is deferred to future work; the grouping only organizes already-picked EIC features A feature table with pre-assigned transition groups already exists — regrouping via DBSCAN would duplicate existing group information

skills.description: Use when you have paired RPLC retention datasets (e.g., RepoRT, PredRet, Metabolome Workbench, MetaboLights sources) sharing compounds across different chromatographic methods and need to measure retention-order replicability or attribute it to specific method differences.

skills.search_text: chromatographic-space-similarity-quantification Use when you have paired RPLC retention datasets (e.g., RepoRT, PredRet, Metabolome Workbench, MetaboLights sources) sharing compounds across different chromatographic methods and need to measure retention-order replicability or attribute it to specific method differences. Datasets are HILIC rather than RPLC — the paper's retention-order replicability analysis (and ROASMI) applies only to the RPLC system The two datasets being compared share too few compounds to form a meaningful paired retention sequence You need absolute RT prediction rather than retention-order replicability quantification Quantifies how similar two chromatographic configurations are (ChrSS) by correlating paired retention sequences via CCRS (correlation coefficient of retention sequences) and relating it to ΔpH, ΔF, and Δ column temperature, to identify which factor drives retention-order replicability in RPLC. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-025-00968-8
skills.summary: Quantifies how similar two chromatographic configurations are (ChrSS) by correlating paired retention sequences via CCRS (correlation coefficient of retention sequences) and relating it to ΔpH, ΔF, and Δ column temperature, to identify which factor drives retention-order replicability in RPLC.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Datasets are HILIC rather than RPLC — the paper's retention-order replicability analysis (and ROASMI) applies only to the RPLC system The two datasets being compared share too few compounds to form a meaningful paired retention sequence You need absolute RT prediction rather than retention-order replicability quantification

skills.when_to_use_negative: When the task is predicting absolute retention times for a single LC system with SVR and no cross-system generalization is intended (SVR cannot exploit data from other systems in the same way). Input is already a peak/feature table rather than raw profile-mode mzML — trace extraction requires raw spectra Data are not LC-IM-MS measurements (no retention-time or ion-mobility dimension) — the RT-dimension CentWave picking and arrival-time traces would not apply Goal is untargeted feature detection across all ions rather than targeted extraction of formulae-derived primary-ion traces http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Targeted extraction of primary-ion m/z traces from a parsed mzML file followed by retention-time CentWave peak picking, as implemented in CCSfind for LC-IM-MS data. skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a peak/feature table rather than raw profile-mode mzML — trace extraction requires raw spectra Data are not LC-IM-MS measurements (no retention-time or ion-mobility dimension) — the RT-dimension CentWave picking and arrival-time traces would not apply Goal is untargeted feature detection across all ions rather than targeted extraction of formulae-derived primary-ion traces

skills.description: Use when deciding whether fine-tuning a pre-trained ROASMI model with a specific reference dataset will yield substantial rank-score gains on a target prediction set, or when grouping retraining results by ChemSS/ChrSS similarity.
skills.name: chromatographic-transferability-assessment
skills.search_text: chromatographic-transferability-assessment Use when deciding whether fine-tuning a pre-trained ROASMI model with a specific reference dataset will yield substantial rank-score gains on a target prediction set, or when grouping retraining results by ChemSS/ChrSS similarity. The prediction set lies in a chemical space outside the elemental restrictions of C, H, N, O, P, S that ROASMI was built for, or in a non-RPLC chromatographic space (e.g., HILIC), since the initial model is limited to RPLC at eluent pH ≈ 2.7. Two compounds' chromatographic peaks are close enough that their retention order may not be consistent across experiments — such pairs should be excluded from identification rather than assessed for transferability. The goal is de novo RT prediction (retention-time regression) rather than retention-order ranking, since ROASMI predicts ordinal scores, not absolute RTs. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Assess whether a retrained ROASMI retention-order model transfers to a new dataset by quantifying rank-score improvements as a function of chemical-space similarity (ChemSS) and chromatographic-space similarity (ChrSS) between the retraining reference and prediction sets. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-025-00968-8
skills.summary: Assess whether a retrained ROASMI retention-order model transfers to a new dataset by quantifying rank-score improvements as a function of chemical-space similarity (ChemSS) and chromatographic-space similarity (ChrSS) between the retraining reference and prediction sets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The prediction set lies in a chemical space outside the elemental restrictions of C, H, N, O, P, S that ROASMI was built for, or in a non-RPLC chromatographic space (e.g., HILIC), since the initial model is limited to RPLC at eluent pH ≈ 2.7. Two compounds' chromatographic peaks are close enough that their retention order may not be consistent across experiments — such pairs should be excluded from identification rather than assessed for transferability. The goal is de novo RT prediction (retention-time regression) rather than retention-order ranking, since ROASMI predicts ordinal scores, not absolute RTs.

skills.description: Use when choosing a GC-MS ionization method or reagent gas for stable-isotope labeling metabolomics and you need to quantify which technique concentrates the [M+H]+ isotopic envelope with least fragmentation.
skills.name: ci-vs-ei-fragmentation-comparison
skills.search_text: ci-vs-ei-fragmentation-comparison Use when choosing a GC-MS ionization method or reagent gas for stable-isotope labeling metabolomics and you need to quantify which technique concentrates the [M+H]+ isotopic envelope with least fragmentation. Data are LC-MS/MS rather than GC-MS, where the CI-vs-EI trade-off and reagent-gas choice described here do not directly apply. The analytes are not derivatizable or are not central carbon metabolism intermediates whose [M+H]+ envelope can be resolved, since the comparison metric relies on that envelope. Only fragment ions (not molecular ions) are needed for targeted quantification, e.g., when using a QqQ in SIM/NS mode where EI fragmentation spectra are deliberately exploited. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0157 Systematic comparison of EI (70 eV and low-energy 15 eV) versus chemical ionization with different reagent gases (methane and isobutane) to identify which ionization source best preserves the protonated [M+H]+ isotopic envelope for detecting isotopologues in GC-MS stable-isotope labeling experiments. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c02998
skills.summary: Systematic comparison of EI (70 eV and low-energy 15 eV) versus chemical ionization with different reagent gases (methane and isobutane) to identify which ionization source best preserves the protonated [M+H]+ isotopic envelope for detecting isotopologues in GC-MS stable-isotope labeling experiments.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are LC-MS/MS rather than GC-MS, where the CI-vs-EI trade-off and reagent-gas choice described here do not directly apply. The analytes are not derivatizable or are not central carbon metabolism intermediates whose [M+H]+ envelope can be resolved, since the comparison metric relies on that envelope. Only fragment ions (not molecular ions) are needed for targeted quantification, e.g., when using a QqQ in SIM/NS mode where EI fragmentation spectra are deliberately exploited.

skills.description: Use when an optimized protonated molecular ion structure (xyz format) must be converted into a user-defined number of collision input files with varied collisional geometry before running CIDMD trajectories.
skills.name: cidmd-collider-trajectory-sampling
skills.search_text: cidmd-collider-trajectory-sampling Use when an optimized protonated molecular ion structure (xyz format) must be converted into a user-defined number of collision input files with varied collisional geometry before running CIDMD trajectories. The molecule has not yet been protonated and geometry-optimized at unrestricted B3LYP/6–31G* — the setup requires an optimized molecular ion xyz as input. skills.search_text: cis-eqtl-target-gene-extraction Use when you have sentinel/proxy variant rsIDs with GRCh37 coordinates and need to flag which local genes are cis-eQTL targets in GTEx tissues, as bottom-up evidence for causal gene prioritization at molecular QTLs. You need to prioritize causal genes at trans-pQTLs — the article notes the top-down/local strategy adopted here 'would call for a different top-down strategy', and cis-eQTL matching assumes the variant acts in cis on local genes You lack registered GTEx access or the GTEx v7 eQTL release — the pipeline depends on the eGene and significant SNP-gene permutation files and cannot substitute other eQTL formats without adaptation The goal is a standalone causal gene call from eQTL data alone — the article shows cis-eQTL targets give 3 false positives per true positive, so this signal must be intersected with positional and annotation evidence http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Parses GTEx v7 cis-eQTL eGene and significant SNP-gene association files to assign sentinel ('lead_eQTL') and proxy variant ('proxy_eQTL') target genes as bottom-up candidate causal genes within the ProGeM prioritization framework. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gky837
skills.summary: Parses GTEx v7 cis-eQTL eGene and significant SNP-gene association files to assign sentinel ('lead_eQTL') and proxy variant ('proxy_eQTL') target genes as bottom-up candidate causal genes within the ProGeM prioritization framework.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need to prioritize causal genes at trans-pQTLs — the article notes the top-down/local strategy adopted here 'would call for a different top-down strategy', and cis-eQTL matching assumes the variant acts in cis on local genes You lack registered GTEx access or the GTEx v7 eQTL release — the pipeline depends on the eGene and significant SNP-gene permutation files and cannot substitute other eQTL formats without adaptation The goal is a standalone causal gene call from eQTL data alone — the article shows cis-eQTL targets give 3 false positives per true positive, so this signal must be intersected with positional and annotation evidence
