skills.search_text: compound-identification-reliability-scoring Use when you have MS2 peak lists that need vetting before metabolite annotation/identification and you need a per-spectrum reliability verdict plus a numeric quality score. Input is already a metabolite annotation/identification result table and no per-spectrum MS2 peak lists are available. The data are MS1-only (no MS2 peak lists) — the service assesses quality of spectra for the MS2 spectral comparison workflow. The goal is filtering/scoring candidate query results by experimental setup and compound properties — that is CMM 2.0's expert-system filter step, not spectral quality assessment. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Assess the reliability of MS2 spectra for compound identification purposes using CMM 3.0's spectral quality-assessment service, exposed via its RESTful API, producing per-spectrum reliability verdicts and numeric quality scores. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.8b00720
skills.summary: Assess the reliability of MS2 spectra for compound identification purposes using CMM 3.0's spectral quality-assessment service, exposed via its RESTful API, producing per-spectrum reliability verdicts and numeric quality scores.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a metabolite annotation/identification result table and no per-spectrum MS2 peak lists are available. The data are MS1-only (no MS2 peak lists) — the service assesses quality of spectra for the MS2 spectral comparison workflow. The goal is filtering/scoring candidate query results by experimental setup and compound properties — that is CMM 2.0's expert-system filter step, not spectral quality assessment.

skills.description: Use when a user-supplied compound list uses heterogeneous names or synonyms and must be mapped to standardized cross-database identifiers (PubChem CID, InChIKey, KEGG, ChEBI, HMDB, DrugBank) before downstream analysis.
skills.name: compound-identifier-mapping
skills.search_text: compound-identifier-mapping Use when a user-supplied compound list uses heterogeneous names or synonyms and must be mapped to standardized cross-database identifiers (PubChem CID, InChIKey, KEGG, ChEBI, HMDB, DrugBank) before downstream analysis. The input is already a harmonized table keyed by InChIKey or PubChem CID with no naming ambiguity. The input is raw spectral data (e.g. mzML peak lists) rather than a list of compound names — identifier mapping is a post-annotation step in this workflow. Compounds lack PubChem/CTS representation and are expected to remain unmatched, making mapping uninformative. http://edamontology.org/topic_3315 Harmonizes compound names in a metabolomics dataset by resolving each name to standard cross-reference identifiers (PubChem CID, Molecular Formula, Molecular Weight, Canonical SMILES, InChIKey, KEGG, ChEBI, HMDB, DrugBank) using the R package webchem, as implemented in the Easy-Amanida workflow. This ensures unambiguous compound naming before meta-analysis of aggregate statistics. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/jrsm.1713
skills.summary: Harmonizes compound names in a metabolomics dataset by resolving each name to standard cross-reference identifiers (PubChem CID, Molecular Formula, Molecular Weight, Canonical SMILES, InChIKey, KEGG, ChEBI, HMDB, DrugBank) using the R package webchem, as implemented in the Easy-Amanida workflow. This ensures unambiguous compound naming before meta-analysis of aggregate statistics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a harmonized table keyed by InChIKey or PubChem CID with no naming ambiguity. The input is raw spectral data (e.g. mzML peak lists) rather than a list of compound names — identifier mapping is a post-annotation step in this workflow. Compounds lack PubChem/CTS representation and are expected to remain unmatched, making mapping uninformative.

skills.description: Use when an untargeted metabolomics dataset holds compound names that must be mapped to KEGG compound identifiers before ORA against KEGG release 96 human pathway sets.
skills.name: compound-identifier-mapping-to-kegg
skills.search_text: compound-identifier-mapping-to-kegg Use when an untargeted metabolomics dataset holds compound names that must be mapped to KEGG compound identifiers before ORA against KEGG release 96 human pathway sets. The dataset already uses KEGG identifiers natively — remapping through MetaboAnalyst would add conversion noise without benefit. The downstream pathway database is Reactome or BioCyc but only KEGG identifiers are needed — map to ChEBI/BioCyc identifiers instead of forcing KEGG IDs. The analysis goal is a comparison of pathway databases rather than KEGG-specific ORA — the identifier harmonisation step must span all three databases (KEGG, Reactome, BioCyc), not just KEGG. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_3391 Converts compound names from metabolomics abundance matrices to KEGG identifiers so they can be matched against KEGG pathway sets, using the MetaboAnalyst 4.0 ID conversion tool with the bioservices package for ChEBI harmonisation. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009105
skills.summary: Converts compound names from metabolomics abundance matrices to KEGG identifiers so they can be matched against KEGG pathway sets, using the MetaboAnalyst 4.0 ID conversion tool with the bioservices package for ChEBI harmonisation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset already uses KEGG identifiers natively — remapping through MetaboAnalyst would add conversion noise without benefit. The downstream pathway database is Reactome or BioCyc but only KEGG identifiers are needed — map to ChEBI/BioCyc identifiers instead of forcing KEGG IDs. The analysis goal is a comparison of pathway databases rather than KEGG-specific ORA — the identifier harmonisation step must span all three databases (KEGG, Reactome, BioCyc), not just KEGG.

skills.description: Use when a metabolite annotation search returns multiple compounds at one m/z — e.g. identically-named or same-formula hits — and you must decide whether rows represent distinct structures or merely the same molecular formula before ranking or exporting annotation tables.
skills.name: compound-identity-collision-handling-smiles-vs-formula
skills.search_text: compound-identity-collision-handling-smiles-vs-formula Use when a metabolite annotation search returns multiple compounds at one m/z — e.g. identically-named or same-formula hits — and you must decide whether rows represent distinct structures or merely the same molecular formula before ranking or exporting annotation tables. Raw peak data — MetaboShiny does not accept unprocessed spectra; preprocessing with XCMS or MSnbase must happen first. Only one compound database is needed and the user does not care about distinguishing isomeric structures — a simpler m/z lookup without SMILES collapse suffices. Data is not mass spectrometry metabolomics, or no compound database with SMILES fields is available. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 When database search returns multiple m/z matches that collapse into one row, MetaboShiny collapses only compounds sharing an identical SMILES into a single row, while compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures (different SMILES) are kept as separate rows. This means each retained row represents a unique chemical structure rather than a unique chemical formula, and isotope/adduct status is used to further prioritize between colliding identities. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-020-01717-8
skills.summary: When database search returns multiple m/z matches that collapse into one row, MetaboShiny collapses only compounds sharing an identical SMILES into a single row, while compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures (different SMILES) are kept as separate rows. This means each retained row represents a unique chemical structure rather than a unique chemical formula, and isotope/adduct status is used to further prioritize between colliding identities.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Raw peak data — MetaboShiny does not accept unprocessed spectra; preprocessing with XCMS or MSnbase must happen first. Only one compound database is needed and the user does not care about distinguishing isomeric structures — a simpler m/z lookup without SMILES collapse suffices. Data is not mass spectrometry metabolomics, or no compound database with SMILES fields is available.

skills.description: Use when a GC-MS library-hit table contains tentative Compound.Name entries with varying Match.Factor values and you must drop unreliable IDs (no strong cross-sample match, no PubChem record, or no canonical SMILES) before aggregating Component.Area across samples.
skills.name: compound-identity-decontamination
skills.search_text: compound-identity-decontamination Use when a GC-MS library-hit table contains tentative Compound.Name entries with varying Match.Factor values and you must drop unreliable IDs (no strong cross-sample match, no PubChem record, or no canonical SMILES) before aggregating Component.Area across samples. Input is already a validated, manually curated compound-area table where every ID has a PubChem CID and canonical SMILES — decontamination would add no value. Data are MS2, MS3, or ion mobility + MS2 spectra: uafR depends on published data and its algorithms 'do not yet apply' to these modes. You need to keep low-match-factor tentative IDs for exploratory review rather than quantitative aggregation — the strong-match and SMILES filters would silently discard them. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 A uafR filtering step (mzExacto with decontaminate = TRUE) that removes GC-MS tentative identifications lacking a strong cross-sample match, a PubChem entry, or a canonical SMILES, so only verifiable compounds are carried into area aggregation and quantification. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pone.0306202
skills.summary: A uafR filtering step (mzExacto with decontaminate = TRUE) that removes GC-MS tentative identifications lacking a strong cross-sample match, a PubChem entry, or a canonical SMILES, so only verifiable compounds are carried into area aggregation and quantification.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a validated, manually curated compound-area table where every ID has a PubChem CID and canonical SMILES — decontamination would add no value. Data are MS2, MS3, or ion mobility + MS2 spectra: uafR depends on published data and its algorithms 'do not yet apply' to these modes. You need to keep low-match-factor tentative IDs for exploratory review rather than quantitative aggregation — the strong-match and SMILES filters would silently discard them.

skills.description: Use when a batch of compounds must be formatted for FIORA spectral prediction (e.g. test compound lists for benchmarking against CFM-ID/ICEBERG, or augmenting spectral libraries) and an fiora-predict-compatible CSV is needed.
skills.name: compound-input-csv-preparation
skills.search_text: compound-input-csv-preparation Use when a batch of compounds must be formatted for FIORA spectral prediction (e.g. test compound lists for benchmarking against CFM-ID/ICEBERG, or augmenting spectral libraries) and an fiora-predict-compatible CSV is needed. Compounds with inconsistencies between SMILES, MOL format and InChiKeys — these are filtered out by FIORA's preprocessing and should be cleaned before inclusion Adducts outside the ionization types FIORA supports, e.g. multi-charge or exotic precursor types beyond [M+H]+, [M-H]- ([M]+/[M]- only for MSnLib-derived use) Spectra with missing collision energies or unclear formats, which were excluded in the paper's pipeline Prepare a CSV query file with the exact header columns 'Name', 'SMILES', 'Precursor_type', 'CE', 'Instrument_type' required by FIORA's fiora-predict CLI, so that tandem mass spectra (MS/MS), retention time (RT), and collision cross section (CCS) predictions can be run batch-wise on GPU or CPU. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-025-57422-4
skills.summary: Prepare a CSV query file with the exact header columns 'Name', 'SMILES', 'Precursor_type', 'CE', 'Instrument_type' required by FIORA's fiora-predict CLI, so that tandem mass spectra (MS/MS), retention time (RT), and collision cross section (CCS) predictions can be run batch-wise on GPU or CPU.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Compounds with inconsistencies between SMILES, MOL format and InChiKeys — these are filtered out by FIORA's preprocessing and should be cleaned before inclusion Adducts outside the ionization types FIORA supports, e.g. multi-charge or exotic precursor types beyond [M+H]+, [M-H]- ([M]+/[M]- only for MSnLib-derived use) Spectra with missing collision energies or unclear formats, which were excluded in the paper's pipeline

skills.description: Use when raw 13C-JRES spectra from 13C-labeled samples must be annotated using compound networks already identified from INADEQUATE spectra in preceding PyINETA steps.
skills.name: compound-label-transfer-between-nmr-experiments
skills.search_text: compound-label-transfer-between-nmr-experiments Use when raw 13C-JRES spectra from 13C-labeled samples must be annotated using compound networks already identified from INADEQUATE spectra in preceding PyINETA steps. Only 13C-JRES data is available with no INADEQUATE networks from prior PyINETA steps — there is no source of compound labels to transfer. JRES peaks already carry compound annotations from another source, making network-based transfer redundant. Samples cannot be 13C-labeled, since the INADEQUATE networks that supply the labels rely on 13C-13C connectivity. http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_3379 PyINETA's optional integration step transfers compound annotations from INADEQUATE peak networks onto peaks of the complementary 13C-JRES experiment, so structural identities established from 13C-13C connectivity also label J-resolved peaks. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c03966
skills.summary: PyINETA's optional integration step transfers compound annotations from INADEQUATE peak networks onto peaks of the complementary 13C-JRES experiment, so structural identities established from 13C-13C connectivity also label J-resolved peaks.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only 13C-JRES data is available with no INADEQUATE networks from prior PyINETA steps — there is no source of compound labels to transfer. JRES peaks already carry compound annotations from another source, making network-based transfer redundant. Samples cannot be 13C-labeled, since the INADEQUATE networks that supply the labels rely on 13C-13C connectivity.

skills.description: Use when a dataset contains multiple spectra (e.g., EI-MS and ESI-MS/MS from MassBank) per compound and a classifier such as Random Forest must be evaluated without compound-level spectral leakage.
skills.name: compound-level-data-split-stratification
skills.search_text: compound-level-data-split-stratification Use when a dataset contains multiple spectra (e.g., EI-MS and ESI-MS/MS from MassBank) per compound and a classifier such as Random Forest must be evaluated without compound-level spectral leakage. Each row in the dataset is an independent compound with exactly one spectrum, so no compound-level grouping is needed The goal is external validation on spectra from new publications or laboratory measurements rather than an internal test estimate The task is prediction on individual EI-MS-only or ESI-MS/MS-only sets, which the article reports gave poor results compared with the combined set Partition mass-spectral training data so that all spectra of the same compound stay within a single fold, using an 80/20 compound-level train/test split repeated 20 times. This prevents spectra from one compound leaking into both train and test partitions, which would inflate classifier performance. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jafc.3c09767
skills.summary: Partition mass-spectral training data so that all spectra of the same compound stay within a single fold, using an 80/20 compound-level train/test split repeated 20 times. This prevents spectra from one compound leaking into both train and test partitions, which would inflate classifier performance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Each row in the dataset is an independent compound with exactly one spectrum, so no compound-level grouping is needed The goal is external validation on spectra from new publications or laboratory measurements rather than an internal test estimate The task is prediction on individual EI-MS-only or ESI-MS/MS-only sets, which the article reports gave poor results compared with the combined set

skills.description: Use when input metabolomics studies report only the compound identifier and a trend label (up-regulated/down-regulated/no trend) rather than p-values, fold-changes, or variance, and a cross-study qualitative meta-analysis per compound is needed.
skills.name: compound-level-vote-aggregation-across-studies
skills.search_text: compound-level-vote-aggregation-across-studies Use when input metabolomics studies report only the compound identifier and a trend label (up-regulated/down-regulated/no trend) rather than p-values, fold-changes, or variance, and a cross-study qualitative meta-analysis per compound is needed. Studies disclose p-values and fold-changes (with N): then compute_amanida's weighted meta-analysis (mode = "quan", Fisher's method for p-values, weighted log fold-change averaging) is the appropriate quantitative route instead of vote-counting. The input requires directional effect sizes or statistical significance measures rather than a rankable qualitative trend — vote-counting yields only summed votes and report counts, no p-value or confidence interval. Identifiers are uncurated compound names without running check_names first when comp.inf = T is desired — the package requires the prior use of check_names before PubChem-based duplicate checking. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Qualitative meta-analysis via vote-counting: each study's trend for a compound is scored (+1 up-regulation, -1 down-regulation, 0 no trend) and votes are summed per compound, with the number of contributing articles recorded. This lets compounds be ranked across studies even when only identifier and trend labels are disclosed. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btab591
skills.summary: Qualitative meta-analysis via vote-counting: each study's trend for a compound is scored (+1 up-regulation, -1 down-regulation, 0 no trend) and votes are summed per compound, with the number of contributing articles recorded. This lets compounds be ranked across studies even when only identifier and trend labels are disclosed.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Studies disclose p-values and fold-changes (with N): then compute_amanida's weighted meta-analysis (mode = "quan", Fisher's method for p-values, weighted log fold-change averaging) is the appropriate quantitative route instead of vote-counting. The input requires directional effect sizes or statistical significance measures rather than a rankable qualitative trend — vote-counting yields only summed votes and report counts, no p-value or confidence interval. Identifiers are uncurated compound names without running check_names first when comp.inf = T is desired — the package requires the prior use of check_names before PubChem-based duplicate checking.

skills.search_text: compound-mass-window-filtering Use when retrieving candidate molecules from a large chemical database (e.g. PubChem) by precursor m/z and you need to quantify or exploit how a high-accuracy ppm mass window narrows the candidate list. skills.search_text: compound-match-ppm-error-prioritization Use when you have a short list of statistically significant m/z values (e.g. t-test hits at 264, 308, 441, 561 m/z) and must rank candidate compound matches from a built database such as HMDB by isotope/adduct status and ppm error. skills.name: compound-metadata-template-parsing
skills.search_text: compound-metadata-template-parsing Use when a batch list of compounds must be imported into a PeakForest database from the supplementary compound-import template (Online Resource 2), where common name, InChI and InChIKey are mandatory per row. Input is raw spectral data (mzML/NMR FID) rather than a compound metadata template — PeakForest stores metadata related to raw data rather than raw data itself Compounds come from automatic extraction/clean-up of uncleaned data — PeakForest does not include data clean-up or extraction tools and requires users to supply completely-cleaned data following SOPs Only one or two compounds need adding — the manual import/curation interface in the PeakForest webapp is simpler than building a batch parsing module http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Parses a structured compound-import template (XLSX) and maps each row to the chemical compound entity of the PeakForest data model, validating mandatory fields (common name, InChI, InChIKey) and emitting structured compound records for database ingestion. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-022-01899-3
skills.summary: Parses a structured compound-import template (XLSX) and maps each row to the chemical compound entity of the PeakForest data model, validating mandatory fields (common name, InChI, InChIKey) and emitting structured compound records for database ingestion.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw spectral data (mzML/NMR FID) rather than a compound metadata template — PeakForest stores metadata related to raw data rather than raw data itself Compounds come from automatic extraction/clean-up of uncleaned data — PeakForest does not include data clean-up or extraction tools and requires users to supply completely-cleaned data following SOPs Only one or two compounds need adding — the manual import/curation interface in the PeakForest webapp is simpler than building a batch parsing module

skills.description: Use when preparing starting-compound sets (e.g. KEGG, EcoCyc, YMDB SMILES/CSV) for a Pickaxe/MINE-Database expansion and you need to constrain network size by compound molecular weight before rule application.
skills.name: compound-molecular-weight-filtering
skills.search_text: compound-molecular-weight-filtering Use when preparing starting-compound sets (e.g. KEGG, EcoCyc, YMDB SMILES/CSV) for a Pickaxe/MINE-Database expansion and you need to constrain network size by compound molecular weight before rule application. You need to control network size around specific target compounds rather than by bulk compound size — use the similarity cutoff or similarity sampling filter (e.g. sampling 2000 compounds from similarity-score distributions) instead The starting compounds are already restricted (e.g. the fig3 exponential-growth script uses a memory/MW cutoff below 300) and re-filtering would double-prune and bias the benchmark You want to filter generated reactions by thermodynamic feasibility (physiological ΔG > 50 kJ/mol via eQuilibrator) — that is a reaction-level filter, not a compound property filter http://edamontology.org/topic_3316 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Prunes a Pickaxe expansion network by retaining only compounds within a specified molecular-weight range (e.g. < 600 g/mol), applied on-the-fly before each rule-application generation so exponential compound growth is curtailed. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-023-05149-8
skills.summary: Prunes a Pickaxe expansion network by retaining only compounds within a specified molecular-weight range (e.g. < 600 g/mol), applied on-the-fly before each rule-application generation so exponential compound growth is curtailed.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need to control network size around specific target compounds rather than by bulk compound size — use the similarity cutoff or similarity sampling filter (e.g. sampling 2000 compounds from similarity-score distributions) instead The starting compounds are already restricted (e.g. the fig3 exponential-growth script uses a memory/MW cutoff below 300) and re-filtering would double-prune and bias the benchmark You want to filter generated reactions by thermodynamic feasibility (physiological ΔG > 50 kJ/mol via eQuilibrator) — that is a reaction-level filter, not a compound property filter

skills.description: Use when a mass spectral library (e.g. the GNPS ALL_GNPS.json file, 154,820 spectra) contains spectra lacking InChIKey annotations and you need structural identifiers for downstream structure-based analyses.
skills.name: compound-name-formula-mass-identifier-linking
skills.search_text: compound-name-formula-mass-identifier-linking Use when a mass spectral library (e.g. the GNPS ALL_GNPS.json file, 154,820 spectra) contains spectra lacking InChIKey annotations and you need structural identifiers for downstream structure-based analyses. When spectra already carry reliable InChIKey annotations (the article's cleaned dataset had 94,121 spectra with InChIKey annotations before the PubChem search) — re-running lookups adds cost without benefit. When the goal is spectral similarity scoring or model training (Spec2Vec embeddings, cosine scores) rather than structural annotation of library entries. When an alternative curated annotated library is already available, e.g. the Zenodo preprocessing outcome under doi 10.5281/zenodo.3979010. http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Cleans GNPS MS/MS library metadata with matchms and then runs an extensive automated PubChem lookup (via pubchempy) by compound name, molecular formula, and parent mass to attach InChIKeys to spectra that initially lack structural annotations, enabling structure-based analyses such as Tanimoto similarity assessment. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008724
skills.summary: Cleans GNPS MS/MS library metadata with matchms and then runs an extensive automated PubChem lookup (via pubchempy) by compound name, molecular formula, and parent mass to attach InChIKeys to spectra that initially lack structural annotations, enabling structure-based analyses such as Tanimoto similarity assessment.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When spectra already carry reliable InChIKey annotations (the article's cleaned dataset had 94,121 spectra with InChIKey annotations before the PubChem search) — re-running lookups adds cost without benefit. When the goal is spectral similarity scoring or model training (Spec2Vec embeddings, cosine scores) rather than structural annotation of library entries. When an alternative curated annotated library is already available, e.g. the Zenodo preprocessing outcome under doi 10.5281/zenodo.3979010.

skills.description: Use when a metabolomics meta-analysis input table contains mixed identifier types or compound synonyms across contributing studies, causing the same compound to appear as multiple rows with split vote counts.
skills.name: compound-name-harmonization
skills.search_text: compound-name-harmonization Use when a metabolomics meta-analysis input table contains mixed identifier types or compound synonyms across contributing studies, causing the same compound to appear as multiple rows with split vote counts. The input identifier list already uses a single, consistent identifier type with no synonyms — harmonization would be a no-op. You have raw individual-level data rather than disclosed aggregate statistics (p-value, fold-change); the amanida pipeline is designed for aggregate-statistics meta-analysis. The task does not require cross-study grouping of compounds (e.g. a single-study analysis where naming harmonization adds no value). http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Harmonizes heterogeneous compound identifiers (common names, synonyms, InChIKeys, SMILES) into a common chemical nomenclature before aggregate-statistics meta-analysis, using the webchem-backed naming combination workflow of the Easy-Amanida Shiny app. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/jrsm.1713
skills.summary: Harmonizes heterogeneous compound identifiers (common names, synonyms, InChIKeys, SMILES) into a common chemical nomenclature before aggregate-statistics meta-analysis, using the webchem-backed naming combination workflow of the Easy-Amanida Shiny app.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input identifier list already uses a single, consistent identifier type with no synonyms — harmonization would be a no-op. You have raw individual-level data rather than disclosed aggregate statistics (p-value, fold-change); the amanida pipeline is designed for aggregate-statistics meta-analysis. The task does not require cross-study grouping of compounds (e.g. a single-study analysis where naming harmonization adds no value).

skills.description: Use when benchmarking TurboPutative's end-to-end processing time against input table size, or when synthetic compound-name/mass tables in TurboPutative's input format are needed to probe runtime scaling in the 500–30,000-row range.
skills.name: compound-name-mass-synthetic-data-generation
skills.search_text: compound-name-mass-synthetic-data-generation Use when benchmarking TurboPutative's end-to-end processing time against input table size, or when synthetic compound-name/mass tables in TurboPutative's input format are needed to probe runtime scaling in the 500–30,000-row range. Input is a real untargeted metabolomics annotation dataset with existing putative annotations and feature intensities — the TPMetrics scoring/80-90% entry-reduction workflow, not a synthetic benchmark, is the target. The goal is annotation curation (Tagger classification, REname isomer/equivalent recognition, RowMerger redundancy removal) rather than runtime benchmarking. The tool under test is not TurboPutative and its input format differs from the TurboPutative web-service table schema. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Builds synthetic TSV benchmark tables of compound-name/mass rows in TurboPutative's accepted input format (500 and 30,000 rows) and times end-to-end submission through the TurboPutative RESTful API services to characterize runtime scaling. metabolomics/v3 10.3389/fmolb.2022.952149
skills.summary: Builds synthetic TSV benchmark tables of compound-name/mass rows in TurboPutative's accepted input format (500 and 30,000 rows) and times end-to-end submission through the TurboPutative RESTful API services to characterize runtime scaling.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a real untargeted metabolomics annotation dataset with existing putative annotations and feature intensities — the TPMetrics scoring/80-90% entry-reduction workflow, not a synthetic benchmark, is the target. The goal is annotation curation (Tagger classification, REname isomer/equivalent recognition, RowMerger redundancy removal) rather than runtime benchmarking. The tool under test is not TurboPutative and its input format differs from the TurboPutative web-service table schema.

skills.description: Use when library spectra carry only a compound name (no SMILES/InChI) and machine-readable structures must be recovered, e.g. many GNPS-library annotations are compound names without SMILES.
skills.name: compound-name-to-smiles-derivation
skills.search_text: compound-name-to-smiles-derivation Use when library spectra carry only a compound name (no SMILES/InChI) and machine-readable structures must be recovered, e.g. many GNPS-library annotations are compound names without SMILES. Annotations already carry a valid SMILES/InChI — the filter targets spectra that are only compound names without SMILES The compound name is absent, ambiguous, or the parent mass is unreliable; the PubChem lookup will not be able to confirm the correct structure via the mass-match check You need to verify fragments match the annotation — the article notes fragment-matching filters are only a possible future expansion, so this skill cannot detect mass-consistent but structurally wrong annotations http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 Derives canonical SMILES, InChI and InChIKey from compound-name-only annotations in mass spectral libraries via PubChem lookup, accepting only structures whose PubChem mass matches the spectrum's parent mass — a matchms library-cleaning filter for annotating otherwise unannotated spectra. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00878-1
skills.summary: Derives canonical SMILES, InChI and InChIKey from compound-name-only annotations in mass spectral libraries via PubChem lookup, accepting only structures whose PubChem mass matches the spectrum's parent mass — a matchms library-cleaning filter for annotating otherwise unannotated spectra.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Annotations already carry a valid SMILES/InChI — the filter targets spectra that are only compound names without SMILES The compound name is absent, ambiguous, or the parent mass is unreliable; the PubChem lookup will not be able to confirm the correct structure via the mass-match check You need to verify fragments match the annotation — the article notes fragment-matching filters are only a possible future expansion, so this skill cannot detect mass-consistent but structurally wrong annotations

skills.description: Use when evaluating a spectral-prediction model on an external public library (e.g., MoNA Q-TOF) while the model was trained on licensed libraries (Agilent PCDL/NIST20) and train/test overlap must be eliminated.
skills.name: compound-overlap-exclusion-across-spectral-libraries
skills.search_text: compound-overlap-exclusion-across-spectral-libraries Use when evaluating a spectral-prediction model on an external public library (e.g., MoNA Q-TOF) while the model was trained on licensed libraries (Agilent PCDL/NIST20) and train/test overlap must be eliminated. When the model was trained only on public data that is already disjoint from the evaluation library, so no overlap exclusion is needed When the goal is training-data curation rather than building a leakage-free external evaluation set When input structures lack InChIKeys or fall outside the model's supported atom types (C, O, N, H, P, S, F, Cl, B, Br, I) or precursor types http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Removes compounds from a public MS/MS evaluation set (e.g., the MoNA Q-TOF subset) that overlap licensed spectral libraries (Agilent PCDL/NIST20), so held-out test spectra are guaranteed disjoint from training data when measuring cross-instrument generalization. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad354
skills.summary: Removes compounds from a public MS/MS evaluation set (e.g., the MoNA Q-TOF subset) that overlap licensed spectral libraries (Agilent PCDL/NIST20), so held-out test spectra are guaranteed disjoint from training data when measuring cross-instrument generalization.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the model was trained only on public data that is already disjoint from the evaluation library, so no overlap exclusion is needed When the goal is training-data curation rather than building a leakage-free external evaluation set When input structures lack InChIKeys or fall outside the model's supported atom types (C, O, N, H, P, S, F, Cl, B, Br, I) or precursor types

skills.description: Use when building ORA inputs for metabolomics: after harmonising metabolite identifiers to KEGG, Reactome (ChEBI), or BioCyc identifiers, before running the right-tailed Fisher's exact test per pathway.
skills.name: compound-pathway-size-filtering
skills.search_text: compound-pathway-size-filtering Use when building ORA inputs for metabolomics: after harmonising metabolite identifiers to KEGG, Reactome (ChEBI), or BioCyc identifiers, before running the right-tailed Fisher's exact test per pathway. Metabolite identifiers have not yet been harmonised to the target pathway database identifiers (KEGG, ChEBI/Reactome, BioCyc), since the size filter presupposes compound-only pathway sets. The goal is an extensive functional comparison of pathway databases themselves, which the authors explicitly state is beyond the scope of this paper. The pathway p-value would be computed for a pathway with 0 overlapping differentially abundant metabolites (k = 0); here the rule is to return 1/NA instead of testing. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Filters the metabolite pathway collection to compound-only pathways containing at least 3 compounds before over-representation analysis, so that Fisher's exact 2x2 contingency tables remain well-posed and trivially small pathways cannot be declared significantly enriched. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009105
skills.summary: Filters the metabolite pathway collection to compound-only pathways containing at least 3 compounds before over-representation analysis, so that Fisher's exact 2x2 contingency tables remain well-posed and trivially small pathways cannot be declared significantly enriched.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Metabolite identifiers have not yet been harmonised to the target pathway database identifiers (KEGG, ChEBI/Reactome, BioCyc), since the size filter presupposes compound-only pathway sets. The goal is an extensive functional comparison of pathway databases themselves, which the authors explicitly state is beyond the scope of this paper. The pathway p-value would be computed for a pathway with 0 overlapping differentially abundant metabolites (k = 0); here the rule is to return 1/NA instead of testing.

skills.description: Use when you have mzML/mzXML/mzData files from untargeted MS-based metabolomics and a list of m/z and RT pairs (e.g. from a long-term QC pool like MetNexs) and need to track compound peaks across batches to expose RT or intensity drift.
skills.name: compound-peak-tracking
skills.search_text: compound-peak-tracking Use when you have mzML/mzXML/mzData files from untargeted MS-based metabolomics and a list of m/z and RT pairs (e.g. from a long-term QC pool like MetNexs) and need to track compound peaks across batches to expose RT or intensity drift. When the goal is postacquisition intensity-drift correction rather than peak tracking/detection — use QC-MXP's tools for correcting intensity drifts instead. When you have no user-defined m/z and RT pairs for the compounds of interest — module_TrackCmp requires such a list; it is not an untargeted feature-finder. When the input is still vendor raw data that has not been converted to mzML/mzXML/mzData — convert first via the ProteoWizard converter. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0219 Detects and tracks chromatographic peaks for user-defined compounds across acquired files by matching against a user-defined list of m/z and retention time (RT) pairs, extracting observed m/z, retention time, intensity, and peak shape to monitor quality in untargeted MS-based metabolomics runs. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c07078
skills.summary: Detects and tracks chromatographic peaks for user-defined compounds across acquired files by matching against a user-defined list of m/z and retention time (RT) pairs, extracting observed m/z, retention time, intensity, and peak shape to monitor quality in untargeted MS-based metabolomics runs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is postacquisition intensity-drift correction rather than peak tracking/detection — use QC-MXP's tools for correcting intensity drifts instead. When you have no user-defined m/z and RT pairs for the compounds of interest — module_TrackCmp requires such a list; it is not an untargeted feature-finder. When the input is still vendor raw data that has not been converted to mzML/mzXML/mzData — convert first via the ProteoWizard converter.

skills.description: Use when handling multiple ESI-MS2 MassBank records of the same compound measured at different collision energies and you need to partition records into per-compound, per-instrument-class groups before spectrum merging.
skills.name: compound-record-grouping-by-instrument-class
skills.search_text: compound-record-grouping-by-instrument-class Use when handling multiple ESI-MS2 MassBank records of the same compound measured at different collision energies and you need to partition records into per-compound, per-instrument-class groups before spectrum merging. Records are EI-MS or FAB-MS data rather than ESI-MS2 measured under multiple CID collision energies Each compound already has a single merged mass spectrum, so no per-energy grouping is needed http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Groups parsed MassBank ESI-MS2 record files by compound identity and instrument class (QqQ vs QqTOF) so that all CID collision-energy scans (10-50 V) of one compound fall into one group, enabling construction of artificially merged reference spectra per compound and instrument class. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/jms.1777
skills.summary: Groups parsed MassBank ESI-MS2 record files by compound identity and instrument class (QqQ vs QqTOF) so that all CID collision-energy scans (10-50 V) of one compound fall into one group, enabling construction of artificially merged reference spectra per compound and instrument class.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Records are EI-MS or FAB-MS data rather than ESI-MS2 measured under multiple CID collision energies Each compound already has a single merged mass spectrum, so no per-energy grouping is needed

skills.description: Use when multiple OMSL files (e.g., GNPS .MGF, MoNA .MSP, MassBank, MS-Dial-VS17) have been integrated or are being compared and you need the fraction of compounds covered by more than one library versus single-library exclusives.
skills.name: compound-redundancy-quantification
skills.search_text: compound-redundancy-quantification Use when multiple OMSL files (e.g., GNPS .MGF, MoNA .MSP, MassBank, MS-Dial-VS17) have been integrated or are being compared and you need the fraction of compounds covered by more than one library versus single-library exclusives. You need spectral-level deduplication rather than compound-level overlap — FragHub's SPLASH-key-based 'update.json' repository is the mechanism for keeping only new spectra, not this compound-membership analysis The libraries have not been harmonized to consistent chemical identifiers; raw SMILES/InChI fields across sources are not directly comparable without RDKit standardization as done in FragHub The goal is annotating unknown spectra rather than characterizing library overlap/redundancy http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Quantifies how many unique chemical identifiers (harmonized InChIKeys) across integrated open mass spectral libraries (OMSLs) are shared between two or more libraries versus exclusive to one, exposing cross-library redundancy before or after FragHub integration. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c02219
skills.summary: Quantifies how many unique chemical identifiers (harmonized InChIKeys) across integrated open mass spectral libraries (OMSLs) are shared between two or more libraries versus exclusive to one, exposing cross-library redundancy before or after FragHub integration.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need spectral-level deduplication rather than compound-level overlap — FragHub's SPLASH-key-based 'update.json' repository is the mechanism for keeping only new spectra, not this compound-membership analysis The libraries have not been harmonized to consistent chemical identifiers; raw SMILES/InChI fields across sources are not directly comparable without RDKit standardization as done in FragHub The goal is annotating unknown spectra rather than characterizing library overlap/redundancy

skills.description: Use when comparing C2MS spectrum-prediction models (e.g. FraGNNet-D4, ICEBERG, MassFormer, NEIMS) on a held-out MS/MS test set and you need retrieval-based compound identification accuracy rather than raw prediction error.
skills.name: compound-retrieval-benchmark-evaluation
skills.search_text: compound-retrieval-benchmark-evaluation Use when comparing C2MS spectrum-prediction models (e.g. FraGNNet-D4, ICEBERG, MassFormer, NEIMS) on a held-out MS/MS test set and you need retrieval-based compound identification accuracy rather than raw prediction error. You are evaluating formula annotation performance as a classification problem rather than full-spectrum retrieval ranking Your unknown spectra come from instruments/adducts outside the paper's scope (the paper flags that performance is not yet established for unmerged spectra, other instrument platforms, or precursor adducts beyond [M+H]+) You only need C2MS prediction error on real spectra without the compound-identification retrieval framing http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Evaluates compound-to-spectrum (C2MS) models on a retrieval-based MS2C task by ranking candidate compounds against an unknown MS/MS spectrum and reporting Top-k accuracy. It quantifies whether predicted spectra improve compound identification over spectral libraries alone. metabolomics/v3 10.48550/arxiv.2404.02360
skills.summary: Evaluates compound-to-spectrum (C2MS) models on a retrieval-based MS2C task by ranking candidate compounds against an unknown MS/MS spectrum and reporting Top-k accuracy. It quantifies whether predicted spectra improve compound identification over spectral libraries alone.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You are evaluating formula annotation performance as a classification problem rather than full-spectrum retrieval ranking Your unknown spectra come from instruments/adducts outside the paper's scope (the paper flags that performance is not yet established for unmerged spectra, other instrument platforms, or precursor adducts beyond [M+H]+) You only need C2MS prediction error on real spectra without the compound-identification retrieval framing

skills.description: Use when a peak (precursor m/z, RT, MS/MS spectrum) must be scored against candidate metabolite annotations, e.g. reproducing reported annotation scores like the sinapate example at m/z 385.1118, RT 1.27 min in negative mode.
skills.name: compound-score-integration
skills.search_text: compound-score-integration Use when a peak (precursor m/z, RT, MS/MS spectrum) must be scored against candidate metabolite annotations, e.g. reproducing reported annotation scores like the sinapate example at m/z 385.1118, RT 1.27 min in negative mode. The task is raw data processing (peak detection, alignment) rather than scoring already-listed candidate metabolite annotations against a peak. The input peak lacks MS/MS fragments or a retention time, so the component scores required by Equation (3) cannot be computed. The metabolite of interest is outside the tool's plant-specific metabolite database, so no candidate annotations can be retrieved at the 25 ppm precursor cutoff. Computes PlantMetSuite's integrated metabolite annotation score (Equation (3)) by combining an MS/MS fragment-match score, a retention-time score, and additional criteria with user-defined weights into a single final score per candidate metabolite. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/plants12152880
skills.summary: Computes PlantMetSuite's integrated metabolite annotation score (Equation (3)) by combining an MS/MS fragment-match score, a retention-time score, and additional criteria with user-defined weights into a single final score per candidate metabolite.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is raw data processing (peak detection, alignment) rather than scoring already-listed candidate metabolite annotations against a peak. The input peak lacks MS/MS fragments or a retention time, so the component scores required by Equation (3) cannot be computed. The metabolite of interest is outside the tool's plant-specific metabolite database, so no candidate annotations can be retrieved at the 25 ppm precursor cutoff.

skills.description: Use when a laboratory needs to ingest LC-MS/MS (or NMR) spectra with their metadata into a local PeakForest database via the prefilled spreadsheet import template, associating each spectrum with a compound and a biological matrix such as human urine.
skills.name: compound-spectra-data-model-mapping
skills.search_text: compound-spectra-data-model-mapping Use when a laboratory needs to ingest LC-MS/MS (or NMR) spectra with their metadata into a local PeakForest database via the prefilled spreadsheet import template, associating each spectrum with a compound and a biological matrix such as human urine. The input is raw spectral data (mzML/netCDF etc.) needing peak detection or clean-up — PeakForest does not include data clean-up or extraction tools and expects completely-cleaned data The goal is large-scale public-repository deposition with automated curation — the curation feature requires centralized, highly-reactive error detection and is 'less easy to deploy in larger-scale public repositories' Only a handful of compounds/spectra exist — a minimum number of compounds and spectra must be imported before a local PeakForest database is fully functional http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 Maps columns of a PeakForest LC-MS/MS Excel-like import template (e.g. the SI urine-matrix template from Online Resources 3–6) onto the PeakForest data-model entities — chemical compounds and spectra — including sample-type/biological-matrix qualifiers, producing clean JSON records compatible with the PeakForest database and Web services. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-022-01899-3
skills.summary: Maps columns of a PeakForest LC-MS/MS Excel-like import template (e.g. the SI urine-matrix template from Online Resources 3–6) onto the PeakForest data-model entities — chemical compounds and spectra — including sample-type/biological-matrix qualifiers, producing clean JSON records compatible with the PeakForest database and Web services.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw spectral data (mzML/netCDF etc.) needing peak detection or clean-up — PeakForest does not include data clean-up or extraction tools and expects completely-cleaned data The goal is large-scale public-repository deposition with automated curation — the curation feature requires centralized, highly-reactive error detection and is 'less easy to deploy in larger-scale public repositories' Only a handful of compounds/spectra exist — a minimum number of compounds and spectra must be imported before a local PeakForest database is fully functional

skills.description: Use when an XCMS feature table from LC/MS or UPLC/ESI-QTOFMS data must be grouped into compound spectra, deisotoped, and annotated with ion species before downstream screens such as stable-isotope label difference searches.
skills.name: compound-spectra-deisotoping-annotation
skills.search_text: compound-spectra-deisotoping-annotation Use when an XCMS feature table from LC/MS or UPLC/ESI-QTOFMS data must be grouped into compound spectra, deisotoped, and annotated with ion species before downstream screens such as stable-isotope label difference searches. Input is already a fully annotated feature table with no ungrouped redundant features — grouping/deisotoping adds little value. Acquisitions lacking chromatographic separation or with saturated MS detector signals, which shift m/z and retention time centroids and truncate peak profiles. Single-polarity datasets when the goal specifically requires cross-polarity annotation verification via combinexsAnnos. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Group LC/MS features into CAMERA compound spectra, deisotope and annotate adducts/fragments with accurate-mass proposals, optionally validating across opposite ionization modes. Reduces feature-list redundancy in untargeted metabolomics so downstream screening (e.g. label-difference feature pairs) operates on annotated, non-isotopic compounds. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/ac202450g
skills.summary: Group LC/MS features into CAMERA compound spectra, deisotope and annotate adducts/fragments with accurate-mass proposals, optionally validating across opposite ionization modes. Reduces feature-list redundancy in untargeted metabolomics so downstream screening (e.g. label-difference feature pairs) operates on annotated, non-isotopic compounds.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a fully annotated feature table with no ungrouped redundant features — grouping/deisotoping adds little value. Acquisitions lacking chromatographic separation or with saturated MS detector signals, which shift m/z and retention time centroids and truncate peak profiles. Single-polarity datasets when the goal specifically requires cross-polarity annotation verification via combinexsAnnos.

skills.description: Use when computing detected vs. correctly annotated compound rates by matching tool-reported identifications against a known standards list via exact InChIKey plus RT (<20 s) and mass (5 ppm) criteria.
skills.name: compound-standards-matching-inchikey
skills.search_text: compound-standards-matching-inchikey Use when computing detected vs. correctly annotated compound rates by matching tool-reported identifications against a known standards list via exact InChIKey plus RT (<20 s) and mass (5 ppm) criteria. The dataset has no curated standards list with InChIKeys and reference RTs (e.g., untargeted discovery samples) — correctness cannot be scored The input is already a validated feature/annotation table with confirmed identities, so re-matching would double-count The spectra are SWATH-DIA rather than DDA ESI+ standards-mixture data, where deconvolution and the benchmark thresholds (20 s RT, 5 ppm) were established http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Validates compound identifications from competing LC-MS/MS annotation pipelines (MetaboAnalystR 4.0 with/without DDA deconvolution, MS-DIAL/MS-FINDER, MZmine/SIRIUS) by exact InChIKey matching against a curated 526-compound standards list, applying retention-time deviation (<20 s) and mass tolerance (5 ppm) filters to compute correct-annotation rates. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-48009-6
skills.summary: Validates compound identifications from competing LC-MS/MS annotation pipelines (MetaboAnalystR 4.0 with/without DDA deconvolution, MS-DIAL/MS-FINDER, MZmine/SIRIUS) by exact InChIKey matching against a curated 526-compound standards list, applying retention-time deviation (<20 s) and mass tolerance (5 ppm) filters to compute correct-annotation rates.

skills.search_text: compound-structure-standardization Use when a metadata sheet of small-molecule samples needs a shared template structure with same column names, standardized structures, and unique sample ids before spectral-library or acquisition work. The metadata sheet already follows the shared template with standardized structures and populated SMILES/InChI/InChIKey fields — re-running cleanup only duplicates work. skills.summary: Harmonizes metadata sheets of compound libraries by running structures through the ChEMBL structure pipeline for salt stripping and canonicalization, then computes RDKit/ChEMBL descriptors (canonical/isomeric SMILES, InChI, InChIKey, logP, monoisotopic mass) and back-fills missing structures from PubChem name search.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The metadata sheet already follows the shared template with standardized structures and populated SMILES/InChI/InChIKey fields — re-running cleanup only duplicates work. skills.description: Decision support for choosing a mass-spectrometry storage format when you need to compare file sizes (and optionally decode cost) of a lossy-precision format like Aird against lossless reference formats (mzML, mgf, mz5) and the original vendor RAW across multiple public datasets.
skills.name: compression-file-size-benchmark-tabulation
skills.search_text: compression-file-size-benchmark-tabulation Decision support for choosing a mass-spectrometry storage format when you need to compare file sizes (and optionally decode cost) of a lossy-precision format like Aird against lossless reference formats (mzML, mgf, mz5) and the original vendor RAW across multiple public datasets. When the goal is to measure decoding/encoding time (3× faster ZDPD claim) or m/z-compression performance of ZDPD alone (49% size reduction vs Zlib) — that needs the compression benchmark skill, not this size-table one. When the input is already a converted (mzML/mgf/mz5/aird) file with no vendor RAW counterpart, since the table's baseline is the RAW size per dataset. skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is to measure decoding/encoding time (3× faster ZDPD claim) or m/z-compression performance of ZDPD alone (49% size reduction vs Zlib) — that needs the compression benchmark skill, not this size-table one. skills.name: compression-ratio-benchmarking
skills.search_text: compression-ratio-benchmarking Use when converting vendor MRM chromatograms to a compressed format (e.g., Aird) and you must quantify storage savings versus vendor and mzML files, or when implementing RT delta + FastPFor + ZSTD encoding. Data are ion mobility or DIA/SWATH spectra rather than MRM chromatograms — the RT-delta chromatogram scheme targets MRM acquisition mode You need lossless raw retention times: RTs are quantized at 1e-5 precision, so finer-resolution RT information is not preserved The goal is faster search-time decoding of m/z arrays (use Aird-Slice/ZDPD-style m/z compression instead of the chromatogram RT pipeline) http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Benchmark the size of encoded mass-spectrometry chromatogram containers against vendor and mzML baselines by delta-quantizing retention times (precision 1e-5), FastPFor-encoding the RT deltas, ZSTD-compressing the result, and reporting vendor/Aird and mzML/Aird size ratios (MRMPro reports >60% and >80% reduction respectively). metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-024-05685-x
skills.summary: Benchmark the size of encoded mass-spectrometry chromatogram containers against vendor and mzML baselines by delta-quantizing retention times (precision 1e-5), FastPFor-encoding the RT deltas, ZSTD-compressing the result, and reporting vendor/Aird and mzML/Aird size ratios (MRMPro reports >60% and >80% reduction respectively).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are ion mobility or DIA/SWATH spectra rather than MRM chromatograms — the RT-delta chromatogram scheme targets MRM acquisition mode You need lossless raw retention times: RTs are quantized at 1e-5 precision, so finer-resolution RT information is not preserved The goal is faster search-time decoding of m/z arrays (use Aird-Slice/ZDPD-style m/z compression instead of the chromatogram RT pipeline)

skills.description: Use when a paper reports a concrete computational throughput or runtime figure (e.g. 60,000 transition pairs/sec) and you must reproduce or sanity-check that number on available hardware before trusting the tool at scale.
skills.name: computational-performance-validation
skills.search_text: computational-performance-validation Use when a paper reports a concrete computational throughput or runtime figure (e.g. 60,000 transition pairs/sec) and you must reproduce or sanity-check that number on available hardware before trusting the tool at scale. The question is about transition-list correctness (fragment masses, collision-energy predictions, blib spectral library output) rather than computation speed — validate content separately, e.g. by exporting a blib file after activating the collision energy module. skills.search_text: condition-grouped-metabolomics-data-handling Use when a metabolite intensity matrix must be organized by condition group and converted into per-condition covariance matrices as the numeric substrate for Jacobian network inference in MInfer. Input is raw or unnormalized metabolomics data that has not passed MetaboAnalyst/MInfer data preparation — the covariance step expects a condition-prepared matrix, not raw intensities. The analysis goal is direct heatmap/3D visualization of interaction networks without Jacobian computation — then visualization functions on existing Jacobian output suffice. skills.name: confidence-model-training
skills.search_text: confidence-model-training Use when GNN-predicted CCS values (e.g. Mol2CCS outputs on METLIN-CCS or CCSBase) must be filtered for reliability, and per-prediction absolute relative error is available on a labeled subset to train a confidence classifier. Predictions already come with calibrated per-sample uncertainty (e.g. Monte Carlo dropout variance alone) and no labeled residuals exist to supervise a classifier. The task is plain CCS prediction accuracy rather than reliability filtering — use Mol2CCS training/splitting workflows instead. Data comes from a chemical space far outside METLIN-CCS or CCSBase; the paper shows model accuracy declines on structurally novel regions, so filtered scores may not transfer. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3336 Trains a random-forest confidence model on Mol2CCS prediction residuals to identify CCS predictions likely to deviate more than 5% from the true value, then filters predictions by confidence score to lower MAE and MRE. This turns raw GNN CCS predictions into reliability-scored outputs before downstream use. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00899-w
skills.summary: Trains a random-forest confidence model on Mol2CCS prediction residuals to identify CCS predictions likely to deviate more than 5% from the true value, then filters predictions by confidence score to lower MAE and MRE. skills.search_text: confidence-score-calibration-binning Use when a frequency- or likelihood-based prioritization score (e.g. DeepMet sampling frequency given an exact mass within ±10 ppm) must be shown to be calibrated before being trusted for metabolite annotation or prospective discovery. The input scores come from MS/MS spectral matching rather than mass-only sampling-frequency prioritization; use the meta-learning annotation-integration approach instead. The model is being applied to evolutionarily distant metabolisms (e.g. plant or bacterial), where the human-metabolite-trained DeepMet prior and its calibration do not transfer and a bespoke model is required. No held-out ground-truth structures are available — calibration of correct vs. incorrect bins cannot be computed without known answers. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Bin sampling-frequency-derived confidence scores for correct vs. incorrect metabolite annotations to verify that DeepMet's structure prioritization prior is well-calibrated. This validates that ranking accuracy (e.g. 29% top-1 in cross-validation) reflects trustworthy, usable confidence values rather than overconfident rankings. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.11.13.623458
skills.summary: Bin sampling-frequency-derived confidence scores for correct vs. incorrect metabolite annotations to verify that DeepMet's structure prioritization prior is well-calibrated. This validates that ranking accuracy (e.g. 29% top-1 in cross-validation) reflects trustworthy, usable confidence values rather than overconfident rankings.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input scores come from MS/MS spectral matching rather than mass-only sampling-frequency prioritization; use the meta-learning annotation-integration approach instead. The model is being applied to evolutionarily distant metabolisms (e.g. plant or bacterial), where the human-metabolite-trained DeepMet prior and its calibration do not transfer and a bespoke model is required. No held-out ground-truth structures are available — calibration of correct vs. incorrect bins cannot be computed without known answers.

Input spectra can already be matched by spectral library search (dot-product cosine similarity) — a library search may suffice, though note COSMIC outperformed it even for de-replication Stereochemistry must be resolved — fragmentation spectra cannot establish stereochemistry, only the two-dimensional structure is considered The score is needed as the probability that an annotation is correct — this is impossible by design of the score http://edamontology.org/topic_3895 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 COSMIC's confidence-score workflow assigns a statistical confidence to in-silico structure annotations by combining kernel density P value estimation with an SVM whose decision values are mapped to Platt posterior probabilities, enabling FDR-controlled metabolite annotation absent from spectral libraries. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41587-021-01045-9

The sequence was produced by the complete randomization algorithm rather than block randomization — runs of consecutive same-group samples are not precluded there, so a zero-violation criterion does not apply. The goal is inter-batch balancing of sample characteristics (age, gender, etc.) across batches, not checking within-batch injection-order adjacency. The randomization dimension is inherently unbalanced and was handled by optimized block randomization with many groups in one dimension, where the paper warns local aggregation can occur under some special numerical distributions. Validates an intra-batch randomized injection sequence by scanning for positions where three consecutive samples share the same treatment/placebo (or other randomization-dimension) group.
