Input is already a processed feature table from MZmine 2 or a GNPS network file — those take a different import route (-t GNPS) and do not need replicate-driven basketing of mzML peak lists No replicate injections exist, so replicate comparison (present in n−1 of n) cannot be performed; NP Analyst can be run on unprocessed data but this typically increases the number of candidate bioactive MS features The goal is downstream bioactivity scoring or visualization rather than generating the unique-feature list — this skill covers only feature basketing upstream of activity mapping http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Builds the consensus list of unique MS features for NP Analyst by first requiring replicated signals (present in n−1 of n replicate injections) and then basketing replicated m/z and retention-time error ranges with R-tree connected-component grouping, averaging features within each component. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acscentsci.1c01108
skills.summary: Builds the consensus list of unique MS features for NP Analyst by first requiring replicated signals (present in n−1 of n replicate injections) and then basketing replicated m/z and retention-time error ranges with R-tree connected-component grouping, averaging features within each component.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a processed feature table from MZmine 2 or a GNPS network file — those take a different import route (-t GNPS) and do not need replicate-driven basketing of mzML peak lists No replicate injections exist, so replicate comparison (present in n−1 of n) cannot be performed; NP Analyst can be run on unprocessed data but this typically increases the number of candidate bioactive MS features The goal is downstream bioactivity scoring or visualization rather than generating the unique-feature list — this skill covers only feature basketing upstream of activity mapping

skills.description: Use when you have RT-aligned, centroided mzML-derived feature maps from multiple LC-MS/MS samples and need a single consensus feature table linking each feature's m/z, RT, adduct and per-sample intensities.
skills.name: consensus-feature-linking
skills.search_text: consensus-feature-linking Use when you have RT-aligned, centroided mzML-derived feature maps from multiple LC-MS/MS samples and need a single consensus feature table linking each feature's m/z, RT, adduct and per-sample intensities. Input is already a consensus feature table or TSV feature matrix (e.g. you are at the re-quantification or annotation stage instead) The dataset is raw vendor files (Thermo .raw, Agilent, Bruker) that have not yet been converted to centroided mzML and undergone feature detection and RT alignment Only a single sample map is available, since linking consensus feature groups across samples requires multiple input maps http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Groups aligned, adduct-annotated LC-MS features across samples into a consensus feature map using OpenMS FeatureLinkerUnlabeledKD, then optionally filters consensus features with too many missing values (minfrac) before exporting a tab-separated feature matrix. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-023-00724-w
skills.summary: Groups aligned, adduct-annotated LC-MS features across samples into a consensus feature map using OpenMS FeatureLinkerUnlabeledKD, then optionally filters consensus features with too many missing values (minfrac) before exporting a tab-separated feature matrix.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a consensus feature table or TSV feature matrix (e.g. you are at the re-quantification or annotation stage instead) The dataset is raw vendor files (Thermo .raw, Agilent, Bruker) that have not yet been converted to centroided mzML and undergone feature detection and RT alignment Only a single sample map is available, since linking consensus feature groups across samples requires multiple input maps

skills.description: Use when you need consensus/aligned peaks across multiple MS/MS spectra of one molecular network component (e.g., GNPS2 FBMN family) to find shared fragments and m/z-shifted peaks from modifications, beyond pairwise cosine.
skills.name: consensus-peak-multiple-spectrum-alignment
skills.search_text: consensus-peak-multiple-spectrum-alignment Use when you need consensus/aligned peaks across multiple MS/MS spectra of one molecular network component (e.g., GNPS2 FBMN family) to find shared fragments and m/z-shifted peaks from modifications, beyond pairwise cosine. Input is already a feature table or quantification matrix rather than raw tandem spectra — MMSA aligns MS/MS peaks, not features You only need a pairwise spectrum comparison (modified cosine score); MSA via MST and topological sorting adds overhead not present in pairwise-only tools Spectra belong to unrelated components rather than one putatively related molecular family from molecular networking http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Compute a global multiple alignment of all tandem MS/MS spectra in a molecular network component using MMSA, yielding non-transitively aligned consensus peak sets (e.g., the rhamnose m/z 135.017 set across a rhamnolipid family) that expose shared core structures and shifted fragments from chemical modifications. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jasms.5c00237
skills.summary: Compute a global multiple alignment of all tandem MS/MS spectra in a molecular network component using MMSA, yielding non-transitively aligned consensus peak sets (e.g., the rhamnose m/z 135.017 set across a rhamnolipid family) that expose shared core structures and shifted fragments from chemical modifications.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a feature table or quantification matrix rather than raw tandem spectra — MMSA aligns MS/MS peaks, not features You only need a pairwise spectrum comparison (modified cosine score); MSA via MST and topological sorting adds overhead not present in pairwise-only tools Spectra belong to unrelated components rather than one putatively related molecular family from molecular networking

skills.description: Use when you have pixel-level DESI-MSI data along a tissue axis (e.g. maize root sections) and need a per-sample list of m/z signatures from untargeted spectra.
skills.name: consensus-peak-picking-with-ppm-tolerance
skills.search_text: consensus-peak-picking-with-ppm-tolerance Use when you have pixel-level DESI-MSI data along a tissue axis (e.g. maize root sections) and need a per-sample list of m/z signatures from untargeted spectra. Input is already a reduced peak/feature table rather than pixel-level imaging spectra — pseudobulk summation and ppm-based consensus calling would be redundant The tissue has no linear developmental axis to interpret, since this consensus-peak step is part of a pipeline (DIMPLE) designed for linear-gradient evaluation You need metabolite annotation/identification — pair the peak list with database search tools (METASPACE, Metlin Classic, LOTUS) rather than expecting it here http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Extract consensus m/z peaks from DESI-MSI imaging runs by summing pixel intensities into a pseudobulk spectrum, then calling peaks within a 2.5 ppm mass tolerance and filtering by background and spatial sparsity. Used in DIMPLE to recover developmental mass signatures from maize root imaging data. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.09.22.677919
skills.summary: Extract consensus m/z peaks from DESI-MSI imaging runs by summing pixel intensities into a pseudobulk spectrum, then calling peaks within a 2.5 ppm mass tolerance and filtering by background and spatial sparsity. Used in DIMPLE to recover developmental mass signatures from maize root imaging data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a reduced peak/feature table rather than pixel-level imaging spectra — pseudobulk summation and ppm-based consensus calling would be redundant The tissue has no linear developmental axis to interpret, since this consensus-peak step is part of a pipeline (DIMPLE) designed for linear-gradient evaluation You need metabolite annotation/identification — pair the peak list with database search tools (METASPACE, Metlin Classic, LOTUS) rather than expecting it here

skills.description: Use when a molecular family (e.g. ~80 rhamnolipid or albicidin MS/MS spectra from GNPS2) needs a global peak alignment that explains which consensus peaks cause spectra to cluster, rather than only pairwise cosine scores.
skills.name: consensus-peak-set-identification
skills.search_text: consensus-peak-set-identification Use when a molecular family (e.g. ~80 rhamnolipid or albicidin MS/MS spectra from GNPS2) needs a global peak alignment that explains which consensus peaks cause spectra to cluster, rather than only pairwise cosine scores. Input is a pairwise spectral comparison or a molecular-network edge score only — MMSA is specifically for the alignment of entire molecular families, not pairwise visualization The analysis requires exact capture of every small peak alignment (e.g. y2 fragments in albicidin) — the greedy multiple alignment does not fully capture smaller peak sets The spectra are C12 HAA-containing rhamnolipid homologs whose shifted peaks (m/z 239.162, 385.219) must be guaranteed in the alignment — MMSA fails to capture those shifted peaks http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 MMSA's consensus-peak-set identification step computes a global multiple alignment of MS/MS spectra within a molecular-network component, producing non-transitively aligned peak sets (m/z + intensity per set) that drive molecular networking formation and expose chemical modifications such as C12 HAA homolog shifts or albicidin modification sites. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jasms.5c00237
skills.summary: MMSA's consensus-peak-set identification step computes a global multiple alignment of MS/MS spectra within a molecular-network component, producing non-transitively aligned peak sets (m/z + intensity per set) that drive molecular networking formation and expose chemical modifications such as C12 HAA homolog shifts or albicidin modification sites.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a pairwise spectral comparison or a molecular-network edge score only — MMSA is specifically for the alignment of entire molecular families, not pairwise visualization The analysis requires exact capture of every small peak alignment (e.g. y2 fragments in albicidin) — the greedy multiple alignment does not fully capture smaller peak sets The spectra are C12 HAA-containing rhamnolipid homologs whose shifted peaks (m/z 239.162, 385.219) must be guaranteed in the alignment — MMSA fails to capture those shifted peaks

skills.description: Use when several MS/MS spectra of the same metabolite with different adducts or charge carriers (e.g., [M+H]+, [M+Na]+, water-loss in-source fragments) are available from a GNPS2 molecular networking task and you need shared/consensus fragment peaks to argue fragmentation consistency.
skills.name: consensus-peak-set-identification-across-adduct-spectra
skills.search_text: consensus-peak-set-identification-across-adduct-spectra Use when several MS/MS spectra of the same metabolite with different adducts or charge carriers (e.g., [M+H]+, [M+Na]+, water-loss in-source fragments) are available from a GNPS2 molecular networking task and you need shared/consensus fragment peaks to argue fragmentation consistency. You only need a pairwise spectral comparison or a single spectrum vs. library match — MMSA is designed for alignment of entire molecular families, not pairwise-only questions You lack a prior molecular networking result (no GNPS2/FBMN task ID, component number, or USIs pointing to specs_ms.mgf) — the tool sources spectra from such tasks rather than raw LC-MS files The key evidence is small or shifted peaks (e.g., adduct-specific shifted fragments like the C12 HAA at m/z 239.162) — the greedy multiple alignment may not fully capture them http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 A Multiple Mass Spectral Alignment (MMSA) workflow that globally aligns all peaks across the MS/MS spectra of one molecular network component (e.g., five phenylalanine-cholic acid adduct spectra, [M+H]+ vs [M+Na]+ and in-source water losses) to identify consensus peak sets demonstrating whether fragmentation chemistry is consistent across adducts. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jasms.5c00237
skills.summary: A Multiple Mass Spectral Alignment (MMSA) workflow that globally aligns all peaks across the MS/MS spectra of one molecular network component (e.g., five phenylalanine-cholic acid adduct spectra, [M+H]+ vs [M+Na]+ and in-source water losses) to identify consensus peak sets demonstrating whether fragmentation chemistry is consistent across adducts.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need a pairwise spectral comparison or a single spectrum vs. library match — MMSA is designed for alignment of entire molecular families, not pairwise-only questions You lack a prior molecular networking result (no GNPS2/FBMN task ID, component number, or USIs pointing to specs_ms.mgf) — the tool sources spectra from such tasks rather than raw LC-MS files The key evidence is small or shifted peaks (e.g., adduct-specific shifted fragments like the C12 HAA at m/z 239.162) — the greedy multiple alignment may not fully capture them

skills.description: Use when a calculated property (e.g. Boltzmann-average CCS from ccs.txt) must be validated against two independent experimental reference sets and a consensus of both, with a percent-error tolerance.
skills.name: consensus-reference-averaging
skills.search_text: consensus-reference-averaging Use when a calculated property (e.g. Boltzmann-average CCS from ccs.txt) must be validated against two independent experimental reference sets and a consensus of both, with a percent-error tolerance. Only one experimental reference set is available, so no consensus average of two reference sets can be formed The comparison target is raw instrument calibration or CCS correction of the TWIMS instrument itself rather than validating computationally predicted CCS values http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Validates in silico CCS predictions by computing percent errors against two independent experimental reference sets (TWIMS measurements and literature database values) and a consensus average of the two, applying a ±3% agreement criterion for 20 benchmark metabolites. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jasms.1c00315
skills.summary: Validates in silico CCS predictions by computing percent errors against two independent experimental reference sets (TWIMS measurements and literature database values) and a consensus average of the two, applying a ±3% agreement criterion for 20 benchmark metabolites.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only one experimental reference set is available, so no consensus average of two reference sets can be formed The comparison target is raw instrument calibration or CCS correction of the TWIMS instrument itself rather than validating computationally predicted CCS values

skills.description: Use when raw LC–MS/MS per-sample MGF files contain redundant, noisy, or duplicate MS2 spectra (e.g., multiple scans of the same precursor, isotopes, or media/blank signals) that must be collapsed into one cleaned consensus spectrum per compound before annotation or BCC ranking.
skills.name: consensus-spectra-clustering-cleaning
skills.search_text: consensus-spectra-clustering-cleaning Use when raw LC–MS/MS per-sample MGF files contain redundant, noisy, or duplicate MS2 spectra (e.g., multiple scans of the same precursor, isotopes, or media/blank signals) that must be collapsed into one cleaned consensus spectrum per compound before annotation or BCC ranking. The input is already a feature table or clean consensus spectra — rerunning clustering would recluster already-collapsed spectra The analysis is targeted MS/MS or spectral library matching of a single spectrum rather than untargeted LC–MS/MS mixture processing Data lack sample-group metadata (blanks, culture media, bioactivity fractions), since cleaning and BCC filtering depend on grouping spectra by sample groups http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Clusters preprocessed MS2 spectra from an LC–MS/MS untargeted metabolomics run into consensus spectra using the NP3-shifted cosine, then cleans and deconvolves them (including automatic [M+H]+ ion selection) to produce clean consensus spectra suitable for library identification and bioactivity correlation scoring. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c05829
skills.summary: Clusters preprocessed MS2 spectra from an LC–MS/MS untargeted metabolomics run into consensus spectra using the NP3-shifted cosine, then cleans and deconvolves them (including automatic [M+H]+ ion selection) to produce clean consensus spectra suitable for library identification and bioactivity correlation scoring.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a feature table or clean consensus spectra — rerunning clustering would recluster already-collapsed spectra The analysis is targeted MS/MS or spectral library matching of a single spectrum rather than untargeted LC–MS/MS mixture processing Data lack sample-group metadata (blanks, culture media, bioactivity fractions), since cleaning and BCC filtering depend on grouping spectra by sample groups

skills.description: Use when consensus spectra have been obtained from GC × GC–MS deconvolution (e.g. GcDUO Module III DuoResults with $cor_spectra) and each peak feature must be assigned a compound identity against an MSP library.
skills.name: consensus-spectra-library-matching
skills.search_text: consensus-spectra-library-matching Use when consensus spectra have been obtained from GC × GC–MS deconvolution (e.g. GcDUO Module III DuoResults with $cor_spectra) and each peak feature must be assigned a compound identity against an MSP library. Input is raw CDF/GC×GC–MS data that still needs peak picking and deconvolution (run GcDUO Modules I–III, e.g. procesData, first) The target compound is absent from the library or its spectrum is too small to deconvolute — as in the fruitybeer dataset where one compound was missing from the in-house library and small signals yielded no annotation Data already contain a full annotated feature table (annotation should precede Module V data integration, not follow it) http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Annotates GC × GC–MS consensus spectra (GcDUO Module IV) by matching them against an in-house MSP spectral library using cosine similarity, with optional retention-index (Kovats) refinement. Identifications are accepted only when similarity exceeds a user-defined match_cutoff (e.g. 0.7). metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bib/bbaf080
skills.summary: Annotates GC × GC–MS consensus spectra (GcDUO Module IV) by matching them against an in-house MSP spectral library using cosine similarity, with optional retention-index (Kovats) refinement. Identifications are accepted only when similarity exceeds a user-defined match_cutoff (e.g. 0.7).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw CDF/GC×GC–MS data that still needs peak picking and deconvolution (run GcDUO Modules I–III, e.g. procesData, first) The target compound is absent from the library or its spectrum is too small to deconvolute — as in the fruitybeer dataset where one compound was missing from the in-house library and small signals yielded no annotation Data already contain a full annotated feature table (annotation should precede Module V data integration, not follow it)

skills.description: Use when a molecule has multiple query MS/MS spectra (e.g. three collision-energy levels from MZmine3 feature extraction) and you need a single ranked candidate list rather than per-spectrum rankings.
skills.name: consensus-spectrum-candidate-ranking
skills.search_text: consensus-spectrum-candidate-ranking Use when a molecule has multiple query MS/MS spectra (e.g. three collision-energy levels from MZmine3 feature extraction) and you need a single ranked candidate list rather than per-spectrum rankings. When each molecule has only one query spectrum — there is no consensus to build; rank candidates directly on that spectrum instead. When the goal is de novo molecule generation or spectrum simulation (MassSpecGym challenges other than retrieval), not candidate ranking. When constituents have inconsistent precursor masses or adducts so a consensus spectrum is not meaningful — rank per spectrum and aggregate instead, but expect lower rank@1 per the article's finding. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 Annotate a molecule with multiple query MS/MS spectra by first aggregating the constituent spectra into a consensus spectrum, then ranking candidate molecules against it with MVP's mol-cs view; this aggregate-then-rank strategy outperforms rank-then-aggregate (e.g. 35.99% vs 26.37% rank@1 for candidates by mass). metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.11.12.688047
skills.summary: Annotate a molecule with multiple query MS/MS spectra by first aggregating the constituent spectra into a consensus spectrum, then ranking candidate molecules against it with MVP's mol-cs view; this aggregate-then-rank strategy outperforms rank-then-aggregate (e.g. 35.99% vs 26.37% rank@1 for candidates by mass).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When each molecule has only one query spectrum — there is no consensus to build; rank candidates directly on that spectrum instead. When the goal is de novo molecule generation or spectrum simulation (MassSpecGym challenges other than retrieval), not candidate ranking. When constituents have inconsistent precursor masses or adducts so a consensus spectrum is not meaningful — rank per spectrum and aggregate instead, but expect lower rank@1 per the article's finding.

skills.description: Use when a molecule has multiple constituent MS/MS spectra (e.g., several collision energies in MassSpecGym) and you need one aggregate query view for candidate ranking instead of rank-then-aggregate scoring.
skills.name: consensus-spectrum-construction
skills.search_text: consensus-spectrum-construction Use when a molecule has multiple constituent MS/MS spectra (e.g., several collision energies in MassSpecGym) and you need one aggregate query view for candidate ranking instead of rank-then-aggregate scoring. When each molecule has only a single spectrum (e.g., the rank-aggregation subset excludes molecules without exactly three spectra), there is nothing to aggregate into a consensus When the goal is rank-then-aggregate scoring of individual spectra rather than an aggregated query view When spectra lack representative-spectrum selection/feature extraction (e.g., no MZmine3 feature handling) so constituent spectra are not directly mergeable http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Constructs a per-molecule consensus MS/MS spectrum from multiple replicate spectra (e.g., different collision energies) so it can be used as an aggregate-then-rank query view in MVP's joint embedding, which outperforms rank aggregation of individual spectra. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.11.12.688047
skills.summary: Constructs a per-molecule consensus MS/MS spectrum from multiple replicate spectra (e.g., different collision energies) so it can be used as an aggregate-then-rank query view in MVP's joint embedding, which outperforms rank aggregation of individual spectra.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When each molecule has only a single spectrum (e.g., the rank-aggregation subset excludes molecules without exactly three spectra), there is nothing to aggregate into a consensus When the goal is rank-then-aggregate scoring of individual spectra rather than an aggregated query view When spectra lack representative-spectrum selection/feature extraction (e.g., no MZmine3 feature handling) so constituent spectra are not directly mergeable

skills.description: Use when clustered MS2 spectra from LC–MS/MS samples must be dereplicated into non-redundant consensus spectra while keeping isomers separated, e.g. NP3 MS Workflow Cleaning steps 3–5 on per-sample MGF input.
skills.name: consensus-spectrum-dereplication
skills.search_text: consensus-spectrum-dereplication Use when clustered MS2 spectra from LC–MS/MS samples must be dereplicated into non-redundant consensus spectra while keeping isomers separated, e.g. NP3 MS Workflow Cleaning steps 3–5 on per-sample MGF input. Raw vendor LC–MS/MS files that have not passed NP3 preprocessing (step 2) — per-sample MGF MS2 spectra and MS1 feature data are required first. Targeted MS/MS library search where the spectra are already individual standards rather than redundant replicate clusters needing dereplication. Datasets where isomer separation is not needed and a full spectral-library-style merge of all similar spectra would be acceptable. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Iteratively merge redundant MS2 spectra from clustered LC–MS/MS features into clean consensus spectra using the NP3-shifted cosine (greedy modified cosine), then export one MGF per ion plus a clean count table for downstream library identification and bioactivity correlation. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c05829
skills.summary: Iteratively merge redundant MS2 spectra from clustered LC–MS/MS features into clean consensus spectra using the NP3-shifted cosine (greedy modified cosine), then export one MGF per ion plus a clean count table for downstream library identification and bioactivity correlation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Raw vendor LC–MS/MS files that have not passed NP3 preprocessing (step 2) — per-sample MGF MS2 spectra and MS1 feature data are required first. Targeted MS/MS library search where the spectra are already individual standards rather than redundant replicate clusters needing dereplication. Datasets where isomer separation is not needed and a full spectral-library-style merge of all similar spectra would be acceptable.

skills.description: Use when benchmarking metabolite annotation models on MassSpecGym and you need to compare aggregate-then-rank (consensus spectrum) versus rank-then-aggregate (individual spectra) candidate retrieval, reporting rank@1 per ranking view and candidate condition.
skills.name: consensus-spectrum-embedding-evaluation
skills.search_text: consensus-spectrum-embedding-evaluation Use when benchmarking metabolite annotation models on MassSpecGym and you need to compare aggregate-then-rank (consensus spectrum) versus rank-then-aggregate (individual spectra) candidate retrieval, reporting rank@1 per ranking view and candidate condition. You are doing de novo molecule generation or spectrum simulation challenges of MassSpecGym rather than the molecule retrieval challenge Your goal is annotation of an individual study's spectra against FoodDB/HMDB/NIST23/GNPS candidate sets with 0.01 Da tolerance, not the standardized MassSpecGym retrieval benchmark You want to evaluate baselines like MIST, ESP, JESTR, or CFM-ID 4.0 that do not expose consensus-spectrum ranking views; those require their own evaluation protocols http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Evaluates cross-modal candidate ranking using a consensus-spectrum embedding view (mol-cs / fp-cs) versus individual-spectrum ranking (mol-s / fp-s) on the MassSpecGym retrieval benchmark, quantified by rank@1 for candidates retrieved by mass and by formula. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.11.12.688047
skills.summary: Evaluates cross-modal candidate ranking using a consensus-spectrum embedding view (mol-cs / fp-cs) versus individual-spectrum ranking (mol-s / fp-s) on the MassSpecGym retrieval benchmark, quantified by rank@1 for candidates retrieved by mass and by formula.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You are doing de novo molecule generation or spectrum simulation challenges of MassSpecGym rather than the molecule retrieval challenge Your goal is annotation of an individual study's spectra against FoodDB/HMDB/NIST23/GNPS candidate sets with 0.01 Da tolerance, not the standardized MassSpecGym retrieval benchmark You want to evaluate baselines like MIST, ESP, JESTR, or CFM-ID 4.0 that do not expose consensus-spectrum ranking views; those require their own evaluation protocols

skills.description: Use when raw MS2 peak lists (.mzXML/.mzML) must be deduplicated into consensus spectra before molecular networking or library search, and the Minimum Cluster Size and precursor mass tolerance need to be justified.
skills.name: consensus-spectrum-generation
skills.search_text: consensus-spectrum-generation Use when raw MS2 peak lists (.mzXML/.mzML) must be deduplicated into consensus spectra before molecular networking or library search, and the Minimum Cluster Size and precursor mass tolerance need to be justified. Input is already a feature table or quantified peak area table — consensus clustering operates on MS2 scans only and yields no quantitative information (classic networking is qualitative) The goal is isomer resolution — MS2 consensus spectra typically cannot differentiate regio- or stereoisomers Feature-Based Molecular Networking with in-source markers needed — this skill targets classic MS-Cluster node formation, not FBMN feature detection http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Reconstruct the MS-Cluster consensus-clustering step of GNPS molecular networking: collapse nearly identical MS2 spectra into consensus spectra (nodes) after GNPS peak filtering, so downstream network construction and spectral library searching operate on one representative spectrum per cluster. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41596-020-0317-5
skills.summary: Reconstruct the MS-Cluster consensus-clustering step of GNPS molecular networking: collapse nearly identical MS2 spectra into consensus spectra (nodes) after GNPS peak filtering, so downstream network construction and spectral library searching operate on one representative spectrum per cluster.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a feature table or quantified peak area table — consensus clustering operates on MS2 scans only and yields no quantitative information (classic networking is qualitative) The goal is isomer resolution — MS2 consensus spectra typically cannot differentiate regio- or stereoisomers Feature-Based Molecular Networking with in-source markers needed — this skill targets classic MS-Cluster node formation, not FBMN feature detection

skills.description: Use when a broad ontology-backed comparison (e.g. 'Digestive Tract' vs 'Bacteria') expands into multiple metadata-combination contrasts and each compound needs one aggregated p-value and one fold-change instead of many pairwise results.
skills.name: conservative-fold-change-aggregation
skills.search_text: conservative-fold-change-aggregation Use when a broad ontology-backed comparison (e.g. 'Digestive Tract' vs 'Bacteria') expands into multiple metadata-combination contrasts and each compound needs one aggregated p-value and one fold-change instead of many pairwise results. When the comparison is a simple pairwise metadata contrast with a single triad pair — no aggregation across n*m pairs is needed For biological metadata combinations with few samples and few studies, where the article warns quantitative comparisons are less robust When compounds have not been pre-processed through the BinBase pipeline (FAME normalization, QC removal, imputation of presence-percentage times minimum detected value) — aggregation on uncurated intensities is not supported http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 A conservative aggregation rule for OGDA meta-analyses that collapses the n*m pairwise Welch t-test results (p-values and fold-changes on log-transformed GC–TOF MS metabolite intensities) into a single p-value and fold-change per compound per query, deliberately reporting the least favorable evidence. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-023-00734-8
skills.summary: A conservative aggregation rule for OGDA meta-analyses that collapses the n*m pairwise Welch t-test results (p-values and fold-changes on log-transformed GC–TOF MS metabolite intensities) into a single p-value and fold-change per compound per query, deliberately reporting the least favorable evidence.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the comparison is a simple pairwise metadata contrast with a single triad pair — no aggregation across n*m pairs is needed For biological metadata combinations with few samples and few studies, where the article warns quantitative comparisons are less robust When compounds have not been pre-processed through the BinBase pipeline (FAME normalization, QC removal, imputation of presence-percentage times minimum detected value) — aggregation on uncurated intensities is not supported

skills.description: Decision support for ontologically grouped differential analysis (OGDA) queries in BinDiscover where a broad term (e.g. 'digestive tract') expands to many metadata combinations and each compound yields multiple pairwise Welch t-test results that must be condensed into one conservative call.
skills.name: conservative-pvalue-foldchange-aggregation
skills.search_text: conservative-pvalue-foldchange-aggregation Decision support for ontologically grouped differential analysis (OGDA) queries in BinDiscover where a broad term (e.g. 'digestive tract') expands to many metadata combinations and each compound yields multiple pairwise Welch t-test results that must be condensed into one conservative call. When comparing a single specific metadata combination (e.g. one organ vs. one organism) rather than a broad ontology term that expands to many combinations — no aggregation across pairs is needed. When quantitative comparison across few samples/studies is intended; the article notes quantitative comparisons are less robust for metadata combinations with few samples and few studies, so conservative aggregation on such sparse pairs may be misleading. When analysing unannotated spectra or chemical artifacts — restrict to the 773 identified metabolites as the article does. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Aggregates per-pair Welch t-test p-values and fold-change matrices across all ontology-expanded metadata-combination pairs per compound using the maximum p-value and minimum fold-change as conservative boundaries, so broad OGDA queries report a single significant/non-significant call per metabolite. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-023-00734-8
skills.summary: Aggregates per-pair Welch t-test p-values and fold-change matrices across all ontology-expanded metadata-combination pairs per compound using the maximum p-value and minimum fold-change as conservative boundaries, so broad OGDA queries report a single significant/non-significant call per metabolite.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When comparing a single specific metadata combination (e.g. one organ vs. one organism) rather than a broad ontology term that expands to many combinations — no aggregation across pairs is needed. When quantitative comparison across few samples/studies is intended; the article notes quantitative comparisons are less robust for metadata combinations with few samples and few studies, so conservative aggregation on such sparse pairs may be misleading. When analysing unannotated spectra or chemical artifacts — restrict to the 773 identified metabolites as the article does.

skills.search_text: contaminant-feature-flagging Use when raw untargeted metabolomics or lipidomics feature-intensity tables contain procedural-blank injections alongside real samples, and features enriched in blanks must be flagged as background contaminants before signal-drift or RSD filtering. When the dataset contains no procedural-blank injections, since the 3x sample-vs-blank criterion cannot be computed When the goal is to correct batch signal drift or detect out-of-control QCpool observations — those are separate QComics steps, not background-contamination flagging When features are already known annotated endogenous metabolites with confirmed spectra, rather than unfiltered feature tables needing contaminant screening http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Flags molecular features as potential contaminants by comparing real-sample intensities against procedural-blank injections, following the QComics background-noise step that flags (rather than deletes) features whose sample mean is not more than three times the procedural-blank mean, and discards only those additionally exhibiting blank RSD > 15%. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c03660
skills.summary: Flags molecular features as potential contaminants by comparing real-sample intensities against procedural-blank injections, following the QComics background-noise step that flags (rather than deletes) features whose sample mean is not more than three times the procedural-blank mean, and discards only those additionally exhibiting blank RSD > 15%.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the dataset contains no procedural-blank injections, since the 3x sample-vs-blank criterion cannot be computed When the goal is to correct batch signal drift or detect out-of-control QCpool observations — those are separate QComics steps, not background-contamination flagging When features are already known annotated endogenous metabolites with confirmed spectra, rather than unfiltered feature tables needing contaminant screening

skills.description: Use when mzML/mzXML/mzData files from untargeted MS-based metabolomics acquisition must be checked for known background contaminants — e.g. to diagnose carryover, contamination from labware, or user-defined compound exposure.
skills.name: contaminant-ion-screening-in-ms-data
skills.search_text: contaminant-ion-screening-in-ms-data Use when mzML/mzXML/mzData files from untargeted MS-based metabolomics acquisition must be checked for known background contaminants — e.g. to diagnose carryover, contamination from labware, or user-defined compound exposure. The input is already a curated feature table or blank-subtracted peak list rather than raw mzML/mzXML vendor output — QC4Metabolomics expects raw file traversal/ingestion via module_Files. The goal is drift correction or intensity normalization (e.g. LOESS on pooled QC samples) rather than detecting discrete contaminant ions; QC4Metabolomics monitors contaminants but does not perform postanalysis intensity-drift correction itself. Target analytes are rare or user-specific compounds not represented in the ~800-contaminant library and no user-defined contaminant list has been supplied — screening will return nothing actionable. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Screens each acquired metabolomics LC-MS file against a built-in library of nearly 800 known contaminant ions to detect contaminant carryover or exposure via QC4Metabolomics, flagging files whose contaminant signal levels exceed user-defined thresholds. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c07078
skills.summary: Screens each acquired metabolomics LC-MS file against a built-in library of nearly 800 known contaminant ions to detect contaminant carryover or exposure via QC4Metabolomics, flagging files whose contaminant signal levels exceed user-defined thresholds.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a curated feature table or blank-subtracted peak list rather than raw mzML/mzXML vendor output — QC4Metabolomics expects raw file traversal/ingestion via module_Files. The goal is drift correction or intensity normalization (e.g. LOESS on pooled QC samples) rather than detecting discrete contaminant ions; QC4Metabolomics monitors contaminants but does not perform postanalysis intensity-drift correction itself. Target analytes are rare or user-specific compounds not represented in the ~800-contaminant library and no user-defined contaminant list has been supplied — screening will return nothing actionable.

skills.description: Use when monitoring background contaminants (e.g. from solvents or sample carryover) across pooled-QC injections in an mzML-based untargeted metabolomics run, where you want time-series, per-sample composition, or heatmap views of contaminant levels.
skills.name: contaminant-peak-detection
skills.search_text: contaminant-peak-detection Use when monitoring background contaminants (e.g. from solvents or sample carryover) across pooled-QC injections in an mzML-based untargeted metabolomics run, where you want time-series, per-sample composition, or heatmap views of contaminant levels. If your goal is general feature detection and peak picking on individual biological samples rather than tracking known background contaminants across a run — module_TrackCmp with a user-defined compound list is the appropriate module instead. If the input data are not untargeted MS-based metabolomics files (e.g. targeted MRM, imaging MS, or NMR), the contaminant list matching against RT/m/z pairs is not applicable. If you need to correct intensity drifts rather than monitor their presence, QC-MXP provides tools for correcting intensity drifts and should be used instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0153 Detects contaminant peaks in untargeted LC-MS metabolomics files by matching observed peaks against a curated list of nearly 800 known contaminant m/z and retention-time pairs, storing diagnostics (observed m/z, retention time, intensity, peak shape) in a mariaDB database and surfacing them on a Shiny web dashboard. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c07078
skills.summary: Detects contaminant peaks in untargeted LC-MS metabolomics files by matching observed peaks against a curated list of nearly 800 known contaminant m/z and retention-time pairs, storing diagnostics (observed m/z, retention time, intensity, peak shape) in a mariaDB database and surfacing them on a Shiny web dashboard.
skills.when_to_use_negative: If your goal is general feature detection and peak picking on individual biological samples rather than tracking known background contaminants across a run — module_TrackCmp with a user-defined compound list is the appropriate module instead. If the input data are not untargeted MS-based metabolomics files (e.g. targeted MRM, imaging MS, or NMR), the contaminant list matching against RT/m/z pairs is not applicable. If you need to correct intensity drifts rather than monitor their presence, QC-MXP provides tools for correcting intensity drifts and should be used instead.

skills.description: Use when HRMS feature data from known contaminant sources (e.g., roadway runoff) mixed at known dilutions is available and the goal is to predict source contribution in unknown mixed environmental samples.
skills.name: contaminant-source-tracking-prediction
skills.search_text: contaminant-source-tracking-prediction Use when HRMS feature data from known contaminant sources (e.g., roadway runoff) mixed at known dilutions is available and the goal is to predict source contribution in unknown mixed environmental samples. When the task is general HRMS feature extraction or annotation from raw .mzML files — this skill operates downstream on a pre-processed, transposed feature dataframe When no dilution/mixing training series of known sources exists — the dm.feature_model workflow requires fingerprint training data with known source gradients When feature grouping (merging isotopes, adducts, in-source fragments) is required first — MSS does not yet implement this, and ungrouped features may confound fingerprint clustering http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Trains a machine-learning model on HRMS 'fingerprint' features from dilution/mixing series (e.g., roadway runoff diluted into other waters) to predict source presence and concentration (apportionment) in unknown downstream mixtures, using the Mass-Suite (MSS) dm module. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-023-00741-9
skills.summary: Trains a machine-learning model on HRMS 'fingerprint' features from dilution/mixing series (e.g., roadway runoff diluted into other waters) to predict source presence and concentration (apportionment) in unknown downstream mixtures, using the Mass-Suite (MSS) dm module.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the task is general HRMS feature extraction or annotation from raw .mzML files — this skill operates downstream on a pre-processed, transposed feature dataframe When no dilution/mixing training series of known sources exists — the dm.feature_model workflow requires fingerprint training data with known source gradients When feature grouping (merging isotopes, adducts, in-source fragments) is required first — MSS does not yet implement this, and ungrouped features may confound fingerprint clustering

skills.description: Use when assembled de novo contigs (e.g. from ALPS over Casanovo predictions) must be scored against a reference antibody sequence to compute per-chain coverage and amino-acid accuracy, including CDR-level evaluation.
skills.name: contig-to-reference-blast-alignment
skills.search_text: contig-to-reference-blast-alignment Use when assembled de novo contigs (e.g. from ALPS over Casanovo predictions) must be scored against a reference antibody sequence to compute per-chain coverage and amino-acid accuracy, including CDR-level evaluation. When the goal is database-search peptide identification rather than scoring database-independent de novo assembly of full-length antibody chains When no reference or ground-truth antibody sequence is available for the target, since coverage and accuracy are defined by contig-to-reference BLAST alignments When the input is raw MS/MS spectra or unfiltered de novo peptide predictions - these must first be sequenced (e.g. with Casanovo), confidence-filtered, and assembled with ALPS before BLAST-based scoring http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0160 Quantifies de novo antibody reconstruction quality by aligning ALPS-assembled peptide contigs to ground-truth antibody sequences with BLAST, converting alignments into per-chain sequence coverage and accuracy metrics for light and heavy chains. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bib/bbac542
skills.summary: Quantifies de novo antibody reconstruction quality by aligning ALPS-assembled peptide contigs to ground-truth antibody sequences with BLAST, converting alignments into per-chain sequence coverage and accuracy metrics for light and heavy chains.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is database-search peptide identification rather than scoring database-independent de novo assembly of full-length antibody chains When no reference or ground-truth antibody sequence is available for the target, since coverage and accuracy are defined by contig-to-reference BLAST alignments When the input is raw MS/MS spectra or unfiltered de novo peptide predictions - these must first be sequenced (e.g. with Casanovo), confidence-filtered, and assembled with ALPS before BLAST-based scoring

skills.description: Use when two annotation or prediction methods have been run on the same query spectra set and you need to quantify overlap vs. uniqueness of correct results to support a complementarity claim.
skills.name: contingency-table-construction
skills.search_text: contingency-table-construction Use when two annotation or prediction methods have been run on the same query spectra set and you need to quantify overlap vs. uniqueness of correct results to support a complementarity claim. The two methods were evaluated on different query sets with no shared query spectra to intersect Per-query correctness labels are unavailable (e.g., only aggregate accuracy percentages were reported) The goal is pairwise correlation of continuous scores rather than a binary correct/incorrect cross-tabulation http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Builds a 2x2 contingency table crossing Boolean correctness labels from two annotation methods (e.g., BAM vs SIRIUS 5.6.3) over a shared query set, then decomposes agreement into correct-in-both, correct-only-in-method-A, and correct-only-in-method-B counts to test complementarity. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c01565
skills.summary: Builds a 2x2 contingency table crossing Boolean correctness labels from two annotation methods (e.g., BAM vs SIRIUS 5.6.3) over a shared query set, then decomposes agreement into correct-in-both, correct-only-in-method-A, and correct-only-in-method-B counts to test complementarity.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The two methods were evaluated on different query sets with no shared query spectra to intersect Per-query correctness labels are unavailable (e.g., only aggregate accuracy percentages were reported) The goal is pairwise correlation of continuous scores rather than a binary correct/incorrect cross-tabulation

skills.description: Decision support for judging whether DeepMASS identifications can be trusted for an unknown: use when you have identification results (e.g. LOOCV on 662 KEGG compounds or external biomarker tests) and need to tabulate validity against presence of a structure-related metabolite in the database.
skills.name: contingency-table-construction-from-identification-results
skills.search_text: contingency-table-construction-from-identification-results Decision support for judging whether DeepMASS identifications can be trusted for an unknown: use when you have identification results (e.g. LOOCV on 662 KEGG compounds or external biomarker tests) and need to tabulate validity against presence of a structure-related metabolite in the database. Input is raw MS/MS spectra needing identification in the first place — run the DeepMASS structural-similarity scoring workflow (example.py) before tabulating validity The unknown has no structurally related metabolite in the database and you expect a valid identification — the skill's premise is that validity depends on structural-neighbor availability You need to extend the identification range of an MS/MS database itself rather than evaluate identification validity of existing results http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Builds a validity-vs-presence contingency table from DeepMASS metabolite identification results to test whether identification of an unknown compound is valid when a structure-related metabolite exists in the reference database. It operationalizes the paper's central claim by cross-tabulating LOOCV and external-test identification outcomes against structural-neighbor database coverage. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.8b05405
skills.summary: Builds a validity-vs-presence contingency table from DeepMASS metabolite identification results to test whether identification of an unknown compound is valid when a structure-related metabolite exists in the reference database. It operationalizes the paper's central claim by cross-tabulating LOOCV and external-test identification outcomes against structural-neighbor database coverage.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw MS/MS spectra needing identification in the first place — run the DeepMASS structural-similarity scoring workflow (example.py) before tabulating validity The unknown has no structurally related metabolite in the database and you expect a valid identification — the skill's premise is that validity depends on structural-neighbor availability You need to extend the identification range of an MS/MS database itself rather than evaluate identification validity of existing results

skills.description: Use when binary or k-means-segregated oncogene activation subgroups (phosphoAKT1-high/low crossed with MYC-high/low) must be tested for association with ordinal clinical variables such as Gleason grade or pathologic stage.
skills.name: contingency-table-construction-oncogene-subgroups
skills.search_text: contingency-table-construction-oncogene-subgroups Use when binary or k-means-segregated oncogene activation subgroups (phosphoAKT1-high/low crossed with MYC-high/low) must be tested for association with ordinal clinical variables such as Gleason grade or pathologic stage. The classification variable is continuous densitometric data (phosphoAKT1/MYC Western blot values) — use k-means clustering first; contingency tables require the pre-binned subgroups. Testing association against the 3 metabolic clusters defined by Silhouette analysis is fine, but testing against >2 unordered subgroup labels with small expected cell counts may violate the 2x2 Fisher setup and needs the 2x4 formulation instead. The question concerns metabolite-level differences between subgroups (GSEA enrichment) rather than subgroup-vs-clinic association — use enrichment scoring, not contingency tables. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Builds 2x2 and 2x4 contingency tables crossing k-means-defined phosphoAKT1/MYC activation subgroups (e.g. phosphoAKT1-high/MYC-low, 21/60, 35%) against clinical covariates such as Gleason grade, then tests independence with Fisher's exact test (GraphPad Prism 5.0 in the paper; scipy.stats.fisher_exact as a scriptable equivalent). metabolomics/v3 10.1158/0008-5472.can-14-1490
skills.summary: Builds 2x2 and 2x4 contingency tables crossing k-means-defined phosphoAKT1/MYC activation subgroups (e.g. phosphoAKT1-high/MYC-low, 21/60, 35%) against clinical covariates such as Gleason grade, then tests independence with Fisher's exact test (GraphPad Prism 5.0 in the paper; scipy.stats.fisher_exact as a scriptable equivalent).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The classification variable is continuous densitometric data (phosphoAKT1/MYC Western blot values) — use k-means clustering first; contingency tables require the pre-binned subgroups. Testing association against the 3 metabolic clusters defined by Silhouette analysis is fine, but testing against >2 unordered subgroup labels with small expected cell counts may violate the 2x2 Fisher setup and needs the 2x4 formulation instead. The question concerns metabolite-level differences between subgroups (GSEA enrichment) rather than subgroup-vs-clinic association — use enrichment scoring, not contingency tables.

skills.description: Use when predicting a continuous phenotypic outcome (e.g. clinically measured bilirubin in serum) from multi-assay LC-MS metabolomics feature tables and you need cross-assay feature importance and significance calls.
skills.name: continuous-outcome-metabolomics-prediction
skills.search_text: continuous-outcome-metabolomics-prediction Use when predicting a continuous phenotypic outcome (e.g. clinically measured bilirubin in serum) from multi-assay LC-MS metabolomics feature tables and you need cross-assay feature importance and significance calls. The outcome is a binary/categorical label (e.g. biological sex or disease status) — use MamsiPls classification mode with metric='auc' and .evaluate_class_model() instead. Data come from a single assay block only — the MB-PLS framework's rationale is modelling interblock relationships across multiple LC-MS assays. Feature tables have not been aligned across assay blocks or lack the assay-prefixed column names needed for cross-assay structural search. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Fit an MB-PLS regression model (MamsiPls, NIPALS, standardised) on multi-assay LC-MS metabolomics data to predict a continuous clinical outcome such as blood bilirubin, using cross-validated latent-variable estimation, MB-VIP feature importance, and permutation-based empirical p-values to identify significant predictors. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c01327
skills.summary: Fit an MB-PLS regression model (MamsiPls, NIPALS, standardised) on multi-assay LC-MS metabolomics data to predict a continuous clinical outcome such as blood bilirubin, using cross-validated latent-variable estimation, MB-VIP feature importance, and permutation-based empirical p-values to identify significant predictors.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The outcome is a binary/categorical label (e.g. biological sex or disease status) — use MamsiPls classification mode with metric='auc' and .evaluate_class_model() instead. Data come from a single assay block only — the MB-PLS framework's rationale is modelling interblock relationships across multiple LC-MS assays. Feature tables have not been aligned across assay blocks or lack the assay-prefixed column names needed for cross-assay structural search.

skills.description: Use when developing or benchmarking a metabolomics algorithm (e.g. PCA, regression) that requires many simulated spectra with a continuous covariate, and no real spectra with known ground-truth concentrations are available.
skills.name: continuous-outcome-spectra-group-generation
skills.search_text: continuous-outcome-spectra-group-generation Use when developing or benchmarking a metabolomics algorithm (e.g. PCA, regression) that requires many simulated spectra with a continuous covariate, and no real spectra with known ground-truth concentrations are available. The analysis target is real patient/sample spectra with measured concentrations rather than simulated data with known ground truth The study design is case-control (discrete outcome, e.g. heart transplant versus healthy) rather than a continuous covariate — use the discrete-outcome grouped mode instead Only a single spectrum is needed (e.g. to inspect one metabolite's peak pattern) — the single-spectrum mode is simpler than setting up a 100-replicate grouped simulation http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Generate groups of simulated 1D 1H NMR spectra whose metabolite concentrations follow a linear regression model against a continuous outcome (e.g. BMI), using MetAssimulo 2.0's grouped-spectra mode with inter-metabolite correlations enabled. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btaf045
skills.summary: Generate groups of simulated 1D 1H NMR spectra whose metabolite concentrations follow a linear regression model against a continuous outcome (e.g. BMI), using MetAssimulo 2.0's grouped-spectra mode with inter-metabolite correlations enabled.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis target is real patient/sample spectra with measured concentrations rather than simulated data with known ground truth The study design is case-control (discrete outcome, e.g. heart transplant versus healthy) rather than a continuous covariate — use the discrete-outcome grouped mode instead Only a single spectrum is needed (e.g. to inspect one metabolite's peak pattern) — the single-spectrum mode is simpler than setting up a 100-replicate grouped simulation

skills.description: Use when you have METASPACE-ML prediction scores for target ions and sampled decoy ions with associated standard deviations (SD), and need per-ion continuous FDR confidence values rather than a single thresholded FDR cutoff.
skills.name: continuous-per-ion-fdr-computation
skills.search_text: continuous-per-ion-fdr-computation Use when you have METASPACE-ML prediction scores for target ions and sampled decoy ions with associated standard deviations (SD), and need per-ion continuous FDR confidence values rather than a single thresholded FDR cutoff. You only need a single global FDR threshold at one significance level rather than continuous per-ion confidence values Decoys were not generated by SD sampling, so no per-decoy standard deviation is available for weighting You are using the older rule-based MSM scoring system (Metabolite Signal Matching), which does not use this target-decoy FDR framework http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Reconstructs METASPACE-ML's computationally-efficient False Discovery Rate estimation by merging target and SD-weighted decoy ions into a single descending ranking and computing a Laplace-smoothed FDR value at every ion position. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-52213-9
skills.summary: Reconstructs METASPACE-ML's computationally-efficient False Discovery Rate estimation by merging target and SD-weighted decoy ions into a single descending ranking and computing a Laplace-smoothed FDR value at every ion position.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need a single global FDR threshold at one significance level rather than continuous per-ion confidence values Decoys were not generated by SD sampling, so no per-decoy standard deviation is available for weighting You are using the older rule-based MSM scoring system (Metabolite Signal Matching), which does not use this target-decoy FDR framework

skills.summary: Integrates feature-group statistical results from msFeaST into a single .json results file consumable by the interactive msFeaST visualization dashboard.

skills.description: Use when comparing one profiler's taxonomic profile against a known ground truth (e.g., a CAMI marine sample) and you need to see exactly which taxa are false positives/false negatives rather than relying on F1 or L1 scores alone.
skills.name: contrast-mode-false-positive-negative-highlighting
skills.search_text: contrast-mode-false-positive-negative-highlighting Use when comparing one profiler's taxonomic profile against a known ground truth (e.g., a CAMI marine sample) and you need to see exactly which taxa are false positives/false negatives rather than relying on F1 or L1 scores alone. No ground-truth profile exists — the article notes TAMPA contrast mode requires a gold standard to classify false positives/negatives; without one use TAMPA's normal mode to compare profiler outputs instead You need visualization of multiple profilers' relative abundances rather than profiler-vs-gold-standard error analysis (use TAMPA normal mode, c=False) Input is amplicon (16S) microbial data — the paper states metacoder-style amplicon approaches aside, TAMPA targets WGS metagenomic taxonomic profiles http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 TAMPA's contrast mode (c=True) renders a taxonomic tree in which false-positive taxa appear as red circles, false-negative taxa as blue circles, and remaining taxa as a white-to-green gradient proportional to relative error, exposing which clades a profiler misses or hallucinates despite good single-value metrics. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/gigascience/giad008
skills.summary: TAMPA's contrast mode (c=True) renders a taxonomic tree in which false-positive taxa appear as red circles, false-negative taxa as blue circles, and remaining taxa as a white-to-green gradient proportional to relative error, exposing which clades a profiler misses or hallucinates despite good single-value metrics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No ground-truth profile exists — the article notes TAMPA contrast mode requires a gold standard to classify false positives/negatives; without one use TAMPA's normal mode to compare profiler outputs instead You need visualization of multiple profilers' relative abundances rather than profiler-vs-gold-standard error analysis (use TAMPA normal mode, c=False) Input is amplicon (16S) microbial data — the paper states metacoder-style amplicon approaches aside, TAMPA targets WGS metagenomic taxonomic profiles

skills.description: Use when reproducing or adapting the FIDDLE ablation study to measure how spectrum noise augmentation, contrastive loss, and post-processing (candidate generation + rescore ranking) each affect top-1/top-5 formula accuracy, missed-atom distributions, and confidence-score ROC AUC.
skills.name: contrastive-learning-ablation
skills.search_text: contrastive-learning-ablation Use when reproducing or adapting the FIDDLE ablation study to measure how spectrum noise augmentation, contrastive loss, and post-processing (candidate generation + rescore ranking) each affect top-1/top-5 formula accuracy, missed-atom distributions, and confidence-score ROC AUC. Working with Orbitrap spectra: the paper notes no data augmentation was applied for Orbitrap training because noise addition lowered spectral similarity, so the DA ablation arm does not transfer Goal is end-to-end formula prediction rather than attribution of performance to training objectives or post-processing components Input spectra are chimeric (co-eluting) or fall outside the training distribution, where FIDDLE's accuracy degrades and ablation deltas would be confounded http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Ablation methodology for quantifying the individual contributions of data augmentation (Gaussian noise, mean 0, sd 0.1), the contrastive-learning objective, and the post-processing steps (candidate formula generation plus confidence-score ranking) to FIDDLE's formula identification performance on the MoNA Q-TOF dataset. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-025-66060-9
skills.summary: Ablation methodology for quantifying the individual contributions of data augmentation (Gaussian noise, mean 0, sd 0.1), the contrastive-learning objective, and the post-processing steps (candidate formula generation plus confidence-score ranking) to FIDDLE's formula identification performance on the MoNA Q-TOF dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Working with Orbitrap spectra: the paper notes no data augmentation was applied for Orbitrap training because noise addition lowered spectral similarity, so the DA ablation arm does not transfer Goal is end-to-end formula prediction rather than attribution of performance to training objectives or post-processing components Input spectra are chimeric (co-eluting) or fall outside the training distribution, where FIDDLE's accuracy degrades and ablation deltas would be confounded

skills.description: Use when you need annotation-free dense vector representations of ion images from preprocessed MSI pixel-by-ion matrices for downstream colocalized-ion or isotope-ion retrieval tasks.
skills.name: contrastive-learning-model-training
skills.search_text: contrastive-learning-model-training Use when you need annotation-free dense vector representations of ion images from preprocessed MSI pixel-by-ion matrices for downstream colocalized-ion or isotope-ion retrieval tasks. When manually labeled training data are available and a supervised classifier is preferable — DeepION is designed for self-supervised representation learning without manual annotation. When the goal is isotope ion identification rather than colocalized ion retrieval and the input characteristics demand the ISO-mode augmentation (intensity-dependent missing value) — do not reuse COL-mode augmentations for that task. When the input is already a reduced feature/embedding table rather than a raw preprocessed MSI pixel-by-ion matrix — the contrastive training pipeline expects unembedded ion images. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Train a SimSiam-style self-supervised contrastive model (DeepION) that learns low-dimensional representations of ion images from mass spectrometry imaging data, using MSI-specific data augmentation and a stop-gradient mechanism to avoid collapse without manual annotation. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c05002
skills.summary: Train a SimSiam-style self-supervised contrastive model (DeepION) that learns low-dimensional representations of ion images from mass spectrometry imaging data, using MSI-specific data augmentation and a stop-gradient mechanism to avoid collapse without manual annotation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When manually labeled training data are available and a supervised classifier is preferable — DeepION is designed for self-supervised representation learning without manual annotation. When the goal is isotope ion identification rather than colocalized ion retrieval and the input characteristics demand the ISO-mode augmentation (intensity-dependent missing value) — do not reuse COL-mode augmentations for that task. When the input is already a reduced feature/embedding table rather than a raw preprocessed MSI pixel-by-ion matrix — the contrastive training pipeline expects unembedded ion images.

skills.description: Use when reproducing the GLEAMS embedder training procedure: you have MassIVE-KB PSM pairs (grouped per precursor charge state) and need to train a Siamese network with contrastive loss to a 32-dimensional embedding space.
skills.name: contrastive-pair-loss-model-training
skills.search_text: contrastive-pair-loss-model-training Use when reproducing the GLEAMS embedder training procedure: you have MassIVE-KB PSM pairs (grouped per precursor charge state) and need to train a Siamese network with contrastive loss to a 32-dimensional embedding space. You only need to apply an already-trained embedding: the released gleams_82c0124b.hdf5 weights exist for this and no retraining is required. Your input is an unlabeled spectra collection with no PSM annotations — pair construction requires peptide-identified spectra to define positives and negatives. You are using non-Linux or non-CUDA hardware; GLEAMS explicitly requires Python 3.8, Linux, and a CUDA-enabled GPU. http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Trains GLEAMS's VGG-inspired Siamese neural network with a contrastive loss on balanced positive/negative MS/MS spectra pairs to produce a 32-dimensional learned embedding in which spectra from the same peptide lie close together. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-022-01496-1
skills.summary: Trains GLEAMS's VGG-inspired Siamese neural network with a contrastive loss on balanced positive/negative MS/MS spectra pairs to produce a 32-dimensional learned embedding in which spectra from the same peptide lie close together.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need to apply an already-trained embedding: the released gleams_82c0124b.hdf5 weights exist for this and no retraining is required. skills.description: Use when you need theoretical isotopic peak envelopes of a user-defined peptide sequence or chemical formula at arbitrary SIP enrichment levels (partial or full labeling), for plotting, PSM scoring, or validating proteomic SIP database-search outputs.
skills.name: convolution-based-isotopic-distribution-modeling
skills.search_text: convolution-based-isotopic-distribution-modeling Use when you need theoretical isotopic peak envelopes of a user-defined peptide sequence or chemical formula at arbitrary SIP enrichment levels (partial or full labeling), for plotting, PSM scoring, or validating proteomic SIP database-search outputs. You need isotopic fine structure (high-resolution isotope fine structure) — the FFT-based envelope method does not account for it; use Aerith's Monte Carlo multinomial simulation instead. The compound is a metabolite whose envelope you need from a known formula — the FFT-based algorithm path, not peptide unit convolution, is the intended method. You need to simulate a 100%-enriched molecular tracer workflow as in the Miso R package — Aerith's value is partial/any-level enrichment, not tracer-based metabolomics. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 Aerith's method for computing theoretical isotopic envelopes of peptide precursors and B/Y fragment ion series by sequentially convolving the isotopic envelopes of monomeric amino-acid units, with user-defined isotopic abundances (e.g., 1.07% natural 13C vs. 50% 13C SIP enrichment) handled via a C++ backend accessed through Rcpp. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c03207
skills.summary: Aerith's method for computing theoretical isotopic envelopes of peptide precursors and B/Y fragment ion series by sequentially convolving the isotopic envelopes of monomeric amino-acid units, with user-defined isotopic abundances (e.g., 1.07% natural 13C vs. 50% 13C SIP enrichment) handled via a C++ backend accessed through Rcpp.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need isotopic fine structure (high-resolution isotope fine structure) — the FFT-based envelope method does not account for it; use Aerith's Monte Carlo multinomial simulation instead. skills.search_text: corason-conserved-core-determination Use when a set of related BGCs (e.g., tauD-expansion clusters) needs a phylogeny-resolved organization beyond BiG-SCAPE GCF clustering, especially when fragmented assemblies or merged adjacent clusters split them into different GCFs. When the BGCs are so divergent that the conserved core collapses to only the query gene — the multi-locus alignment and phylogeny become uninformative. skills.description: Use when comparing a predicted MS/MS spectrum against a measured spectrum (e.g. retrieval-based MS2C ranking with Top-k) and needing to judge whether a cosine score reflects genuine spectral agreement rather than artifacts.
skills.name: cosine-similarity-metric-interpretation
skills.search_text: cosine-similarity-metric-interpretation Use when comparing a predicted MS/MS spectrum against a measured spectrum (e.g. retrieval-based MS2C ranking with Top-k) and needing to judge whether a cosine score reflects genuine spectral agreement rather than artifacts. Spectra come from unmerged acquisitions, different instrument platforms, or precursor adducts other than [M+H]+ Orbitrap-HCD — the paper explicitly flags these as unevaluated conditions The goal is formula annotation for glycans or peptides — the paper excluded these and focused on small molecules You need absolute mass accuracy guarantees; cosine similarity alone does not certify that predicted masses fall within the 10 ppm tolerance of observed peaks http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Interprets cosine similarity scores between measured and predicted MS/MS spectra (as used in FraGNNet's retrieval-based compound identification) as a match-quality metric, accounting for unexplained peaks, OS/IS support, and adduct/instrument-context caveats. metabolomics/v3 10.48550/arxiv.2404.02360
skills.summary: Interprets cosine similarity scores between measured and predicted MS/MS spectra (as used in FraGNNet's retrieval-based compound identification) as a match-quality metric, accounting for unexplained peaks, OS/IS support, and adduct/instrument-context caveats.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Spectra come from unmerged acquisitions, different instrument platforms, or precursor adducts other than [M+H]+ Orbitrap-HCD — the paper explicitly flags these as unevaluated conditions The goal is formula annotation for glycans or peptides — the paper excluded these and focused on small molecules You need absolute mass accuracy guarantees; cosine similarity alone does not certify that predicted masses fall within the 10 ppm tolerance of observed peaks

skills.summary: Compares an experimental MS2 peak list (m/z, intensity pairs) against MassBank reference spectra using the CMM 3.0 MS2 spectral-comparison service, yielding a cosine-similarity-based score per spectrum pair to support metabolite annotation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw instrument data (e.g., mzML/NetCDF) rather than an already peak-picked MS2 m/z–intensity list The task is spectral quality assessment rather than comparison — CMM 3.0 provides a separate spectral quality-assessment service for judging spectrum reliability for compound identification The query target is annotation filtering/scoring by experimental setup and compound properties, which CMM 3.0 handles through its expert-system filter rather than MS2 spectral comparison

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify or remove near-duplicate spectra in an MGF-format MS/MS library (e.g., MassSpecGym or Spectraverse), by flagging same-compound spectra pairs with cosine similarity >= 0.99.

skills.search_text: cosine-similarity-spectra-comparison Use when you need to quantify or remove near-duplicate spectra in an MGF-format MS/MS library (e.g., MassSpecGym or Spectraverse), by flagging same-compound spectra pairs with cosine similarity >= 0.99. Spectra come from different compounds — the near-duplicate criterion applies only within same-compound groups defined by the InChIKey connectivity layer (first 14 characters) and matching ion polarity The goal is de novo structural similarity or fingerprint-based scoring rather than identifying redundant spectra of the same compound Input spectra are not in MGF format and have not been parsed/harmonized with matchms (missing InChIKey or polarity metadata) http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Computes pairwise cosine similarity between MS/MS spectra with matchms and the SpectralEntropy cosine implementation to detect near-duplicate spectra within a spectral library, using the MassSpecGym criterion of cosine similarity >= 0.99 among spectra of the same compound. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c06256
skills.summary: Computes pairwise cosine similarity between MS/MS spectra with matchms and the SpectralEntropy cosine implementation to detect near-duplicate spectra within a spectral library, using the MassSpecGym criterion of cosine similarity >= 0.99 among spectra of the same compound.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Spectra come from different compounds — the near-duplicate criterion applies only within same-compound groups defined by the InChIKey connectivity layer (first 14 characters) and matching ion polarity The goal is de novo structural similarity or fingerprint-based scoring rather than identifying redundant spectra of the same compound Input spectra are not in MGF format and have not been parsed/harmonized with matchms (missing InChIKey or polarity metadata)
