skills.description: Use when assigning or validating molecular formulas from untargeted LC/HRMS MS1 peaks: you have a candidate formula and need to rank or score it by how well its theoretical isotopic envelope matches the observed MS1 isotopic profile.
skills.name: cosine-similarity-spectral-comparison
skills.search_text: cosine-similarity-spectral-comparison Use when assigning or validating molecular formulas from untargeted LC/HRMS MS1 peaks: you have a candidate formula and need to rank or score it by how well its theoretical isotopic envelope matches the observed MS1 isotopic profile. Input is MS2/MSn tandem spectra and the goal is structural or library spectral matching — this skill matches MS1 isotopic profiles only ('The IDSL.UFA pipeline only requires MS1'); use MS2-based tools instead for structure elucidation. Data are low-resolution MS or single-charge spectra lacking a resolvable isotopic envelope, so no meaningful theoretical-vs-experimental isotopic profile comparison is possible. Input is already a fully annotated, formula-assigned feature table and no isotopic-profile scoring or validation is needed. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Scores molecular formula candidates by comparing theoretical MS1 isotopic profiles (computed from IUPAC isotopic abundances, as in IDSL.UFA's IPDB) against experimentally integrated isotopic profile spectra across chromatography using pairwise cosine similarity (PCS), and validates the metric against authentic reference standards. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.2c00563
skills.summary: Scores molecular formula candidates by comparing theoretical MS1 isotopic profiles (computed from IUPAC isotopic abundances, as in IDSL.UFA's IPDB) against experimentally integrated isotopic profile spectra across chromatography using pairwise cosine similarity (PCS), and validates the metric against authentic reference standards.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is MS2/MSn tandem spectra and the goal is structural or library spectral matching — this skill matches MS1 isotopic profiles only ('The IDSL.UFA pipeline only requires MS1'); use MS2-based tools instead for structure elucidation. Data are low-resolution MS or single-charge spectra lacking a resolvable isotopic envelope, so no meaningful theoretical-vs-experimental isotopic profile comparison is possible. Input is already a fully annotated, formula-assigned feature table and no isotopic-profile scoring or validation is needed.

skills.description: Use when matching an observed EI mass spectrum against a library of candidate spectra and you need ranked similarity scores (e.g. recall@10 evaluation) under a molecular-mass filter.
skills.name: cosine-similarity-spectral-comparison
skills.search_text: cosine-similarity-spectral-comparison Use when matching an observed EI mass spectrum against a library of candidate spectra and you need ranked similarity scores (e.g. recall@10 evaluation) under a molecular-mass filter. Query molecules are not yet converted to spectra (e.g. you only have SMILES/InChI) — spectral prediction, not similarity ranking, is needed first. Candidate library spectra have not been generated and mass-filtered, so similarity would be computed against an unfiltered full library, invalidating the NEIMS evaluation protocol. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Rank mass-spectral candidates by computing the weighted cosine similarity (eq 1) between each query spectrum and every spectrum in an augmented reference library, then report recall@10. In NEIMS, library matching restricts candidates to spectra whose molecular mass is within 5 Da of the query before scoring. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acscentsci.9b00085
skills.summary: Rank mass-spectral candidates by computing the weighted cosine similarity (eq 1) between each query spectrum and every spectrum in an augmented reference library, then report recall@10. In NEIMS, library matching restricts candidates to spectra whose molecular mass is within 5 Da of the query before scoring.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Query molecules are not yet converted to spectra (e.g. you only have SMILES/InChI) — spectral prediction, not similarity ranking, is needed first. Candidate library spectra have not been generated and mass-filtered, so similarity would be computed against an unfiltered full library, invalidating the NEIMS evaluation protocol.

skills.search_text: cosine-similarity-spectral-matching Use when dereplicating untargeted LC-MS2 .mzML features against public MS2 spectral libraries (GNPS, HMDB, MassBank) and you need library-level metabolite annotations with per-match similarity scores. Query spectra have fragmentation patterns or peak shifts that break cosine similarity — the authors note cosine metrics fail here and better spectral matching metrics are needed No library spectrum exists for the feature — public spectral databases are not standardized and can only annotate spectra present in them, so compound database dereplication (SIRIUS) is the alternative route Input is already annotated candidates needing ranking/selection — that is final candidate selection via RDKit in MAW-Py, not spectral matching MAW's spectral database dereplication scheme: preprocess MS2 .mzML query spectra and pre-built spectral library R-objects (GNPS, HMDB, MassBank) with the R Spectra package, then match candidates using cosine/dot-product similarity — the GNPS-altered score at a 0.85 threshold and the unaltered dot product for HMDB/MassBank at 0.70 — plus MAW-defined mz_score/int_score metrics. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-023-00695-y
skills.summary: MAW's spectral database dereplication scheme: preprocess MS2 .mzML query spectra and pre-built spectral library R-objects (GNPS, HMDB, MassBank) with the R Spectra package, then match candidates using cosine/dot-product similarity — the GNPS-altered score at a 0.85 threshold and the unaltered dot product for HMDB/MassBank at 0.70 — plus MAW-defined mz_score/int_score metrics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Query spectra have fragmentation patterns or peak shifts that break cosine similarity — the authors note cosine metrics fail here and better spectral matching metrics are needed No library spectrum exists for the feature — public spectral databases are not standardized and can only annotate spectra present in them, so compound database dereplication (SIRIUS) is the alternative route Input is already annotated candidates needing ranking/selection — that is final candidate selection via RDKit in MAW-Py, not spectral matching

skills.search_text: cosine-spectral-similarity-benchmarking Use when tandem-MS fragmentation spectra (fragment m/z lists plus precursor m/z values) are available and the goal is to test whether a new alignment method finds structural associations that cosine-based scoring misses, especially for compounds with multiple structural modifications. Spectra are not in protonation/deprotonation mode — SIMILE is limited to protonation/deprotonation analysis, so other adduct types fall outside this benchmark's scope Only a single scoring method is needed and no head-to-head comparison against cosine similarity is intended; the skill's value is the differential call (SIMILE-significant vs. cosine-hit) per pair Spectra lack precursor m/z or fragment m/z lists, since the pair-specific similarity matrix and matching-ions report both require mzs and pmzs http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Benchmark a tandem-MS spectral alignment/scoring method (SIMILE) against cosine-based similarity scoring (GNPS) on curated compound pairs, recording which structurally related pairs each method uniquely finds and characterizing SIMILE-unique pairs by their mass deltas and maximal common substructure (MCS) categories. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-022-30118-9
skills.summary: Benchmark a tandem-MS spectral alignment/scoring method (SIMILE) against cosine-based similarity scoring (GNPS) on curated compound pairs, recording which structurally related pairs each method uniquely finds and characterizing SIMILE-unique pairs by their mass deltas and maximal common substructure (MCS) categories.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Spectra are not in protonation/deprotonation mode — SIMILE is limited to protonation/deprotonation analysis, so other adduct types fall outside this benchmark's scope Only a single scoring method is needed and no head-to-head comparison against cosine similarity is intended; the skill's value is the differential call (SIMILE-significant vs. cosine-hit) per pair Spectra lack precursor m/z or fragment m/z lists, since the pair-specific similarity matrix and matching-ions report both require mzs and pmzs

skills.description: Use when training a binary classifier on heavily imbalanced chemical labels (e.g. ~5% reactive bonds in EBoMD) where the Jaccard score TP/(TP+FN+FP) is the target metric and a random-forest base learner is desired.
skills.name: cost-sensitive-random-forest-training
skills.search_text: cost-sensitive-random-forest-training Use when training a binary classifier on heavily imbalanced chemical labels (e.g. ~5% reactive bonds in EBoMD) where the Jaccard score TP/(TP+FN+FP) is the target metric and a random-forest base learner is desired. The label distribution is roughly balanced and plain accuracy is the target metric — the 0/0/1/β cost calibration is specifically designed for the 5% reactive / 95% non-reactive EBoMD imbalance. The downstream task is metabolite/byproduct generation from already-predicted bonds (use the MetaboGen SMIRKS-rule workflow instead). Only a small number of η+η (Cyclization) instances is available — the paper notes η+η-forming reactions occurred in only 4 of 828 η-η reactions, so they were excluded from the η-η training set. http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Trains a WEKA random-forest classifier with a 0/0/1/β cost matrix via a super-learner (SL) that grid-searches 189 [β, t, N] combinations by internal 5-fold cross-validation, optimizing the Jaccard score rather than accuracy. Used in CyProduct's CypBoM module to handle the extreme 5%/95% reactive/non-reactive BoM class imbalance. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jcim.1c00144
skills.summary: Trains a WEKA random-forest classifier with a 0/0/1/β cost matrix via a super-learner (SL) that grid-searches 189 [β, t, N] combinations by internal 5-fold cross-validation, optimizing the Jaccard score rather than accuracy. Used in CyProduct's CypBoM module to handle the extreme 5%/95% reactive/non-reactive BoM class imbalance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The label distribution is roughly balanced and plain accuracy is the target metric — the 0/0/1/β cost calibration is specifically designed for the 5% reactive / 95% non-reactive EBoMD imbalance. The downstream task is metabolite/byproduct generation from already-predicted bonds (use the MetaboGen SMIRKS-rule workflow instead). Only a small number of η+η (Cyclization) instances is available — the paper notes η+η-forming reactions occurred in only 4 of 828 η-η reactions, so they were excluded from the η-η training set.

skills.description: Use when a paper reports a peak-to-metabolite funnel (e.g. 691 peaks reduced to 195 metabolites) with an annotation-class breakdown (putative, assigned class, uncertain, unknown) and the counts/percentages must be audited before reuse.
skills.name: count-consistency-verification-of-metabolite-cohorts
skills.search_text: count-consistency-verification-of-metabolite-cohorts Use when a paper reports a peak-to-metabolite funnel (e.g. 691 peaks reduced to 195 metabolites) with an annotation-class breakdown (putative, assigned class, uncertain, unknown) and the counts/percentages must be audited before reuse. The paper reports only a final feature count with no per-criterion exclusion thresholds or annotation-class fractions to reconcile. The input is already a validated feature table (e.g. the 195-metabolite matrix) and the filtering audit has already been performed. The analysis goal is downstream statistical modeling (OPLS-DA, ROC) rather than auditing the filtering funnel itself. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Verifies that the arithmetic of a metabolite filtering/annotation cascade closes: exclusion criteria applied to 691 detected GCxGC-TOFMS peaks must reconcile with the 195 retained metabolites, and the annotation-class breakdown (69+8+18+100=195, percentages summing to 100.0%) must be internally consistent. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pntd.0006215
skills.summary: Verifies that the arithmetic of a metabolite filtering/annotation cascade closes: exclusion criteria applied to 691 detected GCxGC-TOFMS peaks must reconcile with the 195 retained metabolites, and the annotation-class breakdown (69+8+18+100=195, percentages summing to 100.0%) must be internally consistent.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The paper reports only a final feature count with no per-criterion exclusion thresholds or annotation-class fractions to reconcile. The input is already a validated feature table (e.g. the 195-metabolite matrix) and the filtering audit has already been performed. The analysis goal is downstream statistical modeling (OPLS-DA, ROC) rather than auditing the filtering funnel itself.

skills.description: Use when a raw RNA-seq (or miRNA/isoform) count matrix plus phenotype file must be cleaned of low-expression features prior to normalization, batch correction, or differential expression (edgeR/DESeq2/RankProduct).
skills.name: count-matrix-expression-filtering
skills.search_text: count-matrix-expression-filtering Use when a raw RNA-seq (or miRNA/isoform) count matrix plus phenotype file must be cleaned of low-expression features prior to normalization, batch correction, or differential expression (edgeR/DESeq2/RankProduct). Input is already a normalized or batch-corrected expression table rather than a raw count matrix — re-filtering would double-process the data. Analysis of proteomics, lipidomics, or metabolomics raw data where edgeR-style count-based filtering (filterByExp) is not applicable. Filtering is requested for downstream correlation-based pathway enrichment (the correlation-based connection filtering is a distinct, later step in the workflow). http://edamontology.org/topic_0085 Filters a raw gene/miRNA/isoform count matrix to retain only detectable features before normalization and batch-effect correction, using MOI's filterByExp heuristic or a user-chosen expression cutoff configured via mom_filt_method_genes. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioadv/vbae175
skills.summary: Filters a raw gene/miRNA/isoform count matrix to retain only detectable features before normalization and batch-effect correction, using MOI's filterByExp heuristic or a user-chosen expression cutoff configured via mom_filt_method_genes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a normalized or batch-corrected expression table rather than a raw count matrix — re-filtering would double-process the data. Analysis of proteomics, lipidomics, or metabolomics raw data where edgeR-style count-based filtering (filterByExp) is not applicable. Filtering is requested for downstream correlation-based pathway enrichment (the correlation-based connection filtering is a distinct, later step in the workflow).

skills.search_text: count-matrix-statistical-testing Use when you have a filtered, normalized, batch-corrected gene or isoform count matrix plus a phenotype file and need differential expression testing between conditions, or Salmon quant.sf files needing isoform switch analysis. skills.description: Use when metabolite data has already been condition-prepared with MInfer's prepare_data and a per-condition covariance matrix must be generated and exported as the cov argument for calculate_jacobian.
skills.name: covariance-matrix-io-for-network-inference
skills.search_text: covariance-matrix-io-for-network-inference Use when metabolite data has already been condition-prepared with MInfer's prepare_data and a per-condition covariance matrix must be generated and exported as the cov argument for calculate_jacobian. The input is raw metabolite data (met_input) that has not yet been condition-grouped by prepare_data — generate_covariance consumes the prepared object, not raw intensities. The goal is the interaction network itself — once the covariance matrix exists, proceed to calculate_jacobian rather than re-running covariance generation. Data spans multiple conditions (e.g. 6C and 16C) — each condition requires its own generate_covariance call (cov_6C and cov_16C); do not pool conditions into a single call. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Computes and exports the per-condition covariance matrix in MInfer's workflow: generate_covariance turns a condition-prepared metabolite matrix (e.g. data_6C with num_tp = 1) into the square, symmetric covariance matrix that serves as the cov input to calculate_jacobian for Jacobian-based metabolite network inference. metabolomics/v3 10.1016/j.cmpb.2025.108672
skills.summary: Computes and exports the per-condition covariance matrix in MInfer's workflow: generate_covariance turns a condition-prepared metabolite matrix (e.g. data_6C with num_tp = 1) into the square, symmetric covariance matrix that serves as the cov input to calculate_jacobian for Jacobian-based metabolite network inference.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw metabolite data (met_input) that has not yet been condition-grouped by prepare_data — generate_covariance consumes the prepared object, not raw intensities. The goal is the interaction network itself — once the covariance matrix exists, proceed to calculate_jacobian rather than re-running covariance generation. Data spans multiple conditions (e.g. 6C and 16C) — each condition requires its own generate_covariance call (cov_6C and cov_16C); do not pool conditions into a single call.

skills.description: Use when a missing-value imputation benchmark needs a complete simulated metabolomics data matrix with realistic covariance and group structure, so MNAR patterns can be injected and imputation accuracy be measured against known truth.
skills.name: covariance-matrix-svd-preservation
skills.search_text: covariance-matrix-svd-preservation Use when a missing-value imputation benchmark needs a complete simulated metabolomics data matrix with realistic covariance and group structure, so MNAR patterns can be injected and imputation accuracy be measured against known truth. When the goal is to impute already missing values in a real dataset — this skill only generates a complete simulation with no missing values. When the target data structure is not covariance-based multivariate normal (e.g. count data or compositional data), since the generator assumes a multivariate normal draw with covariance Cov. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Generates a simulated metabolomics dataset by computing a covariance matrix from a real targeted metabolomics dataset (P=76 FFAs and BAs), then repeatedly drawing multivariate-normal sample blocks with per-variable means N(0, 0.5^2) while preserving the covariance via SVD, producing a complete data_sim.csv matrix without missing values. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005973
skills.summary: Generates a simulated metabolomics dataset by computing a covariance matrix from a real targeted metabolomics dataset (P=76 FFAs and BAs), then repeatedly drawing multivariate-normal sample blocks with per-variable means N(0, 0.5^2) while preserving the covariance via SVD, producing a complete data_sim.csv matrix without missing values.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is to impute already missing values in a real dataset — this skill only generates a complete simulation with no missing values. When the target data structure is not covariance-based multivariate normal (e.g. count data or compositional data), since the generator assumes a multivariate normal draw with covariance Cov.

skills.description: Use when performing transcriptomics differential expression testing on RNA-seq count matrices where sample metadata contains confounders (e.g. CONDITION, SEX, AGE columns) that must be included in the design formula before filtering significant genes.
skills.name: covariate-adjusted-glm-modeling
skills.search_text: covariate-adjusted-glm-modeling Use when performing transcriptomics differential expression testing on RNA-seq count matrices where sample metadata contains confounders (e.g. CONDITION, SEX, AGE columns) that must be included in the design formula before filtering significant genes. The input is already a normalized feature/abundance table rather than raw RNA-seq counts requiring a DESeq2 negative-binomial model The metabolomics module is needed — BiomiX quantifies peak differences via the Wilcoxon test with FDR correction, not a covariate-adjusted GLM Only QC/exploration is required (scatterplots, PCA, correlation heatmaps, UMAP) — the preview-QC Shiny interface handles this without GLM fitting http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Fit a negative-binomial generalized linear model (DESeq2) with the biological condition of interest plus nuisance covariates (e.g. SEX and AGE) in the design formula, to identify differentially expressed genes while correcting for unwanted variation, as demonstrated in BiomiX's transcriptomics pipeline on the PTB whole-blood dataset (ENA PRJNA971365). metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-024-06022-y
skills.summary: Fit a negative-binomial generalized linear model (DESeq2) with the biological condition of interest plus nuisance covariates (e.g. SEX and AGE) in the design formula, to identify differentially expressed genes while correcting for unwanted variation, as demonstrated in BiomiX's transcriptomics pipeline on the PTB whole-blood dataset (ENA PRJNA971365).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a normalized feature/abundance table rather than raw RNA-seq counts requiring a DESeq2 negative-binomial model The metabolomics module is needed — BiomiX quantifies peak differences via the Wilcoxon test with FDR correction, not a covariate-adjusted GLM Only QC/exploration is required (scatterplots, PCA, correlation heatmaps, UMAP) — the preview-QC Shiny interface handles this without GLM fitting

skills.description: Use when a metabolomics or proteomics feature table has study covariates (metadata beyond the primary group label) and you need to test whether covariate adjustment changes which features are statistically significant versus plain ANOVA/t-tests.

skills.search_text: covariate-adjusted-linear-modeling-ancova Use when a metabolomics or proteomics feature table has study covariates (metadata beyond the primary group label) and you need to test whether covariate adjustment changes which features are statistically significant versus plain ANOVA/t-tests. The analysis goal is only plain two-group or multi-group testing with no covariates of interest — POMA's univariate tests alone suffice The data are raw spectra requiring upstream MS processing — the paper directs that work to the RforMassSpectrometry packages before migrating to POMA for statistical analysis The metadata file lacks covariate columns beyond the group label, so no adjusted model can be fit Method for reanalyzing POMAShiny/POMA univariate metabolomics results (e.g. ST000284 three-group targeted metabolomics data) with covariate-adjusted linear models (ANCOVA and the limma framework) and comparing significant feature sets against plain t-test/ANOVA results. The paper claims that covariate-combining methods such as ANCOVA or limma improve the accuracy and understanding of POMAShiny analyses.

skills.description: Use when a lipidomics dataset (e.g. Metabolomics Workbench study ST001111) has loaded clinical variables and the differential-abundance contrast may be confounded by a covariate such as Race, requiring a factorial model like ~ Race + SampleType.
skills.name: covariate-adjusted-lipidomics-statistics
skills.search_text: covariate-adjusted-lipidomics-statistics Use when a lipidomics dataset (e.g. Metabolomics Workbench study ST001111) has loaded clinical variables and the differential-abundance contrast may be confounded by a covariate such as Race, requiring a factorial model like ~ Race + SampleType. The analysis is a simple two-group comparison with no confounding variable to adjust for — use lipidr's univariate two-group differential analysis instead of a factorial de_design model. The data are not lipidomics intensities with sample annotation (e.g. already a feature table without clinical variables loaded) — the design matrix must be built from loaded clinical variables. The dataset lacks any loaded clinical covariates; de_design requires sample annotation containing both the coefficient of interest and the adjustment covariate. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Perform covariate-adjusted differential abundance analysis of lipid molecules in a lipidomics dataset using lipidr's limma-based de_design function, so the effect of a primary variable (e.g. SampleType Cancer vs Benign) is estimated while correcting for confounders (e.g. Race), then export significant molecules as CSV and inspect them with a volcano plot. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.0c00082
skills.summary: Perform covariate-adjusted differential abundance analysis of lipid molecules in a lipidomics dataset using lipidr's limma-based de_design function, so the effect of a primary variable (e.g. SampleType Cancer vs Benign) is estimated while correcting for confounders (e.g. Race), then export significant molecules as CSV and inspect them with a volcano plot.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis is a simple two-group comparison with no confounding variable to adjust for — use lipidr's univariate two-group differential analysis instead of a factorial de_design model. The data are not lipidomics intensities with sample annotation (e.g. already a feature table without clinical variables loaded) — the design matrix must be built from loaded clinical variables. The dataset lacks any loaded clinical covariates; de_design requires sample annotation containing both the coefficient of interest and the adjustment covariate.

skills.description: Use when the goal is a supervised classification model (e.g., breast cancer vs. control) from metabolomics and/or gene-expression data where covariate adjustment and feature filtering must be demonstrated against reference metrics like Q2Y = 0.701.
skills.name: covariate-adjusted-prediction-modeling
skills.search_text: covariate-adjusted-prediction-modeling Use when the goal is a supervised classification model (e.g., breast cancer vs. control) from metabolomics and/or gene-expression data where covariate adjustment and feature filtering must be demonstrated against reference metrics like Q2Y = 0.701. The task is unsupervised dimensionality reduction or exploratory visualization rather than class prediction — use PCA/other reduction modules instead. skills.summary: Builds covariate-adjusted PLS/PLS-DA classification models in SMART 2.0, applying a dual-filtering variable selection strategy (pFDR < 0.05 combined with a top-10 VIP cutoff) to maximize cross-validated predictive accuracy (Q2Y) on integrated multiomics data such as the breast cancer gene-expression and metabolomics datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is unsupervised dimensionality reduction or exploratory visualization rather than class prediction — use PCA/other reduction modules instead. Input data are raw LC-MS vendor files (.raw, .d, mzXML) that still require SMART's data import, peak analysis, and preprocessing modules before any PLS-DA modeling is meaningful. The dataset lacks a categorical phenotype and covariates, so no covariate-adjusted PLS-DA comparison can be constructed.

skills.description: Use when scanning ~249 NMR metabolic biomarkers (plus derived ratios) for associations with incident CAD or stroke in UK Biobank, and results must be adjusted for age and sex with prevalent cases and lipid-lowering medication users excluded.
skills.name: covariate-adjustment-confounder-control
skills.search_text: covariate-adjustment-confounder-control Use when scanning ~249 NMR metabolic biomarkers (plus derived ratios) for associations with incident CAD or stroke in UK Biobank, and results must be adjusted for age and sex with prevalent cases and lipid-lowering medication users excluded. When estimating effects of lipid-lowering medication itself — the skill excludes medication users as a confounder-control strategy rather than modeling medication as an exposure. Adjusts biomarker-disease association analyses in the UK Biobank NMR metabolomics data for core demographic confounders (age, sex) and removes the major systematic biological influence of lipid-lowering medication use by exclusion, when scanning biomarker associations with incident coronary artery disease and stroke via Cox proportional hazards models. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41597-023-01949-y
skills.summary: Adjusts biomarker-disease association analyses in the UK Biobank NMR metabolomics data for core demographic confounders (age, sex) and removes the major systematic biological influence of lipid-lowering medication use by exclusion, when scanning biomarker associations with incident coronary artery disease and stroke via Cox proportional hazards models.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When estimating effects of lipid-lowering medication itself — the skill excludes medication users as a confounder-control strategy rather than modeling medication as an exposure. When running remove_technical_variation() itself — the README warns that no prefiltering of samples or columns should be performed before that function; exclusion steps belong to downstream association analysis. skills.search_text: cox-proportional-hazards-survival-analysis Use when cohort-level survival summary statistics (e.g. 226 Nightingale NMR metabolic biomarkers vs. all-cause mortality) must be combined across cohorts via fixed-effect meta-analysis to select an independent, significant biomarker set. The goal is clinical patient classification: the article notes the score built from per-cohort scaled biomarker values 'is not yet suitable for classification of patients in the clinic'; a concentration-unit score from individual-level data is needed instead. Biomarker values are already transformed/scaled — applying x+1, log-transform, and per-cohort scaling again would double-transform the data. The question is predictive performance benchmarking (C-statistic, IDI against conventional risk factors) rather than identification of independently associated biomarkers. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Per-cohort Cox proportional hazards modelling with age at blood sampling as the time scale, followed by fixed-effect meta-analysis and a forward-backward stepwise selection on Bonferroni-corrected P values, to identify circulating metabolic biomarkers independently associated with all-cause mortality. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-019-11311-9

The question is predictive performance benchmarking (C-statistic, IDI against conventional risk factors) rather than identification of independently associated biomarkers.

skills.search_text: cpp-cython-interface-wrapping Use when a Python analysis pipeline needs to call compiled C++ code — e.g. an optimized spectrum/MGF parser for MS data — and raw-file parsing dominates runtime (peak information takes up over 95% of the data volume in raw files). The bottleneck is not native parsing — e.g. when spectral clustering or distance computation dominates and GPU kernels (HyperSpec's HD encoding / Hamming distance) are the right optimization target instead. The data are already numerical peak arrays or preprocessed spectra; re-wrapping a parser would add overhead with no benefit. The target environment cannot compile native extensions (no C++14 toolchain, no CUDA/NVIDIA GPU setup for the surrounding HyperSpec pipeline, or no Cython available), in which case a pure-Python or prebuilt-binary route is safer. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 Wrap a high-performance C++ parser (built with the Spirit X3 parser in Boost C++14) into Cython interfaces callable from Python, so a fast MGF spectrum parser can be exposed to a Python pipeline without giving up native parsing speed on large MS files. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.2c00612
skills.summary: Wrap a high-performance C++ parser (built with the Spirit X3 parser in Boost C++14) into Cython interfaces callable from Python, so a fast MGF spectrum parser can be exposed to a Python pipeline without giving up native parsing speed on large MS files.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The bottleneck is not native parsing — e.g. when spectral clustering or distance computation dominates and GPU kernels (HyperSpec's HD encoding / Hamming distance) are the right optimization target instead. The target environment cannot compile native extensions (no C++14 toolchain, no CUDA/NVIDIA GPU setup for the surrounding HyperSpec pipeline, or no Cython available), in which case a pure-Python or prebuilt-binary route is safer.

skills.description: Use when the goal is metabolite presence/absence identification from 1H NMR spectra using a nine-metabolite reference set, and simulated augmented spectra (NMRQNet pipeline) are available for training and testing.
skills.name: crnn-metabolite-identification-model-training
skills.search_text: crnn-metabolite-identification-model-training Use when the goal is metabolite presence/absence identification from 1H NMR spectra using a nine-metabolite reference set, and simulated augmented spectra (NMRQNet pipeline) are available for training and testing. The task is quantification (reconstructing spectra and estimating relative concentrations, scored by RMSE/Pearson correlation) rather than presence/absence identification. The input spectra are experimental plasma samples (e.g. EDTA/heparin/citrate plasma) rather than NMRQNet-simulated spectra; this skill's 92% accuracy applies to the simulated test set. The metabolite library differs substantially from the nine-metabolite reference set, so the reported 0.978–0.995 per-metabolite accuracies no longer apply. http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 Trains NMRQNet's CRNN (CNN + GRU) model on simulated nine-metabolite 1H NMR spectra to predict presence/absence of each metabolite, and evaluates per-metabolite and overall identification accuracy on a held-out simulated test set. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2023.03.01.530642
skills.summary: Trains NMRQNet's CRNN (CNN + GRU) model on simulated nine-metabolite 1H NMR spectra to predict presence/absence of each metabolite, and evaluates per-metabolite and overall identification accuracy on a held-out simulated test set.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is quantification (reconstructing spectra and estimating relative concentrations, scored by RMSE/Pearson correlation) rather than presence/absence identification. The metabolite library differs substantially from the nine-metabolite reference set, so the reported 0.978–0.995 per-metabolite accuracies no longer apply.

skills.description: Decision support for validating disease-metabolite associations when targeted quantitative measurements (e.g. conjugated bile acid mg/kg from LC-MS/MS fecal extracts) are available alongside binary phenotype labels such as active vs inactive Crohn's disease status.
skills.name: crohn-disease-phenotype-association-testing
skills.search_text: crohn-disease-phenotype-association-testing Decision support for validating disease-metabolite associations when targeted quantitative measurements (e.g. conjugated bile acid mg/kg from LC-MS/MS fecal extracts) are available alongside binary phenotype labels such as active vs inactive Crohn's disease status. When the goal is discovery of candidate compounds rather than testing pre-specified analytes — use reverse metabolomics (synthesized standards + MASST searches of public data) instead, since this skill requires a defined analyte panel with absolute concentrations. When the outcome variable is multi-class or continuous (e.g. a continuous disease-activity score) rather than a two-group phenotype split like active vs inactive, where a one-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum design does not apply. When concentrations are relative (peak-area-only) without internal-standard normalization and matrix-matched calibration, since the reported CD-only increase of conjugated bile acids was quantified in mg/kg against a sulfadimethoxine standard. http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 http://edamontology.org/topic_3337 Statistical association testing that links targeted metabolite concentrations to Crohn's disease phenotype, e.g. one-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests of 19 conjugated bile acids quantified in mg/kg from the MSV000092337 Q-ToF fecal cohort, to confirm reverse-metabolomics discoveries across human IBD cohorts. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41586-023-06906-8
skills.summary: Statistical association testing that links targeted metabolite concentrations to Crohn's disease phenotype, e.g. one-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests of 19 conjugated bile acids quantified in mg/kg from the MSV000092337 Q-ToF fecal cohort, to confirm reverse-metabolomics discoveries across human IBD cohorts.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is discovery of candidate compounds rather than testing pre-specified analytes — use reverse metabolomics (synthesized standards + MASST searches of public data) instead, since this skill requires a defined analyte panel with absolute concentrations. When the outcome variable is multi-class or continuous (e.g. a continuous disease-activity score) rather than a two-group phenotype split like active vs inactive, where a one-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum design does not apply. When concentrations are relative (peak-area-only) without internal-standard normalization and matrix-matched calibration, since the reported CD-only increase of conjugated bile acids was quantified in mg/kg against a sulfadimethoxine standard.

skills.search_text: cross-cohort-risk-score-validation Use when a risk score's weights are fitted in a training cohort (e.g. Estonian Biobank, Supplementary Table 4) and must be tested for 5- and 10-year mortality prediction in a separate validation cohort (e.g. FINRISK 1997, 7603 individuals, 1213 deaths). The goal is clinical patient classification — the score is based on scaled biomarker values created separately per cohort, so it is not yet suitable for classifying patients in the clinic The same cohort is used for both weight estimation and predictive testing — this inflates performance (the paper derives weights in the Estonian Biobank specifically to avoid overestimation) The outcome is a short-term endpoint rather than intermediate- and long-term (5–10 years) all-cause mortality http://edamontology.org/topic_3053 Trains a weighted mortality risk score in one biobank cohort and validates its predictive accuracy out-of-cohort, mirroring the Deelen et al. design where Cox-derived weights from the Estonian Biobank were tested in FINRISK 1997 using Harrell C-statistics and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI). metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-019-11311-9
skills.summary: Trains a weighted mortality risk score in one biobank cohort and validates its predictive accuracy out-of-cohort, mirroring the Deelen et al. design where Cox-derived weights from the Estonian Biobank were tested in FINRISK 1997 using Harrell C-statistics and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is clinical patient classification — the score is based on scaled biomarker values created separately per cohort, so it is not yet suitable for classifying patients in the clinic The same cohort is used for both weight estimation and predictive testing — this inflates performance (the paper derives weights in the Estonian Biobank specifically to avoid overestimation) The outcome is a short-term endpoint rather than intermediate- and long-term (5–10 years) all-cause mortality

skills.description: Use when evaluating whether a domain-specific MS data compressor (e.g. ZDPD, Stack-ZDPD, ZDVB) beats a general-purpose codec like Zlib on the same m/z arrays, using size ratio and decoding-time ratio as the metrics.
skills.name: cross-compressor-size-ratio-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-compressor-size-ratio-analysis Use when evaluating whether a domain-specific MS data compressor (e.g. ZDPD, Stack-ZDPD, ZDVB) beats a general-purpose codec like Zlib on the same m/z arrays, using size ratio and decoding-time ratio as the metrics. When compressing intensity arrays rather than m/z arrays — the ZDPD-vs-Zlib result is specific to m/z data; Aird uses separate strategies for intensity (e.g. Log10 compressor, Ignore Zero Intensity Point filtering) When the goal is a lossless byte-identical format comparison, since ZDPD relies on controllable-precision quantization of floating-point m/z to integers before compression When evaluating the newest Aird compressors — Stack-ZDPD and ZDVB supersede the ZDPD kernel (5–20% and 10–20% better compression respectively), so a ZDPD-only baseline understates current Aird performance http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Benchmark methodology for comparing a specialized m/z compressor (Aird's ZDPD: delta coding + FastPfor + Zlib wrapper) against a general-purpose baseline (Zlib-only, level 6) by measuring compressed byte size and decoding wall-clock time over the same spectra. The paper reports ZDPD reaches ~55% of Zlib-only m/z size while decoding in ~33% of Zlib's time via SIMD. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-021-04490-0
skills.summary: Benchmark methodology for comparing a specialized m/z compressor (Aird's ZDPD: delta coding + FastPfor + Zlib wrapper) against a general-purpose baseline (Zlib-only, level 6) by measuring compressed byte size and decoding wall-clock time over the same spectra. The paper reports ZDPD reaches ~55% of Zlib-only m/z size while decoding in ~33% of Zlib's time via SIMD.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When compressing intensity arrays rather than m/z arrays — the ZDPD-vs-Zlib result is specific to m/z data; Aird uses separate strategies for intensity (e.g. Log10 compressor, Ignore Zero Intensity Point filtering) When the goal is a lossless byte-identical format comparison, since ZDPD relies on controllable-precision quantization of floating-point m/z to integers before compression When evaluating the newest Aird compressors — Stack-ZDPD and ZDVB supersede the ZDPD kernel (5–20% and 10–20% better compression respectively), so a ZDPD-only baseline understates current Aird performance

skills.description: Use when MOCCal is applied to datasets acquired under altered instrument settings (e.g. ramped traveling wave velocity instead of static) and you must quantify whether class-assignment rates and calibration errors remain comparable before trusting downstream CCS values.
skills.name: cross-condition-performance-comparison-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-condition-performance-comparison-analysis Use when MOCCal is applied to datasets acquired under altered instrument settings (e.g. ramped traveling wave velocity instead of static) and you must quantify whether class-assignment rates and calibration errors remain comparable before trusting downstream CCS values. Input is a single-condition dataset with no reference condition processed under the same MOCCal pipeline — there is nothing to compare The goal is feature identification or CCS calibration itself rather than assessing robustness across acquisition settings (use the MOCCal calibration skill instead) Data are not traveling-wave IM-MS acquisitions (MOCCal is built around TWIM power-law calibrations and arrival-time extraction) http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 A structured side-by-side benchmarking procedure that evaluates whether MOCCal's biomolecular class assignment and TWCCSN2 calibration accuracy are stable across instrument acquisition conditions, e.g. static 600 m/s traveling wave versus ramped wave velocity, using the identical calibration pipeline on each dataset. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c04290
skills.summary: A structured side-by-side benchmarking procedure that evaluates whether MOCCal's biomolecular class assignment and TWCCSN2 calibration accuracy are stable across instrument acquisition conditions, e.g. static 600 m/s traveling wave versus ramped wave velocity, using the identical calibration pipeline on each dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a single-condition dataset with no reference condition processed under the same MOCCal pipeline — there is nothing to compare The goal is feature identification or CCS calibration itself rather than assessing robustness across acquisition settings (use the MOCCal calibration skill instead) Data are not traveling-wave IM-MS acquisitions (MOCCal is built around TWIM power-law calibrations and arrival-time extraction)

skills.description: Use when comparing batch-correction methods on multi-batch untargeted metabolomics data (e.g. the Cherkaoui et al. cancer-cell-line dataset) and you need quantitative metrics to rank methods or test robustness of normalization hyperparameters.
skills.name: cross-correlation-batch-correction-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-correlation-batch-correction-evaluation Use when comparing batch-correction methods on multi-batch untargeted metabolomics data (e.g. the Cherkaoui et al. cancer-cell-line dataset) and you need quantitative metrics to rank methods or test robustness of normalization hyperparameters. Data are single-batch with no replicate reference samples across batches, so cross-correlation of interbatch replicates cannot be computed Evaluating performance claims on datasets other than multi-batch untargeted metabolomics (the metrics rely on replicate measurements across batches of MS data) You need per-feature differential analysis rather than method-level normalization quality ranking http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Evaluation methodology from the RALPS paper (Dmitrenko et al., Bioinformatics 2023) that judges multi-batch metabolomics normalization quality by computing cross-correlation improvement of replicate measurements across batches, spectral preservation, and the fraction of negative values in normalized matrices. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad096
skills.summary: Evaluation methodology from the RALPS paper (Dmitrenko et al., Bioinformatics 2023) that judges multi-batch metabolomics normalization quality by computing cross-correlation improvement of replicate measurements across batches, spectral preservation, and the fraction of negative values in normalized matrices.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are single-batch with no replicate reference samples across batches, so cross-correlation of interbatch replicates cannot be computed Evaluating performance claims on datasets other than multi-batch untargeted metabolomics (the metrics rely on replicate measurements across batches of MS data) You need per-feature differential analysis rather than method-level normalization quality ranking

skills.description: Use when raw LC/MS data in mzML format must be converted into a drift-corrected MS1 feature table without user-tuned parameters, QC samples, or prior knowledge of retention-time drift.
skills.name: cross-correlation-rt-drift-alignment
skills.search_text: cross-correlation-rt-drift-alignment Use when raw LC/MS data in mzML format must be converted into a drift-corrected MS1 feature table without user-tuned parameters, QC samples, or prior knowledge of retention-time drift. The input is already a feature table (e.g., the CSV matrices consumed by mzEmbed pretraining/finetuning) rather than raw mzML files — mzLearn's detection/alignment stage operates on raw LC/MS data The goal includes de-isotoping, compound annotation, or MS/MS identification — mzLearn outputs are limited to the ion MS1 level and these must be handled by downstream workflows You need a fast, interactive run: iterative learning can take up to 2.5 days on a single machine with no parallel multi-node processing implemented http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 mzLearn's data-driven MS1 signal detection and alignment core: it recursively partitions rt/m/z space into dynamically resized patches, filters them by auto-correlation, aligns them across LC/MS files by sliding cross-correlation, and learns thresholds from highest-quality 'pin' patches — requiring no user-set parameters or QC samples. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.01.26.634927
skills.summary: mzLearn's data-driven MS1 signal detection and alignment core: it recursively partitions rt/m/z space into dynamically resized patches, filters them by auto-correlation, aligns them across LC/MS files by sliding cross-correlation, and learns thresholds from highest-quality 'pin' patches — requiring no user-set parameters or QC samples.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a feature table (e.g., the CSV matrices consumed by mzEmbed pretraining/finetuning) rather than raw mzML files — mzLearn's detection/alignment stage operates on raw LC/MS data The goal includes de-isotoping, compound annotation, or MS/MS identification — mzLearn outputs are limited to the ion MS1 level and these must be handled by downstream workflows You need a fast, interactive run: iterative learning can take up to 2.5 days on a single machine with no parallel multi-node processing implemented

skills.description: Use when a series of 1D NMR spectra must be aligned prior to multivariate analysis and individual segments show chemical-shift offsets relative to a designated reference spectrum.
skills.name: cross-correlation-shift-estimation
skills.search_text: cross-correlation-shift-estimation Use when a series of 1D NMR spectra must be aligned prior to multivariate analysis and individual segments show chemical-shift offsets relative to a designated reference spectrum. The segment has no reference signal — MetaboLabPy performs no alignment when reference signal is lacking in the chosen region The input is 2D-NMR data or a metabolite identification/isotopomer task — use the metabolabpytools package for isotopomer distributions from NMR multiplet and GC-MS data instead Spectra are already shift-aligned and the goal is another pre-processing step such as spectral scaling or variance stabilisation http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 Estimates the optimum chemical-shift offset for each spectrum in a 1D-NMR series by simple cross-correlation of a user-selected spectral segment against a chosen reference spectrum, as implemented in MetaboLabPy's segmental alignment. It removes pH/instrument-induced shift variation before multivariate statistical analysis of metabolomics spectra. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo15010048
skills.summary: Estimates the optimum chemical-shift offset for each spectrum in a 1D-NMR series by simple cross-correlation of a user-selected spectral segment against a chosen reference spectrum, as implemented in MetaboLabPy's segmental alignment. It removes pH/instrument-induced shift variation before multivariate statistical analysis of metabolomics spectra.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The segment has no reference signal — MetaboLabPy performs no alignment when reference signal is lacking in the chosen region The input is 2D-NMR data or a metabolite identification/isotopomer task — use the metabolabpytools package for isotopomer distributions from NMR multiplet and GC-MS data instead Spectra are already shift-aligned and the goal is another pre-processing step such as spectral scaling or variance stabilisation

skills.description: Use when a CRNN (or similar) initial NMR reconstruction exhibits a global positional offset relative to the target plasma spectrum and metabolite candidates must be aligned before local optimization.
skills.name: cross-correlation-spectral-alignment
skills.search_text: cross-correlation-spectral-alignment Use when a CRNN (or similar) initial NMR reconstruction exhibits a global positional offset relative to the target plasma spectrum and metabolite candidates must be aligned before local optimization. The offset is a local or per-metabolite misalignment rather than a global positional offset of the whole spectrum — this step applies one shift to all metabolite candidates and defers finer alignment to NMRQNet's local optimization. Input spectra are already positionally aligned to the target, so a -150 to +150 step shift search would be redundant. Data are not 1H NMR plasma spectra in the NMRQNet csv format (e.g. raw FID files or feature tables). http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 A global positional correction step from NMRQNet that aligns a CRNN initial reconstruction to its target plasma 1H NMR spectrum by sliding the reconstruction over shifts from -150 to +150 steps and selecting the shift whose 30-region accumulated correlation with the target is maximal. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2023.03.01.530642
skills.summary: A global positional correction step from NMRQNet that aligns a CRNN initial reconstruction to its target plasma 1H NMR spectrum by sliding the reconstruction over shifts from -150 to +150 steps and selecting the shift whose 30-region accumulated correlation with the target is maximal.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The offset is a local or per-metabolite misalignment rather than a global positional offset of the whole spectrum — this step applies one shift to all metabolite candidates and defers finer alignment to NMRQNet's local optimization. Input spectra are already positionally aligned to the target, so a -150 to +150 step shift search would be redundant. Data are not 1H NMR plasma spectra in the NMRQNet csv format (e.g. raw FID files or feature tables).

skills.description: Use when evaluating annotation coverage of an integrated pathway database: you need to compute per-source-database uniqueness and multi-database overlap percentages for metabolite and gene analytes, e.g. to reproduce Figure-2-style coverage statistics from the RaMP MySQL dump.
skills.name: cross-database-analyte-overlap-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-database-analyte-overlap-analysis Use when evaluating annotation coverage of an integrated pathway database: you need to compute per-source-database uniqueness and multi-database overlap percentages for metabolite and gene analytes, e.g. to reproduce Figure-2-style coverage statistics from the RaMP MySQL dump. When the goal is pathway or chemical enrichment testing rather than coverage statistics — use RaMP's runFisherTest / runCombinedFisherTest / FilterFishersResults pipeline instead When working with RaMP-DB 3.0, which draws annotations from more than four sources (HMDB, KEGG via HMDB, Lipid-MAPS, WikiPathways, Reactome, CheBI, PFOCR, RefMet, Rhea) — the four-database overlap framing and 0.05%/13.2% figures no longer apply When analyte identifiers have not been reconciled/synonym-mapped across source databases — unmatched IDs would silently deflate cross-database overlap counts http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Quantifies how many metabolites and genes in the RaMP relational pathway database are annotated by exactly one versus multiple source databases (KEGG, Reactome, HMDB, WikiPathways), including the fraction shared across all four. This exposes the annotation coverage gaps that motivate RaMP's integrated, multi-source design. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo8010016
skills.summary: Quantifies how many metabolites and genes in the RaMP relational pathway database are annotated by exactly one versus multiple source databases (KEGG, Reactome, HMDB, WikiPathways), including the fraction shared across all four. This exposes the annotation coverage gaps that motivate RaMP's integrated, multi-source design.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is pathway or chemical enrichment testing rather than coverage statistics — use RaMP's runFisherTest / runCombinedFisherTest / FilterFishersResults pipeline instead When working with RaMP-DB 3.0, which draws annotations from more than four sources (HMDB, KEGG via HMDB, Lipid-MAPS, WikiPathways, Reactome, CheBI, PFOCR, RefMet, Rhea) — the four-database overlap framing and 0.05%/13.2% figures no longer apply When analyte identifiers have not been reconciled/synonym-mapped across source databases — unmatched IDs would silently deflate cross-database overlap counts

skills.description: Use when evaluating CCS prediction models on CCSBase and/or METLIN-CCS data — same-database, cross-database (train-metlin-test-ccsbase), or combined-dataset splits — to quantify generalizability via R2, RMSE, and MRE.
skills.name: cross-database-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cross-database-benchmarking Use when evaluating CCS prediction models on CCSBase and/or METLIN-CCS data — same-database, cross-database (train-metlin-test-ccsbase), or combined-dataset splits — to quantify generalizability via R2, RMSE, and MRE. The goal is predicting CCS for new compounds with an already-trained model rather than benchmarking model performance against reference databases The CCS data comes from a different database or adduct set outside CCSBase/METLIN-CCS (e.g. non-[M+H]+, [M+Na]+, [M-H]- adducts), so the trained models and splits are not applicable The focus is confidence-model filtering or applicability-domain analysis rather than head-to-head model benchmarking http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_3335 Benchmark GNN-based CCS prediction models (SigmaCCS, GraphCCS, Mol2CCS) under matched training/evaluation configurations on the CCSBase (v1.3) and METLIN-CCS databases to quantify in-domain accuracy and cross-database generalizability. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00899-w
skills.summary: Benchmark GNN-based CCS prediction models (SigmaCCS, GraphCCS, Mol2CCS) under matched training/evaluation configurations on the CCSBase (v1.3) and METLIN-CCS databases to quantify in-domain accuracy and cross-database generalizability.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is predicting CCS for new compounds with an already-trained model rather than benchmarking model performance against reference databases The CCS data comes from a different database or adduct set outside CCSBase/METLIN-CCS (e.g. non-[M+H]+, [M+Na]+, [M-H]- adducts), so the trained models and splits are not applicable The focus is confidence-model filtering or applicability-domain analysis rather than head-to-head model benchmarking

skills.description: Use when a source article discusses multiple tools or databases side by side with respect to one capability (e.g., programmatic sample-level meta-analysis) and the design choices behind each must be compared and valenced in a tabular output.
skills.name: cross-database-comparison-tabulation
skills.search_text: cross-database-comparison-tabulation Use when a source article discusses multiple tools or databases side by side with respect to one capability (e.g., programmatic sample-level meta-analysis) and the design choices behind each must be compared and valenced in a tabular output. The article discusses only one tool with no side-by-side comparison, so no cross-tool valence contrast is possible. The authors describe tools only generically without attributing specific design choices (e.g., vocabulary constraints, API availability) that can be individually classified. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Extracts and tabulates individual design choices that authors attribute to each of several related tools/databases (here Metabolomics Workbench, ReDU, and MetaboLights), classifying each choice as favorable or hindering for a stated purpose such as programmatic sample-level meta-analysis. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo13080941
skills.summary: Extracts and tabulates individual design choices that authors attribute to each of several related tools/databases (here Metabolomics Workbench, ReDU, and MetaboLights), classifying each choice as favorable or hindering for a stated purpose such as programmatic sample-level meta-analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The article discusses only one tool with no side-by-side comparison, so no cross-tool valence contrast is possible. The authors describe tools only generically without attributing specific design choices (e.g., vocabulary constraints, API availability) that can be individually classified.

skills.search_text: cross-database-consistency-benchmarking Use when you need to quantify how reliably MetaFetcheR maps identifiers within one of the five supported small-compound databases (HMDB, ChEBI, PubChem, KEGG, LIPID MAPS), by measuring consistency, ambiguity, and unresolved rates over random samples. skills.description: Use when integrating pathway/annotation records from HMDB XML, KEGG REST responses, Reactome ChEBI/UniProt mappings, or WikiPathways GPML files whose metabolite and gene identifiers use different, overlapping schemes.
skills.name: cross-database-identifier-mapping
skills.search_text: cross-database-identifier-mapping Use when integrating pathway/annotation records from HMDB XML, KEGG REST responses, Reactome ChEBI/UniProt mappings, or WikiPathways GPML files whose metabolite and gene identifiers use different, overlapping schemes. skills.description: Use when assembling a unified reaction-rule/metabolite-structure resource from separately maintained databases (e.g., RetroRules rules lacking mass shifts, LOTUS entries not in SQLite) before rule- or mass-based metabolite annotation.
skills.name: cross-database-identifier-mapping
skills.search_text: cross-database-identifier-mapping Use when assembling a unified reaction-rule/metabolite-structure resource from separately maintained databases (e.g., RetroRules rules lacking mass shifts, LOTUS entries not in SQLite) before rule- or mass-based metabolite annotation. Mass features already have assigned molecular structures — annotation via adduct/LOTUS lookups would be redundant. The goal is MS/MS spectral-library or molecular-network-based annotation, which MEANtools does not currently support. Analysis targets multi-substrate reactions or stereoisomeric conversions — RetroRules-based rules are single-substrate and MEANtools filters stereomeric rules. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Cross-references reaction and metabolite identifiers between public databases (RetroRules↔MetaNetX↔Rhea/KEGG orthology, and LOTUS converted to SQLite) so that reaction rules, mass shifts, enzyme associations, and metabolite structures become interoperable within MEANtools. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pbio.3003307
skills.summary: Cross-references reaction and metabolite identifiers between public databases (RetroRules↔MetaNetX↔Rhea/KEGG orthology, and LOTUS converted to SQLite) so that reaction rules, mass shifts, enzyme associations, and metabolite structures become interoperable within MEANtools.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Mass features already have assigned molecular structures — annotation via adduct/LOTUS lookups would be redundant. The goal is MS/MS spectral-library or molecular-network-based annotation, which MEANtools does not currently support. Analysis targets multi-substrate reactions or stereoisomeric conversions — RetroRules-based rules are single-substrate and MEANtools filters stereomeric rules.

skills.name: cross-database-identifier-mapping-interpretation
skills.search_text: cross-database-identifier-mapping-interpretation Use when you have a merged/harmonized metabolite table (e.g. the 391-entry urinary asthma metabolite MMS output) and need to report or audit what percentage of entries carry each non-systematic identifier before interpreting or comparing annotations across databases. The table is a raw per-study metabolite list that has not yet gone through InChIKey-based merging and the three-step MMS curation process — coverage on uncurated data will not match the merged-dataset benchmarks You need to obtain/retrieve the identifiers themselves (MMS Step 2 attribute retrieval) rather than quantify the coverage of identifier columns that already exist The analysis concerns systematic identifiers (e.g. InChIKey) or chemical property descriptors rather than the eight non-systematic identifier attributes Quantifies how completely each non-systematic metabolite identifier (CAS, RefMet accepted name, ChEBI, HMDB, KEGG, BinVestigate, DrugBank, LipidMaps) annotates a merged metabolite dataset, following Step 2 (attribute retrieval from the InChIKey) of the Metabolites Merging Strategy (MMS). It turns identifier columns into interpretable coverage percentages that reveal which databases can realistically support downstream interstudy comparison. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo13121167
skills.summary: Quantifies how completely each non-systematic metabolite identifier (CAS, RefMet accepted name, ChEBI, HMDB, KEGG, BinVestigate, DrugBank, LipidMaps) annotates a merged metabolite dataset, following Step 2 (attribute retrieval from the InChIKey) of the Metabolites Merging Strategy (MMS). It turns identifier columns into interpretable coverage percentages that reveal which databases can realistically support downstream interstudy comparison.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The table is a raw per-study metabolite list that has not yet gone through InChIKey-based merging and the three-step MMS curation process — coverage on uncurated data will not match the merged-dataset benchmarks You need to obtain/retrieve the identifiers themselves (MMS Step 2 attribute retrieval) rather than quantify the coverage of identifier columns that already exist The analysis concerns systematic identifiers (e.g. InChIKey) or chemical property descriptors rather than the eight non-systematic identifier attributes

skills.description: Use when a sparse metabolite table has known primary identifiers (e.g. HMDB IDs) but empty fields for other databases, and you need complete cross-database mapping for pathway enrichment or annotation.
skills.name: cross-database-identifier-resolution
skills.search_text: cross-database-identifier-resolution Use when a sparse metabolite table has known primary identifiers (e.g. HMDB IDs) but empty fields for other databases, and you need complete cross-database mapping for pathway enrichment or annotation. You need stable unique cross-database identifiers: unique MetaFetcheR identifiers are only a planned future feature, not currently available You need a fully automated one-shot mapper: ambiguous multi-mapped entries require the user to choose the representative identifier among the discovered ones You cannot set up a local PostgreSQL database or lack access to HMDB/ChEBI/LIPID MAPS dump files, since the cache is the foundation of the algorithm http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Resolve metabolite identifiers across HMDB, ChEBI, PubChem, KEGG and LIPID MAPS using MetaFetcheR's queue-based algorithm, backed by a local PostgreSQL cache populated from database dump files and on-the-fly HTTP calls. The skill targets filling empty (missing) identifier fields exhaustively so metabolite records can be linked across five small-compound databases. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2021.02.28.433248
skills.summary: Resolve metabolite identifiers across HMDB, ChEBI, PubChem, KEGG and LIPID MAPS using MetaFetcheR's queue-based algorithm, backed by a local PostgreSQL cache populated from database dump files and on-the-fly HTTP calls. The skill targets filling empty (missing) identifier fields exhaustively so metabolite records can be linked across five small-compound databases.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need stable unique cross-database identifiers: unique MetaFetcheR identifiers are only a planned future feature, not currently available You need a fully automated one-shot mapper: ambiguous multi-mapped entries require the user to choose the representative identifier among the discovered ones You cannot set up a local PostgreSQL database or lack access to HMDB/ChEBI/LIPID MAPS dump files, since the cache is the foundation of the algorithm

skills.search_text: cross-database-identifier-retrieval Use when a metabolomics input table lists compounds under inconsistent names or synonyms and the rows must be keyed to unambiguous database identifiers (CID, InChIKey, KEGG, ChEBI, HMDB, DrugBank) before downstream aggregation or meta-analysis. skills.summary: Harmonizes compound names in a user-supplied metabolomics dataset by retrieving cross-database identifiers (PubChem CID, Molecular Formula, Molecular Weight, Canonical SMILES, InChIKey, KEGG, ChEBI, HMDB, DrugBank) using webchem's PubChem retrieval and identifier-conversion functions in R.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input rows already carry unambiguous identifiers (e.g. InChIKey or CID) for every compound, so no name-to-identifier resolution is needed The analysis goal is raw-signal processing or feature detection rather than harmonizing compound naming prior to meta-analysis of aggregate statistics Compounds are not chemical entities resolvable in PubChem (e.g. purely descriptive clinical variables)

skills.description: Use when comparing adduct or molecule inventories across multiple published databases to quantify overlap, novel additions, and exclusions via set operations on harmonized names, formulas, and monoisotopic masses.
skills.name: cross-database-overlap-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-database-overlap-analysis Use when comparing adduct or molecule inventories across multiple published databases to quantify overlap, novel additions, and exclusions via set operations on harmonized names, formulas, and monoisotopic masses. The task is annotating new HRMS/MS spectra against the adduct database rather than comparing database contents — use the spectral-library/annotation workflow instead The databases use incompatible identifier schemes with no available molecular formulas or monoisotopic masses for harmonization, making set operations unreliable Quantifies overlap and extension between the curated 279-entry literature DNA adduct database and prior published adduct databases (Hemeryck et al. 2015, Carrà et al. 2019a, Guo et al. 2017) using set operations on systematically harmonized identifiers, yielding counts of novel additions and confidence-based exclusions (Figure 3A Venn, Supplementary Table S4). metabolomics/v3 10.3389/fchem.2022.908572
skills.summary: Quantifies overlap and extension between the curated 279-entry literature DNA adduct database and prior published adduct databases (Hemeryck et al. 2015, Carrà et al. 2019a, Guo et al. 2017) using set operations on systematically harmonized identifiers, yielding counts of novel additions and confidence-based exclusions (Figure 3A Venn, Supplementary Table S4).

skills.search_text: cross-database-record-count-verification Use when reproducing a data-processing pipeline from a manuscript and you need to confirm the cleaned dataset size matches the reported figure (e.g., CCSBase 16,989 → 13,617 points) before any model training. The database version differs from the one cited in the paper (e.g., a newer CCSBase release) — the exact count invariant 16,989 → 13,617 will not hold and should not be treated as an error signal You are evaluating model prediction accuracy or generalizability rather than verifying data preprocessing provenance The dataset is already standardized (e.g., using the Zenodo-published predictions/splits at 10.5281/zenodo.11199061) — re-counting would be redundant http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 Verifies that a database preprocessing/standardization chain (deduplication, filtering, aggregation) reproduces the exact record counts reported in a paper — here, confirming CCSBase v1.3 shrinks from 16,989 raw CCS values to 13,617 cleaned data points before model training. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00899-w

skills.when_to_use_negative: The database version differs from the one cited in the paper (e.g., a newer CCSBase release) — the exact count invariant 16,989 → 13,617 will not hold and should not be treated as an error signal You are evaluating model prediction accuracy or generalizability rather than verifying data preprocessing provenance The dataset is already standardized (e.g., using the Zenodo-published predictions/splits at 10.5281/zenodo.11199061) — re-counting would be redundant

skills.name: cross-database-set-overlap-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-database-set-overlap-analysis Use when you need to quantify how many entries of an in-house metabolite/lipid library overlap with a public reference database, e.g., verifying claims that CMM 3.0's oxidized lipids are 'not present in other sources'. The goal is annotating experimental spectra from m/z or MS2 data rather than auditing library contents — use CMM 3.0's annotation, spectral-comparison, or spectral quality-assessment services instead. The two databases cannot be reconciled to a shared identifier/abbreviated-name nomenclature (no PC-class or oxidation-level normalization possible), making set membership meaningless. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Set-membership comparison that quantifies how many entries of CMM 3.0's in-house oxidized lipid library overlap a public reference (LIPID MAPS), yielding per-entry presence/absence records that substantiate the claim that CMM 3.0 added oxidized lipids 'not present in other sources'. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.8b00720
skills.summary: Set-membership comparison that quantifies how many entries of CMM 3.0's in-house oxidized lipid library overlap a public reference (LIPID MAPS), yielding per-entry presence/absence records that substantiate the claim that CMM 3.0 added oxidized lipids 'not present in other sources'.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is annotating experimental spectra from m/z or MS2 data rather than auditing library contents — use CMM 3.0's annotation, spectral-comparison, or spectral quality-assessment services instead. skills.description: Use when the same physical mass spectrum must be reconciled across MassBank, MoNA, GNPS, HMDB, MetaboLights, or mzCloud entries whose accession IDs differ, and a database-independent identifier is needed to confirm they refer to the same spectrum.
skills.name: cross-database-spectral-record-retrieval
skills.search_text: cross-database-spectral-record-retrieval Use when the same physical mass spectrum must be reconciled across MassBank, MoNA, GNPS, HMDB, MetaboLights, or mzCloud entries whose accession IDs differ, and a database-independent identifier is needed to confirm they refer to the same spectrum. When the goal is to distinguish two spectra that each contain only a single ion of the same mass — the SPLASH was observed to collide for such spectra, so the identifier cannot discriminate them. When the input is not a mass spectrum but a chemical structure identifier — the article positions InChIKey as the analogous identifier for structures, so InChI-based tools are the correct choice there. When spectra come from libraries like NIST that cannot be publicly released and are therefore absent from the MoNA-hosted SPLASH dataset — no hash can be computed without access to the underlying peak list. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3360 Resolves identical mass spectra recorded under different database-specific identifiers (e.g. PR100026 in MassBank/MoNA, 5464 in HMDB, CCMSLIB00000222858 in GNPS) by applying the SPLASH spectral hash to each record and matching on the resulting four-block identifier rather than on database accession numbers. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/nbt.3689
skills.summary: Resolves identical mass spectra recorded under different database-specific identifiers (e.g. PR100026 in MassBank/MoNA, 5464 in HMDB, CCMSLIB00000222858 in GNPS) by applying the SPLASH spectral hash to each record and matching on the resulting four-block identifier rather than on database accession numbers.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is to distinguish two spectra that each contain only a single ion of the same mass — the SPLASH was observed to collide for such spectra, so the identifier cannot discriminate them. When the input is not a mass spectrum but a chemical structure identifier — the article positions InChIKey as the analogous identifier for structures, so InChI-based tools are the correct choice there. When spectra come from libraries like NIST that cannot be publicly released and are therefore absent from the MoNA-hosted SPLASH dataset — no hash can be computed without access to the underlying peak list.

skills.summary: Benchmarks a feature alignment algorithm against native alignment methods (XCMS, MZmine2, OpenMS) across multiple public LC-MS metabolomics benchmark datasets, computing feature accuracy (F_ACC) and analyte accuracy (A_ACC) against manually annotated library analytes per dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is method development on a single dataset without manually annotated library analytes — no ground truth exists to compute F_ACC/A_ACC deltas The input is raw MS data rather than already-extracted feature lists; feature extraction, not cross-software alignment comparison, is the bottleneck Only one instrument/platform is in scope and the goal is a quick sanity check rather than cross-dataset robustness validation

skills.description: Use when a spectral/annotation method's accuracy claim must be validated across two or more independent test sets (e.g. NPLIB1 vs MassSpecGym) rather than a single benchmark.
skills.name: cross-dataset-benchmark-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-benchmark-comparison Use when a spectral/annotation method's accuracy claim must be validated across two or more independent test sets (e.g. NPLIB1 vs MassSpecGym) rather than a single benchmark. skills.summary: Evaluates formula-annotation tools (MIST-CF, BUDDY) and a downstream de novo structure generator (DiffMS) side-by-side on two public benchmarks, NPLIB1 (CANOPUS/GNPS subset) and MassSpecGym, so that performance conclusions are not tied to a single dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Spectra lack the high-resolution MS1 peak lists needed for formula annotation, so ranked formula candidates cannot be produced. The datasets being compared have different annotation conventions or split definitions, so accuracy figures would not be comparable. skills.search_text: cross-dataset-clustering-ordering-comparison Use when you have clustered spectra from ≥2 MS/MS clustering tools on ≥2 metabolomics datasets and need MS-RT purity/N10 scores to test whether tool rankings (e.g. Falcon vs MaRaCluster) transfer across instruments.
