skills.when_to_use_negative: Evaluation is on proteomics data where FDR-controlled database-search identifications exist — use the DB-Search comparison (src/clustering_eval_compare_DB) instead of MS-RT, which is a surrogate designed for metabolomics where 'FDR controlled identifications are not currently practical' Only one clustering tool or one dataset is available — a cross-tool, cross-dataset ordering comparison needs at least two tools and datasets to be meaningful Vendor raw files have not yet been converted — run msconvert/ThermoRawFileParser conversion and clustering first; this skill is the downstream evaluation step

skills.description: Use when two LC–MS metabolomics feature tables have already been matched (e.g., 4953 unique matches via M2S) and you must verify correctness using the subset of features annotated at MSI confidence level 2.
skills.name: cross-dataset-feature-match-audit
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-feature-match-audit Use when two LC–MS metabolomics feature tables have already been matched (e.g., 4953 unique matches via M2S) and you must verify correctness using the subset of features annotated at MSI confidence level 2. Input is a raw LC–MS file or unfiltered peak list — this audit assumes M2S matching has already run and produced a final match table. Features lack manual annotations at MSI confidence level 2 (accuracy is limited by the number of annotations available in the datasets). You need to re-run the matching itself; use the M2S matching pipeline instead of this post-hoc audit. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Audit how many and what fraction of manually annotated metabolomic features were correctly matched when two untargeted LC–MS metabolomics datasets (e.g., MESA vs Rotterdam) are joined via the M2S correspondence method. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c03592
skills.summary: Audit how many and what fraction of manually annotated metabolomic features were correctly matched when two untargeted LC–MS metabolomics datasets (e.g., MESA vs Rotterdam) are joined via the M2S correspondence method.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a raw LC–MS file or unfiltered peak list — this audit assumes M2S matching has already run and produced a final match table. Features lack manual annotations at MSI confidence level 2 (accuracy is limited by the number of annotations available in the datasets). You need to re-run the matching itself; use the M2S matching pipeline instead of this post-hoc audit.

skills.description: Use when two peak-picked, conventionally aligned untargeted LC-MS feature tables acquired under non-identical conditions (different gradients, instruments, or laboratories) must have their overlapping features identified and concatenated.
skills.name: cross-dataset-feature-matching
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-feature-matching Use when two peak-picked, conventionally aligned untargeted LC-MS feature tables acquired under non-identical conditions (different gradients, instruments, or laboratories) must have their overlapping features identified and concatenated. Datasets acquired from excessively disparate chromatographic techniques (e.g., an RPLC dataset aligned to a HILIC dataset), since elution order is not preserved and HILIC sets are harder to align Datasets in different ionization modes (positive vs negative) or with biologically dissimilar samples lacking overlap in metabolomic composition Abundance values normalized or transformed in a way that removes ranked abundance order information, which the similarity scoring depends on http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Match overlapping <m/z, retention time> features across two disparately acquired untargeted LC-HRMS metabolomics datasets using metabCombiner: m/z grouping, RT mapping spline fitting, and weighted feature pair alignment (FPA) scoring, followed by concatenation of abundances into a combined table. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c03693
skills.summary: Match overlapping <m/z, retention time> features across two disparately acquired untargeted LC-HRMS metabolomics datasets using metabCombiner: m/z grouping, RT mapping spline fitting, and weighted feature pair alignment (FPA) scoring, followed by concatenation of abundances into a combined table.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Datasets acquired from excessively disparate chromatographic techniques (e.g., an RPLC dataset aligned to a HILIC dataset), since elution order is not preserved and HILIC sets are harder to align Datasets in different ionization modes (positive vs negative) or with biologically dissimilar samples lacking overlap in metabolomic composition Abundance values normalized or transformed in a way that removes ranked abundance order information, which the similarity scoring depends on

skills.description: Use when integrating two untargeted LC-MS metabolomics peak tables (e.g. MESA reference vs Rotterdam target) that share RT, m/z, and FI dimensions but were acquired in separate runs, and you need unique feature correspondence without MS/MS or annotation-level matching.
skills.name: cross-dataset-feature-matching
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-feature-matching Use when integrating two untargeted LC-MS metabolomics peak tables (e.g. MESA reference vs Rotterdam target) that share RT, m/z, and FI dimensions but were acquired in separate runs, and you need unique feature correspondence without MS/MS or annotation-level matching. When the two datasets are peak lists from the same acquisition run (within-batch feature grouping), not inter-batch/inter-study alignment When features lack reliable intensity (e.g. pure MS1 presence/absence only) and the FI-dimension residual-driven uniqueness resolution is not informative When MS/MS spectral matching or known-annotation-based correspondence is available and preferred over RT/MZ/FI shift modeling http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Match untargeted LC-MS metabolomic features across two similar datasets or batches using only retention time, m/z, and optionally feature intensity (FI), via the M2S three-step procedure (candidate matching, robust inter-dataset shift modeling with neighbor definitions, unique correspondence resolution). metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c03592
skills.summary: Match untargeted LC-MS metabolomic features across two similar datasets or batches using only retention time, m/z, and optionally feature intensity (FI), via the M2S three-step procedure (candidate matching, robust inter-dataset shift modeling with neighbor definitions, unique correspondence resolution).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the two datasets are peak lists from the same acquisition run (within-batch feature grouping), not inter-batch/inter-study alignment When features lack reliable intensity (e.g. pure MS1 presence/absence only) and the FI-dimension residual-driven uniqueness resolution is not informative When MS/MS spectral matching or known-annotation-based correspondence is available and preferred over RT/MZ/FI shift modeling

skills.description: Use when you have completed feature matching between two LC-MS metabolomics datasets and need to quantify match correctness — e.g. via annotated feature concordance or a simulated dataset with known embedded correspondences.
skills.name: cross-dataset-feature-matching-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-feature-matching-evaluation Use when you have completed feature matching between two LC-MS metabolomics datasets and need to quantify match correctness — e.g. via annotated feature concordance or a simulated dataset with known embedded correspondences. Input is raw LC-MS data that has not yet been peak-picked with XCMS and quality-controlled (QC dilution series R2 <0.7 threshold) — matching evaluation presupposes a completed match set. Only a single dataset is available with no second dataset or simulated pair to match against — the skill requires two feature tables or a known correspondence set. The goal is metabolite annotation itself rather than assessing the quality of feature correspondences — use annotation workflows (e.g. LIPID MAPS, METLIN, HMDB searches) instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Evaluate how well M2S matched features between two untargeted LC-MS metabolomics datasets using six orthogonal validation strategies, including ground-truth comparison on simulated data with embedded correspondences and manual annotation concordance. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c03592
skills.summary: Evaluate how well M2S matched features between two untargeted LC-MS metabolomics datasets using six orthogonal validation strategies, including ground-truth comparison on simulated data with embedded correspondences and manual annotation concordance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw LC-MS data that has not yet been peak-picked with XCMS and quality-controlled (QC dilution series R2 <0.7 threshold) — matching evaluation presupposes a completed match set. Only a single dataset is available with no second dataset or simulated pair to match against — the skill requires two feature tables or a known correspondence set. The goal is metabolite annotation itself rather than assessing the quality of feature correspondences — use annotation workflows (e.g. LIPID MAPS, METLIN, HMDB searches) instead.

skills.description: Use when you need to test whether a CCS prediction model's reported accuracy transfers beyond its training dataset's chemical space, using METLIN-CCS (~27k structures) and CCSBase v1.3 (16,989 values) as train/test pairs.
skills.name: cross-dataset-generalization-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-generalization-evaluation Use when you need to test whether a CCS prediction model's reported accuracy transfers beyond its training dataset's chemical space, using METLIN-CCS (~27k structures) and CCSBase v1.3 (16,989 values) as train/test pairs. When the goal is in-distribution accuracy on a single homogeneous dataset rather than quantifying the generalization gap across chemical spaces. When the molecule classes of interest fall outside small-molecule synthetic chemistry, since METLIN-CCS is based on synthetic structures and the evaluation is restricted to specific regions of chemical space. When experimental CCS references for the target chemical space are unavailable, as only a few thousand high-quality experimental values exist and lack of data availability is a major field challenge. http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Benchmarks CCS prediction models (SigmaCCS, GraphCCS, Mol2CCS) by training on one CCS database (METLIN-CCS or CCSBase v1.3) and testing on the other, to quantify how performance degrades outside the training chemical space. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00899-w
skills.summary: Benchmarks CCS prediction models (SigmaCCS, GraphCCS, Mol2CCS) by training on one CCS database (METLIN-CCS or CCSBase v1.3) and testing on the other, to quantify how performance degrades outside the training chemical space.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is in-distribution accuracy on a single homogeneous dataset rather than quantifying the generalization gap across chemical spaces. When the molecule classes of interest fall outside small-molecule synthetic chemistry, since METLIN-CCS is based on synthetic structures and the evaluation is restricted to specific regions of chemical space. When experimental CCS references for the target chemical space are unavailable, as only a few thousand high-quality experimental values exist and lack of data availability is a major field challenge.

skills.description: Use when a trained GNN CCS predictor must be evaluated on a structurally different database than its training set (e.g. CCSBase→METLIN-CCS or METLIN-CCS→CCSBase) and per-model R2/MAE/MRE must be compiled into a cross-database comparison table.
skills.name: cross-dataset-generalization-metrics-aggregation
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-generalization-metrics-aggregation Use when a trained GNN CCS predictor must be evaluated on a structurally different database than its training set (e.g. CCSBase→METLIN-CCS or METLIN-CCS→CCSBase) and per-model R2/MAE/MRE must be compiled into a cross-database comparison table. When evaluating in-distribution performance (train and test on the same database split, e.g. train-metlin-test-metlin) — the skill targets cross-chemical-space generalization, not standard held-out accuracy When the goal is to improve generalization by adding features (fingerprints, descriptors, instrument type in Mol2CCS) rather than to quantify the generalization gap itself When the datasets are not structurally distinct CCS databases — aggregating metrics across random splits of one database will not reproduce the reported generalization drop http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Aggregates R2, MAE, and MRE metrics from cross-database CCS prediction runs — training GNN models (SigmaCCS, GraphCCS, Mol2CCS) on one CCS database (e.g. CCSBase) and evaluating on a structurally different one (e.g. METLIN-CCS) — to quantify generalization failure matching the paper's Fig. 3. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00899-w
skills.summary: Aggregates R2, MAE, and MRE metrics from cross-database CCS prediction runs — training GNN models (SigmaCCS, GraphCCS, Mol2CCS) on one CCS database (e.g. CCSBase) and evaluating on a structurally different one (e.g. METLIN-CCS) — to quantify generalization failure matching the paper's Fig. 3.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When evaluating in-distribution performance (train and test on the same database split, e.g. train-metlin-test-metlin) — the skill targets cross-chemical-space generalization, not standard held-out accuracy When the goal is to improve generalization by adding features (fingerprints, descriptors, instrument type in Mol2CCS) rather than to quantify the generalization gap itself When the datasets are not structurally distinct CCS databases — aggregating metrics across random splits of one database will not reproduce the reported generalization drop

skills.summary: Aggregates per-dataset average precision (AP) of target-vs-decoy ion rankings into mean average precision (MAP) across many testing datasets, enabling benchmarking of METASPACE-ML against the rule-based MSM scorer on animal and plant imaging MS datasets.

skills.description: Use when multiple replicate DESI-MSI datasets of the same tissue type (e.g., root sections) have each been processed along a linear developmental gradient and you need a pooled, de-replicated mass signature list for cross-sample clustering and variety comparison.
skills.name: cross-dataset-mass-signature-pooling
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-mass-signature-pooling Use when multiple replicate DESI-MSI datasets of the same tissue type (e.g., root sections) have each been processed along a linear developmental gradient and you need a pooled, de-replicated mass signature list for cross-sample clustering and variety comparison. The datasets are not organized along a linear developmental axis — DIMPLE was designed specifically to leverage the linear developmental axis of the maize root and does not apply to arbitrary 2D tissue geometry. You need metabolite annotation/identification rather than pattern discovery — the article notes the majority of mass signatures remain unannotated and recommends dedicated database searching (METASPACE, Metlin Classic, LOTUS). You have only a single replicate and no cross-dataset de-replication or variety comparison is needed. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Pool mass signatures detected by DIMPLE across replicate DESI-MSI root datasets (e.g., Oaxacan Green OG1, OG5, OG2-P11-0 at ~50 µm spatial resolution), collapse redundant detections into a unique signature list, and cluster signatures by developmental enrichment pattern along the linear root axis. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.09.22.677919
skills.summary: Pool mass signatures detected by DIMPLE across replicate DESI-MSI root datasets (e.g., Oaxacan Green OG1, OG5, OG2-P11-0 at ~50 µm spatial resolution), collapse redundant detections into a unique signature list, and cluster signatures by developmental enrichment pattern along the linear root axis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The datasets are not organized along a linear developmental axis — DIMPLE was designed specifically to leverage the linear developmental axis of the maize root and does not apply to arbitrary 2D tissue geometry. skills.when_to_use_negative: The data contain real MS/MS scans — standard MS/MS library search (e.g. GNPS library via ms1-id reverse matching) is the appropriate route, not cross-dataset pseudo-MS/MS matching The goal is first-pass structural annotation of a single dataset (use the ms1-id lcms/msi workflows) rather than validating or propagating an existing annotation across datasets The target dataset has no pre-generated pseudo MS/MS pool and in-source-fragment clustering cannot be performed

skills.description: Use when two ICA decompositions of different cancer transcriptomic datasets must be compared component-wise to assess reproducibility, and no one-to-one component ordering exists between them.

skills.search_text: cross-dataset-metagene-network-construction Use when two ICA decompositions of different cancer transcriptomic datasets must be compared component-wise to assess reproducibility, and no one-to-one component ordering exists between them. The decompositions share an established component ordering, so direct per-component comparison suffices and RBH matching is unnecessary. The task is assessing ICA stability within a single dataset (e.g. via stability analysis in BIODICA), not reproducibility across two independent datasets. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_2640 Builds an RBH (reciprocal best hit) network linking metagenes (sk gene-weight vectors) from two ICA decompositions of different transcriptomic datasets, then quantifies reproducibility of components via network metrics such as modularity and average clustering coefficient. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/ijms20184414
skills.summary: Builds an RBH (reciprocal best hit) network linking metagenes (sk gene-weight vectors) from two ICA decompositions of different transcriptomic datasets, then quantifies reproducibility of components via network metrics such as modularity and average clustering coefficient.

skills.description: Use when you must quantify how much a model component (e.g. predicted fingerprint input) contributes by re-running the identical generation/re-ranking pipeline with that component removed on held-out spectra from multiple reference datasets.
skills.name: cross-dataset-model-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-model-benchmarking Use when you must quantify how much a model component (e.g. predicted fingerprint input) contributes by re-running the identical generation/re-ranking pipeline with that component removed on held-out spectra from multiple reference datasets. You want the full fingerprint-guided model's performance rather than the fingerprint-input ablation — run the guided pipeline instead. Spectra are in negative-ion mode: MSNovelist is trained only for positive-mode data, so benchmark numbers will not reflect true performance. MS2 spectra have fewer than three fragment ions; the pipeline processes a minimum of three fragment ions and richer spectra are desirable. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Benchmark a fingerprint-free (naïve) de novo structure generator against the full fingerprint-guided MSNovelist model by running an identical generation-plus-Platt-reranking pipeline over GNPS and CASMI MS2 spectra and measuring structure retrieval and top-1 rates per 10-fold cross-validation split. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-022-01486-3
skills.summary: Benchmark a fingerprint-free (naïve) de novo structure generator against the full fingerprint-guided MSNovelist model by running an identical generation-plus-Platt-reranking pipeline over GNPS and CASMI MS2 spectra and measuring structure retrieval and top-1 rates per 10-fold cross-validation split.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You want the full fingerprint-guided model's performance rather than the fingerprint-input ablation — run the guided pipeline instead. Spectra are in negative-ion mode: MSNovelist is trained only for positive-mode data, so benchmark numbers will not reflect true performance. MS2 spectra have fewer than three fragment ions; the pipeline processes a minimum of three fragment ions and richer spectra are desirable.

skills.search_text: cross-dataset-model-transfer-validation Use when ML models trained on one cell-line panel (e.g. CCLE) have produced top features, and you need to confirm those features generalize by measuring their importance in independent datasets such as NCI60 or single-cell data. When the goal is direct prediction of metabolites from another data source — the article notes models are 'not directly transferrable' due to differences between in vitro and in vivo conditions, cell line panels, and limited feature overlap When you only need model performance (Pearson's correlation) on the training data rather than generalization of feature importance in independent data http://edamontology.org/topic_3524 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Validates that features selected by machine-learning models trained on one omics dataset (e.g. CCLE-trained random forest metabolite models) are genuinely informative by testing whether they show significantly higher feature importance in independent datasets (NCI60, single-cell transcriptomics) than expected by chance. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.08.17.608400
skills.summary: Validates that features selected by machine-learning models trained on one omics dataset (e.g. CCLE-trained random forest metabolite models) are genuinely informative by testing whether they show significantly higher feature importance in independent datasets (NCI60, single-cell transcriptomics) than expected by chance.

skills.description: Use when a published method reports a concrete runtime on named hardware (e.g. compareMS2 2.0's 40 min for 10 pairwise serum dataset comparisons on an Intel Xeon W-2135 at 3.70 GHz) and a re-run's performance must be assessed on possibly different machines.
skills.name: cross-hardware-performance-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-hardware-performance-comparison Use when a published method reports a concrete runtime on named hardware (e.g. compareMS2 2.0's 40 min for 10 pairwise serum dataset comparisons on an Intel Xeon W-2135 at 3.70 GHz) and a re-run's performance must be assessed on possibly different machines. The published article reports no runtime or hardware configuration for the step being reproduced, so there is no qualified baseline to compare against. The workload differs from the article's benchmark inputs (e.g. datasets with far fewer or more tandem mass spectra than the 42,629–47,626 range), making the 40 min baseline inapplicable. The goal is algorithmic correctness validation rather than performance assessment — use the article's phylogenetic tree reconstruction in compareMS2 and MEGA11 for that instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_3360 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Benchmark a compute step's wall-clock runtime against the hardware-qualified baseline reported in the source article, here the 40 min compareMS2 2.0 runtime for 10 pairwise LC-MS/MS dataset comparisons on an Intel Xeon W-2135 at 3.70 GHz. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.2c00457
skills.summary: Benchmark a compute step's wall-clock runtime against the hardware-qualified baseline reported in the source article, here the 40 min compareMS2 2.0 runtime for 10 pairwise LC-MS/MS dataset comparisons on an Intel Xeon W-2135 at 3.70 GHz.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The published article reports no runtime or hardware configuration for the step being reproduced, so there is no qualified baseline to compare against. The workload differs from the article's benchmark inputs (e.g. datasets with far fewer or more tandem mass spectra than the 42,629–47,626 range), making the 40 min baseline inapplicable. The goal is algorithmic correctness validation rather than performance assessment — use the article's phylogenetic tree reconstruction in compareMS2 and MEGA11 for that instead.

skills.description: Use when testing whether a formula-prediction model trained on one instrument's MS/MS spectra (e.g. Orbitrap) generalizes to another (e.g. Q-TOF) on identical compound sets.
skills.name: cross-instrument-generalization-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-instrument-generalization-evaluation Use when testing whether a formula-prediction model trained on one instrument's MS/MS spectra (e.g. Orbitrap) generalizes to another (e.g. Q-TOF) on identical compound sets. The analysis goal is top-1/top-5 accuracy benchmarking against SIRIUS or BUDDY rather than instrument-transfer behavior The compound sets differ between the two instruments (matched same-compound pairs are required for a fair 2x2 comparison) The spectra come from other instrument families (e.g. ion trap) not covered by the Q-TOF/Orbitrap training data http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Reproduces FIDDLE's cross-instrument validation by training separate TCN models on matched Q-TOF (MoNA) and Orbitrap (NIST23, downsampled) spectra of the same compounds, then evaluating each checkpoint on both instrument types to assemble the 2x2 missed-atom matrix of Fig. 4j. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-025-66060-9
skills.summary: Reproduces FIDDLE's cross-instrument validation by training separate TCN models on matched Q-TOF (MoNA) and Orbitrap (NIST23, downsampled) spectra of the same compounds, then evaluating each checkpoint on both instrument types to assemble the 2x2 missed-atom matrix of Fig. 4j.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is top-1/top-5 accuracy benchmarking against SIRIUS or BUDDY rather than instrument-transfer behavior The compound sets differ between the two instruments (matched same-compound pairs are required for a fair 2x2 comparison) The spectra come from other instrument families (e.g. ion trap) not covered by the Q-TOF/Orbitrap training data

skills.description: Use when you need to measure how well MS2 reference spectra acquired on one instrument type identify compounds queried from another (e.g. QS=[QqQ] vs TS=[QqTOF]), and to evaluate whether merged ESI-MS2 target sets improve precision at a fixed similarity-score cutoff.
skills.name: cross-instrument-spectral-matching
skills.search_text: cross-instrument-spectral-matching Use when you need to measure how well MS2 reference spectra acquired on one instrument type identify compounds queried from another (e.g. QS=[QqQ] vs TS=[QqTOF]), and to evaluate whether merged ESI-MS2 target sets improve precision at a fixed similarity-score cutoff. Your queries and targets come from the same instrument and identical acquisition conditions — the unmerged cross-instrument baseline and merged-set evaluation do not apply. Your spectra are EI-MS or GC-MS volatility data; the weighted cosine exponents here are optimized for ESI-MS2 data only. You need a screening result rather than a precision/recall benchmark of a spectral-search reference library. http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Cross-searches ESI-MS2 query spectra from one instrument (QqQ or QqTOF) against reference/target spectra from another using MassBank's weighted cosine correlation similarity score, optionally with merged collision-energy spectra, to quantify precision/recall/F-value of compound identification. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/jms.1777
skills.summary: Cross-searches ESI-MS2 query spectra from one instrument (QqQ or QqTOF) against reference/target spectra from another using MassBank's weighted cosine correlation similarity score, optionally with merged collision-energy spectra, to quantify precision/recall/F-value of compound identification.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your queries and targets come from the same instrument and identical acquisition conditions — the unmerged cross-instrument baseline and merged-set evaluation do not apply. Your spectra are EI-MS or GC-MS volatility data; the weighted cosine exponents here are optimized for ESI-MS2 data only. You need a screening result rather than a precision/recall benchmark of a spectral-search reference library.

skills.description: Use when flow injection–Orbitrap MSn data have been acquired in both positive and negative ionization modes, per-mode feature lists (e.g. from mzmine) and cleaned metadata exist, and the goal is to quantify how many unique compounds are detected in positive-only, negative-only, and both modes.
skills.name: cross-ionization-mode-compound-set-intersection
skills.search_text: cross-ionization-mode-compound-set-intersection Use when flow injection–Orbitrap MSn data have been acquired in both positive and negative ionization modes, per-mode feature lists (e.g. from mzmine) and cleaned metadata exist, and the goal is to quantify how many unique compounds are detected in positive-only, negative-only, and both modes. Input is already a feature table with ionization-mode labels and a compound identifier column — no join or set-intersection work is needed Data were acquired in a single ionization mode only — the cross-mode intersection is undefined and per-mode counts alone suffice Metadata have not passed the metadata cleanup flow and lack consistent column names (unique sample id, plate_id, well location) — the feature-to-compound join would be ambiguous http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Compute the distribution of unique compound detections across positive-only, negative-only, and both ionization modes by joining mzmine feature lists against cleaned flow injection–Orbitrap MSn metadata and intersecting the per-mode compound identifier sets; this yields the 30,008-unique-compound coverage breakdown central to the MSnLib resource. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-025-02813-0
skills.summary: Compute the distribution of unique compound detections across positive-only, negative-only, and both ionization modes by joining mzmine feature lists against cleaned flow injection–Orbitrap MSn metadata and intersecting the per-mode compound identifier sets; this yields the 30,008-unique-compound coverage breakdown central to the MSnLib resource.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a feature table with ionization-mode labels and a compound identifier column — no join or set-intersection work is needed Data were acquired in a single ionization mode only — the cross-mode intersection is undefined and per-mode counts alone suffice Metadata have not passed the metadata cleanup flow and lack consistent column names (unique sample id, plate_id, well location) — the feature-to-compound join would be ambiguous

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify whether dual-ionization-mode training trades off within-mode prediction accuracy, by benchmarking single-mode ablations on held-out same-mode spectrum pairs per Tanimoto bin.
skills.name: cross-ionization-mode-loss-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-ionization-mode-loss-evaluation Use when you need to quantify whether dual-ionization-mode training trades off within-mode prediction accuracy, by benchmarking single-mode ablations on held-out same-mode spectrum pairs per Tanimoto bin. Your goal is cross-mode (positive-vs-negative) similarity prediction — single-mode ablation models cannot make cross-ionization-mode predictions at all Your dataset is small (< ~100,000 spectra); the README warns pair sampling can be suboptimal and the ablation comparison would be confounded by sampling artifacts You only need final similarity matrices from the pre-trained model rather than a training-strategy ablation Trains single-ionization-mode Siamese models (positive-only and negative-only) with identical hyperparameters to the dual-mode MS2DeepScore 2.0 model, then compares within-mode losses per Tanimoto bin to isolate how joint training affects accuracy. This reproduces the Suppl. Fig 4.1-4.3 ablation that justifies (or questions) dual-mode training. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.03.25.586580
skills.summary: Trains single-ionization-mode Siamese models (positive-only and negative-only) with identical hyperparameters to the dual-mode MS2DeepScore 2.0 model, then compares within-mode losses per Tanimoto bin to isolate how joint training affects accuracy. This reproduces the Suppl. Fig 4.1-4.3 ablation that justifies (or questions) dual-mode training.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your goal is cross-mode (positive-vs-negative) similarity prediction — single-mode ablation models cannot make cross-ionization-mode predictions at all Your dataset is small (< ~100,000 spectra); the README warns pair sampling can be suboptimal and the ablation comparison would be confounded by sampling artifacts You only need final similarity matrices from the pre-trained model rather than a training-strategy ablation

skills.description: Use when you have MS/MS spectra acquired in both positive and negative ionization modes (e.g. mgf/msp from LC-MS metabolomics) and want a single molecular network spanning both modes rather than separate per-mode networks.
skills.name: cross-ionization-mode-molecular-networking
skills.search_text: cross-ionization-mode-molecular-networking Use when you have MS/MS spectra acquired in both positive and negative ionization modes (e.g. mgf/msp from LC-MS metabolomics) and want a single molecular network spanning both modes rather than separate per-mode networks. Your spectra are all from a single ionization mode only — plain within-mode spectral-similarity networking suffices and cross-mode training is unnecessary overhead Input spectra are low quality with limited fragmentation, chimeric, or strongly dissimilar to the training libraries — the paper predicts poor MS2DeepScore scores for such spectra, so network edges would be unreliable You only need library-based annotation (e.g. MS2Query-style search) rather than network-level exploration of chemical space http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Builds molecular networks that integrate tandem mass spectra from both positive and negative ionization modes into one unified graph, using MS2DeepScore 2.0-predicted chemical similarities instead of mode-restricted spectral cosine scores. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.03.25.586580
skills.summary: Builds molecular networks that integrate tandem mass spectra from both positive and negative ionization modes into one unified graph, using MS2DeepScore 2.0-predicted chemical similarities instead of mode-restricted spectral cosine scores.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your spectra are all from a single ionization mode only — plain within-mode spectral-similarity networking suffices and cross-mode training is unnecessary overhead Input spectra are low quality with limited fragmentation, chimeric, or strongly dissimilar to the training libraries — the paper predicts poor MS2DeepScore scores for such spectra, so network edges would be unreliable You only need library-based annotation (e.g. MS2Query-style search) rather than network-level exploration of chemical space

skills.description: Use when positive and negative ionization mode MS/MS spectra of structurally identical or related compounds must be compared, and classical spectrum similarity scores (cosine, modified cosine) miss cross-mode similarity.
skills.name: cross-ionization-mode-similarity-prediction
skills.search_text: cross-ionization-mode-similarity-prediction Use when positive and negative ionization mode MS/MS spectra of structurally identical or related compounds must be compared, and classical spectrum similarity scores (cosine, modified cosine) miss cross-mode similarity. When all spectra are within a single ionization mode and classical spectral similarity scores suffice — the cross-mode capability is the reason to use this model When the analysis depends on adduct information: the default model excludes adduct input because not all preprocessing tools generate reliable adduct information, which could reduce performance When training a custom model on a small dataset (<100,000 spectra) without first merging with larger public libraries — pair sampling can be suboptimal if not re-checked and re-optimized http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 MS2DeepScore 2.0 is a Siamese neural network, implemented in PyTorch and trained on >500,000 MS/MS spectra from GNPS, MoNA, MassBank and MSnLib, that predicts Tanimoto chemical similarity between tandem mass spectra acquired in both the same and different ionization modes. It enables unified positive/negative-mode molecular networking where classical scores (cosine, modified cosine) fail across polarities. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.03.25.586580
skills.summary: MS2DeepScore 2.0 is a Siamese neural network, implemented in PyTorch and trained on >500,000 MS/MS spectra from GNPS, MoNA, MassBank and MSnLib, that predicts Tanimoto chemical similarity between tandem mass spectra acquired in both the same and different ionization modes. It enables unified positive/negative-mode molecular networking where classical scores (cosine, modified cosine) fail across polarities.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When all spectra are within a single ionization mode and classical spectral similarity scores suffice — the cross-mode capability is the reason to use this model When the analysis depends on adduct information: the default model excludes adduct input because not all preprocessing tools generate reliable adduct information, which could reduce performance When training a custom model on a small dataset (<100,000 spectra) without first merging with larger public libraries — pair sampling can be suboptimal if not re-checked and re-optimized

skills.description: Use when constructing training pairs for a Siamese spectral-similarity model (e.g. MS2DeepScore) from spectra spanning both ionization modes, especially when raw pair enumeration would over-represent high-frequency molecules or easy (very high/very low) Tanimoto bins.
skills.name: cross-ionization-mode-spectra-pair-sampling
skills.search_text: cross-ionization-mode-spectra-pair-sampling Use when constructing training pairs for a Siamese spectral-similarity model (e.g. MS2DeepScore) from spectra spanning both ionization modes, especially when raw pair enumeration would over-represent high-frequency molecules or easy (very high/very low) Tanimoto bins. You are training a model on a single ionization mode only, e.g. reproducing a DreaMS-style positive-mode model — the cross-mode balancing logic is not needed The spectrum set is tiny (< ~100,000 spectra): the article/README recommend merging custom data with larger public libraries or fine-tuning the pre-trained model instead of retraining from scratch with re-optimized pair sampling Pairs are needed only for evaluation on a held-out test set — sampling balance is a training-time bias-control step, not an evaluation requirement http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_3334 A balanced pair-sampling algorithm for building Siamese-network training sets from tandem MS spectra in both positive and negative ionization modes. It stratifies spectrum pairs over Tanimoto similarity bins to reduce the sampling bias that would otherwise dominate MS2DeepScore 2.0 training. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.03.25.586580
skills.summary: A balanced pair-sampling algorithm for building Siamese-network training sets from tandem MS spectra in both positive and negative ionization modes. It stratifies spectrum pairs over Tanimoto similarity bins to reduce the sampling bias that would otherwise dominate MS2DeepScore 2.0 training.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You are training a model on a single ionization mode only, e.g. reproducing a DreaMS-style positive-mode model — the cross-mode balancing logic is not needed The spectrum set is tiny (< ~100,000 spectra): the article/README recommend merging custom data with larger public libraries or fine-tuning the pre-trained model instead of retraining from scratch with re-optimized pair sampling Pairs are needed only for evaluation on a held-out test set — sampling balance is a training-time bias-control step, not an evaluation requirement

skills.description: Use when positive- and negative-ionization-mode MS/MS spectra must be compared in one unified analysis, or when evaluating whether spectral metadata (precursor m/z, ionmode, adduct, instrument type) improves similarity prediction.

skills.search_text: cross-ionization-mode-spectral-similarity-modeling Use when positive- and negative-ionization-mode MS/MS spectra must be compared in one unified analysis, or when evaluating whether spectral metadata (precursor m/z, ionmode, adduct, instrument type) improves similarity prediction. skills.description: Use when two or more replicate experiments (e.g., within-lab biological replicates or between-lab same-platform comparisons of RNA-seq read counts) need reproducibility assessment as gene rank lists with error control at a target FDR.
skills.name: cross-laboratory-rank-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-laboratory-rank-comparison Use when two or more replicate experiments (e.g., within-lab biological replicates or between-lab same-platform comparisons of RNA-seq read counts) need reproducibility assessment as gene rank lists with error control at a target FDR. skills.search_text: cross-layer-edge-counting-and-sign-summary Use when a built multi-omics network (e.g. microbiome x transcriptome, chemicals x genes) must be summarized per layer pair, to test whether exposure classes show distinct correlation-sign patterns and to report node/edge counts per layer pair. The network has not yet been built or filtered (no correlation threshold/p-value adjustment applied) — run c_net_calculate and c_net_build first The question concerns intra-layer topology (module detection, degree centrality) rather than cross-layer association counts and sign patterns Associations are non-correlation-based (e.g. non-linear or directed causal edges), which the article notes correlation-based network optimization may overlook http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Quantify how many nodes and edges link each pair of omics layers in a MetaNet multi-omics network and summarize the sign (positive/negative) distribution of cross-layer correlations, as demonstrated in the Case 2 exposome-transcriptome analysis. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.06.26.661636
skills.summary: Quantify how many nodes and edges link each pair of omics layers in a MetaNet multi-omics network and summarize the sign (positive/negative) distribution of cross-layer correlations, as demonstrated in the Case 2 exposome-transcriptome analysis.

skills.description: Use when you have one aligned MS/MS feature list (e.g., an MS-Dial peak table) and need to quantify how many features each candidate spectral library can annotate, to choose or justify a library.
skills.name: cross-library-annotation-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-library-annotation-comparison Use when you have one aligned MS/MS feature list (e.g., an MS-Dial peak table) and need to quantify how many features each candidate spectral library can annotate, to choose or justify a library. Input is already a single annotation result and no library comparison is needed Libraries cannot be exported to a common format compatible with the search tool (FragHub supports .MSP, .MGF, .JSON, .CSV, .XML) The feature list has not been filtered for blanks and reproducibility, so unfiltered noise inflates all annotation counts non-comparably http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 A benchmarking skill for feature-level MS/MS annotation in which an identical aligned feature list is searched against each candidate spectral library independently and per-library annotation counts are tabulated to quantify coverage differences. In the FragHub paper this benchmark compared FragHub's unified library against individual libraries (MassBank, GNPS, MoNA, MS-Dial-VS17) on the 435-feature A. thaliana PI-mode feature list. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c02219
skills.summary: A benchmarking skill for feature-level MS/MS annotation in which an identical aligned feature list is searched against each candidate spectral library independently and per-library annotation counts are tabulated to quantify coverage differences. In the FragHub paper this benchmark compared FragHub's unified library against individual libraries (MassBank, GNPS, MoNA, MS-Dial-VS17) on the 435-feature A. thaliana PI-mode feature list.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a single annotation result and no library comparison is needed Libraries cannot be exported to a common format compatible with the search tool (FragHub supports .MSP, .MGF, .JSON, .CSV, .XML) The feature list has not been filtered for blanks and reproducibility, so unfiltered noise inflates all annotation counts non-comparably

skills.description: Use when you must decide whether ML models trained on molecular descriptors (e.g., CDK descriptors for retention-time prediction) will generalize to a test or validation library with a different chemical profile.
skills.name: cross-library-compound-overlap-assessment
skills.search_text: cross-library-compound-overlap-assessment Use when you must decide whether ML models trained on molecular descriptors (e.g., CDK descriptors for retention-time prediction) will generalize to a test or validation library with a different chemical profile. Compounds lie outside the training chemical landscape by design (e.g., complex high-molecular-weight lipids such as triacylglycerols or phosphatidylcholines were excluded from training, so overlap conclusions would not apply to them) The goal is model building or error estimation (MAE), not structural generalizability screening — this skill is a diagnostic precursor, not a prediction workflow Descriptors cannot be computed for a large fraction of compounds (e.g., salts or metal-containing structures not first standardized), making the PCA basis unrepresentative Assesses whether training, test, and external validation compound sets (e.g., HILIC 880/143/377 and RPLC PlaSMA 398/96/358 compounds) occupy overlapping chemical space by running PCA on standardized 2D CDK molecular descriptors, so that retention-time prediction models can be judged generalizable before being built. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.9b05765
skills.summary: Assesses whether training, test, and external validation compound sets (e.g., HILIC 880/143/377 and RPLC PlaSMA 398/96/358 compounds) occupy overlapping chemical space by running PCA on standardized 2D CDK molecular descriptors, so that retention-time prediction models can be judged generalizable before being built.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Compounds lie outside the training chemical landscape by design (e.g., complex high-molecular-weight lipids such as triacylglycerols or phosphatidylcholines were excluded from training, so overlap conclusions would not apply to them) The goal is model building or error estimation (MAE), not structural generalizability screening — this skill is a diagnostic precursor, not a prediction workflow Descriptors cannot be computed for a large fraction of compounds (e.g., salts or metal-containing structures not first standardized), making the PCA basis unrepresentative

skills.description: Use when compiling a training .msp set (e.g., from MoNA or GNPS) while an independent evaluation set will be annotated via reference libraries such as NIST 20 or in-silico LipidBlast; overlapping compounds must be removed.
skills.name: cross-library-compound-overlap-removal
skills.search_text: cross-library-compound-overlap-removal Use when compiling a training .msp set (e.g., from MoNA or GNPS) while an independent evaluation set will be annotated via reference libraries such as NIST 20 or in-silico LipidBlast; overlapping compounds must be removed. When the evaluation set is not annotated via reference libraries (e.g., only spectral-similarity search without external libraries), removing overlaps yields no methodological benefit. When the training pool is already small and you cannot afford to lose candidate blocks, overlap removal may over-thin the dataset; consider expanding the training pool instead of removing more compounds. When building a general-purpose reference library where broad compound coverage is the goal — exclusion is specific to train/evaluation disjunction, not library construction. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 A data-curation step for training deep learning MS/MS models (e.g., IDSL_MINT) that excludes spectra of compounds already covered in libraries used to annotate the independent evaluation set, preventing leakage between training and benchmark data. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00804-5
skills.summary: A data-curation step for training deep learning MS/MS models (e.g., IDSL_MINT) that excludes spectra of compounds already covered in libraries used to annotate the independent evaluation set, preventing leakage between training and benchmark data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the evaluation set is not annotated via reference libraries (e.g., only spectral-similarity search without external libraries), removing overlaps yields no methodological benefit. When the training pool is already small and you cannot afford to lose candidate blocks, overlap removal may over-thin the dataset; consider expanding the training pool instead of removing more compounds. When building a general-purpose reference library where broad compound coverage is the goal — exclusion is specific to train/evaluation disjunction, not library construction.

skills.description: Use when you have MS/MS search results from the same features against multiple in-silico lipidomics libraries and need to quantify which lipid classes or adducts each library covers, or which classes are unique to a single library.
skills.name: cross-library-coverage-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-library-coverage-comparison Use when you have MS/MS search results from the same features against multiple in-silico lipidomics libraries and need to quantify which lipid classes or adducts each library covers, or which classes are unique to a single library. Input is a single-library search result — there is no second library to cross-compare coverage against Goal is scoring individual feature identifications rather than characterizing whole-library class coverage (use RBP/hypergeometric score thresholding workflows instead) Data are metabolomics (non-lipid) spectral matches; the class/adduct enumeration schema described here is lipid-class-specific http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Systematically compares the per-lipid-class and per-adduct coverage of two or more in-silico MS/MS spectral libraries (e.g., CalicoLipids vs MS-DIAL) as searched in MAVEN2, building a class-by-library count matrix of library entries and annotated features and flagging classes represented in only one library. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo12080684
skills.summary: Systematically compares the per-lipid-class and per-adduct coverage of two or more in-silico MS/MS spectral libraries (e.g., CalicoLipids vs MS-DIAL) as searched in MAVEN2, building a class-by-library count matrix of library entries and annotated features and flagging classes represented in only one library.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a single-library search result — there is no second library to cross-compare coverage against Goal is scoring individual feature identifications rather than characterizing whole-library class coverage (use RBP/hypergeometric score thresholding workflows instead) Data are metabolomics (non-lipid) spectral matches; the class/adduct enumeration schema described here is lipid-class-specific

skills.description: Use when annotations of the same LC-MS/MS features were produced with two different spectral libraries and you need library-specific hypergeometric score cutoffs to separate authentic from spurious identifications.
skills.name: cross-library-lipidomics-benchmark-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-library-lipidomics-benchmark-comparison Use when annotations of the same LC-MS/MS features were produced with two different spectral libraries and you need library-specific hypergeometric score cutoffs to separate authentic from spurious identifications. Input is already a feature table annotated with only one spectral library — no cross-library agreement/disagreement histograms can be built The comparison targets experimental (measured) spectral libraries rather than in-silico lipid libraries, since score distributions differ by library construction The goal is general compound identification rather than deriving library-specific score thresholds for aligning annotations http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Benchmark lipid annotations produced by MAVEN2 spectral matching against two MS/MS fragmentation libraries (CalicoLipids in-silico library and MS-DIAL), collapsing agreement/disagreement score histograms into library-specific Retention Balance Point (RBP) hypergeometric-score thresholds (22.8 for CalicoLipids, 13.9 for MS-DIAL). metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo12080684
skills.summary: Benchmark lipid annotations produced by MAVEN2 spectral matching against two MS/MS fragmentation libraries (CalicoLipids in-silico library and MS-DIAL), collapsing agreement/disagreement score histograms into library-specific Retention Balance Point (RBP) hypergeometric-score thresholds (22.8 for CalicoLipids, 13.9 for MS-DIAL).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a feature table annotated with only one spectral library — no cross-library agreement/disagreement histograms can be built The comparison targets experimental (measured) spectral libraries rather than in-silico lipid libraries, since score distributions differ by library construction The goal is general compound identification rather than deriving library-specific score thresholds for aligning annotations

skills.description: Reference for aggregating multiple MS/MS spectral libraries (e.g., NIST20, METLIN, GNPS, MSDIAL) into a deduplicated reference set, and for quantifying pairwise or multiway overlap via InChIKey prefix matching before assigning each compound to a single source library.
skills.name: cross-library-overlap-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-library-overlap-analysis Reference for aggregating multiple MS/MS spectral libraries (e.g., NIST20, METLIN, GNPS, MSDIAL) into a deduplicated reference set, and for quantifying pairwise or multiway overlap via InChIKey prefix matching before assigning each compound to a single source library. Input is a single spectral library — overlap analysis requires at least two sources to be meaningful. Compounds lack InChIKey identifiers or use incomplete InChIKeys shorter than 14 characters, preventing connectivity-layer matching. You need to resolve duplicates by spectral similarity rather than a fixed library priority order. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 This skill quantifies compound overlap across multiple MS/MS spectral reference libraries (NIST20, Agilent METLIN, GNPS, MSDIAL) by matching the first 14 characters of InChIKey identifiers, then applies a deterministic priority hierarchy (NIST20 > Agilent METLIN > GNPS > MSDIAL) to resolve duplicates and produce a deduplicated compound database. It exists because naive merging of libraries inflates compound counts through cross-source duplication. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.02.07.637102
skills.summary: This skill quantifies compound overlap across multiple MS/MS spectral reference libraries (NIST20, Agilent METLIN, GNPS, MSDIAL) by matching the first 14 characters of InChIKey identifiers, then applies a deterministic priority hierarchy (NIST20 > Agilent METLIN > GNPS > MSDIAL) to resolve duplicates and produce a deduplicated compound database. It exists because naive merging of libraries inflates compound counts through cross-source duplication.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a single spectral library — overlap analysis requires at least two sources to be meaningful. Compounds lack InChIKey identifiers or use incomplete InChIKeys shorter than 14 characters, preventing connectivity-layer matching. You need to resolve duplicates by spectral similarity rather than a fixed library priority order.

skills.description: Use when choosing a Python library for a fixed spectrum-processing pipeline (m/z trimming, precursor removal, intensity filtering, scaling) and per-spectrum runtime on identical spectra must be measured and compared across libraries.
skills.name: cross-library-performance-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-library-performance-comparison Use when choosing a Python library for a fixed spectrum-processing pipeline (m/z trimming, precursor removal, intensity filtering, scaling) and per-spectrum runtime on identical spectra must be measured and compared across libraries. The spectra have not been read from an MGF/mzML file or the libraries are not pinned (e.g. spectrum_utils 0.3.0, pymzML 2.4.4, pyOpenMS 2.4.0) — version differences invalidate the comparison. The processing pipelines are not step-for-step equivalent (different m/z window, precursor tolerance, intensity threshold, or peak cap) — comparing non-identical operations is not a fair runtime benchmark. Only a first-call measurement is taken: the spectrum_utils first invocation is dominated by Numba JIT compilation, so skipping the warm-up exclusion misrepresents steady-state runtime. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Benchmark per-spectrum processing runtime of spectrum_utils against functionally equivalent pymzML and pyOpenMS pipelines on the same spectra (e.g. iPRG2012 MGF), recording the Numba JIT first-call outlier for spectrum_utils and producing log-scaled runtime comparison boxplots. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.9b04884
skills.summary: Benchmark per-spectrum processing runtime of spectrum_utils against functionally equivalent pymzML and pyOpenMS pipelines on the same spectra (e.g. iPRG2012 MGF), recording the Numba JIT first-call outlier for spectrum_utils and producing log-scaled runtime comparison boxplots.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The spectra have not been read from an MGF/mzML file or the libraries are not pinned (e.g. spectrum_utils 0.3.0, pymzML 2.4.4, pyOpenMS 2.4.0) — version differences invalidate the comparison. The processing pipelines are not step-for-step equivalent (different m/z window, precursor tolerance, intensity threshold, or peak cap) — comparing non-identical operations is not a fair runtime benchmark. Only a first-call measurement is taken: the spectrum_utils first invocation is dominated by Numba JIT compilation, so skipping the warm-up exclusion misrepresents steady-state runtime.

skills.description: Use when a matchms library-cleaning workflow (fixed filter order + settings captured in YAML) must be validated as a portable configuration on a different public spectral library, e.g., porting the GNPS setup to MassBank or MoNA.
skills.name: cross-library-pipeline-portability-testing
skills.search_text: cross-library-pipeline-portability-testing Use when a matchms library-cleaning workflow (fixed filter order + settings captured in YAML) must be validated as a portable configuration on a different public spectral library, e.g., porting the GNPS setup to MassBank or MoNA. Input is a raw LC-MS/MS sample dataset needing peak picking rather than an existing annotated spectral library — that is handled by tools like MZMine, MSDial, or OpenMS, not this skill The goal is to validate chemical annotations against measured fragments — the article states such fragment-matching plausibility checks are not yet implemented and are only a possible future expansion Only a one-off cleaning of a single library is needed with no intent to replicate the configuration elsewhere — then a simpler pipeline configuration without the portability/reproducibility framing suffices http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Tests whether a fixed matchms library-cleaning pipeline configuration, captured in a shareable YAML file, can be reused unchanged to clean other public mass spectral libraries beyond the one it was developed on (GNPS), here MassBank and MoNA. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00878-1
skills.summary: Tests whether a fixed matchms library-cleaning pipeline configuration, captured in a shareable YAML file, can be reused unchanged to clean other public mass spectral libraries beyond the one it was developed on (GNPS), here MassBank and MoNA.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a raw LC-MS/MS sample dataset needing peak picking rather than an existing annotated spectral library — that is handled by tools like MZMine, MSDial, or OpenMS, not this skill The goal is to validate chemical annotations against measured fragments — the article states such fragment-matching plausibility checks are not yet implemented and are only a possible future expansion Only a one-off cleaning of a single library is needed with no intent to replicate the configuration elsewhere — then a simpler pipeline configuration without the portability/reproducibility framing suffices

skills.description: Decision support for extending an MTI/internal-standard-calibrated MSI-CE-MS annotation pipeline beyond its validated serum matrix to urine, saliva, stool, or serial-injection isocratic LC-MS data.
skills.name: cross-matrix-metabolomics-method-transfer
skills.search_text: cross-matrix-metabolomics-method-transfer Decision support for extending an MTI/internal-standard-calibrated MSI-CE-MS annotation pipeline beyond its validated serum matrix to urine, saliva, stool, or serial-injection isocratic LC-MS data. Data are already from serum MSI-CE-MS runs — PeakMeister's serum validation (median annotation accuracy >99.9%, median CV = 16.0%) already covers this case directly Untargeted metabolomic feature finding is the goal — PeakMeister requires a targeted mass list and is designed for targeted full-scan MSI-CE-MS pre-processing Late-migrating analytes lacking two flanking or stable-isotope internal standards, or low-abundance signals near the detection limit, dominate the panel — these were prone to peak misannotation even in serum and need special handling before matrix transfer http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Evaluates whether the MTI-based PeakMeister preprocessing workflow, validated for serum MSI-CE-MS (median annotation accuracy >99.9%), can be transferred to other sample matrices (urine, saliva, stool) by benchmarking annotation accuracy and peak-area MAE against ground truth. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c03513
skills.summary: Evaluates whether the MTI-based PeakMeister preprocessing workflow, validated for serum MSI-CE-MS (median annotation accuracy >99.9%), can be transferred to other sample matrices (urine, saliva, stool) by benchmarking annotation accuracy and peak-area MAE against ground truth.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are already from serum MSI-CE-MS runs — PeakMeister's serum validation (median annotation accuracy >99.9%, median CV = 16.0%) already covers this case directly Untargeted metabolomic feature finding is the goal — PeakMeister requires a targeted mass list and is designed for targeted full-scan MSI-CE-MS pre-processing Late-migrating analytes lacking two flanking or stable-isotope internal standards, or low-abundance signals near the detection limit, dominate the panel — these were prone to peak misannotation even in serum and need special handling before matrix transfer

skills.description: Use when an annotation workflow validated on one matrix (e.g. human serum) must be tested on other biological matrices or instrument types, with precision/recall computed against expert manual annotations.
skills.name: cross-matrix-workflow-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cross-matrix-workflow-benchmarking Use when an annotation workflow validated on one matrix (e.g. human serum) must be tested on other biological matrices or instrument types, with precision/recall computed against expert manual annotations. The data are the original human serum development datasets — use the primary workflow evaluation, not the cross-matrix benchmark The goal is validating on higher mass accuracy instruments (e.g. Orbitrap) or non-AIF DIA schemes such as SWATH — explicitly untested/unsupported per the paper Input is MS/MS spectra for spectral-library matching rather than AIF pseudo-MS/MS feature annotation http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Benchmark a metabolite annotation workflow beyond its development matrix by running it on external validation datasets from different biological matrices and instrument types (adipose tissue ESI+/ESI−, amniotic fluid MTBLS666, urine MTBLS816) and computing per-dataset precision and recall against expert manual annotations. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c03032
skills.summary: Benchmark a metabolite annotation workflow beyond its development matrix by running it on external validation datasets from different biological matrices and instrument types (adipose tissue ESI+/ESI−, amniotic fluid MTBLS666, urine MTBLS816) and computing per-dataset precision and recall against expert manual annotations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are the original human serum development datasets — use the primary workflow evaluation, not the cross-matrix benchmark The goal is validating on higher mass accuracy instruments (e.g. Orbitrap) or non-AIF DIA schemes such as SWATH — explicitly untested/unsupported per the paper Input is MS/MS spectra for spectral-library matching rather than AIF pseudo-MS/MS feature annotation

skills.description: Use when an untargeted metabolomics dataset has both a computational metabolite prediction (e.g., mummichog on a significant m/z feature list) and an independent targeted annotation, and you need to measure their agreement to validate the prediction approach.
skills.name: cross-method-annotation-agreement-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-method-annotation-agreement-evaluation Use when an untargeted metabolomics dataset has both a computational metabolite prediction (e.g., mummichog on a significant m/z feature list) and an independent targeted annotation, and you need to measure their agreement to validate the prediction approach. The input is already an annotated feature table with confirmed metabolite identities — no computational prediction needs benchmarking Only one annotation method exists (no independent targeted annotation or standard-based identification to compare against) The goal is de novo metabolite identification rather than benchmarking a prediction method — mummichog 'is not designed to replace tandem mass spectrometry in metabolite identification' http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 Quantify the overlap between metabolites predicted computationally by mummichog from an untargeted feature table and those identified by an independent targeted annotation method (e.g., MAVEN with authentic standards), to benchmark the accuracy of network-based prediction without a priori metabolite identification. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003123
skills.summary: Quantify the overlap between metabolites predicted computationally by mummichog from an untargeted feature table and those identified by an independent targeted annotation method (e.g., MAVEN with authentic standards), to benchmark the accuracy of network-based prediction without a priori metabolite identification.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already an annotated feature table with confirmed metabolite identities — no computational prediction needs benchmarking Only one annotation method exists (no independent targeted annotation or standard-based identification to compare against) The goal is de novo metabolite identification rather than benchmarking a prediction method — mummichog 'is not designed to replace tandem mass spectrometry in metabolite identification'

skills.description: Use when two or more microbiome-metabolome prediction models (e.g., MiMeNet vs. MelonnPan vs. NED) must be compared under an identical cross-validation protocol on paired community profiles.
skills.name: cross-method-benchmark-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-method-benchmark-comparison Use when two or more microbiome-metabolome prediction models (e.g., MiMeNet vs. MelonnPan vs. NED) must be compared under an identical cross-validation protocol on paired community profiles. When only one method exists or the question is a single model's predictive accuracy rather than a head-to-head comparison — the cross-method setup adds no information. When datasets lack paired microbial and metabolite samples from the same specimens; cross-model benchmarking on mismatched pairs is meaningless. When the metabolites of interest are unannotated and cannot be evaluated by the annotated-metabolite-only protocols used in the MelonnPan comparison. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Head-to-head benchmarking of MiMeNet's MLPNN metabolite predictions against MelonnPan's Elastic Net linear models using shared 10-iteration 10-fold cross-validation across IBD (PRISM), cystic fibrosis, and soil datasets plus an external IBD test set. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009021
skills.summary: Head-to-head benchmarking of MiMeNet's MLPNN metabolite predictions against MelonnPan's Elastic Net linear models using shared 10-iteration 10-fold cross-validation across IBD (PRISM), cystic fibrosis, and soil datasets plus an external IBD test set.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When only one method exists or the question is a single model's predictive accuracy rather than a head-to-head comparison — the cross-method setup adds no information. When datasets lack paired microbial and metabolite samples from the same specimens; cross-model benchmarking on mismatched pairs is meaningless. When the metabolites of interest are unannotated and cannot be evaluated by the annotated-metabolite-only protocols used in the MelonnPan comparison.

skills.description: Use when a new method (e.g. NPFimg) claims lower error rates of signal acquisition or marker identification than a baseline (e.g. XCMS) and the same raw chromatography–MS data can be processed by both.
skills.name: cross-method-benchmark-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-method-benchmark-comparison Use when a new method (e.g. NPFimg) claims lower error rates of signal acquisition or marker identification than a baseline (e.g. XCMS) and the same raw chromatography–MS data can be processed by both. The input is already a processed feature/marker table — benchmarking requires running both methods end-to-end on the same raw MS maps so peak-picking behavior differs only by method. Only one method can be executed on the data (e.g. XCMS cannot be applied to the data format, or the image-based method lacks a suitable input representation) — a comparison needs both arms on identical inputs. The evaluation goal is runtime/memory benchmarking rather than error rates of signal acquisition and marker identification — the paper's claim is about correctness (lower error rates), not speed. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Benchmark a newly proposed chromatography–MS data-processing method against an established baseline (here, NPFimg vs XCMS) by running both on the same GC–MS datasets and quantifying error rates of signal acquisition and marker identification. This skill converts a paper's comparative claim into a reproducible head-to-head comparison table. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c03163
skills.summary: Benchmark a newly proposed chromatography–MS data-processing method against an established baseline (here, NPFimg vs XCMS) by running both on the same GC–MS datasets and quantifying error rates of signal acquisition and marker identification. This skill converts a paper's comparative claim into a reproducible head-to-head comparison table.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a processed feature/marker table — benchmarking requires running both methods end-to-end on the same raw MS maps so peak-picking behavior differs only by method. Only one method can be executed on the data (e.g. XCMS cannot be applied to the data format, or the image-based method lacks a suitable input representation) — a comparison needs both arms on identical inputs. The evaluation goal is runtime/memory benchmarking rather than error rates of signal acquisition and marker identification — the paper's claim is about correctness (lower error rates), not speed.

skills.description: Use when two computational prediction methods must be compared on the same external test data and headline metrics (R2, RMSE, Median RE) are needed to judge which performs better without training-set leakage.
skills.name: cross-method-benchmark-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-method-benchmark-comparison Use when two computational prediction methods must be compared on the same external test data and headline metrics (R2, RMSE, Median RE) are needed to judge which performs better without training-set leakage. The comparison set contains molecules present in either method's training set — deduplication against both training sets is required first to exclude data leakage Molecules contain elements outside C, H, O, N, P, S, F, Cl, Br, I, Co, As, Se, or adducts other than [M+H]+, [M-H]-, [M+Na]+, since SigmaCCS cannot predict them Only one method's predictions are available — without matched predictions from both methods on identical entries, the benchmark is not meaningful http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Benchmark two CCS prediction methods (SigmaCCS vs CCSbase) on a shared, deduplicated external test set by computing R2, RMSE, and Median relative error against experimental CCS values, eliminating data-leakage confounds before comparing metrics. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s42004-023-00939-w
skills.summary: Benchmark two CCS prediction methods (SigmaCCS vs CCSbase) on a shared, deduplicated external test set by computing R2, RMSE, and Median relative error against experimental CCS values, eliminating data-leakage confounds before comparing metrics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The comparison set contains molecules present in either method's training set — deduplication against both training sets is required first to exclude data leakage Molecules contain elements outside C, H, O, N, P, S, F, Cl, Br, I, Co, As, Se, or adducts other than [M+H]+, [M-H]-, [M+Na]+, since SigmaCCS cannot predict them Only one method's predictions are available — without matched predictions from both methods on identical entries, the benchmark is not meaningful

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify how robust a CCS calibration/feature-class-assignment pipeline is to calibration error and whether it outperforms single-trendline or IMSCal baselines.
skills.name: cross-method-calibration-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-method-calibration-comparison Use when you need to quantify how robust a CCS calibration/feature-class-assignment pipeline is to calibration error and whether it outperforms single-trendline or IMSCal baselines. You only need routine CCS calibration of already-identified features; use MOCCal's standard calibration path rather than this robustness benchmark.
