skills.summary: Compute per-run MS2/MS1 total ion current (TIC) ratios from MetaXtract scan-header exports and flag underperforming acquisitions against a configurable threshold, enabling identification-free, near real-time QC gating before database searching.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is not Thermo Fisher RAW data — MetaXtract currently supports only Thermo RAW files; additional vendor formats are not yet supported Database-search-derived QC metrics are required, e.g. identification-based metrics like those MSQC computes from search results — this skill is identification-free and uses only acquisition-side TIC signals You need fine-grained, scan-level anomaly localization rather than a single per-run ratio gate — this skill aggregates TIC over the whole run

skills.description: Use when integrating two spatial omics modalities (e.g. 10X Visium spatial transcriptome and MALDI-MSI metabolome) that share no features, and you need a cross-omics correlated feature to guide spot-to-spot alignment.
skills.name: cross-omics-feature-pair-conversion
skills.search_text: cross-omics-feature-pair-conversion Use when integrating two spatial omics modalities (e.g. 10X Visium spatial transcriptome and MALDI-MSI metabolome) that share no features, and you need a cross-omics correlated feature to guide spot-to-spot alignment. When the spatial transcriptome and MALDI-MSI data already share a common feature space (shared genes/metabolites), the cross-omics feature-pair conversion step is unnecessary and simpler direct alignment suffices. When the goal is purely morphological (image-based) alignment of spatial coordinates without leveraging cross-omics co-variation, use the manual_gross_alignment or icp_3d_alignment path alone instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Identify gene–metabolite (m/z) feature pairs with high Pearson correlation across paired spatial transcriptome and MALDI-MSI spot maps, then convert those pairs into a single canonical-correlation variate (fcca) that is appended as an extra feature dimension to both datasets before alignment. This enables haCCA to anchor spot-to-spot integration on cross-omics co-variation rather than shared features alone. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.08.20.608773
skills.summary: Identify gene–metabolite (m/z) feature pairs with high Pearson correlation across paired spatial transcriptome and MALDI-MSI spot maps, then convert those pairs into a single canonical-correlation variate (fcca) that is appended as an extra feature dimension to both datasets before alignment. This enables haCCA to anchor spot-to-spot integration on cross-omics co-variation rather than shared features alone.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the spatial transcriptome and MALDI-MSI data already share a common feature space (shared genes/metabolites), the cross-omics feature-pair conversion step is unnecessary and simpler direct alignment suffices. When the goal is purely morphological (image-based) alignment of spatial coordinates without leveraging cross-omics co-variation, use the manual_gross_alignment or icp_3d_alignment path alone instead.

skills.description: Use when merging or enriching multi-omics results (e.g. isoforms, miRNAs, proteins, lipids from MOI Salmon/isoformSwitchAnalyzeR outputs) that must be converted to gene-level features before pathway analysis.
skills.name: cross-omics-identifier-mapping
skills.search_text: cross-omics-identifier-mapping Use when merging or enriching multi-omics results (e.g. isoforms, miRNAs, proteins, lipids from MOI Salmon/isoformSwitchAnalyzeR outputs) that must be converted to gene-level features before pathway analysis. Input features are already gene-level mRNAs only with no miRNA, isoform, protein, or lipid layers to reconcile — no translation is needed Downstream analysis does not require pathway enrichment or cross-layer integration (e.g. layer-specific QC like FASTQC/Trim Galore) http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Translates heterogeneous omics feature identifiers (miRNAs, isoforms, proteins, lipids, mRNAs) into a unified gene-level namespace so that downstream pathway enrichment and integration operate on comparable features. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioadv/vbae175
skills.summary: Translates heterogeneous omics feature identifiers (miRNAs, isoforms, proteins, lipids, mRNAs) into a unified gene-level namespace so that downstream pathway enrichment and integration operate on comparable features.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input features are already gene-level mRNAs only with no miRNA, isoform, protein, or lipid layers to reconcile — no translation is needed Downstream analysis does not require pathway enrichment or cross-layer integration (e.g. layer-specific QC like FASTQC/Trim Galore)

skills.description: Use when multiple aligned omics feature matrices (e.g. mRNA, miRNA, isoform, proteomics, lipidomics tables) are available after MOI's MCIA integration step and noisy feature-to-feature connections must be filtered out before pathway enrichment analysis.
skills.name: cross-omics-pearson-spearman-correlation
skills.search_text: cross-omics-pearson-spearman-correlation Use when multiple aligned omics feature matrices (e.g. mRNA, miRNA, isoform, proteomics, lipidomics tables) are available after MOI's MCIA integration step and noisy feature-to-feature connections must be filtered out before pathway enrichment analysis. Input is raw sequencing data (FASTQ/SRA runs) — correlation comes after QC (FASTQC, Trim Galore), Salmon quantification, and count-matrix filtering/normalization/batch correction, not before The goal is the primary data-driven integration of samples across omics — MOI uses MCIA for that, reporting the sample-space PCA and pseudo-eigen values; correlation is a downstream connection-filtering step Only a single omics layer is available — pairwise cross-omics correlation requires at least two aligned feature matrices http://edamontology.org/topic_3360 Compute pairwise Pearson or Spearman correlations between per-omics feature matrices (genes, miRNAs, isoforms, proteins, lipids) within the MultiOmicsIntegrator (MOI) pipeline to filter illuminating connections and mitigate noise before downstream pathway enrichment with clusterProfiler or BioTranslator. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioadv/vbae175
skills.summary: Compute pairwise Pearson or Spearman correlations between per-omics feature matrices (genes, miRNAs, isoforms, proteins, lipids) within the MultiOmicsIntegrator (MOI) pipeline to filter illuminating connections and mitigate noise before downstream pathway enrichment with clusterProfiler or BioTranslator.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sequencing data (FASTQ/SRA runs) — correlation comes after QC (FASTQC, Trim Galore), Salmon quantification, and count-matrix filtering/normalization/batch correction, not before The goal is the primary data-driven integration of samples across omics — MOI uses MCIA for that, reporting the sample-space PCA and pseudo-eigen values; correlation is a downstream connection-filtering step Only a single omics layer is available — pairwise cross-omics correlation requires at least two aligned feature matrices

skills.description: Use when per-metabolite model feature importances are available for multiple omics feature sets and you need to identify globally influential regulators, e.g. confirming YAP1 as a top predictor across 4 omic layers.
skills.name: cross-omics-regulator-consistency-check
skills.search_text: cross-omics-regulator-consistency-check Use when per-metabolite model feature importances are available for multiple omics feature sets and you need to identify globally influential regulators, e.g. confirming YAP1 as a top predictor across 4 omic layers. Only one omics feature set is available — no cross-omics consistency can be assessed. The goal is single-metabolite feature importance (use Shapley analysis per metabolite instead), not global metabolome-wide regulator ranking. Input is raw omics data rather than trained-model importances; models must first be trained and their feature importances extracted (see ML_function.ipynb). http://edamontology.org/topic_3339 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Aggregates per-metabolite random-forest feature importances across the eight biomolecular feature classes (transcriptomics, proteomics, methylation, phosphoproteomics, miRNA, lncRNA, CNV, histone PTMs) from the 225 CCLE metabolite models in Metab8D to rank global metabolome regulators and count how many models each feature tops in each omics class. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.08.17.608400
skills.summary: Aggregates per-metabolite random-forest feature importances across the eight biomolecular feature classes (transcriptomics, proteomics, methylation, phosphoproteomics, miRNA, lncRNA, CNV, histone PTMs) from the 225 CCLE metabolite models in Metab8D to rank global metabolome regulators and count how many models each feature tops in each omics class.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only one omics feature set is available — no cross-omics consistency can be assessed. The goal is single-metabolite feature importance (use Shapley analysis per metabolite instead), not global metabolome-wide regulator ranking. Input is raw omics data rather than trained-model importances; models must first be trained and their feature importances extracted (see ML_function.ipynb).

skills.description: Reference for comparing chemical-class coverage, spectral redundancy (median spectra per compound), and compound counts across multiple open mass spectral libraries before integrating them or choosing which OMSL to use.
skills.name: cross-omsl-comparative-statistics
skills.search_text: cross-omsl-comparative-statistics Reference for comparing chemical-class coverage, spectral redundancy (median spectra per compound), and compound counts across multiple open mass spectral libraries before integrating them or choosing which OMSL to use. You only need to integrate/harmonize library files — that is FragHub's parsing, SPLASH-key deduplication and filtering job, not comparative statistics. The input is already a merged FragHub output table with class annotations; re-deriving class distributions from raw files would duplicate work. You need collision-energy comparison across libraries — the paper explicitly states collision energies were not harmonized due to ~70 nonstandardized formats. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0089 A comparative-statistics skill that characterizes the chemical-class composition and spectral redundancy of multiple Open Mass Spectra Libraries (GNPS, MassBank, MoNA, MS-Dial-VS17) by counting spectra per compound InChIKey and annotating compounds with NPClassifier pathways/superclasses. It quantifies how unevenly chemical space (fatty acids, alkaloids, carbohydrates/peptides) and spectra-per-compound medians (e.g. GNPS 2 vs MassBank 12) are distributed across OMSLs. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c02219
skills.summary: A comparative-statistics skill that characterizes the chemical-class composition and spectral redundancy of multiple Open Mass Spectra Libraries (GNPS, MassBank, MoNA, MS-Dial-VS17) by counting spectra per compound InChIKey and annotating compounds with NPClassifier pathways/superclasses. It quantifies how unevenly chemical space (fatty acids, alkaloids, carbohydrates/peptides) and spectra-per-compound medians (e.g. GNPS 2 vs MassBank 12) are distributed across OMSLs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need to integrate/harmonize library files — that is FragHub's parsing, SPLASH-key deduplication and filtering job, not comparative statistics. The input is already a merged FragHub output table with class annotations; re-deriving class distributions from raw files would duplicate work. You need collision-energy comparison across libraries — the paper explicitly states collision energies were not harmonized due to ~70 nonstandardized formats.

skills.description: Use when the goal is to compare metabolisms of two or more KEGG organisms via similarity indexes (set/multiset reaction sets) or to check whether index-based groupings reproduce known evolutionary relationships.
skills.name: cross-organism-metabolic-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-organism-metabolic-comparison Use when the goal is to compare metabolisms of two or more KEGG organisms via similarity indexes (set/multiset reaction sets) or to check whether index-based groupings reproduce known evolutionary relationships. When the input is raw genomic/experimental data rather than KEGG organisms — MetNet does not yet accept genomic data and reconstructs metabolism only from the KEGG database When a single organism must be reconstructed without any comparison — MetNet is built around pairwise (and derived multi-pair) comparison of two or more KEGG organisms When metabolism must be reconstructed from non-KEGG sources (e.g. BioCyc, BioModels) or from newly annotated genomes, since reconstruction is based uniquely on KEGG's reference pathways http://edamontology.org/topic_3391 Reconstruct the metabolic networks of KEGG organisms with MetNet and compare them quantitatively and visually using two-level similarity indexes (structural Ssim, pathway Psim/PsimW, combined Csim), optionally extending pairwise comparisons to a whole organism set via distance-matrix clustering. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pone.0246962
skills.summary: Reconstruct the metabolic networks of KEGG organisms with MetNet and compare them quantitatively and visually using two-level similarity indexes (structural Ssim, pathway Psim/PsimW, combined Csim), optionally extending pairwise comparisons to a whole organism set via distance-matrix clustering.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is raw genomic/experimental data rather than KEGG organisms — MetNet does not yet accept genomic data and reconstructs metabolism only from the KEGG database When a single organism must be reconstructed without any comparison — MetNet is built around pairwise (and derived multi-pair) comparison of two or more KEGG organisms When metabolism must be reconstructed from non-KEGG sources (e.g. BioCyc, BioModels) or from newly annotated genomes, since reconstruction is based uniquely on KEGG's reference pathways

skills.description: Use when two KEGG-coded organisms with suspected metabolic interdependence (e.g. host–endosymbiont pairs) need their metabolisms reconstructed from KGML data and compared pathway-by-pathway to reveal complementation.
skills.name: cross-organism-metabolic-complementation-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-organism-metabolic-complementation-analysis Use when two KEGG-coded organisms with suspected metabolic interdependence (e.g. host–endosymbiont pairs) need their metabolisms reconstructed from KGML data and compared pathway-by-pathway to reveal complementation. You need to reconstruct a metabolism from annotated genomic/experimental data rather than KEGG — MetNet is based uniquely on the KEGG database and does not currently support input of genomic data The organism pair is not available under KEGG organism codes, or you need a graphical-visualisation-driven comparison rather than the command-line two-organism functional comparison The goal is single-organism network reconstruction without a pairwise comparison (tools like AutoKEGGRec or KBase address that) http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Reconstructs the metabolic networks of two KEGG organisms with MetNet and compares them at the functional level using per-pathway Pi similarity indexes (SimPi) and the global Psim/PsimW indexes, then builds a complementarity inventory to test whether low global similarity reflects complementary metabolisms (e.g. aphid apis vs. symbiont bap). metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pone.0246962
skills.summary: Reconstructs the metabolic networks of two KEGG organisms with MetNet and compares them at the functional level using per-pathway Pi similarity indexes (SimPi) and the global Psim/PsimW indexes, then builds a complementarity inventory to test whether low global similarity reflects complementary metabolisms (e.g. aphid apis vs. symbiont bap).
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need to reconstruct a metabolism from annotated genomic/experimental data rather than KEGG — MetNet is based uniquely on the KEGG database and does not currently support input of genomic data The organism pair is not available under KEGG organism codes, or you need a graphical-visualisation-driven comparison rather than the command-line two-organism functional comparison The goal is single-organism network reconstruction without a pairwise comparison (tools like AutoKEGGRec or KBase address that)

skills.description: Use when two organism-specific MPI classifiers must be compared on identical shared metabolite-protein pairs to test whether predictions are consistent across metabolic networks.
skills.name: cross-organism-metabolite-protein-interaction-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-organism-metabolite-protein-interaction-evaluation Use when two organism-specific MPI classifiers must be compared on identical shared metabolite-protein pairs to test whether predictions are consistent across metabolic networks. When the goal is standard within-organism classifier evaluation (use evaluate.py per gold standard instead) When evaluating performance on subsystem-specific exclusions such as Alternate Carbon Metabolism or Cofactor and Prosthetic Group Biosynthesis (use subsys.py) When input features are molecular fingerprints (fp) rather than shadow prices — this cross-organism agreement task is framed around shadow-price features http://edamontology.org/topic_0128 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Trains organism-specific random forest classifiers on shadow-price features from two GEMs (iJO1366 for E. coli, Yeast-GEM/Yeast8 for S. cerevisiae), excludes metabolite-protein pairs shared between the GEMs, applies each model to the shared pairs, and quantifies cross-organism prediction agreement via accuracy and cosine similarity of prediction vectors. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioadv/vbad098
skills.summary: Trains organism-specific random forest classifiers on shadow-price features from two GEMs (iJO1366 for E. coli, Yeast-GEM/Yeast8 for S. cerevisiae), excludes metabolite-protein pairs shared between the GEMs, applies each model to the shared pairs, and quantifies cross-organism prediction agreement via accuracy and cosine similarity of prediction vectors.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is standard within-organism classifier evaluation (use evaluate.py per gold standard instead) When evaluating performance on subsystem-specific exclusions such as Alternate Carbon Metabolism or Cofactor and Prosthetic Group Biosynthesis (use subsys.py) When input features are molecular fingerprints (fp) rather than shadow prices — this cross-organism agreement task is framed around shadow-price features

skills.description: Use when two (or a set of) KEGG organisms' metabolisms must be compared at the structural/topological level and a qualitative visual judgement of network shape difference (e.g. complex host vs. simple symbiont) is the deliverable.
skills.name: cross-organism-topology-visual-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-organism-topology-visual-comparison Use when two (or a set of) KEGG organisms' metabolisms must be compared at the structural/topological level and a qualitative visual judgement of network shape difference (e.g. complex host vs. simple symbiont) is the deliverable. The analysis goal is a quantitative, pathway-by-pathway or global similarity score rather than a qualitative visual topology comparison (use MetNet's similarity measures instead). The input is raw genomic data rather than KEGG organisms: MetNet's reconstruction is based uniquely on the KEGG database and does not currently support input of genomic data. Only a single organism's network needs to be reconstructed or visualized with no cross-organism comparison. http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 Renders and visually compares the structural-level (graph-based) metabolic network topologies of two KEGG organisms reconstructed by MetNet, where pathways are nodes and edges connect pathways sharing at least one non-ubiquitous compound. This qualitative visual inspection complements MetNet's quantitative similarity indexes. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pone.0246962
skills.summary: Renders and visually compares the structural-level (graph-based) metabolic network topologies of two KEGG organisms reconstructed by MetNet, where pathways are nodes and edges connect pathways sharing at least one non-ubiquitous compound. This qualitative visual inspection complements MetNet's quantitative similarity indexes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is a quantitative, pathway-by-pathway or global similarity score rather than a qualitative visual topology comparison (use MetNet's similarity measures instead). The input is raw genomic data rather than KEGG organisms: MetNet's reconstruction is based uniquely on the KEGG database and does not currently support input of genomic data. Only a single organism's network needs to be reconstructed or visualized with no cross-organism comparison.

skills.description: Use when selecting an R package to import/export spectral libraries in NIST msp or MoNA/GNPS dialects, and you need a reproducible support matrix rather than documentation claims.
skills.name: cross-package-capability-matrix-compilation
skills.search_text: cross-package-capability-matrix-compilation Use when selecting an R package to import/export spectral libraries in NIST msp or MoNA/GNPS dialects, and you need a reproducible support matrix rather than documentation claims. The input is already a processed feature table or quantification matrix rather than a spectral-library exchange file (msp/mgf) — this skill only tests spectral-database readers and writers. You need a single production-ready conversion rather than a comparative benchmark — pick the one package that already passes the dialect check instead of re-running the full matrix. The target format is neither NIST msp nor MoNA/GNPS mgf (e.g. native instrument formats), since the workflow's dialects and attribute round-trip checks do not cover it. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Systematically benchmarks metabolomics R packages (e.g. metaMS, OrgMassSpecR, enviGCMS, TargetSearch, MSnbase/MSnio, compMS2Miner) for their ability to read and write spectral-library exchange dialects such as NIST msp and GNPS mgf, and condenses the results into a package x dialect/attribute capability matrix. It reproduces the review-style comparisons of Table 3 and Table S1 with measurable parse success, attribute round-trip survival, and export runtimes. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo9100200
skills.summary: Systematically benchmarks metabolomics R packages (e.g. metaMS, OrgMassSpecR, enviGCMS, TargetSearch, MSnbase/MSnio, compMS2Miner) for their ability to read and write spectral-library exchange dialects such as NIST msp and GNPS mgf, and condenses the results into a package x dialect/attribute capability matrix. It reproduces the review-style comparisons of Table 3 and Table S1 with measurable parse success, attribute round-trip survival, and export runtimes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a processed feature table or quantification matrix rather than a spectral-library exchange file (msp/mgf) — this skill only tests spectral-database readers and writers. You need a single production-ready conversion rather than a comparative benchmark — pick the one package that already passes the dialect check instead of re-running the full matrix. The target format is neither NIST msp nor MoNA/GNPS mgf (e.g. native instrument formats), since the workflow's dialects and attribute round-trip checks do not cover it.

skills.description: Use when comparing computational efficiency (elapsed time, memory allocation) of alternative R packages performing the same network-construction task on identically sized, identically seeded inputs, e.g. to substantiate claims like 'up to 100-fold faster'.
skills.name: cross-package-runtime-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cross-package-runtime-benchmarking Use when comparing computational efficiency (elapsed time, memory allocation) of alternative R packages performing the same network-construction task on identically sized, identically seeded inputs, e.g. to substantiate claims like 'up to 100-fold faster'. The goal is benchmarking wall-clock speed rather than network quality — topology or biological validity of resulting networks is out of scope Datasets exceed ~1,000 features per tool but the packages' own documented limits differ; scaling beyond the paper's tested sizes (e.g. >10,000 features) was not validated here http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 A reproducible runtime/memory benchmarking skill that times equivalent network-construction calls from R packages such as MetaNet, WGCNA, microeco, ggClusterNet, and NetCoMi on identically seeded synthetic count matrices of graded sizes (50–1,000 features), using bench::mark over repeated runs to quantify per-package speed and memory scaling. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.06.26.661636
skills.summary: A reproducible runtime/memory benchmarking skill that times equivalent network-construction calls from R packages such as MetaNet, WGCNA, microeco, ggClusterNet, and NetCoMi on identically seeded synthetic count matrices of graded sizes (50–1,000 features), using bench::mark over repeated runs to quantify per-package speed and memory scaling.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is benchmarking wall-clock speed rather than network quality — topology or biological validity of resulting networks is out of scope Datasets exceed ~1,000 features per tool but the packages' own documented limits differ; scaling beyond the paper's tested sizes (e.g. >10,000 features) was not validated here

skills.description: Use when two peak-intensity/height data matrices were generated from the same raw LC/HRMS study by different pipelines (e.g. IDSL.IPA vs MS-DIAL) and you need a statistically grounded comparison of how many features each detects as associated with a phenotype.
skills.name: cross-pipeline-matrix-comparison-idsl-ipa-vs-msdial
skills.search_text: cross-pipeline-matrix-comparison-idsl-ipa-vs-msdial Use when two peak-intensity/height data matrices were generated from the same raw LC/HRMS study by different pipelines (e.g. IDSL.IPA vs MS-DIAL) and you need a statistically grounded comparison of how many features each detects as associated with a phenotype. The two matrices come from the same pipeline and only differ in parameters - the comparison would measure parameter tuning, not pipeline sensitivity Peak matrices have not been aligned to a common sample-ID key, so per-peak phenotypic correlations would be computed on mismatched samples Input is already a set of annotated/formula-assigned peaks and the goal is formula or structural annotation rather than quantifying pipeline detection sensitivity http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0219 Benchmark skill that compares feature matrices generated by two untargeted LC/HRMS peak-picking pipelines (IDSL.IPA and MS-DIAL) by mapping both onto the same phenotype and testing peak-level statistical associations, e.g. Spearman correlations against birth weight in the 499-sample MTBLS1684 cord-blood study. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.2c00120
skills.summary: Benchmark skill that compares feature matrices generated by two untargeted LC/HRMS peak-picking pipelines (IDSL.IPA and MS-DIAL) by mapping both onto the same phenotype and testing peak-level statistical associations, e.g. Spearman correlations against birth weight in the 499-sample MTBLS1684 cord-blood study.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The two matrices come from the same pipeline and only differ in parameters - the comparison would measure parameter tuning, not pipeline sensitivity Peak matrices have not been aligned to a common sample-ID key, so per-peak phenotypic correlations would be computed on mismatched samples Input is already a set of annotated/formula-assigned peaks and the goal is formula or structural annotation rather than quantifying pipeline detection sensitivity

skills.description: Use when an unassigned LC-HRMS signal recurs across two or more instruments/modes and you need to pull its spectral and compound records from a spectral database and tabulate platform-by-platform annotations with MSI confidence levels.
skills.name: cross-platform-annotation-table-compilation
skills.search_text: cross-platform-annotation-table-compilation Use when an unassigned LC-HRMS signal recurs across two or more instruments/modes and you need to pull its spectral and compound records from a spectral database and tabulate platform-by-platform annotations with MSI confidence levels. The target signal was observed on only a single instrument/platform and no cross-platform comparison is required You need to store or clean raw spectral data — PeakForest stores metadata related to raw data rather than raw data itself and requires users to supply completely-cleaned data Annotations are already available in a compiled feature table; re-querying PeakForest records would duplicate existing work http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Compiles metabolite annotations observed across multiple LC-HRMS platforms (e.g. Orbitrap Fusion and Q-ToF Impact II) into a single structured table, using PeakForest REST/Web services to retrieve spectrum and compound records for cross-platform signals such as the recurrent m/z 247.1441 in positive-mode NIST plasma annotated as hypaphorine (MSI level 2). metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-022-01899-3
skills.summary: Compiles metabolite annotations observed across multiple LC-HRMS platforms (e.g. Orbitrap Fusion and Q-ToF Impact II) into a single structured table, using PeakForest REST/Web services to retrieve spectrum and compound records for cross-platform signals such as the recurrent m/z 247.1441 in positive-mode NIST plasma annotated as hypaphorine (MSI level 2).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The target signal was observed on only a single instrument/platform and no cross-platform comparison is required You need to store or clean raw spectral data — PeakForest stores metadata related to raw data rather than raw data itself and requires users to supply completely-cleaned data Annotations are already available in a compiled feature table; re-querying PeakForest records would duplicate existing work

skills.description: Use when IM-MS lipidomics data from two ion-mobility technologies (trapped IM and drift-tube IM) must be compared, e.g., to compute mean absolute CCSN2 bias per ionization mode or to decide whether class-adduct-specific CCS correction is needed.
skills.name: cross-platform-ccs-comparison-tims-dtims
skills.search_text: cross-platform-ccs-comparison-tims-dtims Use when IM-MS lipidomics data from two ion-mobility technologies (trapped IM and drift-tube IM) must be compared, e.g., to compute mean absolute CCSN2 bias per ionization mode or to decide whether class-adduct-specific CCS correction is needed. Input CCS data are from a single IM technology with no DTIM reference and no U13C-labeled internal standards spiked in — internal standardization cannot be performed Lipid classes fall outside the supported list (AcCa, Cer, Co, DG, HexCer, LPC, LPE, PA, PC, PE, PG, PI, PS, SPH, TG) or use adducts not permitted for that class Goal is absolute CCS prediction rather than bias assessment/correction against a DTCCSN2 library http://edamontology.org/topic_0157 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Quantify and interpret CCSN2 bias between TIM-MS (e.g., timsTOF Pro) and DTIM-MS (Agilent 6560) lipid measurements using a U13C-labeled yeast lipid DTCCSN2 library, enabling cross-platform CCS quality control and class-specific correction in MobiLipid. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c01253
skills.summary: Quantify and interpret CCSN2 bias between TIM-MS (e.g., timsTOF Pro) and DTIM-MS (Agilent 6560) lipid measurements using a U13C-labeled yeast lipid DTCCSN2 library, enabling cross-platform CCS quality control and class-specific correction in MobiLipid.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input CCS data are from a single IM technology with no DTIM reference and no U13C-labeled internal standards spiked in — internal standardization cannot be performed Lipid classes fall outside the supported list (AcCa, Cer, Co, DG, HexCer, LPC, LPE, PA, PC, PE, PG, PI, PS, SPH, TG) or use adducts not permitted for that class Goal is absolute CCS prediction rather than bias assessment/correction against a DTCCSN2 library

skills.description: Use when a machine-learning peak-quality classifier trained on one LC-MS platform/dataset must be tested on independent datasets from a different platform or ionization mode, and cross-dataset generalization (Accuracy, Pass/Fail F-measure) needs to be quantified.
skills.name: cross-platform-classifier-generalization-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-platform-classifier-generalization-evaluation Use when a machine-learning peak-quality classifier trained on one LC-MS platform/dataset must be tested on independent datasets from a different platform or ionization mode, and cross-dataset generalization (Accuracy, Pass/Fail F-measure) needs to be quantified. skills.search_text: cross-polarity-annotation-verification Use when LC/MS datasets were acquired in both positive and negative ESI ion modes, xsAnnotate objects exist for each polarity, and single-mode ion annotations need cross-verification to improve molecular mass annotation rates. Data were acquired in a single ionization mode only, so no opposite-polarity spectra exist to match. You only need within-mode isotope/adduct grouping and annotation; use CAMERA's single-polarity workflow (findIsotopes, calcCiS/calcCaS, calcPC) rather than combinexsAnnos. The candidate ion combinations involve rare or untrusted adducts — including them risks overriding correct single-polarity annotations, since cross-polarity rules take precedence. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 CAMERA's annotation-verification approach that matches compound spectra measured in opposite ionization modes against a cross-polarity rule table, keeping only common and trusted adduct/ion combinations to confirm or override single-polarity annotations and raise the molecular-mass annotation rate. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/ac202450g
skills.summary: CAMERA's annotation-verification approach that matches compound spectra measured in opposite ionization modes against a cross-polarity rule table, keeping only common and trusted adduct/ion combinations to confirm or override single-polarity annotations and raise the molecular-mass annotation rate.

skills.search_text: cross-run-ccs-reproducibility-assessment Use when a large batch of IMS-MS runs (e.g. 7106 RapidFire SPE-IMS-MS runs) yields a repeat analyte measurement and you need to quantify CCS variance across runs, or to compare calibration variants (conventional vs. pressure/temperature-corrected single-field) by their %RSD. skills.summary: Aggregate component peak areas for tentative compound identifications across every sample in a GC-MS experiment using the uafR R package (spreadOut + mzExacto), replacing weeks-to-months of manual peak-area selection and integration with a reproducible R workflow.

skills.description: Use when you have peak/feature tables per sample from multidimensional MS acquisitions and need one feature list matched across all study samples, QC pools, and blanks using simultaneous m/z, drift time, and retention time tolerances.
skills.name: cross-sample-feature-alignment
skills.search_text: cross-sample-feature-alignment Use when you have peak/feature tables per sample from multidimensional MS acquisitions and need one feature list matched across all study samples, QC pools, and blanks using simultaneous m/z, drift time, and retention time tolerances. Input is already a collapsed, cross-sample aligned feature table — re-running alignment would merge distinct features and lose per-sample resolution. You only have raw spectra (e.g. Bruker .d or Waters .raw acquisitions) and no per-sample peak tables yet; feature detection must precede alignment. Data are 1D or 2D (e.g. LC-MS only, no drift time); the multidimensional partition/maximum-linkage approach is designed for N-dimensional (e.g. LC-IMS-MS/MS) coordinates and gains little over m/z versus RT alignment. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Aligns per-sample feature tables from high-dimensional mass spectrometry data (e.g. LC-IMS-MS/MS in m/z, drift time, retention time) across study samples by clustering features with maximum linkage, producing a single table of features matched across samples. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c05017
skills.summary: Aligns per-sample feature tables from high-dimensional mass spectrometry data (e.g. LC-IMS-MS/MS in m/z, drift time, retention time) across study samples by clustering features with maximum linkage, producing a single table of features matched across samples.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a collapsed, cross-sample aligned feature table — re-running alignment would merge distinct features and lose per-sample resolution. skills.description: Use when you have per-sample deconvolution results from untargeted GC×GC–MS data (e.g. GcDUO Module III output) and need to merge duplicate features into cross-sample consensus features with consensus spectra before annotation or integration.
skills.name: cross-sample-feature-grouping
skills.search_text: cross-sample-feature-grouping Use when you have per-sample deconvolution results from untargeted GC×GC–MS data (e.g. GcDUO Module III output) and need to merge duplicate features into cross-sample consensus features with consensus spectra before annotation or integration. Only one sample is available — cross-sample grouping and consensus spectra cannot be formed; consensus spectra require common features between samples Input is already an aligned/annotated feature table — grouping precedes annotation (duoID) and integration (ConsProcessing), so re-grouping would duplicate work Features were produced by a different deconvolution pipeline whose spectra are not dot-product comparable with the per-sample PARAFAC-extracted spectra http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Groups per-sample deconvolved GC×GC–MS features into consensus features by matching retention time and top m/z fragment with a dot-product spectral similarity cutoff of 60%, then computes the mean consensus spectrum per grouped feature. This bridges per-sample PARAFAC deconvolution and downstream annotation/quantification. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bib/bbaf080
skills.summary: Groups per-sample deconvolved GC×GC–MS features into consensus features by matching retention time and top m/z fragment with a dot-product spectral similarity cutoff of 60%, then computes the mean consensus spectrum per grouped feature. This bridges per-sample PARAFAC deconvolution and downstream annotation/quantification.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only one sample is available — cross-sample grouping and consensus spectra cannot be formed; consensus spectra require common features between samples Input is already an aligned/annotated feature table — grouping precedes annotation (duoID) and integration (ConsProcessing), so re-grouping would duplicate work Features were produced by a different deconvolution pipeline whose spectra are not dot-product comparable with the per-sample PARAFAC-extracted spectra

skills.description: Use when running the TIC peak detection stage of AutoTuner and you must supply the Group difference value, the sole parameter estimated through a manual, non-automatable cross-sample comparison rather than statistical inference on raw data.
skills.name: cross-sample-group-difference-estimation
skills.search_text: cross-sample-group-difference-estimation Use when running the TIC peak detection stage of AutoTuner and you must supply the Group difference value, the sole parameter estimated through a manual, non-automatable cross-sample comparison rather than statistical inference on raw data. Estimating any of the seven continuous centWave parameters (ppm, S/N Threshold, Scan count, Noise, Prefilter intensity, Minimum/Maximum Peak-width) — these come from AutoTuner's single-step statistical inference, not this manual comparison You expect a fully automated, statistically validated estimate — this parameter is explicitly non-automatable and its robustness could not be checked in the Monte Carlo experiment Input is already a feature table — AutoTuner operates on raw converted data (.mzML/.mzXML/.CDF) prior to feature-table generation Estimates the XCMS Group difference parameter—the one non-automatable parameter in AutoTuner—by manually comparing TIC peak detections across samples in different experimental factor groups, yielding the value that is later aggregated (as a cross-sample maximum) into the final eight-parameter centWave/grouping parameter set. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/812370
skills.summary: Estimates the XCMS Group difference parameter—the one non-automatable parameter in AutoTuner—by manually comparing TIC peak detections across samples in different experimental factor groups, yielding the value that is later aggregated (as a cross-sample maximum) into the final eight-parameter centWave/grouping parameter set.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Estimating any of the seven continuous centWave parameters (ppm, S/N Threshold, Scan count, Noise, Prefilter intensity, Minimum/Maximum Peak-width) — these come from AutoTuner's single-step statistical inference, not this manual comparison You expect a fully automated, statistically validated estimate — this parameter is explicitly non-automatable and its robustness could not be checked in the Monte Carlo experiment Input is already a feature table — AutoTuner operates on raw converted data (.mzML/.mzXML/.CDF) prior to feature-table generation

skills.description: Use when you have per-sample spin system feature tables (from combined TOCSY/HSQC peak picking) for a sample set and need pairwise sample similarity to drive network-based dereplication or bioactive metabolite prioritization.
skills.name: cross-sample-nmr-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-sample-nmr-comparison Use when you have per-sample spin system feature tables (from combined TOCSY/HSQC peak picking) for a sample set and need pairwise sample similarity to drive network-based dereplication or bioactive metabolite prioritization. Input is raw spectra rather than spin system feature tables — run MADByTE peak picking, filtering (solvent/water removal at ±0.02 ppm in 1H, illegitimate HSQC region removal, TOCSY <2.5 ppm quadrant exclusion) and spin system construction first Compounds with exclusively shielded 1H signals (e.g. sterols, low MW isoprenoids, lipids, volatile terpenes) — TOCSY cross-peaks with both F1 and F2 < 2.5 ppm are excluded, so these features will be absent from the comparison Single-sample analysis — pairwise comparison requires multiple samples to populate the matrix http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 Compares spin system feature tables between samples in an NMR sample set to build an asymmetric pairwise similarity (correlation) matrix, where each off-diagonal entry takes the higher of the two directional scores (A vs B or B vs A) that defines edges in the downstream chemical similarity network. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jnatprod.0c01076
skills.summary: Compares spin system feature tables between samples in an NMR sample set to build an asymmetric pairwise similarity (correlation) matrix, where each off-diagonal entry takes the higher of the two directional scores (A vs B or B vs A) that defines edges in the downstream chemical similarity network.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw spectra rather than spin system feature tables — run MADByTE peak picking, filtering (solvent/water removal at ±0.02 ppm in 1H, illegitimate HSQC region removal, TOCSY <2.5 ppm quadrant exclusion) and spin system construction first Compounds with exclusively shielded 1H signals (e.g. sterols, low MW isoprenoids, lipids, volatile terpenes) — TOCSY cross-peaks with both F1 and F2 < 2.5 ppm are excluded, so these features will be absent from the comparison Single-sample analysis — pairwise comparison requires multiple samples to populate the matrix

skills.description: Use when building peak groups from LC-MS/MS lipidomics or metabolomics data (e.g., mzML files) where MS/MS scans must be aggregated across samples and assigned to finalized peak groups.
skills.name: cross-sample-overlapping-slice-merging
skills.search_text: cross-sample-overlapping-slice-merging Use when building peak groups from LC-MS/MS lipidomics or metabolomics data (e.g., mzML files) where MS/MS scans must be aggregated across samples and assigned to finalized peak groups. Input is already a feature/peak table — merging operates on raw MS1/MS2 scans in mzML space Data contain only MS1 scans (no fragmentation scans), since slice formation depends on MS2 precursor isolation windows http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 MAVEN2's MS/MS peak-grouping pipeline: fragmentation (MS2) scans are grouped into (m/z, retention time) slices around precursor isolation windows, overlapping slices are progressively merged across all samples, and the merged slices are then used to form peak groups with MS/MS scans attached afterward by retention time proximity. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo12080684
skills.summary: MAVEN2's MS/MS peak-grouping pipeline: fragmentation (MS2) scans are grouped into (m/z, retention time) slices around precursor isolation windows, overlapping slices are progressively merged across all samples, and the merged slices are then used to form peak groups with MS/MS scans attached afterward by retention time proximity.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a feature/peak table — merging operates on raw MS1/MS2 scans in mzML space Data contain only MS1 scans (no fragmentation scans), since slice formation depends on MS2 precursor isolation windows

skills.description: Use when you have per-sample peak lists (e.g. m/z values from SIM-stitched DIMS or XCMS feature tables) and need one aligned peak table across all biological and blank samples before filtering or statistics.
skills.name: cross-sample-peak-alignment
skills.search_text: cross-sample-peak-alignment Use when you have per-sample peak lists (e.g. m/z values from SIM-stitched DIMS or XCMS feature tables) and need one aligned peak table across all biological and blank samples before filtering or statistics. Input is already an aligned peak/feature table — re-aligning would duplicate features or split true matches. You are still at the raw-transient stage (.dat/Thermo .RAW files) — alignment requires per-sample peak lists produced after Mass Calibration and SIM-stitching. You need to combine peaks within a single sample across SIM windows — that is SIM-stitching, not cross-sample alignment. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Align peak lists (m/z values) across all samples so that identical metabolite features detected independently in each sample are matched into a single row of an aligned peak table, ready for data cleansing and statistics. In the Galaxy-M DIMS workflow this is performed by the Align Samples tool on the SIM-stitched peak lists. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13742-016-0115-8
skills.summary: Align peak lists (m/z values) across all samples so that identical metabolite features detected independently in each sample are matched into a single row of an aligned peak table, ready for data cleansing and statistics. The feature table already contains cross-software annotations and you only need to re-run LipidMatch scoring The task is annotation of a lipid class (e.g., cardiolipins) that MS-DIAL and Greazy libraries do not cover — cross-validation is unavailable for those types Only a single identification level (e.g., precursor-m/z-only, level 4) is at stake, where corroboration by other tools is not informative http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 Append and compare lipid identifications from LipidMatch, MS-DIAL, and Greazy on the same UHPLC-HRMS/MS feature table, then compute cross-software corroboration rates (e.g., 92% positive-mode, 98% negative-mode agreement) to vet rule-based annotations. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-017-1744-3

skills.description: Use when you have lipid annotations from two or more open-source lipidomics software aligned to the same features and need to quantify cross-software agreement or benchmark one annotator against the others.

You have annotations from only a single software and no second annotation source to reconcile against You need rule-based fragment-level lipid identification itself rather than post-hoc comparison of existing annotations (run LipidMatch's MS/MS filter pipeline instead) Features lack retention time or m/z alignment windows required for cross-software feature matching (e.g., direct infusion data without RT) Reconciles lipid identifications produced by multiple annotation engines (LipidMatch, MS-DIAL, Greazy) by appending all identifications onto a shared MZmine feature table, then measures how many of one tool's fatty acyl assignments are corroborated by at least one other tool per ion polarity. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-017-1744-3
skills.summary: Reconciles lipid identifications produced by multiple annotation engines (LipidMatch, MS-DIAL, Greazy) by appending all identifications onto a shared MZmine feature table, then measures how many of one tool's fatty acyl assignments are corroborated by at least one other tool per ion polarity.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have annotations from only a single software and no second annotation source to reconcile against You need rule-based fragment-level lipid identification itself rather than post-hoc comparison of existing annotations (run LipidMatch's MS/MS filter pipeline instead) Features lack retention time or m/z alignment windows required for cross-software feature matching (e.g., direct infusion data without RT)

skills.description: Use when one raw LC-MS mzML file must be processed independently by MS-DIAL, MZmine3, xcms, and MassCube so their exported feature tables can be matched against a ground-truth list to benchmark peak-detection accuracy.
skills.name: cross-software-feature-table-harmonization
skills.search_text: cross-software-feature-table-harmonization Use when one raw LC-MS mzML file must be processed independently by MS-DIAL, MZmine3, xcms, and MassCube so their exported feature tables can be matched against a ground-truth list to benchmark peak-detection accuracy. Input is already a processed feature table — harmonization requires each tool to process the identical raw mzML itself, so pre-extracted features defeat the benchmark. The goal is metabolite identification rather than peak-detection benchmarking; MassCube does not directly perform metabolite identification and this skill only compares detection accuracy. Real experimental data without a known truth list — the accuracy counts depend on the 27,000-feature synthetic ground truth, and real data have characteristics (varying scan numbers across peaks, peak tailing) that are difficult to capture systematically with synthetic data. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Harmonize LC-MS feature tables by running MS-DIAL 4.9, MZmine 3.90, xcms 4.0.0, and MassCube independently on the identical raw mzML file, then matching each tool's detected features to a ground-truth list to benchmark peak-detection accuracy (MassCube 96.5% vs 85.4-88.4% for the others). metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-025-60640-5
skills.summary: Harmonize LC-MS feature tables by running MS-DIAL 4.9, MZmine 3.90, xcms 4.0.0, and MassCube independently on the identical raw mzML file, then matching each tool's detected features to a ground-truth list to benchmark peak-detection accuracy (MassCube 96.5% vs 85.4-88.4% for the others).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a processed feature table — harmonization requires each tool to process the identical raw mzML itself, so pre-extracted features defeat the benchmark. Real experimental data without a known truth list — the accuracy counts depend on the 27,000-feature synthetic ground truth, and real data have characteristics (varying scan numbers across peaks, peak tailing) that are difficult to capture systematically with synthetic data.

skills.description: Use when you have a replicate series of 1D-NMR spectra (e.g. metabolite mix replicates or Daphnia extract CryoProbe spectra) and must decide which software's automatic phase correction yields the most reproducible phases across the series.
skills.name: cross-software-phasing-benchmark-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-software-phasing-benchmark-comparison Use when you have a replicate series of 1D-NMR spectra (e.g. metabolite mix replicates or Daphnia extract CryoProbe spectra) and must decide which software's automatic phase correction yields the most reproducible phases across the series. skills.description: Use when evaluating DeepSAT annotation robustness on paired HSQC spectra of identical compounds recorded in different NMR solvents, or when choosing whether solvent changes threaten structure-identification reliability.
skills.name: cross-solvent-annotation-consistency-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-solvent-annotation-consistency-analysis Use when evaluating DeepSAT annotation robustness on paired HSQC spectra of identical compounds recorded in different NMR solvents, or when choosing whether solvent changes threaten structure-identification reliability.
