skills.summary: Assess how stable DeepSAT's 1H-13C HSQC structure identification is when the same natural products are re-measured in a different deuterated solvent (methanol-d4 vs chloroform-d), quantifying the fraction of correct annotations retained across solvent conditions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When spectra are measured in a single solvent only — no cross-solvent retention can be computed and standard single-condition DeepSAT evaluation applies instead. When the goal is interpretability of which substructures drive predictions (occlusion sensitivity) rather than solvent-robustness quantification. When comparing against SMART 2.0 or other NMR search tools on general performance — this skill is specifically the solvent-change robustness evaluation.

skills.description: Use when aggregating molecule entries from multiple public datasets (e.g. AfroDB, ChEBI NPs, BitterDB, AnalytiCon Discovery NPs) and you must detect cross-source duplicates, merge them without losing annotations, and reconcile per-source counts against release-level unique totals.
skills.name: cross-source-duplicate-reconciliation
skills.search_text: cross-source-duplicate-reconciliation Use when aggregating molecule entries from multiple public datasets (e.g. AfroDB, ChEBI NPs, BitterDB, AnalytiCon Discovery NPs) and you must detect cross-source duplicates, merge them without losing annotations, and reconcile per-source counts against release-level unique totals. The dataset contains structures from only a single source with no expected overlap — use a simple format/valence QC pipeline instead of cross-source deduplication. You need stereochemistry-aware deduplication that keeps stereoisomers as separate unique entries; this skill deliberately collapses records on the stereo-less InChIKey, so it is wrong if the target schema treats stereoisomers as distinct NPs. Structures fail the basic QC thresholds (e.g. >210 heavy atoms, multiple disconnected components, pseudo-atoms) before any InChI can be computed reliably — deduplication must wait until the parsing/QC stage passes. http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Reconcile chemical entries aggregated from many public natural-product sources by unifying duplicates on stereo-less InChIKey identity, merging records into a highly annotated parent entry, and verifying the summed per-source counts against the resulting unique flat and stereo-preserving totals (e.g. 406,076 flat and 730,441 stereo NPs in the October 2020 COCONUT release). metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-020-00478-9
skills.summary: Reconcile chemical entries aggregated from many public natural-product sources by unifying duplicates on stereo-less InChIKey identity, merging records into a highly annotated parent entry, and verifying the summed per-source counts against the resulting unique flat and stereo-preserving totals (e.g. 406,076 flat and 730,441 stereo NPs in the October 2020 COCONUT release).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset contains structures from only a single source with no expected overlap — use a simple format/valence QC pipeline instead of cross-source deduplication. You need stereochemistry-aware deduplication that keeps stereoisomers as separate unique entries; this skill deliberately collapses records on the stereo-less InChIKey, so it is wrong if the target schema treats stereoisomers as distinct NPs. Structures fail the basic QC thresholds (e.g. >210 heavy atoms, multiple disconnected components, pseudo-atoms) before any InChI can be computed reliably — deduplication must wait until the parsing/QC stage passes.

skills.description: Use when you have a merged/harmonized metabolite table from multiple information sources (e.g. an MMS InChIKey-merged list) and need to reduce false positives before pathway enrichment by keeping only compounds supported by ≥2 sources.
skills.name: cross-source-metabolite-frequency-filtering
skills.search_text: cross-source-metabolite-frequency-filtering Use when you have a merged/harmonized metabolite table from multiple information sources (e.g. an MMS InChIKey-merged list) and need to reduce false positives before pathway enrichment by keeping only compounds supported by ≥2 sources. You have a single-source list (no frequency information) — no filtering is possible. You want maximum sensitivity with no confidence filter (the ≥2-source cutoff is a confidence requirement). The target downstream tool needs raw counts rather than a filtered compound list. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 This skill applies a minimum-source-frequency filter to a harmonized metabolite list (e.g. MMS output) so that only compounds corroborated by at least two information sources are carried into downstream analyses such as pathway enrichment, improving confidence in the merged dataset. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo13121167
skills.summary: This skill applies a minimum-source-frequency filter to a harmonized metabolite list (e.g. MMS output) so that only compounds corroborated by at least two information sources are carried into downstream analyses such as pathway enrichment, improving confidence in the merged dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have a single-source list (no frequency information) — no filtering is possible. You want maximum sensitivity with no confidence filter (the ≥2-source cutoff is a confidence requirement). The target downstream tool needs raw counts rather than a filtered compound list.

skills.description: Use when multiple metabolite datasets from different sources (e.g. Metabolomics Workbench studies, HMDB, literature tables) must be merged on a common key and annotated with identifiers and ontology for intercomparison.
skills.name: cross-source-metabolite-harmonization
skills.search_text: cross-source-metabolite-harmonization Use when multiple metabolite datasets from different sources (e.g. Metabolomics Workbench studies, HMDB, literature tables) must be merged on a common key and annotated with identifiers and ontology for intercomparison. Input is already a single harmonized table with systematic identifiers — merging would only add redundant curation overhead. Only one dataset source is involved and no interstudy comparison is needed; the merge key and deduplication machinery add no value. Compounds cannot be translated to InChIKeys via PubChem or CTS — the merge key is undefined and rows cannot be joined reliably. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 Implements the three-step Metabolites Merging Strategy (MMS) to harmonize multiple metabolite datasets by translating names to InChIKeys, retrieving attributes per InChIKey, and applying a three-step curation process, enabling interstudy comparability of metabolomics datasets. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo13121167
skills.summary: Implements the three-step Metabolites Merging Strategy (MMS) to harmonize multiple metabolite datasets by translating names to InChIKeys, retrieving attributes per InChIKey, and applying a three-step curation process, enabling interstudy comparability of metabolomics datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a single harmonized table with systematic identifiers — merging would only add redundant curation overhead. Only one dataset source is involved and no interstudy comparison is needed; the merge key and deduplication machinery add no value. Compounds cannot be translated to InChIKeys via PubChem or CTS — the merge key is undefined and rows cannot be joined reliably.

skills.description: Use when you need to measure how much metabolite content is shared between pathway definitions from different databases (e.g., KEGG vs Reactome vs WikiPathways) to assess redundancy before enrichment analysis or pathway clustering.
skills.name: cross-source-pathway-mapping
skills.search_text: cross-source-pathway-mapping Use when you need to measure how much metabolite content is shared between pathway definitions from different databases (e.g., KEGG vs Reactome vs WikiPathways) to assess redundancy before enrichment analysis or pathway clustering. Input is a metabolite list requiring pathway enrichment (use RaMP's runFisherTest/runCombinedFisherTest instead, not overlap matrices) The analysis needs gene/protein pathway overlap rather than metabolite-only overlap (the 'together' parameter would need combined analytes, not metabolites-only) You need a single pathway's membership query rather than cross-source redundancy assessment (use rampFastPathFromSource or getPathwayFromAnalyte) http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Quantifies pairwise metabolite-content overlap between pathway definitions drawn from different source databases (KEGG, Reactome, WikiPathways) integrated in RaMP, using the Jaccard index to expose pathway redundancy across sources. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo8010016
skills.summary: Quantifies pairwise metabolite-content overlap between pathway definitions drawn from different source databases (KEGG, Reactome, WikiPathways) integrated in RaMP, using the Jaccard index to expose pathway redundancy across sources.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a metabolite list requiring pathway enrichment (use RaMP's runFisherTest/runCombinedFisherTest instead, not overlap matrices) The analysis needs gene/protein pathway overlap rather than metabolite-only overlap (the 'together' parameter would need combined analytes, not metabolites-only) You need a single pathway's membership query rather than cross-source redundancy assessment (use rampFastPathFromSource or getPathwayFromAnalyte)

skills.description: Use when you have de novo sequencing predictions on annotated MS/MS spectra from several species or heterogeneous samples and need a standardized peptide- and amino-acid-level accuracy comparison across models or training datasets.
skills.name: cross-species-benchmark-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-species-benchmark-comparison Use when you have de novo sequencing predictions on annotated MS/MS spectra from several species or heterogeneous samples and need a standardized peptide- and amino-acid-level accuracy comparison across models or training datasets. Input spectra are unlabeled or from a single homogeneous species with no ground-truth peptide annotations — precision cannot be computed without annotated MGF ground truth. The goal is sequence database searching with a known protein database (Casanovo-DB mode), not de novo accuracy benchmarking across tools or training sets. Evaluating spectra containing modifications absent from the benchmark's annotation vocabulary (e.g. non-enzymatic immunopeptidomics PTMs) — use the fine-tuned non-enzymatic Casanovo model instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Evaluate de novo peptide sequencing models on a multi-species annotated MGF benchmark (MassIVE dataset MSV000090982), computing peptide-level and amino acid-level average precision plus precursor mass accuracy so that performance can be compared across tools and training sets. The published benchmark shows a MassIVE-KB-trained Casanovo reaching peptide-level AP ≈0.95 on nine species. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-49731-x
skills.summary: Evaluate de novo peptide sequencing models on a multi-species annotated MGF benchmark (MassIVE dataset MSV000090982), computing peptide-level and amino acid-level average precision plus precursor mass accuracy so that performance can be compared across tools and training sets. The published benchmark shows a MassIVE-KB-trained Casanovo reaching peptide-level AP ≈0.95 on nine species.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra are unlabeled or from a single homogeneous species with no ground-truth peptide annotations — precision cannot be computed without annotated MGF ground truth. The goal is sequence database searching with a known protein database (Casanovo-DB mode), not de novo accuracy benchmarking across tools or training sets. Evaluating spectra containing modifications absent from the benchmark's annotation vocabulary (e.g. non-enzymatic immunopeptidomics PTMs) — use the fine-tuned non-enzymatic Casanovo model instead.

skills.description: Use when comparing two de novo sequencing models (e.g., two Casanovo variants trained on different training sets) with a controlled cross-species evaluation, or when reporting peptide precision and average precision on held-out species from MSV000090982.
skills.name: cross-species-benchmark-peptide-precision-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-species-benchmark-peptide-precision-evaluation Use when comparing two de novo sequencing models (e.g., two Casanovo variants trained on different training sets) with a controlled cross-species evaluation, or when reporting peptide precision and average precision on held-out species from MSV000090982. You need protein-level or FDR-estimated identifications rather than de novo precision metrics — database searching (e.g., 'casanovo db_search') targets a different question. The comparison question is about model architecture rather than training-set size or quality — cross-species precision evaluation here is designed for matched-training-set comparisons. Your test data are DIA spectra or non-enzymatic (immunopeptidomics) spectra requiring the fine-tuned non-enzymatic Casanovo variant instead of the standard benchmark protocol. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Evaluate a de novo peptide sequencing model by cross-validated testing on a multi-species benchmark of annotated MGF files, computing peptide precision and average precision for each held-out species. This protocol enables size- and quality-matched model comparisons such as downsampled MassIVE-KB-trained Casanovo versus a size-matched baseline. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-49731-x
skills.summary: Evaluate a de novo peptide sequencing model by cross-validated testing on a multi-species benchmark of annotated MGF files, computing peptide precision and average precision for each held-out species. This protocol enables size- and quality-matched model comparisons such as downsampled MassIVE-KB-trained Casanovo versus a size-matched baseline.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need protein-level or FDR-estimated identifications rather than de novo precision metrics — database searching (e.g., 'casanovo db_search') targets a different question. The comparison question is about model architecture rather than training-set size or quality — cross-species precision evaluation here is designed for matched-training-set comparisons. Your test data are DIA spectra or non-enzymatic (immunopeptidomics) spectra requiring the fine-tuned non-enzymatic Casanovo variant instead of the standard benchmark protocol.

skills.description: Use when you have unannotated LC-MS/MS tandem mass spectra (e.g. MGF files from serum tryptic digests) from multiple species or individuals and need to quantify shared peptide content — without database search — as a distance for phylogenetic reconstruction or species identification.
skills.name: cross-species-peptide-overlap-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-species-peptide-overlap-analysis Use when you have unannotated LC-MS/MS tandem mass spectra (e.g. MGF files from serum tryptic digests) from multiple species or individuals and need to quantify shared peptide content — without database search — as a distance for phylogenetic reconstruction or species identification. When translated genome sequences or spectral libraries are available and an identification-based comparison (database search like Mascot/Comet or spectral library search like SpectraST) is preferred over direct spectral comparison When the input is not tandem mass spectra (e.g. MS1 feature tables, protein abundance matrices) — compareMS2 operates on MS2 spectra When the goal is absolute protein identification or quantification rather than unannotated pairwise similarity between samples http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_0194 Quantify the fraction of shared peptides between biological samples by comparing unannotated tandem mass spectra directly with compareMS2, inverting the dot-product-derived similarity into a distance metric, and averaging over individuals per species to support molecular phylogenetics without any peptide identification. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/rcm.6162
skills.summary: Quantify the fraction of shared peptides between biological samples by comparing unannotated tandem mass spectra directly with compareMS2, inverting the dot-product-derived similarity into a distance metric, and averaging over individuals per species to support molecular phylogenetics without any peptide identification.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When translated genome sequences or spectral libraries are available and an identification-based comparison (database search like Mascot/Comet or spectral library search like SpectraST) is preferred over direct spectral comparison When the input is not tandem mass spectra (e.g. MS1 feature tables, protein abundance matrices) — compareMS2 operates on MS2 spectra When the goal is absolute protein identification or quantification rather than unannotated pairwise similarity between samples

skills.description: Use when multiple 1D NMR spectra (e.g. 40 wine spectra of 8712 points, or 31 mouse-urine spectra) need their per-spectrum wavelet peaks matched across samples to form a shared feature matrix, avoiding binning.
skills.name: cross-spectrum-peak-grouping
skills.search_text: cross-spectrum-peak-grouping Use when multiple 1D NMR spectra (e.g. 40 wine spectra of 8712 points, or 31 mouse-urine spectra) need their per-spectrum wavelet peaks matched across samples to form a shared feature matrix, avoiding binning. The input is already a binned/bucketed or otherwise summarized feature table rather than raw spectra with per-spectrum peaks Only a single spectrum is available, so there is no cross-spectrum grouping to perform The goal is spectral alignment of severely shifted raw spectra rather than peak-based feature extraction — alignment algorithms may be suboptimal and speaq 2.0's peak-based route avoids binning instead http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 The speaq 2.0 peak-grouping step aligns wavelet-detected peaks across multiple 1D NMR spectra into common peak groups, replacing binning/bucketing so that a feature/sample/peak-value matrix can be built without bin-boundary information loss. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1006018
skills.summary: The speaq 2.0 peak-grouping step aligns wavelet-detected peaks across multiple 1D NMR spectra into common peak groups, replacing binning/bucketing so that a feature/sample/peak-value matrix can be built without bin-boundary information loss.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a binned/bucketed or otherwise summarized feature table rather than raw spectra with per-spectrum peaks Only a single spectrum is available, so there is no cross-spectrum grouping to perform The goal is spectral alignment of severely shifted raw spectra rather than peak-based feature extraction — alignment algorithms may be suboptimal and speaq 2.0's peak-based route avoids binning instead

skills.description: Use when mass spectrometry imaging datasets from multiple mouse strains have been annotated per organ and you need to test whether the organ-specific metabolite distribution pattern is conserved across strains.
skills.name: cross-strain-metabolic-distribution-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-strain-metabolic-distribution-comparison Use when mass spectrometry imaging datasets from multiple mouse strains have been annotated per organ and you need to test whether the organ-specific metabolite distribution pattern is conserved across strains. When the analysis goal is discovering differential metabolites or pathway perturbations rather than verifying spatial distribution conservation — use differential expression/pathway skills instead. When input data are raw MSI peak lists that have not yet been annotated with organ-specific databases via MSIannotator; this skill operates on already-annotated metabolite sets. When only a single organ or a single mouse strain is available, since the core claim (organ-specificity spanning strains) requires multi-organ, multi-strain sets. http://edamontology.org/topic_3292 http://edamontology.org/topic_0153 Verifies that organ-specific metabolite distributions detected by AFADESI-MSI hold across different mouse strains, using set operations over organ-partitioned metabolite databases to compare per-organ metabolite sets between strains. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.2c00557
skills.summary: Verifies that organ-specific metabolite distributions detected by AFADESI-MSI hold across different mouse strains, using set operations over organ-partitioned metabolite databases to compare per-organ metabolite sets between strains.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the analysis goal is discovering differential metabolites or pathway perturbations rather than verifying spatial distribution conservation — use differential expression/pathway skills instead. When input data are raw MSI peak lists that have not yet been annotated with organ-specific databases via MSIannotator; this skill operates on already-annotated metabolite sets. When only a single organ or a single mouse strain is available, since the core claim (organ-specificity spanning strains) requires multi-organ, multi-strain sets.

skills.description: Use when an annotated LC-MS/MS feature table (e.g. from GNPS2 FBMN with ChemWalker and SIRIUS annotations) must be assigned metabolic pathways via KEGG cross-referencing and compared across strains to find common pathways.
skills.name: cross-strain-metabolome-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-strain-metabolome-comparison Use when an annotated LC-MS/MS feature table (e.g. from GNPS2 FBMN with ChemWalker and SIRIUS annotations) must be assigned metabolic pathways via KEGG cross-referencing and compared across strains to find common pathways. The input is a raw MS file or an unannotated MZmine feature list — pathway cross-referencing requires compounds already annotated through GNPS2 FBMN, ChemWalker, and SIRIUS Only one strain is available — the skill's core output is a cross-strain comparison of shared pathways, which cannot be computed from a single feature table The goal is spectral library matching or annotation propagation itself (use GNPS2 FBMN/ChemWalker workflows directly) rather than assigning KEGG pathways to already-annotated compounds Maps annotated molecular features from multiple bacterial strains (here actinomycetes BRA006, BRA010, BRA177) to KEGG compound entries, attaches their KEGG pathway assignments, and compares pathways across strains to find shared pathways with differing intermediates, such as purine metabolism. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.08.07.607073
skills.summary: Maps annotated molecular features from multiple bacterial strains (here actinomycetes BRA006, BRA010, BRA177) to KEGG compound entries, attaches their KEGG pathway assignments, and compares pathways across strains to find shared pathways with differing intermediates, such as purine metabolism.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a raw MS file or an unannotated MZmine feature list — pathway cross-referencing requires compounds already annotated through GNPS2 FBMN, ChemWalker, and SIRIUS Only one strain is available — the skill's core output is a cross-strain comparison of shared pathways, which cannot be computed from a single feature table The goal is spectral library matching or annotation propagation itself (use GNPS2 FBMN/ChemWalker workflows directly) rather than assigning KEGG pathways to already-annotated compounds

skills.description: Use when you have publicly available LC/HRMS studies with MSI 1–3 peak annotations plus a tool that produces ranked molecular-formula assignments per peak, and you need to quantify top-hit and top-5-hit recovery rates to compare formula-annotation performance across studies.
skills.name: cross-study-annotation-rate-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cross-study-annotation-rate-benchmarking Use when you have publicly available LC/HRMS studies with MSI 1–3 peak annotations plus a tool that produces ranked molecular-formula assignments per peak, and you need to quantify top-hit and top-5-hit recovery rates to compare formula-annotation performance across studies. The tool under test requires MS2 spectra or MS/MS-based formula assignment; IDSL.UFA operates on MS1-only data via isotopic profile matching. The goal is de novo formula enumeration without a reference chemical database; use IDSL.UFAx (exhaustive chemical enumeration over C, B, Br, Cl, K, S, Si, N, H, As, F, I, Na, O, P) instead. The studies lack public MSI 1–3 annotations to serve as ground-truth true positives, making top-hit/top-five recovery rates unmeasurable. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 Benchmarking protocol that quantifies how many MSI 1–3 annotated LC/HRMS peaks from public metabolomics studies (e.g. ST001154, ST001683, MTBLS1684, MTBLS2542) receive a molecular formula as the top hit and within the top five hits from an isotopic-profile formula-annotation tool (IDSL.UFA) run against a fixed IPDB (IDSL.ExposomeDB). metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.2c00563
skills.summary: Benchmarking protocol that quantifies how many MSI 1–3 annotated LC/HRMS peaks from public metabolomics studies (e.g. ST001154, ST001683, MTBLS1684, MTBLS2542) receive a molecular formula as the top hit and within the top five hits from an isotopic-profile formula-annotation tool (IDSL.UFA) run against a fixed IPDB (IDSL.ExposomeDB).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The tool under test requires MS2 spectra or MS/MS-based formula assignment; IDSL.UFA operates on MS1-only data via isotopic profile matching. The goal is de novo formula enumeration without a reference chemical database; use IDSL.UFAx (exhaustive chemical enumeration over C, B, Br, Cl, K, S, Si, N, H, As, F, I, Na, O, P) instead. The studies lack public MSI 1–3 annotations to serve as ground-truth true positives, making top-hit/top-five recovery rates unmeasurable.

skills.description: Use when a pipeline re-run on a public dataset must be validated against the original publication: you have annotated, quality-filtered features (annotation, fold change, p-value) and need to check which ones the original study did or did not report.
skills.name: cross-study-feature-comparison-literature-check
skills.search_text: cross-study-feature-comparison-literature-check Use when a pipeline re-run on a public dataset must be validated against the original publication: you have annotated, quality-filtered features (annotation, fold change, p-value) and need to check which ones the original study did or did not report. Input is already a curated feature table whose features you do not need to compare against any published reference — skip the literature check and proceed to downstream statistics. The dataset has no published reference study (no Table/analyte list to cross-reference); the comparison step has nothing to validate against. The peak table has not yet been through result integration (classifier quality still unmapped to individual peaks), so annotations and statistics do not reflect the final high-quality peak set. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Compare a reprocessed metabolomics feature table against a published reference study to identify novel significantly different features that the original analysis missed. In the WiPP paper this means extracting annotated features (e.g. a hexose) from the final high-quality peak set and cross-referencing them against the original article's reported analytes table. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo9090171
skills.summary: Compare a reprocessed metabolomics feature table against a published reference study to identify novel significantly different features that the original analysis missed. In the WiPP paper this means extracting annotated features (e.g. a hexose) from the final high-quality peak set and cross-referencing them against the original article's reported analytes table.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a curated feature table whose features you do not need to compare against any published reference — skip the literature check and proceed to downstream statistics. The dataset has no published reference study (no Table/analyte list to cross-reference); the comparison step has nothing to validate against. The peak table has not yet been through result integration (classifier quality still unmapped to individual peaks), so annotations and statistics do not reflect the final high-quality peak set.

skills.description: Use when pooling RNA-Seq/microarray data from multiple studies (e.g. TCGA + GTEx via PMR) and you must restrict the feature matrix to genes reported in every contributing study, plus drop undersampled organ types and samples lacking metadata.
skills.name: cross-study-gene-intersection-filtering
skills.search_text: cross-study-gene-intersection-filtering Use when pooling RNA-Seq/microarray data from multiple studies (e.g. TCGA + GTEx via PMR) and you must restrict the feature matrix to genes reported in every contributing study, plus drop undersampled organ types and samples lacking metadata. The input is a single-study dataset with no cross-study gene reporting discrepancies, so an intersection step would remove nothing informative Samples are already deduplicated and every gene is annotated in all contributing studies — rebuilding the intersection would be redundant The analysis goal is method development on raw sequencing data rather than curated expression matrices http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Assemble a pooled multi-study expression dataset (e.g. the Hu-cancer-RNASeq-dataset from the Wang et al. combined TCGA/GTEx RNA-Seq resource) by intersecting genes across all contributing studies and applying sample-level filters, then encode the result as a MetaOmGraph (MOG) project for interactive exploratory analysis. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkz1209
skills.summary: Assemble a pooled multi-study expression dataset (e.g. the Hu-cancer-RNASeq-dataset from the Wang et al. combined TCGA/GTEx RNA-Seq resource) by intersecting genes across all contributing studies and applying sample-level filters, then encode the result as a MetaOmGraph (MOG) project for interactive exploratory analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a single-study dataset with no cross-study gene reporting discrepancies, so an intersection step would remove nothing informative Samples are already deduplicated and every gene is annotated in all contributing studies — rebuilding the intersection would be redundant The analysis goal is method development on raw sequencing data rather than curated expression matrices

skills.summary: Quantifies how metabolites shared across studies in an MMS-merged urinary asthma metabolomics dataset are reported: whether the reported name matches the PubChem title name, and how many compounds would have been missed if datasets were merged by name alone instead of InChIKeys.

skills.description: Use when the goal is to reproduce/validate a prior metabolomics finding: paired within-subject measurements across conditions (e.g., venous vs arterial blood over time points) plus a published list of top significant metabolites to compare against.
skills.name: cross-study-metabolite-overlap-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-study-metabolite-overlap-comparison Use when the goal is to reproduce/validate a prior metabolomics finding: paired within-subject measurements across conditions (e.g., venous vs arterial blood over time points) plus a published list of top significant metabolites to compare against. The data are unprocessed raw metabolomics data — MeTEor expects pre-processed data in long format; start with the data-cleaning/imputation workflow instead (raw_example_data handling is separate). The analysis is a between-subjects comparison without repeated within-subject measurements — repeated measures ANOVA is inappropriate; consider MeTEor's mixed ANOVA, linear mixed models, or Friedman test modules instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Runs a repeated measures ANOVA in MeTEor on longitudinal metabolomics data (here the covid_data dataset of venous vs arterial samples from COVID-19 patients), ranks metabolites by significance for feature selection, and compares the top-ranked features against the most significant metabolites reported in a prior study (More et al. 2022) to quantify replication overlap. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioadv/vbae178
skills.summary: Runs a repeated measures ANOVA in MeTEor on longitudinal metabolomics data (here the covid_data dataset of venous vs arterial samples from COVID-19 patients), ranks metabolites by significance for feature selection, and compares the top-ranked features against the most significant metabolites reported in a prior study (More et al. 2022) to quantify replication overlap.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are unprocessed raw metabolomics data — MeTEor expects pre-processed data in long format; start with the data-cleaning/imputation workflow instead (raw_example_data handling is separate). The analysis is a between-subjects comparison without repeated within-subject measurements — repeated measures ANOVA is inappropriate; consider MeTEor's mixed ANOVA, linear mixed models, or Friedman test modules instead.

skills.description: Use when an automated GC-MS re-analysis of an already-published dataset must be validated by reproducing the original study's between-treatment significance pattern (e.g., NMDS of compound areas).
skills.name: cross-study-significance-pattern-verification
skills.search_text: cross-study-significance-pattern-verification Use when an automated GC-MS re-analysis of an already-published dataset must be validated by reproducing the original study's between-treatment significance pattern (e.g., NMDS of compound areas). The source data are MS2, MS3, or ion mobility + MS2 acquisitions — uafR's algorithms depend on published spectra and do not apply to these contexts Data were acquired on instruments uafR has not been tested on (Q-TOF, Orbitrap, TimsTOF HT, Astral) or are LC-MS rather than GC-MS data There is no previously published analysis with a reported significance pattern to compare against, or the original study used a different compound-annotation framework whose design cannot be mirrored Re-runs an ordination-based between-treatment test (NMDS on GC-MS compound areas processed by uafR) against a previously published study's statistical framework to verify that the automated pipeline reproduces the original pattern of significance. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pone.0306202
skills.summary: Re-runs an ordination-based between-treatment test (NMDS on GC-MS compound areas processed by uafR) against a previously published study's statistical framework to verify that the automated pipeline reproduces the original pattern of significance.

skills.description: Use when an .msp CSA library built from one study's MS1-only data is available and the goal is to annotate peaks in an independent untargeted LC/HRMS study beyond the compounds already recovered by MS/MS spectral library search.
skills.name: cross-study-spectral-library-transfer
skills.search_text: cross-study-spectral-library-transfer Use when an .msp CSA library built from one study's MS1-only data is available and the goal is to annotate peaks in an independent untargeted LC/HRMS study beyond the compounds already recovered by MS/MS spectral library search. The query study has no composite spectra (.msp) yet and the task is to build the CSA library from raw LC/HRMS files — use the IDSL.IPA + IDSL.CSA library-creation workflow first The goal is de novo identification with no reference spectral library from a related study available You need confirmatory compound identification; CSA matches are MS1-derived composite spectra similarities, not MS2-based confirmations http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Search a composite spectra (CSA) .msp library generated from one untargeted LC/HRMS metabolomics study against CSA spectra variants exported from a different study using IDSL.FSA, recovering cross-study compound annotations that MS/MS library searches (e.g. NIST 2020) miss. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c00376
skills.summary: Search a composite spectra (CSA) .msp library generated from one untargeted LC/HRMS metabolomics study against CSA spectra variants exported from a different study using IDSL.FSA, recovering cross-study compound annotations that MS/MS library searches (e.g. NIST 2020) miss.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The query study has no composite spectra (.msp) yet and the task is to build the CSA library from raw LC/HRMS files — use the IDSL.IPA + IDSL.CSA library-creation workflow first The goal is de novo identification with no reference spectral library from a related study available You need confirmatory compound identification; CSA matches are MS1-derived composite spectra similarities, not MS2-based confirmations

skills.description: Use when per-RAW-file metadata QC tables (file-based-details TSVs from MetaXtract) must be combined with identification-level results to confirm or refute instrument underperformance signals such as depressed MS2 TIC with preserved MS1 TIC.
skills.name: cross-table-merge-by-filename

skills.description: Use when you need to justify a new meta-learning/transfer model by comparing it against SVM, random forest, LeNet, and ANN baselines trained on identical single-cell mass-spectrometry splits, especially when training cell counts are small.
skills.name: cross-task-transfer-benchmark-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-task-transfer-benchmark-comparison Use when you need to justify a new meta-learning/transfer model by comparing it against SVM, random forest, LeNet, and ANN baselines trained on identical single-cell mass-spectrometry splits, especially when training cell counts are small. The goal is to evaluate MetaPhenotype itself or tune its meta-learning hyperparameters (adaptation shots, epochs) — this skill only reproduces the conventional-classifier baselines reported in the paper, not the meta-learning pipeline. Input data have not gone through the SCMS pretreatment pipeline (noise/background subtraction, TIC normalization, Geena2 peak alignment at 10 ppm mass tolerance, missing-value removal); training classifiers on unaligned raw peak lists is out of scope. The dataset is large and conventional deep learning is appropriate — the paper's premise is that ambient SCMS yields relatively small cell numbers, so when data are plentiful this benchmark adds little beyond what standard supervised pipelines already provide. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Benchmarks conventional ML classifiers (SVM, random forest, LeNet-style 1D-CNN, and a fully connected ANN) against a meta-learning model on the same pretreated single-cell mass-spectrometry feature splits, quantifying how much phenotype-classification performance is attributable to the meta-learning approach rather than any classifier. It grounds claims of transferability by exposing how baselines degrade (<60% accuracy, AUROC 0.4–0.6) when SCMS training data are limited. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c02038
skills.summary: Benchmarks conventional ML classifiers (SVM, random forest, LeNet-style 1D-CNN, and a fully connected ANN) against a meta-learning model on the same pretreated single-cell mass-spectrometry feature splits, quantifying how much phenotype-classification performance is attributable to the meta-learning approach rather than any classifier. It grounds claims of transferability by exposing how baselines degrade (<60% accuracy, AUROC 0.4–0.6) when SCMS training data are limited.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to evaluate MetaPhenotype itself or tune its meta-learning hyperparameters (adaptation shots, epochs) — this skill only reproduces the conventional-classifier baselines reported in the paper, not the meta-learning pipeline. Input data have not gone through the SCMS pretreatment pipeline (noise/background subtraction, TIC normalization, Geena2 peak alignment at 10 ppm mass tolerance, missing-value removal); training classifiers on unaligned raw peak lists is out of scope. The dataset is large and conventional deep learning is appropriate — the paper's premise is that ambient SCMS yields relatively small cell numbers, so when data are plentiful this benchmark adds little beyond what standard supervised pipelines already provide.

skills.search_text: cross-tool-error-frequency-tabulation Use when comparing de novo peptide sequencing predictions (e.g. pNovo 3, SMSNet, PointNovo, Casanovo) against pseudo-ground-truth PSMs and you need to characterize which error types dominate each tool's incorrect predictions. When you only need peptide recall/precision metrics for each tool rather than a breakdown of why incorrect predictions failed When the input spectra lack a database-search-derived pseudo-ground truth (MS-GF+/X!Tandem PSMs at 1% FDR), since error categories cannot be assigned without reference peptides When evaluating protein/antibody assembly quality (e.g. ALPS sequence coverage) rather than per-peptide prediction errors http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Tabulates the relative frequencies of error types among incorrect de novo peptide sequence predictions across multiple de novo sequencing tools, using a mass-based residue-matching criterion to classify mismatches into defined error categories (e.g. inversions, substitutions, >6 wrongly assigned amino acids). metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bib/bbac542
skills.summary: Tabulates the relative frequencies of error types among incorrect de novo peptide sequence predictions across multiple de novo sequencing tools, using a mass-based residue-matching criterion to classify mismatches into defined error categories (e.g. inversions, substitutions, >6 wrongly assigned amino acids).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When you only need peptide recall/precision metrics for each tool rather than a breakdown of why incorrect predictions failed When the input spectra lack a database-search-derived pseudo-ground truth (MS-GF+/X!Tandem PSMs at 1% FDR), since error categories cannot be assigned without reference peptides When evaluating protein/antibody assembly quality (e.g. ALPS sequence coverage) rather than per-peptide prediction errors

skills.description: Use when multiple LC-MS processing tools (asari, XCMS, MZmine with wavelet or local-minimum peak detection) report very different feature counts on the same dataset and you must determine whether the extra features are genuine or low-quality non-reproducible peaks.
skills.name: cross-tool-feature-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-tool-feature-comparison Use when multiple LC-MS processing tools (asari, XCMS, MZmine with wavelet or local-minimum peak detection) report very different feature counts on the same dataset and you must determine whether the extra features are genuine or low-quality non-reproducible peaks. The data are low-resolution or from non-Orbitrap platforms without re-optimized settings, since the underlying processing tools were mostly tested on Orbitrap data The goal is tuning a single tool's parameters rather than a tool-independent, fair comparison of feature quality across tools Only one tool's feature table is available and no shared raw (mzML) data exist to extract comparable EICs across tools http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Fairly compares LC-MS feature tables produced by asari, XCMS and MZmine by recomputing a tool-independent Gaussian peak-shape fitness score on each reported peak, showing that large differences in reported feature counts arise from low-quality peaks rather than better coverage. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-023-39889-1
skills.summary: Fairly compares LC-MS feature tables produced by asari, XCMS and MZmine by recomputing a tool-independent Gaussian peak-shape fitness score on each reported peak, showing that large differences in reported feature counts arise from low-quality peaks rather than better coverage.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are low-resolution or from non-Orbitrap platforms without re-optimized settings, since the underlying processing tools were mostly tested on Orbitrap data The goal is tuning a single tool's parameters rather than a tool-independent, fair comparison of feature quality across tools Only one tool's feature table is available and no shared raw (mzML) data exist to extract comparable EICs across tools

skills.description: Decision support for selecting an LC/MS signal-detection/peak-picking tool: you have raw mzML files, candidate peak-detection algorithms (e.g. mzLearn, XCMS, ASARI), and need objective per-dataset feature counts plus TP/FP rates to compare them.
skills.name: cross-tool-feature-count-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-tool-feature-count-comparison Decision support for selecting an LC/MS signal-detection/peak-picking tool: you have raw mzML files, candidate peak-detection algorithms (e.g. mzLearn, XCMS, ASARI), and need objective per-dataset feature counts plus TP/FP rates to compare them. When the goal is downstream annotation or biological interpretation of already-detected features (e.g. de-isotoping, MS/MS identification) — the article states mzLearn results are at the ion MS1 level and it does not perform de-isotoping or MS/MS identification When the inputs are already normalized feature intensity matrices rather than raw mzML files — this skill compares tool behavior on raw signal-detection, not downstream modeling on existing tables When datasets are so small that feature counts alone cannot distinguish true signal from noise — the article's benchmarks span 15 public datasets and 20,548 blood samples, and per-dataset TP/FP estimates require enough peaks to be stable http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Benchmarking skill that tabulates the number of MS1 signals detected by different LC/MS peak-detection tools (mzLearn, XCMS, ASARI) on the same raw mzML datasets and compares their true-positive and false-positive rates against peak-shape ground truth, to justify tool choice for feature-detection pipelines. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.01.26.634927
skills.summary: Benchmarking skill that tabulates the number of MS1 signals detected by different LC/MS peak-detection tools (mzLearn, XCMS, ASARI) on the same raw mzML datasets and compares their true-positive and false-positive rates against peak-shape ground truth, to justify tool choice for feature-detection pipelines.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is downstream annotation or biological interpretation of already-detected features (e.g. de-isotoping, MS/MS identification) — the article states mzLearn results are at the ion MS1 level and it does not perform de-isotoping or MS/MS identification When the inputs are already normalized feature intensity matrices rather than raw mzML files — this skill compares tool behavior on raw signal-detection, not downstream modeling on existing tables When datasets are so small that feature counts alone cannot distinguish true signal from noise — the article's benchmarks span 15 public datasets and 20,548 blood samples, and per-dataset TP/FP estimates require enough peaks to be stable

skills.description: Use when you need to benchmark a peak-picking/grouping workflow against an established tool like MetaboAnalyst on the same raw NMR spectra, and must quantify differences in feature resolution and overlap of statistically significant features.
skills.name: cross-tool-feature-mapping-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-tool-feature-mapping-comparison Use when you need to benchmark a peak-picking/grouping workflow against an established tool like MetaboAnalyst on the same raw NMR spectra, and must quantify differences in feature resolution and overlap of statistically significant features. Input is already a feature table produced by a single tool and no cross-tool benchmarking comparison is required The NMR data require binning/bucketing as the mandated summarization approach rather than peak picking plus grouping (speaq 2.0 explicitly avoids the binning step) http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 A benchmarking protocol for comparing feature matrices produced by different NMR peak-grouping implementations — here speaq 2.0 (677 features) versus MetaboAnalyst (245 features) on the onion intake in mice dataset — by running identical differential analyses (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR) on both matrices and cross-mapping the highly significant features. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1006018
skills.summary: A benchmarking protocol for comparing feature matrices produced by different NMR peak-grouping implementations — here speaq 2.0 (677 features) versus MetaboAnalyst (245 features) on the onion intake in mice dataset — by running identical differential analyses (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR) on both matrices and cross-mapping the highly significant features.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a feature table produced by a single tool and no cross-tool benchmarking comparison is required The NMR data require binning/bucketing as the mandated summarization approach rather than peak picking plus grouping (speaq 2.0 explicitly avoids the binning step)

skills.description: Use when reproducing published untargeted metabolomics feature detection with a different tool and quantifying what fraction of the published (XCMS/CAMERA) features is recovered, separately per ionization mode, from public MetaboLights raw data.
skills.name: cross-tool-feature-matching-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cross-tool-feature-matching-benchmarking Use when reproducing published untargeted metabolomics feature detection with a different tool and quantifying what fraction of the published (XCMS/CAMERA) features is recovered, separately per ionization mode, from public MetaboLights raw data. Input is already a feature/consensus table — this skill starts from vendor raw or centroided mzML files and requires running feature detection first No published or ground-truth feature list exists for the dataset, so no cross-tool recall fraction can be computed The goal is molecular annotation (SIRIUS/CSI:FingerID/GNPS FBMN) rather than benchmarking feature-detection and quantification coverage http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Benchmark an alternative untargeted metabolomics feature-detection workflow (e.g., OpenMS-based UmetaFlow) against a published XCMS/CAMERA analysis by matching detected features to published feature lists via m/z and retention-time tolerance, computing per-mode detection fractions and intensity-pattern agreement. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-023-00724-w
skills.summary: Benchmark an alternative untargeted metabolomics feature-detection workflow (e.g., OpenMS-based UmetaFlow) against a published XCMS/CAMERA analysis by matching detected features to published feature lists via m/z and retention-time tolerance, computing per-mode detection fractions and intensity-pattern agreement.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a feature/consensus table — this skill starts from vendor raw or centroided mzML files and requires running feature detection first No published or ground-truth feature list exists for the dataset, so no cross-tool recall fraction can be computed The goal is molecular annotation (SIRIUS/CSI:FingerID/GNPS FBMN) rather than benchmarking feature-detection and quantification coverage

skills.description: Use when choosing between two visualization tools for large ordination datasets: generate equivalent outputs from both on the same samples and metadata, then measure and compare total output file size on disk.
skills.name: cross-tool-file-size-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cross-tool-file-size-benchmarking Use when choosing between two visualization tools for large ordination datasets: generate equivalent outputs from both on the same samples and metadata, then measure and compare total output file size on disk. The dataset is small or the output size is not a deciding factor — the 1.3% ratio argument matters mainly for thousands of samples and many metadata columns The candidate tools do not produce comparable outputs (e.g., one produces interactive 3D plots and the other a numeric summary), so the size ratio would not be a fair comparison You need publication-quality static figures rather than web-shareable interactive visualizations, which is the trade-off this benchmark quantifies http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Benchmarks the on-disk output size of competing visualization tools (e.g., EMPeror vs. KiNG) on an identical PCoA dataset and metadata mapping, quantifying the ratio to justify adoption of a lightweight tool. In the source study, EMPeror files were 26 MB versus 1.85 GB for KiNG (1.3% of original size). metabolomics/v3 10.1186/2047-217x-2-16
skills.summary: Benchmarks the on-disk output size of competing visualization tools (e.g., EMPeror vs. KiNG) on an identical PCoA dataset and metadata mapping, quantifying the ratio to justify adoption of a lightweight tool. In the source study, EMPeror files were 26 MB versus 1.85 GB for KiNG (1.3% of original size).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset is small or the output size is not a deciding factor — the 1.3% ratio argument matters mainly for thousands of samples and many metadata columns The candidate tools do not produce comparable outputs (e.g., one produces interactive 3D plots and the other a numeric summary), so the size ratio would not be a fair comparison You need publication-quality static figures rather than web-shareable interactive visualizations, which is the trade-off this benchmark quantifies

skills.description: Use when you have a labeled MS/MS challenge dataset (e.g., CASMI 2022, 304 positive-mode spectra) and need to compare formula-annotation accuracy of two or more tools under identical inputs.
skills.name: cross-tool-formula-accuracy-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cross-tool-formula-accuracy-benchmarking Use when you have a labeled MS/MS challenge dataset (e.g., CASMI 2022, 304 positive-mode spectra) and need to compare formula-annotation accuracy of two or more tools under identical inputs. Evaluating negative-mode spectra — the released models were trained only for positive-mode data Input spectra lack ground-truth formula/adduct assignments, so no accuracy comparison is possible The goal is de novo prediction on new data rather than scoring tool performance against a labeled benchmark http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Head-to-head evaluation of chemical formula prediction tools (e.g., MIST-CF vs SIRIUS/CSI:FingerID) on a shared, ground-truthed spectrum set such as the CASMI2022 positive-mode challenge, scoring joint formula+adduct and formula-only top-1 accuracy against Table 2 baselines. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jcim.3c01082
skills.summary: Head-to-head evaluation of chemical formula prediction tools (e.g., MIST-CF vs SIRIUS/CSI:FingerID) on a shared, ground-truthed spectrum set such as the CASMI2022 positive-mode challenge, scoring joint formula+adduct and formula-only top-1 accuracy against Table 2 baselines.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Evaluating negative-mode spectra — the released models were trained only for positive-mode data Input spectra lack ground-truth formula/adduct assignments, so no accuracy comparison is possible The goal is de novo prediction on new data rather than scoring tool performance against a labeled benchmark

skills.description: Use when evaluating whether a data-driven formula prediction model (e.g., a formula transformer trained on MS/MS spectra) outperforms a classical tree-based competitor on the same spectra, and you need accuracy, coverage, and concordance metrics on identical inputs.
skills.name: cross-tool-formula-annotation-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-tool-formula-annotation-comparison Use when evaluating whether a data-driven formula prediction model (e.g., a formula transformer trained on MS/MS spectra) outperforms a classical tree-based competitor on the same spectra, and you need accuracy, coverage, and concordance metrics on identical inputs. Input spectra are negative-mode data: MIST-CF models were trained only on positive-mode data, so this comparison is invalid for negative ionization. The goal is Prospective structure or fingerprint prediction (e.g., CSI:FingerID or MIST fingerprint scoring) rather than de novo chemical formula annotation accuracy comparison. No NIST20 license is available and only the public NPLIB1/CANOPUS-trained model is used, but the reference claims Orbitrap or higher-resolution performance parity — the public model is explicitly less performant than the NIST20-trained model. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Benchmark a learned de novo chemical formula annotation model (MIST-CF, 10 ppm candidate masses with FastFilter top-256 down-selection) head-to-head against a fragmentation-tree baseline (SIRIUS 5.6.3, 300 s tree/compound timeouts) on a shared test set such as NPLIB1, reporting top-1 formula accuracy, joint formula+adduct accuracy, failure rate, and per-spectrum concordance. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jcim.3c01082
skills.summary: Benchmark a learned de novo chemical formula annotation model (MIST-CF, 10 ppm candidate masses with FastFilter top-256 down-selection) head-to-head against a fragmentation-tree baseline (SIRIUS 5.6.3, 300 s tree/compound timeouts) on a shared test set such as NPLIB1, reporting top-1 formula accuracy, joint formula+adduct accuracy, failure rate, and per-spectrum concordance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra are negative-mode data: MIST-CF models were trained only on positive-mode data, so this comparison is invalid for negative ionization. The goal is Prospective structure or fingerprint prediction (e.g., CSI:FingerID or MIST fingerprint scoring) rather than de novo chemical formula annotation accuracy comparison. No NIST20 license is available and only the public NPLIB1/CANOPUS-trained model is used, but the reference claims Orbitrap or higher-resolution performance parity — the public model is explicitly less performant than the NIST20-trained model.

skills.description: Use when comparing MS/MS spectral prediction quality across in silico fragmentation tools (e.g., FIORA vs ICEBERG vs CFM-ID) and assessing generalization to compounds structurally dissimilar from the training set via sqrt-weighted cosine similarity stratified by maximum Tanimoto similarity.
skills.name: cross-tool-fragmentation-prediction-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-tool-fragmentation-prediction-evaluation Use when comparing MS/MS spectral prediction quality across in silico fragmentation tools (e.g., FIORA vs ICEBERG vs CFM-ID) and assessing generalization to compounds structurally dissimilar from the training set via sqrt-weighted cosine similarity stratified by maximum Tanimoto similarity. No experimentally measured reference spectra exist for the test compounds — the sqrt-weighted cosine metric requires scoring predictions against reference spectra. The goal is retention time (RT) or collision cross section (CCS) prediction rather than MS/MS spectral quality benchmarking. Only a single tool's predictions are being validated without comparison baselines — this skill is specifically a cross-tool evaluation stratified by training-set similarity. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Benchmark in silico fragmentation tools (FIORA, ICEBERG, CFM-ID) by scoring predicted MS/MS spectra against reference spectra with the sqrt-weighted cosine similarity, then stratify performance by each test compound's maximum Tanimoto similarity to the training set. This is how the article demonstrates FIORA's robustness on structurally dissimilar compounds (median cosine 0.63 in the 0.2–0.3 Tanimoto bin) while outperforming ICEBERG and CFM-ID. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-025-57422-4
skills.summary: Benchmark in silico fragmentation tools (FIORA, ICEBERG, CFM-ID) by scoring predicted MS/MS spectra against reference spectra with the sqrt-weighted cosine similarity, then stratify performance by each test compound's maximum Tanimoto similarity to the training set. This is how the article demonstrates FIORA's robustness on structurally dissimilar compounds (median cosine 0.63 in the 0.2–0.3 Tanimoto bin) while outperforming ICEBERG and CFM-ID.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No experimentally measured reference spectra exist for the test compounds — the sqrt-weighted cosine metric requires scoring predictions against reference spectra. The goal is retention time (RT) or collision cross section (CCS) prediction rather than MS/MS spectral quality benchmarking. Only a single tool's predictions are being validated without comparison baselines — this skill is specifically a cross-tool evaluation stratified by training-set similarity.

Only one tool has processed the data and no cross-tool reference or replicate result exists to correlate against The analysis goal is peak picking quality itself rather than consistency of quantification outputs between tools Transitions lack matched identities or a shared file set between the two tool outputs, making area-level correlation meaningless http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Benchmark quantification consistency between two MRM data analysis tools (e.g., MRMPro and Skyline) by extracting peak areas for matched transitions across a shared file set and comparing fitted calibration curves via R-square values, flagging discrepancies to baseline-determination or peak-integration errors. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-024-05685-x

skills.when_to_use_negative: Only one tool has processed the data and no cross-tool reference or replicate result exists to correlate against The analysis goal is peak picking quality itself rather than consistency of quantification outputs between tools Transitions lack matched identities or a shared file set between the two tool outputs, making area-level correlation meaningless

skills.description: Decision support for choosing among CYP450 SoM or byproduct predictors: when a practitioner has a common evaluation test set (e.g., EBoMD2, the BioTransformer hold-out 13321_2018_324_MOESM6_ESM.sdf, or the HDFAME 60Reactants.
skills.name: cross-tool-metabolite-prediction-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-tool-metabolite-prediction-comparison Decision support for choosing among CYP450 SoM or byproduct predictors: when a practitioner has a common evaluation test set (e.g., EBoMD2, the BioTransformer hold-out 13321_2018_324_MOESM6_ESM.sdf, or the HDFAME 60Reactants. If no ground-truth SoM/metabolite annotation is available for the test compounds — Jaccard scoring requires labeled positives to compute TP, FN, and FP. If the goal is to evaluate one tool's internal performance rather than cross-tool comparison — a single-tool evaluation does not need a per-tool/per-isoform Jaccard matrix. If the evaluation set contains compounds that some tools (via CypReact filter) classify as non-reactants and you do not wish to penalize filtered-out predictions — this skill assumes common treatment of reactant/non-reactant classifications across tools. http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 http://edamontology.org/topic_3336 Benchmark multiple in silico CYP450 metabolism predictors by scoring their outputs on common datasets against the Jaccard similarity TP/(TP+FN+FP), then tabulate per-tool/per-isoform performance to quantify relative advantages (e.g., CypBoM's Jaccard being 25% better than FAME2's and 36% better than FAME3's for SoMs). metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jcim.1c00144
skills.summary: Benchmark multiple in silico CYP450 metabolism predictors by scoring their outputs on common datasets against the Jaccard similarity TP/(TP+FN+FP), then tabulate per-tool/per-isoform performance to quantify relative advantages (e.g., CypBoM's Jaccard being 25% better than FAME2's and 36% better than FAME3's for SoMs).
skills.when_to_use_negative: If no ground-truth SoM/metabolite annotation is available for the test compounds — Jaccard scoring requires labeled positives to compute TP, FN, and FP. If the goal is to evaluate one tool's internal performance rather than cross-tool comparison — a single-tool evaluation does not need a per-tool/per-isoform Jaccard matrix. If the evaluation set contains compounds that some tools (via CypReact filter) classify as non-reactants and you do not wish to penalize filtered-out predictions — this skill assumes common treatment of reactant/non-reactant classifications across tools.

skills.search_text: cross-tool-parameter-benchmarking Use when two or more parameter-optimization tools (e.g., AutoTuner, IPO) have produced centWave parameter sets for the same raw LC-MS dataset and the analysis goal is to compare how each choice changes feature counts. The input is already a processed feature table rather than raw instrument data — parameter estimation must occur on raw data prior to analysis Fewer than 3 samples are available — AutoTuner requires at least 3 samples of raw data, and the paper recommends 9-12 samples for stable parameter estimates The question is feature identification/annotation rather than benchmarking parameter-selection methods; the article states identifying each distinct feature was beyond its scope Benchmark metabolomics peak-picking parameter sets produced by competing selection tools (AutoTuner vs IPO) by running each parameter set through the identical XCMS centWave pipeline and quantifying unique and shared features in the resulting feature tables per ionization mode. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/812370
skills.summary: Benchmark metabolomics peak-picking parameter sets produced by competing selection tools (AutoTuner vs IPO) by running each parameter set through the identical XCMS centWave pipeline and quantifying unique and shared features in the resulting feature tables per ionization mode.

skills.description: Use when two or more GC–MS peak-picking or deconvolution tools (e.g. eRah, XCMS centWave, MetAlign) have produced per-sample quantification tables and you need to quantify their agreement by correlating peak areas/intensities per compound across samples.

skills.search_text: cross-tool-peak-area-correlation-analysis Use when two or more GC–MS peak-picking or deconvolution tools (e.g. eRah, XCMS centWave, MetAlign) have produced per-sample quantification tables and you need to quantify their agreement by correlating peak areas/intensities per compound across samples. skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a single tool's peak table and no second tool's quantification exists to compare against The goal is to evaluate identification accuracy (spectral match scores, library hits) rather than quantitative agreement of peak areas Samples or compound sets are not shared across tools, so no per-sample per-compound pairing is possible

skills.description: Use when a novel peak-picking pipeline for untargeted LC/HRMS data needs quantitative benchmarking against MZmine 2, xcms-CAMERA, or MS-DIAL on a shared raw test file.
skills.name: cross-tool-peak-count-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cross-tool-peak-count-benchmarking Use when a novel peak-picking pipeline for untargeted LC/HRMS data needs quantitative benchmarking against MZmine 2, xcms-CAMERA, or MS-DIAL on a shared raw test file. When the input is already a processed/aligned peak table rather than raw LC/HRMS acquisitions — re-running peak detection tools on peak tables will not yield comparable raw counts. skills.summary: Benchmark a new peak-detection pipeline against established untargeted LC/HRMS tools (MZmine 2, xcms-CAMERA, MS-DIAL) by running all four on the same raw file and comparing total peak counts, fold ratios, and threshold-failure rates.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is already a processed/aligned peak table rather than raw LC/HRMS acquisitions — re-running peak detection tools on peak tables will not yield comparable raw counts. When the goal is quantifying alignment/annotation quality across tools rather than raw peak-detection sensitivity — this skill measures only peak counts and threshold failures, not retention-time alignment or annotation accuracy. When baseline tools require vendor-specific file formats not available for the study (e.g. MZmine 2 or MS-DIAL may not parse Agilent .d directly) — the file must be convertible/parseable by all four tools before benchmarking.

skills.description: Use when the same set of MS/MS spectra has been annotated by two independent classifiers (e.g. CANOPUS and MolNetEnhancer) and you need to tabulate per-class disagreement before choosing one tool's output for downstream scoring such as NPClassScore.

skills.search_text: cross-tool-prediction-discrepancy-analysis Use when the same set of MS/MS spectra has been annotated by two independent classifiers (e.g. CANOPUS and MolNetEnhancer) and you need to tabulate per-class disagreement before choosing one tool's output for downstream scoring such as NPClassScore. skills.summary: Quantifies where two structure-based ontology prediction tools (CANOPUS via SIRIUS and MolNetEnhancer) disagree on ClassyFire superclass assignments for the same GNPS molecular networking MS/MS spectra, using the Streptomyces/Salinispora dataset as the reference case.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When you already have a single trusted annotation source and only need a classification ranking rather than an inter-tool agreement assessment. When the spectra exceed the CANOPUS 850 Da mass cut-off or lack structure-based classes, since missing predictions distort the intersection count. When the analysis goal is BGC–spectrum linking (e.g. NPClassScore/Metcalf scoring) rather than evaluating which ontology predictor to use.

skills.description: Use when a new in silico reactant-prediction or site-of-metabolism tool must be benchmarked against CypReact, ADMET Predictor, or SMARTCyp on the 1632-molecule CYP450 reactant dataset using per-enzyme AUROC.
skills.name: cross-tool-prediction-performance-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-tool-prediction-performance-comparison Use when a new in silico reactant-prediction or site-of-metabolism tool must be benchmarked against CypReact, ADMET Predictor, or SMARTCyp on the 1632-molecule CYP450 reactant dataset using per-enzyme AUROC. The goal is predicting a single site of metabolism (SoM) per molecule rather than binary reactant classification per CYP450 enzyme — SMARTCyp's original mode, not this reactant-prediction comparison. ADMET Predictor must be computed de novo but no license is available — it is commercial, so only its reported average AUROC of 0.75 can be recorded for comparison. The molecule set differs from the 1632-molecule benchmark and no cross-validation protocol is being reproduced — AUROC averages are then not comparable to the published 0.83–0.92 / 0.75 / 0.53 figures. http://edamontology.org/topic_3316 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Benchmarks reactant-prediction software for the nine human CYP450 enzymes by computing per-enzyme AUROCs on the 1632-molecule benchmark and comparing tool averages (e.g. CypReact 0.83–0.92 vs ADMET Predictor 0.75 vs SMARTCyp 0.53). It establishes whether a new tool significantly outperforms published baselines. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jcim.8b00035
skills.summary: Benchmarks reactant-prediction software for the nine human CYP450 enzymes by computing per-enzyme AUROCs on the 1632-molecule benchmark and comparing tool averages (e.g. CypReact 0.83–0.92 vs ADMET Predictor 0.75 vs SMARTCyp 0.53). It establishes whether a new tool significantly outperforms published baselines.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is predicting a single site of metabolism (SoM) per molecule rather than binary reactant classification per CYP450 enzyme — SMARTCyp's original mode, not this reactant-prediction comparison. ADMET Predictor must be computed de novo but no license is available — it is commercial, so only its reported average AUROC of 0.75 can be recorded for comparison. The molecule set differs from the 1632-molecule benchmark and no cross-validation protocol is being reproduced — AUROC averages are then not comparable to the published 0.83–0.92 / 0.75 / 0.53 figures.

skills.description: Use when you have a manually labeled set of Pass/Fail peaks from an untargeted LC–MS metabolomics dataset and need to train, cross-validate, and statistically select among competing classifiers rather than trust a single model.
skills.name: cross-validated-classifier-training
skills.search_text: cross-validated-classifier-training Use when you have a manually labeled set of Pass/Fail peaks from an untargeted LC–MS metabolomics dataset and need to train, cross-validate, and statistically select among competing classifiers rather than trust a single model. Your data is vendor-processed output in a uniquely formatted file — MetaClean requires an XCMS object input and is not amenable to such formats in its current form. You have no labeled Pass/Fail peaks and cannot obtain expert annotations — fivefold cross-validation training of the classifier requires labeled examples. Your dataset contains many low-abundance Pass peaks resembling background noise but your training set lacks such examples — the classifier was shown to be conservative and performed worse on the low-quality class when trained without them. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Trains and selects a peak-quality classifier by pairing three sets of peak-quality metrics (Zhang et al. M4, TargetedMSQC-derived M7, and combined M11) with eight machine learning algorithms under a rigorous fivefold cross-validation framework, then statistically comparing candidates to pick the best classifier (here, AdaBoost on M11) for flagging low-quality peaks in untargeted LC–MS metabolomics. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-020-01738-3
skills.summary: Trains and selects a peak-quality classifier by pairing three sets of peak-quality metrics (Zhang et al. M4, TargetedMSQC-derived M7, and combined M11) with eight machine learning algorithms under a rigorous fivefold cross-validation framework, then statistically comparing candidates to pick the best classifier (here, AdaBoost on M11) for flagging low-quality peaks in untargeted LC–MS metabolomics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your data is vendor-processed output in a uniquely formatted file — MetaClean requires an XCMS object input and is not amenable to such formats in its current form. You have no labeled Pass/Fail peaks and cannot obtain expert annotations — fivefold cross-validation training of the classifier requires labeled examples. Your dataset contains many low-abundance Pass peaks resembling background noise but your training set lacks such examples — the classifier was shown to be conservative and performed worse on the low-quality class when trained without them.

skills.search_text: cross-validated-knn-imputation Use when a benchmark requires KNNimpute error rates on data with artificially introduced missing values (10%, 20% or 30% MCAR) but no a priori neighbour count k is given, so k_ must be chosen by cross-validation. The goal is a single off-the-shelf imputation without benchmarking: the cross-validation over k (Algorithm 2) exists only to give KNNimpute a fair, parameter-tuned comparison against missForest, which has no k-like parameter The data are mixed-type and you need a method that handles variable types natively without the {-1,1} dummy-coding workaround — missForest or MICE are the paper's choices there The data contain no missing values (or missingness is not MCAR in the 10–30% range the evaluation assumes) http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Reproduces the KNNimpute baseline (Troyanskaya et al. 2001) from Stekhoven & Bühlmann (2011) as a cross-validated competitor: the neighbour count k_best is selected by cross-validation (Algorithm 2) over a candidate range K, imputation is done on standardized data, and the imputed matrix is retransformed to the original scales before computing NRMSE (continuous data) or PFC (dummy-coded categorical data). metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btr597
skills.summary: Reproduces the KNNimpute baseline (Troyanskaya et al. 2001) from Stekhoven & Bühlmann (2011) as a cross-validated competitor: the neighbour count k_best is selected by cross-validation (Algorithm 2) over a candidate range K, imputation is done on standardized data, and the imputed matrix is retransformed to the original scales before computing NRMSE (continuous data) or PFC (dummy-coded categorical data).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is a single off-the-shelf imputation without benchmarking: the cross-validation over k (Algorithm 2) exists only to give KNNimpute a fair, parameter-tuned comparison against missForest, which has no k-like parameter The data are mixed-type and you need a method that handles variable types natively without the {-1,1} dummy-coding workaround — missForest or MICE are the paper's choices there The data contain no missing values (or missingness is not MCAR in the 10–30% range the evaluation assumes)

skills.description: Use when fitting a PathIntegrate Multi-View MB-PLS (or comparable PLS-based multi-omics model) and the latent-variable count must be tuned to avoid over- or under-fitting before pathway importance is interpreted.
skills.name: cross-validated-latent-variable-selection
skills.search_text: cross-validated-latent-variable-selection Use when fitting a PathIntegrate Multi-View MB-PLS (or comparable PLS-based multi-omics model) and the latent-variable count must be tuned to avoid over- or under-fitting before pathway importance is interpreted. The task is a purely unsupervised decomposition with no outcome variable, so AUC-based tuning is undefined. skills.search_text: cross-validation-evaluation-data-processing Use when MS/MS spectra plus structure labels (e.g., GNPS cross-validation data) must be scored against database structure candidates to produce a top-k correct-identification curve for a structure identification tool. The evaluation requires an updated CSI:FingerID version's identification rate rather than replicating the original CSI:FingerID 1.1 release setup. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Reproduces the structure-disjoint cross-validation evaluation of CSI:FingerID structure identification on GNPS MS/MS spectra, computing the top-k identification curve against PubChem search candidates and confirming the reported 40.4% top-1 correct identification rate of CSI:FingerID 1.1. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-019-0344-8
skills.summary: Reproduces the structure-disjoint cross-validation evaluation of CSI:FingerID structure identification on GNPS MS/MS spectra, computing the top-k identification curve against PubChem search candidates and confirming the reported 40.4% top-1 correct identification rate of CSI:FingerID 1.1.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is de novo fragmentation tree or molecular formula assignment without evaluating structure identification accuracy against a labeled benchmark.
