skills.description: Use when reproducing the DeepMet training protocol: you have a pre-trained SMILES language model, a known-metabolite structure set (HMDB), and need per-fold fine-tuned generators whose withheld 10% mimics unknown metabolites.
skills.name: cross-validation-fold-model-fine-tuning
skills.search_text: cross-validation-fold-model-fine-tuning Use when reproducing the DeepMet training protocol: you have a pre-trained SMILES language model, a known-metabolite structure set (HMDB), and need per-fold fine-tuned generators whose withheld 10% mimics unknown metabolites. If you only want to annotate metabolomics data with an already-trained model — the article provides the trained DeepMet model for that purpose, so no fine-tuning is needed If the target organism is evolutionarily distant from humans (e.g. plant or bacterial metabolism) — the article notes such applications 'will likely require' bespoke models rather than the human-metabolite-trained folds If the task is candidate prioritization or MS/MS annotation rather than model training — use the mass-to-charge filtering and meta-learning skills instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Fine-tunes a pre-trained chemical language model (a 3-layer LSTM, hidden size 1024, embedding 128) independently on each cross-validation fold of known metabolite structures (e.g. HMDB), holding out 10% of metabolites per fold to simulate discovery of unknown metabolites. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.11.13.623458
skills.summary: Fine-tunes a pre-trained chemical language model (a 3-layer LSTM, hidden size 1024, embedding 128) independently on each cross-validation fold of known metabolite structures (e.g. HMDB), holding out 10% of metabolites per fold to simulate discovery of unknown metabolites.
skills.when_to_use_negative: If you only want to annotate metabolomics data with an already-trained model — the article provides the trained DeepMet model for that purpose, so no fine-tuning is needed If the target organism is evolutionarily distant from humans (e.g. plant or bacterial metabolism) — the article notes such applications 'will likely require' bespoke models rather than the human-metabolite-trained folds If the task is candidate prioritization or MS/MS annotation rather than model training — use the mass-to-charge filtering and meta-learning skills instead

skills.description: Use when training per-feature-set ML models (e.g., random forest regressors on CCLE omics) where scaling must be fit only on training folds of a 5-fold CV scheme to avoid leakage into held-out metabolite predictions.
skills.name: cross-validation-fold-normalization
skills.search_text: cross-validation-fold-normalization Use when training per-feature-set ML models (e.g., random forest regressors on CCLE omics) where scaling must be fit only on training folds of a 5-fold CV scheme to avoid leakage into held-out metabolite predictions. Models are not directly transferrable to predicting metabolomics from other sources due to differences between in vitro and in vivo conditions and limited feature overlap — do not apply CCLE-derived fold scaling statistics to NCI60 or single-cell data Binary mutation features were excluded from random forest model results due to their binary structure, so Z-score scaling of the mutation feature set is not meaningful for the final Metab8D models http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Z-score normalization of CCLE omics feature matrices performed inside each 5-fold cross-validation training split, as used by Metab8D/Recon8D random forest metabolite models to prevent information leakage from held-out folds into scaling parameters. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.08.17.608400
skills.summary: Z-score normalization of CCLE omics feature matrices performed inside each 5-fold cross-validation training split, as used by Metab8D/Recon8D random forest metabolite models to prevent information leakage from held-out folds into scaling parameters.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Models are not directly transferrable to predicting metabolomics from other sources due to differences between in vitro and in vivo conditions and limited feature overlap — do not apply CCLE-derived fold scaling statistics to NCI60 or single-cell data Binary mutation features were excluded from random forest model results due to their binary structure, so Z-score scaling of the mutation feature set is not meaningful for the final Metab8D models

skills.description: Use when matched multiomic (CCLE-style) feature tables and a metabolite abundance matrix are available and the goal is to benchmark how well each omics class individually predicts each metabolite via cross-validated ML.
skills.name: cross-validation-metabolite-predictability-assessment
skills.search_text: cross-validation-metabolite-predictability-assessment Use when matched multiomic (CCLE-style) feature tables and a metabolite abundance matrix are available and the goal is to benchmark how well each omics class individually predicts each metabolite via cross-validated ML. Predicting metabolomics from non-cell-line sources (e.g., in vivo tissue): models trained on cell lines in culture are not directly transferrable due to in vitro/in vivo differences and limited feature overlap Feature importance interpretation or network construction — use the separate Shapley analysis / Metab8D_network.xlsx workflow instead of the accuracy-benchmarking run Input omics have very few matched samples (cell lines); per the paper, omics with too few samples may not perform as well and accuracies are not comparable across unequal sample sizes http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3473 Trains per-metabolite random forest regression models on each multiomic feature set from the CCLE cell line panel and scores predictability of the 225-metabolite panel via cross-validated Pearson correlations, quantifying which omics class (e.g., transcriptomics) best predicts metabolomic variation. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.08.17.608400
skills.summary: Trains per-metabolite random forest regression models on each multiomic feature set from the CCLE cell line panel and scores predictability of the 225-metabolite panel via cross-validated Pearson correlations, quantifying which omics class (e.g., transcriptomics) best predicts metabolomic variation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Predicting metabolomics from non-cell-line sources (e.g., in vivo tissue): models trained on cell lines in culture are not directly transferrable due to in vitro/in vivo differences and limited feature overlap Feature importance interpretation or network construction — use the separate Shapley analysis / Metab8D_network.xlsx workflow instead of the accuracy-benchmarking run Input omics have very few matched samples (cell lines); per the paper, omics with too few samples may not perform as well and accuracies are not comparable across unequal sample sizes

skills.description: Use when comparing versions of an in silico MS/MS spectral prediction model on a shared experimental dataset and you need fold-matched, per-energy-level metrics (Dice, Precision, Recall, Dot Product) with significance testing.
skills.name: cross-validation-model-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-validation-model-evaluation Use when comparing versions of an in silico MS/MS spectral prediction model on a shared experimental dataset and you need fold-matched, per-energy-level metrics (Dice, Precision, Recall, Dot Product) with significance testing. The task is compound identification (MS2C) benchmarking rather than spectral-prediction accuracy comparison — the CASMI 2016 identification evaluation uses a different scoring setup. Spectra come from non-QTOF instruments, which CFM-ID does not currently handle. Only a single train/test split is needed and fold-matched variance/significance estimation is not required — a simple holdout evaluation suffices. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Benchmark protocol for comparing spectral-prediction model versions (e.g., CFM-ID 4.0 vs 2.0/3.0) under a matched 10-fold cross-validation framework on Metlin ESI-MS/MS data, scoring Dice, Precision, Recall, and Stein's Dot Product per energy level and ionization mode. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c01465
skills.summary: Benchmark protocol for comparing spectral-prediction model versions (e.g., CFM-ID 4.0 vs 2.0/3.0) under a matched 10-fold cross-validation framework on Metlin ESI-MS/MS data, scoring Dice, Precision, Recall, and Stein's Dot Product per energy level and ionization mode.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is compound identification (MS2C) benchmarking rather than spectral-prediction accuracy comparison — the CASMI 2016 identification evaluation uses a different scoring setup. Spectra come from non-QTOF instruments, which CFM-ID does not currently handle. Only a single train/test split is needed and fold-matched variance/significance estimation is not required — a simple holdout evaluation suffices.

skills.summary: Reproduces the RT-Transformer paper's compound-annotation performance statistics by transfer-learning a retention-time model on Metabobase/MoNa data and filtering MS-Finder candidate lists by predicted RT deviation, verifying headline numbers (93 correct, 10 erroneously filtered, 11-position average rank improvement, 52.64% filtered).

skills.description: Use when you hold a table of generative-model outputs with sampling frequencies and want to test whether frequency alone prioritizes withheld cross-validation metabolites or newly released HMDB structures over generated decoys.

skills.search_text: cross-validation-rank-statistics-evaluation Use when you hold a table of generative-model outputs with sampling frequencies and want to test whether frequency alone prioritizes withheld cross-validation metabolites or newly released HMDB structures over generated decoys. When the query structures were part of the model's training data — ranks would be inflated; only withheld test-fold metabolites or post-training releases like HMDB v5.0 additions give a fair ROC When prioritization should use analytical evidence (mass-to-charge ratio, MS/MS spectra) rather than sampling frequency alone — this skill isolates the frequency-only signal When applying to evolutionarily distant metabolomes (plant or bacterial metabolism), since DeepMet was trained and evaluated on human metabolite structures http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Evaluates whether a chemical language model's sampling frequency can rank withheld or newly discovered metabolites above its generated background, using rank-based ROC/AUC analysis and hypergeometric enrichment against HMDB. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.11.13.623458

skills.when_to_use_negative: When the query structures were part of the model's training data — ranks would be inflated; only withheld test-fold metabolites or post-training releases like HMDB v5.0 additions give a fair ROC When prioritization should use analytical evidence (mass-to-charge ratio, MS/MS spectra) rather than sampling frequency alone — this skill isolates the frequency-only signal When applying to evolutionarily distant metabolomes (plant or bacterial metabolism), since DeepMet was trained and evaluated on human metabolite structures

skills.description: Use when a GC-MS (or analogous LC-MS) metabolomics study provides a pooled-QC training block plus an external validation QC set, and you need to measure how well a normalization method controls batch drift via RSD precision.
skills.name: cross-validation-rsd-precision-assessment
skills.search_text: cross-validation-rsd-precision-assessment Use when a GC-MS (or analogous LC-MS) metabolomics study provides a pooled-QC training block plus an external validation QC set, and you need to measure how well a normalization method controls batch drift via RSD precision. The dataset contains only pooled QC samples with no independent external validation QC pools — RSDs on training QCs alone (e.g., SERRF's 19% median RSD) overstate real precision, as shown by the 34% median RSD on BioIVT validation. Only a small number of QC samples are available that cannot support five-fold cross-validation splits. The aim is absolute quantification rather than precision assessment of a drift-correction/normalization method. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Quantifies normalization precision in large-scale untargeted GC-MS metabolomics by computing per-metabolite relative standard deviations (RSDs) under five-fold cross-validation on training pooled QC samples and on an independent external validation QC block, then benchmarking coverage of compounds below a 30% RSD threshold. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo13080944
skills.summary: Quantifies normalization precision in large-scale untargeted GC-MS metabolomics by computing per-metabolite relative standard deviations (RSDs) under five-fold cross-validation on training pooled QC samples and on an independent external validation QC block, then benchmarking coverage of compounds below a 30% RSD threshold.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset contains only pooled QC samples with no independent external validation QC pools — RSDs on training QCs alone (e.g., SERRF's 19% median RSD) overstate real precision, as shown by the 34% median RSD on BioIVT validation. Only a small number of QC samples are available that cannot support five-fold cross-validation splits. The aim is absolute quantification rather than precision assessment of a drift-correction/normalization method.

skills.description: Use when normalizing LC-MS metabolomics run-order data with Metanorm and you must decide between GCV and LOOCV smoother selection, or need to demonstrate that downstream differential abundance results are insensitive to that choice.
skills.name: cross-validation-span-selection-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-validation-span-selection-comparison Use when normalizing LC-MS metabolomics run-order data with Metanorm and you must decide between GCV and LOOCV smoother selection, or need to demonstrate that downstream differential abundance results are insensitive to that choice. When the goal is to compare different normalization methods against each other (e.g. robust methods vs QC-RLSC DAM overlap) rather than to compare the two span-selection schemes within one method When the input data are already normalized or when no QC samples exist to anchor QC-based drift fitting, since metanorm() requires an unnormalized matrix and representative QC runs for QCcheck = TRUE When a single normalization run suffices and no sensitivity assessment of span/smoother selection is needed — running both cv schemes doubles computation, which is a real cost for the slower tGAM model http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Compares the two span/smoother selection schemes supported by the Metanorm metanorm() function — cross-validated generalized cross-validation (GCV) and leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV), selected via the cv argument — by running each normalization method under both schemes and verifying that differential abundance testing outcomes and p-value orderings remain comparable. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.09.30.679445
skills.summary: Compares the two span/smoother selection schemes supported by the Metanorm metanorm() function — cross-validated generalized cross-validation (GCV) and leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV), selected via the cv argument — by running each normalization method under both schemes and verifying that differential abundance testing outcomes and p-value orderings remain comparable.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is to compare different normalization methods against each other (e.g. robust methods vs QC-RLSC DAM overlap) rather than to compare the two span-selection schemes within one method When the input data are already normalized or when no QC samples exist to anchor QC-based drift fitting, since metanorm() requires an unnormalized matrix and representative QC runs for QCcheck = TRUE When a single normalization run suffices and no sensitivity assessment of span/smoother selection is needed — running both cv schemes doubles computation, which is a real cost for the slower tGAM model

skills.description: Use when benchmarking an in silico structure annotation workflow's confidence scoring against known ground-truth reference spectra, comparing merged vs single collision-energy MS/MS performance, or reproducing hop-plot/ROC evaluations.
skills.name: cross-validation-spectral-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cross-validation-spectral-benchmarking Use when benchmarking an in silico structure annotation workflow's confidence scoring against known ground-truth reference spectra, comparing merged vs single collision-energy MS/MS performance, or reproducing hop-plot/ROC evaluations. Evaluating annotations on biological samples with no ground truth — the article notes evaluations were carried out using reference measurements because correct answers for biological datasets are unknown Spectral library de-replication or sample-level annotation of real LC–MS/MS runs rather than benchmarking against known reference structures Datasets lacking all three collision energies per compound, or where spectra contain at most one peak at some collision energy/noise level (such compounds must be discarded per the protocol) http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Structure-disjoint benchmarking of COSMIC confidence scores via ten-fold cross-validation on Orbitrap reference data (n = 3,721) and an independent QTOF set (n = 3,013), evaluated with hop plots of correct hits versus annotation rate across collision energies (10/20/40 eV, merged) and noise levels. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41587-021-01045-9
skills.summary: Structure-disjoint benchmarking of COSMIC confidence scores via ten-fold cross-validation on Orbitrap reference data (n = 3,721) and an independent QTOF set (n = 3,013), evaluated with hop plots of correct hits versus annotation rate across collision energies (10/20/40 eV, merged) and noise levels.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Evaluating annotations on biological samples with no ground truth — the article notes evaluations were carried out using reference measurements because correct answers for biological datasets are unknown Spectral library de-replication or sample-level annotation of real LC–MS/MS runs rather than benchmarking against known reference structures Datasets lacking all three collision energies per compound, or where spectra contain at most one peak at some collision energy/noise level (such compounds must be discarded per the protocol)

skills.description: Use when training CCS-prediction SVR models on McLean Unified CCS Compendium adduct data ([M-H]-, [M+H]+, [M+Na]+) and you need unbiased split-level performance reporting via a median-RMSEV model rather than a single arbitrary split.
skills.name: cross-validation-split-sampling-and-median-model-selection
skills.search_text: cross-validation-split-sampling-and-median-model-selection Use when training CCS-prediction SVR models on McLean Unified CCS Compendium adduct data ([M-H]-, [M+H]+, [M+Na]+) and you need unbiased split-level performance reporting via a median-RMSEV model rather than a single arbitrary split. skills.summary: Runs the G.A.M.E. command-line solver (csccp-solver-cli) to solve the chemical substituent core combinatorial problem (CSCCP) via a CUDA/GPU-parallelized iterative dynamic programming (idp) kernel, predicting top-ranked probable molecular structures matching a targeted molecular weight at up to five decimal digits of mass precision.

skills.name: csi-fingerid-fingerprint-prediction
skills.search_text: csi-fingerid-fingerprint-prediction Use when an MS2 spectrum (mgf, .ms, or preprocessed SIRIUS workspace) needs a predicted structural fingerprint xF — either to rank candidate structures by modified Platt score or to serve as the blueprint input for MSNovelist de novo generation. Negative-mode MS2 spectra — MSNovelist/CSI:FingerID performance is lower there since MSNovelist is trained only on positive-mode data Spectra with fewer than three fragment ions — the pipeline requires a minimum of three fragment ions, and richer spectra are desirable Spectra at high m/z with unreliable formula assignment — SIRIUS formula error rates rise to >50% for compounds up to m/z 800, which propagates into fingerprint prediction http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Predicts a structural fingerprint (xF) from an MS2 tandem mass spectrum using CSI:FingerID, after SIRIUS assigns the molecular formula (xM). The fingerprint acts both as a database-search target and as the structural blueprint that MSNovelist's encoder–decoder consumes for de novo SMILES generation. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-022-01486-3
skills.summary: Predicts a structural fingerprint (xF) from an MS2 tandem mass spectrum using CSI:FingerID, after SIRIUS assigns the molecular formula (xM). The fingerprint acts both as a database-search target and as the structural blueprint that MSNovelist's encoder–decoder consumes for de novo SMILES generation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Negative-mode MS2 spectra — MSNovelist/CSI:FingerID performance is lower there since MSNovelist is trained only on positive-mode data Spectra with fewer than three fragment ions — the pipeline requires a minimum of three fragment ions, and richer spectra are desirable Spectra at high m/z with unreliable formula assignment — SIRIUS formula error rates rise to >50% for compounds up to m/z 800, which propagates into fingerprint prediction

skills.description: Use when a large targeted-metabolomics run is split into batches with QC samples injected in acquisition order and you need to remove batch-effect drift from MRM quantitation, using the QC-RLSC approach of MRMQuant.
skills.name: cubic-spline-injection-order-interpolation
skills.search_text: cubic-spline-injection-order-interpolation Use when a large targeted-metabolomics run is split into batches with QC samples injected in acquisition order and you need to remove batch-effect drift from MRM quantitation, using the QC-RLSC approach of MRMQuant. When the dataset contains no QC samples injected across batches - MRMQuant conducts batch-effect correction only if quality control (QC) samples are included in the sample files. When the input is a raw MRM signal (mzML/abf) that has not yet been peak-detected and quantitated - this skill operates on the quantitated abundances, not on raw traces. When you need deconvolution of coeluted isomer peaks or peak-tip detection - that is a separate MRMQuant step, not the batch-effect correction itself. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0219 MRMQuant's QC-RLSC batch-effect correction uses a cubic-spline interpolation/extrapolation of a LOESS curve fitted to QC-sample abundances (ordered by acquisition/injection order) to remove systematic response drift across sample batches. The interpolated trend is used to compute correction ratios that restore the abundances to the reference scale. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c02462
skills.summary: MRMQuant's QC-RLSC batch-effect correction uses a cubic-spline interpolation/extrapolation of a LOESS curve fitted to QC-sample abundances (ordered by acquisition/injection order) to remove systematic response drift across sample batches. The interpolated trend is used to compute correction ratios that restore the abundances to the reference scale.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the dataset contains no QC samples injected across batches - MRMQuant conducts batch-effect correction only if quality control (QC) samples are included in the sample files. When the input is a raw MRM signal (mzML/abf) that has not yet been peak-detected and quantitated - this skill operates on the quantitated abundances, not on raw traces. When you need deconvolution of coeluted isomer peaks or peak-tip detection - that is a separate MRMQuant step, not the batch-effect correction itself.

skills.description: Use when a raw 1D NMR spectrum (ppm scale + intensity array) shows a rolling or offset baseline and peak shapes must be preserved while flattening signal-free regions to zero intensity.
skills.name: cubic-spline-interpolation
skills.search_text: cubic-spline-interpolation Use when a raw 1D NMR spectrum (ppm scale + intensity array) shows a rolling or offset baseline and peak shapes must be preserved while flattening signal-free regions to zero intensity. The spectrum is 2D or the task is isotopomer/HSQC + GC-MS analysis — the SplineBaseline workflow and its linear-spline fallback are defined for 1D NMR spectra The baseline is already flat around zero in signal-free regions — spline subtraction would add variance rather than remove baseline error Baseline anchors are needed inside dense resonance regions where signal-free points cannot be selected — over-correction risk is precisely what the fallback mitigates, not eliminates http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 Fits a cubic spline (scipy.interpolate.CubicSpline) through sparse baseline points selected in signal-free regions of a 1D NMR spectrum, with a linear-spline fallback that inserts intermediate baseline points along straight lines when adjacent anchors are more than a configured maximum number of data points apart, preventing over-correction in dense spectral regions. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo15010048
skills.summary: Fits a cubic spline (scipy.interpolate.CubicSpline) through sparse baseline points selected in signal-free regions of a 1D NMR spectrum, with a linear-spline fallback that inserts intermediate baseline points along straight lines when adjacent anchors are more than a configured maximum number of data points apart, preventing over-correction in dense spectral regions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The spectrum is 2D or the task is isotopomer/HSQC + GC-MS analysis — the SplineBaseline workflow and its linear-spline fallback are defined for 1D NMR spectra The baseline is already flat around zero in signal-free regions — spline subtraction would add variance rather than remove baseline error Baseline anchors are needed inside dense resonance regions where signal-free points cannot be selected — over-correction risk is precisely what the fallback mitigates, not eliminates

skills.description: Use when comparing the precision of corrected vs raw LC-MS/GC-MS metabolomics or proteomics feature tables by measuring how many features fall below successive RSD (CV%) thresholds in QC samples.
skills.name: cumulative-frequency-distribution-plotting
skills.search_text: cumulative-frequency-distribution-plotting Use when comparing the precision of corrected vs raw LC-MS/GC-MS metabolomics or proteomics feature tables by measuring how many features fall below successive RSD (CV%) thresholds in QC samples. The input is already a summary table of RSD bins or percentages — the skill expects per-feature QC intensity values so RSDs can be computed from scratch. There are too few QC injections (e.g. fewer than a handful) to give a stable CV estimate per feature; the article relies on QC repeated every 5–8 subject samples across batches. The goal is subject-sample (biological) variability, not QC (technical) precision — the cumulative RSD plot is specifically computed across aliquoted QC injections. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Plot the cumulative frequency distribution of QC-sample feature RSDs (CV%) across binned cutoffs (e.g. CV<5%, 10%, ... 100%) to quantify how a signal-drift correction method, such as QC-RFSC, improves metabolomics/proteomics data precision versus raw data and alternative correction algorithms. metabolomics/v3 10.1016/j.aca.2018.08.002
skills.summary: Plot the cumulative frequency distribution of QC-sample feature RSDs (CV%) across binned cutoffs (e.g. CV<5%, 10%, ... 100%) to quantify how a signal-drift correction method, such as QC-RFSC, improves metabolomics/proteomics data precision versus raw data and alternative correction algorithms.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a summary table of RSD bins or percentages — the skill expects per-feature QC intensity values so RSDs can be computed from scratch. There are too few QC injections (e.g. fewer than a handful) to give a stable CV estimate per feature; the article relies on QC repeated every 5–8 subject samples across batches. The goal is subject-sample (biological) variability, not QC (technical) precision — the cumulative RSD plot is specifically computed across aliquoted QC injections.

The query spectrum already matches a spectral library entry — dereplication, not de novo vs database comparison, is the right decision path The spectrum's molecular formula is not high-confidence (below the ≥80% explained peaks, ≥90% explained intensity, ≥0.9 ZODIAC thresholds), so de novo and database candidates are not comparable under equal constraints The database search and the de novo generation were run with different fingerprints or scoring — comparing scores across different scoring schemes is invalid http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Compares the top de novo structure score generated by MSNovelist against the best structural-database (PubChem/KEGG) candidate for the same MS2 spectrum, both scored with the modified Platt fingerprint-match score, to decide whether the de novo prediction is the better explanation of the spectrum. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-022-01486-3
skills.summary: Compares the top de novo structure score generated by MSNovelist against the best structural-database (PubChem/KEGG) candidate for the same MS2 spectrum, both scored with the modified Platt fingerprint-match score, to decide whether the de novo prediction is the better explanation of the spectrum.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The query spectrum already matches a spectral library entry — dereplication, not de novo vs database comparison, is the right decision path The spectrum's molecular formula is not high-confidence (below the ≥80% explained peaks, ≥90% explained intensity, ≥0.9 ZODIAC thresholds), so de novo and database candidates are not comparable under equal constraints The database search and the de novo generation were run with different fingerprints or scoring — comparing scores across different scoring schemes is invalid

skills.description: Use when building a unified chemical inventory from multiple databases and literature sources (e.g., exposome source lists) and you need a deduplicated, structurally annotated parent-chemical list.
skills.name: database-chemical-list-fusion
skills.search_text: database-chemical-list-fusion Use when building a unified chemical inventory from multiple databases and literature sources (e.g., exposome source lists) and you need a deduplicated, structurally annotated parent-chemical list. The analysis targets biotransformation metabolites rather than parent chemicals — metabolite prediction is handled separately with BioTransformer, not by database fusion. Chemicals of interest are inorganic compounds, metals, or organic mixtures — these are explicitly filtered out during the fusion workflow. A chemical lacks a CASRN — the U.S. EPA Chemistry Dashboard cannot retrieve diverse types of relevant domain data for it, so downstream annotation will fail. http://edamontology.org/topic_3334 Fuses chemical entries from multiple public databases and literature sources into a single deduplicated human exposome chemical inventory keyed by CASRN, filtering out inorganic compounds, organic mixtures, and metals. This produced the >20,000-chemical (20,756 unique CASRN) list underlying the prioritized HExpMetDB resource. metabolomics/v3 10.1289/ehp7722
skills.summary: Fuses chemical entries from multiple public databases and literature sources into a single deduplicated human exposome chemical inventory keyed by CASRN, filtering out inorganic compounds, organic mixtures, and metals. This produced the >20,000-chemical (20,756 unique CASRN) list underlying the prioritized HExpMetDB resource.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis targets biotransformation metabolites rather than parent chemicals — metabolite prediction is handled separately with BioTransformer, not by database fusion. Chemicals of interest are inorganic compounds, metals, or organic mixtures — these are explicitly filtered out during the fusion workflow. A chemical lacks a CASRN — the U.S. EPA Chemistry Dashboard cannot retrieve diverse types of relevant domain data for it, so downstream annotation will fail.

skills.description: Use when a paper reports an aggregate count for a curated reference database (records and unique entities) and you must reproduce the build, reconcile the total, and retain source provenance.
skills.name: database-count-verification-and-provenance-tracking
skills.search_text: database-count-verification-and-provenance-tracking Use when a paper reports an aggregate count for a curated reference database (records and unique entities) and you must reproduce the build, reconcile the total, and retain source provenance. Your input is already a merged, deduplicated feature or annotation table — counting rows there verifies nothing about the underlying database build You only need to run compound identification against an existing reference library (use the MS2 Peak Annotation module directly rather than rebuilding the database) The claim you are verifying concerns a single-source database with no overlapping/duplicate entries, where a simple row count suffices http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Reproduce and verify the size of a merged multi-source reference database (e.g. MetaboAnalyst 6.0's curated MS2 spectral library: 10,420,215 MS2 records over 1,551,012 unique compounds) while tracking per-source provenance and deduplication decisions. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkae253
skills.summary: Reproduce and verify the size of a merged multi-source reference database (e.g. MetaboAnalyst 6.0's curated MS2 spectral library: 10,420,215 MS2 records over 1,551,012 unique compounds) while tracking per-source provenance and deduplication decisions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your input is already a merged, deduplicated feature or annotation table — counting rows there verifies nothing about the underlying database build You only need to run compound identification against an existing reference library (use the MS2 Peak Annotation module directly rather than rebuilding the database) The claim you are verifying concerns a single-source database with no overlapping/duplicate entries, where a simple row count suffices

skills.description: Use when you have an integrated multi-source annotation database and need per-database annotation coverage and cross-source overlap statistics for metabolites vs. genes.
skills.name: database-coverage-quantification
skills.search_text: database-coverage-quantification Use when you have an integrated multi-source annotation database and need per-database annotation coverage and cross-source overlap statistics for metabolites vs. genes. Your goal is pathway over-representation/enrichment testing rather than characterizing database annotation coverage — use runFisherTest / runCombinedFisherTest instead. You need up-to-date annotations from the expanded RaMP-DB 3.0 sources (ChEBI, Lipid-MAPS, RefMet, Rhea, PFOCR) rather than reproducing the original four-database coverage analysis. The analytes you care about are not mapped into the integrated database's analyte-pathway tables (e.g., you only have raw source files and no MySQL dump loaded). http://edamontology.org/topic_0089 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Quantifies how completely each source database (KEGG, Reactome, HMDB, WikiPathways) annotates metabolites and genes within an integrated pathway database like RaMP, and computes cross-database overlap including the fraction of analytes annotated by all four sources. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo8010016
skills.summary: Quantifies how completely each source database (KEGG, Reactome, HMDB, WikiPathways) annotates metabolites and genes within an integrated pathway database like RaMP, and computes cross-database overlap including the fraction of analytes annotated by all four sources.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your goal is pathway over-representation/enrichment testing rather than characterizing database annotation coverage — use runFisherTest / runCombinedFisherTest instead. You need up-to-date annotations from the expanded RaMP-DB 3.0 sources (ChEBI, Lipid-MAPS, RefMet, Rhea, PFOCR) rather than reproducing the original four-database coverage analysis. The analytes you care about are not mapped into the integrated database's analyte-pathway tables (e.g., you only have raw source files and no MySQL dump loaded).

skills.description: Use when the goal is to quantify how many novel compounds and reactions a reaction-rule network expansion (e.g., top 500 JN1224min rules, one generation, compounds <600 g/mol) produces from a compound database.
skills.name: database-expansion-count-tabulation
skills.search_text: database-expansion-count-tabulation Use when the goal is to quantify how many novel compounds and reactions a reaction-rule network expansion (e.g., top 500 JN1224min rules, one generation, compounds <600 g/mol) produces from a compound database. The task targets filtered or sampled networks (e.g., similarity cutoff, similarity sampling, metabolomics, or thermodynamics filters) rather than a full unfiltered one-generation expansion whose counts should match the paper's results table The goal is multi-generation expansion or rule sets other than the top 500 JN1224min rules (e.g., the top 50 rules / two-generation EcoCyc run in the paper), since counts will not match the reported values Only pathway design or metabolomics peak annotation is needed — Pickaxe supports those applications, but this skill specifically produces count tabulation for expansion validation http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 http://edamontology.org/topic_3361 Reproduces one-generation rule-based expansion of biological compound databases (KEGG, EcoCyc, YMDB) with Pickaxe and tabulates per-database counts of starting compounds, generated compounds, and generated reactions into a results table for validation against published values. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-023-05149-8
skills.summary: Reproduces one-generation rule-based expansion of biological compound databases (KEGG, EcoCyc, YMDB) with Pickaxe and tabulates per-database counts of starting compounds, generated compounds, and generated reactions into a results table for validation against published values.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task targets filtered or sampled networks (e.g., similarity cutoff, similarity sampling, metabolomics, or thermodynamics filters) rather than a full unfiltered one-generation expansion whose counts should match the paper's results table The goal is multi-generation expansion or rule sets other than the top 500 JN1224min rules (e.g., the top 50 rules / two-generation EcoCyc run in the paper), since counts will not match the reported values Only pathway design or metabolomics peak annotation is needed — Pickaxe supports those applications, but this skill specifically produces count tabulation for expansion validation

skills.description: Use when a categorate() result for GC-MS compounds must be narrowed to chemicals meeting user-defined database-membership (LOTUS, KEGG, FEMA, FDA_SPL, reactives), structural-property (MW, Rings, Groups, Atoms, NCharges), or library-group criteria before downstream extraction.
skills.name: database-label-filtering
skills.search_text: database-label-filtering Use when a categorate() result for GC-MS compounds must be narrowed to chemicals meeting user-defined database-membership (LOTUS, KEGG, FEMA, FDA_SPL, reactives), structural-property (MW, Rings, Groups, Atoms, NCharges), or library-group criteria before downstream extraction. Input is already a filtered compound list or a raw GC-MS hit table rather than a categorate() result — use spreadOut()/mzExacto() directly instead. The goal is to keep every tentative compound without database/structural/library criteria; exactoThese() subsetting is unnecessary and would drop compounds. Working with MS2, MS3, or ion mobility + MS2 data, where uafR's published-data-dependent filtering does not yet apply. http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Subsets chemicals of interest from the categorate() output using exactoThese() according to a user-specified information set (e.g. Database, FMCS, or Library) and matching criteria, enabling targeted downstream GC-MS extraction of the filtered compound set. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pone.0306202
skills.summary: Subsets chemicals of interest from the categorate() output using exactoThese() according to a user-specified information set (e.g. Database, FMCS, or Library) and matching criteria, enabling targeted downstream GC-MS extraction of the filtered compound set.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a filtered compound list or a raw GC-MS hit table rather than a categorate() result — use spreadOut()/mzExacto() directly instead. The goal is to keep every tentative compound without database/structural/library criteria; exactoThese() subsetting is unnecessary and would drop compounds. Working with MS2, MS3, or ion mobility + MS2 data, where uafR's published-data-dependent filtering does not yet apply.

skills.description: Use when you have estimated m/z values from LC-MS metabolomics data and need to assign compound identities via m/z matching against HMDB or MassBank at ppm-level tolerances.
skills.name: database-query-interpretation
skills.search_text: database-query-interpretation Use when you have estimated m/z values from LC-MS metabolomics data and need to assign compound identities via m/z matching against HMDB or MassBank at ppm-level tolerances. The goal is unambiguous one-to-one compound identification from m/z alone with no prior drug/metabolite information — identical m/z values from other metabolites make this infeasible The target compounds are not present in HMDB or MassBank (e.g., heroin and nimetazepam are absent from HMDB and SMART 2.0 cannot detect them) Only a single mass tolerance has been tested and low-abundance or borderline peaks require re-evaluation of peak detection parameters before identification is meaningful http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Identify metabolites/peaks by querying estimated m/z values against spectral or metabolite databases (HMDB, MassBank) at defined mass tolerances, then interpreting match counts against expected results. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c03225
skills.summary: Identify metabolites/peaks by querying estimated m/z values against spectral or metabolite databases (HMDB, MassBank) at defined mass tolerances, then interpreting match counts against expected results.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is unambiguous one-to-one compound identification from m/z alone with no prior drug/metabolite information — identical m/z values from other metabolites make this infeasible The target compounds are not present in HMDB or MassBank (e.g., heroin and nimetazepam are absent from HMDB and SMART 2.0 cannot detect them) Only a single mass tolerance has been tested and low-abundance or borderline peaks require re-evaluation of peak detection parameters before identification is meaningful

skills.description: Use when benchmarking a de novo structure-annotation model against database-search baselines (HSS, SSS, BDC) on EI-MS spectra, or when re-deriving headline metrics like Acc1 = 0.43 or win rate = 0.76 from deposited predictions.
skills.name: database-search-baseline-reproduction
skills.search_text: database-search-baseline-reproduction Use when benchmarking a de novo structure-annotation model against database-search baselines (HSS, SSS, BDC) on EI-MS spectra, or when re-deriving headline metrics like Acc1 = 0.43 or win rate = 0.76 from deposited predictions. Input spectra are tandem MS/MS rather than gas chromatography electron ionization (GC-EI) mass spectra — the comparison and the underlying model are specific to EI-MS The goal is to generate new predictions rather than re-evaluate the deposited ones — that requires an NIST 20 license and the full training pipeline, not just the evaluation notebooks The task needs explainability or peak-level justification of candidate rankings — the paper notes SpecTUS lacks intermediate representations such as peak annotations or fragmentation trees http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 Reproduces the SpecTUS-vs-database-search comparison (hybrid similarity search HSS, similarity search SSS, Blackwell's data compound BDC) on the 28,267-spectrum NIST 20 test split, computing top-k accuracy, Morgan-fingerprint Tanimoto similarity, and SpecTUS-vs-HSS win rates for k = 1, 10, and 50. metabolomics/v3 10.48550/arxiv.2502.05114
skills.summary: Reproduces the SpecTUS-vs-database-search comparison (hybrid similarity search HSS, similarity search SSS, Blackwell's data compound BDC) on the 28,267-spectrum NIST 20 test split, computing top-k accuracy, Morgan-fingerprint Tanimoto similarity, and SpecTUS-vs-HSS win rates for k = 1, 10, and 50.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra are tandem MS/MS rather than gas chromatography electron ionization (GC-EI) mass spectra — the comparison and the underlying model are specific to EI-MS The goal is to generate new predictions rather than re-evaluate the deposited ones — that requires an NIST 20 license and the full training pipeline, not just the evaluation notebooks The task needs explainability or peak-level justification of candidate rankings — the paper notes SpecTUS lacks intermediate representations such as peak annotations or fragmentation trees

skills.description: Use when preparing HMDB, GNPS, or CASMI MS/MS spectral datasets for formula-ranking benchmarks and you must quantify how many spectra/metabolites survive the CHONSP, <1500 Da, precursor-type, and >=3-peak selection criteria.
skills.name: database-spectrum-selection-statistics
skills.search_text: database-spectrum-selection-statistics Use when preparing HMDB, GNPS, or CASMI MS/MS spectral datasets for formula-ranking benchmarks and you must quantify how many spectra/metabolites survive the CHONSP, <1500 Da, precursor-type, and >=3-peak selection criteria. Compounds containing elements beyond C, H, O, N, S, and P, or forming adducts other than [M+H]+/[M-H]- — the criteria (and FSA itself) were validated only on CHONSP compounds with these precursors Spectra with fewer than three centroid peaks — they will be discarded by criterion 4, so downstream ranking results would be meaningless When the goal is formula ranking of already-qualified spectra rather than dataset qualification statistics — use FSA ranking directly instead Applies the paper's four dataset-qualification criteria (CHONSP-only formulas with mandatory C and H, mass < 1500 Da, [M+H]+/[M-H]- precursors, at least three peaks) to raw HMDB, GNPS, and CASMI MS/MS spectra, and reports per-dataset qualified spectra/compound counts to reproduce Table 1. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-025-02379-0
skills.summary: Applies the paper's four dataset-qualification criteria (CHONSP-only formulas with mandatory C and H, mass < 1500 Da, [M+H]+/[M-H]- precursors, at least three peaks) to raw HMDB, GNPS, and CASMI MS/MS spectra, and reports per-dataset qualified spectra/compound counts to reproduce Table 1.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Compounds containing elements beyond C, H, O, N, S, and P, or forming adducts other than [M+H]+/[M-H]- — the criteria (and FSA itself) were validated only on CHONSP compounds with these precursors Spectra with fewer than three centroid peaks — they will be discarded by criterion 4, so downstream ranking results would be meaningless When the goal is formula ranking of already-qualified spectra rather than dataset qualification statistics — use FSA ranking directly instead

skills.description: Use when building or documenting a multiomics database and you need to enumerate its constituent data types (e.g. epigenomics marks), organizational modules, and user-facing functionalities into a structured schema.
skills.name: database-taxonomy-structuring
skills.search_text: database-taxonomy-structuring Use when building or documenting a multiomics database and you need to enumerate its constituent data types (e.g. epigenomics marks), organizational modules, and user-facing functionalities into a structured schema. Input is raw omics data files (FASTQ, VCF) rather than textual descriptions of database organization — data curation, not taxonomy structuring, is needed. The database already publishes a machine-readable schema or API spec; reuse it instead of re-deriving the taxonomy from prose. Only a single data type is in scope (e.g. one histone mark), where a full module/functionality taxonomy adds no value. http://edamontology.org/topic_3071 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Structures a multiomics database's content into an explicit taxonomy of data types, modules, and functionalities, as done for GutUDB's eight omics types, four modules (SPECIES, DISEASES, OMICS, THERAPY), and four core functionalities (Browse, Query, Visualization, Download). metabolomics/v3 10.1002/imt2.195
skills.summary: Structures a multiomics database's content into an explicit taxonomy of data types, modules, and functionalities, as done for GutUDB's eight omics types, four modules (SPECIES, DISEASES, OMICS, THERAPY), and four core functionalities (Browse, Query, Visualization, Download).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw omics data files (FASTQ, VCF) rather than textual descriptions of database organization — data curation, not taxonomy structuring, is needed. The database already publishes a machine-readable schema or API spec; reuse it instead of re-deriving the taxonomy from prose. Only a single data type is in scope (e.g. one histone mark), where a full module/functionality taxonomy adds no value.

skills.search_text: dataset-centering-and-scaling-for-neural-networks Use when training Keras or BRNN neural networks on chemical descriptor matrices for retention time prediction, where features on different scales (e.g., XLogP vs. atom counts vs. pKa) must be centered and scaled first. When fitting tree-based Retip models (random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM) that do not require centered/scaled inputs for the neural-network-specific rationale to apply When predicting on compounds far outside the chemical landscape of the training set, since scaling cannot fix descriptor extrapolation errors the article warns about When the input is already a normalized/scaled feature table rather than raw getCD() descriptor output http://edamontology.org/topic_3398 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Center and scale molecular-descriptor training sets (e.g., Retip's HILIC 880-compound and RPLC 398-compound sets) with Retip's cesc() function before fitting neural network retention-time models such as Keras. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.9b05765

skills.description: Use when reproducing or auditing a claim that depends on exact dataset frequencies, such as the CyProduct paper's finding that η+η-forming reactions occur in only 4 of 828 η-η BoM records and all 4 are Cyclization.
skills.name: dataset-count-verification
skills.search_text: dataset-count-verification Use when reproducing or auditing a claim that depends on exact dataset frequencies, such as the CyProduct paper's finding that η+η-forming reactions occur in only 4 of 828 η-η BoM records and all 4 are Cyclization. When the goal is to train or score a CypBoM classifier on the BoM records — use the model-training skill instead; counting is only a consistency check. When the input SDF lacks annotated BoM fields (e.g. a raw Zaretzki SoM dataset without the literature curation that produced BoMs) — the tally cannot be computed from unconverted SoM data. When auditing counts of a different dataset (e.g. EBoMD2 hold-out, 60Reactants.sdf, 30NonReactants.sdf) whose published totals are not the 828/1348/86/·+η·4 figures. http://edamontology.org/topic_3336 Tallies annotated bond-of-metabolism (BoM) records in the EBoMD/EBoMD2 SDF datasets and cross-checks the counts (e.g. 828 η-η BoMs, 1348 η-H, 86 η-SPN, 4 η+η Cyclization cases) against values reported in the CyProduct paper, flagging any mismatch as a reproduction failure. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jcim.1c00144
skills.summary: Tallies annotated bond-of-metabolism (BoM) records in the EBoMD/EBoMD2 SDF datasets and cross-checks the counts (e.g. 828 η-η BoMs, 1348 η-H, 86 η-SPN, 4 η+η Cyclization cases) against values reported in the CyProduct paper, flagging any mismatch as a reproduction failure.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is to train or score a CypBoM classifier on the BoM records — use the model-training skill instead; counting is only a consistency check. When the input SDF lacks annotated BoM fields (e.g. a raw Zaretzki SoM dataset without the literature curation that produced BoMs) — the tally cannot be computed from unconverted SoM data. When auditing counts of a different dataset (e.g. EBoMD2 hold-out, 60Reactants.sdf, 30NonReactants.sdf) whose published totals are not the 828/1348/86/·+η·4 figures.

skills.description: Use when a generative model produces multiple candidate molecular graphs per spectrum and you need deterministic top-k predictions with accuracy, MCES-distance, and Tanimoto-similarity metrics on benchmarks like NPLIB1 or MassSpecGym.
skills.name: dataset-frequency-ranking-postprocessing
skills.search_text: dataset-frequency-ranking-postprocessing Use when a generative model produces multiple candidate molecular graphs per spectrum and you need deterministic top-k predictions with accuracy, MCES-distance, and Tanimoto-similarity metrics on benchmarks like NPLIB1 or MassSpecGym. Evaluating autoregressive/SMILES baselines such as MSNovelist, where ranking is by beam-search log-likelihood rather than sampled-structure frequency When you need full candidate diversity rather than the most frequent structures — frequency ranking collapses 100 samples to top-k http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3473 Post-generation evaluation procedure for de novo molecule generation from mass spectra: sample many candidate molecules per spectrum (100 per spectrum in DiffMS), filter invalid/disconnected structures, and rank by frequency to produce top-k predictions scored against ground truth. metabolomics/v3 10.48550/arxiv.2502.09571
skills.summary: Post-generation evaluation procedure for de novo molecule generation from mass spectra: sample many candidate molecules per spectrum (100 per spectrum in DiffMS), filter invalid/disconnected structures, and rank by frequency to produce top-k predictions scored against ground truth.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Evaluating autoregressive/SMILES baselines such as MSNovelist, where ranking is by beam-search log-likelihood rather than sampled-structure frequency When you need full candidate diversity rather than the most frequent structures — frequency ranking collapses 100 samples to top-k

skills.description: Use when a database release report must state how many records were added since the previous version, expressed both as absolute counts (851 new BGCs) and as percentage growth (73% from 1170 to 2021), broken down by class.

skills.search_text: dataset-growth-quantification Use when a database release report must state how many records were added since the previous version, expressed both as absolute counts (851 new BGCs) and as percentage growth (73% from 1170 to 2021), broken down by class. skills.summary: Merge DDA-derived and DIA-(SWATH)-derived metabolic feature lists into a single metabolite-intensity table and export combined MS2 spectra tagged by acquisition source, using DaDIA.R on top of XCMS peak detection.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a merged feature table or annotation result — DaDIA.R expects raw mzXML acquisitions per mode Data were acquired in a single mode only (pure DDA or pure DIA with no paired counterpart), since the merge step requires both feature lists Running XCMS older than version 3.11.4, which the article states is required to run DaDIA.R

skills.description: Use when you hold paired vendor raw files (.raw, .d, .wiff) acquired in both DDA and DIA modes on the same instrument (e.g. QE HF-X) and need to compare DDA- vs DIA-based QC metric sensitivity around recorded maintenance events.
skills.name: dda-dia-paired-file-processing
skills.search_text: dda-dia-paired-file-processing Use when you hold paired vendor raw files (.raw, .d, .wiff) acquired in both DDA and DIA modes on the same instrument (e.g. QE HF-X) and need to compare DDA- vs DIA-based QC metric sensitivity around recorded maintenance events. Input is already an extracted metric/feature table — proceed directly to the ratio-of-change and maintenance-event alignment step instead of reprocessing raw files You only have DIA data without paired DDA acquisitions, so the DDA-vs-DIA sensitivity comparison cannot be made QC assessment for SRM/targeted experiments — the article notes SRM-based QC tools cannot be directly applied to large-scale quantitative proteomics experiments, and this skill targets DDA/DIA raw-file processing http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Paired DDA and DIA vendor raw files are converted to mzXML with msConvert, DIA files are quantified with DIA-NN (v1.7.15) at 1% FDR at both peptide precursor and protein levels, and numerical QC metrics are extracted per file so that DDA vs DIA sensitivity to LC-MS system faults can be compared around maintenance events. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-54871-1
skills.summary: Paired DDA and DIA vendor raw files are converted to mzXML with msConvert, DIA files are quantified with DIA-NN (v1.7.15) at 1% FDR at both peptide precursor and protein levels, and numerical QC metrics are extracted per file so that DDA vs DIA sensitivity to LC-MS system faults can be compared around maintenance events.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already an extracted metric/feature table — proceed directly to the ratio-of-change and maintenance-event alignment step instead of reprocessing raw files You only have DIA data without paired DDA acquisitions, so the DDA-vs-DIA sensitivity comparison cannot be made QC assessment for SRM/targeted experiments — the article notes SRM-based QC tools cannot be directly applied to large-scale quantitative proteomics experiments, and this skill targets DDA/DIA raw-file processing

skills.description: Use when processing combined DDA and DIA-(SWATH) mzXML files (e.g. human urine samples) through DaDIA.R and you need to report what fraction of MS2 spectra originates from each acquisition mode and their quality distribution.
skills.name: dda-dia-provenance-fraction-analysis
skills.search_text: dda-dia-provenance-fraction-analysis Use when processing combined DDA and DIA-(SWATH) mzXML files (e.g. human urine samples) through DaDIA.R and you need to report what fraction of MS2 spectra originates from each acquisition mode and their quality distribution. Input is a single acquisition mode only (pure DDA or pure DIA/SWATH without pooled-QC DDA mzXML files) — the provenance split is undefined. MS2 spectra have not yet been extracted and deconvolved from the raw mzXML files (use the DaDIA.R feature-extraction and MS2 deconvolution steps first). The analysis targets chromatographic feature counts or rescued-feature true/false-positive rates rather than MS2 spectral provenance and dot-product quality fractions. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Quantifies the DDA-versus-DIA provenance split of MS2 spectra generated by the DaDIA hybrid acquisition workflow, and computes the high-/low-quality spectral fractions by dot-product scoring against the MoNA library. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c05022
skills.summary: Quantifies the DDA-versus-DIA provenance split of MS2 spectra generated by the DaDIA hybrid acquisition workflow, and computes the high-/low-quality spectral fractions by dot-product scoring against the MoNA library.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a single acquisition mode only (pure DDA or pure DIA/SWATH without pooled-QC DDA mzXML files) — the provenance split is undefined. MS2 spectra have not yet been extracted and deconvolved from the raw mzXML files (use the DaDIA.R feature-extraction and MS2 deconvolution steps first). The analysis targets chromatographic feature counts or rescued-feature true/false-positive rates rather than MS2 spectral provenance and dot-product quality fractions.

skills.description: Use when prototyping or simulating a DDA acquisition strategy for untargeted LC-MS/MS metabolomics: full-scan mzML input, a duty cycle to define, and a goal of improving coverage of picked peaks over a TopN baseline.
skills.name: dda-duty-cycle-scheduling
skills.search_text: dda-duty-cycle-scheduling Use when prototyping or simulating a DDA acquisition strategy for untargeted LC-MS/MS metabolomics: full-scan mzML input, a duty cycle to define, and a goal of improving coverage of picked peaks over a TopN baseline. The input is already an acquired MS2 dataset or a feature table — this skill schedules acquisition, it does not re-analyze existing spectra. The goal is DIA (data-independent) acquisition rather than DDA ion prioritization; the article notes the DDA-vs-DIA question is out of scope for its DDA coverage objective. Real instrument timing without an instrument API is required — in silico ViMMS schedules must be validated separately on real hardware via IAPI. http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Schedules data-dependent acquisition duty cycles in which one MS1 survey scan is followed by up to N MS2 fragmentation scans, using ROI-based ion prioritization (e.g., SmartROI availability rules) instead of naive TopN intensity ranking, so that more unique peaks get fragmented per injection. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c03895
skills.summary: Schedules data-dependent acquisition duty cycles in which one MS1 survey scan is followed by up to N MS2 fragmentation scans, using ROI-based ion prioritization (e.g., SmartROI availability rules) instead of naive TopN intensity ranking, so that more unique peaks get fragmented per injection.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already an acquired MS2 dataset or a feature table — this skill schedules acquisition, it does not re-analyze existing spectra. The goal is DIA (data-independent) acquisition rather than DDA ion prioritization; the article notes the DDA-vs-DIA question is out of scope for its DDA coverage objective. Real instrument timing without an instrument API is required — in silico ViMMS schedules must be validated separately on real hardware via IAPI.

skills.description: Use when you have MZmine feature tables from a full-scan run and a DDA run of the same strains, plus a RegFilter-generated SPL, and you need to quantify which SPL ions were not fragmented by DDA.
skills.name: dda-fragmentation-coverage-assessment
skills.search_text: dda-fragmentation-coverage-assessment Use when you have MZmine feature tables from a full-scan run and a DDA run of the same strains, plus a RegFilter-generated SPL, and you need to quantify which SPL ions were not fragmented by DDA. The input is a raw instrument file (.raw or .mzXML) that has not yet been preprocessed by MZmine into aligned feature tables with row ID, row m/z, row retention time, and peak area columns. No RegFilter SPL or other targeted precursor list exists — without a candidate list there is no 'list-only' set to compare against the DDA fragmented precursors. The goal is annotation or molecular networking (FBMN, SIRIUS, ChemWalker) rather than assessing DDA fragmentation coverage of a precursor list. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Quantifies how well a targeted scheduled precursor list (SPL) from RegFilter overlaps with what data-dependent acquisition (DDA) actually fragmented, by aligning MZmine full-scan and MS/MS feature tables and computing per-strain fractions of list-only ions, including how many were full-scan base peaks that DDA missed. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.08.07.607073
skills.summary: Quantifies how well a targeted scheduled precursor list (SPL) from RegFilter overlaps with what data-dependent acquisition (DDA) actually fragmented, by aligning MZmine full-scan and MS/MS feature tables and computing per-strain fractions of list-only ions, including how many were full-scan base peaks that DDA missed.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a raw instrument file (.raw or .mzXML) that has not yet been preprocessed by MZmine into aligned feature tables with row ID, row m/z, row retention time, and peak area columns. No RegFilter SPL or other targeted precursor list exists — without a candidate list there is no 'list-only' set to compare against the DDA fragmented precursors. The goal is annotation or molecular networking (FBMN, SIRIUS, ChemWalker) rather than assessing DDA fragmentation coverage of a precursor list.

skills.description: Use when you need to assess the sensitivity of a JPA feature-extraction workflow to peak-picking thresholds, e.g., comparing default (ppm=10, snthresh=6) versus tolerant (ppm=30, S/N=3) settings on the same raw mzXML files.
skills.name: dda-metabolomics-dataset-reprocessing
skills.search_text: dda-metabolomics-dataset-reprocessing Use when you need to assess the sensitivity of a JPA feature-extraction workflow to peak-picking thresholds, e.g., comparing default (ppm=10, snthresh=6) versus tolerant (ppm=30, S/N=3) settings on the same raw mzXML files. The dataset is full-scan or DIA data — the README explicitly warns 'Please do not use this function when processing full-scan or DIA data set!' for MR feature extraction The input is already a processed feature table rather than raw mzXML files (use custom.featureTable instead of reprocessing raw data) A single-pass feature extraction is sufficient and no parameter-sensitivity comparison is required http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Reprocess the same LC-MS/MS (DDA) mzXML dataset twice through the JPA pipeline — once with default JPA parameters (ppm=10, snthresh=6) and once with tolerant thresholds (ppm=30, S/N=3) — to quantify how peak-picking (JPA-PP) and MS2-recognition (JPA-MR) feature counts and fidelity rates shift with parameter tolerance. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo12030212
skills.summary: Reprocess the same LC-MS/MS (DDA) mzXML dataset twice through the JPA pipeline — once with default JPA parameters (ppm=10, snthresh=6) and once with tolerant thresholds (ppm=30, S/N=3) — to quantify how peak-picking (JPA-PP) and MS2-recognition (JPA-MR) feature counts and fidelity rates shift with parameter tolerance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset is full-scan or DIA data — the README explicitly warns 'Please do not use this function when processing full-scan or DIA data set!' for MR feature extraction The input is already a processed feature table rather than raw mzXML files (use custom.featureTable instead of reprocessing raw data) A single-pass feature extraction is sufficient and no parameter-sensitivity comparison is required

skills.description: Use when converting DDA vendor MS data to the Aird format and you need to construct the metadata correlation index that groups MS1 spectra into contiguous blocks with their associated MS2 spectra for fast random access.
skills.name: dda-ms1-ms2-group-index-construction
skills.search_text: dda-ms1-ms2-group-index-construction Use when converting DDA vendor MS data to the Aird format and you need to construct the metadata correlation index that groups MS1 spectra into contiguous blocks with their associated MS2 spectra for fast random access. Data were acquired in DIA/SWATH mode — build the precursor m/z range-MS2 group index instead of the MS1-MS2 group index The acquisition mode is PRM or a format Aird does not yet support (e.g. ScanningSWATH or Ion Mobility are under development) The goal is to read an existing Aird file rather than produce the index — use AirdSDK's reader instead of rebuilding the index http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Build the MS1-MS2 group index that Aird stores in its JSON metadata for DDA data, reordering spectra so each MS1 block sits adjacent to its corresponding MS2 group with recorded start positions, enabling faster block reads during analysis. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-021-04490-0
skills.summary: Build the MS1-MS2 group index that Aird stores in its JSON metadata for DDA data, reordering spectra so each MS1 block sits adjacent to its corresponding MS2 group with recorded start positions, enabling faster block reads during analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data were acquired in DIA/SWATH mode — build the precursor m/z range-MS2 group index instead of the MS1-MS2 group index The acquisition mode is PRM or a format Aird does not yet support (e.g. ScanningSWATH or Ion Mobility are under development) The goal is to read an existing Aird file rather than produce the index — use AirdSDK's reader instead of rebuilding the index

skills.description: Use when a DDA MS/MS dataset has been converted to MZA (HDF5) and you need to pull out the fragmented MS2 spectrum (with m/z, intensity, and ion mobility arrival time where present) for a specific precursor identified in the metadata.
skills.name: dda-msms-precursor-spectrum-retrieval
skills.search_text: dda-msms-precursor-spectrum-retrieval Use when a DDA MS/MS dataset has been converted to MZA (HDF5) and you need to pull out the fragmented MS2 spectrum (with m/z, intensity, and ion mobility arrival time where present) for a specific precursor identified in the metadata. The data is still in a proprietary vendor format (.raw, .d, mzML) and has not yet been converted to MZA — use the mza converter first The file was not acquired in DDA mode or contains no MS2 spectra (MSLevel 1 only) — there is no MS/MS spectrum to retrieve You need centroided peak lists or identifications rather than raw spectrum arrays — mzapy provides raw data extraction, not database search results http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Retrieves the MS/MS (MS2) spectrum for a named precursor from a DDA mass spectrometry file converted to the MZA HDF5 format, using the mzapy.dda.MsmsReaderDda class. Handles identification of the precursor's scans from the MZA metadata table, optional removal of erroneous scans, and extraction of m/z, intensity, and ion mobility arrival-time arrays. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c01653
skills.summary: Retrieves the MS/MS (MS2) spectrum for a named precursor from a DDA mass spectrometry file converted to the MZA HDF5 format, using the mzapy.dda.MsmsReaderDda class. Handles identification of the precursor's scans from the MZA metadata table, optional removal of erroneous scans, and extraction of m/z, intensity, and ion mobility arrival-time arrays.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data is still in a proprietary vendor format (.raw, .d, mzML) and has not yet been converted to MZA — use the mza converter first The file was not acquired in DDA mode or contains no MS2 spectra (MSLevel 1 only) — there is no MS/MS spectrum to retrieve You need centroided peak lists or identifications rather than raw spectrum arrays — mzapy provides raw data extraction, not database search results

skills.description: Use when raw DDA LC-MS/MS data (e.g. a Metabolomics WorkBench study such as ST002044) must be converted into deconvolved, unique MS/MS spectra in NIST .msp format for library matching or model training/evaluation.
skills.name: dda-msms-spectrum-deconvolution
skills.search_text: dda-msms-spectrum-deconvolution Use when raw DDA LC-MS/MS data (e.g. a Metabolomics WorkBench study such as ST002044) must be converted into deconvolved, unique MS/MS spectra in NIST .msp format for library matching or model training/evaluation. Input is already a deconvolved .msp/.mgf library or a feature table — no peak-picking/deconvolution is needed Data are DIA/SWATH or otherwise lack precursor-isolated MS2 scans, since IDSL.CSA associates fragment spectra with precursor MS1 features Goal is MS/MS prediction or fingerprint inference rather than spectrum extraction — use IDSL_MINT training/prediction instead Deconvolution of DDA LC-MS/MS data: chromatographic peak-picking with IDSL.IPA followed by MS/MS deconvolution with IDSL.CSA to associate fragment spectra with precursor MS1 features, producing unique, deduplicated spectra in NIST .msp format (separately per ionization mode). This step supplies the .msp inputs for downstream fingerprint-prediction models such as IDSL_MINT. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00804-5
skills.summary: Deconvolution of DDA LC-MS/MS data: chromatographic peak-picking with IDSL.IPA followed by MS/MS deconvolution with IDSL.CSA to associate fragment spectra with precursor MS1 features, producing unique, deduplicated spectra in NIST .msp format (separately per ionization mode). This step supplies the .msp inputs for downstream fingerprint-prediction models such as IDSL_MINT.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a deconvolved .msp/.mgf library or a feature table — no peak-picking/deconvolution is needed Data are DIA/SWATH or otherwise lack precursor-isolated MS2 scans, since IDSL.CSA associates fragment spectra with precursor MS1 features Goal is MS/MS prediction or fingerprint inference rather than spectrum extraction — use IDSL_MINT training/prediction instead

skills.description: Use when processing centroided DDA LC-MS/MS data (e.g. mzML from a standards mixture or clinical sample) where chimeric spectra must be deconvolved before MS2-based compound identification in R.
skills.name: dda-spectra-deconvolution
skills.search_text: dda-spectra-deconvolution Use when processing centroided DDA LC-MS/MS data (e.g. mzML from a standards mixture or clinical sample) where chimeric spectra must be deconvolved before MS2-based compound identification in R. Input is SWATH-DIA data — use PerformDIADeconvolution (or reconstructChromPeakSpectra) instead, which relinks precursors with fragment ions from isolation windows Input is already a deconvoluted MS2 feature/annotation table rather than raw DDA spectra — re-deconvolution is unnecessary and the workflow starts from mzML The goal is MS1-only quantification without compound annotation, where MS2 processing adds no value http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Deconvolve chimeric DDA MS2 spectra in MetaboAnalystR 4.0 using an auto-optimized elastic-net model over candidate spectra, then build replicate consensus spectra and search them against MS2 reference libraries to improve compound identification and matching scores. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-48009-6
skills.summary: Deconvolve chimeric DDA MS2 spectra in MetaboAnalystR 4.0 using an auto-optimized elastic-net model over candidate spectra, then build replicate consensus spectra and search them against MS2 reference libraries to improve compound identification and matching scores.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is SWATH-DIA data — use PerformDIADeconvolution (or reconstructChromPeakSpectra) instead, which relinks precursors with fragment ions from isolation windows Input is already a deconvoluted MS2 feature/annotation table rather than raw DDA spectra — re-deconvolution is unnecessary and the workflow starts from mzML The goal is MS1-only quantification without compound annotation, where MS2 processing adds no value

skills.description: Use when processing centroided DDA mzML data in which many MS2 spectra are chimeric (multiple ions co-isolated in the isolation window, 'over half' per the paper) and clean, precursor-specific MS2 spectra are needed for downstream library search.
skills.name: dda-spectral-deconvolution
skills.search_text: dda-spectral-deconvolution Use when processing centroided DDA mzML data in which many MS2 spectra are chimeric (multiple ions co-isolated in the isolation window, 'over half' per the paper) and clean, precursor-specific MS2 spectra are needed for downstream library search. Data are SWATH-DIA: use the DIA/SWATH deconvolution path (PerformDIADeconvolution / reconstructChromPeakSpectra) instead, which relinks precursors with fragment ions MS2 spectra are already clean/consensus spectra (e.g., after PerformSpectrumConsenus frequency-based filtering) — deconvolution targets chimeric DDA acquisitions Only LC-MS1 feature detection and quantification is needed; that is handled by the auto-optimized feature detection module, not DDA deconvolution http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 MetaboAnalystR 4.0's auto-optimized DDA chimeric-spectra deconvolution: it assigns MS2 spectra to MS1 features, detects chimeric acquisitions, and uses a self-tuned elastic-net regression over candidate component spectra to extract a clean spectrum for the main (precursor) ion. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-48009-6
skills.summary: MetaboAnalystR 4.0's auto-optimized DDA chimeric-spectra deconvolution: it assigns MS2 spectra to MS1 features, detects chimeric acquisitions, and uses a self-tuned elastic-net regression over candidate component spectra to extract a clean spectrum for the main (precursor) ion.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are SWATH-DIA: use the DIA/SWATH deconvolution path (PerformDIADeconvolution / reconstructChromPeakSpectra) instead, which relinks precursors with fragment ions MS2 spectra are already clean/consensus spectra (e.g., after PerformSpectrumConsenus frequency-based filtering) — deconvolution targets chimeric DDA acquisitions Only LC-MS1 feature detection and quantification is needed; that is handled by the auto-optimized feature detection module, not DDA deconvolution

skills.description: Use when entries from a generated lipid/precursor library must be targeted for DDA on an Orbitrap and an Excalibur-compatible precursor list (.CSV) — not an '.MSP' spectral library — is the required deliverable.
skills.name: dda-target-selection
skills.search_text: dda-target-selection Use when entries from a generated lipid/precursor library must be targeted for DDA on an Orbitrap and an Excalibur-compatible precursor list (.CSV) — not an '.MSP' spectral library — is the required deliverable. skills.summary: Exports a curated subset of in silico lipid precursor entries from the Lipid Spectrum Generator as an Excalibur-compatible precursor list (.CSV) targeting data-dependent acquisition (DDA) on Orbitrap instruments; a Skyline-compatible transition list is the alternative .CSV output.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The downstream consumer requires an '.MSP' spectral library (fragmentation spectra), not an acquisition target list — in that case select '.MSP' instead. skills.search_text: dda-vs-dadia-workflow-comparison Decision support for choosing between DDA and DaDIA acquisition when you have paired LC-MS runs of individual biological samples and pooled QC samples and need to compare significant-feature detection, MS2 coverage, and metabolite annotation counts.
