skills.description: Use when an eigen-analysis-based p-value adjustment method originally defined on Pearson correlations must be re-expressed on distance correlations for metabolomics features, or when Meff estimates need to account for nonlinear dependence structure.
skills.name: distance-correlation-computation
skills.search_text: distance-correlation-computation Use when an eigen-analysis-based p-value adjustment method originally defined on Pearson correlations must be re-expressed on distance correlations for metabolomics features, or when Meff estimates need to account for nonlinear dependence structure. The goal is plain Pearson-correlation-based Meff correction (PrsCo) and no nonlinear dependence is expected — the distance correlation adds computation without benefit. Input is not a numeric samples-by-features metabolomics matrix (e.g., already an adjusted p-value table), since pairwise distance correlations require raw feature values per sample. The downstream estimator does not require a non-negative-definite matrix and you cannot apply nearestSPD projection, as eigen-analysis-based Meff methods need valid eigen-decompositions. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Compute all pairwise distance correlations (DisCo) among M metabolite features to build an M-by-M distance-correlation matrix that captures nonlinear dependence, then project it to the nearest non-negative-definite matrix (nearestSPD, eigenvalue threshold 1e-12) so eigen-analysis-based Meff estimation can be applied. This is the core operation enabling the DisCo P-ad multiple-testing correction for metabolomics. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo15010028
skills.summary: Compute all pairwise distance correlations (DisCo) among M metabolite features to build an M-by-M distance-correlation matrix that captures nonlinear dependence, then project it to the nearest non-negative-definite matrix (nearestSPD, eigenvalue threshold 1e-12) so eigen-analysis-based Meff estimation can be applied. This is the core operation enabling the DisCo P-ad multiple-testing correction for metabolomics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is plain Pearson-correlation-based Meff correction (PrsCo) and no nonlinear dependence is expected — the distance correlation adds computation without benefit. Input is not a numeric samples-by-features metabolomics matrix (e.g., already an adjusted p-value table), since pairwise distance correlations require raw feature values per sample. The downstream estimator does not require a non-negative-definite matrix and you cannot apply nearestSPD projection, as eigen-analysis-based Meff methods need valid eigen-decompositions.

skills.description: Use when you must reproduce or validate a LipidSpace-style structural lipid space: a set of lipid species (e.g. a homologous PC series) needs a pairwise structural distance matrix embedded by PCA, or an arc-like sequential PC1/PC2 ordering must be verified.
skills.name: distance-matrix-pca-embedding
skills.search_text: distance-matrix-pca-embedding Use when you must reproduce or validate a LipidSpace-style structural lipid space: a set of lipid species (e.g. a homologous PC series) needs a pairwise structural distance matrix embedded by PCA, or an arc-like sequential PC1/PC2 ordering must be verified. The input is already a feature/abundance table and quantitative information should shape the model - the article notes quantitative information is not added to these structural comparison models, so low-abundant species are weighted equally. Lipid names cannot be parsed into fully resolved structures (e.g. sum-composition level species without headgroup/acyl detail), since the MCS comparison needs molecular graphs. You need exact name-identifier matching between lipidomes rather than structural similarity - LipidSpace explicitly targets the structural-comparison use case instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Reproduces LipidSpace's structural space model: pairwise lipid structural distances are computed via maximum common subgraph (MCS/LaWeCSE headgroups plus sn-order-aware fatty acyl comparison) combined with the Jaccard index, then embedded by PCA on the n x n distance matrix using the Lanczos method. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c02449
skills.summary: Reproduces LipidSpace's structural space model: pairwise lipid structural distances are computed via maximum common subgraph (MCS/LaWeCSE headgroups plus sn-order-aware fatty acyl comparison) combined with the Jaccard index, then embedded by PCA on the n x n distance matrix using the Lanczos method.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a feature/abundance table and quantitative information should shape the model - the article notes quantitative information is not added to these structural comparison models, so low-abundant species are weighted equally. Lipid names cannot be parsed into fully resolved structures (e.g. sum-composition level species without headgroup/acyl detail), since the MCS comparison needs molecular graphs. You need exact name-identifier matching between lipidomes rather than structural similarity - LipidSpace explicitly targets the structural-comparison use case instead.

skills.search_text: distance-preservation-scoring-of-embeddings Use when a 2D t-SNE embedding of spectral or feature-distance data must be tuned — choose a perplexity from a grid by comparing each embedding's distance-preservation performance rather than picking a default value. The input is already a 2D embedding or a low-dimensional coordinate table — no distance-preservation tuning is needed. The pairwise distance structure is not shared with the clustering (e.g. the embedding is computed on raw intensities rather than the spectral-similarity distance matrix), so distance-preservation scores would not reflect the clustering-relevant structure. Only a single perplexity is required without evaluation — e.g. the embedding is purely illustrative and no perplexity tuning grid is part of the workflow. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Sweep a grid of t-SNE perplexity values and score each candidate 2D embedding by how well it preserves the high-dimensional pairwise distance structure (e.g. the mass-spectral feature distance matrix used in msFeaST), then select the perplexity with the best distance-preservation score. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae584

skills.description: Use when raw 1D NMR FID data (Bruker or Agilent/Varian, or nmrML) must be processed through calibration, baseline correction, realignment, and binning via NMRProcFlow deployed as a local Docker web application.
skills.name: dockerized-nmr-workflow-execution
skills.search_text: dockerized-nmr-workflow-execution Use when raw 1D NMR FID data (Bruker or Agilent/Varian, or nmrML) must be processed through calibration, baseline correction, realignment, and binning via NMRProcFlow deployed as a local Docker web application. Input is already a processed feature/bucket table rather than raw 1D NMR FID or nmrML spectra The goal is a fully automated, non-interactive batch pipeline — the article states batch-mode black-box workflows 'have not yet reached full maturity' and interactive processing is preferred Data are 2D NMR spectra — NMRProcFlow is dedicated to 1D (1H & 13C) spectra processing Run the NMRProcFlow 1D NMR (1H & 13C) metabolomics spectra-processing workflow interactively inside the 'npflow' Docker image, with raw spectra staged in the shared /opt/data volume and the NMR spectra viewer as the central working interface. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-017-1178-y
skills.summary: Run the NMRProcFlow 1D NMR (1H & 13C) metabolomics spectra-processing workflow interactively inside the 'npflow' Docker image, with raw spectra staged in the shared /opt/data volume and the NMR spectra viewer as the central working interface.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a processed feature/bucket table rather than raw 1D NMR FID or nmrML spectra The goal is a fully automated, non-interactive batch pipeline — the article states batch-mode black-box workflows 'have not yet reached full maturity' and interactive processing is preferred Data are 2D NMR spectra — NMRProcFlow is dedicated to 1D (1H & 13C) spectra processing

skills.description: Use when a runtime benchmark must compare prediction tools with heterogeneous installs (CFM-ID via Docker, ICEBERG via its repo, FIORA natively) over an identical compound list, and per-spectrum prediction times must be tabulated.
skills.name: dockerized-tool-execution
skills.search_text: dockerized-tool-execution Use when a runtime benchmark must compare prediction tools with heterogeneous installs (CFM-ID via Docker, ICEBERG via its repo, FIORA natively) over an identical compound list, and per-spectrum prediction times must be tabulated. When the goal is prediction quality (spectral similarity) rather than runtime — the article's benchmarking of prediction quality uses separate CASMI 2016/2022 workflows with collision-energy matching. When retraining CFM-ID is required — the authors found 'Retraining CFM-ID with our dataset was found computationally infeasible', so Dockerized CFM-ID is only usable for prediction as-is. When compounds require multi-step fragmentation — FIORA lacks multi-step fragmentation, so a runtime comparison of single-step prediction does not cover that use case. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Benchmark external fragmentation-prediction tools by running them inside their published Docker containers (e.g., the wishartlab/cfmid Docker image for CFM-ID) alongside native repositories like ICEBERG's ms-pred, recording wall-clock runtimes over the same test compound set to reproduce the FIORA runtime comparison (Table 2). metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-025-57422-4
skills.summary: Benchmark external fragmentation-prediction tools by running them inside their published Docker containers (e.g., the wishartlab/cfmid Docker image for CFM-ID) alongside native repositories like ICEBERG's ms-pred, recording wall-clock runtimes over the same test compound set to reproduce the FIORA runtime comparison (Table 2).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is prediction quality (spectral similarity) rather than runtime — the article's benchmarking of prediction quality uses separate CASMI 2016/2022 workflows with collision-energy matching. When retraining CFM-ID is required — the authors found 'Retraining CFM-ID with our dataset was found computationally infeasible', so Dockerized CFM-ID is only usable for prediction as-is. When compounds require multi-step fragmentation — FIORA lacks multi-step fragmentation, so a runtime comparison of single-step prediction does not cover that use case.

skills.description: Use when comparing BGC detection tools at matched domain-level stringency: you have per-domain prediction scores and labeled calibration data, and need cutoffs at defined FPR/TPR operating points before merging domains into clusters.
skills.name: domain-level-score-threshold-calibration
skills.search_text: domain-level-score-threshold-calibration Use when comparing BGC detection tools at matched domain-level stringency: you have per-domain prediction scores and labeled calibration data, and need cutoffs at defined FPR/TPR operating points before merging domains into clusters. You only need product-class or activity classification of already-detected BGCs (use the random forest classifiers, not threshold calibration) Input is rule-based detector output such as antiSMASH cluster predictions that lack continuous per-domain scores to threshold No labeled genome annotations are available to estimate FPR/TPR operating points http://edamontology.org/topic_0797 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Calibration of per-Pfam-domain detection score thresholds to fixed operating points — a stringent 10% false positive rate and a lenient 80% true positive rate — used in the DeepBGC paper to compare BGC-level precision against ClusterFinder on nine manually annotated bacterial genomes. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkz654
skills.summary: Calibration of per-Pfam-domain detection score thresholds to fixed operating points — a stringent 10% false positive rate and a lenient 80% true positive rate — used in the DeepBGC paper to compare BGC-level precision against ClusterFinder on nine manually annotated bacterial genomes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need product-class or activity classification of already-detected BGCs (use the random forest classifiers, not threshold calibration) Input is rule-based detector output such as antiSMASH cluster predictions that lack continuous per-domain scores to threshold No labeled genome annotations are available to estimate FPR/TPR operating points

skills.description: Use when computing pairwise distances between biosynthetic gene clusters at scale and the distance must capture both Pfam domain copy-number differences and domain sequence identity, e.g. for GCF network construction from antiSMASH output.
skills.name: domain-sequence-similarity-scoring
skills.search_text: domain-sequence-similarity-scoring Use when computing pairwise distances between biosynthetic gene clusters at scale and the distance must capture both Pfam domain copy-number differences and domain sequence identity, e.g. for GCF network construction from antiSMASH output. Input gene clusters are not antiSMASH-processed GenBank files with Pfam domain annotations, so no domain sequences exist to align to profile HMMs The analysis goal is a high-resolution multi-locus phylogeny of a gene cluster family (CORASON-style conserved-core analysis), where full alignment methods like Muscle or MAFFT are used instead Only a handful of BGCs are compared and full all-vers-all sequence alignment cost is negligible http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Computes the Domain Sequence Similarity (DSS) index of BiG-SCAPE's pairwise BGC distance by aligning each predicted domain sequence to its Pfam profile HMM with hmmalign, then scoring matched domain pairs for copy-number differences and sequence identity. This profile-based approach avoids the quadratic all-vers-all sequence comparison bottleneck in large-scale BGC comparisons. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41589-019-0400-9
skills.summary: Computes the Domain Sequence Similarity (DSS) index of BiG-SCAPE's pairwise BGC distance by aligning each predicted domain sequence to its Pfam profile HMM with hmmalign, then scoring matched domain pairs for copy-number differences and sequence identity. This profile-based approach avoids the quadratic all-vers-all sequence comparison bottleneck in large-scale BGC comparisons.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input gene clusters are not antiSMASH-processed GenBank files with Pfam domain annotations, so no domain sequences exist to align to profile HMMs The analysis goal is a high-resolution multi-locus phylogeny of a gene cluster family (CORASON-style conserved-core analysis), where full alignment methods like Muscle or MAFFT are used instead Only a handful of BGCs are compared and full all-vers-all sequence alignment cost is negligible

skills.description: Use when a predictor's claimed improvement must be verified per application domain — e.g. testing whether adding a rule-based module (MSRB) helps on foodomics/metabolomics-like molecule sets but not exposomics-like ones.
skills.name: domain-stratified-benchmark-comparison
skills.search_text: domain-stratified-benchmark-comparison Use when a predictor's claimed improvement must be verified per application domain — e.g. testing whether adding a rule-based module (MSRB) helps on foodomics/metabolomics-like molecule sets but not exposomics-like ones. The goal is a single domain-agnostic accuracy figure on one held-out test set — domain-stratified resampling would distort the aggregate benchmark rather than serve it. No experimental reference spectra are available — the Dice-coefficient comparison against Metlin experimental spectra cannot be performed. The evaluated module's scope does not overlap the stratification axis (e.g. rule-based modules covering only acylcarnitines, acylcholines, flavonols, flavones, flavanones, and flavonoid glycosides will show no gain on exposomics-like non-modular compound sets). Validates whether a predictor improvement holds per research domain by building evaluation subsets that replicate domain-specific chemical-class distributions, then comparing metric scores (Dice) per domain between model variants. Used in CFM-ID 4.0 to test the MSRB rule-based module against the MSML machine-learned module. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c01465
skills.summary: Validates whether a predictor improvement holds per research domain by building evaluation subsets that replicate domain-specific chemical-class distributions, then comparing metric scores (Dice) per domain between model variants. Used in CFM-ID 4.0 to test the MSRB rule-based module against the MSML machine-learned module.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is a single domain-agnostic accuracy figure on one held-out test set — domain-stratified resampling would distort the aggregate benchmark rather than serve it. No experimental reference spectra are available — the Dice-coefficient comparison against Metlin experimental spectra cannot be performed. The evaluated module's scope does not overlap the stratification axis (e.g. rule-based modules covering only acylcarnitines, acylcholines, flavonols, flavones, flavanones, and flavonoid glycosides will show no gain on exposomics-like non-modular compound sets).

skills.description: Use when metabolomics feature abundances (e.g., LC-MS peak tables) are measured across multiple dose levels of an exposure and you need fitted dose-response curves and per-feature benchmark dose (BMD) values for chemical risk assessment.
skills.name: dose-response-curve-fitting
skills.search_text: dose-response-curve-fitting Use when metabolomics feature abundances (e.g., LC-MS peak tables) are measured across multiple dose levels of an exposure and you need fitted dose-response curves and per-feature benchmark dose (BMD) values for chemical risk assessment. The data contain only a single dose vs. control comparison (no multi-level dose gradient), so no dose-response curve can be fitted and plain differential analysis should be used instead The input is raw MS spectra rather than a processed feature table — use the Spectra Processing module (asari/OptiLCMS) first; this skill assumes normalized, dose-annotated features The goal is causal metabolite-phenotype inference (Mendelian randomization) or multi-factor statistical analysis rather than exposure dose-response modeling http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Fit dose-response curves to metabolomics features measured across multiple exposure levels and compute per-feature benchmark dose (BMD) values using the MetaboAnalyst 6.0 Dose-Response Analysis module, exemplified by the etomoxir BT549 breast cancer cell case study. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkae253
skills.summary: Fit dose-response curves to metabolomics features measured across multiple exposure levels and compute per-feature benchmark dose (BMD) values using the MetaboAnalyst 6.0 Dose-Response Analysis module, exemplified by the etomoxir BT549 breast cancer cell case study.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data contain only a single dose vs. control comparison (no multi-level dose gradient), so no dose-response curve can be fitted and plain differential analysis should be used instead The input is raw MS spectra rather than a processed feature table — use the Spectra Processing module (asari/OptiLCMS) first; this skill assumes normalized, dose-annotated features The goal is causal metabolite-phenotype inference (Mendelian randomization) or multi-factor statistical analysis rather than exposure dose-response modeling

skills.search_text: dose-response-curve-visualization Use when a multiclass metabolomics dataset contains spiked reference metabolites with known dose levels and you must visually verify whether a ranked processing workflow (e.g., HAM+NON+CUT+[CON-RAN] vs KNN+NON+LOG+[VAS-LIN]) preserves the true dose gradient. skills.description: Use when you need to prioritize chemicals by risk from exposure estimates plus predicted acute toxicity (LD50) data, and no measured chronic reference dose or BMD is available for most compounds.
skills.name: dose-response-threshold-estimation
skills.search_text: dose-response-threshold-estimation Use when you need to prioritize chemicals by risk from exposure estimates plus predicted acute toxicity (LD50) data, and no measured chronic reference dose or BMD is available for most compounds. The goal is chronic or subchronic risk assessment — the LD50-based approach may underestimate chronic/subchronic toxicity risk. Chemicals lack SEEM exposure estimates (the SEEM database was unable to cover all compounds in the study). Ameasured, chemical-specific reference dose or in vivo toxicity data are available; a measured BMD is preferable to an LD50-derived probabilistic surrogate. Derives probabilistic reference dose thresholds (HDMI) from predicted oral LD50 values with applied uncertainty factors, then computes a probabilistic hazard quotient (PrHQ = EHE/HDMI) to risk-rank chemicals in the human exposome database. metabolomics/v3 10.1289/ehp7722
skills.summary: Derives probabilistic reference dose thresholds (HDMI) from predicted oral LD50 values with applied uncertainty factors, then computes a probabilistic hazard quotient (PrHQ = EHE/HDMI) to risk-rank chemicals in the human exposome database.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is chronic or subchronic risk assessment — the LD50-based approach may underestimate chronic/subchronic toxicity risk. Chemicals lack SEEM exposure estimates (the SEEM database was unable to cover all compounds in the study). Ameasured, chemical-specific reference dose or in vivo toxicity data are available; a measured BMD is preferable to an LD50-derived probabilistic surrogate.

skills.description: Use when you need a conventional cosine/dot-product similarity score between two centroided MS/MS spectra, e.g. as the baseline against which entropy-similarity robustness or library-search performance is compared.
skills.name: dot-product-similarity-scoring
skills.search_text: dot-product-similarity-scoring Use when you need a conventional cosine/dot-product similarity score between two centroided MS/MS spectra, e.g. as the baseline against which entropy-similarity robustness or library-search performance is compared. As the primary library-search score for noisy or ion-rich spectra: the paper shows dot product similarity is markedly more affected by added noise ions than entropy similarity On spectra that have not been centroided, precursor-filtered, and intensity-normalized (sum = 1), since peak alignment at 0.05 Da assumes cleaned input When a single score cutoff is expected to prevent false positives — the paper states even entropy similarity cannot define such a threshold, and dot product fares worse http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Computes the classic dot product (cosine) similarity between two centroided, intensity-normalized MS/MS peak lists — the conventional library-matching baseline that Li et al. benchmark spectral entropy similarity against under added Poisson noise. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-021-01331-z
skills.summary: Computes the classic dot product (cosine) similarity between two centroided, intensity-normalized MS/MS peak lists — the conventional library-matching baseline that Li et al. benchmark spectral entropy similarity against under added Poisson noise.
skills.when_to_use_negative: As the primary library-search score for noisy or ion-rich spectra: the paper shows dot product similarity is markedly more affected by added noise ions than entropy similarity On spectra that have not been centroided, precursor-filtered, and intensity-normalized (sum = 1), since peak alignment at 0.05 Da assumes cleaned input When a single score cutoff is expected to prevent false positives — the paper states even entropy similarity cannot define such a threshold, and dot product fares worse

skills.description: Use when annotating MS2 spectra of LC-MS metabolomic features (e.g. DDA, DIA(SWATH), or DaDIA data on a Bruker Impact II UHR-QqTOF) by spectral library matching, or when binning spectra into high- vs low-quality classes using a dot-product threshold.
skills.name: dot-product-spectral-library-matching
skills.search_text: dot-product-spectral-library-matching Use when annotating MS2 spectra of LC-MS metabolomic features (e.g. DDA, DIA(SWATH), or DaDIA data on a Bruker Impact II UHR-QqTOF) by spectral library matching, or when binning spectra into high- vs low-quality classes using a dot-product threshold. The analysis goal is feature detection or peak picking — use XCMS centWave-based peak picking instead; dot-product matching is applied only after MS2 spectra have been extracted from features. Input data are already annotated metabolite tables with confidence levels — no further spectral matching is needed at that stage. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Grades experimental MS2 spectra against a standard reference library by computing dot-product (cosine) scores between matched fragment peaks; in the DaDIA urine study, 91 819 MoNA MS2 spectra served as the reference and a score cutoff of 0.7 separated high- from low-quality spectra for metabolite annotation. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c05022
skills.summary: Grades experimental MS2 spectra against a standard reference library by computing dot-product (cosine) scores between matched fragment peaks; in the DaDIA urine study, 91 819 MoNA MS2 spectra served as the reference and a score cutoff of 0.7 separated high- from low-quality spectra for metabolite annotation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is feature detection or peak picking — use XCMS centWave-based peak picking instead; dot-product matching is applied only after MS2 spectra have been extracted from features. Input data are already annotated metabolite tables with confidence levels — no further spectral matching is needed at that stage.

skills.description: Use when matching an unknown ESI-MS/MS spectrum against a set of predicted spectra from candidate chemical structures to produce a compound-identification ranking (e.g. CASMI challenge submissions or library search with CFM-ID).
skills.name: dot-product-spectral-matching-scoring
skills.search_text: dot-product-spectral-matching-scoring Use when matching an unknown ESI-MS/MS spectrum against a set of predicted spectra from candidate chemical structures to produce a compound-identification ranking (e.g. CASMI challenge submissions or library search with CFM-ID). The spectrum is from a non-QTOF instrument (e.g. Orbitrap collision energy curves) unless the energy levels are first converted to the QTOF levels CFM-ID was trained on (10, 20, 40 eV). The input is a peak table or extracted ion chromatogram rather than a per-fragment MS/MS spectrum, since the Dot Product requires an intensity-vector representation of the fragmentation pattern. Metadata (e.g. citation frequency) is unavailable and the candidates are all chemically plausible — the skill will still rank but with lower discrimination. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 A scoring skill that compares an experimentally acquired ESI-MS/MS spectrum against in-silico predicted spectra from candidate structures using the modified Dot Product function from CFM-ID, ranking candidates by spectral similarity to identify the top-hit compound. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c01465
skills.summary: A scoring skill that compares an experimentally acquired ESI-MS/MS spectrum against in-silico predicted spectra from candidate structures using the modified Dot Product function from CFM-ID, ranking candidates by spectral similarity to identify the top-hit compound.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The spectrum is from a non-QTOF instrument (e.g. Orbitrap collision energy curves) unless the energy levels are first converted to the QTOF levels CFM-ID was trained on (10, 20, 40 eV). The input is a peak table or extracted ion chromatogram rather than a per-fragment MS/MS spectrum, since the Dot Product requires an intensity-vector representation of the fragmentation pattern. Metadata (e.g. citation frequency) is unavailable and the candidates are all chemically plausible — the skill will still rank but with lower discrimination.

skills.description: Use when dereplicating query MS/MS spectra (with precursor charge, precursor m/z, and peak lists) against accumulated reference library spectra and a peak-level similarity score such as a normalized dot product is needed for identification.
skills.name: dot-product-spectral-scoring
skills.search_text: dot-product-spectral-scoring Use when dereplicating query MS/MS spectra (with precursor charge, precursor m/z, and peak lists) against accumulated reference library spectra and a peak-level similarity score such as a normalized dot product is needed for identification. The goal is spectral-spectrum similarity networking between query spectra (molecular networking), not library identification — use the MSCluster clustering plus top-K mutual-neighbor edge construction workflow instead The variant search needs to tolerate systematic fragment shifts from precursor mass differences — that requires the modification-tolerant search with additional delta +/- fragment tolerance edges, not the exact match Input MS/MS spectra have MS1 precursor intensity <1E4 or precursor m/z ppm error >=50 versus theoretical mass, which are excluded in the reference workflow's putative identification filter http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 GNPS-style exact spectral library matching in which library-to-query peak correspondences are found by maximum bipartite matching under a fragment mass tolerance and each match is scored with a normalized dot product to derePLICATE natural products from MS/MS spectra. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/nbt.3597
skills.summary: GNPS-style exact spectral library matching in which library-to-query peak correspondences are found by maximum bipartite matching under a fragment mass tolerance and each match is scored with a normalized dot product to derePLICATE natural products from MS/MS spectra.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is spectral-spectrum similarity networking between query spectra (molecular networking), not library identification — use the MSCluster clustering plus top-K mutual-neighbor edge construction workflow instead The variant search needs to tolerate systematic fragment shifts from precursor mass differences — that requires the modification-tolerant search with additional delta +/- fragment tolerance edges, not the exact match Input MS/MS spectra have MS1 precursor intensity <1E4 or precursor m/z ppm error >=50 versus theoretical mass, which are excluded in the reference workflow's putative identification filter

skills.search_text: dot-product-spectral-similarity-scoring Use when annotating LC-MS/MS or LC-MSn lipid features against an in-silico spectral library (e.g. LipiDex 2 Library Generator output) and you need to score match quality of MS2 and MS3+ spectra before applying identification thresholds. skills.search_text: drug-analog-spectra-filtering Use when converting raw drug-analog matches (from GNPS Drug Library spectra vs. untargeted metabolomics data) into a reliable propagated analog library, i.e., when analog spectra must be filtered to keep only chemically explainable, non-duplicate, exposure-informative MS/MS hits. Input is profile (non-centroided) spectra — the pipeline is designed for centroided .imzML import Data are already processed into a feature table or quantitative concentration maps — no peak alignment is needed A fixed absolute-mass binning is required by a downstream tool that cannot consume ppm-constant bins http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Aligns centroided m/z peaks across all pixels of an MSI dataset using a dynamic binning algorithm that maintains constant resolution in ppm over the entire mass range, as implemented in LipidQMap prior to recalibration and lipid annotation. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.10.15.682422
skills.summary: Aligns centroided m/z peaks across all pixels of an MSI dataset using a dynamic binning algorithm that maintains constant resolution in ppm over the entire mass range, as implemented in LipidQMap prior to recalibration and lipid annotation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is profile (non-centroided) spectra — the pipeline is designed for centroided .imzML import Data are already processed into a feature table or quantitative concentration maps — no peak alignment is needed A fixed absolute-mass binning is required by a downstream tool that cannot consume ppm-constant bins

skills.description: Use when a complete LC-MS/MS run has per-spectrum scored candidate lists (e.g. from IOKR, queried from PubChem) plus a trained retention-order model, and you need a joint metabolite assignment consistent with predicted elution order.
skills.name: dynamic-programming-shortest-path-optimization
skills.search_text: dynamic-programming-shortest-path-optimization Use when a complete LC-MS/MS run has per-spectrum scored candidate lists (e.g. from IOKR, queried from PubChem) plus a trained retention-order model, and you need a joint metabolite assignment consistent with predicted elution order. Identifying a single MS/MS spectrum in isolation — the graph formulation requires multiple spectra from a complete LC-MS/MS run ordered by retention time No retention-order predictor output (RankSVM weight vector w and feature map phi) is available — then only the D=0 IOKR-only baseline applies and the shortest-path machinery adds nothing Observed retention times of adjacent layers are equal — the hinge penalty is zero there, so the path degenerates to IOKR score comparison for those transitions http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Joint metabolite identification across a complete LC-MS/MS run by building a layered directed graph over IOKR candidate lists (one layer per MS/MS spectrum, ordered by increasing retention time) and recovering the minimum-weight path with a Bellman-style dynamic programming pass. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/bty590
skills.summary: Joint metabolite identification across a complete LC-MS/MS run by building a layered directed graph over IOKR candidate lists (one layer per MS/MS spectrum, ordered by increasing retention time) and recovering the minimum-weight path with a Bellman-style dynamic programming pass.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Identifying a single MS/MS spectrum in isolation — the graph formulation requires multiple spectra from a complete LC-MS/MS run ordered by retention time No retention-order predictor output (RankSVM weight vector w and feature map phi) is available — then only the D=0 IOKR-only baseline applies and the shortest-path machinery adds nothing Observed retention times of adjacent layers are equal — the hinge penalty is zero there, so the path degenerates to IOKR score comparison for those transitions

skills.description: Use when a metabolomics concentration table (post-normalization, post-imputation) still shows skewed, heavy-tailed distributions that would violate normality assumptions in downstream PCA or group-comparison analyses.
skills.name: dynamic-range-compression
skills.search_text: dynamic-range-compression Use when a metabolomics concentration table (post-normalization, post-imputation) still shows skewed, heavy-tailed distributions that would violate normality assumptions in downstream PCA or group-comparison analyses. The input is raw, un-normalized data with missing values that still need Viime's automatic MCAR/MNAR imputation and normalization first The data are already approximately normal and the dynamic range is modest — Viime marks this step as optional and applying a transform unnecessarily can distort relative concentration patterns The goal is to modify ID, factor, group, or other metadata columns rather than metabolite concentration values http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 An optional Viime data-treatment step that applies an element-wise transformation (Log10, Log2, square root, or cube root) to metabolomics concentration data, bringing the distribution closer to normality and compressing the dynamic range before scaling and analysis. metabolomics/v3 10.21105/joss.02410
skills.summary: An optional Viime data-treatment step that applies an element-wise transformation (Log10, Log2, square root, or cube root) to metabolomics concentration data, bringing the distribution closer to normality and compressing the dynamic range before scaling and analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw, un-normalized data with missing values that still need Viime's automatic MCAR/MNAR imputation and normalization first The data are already approximately normal and the dynamic range is modest — Viime marks this step as optional and applying a transform unnecessarily can distort relative concentration patterns The goal is to modify ID, factor, group, or other metadata columns rather than metabolite concentration values

skills.description: Use when raw LC-MS serum metabolomics data (mzML or .npy) must be classified into lung cancer / benign lung nodule / healthy groups, and the target is early-stage (stage-I) adenocarcinoma detection accuracy.
skills.name: early-stage-lung-adenocarcinoma-detection
skills.search_text: early-stage-lung-adenocarcinoma-detection Use when raw LC-MS serum metabolomics data (mzML or .npy) must be classified into lung cancer / benign lung nodule / healthy groups, and the target is early-stage (stage-I) adenocarcinoma detection accuracy. The input is already a peak-picked, aligned, annotated feature table — DeepMSProfiler is designed for end-to-end analysis of raw metabolic signals without peak extraction/alignment The goal is biomarker/feature interpretation (metabolite-protein networks) rather than sample classification — use run_feature/show_feature RISE heatmaps instead of prediction-only mode Only the public demo data is available and the pre-trained serum model has not been obtained from the author — training from scratch on the small demo set will not reproduce the 0.961 figure http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Reproduce DeepMSProfiler's tri-class ensemble (DenseNet121, 10 runs, adam, lr 1e-04) inference on raw LC-MS serum data to detect stage-I lung adenocarcinoma, which the paper reports at 96.1% accuracy with AUC 0.99 on independent testing samples. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-51433-3
skills.summary: Reproduce DeepMSProfiler's tri-class ensemble (DenseNet121, 10 runs, adam, lr 1e-04) inference on raw LC-MS serum data to detect stage-I lung adenocarcinoma, which the paper reports at 96.1% accuracy with AUC 0.99 on independent testing samples.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a peak-picked, aligned, annotated feature table — DeepMSProfiler is designed for end-to-end analysis of raw metabolic signals without peak extraction/alignment The goal is biomarker/feature interpretation (metabolite-protein networks) rather than sample classification — use run_feature/show_feature RISE heatmaps instead of prediction-only mode Only the public demo data is available and the pre-trained serum model has not been obtained from the author — training from scratch on the small demo set will not reproduce the 0.961 figure

skills.description: Use when training a neural ranking/retention model from molecular embeddings where a pairwise binary cross-entropy loss must be tuned and monitored to avoid overfitting on limited reference retention data.
skills.name: early-stopping-hyperparameter-tuning
skills.search_text: early-stopping-hyperparameter-tuning Use when training a neural ranking/retention model from molecular embeddings where a pairwise binary cross-entropy loss must be tuned and monitored to avoid overfitting on limited reference retention data. When the input is already a set of predicted retention scores rather than a pairwise elution-order training problem — use ROASMI's ROASMI_predict.py instead. When the chromatographic system is HILIC rather than RPLC; the paper states that constructing retention models with generalizability under HILIC remains future work. When the task is to distinguish coexisting isomers or integrate retention scores with MS/MS scores (Identify.py); those are downstream skills, not the training step. http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Trains ROASMI's RankNet retention-order module on pairwise elution probabilities using the chemprop D-MPNN embeddings, tuning hyperparameters per the paper's Table 1 and applying early stopping on validation pairwise loss to prevent overfitting. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-025-00968-8
skills.summary: Trains ROASMI's RankNet retention-order module on pairwise elution probabilities using the chemprop D-MPNN embeddings, tuning hyperparameters per the paper's Table 1 and applying early stopping on validation pairwise loss to prevent overfitting.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is already a set of predicted retention scores rather than a pairwise elution-order training problem — use ROASMI's ROASMI_predict.py instead. When the chromatographic system is HILIC rather than RPLC; the paper states that constructing retention models with generalizability under HILIC remains future work. When the task is to distinguish coexisting isomers or integrate retention scores with MS/MS scores (Identify.py); those are downstream skills, not the training step.

skills.description: Use when fine-tuning a generative chemical language model on a train fold (e.g., 90% of known metabolites) and you need an automatic, loss-based stopping criterion rather than a fixed number of epochs.
skills.name: early-stopping-model-selection
skills.search_text: early-stopping-model-selection Use when fine-tuning a generative chemical language model on a train fold (e.g., 90% of known metabolites) and you need an automatic, loss-based stopping criterion rather than a fixed number of epochs. The model will be used purely generatively after pretraining and no labeled/fine-tuning split exists — there is no validation loss to monitor, so early stopping is inapplicable Input is a fixed-epoch benchmark reproduction where the paper specifies an exact epoch count and no validation-based stopping criterion http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Selects when to stop fine-tuning a chemical language model (e.g., DeepMet's 3-layer LSTM) by monitoring validation loss and halting training before overfitting, then exporting the checkpoint and loss curve. In the DeepMet workflow this is applied per HMDB cross-validation fold and per training seed. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.11.13.623458

skills.description: Use when reconstructing SigmaCCS- or Mol2CCS-style CCS predictors from SMILES+adduct inputs, i.e. when the architecture must combine graph-based ECC layers with a parallel dense feature branch.
skills.name: ecc-layer-implementation
skills.search_text: ecc-layer-implementation Use when reconstructing SigmaCCS- or Mol2CCS-style CCS predictors from SMILES+adduct inputs, i.e. when the architecture must combine graph-based ECC layers with a parallel dense feature branch. Input is already a feature table without SMILES/molecular graphs — the ECC layers require graph construction from SMILES and adduct The task is benchmarking existing pretrained GNNs (SigmaCCS, GraphCCS) rather than implementing/reconstructing the architecture The prediction problem does not involve collision cross section (e.g. retention time or MS/MS spectra), since the ECC configuration here is tuned for CCS prediction http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_3332 Implements the edge-conditioned convolution (ECC) graph neural network layers of SigmaCCS, and their extension in Mol2CCS where ECC outputs are concatenated with a parallel four-layer fully connected module (256/512/512/256 neurons, dropout 0.1) that ingests molecular fingerprints, descriptors, molecule types and instrument type. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00899-w
skills.summary: Implements the edge-conditioned convolution (ECC) graph neural network layers of SigmaCCS, and their extension in Mol2CCS where ECC outputs are concatenated with a parallel four-layer fully connected module (256/512/512/256 neurons, dropout 0.1) that ingests molecular fingerprints, descriptors, molecule types and instrument type.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a feature table without SMILES/molecular graphs — the ECC layers require graph construction from SMILES and adduct The task is benchmarking existing pretrained GNNs (SigmaCCS, GraphCCS) rather than implementing/reconstructing the architecture The prediction problem does not involve collision cross section (e.g. retention time or MS/MS spectra), since the ECC configuration here is tuned for CCS prediction

skills.description: Use when building or rebuilding a curated pHMM feature library restricted to biosynthetic protein families (e.g., for BiG-SLiCE feature set 1) from a full Pfam release plus antiSMASH domain models.
skills.name: ecdomainminer-biosynthetic-domain-mining
skills.search_text: ecdomainminer-biosynthetic-domain-mining Use when building or rebuilding a curated pHMM feature library restricted to biosynthetic protein families (e.g., for BiG-SLiCE feature set 1) from a full Pfam release plus antiSMASH domain models. The goal is broad domain annotation of all protein families rather than a biosynthesis-restricted feature space — the curated list deliberately discards non-biosynthetic Pfam domains. A newer BiG-SLiCE release is already in use whose pHMM databases target PFAM 35.0 and antiSMASH v7.0.0 class definitions — do not re-assemble the older v32/antiSMASH 5.0 set unless reproducing the original study. Downstream analysis requires pairwise BGC similarity networks (e.g., BiG-SCAPE-style comparison) rather than Euclidean-space feature projection. http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Constructs a reduced 'biosynthetic-Pfam' pHMM library (feature set 1) by filtering all Pfam domains down to biosynthetically related protein families via ECDomainMiner plus manual curation, then merging antiSMASH pHMM models and packaging the result into the BiG-SLiCE HMM database. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/gigascience/giaa154
skills.summary: Constructs a reduced 'biosynthetic-Pfam' pHMM library (feature set 1) by filtering all Pfam domains down to biosynthetically related protein families via ECDomainMiner plus manual curation, then merging antiSMASH pHMM models and packaging the result into the BiG-SLiCE HMM database.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is broad domain annotation of all protein families rather than a biosynthesis-restricted feature space — the curated list deliberately discards non-biosynthetic Pfam domains. A newer BiG-SLiCE release is already in use whose pHMM databases target PFAM 35.0 and antiSMASH v7.0.0 class definitions — do not re-assemble the older v32/antiSMASH 5.0 set unless reproducing the original study. Downstream analysis requires pairwise BGC similarity networks (e.g., BiG-SCAPE-style comparison) rather than Euclidean-space feature projection.

skills.description: Use when you have molecular structures (SMILES strings or SDF files) and need fixed-length ECFP representations as model inputs for in-silico EI mass spectrum prediction with NEIMS or similar fingerprint-based models.
skills.name: ecfp-fingerprint-generation
skills.search_text: ecfp-fingerprint-generation Use when you have molecular structures (SMILES strings or SDF files) and need fixed-length ECFP representations as model inputs for in-silico EI mass spectrum prediction with NEIMS or similar fingerprint-based models. Molecules failing the article's filters: mass >= 1000 Da, elements outside the 11 common elements (H, C, O, N, P, S, Cl, F, Br, I, Si), ionic compounds, or LogP outside -12 to 24 When experimental EI mass spectra are already available — direct library matching against measured spectra (e.g., NIST 2017) is preferable Non-Windows environments for the packaged FastEI GUI, which the README states only supports Windows 64-bit (tested on Windows 7 and 10) http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 Generate extended circular fingerprints (ECFPs) from molecular structures with RDKit so they can be fed into the NEIMS fully connected neural network to predict EI-MS spectra, enabling large-scale in-silico spectral library construction. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-023-39279-7
skills.summary: Generate extended circular fingerprints (ECFPs) from molecular structures with RDKit so they can be fed into the NEIMS fully connected neural network to predict EI-MS spectra, enabling large-scale in-silico spectral library construction.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Molecules failing the article's filters: mass >= 1000 Da, elements outside the 11 common elements (H, C, O, N, P, S, Cl, F, Br, I, Si), ionic compounds, or LogP outside -12 to 24 When experimental EI mass spectra are already available — direct library matching against measured spectra (e.g., NIST 2017) is preferable Non-Windows environments for the packaged FastEI GUI, which the README states only supports Windows 64-bit (tested on Windows 7 and 10)

skills.description: Use when molecules must be featurized as fixed-length count/circular fingerprints to feed a spectral-prediction or molecular ML model, e.g., encoding NIST 2017 library molecules for NEIMS inference.
skills.name: ecfp-fingerprint-generation
skills.search_text: ecfp-fingerprint-generation Use when molecules must be featurized as fixed-length count/circular fingerprints to feed a spectral-prediction or molecular ML model, e.g., encoding NIST 2017 library molecules for NEIMS inference. The downstream model expects a different molecular representation (e.g., graph-convolutional features — the paper notes bond-centered graph representations would likely improve accuracy) Isotopologue-resolved spectra are the target: NEIMS cannot model isotope intensity peaks regardless of fingerprinting The task requires interpreting individual substructural contributions rather than fixed-length featurization for regression http://edamontology.org/topic_0081 http://edamontology.org/topic_3420 Converts small molecules (SMILES/SDF/InChI) into additive Extended Circular Fingerprints (ECFPs) of length 4096 with radius 2 using RDKit, the input representation required by the NEIMS neural network for mass spectra prediction. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acscentsci.9b00085
skills.summary: Converts small molecules (SMILES/SDF/InChI) into additive Extended Circular Fingerprints (ECFPs) of length 4096 with radius 2 using RDKit, the input representation required by the NEIMS neural network for mass spectra prediction.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The downstream model expects a different molecular representation (e.g., graph-convolutional features — the paper notes bond-centered graph representations would likely improve accuracy) Isotopologue-resolved spectra are the target: NEIMS cannot model isotope intensity peaks regardless of fingerprinting The task requires interpreting individual substructural contributions rather than fixed-length featurization for regression

skills.description: Use when a neural-network or regression model needs a fixed-length molecular representation computed from SMILES/SDF structures, e.g. to predict electron-ionization mass spectra in the NEIMS pipeline.
skills.name: ecfp-molecular-fingerprint-featurization
skills.search_text: ecfp-molecular-fingerprint-featurization Use when a neural-network or regression model needs a fixed-length molecular representation computed from SMILES/SDF structures, e.g. to predict electron-ionization mass spectra in the NEIMS pipeline. The task requires modeling isotope intensity peaks in ion fragments — the article states NEIMS lacks a method for this Binary (presence/absence) ECFP bits suffice and substructure occurrence counts are not needed — the additive fingerprint is specifically chosen to preserve counts The ionization method is not electron ionization and no retraining data exists for that method — the featurization is coupled to an EI-trained MLP head http://edamontology.org/topic_0081 http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 Converts small-molecule structures (SDF/SMILES) into additive Extended Circular Fingerprints (ECFPs) of length 4096 with radius 2 via RDKit, providing the fixed-size input vector that the NEIMS MLP consumes to regress mass-spectral intensity at every integral m/z bin. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acscentsci.9b00085
skills.summary: Converts small-molecule structures (SDF/SMILES) into additive Extended Circular Fingerprints (ECFPs) of length 4096 with radius 2 via RDKit, providing the fixed-size input vector that the NEIMS MLP consumes to regress mass-spectral intensity at every integral m/z bin.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task requires modeling isotope intensity peaks in ion fragments — the article states NEIMS lacks a method for this Binary (presence/absence) ECFP bits suffice and substructure occurrence counts are not needed — the additive fingerprint is specifically chosen to preserve counts The ionization method is not electron ionization and no retraining data exists for that method — the featurization is coupled to an EI-trained MLP head

skills.description: Use when building gene-gene interaction edge lists for topology-based pathway enrichment, starting from a gene identifier set (e.g. breastcancer2012 row names) and pathway databases such as 'kegg' and 'reactome'.
skills.name: edge-list-construction
skills.search_text: edge-list-construction Use when building gene-gene interaction edge lists for topology-based pathway enrichment, starting from a gene identifier set (e.g. breastcancer2012 row names) and pathway databases such as 'kegg' and 'reactome'. The input data has not yet been filtered to keep only variables belonging to at least one tested pathway (the netgsa README notes variables in the input data matrix should be filtered to tested pathways before running NetGSA). The analysis goal is network visualization rather than interaction retrieval — Cytoscape-based visualization via netgsa is the appropriate path instead. The pathway interactions of interest are already available as a prepared adjacency matrix, in which case adjacency assembly (not database retrieval) is needed. http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Reconstructs the netgsa obtainEdgeList retrieval step, which pulls pairwise gene-gene interactions from user-specified pathway databases (KEGG, Reactome) via graphite and assembles them into a 4-column edge list aligned to the input gene identifier space. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008979
skills.summary: Reconstructs the netgsa obtainEdgeList retrieval step, which pulls pairwise gene-gene interactions from user-specified pathway databases (KEGG, Reactome) via graphite and assembles them into a 4-column edge list aligned to the input gene identifier space.

The analysis goal is network visualization rather than interaction retrieval — Cytoscape-based visualization via netgsa is the appropriate path instead. The pathway interactions of interest are already available as a prepared adjacency matrix, in which case adjacency assembly (not database retrieval) is needed.

skills.search_text: edge-list-export-and-validation Use when a top-prioritized feature from globaltest-based msFeaST testing must be interrogated in network context: extract its k-nearest spectral neighbors as a weighted edge list and verify cross-cluster connectivity. skills.description: Use when estimating weighted adjacency matrices for pathway enrichment from a gene-gene edge list whose connected components exceed 1,000 genes, and a tractable block-diagonal adjacency structure is needed for NetGSA.
skills.name: edge-loss-algorithm-selection
skills.search_text: edge-loss-algorithm-selection Use when estimating weighted adjacency matrices for pathway enrichment from a gene-gene edge list whose connected components exceed 1,000 genes, and a tractable block-diagonal adjacency structure is needed for NetGSA. The network has no connected component larger than 1,000 genes, so no clustering-based block decomposition is needed The adjacency matrices across groups are already provided as per-group lists of smaller matrices to NetGSA, bypassing the need to re-estimate a block-diagonal structure The goal is differential expression or non-topology-based enrichment (e.g. SPIA, PRS) that does not require an estimated adjacency matrix A clustering-based procedure from netgsa's prepareAdjMat that partitions large gene networks into blocks using igraph community-detection algorithms, selecting the algorithm with the smallest edge loss so that weighted adjacency matrices can be estimated per cluster and reassembled as a block-diagonal matrix. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008979
skills.summary: A clustering-based procedure from netgsa's prepareAdjMat that partitions large gene networks into blocks using igraph community-detection algorithms, selecting the algorithm with the smallest edge loss so that weighted adjacency matrices can be estimated per cluster and reassembled as a block-diagonal matrix.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The network has no connected component larger than 1,000 genes, so no clustering-based block decomposition is needed The adjacency matrices across groups are already provided as per-group lists of smaller matrices to NetGSA, bypassing the need to re-estimate a block-diagonal structure The goal is differential expression or non-topology-based enrichment (e.g. SPIA, PRS) that does not require an estimated adjacency matrix

skills.description: Use when you have an annotated MALDI/MSI m/z intensity matrix plus spatial cluster labels (e.g. tissue regions) and need a reproducible ranked list of m/z peaks that differ significantly between those regions.
skills.name: edger-differential-abundance-testing
skills.search_text: edger-differential-abundance-testing Use when you have an annotated MALDI/MSI m/z intensity matrix plus spatial cluster labels (e.g. tissue regions) and need a reproducible ranked list of m/z peaks that differ significantly between those regions. Input is already a single-cell/single-ROI feature table from LC-MS with biological replicates — standard edgeR replicate designs apply instead of pixel pseudo-bulking. The goal is metabolite annotation of m/z values rather than testing for differential abundance — use SpaMTP's annotation pipeline (AnnotateBigData, BuildMZAnnotationIndex) instead. Clusters have not yet been defined on the MSI data — run SpaMTP's integrative clustering / SelectROIs first, since differential testing requires region labels. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 SpaMTP-style differential peak expression testing: m/z intensities are pseudo-bulked per spatial region/cluster (pixels randomly pooled with a fixed seed and summed) and tested with edgeR to produce a ranked table of differentially expressed metabolite peaks with fold-change and FDR statistics. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.10.31.621429
skills.summary: SpaMTP-style differential peak expression testing: m/z intensities are pseudo-bulked per spatial region/cluster (pixels randomly pooled with a fixed seed and summed) and tested with edgeR to produce a ranked table of differentially expressed metabolite peaks with fold-change and FDR statistics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a single-cell/single-ROI feature table from LC-MS with biological replicates — standard edgeR replicate designs apply instead of pixel pseudo-bulking. The goal is metabolite annotation of m/z values rather than testing for differential abundance — use SpaMTP's annotation pipeline (AnnotateBigData, BuildMZAnnotationIndex) instead. Clusters have not yet been defined on the MSI data — run SpaMTP's integrative clustering / SelectROIs first, since differential testing requires region labels.

skills.search_text: edited-mrs-sequence-parameter-configuration Use when generating a vendor- and sequence-specific simulated basis set for an edited MRS experiment (MEGA-PRESS, HERMES, HERCULES) and you need to map your scanner acquisition parameters onto MRSCloud's simMRS.json options. Plasma anticoagulated with heparin or citrate instead of EDTA — NMRQNet provides a separate tutorial (tutorial_for_other_plasma.ipynb) for those samples Spectra that have already undergone EDTA free-peak removal and preprocessing in a prior run Non-plasma biofluids — the article notes the biofluid-specific analysis pipeline was not yet developed, so this plasma-specific step does not generalize http://edamontology.org/topic_3678 http://edamontology.org/topic_3334 A preprocessing step in the NMRQNet pipeline that removes EDTA-anticoagulant free peaks from EDTA-plasma 1H NMR spectra before CRNN component fitting, so that the 65-component quantification (38 metabolites, 24 lipoprotein clusters, anticoagulants, DSS) is not contaminated by the anticoagulant's own spectral features. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2023.03.01.530642

skills.when_to_use_negative: Plasma anticoagulated with heparin or citrate instead of EDTA — NMRQNet provides a separate tutorial (tutorial_for_other_plasma.ipynb) for those samples Spectra that have already undergone EDTA free-peak removal and preprocessing in a prior run Non-plasma biofluids — the article notes the biofluid-specific analysis pipeline was not yet developed, so this plasma-specific step does not generalize

skills.description: Use when you have M metabolite features with a features-by-samples matrix (e.g. 761 metabolites x 1054 COPDGene subjects) and need to correct marginal association p-values via an effective-number-of-tests (Meff) estimate instead of raw M.
skills.name: effective-number-of-tests-estimation
skills.search_text: effective-number-of-tests-estimation Use when you have M metabolite features with a features-by-samples matrix (e.g. 761 metabolites x 1054 COPDGene subjects) and need to correct marginal association p-values via an effective-number-of-tests (Meff) estimate instead of raw M. Input is already a set of p-values with no feature matrix — eigen-analysis-based Meff estimators require the features' correlation structure, not just p-values Only a handful of features/tests — Bonferroni (Meff = M) suffices and eigen-analysis corrections add no benefit The correlation matrix is used for direct coefficient interpretation rather than p-value adjustment; nearestSPD projection alters eigenvalues and is intended only to enable valid eigen-analysis http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Estimate the effective number of tests (Meff) in high-dimensional metabolomics multiple testing using seven estimators — Bonferroni, Šidák, Nyholt, Li and Ji, Gao, Galwey, Peluso — of which five derive Meff from eigen-analysis of an M-by-M correlation matrix, optionally recomputed on distance correlations as in DisCo P-ad. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo15010028
skills.summary: Estimate the effective number of tests (Meff) in high-dimensional metabolomics multiple testing using seven estimators — Bonferroni, Šidák, Nyholt, Li and Ji, Gao, Galwey, Peluso — of which five derive Meff from eigen-analysis of an M-by-M correlation matrix, optionally recomputed on distance correlations as in DisCo P-ad.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a set of p-values with no feature matrix — eigen-analysis-based Meff estimators require the features' correlation structure, not just p-values Only a handful of features/tests — Bonferroni (Meff = M) suffices and eigen-analysis corrections add no benefit The correlation matrix is used for direct coefficient interpretation rather than p-value adjustment; nearestSPD projection alters eigenvalues and is intended only to enable valid eigen-analysis

skills.description: Use when a single LC-MS/MS feature (node) in the t-SNE overview needs its local neighborhood examined — i.e., the user wants to see which features are adjacent under a given similarity threshold, and optionally expand that neighborhood by regenerating under new constraints.
skills.name: ego-network-subgraph-extraction
skills.search_text: ego-network-subgraph-extraction Use when a single LC-MS/MS feature (node) in the t-SNE overview needs its local neighborhood examined — i.e., the user wants to see which features are adjacent under a given similarity threshold, and optionally expand that neighborhood by regenerating under new constraints. When the goal is a global molecular-network overview across the whole feature set — specXplore's t-SNE plus edge overlays are explicitly designed for localized, ego-centric exploration, not exhaustive network rendering (the paper warns that liberal settings cause difficulties beyond ~5000 features). When the input is raw vendor data or an mzML file — specXplore currently requires a preprocessed .mgf file with a 'feature_id' key; feature lists without a valid identifier cannot be used until renamed. When an unsupervised global clustering (e.g. k-medoid) assignment is the deliverable rather than a node-neighbor adjacency; the ego view is a per-node overlay, not a partition. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Extracts the local ego-network (all nodes adjacent to a selected reference node) from an ms2deepscore pairwise similarity matrix, thresholded and connectivity-limited, as an edge overlay for the specXplore t-SNE dashboard. This enables localized connectivity exploration around a single LC-MS/MS feature of interest. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c04444
skills.summary: Extracts the local ego-network (all nodes adjacent to a selected reference node) from an ms2deepscore pairwise similarity matrix, thresholded and connectivity-limited, as an edge overlay for the specXplore t-SNE dashboard. This enables localized connectivity exploration around a single LC-MS/MS feature of interest.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is a global molecular-network overview across the whole feature set — specXplore's t-SNE plus edge overlays are explicitly designed for localized, ego-centric exploration, not exhaustive network rendering (the paper warns that liberal settings cause difficulties beyond ~5000 features). When the input is raw vendor data or an mzML file — specXplore currently requires a preprocessed .mgf file with a 'feature_id' key; feature lists without a valid identifier cannot be used until renamed. When an unsupervised global clustering (e.g. k-medoid) assignment is the deliverable rather than a node-neighbor adjacency; the ego view is a per-node overlay, not a partition.

skills.description: Use when query EI mass spectra must be identified against a million-scale in-silico library where exact nearest-neighbor matching is too slow, and recall@1/recall@10 accuracy plus per-query wall time must be benchmarked.
skills.name: ei-mass-spectrum-embedding-similarity-search
skills.search_text: ei-mass-spectrum-embedding-similarity-search Use when query EI mass spectra must be identified against a million-scale in-silico library where exact nearest-neighbor matching is too slow, and recall@1/recall@10 accuracy plus per-query wall time must be benchmarked. skills.summary: FastEI-style EI mass spectrum matching that embeds spectra with a Word2vec model and searches a million-scale in-silico library (~2,146,690 spectra) via an hnswlib HNSW index, achieving 80.4% recall@10 (88.3% with a 5 Da mass filter) with ~100x speedup over exact weighted cosine similarity (WCS).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The compound of interest is already covered by an experimental library such as NIST 2017, where standard library matching suffices and only ~20% of GC-MS compounds were historically identifiable Query spectra are not electron ionization spectra (e.g., LC-MS/MS tandem spectra), since the in-silico library and embeddings are EI-specific Very small candidate sets where exhaustive weighted cosine similarity is cheap enough that HNSW approximate search provides no speed benefit

skills.description: Use when a PS2MS-style synthetic NPS database already exists and you want to evaluate whether a different in silico EI spectrum predictor (e.g., RASSP) improves or degrades ranked identification of GC/EI-MS queries relative to the NEIMS baseline.
skills.name: ei-mass-spectrum-prediction-model-substitution
skills.search_text: ei-mass-spectrum-prediction-model-substitution Use when a PS2MS-style synthetic NPS database already exists and you want to evaluate whether a different in silico EI spectrum predictor (e.g., RASSP) improves or degrades ranked identification of GC/EI-MS queries relative to the NEIMS baseline. The analyte spectrum already matches an established reference spectrum (NIST, Wiley, SWGDRUG) in conventional library screening — PS2MS-style prediction is only triggered when no reference match is found. The goal is de novo structure prediction of an NPS from its spectrum, rather than re-scoring and ranking an already-enumerated candidate subset with a substituted spectrum predictor. The EI spectra come from a source where no candidate SMILES set has been enumerated/filtered, so there is nothing to predict spectra for. http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Substitutes an alternative EI-MS prediction model (RASSP) for NEIMS within the PS2MS matching pipeline to test how the choice of spectrum predictor affects candidate ranking. It re-runs cosine + Jaccard spectrum similarity and SMSF fingerprint-integrated ranking on SWGDRUG queries, then benchmarks top-1/top-20 rates against the NEIMS baseline. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c05019

skills.description: Use when you have GC-EI mass spectra (e.g. from an msp file or synthetic NEIMS/RASSP test splits) and need de novo molecular structure reconstruction via the pretrained SpecTUS model without reference spectral libraries.
skills.name: ei-ms-spectral-transformer-inference
skills.search_text: ei-ms-spectral-transformer-inference Use when you have GC-EI mass spectra (e.g. from an msp file or synthetic NEIMS/RASSP test splits) and need de novo molecular structure reconstruction via the pretrained SpecTUS model without reference spectral libraries. You need reference-library matching or spectral similarity search against known EI-MS databases (e.g. hybrid search) rather than de novo structure prediction. The task is finetuning or training SpecTUS itself on NIST20 — this skill covers inference with the released pretrained checkpoint only (the final NIST20-finetuned model is not shareable). Spectra exceed model thresholds: max m/z 500, max 300 peaks per spectrum, SMILES > 100 characters. http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 Runs autoregressive inference with the pretrained SpecTUS transformer checkpoint to translate GC-EI-MS spectra directly into ranked SMILES candidate structures, producing top-1/top-10 predictions evaluated by exact reconstruction (Acc1/Acc10) and Morgan-fingerprint Tanimoto similarity (Sim1/Sim10). metabolomics/v3 10.48550/arxiv.2502.05114
skills.summary: Runs autoregressive inference with the pretrained SpecTUS transformer checkpoint to translate GC-EI-MS spectra directly into ranked SMILES candidate structures, producing top-1/top-10 predictions evaluated by exact reconstruction (Acc1/Acc10) and Morgan-fingerprint Tanimoto similarity (Sim1/Sim10).
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need reference-library matching or spectral similarity search against known EI-MS databases (e.g. hybrid search) rather than de novo structure prediction. Spectra exceed model thresholds: max m/z 500, max 300 peaks per spectrum, SMILES > 100 characters.

skills.name: ei-ms-spectrum-encoding
skills.search_text: ei-ms-spectrum-encoding Use when preprocessing intensity-binned EI-MS peaks (m/z <= 500, <= 300 peaks) for transformer-based de novo SMILES translation, or when choosing a peak/intensity encoding scheme for a spectral translation model. skills.summary: Encodes a low-resolution GC-EI-MS spectrum for SpecTUS by representing each peak as the sum of its m/z and intensity embeddings, with intensity binning tuned via ablation, and decodes the structure autoregressively as character-level SMILES.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is an MS/MS spectrum or requires precursor ion mass or molecular formula cues — SpecTUS was trained for GC-EI-MS and does not use those inputs Spectrum violates model constraints (m/z above 500, more than 300 peaks, or expected SMILES longer than 100 characters) — such data was excluded by the model's filters A explainable intermediate representation (peak annotations, fragmentation trees) or reference spectra for candidates is required — SpecTUS provides none

skills.search_text: eic-peak-shape-correlation-deconvolution Use when raw LC-MS all-ion fragmentation (AIF) centroid chromatograms are available and parent–fragment ion relationships must be deconvoluted from peak-shape correlation before fragment-library matching or feature annotation. skills.description: Use when scoring extracted ion chromatogram (EIC) quality prior to peak detection in LC/MS metabolomics workflows, or when benchmarking the MCQ index against alternatives (e.g., the global zigzag index) on normal, high-background, or single-peak EIC profiles.
skills.name: eic-quality-index-computation
skills.search_text: eic-quality-index-computation Use when scoring extracted ion chromatogram (EIC) quality prior to peak detection in LC/MS metabolomics workflows, or when benchmarking the MCQ index against alternatives (e.g., the global zigzag index) on normal, high-background, or single-peak EIC profiles. The EICs to evaluate have high background signals or contain only a single peak — the paper shows MCQ cannot fairly evaluate these cases; use the EIC-related global zigzag index instead. The goal is evaluating detected chromatographic peak quality rather than EIC quality — that stage uses separate metrics (sharpness, Gaussian similarity, SNR, peak significance level, TPASR, local peak-related zigzag index) applied after peak detection. Selecting and aligning analyte components is the primary objective rather than general EIC quality assessment — although MCQ is suited to that narrower task, it is not a general EIC quality metric. http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Computes the mass chromatographic quality (MCQ) index for extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) by combining a spike detection index (original vs. smoothed signal similarity) and a background detection index (original vs. mean-subtracted signal similarity), yielding a bounded 0–1.0 quality score per EIC. It serves as the comparator baseline for the paper's proposed global zigzag index and is demonstrated to fail on high-background and single-peak EICs. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/1471-2105-15-s11-s5
skills.summary: Computes the mass chromatographic quality (MCQ) index for extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) by combining a spike detection index (original vs. smoothed signal similarity) and a background detection index (original vs. mean-subtracted signal similarity), yielding a bounded 0–1.0 quality score per EIC. It serves as the comparator baseline for the paper's proposed global zigzag index and is demonstrated to fail on high-background and single-peak EICs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The EICs to evaluate have high background signals or contain only a single peak — the paper shows MCQ cannot fairly evaluate these cases; use the EIC-related global zigzag index instead. The goal is evaluating detected chromatographic peak quality rather than EIC quality — that stage uses separate metrics (sharpness, Gaussian similarity, SNR, peak significance level, TPASR, local peak-related zigzag index) applied after peak detection. Selecting and aligning analyte components is the primary objective rather than general EIC quality assessment — although MCQ is suited to that narrower task, it is not a general EIC quality metric.

skills.description: Use when filtering extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) from LC/MS metabolomics profiles before peak detection — especially when EICs contain high background signals or only a single peak, where the MCQ index scores unfairly and cutoff thresholds must be tuned.
skills.name: eic-quality-threshold-classification
skills.search_text: eic-quality-threshold-classification Use when filtering extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) from LC/MS metabolomics profiles before peak detection — especially when EICs contain high background signals or only a single peak, where the MCQ index scores unfairly and cutoff thresholds must be tuned.
