Annotations already exist for every m/z value in the SPM assay and only downstream clustering/integration is needed — no re-annotation is required. skills.search_text: fold-change-computation Use when sex-stratified tumor-vs-normal metabolomics expression data are loaded in the massdataset framework and per-feature fold change plus univariate significance statistics are needed to build volcano plots. Input is raw LC-MS data (e.g. mzML) that still needs peak picking, data cleaning, or quality control — tidyMass raw-data-processing and filter steps must run first before fold-change testing The input is already a finished differential-expression table with fold change and adjusted p-values — no recomputation is needed, only downstream visualization The experimental design is not a two-group (tumor vs normal) comparison, e.g. multi-factor or longitudinal designs requiring a different statistical model http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Computes per-feature fold change between tumor and normal sample groups (separately for male and female CRC cohorts) within the tidyMass/massStat statistical-analysis stage, producing volcano-plot source tables with fold change, p-value, and adjusted p-value columns. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-022-32155-w
skills.summary: Computes per-feature fold change between tumor and normal sample groups (separately for male and female CRC cohorts) within the tidyMass/massStat statistical-analysis stage, producing volcano-plot source tables with fold change, p-value, and adjusted p-value columns.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw LC-MS data (e.g. mzML) that still needs peak picking, data cleaning, or quality control — tidyMass raw-data-processing and filter steps must run first before fold-change testing The input is already a finished differential-expression table with fold change and adjusted p-values — no recomputation is needed, only downstream visualization The experimental design is not a two-group (tumor vs normal) comparison, e.g. multi-factor or longitudinal designs requiring a different statistical model

skills.description: Use when a metabolomics count data frame has exactly two experimental groups to contrast (e.g., a Treatment factor with numerator/denominator levels like 'Strep' vs 'Mock') and per-metabolite fold-change and t-test statistics are needed.
skills.name: fold-change-computation-between-experimental-groups
skills.search_text: fold-change-computation-between-experimental-groups Use when a metabolomics count data frame has exactly two experimental groups to contrast (e.g., a Treatment factor with numerator/denominator levels like 'Strep' vs 'Mock') and per-metabolite fold-change and t-test statistics are needed. The design has more than two experimental groups — use the omu_anova (anova_function) alternative instead The goal is assigning KEGG compound hierarchy metadata or counting significant metabolites per KEGG category (assign_hierarchy / count_fold_changes) rather than two-group testing The input is not metabolomics count data and has not been made appropriate for the model via omu's transform functions http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Per-metabolite two-group statistical testing with fold-change calculation using the omu R package's omu_summary function, which computes group means, standard error, standard deviation, fold change, log2 fold change, p values, and Benjamini & Hochberg adjusted p values for every metabolite in metabolomics count data. metabolomics/v3 10.1128/mra.00129-19
skills.summary: Per-metabolite two-group statistical testing with fold-change calculation using the omu R package's omu_summary function, which computes group means, standard error, standard deviation, fold change, log2 fold change, p values, and Benjamini & Hochberg adjusted p values for every metabolite in metabolomics count data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The design has more than two experimental groups — use the omu_anova (anova_function) alternative instead The goal is assigning KEGG compound hierarchy metadata or counting significant metabolites per KEGG category (assign_hierarchy / count_fold_changes) rather than two-group testing The input is not metabolomics count data and has not been made appropriate for the model via omu's transform functions

skills.description: Use when a feature table from LC-MS preprocessing (e.g. an Asari preferred_Feature_table.tsv) contains features likely arising from background ions or contaminants, and a sample_type annotation (e.g. 'Blank' vs 'Unknown') is available to separate blanks from study samples.
skills.name: fold-change-intensity-comparison
skills.search_text: fold-change-intensity-comparison Use when a feature table from LC-MS preprocessing (e.g. an Asari preferred_Feature_table.tsv) contains features likely arising from background ions or contaminants, and a sample_type annotation (e.g. 'Blank' vs 'Unknown') is available to separate blanks from study samples. The input data is raw .mzML or .raw — preprocessing into a feature table (e.g. with Asari) must happen first The goal is correcting batch effects or missing values rather than background contamination — pcpfm provides separate batch correction and missing value imputation operations No blank samples (or sample_type annotations distinguishing blanks) exist in the experiment metadata, so no blank-vs-sample intensity comparison is possible http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 A blank-masking filter that removes background/contaminant features by comparing feature intensities between blank and study samples, retaining only features whose sample intensity is at least a set ratio (default 3x) above the blank intensity. This is the blank masking operation of the pcpfm metabolomics pipeline. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011912
skills.summary: A blank-masking filter that removes background/contaminant features by comparing feature intensities between blank and study samples, retaining only features whose sample intensity is at least a set ratio (default 3x) above the blank intensity. This is the blank masking operation of the pcpfm metabolomics pipeline.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input data is raw .mzML or .raw — preprocessing into a feature table (e.g. with Asari) must happen first The goal is correcting batch effects or missing values rather than background contamination — pcpfm provides separate batch correction and missing value imputation operations No blank samples (or sample_type annotations distinguishing blanks) exist in the experiment metadata, so no blank-vs-sample intensity comparison is possible

skills.description: Use when a metabolomics meta-analysis has only per-study fold-changes (no standard deviations or raw data) and per-compound combined effect sizes must be computed from heterogeneous study reports.
skills.name: fold-change-log2-transformation
skills.search_text: fold-change-log2-transformation Use when a metabolomics meta-analysis has only per-study fold-changes (no standard deviations or raw data) and per-compound combined effect sizes must be computed from heterogeneous study reports. Raw data or standard deviations are available for each study — an inverse-variance meta-analysis is then preferable to the weighted fold-change average Only qualitative trend labels (up/down-regulated) are reported — use amanida_vote vote-counting instead of fold-change combination Identifiers have not been curated/harmonized to PubChem IDs (via check_names) — duplicate or mismatched compound names will corrupt the per-compound combination http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Log2-transform per-study fold-change values and combine them via a weighted average (weights proportional to study size n) for metabolomics meta-analysis with amanida, including orientation reversal of inverted comparisons and NA-skipping of missing entries. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btab591
skills.summary: Log2-transform per-study fold-change values and combine them via a weighted average (weights proportional to study size n) for metabolomics meta-analysis with amanida, including orientation reversal of inverted comparisons and NA-skipping of missing entries.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Raw data or standard deviations are available for each study — an inverse-variance meta-analysis is then preferable to the weighted fold-change average Only qualitative trend labels (up/down-regulated) are reported — use amanida_vote vote-counting instead of fold-change combination Identifiers have not been curated/harmonized to PubChem IDs (via check_names) — duplicate or mismatched compound names will corrupt the per-compound combination

skills.description: Use when comparing metabolite abundance/intensity between two groups (factor1 vs factor2 from a metadata factor column) and per-metabolite fold change, log2FC, and significance values are needed before enrichment analysis.
skills.name: fold-change-log2fc-calculation
skills.search_text: fold-change-log2fc-calculation Use when comparing metabolite abundance/intensity between two groups (factor1 vs factor2 from a metadata factor column) and per-metabolite fold change, log2FC, and significance values are needed before enrichment analysis. When more than two experimental groups must be compared simultaneously — use MetENP's anova_ana for multi-group ANOVA instead of the two-group t-test fold-change workflow When the goal is enrichment scoring of metabolite classes or KEGG pathways rather than identifying significantly altered metabolites — fold change calculation is only the upstream step http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Per-metabolite fold change and log2 fold change computation between two experimental groups as performed by MetENP's significant_met function, alongside raw and adjusted p-values from a chosen statistical test. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2020.11.20.391912
skills.summary: Per-metabolite fold change and log2 fold change computation between two experimental groups as performed by MetENP's significant_met function, alongside raw and adjusted p-values from a chosen statistical test.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When more than two experimental groups must be compared simultaneously — use MetENP's anova_ana for multi-group ANOVA instead of the two-group t-test fold-change workflow When the goal is enrichment scoring of metabolite classes or KEGG pathways rather than identifying significantly altered metabolites — fold change calculation is only the upstream step

skills.description: Use when filtering up/down-regulated ions between two MSI ROIs and you need the direction/magnitude of change (parameter c) computed on null-discarded median concentrations, combined with the null-ratio (a) and Mann-Whitney U (b) parameters.
skills.name: fold-change-median-calculation
skills.search_text: fold-change-median-calculation Use when filtering up/down-regulated ions between two MSI ROIs and you need the direction/magnitude of change (parameter c) computed on null-discarded median concentrations, combined with the null-ratio (a) and Mann-Whitney U (b) parameters. When you only need a binary significant/non-significant call and can ignore undetected peaks — the paper's rationale for the median fold-change on null-segregated data is the elevated number of undetected MS ions in a high percentage of pixels; classical p-value/FC alone misses that difficulty. When the input is already a summary feature table rather than a pixel-by-ion rMSIproc peak matrix — the fold-change is defined per ion over pixel-level null-segregated concentrations of two ROIs. When comparing more than two ROIs in a single test — the workflow defines fold-change between a pair of regions at a time. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Computes parameter (c) of the rMSIKeyIon three-parameter ion filter: the fold-change of medians of null-segregated ion concentrations between two regions of interest (ROIs) in an MSI peak matrix, after undetected (null) peaks are discarded. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo9080162
skills.summary: Computes parameter (c) of the rMSIKeyIon three-parameter ion filter: the fold-change of medians of null-segregated ion concentrations between two regions of interest (ROIs) in an MSI peak matrix, after undetected (null) peaks are discarded.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When you only need a binary significant/non-significant call and can ignore undetected peaks — the paper's rationale for the median fold-change on null-segregated data is the elevated number of undetected MS ions in a high percentage of pixels; classical p-value/FC alone misses that difficulty. When the input is already a summary feature table rather than a pixel-by-ion rMSIproc peak matrix — the fold-change is defined per ion over pixel-level null-segregated concentrations of two ROIs. When comparing more than two ROIs in a single test — the workflow defines fold-change between a pair of regions at a time.

skills.description: Use when you have WiPP's merged, classified peak table for a two-condition GC-MS dataset and need per-feature fold change and p-value to compare against a previously published feature list.
skills.name: fold-change-pvalue-extraction-from-peak-tables
skills.search_text: fold-change-pvalue-extraction-from-peak-tables Use when you have WiPP's merged, classified peak table for a two-condition GC-MS dataset and need per-feature fold change and p-value to compare against a previously published feature list. You only have raw GC-MS data and have not yet run WiPP's peak picking and result integration — this skill operates on the merged final peak table, not raw mzML/NetCDF files. The dataset has more than two experimental conditions or no predefined two-group comparison — fold change and p-value extraction as described assumes a two-condition contrast. Features lack WiPP annotation (no retention-index support or no class assignment) — statistics on unannotated features cannot be cross-referenced against a published analyte table. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Extracts condition-wise fold changes (HCC vs cirrhosis) and p-values for an annotated GC-MS feature (e.g. a hexose) from the final high-quality peak table produced by WiPP's result integration, and records it for cross-checking against the original published analysis. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo9090171
skills.summary: Extracts condition-wise fold changes (HCC vs cirrhosis) and p-values for an annotated GC-MS feature (e.g. a hexose) from the final high-quality peak table produced by WiPP's result integration, and records it for cross-checking against the original published analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only have raw GC-MS data and have not yet run WiPP's peak picking and result integration — this skill operates on the merged final peak table, not raw mzML/NetCDF files. The dataset has more than two experimental conditions or no predefined two-group comparison — fold change and p-value extraction as described assumes a two-condition contrast. Features lack WiPP annotation (no retention-index support or no class assignment) — statistics on unannotated features cannot be cross-referenced against a published analyte table.

skills.description: Use when you have raw MS1 LC-HRMS feature-intensity data from a treated-vs-inactivated-control incubation design (e.g., pesticide vs heat-inactivated S9) and need to isolate biotransformation-derived differential features before reaction-based annotation.
skills.name: fold-change-signal-to-noise-statistical-filtering
skills.search_text: fold-change-signal-to-noise-statistical-filtering Use when you have raw MS1 LC-HRMS feature-intensity data from a treated-vs-inactivated-control incubation design (e.g., pesticide vs heat-inactivated S9) and need to isolate biotransformation-derived differential features before reaction-based annotation. Data has no treated-vs-inactivated-control contrast (e.g., single-group profiling or human cohort screening), since fold-change(PG/CG) and SNR cannot be computed as defined The goal is MS2-level annotation or spectrum networking — those belong to the CMDN SSN layer, not DMS filtering You are running a traditional 'bottom-up' workflow relying on reference spectral libraries rather than top-down differential screening of unknown biotransformed metabolites http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 The differential metabolite space (DMS) screening step of the CMDN framework: MS1 LC-HRMS features from human liver S9 incubations are aligned in MS-Dial and differentially expressed metabolites between the pesticide group (PG) and heat-inactivated control group (CG) are retained via unadjusted Student's t test with fold-change(PG/CG) ≥ 2, signal-to-noise ≥ 10, and p ≤ 0.05. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.est.5c08558
skills.summary: The differential metabolite space (DMS) screening step of the CMDN framework: MS1 LC-HRMS features from human liver S9 incubations are aligned in MS-Dial and differentially expressed metabolites between the pesticide group (PG) and heat-inactivated control group (CG) are retained via unadjusted Student's t test with fold-change(PG/CG) ≥ 2, signal-to-noise ≥ 10, and p ≤ 0.05.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data has no treated-vs-inactivated-control contrast (e.g., single-group profiling or human cohort screening), since fold-change(PG/CG) and SNR cannot be computed as defined The goal is MS2-level annotation or spectrum networking — those belong to the CMDN SSN layer, not DMS filtering You are running a traditional 'bottom-up' workflow relying on reference spectral libraries rather than top-down differential screening of unknown biotransformed metabolites

skills.description: Use when two spatially defined pixel groups (e.g., UMAP-kmeans clusters 6/1 vs 23/12) must be compared per ion peak in a 14,260-pixel × 3,044-ion spatial metabolomics feature matrix, and you need fold-change/significance-filtered differential metabolites to feed pathway enrichment.
skills.name: fold-change-significance-filtering
skills.search_text: fold-change-significance-filtering Use when two spatially defined pixel groups (e.g., UMAP-kmeans clusters 6/1 vs 23/12) must be compared per ion peak in a 14,260-pixel × 3,044-ion spatial metabolomics feature matrix, and you need fold-change/significance-filtered differential metabolites to feed pathway enrichment. Input is raw mass-spectrometry imaging data rather than a pre-built pixel × ion feature matrix — run SMAnalyst QC (background consistency QC1, noise ion filtering QC2 with score ≥ 30) and annotation first Regions are not defined by pixel clusters but by manually drawn ROIs of different biological origin where a Wilcoxon rank-sum on pixel-level samples is inappropriate The goal is peak picking or marker-ion discovery from latent features rather than two-group differential testing — SmartGate's graph-attention autoencoder covers that case instead http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 A statistical filtering skill that identifies metabolite ions differentially abundant between two spatial regions by combining a non-parametric Wilcoxon rank-sum test with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control and a dual fold-change cutoff (FC > 2 or < 0.5). In the SMAnalyst mouse-brain workflow it separates midbrain (MB) from hippocampal (HIP) metabolites for downstream pathway enrichment. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/biom15111562
skills.summary: A statistical filtering skill that identifies metabolite ions differentially abundant between two spatial regions by combining a non-parametric Wilcoxon rank-sum test with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control and a dual fold-change cutoff (FC > 2 or < 0.5). In the SMAnalyst mouse-brain workflow it separates midbrain (MB) from hippocampal (HIP) metabolites for downstream pathway enrichment.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw mass-spectrometry imaging data rather than a pre-built pixel × ion feature matrix — run SMAnalyst QC (background consistency QC1, noise ion filtering QC2 with score ≥ 30) and annotation first Regions are not defined by pixel clusters but by manually drawn ROIs of different biological origin where a Wilcoxon rank-sum on pixel-level samples is inappropriate The goal is peak picking or marker-ion discovery from latent features rather than two-group differential testing — SmartGate's graph-attention autoencoder covers that case instead

skills.description: Use when a metabolomics abundance matrix has been differentially analyzed between two groups (e.g. control vs mutant lung cancer) and you need a significant-metabolite list as input to pathway enrichment.
skills.name: fold-change-significance-filtering
skills.search_text: fold-change-significance-filtering Use when a metabolomics abundance matrix has been differentially analyzed between two groups (e.g. control vs mutant lung cancer) and you need a significant-metabolite list as input to pathway enrichment. Input is already a defined query set of metabolites (e.g. a hand-curated list of KEGG IDs) and no differential analysis was performed — pass it directly via inputMetabolites instead The goal is MetSEA on a full ranked metabolite list rather than over-representation on a selected significant subset, since MetSEA uses summary statistics like log2fc and p-values rather than a filtered query set http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Selects a significant-metabolite query set from a metabolomics differential analysis by filtering on absolute fold change ≥ 1 and Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value < 0.05; these filtered metabolites then feed Fisher's Exact Test pathway enrichment in EnrichMet. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.08.28.672951
skills.summary: Selects a significant-metabolite query set from a metabolomics differential analysis by filtering on absolute fold change ≥ 1 and Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value < 0.05; these filtered metabolites then feed Fisher's Exact Test pathway enrichment in EnrichMet.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a defined query set of metabolites (e.g. a hand-curated list of KEGG IDs) and no differential analysis was performed — pass it directly via inputMetabolites instead The goal is MetSEA on a full ranked metabolite list rather than over-representation on a selected significant subset, since MetSEA uses summary statistics like log2fc and p-values rather than a filtered query set

skills.description: Use when you have a metabolomics abundance matrix with case/control (disease vs wild-type) groups and need to identify differentially abundant metabolites with direction and statistical significance, e.g. 35 DA metabolites and 10 dysregulated pathways.
skills.name: fold-change-statistical-testing
skills.search_text: fold-change-statistical-testing Use when you have a metabolomics abundance matrix with case/control (disease vs wild-type) groups and need to identify differentially abundant metabolites with direction and statistical significance, e.g. 35 DA metabolites and 10 dysregulated pathways. Input is already a curated list of differentially abundant metabolites and only pathway enrichment is needed — go straight to hypergeometric over-representation instead. The data are raw mass-spectrometry peaks needing peak detection/normalization; differential testing must come after preprocessing, not replace it. No biological replicates or group labels exist, so fold-change and p-value testing between conditions is not defined. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Compute per-metabolite log2 fold changes and abundance-difference p-values between case and control groups, then flag metabolites as differentially abundant (e.g. p < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 1) as performed in PlantMetSuite's acd5 vs Col-0 case study. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/plants12152880
skills.summary: Compute per-metabolite log2 fold changes and abundance-difference p-values between case and control groups, then flag metabolites as differentially abundant (e.g. p < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 1) as performed in PlantMetSuite's acd5 vs Col-0 case study.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a curated list of differentially abundant metabolites and only pathway enrichment is needed — go straight to hypergeometric over-representation instead. The data are raw mass-spectrometry peaks needing peak detection/normalization; differential testing must come after preprocessing, not replace it. No biological replicates or group labels exist, so fold-change and p-value testing between conditions is not defined.

skills.description: Use when individual metabolomics studies report only fold-change (no raw data, error, or variance) for the same compounds and you need a case-vs-control combined effect size, e.g. input tables with Id, P-value, Fold-change, N, Reference columns.
skills.name: fold-change-weighted-averaging
skills.search_text: fold-change-weighted-averaging Use when individual metabolomics studies report only fold-change (no raw data, error, or variance) for the same compounds and you need a case-vs-control combined effect size, e.g. input tables with Id, P-value, Fold-change, N, Reference columns. When raw data or standard deviations are available for each study — then conventional meta-analysis methods that use variance are appropriate instead When studies report only qualitative trend labels (up/down-regulated) with no fold-change values — use amanida's vote-counting (amanida_vote) instead When the comparison orientation is unknown, since -1/value reversal of control/case entries cannot be assigned correctly http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Combines per-study fold-change values reported for metabolomics compounds into a single per-compound estimate by log2-transforming the fold-changes and averaging them with weights proportional to study size (n), as implemented in the amanida R package for meta-analysis without standard deviations. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btab591
skills.summary: Combines per-study fold-change values reported for metabolomics compounds into a single per-compound estimate by log2-transforming the fold-changes and averaging them with weights proportional to study size (n), as implemented in the amanida R package for meta-analysis without standard deviations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When raw data or standard deviations are available for each study — then conventional meta-analysis methods that use variance are appropriate instead When studies report only qualitative trend labels (up/down-regulated) with no fold-change values — use amanida's vote-counting (amanida_vote) instead When the comparison orientation is unknown, since -1/value reversal of control/case entries cannot be assigned correctly

skills.description: Use when a metabolomics feature table has rich sample metadata organized as a multi-level ontology (e.g. food sample types in Global FoodOmics) and you need to quantify, per ontology level, whether fingerprint-tree-informed sample dissimilarities reveal structure that tree-agnostic metrics miss.
skills.name: food-ontology-level-comparison
skills.search_text: food-ontology-level-comparison Use when a metabolomics feature table has rich sample metadata organized as a multi-level ontology (e.g. food sample types in Global FoodOmics) and you need to quantify, per ontology level, whether fingerprint-tree-informed sample dissimilarities reveal structure that tree-agnostic metrics miss. The dataset lacks multi-level sample-type ontology metadata, so 'within-food vs between-food' comparison per level cannot be defined Features carry only MS1 spectra with no predicted fingerprints and no MS/MS library matches — the chemical hierarchy and hence fingerprint-based UniFrac cannot be built (the article notes features with only MS1 are not considered) The analysis goal is simply a single global clustering of samples rather than a per-ontology-level comparison across multiple metrics http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Assess whether a Qemistree fingerprint-based chemical hierarchy captures chemically meaningful sample clustering at each level of a food ontology (levels 1–4) by comparing weighted UniFrac, Bray-Curtis, CSCS, and MS/MS cosine-score hierarchy dissimilarities across within-food vs between-food sample pairs, and compile the per-metric per-level counts into an Extended Data Table 4-style comparison. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41589-020-00677-3
skills.summary: Assess whether a Qemistree fingerprint-based chemical hierarchy captures chemically meaningful sample clustering at each level of a food ontology (levels 1–4) by comparing weighted UniFrac, Bray-Curtis, CSCS, and MS/MS cosine-score hierarchy dissimilarities across within-food vs between-food sample pairs, and compile the per-metric per-level counts into an Extended Data Table 4-style comparison.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset lacks multi-level sample-type ontology metadata, so 'within-food vs between-food' comparison per level cannot be defined Features carry only MS1 spectra with no predicted fingerprints and no MS/MS library matches — the chemical hierarchy and hence fingerprint-based UniFrac cannot be built (the article notes features with only MS1 are not considered) The analysis goal is simply a single global clustering of samples rather than a per-ontology-level comparison across multiple metrics

skills.description: Use when a Qemistree chemical hierarchy (qemistree.qza) merged with feature data across heterogeneous samples needs class-level interpretation — e.g., checking whether a ClassyFire class forms a subtree restricted to particular metadata groups (animal vs plant products, honey).
skills.name: foodomics-class-subtree-interpretation
skills.search_text: foodomics-class-subtree-interpretation Use when a Qemistree chemical hierarchy (qemistree.qza) merged with feature data across heterogeneous samples needs class-level interpretation — e.g., checking whether a ClassyFire class forms a subtree restricted to particular metadata groups (animal vs plant products, honey). Input features are still raw MS1/MS2 peak lists without a merged Qemistree hierarchy or SIRIUS/CSI:FingerID fingerprints — run compute-fragmentation-trees through make-hierarchy first. Structural annotations come only from spectral matches with low coverage (typically 1–20% of features), insufficient to summarize complex-sample chemistry; use fingerprint-based subtrees instead of match-only interpretation. The goal is abundance/differential testing between groups rather than taxonomic containment of chemical classes within the hierarchy. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0218 Interpreting ClassyFire-annotated Qemistree chemical hierarchies by reading class-level subtrees (e.g., acyl-carnitines, flavonoids) against sample metadata to detect class-specific chemical signatures discriminating sample types such as animal-derived vs plant-derived food products. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41589-020-00677-3
skills.summary: Interpreting ClassyFire-annotated Qemistree chemical hierarchies by reading class-level subtrees (e.g., acyl-carnitines, flavonoids) against sample metadata to detect class-specific chemical signatures discriminating sample types such as animal-derived vs plant-derived food products.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input features are still raw MS1/MS2 peak lists without a merged Qemistree hierarchy or SIRIUS/CSI:FingerID fingerprints — run compute-fragmentation-trees through make-hierarchy first. Structural annotations come only from spectral matches with low coverage (typically 1–20% of features), insufficient to summarize complex-sample chemistry; use fingerprint-based subtrees instead of match-only interpretation. The goal is abundance/differential testing between groups rather than taxonomic containment of chemical classes within the hierarchy.

skills.description: Use when a community FBA/FVA solution predicts exchange fluxes (e.g., H2 and CO2 uptake) that were absent from the original analysis, suggesting a thermodynamically infeasible cycle rather than a biological interaction.
skills.name: formate-hydrogen-shuttle-loop-identification
skills.search_text: formate-hydrogen-shuttle-loop-identification Use when a community FBA/FVA solution predicts exchange fluxes (e.g., H2 and CO2 uptake) that were absent from the original analysis, suggesting a thermodynamically infeasible cycle rather than a biological interaction. The model is a single-organism model rather than a PyCoMo compartmentalized community model with member-prefixed metabolites and compartments The analysis goal is enumerating elementary flux modes rather than diagnosing a specific spurious exchange flux between two community members http://edamontology.org/topic_2259 A diagnostic workflow for isolating thermodynamically infeasible cross-feeding cycles in PyCoMo-generated community metabolic models, exemplified by the spurious D. vulgaris H2 uptake driven by a formate/H2/CO2 shuttle with M. hungatei in the Koch et al. (2019) biogas community. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae153
skills.summary: A diagnostic workflow for isolating thermodynamically infeasible cross-feeding cycles in PyCoMo-generated community metabolic models, exemplified by the spurious D. vulgaris H2 uptake driven by a formate/H2/CO2 shuttle with M. hungatei in the Koch et al. (2019) biogas community.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The model is a single-organism model rather than a PyCoMo compartmentalized community model with member-prefixed metabolites and compartments The analysis goal is enumerating elementary flux modes rather than diagnosing a specific spurious exchange flux between two community members

skills.description: Use when the true chemical formula may be unknown in an elucidation setting and you need to quantify top-1/top-5 formula annotation accuracy on NPLIB1/MassSpecGym test spectra before conditioning DiffMS on predicted formulae.
skills.name: formula-accuracy-evaluation
skills.search_text: formula-accuracy-evaluation Use when the true chemical formula may be unknown in an elucidation setting and you need to quantify top-1/top-5 formula annotation accuracy on NPLIB1/MassSpecGym test spectra before conditioning DiffMS on predicted formulae. When ground-truth formulae are available for the spectra you plan to condition DiffMS on — use them directly, since predicted formulae give slightly lower accuracy When high-resolution MS1 data with isotopic traces are available and isotope-aware inference is required — note MIST-CF does not consider isotope distributions When the goal is fingerprint prediction rather than formula annotation — MIST predicts 4,096-bit Morgan fingerprints (radius 2) via mist-predict-fingerprints, not formulae http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Evaluates how reliably out-of-the-box formula annotation tools (MIST-CF, BUDDY) recover the true chemical formula from MS/MS spectra on the NPLIB1 and MassSpecGym benchmarks, by computing top-1/top-5 annotation accuracy against known ground-truth formulae. This establishes whether DiffMS de novo structure elucidation can retain performance when supplied predicted formulae (top-5 per spectrum) instead of ground truth. metabolomics/v3 10.48550/arxiv.2502.09571
skills.summary: Evaluates how reliably out-of-the-box formula annotation tools (MIST-CF, BUDDY) recover the true chemical formula from MS/MS spectra on the NPLIB1 and MassSpecGym benchmarks, by computing top-1/top-5 annotation accuracy against known ground-truth formulae. This establishes whether DiffMS de novo structure elucidation can retain performance when supplied predicted formulae (top-5 per spectrum) instead of ground truth.

skills.search_text: formula-encoder-dimensionality-verification Use when reimplementing, porting, or regression-testing the MIST-CF counts-based formula encoder, or when feeding formula candidates into the Chemical Formula Transformer and you must confirm the encoding is exactly 144-dimensional and non-negative before training or inference. Input is raw MS/MS spectra or peak lists — this skill validates the formula-count encoder only, not the spectrum/subformula encodings Formulas contain elements outside the fixed 18-element set considered by MIST-CF, so counts cannot be mapped to the 144-dim layout A quantitative accuracy benchmark of the encoder is required — the paper validates it only qualitatively (shape and non-negativity) http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Verifies the sinusoidal counts-based formula embedding (Equation 5) used by MIST-CF: each of the 18 considered elements gets an 8-dimensional integer encoding (log2(256)), flattened to a 144-dimensional, strictly non-negative vector Enc(F). This check guards the interface between formula candidate parsing and the Chemical Formula Transformer. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jcim.3c01082
skills.summary: Verifies the sinusoidal counts-based formula embedding (Equation 5) used by MIST-CF: each of the 18 considered elements gets an 8-dimensional integer encoding (log2(256)), flattened to a 144-dimensional, strictly non-negative vector Enc(F). This check guards the interface between formula candidate parsing and the Chemical Formula Transformer.

skills.description: Use when you have qualified MS/MS spectra paired with known molecular formulas and need to quantify how often a formula-ranking tool places the true formula at rank#1, within top-3/top-5, and how long it takes per spectrum.
skills.name: formula-ranking-accuracy-evaluation
skills.search_text: formula-ranking-accuracy-evaluation Use when you have qualified MS/MS spectra paired with known molecular formulas and need to quantify how often a formula-ranking tool places the true formula at rank#1, within top-3/top-5, and how long it takes per spectrum. The goal is structural identification or spectral similarity matching, not formula ranking — FSA has not utilized structural information and its rank#1 accuracy is not comparable to state-of-the-art identification tools like Buddy and SIRIUS. Compounds contain elements beyond C, H, O, N, S, P or rely on diverse adduct types — FSA has only been validated on datasets with compounds composed of C, H, O, N, S, and P. Spectra lack ground-truth formulas, so rank-of-true-formula cannot be computed for accuracy metrics. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Benchmark molecular-formula ranking accuracy (rank#1, top-3, top-5) and runtime of formula-assignment tools such as FSA, SIRIUS, and Buddy on MS/MS datasets with ground-truth formulas, reproducing table-style accuracy/speed comparisons. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-025-02379-0
skills.summary: Benchmark molecular-formula ranking accuracy (rank#1, top-3, top-5) and runtime of formula-assignment tools such as FSA, SIRIUS, and Buddy on MS/MS datasets with ground-truth formulas, reproducing table-style accuracy/speed comparisons.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is structural identification or spectral similarity matching, not formula ranking — FSA has not utilized structural information and its rank#1 accuracy is not comparable to state-of-the-art identification tools like Buddy and SIRIUS. Compounds contain elements beyond C, H, O, N, S, P or rely on diverse adduct types — FSA has only been validated on datasets with compounds composed of C, H, O, N, S, and P. Spectra lack ground-truth formulas, so rank-of-true-formula cannot be computed for accuracy metrics.

skills.description: Use when replicating or validating FSA formula-ranking behavior — e.g. sweeping the MaxComb setting for rank#1 accuracy, or verifying a worked metabolite example such as salbutamol (HMDB0001937) precursor C13H21NO3 scoring 1.8333.
skills.name: formula-ranking-score-validation
skills.search_text: formula-ranking-score-validation Use when replicating or validating FSA formula-ranking behavior — e.g. sweeping the MaxComb setting for rank#1 accuracy, or verifying a worked metabolite example such as salbutamol (HMDB0001937) precursor C13H21NO3 scoring 1.8333. skills.summary: Validates the FSA (formula subset analysis) precursor-formula ranking by reproducing the MaxComb=1 rule (dropping fragments carrying multiple maximum-difference-redundancy, MDR, combinations) and checking the salbutamol worked example, where fragment formula C13H21NO3 must score 1.8333 (5/6 + 1 per Eq. 4) and rank #1.

skills.search_text: forward-variable-selection Use when you have manually labeled true/false peak examples and many candidate shape parameters (e.g., 59 peak group parameters from duration, height, area, FWHM, tailing factor, asymmetry) and need a small interpretable logistic regression model. skills.search_text: four-dimensional-metabolomics-database-construction Use when building an in-silico LC-IM-MS/MS reference library in which each derivatized sterol (or other C=C-bearing lipid) entry must carry all four 4D fields: m/z, retention time, CCS, and fragment ions. skills.summary: Assembles a large-scale 4D information database of derivatized sterol lipids (n = 4891) by combining per-molecule m/z, retention time (pretrained GNN), collision cross section (QCC-assisted scikit-learn SVR), and RDkit-predicted N-Me fragment ions into a single searchable table. skills.when_to_use_negative: The target molecules lack C=C bonds or are outside the sterol lipid class — the MS/MS calculation script recognizes double bond positions and was only tested on sterol lipids, though theoretically applicable to all molecules containing C=C bonds An experimentally measured spectral/RT/CCS library already exists for the analytes of interest — the 4D database is an in-silico prediction resource, not a replacement for measured standards The analysis does not involve N-Me derivatization — the fragment ion prediction logic is specific to N-Me fragmentation patterns

The downstream task is MS1 mass matching or MS2 spectral similarity comparison of already-derivatized m/z features, not enumerating reactive functional groups on database structures The matrix is a conventional (non-derivatizing) MALDI matrix, so no functional-group-specific target subsetting applies Candidate molecules have no parseable structural representation (SMILES/SDF), since SMARTS matching cannot be performed http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Validates a derivatization-site enumeration pipeline (e.g. Met-ID's FMP-10 functional-group filter) by reproducing the paper's four-isomer benchmark, where RDKit substructure counting must yield 0 sites for enbucrilate, 2 for p-octopamine, 2 for norfenefrine, and 3 for dopamine. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c00633
skills.summary: Validates a derivatization-site enumeration pipeline (e.g. Met-ID's FMP-10 functional-group filter) by reproducing the paper's four-isomer benchmark, where RDKit substructure counting must yield 0 sites for enbucrilate, 2 for p-octopamine, 2 for norfenefrine, and 3 for dopamine.

The input is already uniformly sampled and fully processed frequency-domain data — direct Fourier transformation of conventionally acquired data suffices without SMILE iteration The goal is peak deconvolution or line-shape fitting on an existing spectrum (use DEEP Picker/Voigt Fitter instead of reconstruction) Data are 1D spectra without a NUS schedule, where reconstruction offers no benefit http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_3419 Reconstructs non-uniformly sampled (NUS) multidimensional NMR spectra using fast direct-FT for a first-pass uniformly sampled spectrum and iterative SMILE reconstruction for higher fidelity, as implemented in COLMARvista's WebAssembly pipeline for Bruker `fid`/`ser` FID data. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s10858-025-00465-y

skills.description: Use when auditing a metabCombiner combined table reduction: you must remove misaligned feature pair alignments (FPAs) via labelRows() thresholds and verify the resulting row counts against expected removal statistics.
skills.name: fpa-count-verification-across-datasets
skills.search_text: fpa-count-verification-across-datasets Use when auditing a metabCombiner combined table reduction: you must remove misaligned feature pair alignments (FPAs) via labelRows() thresholds and verify the resulting row counts against expected removal statistics. The datasets were acquired from excessively disparate chromatographic techniques, such as an RPLC dataset paired with a HILIC dataset — the elution order is not preserved and the paper says such pairs are not suitable. The input datasets were acquired in different ionization modes (positive vs. negative), which the paper lists as a prerequisite for metabCombiner. The combined table is already reduced and only needs downstream batch-effect correction, not another FPA removal pass. Verifies the metabCombiner 'Combined Table Reduction' step by tracking how many feature pair alignments (FPAs) survive labelRows() filtering — on the plasma20/plasma30 pair, 6765 of 14024 FPAs are removed automatically plus ~400 by inspection, leaving fewer than 6900 rows in the final combined table. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c03693
skills.summary: Verifies the metabCombiner 'Combined Table Reduction' step by tracking how many feature pair alignments (FPAs) survive labelRows() filtering — on the plasma20/plasma30 pair, 6765 of 14024 FPAs are removed automatically plus ~400 by inspection, leaving fewer than 6900 rows in the final combined table.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The datasets were acquired from excessively disparate chromatographic techniques, such as an RPLC dataset paired with a HILIC dataset — the elution order is not preserved and the paper says such pairs are not suitable. The input datasets were acquired in different ionization modes (positive vs. negative), which the paper lists as a prerequisite for metabCombiner. The combined table is already reduced and only needs downstream batch-effect correction, not another FPA removal pass.

skills.description: Use when multiple .MSP, .MGF, .JSON, .CSV or .XML open mass spectral libraries (or an MZmine-generated in-house library) must be concatenated, metadata-harmonized, filtered, and exported for dereplication tools like MS-Dial, MZmine, or Flash Entropy Search.
skills.name: fraghub-library-integration-processing
skills.search_text: fraghub-library-integration-processing Use when multiple .MSP, .MGF, .JSON, .CSV or .XML open mass spectral libraries (or an MZmine-generated in-house library) must be concatenated, metadata-harmonized, filtered, and exported for dereplication tools like MS-Dial, MZmine, or Flash Entropy Search. Input is already a FragHub-standardized output directory with update.json SPLASH keys — reprocessing it from scratch would require resetting the project first. Spectra lack both InChI and SMILES, or lack a valid precursor m/z — these inconsistent spectra are automatically removed, so the skill cannot recover unidentifiable entries. The goal is to harmonize collision energy annotations across libraries — FragHub explicitly does not harmonize collision energies because ~70 nonstandardized formats exist. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Method for converting open or in-house mass spectral libraries (e.g. GNPS .MGF, MoNA .MSP/.SDF/.JSON, MassBank, MS-Dial exports, MZmine spectral-library-generation output) into a single FragHub-standardized, filtered, SPLASH-keyed library harmonized by RDKit and PSI-MS controlled vocabulary, segregated by ionization mode, LC/GC, and experimental vs in-silico origin. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c02219
skills.summary: Method for converting open or in-house mass spectral libraries (e.g. GNPS .MGF, MoNA .MSP/.SDF/.JSON, MassBank, MS-Dial exports, MZmine spectral-library-generation output) into a single FragHub-standardized, filtered, SPLASH-keyed library harmonized by RDKit and PSI-MS controlled vocabulary, segregated by ionization mode, LC/GC, and experimental vs in-silico origin.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a FragHub-standardized output directory with update.json SPLASH keys — reprocessing it from scratch would require resetting the project first. Spectra lack both InChI and SMILES, or lack a valid precursor m/z — these inconsistent spectra are automatically removed, so the skill cannot recover unidentifiable entries. The goal is to harmonize collision energy annotations across libraries — FragHub explicitly does not harmonize collision energies because ~70 nonstandardized formats exist.

The glycans of interest are O-linked — the app's scope is limited to N-linked glycans De novo glycan identification is needed for species not in the database — the app only identifies glycans already located in the database Multiple mzXML files must be processed simultaneously — this is a planned future improvement, not implemented Annotate MS2 fragmentation spectra for a selected glycan–RT pair by matching observed fragment peaks against a curated MS2 Fragment Database within a mass-accuracy tolerance, keeping peaks above a relative-intensity threshold, and labeling each m/z with up to two candidate fragments including adduct forms (+Na, +K, -OH). metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-023-05346-5

skills.when_to_use_negative: The glycans of interest are O-linked — the app's scope is limited to N-linked glycans De novo glycan identification is needed for species not in the database — the app only identifies glycans already located in the database Multiple mzXML files must be processed simultaneously — this is a planned future improvement, not implemented

skills.description: Use when reconstructing GLEAMS' per-spectrum input encoding: fragment peaks from an mzML/peak file must be converted to fixed-length binned intensity features (2449 bins, 50.5–2500 m/z, square-root transformed) before feeding the neural network.
skills.name: fragment-intensity-binning-sqrt-transform
skills.search_text: fragment-intensity-binning-sqrt-transform Use when reconstructing GLEAMS' per-spectrum input encoding: fragment peaks from an mzML/peak file must be converted to fixed-length binned intensity features (2449 bins, 50.5–2500 m/z, square-root transformed) before feeding the neural network. You already have the 32-dimensional GLEAMS embedding output — the neural network, not this raw feature encoding, is the relevant stage then (use `gleams embed`). You need spectral similarity for direct library matching rather than network input — GLEAMS embeddings or a tool like ANN-SoLo operate on the embedded/clustered representations instead. Training configuration changes (e.g. bin count or m/z range edited in gleams/config.py) would invalidate the fixed 2449-bin/50.5–2500 m/z scheme; do not assume these constants hold for custom configurations. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Encodes the fragment-ion content of a single MS/MS spectrum as part of GLEAMS' 3010-dimensional input feature vector by binning peak intensities into 2449 bins over the 50.5–2500 m/z range and applying a square-root transform, followed by concatenation with Gray-coded precursor features and 500 reference-spectrum similarities. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-022-01496-1
skills.summary: Encodes the fragment-ion content of a single MS/MS spectrum as part of GLEAMS' 3010-dimensional input feature vector by binning peak intensities into 2449 bins over the 50.5–2500 m/z range and applying a square-root transform, followed by concatenation with Gray-coded precursor features and 500 reference-spectrum similarities.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You already have the 32-dimensional GLEAMS embedding output — the neural network, not this raw feature encoding, is the relevant stage then (use `gleams embed`). You need spectral similarity for direct library matching rather than network input — GLEAMS embeddings or a tool like ANN-SoLo operate on the embedded/clustered representations instead. Training configuration changes (e.g. bin count or m/z range edited in gleams/config.py) would invalidate the fixed 2449-bin/50.5–2500 m/z scheme; do not assume these constants hold for custom configurations.

skills.name: fragment-intensity-heatmap-construction
skills.search_text: fragment-intensity-heatmap-construction Use when after selecting a feature or feature group of interest (e.g. from the t-SNE overview or k-medoid clustering in the specXplore dashboard), you need a single-figure overview of how fragment ions and neutral losses overlap across the multiple MS/MS spectra of that group. When the goal is to inspect the global pairwise spectral similarity structure (e.g. a full ms2deepscore similarity matrix or t-SNE overview of the whole feature set) rather than the fragmentation content of a small local group of spectra. When no MS/MS peak lists are available — e.g. only MS1 feature intensities or a feature table without .mgf-derived fragment spectra — since the heatmap cells must be filled with fragment intensities from the spectra. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Construct a fragmentation-overlap (fragmap) heatmap that renders, per spectrum of a selected feature or feature group, binned and factorized fragment m/z positions colored by fragment intensity, with neutral-loss blocks overlaid so shared fragmentation patterns become readable across all selected spectra. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c04444
skills.summary: Construct a fragmentation-overlap (fragmap) heatmap that renders, per spectrum of a selected feature or feature group, binned and factorized fragment m/z positions colored by fragment intensity, with neutral-loss blocks overlaid so shared fragmentation patterns become readable across all selected spectra.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is to inspect the global pairwise spectral similarity structure (e.g. a full ms2deepscore similarity matrix or t-SNE overview of the whole feature set) rather than the fragmentation content of a small local group of spectra. When no MS/MS peak lists are available — e.g. only MS1 feature intensities or a feature table without .mgf-derived fragment spectra — since the heatmap cells must be filled with fragment intensities from the spectra.

skills.description: Use when building targeted lipidomics PRM/MRM assays that need optimal collision energies per fragment from CE-dependent intensity measurements on Thermo QExactive HF or Agilent QTOF instruments.
skills.name: fragment-intensity-nonlinear-regression-fitting
skills.search_text: fragment-intensity-nonlinear-regression-fitting Use when building targeted lipidomics PRM/MRM assays that need optimal collision energies per fragment from CE-dependent intensity measurements on Thermo QExactive HF or Agilent QTOF instruments. CE-dependent measurements for the lipid class of interest are unavailable — LipidCreator CE models are currently exclusive to lipid mediators and expansion requires availability of more structurally diverse lipid standards The user needs a scoring algorithm to determine false discovery rates or to resolve coeluting/isobaric lipids and peak area integration — LipidCreator intentionally does not address these Target organisms are bacteria such as E. coli or archaea, where rare lipidome-wide studies and explicit lack of standards for acyl-PG, acyl-PE, and di-/tetraacyl cardiolipins limit standard availability http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Fit fragment-specific nonlinear regression models (extended log-normal kernel) to collision-energy-dependent relative fragment intensities from QExactive HF and QTOF standards, enabling model-based collision energy prediction for targeted lipidomics transitions in LipidCreator. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-020-15960-z
skills.summary: Fit fragment-specific nonlinear regression models (extended log-normal kernel) to collision-energy-dependent relative fragment intensities from QExactive HF and QTOF standards, enabling model-based collision energy prediction for targeted lipidomics transitions in LipidCreator.
skills.when_to_use_negative: CE-dependent measurements for the lipid class of interest are unavailable — LipidCreator CE models are currently exclusive to lipid mediators and expansion requires availability of more structurally diverse lipid standards The user needs a scoring algorithm to determine false discovery rates or to resolve coeluting/isobaric lipids and peak area integration — LipidCreator intentionally does not address these Target organisms are bacteria such as E. coli or archaea, where rare lipidome-wide studies and explicit lack of standards for acyl-PG, acyl-PE, and di-/tetraacyl cardiolipins limit standard availability

skills.search_text: fragment-intensity-threshold-binning Use when you have a feature-lipid candidate table from exact-mass MS1 matching and need to decide which experimental fragments in ddMS2-topN .ms2 data are trustworthy evidence for confirming each lipid. The input is raw vendor files without prior peak picking and .ms2 conversion, since the skill operates on pre-processed .ms2 scan data. You only need precursor m/z-level identifications and have no MS/MS data, since the binarization depends on fragment-level evidence. skills.search_text: fragment-ion-cross-collision-energy-alignment Use when MS/MS spectra for the same compound were acquired at multiple collision energies and you need to link identical fragment ions across CEs to construct per-fragment longitudinal intensity vectors before similarity scoring. skills.description: Use when you have validated peptide-spectrum matches (with known peptide sequences) plus de novo tool predictions and need to quantify missing fragment ions, noise peak fractions, or how these spectrum properties drive peptide recall.
skills.name: fragment-ion-peak-annotation
skills.search_text: fragment-ion-peak-annotation Use when you have validated peptide-spectrum matches (with known peptide sequences) plus de novo tool predictions and need to quantify missing fragment ions, noise peak fractions, or how these spectrum properties drive peptide recall. Spectra lack validated reference peptide sequences, so expected cleavage sites and the eight theoretical ion types cannot be enumerated. High-resolution data where a 0.5 Da tolerance is inappropriate or where the analysis goal is database-search PSM scoring rather than de novo error analysis. skills.search_text: fragment-ion-similarity-scoring Use when comparing two fragmentation spectra whose fragment m/z values do not match exactly and whose precursor ion neutral losses differ (e.g., structurally related compounds with multiple modifications), where cosine scoring fails. Spectra are from compounds differing by only one localized modification — cosine-based scoring is the article's recommended complement and may be more appropriate for some molecule classes. Analysis requires adducts other than [M+H]+/[M-H]- — SIMILE is currently limited to protonation/deprotonation analysis. Only a global, dataset-wide fragment substitution matrix is needed — this skill produces a pair-specific, context-sensitive matrix, not a reusable global one. Computes a pair-specific fragment ion similarity matrix S from two tandem MS spectra by building an (m+n)×(m+n) pairwise m/z-difference count matrix, row-normalizing it into transition probabilities, and taking the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of the normalized graph Laplacian to get an average-commute-time similarity between all fragment ions. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-022-30118-9

This is the final observation/decoding step of the RASSP EI–MS prediction pipeline, producing spectra at 1 Da or 0.1 Da resolution. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.2c02093

skills.description: Use when you have repeated (e.g., 10-fold or fivefold CV) F-measure/Accuracy scores for multiple competing models across folds and must rank them and identify statistically significant pairwise winners, such as selecting among 24 classifiers built from peak-quality metric sets M4, M7 and M11.
skills.name: friedman-nemenyi-multiple-comparison-testing
skills.search_text: friedman-nemenyi-multiple-comparison-testing Use when you have repeated (e.g., 10-fold or fivefold CV) F-measure/Accuracy scores for multiple competing models across folds and must rank them and identify statistically significant pairwise winners, such as selecting among 24 classifiers built from peak-quality metric sets M4, M7 and M11. You have only a single train/test split or unpaired scores — Friedman–Nemenyi requires repeated, matched measurements (e.g., 10 CV runs) across all classifiers on the same folds. You are comparing a single classifier against a baseline rather than ranking a full set of ≥ 3 models — a Wilcoxon Rank Sum test (as MetaClean used for pairwise metric-set comparison) is the appropriate choice. Input is raw peak-quality metric data or an unprocessed XCMS feature table rather than aggregated per-fold evaluation measures — pre-compute F-measures/Accuracy first. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Two-round statistical comparison (intra-metric set, then inter-metric set) of candidate classifiers using Friedman's test followed by Nemenyi's post-hoc test on cross-validated evaluation measures, used in MetaClean to select the global peak-quality classifier (AdaBoost with the M11 metric set). metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-020-01738-3
skills.summary: Two-round statistical comparison (intra-metric set, then inter-metric set) of candidate classifiers using Friedman's test followed by Nemenyi's post-hoc test on cross-validated evaluation measures, used in MetaClean to select the global peak-quality classifier (AdaBoost with the M11 metric set).
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have only a single train/test split or unpaired scores — Friedman–Nemenyi requires repeated, matched measurements (e.g., 10 CV runs) across all classifiers on the same folds. When only a single train/test split or one fold is available — Friedman's test requires repeated performance statistics across multiple CV runs (Demsar 2006), not a single paired comparison. skills.summary: A two-round statistical comparison procedure using Friedman's test followed by Nemenyi's post-hoc test (via the scmamp package) to rank candidate classifiers across metric sets and select the global best-performing model, as implemented in MetaClean to choose AdaBoost with the M11 peak-quality metric set.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only two classifiers are being compared — a Wilcoxon Rank Sum (or paired) test per metric-pair is what the paper used for pairwise metric-set differences, not Friedman-Nemenyi Performance estimates are not paired across folds/repetitions (independent samples), since Friedman's test assumes a repeated-measures/blocked design You need per-metric-set pairwise significance between metric sets rather than a global ranking — the paper found only moderately significant Wilcoxon p-values between metric pairs, indicating the two-round Nemenyi approach is overkill for that narrow question

skills.search_text: ft-icr-ms-pairwise-mass-difference-matching Decision support for building ab initio biochemical transformation networks from FT-ICR MS peak tables that already have assigned molecular formulas; triggered when you need putative biotic/abiotic edges (e.g., CH2, N2 gains/losses) per sample. Input is raw FT-ICR MS spectra without molecular formula assignment — MetaboDirect requires formula-assigned peak abundance data produced by upstream tools (e.g., MFAssignR or Formularity). The input data is LC-MS/MS or DI-MS where isomers are separated; this skill targets direct injection FT-ICR MS peak tables and does not resolve chemical isomers. You need transformation edges with strict stoichiometric validation beyond mass-difference tolerance; this approach matches mass differences at ≤1 ppm and does not independently confirm biochemical plausibility beyond the reference keys. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Computes all pairwise m/z differences among FT-ICR MS-detected peaks in each sample, matches them against a reference biochemical transformation key file at ≤1 ppm error, and exports per-sample edge files plus transformation counts for building molecular transformation networks. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s40168-023-01476-3
skills.summary: Computes all pairwise m/z differences among FT-ICR MS-detected peaks in each sample, matches them against a reference biochemical transformation key file at ≤1 ppm error, and exports per-sample edge files plus transformation counts for building molecular transformation networks.

skills.description: Use when you have raw low-resolution FT-ICR transients (e.g., 64k-point MALDI FT-ICR MSI or SCMS acquisitions) and need high-resolution, high-SNR spectra without the acquisition time of full 1M-point transients.

skills.search_text: ft-icr-transient-reconstruction Use when you have raw low-resolution FT-ICR transients (e.g., 64k-point MALDI FT-ICR MSI or SCMS acquisitions) and need high-resolution, high-SNR spectra without the acquisition time of full 1M-point transients. Input is already a high-resolution (1M-point) transient — reconstruction provides no benefit and the model is not trained for this domain. The goal is a rapid visual spectrum with no need for high mass resolution; traditional FT of the 64k transient suffices when only coarse peak lists are required. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Applies the MEISTER trained decoder/regressor to reconstruct high-mass-resolving (1M-point, ~160,000 resolution at m/z 400) FT-ICR mass spectra from short-transient (64,000-point, ~10,000 resolution) raw time-domain data, delivering ~15× throughput acceleration and large SNR gains over conventional Fourier-transform processing. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-024-02171-3
skills.summary: Applies the MEISTER trained decoder/regressor to reconstruct high-mass-resolving (1M-point, ~160,000 resolution at m/z 400) FT-ICR mass spectra from short-transient (64,000-point, ~10,000 resolution) raw time-domain data, delivering ~15× throughput acceleration and large SNR gains over conventional Fourier-transform processing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a high-resolution (1M-point) transient — reconstruction provides no benefit and the model is not trained for this domain. Datasets come from excessively disparate chromatographic techniques (e.g. RPLC vs HILIC) where elution order is not preserved — the RT mapping itself, and hence its error metrics, are not meaningful. Abundance or RT values have been normalized or transformed so that ranked abundance/RT order information is destroyed, invalidating the anchor-based evaluation. Evaluating fit_loess rather than GAM models — the scaled-t family rationale and mgcv backing described here apply to fit_gam specifically. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Evaluate the quality of a fit_gam (GAM) retention-time mapping model by computing mean absolute prediction error on held-out known-feature anchors, using the scaled-t family to resist outlier influence. Only one experimental condition is present — use the group's single-group tool CorrelationCalculator instead of the two-condition joint estimation Pathway-database enrichment is the goal and metabolites are well-annotated endogenous compounds mappable to KEGG — the data-driven GGM approach targets exogenous, secondary, and unknown metabolites that pathway analysis cannot map The dataset has far more samples than features so unregularized partial correlation estimation is feasible without the GLASSO penalty http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Jointly estimate partial-correlation (Gaussian graphical model) networks for two experimental conditions from metabolomics peak-intensity data using GLASSO regularization with a tuned or approximated lambda penalty, as implemented in the DNEA R package. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-024-05994-1
skills.summary: Jointly estimate partial-correlation (Gaussian graphical model) networks for two experimental conditions from metabolomics peak-intensity data using GLASSO regularization with a tuned or approximated lambda penalty, as implemented in the DNEA R package.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only one experimental condition is present — use the group's single-group tool CorrelationCalculator instead of the two-condition joint estimation Pathway-database enrichment is the goal and metabolites are well-annotated endogenous compounds mappable to KEGG — the data-driven GGM approach targets exogenous, secondary, and unknown metabolites that pathway analysis cannot map The dataset has far more samples than features so unregularized partial correlation estimation is feasible without the GLASSO penalty

skills.description: Use when estimating partial-correlation metabolite-metabolite networks under p >> n with DNEA, after BIC tuning of lambda, and before getNetworks(), to stabilize edge inclusion via resampling.
skills.name: gaussian-graphical-model-resampling
skills.search_text: gaussian-graphical-model-resampling Use when estimating partial-correlation metabolite-metabolite networks under p >> n with DNEA, after BIC tuning of lambda, and before getNetworks(), to stabilize edge inclusion via resampling. When analyzing a single experimental group — DNEA's stability selection is built for joint estimation across two conditions and subsampling equalization of two groups When the input is raw peak-intensity data that has not been pre-processed, feature-aggregated (aggregateFeatures), and lambda-tuned (BICtune) — selection probabilities would be conditioned on an untuned penalty When the goal is marginal correlation networks for exploratory co-occurrence — partial-correlation GGMs target direct associations and the resampling machinery is unnecessary overhead http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Stability-selection step of the DNEA workflow that repeatedly refits GLASSO-based Gaussian graphical models on randomly subsampled data (1000 replicates via BiocParallel) to compute per-edge selection probabilities, which then weight the regularization parameter for final network estimation. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-024-05994-1
skills.summary: Stability-selection step of the DNEA workflow that repeatedly refits GLASSO-based Gaussian graphical models on randomly subsampled data (1000 replicates via BiocParallel) to compute per-edge selection probabilities, which then weight the regularization parameter for final network estimation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When analyzing a single experimental group — DNEA's stability selection is built for joint estimation across two conditions and subsampling equalization of two groups When the input is raw peak-intensity data that has not been pre-processed, feature-aggregated (aggregateFeatures), and lambda-tuned (BICtune) — selection probabilities would be conditioned on an untuned penalty When the goal is marginal correlation networks for exploratory co-occurrence — partial-correlation GGMs target direct associations and the resampling machinery is unnecessary overhead

skills.description: Use when fitting a semi-parametric kernel machine regression g(Y)=Xβ+h(Z)+ϵ on pathway metabolite features and need a Gaussian kernel whose bandwidth is calibrated from the data.
skills.name: gaussian-kernel-bandwidth-calibration
skills.search_text: gaussian-kernel-bandwidth-calibration Use when fitting a semi-parametric kernel machine regression g(Y)=Xβ+h(Z)+ϵ on pathway metabolite features and need a Gaussian kernel whose bandwidth is calibrated from the data. The pathway graph is disconnected and has not been regularized — the article notes the unregularized normalized Laplacian hindered testing performance on disconnected graphs Very large cohorts (over 1,000 observations) where p-values from the compared methods were indistinguishable from one another, so the pathway-smoothed kernel adds little practical gain http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3366 Constructs the Gaussian (radial basis) kernel for PaIRKAT's kernel machine regression using metabolite features smoothed through the regularized normalized Laplacian of a pathway graph, with the bandwidth parameter set to the median pairwise distance. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2021.04.23.440821
skills.summary: Constructs the Gaussian (radial basis) kernel for PaIRKAT's kernel machine regression using metabolite features smoothed through the regularized normalized Laplacian of a pathway graph, with the bandwidth parameter set to the median pairwise distance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The pathway graph is disconnected and has not been regularized — the article notes the unregularized normalized Laplacian hindered testing performance on disconnected graphs Very large cohorts (over 1,000 observations) where p-values from the compared methods were indistinguishable from one another, so the pathway-smoothed kernel adds little practical gain
