skills.search_text: hierarchical-unwanted-variation-normalisation Use when a large-scale metabolomics matrix spans multiple 96-well plates/batches with embedded replicate structure (pooled QC, short replicates, batch replicates) and you must correct signal drift and inter-batch unwanted variation while retaining biological signal. When there is only a single batch and no embedded intra- or inter-batch replicates — hierarchical merging of neighbouring batches and RUV-III batch correction have no replicate structure to estimate unwanted variation from. When the input is a missing-value-laden matrix without an imputation step — hRUV expects data without missing values, so imputation (e.g. knn/impute) is required first. When the goal is drift correction only on pooled-QC-identical assumptions for a small study — existing single-step normalisation methods may suffice and hierarchical RUV is unnecessary. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0219 Normalises multi-batch large-scale metabolomics data (e.g. BioHEART-CT plasma LC-MS/MS abundances) by progressively merging RUV-III adjustments across neighbouring batches using embedded intra-batch (pooled QC, short) and inter-batch sample replicates, as implemented in the hRUV R package. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2020.12.21.423723
skills.summary: Normalises multi-batch large-scale metabolomics data (e.g. BioHEART-CT plasma LC-MS/MS abundances) by progressively merging RUV-III adjustments across neighbouring batches using embedded intra-batch (pooled QC, short) and inter-batch sample replicates, as implemented in the hRUV R package.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When there is only a single batch and no embedded intra- or inter-batch replicates — hierarchical merging of neighbouring batches and RUV-III batch correction have no replicate structure to estimate unwanted variation from. When the input is a missing-value-laden matrix without an imputation step — hRUV expects data without missing values, so imputation (e.g. knn/impute) is required first. Input is raw MS/MS spectra (e.g. an .mgf file) rather than an already computed GNPS molecular network — mine the spectra first with mineMS2 or GNPS before extracting components The goal is de novo fragmentation pattern mining from spectra, not selecting spectra subsets from an existing network — use the mineMS2 frequent-subgraph mining workflow (discretizeMzDifferences, graph building, subgraph mining) instead Probabilistic motif discovery (MS2LDA-style distributions of fragments and losses) is desired rather than exact graph-based similarity extraction from a GNPS network http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Extracts high-similarity spectrum pairs from a precomputed GNPS molecular network by thresholding the edge similarity attribute (pairThreshold=0.9 in the mineMS2 Penicillium nordicum workflow), alongside connected components and disjoint cliques, using findGNPSComponents on a simplified igraph object. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-025-01051-y

skills.description: Use when a spectral mixture reconstruction has been cast as a minimum cost flow LP on the mcfNMR network (compound hubs, peak nodes, capacity-limited mixture nodes, absorption sink) and must be solved to optimality to obtain flow assignments and concentration factors.
skills.name: highs-lp-solver-via-scipy-interface
skills.search_text: highs-lp-solver-via-scipy-interface Use when a spectral mixture reconstruction has been cast as a minimum cost flow LP on the mcfNMR network (compound hubs, peak nodes, capacity-limited mixture nodes, absorption sink) and must be solved to optimality to obtain flow assignments and concentration factors. Peak matching is purely local (assignment radius) rather than global EMD-style redistribution, so do not use this LP formulation when a global Wasserstein-distance transport over the full spectrum without capacity limits is intended. The compound library lacks spectra of some mixture constituents, since a complete reconstruction requires knowledge of every constituent's peak pattern and unknown compounds cannot be recovered by the flow. The problem is not a linear program but a nonlinear or combinatorial optimization (e.g. direct discrete peak classification), which HiGHS via SciPy cannot handle. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Solves the mcfNMR minimum cost flow linear program (eq 8) using the HiGHS optimization backend invoked through the SciPy interface, yielding the optimal flow assignment from which compound concentration factors alpha_k and detection indicators are extracted. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c01652
skills.summary: Solves the mcfNMR minimum cost flow linear program (eq 8) using the HiGHS optimization backend invoked through the SciPy interface, yielding the optimal flow assignment from which compound concentration factors alpha_k and detection indicators are extracted.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Peak matching is purely local (assignment radius) rather than global EMD-style redistribution, so do not use this LP formulation when a global Wasserstein-distance transport over the full spectrum without capacity limits is intended. The compound library lacks spectra of some mixture constituents, since a complete reconstruction requires knowledge of every constituent's peak pattern and unknown compounds cannot be recovered by the flow. The problem is not a linear program but a nonlinear or combinatorial optimization (e.g. direct discrete peak classification), which HiGHS via SciPy cannot handle.

skills.description: Use when you have raw mzML files from HILIC positive-mode serum/plasma LC/MS studies (ideally multiple studies) and need a feature matrix suitable for downstream ML: signal detection without manual parameters, cross-study alignment, RT drift correction, and filtering to reproducible features.

The data are negative-mode, reversed-phase, or otherwise non-HILIC-positive LC/MS — the article states the current pre-trained model was developed specifically for HILIC positive mode. You need de-isotoping or MS/MS-level compound identification — mzLearn outputs are limited to the ion MS1 level, and mapping to MS/MS spectra must be carried out with downstream workflows. You already have a processed feature table and only need downstream annotation — this skill covers raw-mzML-to-feature-matrix generation and alignment, not annotation itself. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0153 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 A cross-study processing and pretraining pipeline for HILIC positive-mode LC/MS serum untargeted metabolomics: raw mzML files are run through mzLearn's zero-parameter signal detection, aligned across studies, filtered to robust peak groups, and used to pretrain a VAE whose encoder can be fine-tuned on new cohorts. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.01.26.634927
skills.summary: A cross-study processing and pretraining pipeline for HILIC positive-mode LC/MS serum untargeted metabolomics: raw mzML files are run through mzLearn's zero-parameter signal detection, aligned across studies, filtered to robust peak groups, and used to pretrain a VAE whose encoder can be fine-tuned on new cohorts.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are negative-mode, reversed-phase, or otherwise non-HILIC-positive LC/MS — the article states the current pre-trained model was developed specifically for HILIC positive mode. You need de-isotoping or MS/MS-level compound identification — mzLearn outputs are limited to the ion MS1 level, and mapping to MS/MS spectra must be carried out with downstream workflows. You already have a processed feature table and only need downstream annotation — this skill covers raw-mzML-to-feature-matrix generation and alignment, not annotation itself.

skills.when_to_use_negative: The analytes are complex, high molecular weight lipids such as triacylglycerols or phosphatidylcholines — these were largely excluded from the training set and predictions may be erroneous The compounds lie outside the chemical landscape of the training set (the article warns predictions 'may be more erroneous' and accuracy is limited by training-set size and chemical diversity) You need to discriminate closely eluting isomers in short ~12 min UPLC methods, since 1 min prediction errors preclude this and ~1 min windows excluded about 25% of true positives

skills.description: Use when you have fitted Retip Keras RT-prediction models (HILIC and/or RPLC descriptor tables from Retip getCD() plus ChemAxon pKa) and need to rank descriptor importances to explain retention mechanisms per chromatographic mode.
skills.name: hilic-versus-rplc-descriptor-mechanism-interpretation
skills.search_text: hilic-versus-rplc-descriptor-mechanism-interpretation Use when you have fitted Retip Keras RT-prediction models (HILIC and/or RPLC descriptor tables from Retip getCD() plus ChemAxon pKa) and need to rank descriptor importances to explain retention mechanisms per chromatographic mode. You need accurate retention predictions for new compounds rather than model interpretation — importance ranking does not improve MAE, which remains about ±1 min (0.78 min HILIC, 0.57 min RPLC). Your compounds fall outside the chemical landscape of the Fiehn HILIC/RPLC training sets (e.g. complex high-molecular-weight lipids such as triacylglycerols or phosphatidylcholines, which were largely excluded) — the learned descriptor importances may not transfer. skills.summary: Interpret trained Retip Keras retention-time models by extracting and ranking relative chemical-descriptor importances separately for the HILIC (880-compound Fiehn training set) and RPLC (398-compound training set) models, revealing which molecular properties (e.g. XLogP, ALogP, Basic Group Count, pKa) drive retention on each chromatographic mode.

skills.summary: Module 1 of the metGWAS 1.0 R workflow: after filtering MetaboAnalyst KEGG pathway over-representation results to FDR (q-value) ≤ 0.05, the metabolites of each significant pathway are retrieved from the KEGG database via an RSelenium browser call-out and mapped to HMDB IDs using the MetaboAnalyst name_map table. These per-pathway HMDB metabolite sets are the identifier space through which metGWAS 1.0 subsequently maps metabolites to interacting genes via the Human Metabolome Database.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No pathway in pathway_results.csv passes the FDR ≤ 0.05 threshold — the selection step yields nothing and the KEGG call-out should not be run Input metabolomics data is not a MetaboAnalyst output set (no name_map.csv) — the KEGG-to-HMDB mapping central to this skill cannot be performed The goal is building genomic gene sets from the GWAS Catalog network rather than annotating the metabolites of selected KEGG pathways

skills.description: Use when building a reference metabolite library from HMDB NMR assignments — i.e., extracting per-metabolite chemical shift peaks (ppm) and SRRM multiplet regions needed for spectral region-of-interest (ROI) matching in untargeted NMR metabolomics.
skills.name: hmdb-chemical-shift-parsing
skills.search_text: hmdb-chemical-shift-parsing Use when building a reference metabolite library from HMDB NMR assignments — i.e., extracting per-metabolite chemical shift peaks (ppm) and SRRM multiplet regions needed for spectral region-of-interest (ROI) matching in untargeted NMR metabolomics. You need automated ROI identification or absolute metabolite quantification — ROIAL-NMR explicitly treats both as beyond its scope You need a reference database beyond what HMDB NMR assignments cover — note that ROIAL-NMR can also ingest BMRB and other NMR-assignment databases, so forcing everything through HMDB parsing may be the wrong path You need auto-synced chemical shift databases — periodic/automatic synchronization of NMR chemical shift databases is planned but not yet implemented http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 Parse 1H NMR chemical shift assignments from the Human Metabolome Database (HMDB) into program-specific metabolic libraries of chemical shift values and spectral region resonance multiplets (SRRMs) for 891 metabolites, organized by biosample type (serum, plasma, CSF, feces, saliva, sweat, urine), so that downstream ROI-matching (ROIAL-NMR) can identify potential metabolites within ~5 seconds. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/nbm.70131
skills.summary: Parse 1H NMR chemical shift assignments from the Human Metabolome Database (HMDB) into program-specific metabolic libraries of chemical shift values and spectral region resonance multiplets (SRRMs) for 891 metabolites, organized by biosample type (serum, plasma, CSF, feces, saliva, sweat, urine), so that downstream ROI-matching (ROIAL-NMR) can identify potential metabolites within ~5 seconds.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need automated ROI identification or absolute metabolite quantification — ROIAL-NMR explicitly treats both as beyond its scope You need a reference database beyond what HMDB NMR assignments cover — note that ROIAL-NMR can also ingest BMRB and other NMR-assignment databases, so forcing everything through HMDB parsing may be the wrong path You need auto-synced chemical shift databases — periodic/automatic synchronization of NMR chemical shift databases is planned but not yet implemented

skills.description: Use when an MS1 metabolite-annotation workflow needs a reference library of monoisotopic compound masses retrieved from public HMDB to match query m/z values (neutral mass plus adduct shift) against.
skills.name: hmdb-compound-mass-retrieval
skills.search_text: hmdb-compound-mass-retrieval Use when an MS1 metabolite-annotation workflow needs a reference library of monoisotopic compound masses retrieved from public HMDB to match query m/z values (neutral mass plus adduct shift) against. The task is MS2 spectral comparison or spectral quality assessment — CMM 3.0 provides dedicated services for those, distinct from MS1 mass-based candidate retrieval. Annotating oxidized glycerophosphocholines / oxidized lipids: CMM adds an in-house library of oxidized lipids 'not present in other sources', so HMDB retrieval alone will miss them. Input is already a scored/filtered candidate table — this skill only provisions the reference masses upstream of the expert-system filtering step. http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Retrieves monoisotopic compound masses from the public HMDB (Human Metabolome Database) to build the reference mass library that CEU Mass Mediator matches MS1 query m/z values (neutral mass plus adduct shift) against. This provisioning step feeds CMM's expert-system filtering and scoring of candidate metabolite annotations. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.8b00720
skills.summary: Retrieves monoisotopic compound masses from the public HMDB (Human Metabolome Database) to build the reference mass library that CEU Mass Mediator matches MS1 query m/z values (neutral mass plus adduct shift) against. This provisioning step feeds CMM's expert-system filtering and scoring of candidate metabolite annotations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is MS2 spectral comparison or spectral quality assessment — CMM 3.0 provides dedicated services for those, distinct from MS1 mass-based candidate retrieval. Annotating oxidized glycerophosphocholines / oxidized lipids: CMM adds an in-house library of oxidized lipids 'not present in other sources', so HMDB retrieval alone will miss them. Input is already a scored/filtered candidate table — this skill only provisions the reference masses upstream of the expert-system filtering step.

skills.search_text: hmdb-data-ingestion Use when a metabolomics annotation workflow needs a local, reproducible reference database of compounds plus experimental MS2 spectra built from an HMDB release, rather than querying HMDB online. When an existing CompDb.Hsapiens.HMDB.5.0.sqlite is already available — the correct step is to load it with CompDb(), not rebuild it from HMDB sources. When the annotation target database is not HMDB (e.g. MassBank or GNPS-derived libraries); other backends such as MsBackendMassbank or MsBackendMgf cover those formats. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Builds a portable, self-contained CompoundDb (CompDb) SQLite reference annotation database from the Human Metabolome Database (HMDB) version 5.0 data release, containing compound annotations and experimental (non-predicted) MS2 spectra for downstream MS1/MS2 metabolomics annotation in R. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo12020173
skills.summary: Builds a portable, self-contained CompoundDb (CompDb) SQLite reference annotation database from the Human Metabolome Database (HMDB) version 5.0 data release, containing compound annotations and experimental (non-predicted) MS2 spectra for downstream MS1/MS2 metabolomics annotation in R.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When an existing CompDb.Hsapiens.HMDB.5.0.sqlite is already available — the correct step is to load it with CompDb(), not rebuild it from HMDB sources. When the goal is to annotate experimental spectra against a reference (MS2 spectral matching via matchSpectra); this skill only creates the reference database, it does not perform matching. When the annotation target database is not HMDB (e.g. MassBank or GNPS-derived libraries); other backends such as MsBackendMassbank or MsBackendMgf cover those formats.

skills.name: hmdb-metabolite-database-querying
skills.search_text: hmdb-metabolite-database-querying Use when you have user-defined proton NMR spectral ROIs (e.g., 0.5–4.5 ppm biofluid regions) and need to identify candidate metabolites by matching HMDB chemical shift peaks and SRRMs, avoiding over-identification in crowded spectra. When the goal is absolute quantification of compounds — the article states 'absolute quantification of the compounds is not the primary aim of the program'. When ROIs need to be identified automatically from spectra — 'Automated identification of ROIs is beyond the scope of the current version of the program'. skills.summary: Query the Human Metabolome Database (HMDB) for metabolite-specific chemical shift peaks and SRRMs (metabolite-specific resonance ranges), then score candidates against user-defined NMR ROIs using a match-ratio rule (retain metabolites with ≥50% of SRRMs matched to analyzed ROIs) so metabolites present in multiple spectral regions are not over-identified.

When validating the accuracy of user-defined ROIs — 'ROIAL-NMR was not built to test the accuracy of the user-defined ROIs'.

skills.description: Use when a metabolomics result has been annotated with HMDB IDs and you must build the metabolite-interacting gene set (UniProt IDs → current human gene symbols) that metGWAS 1.0 needs for its hypergeometric over-representation test.
skills.name: hmdb-protein-interaction-retrieval
skills.search_text: hmdb-protein-interaction-retrieval Use when a metabolomics result has been annotated with HMDB IDs and you must build the metabolite-interacting gene set (UniProt IDs → current human gene symbols) that metGWAS 1.0 needs for its hypergeometric over-representation test. Input metabolites lack HMDB IDs (e.g., only KEGG or InChIKey annotations), so their HMDB pages cannot be located by ID search. You already have paired metabolomics-GWAS data; this skill addresses the unpaired, standalone setting that is limited to genes with known metabolite interactions. The needed output is the genomic gene set from the GWAS Catalog network (GWASnetwork_discoverableGenesOnly_2021_10_14.RData), which this HMDB-retrieval module does not produce. http://edamontology.org/topic_3489 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Module 2 of the metGWAS 1.0 R workflow: it builds the metabolic gene set by searching each input metabolite's HMDB ID in the Human Metabolome Database (via RSelenium browser automation), harvesting the interacting proteins annotated as UniProt IDs, and mapping them to current human gene symbols for downstream hypergeometric over-representation analysis against GWAS Catalog-derived gene sets. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad523
skills.summary: Module 2 of the metGWAS 1.0 R workflow: it builds the metabolic gene set by searching each input metabolite's HMDB ID in the Human Metabolome Database (via RSelenium browser automation), harvesting the interacting proteins annotated as UniProt IDs, and mapping them to current human gene symbols for downstream hypergeometric over-representation analysis against GWAS Catalog-derived gene sets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input metabolites lack HMDB IDs (e.g., only KEGG or InChIKey annotations), so their HMDB pages cannot be located by ID search. You already have paired metabolomics-GWAS data; this skill addresses the unpaired, standalone setting that is limited to genes with known metabolite interactions. The needed output is the genomic gene set from the GWAS Catalog network (GWASnetwork_discoverableGenesOnly_2021_10_14.RData), which this HMDB-retrieval module does not produce.

skills.name: hmdb-reference-database-querying
skills.search_text: hmdb-reference-database-querying Use when an annotation step needs candidate metabolites with exact masses and formulas from HMDB 5.0, e.g. to feed m/z-based matching of chromatographic peaks via matchMz/Mass2MzParam. When the annotation strategy needs MS2 fragment spectra rather than exact-mass/m-z lookup — Spectra/MsBackendMassbank or reference spectral libraries are the appropriate reference instead of the HMDB CompDb When the target compounds are not metabolite-like/small molecules covered by HMDB 5.0; CompoundDb supports creating custom databases for other compound sets When a lightweight m/z-only search against a flat text list (e.g. std_ions.txt) suffices — building/querying a full CompDb adds overhead http://edamontology.org/topic_0218 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Loading and querying a CompoundDb-built HMDB 5.0 reference database (CompDb.Hsapiens.HMDB.5.0.sqlite) to supply compound identifiers, exact masses, formulas and names that downstream MetaboAnnotation matching (e.g. matchMz with Mass2MzParam) consumes as annotation targets. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo12020173
skills.summary: Loading and querying a CompoundDb-built HMDB 5.0 reference database (CompDb.Hsapiens.HMDB.5.0.sqlite) to supply compound identifiers, exact masses, formulas and names that downstream MetaboAnnotation matching (e.g. matchMz with Mass2MzParam) consumes as annotation targets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the annotation strategy needs MS2 fragment spectra rather than exact-mass/m-z lookup — Spectra/MsBackendMassbank or reference spectral libraries are the appropriate reference instead of the HMDB CompDb When the target compounds are not metabolite-like/small molecules covered by HMDB 5.0; CompoundDb supports creating custom databases for other compound sets When a lightweight m/z-only search against a flat text list (e.g. std_ions.txt) suffices — building/querying a full CompDb adds overhead

skills.description: Use when preparing HMDB-derived SMILES datasets in the {SMILES String: [[Question, Answer], ...]} format so each metabolite yields a molecular graph and image that downstream GNN/CNN encoders can encode for MetaboliteChat training.
skills.name: hmdb-smiles-dataset-preparation
skills.search_text: hmdb-smiles-dataset-preparation Use when preparing HMDB-derived SMILES datasets in the {SMILES String: [[Question, Answer], ...]} format so each metabolite yields a molecular graph and image that downstream GNN/CNN encoders can encode for MetaboliteChat training. The molecular graphs and images have already been generated and the pretrained checkpoints are in place — re-running the featurisation is redundant The dataset is not SMILES-keyed HMDB metabolite data (e.g. non-molecular text corpora) — RDKit cannot parse it into molecular graphs You are only running inference with the released checkpoint (152,222-metabolite model) and not rebuilding the training dataset http://edamontology.org/topic_3334 http://edamontology.org/topic_3316 Converts HMDB-derived SMILES instruction-tuning data (keyed {SMILES String: [[Question, Answer], ...]}) into per-molecule molecular graphs and rendered molecular images using RDKit inside a dedicated rdkit conda environment, so pretrained GNN and CNN encoders can featurize them for MetaboliteChat's projection layer. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.11.07.687008
skills.summary: Converts HMDB-derived SMILES instruction-tuning data (keyed {SMILES String: [[Question, Answer], ...]}) into per-molecule molecular graphs and rendered molecular images using RDKit inside a dedicated rdkit conda environment, so pretrained GNN and CNN encoders can featurize them for MetaboliteChat's projection layer.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The molecular graphs and images have already been generated and the pretrained checkpoints are in place — re-running the featurisation is redundant The dataset is not SMILES-keyed HMDB metabolite data (e.g. non-molecular text corpora) — RDKit cannot parse it into molecular graphs You are only running inference with the released checkpoint (152,222-metabolite model) and not rebuilding the training dataset

skills.description: Use when untargeted 1H NMR spectra have user-defined ROIs (e.g. 0.5-4.5 ppm curve-fitted peaks) and metabolites must be identified by matching HMDB chemical shifts and SRRMs within those ROIs rather than by whole-spectrum database search.
skills.name: hmdb-spectral-database-matching
skills.search_text: hmdb-spectral-database-matching Use when untargeted 1H NMR spectra have user-defined ROIs (e.g. 0.5-4.5 ppm curve-fitted peaks) and metabolites must be identified by matching HMDB chemical shifts and SRRMs within those ROIs rather than by whole-spectrum database search. You need automated ROI detection — automated identification of ROIs is beyond the scope of the current version; ROIs must be supplied by the user. You need absolute quantification — absolute quantification of compounds is not the primary aim of the program. You want to validate or test the accuracy of user-defined ROIs — ROIAL-NMR was not built for that purpose, and user variability in ROI creation can yield variable results. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 ROI-based metabolite identification for untargeted 1H NMR (ROIAL-NMR): candidates are proposed by matching user-defined spectral regions-of-interest against HMDB chemical shift values and metabolite-specific SRRMs for 891 metabolites, then filtered by match ratio, significance, and 5 uM concentration cutoffs. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/nbm.70131
skills.summary: ROI-based metabolite identification for untargeted 1H NMR (ROIAL-NMR): candidates are proposed by matching user-defined spectral regions-of-interest against HMDB chemical shift values and metabolite-specific SRRMs for 891 metabolites, then filtered by match ratio, significance, and 5 uM concentration cutoffs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need automated ROI detection — automated identification of ROIs is beyond the scope of the current version; ROIs must be supplied by the user. You need absolute quantification — absolute quantification of compounds is not the primary aim of the program. You want to validate or test the accuracy of user-defined ROIs — ROIAL-NMR was not built for that purpose, and user variability in ROI creation can yield variable results.

skills.description: Use when a metabolomics matrix's columns are raw metabolite names (e.g., plasma_breast_cancer.csv) that must be converted to standard HMDB IDs before pathway mapping or PDS-score computation in Lilikoi.
skills.name: hmdb-standard-id-lookup
skills.search_text: hmdb-standard-id-lookup Use when a metabolomics matrix's columns are raw metabolite names (e.g., plasma_breast_cancer.csv) that must be converted to standard HMDB IDs before pathway mapping or PDS-score computation in Lilikoi. Input metabolites are already identified by standard HMDB/PubChem/METLIN IDs and only need pathway assignment, not name standardization You need group-level pathway enrichment (MetPA, IMPaLA, MPEA style) rather than sample-level ID standardization feeding a personalized PDS pipeline A very small fraction of query names will survive matching and the mapping step would add noise rather than value (expect ~20% of names to remain unmapped) http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Standardizes user-provided metabolite names to standard HMDB IDs using Lilikoi's feature-pathway mapper, which chains exact matching, synonym-database lookup, and Levenshtein-distance fuzzy matching, and then maps IDs to pathways via lilikoi.metab_to_pathway. This is the first step of the Lilikoi metabolomics pipeline and gates all downstream pathway-based modeling. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/gigascience/giy136
skills.summary: Standardizes user-provided metabolite names to standard HMDB IDs using Lilikoi's feature-pathway mapper, which chains exact matching, synonym-database lookup, and Levenshtein-distance fuzzy matching, and then maps IDs to pathways via lilikoi.metab_to_pathway. This is the first step of the Lilikoi metabolomics pipeline and gates all downstream pathway-based modeling.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input metabolites are already identified by standard HMDB/PubChem/METLIN IDs and only need pathway assignment, not name standardization You need group-level pathway enrichment (MetPA, IMPaLA, MPEA style) rather than sample-level ID standardization feeding a personalized PDS pipeline A very small fraction of query names will survive matching and the mapping step would add noise rather than value (expect ~20% of names to remain unmapped)

skills.name: hmdb-structure-database-parsing
skills.search_text: hmdb-structure-database-parsing Use when annotating MALDI-MSI m/z features against a derivatizing matrix (e.g. FMP-10) and you need HMDB/LIPID MAPS structures filtered to compounds bearing matrix-reactive functional groups. The MALDI-MSI dataset uses a conventional matrix where annotation is based on common [M+H]+ / [M-H]- ions rather than on-tissue derivatization The target database is Metlin or GNPS (LC-MS oriented) rather than the HMDB/LIPID MAPS structures Met-ID parses into SQLite You already have a derivatized-candidate subset or site-count table and only need MS2 spectral comparison or mass recalibration http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Parses HMDB (and LIPID MAPS) metabolite structure records into sanitized RDKit molecular objects and SQLite tables so that derivatizing-matrix annotation (e.g. FMP-10) can filter candidates by derivatizable functional groups. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c00633
skills.summary: Parses HMDB (and LIPID MAPS) metabolite structure records into sanitized RDKit molecular objects and SQLite tables so that derivatizing-matrix annotation (e.g. FMP-10) can filter candidates by derivatizable functional groups.

skills.search_text: hmdb-subclass-annotation-mapping Use when you have a list of metabolite annotations uniquely captured by METASPACE-ML at the 10% FDR threshold (split by animal vs. plant datasets) and need to identify which HMDB chemical taxonomy subclasses are significantly overrepresented. skills.summary: Maps METASPACE-ML-exclusive metabolite annotations (identified at 10% FDR in imaging MS datasets) to HMDB chemical taxonomy subclasses and tests each subclass for overrepresentation with a one-tailed Fisher exact test, comparing animal-tissue versus plant datasets.

skills.description: Use when a structure-generating model predates a database version bump (e.g., HMDB v4→v5) and you want to test whether its sampling frequency ranks newly added, previously unknown metabolites above other generated molecules.
skills.name: hmdb-version-diff-prospective-evaluation
skills.search_text: hmdb-version-diff-prospective-evaluation Use when a structure-generating model predates a database version bump (e.g., HMDB v4→v5) and you want to test whether its sampling frequency ranks newly added, previously unknown metabolites above other generated molecules. The model was trained on the same database version you are evaluating against — any 'prospective' gain would be circular; only metabolites newly added after training (HMDB v4→v5 diff) qualify. You lack the model's sampling frequencies or generated-structure database — the ROC and enrichment analysis cannot be computed from reference lists alone. You need to evaluate metabolites from evolutionarily distant organisms (e.g., plant or bacterial metabolism), where the article notes a bespoke model trained on human metabolite structures is likely required. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Evaluates whether a generative chemical language model's sampling frequencies prospectively anticipate metabolites discovered after model training, by diffing metabolites newly added in a later database release (HMDB v5.0) against the released set of generated structures and computing enrichment/ROC metrics. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.11.13.623458
skills.summary: Evaluates whether a generative chemical language model's sampling frequencies prospectively anticipate metabolites discovered after model training, by diffing metabolites newly added in a later database release (HMDB v5.0) against the released set of generated structures and computing enrichment/ROC metrics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The model was trained on the same database version you are evaluating against — any 'prospective' gain would be circular; only metabolites newly added after training (HMDB v4→v5 diff) qualify. You lack the model's sampling frequencies or generated-structure database — the ROC and enrichment analysis cannot be computed from reference lists alone. You need to evaluate metabolites from evolutionarily distant organisms (e.g., plant or bacterial metabolism), where the article notes a bespoke model trained on human metabolite structures is likely required.

The goal is production BGC detection in new genomes — the HMM is the weaker comparator and the paper shows DeepBGC outperforms it in both accuracy and novel-class detection Input is raw nucleotide sequence rather than Pfam-annotated domain TSVs; sequences must first be prepared (e.g. deepbgc prepare) into Pfam TSV format Evaluating extrapolation to BGC classes absent from training data — that requires the leave-class-out analysis, not this cross-validation setup http://edamontology.org/topic_0797 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Trains and scores a Hidden Markov Model BGC detector (ClusterFinder) on Pfam-domain training matrices as the classical machine-learning baseline against which DeepBGC's BiLSTM RNN detector is compared in 10-fold cross-validation on MIBiG positives vs artificial negatives. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkz654

skills.description: Use when processing untargeted LC-HRMS/MS data (e.g. aqueous film forming foam or environmental samples) to discover PFAS homologous series and assign per-compound confidence levels beyond a small targeted PFOA/PFOS panel.
skills.name: homologous-series-matching
skills.search_text: homologous-series-matching Use when processing untargeted LC-HRMS/MS data (e.g. aqueous film forming foam or environmental samples) to discover PFAS homologous series and assign per-compound confidence levels beyond a small targeted PFOA/PFOS panel. The original FluoroMatch release's suspect-screening approach is the right choice when you only want to target compounds with available MS/MS spectra rather than discover unknown/uncommon PFAS. Analysis is general small-molecule or lipid non-targeted screening; here the pipeline is PFAS-specific unless Lipid <- TRUE is set for lipids. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 Automated detection and structural annotation of PFAS homologous series in LC-HRMS/MS data using FluoroMatch 2.0, which chains feature detection, blank/mass-defect filtering, exact mass matching, retention-time pattern analysis, and class-based MS/MS screening to replace tedious manual series surveying. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s00216-021-03392-7
skills.summary: Automated detection and structural annotation of PFAS homologous series in LC-HRMS/MS data using FluoroMatch 2.0, which chains feature detection, blank/mass-defect filtering, exact mass matching, retention-time pattern analysis, and class-based MS/MS screening to replace tedious manual series surveying.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The original FluoroMatch release's suspect-screening approach is the right choice when you only want to target compounds with available MS/MS spectra rather than discover unknown/uncommon PFAS. Analysis is general small-molecule or lipid non-targeted screening; here the pipeline is PFAS-specific unless Lipid <- TRUE is set for lipids.

skills.search_text: hrms-eic-extraction-from-mzml Use when you have raw HRMS peak data in mzML plus a validated compound list (CSV) of target or suspect masses, and you need EICs, MS2 scans, and per-peak quality flags before full identification. The input is already a processed feature table or peak list rather than raw vendor-independent mzML data — no extraction from raw scans is needed. You need untargeted peak detection across the full feature space (not just preselected compound/mass lists); tools like xcms, RforMassSpectrometry or patRoon are designed for that, whereas this skill extracts only listed masses. You need full compound identification rather than prescreening/QC — this skill only flags quality and selects representative MS2 spectra for downstream tools such as MetFrag. http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Extract MS1 extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) and corresponding MS2 spectral scans for a preselected list of compounds or masses from a high-resolution mass spectrometry mzML file using MSnbase/mzR, then apply threshold-based quality assessment per MS1 parent data point. This is the extraction and prescreening stage of vendor-independent first-look HRMS inspection workflows such as Shinyscreen. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-025-01044-x

This is the extraction and prescreening stage of vendor-independent first-look HRMS inspection workflows such as Shinyscreen.

skills.description: Use when a pre-processed HRMS feature table (e.g., Agilent .csv export, features x samples) needs grouping by abundance-trend similarity — e.g., to flag candidate transformation products across a time course or isolate contaminant source fingerprints from dilution/mixing series.
skills.name: hrms-feature-clustering
skills.search_text: hrms-feature-clustering Use when a pre-processed HRMS feature table (e.g., Agilent .csv export, features x samples) needs grouping by abundance-trend similarity — e.g., to flag candidate transformation products across a time course or isolate contaminant source fingerprints from dilution/mixing series. Input is still raw .mzML data — run mssmain.get_scans and mssmain.peak_pick (with peak width, replicated-peak, and background-subtraction filters) to build the feature table first The goal is feature annotation or MS/MS identification (use mss.frag with MoNA MassBank searching), not grouping by abundance trend Feature labels are already known and a supervised approach is intended — use dm.feature_model regression instead of unsupervised clustering http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Unsupervised clustering of HRMS non-targeted analysis feature tables using the Mass-Suite (MSS) dm.ms_cluster function, which Z-score normalizes feature abundances and groups features with similar abundance trends via DBSCAN (or OPTICS) to support transformation-product prioritization and source-fingerprint discovery. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-023-00741-9
skills.summary: Unsupervised clustering of HRMS non-targeted analysis feature tables using the Mass-Suite (MSS) dm.ms_cluster function, which Z-score normalizes feature abundances and groups features with similar abundance trends via DBSCAN (or OPTICS) to support transformation-product prioritization and source-fingerprint discovery.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is still raw .mzML data — run mssmain.get_scans and mssmain.peak_pick (with peak width, replicated-peak, and background-subtraction filters) to build the feature table first The goal is feature annotation or MS/MS identification (use mss.frag with MoNA MassBank searching), not grouping by abundance trend Feature labels are already known and a supervised approach is intended — use dm.feature_model regression instead of unsupervised clustering

skills.search_text: hrms-feature-list-overlap-analysis Use when you have feature lists (m/z–RT pairs with peak areas) from one HRMS peak-picking tool and equivalent lists from comparison tools run on identical .mzML files of known-composition standards, and need a cross-platform overlap fraction to validate extraction performance. skills.description: Use when a non-target LC/GC-HRMS feature list (e.g. external_feature_list.xlsx from FeatureFinding with its mzML file) must be prioritized for PFAS by reducing matrix features using the MD/C-m/C data-reduction dimensions.
skills.name: hrms-feature-table-processing
skills.search_text: hrms-feature-table-processing Use when a non-target LC/GC-HRMS feature list (e.g. external_feature_list.xlsx from FeatureFinding with its mzML file) must be prioritized for PFAS by reducing matrix features using the MD/C-m/C data-reduction dimensions. Input is raw MS data rather than a feature list — use PFΔScreen's FeatureFinding tab first (or vendor feature finding) before external-feature-table MD/C-m/C processing Analysis goal is homologous-series detection rather than per-feature MD/C-m/C reduction — KMD analysis with (CF2)n and CF2O repeating units (±2 mDa, ≥3 homologues) is the appropriate technique Sample matrix is dominated by features with m/C < 30 and negative MD/C that are not PFAS — the m/C = 30 / MD/C < +0.003 cutoffs may wrongly discard or retain features; parameters must be adjusted per sample http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Processes HRMS feature tables through the MD/C-m/C framework of PFΔScreen: per-feature carbon number, mass-per-carbon (m/C) and mass-defect-per-carbon (MD/C) are computed under the CH2-scaled Kendrick framework and used with cutoffs (m/C = 30, MD/C < +0.003) to reduce non-target features to potential PFAS far more efficiently than a mass-defect window alone. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s00216-023-05070-2
skills.summary: Processes HRMS feature tables through the MD/C-m/C framework of PFΔScreen: per-feature carbon number, mass-per-carbon (m/C) and mass-defect-per-carbon (MD/C) are computed under the CH2-scaled Kendrick framework and used with cutoffs (m/C = 30, MD/C < +0.003) to reduce non-target features to potential PFAS far more efficiently than a mass-defect window alone.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw MS data rather than a feature list — use PFΔScreen's FeatureFinding tab first (or vendor feature finding) before external-feature-table MD/C-m/C processing Analysis goal is homologous-series detection rather than per-feature MD/C-m/C reduction — KMD analysis with (CF2)n and CF2O repeating units (±2 mDa, ≥3 homologues) is the appropriate technique Sample matrix is dominated by features with m/C < 30 and negative MD/C that are not PFAS — the m/C = 30 / MD/C < +0.003 cutoffs may wrongly discard or retain features; parameters must be adjusted per sample

skills.name: hrms-low-energy-mslevel-filtering
skills.search_text: hrms-low-energy-mslevel-filtering Use when you have HRMS data in Apache Parquet format (from arcMS/HDMSE conversion) and need to extract an EIC, TIC or MS spectrum for a specific m/z window or scan subset without loading the full file into memory. Input is an mzML, UNIFI-native or HDF5 file that has not yet been converted to Parquet (use arcMS conversion first, e.g. convert_one_sample_data()) You need high-collision-energy (MS2 / high-energy) fragment data rather than MS1-level traces — this skill explicitly filters to mslevel == "1" The whole dataset already fits in RAM and a simple in-memory dplyr or pure Arrow query is fast enough (the article notes pure Arrow binned queries can take ~30s–1 min, so a small in-memory file does not need DuckDB) http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0219 Extracts chromatograms or spectra from Parquet-stored HRMS data by filtering to low-collision-energy (mslevel == 1) scans and windowing m/z values (e.g. 216.0016–216.2016 for atrazine), querying the on-disk Arrow dataset through DuckDB without loading the ~200–400 MB profile-mode file into RAM. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioadv/vbae160
skills.summary: Extracts chromatograms or spectra from Parquet-stored HRMS data by filtering to low-collision-energy (mslevel == 1) scans and windowing m/z values (e.g. 216.0016–216.2016 for atrazine), querying the on-disk Arrow dataset through DuckDB without loading the ~200–400 MB profile-mode file into RAM.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is an mzML, UNIFI-native or HDF5 file that has not yet been converted to Parquet (use arcMS conversion first, e.g. convert_one_sample_data()) You need high-collision-energy (MS2 / high-energy) fragment data rather than MS1-level traces — this skill explicitly filters to mslevel == "1" The whole dataset already fits in RAM and a simple in-memory dplyr or pure Arrow query is fast enough (the article notes pure Arrow binned queries can take ~30s–1 min, so a small in-memory file does not need DuckDB)

skills.search_text: http-request-throttling Use when a script iterates over many PUG-View URLs — pagination pages of a bulk heading request or one request per record identifier — and must avoid tripping PubChem's 5 req/s, 400 req/min, 300 s/min usage limits. The task is a single one-off PUG-View request (e.g. one CID's JSON full-record retrieval); with no loop there is nothing to throttle. The needed data are specialized (especially tabular) data served by other backend service(s) that are not currently accessible through PUG-View. You expect annotation data under multiple headings for one compound in a single call — instead request the full annotation data retrieval; throttling only paces the per-request loop, it does not merge heading queries. Paces loops of HTTP requests against PubChem's PUG-View REST service so bulk annotation retrieval stays inside PubChem's published usage limits (no more than 5 requests per second, 400 per minute, 300 s running time per minute).
