The spectra being matched originate directly from human samples — microbeMASST and the metadataMASST joins are designed to trace spectra found in non-human or model-organism data into public human datasets; if the input is already human-derived, stratification by human sample context is redundant No ReDU sample metadata is available or linkable for the matched datasets — without metadata terms describing sample context (body site, disease state) the stratification cannot be performed and only raw match counts are available The search has not yet completed all re-runs of jobs.py with skip_existing=True — matches missing because the Fast Search API failed on some entries would produce an undercount of human-context matches http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_2640 Stratifies MS/MS spectral matches returned by a MASST batch search by human sample context (e.g. stool, blood, oral cavity, breast milk) and disease cohort (T2D, IBD, AD) by joining _matches.tsv and _datasets.tsv outputs to ReDU sample metadata. Used to trace microbe-derived spectra found in animal models into public human datasets and identify in which body sites and disease states they are detected. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41564-023-01575-9
skills.summary: Stratifies MS/MS spectral matches returned by a MASST batch search by human sample context (e.g. stool, blood, oral cavity, breast milk) and disease cohort (T2D, IBD, AD) by joining _matches.tsv and _datasets.tsv outputs to ReDU sample metadata. Used to trace microbe-derived spectra found in animal models into public human datasets and identify in which body sites and disease states they are detected.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The spectra being matched originate directly from human samples — microbeMASST and the metadataMASST joins are designed to trace spectra found in non-human or model-organism data into public human datasets; if the input is already human-derived, stratification by human sample context is redundant No ReDU sample metadata is available or linkable for the matched datasets — without metadata terms describing sample context (body site, disease state) the stratification cannot be performed and only raw match counts are available The search has not yet completed all re-runs of jobs.py with skip_existing=True — matches missing because the Fast Search API failed on some entries would produce an undercount of human-context matches

skills.description: Use when you have a HUMAnN functional-profile matrix (e.g., KEGG pathways) plus a LEfSe result file and need to render them as an annotated GraPhlAn circular functional tree.
skills.name: humann-output-conversion
skills.search_text: humann-output-conversion Use when you have a HUMAnN functional-profile matrix (e.g., KEGG pathways) plus a LEfSe result file and need to render them as an annotated GraPhlAn circular functional tree. Input is a taxonomic abundance profile you want as a heat-map — use hclust2 instead of a functional-tree conversion You need interactive exploration of large phylogenies rather than a static publication figure — iTOL or Krona may be more appropriate Input files are not MetaPhlAn/LEfSe/HUMAnN outputs and lack the hierarchical pathway naming export2graphlan expects http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Convert HUMAnN-derived KEGG functional profiles and LEfSe biomarker results into GraPhlAn tree and annotation files using export2graphlan, enabling circular visualization of functional-ontology contrasts such as the HMP vs MetaHIT gut metagenome tree (Fig. 4). metabolomics/v3 10.7717/peerj.1029
skills.summary: Convert HUMAnN-derived KEGG functional profiles and LEfSe biomarker results into GraPhlAn tree and annotation files using export2graphlan, enabling circular visualization of functional-ontology contrasts such as the HMP vs MetaHIT gut metagenome tree (Fig. 4).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a taxonomic abundance profile you want as a heat-map — use hclust2 instead of a functional-tree conversion You need interactive exploration of large phylogenies rather than a static publication figure — iTOL or Krona may be more appropriate Input files are not MetaPhlAn/LEfSe/HUMAnN outputs and lack the hierarchical pathway naming export2graphlan expects

skills.description: Use when comparing a predicted high-resolution MS/MS spectrum to a reference spectrum where peak mass accuracy matters — e.g. evaluating fragment-annotated models on Orbitrap [M+H]+ HCD data where 0.01 Da binning would blur small mass offsets.
skills.name: hungarian-matching-peak-alignment-ppm-tolerance
skills.search_text: hungarian-matching-peak-alignment-ppm-tolerance Use when comparing a predicted high-resolution MS/MS spectrum to a reference spectrum where peak mass accuracy matters — e.g. evaluating fragment-annotated models on Orbitrap [M+H]+ HCD data where 0.01 Da binning would blur small mass offsets. When the metric of interest is deliberately mass-accuracy-insensitive — use binned cosine C_BIN (0.01 Da bins) instead, as the paper reports both When spectra come from low-resolution instruments or other adducts/instrument platforms, since the 10 ppm threshold was calibrated on Orbitrap [M+H]+ HCD data When peaks must be interpreted as formula annotations rather than just scored — the paper excludes formula annotations more than 10 ppm from peak mass, a related but distinct filter http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Scores predicted vs. real MS/MS spectra by optimally matching peaks with the Hungarian algorithm under a 10 ppm mass tolerance, yielding the C_HUN similarity metric used alongside binned cosine (C_BIN) to benchmark C2MS models like FraGNNet against ICEBERG, GrAFF-MS, MassFormer, and NEIMS. metabolomics/v3 10.48550/arxiv.2404.02360
skills.summary: Scores predicted vs. real MS/MS spectra by optimally matching peaks with the Hungarian algorithm under a 10 ppm mass tolerance, yielding the C_HUN similarity metric used alongside binned cosine (C_BIN) to benchmark C2MS models like FraGNNet against ICEBERG, GrAFF-MS, MassFormer, and NEIMS.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the metric of interest is deliberately mass-accuracy-insensitive — use binned cosine C_BIN (0.01 Da bins) instead, as the paper reports both When spectra come from low-resolution instruments or other adducts/instrument platforms, since the 10 ppm threshold was calibrated on Orbitrap [M+H]+ HCD data When peaks must be interpreted as formula annotations rather than just scored — the paper excludes formula annotations more than 10 ppm from peak mass, a related but distinct filter

skills.description: Use when MRM ion chromatograms need automated peak-tip detection, left/right boundary tracing, and coelution flagging before quantitation — e.g. noisy, unevenly sampled, or isomeric (coeluted) peaks that must be resolved rather than merged.
skills.name: hwhm-coelution-boundary-determination
skills.search_text: hwhm-coelution-boundary-determination Use when MRM ion chromatograms need automated peak-tip detection, left/right boundary tracing, and coelution flagging before quantitation — e.g. noisy, unevenly sampled, or isomeric (coeluted) peaks that must be resolved rather than merged. Input data have already been peak-detected and boundary-assigned by another tool (e.g. Skyline or MRMkit output) — this skill would re-detect tips and could disagree with the prior assignments. The chromatogram contains no coeluted isomers and the goal is only absolute quantitation from a standard curve, not boundary refinement. The data are unprocessed raw vendor files that have not yet been converted to mzML/.abf by msconvert. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0153 Determines peak boundaries and coelution status for each MRM ion chromatogram by tracing peak tips with MATLAB findpeaks, computing the half-width at half-maximum (HWHM), and flagging coelution when a neighboring peak intrudes within 2.5× the HWHM of the candidate peak. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c02462
skills.summary: Determines peak boundaries and coelution status for each MRM ion chromatogram by tracing peak tips with MATLAB findpeaks, computing the half-width at half-maximum (HWHM), and flagging coelution when a neighboring peak intrudes within 2.5× the HWHM of the candidate peak.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data have already been peak-detected and boundary-assigned by another tool (e.g. Skyline or MRMkit output) — this skill would re-detect tips and could disagree with the prior assignments. The chromatogram contains no coeluted isomers and the goal is only absolute quantitation from a standard curve, not boundary refinement. The data are unprocessed raw vendor files that have not yet been converted to mzML/.abf by msconvert.

skills.description: Use when a recursive bond-breaking fragmentation DAG has nodes annotated with heavy-atom formulae f_n and attached hydrogen counts h_n, and you must map predicted fragments onto observed MS/MS peaks via formula masses (e.g. on NIST20 spectra).
skills.name: hydrogen-count-tolerance-formula-enumeration
skills.search_text: hydrogen-count-tolerance-formula-enumeration Use when a recursive bond-breaking fragmentation DAG has nodes annotated with heavy-atom formulae f_n and attached hydrogen counts h_n, and you must map predicted fragments onto observed MS/MS peaks via formula masses (e.g. on NIST20 spectra). Formula annotation analysis of glycan or peptide spectra — the paper explicitly excluded these and focused on small molecules Explaining OS (Outside of the Support) peaks arising from complex chemistry such as cyclizations — the algorithm fails to account for these fragments, so hydrogen-tolerant enumeration will not cover them Cases where only a single fragment is possible for a formula — these degenerate single-fragment formulae are excluded from the agreement analysis For each node n of the approximate fragmentation DAG G_F^d, enumerate the hydrogen-tolerant formula set {f_n^{-j},...,f_n^{j}} with tolerance j=4 around the node's heavy-atom formula f_n, and compute each variant's monoisotopic mass. This bridges the fragment distribution predicted over the DAG to concrete MS/MS peak masses. metabolomics/v3 10.48550/arxiv.2404.02360
skills.summary: For each node n of the approximate fragmentation DAG G_F^d, enumerate the hydrogen-tolerant formula set {f_n^{-j},...,f_n^{j}} with tolerance j=4 around the node's heavy-atom formula f_n, and compute each variant's monoisotopic mass. This bridges the fragment distribution predicted over the DAG to concrete MS/MS peak masses.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Formula annotation analysis of glycan or peptide spectra — the paper explicitly excluded these and focused on small molecules Explaining OS (Outside of the Support) peaks arising from complex chemistry such as cyclizations — the algorithm fails to account for these fragments, so hydrogen-tolerant enumeration will not cover them Cases where only a single fragment is possible for a formula — these degenerate single-fragment formulae are excluded from the agreement analysis

skills.description: Use when you have ICEBERG-generated fragmentation DAGs with per-peak hydrogen-shift annotations and want to verify that bond-breakage patterns and peak-to-fragment assignments align with chemical intuition.
skills.name: hydrogen-rearrangement-shift-assignment
skills.search_text: hydrogen-rearrangement-shift-assignment Use when you have ICEBERG-generated fragmentation DAGs with per-peak hydrogen-shift annotations and want to verify that bond-breakage patterns and peak-to-fragment assignments align with chemical intuition. When the input is experimental spectra with no predicted fragmentation DAG — there are no per-peak hydrogen-shift annotations to audit. When throughput matters: ICEBERG costs roughly 1 CPU second per molecule, nearly an order of magnitude more than SCARF, so large-scale sweeps may warrant the faster formula-level models instead. When you need proven ground-truth fragmentation explanations — the article states there are no guarantees that generated fragment explanations are the correct physical explanations. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0089 Interpret ICEBERG's per-peak fragment attributions by extracting annotated hydrogen-rearrangement fields for intense peaks and auditing whether shifts like -1H correspond to chemically intuitive neutral losses (e.g. H2O), alongside aggregating predicted broken-bond types. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c04654
skills.summary: Interpret ICEBERG's per-peak fragment attributions by extracting annotated hydrogen-rearrangement fields for intense peaks and auditing whether shifts like -1H correspond to chemically intuitive neutral losses (e.g. H2O), alongside aggregating predicted broken-bond types.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is experimental spectra with no predicted fragmentation DAG — there are no per-peak hydrogen-shift annotations to audit. When throughput matters: ICEBERG costs roughly 1 CPU second per molecule, nearly an order of magnitude more than SCARF, so large-scale sweeps may warrant the faster formula-level models instead. When you need proven ground-truth fragmentation explanations — the article states there are no guarantees that generated fragment explanations are the correct physical explanations.

skills.description: Use when building a synthetic compound database from a known illicit-drug template (e.g., cathinone) and no reference spectra exist for emerging NPS analogs.
skills.name: hydrogen-site-functional-group-substitution
skills.search_text: hydrogen-site-functional-group-substitution Use when building a synthetic compound database from a known illicit-drug template (e.g., cathinone) and no reference spectra exist for emerging NPS analogs. When the analyte's mass spectrum already matches an established reference spectrum (NIST, Wiley, SWGDRUG) — PS2MS enumeration is only triggered when no reference match is found When the chemical structure of the NPS is already known — in silico EI-MS prediction via NEIMS can be applied directly without derivative enumeration When the target drug class has a core structure other than the preselected template (here cathinone) — the substitution is defined on a specific drug template's hydrogen sites http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 Enumerates candidate derivatives of a known drug core (e.g., cathinone) by recursively replacing hydrogen atoms with functional-group R-groups using RDKit, then prunes the combinatorial space with SCScore-based synthesis-difficulty thresholds and Virshup drug-like criteria to build PS2MS's synthetic NPS database. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c05019
skills.summary: Enumerates candidate derivatives of a known drug core (e.g., cathinone) by recursively replacing hydrogen atoms with functional-group R-groups using RDKit, then prunes the combinatorial space with SCScore-based synthesis-difficulty thresholds and Virshup drug-like criteria to build PS2MS's synthetic NPS database.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the analyte's mass spectrum already matches an established reference spectrum (NIST, Wiley, SWGDRUG) — PS2MS enumeration is only triggered when no reference match is found When the chemical structure of the NPS is already known — in silico EI-MS prediction via NEIMS can be applied directly without derivative enumeration When the target drug class has a core structure other than the preselected template (here cathinone) — the substitution is defined on a specific drug template's hydrogen sites

skills.description: Use when preprocessed, quantized peak m/z and intensity vectors must be converted into fixed-length binary hypervectors prior to Hamming-distance-based clustering of large MS/MS data sets.
skills.name: hyperdimensional-vector-encoding
skills.search_text: hyperdimensional-vector-encoding Use when preprocessed, quantized peak m/z and intensity vectors must be converted into fixed-length binary hypervectors prior to Hamming-distance-based clustering of large MS/MS data sets. The spectra have not yet been preprocessed and bucket-divided (peaks not quantized/normalized) — encoding expects quantized m/z and intensity vectors per bucket The downstream analysis requires real-valued spectral similarity rather than binary Hamming distances Clustering must preserve exact spectrum distances: HDC encoding trades some information for speed, and the authors note an optimized distance function for comparing spectrum HVs is not yet derived http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Encodes preprocessed MS/MS spectra as binary hypervectors (HVs) of configurable dimension D using level-ID hyperdimensional computing, bit-packed into 32-bit integers for an 8-fold memory reduction, with GPU (CUDA/Numba/CuPy) batched encoding in HyperSpec. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.2c00612
skills.summary: Encodes preprocessed MS/MS spectra as binary hypervectors (HVs) of configurable dimension D using level-ID hyperdimensional computing, bit-packed into 32-bit integers for an 8-fold memory reduction, with GPU (CUDA/Numba/CuPy) batched encoding in HyperSpec.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The spectra have not yet been preprocessed and bucket-divided (peaks not quantized/normalized) — encoding expects quantized m/z and intensity vectors per bucket The downstream analysis requires real-valued spectral similarity rather than binary Hamming distances Clustering must preserve exact spectrum distances: HDC encoding trades some information for speed, and the authors note an optimized distance function for comparing spectrum HVs is not yet derived

skills.description: Use when you have a list of metabolite annotations (with HMDB identifiers) unique to one annotation method and need to test which chemical taxonomy subclasses are overrepresented, comparing subset counts against a full background annotation set.
skills.name: hypergeometric-enrichment-analysis
skills.search_text: hypergeometric-enrichment-analysis Use when you have a list of metabolite annotations (with HMDB identifiers) unique to one annotation method and need to test which chemical taxonomy subclasses are overrepresented, comparing subset counts against a full background annotation set. The annotation list has no HMDB identifiers or no chemical taxonomy mapping, since subclass contingency tables cannot be constructed You need differential-abundance testing of metabolite intensities across biological conditions rather than overrepresentation of annotation classes The comparison set is not a proper subset of a defined background (exclusive annotations are not contained in the group's full annotation list), invalidating the hypergeometric assumption http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 One-tailed Fisher exact (hypergeometric tail) overrepresentation testing of HMDB chemical-taxonomy subclasses among METASPACE-ML-exclusive annotations at 10% FDR, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, used to identify which metabolite classes are better annotated by machine-learning FDR estimation in animal versus plant imaging mass spectrometry datasets. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-52213-9
skills.summary: One-tailed Fisher exact (hypergeometric tail) overrepresentation testing of HMDB chemical-taxonomy subclasses among METASPACE-ML-exclusive annotations at 10% FDR, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, used to identify which metabolite classes are better annotated by machine-learning FDR estimation in animal versus plant imaging mass spectrometry datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The annotation list has no HMDB identifiers or no chemical taxonomy mapping, since subclass contingency tables cannot be constructed You need differential-abundance testing of metabolite intensities across biological conditions rather than overrepresentation of annotation classes The comparison set is not a proper subset of a defined background (exclusive annotations are not contained in the group's full annotation list), invalidating the hypergeometric assumption

skills.description: Use when performing ORA on metabolomics data and per-pathway enrichment p-values are needed from a pathway collection, a list of metabolites of interest, and a background compound set.
skills.name: hypergeometric-enrichment-pvalue-computation
skills.search_text: hypergeometric-enrichment-pvalue-computation Use when performing ORA on metabolomics data and per-pathway enrichment p-values are needed from a pathway collection, a list of metabolites of interest, and a background compound set. The input is not a metabolic pathway/metabolite-set enrichment problem — this skill computes enrichment p-values, not general hypergeometric draws or GSEA-style rank-based scores. The pathway contains fewer than 3 compounds: the reference workflow states 'Only pathways containing at least 3 compounds were used as input for ORA.' No metabolites of interest overlap the pathway (k = 0): the reference implementation skips p-value calculation in this case. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3524 Computes per-pathway over-representation p-values for metabolomics ORA using a right-tailed Fisher's exact test based on the hypergeometric distribution, as implemented in the metabolomics-ORA reference workflow. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009105
skills.summary: Computes per-pathway over-representation p-values for metabolomics ORA using a right-tailed Fisher's exact test based on the hypergeometric distribution, as implemented in the metabolomics-ORA reference workflow.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is not a metabolic pathway/metabolite-set enrichment problem — this skill computes enrichment p-values, not general hypergeometric draws or GSEA-style rank-based scores. The pathway contains fewer than 3 compounds: the reference workflow states 'Only pathways containing at least 3 compounds were used as input for ORA.' No metabolites of interest overlap the pathway (k = 0): the reference implementation skips p-value calculation in this case.

skills.description: Use when comparing two feature tables generated with different XCMS/centWave parameters (AutoTuner vs IPO) and you need to test whether a parameter-specific subset is enriched or depleted for MS2 spectra.
skills.name: hypergeometric-enrichment-testing
skills.search_text: hypergeometric-enrichment-testing Use when comparing two feature tables generated with different XCMS/centWave parameters (AutoTuner vs IPO) and you need to test whether a parameter-specific subset is enriched or depleted for MS2 spectra. When the input is already a single feature table without a comparison subset (e.g. no AutoTuner vs IPO contrast) — there is no hypergeometric population/success structure to test When MS2 spectrum counts have not been generated or cannot be linked to individual features — the test requires per-feature MS2 association When features cannot be partitioned into specific vs intersect sets (e.g. no shared identifiers between the two tables) — normalization and the hypergeometric denominator would be undefined http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Assess whether IPO-specific features in a culture dataset are depleted of MS2 spectra relative to the intersect of AutoTuner- and IPO-derived feature tables, using normalized counts and a hypergeometric test (stats::phyper) per ionization mode. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/812370
skills.summary: Assess whether IPO-specific features in a culture dataset are depleted of MS2 spectra relative to the intersect of AutoTuner- and IPO-derived feature tables, using normalized counts and a hypergeometric test (stats::phyper) per ionization mode.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is already a single feature table without a comparison subset (e.g. no AutoTuner vs IPO contrast) — there is no hypergeometric population/success structure to test When MS2 spectrum counts have not been generated or cannot be linked to individual features — the test requires per-feature MS2 association When features cannot be partitioned into specific vs intersect sets (e.g. no shared identifiers between the two tables) — normalization and the hypergeometric denominator would be undefined

skills.description: Use when a standalone (unpaired) metabolomics dataset of disease-associated metabolites must be statistically evaluated against GWAS Catalog-derived gene sets to find novel metabolite-gene associations via a hypergeometric test.
skills.name: hypergeometric-enrichment-testing
skills.search_text: hypergeometric-enrichment-testing Use when a standalone (unpaired) metabolomics dataset of disease-associated metabolites must be statistically evaluated against GWAS Catalog-derived gene sets to find novel metabolite-gene associations via a hypergeometric test. The metabolomics and GWAS data are paired (from the same metabolomics-GWAS study) — metGWAS 1.0 is designed for evaluating independent, standalone studies The large GWAS network file GWASnetwork_discoverableGenesOnly_2021_10_14.RData has not been downloaded — it is not included in the supplementary material and the workflow cannot run without it The metabolite list has not been mapped to interacting proteins/genes — the hypergeometric comparison operates on metabolic gene sets derived via online databases, not raw metabolite names http://edamontology.org/topic_3388 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Run hypergeometric over-representation testing as implemented in metGWAS 1.0, which statistically compares metabolic gene sets (disease-associated metabolites mapped to interacting proteins) against genomic gene sets from a network representation of the GWAS Catalog. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad523
skills.summary: Run hypergeometric over-representation testing as implemented in metGWAS 1.0, which statistically compares metabolic gene sets (disease-associated metabolites mapped to interacting proteins) against genomic gene sets from a network representation of the GWAS Catalog.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The metabolomics and GWAS data are paired (from the same metabolomics-GWAS study) — metGWAS 1.0 is designed for evaluating independent, standalone studies The large GWAS network file GWASnetwork_discoverableGenesOnly_2021_10_14.RData has not been downloaded — it is not included in the supplementary material and the workflow cannot run without it The metabolite list has not been mapped to interacting proteins/genes — the hypergeometric comparison operates on metabolic gene sets derived via online databases, not raw metabolite names

skills.description: Use when a list of significant metabolites (e.g. Log2FC > 1.5, BH-adjusted p < 0.05) must be mapped to KEGG pathways to identify over-represented biological processes after batch correction.
skills.name: hypergeometric-enrichment-testing
skills.search_text: hypergeometric-enrichment-testing Use when a list of significant metabolites (e.g. Log2FC > 1.5, BH-adjusted p < 0.05) must be mapped to KEGG pathways to identify over-represented biological processes after batch correction. When the input is a full metabolite abundance matrix rather than a curated list of significant hits — MSEA here requires an already-filtered differential list. When the goal is gene set enrichment (e.g. GO or Reactome gene sets); this workflow is specific to metabolite identifiers (HMDB/KEGG compound IDs) and KEGG pathway over-representation. When the metabolite list has not yet been batch-effect corrected (e.g. via dbnorm ber/ComBat), as raw lists contained too few metabolites from lipid pathways to trigger enrichment. http://edamontology.org/topic_3345 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Downstream metabolite set enrichment analysis (MSEA) via ConsensusPathDB, applying a hypergeometric over-representation test against KEGG pathways with FDR (q-value) correction, as used to identify lipid metabolism pathways enriched among HFD-dysregulated metabolites. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41598-021-84824-3
skills.summary: Downstream metabolite set enrichment analysis (MSEA) via ConsensusPathDB, applying a hypergeometric over-representation test against KEGG pathways with FDR (q-value) correction, as used to identify lipid metabolism pathways enriched among HFD-dysregulated metabolites.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is a full metabolite abundance matrix rather than a curated list of significant hits — MSEA here requires an already-filtered differential list. When the goal is gene set enrichment (e.g. GO or Reactome gene sets); this workflow is specific to metabolite identifiers (HMDB/KEGG compound IDs) and KEGG pathway over-representation. When the metabolite list has not yet been batch-effect corrected (e.g. via dbnorm ber/ComBat), as raw lists contained too few metabolites from lipid pathways to trigger enrichment.

skills.description: Use when validating unlabeled or SIP-labeled peptide-spectrum matches in proteomic SIP data: you have observed MS/MS spectra paired with theoretical fragment spectra for a candidate peptide and need per-PSM scores (MVH, Xcorr, WDP, spectral entropy).
skills.name: hypergeometric-fragment-peak-matching
skills.search_text: hypergeometric-fragment-peak-matching Use when validating unlabeled or SIP-labeled peptide-spectrum matches in proteomic SIP data: you have observed MS/MS spectra paired with theoretical fragment spectra for a candidate peptide and need per-PSM scores (MVH, Xcorr, WDP, spectral entropy). The goal is simulating or visualizing isotopic envelopes of metabolites or peptides at the MS1 level (use Aerith's FFT-based or Monte Carlo envelope simulation instead) The task is RAW file conversion to .FT1/.FT2 or mzML (use Raxport or ThermoRawFileParser) No theoretical fragment spectrum exists for the candidate peptide, so observed peaks cannot be matched to b/y ion series http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Scores peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) in Aerith's proteomic SIP workflow by matching observed MS/MS fragment peaks to theoretical b/y ion series and computing a multivariate hypergeometric (MVH) score, alongside Xcorr, WDP, and spectral entropy similarity scores written to psm_scores.csv. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c03207
skills.summary: Scores peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) in Aerith's proteomic SIP workflow by matching observed MS/MS fragment peaks to theoretical b/y ion series and computing a multivariate hypergeometric (MVH) score, alongside Xcorr, WDP, and spectral entropy similarity scores written to psm_scores.csv.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is simulating or visualizing isotopic envelopes of metabolites or peptides at the MS1 level (use Aerith's FFT-based or Monte Carlo envelope simulation instead) The task is RAW file conversion to .FT1/.FT2 or mzML (use Raxport or ThermoRawFileParser) No theoretical fragment spectrum exists for the candidate peptide, so observed peaks cannot be matched to b/y ion series

skills.description: Use when tokenised BGCs (genes as (sub)Pfam domain combinations) are available and gene-pair co-occurrence significance must be quantified to build sub-cluster interaction graphs.
skills.name: hypergeometric-gene-interaction-pvalue-computation
skills.search_text: hypergeometric-gene-interaction-pvalue-computation Use when tokenised BGCs (genes as (sub)Pfam domain combinations) are available and gene-pair co-occurrence significance must be quantified to build sub-cluster interaction graphs. The analysis goal is topic-model-based sub-cluster detection (PRESTO-TOP), which uses an LDA bag-of-words model where original gene order is not considered and no pairwise p-values are computed. Only a small dataset (e.g. the Streptomyces/Salinispora dataset) is available, where graph-based filtering rather than genome-scale pairwise statistics was used for visualisation purposes. http://edamontology.org/topic_0084 http://edamontology.org/topic_0160 A per-gene-pair statistical test in iPRESTO's PRESTO-STAT that quantifies whether two (sub)Pfam-tokenised genes co-occur within BGCs more often than expected by chance, using hypergeometric p-values for both adjacency and co-localisation interactions on the antiSMASH-DB dataset. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1010462
skills.summary: A per-gene-pair statistical test in iPRESTO's PRESTO-STAT that quantifies whether two (sub)Pfam-tokenised genes co-occur within BGCs more often than expected by chance, using hypergeometric p-values for both adjacency and co-localisation interactions on the antiSMASH-DB dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is topic-model-based sub-cluster detection (PRESTO-TOP), which uses an LDA bag-of-words model where original gene order is not considered and no pairwise p-values are computed. Only a small dataset (e.g. the Streptomyces/Salinispora dataset) is available, where graph-based filtering rather than genome-scale pairwise statistics was used for visualisation purposes.

skills.description: Use when a metabolite-interacting gene set (e.g., from KEGG-pathway metabolites mapped via HMDB) must be statistically tested against a disease/trait-specific GWAS subnetwork gene set extracted from the GWAS Catalog.
skills.name: hypergeometric-overrepresentation-testing
skills.search_text: hypergeometric-overrepresentation-testing Use when a metabolite-interacting gene set (e.g., from KEGG-pathway metabolites mapped via HMDB) must be statistically tested against a disease/trait-specific GWAS subnetwork gene set extracted from the GWAS Catalog. The metabolomics and GWAS data are paired from the same cohort — a direct metabolomics-GWAS (mGWAS) association analysis is more appropriate than the unpaired over-representation approach. skills.search_text: icoshift-spectral-peak-alignment Use when a set of 1H-NMR spectra (already phase-corrected, internally referenced, baseline-corrected, region-removed) still shows peak drift between samples, and binned feature tables would blur shifted metabolite peaks if alignment were skipped. skills.search_text: igraph-community-detection Use when a partial-correlation network estimated from two-condition metabolomics data (e.g., TEDDY-style GLASSO networks) needs to be partitioned into metabolic modules via consensus clustering before subnetwork enrichment testing. The goal is pathway enrichment of well-annotated endogenous metabolites that map to KEGG/pathway databases — data-driven module detection is designed for datasets with exogenous, secondary, or unknown metabolites The network is a single-group or marginal-correlation network where indirect correlations confound the identification of biologically relevant interactions The network has not yet been estimated/filtered (clusterNet() expects a DNEA object with networks from getNetworks(), optionally pruned by filterNetworks()) http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Identifies metabolic modules (subnetworks) in an estimated metabolite network by consensus clustering over seven igraph community-detection algorithms, as implemented in the DNEA R package's clusterNet() function. Agreement across algorithms (tau threshold) determines final subnetwork membership, which is appended to the node list for downstream NetGSA enrichment testing. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-024-05994-1
skills.summary: Identifies metabolic modules (subnetworks) in an estimated metabolite network by consensus clustering over seven igraph community-detection algorithms, as implemented in the DNEA R package's clusterNet() function. Agreement across algorithms (tau threshold) determines final subnetwork membership, which is appended to the node list for downstream NetGSA enrichment testing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is pathway enrichment of well-annotated endogenous metabolites that map to KEGG/pathway databases — data-driven module detection is designed for datasets with exogenous, secondary, or unknown metabolites The network is a single-group or marginal-correlation network where indirect correlations confound the identification of biologically relevant interactions The network has not yet been estimated/filtered (clusterNet() expects a DNEA object with networks from getNetworks(), optionally pruned by filterNetworks())

skills.description: Use when processing feature quantification tables (.csv), MS2 spectral summaries (.mgf), and IIN edges files from ion identity molecular networking, and the goal is to expand spectral library coverage by extracting consensus MS2 spectra of unannotated ion species linked to annotated features.
skills.name: iimn-annotation-propagation
skills.search_text: iimn-annotation-propagation Use when processing feature quantification tables (.csv), MS2 spectral summaries (.mgf), and IIN edges files from ion identity molecular networking, and the goal is to expand spectral library coverage by extracting consensus MS2 spectra of unannotated ion species linked to annotated features. The feature table lacks IIN edges (e.g., plain FBMN output without ion identity networking) — there is no connectivity to propagate annotations along. No feature in the network meets the library-match threshold (cosine >0.9, 4–6 shared fragments) or corresponds to an authentic standard — propagation would be ungrounded. Features have poor MS2 spectra with fewer than four signals or fewer than three signals above 0.1% relative intensity — they are filtered out rather than used as library entries. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Propagates high-confidence GNPS spectral library annotations (cosine >0.9 with 4–6 shared fragments, or authentic standards) across connected ion identity features within IIMN networks, yielding propagated consensus MS2 library spectra entries (e.g., GNPS-IIMN-PROPOGATED with 2657 entries covering adducts, multimers, and in-source fragments). metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-021-23953-9
skills.summary: Propagates high-confidence GNPS spectral library annotations (cosine >0.9 with 4–6 shared fragments, or authentic standards) across connected ion identity features within IIMN networks, yielding propagated consensus MS2 library spectra entries (e.g., GNPS-IIMN-PROPOGATED with 2657 entries covering adducts, multimers, and in-source fragments).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The feature table lacks IIN edges (e.g., plain FBMN output without ion identity networking) — there is no connectivity to propagate annotations along. No feature in the network meets the library-match threshold (cosine >0.9, 4–6 shared fragments) or corresponds to an authentic standard — propagation would be ungrounded. Features have poor MS2 spectra with fewer than four signals or fewer than three signals above 0.1% relative intensity — they are filtered out rather than used as library entries.

skills.description: Use when starting from an original raw LC-IM-MS instrument file (e.g., Agilent .d from a MassIVE deposit) and you need the acquisition settings — electric field strength, pressure, temperature, voltages — before or alongside downstream processing.
skills.name: im-ms-acquisition-metadata-extraction
skills.search_text: im-ms-acquisition-metadata-extraction Use when starting from an original raw LC-IM-MS instrument file (e.g., Agilent .d from a MassIVE deposit) and you need the acquisition settings — electric field strength, pressure, temperature, voltages — before or alongside downstream processing. The goal is signal processing (smoothing, saturation repair, demultiplexing, LC compression/IM interpolation) rather than extracting acquisition parameters — use the PreProcessor's preprocessing modules instead. The data is already in an open, processed format without the vendor instrument file, so the acquisition settings cannot be read from the source. The instrument data is not in a format the PreProcessor ingests (e.g., non-Agilent, non-UIMF vendor formats); the article notes conversion to UIMF as an intermediate step may be needed for other IM-MS instrumentation. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Exports the IM-MS acquisition settings and parameters (electric field strength, pressure, temperature, voltages) embedded in raw instrument files using the PNNL PreProcessor's metadata export module, producing a metadata text file that lets users examine instrument performance relative to the collected data. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.1c00425
skills.summary: Exports the IM-MS acquisition settings and parameters (electric field strength, pressure, temperature, voltages) embedded in raw instrument files using the PNNL PreProcessor's metadata export module, producing a metadata text file that lets users examine instrument performance relative to the collected data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is signal processing (smoothing, saturation repair, demultiplexing, LC compression/IM interpolation) rather than extracting acquisition parameters — use the PreProcessor's preprocessing modules instead. The data is already in an open, processed format without the vendor instrument file, so the acquisition settings cannot be read from the source. The instrument data is not in a format the PreProcessor ingests (e.g., non-Agilent, non-UIMF vendor formats); the article notes conversion to UIMF as an intermediate step may be needed for other IM-MS instrumentation.

skills.description: Use when building a chemically informed database from drift tube LC-IM-MS mzML files and you must generate theoretical m/z targets (monoisotopic mass, isotopologue pattern A/A+1/A+2) for primary ions and adducts of known molecular formulae, then confirm them by isotopologue matching after peak.
skills.name: im-ms-database-ion-annotation
skills.search_text: im-ms-database-ion-annotation Use when building a chemically informed database from drift tube LC-IM-MS mzML files and you must generate theoretical m/z targets (monoisotopic mass, isotopologue pattern A/A+1/A+2) for primary ions and adducts of known molecular formulae, then confirm them by isotopologue matching after peak. Input is not profile-mode drift tube IM-MS mzML data (CCSfind is built for LC-DTIM-MS drift tube measurements) No molecular formulae are available for the compounds — the tool requires a list of formulae to generate theoretical targets and cannot annotate unknowns de novo Only a processed feature/peak table exists; isotopologue matching confirmation here operates after peak picking on parsed mzML, not on already-summarized features Chemically informed annotation of LC-IM-MS database entries: theoretical monoisotopic masses and isotopologue distributions for primary and adduct ions are computed from input molecular formulae (via the molmass library), then used by CCSfind to target and confirm ion species in drift tube IM-MS mzML data. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/jms.5040
skills.summary: Chemically informed annotation of LC-IM-MS database entries: theoretical monoisotopic masses and isotopologue distributions for primary and adduct ions are computed from input molecular formulae (via the molmass library), then used by CCSfind to target and confirm ion species in drift tube IM-MS mzML data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is not profile-mode drift tube IM-MS mzML data (CCSfind is built for LC-DTIM-MS drift tube measurements) No molecular formulae are available for the compounds — the tool requires a list of formulae to generate theoretical targets and cannot annotate unknowns de novo Only a processed feature/peak table exists; isotopologue matching confirmation here operates after peak picking on parsed mzML, not on already-summarized features

skills.description: Use when processing LC-DTIM-MS mzML files of small molecules where isomeric ion species (e.g., protomers or conformers) must be separated in the IM dimension and DTCCS(N2) values assigned after RT confirmation of a primary ion.
skills.name: im-ms-isomeric-ion-separation
skills.search_text: im-ms-isomeric-ion-separation Use when processing LC-DTIM-MS mzML files of small molecules where isomeric ion species (e.g., protomers or conformers) must be separated in the IM dimension and DTCCS(N2) values assigned after RT confirmation of a primary ion. Input is not drift-tube IM-MS data (the tool is built for drift tube IM-MS measurements; e.g., TWIMS data would need a different calibration approach) No single-field CCS calibration coefficients (Tfix, Beta) are available for the data file, so arrival times cannot be converted to DTCCS(N2) The goal is untargeted feature finding without prior molecular formulae or confirmed RT windows — CCSfind is chemically informed and requires targeted formulae http://edamontology.org/topic_0153 http://edamontology.org/topic_3361 This skill covers the CCSfind workflow for resolving isomeric ion species (protomers, conformers) of small molecules in drift-tube LC-IM-MS data: after retention-time confirmation, targeted adduct ions are extracted over the confirmed RT window, a second peak-detection pass is run in the arrival-time (IM) dimension, and arrival times are converted to DTCCS(N2) using single-field calibration coefficients (Tfix, beta) with nitrogen as drift gas. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/jms.5040
skills.summary: This skill covers the CCSfind workflow for resolving isomeric ion species (protomers, conformers) of small molecules in drift-tube LC-IM-MS data: after retention-time confirmation, targeted adduct ions are extracted over the confirmed RT window, a second peak-detection pass is run in the arrival-time (IM) dimension, and arrival times are converted to DTCCS(N2) using single-field calibration coefficients (Tfix, beta) with nitrogen as drift gas.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is not drift-tube IM-MS data (the tool is built for drift tube IM-MS measurements; e.g., TWIMS data would need a different calibration approach) No single-field CCS calibration coefficients (Tfix, Beta) are available for the data file, so arrival times cannot be converted to DTCCS(N2) The goal is untargeted feature finding without prior molecular formulae or confirmed RT windows — CCSfind is chemically informed and requires targeted formulae

skills.description: Use when TIM-MS (or another IM-MS platform) lipidomics data have been spiked with U13C-labeled yeast extract internal standards and you need to monitor and/or correct CCSN2 bias without measuring additional external calibrants.
skills.name: im-ms-lipidomics-ccs-quality-control
skills.search_text: im-ms-lipidomics-ccs-quality-control Use when TIM-MS (or another IM-MS platform) lipidomics data have been spiked with U13C-labeled yeast extract internal standards and you need to monitor and/or correct CCSN2 bias without measuring additional external calibrants. Input data have not been spiked with U13C-labeled yeast extract internal standards — the library-based bias calculation and correction cannot be applied A lipid class-adduct combination contains fewer than 3 U13C-labeled lipids — CCS correction via linear regression is not possible for that combination The adduct or lipid class of the input does not appear in the permitted table (e.g. AcCa with [M+NH4], SPH with [M-H]) or uses an adduct outside [M+H], [M+NH4], [M+Na], [M-H], [M+HCOO] http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Internal CCS quality control for IM-MS lipidomics that calculates CCS bias between measured TIM CCS N2 values and a DTCCSN2 library of U13C-labeled yeast lipids, then optionally corrects CCS values with lipid class- and adduct-specific linear correction functions. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c01253
skills.summary: Internal CCS quality control for IM-MS lipidomics that calculates CCS bias between measured TIM CCS N2 values and a DTCCSN2 library of U13C-labeled yeast lipids, then optionally corrects CCS values with lipid class- and adduct-specific linear correction functions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data have not been spiked with U13C-labeled yeast extract internal standards — the library-based bias calculation and correction cannot be applied A lipid class-adduct combination contains fewer than 3 U13C-labeled lipids — CCS correction via linear regression is not possible for that combination The adduct or lipid class of the input does not appear in the permitted table (e.g. AcCa with [M+NH4], SPH with [M-H]) or uses an adduct outside [M+H], [M+NH4], [M+Na], [M-H], [M+HCOO]

skills.description: Use when raw LC-IM-MS TOF profile data (e.g., Agilent 6560 .d files, All Ions mode) shows poor peak definition of low-abundance ions or saturation-truncated high-abundance peaks, and you must judge whether preprocessing improved peak quality.
skills.name: im-ms-peak-quality-assessment
skills.search_text: im-ms-peak-quality-assessment Use when raw LC-IM-MS TOF profile data (e.g., Agilent 6560 .d files, All Ions mode) shows poor peak definition of low-abundance ions or saturation-truncated high-abundance peaks, and you must judge whether preprocessing improved peak quality. Input is already a centroided or feature table output (e.g., from MS-DIAL, Skyline, OpenMS, or Lipid Annotator) rather than raw profile-mode LC-IM-MS data Data are not IM-MS TOF data or cannot be handled in the original instrument format or via UIMF conversion, since the enhancements target LC-IM-MS raw data The goal is detector-saturation repair of truncated high-abundance peaks rather than smoothing/peak-shape assessment of low-abundance ions http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Assessing whether preprocessing of raw LC-IM-MS TOF data (e.g., multidimensional smoothing with the PNNL PreProcessor) improves peak shapes of poorly defined low-abundance signals and extends the dynamic range, using replicate feature-detection and downstream annotation metrics as evidence. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.1c00425
skills.summary: Assessing whether preprocessing of raw LC-IM-MS TOF data (e.g., multidimensional smoothing with the PNNL PreProcessor) improves peak shapes of poorly defined low-abundance signals and extends the dynamic range, using replicate feature-detection and downstream annotation metrics as evidence.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a centroided or feature table output (e.g., from MS-DIAL, Skyline, OpenMS, or Lipid Annotator) rather than raw profile-mode LC-IM-MS data Data are not IM-MS TOF data or cannot be handled in the original instrument format or via UIMF conversion, since the enhancements target LC-IM-MS raw data The goal is detector-saturation repair of truncated high-abundance peaks rather than smoothing/peak-shape assessment of low-abundance ions

skills.description: Use when raw LC-IM-MS time-of-flight profile data (Agilent .d or UIMF) contains random, isolated high-intensity points that are not part of a chromatographic or drift-time peak, and the goal is to reduce file size and background before feature finding.
skills.name: im-ms-spike-removal
skills.search_text: im-ms-spike-removal Use when raw LC-IM-MS time-of-flight profile data (Agilent .d or UIMF) contains random, isolated high-intensity points that are not part of a chromatographic or drift-time peak, and the goal is to reduce file size and background before feature finding. When the input is already centroided or a feature table — spike removal operates on raw profile-mode data points and their IM/MS-dimensional neighbors, so a centroided or feature-level input cannot be filtered this way When genuine low-abundance, low-signal-to-noise peaks must be preserved — removing isolated points may delete legitimate low-abundance signals rather than random noise http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Removes isolated 'spike' raw data points from LC-IM-MS MS-files by deleting points that exceed the intensity threshold but lack adjacent neighbors in the IM and MS dimensions, as implemented in the PNNL PreProcessor. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.1c00425
skills.summary: Removes isolated 'spike' raw data points from LC-IM-MS MS-files by deleting points that exceed the intensity threshold but lack adjacent neighbors in the IM and MS dimensions, as implemented in the PNNL PreProcessor.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is already centroided or a feature table — spike removal operates on raw profile-mode data points and their IM/MS-dimensional neighbors, so a centroided or feature-level input cannot be filtered this way When genuine low-abundance, low-signal-to-noise peaks must be preserved — removing isolated points may delete legitimate low-abundance signals rather than random noise

Your analytical database only needs to store summary CCS values, not the full mobility spectra (CCS distributions) per compound Input is not drift tube IM-MS (LC-DTIM-MS) profile mzML data with known CCS calibration coefficients and drift gas identity http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Encodes reviewed CCSfind results—including EICs, full normalized ion mobility spectra, DTCCS N2 values, experimental settings, and PubChem CID links—into SQL-format database entries so the full IM-MS dataset remains retrievable, at a reported storage cost of ~200 KB per entry. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/jms.5040

skills.search_text: image-coordinate-similarity-registration Use when detected target pixel positions from an optical image (flatbed scanner or cell phone camera) must be converted to instrument-relative coordinates via fiducial registration, e.g. to generate macroMS device geometry files for optically guided MALDI-TOF targeting. Samples smaller than 300 μm, where the article states microMS is more effective Images with distortion beyond the 'moderate distortion and imperfect perspective' that macroMS's optical correction tools are designed to resolve Target sets exceeding the ~10,000 target upper limit reported for macroMS Fits a similarity transform (translation, rotation, uniform scale) plus perspective correction from three fiducial marks to map optical image pixel coordinates into the instrument-relative coordinate system used by macroMS, producing the custom geometry file consumed by the MS device. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jasms.1c00013

skills.description: Use when target coordinates are derived from optical images acquired with imperfect devices (flatbed scanners, cell phone cameras) that introduce moderate distortion or imperfect perspective before MS targeting.
skills.name: image-grid-registration
skills.search_text: image-grid-registration Use when target coordinates are derived from optical images acquired with imperfect devices (flatbed scanners, cell phone cameras) that introduce moderate distortion or imperfect perspective before MS targeting. Samples are smaller than 300 μm — the article states microMS is more effective at that scale The image geometry is already known-good (e.g., coordinates generated directly by instrument software with no optical distortion) Corrects optical distortion and imperfect perspective in macroscopic sample images so that MALDI-TOF target coordinates are accurate, by combining a four-point perspective warp with a reference-grid distortion map, as implemented in macroMS. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jasms.1c00013
skills.summary: Corrects optical distortion and imperfect perspective in macroscopic sample images so that MALDI-TOF target coordinates are accurate, by combining a four-point perspective warp with a reference-grid distortion map, as implemented in macroMS.

skills.search_text: image-interpolation-algorithm-selection Use when a low-resolution MSI composite or cluster image must be resampled to the pixel dimensions of a co-registered H&E (or other histology) image and you need to select or justify an interpolation method. The MSI and histology images are already at matching dimensions and no resampling is needed (use the registration workflow instead) The task is geometric co-registration (linear/non-linear registration, Figure S7) rather than simple pixel upscaling of the composite image Only one interpolation method is prescribed by the downstream pipeline and no comparison/selection is required Comparative benchmarking of the four interpolation algorithms supported by MSIght (bilinear, bicubic, nearest neighbor, and Lanczos) for upscaling an MSI composite cluster image to match H&E image dimensions, as in the paper's supplementary Figure S5. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.4c01140
skills.summary: Comparative benchmarking of the four interpolation algorithms supported by MSIght (bilinear, bicubic, nearest neighbor, and Lanczos) for upscaling an MSI composite cluster image to match H&E image dimensions, as in the paper's supplementary Figure S5.

skills.description: Use when raw GC-MS or LC-MS two-dimensional MS maps (m/z vs retention time) must be characterized comprehensively without peak picking, and multivariate marker features need to be identified and visualized, even at parts-per-billion analyte concentrations.
skills.name: image-processing-based-chemometrics
skills.search_text: image-processing-based-chemometrics Use when raw GC-MS or LC-MS two-dimensional MS maps (m/z vs retention time) must be characterized comprehensively without peak picking, and multivariate marker features need to be identified and visualized, even at parts-per-billion analyte concentrations. Input is already a curated peak/feature table where peak picking has been performed and validated - NPFimg's value is bypassing the peak picking process, which suffers from false peak detections. The goal is a targeted analysis of a small set of known analytes rather than untargeted identification of multivariate marker features across a 2D MS map. Only a 1D spectrum is available with no two-dimensional m/z vs retention time map, since the method processes 2D MS maps. Identifies multivariate chemo-/biomarker features from chromatography-MS data by converting the two-dimensional MS map (m/z vs retention time) into an image and applying image processing plus machine learning, avoiding the conventional peak picking process that suffers from false peak detections. Implemented in NPFimg and demonstrated on GC-MS aroma odor and human breath data down to the parts per billion level. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c03163
skills.summary: Identifies multivariate chemo-/biomarker features from chromatography-MS data by converting the two-dimensional MS map (m/z vs retention time) into an image and applying image processing plus machine learning, avoiding the conventional peak picking process that suffers from false peak detections. Implemented in NPFimg and demonstrated on GC-MS aroma odor and human breath data down to the parts per billion level.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a curated peak/feature table where peak picking has been performed and validated - NPFimg's value is bypassing the peak picking process, which suffers from false peak detections. The goal is a targeted analysis of a small set of known analytes rather than untargeted identification of multivariate marker features across a 2D MS map. Only a 1D spectrum is available with no two-dimensional m/z vs retention time map, since the method processes 2D MS maps.

skills.description: Use when a pipeline encodes spectra into fixed-size images and you must decide which input resolution balances validation accuracy against training cost before committing to a production model.
skills.name: image-resolution-scaling-benchmarking
skills.search_text: image-resolution-scaling-benchmarking Use when a pipeline encodes spectra into fixed-size images and you must decide which input resolution balances validation accuracy against training cost before committing to a production model. The input is already a feature table or spectral peak list — this skill applies only to image-encoded model inputs, not to tabular ML baselines like Random Forest. You have a single pre-chosen image size and no need to compare resolutions — running the full resolution sweep adds compute without decision value. The downstream task is not image-based deep learning (e.g. PCA or OPLS-DA on feature matrices), where resolution scaling is not a tunable parameter. http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Benchmarks CNN predictive performance on molecular fingerprint images rendered at multiple input resolutions (e.g. 75×70, 150×140, 300×280 px) to find the accuracy-versus-computational-efficiency sweet spot for a fixed architecture. metabolomics/v3 10.48550/arxiv.2510.09716
skills.summary: Benchmarks CNN predictive performance on molecular fingerprint images rendered at multiple input resolutions (e.g. 75×70, 150×140, 300×280 px) to find the accuracy-versus-computational-efficiency sweet spot for a fixed architecture.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a feature table or spectral peak list — this skill applies only to image-encoded model inputs, not to tabular ML baselines like Random Forest. You have a single pre-chosen image size and no need to compare resolutions — running the full resolution sweep adds compute without decision value. The downstream task is not image-based deep learning (e.g. PCA or OPLS-DA on feature matrices), where resolution scaling is not a tunable parameter.

skills.description: Use when an imported elemental image contains isolated pixels of extremely low or high signal from instrument noise that would distort visualization or quantification, and the goal is targeted spike removal while leaving valid pixels untouched.
skills.name: image-threshold-outlier-replacement
skills.search_text: image-threshold-outlier-replacement Use when an imported elemental image contains isolated pixels of extremely low or high signal from instrument noise that would distort visualization or quantification, and the goal is targeted spike removal while leaving valid pixels untouched. Input is already a clean image with no isolated extreme-pixel artifacts — applying the filter would risk replacing valid high-signal features with local background values Noise is a broad drift or background trend across the whole acquisition rather than isolated spikes — use Pew2's drift correction tool instead Data is spot-wise or line-by-line with continuous intensity variation rather than a 2D image; the local window filter assumes spatial neighborhood structure in an image http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Removes instrumental noise spikes from LA-ICP-MS elemental images by comparing each pixel value to a local mean or median and replacing outliers exceeding a user-defined threshold with the local value, as implemented in Pew2's filtering tool. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c02138
skills.summary: Removes instrumental noise spikes from LA-ICP-MS elemental images by comparing each pixel value to a local mean or median and replacing outliers exceeding a user-defined threshold with the local value, as implemented in Pew2's filtering tool.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a clean image with no isolated extreme-pixel artifacts — applying the filter would risk replacing valid high-signal features with local background values Noise is a broad drift or background trend across the whole acquisition rather than isolated spikes — use Pew2's drift correction tool instead Data is spot-wise or line-by-line with continuous intensity variation rather than a 2D image; the local window filter assumes spatial neighborhood structure in an image

skills.name: imaging-mass-cytometry-single-cell-segmentation
skills.search_text: imaging-mass-cytometry-single-cell-segmentation Use when raw multiplexed IMC image stacks must be converted into per-cell segmentation masks (nuclear and whole-cell) so that single-cell protein/metabolite intensities and spatial locations can be extracted and cell counts reported. skills.description: Use when raw MSI data in .imzML/.ibd format (e.g. test_POS files from MetaboLights MTBLS487) must be converted into a normalised, deisotoped, lipid-annotated feature matrix before PCA, k-means clustering, or single-ion image generation.
skills.name: imaging-mass-spectrometry-preprocessing
skills.search_text: imaging-mass-spectrometry-preprocessing Use when raw MSI data in .imzML/.ibd format (e.g. test_POS files from MetaboLights MTBLS487) must be converted into a normalised, deisotoped, lipid-annotated feature matrix before PCA, k-means clustering, or single-ion image generation. The input is already a normalised feature table (image.norm.csv) and you only need downstream PCA, clustering or ion slicing — use process=F instead of re-preprocessing Data are not in imzML format and cannot readily be converted — massPix supports .imzML files only The analytes of interest are outside massPix's covered lipid classes (DAG, TAG, PC, PE, PS, PG, PI, PA, LysoPC, CE, SM, Cer, FFA) and their anticipated adducts Preprocessing of imzML mass spectrometry imaging data into a normalised, lipid-annotated pixel-by-feature matrix using the massPix R package: intensity/mz thresholding, 10 ppm mass binning, filtering of sparse features, deisotoping, accurate-mass lipid annotation, and TIC normalisation. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-017-1252-5
skills.summary: Preprocessing of imzML mass spectrometry imaging data into a normalised, lipid-annotated pixel-by-feature matrix using the massPix R package: intensity/mz thresholding, 10 ppm mass binning, filtering of sparse features, deisotoping, accurate-mass lipid annotation, and TIC normalisation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a normalised feature table (image.norm.csv) and you only need downstream PCA, clustering or ion slicing — use process=F instead of re-preprocessing Data are not in imzML format and cannot readily be converted — massPix supports .imzML files only The analytes of interest are outside massPix's covered lipid classes (DAG, TAG, PC, PE, PS, PG, PI, PA, LysoPC, CE, SM, Cer, FFA) and their anticipated adducts

skills.description: Use when comparing two imaging-MS metabolite annotation engines on the same dataset set and you need per-dataset annotation counts at specified FDR cutoffs (e.g., 5% and 10%), summarized by sample-type or instrument-context medians.
skills.name: imaging-ms-annotation-count-benchmarking-across-fdr-thresholds
skills.search_text: imaging-ms-annotation-count-benchmarking-across-fdr-thresholds Use when comparing two imaging-MS metabolite annotation engines on the same dataset set and you need per-dataset annotation counts at specified FDR cutoffs (e.g., 5% and 10%), summarized by sample-type or instrument-context medians. You only need to inspect or browse a single dataset's annotations interactively rather than benchmark two engines across a dataset collection Your annotations come from an engine or FDR estimation scheme other than METASPACE-ML vs. MSM, where the target/decoy FDR-based count comparison is not meaningful The dataset lacks both ML and MSM annotation runs at matched FDR levels, so paired per-dataset differences cannot be computed http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 A benchmarking skill that quantifies how many more confident metabolite annotations the machine-learning METASPACE-ML engine delivers versus the rule-based MSM scoring, per dataset, at FDR thresholds of 10% and 5%, across animal, plant, Orbitrap, and FT-ICR testing contexts. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-52213-9
skills.summary: A benchmarking skill that quantifies how many more confident metabolite annotations the machine-learning METASPACE-ML engine delivers versus the rule-based MSM scoring, per dataset, at FDR thresholds of 10% and 5%, across animal, plant, Orbitrap, and FT-ICR testing contexts.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need to inspect or browse a single dataset's annotations interactively rather than benchmark two engines across a dataset collection Your annotations come from an engine or FDR estimation scheme other than METASPACE-ML vs. MSM, where the target/decoy FDR-based count comparison is not meaningful The dataset lacks both ML and MSM annotation runs at matched FDR levels, so paired per-dataset differences cannot be computed

skills.description: Use when reproducing or auditing reported counts of metabolite annotations in METASPACE imaging-MS datasets — e.g. how many DHB matrix-cluster ions are annotated at a given FDR and how many are classified off-sample.
skills.name: imaging-ms-annotation-count-summarization
skills.search_text: imaging-ms-annotation-count-summarization Use when reproducing or auditing reported counts of metabolite annotations in METASPACE imaging-MS datasets — e.g. how many DHB matrix-cluster ions are annotated at a given FDR and how many are classified off-sample. Input is raw MALDI imaging mass spectrometry data that has not been annotated in METASPACE — run the annotation engine first Goal is pixel-level segmentation of off-sample regions rather than whole-image off-sample classification and count summarization Datasets were not acquired with the DHB matrix in positive ion mode — the 353 cluster formulas and reported counts are DHB-specific Reproduces the paper's DHB matrix-cluster off-sample recognition statistics by re-annotating 31 MALDI positive-mode datasets in METASPACE against HMDB v4 at FDR <= 50%, classifying ion images with the ResNet50 off-sample model, and exporting summary counts (6677 annotations; 3134 ~47% off-sample; ~5% of 58,203; 4.3% isomeric) to a CSV table. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-020-3425-x
skills.summary: Reproduces the paper's DHB matrix-cluster off-sample recognition statistics by re-annotating 31 MALDI positive-mode datasets in METASPACE against HMDB v4 at FDR <= 50%, classifying ion images with the ResNet50 off-sample model, and exporting summary counts (6677 annotations; 3134 ~47% off-sample; ~5% of 58,203; 4.3% isomeric) to a CSV table.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw MALDI imaging mass spectrometry data that has not been annotated in METASPACE — run the annotation engine first Goal is pixel-level segmentation of off-sample regions rather than whole-image off-sample classification and count summarization Datasets were not acquired with the DHB matrix in positive ion mode — the 353 cluster formulas and reported counts are DHB-specific

skills.description: Use when a labeled set of imaging MS ion images tagged on-/off-sample exists and several classifiers (deep learning, biclustering, co-localization) must be cross-validated and compared per-fold on F1, precision, and recall.
skills.name: imaging-ms-off-sample-classification-evaluation
skills.search_text: imaging-ms-off-sample-classification-evaluation Use when a labeled set of imaging MS ion images tagged on-/off-sample exists and several classifiers (deep learning, biclustering, co-localization) must be cross-validated and compared per-fold on F1, precision, and recall. The goal is pixel-level segmentation of off-sample regions — this skill only classifies whole ion images and explicitly does not solve the segmentation problem No expert-labeled gold standard exists and none can be curated, since the baselines and evaluation require on-/off-sample ground truth tags Data are raw instrument files rather than METASPACE-annotated ion images, since the biclustering baseline depends on the pixel-annotation export http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Reproduce the Table 1 benchmark comparing residual deep learning, semi-automated spatio-molecular biclustering, and molecular co-localization for recognizing off-sample ion images, evaluating each with grouped five-fold cross-validation on the 23,238-image expert-tagged gold standard and reporting off-sample/on-sample F1-score, precision, and recall. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-020-3425-x
skills.summary: Reproduce the Table 1 benchmark comparing residual deep learning, semi-automated spatio-molecular biclustering, and molecular co-localization for recognizing off-sample ion images, evaluating each with grouped five-fold cross-validation on the 23,238-image expert-tagged gold standard and reporting off-sample/on-sample F1-score, precision, and recall.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is pixel-level segmentation of off-sample regions — this skill only classifies whole ion images and explicitly does not solve the segmentation problem No expert-labeled gold standard exists and none can be curated, since the baselines and evaluation require on-/off-sample ground truth tags Data are raw instrument files rather than METASPACE-annotated ion images, since the biclustering baseline depends on the pixel-annotation export

skills.description: Use when you need user-defined 'relevant'/'other' training classes for MS2DeepScore-based spectrum classifiers, by labeling spectral-library entries via SMARTS substructure queries.
skills.name: imbalanced-dataset-construction
skills.search_text: imbalanced-dataset-construction Use when you need user-defined 'relevant'/'other' training classes for MS2DeepScore-based spectrum classifiers, by labeling spectral-library entries via SMARTS substructure queries. You already have curated labeled training spectra (e.g., reference standards); the filtering GUI is only needed to derive labels from structures by SMARTS matching. Your downstream analysis requires balanced training data — the article states the package 'is not capable of resolving' the imbalance failure mode. Your target structures cannot be captured by SMARTS substructure queries (labeling is structure-based, not spectrum-similarity based). http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 Constructs a deliberately imbalanced binary training set for HR-MS/MS spectrum classification by SMARTS substructure-filtering a spectral library into a small 'relevant' class and a much larger 'other' class (e.g., 655 (iso-)flavonoid vs. 10000 non-(iso-)flavonoid spectra from MSnLib v6). metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioadv/vbag111
skills.summary: Constructs a deliberately imbalanced binary training set for HR-MS/MS spectrum classification by SMARTS substructure-filtering a spectral library into a small 'relevant' class and a much larger 'other' class (e.g., 655 (iso-)flavonoid vs. 10000 non-(iso-)flavonoid spectra from MSnLib v6).
skills.when_to_use_negative: You already have curated labeled training spectra (e.g., reference standards); the filtering GUI is only needed to derive labels from structures by SMARTS matching. Your downstream analysis requires balanced training data — the article states the package 'is not capable of resolving' the imbalance failure mode. Your target structures cannot be captured by SMARTS substructure queries (labeling is structure-based, not spectrum-similarity based).

skills.description: Use when comparing missing-value imputation methods on complete benchmark data where values can be removed completely at random (10%, 20%, 30%) and true values are known, so NRMSE (continuous) and PFC (categorical) error rates can be computed per simulation.
skills.name: imputation-error-quantification
skills.search_text: imputation-error-quantification Use when comparing missing-value imputation methods on complete benchmark data where values can be removed completely at random (10%, 20%, 30%) and true values are known, so NRMSE (continuous) and PFC (categorical) error rates can be computed per simulation. True values are unavailable for the missing entries (e.g. naturally occurring missingness), so NRMSE/PFC against ground truth cannot be computed — only OOB estimates remain, and the article treats these as an informal per-variable reliability check rather than formal error assessment Missingness is not completely at random; the evaluation framework here is built solely on artificially introduced MCAR values of 10% to 30% MissPALasso is being run on very high-dimensional data (e.g. the Insulin dataset, p=12,626), where the article states computation is not feasible http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Quantifies imputation accuracy of missForest against baselines (KNNimpute, MissPALasso, MICE, dummy-coded KNNimpute) using NRMSE for continuous variables and PFC for categorical variables over 50 simulations with 10–30% artificially removed values, plus random-forest out-of-bag error as a test-set-free error estimate. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btr597
skills.summary: Quantifies imputation accuracy of missForest against baselines (KNNimpute, MissPALasso, MICE, dummy-coded KNNimpute) using NRMSE for continuous variables and PFC for categorical variables over 50 simulations with 10–30% artificially removed values, plus random-forest out-of-bag error as a test-set-free error estimate.

skills.description: Use when a wide-format feature table (samples as columns, features as rows) contains missing entries that must be filled before downstream statistics, and each imputed feature needs a binary indicator flag for provenance.
skills.name: imputation-flag-annotation
skills.search_text: imputation-flag-annotation Use when a wide-format feature table (samples as columns, features as rows) contains missing entries that must be filled before downstream statistics, and each imputed feature needs a binary indicator flag for provenance. The input is not a feature table (e.g. raw peak-picking output); the standard workflow places imputation after data preprocessing, following feature identification. A single imputed value per missing entry must be traceable across reruns and the method must be stochastic — the KNN route described here is deterministic, returning the same result for a given dataset. The missingness is so pervasive that imputation would fabricate the majority of the table rather than fill sparse gaps; use flagging/filtering tools (e.g. Threshold Based Flags) to drop such features first. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Fills missing values in metabolomics feature tables using SECIMTools' Imputation tool — group mean, group median, or K-nearest-neighbor (KNN) — and emits a flag column marking imputed features per the SECIMTools flag-file convention. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-018-2134-1
skills.summary: Fills missing values in metabolomics feature tables using SECIMTools' Imputation tool — group mean, group median, or K-nearest-neighbor (KNN) — and emits a flag column marking imputed features per the SECIMTools flag-file convention.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is not a feature table (e.g. raw peak-picking output); the standard workflow places imputation after data preprocessing, following feature identification. A single imputed value per missing entry must be traceable across reruns and the method must be stochastic — the KNN route described here is deterministic, returning the same result for a given dataset. The missingness is so pervasive that imputation would fabricate the majority of the table rather than fill sparse gaps; use flagging/filtering tools (e.g. Threshold Based Flags) to drop such features first.

skills.search_text: imputation-method-benchmarking Use when selecting a missing value imputation method for MNAR left-censored metabolomics (LOD/LOQ-caused) data, or when building an evaluation pipeline that must rank candidate imputers by TPR, RMSE, or SOR metrics. skills.when_to_use_negative: When missing values are predominantly MCAR/MAR (e.g. post-missing-retrieval non-targeted GC/MS data), since the benchmark's MNAR-generation and left-censored truncation bounds (lo=-Inf, hi='min') are designed for MNAR left-censored situations. When the goal is simply to impute a single dataset with an already-validated method, rather than to compare or rank multiple imputation methods. When the data are non-omics without left-censored (LOD/LOQ) structure, since GSimp's truncation-bounded Gibbs sampler and the MNAR benchmark design are specific to that setting.
