skills.name: inverted-comparison-orientation-correction
skills.search_text: inverted-comparison-orientation-correction Use when pooling fold-changes from multiple metabolomics studies where some reports give the inverted ratio (control/case instead of case/control), and a case-vs-control-consistent combined estimate per compound is required. When raw intensity data and standard deviations are available — use standard effect-size meta-analysis instead of amanida's fold-change-only weighted average When the input is trend/behaviour labels only (qualitative data) — use amanida's vote-counting, not fold-change orientation correction When identifiers have not been curated/harmonized — amanida requires identifier curation and PubChem ID harmonization (check_names) before meta-analysis http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Before combining fold-changes across metabolomics studies in amanida, detect studies that report the inverse comparison orientation (control/case) and reverse their fold-change values via -1/value, so that all per-compound values share the case-vs-control direction prior to log2 transformation and study-size-weighted averaging. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btab591
skills.summary: Before combining fold-changes across metabolomics studies in amanida, detect studies that report the inverse comparison orientation (control/case) and reverse their fold-change values via -1/value, so that all per-compound values share the case-vs-control direction prior to log2 transformation and study-size-weighted averaging.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When raw intensity data and standard deviations are available — use standard effect-size meta-analysis instead of amanida's fold-change-only weighted average When the input is trend/behaviour labels only (qualitative data) — use amanida's vote-counting, not fold-change orientation correction When identifiers have not been curated/harmonized — amanida requires identifier curation and PubChem ID harmonization (check_names) before meta-analysis

skills.description: Use when you have paired microbial genome-mining (AntiSMASH BGC/GCF) and metabolomics (GNPS spectral) data loaded in NPLinker and need a kernel-regression score to rank candidate BGC–spectrum links, e.g. against a validated link subset.
skills.name: iokr-kernel-regression-link-scoring
skills.search_text: iokr-kernel-regression-link-scoring Use when you have paired microbial genome-mining (AntiSMASH BGC/GCF) and metabolomics (GNPS spectral) data loaded in NPLinker and need a kernel-regression score to rank candidate BGC–spectrum links, e.g. against a validated link subset. The goal is not link scoring but data preparation, e.g. GNPS download/extraction, AntiSMASH BGC preparation, or BigScape GCF clustering, which NPLinker provides as separate upstream steps No paired genomics and metabolomics data are available for the strains, so candidate BGC–spectrum links cannot be constructed You need a validated standardised hypergeometric-style score rather than the novel kernel-regression score; combine IOKR with complementary scoring functions instead of using it alone as ground truth http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Applies NPLinker's Input-Output Kernel Regression (IOKR) scoring method to prioritise links between BGC/GCF objects and MS2 spectra from integrated genomics–metabolomics data, producing per-link scores that can be compared against literature-validated links. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008920
skills.summary: Applies NPLinker's Input-Output Kernel Regression (IOKR) scoring method to prioritise links between BGC/GCF objects and MS2 spectra from integrated genomics–metabolomics data, producing per-link scores that can be compared against literature-validated links.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is not link scoring but data preparation, e.g. GNPS download/extraction, AntiSMASH BGC preparation, or BigScape GCF clustering, which NPLinker provides as separate upstream steps No paired genomics and metabolomics data are available for the strains, so candidate BGC–spectrum links cannot be constructed You need a validated standardised hypergeometric-style score rather than the novel kernel-regression score; combine IOKR with complementary scoring functions instead of using it alone as ground truth

skills.description: Use when ranking candidate GCF-to-molecular-family links in NPLinker output and you want to combine the standardised strain correlation score with IOKR scores to improve the rank of validated links.
skills.name: iokr-link-prediction-scoring
skills.search_text: iokr-link-prediction-scoring Use when ranking candidate GCF-to-molecular-family links in NPLinker output and you want to combine the standardised strain correlation score with IOKR scores to improve the rank of validated links. You have no validated (ground-truth) GCF–molecular-family links to evaluate ranks against, so the priority-ranking comparison cannot be judged. Your input is not GNPS molecular networking data paired with antiSMASH/BigScape GCFs and a strain_mappings.json — NPLinker requires this data layout. You need a single pre-existing score rather than a combination; the metcalf correlation score alone or IOKR alone may suffice and is simpler to compute. http://edamontology.org/topic_3407 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Score GCF–molecular-family links with Input-Output Kernel Regression (IOKR), standardise these alongside strain-correlation (metcalf) scores, and combine them via sign-weighted ℓp sums (ℓ1, ℓ2, ℓ1.5) to rank candidate links, so that validated GCF–metabolite links are prioritised better than by either score alone. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008920
skills.summary: Score GCF–molecular-family links with Input-Output Kernel Regression (IOKR), standardise these alongside strain-correlation (metcalf) scores, and combine them via sign-weighted ℓp sums (ℓ1, ℓ2, ℓ1.5) to rank candidate links, so that validated GCF–metabolite links are prioritised better than by either score alone.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have no validated (ground-truth) GCF–molecular-family links to evaluate ranks against, so the priority-ranking comparison cannot be judged. Your input is not GNPS molecular networking data paired with antiSMASH/BigScape GCFs and a strain_mappings.json — NPLinker requires this data layout. You need a single pre-existing score rather than a combination; the metcalf correlation score alone or IOKR alone may suffice and is simpler to compute.

skills.description: Use when you have per-dataset IIMN/FBMN-IIN output (feature quantification table plus IIN edges CSVs) from MZmine-processed LC-MS/MS datasets and need relative adduct percentages per dataset or per sample-type group.
skills.name: ion-adduct-abundance-quantification
skills.search_text: ion-adduct-abundance-quantification Use when you have per-dataset IIMN/FBMN-IIN output (feature quantification table plus IIN edges CSVs) from MZmine-processed LC-MS/MS datasets and need relative adduct percentages per dataset or per sample-type group. Input is raw LC-MS/MS data or an unprocessed feature table that has not yet gone through MS1-based feature grouping and ion identity annotation — first run the IIMN workflow Analysis relies only on MS2 spectral similarity networks without MS1 ion-identity edges, since adduct species assignments come from the MS1-based IIN layer Single-dataset analysis with no sample-type grouping, where per-dataset adduct percentages cannot be contrasted between groups http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Quantifies the relative ion-formation (adduct) percentages of [M+H]+, [M+Na]+, [M+NH4]+ and related species from MS1-based ion identity networking (IIN) edges produced by the IIMN/FBMN workflow, and compares them across datasets grouped by sample type (e.g., marine vs non-marine). metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-021-23953-9
skills.summary: Quantifies the relative ion-formation (adduct) percentages of [M+H]+, [M+Na]+, [M+NH4]+ and related species from MS1-based ion identity networking (IIN) edges produced by the IIMN/FBMN workflow, and compares them across datasets grouped by sample type (e.g., marine vs non-marine).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw LC-MS/MS data or an unprocessed feature table that has not yet gone through MS1-based feature grouping and ion identity annotation — first run the IIMN workflow Analysis relies only on MS2 spectral similarity networks without MS1 ion-identity edges, since adduct species assignments come from the MS1-based IIN layer Single-dataset analysis with no sample-type grouping, where per-dataset adduct percentages cannot be contrasted between groups

skills.description: Use when IM-MS data contains adduct types (e.g. [M−H]−, [M+H]+, [M+Na]+, or uncommon dimers like [2M+H]+ / [2M−H]−) for which CCS predictions are needed to filter or annotate candidate structures.
skills.name: ion-adduct-annotation
skills.search_text: ion-adduct-annotation Use when IM-MS data contains adduct types (e.g. [M−H]−, [M+H]+, [M+Na]+, or uncommon dimers like [2M+H]+ / [2M−H]−) for which CCS predictions are needed to filter or annotate candidate structures. Input is already a curated, adduct-matched CCS dataset — CCSP 2.0's published models are only built for [M−H]−, [M+H]+, [M+Na]+, and [M+K]+; other adducts require user-curated training sets. The analysis goal is multi-adduct CCS filtering or fragment-ion CCS prediction in tandem MS; the paper lists these as future work, not supported by the current tool. http://edamontology.org/topic_0157 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 A method for annotating ion-mobility–derived CCS values to candidate ion adducts using CCSP 2.0's linear SVR models, including the ability to build user-curated training sets for adduct types like dimers ([2M+H]+, [2M−H]−) not covered by the published [M−H]−, [M+H]+, and [M+Na]+ models. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.2c03491
skills.summary: A method for annotating ion-mobility–derived CCS values to candidate ion adducts using CCSP 2.0's linear SVR models, including the ability to build user-curated training sets for adduct types like dimers ([2M+H]+, [2M−H]−) not covered by the published [M−H]−, [M+H]+, and [M+Na]+ models.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a curated, adduct-matched CCS dataset — CCSP 2.0's published models are only built for [M−H]−, [M+H]+, [M+Na]+, and [M+K]+; other adducts require user-curated training sets. The analysis goal is multi-adduct CCS filtering or fragment-ion CCS prediction in tandem MS; the paper lists these as future work, not supported by the current tool.

skills.description: Use when a dataset has been processed through the MZmine metaCorrelate IIMN workflow and you need to measure how much annotation improves by propagating library matches to neighboring ion identity nodes.
skills.name: ion-adduct-annotation-propagation-statistics
skills.search_text: ion-adduct-annotation-propagation-statistics Use when a dataset has been processed through the MZmine metaCorrelate IIMN workflow and you need to measure how much annotation improves by propagating library matches to neighboring ion identity nodes. Input data has not been processed through the MZmine metaCorrelate IIMN workflow — without IIN edges there is no neighbor propagation to measure The goal is de novo molecular formula or compound-class annotation (e.g., SIRIUS/CANOPUS/Qemistree) rather than propagation of existing GNPS spectral library matches across ion identity edges Only a single raw file is available with no aligned feature list — consensus MS2 spectra and aligned feature rows are prerequisites for computing propagation gain http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Quantifies the annotation gain achieved by propagating spectral library matches across Ion Identity Network (IIN) edges in ion identity molecular networking, computing per-dataset MS2 (~6%) and MS1 (~12%) annotation rates plus mean propagation gain (~35%). metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-021-23953-9
skills.summary: Quantifies the annotation gain achieved by propagating spectral library matches across Ion Identity Network (IIN) edges in ion identity molecular networking, computing per-dataset MS2 (~6%) and MS1 (~12%) annotation rates plus mean propagation gain (~35%).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data has not been processed through the MZmine metaCorrelate IIMN workflow — without IIN edges there is no neighbor propagation to measure The goal is de novo molecular formula or compound-class annotation (e.g., SIRIUS/CANOPUS/Qemistree) rather than propagation of existing GNPS spectral library matches across ion identity edges Only a single raw file is available with no aligned feature list — consensus MS2 spectra and aligned feature rows are prerequisites for computing propagation gain

skills.description: Use when IMS-MS data were acquired in stepped-field DTIMS mode (e.g., Agilent 6560 with multiple electric fields per ion) and per-ion CCS values must be computed from arrival-time vs P/V regressions rather than single-field calibration.
skills.name: ion-arrival-time-field-regression
skills.search_text: ion-arrival-time-field-regression Use when IMS-MS data were acquired in stepped-field DTIMS mode (e.g., Agilent 6560 with multiple electric fields per ion) and per-ion CCS values must be computed from arrival-time vs P/V regressions rather than single-field calibration. Data were acquired in single-field DTIMS mode (e.g., RapidFire-DTIMS) or on traveling-wave instruments (Bruker timsTOF, Waters Synapt, SLIM) — those require AutoCCS's single-field or TWIMS calibration modes instead Ions are observed across fewer than the required number of electric fields (below the --threshold_n_fields 5 cutoff) and cannot support a stable arrival-time vs P/V regression http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Determines ion drift times and collision cross sections (CCS) from stepped-field DTIMS-MS data by regressing arrival time versus electric field (P/V) across multiple field steps, following Stow et al. 2017, as automated in AutoCCS. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btab429
skills.summary: Determines ion drift times and collision cross sections (CCS) from stepped-field DTIMS-MS data by regressing arrival time versus electric field (P/V) across multiple field steps, following Stow et al. 2017, as automated in AutoCCS.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data were acquired in single-field DTIMS mode (e.g., RapidFire-DTIMS) or on traveling-wave instruments (Bruker timsTOF, Waters Synapt, SLIM) — those require AutoCCS's single-field or TWIMS calibration modes instead Ions are observed across fewer than the required number of electric fields (below the --threshold_n_fields 5 cutoff) and cannot support a stable arrival-time vs P/V regression

skills.description: Use when an aligned multi-sample feature table (with m/z, drift time, and retention time dimensions) needs isotopic signature detection and charge-state annotation, as required before identifications rely on isotopic evidence.
skills.name: ion-charge-state-assignment
skills.search_text: ion-charge-state-assignment Use when an aligned multi-sample feature table (with m/z, drift time, and retention time dimensions) needs isotopic signature detection and charge-state annotation, as required before identifications rely on isotopic evidence. Input is a raw instrument acquisition file (e.g. Agilent 6560 IMS-MS dumps) rather than an already detected-and-aligned feature table — feature detection and alignment must be performed first. The isotopic pattern of interest is not the C13 spacing (1.003355 Da); the skill's documented search is parameterized around that delta and ≤5 substitutions. Only 1 or 2 isotopologue members are present, since the documented first screening requires signatures with at least 3 members. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Assigns ion charge states to detected features by detecting isotopologues (e.g. C13 spacing of 1.003355 Da) in aligned LC-IMS-MS feature tables with DEIMoS's isotope detection, then inferring charge from the observed isotopologue spacing. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c05017
skills.summary: Assigns ion charge states to detected features by detecting isotopologues (e.g. C13 spacing of 1.003355 Da) in aligned LC-IMS-MS feature tables with DEIMoS's isotope detection, then inferring charge from the observed isotopologue spacing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a raw instrument acquisition file (e.g. Agilent 6560 IMS-MS dumps) rather than an already detected-and-aligned feature table — feature detection and alignment must be performed first. The isotopic pattern of interest is not the C13 spacing (1.003355 Da); the skill's documented search is parameterized around that delta and ≤5 substitutions. Only 1 or 2 isotopologue members are present, since the documented first screening requires signatures with at least 3 members.

skills.description: Use when processing LC-MS/MS MRM ion chromatograms where a background intensity level is needed to define smoothing windows or section extents prior to peak detection and quantitation.
skills.name: ion-chromatogram-background-estimation
skills.search_text: ion-chromatogram-background-estimation Use when processing LC-MS/MS MRM ion chromatograms where a background intensity level is needed to define smoothing windows or section extents prior to peak detection and quantitation. The input is not an MRM ion chromatogram but already a peak/intensity table from a prior quantitation step. A fixed global baseline is required instead of a section-adaptive background, e.g. when comparing against tools like TargetLynx that connect nearby valleys. The chromatogram data is of a non-MRM acquisition where dwell time is uniform and the dynamic dwell-time smoothing rationale does not apply. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Estimates the background intensity of an ion chromatogram as its 30th-percentile signal intensity, a threshold MRMQuant uses for dynamic signal smoothing and section-adaptive adjustment of chromatogram sections. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c02462
skills.summary: Estimates the background intensity of an ion chromatogram as its 30th-percentile signal intensity, a threshold MRMQuant uses for dynamic signal smoothing and section-adaptive adjustment of chromatogram sections.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is not an MRM ion chromatogram but already a peak/intensity table from a prior quantitation step. A fixed global baseline is required instead of a section-adaptive background, e.g. when comparing against tools like TargetLynx that connect nearby valleys. The chromatogram data is of a non-MRM acquisition where dwell time is uniform and the dynamic dwell-time smoothing rationale does not apply.

skills.description: Use when MRM ion chromatograms contain coeluted peaks (2–3 isomers sharing one chromatogram) and per-compound peak abundances must be computed automatically rather than attributed wholly to one targeted compound.
skills.name: ion-chromatogram-peak-abundance-quantitation
skills.search_text: ion-chromatogram-peak-abundance-quantitation Use when MRM ion chromatograms contain coeluted peaks (2–3 isomers sharing one chromatogram) and per-compound peak abundances must be computed automatically rather than attributed wholly to one targeted compound. The chromatogram contains a single well-separated peak with no coelution — simpler integration suffices The input is already a processed feature/abundance table rather than raw or converted MRM chromatogram data Saturated peaks needing regression-based absolute quantitation are the target — those are excluded from regression rather than deconvolved http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Computes per-peak abundances from MRM ion chromatograms by fitting Gaussian models at findpeaks-detected tip locations and deconvolving coeluted peaks so each isomer receives its own abundance value. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c02462
skills.summary: Computes per-peak abundances from MRM ion chromatograms by fitting Gaussian models at findpeaks-detected tip locations and deconvolving coeluted peaks so each isomer receives its own abundance value.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The chromatogram contains a single well-separated peak with no coelution — simpler integration suffices The input is already a processed feature/abundance table rather than raw or converted MRM chromatogram data Saturated peaks needing regression-based absolute quantitation are the target — those are excluded from regression rather than deconvolved

skills.description: Use when input is a pixel-by-ion feature matrix from an imaging mass spectrometry run (CSV with X/Y pixel coordinates plus per-pixel ion intensities) and noise ions must be removed during quality control before metabolite annotation or spatial pattern analysis.
skills.name: ion-feature-matrix-processing
skills.search_text: ion-feature-matrix-processing Use when input is a pixel-by-ion feature matrix from an imaging mass spectrometry run (CSV with X/Y pixel coordinates plus per-pixel ion intensities) and noise ions must be removed during quality control before metabolite annotation or spatial pattern analysis. Input is raw instrument data (e.g. IMZML/MS runs) rather than a processed pixel-by-ion feature matrix in the SMAnalyst CSV layout The goal is annotation or differential analysis itself rather than the QC2 noise-ion filtering stage of the workflow Data are non-spatial bulk metabolomics measurements, since the quadrat test's CSR assessment requires spatial pixel coordinates http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Processing step for spatial metabolomics feature matrices in which each ion's spatial distribution across pixels is tested for departure from Complete Spatial Randomness (spatstat quadrat test) and converted into a noise score (-log10 p-value), then filtered at SMAnalyst's default threshold of score ≥30 to separate noise ions from ions retained for downstream analysis. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/biom15111562
skills.summary: Processing step for spatial metabolomics feature matrices in which each ion's spatial distribution across pixels is tested for departure from Complete Spatial Randomness (spatstat quadrat test) and converted into a noise score (-log10 p-value), then filtered at SMAnalyst's default threshold of score ≥30 to separate noise ions from ions retained for downstream analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw instrument data (e.g. IMZML/MS runs) rather than a processed pixel-by-ion feature matrix in the SMAnalyst CSV layout The goal is annotation or differential analysis itself rather than the QC2 noise-ion filtering stage of the workflow Data are non-spatial bulk metabolomics measurements, since the quadrat test's CSR assessment requires spatial pixel coordinates

skills.name: ion-form-benchmark-comparison
skills.search_text: ion-form-benchmark-comparison Use when you have a curated LC-MS peak benchmark (e.g. Demo_MetDNA2_NIST_urine_pos) and need to compare rule-based isotope/adduct annotation (CAMERA) against knowledge-guided network-based ion form assignment (KGMN, MetDNA2Vis). Input is raw LC-MS vendor data without a curated peak table — ion form annotation comparison requires an already peak-picked, manually curated benchmark table The goal is metabolite identification/structural annotation of unknowns (KGMN three-layer annotation) rather than evaluating ion form (isotope/adduct/in-source fragment) annotation accuracy The sample class is non-model organisms or environmental/exposomics profiles where the article advises caution applying KGMN http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Benchmark KGMN's global peak correlation network against CAMERA for ion form annotation on the manually curated benchmark peak dataset (Demo_MetDNA2_NIST_urine_pos), reproducing the reported counts (3374 CAMERA vs 2297 KGMN ion forms) and correct annotation rates (97.5% vs 81.7%). metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-022-34537-6
skills.summary: Benchmark KGMN's global peak correlation network against CAMERA for ion form annotation on the manually curated benchmark peak dataset (Demo_MetDNA2_NIST_urine_pos), reproducing the reported counts (3374 CAMERA vs 2297 KGMN ion forms) and correct annotation rates (97.5% vs 81.7%).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw LC-MS vendor data without a curated peak table — ion form annotation comparison requires an already peak-picked, manually curated benchmark table The goal is metabolite identification/structural annotation of unknowns (KGMN three-layer annotation) rather than evaluating ion form (isotope/adduct/in-source fragment) annotation accuracy The sample class is non-model organisms or environmental/exposomics profiles where the article advises caution applying KGMN

skills.description: Use when a feature quantification table, IIN edges file, or GNPS library (e.g., GNPS-IIMN-PROPOGATED) contains ion-identity annotation strings with inconsistent spellings or ordering that must be normalized before grouping, counting, or comparing adduct abundances.
skills.name: ion-identity-annotation-parsing
skills.search_text: ion-identity-annotation-parsing Use when a feature quantification table, IIN edges file, or GNPS library (e.g., GNPS-IIMN-PROPOGATED) contains ion-identity annotation strings with inconsistent spellings or ordering that must be normalized before grouping, counting, or comparing adduct abundances. The annotation column already contains canonical bracketed strings from a single harmonized source — re-parsing adds no information The data are raw MS/MS spectra or MGF peak lists without MS1-based ion-identity grouping (IIN) results, so no adduct annotations exist to parse The goal is MS2 spectral similarity networking or library matching, which operates on fragmentation spectra, not ion-identity strings http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Parses and harmonizes ion-identity/adduct annotation strings (e.g., 'M + H', '[M+Na]+') that appear in GNPS-IIMN and IIN feature tables, collapsing spelling variants into one canonical bracketed identity so downstream adduct-level statistics are computed on true ion identities rather than on redundant string variants. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-021-23953-9
skills.summary: Parses and harmonizes ion-identity/adduct annotation strings (e.g., 'M + H', '[M+Na]+') that appear in GNPS-IIMN and IIN feature tables, collapsing spelling variants into one canonical bracketed identity so downstream adduct-level statistics are computed on true ion identities rather than on redundant string variants.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The annotation column already contains canonical bracketed strings from a single harmonized source — re-parsing adds no information The data are raw MS/MS spectra or MGF peak lists without MS1-based ion-identity grouping (IIN) results, so no adduct annotations exist to parse The goal is MS2 spectral similarity networking or library matching, which operates on fragmentation spectra, not ion-identity strings

skills.description: Use when you have an aligned LC-MS/MS feature list with consensus MS2 spectra and redundant unconnected nodes (adducts/isotopes of one compound), and you want MS1 ion-identity edges to propagate annotations in GNPS FBMN.
skills.name: ion-identity-network-construction
skills.search_text: ion-identity-network-construction Use when you have an aligned LC-MS/MS feature list with consensus MS2 spectra and redundant unconnected nodes (adducts/isotopes of one compound), and you want MS1 ion-identity edges to propagate annotations in GNPS FBMN. When you already hold a merged/collapsed feature table per compound with no adduct/isotope redundancy — IIN grouping would be redundant When the data lack MS1 peak-shape information across samples, since grouping depends on RT tolerance (0.1 min), Pearson shape correlation (>=0.85, >=5 points), and overlapping intensity (>=50%, >=2 samples) When the analysis is purely MS2 spectral-similarity networking (e.g., classical GNPS METABOLOMICS-SNETS-V2) without an aligned feature table to upload http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3361 Builds MS1-based ion identity networks (IIN) that group and connect adducts, isotopes, and multimers of the same compound across an aligned LC-MS/MS feature list, so that MS2 spectral library matches can be propagated over IIN edges in GNPS Feature-Based Molecular Networking (FBMN) — raising annotation rates by an average of 35% across 24 public datasets. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-021-23953-9
skills.summary: Builds MS1-based ion identity networks (IIN) that group and connect adducts, isotopes, and multimers of the same compound across an aligned LC-MS/MS feature list, so that MS2 spectral library matches can be propagated over IIN edges in GNPS Feature-Based Molecular Networking (FBMN) — raising annotation rates by an average of 35% across 24 public datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When you already hold a merged/collapsed feature table per compound with no adduct/isotope redundancy — IIN grouping would be redundant When the data lack MS1 peak-shape information across samples, since grouping depends on RT tolerance (0.1 min), Pearson shape correlation (>=0.85, >=5 points), and overlapping intensity (>=50%, >=2 samples) When the analysis is purely MS2 spectral-similarity networking (e.g., classical GNPS METABOLOMICS-SNETS-V2) without an aligned feature table to upload

skills.description: Use when the analysis goal is to reproduce or verify the graph-level statistics of a GNPS FBMN job (feature count, IIN group count, node count, singleton count, edge count) from the deposited MZmine quant table and GNPS job ID.
skills.name: ion-identity-network-group-counting
skills.search_text: ion-identity-network-group-counting Use when the analysis goal is to reproduce or verify the graph-level statistics of a GNPS FBMN job (feature count, IIN group count, node count, singleton count, edge count) from the deposited MZmine quant table and GNPS job ID. skills.search_text: ion-mobility-spectrum-conversion Use when raw IM-MS data (Agilent .d, Bruker TimsTOF .d, Thermo .raw, or mzML) must be converted to a cross-platform HDF5 structure for Python/R access, especially when the ion mobility dimension must be preserved. The goal is LC-MS proteomics feature extraction with lossy representations or IM dimension support is irrelevant — the paper notes MS2AI is limited to LC-MS proteomics and does not support the IM dimension, whereas MZA preserves it. The input is already an .mza file or another HDF5-based structure — data access via h5py/rhdf5 scripts suffices; no reconversion is needed. Vendor-specific processing is required that the stand-alone converter does not expose beyond file/extension/intensityThreshold parameters. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Convert multidimensional ion mobility mass spectrometry (IM-MS) data, including mzML inputs, into the MZA HDF5 file structure using the MZA converter, storing IM spectra as m/z bin indexes into a shared Full_mz_array plus per-spectrum intensity arrays and a metadata table. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.2c00313
skills.summary: Convert multidimensional ion mobility mass spectrometry (IM-MS) data, including mzML inputs, into the MZA HDF5 file structure using the MZA converter, storing IM spectra as m/z bin indexes into a shared Full_mz_array plus per-spectrum intensity arrays and a metadata table.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is LC-MS proteomics feature extraction with lossy representations or IM dimension support is irrelevant — the paper notes MS2AI is limited to LC-MS proteomics and does not support the IM dimension, whereas MZA preserves it. The input is already an .mza file or another HDF5-based structure — data access via h5py/rhdf5 scripts suffices; no reconversion is needed. Vendor-specific processing is required that the stand-alone converter does not expose beyond file/extension/intensityThreshold parameters.

skills.description: Use when preparing or validating an organ-specific metabolite database for MSI annotation, where measured m/z values must be matched against theoretical adduct m/z per ionization mode and per organ.
skills.name: ion-mode-database-partitioning
skills.search_text: ion-mode-database-partitioning Use when preparing or validating an organ-specific metabolite database for MSI annotation, where measured m/z values must be matched against theoretical adduct m/z per ionization mode and per organ. The MSI dataset is not organ-specific or its detection mode is unknown — mixing modes or organs would violate the consistency check MSIannotator requires. The task is annotating non-MSI LC-MS data, where adduct-form differences between LC-MS and AFADESI-MSI have not been evaluated and this database's partitioning does not apply. Only a single pooled (non-partitioned) metabolite list is available and per-organ splitting has not been performed; the skill requires the 11-sheet structure. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Organize an MSI metabolite reference database into positive-mode and negative-mode sheets and further split them per organ (brain, liver, kidney, heart, spleen, lung, muscle, pancreas, serum) so annotation runs only against the adduct forms and metabolites relevant to the tissue and ionization mode of the MSI data. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.2c00557
skills.summary: Organize an MSI metabolite reference database into positive-mode and negative-mode sheets and further split them per organ (brain, liver, kidney, heart, spleen, lung, muscle, pancreas, serum) so annotation runs only against the adduct forms and metabolites relevant to the tissue and ionization mode of the MSI data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The MSI dataset is not organ-specific or its detection mode is unknown — mixing modes or organs would violate the consistency check MSIannotator requires. The task is annotating non-MSI LC-MS data, where adduct-form differences between LC-MS and AFADESI-MSI have not been evaluated and this database's partitioning does not apply. Only a single pooled (non-partitioned) metabolite list is available and per-organ splitting has not been performed; the skill requires the 11-sheet structure.

skills.search_text: ion-mode-feature-counting Use when you have UPLC-HRMS peak lists acquired in both positive and negative ESI modes and need a non-targeted count of genuine sample components per mode, reconciled against background-subtracted totals. skills.summary: Counts and reconciles UPLC-HRMS chemical components per electrospray ionization mode after PATBS background subtraction, producing a mode-wise prototype inventory (e.g. CKXR: 199 total; 96 positive / 136 negative / 33 in both modes) with database-annotated identities and abundance ranking.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The peak table has already been background-subtracted and filtered, so PATBS would double-process the data and distort mode-wise counts Only one ion mode was acquired, so the positive/negative/both-mode reconciliation (96/136/33) cannot be performed The goal is targeted quantification of pre-selected analytes rather than non-targeted fingerprint component enumeration

skills.name: ion-mode-partition-analysis
skills.search_text: ion-mode-partition-analysis Use when a metabolomics paper reports ion-mode-specific or organ-specific metabolite counts (e.g. positive/negative mode totals, deduplicated unique-metabolite totals) and a companion database file must be counted and reconciled against those claims. The goal is metabolite annotation of MSI peaks, not verifying database coverage counts — use MSIannotator.m on MSIdata and Database instead. The database file's sheets do not follow the documented layout (metabolite names in first column, organ/mode sheet structure), so sheet-level counts would not map to the reported partitions. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 This skill verifies and reconciles metabolite counts partitioned by ion mode and organ against a paper's reported totals, using the MSIannotator 'Organ specific metabolite database.xlsx' (1298 metabolites in positive mode Sheet1, 515 in negative mode Sheet2, split across organ sheets Sheet3-Sheet11) and the DDA LC-MS/MS figure of 1620 unique metabolites from eight mouse organs and serum. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.2c00557
skills.summary: This skill verifies and reconciles metabolite counts partitioned by ion mode and organ against a paper's reported totals, using the MSIannotator 'Organ specific metabolite database.xlsx' (1298 metabolites in positive mode Sheet1, 515 in negative mode Sheet2, split across organ sheets Sheet3-Sheet11) and the DDA LC-MS/MS figure of 1620 unique metabolites from eight mouse organs and serum.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is metabolite annotation of MSI peaks, not verifying database coverage counts — use MSIannotator.m on MSIdata and Database instead. The database file's sheets do not follow the documented layout (metabolite names in first column, organ/mode sheet structure), so sheet-level counts would not map to the reported partitions.

skills.summary: A validation step that ensures the metabolite database selected for MSIannotator annotation matches both the organ being imaged and the ionization detection mode (positive or negative) of the preprocessed MSI dataset, preventing false metabolite assignments from mode-organ mismatched adduct-ion tables.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When running annotation on already-validated, organ- and mode-matched Database.xlsx and MSIdata.xlsx example inputs — the check is already satisfied and adds no information. skills.description: Use when comparing predicted versus experimental MS/MS spectra acquired under both positive and negative ionization modes, so that mean cosine similarity and significance tests are reported per mode rather than pooled.
skills.name: ion-mode-stratified-analysis
skills.search_text: ion-mode-stratified-analysis Use when comparing predicted versus experimental MS/MS spectra acquired under both positive and negative ionization modes, so that mean cosine similarity and significance tests are reported per mode rather than pooled. Spectra are acquired under only one ionization mode — stratification is unnecessary; pool directly Precursor/adduct labels are missing or ambiguous in the MGF/PKL records, so [M+H]+ and [M−H]− cannot be assigned reliably Input is a single spectral similarity summary already collapsed across modes — re-stratification from pooled means alone is not possible without per-compound values http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Stratify MS/MS prediction accuracy by ion mode — [M+H]+ versus [M−H]− — and aggregate per-compound cosine similarities separately in each mode, because model performance differs sharply between them (e.g. 3DMolMS 0.691 pos vs 0.478 neg; CFM-ID 0.076 pos vs 0.291 neg). metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad354
skills.summary: Stratify MS/MS prediction accuracy by ion mode — [M+H]+ versus [M−H]− — and aggregate per-compound cosine similarities separately in each mode, because model performance differs sharply between them (e.g. 3DMolMS 0.691 pos vs 0.478 neg; CFM-ID 0.076 pos vs 0.291 neg).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Spectra are acquired under only one ionization mode — stratification is unnecessary; pool directly Precursor/adduct labels are missing or ambiguous in the MGF/PKL records, so [M+H]+ and [M−H]− cannot be assigned reliably Input is a single spectral similarity summary already collapsed across modes — re-stratification from pooled means alone is not possible without per-compound values

skills.description: Use when HPTLC-HRMS data contains many EICs mixing analyte ions with background ions and the goal is to partition ion tracks into interesting vs background clusters before structure elucidation.
skills.name: ion-of-interest-vs-background-partitioning
skills.search_text: ion-of-interest-vs-background-partitioning Use when HPTLC-HRMS data contains many EICs mixing analyte ions with background ions and the goal is to partition ion tracks into interesting vs background clusters before structure elucidation. When the input is already a curated feature table whose ions have already been partitioned into interesting vs background clusters — this skill targets raw EIC-level partitioning from HPTLC-HRMS mzXML data. When the data does not come from HPTLC-HRMS (e.g. standard LC-MS/MS feature lists without planar chromatography tracks), as the EIC clusterisation and background-removal rationale is specific to planar chromatography signal highlighting. When a fully automated, non-interactive clustering is required without expert visual review, since run_eicCluster() explicitly launches an interactive Shiny app for user analysis. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Clusters extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) from HPTLC-HRMS runs so that ions carrying the analyte signal of interest can be visually and computationally separated from background ions, easing structure elucidation in planar chromatography. metabolomics/v3 10.1016/j.chroma.2018.09.050
skills.summary: Clusters extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) from HPTLC-HRMS runs so that ions carrying the analyte signal of interest can be visually and computationally separated from background ions, easing structure elucidation in planar chromatography.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is already a curated feature table whose ions have already been partitioned into interesting vs background clusters — this skill targets raw EIC-level partitioning from HPTLC-HRMS mzXML data. When the data does not come from HPTLC-HRMS (e.g. standard LC-MS/MS feature lists without planar chromatography tracks), as the EIC clusterisation and background-removal rationale is specific to planar chromatography signal highlighting. When a fully automated, non-interactive clustering is required without expert visual review, since run_eicCluster() explicitly launches an interactive Shiny app for user analysis.

skills.description: Use when reference and target LC-HRMS feature lists contain the same metabolites detected as different ion species/adducts, and peak matching fails or must be tested against an adduct swap.

skills.search_text: ion-species-mz-transformation Use when reference and target LC-HRMS feature lists contain the same metabolites detected as different ion species/adducts, and peak matching fails or must be tested against an adduct swap. Reference and target features are already recorded as the same ion species, so no adduct transformation is needed before alignment The input is already a post-alignment combined data matrix rather than an unaligned reference/target feature list http://edamontology.org/topic_3391 Transform LC-HRMS feature m/z values between ion species (e.g., simulated A1-to-A2 adduct swap) so that MetMatch can align reference and target feature lists whose metabolites are detected as differently formed ion species. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo6040039

skills.description: Use when LC/MS peak lists (e.g. XCMS feature tables) contain co-eluting features whose m/z differences match known adducts or losses and you need to reduce feature redundancy and identify quasi-molecular ions.
skills.name: ion-species-rule-matching
skills.search_text: ion-species-rule-matching Use when LC/MS peak lists (e.g. XCMS feature tables) contain co-eluting features whose m/z differences match known adducts or losses and you need to reduce feature redundancy and identify quasi-molecular ions. When the input is an already-annotated or targeted feature table where every feature's ion species is known - the rule-matching step would re-derive what is already present. When the goal is a first-pass isotope grouping step rather than ion-species annotation; use CAMERA's findIsotopes/findIsotopesWithValidation or grouping algorithms (calcCiS, calcCaS, calcPC.lpc, calcPC.hcs) instead. When the compound spectrum contains only the molecular ion and fragment ions with no further adducts and the neutral loss is not in the rule set - direct annotation is not possible in that case. When data are saturated (detector over-range causes m/z and RT centroid shifts), because matching rules to shifted m/z differences would produce incorrect annotations. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0219 Dynamic rule-based matching of within-spectrum m/z differences to ion species (adducts, neutral losses, cluster ions), so LC/MS features from the same analyte are annotated with a single ion species and quasi-molecular ion instead of being treated as unrelated features. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/ac202450g
skills.summary: Dynamic rule-based matching of within-spectrum m/z differences to ion species (adducts, neutral losses, cluster ions), so LC/MS features from the same analyte are annotated with a single ion species and quasi-molecular ion instead of being treated as unrelated features.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is an already-annotated or targeted feature table where every feature's ion species is known - the rule-matching step would re-derive what is already present. When the goal is a first-pass isotope grouping step rather than ion-species annotation; use CAMERA's findIsotopes/findIsotopesWithValidation or grouping algorithms (calcCiS, calcCaS, calcPC.lpc, calcPC.hcs) instead. When the compound spectrum contains only the molecular ion and fragment ions with no further adducts and the neutral loss is not in the rule set - direct annotation is not possible in that case. When data are saturated (detector over-range causes m/z and RT centroid shifts), because matching rules to shifted m/z differences would produce incorrect annotations.

skills.search_text: ion-species-spectrum-aggregation Use when building or extending MS/MS spectral libraries from feature-based molecular networking outputs, specifically to propagate a high-confidence library match (cosine >0.9) to other ion species (adducts, multimers, in-source fragments) of the same compound. When the goal is de novo spectral annotation of features lacking any library match — propagation only works within IINs that contain a feature matched to the GNPS spectral libraries at cosine >0.9 When MS1 ion identity networks have not been built (no IIN edges .csv files) — IIMN feature relationships are required to link ion species of the same compound When working with raw MS/MS vendor data directly; the workflow expects feature-finding tool exports (feature quantification table, .mgf, IIN edges) from MZmine, MS-DIAL, or XCMS http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Extracts consensus MS2 spectra of ion-identity features inside matched IINs to propagate high-confidence library annotations to connected ion species, yielding the GNPS-IIMN-PROPOGATED spectral library with 2657 entries (538 new entries from 24 public datasets). metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-021-23953-9

skills.description: Use when curating large molecule sets (SDF/SMILES from databases like NIST, ChEMBL, HMDB) before spectrum prediction, and neutral-only compounds are required for EI-MS library building.
skills.name: ionic-compound-exclusion
skills.search_text: ionic-compound-exclusion Use when curating large molecule sets (SDF/SMILES from databases like NIST, ChEMBL, HMDB) before spectrum prediction, and neutral-only compounds are required for EI-MS library building. The target library explicitly admits charged or zwitterionic species (e.g., LC-MS metabolomics libraries where ionizable metabolites from HMDB are the focus) The dataset has already passed through this pipeline — re-running exclusion after deduplication (rule 5) is redundant since each molecule appears in only one filtered set http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 Filter rule (3) of the five-step curation pipeline used to build f-NIST, f-ChEMBL, and f-HMDB: molecules flagged as ionic compounds — charged species and salt/counter-ion representations — are excluded so the in-silico EI-MS library contains only neutral molecules amenable to GC-EI-MS. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-023-39279-7
skills.summary: Filter rule (3) of the five-step curation pipeline used to build f-NIST, f-ChEMBL, and f-HMDB: molecules flagged as ionic compounds — charged species and salt/counter-ion representations — are excluded so the in-silico EI-MS library contains only neutral molecules amenable to GC-EI-MS.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The target library explicitly admits charged or zwitterionic species (e.g., LC-MS metabolomics libraries where ionizable metabolites from HMDB are the focus) The dataset has already passed through this pipeline — re-running exclusion after deduplication (rule 5) is redundant since each molecule appears in only one filtered set

skills.description: Use when raw untargeted metabolomics LC-MS/MS data must be processed with two distinct peak-picking parameter sets (e.g., AutoTuner- vs. IPO-derived centWave parameters) and downstream feature-table differences need to be quantified per ionization mode.

skills.search_text: ionization-mode-feature-count-comparison Use when raw untargeted metabolomics LC-MS/MS data must be processed with two distinct peak-picking parameter sets (e.g., AutoTuner- vs. IPO-derived centWave parameters) and downstream feature-table differences need to be quantified per ionization mode. The analysis goal is adduct/isotope annotation rather than comparing ISF feature percentages across MS parameter values.

skills.description: Use when assessing the robustness of metabolomics ORA results to metabolite misidentification: you have a differential metabolite list, a background compound set, and KEGG pathway sets, and need to quantify pathway loss/gain under simulated misidentification at a chosen rate (e.g. 4%).
skills.name: isobaric-compound-mass-matching
skills.search_text: isobaric-compound-mass-matching Use when assessing the robustness of metabolomics ORA results to metabolite misidentification: you have a differential metabolite list, a background compound set, and KEGG pathway sets, and need to quantify pathway loss/gain under simulated misidentification at a chosen rate (e.g. 4%). You need a true annotation-correction tool: this is an in-silico simulation of misidentification impact, not a method for identifying or correcting misidentified metabolites. You need to compare pathway databases or benchmark against a ground-truth set of enriched pathways — the study explicitly lacks a ground-truth dataset where the identities of enriched pathways are known. Your dataset is not MS-based untargeted metabolomics with compound identifiers mappable to KEGG (the study was limited to five MS-based untargeted metabolomics datasets). http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Simulates metabolite misidentification by replacing a fraction of compounds in a differential metabolite list with approximately isobaric KEGG compounds (molecular weight within ±20 ppm) or identical-chemical-formula counterparts, then quantifies the resulting pathway loss and gain rates in over-representation analysis (ORA). metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009105
skills.summary: Simulates metabolite misidentification by replacing a fraction of compounds in a differential metabolite list with approximately isobaric KEGG compounds (molecular weight within ±20 ppm) or identical-chemical-formula counterparts, then quantifies the resulting pathway loss and gain rates in over-representation analysis (ORA).
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need a true annotation-correction tool: this is an in-silico simulation of misidentification impact, not a method for identifying or correcting misidentified metabolites. You need to compare pathway databases or benchmark against a ground-truth set of enriched pathways — the study explicitly lacks a ground-truth dataset where the identities of enriched pathways are known. Your dataset is not MS-based untargeted metabolomics with compound identifiers mappable to KEGG (the study was limited to five MS-based untargeted metabolomics datasets).

skills.description: Use when centroided MSI lipid ion images contain unresolved isobaric overlaps — [X+2:Y+3][M+H]+ overlapped with [X:Y][M+Na]+, or Type II same-class double-bond isobars (e.g. PC 34:0 vs PC 34:1) — that cannot be mass-resolved (Δm/z 0.0025 needs resolution ≥600,000).
skills.name: isobaric-overlap-correction-msi
skills.search_text: isobaric-overlap-correction-msi Use when centroided MSI lipid ion images contain unresolved isobaric overlaps — [X+2:Y+3][M+H]+ overlapped with [X:Y][M+Na]+, or Type II same-class double-bond isobars (e.g. PC 34:0 vs PC 34:1) — that cannot be mass-resolved (Δm/z 0.0025 needs resolution ≥600,000). When the mass spectrometer can directly resolve the Na/H isobaric Δm/z of 0.0025 (resolution ≥600,000) or ion-mobility (e.g. timsTOF fleX TIMS) separation is available — use resolved images instead of mathematical correction. When no co-sprayed class-specific internal standards are available, the sodiated-to-protonated adduct ratio (RANa) needed for Na/H deconvolution cannot be estimated. When isobaric overlaps involve lipid pairs that are not same-class single-double-bond pairs (Type II correction subtracts isotope contributions only within such pairs). http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 LipidQMap's mathematical correction of isobaric overlaps in quantitative MSI lipidomics: Na/H adduct deconvolution using standard-derived sodiated-to-protonated adduct ratios (RANa) and Type II double-bond overlap correction using predicted isotope patterns. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.10.15.682422
skills.summary: LipidQMap's mathematical correction of isobaric overlaps in quantitative MSI lipidomics: Na/H adduct deconvolution using standard-derived sodiated-to-protonated adduct ratios (RANa) and Type II double-bond overlap correction using predicted isotope patterns.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the mass spectrometer can directly resolve the Na/H isobaric Δm/z of 0.0025 (resolution ≥600,000) or ion-mobility (e.g. timsTOF fleX TIMS) separation is available — use resolved images instead of mathematical correction. When no co-sprayed class-specific internal standards are available, the sodiated-to-protonated adduct ratio (RANa) needed for Na/H deconvolution cannot be estimated. When isobaric overlaps involve lipid pairs that are not same-class single-double-bond pairs (Type II correction subtracts isotope contributions only within such pairs).

skills.description: Decision support for choosing a GC-MS ionization configuration (isobutane CI vs methane CI vs EI at 70 or 15 eV) when metabolites fragment excessively or the [M+H]+ isotopic envelope is too weak for isotopologue quantification.
skills.name: isobutane-ci-fragmentation-evaluation
skills.search_text: isobutane-ci-fragmentation-evaluation Decision support for choosing a GC-MS ionization configuration (isobutane CI vs methane CI vs EI at 70 or 15 eV) when metabolites fragment excessively or the [M+H]+ isotopic envelope is too weak for isotopologue quantification. The analytes are not volatile small metabolites amenable to GC after methoxyamination/silylation derivatization — CI-isobutane protonation behavior may not transfer The goal is isotope ratio fidelity measurement at high resolution rather than choosing an ionization reagent gas; the article addresses reagent-gas selection, not HRMS isotope-ratio calibration Data are already processed isotopologue tables (e.g. isoSCAN output); this skill evaluates acquisition ionization, not downstream isotopologue quantification http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0157 A GC-MS method-validation skill for comparing chemical ionization reagent gases and ionization modes by assessing where metabolite abundance concentrates in the isotopic envelope, to select the configuration that best preserves intact protonated molecular ions [M+H]+ for stable-isotope tracing. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c02998
skills.summary: A GC-MS method-validation skill for comparing chemical ionization reagent gases and ionization modes by assessing where metabolite abundance concentrates in the isotopic envelope, to select the configuration that best preserves intact protonated molecular ions [M+H]+ for stable-isotope tracing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analytes are not volatile small metabolites amenable to GC after methoxyamination/silylation derivatization — CI-isobutane protonation behavior may not transfer The goal is isotope ratio fidelity measurement at high resolution rather than choosing an ionization reagent gas; the article addresses reagent-gas selection, not HRMS isotope-ratio calibration Data are already processed isotopologue tables (e.g. isoSCAN output); this skill evaluates acquisition ionization, not downstream isotopologue quantification

skills.description: Use when you have Salmon quant.sf transcript quantifications and phenotype groups, and need to identify isoform switches (changes in isoform usage between conditions) plus functional consequences of the switched isoforms.
skills.name: isoform-switch-detection
skills.search_text: isoform-switch-detection Use when you have Salmon quant.sf transcript quantifications and phenotype groups, and need to identify isoform switches (changes in isoform usage between conditions) plus functional consequences of the switched isoforms. You only need gene-level differential expression from a normalized count matrix — use the edgeR/DESeq2/RankProd module instead of the isoformSwitchAnalyzeR sub-workflow. Your quantifications are gene-level counts or alignment-based (no Salmon quant.sf transcript-level output), since this skill operates directly on Salmon quantification files. No transcriptome annotation is available to map switched isoforms to coding sequences, making CPAT/Pfam/signalP annotation impossible. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Detect genome-wide isoform switches and perform isoform- and gene-level differential expression with isoformSwitchAnalyzeR on Salmon quant.sf files, then functionally annotate switched transcripts for coding potential (CPAT), protein domains (Pfam), and signal sequences (signalP) within the MultiOmicsIntegrator (MOI) pipeline. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioadv/vbae175
skills.summary: Detect genome-wide isoform switches and perform isoform- and gene-level differential expression with isoformSwitchAnalyzeR on Salmon quant.sf files, then functionally annotate switched transcripts for coding potential (CPAT), protein domains (Pfam), and signal sequences (signalP) within the MultiOmicsIntegrator (MOI) pipeline.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need gene-level differential expression from a normalized count matrix — use the edgeR/DESeq2/RankProd module instead of the isoformSwitchAnalyzeR sub-workflow. Your quantifications are gene-level counts or alignment-based (no Salmon quant.sf transcript-level output), since this skill operates directly on Salmon quantification files. No transcriptome annotation is available to map switched isoforms to coding sequences, making CPAT/Pfam/signalP annotation impossible.

skills.description: Use when a batch of raw MS runs (Agilent 'd', Thermo '.raw', Bruker 'd', or mzML) has had precursor-ion peak metrics extracted and individual anomalous runs per metric and per sample group must be identified and visualized.
skills.name: isolation-forest-anomaly-detection
skills.search_text: isolation-forest-anomaly-detection Use when a batch of raw MS runs (Agilent 'd', Thermo '.raw', Bruker 'd', or mzML) has had precursor-ion peak metrics extracted and individual anomalous runs per metric and per sample group must be identified and visualized. When the goal is a single combined QC score for the batch — PeakQC's anomaly detection operates per metric/per group rather than producing a combined QC score When input is still raw vendor spectra and peak metrics have not yet been extracted (run the full PeakQC pipeline first: raw data conversion, MS1 time-versus-m/z images, PCA, metric extraction) When identification-based QC is sufficient, e.g. counting spectral matches in proteomics; such tools do little to pinpoint specific causes of performance deterioration, which is the gap this skill addresses Anomaly detection of MS run quality in which PeakQC fits an Isolation Forest model separately for each precursor-ion peak metric (mass error, retention time error, arrival time error) within each sample group, flagging runs whose metric values are outliers relative to their group. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jasms.4c00146
skills.summary: Anomaly detection of MS run quality in which PeakQC fits an Isolation Forest model separately for each precursor-ion peak metric (mass error, retention time error, arrival time error) within each sample group, flagging runs whose metric values are outliers relative to their group.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is a single combined QC score for the batch — PeakQC's anomaly detection operates per metric/per group rather than producing a combined QC score When input is still raw vendor spectra and peak metrics have not yet been extracted (run the full PeakQC pipeline first: raw data conversion, MS1 time-versus-m/z images, PCA, metric extraction) When identification-based QC is sufficient, e.g. counting spectral matches in proteomics; such tools do little to pinpoint specific causes of performance deterioration, which is the gap this skill addresses

skills.description: Use when a batch of MS runs (metabolomics, lipidomics, proteomics, or multiomics) needs automated per-metric outlier detection and you must visually pinpoint which runs and which ion metrics (mass, RT, arrival time errors, etc.) are defective.
skills.name: isolation-forest-outlier-visualization
skills.search_text: isolation-forest-outlier-visualization Use when a batch of MS runs (metabolomics, lipidomics, proteomics, or multiomics) needs automated per-metric outlier detection and you must visually pinpoint which runs and which ion metrics (mass, RT, arrival time errors, etc.) are defective. Input is already an identification-based QC summary (e.g., total number of spectral matches) and the goal is to interpret identification counts rather than inspect specific precursor-ion metrics — the article notes identification-based tools 'do little to pinpoint the specific causes of performance deterioration'. Data does not contain the precursor-ion peak metrics needed (no extracted mass, RT, or arrival time errors), so Isolation Forest has no per-metric features to score. The question is general batch quality assessment rather than pinpointing defective runs/metrics — PeakQC's PCA-on-MS1 step is the appropriate prior step in that case. http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 A PeakQC pipeline step that applies the Isolation Forest algorithm to flag outlier peak metrics for individual precursor ions per sample group, then renders the flagged defective MS runs and their defective metrics as error heatmaps exported as JPG and PDF files alongside CSV reports. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jasms.4c00146
skills.summary: A PeakQC pipeline step that applies the Isolation Forest algorithm to flag outlier peak metrics for individual precursor ions per sample group, then renders the flagged defective MS runs and their defective metrics as error heatmaps exported as JPG and PDF files alongside CSV reports.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already an identification-based QC summary (e.g., total number of spectral matches) and the goal is to interpret identification counts rather than inspect specific precursor-ion metrics — the article notes identification-based tools 'do little to pinpoint the specific causes of performance deterioration'. Data does not contain the precursor-ion peak metrics needed (no extracted mass, RT, or arrival time errors), so Isolation Forest has no per-metric features to score. The question is general batch quality assessment rather than pinpointing defective runs/metrics — PeakQC's PCA-on-MS1 step is the appropriate prior step in that case.

skills.description: Use when TP components produced by patRoon 2.0 componentization (parent feature linked with corresponding TP features) must be prioritized, and suspected isomeric TPs or duplicate TPs arising from multiple pathways through the same parent must be filtered before reporting.
skills.name: isomer-and-duplicate-removal
skills.search_text: isomer-and-duplicate-removal Use when TP components produced by patRoon 2.0 componentization (parent feature linked with corresponding TP features) must be prioritized, and suspected isomeric TPs or duplicate TPs arising from multiple pathways through the same parent must be filtered before reporting. When the input is raw LC-HRMS data or a feature table that has not yet passed through the patRoon TP screening and componentization steps — prioritization filters operate on TP components, not raw features When only a single filter dimension is needed and the components have already been prioritized (e.g., isomers already resolved chromatographically and confirmed) patRoon 2.0 prioritization filters that refine TP components after componentization: the remove-isomers filter drops isomers that MS alone cannot distinguish, and the duplicates filter removes duplicate TPs formed from the same parent through different pathways. metabolomics/v3 10.21105/joss.04029
skills.summary: patRoon 2.0 prioritization filters that refine TP components after componentization: the remove-isomers filter drops isomers that MS alone cannot distinguish, and the duplicates filter removes duplicate TPs formed from the same parent through different pathways.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is raw LC-HRMS data or a feature table that has not yet passed through the patRoon TP screening and componentization steps — prioritization filters operate on TP components, not raw features When only a single filter dimension is needed and the components have already been prioritized (e.g., isomers already resolved chromatographically and confirmed)

skills.description: Use when MS-FINDER formula assignment returns multiple isomeric candidate structures for HILIC MS/MS features and you have (or can predict) Retip retention times to exclude RT-inconsistent candidates.
skills.name: isomer-candidate-ranking
skills.search_text: isomer-candidate-ranking Use when MS-FINDER formula assignment returns multiple isomeric candidate structures for HILIC MS/MS features and you have (or can predict) Retip retention times to exclude RT-inconsistent candidates. Chromatography is a reversed-phase or otherwise altered method for which no Retip model was trained, or the analytes (e.g., high-molecular-weight lipids like triacylglycerols or phosphatidylcholines) lie outside the training set's chemical landscape You need to discriminate closely eluting positional isomers in fast UPLC methods (e.g., 12 min runs), where 1 min prediction errors are too coarse Each formula already has a single, uniquely matched candidate structure confirmed by an authentic standard — RT filtering adds no information and can wrongly exclude true positives http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Ranks and prunes isomeric candidate structures from MS-FINDER compound identification by comparing Retip-predicted HILIC retention times against experimental RT within a ±1 min window, yielding large reductions (e.g., 68%) in candidate lists. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.9b05765
skills.summary: Ranks and prunes isomeric candidate structures from MS-FINDER compound identification by comparing Retip-predicted HILIC retention times against experimental RT within a ±1 min window, yielding large reductions (e.g., 68%) in candidate lists.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Chromatography is a reversed-phase or otherwise altered method for which no Retip model was trained, or the analytes (e.g., high-molecular-weight lipids like triacylglycerols or phosphatidylcholines) lie outside the training set's chemical landscape You need to discriminate closely eluting positional isomers in fast UPLC methods (e.g., 12 min runs), where 1 min prediction errors are too coarse Each formula already has a single, uniquely matched candidate structure confirmed by an authentic standard — RT filtering adds no information and can wrongly exclude true positives

skills.description: Use when a spatial metabolomics peak list (e.g. exported from imzML) needs metabolite names assigned to detected m/z values without relying on METASPACE/pySM, and all isomeric candidates per peak must be preserved.
skills.name: isomer-candidate-summarisation
skills.search_text: isomer-candidate-summarisation Use when a spatial metabolomics peak list (e.g. exported from imzML) needs metabolite names assigned to detected m/z values without relying on METASPACE/pySM, and all isomeric candidates per peak must be preserved. When data come from high-resolution instruments (FT-ICR, orbitrap) where METASPACE/pySM's FDR-controlled annotation applies — SpaMTP was built because those tools 'do not yet apply to most data obtained with time-of-flight (TOF) analysers' When already-annotated data need downstream statistics (pathway analysis, differential expression) — use SpaMTP's CalculateAnnotationStatistics or AnnotateBigData refinement functions instead of re-annotating When confident structural ID beyond MSI level 4 is required — this step cannot disambiguate isomers without additional evidence (e.g. pseudo-MS/MS via MS1-ID/GNPS) SpaMTP's platform-agnostic exact-mass m/z annotation step: peaks are matched against adduct-expanded compound databases and every possible isomer per matched m/z is reported, corresponding to a level 4 Metabolomics Standards Initiative annotation. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.10.31.621429
skills.summary: SpaMTP's platform-agnostic exact-mass m/z annotation step: peaks are matched against adduct-expanded compound databases and every possible isomer per matched m/z is reported, corresponding to a level 4 Metabolomics Standards Initiative annotation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When data come from high-resolution instruments (FT-ICR, orbitrap) where METASPACE/pySM's FDR-controlled annotation applies — SpaMTP was built because those tools 'do not yet apply to most data obtained with time-of-flight (TOF) analysers' When already-annotated data need downstream statistics (pathway analysis, differential expression) — use SpaMTP's CalculateAnnotationStatistics or AnnotateBigData refinement functions instead of re-annotating When confident structural ID beyond MSI level 4 is required — this step cannot disambiguate isomers without additional evidence (e.g. pseudo-MS/MS via MS1-ID/GNPS)

skills.description: Use when matching LC-HRMS metabolite features from in vivo samples against a prototype list, and same-nominal-mass components must be classified as prototype matches vs. chromatographically distinct isomers.
skills.name: isomer-discrimination-by-rt
skills.search_text: isomer-discrimination-by-rt Use when matching LC-HRMS metabolite features from in vivo samples against a prototype list, and same-nominal-mass components must be classified as prototype matches vs. chromatographically distinct isomers. The metabolite candidates are already characterized and only downstream MS1/MS2 mass-defect or MS2-fragment-similarity scoring (later MDRB steps) is needed. RT is not comparable between the prototype and metabolite lists (e.g., different LC columns, gradients, or instruments), since the ±25 s window assumes co-elution of the same component in both runs. Data are single-run features with no paired in vitro prototype list to bridge against — MTSF-style prototype-database matching or de novo annotation is more appropriate. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Discriminates true prototype components from same-mass isomers when bridging in vivo mouse metabolite features to an in vitro prototype list (MDRB step 1): matching uses accurate m/z within ±5 ppm, and retention time within ±25 s separates a prototype match from a candidate isomer. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13020-024-01031-8
skills.summary: Discriminates true prototype components from same-mass isomers when bridging in vivo mouse metabolite features to an in vitro prototype list (MDRB step 1): matching uses accurate m/z within ±5 ppm, and retention time within ±25 s separates a prototype match from a candidate isomer.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The metabolite candidates are already characterized and only downstream MS1/MS2 mass-defect or MS2-fragment-similarity scoring (later MDRB steps) is needed. RT is not comparable between the prototype and metabolite lists (e.g., different LC columns, gradients, or instruments), since the ±25 s window assumes co-elution of the same component in both runs. Data are single-run features with no paired in vitro prototype list to bridge against — MTSF-style prototype-database matching or de novo annotation is more appropriate.
