skills.description: Use when you have raw LC/MS untargeted metabolomics data in mzML format (e.g., HILIC positive-mode serum studies) and need to detect metabolite signals without user-set parameters, QC samples, or manual threshold tuning.
skills.name: lcms-ms1-signal-detection
skills.search_text: lcms-ms1-signal-detection Use when you have raw LC/MS untargeted metabolomics data in mzML format (e.g., HILIC positive-mode serum studies) and need to detect metabolite signals without user-set parameters, QC samples, or manual threshold tuning. When you need de-isotoping, MS/MS identification, or compound annotation — mzLearn outputs are limited to the ion MS1 level and does not perform these steps. When working with LC modes other than HILIC positive mode (e.g., reversed-phase or negative mode), since the current pre-trained model and mzLearn pretraining set were developed specifically for HILIC positive mode. When a parameterized classical pipeline is required for reproducibility audits that demand explicit user-set thresholds, as mzLearn is designed to be zero-parameter. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 mzLearn is a data-driven, zero-parameter MS1 signal-detection and alignment algorithm for LC/MS untargeted metabolomics that runs directly on mzML files, iteratively learns signal characteristics and drift maps via synthetic QC samples, and outperforms XCMS and ASARI in sensitivity and false-positive control. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.01.26.634927
skills.summary: mzLearn is a data-driven, zero-parameter MS1 signal-detection and alignment algorithm for LC/MS untargeted metabolomics that runs directly on mzML files, iteratively learns signal characteristics and drift maps via synthetic QC samples, and outperforms XCMS and ASARI in sensitivity and false-positive control.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When you need de-isotoping, MS/MS identification, or compound annotation — mzLearn outputs are limited to the ion MS1 level and does not perform these steps. When working with LC modes other than HILIC positive mode (e.g., reversed-phase or negative mode), since the current pre-trained model and mzLearn pretraining set were developed specifically for HILIC positive mode. When a parameterized classical pipeline is required for reproducibility audits that demand explicit user-set thresholds, as mzLearn is designed to be zero-parameter.

When only a single EIC quality metric is needed for component selection and alignment without concern for high-background or single-peak EICs — the MCQ index alone is suited for selecting and aligning analyte components but cannot fairly evaluate EICs with high background signals or those containing only a single peak. When the goal is automatic machine-learning-based peak identification (e.g. SVM) — this requires a curated training set of good and bad representative peaks that does not yet exist. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Quantifies background-signal and single-peak artifacts in extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) from LC/MS metabolomics profiles by modeling EIC noise via the mass chromatographic quality (MCQ) index and its global zigzag index alternative, enabling filtering of bad EICs before downstream chromatographic peak detection. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/1471-2105-15-s11-s5
skills.summary: Quantifies background-signal and single-peak artifacts in extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) from LC/MS metabolomics profiles by modeling EIC noise via the mass chromatographic quality (MCQ) index and its global zigzag index alternative, enabling filtering of bad EICs before downstream chromatographic peak detection.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is already a detected chromatographic peak list rather than raw EIC intensities — use peak quality evaluation and filtering (sharpness, Gaussian similarity, SNR, peak significance level, TPASR, local peak-related zigzag index) instead. When only a single EIC quality metric is needed for component selection and alignment without concern for high-background or single-peak EICs — the MCQ index alone is suited for selecting and aligning analyte components but cannot fairly evaluate EICs with high background signals or those containing only a single peak. When the goal is automatic machine-learning-based peak identification (e.g. SVM) — this requires a curated training set of good and bad representative peaks that does not yet exist.

skills.summary: Annotate LC-MS peaks to KEGG compounds via mWISE by matching m/z against a default adduct/fragment set, clustering candidate features with spectral clustering (DBSCAN-optimized) plus a cluster-based filter, and prioritizing a final top-three list per peak using diffusion scores in the FELLA or RClass networks.

skills.search_text: lcms-peak-quality-classification Use when unaligned or aligned mzMine2/XCMS feature tables must be labelled and filtered to remove false-positive MS1 peaks before downstream statistical analysis of large-scale LC-MS metabolomics data. The goal is to remove peaks from non-lipid metabolites or peaks that need identity and reproducibility assessment — NeatMS gives no information on peak identity or reproducibility A curated library panel of metabolites of interest is required to classify peaks rather than remove chemical noise http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Classifies untargeted LC-MS peaks as High_quality, Low_quality, or Noise using NeatMS's pretrained neural network, then filters out false-positive MS1 peaks reported by upstream pipelines such as mzMine2 and XCMS. Rationale: label-driven peak curation with a probability threshold (0.22 for the default model) outperforms rule-based noise removal on large-scale metabolomics data. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c02220
skills.summary: Classifies untargeted LC-MS peaks as High_quality, Low_quality, or Noise using NeatMS's pretrained neural network, then filters out false-positive MS1 peaks reported by upstream pipelines such as mzMine2 and XCMS. Rationale: label-driven peak curation with a probability threshold (0.22 for the default model) outperforms rule-based noise removal on large-scale metabolomics data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to remove peaks from non-lipid metabolites or peaks that need identity and reproducibility assessment — NeatMS gives no information on peak identity or reproducibility A curated library panel of metabolites of interest is required to classify peaks rather than remove chemical noise

skills.description: Use when detected chromatographic peaks from LC/MS metabolomics data must be classified as good or bad, and single-metric cutoff filtering is insufficient — combine multiple peak quality metrics as ML features.
skills.name: lcms-peak-quality-feature-engineering
skills.search_text: lcms-peak-quality-feature-engineering Use when detected chromatographic peaks from LC/MS metabolomics data must be classified as good or bad, and single-metric cutoff filtering is insufficient — combine multiple peak quality metrics as ML features. When evaluating extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) rather than detected peaks — the paper shows EICs with high background signals or containing only a single peak cannot be fairly evaluated by the MCQ index and instead need the EIC-related global zigzag index When no curated training set of good and bad representative peaks exists — the article explicitly notes machine-learning-based peak identification via SVM is not yet implemented because such training samples are lacking When a single metric with an optimized cutoff threshold suffices for the filtering task and interpretability of a simple threshold rule is preferred http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 Engineer chromatographic peak-quality feature vectors for LC/MS metabolomics peaks by computing the six quality metrics (sharpness, Gaussian similarity, SNR, peak significance level, TPASR, and local zigzag index) in Matlab, then normalize and combine them for SVM-based good/bad peak classification instead of applying single-metric cutoff thresholds. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/1471-2105-15-s11-s5
skills.summary: Engineer chromatographic peak-quality feature vectors for LC/MS metabolomics peaks by computing the six quality metrics (sharpness, Gaussian similarity, SNR, peak significance level, TPASR, and local zigzag index) in Matlab, then normalize and combine them for SVM-based good/bad peak classification instead of applying single-metric cutoff thresholds.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When evaluating extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) rather than detected peaks — the paper shows EICs with high background signals or containing only a single peak cannot be fairly evaluated by the MCQ index and instead need the EIC-related global zigzag index When no curated training set of good and bad representative peaks exists — the article explicitly notes machine-learning-based peak identification via SVM is not yet implemented because such training samples are lacking When a single metric with an optimized cutoff threshold suffices for the filtering task and interpretability of a simple threshold rule is preferred

skills.description: Use when running the Nextflow4MS-DIAL pipeline on .mzML LC-HRMS input and you need MS-DIAL's peak table to flow into MS-FLO automatically without manual file copying or manual re-parameterization between the two tools.
skills.name: lcms-peak-table-automated-transfer
skills.search_text: lcms-peak-table-automated-transfer Use when running the Nextflow4MS-DIAL pipeline on .mzML LC-HRMS input and you need MS-DIAL's peak table to flow into MS-FLO automatically without manual file copying or manual re-parameterization between the two tools. When the input is already a finished, manually curated feature table — this skill's purpose is automated intermediate handoff between MS-DIAL and MS-FLO, not post-hoc table refinement. When working outside the Nextflow4MS-DIAL framework (e.g., calling MS-FLO standalone from a separate script) — no containerized, workflow-managed transfer occurs, undermining the reproducibility this skill provides. When the raw data are not .mzML or .abf LC-HRMS files, since the workflow only accepts those formats and the handoff depends on MS-DIAL's peak-table output from them. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Automates handoff of MS-DIAL-generated peak tables (in .msdial/.tsv form) to MS-FLO inside the Nextflow4MS-DIAL workflow, eliminating manual copying of intermediate feature tables so that downstream duplicate/adduct/isotope flagging, peak alignment, and contaminant ion removal run unattended. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jasms.4c00364
skills.summary: Automates handoff of MS-DIAL-generated peak tables (in .msdial/.tsv form) to MS-FLO inside the Nextflow4MS-DIAL workflow, eliminating manual copying of intermediate feature tables so that downstream duplicate/adduct/isotope flagging, peak alignment, and contaminant ion removal run unattended.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is already a finished, manually curated feature table — this skill's purpose is automated intermediate handoff between MS-DIAL and MS-FLO, not post-hoc table refinement. When working outside the Nextflow4MS-DIAL framework (e.g., calling MS-FLO standalone from a separate script) — no containerized, workflow-managed transfer occurs, undermining the reproducibility this skill provides. When the raw data are not .mzML or .abf LC-HRMS files, since the workflow only accepts those formats and the handoff depends on MS-DIAL's peak-table output from them.

skills.description: Use when starting from raw .mzML (or .abf) LC-HRMS metabolomics files and you need a reproducible, containerized peak-detection/alignment pipeline that yields a filtered MS-DIAL plus MS-FLO peak table (.tsv).

skills.summary: Generate feature/peak tables from untargeted LC-MS metabolomics raw data by running containerized MS-DIAL (peak detection, alignment, m/z and retention-time assignment) followed by MS-FLO quality filtering (duplicate, adduct/isotope flagging, contaminant ion removal), as implemented in the Nextflow4MS-DIAL workflow.

skills.search_text: lcms-qc-normalization-benchmarking Use when comparing the computational cost of QC sample-based normalization methods on targeted (e.g., 53-compound) vs untargeted (e.g., 8913-feature) metabolomics matrices, or when deciding which normalization method is feasible for high-throughput use. skills.summary: Benchmarks the computational run time of QC-based LC-MS metabolomics normalization methods (Metanorm's rLOESS, rGAM, tGAM, QC-RLSC, QC-RSC, plus external TIGER and SERFF) across targeted and untargeted datasets, quantifying how parallelization and dataset size affect wall-clock time.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to assess normalization quality (replicate concordance, drift/batch-effect reduction) rather than computational cost — use performance evaluation on QC/replicate samples instead The dataset contains fewer features than can reveal scaling behavior (timing curves must scale with dataset size to be meaningful) The normalization method of interest is not QC sample-based (e.g., sample-based only normalization outside the Metanorm/TIGER/SERFF scope)

You only have a single MS/MS spectrum to identify (no complete LC-MS/MS run with retention ordering across spectra) — the graph-based joint identification needs multiple ordered layers You lack a trained retention-order predictor (RankSVM w) and only have MS/MS scores — then D=0 recovers the plain IOKR baseline and adds nothing Molecules have retention times too small to interact with the chromatographic system — these were removed during preprocessing and would corrupt the order graph http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Evaluates metabolite identification accuracy over a complete LC-MS/MS run by combining IOKR MS/MS candidate scores with predicted retention orders via a dynamic-programming shortest-path search, sweeping the trade-off constant D to quantify improvement over the IOKR-only baseline. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/bty590
skills.summary: Evaluates metabolite identification accuracy over a complete LC-MS/MS run by combining IOKR MS/MS candidate scores with predicted retention orders via a dynamic-programming shortest-path search, sweeping the trade-off constant D to quantify improvement over the IOKR-only baseline.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only have a single MS/MS spectrum to identify (no complete LC-MS/MS run with retention ordering across spectra) — the graph-based joint identification needs multiple ordered layers You lack a trained retention-order predictor (RankSVM w) and only have MS/MS scores — then D=0 recovers the plain IOKR baseline and adds nothing Molecules have retention times too small to interact with the chromatographic system — these were removed during preprocessing and would corrupt the order graph

skills.description: Use when you need the health/safety (LCSS) annotation content for a single PubChem compound record, organized by the LCSS table of contents, as a JSON payload from PUG-View.
skills.name: lcss-optional-parameter-usage
skills.search_text: lcss-optional-parameter-usage Use when you need the health/safety (LCSS) annotation content for a single PubChem compound record, organized by the LCSS table of contents, as a JSON payload from PUG-View. You need to query multiple compound record identifiers in one call — a PUG-View request cannot take multiple input record identifiers You need specific individual computed compound properties — PUG-REST is best suited for that, not PUG-View You need annotation data under multiple headings for a compound in a single request (without retrieving the full annotation data), or specialized tabular data that come from other backend services and are not currently accessible through PUG-View http://edamontology.org/topic_3315 Retrieves a compound's Laboratory Chemical Safety Summary (LCSS) annotations from PubChem via a PUG-View data request using the optional toc parameter set to LCSS+TOC, which reorganizes the record annotations by the LCSS table of contents instead of the default one. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-019-0375-2
skills.summary: Retrieves a compound's Laboratory Chemical Safety Summary (LCSS) annotations from PubChem via a PUG-View data request using the optional toc parameter set to LCSS+TOC, which reorganizes the record annotations by the LCSS table of contents instead of the default one.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need to query multiple compound record identifiers in one call — a PUG-View request cannot take multiple input record identifiers You need specific individual computed compound properties — PUG-REST is best suited for that, not PUG-View You need annotation data under multiple headings for a compound in a single request (without retrieving the full annotation data), or specialized tabular data that come from other backend services and are not currently accessible through PUG-View

skills.description: Use when counting independent genetic association signals from PLINK2 GWAS summary statistics, e.g. comparing genome-wide significant locus counts between pre- and post-QC versions of NMR biomarker data.
skills.name: ld-block-locus-partitioning
skills.search_text: ld-block-locus-partitioning Use when counting independent genetic association signals from PLINK2 GWAS summary statistics, e.g. comparing genome-wide significant locus counts between pre- and post-QC versions of NMR biomarker data. The input is raw UK Biobank NMR field data that has not yet passed through ukbnmr remove_technical_variation() and the goal is QC correction rather than locus counting GWAS has not been run or summary statistics lack P-values, so there are no significant SNPs to partition You need SNP-level rather than locus-level association summaries (SNPs within a block are deliberately collapsed) http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 Partitions genome-wide significant SNPs (P < 5e-8) from GWAS summary statistics into independent loci using LD blocks, enabling accurate locus-level counting of genetic associations before and after technical-variation removal. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41597-023-01949-y
skills.summary: Partitions genome-wide significant SNPs (P < 5e-8) from GWAS summary statistics into independent loci using LD blocks, enabling accurate locus-level counting of genetic associations before and after technical-variation removal.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw UK Biobank NMR field data that has not yet passed through ukbnmr remove_technical_variation() and the goal is QC correction rather than locus counting GWAS has not been run or summary statistics lack P-values, so there are no significant SNPs to partition You need SNP-level rather than locus-level association summaries (SNPs within a block are deliberately collapsed)

skills.description: Use when running a two-sample Mendelian randomization analysis (e.g. an mGWAS metabolite as exposure against a GWAS outcome such as finn-b-E4_DM2) and the selected instrument SNPs need pruning of correlated variants before harmonization.
skills.name: ld-clumping-of-instrument-variants
skills.search_text: ld-clumping-of-instrument-variants Use when running a two-sample Mendelian randomization analysis (e.g. an mGWAS metabolite as exposure against a GWAS outcome such as finn-b-E4_DM2) and the selected instrument SNPs need pruning of correlated variants before harmonization. When the input is already a pruned, LD-independent variant list and no correlation structure exists among the instrument SNPs When the analysis goal is raw mGWAS/GWAS association testing rather than Mendelian randomization — clumping is only relevant for constructing valid MR instrument sets When instrument variants come from a single reference panel with no LD structure to account for (e.g. rare independent variants already selected by significance threshold alone) http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 http://edamontology.org/topic_3393 Removes correlated SNPs from the instrument set selected for a metabolite–phenotype Mendelian randomization analysis, so that only linkage-disequilibrium-independent variants contribute to the two-sample MR effect estimate in the MetaboAnalyst 6.0 Causal Analysis module. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkae253
skills.summary: Removes correlated SNPs from the instrument set selected for a metabolite–phenotype Mendelian randomization analysis, so that only linkage-disequilibrium-independent variants contribute to the two-sample MR effect estimate in the MetaboAnalyst 6.0 Causal Analysis module.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is already a pruned, LD-independent variant list and no correlation structure exists among the instrument SNPs When the analysis goal is raw mGWAS/GWAS association testing rather than Mendelian randomization — clumping is only relevant for constructing valid MR instrument sets When instrument variants come from a single reference panel with no LD structure to account for (e.g. rare independent variants already selected by significance threshold alone)

skills.description: Use when ranking thousands of exposome chemicals by risk and only predicted LD50 toxicity (no measured reference dose) is available, requiring LD50-to-BMD10 conversion with uncertainty factors.
skills.name: ld50-to-bmd10-uncertainty-factor-derivation
skills.search_text: ld50-to-bmd10-uncertainty-factor-derivation Use when ranking thousands of exposome chemicals by risk and only predicted LD50 toxicity (no measured reference dose) is available, requiring LD50-to-BMD10 conversion with uncertainty factors. Measured chronic/subchronic toxicity data or reference doses (e.g., RfD, BMD from guideline studies) are available — the LD50-based approach may underestimate chronic and subchronic toxicity risk The chemical lacks a CASRN and thus cannot be retrieved through the U.S. EPA Chemistry Dashboard-based HTS workflow The analysis requires internal (IVIVE-based) rather than external exposure — the PrHQ here is computed from external exposure only Converts predicted rat oral LD50 values (from TEST) into probabilistic BMD10-derived reference doses by applying chemical-specific uncertainty factors (Equations 1–3) to obtain the human dose of minimal incidence (HDMI), enabling probabilistic hazard quotient (PrHQ) risk ranking across the human exposome database. metabolomics/v3 10.1289/ehp7722
skills.summary: Converts predicted rat oral LD50 values (from TEST) into probabilistic BMD10-derived reference doses by applying chemical-specific uncertainty factors (Equations 1–3) to obtain the human dose of minimal incidence (HDMI), enabling probabilistic hazard quotient (PrHQ) risk ranking across the human exposome database.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Measured chronic/subchronic toxicity data or reference doses (e.g., RfD, BMD from guideline studies) are available — the LD50-based approach may underestimate chronic and subchronic toxicity risk The chemical lacks a CASRN and thus cannot be retrieved through the U.S. EPA Chemistry Dashboard-based HTS workflow The analysis requires internal (IVIVE-based) rather than external exposure — the PrHQ here is computed from external exposure only

skills.description: Use when training an LDA topic model over bag-of-words BGC (sub)Pfam tokenisations (e.g. iPRESTO PRESTO-TOP) and you must verify topic quality (u_mass coherence) and training convergence before using the motifs downstream.
skills.name: lda-coherence-scoring-and-convergence-checking
skills.search_text: lda-coherence-scoring-and-convergence-checking Use when training an LDA topic model over bag-of-words BGC (sub)Pfam tokenisations (e.g. iPRESTO PRESTO-TOP) and you must verify topic quality (u_mass coherence) and training convergence before using the motifs downstream. Gene order within the BGC is biologically important — LDA assumes a bag-of-words model where original gene order is not considered; use the PRESTO-STAT statistical method, which represents tokenised genes in their original order The corpus is too small to support a 1,000-topic model (e.g. the small Streptomyces/Salinispora dataset), where topic granularity and coherence estimates become unreliable You need de novo sub-cluster detection rather than quality assessment of an already-trained topic model http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Quality-assessment procedure for the PRESTO-TOP Latent Dirichlet Allocation topic model used in iPRESTO: it computes the u_mass coherence score over the learned sub-cluster motifs and monitors log-likelihood convergence on held-out BGCs to confirm the 1,000-topic model is stable before motif filtering and validation. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1010462
skills.summary: Quality-assessment procedure for the PRESTO-TOP Latent Dirichlet Allocation topic model used in iPRESTO: it computes the u_mass coherence score over the learned sub-cluster motifs and monitors log-likelihood convergence on held-out BGCs to confirm the 1,000-topic model is stable before motif filtering and validation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Gene order within the BGC is biologically important — LDA assumes a bag-of-words model where original gene order is not considered; use the PRESTO-STAT statistical method, which represents tokenised genes in their original order The corpus is too small to support a 1,000-topic model (e.g. the small Streptomyces/Salinispora dataset), where topic granularity and coherence estimates become unreliable You need de novo sub-cluster detection rather than quality assessment of an already-trained topic model

skills.description: Use when you have a corpus of unlabelled MS2 spectra (e.g. ~1,000 MS peaks per sample per ionization mode from complex mixtures) and want unsupervised discovery of conserved fragment/neutral-loss substructures plus per-spectrum motif loadings.
skills.name: lda-topic-model-inference-on-mass-spectra
skills.search_text: lda-topic-model-inference-on-mass-spectra Use when you have a corpus of unlabelled MS2 spectra (e.g. ~1,000 MS peaks per sample per ionization mode from complex mixtures) and want unsupervised discovery of conserved fragment/neutral-loss substructures plus per-spectrum motif loadings. Spectra come from simple mixtures with information-poor MS2 spectra rather than complex mixtures fragmented with ramped or stepped collision energy — the article notes MS2LDA works best with a large number of fragmented metabolites The goal is direct automated library annotation of spectra including neutral losses — losses are not currently supported by spectral matching tools and had to be omitted Computation budget is minimal and a simpler targeted/similarity tool would suffice — MS2LDA is computationally more costly than simpler tools, though not prohibitively so http://edamontology.org/topic_3395 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Applies unsupervised Latent Dirichlet Allocation (as implemented in MS2LDA) to MS2 fragmentation spectra, represented as bags of fragments and neutral losses, to learn recurring substructures (Mass2Motifs) and decompose each spectrum into these motifs without training data. metabolomics/v3 10.1073/pnas.1608041113
skills.summary: Applies unsupervised Latent Dirichlet Allocation (as implemented in MS2LDA) to MS2 fragmentation spectra, represented as bags of fragments and neutral losses, to learn recurring substructures (Mass2Motifs) and decompose each spectrum into these motifs without training data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Spectra come from simple mixtures with information-poor MS2 spectra rather than complex mixtures fragmented with ramped or stepped collision energy — the article notes MS2LDA works best with a large number of fragmented metabolites The goal is direct automated library annotation of spectra including neutral losses — losses are not currently supported by spectral matching tools and had to be omitted Computation budget is minimal and a simpler targeted/similarity tool would suffice — MS2LDA is computationally more costly than simpler tools, though not prohibitively so

skills.description: Use when you have a trained LDA topic model over MS/MS fragmentation data (e.g., ms2lda.bin with motifset.json) and need interactive exploration of inferred topics and their fragment/neutral-loss terms before structural characterization.
skills.name: lda-topic-model-visualization
skills.search_text: lda-topic-model-visualization Use when you have a trained LDA topic model over MS/MS fragmentation data (e.g., ms2lda.bin with motifset.json) and need interactive exploration of inferred topics and their fragment/neutral-loss terms before structural characterization. The analysis goal is structural characterization of already-selected motifs (annotation via spectral matching), not interactive exploration of the topic model output. Input spectra are simple or information-poor (few fragments, no ramped/stepped collision energy) — the paper states MS2LDA 'works best for complex mixtures where a large number of metabolites are fragmented and information-rich MS2 spectra are available'. You only need a static figure of the spectral network; the SI shows a subset network produced by MS2LDAvis, but the interactive module is for exploration, not final publication rendering. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Reconstructs the MS2LDAvis interactive exploration module — a customization of LDAvis (Sievert & Shirley 2014) — so that trained LDA topic-model output (Mass2Motifs, their fragment/neutral-loss term distributions, and spectra-level topic loadings) can be inspected in a 2D inter-topic bubble plot with a lambda relevance slider for ranking terms per motif. metabolomics/v3 10.1073/pnas.1608041113
skills.summary: Reconstructs the MS2LDAvis interactive exploration module — a customization of LDAvis (Sievert & Shirley 2014) — so that trained LDA topic-model output (Mass2Motifs, their fragment/neutral-loss term distributions, and spectra-level topic loadings) can be inspected in a 2D inter-topic bubble plot with a lambda relevance slider for ranking terms per motif.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is structural characterization of already-selected motifs (annotation via spectral matching), not interactive exploration of the topic model output. Input spectra are simple or information-poor (few fragments, no ramped/stepped collision energy) — the paper states MS2LDA 'works best for complex mixtures where a large number of metabolites are fragmented and information-rich MS2 spectra are available'. You only need a static figure of the spectral network; the SI shows a subset network produced by MS2LDAvis, but the interactive module is for exploration, not final publication rendering.

skills.description: Use when you have antiSMASH-predicted BGCs tokenised into (sub)Pfam domain combinations and need unsupervised discovery of sub-cluster motifs without relying on gene order.
skills.name: lda-topic-modeling-of-bgc-domain-combinations
skills.search_text: lda-topic-modeling-of-bgc-domain-combinations Use when you have antiSMASH-predicted BGCs tokenised into (sub)Pfam domain combinations and need unsupervised discovery of sub-cluster motifs without relying on gene order. When gene order matters for the sub-cluster signal — the LDA (PRESTO-TOP) bag-of-words representation discards gene order; the statistical method (PRESTO-STAT) that preserves tokenised gene order is the appropriate alternative When you need per-clade functional resolution of highly frequent Pfam domains rather than domain-combination motifs — build per-clade subPfam pHMM models instead When BGCs have already been assigned to sub-clusters or a feature table of domain combinations exists — retraining LDA from scratch is unnecessary Train an LDA topic model (PRESTO-TOP from iPRESTO) on bag-of-words vectors of (sub)Pfam domain combinations from BGCs to discover biosynthetic sub-cluster motifs, validated against experimentally verified SubClusterBlast sub-clusters. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1010462
skills.summary: Train an LDA topic model (PRESTO-TOP from iPRESTO) on bag-of-words vectors of (sub)Pfam domain combinations from BGCs to discover biosynthetic sub-cluster motifs, validated against experimentally verified SubClusterBlast sub-clusters.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When gene order matters for the sub-cluster signal — the LDA (PRESTO-TOP) bag-of-words representation discards gene order; the statistical method (PRESTO-STAT) that preserves tokenised gene order is the appropriate alternative When you need per-clade functional resolution of highly frequent Pfam domains rather than domain-combination motifs — build per-clade subPfam pHMM models instead When BGCs have already been assigned to sub-clusters or a feature table of domain combinations exists — retraining LDA from scratch is unnecessary

skills.description: Use when training or evaluating ESP's MLP/GNN base models where spectral-peak dependencies and topic-structured co-occurrence should be exploited — e.g. flags like disable_mt_lda=False, mt_lda_weight, correlation_mat_rank appear in the config.
skills.name: lda-topic-multitask-head-training
skills.search_text: lda-topic-multitask-head-training Use when training or evaluating ESP's MLP/GNN base models where spectral-peak dependencies and topic-structured co-occurrence should be exploited — e.g. flags like disable_mt_lda=False, mt_lda_weight, correlation_mat_rank appear in the config. When you only want the plain MLP or GNN baselines for comparison — the baselines are defined with these enhancements ablated via --disable_* flags When input spectra are not at the paper's 1000-bin resolution (resolution parameter controls bins: 1000/resolution), since the mixing matrix and topic head shapes depend on it When no LDA spectral-topic labels are available for the dataset, as the multi-task head requires topic supervision Trains ESP base models (MLP and GNN spectral predictors) with an auxiliary multi-task head that predicts LDA spectral-topic distributions alongside the 1000-bin spectrum, and couples peaks via a rank-limited learnable correlation mixing matrix. This is one of the two enhancement techniques that lift ESP 23.7%/37.2% in average rank over the MLP/GNN baselines. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae490
skills.summary: Trains ESP base models (MLP and GNN spectral predictors) with an auxiliary multi-task head that predicts LDA spectral-topic distributions alongside the 1000-bin spectrum, and couples peaks via a rank-limited learnable correlation mixing matrix. This is one of the two enhancement techniques that lift ESP 23.7%/37.2% in average rank over the MLP/GNN baselines.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When you only want the plain MLP or GNN baselines for comparison — the baselines are defined with these enhancements ablated via --disable_* flags When input spectra are not at the paper's 1000-bin resolution (resolution parameter controls bins: 1000/resolution), since the mixing matrix and topic head shapes depend on it When no LDA spectral-topic labels are available for the dataset, as the multi-task head requires topic supervision

skills.description: Use when importing a lipidome quantity table (csv/xlsx, pivot or flat, or mzTab-M) and you need a global QC verdict on whether quantitative values plausibly span several orders of magnitude before downstream analysis.
skills.name: leading-digit-distribution-comparison-statistics
skills.search_text: leading-digit-distribution-comparison-statistics Use when importing a lipidome quantity table (csv/xlsx, pivot or flat, or mzTab-M) and you need a global QC verdict on whether quantitative values plausibly span several orders of magnitude before downstream analysis. The input is raw mass-spectrometric peak data rather than a tabulated lipidome quantity table — this check operates on lipid quantity values after lipid search-engine identification (e.g., LipidXplorer, LDA, MS-DIAL output). The goal is per-lipid or per-sample variance QC rather than a dataset-level plausibility check on quantitative value ranges — Benford conformance is a global leading-digit test, not a replicate or batch QC method. Quantities are ratios, log-transformed, or otherwise rescaled so leading digits no longer reflect measurement magnitude — the test presumes raw quantitative values spanning orders of magnitude. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Quality control check, as implemented in LipidSpace's built-in QC, that tests whether the leading-digit distribution of lipid quantity values in a loaded lipidome conforms to Benford's law (expected frequency of digit d = log10(1 + 1/d)), flagging datasets whose quantities span too narrow a range or are over-imputed. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c02449
skills.summary: Quality control check, as implemented in LipidSpace's built-in QC, that tests whether the leading-digit distribution of lipid quantity values in a loaded lipidome conforms to Benford's law (expected frequency of digit d = log10(1 + 1/d)), flagging datasets whose quantities span too narrow a range or are over-imputed.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw mass-spectrometric peak data rather than a tabulated lipidome quantity table — this check operates on lipid quantity values after lipid search-engine identification (e.g., LipidXplorer, LDA, MS-DIAL output). The goal is per-lipid or per-sample variance QC rather than a dataset-level plausibility check on quantitative value ranges — Benford conformance is a global leading-digit test, not a replicate or batch QC method. Quantities are ratios, log-transformed, or otherwise rescaled so leading digits no longer reflect measurement magnitude — the test presumes raw quantitative values spanning orders of magnitude.

skills.description: Use when planning or justifying a custom AnnoMe/MS2DeepScore classifier training run and you must decide whether your number of annotated 'relevant'-class reference spectra is sufficient or can be trimmed.
skills.name: learning-curve-performance-analysis
skills.search_text: learning-curve-performance-analysis Use when planning or justifying a custom AnnoMe/MS2DeepScore classifier training run and you must decide whether your number of annotated 'relevant'-class reference spectra is sufficient or can be trimmed. When the training dataset is highly imbalanced — the AnnoMe README states classification of MS/MS spectra into substance classes will most often fail and the package cannot resolve this issue, so a learning curve will not rescue it When the analysis goal is filtering or prioritizing an inference extract (e.g. Paulownia tomentosa or Glycyrrhizza uralensis spectra) rather than assessing training-data sufficiency When embeddings have not yet been computed — MS2DeepScore generation is the time-limiting step (4 hours on a standard laptop), so run embedding generation first before any subsampling Quantifies how much annotated 'relevant'-class HR-MS/MS training data an AnnoMe classifier actually needs by randomly reducing the training set in 10% decrements (100%→50%) and tracking the 'relevant'-class recall plateau. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioadv/vbag111
skills.summary: Quantifies how much annotated 'relevant'-class HR-MS/MS training data an AnnoMe classifier actually needs by randomly reducing the training set in 10% decrements (100%→50%) and tracking the 'relevant'-class recall plateau.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the training dataset is highly imbalanced — the AnnoMe README states classification of MS/MS spectra into substance classes will most often fail and the package cannot resolve this issue, so a learning curve will not rescue it When the analysis goal is filtering or prioritizing an inference extract (e.g. Paulownia tomentosa or Glycyrrhizza uralensis spectra) rather than assessing training-data sufficiency When embeddings have not yet been computed — MS2DeepScore generation is the time-limiting step (4 hours on a standard laptop), so run embedding generation first before any subsampling

skills.description: Use when quantifying how much target-system training data a RankSVM or SVR retention-order predictor needs, by sweeping target-system training percentages and plotting accuracy curves for single-system vs multi-system regimes.
skills.name: learning-curve-visualization
skills.search_text: learning-curve-visualization Use when quantifying how much target-system training data a RankSVM or SVR retention-order predictor needs, by sweeping target-system training percentages and plotting accuracy curves for single-system vs multi-system regimes. When the goal is a single accuracy number per system rather than accuracy as a function of training-set size — use the baseline_single or all_on_one scenarios (Tables 3 and 4) instead. When the input representation is MACCS binary fingerprints with the Tanimoto kernel rather than counting fingerprints with MinMax — the Figure 4 comparison targets counting vs binary fingerprint differences, so mixing representations invalidates the curve comparison. When retention times have not been pre-processed (lowest RT kept, molecules with >5% RT spread removed); unprocessed PredRet measurements will distort the pairwise accuracy estimates. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Plots pairwise retention-order prediction accuracy as a function of the percentage of target-system retention time data used for training, contrasting single-system (baseline_single_perc, stroked lines) with all-systems training (all_on_one_perc, solid lines) to reproduce Figure 4. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/bty590
skills.summary: Plots pairwise retention-order prediction accuracy as a function of the percentage of target-system retention time data used for training, contrasting single-system (baseline_single_perc, stroked lines) with all-systems training (all_on_one_perc, solid lines) to reproduce Figure 4.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is a single accuracy number per system rather than accuracy as a function of training-set size — use the baseline_single or all_on_one scenarios (Tables 3 and 4) instead. When the input representation is MACCS binary fingerprints with the Tanimoto kernel rather than counting fingerprints with MinMax — the Figure 4 comparison targets counting vs binary fingerprint differences, so mixing representations invalidates the curve comparison. When retention times have not been pre-processed (lowest RT kept, molecules with >5% RT spread removed); unprocessed PredRet measurements will distort the pairwise accuracy estimates.

skills.description: Use when you need to show how model performance (precision, recall) scales with training-set size — e.g., to justify a dataset's size or demonstrate diminishing returns on a spectral classification task.
skills.name: learning-curve-visualization
skills.search_text: learning-curve-visualization Use when you need to show how model performance (precision, recall) scales with training-set size — e.g., to justify a dataset's size or demonstrate diminishing returns on a spectral classification task. You want absolute model performance rather than performance-vs-data-size scaling — evaluate the single trained BitterMasS model instead The spectra are negative ion mode or not EI-MS/ESI-MS/MS positive-mode spectra, outside BitterMasS's stated applicability ('the model makes predictions based on EI-MS or ESI-MS/MS spectra obtained in positive ion mode') http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Retrain a fixed classifier (here BitterMasS, a Random Forest over 5414 MassBank EI-MS/ESI-MS/MS spectra) on progressively larger training subsets and plot precision/recall versus training-set size to characterize diminishing returns, reproducing Figure S6 of the BitterMasS paper. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jafc.3c09767
skills.summary: Retrain a fixed classifier (here BitterMasS, a Random Forest over 5414 MassBank EI-MS/ESI-MS/MS spectra) on progressively larger training subsets and plot precision/recall versus training-set size to characterize diminishing returns, reproducing Figure S6 of the BitterMasS paper.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You want absolute model performance rather than performance-vs-data-size scaling — evaluate the single trained BitterMasS model instead The spectra are negative ion mode or not EI-MS/ESI-MS/MS positive-mode spectra, outside BitterMasS's stated applicability ('the model makes predictions based on EI-MS or ESI-MS/MS spectra obtained in positive ion mode')

skills.description: Use when overlaid 1D 1H NMR spectra show uncontrolled chemical shift variations between spectra in specific ppm areas, and peaks must be re-aligned before binning or statistical analysis of metabolomics data.
skills.name: least-square-spectral-alignment
skills.search_text: least-square-spectral-alignment Use when overlaid 1D 1H NMR spectra show uncontrolled chemical shift variations between spectra in specific ppm areas, and peaks must be re-aligned before binning or statistical analysis of metabolomics data. Input spectra have not yet undergone ppm scale calibration or baseline correction — realignment is one step within the NMRProcFlow processing sequence that includes calibration of the ppm scale and base line correction The spectral region contains intertwined peaks and the spectra do not have the same amount of peaks in that region — Parametric Time Warping will not produce a good result in this case http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Realignment of resonances showing uncontrolled chemical shift variations across a set of 1D 1H NMR spectra, applied interactively to selected ppm areas in NMRProcFlow using the Least-Square algorithm, with Parametric Time Warping as the fallback for regions of intertwined peaks. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-017-1178-y
skills.summary: Realignment of resonances showing uncontrolled chemical shift variations across a set of 1D 1H NMR spectra, applied interactively to selected ppm areas in NMRProcFlow using the Least-Square algorithm, with Parametric Time Warping as the fallback for regions of intertwined peaks.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra have not yet undergone ppm scale calibration or baseline correction — realignment is one step within the NMRProcFlow processing sequence that includes calibration of the ppm scale and base line correction The spectral region contains intertwined peaks and the spectra do not have the same amount of peaks in that region — Parametric Time Warping will not produce a good result in this case

skills.description: Use when a 1D signal (e.g., an extracted ion chromatogram or arrival time distribution from MZA/HDF5 data) contains Gaussian-shaped peaks whose centers, heights, and widths must be quantified, not just located.
skills.name: least-squares-curve-fitting
skills.search_text: least-squares-curve-fitting Use when a 1D signal (e.g., an extracted ion chromatogram or arrival time distribution from MZA/HDF5 data) contains Gaussian-shaped peaks whose centers, heights, and widths must be quantified, not just located. skills.description: Use when targeted metabolomics datasets contain left-censored missing values caused by LOD/LOQ (MNAR) and a robust imputation method is needed before univariate t-tests, PLS-DA, or differential-variable detection.
skills.name: left-censored-metabolomics-imputation
skills.search_text: left-censored-metabolomics-imputation Use when targeted metabolomics datasets contain left-censored missing values caused by LOD/LOQ (MNAR) and a robust imputation method is needed before univariate t-tests, PLS-DA, or differential-variable detection. Missingness is MCAR/MAR rather than left-censored MNAR — with non-informative bounds (+∞, -∞) GSimp extends to MCAR/MAR, but the default lo=-Inf/hi='min' setting targets left-censored values. Data still contains raw un-retrieved missing values in non-targeted GC/MS studies — the paper recommends missing retrieval from raw spectral data first, assuming the majority of missing values are MCAR/MAR before manual retrieval. Upper truncation is stricter than needed — when the minimum is too strict, quantile bounds (e.g. hi=sapply(data, function(x) quantile(x, .1, na.rm=T))) or known LOQ/LOD values should be used instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 GSimp is an iterative Gibbs sampler based imputation approach for left-censored (MNAR) missing values in targeted metabolomics data, where an elastic-net prediction model (glmnet) is embedded in the Gibbs sampler. It is compared against QRILC and kNN-TN using an imputation evaluation pipeline covering accuracy, distribution, univariate/multivariate analyses, and statistical sensitivity. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005973
skills.summary: GSimp is an iterative Gibbs sampler based imputation approach for left-censored (MNAR) missing values in targeted metabolomics data, where an elastic-net prediction model (glmnet) is embedded in the Gibbs sampler. It is compared against QRILC and kNN-TN using an imputation evaluation pipeline covering accuracy, distribution, univariate/multivariate analyses, and statistical sensitivity.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Missingness is MCAR/MAR rather than left-censored MNAR — with non-informative bounds (+∞, -∞) GSimp extends to MCAR/MAR, but the default lo=-Inf/hi='min' setting targets left-censored values. Data still contains raw un-retrieved missing values in non-targeted GC/MS studies — the paper recommends missing retrieval from raw spectral data first, assuming the majority of missing values are MCAR/MAR before manual retrieval. Upper truncation is stricter than needed — when the minimum is too strict, quantile bounds (e.g. hi=sapply(data, function(x) quantile(x, .1, na.rm=T))) or known LOQ/LOD values should be used instead.

skills.description: Use when a targeted metabolomics (LC/MS or GC/MS) data matrix contains left-censored MNAR missing values caused by LOD/LOQ, and prediction-based imputation bounded by the censoring point is needed before downstream univariate or multivariate analysis.
skills.name: left-censored-missing-value-imputation
skills.search_text: left-censored-missing-value-imputation Use when a targeted metabolomics (LC/MS or GC/MS) data matrix contains left-censored MNAR missing values caused by LOD/LOQ, and prediction-based imputation bounded by the censoring point is needed before downstream univariate or multivariate analysis. Missingness is MCAR/MAR (e.g., non-targeted profiling data without missing retrieval) unless non-informative bounds lo=-Inf, hi=Inf are deliberately supplied Values are right-censored rather than left-censored — use 'rsym' initialization with an informative lower truncation point instead of the default left-censored configuration The dataset is expected to require heavy computation without parallelization — the sequential least-to-most-missing ordering and 20x100 iterations can be slow; use the parallel version for large-scale datasets http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 GSimp is a Gibbs sampler based left-censored missing value imputation approach for MNAR missing values in targeted metabolomics data, where an elastic net prediction model (glmnet) is embedded in an iterative Gibbs sampler that draws imputed values from truncated normal distributions bounded by the censoring point. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005973
skills.summary: GSimp is a Gibbs sampler based left-censored missing value imputation approach for MNAR missing values in targeted metabolomics data, where an elastic net prediction model (glmnet) is embedded in an iterative Gibbs sampler that draws imputed values from truncated normal distributions bounded by the censoring point.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Missingness is MCAR/MAR (e.g., non-targeted profiling data without missing retrieval) unless non-informative bounds lo=-Inf, hi=Inf are deliberately supplied Values are right-censored rather than left-censored — use 'rsym' initialization with an informative lower truncation point instead of the default left-censored configuration The dataset is expected to require heavy computation without parallelization — the sequential least-to-most-missing ordering and 20x100 iterations can be slow; use the parallel version for large-scale datasets

No independent cohort is available for external validation — only in-sample accuracy can be reported. http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_3360 Train a LightGBM classifier on a small set of lipid features (e.g. the 10 featured lipids selected by random-forest Gini importance) to classify clinical cohorts, tuned with learning_rate=0.01 and max_depth=5, and evaluate via accuracy and ROC/AUC. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-025-59683-5
skills.summary: Train a LightGBM classifier on a small set of lipid features (e.g. the 10 featured lipids selected by random-forest Gini importance) to classify clinical cohorts, tuned with learning_rate=0.01 and max_depth=5, and evaluate via accuracy and ROC/AUC.

skills.search_text: likelihood-array-postprocessing-threshold-and-power-scaling Use when a ModiFinder per-atom likelihood array Ω has been computed and must be cleaned/sharpened prior to evaluation (e.g. Average-distance scoring) or visualization, to suppress low-confidence atoms and emphasize top candidates. When the raw Ω is needed for untransformed inspection of diffuse/ambiguous likelihoods, since thresholding and power-4 scaling deliberately discard low-score atoms and flatten spread When scoring spectra that have not passed ModiFinder's upstream steps (MS/MS alignment, 40 ppm substructure assignment, peak filtering), since the raw array would not be a valid input http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Applies ModiFinder's final post-processing to the per-atom modification-site likelihood array Ω: zeroing atom scores below 0.5, raising values to the power of 4, and renormalizing, to sharpen contrast among high-scoring candidate atoms before downstream evaluation. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jasms.4c00061
