skills.description: Use when you have two (or three) replicate rank lists over the same n genes and need an error-controlled call set of reproducible signals without parametric assumptions on the dependence structure of reproducible genes.
skills.name: marginal-false-discovery-rate-estimation
skills.search_text: marginal-false-discovery-rate-estimation Use when you have two (or three) replicate rank lists over the same n genes and need an error-controlled call set of reproducible signals without parametric assumptions on the dependence structure of reproducible genes. You want a parametric model of the dependence structure among reproducible signals (e.g. the copula mixture model of Li et al. 2011) rather than a nonparametric FDR-controlled call set — the copula model fits dependence via (mu_A, rho, pi1), while MaRR makes no parametric assumptions. There is only one experiment / no replicate rank lists to compare, so no maximum rank statistic M_g can be formed. You need a decision boundary sensitive to signals far off the diagonal y=x; note the MaRR region {M_g <= N-hat} is square and, in the near-perfect-correlation setting (r0 = 0.95, pi1 = 0.80), the copula mixture model instead captures tail-shaped regions — choose the method matching the boundary shape you want. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Computes the marginal false discovery rate mFDR-hat(i) = (i-k-hat)^2 / (Q(i)(n-k-hat)) from the maximum rank statistic M_g = max{Rgx, Rgy} in the MaRR procedure, and selects the threshold N-hat = max{i : mFDR-hat(i) <= alpha} so genes with M_g <= N-hat are declared reproducible at nominal alpha (0.05 or 0.01) with no tuning parameters. metabolomics/v3 10.1080/01621459.2017.1397521
skills.summary: Computes the marginal false discovery rate mFDR-hat(i) = (i-k-hat)^2 / (Q(i)(n-k-hat)) from the maximum rank statistic M_g = max{Rgx, Rgy} in the MaRR procedure, and selects the threshold N-hat = max{i : mFDR-hat(i) <= alpha} so genes with M_g <= N-hat are declared reproducible at nominal alpha (0.05 or 0.01) with no tuning parameters.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You want a parametric model of the dependence structure among reproducible signals (e.g. the copula mixture model of Li et al. 2011) rather than a nonparametric FDR-controlled call set — the copula model fits dependence via (mu_A, rho, pi1), while MaRR makes no parametric assumptions. There is only one experiment / no replicate rank lists to compare, so no maximum rank statistic M_g can be formed. You need a decision boundary sensitive to signals far off the diagonal y=x; note the MaRR region {M_g <= N-hat} is square and, in the near-perfect-correlation setting (r0 = 0.95, pi1 = 0.80), the copula mixture model instead captures tail-shaped regions — choose the method matching the boundary shape you want.

skills.description: Use when you need to explain or quantify why Pearson-correlation metabolite networks are denser than GLASSO-based partial correlation networks built from the same peak-intensity table, e.g. reproducing the DNEA paper's MetaBox2 vs DNEA edge-count comparison (576 vs 172 edges).
skills.name: marginal-versus-partial-correlation-network-comparison
skills.search_text: marginal-versus-partial-correlation-network-comparison Use when you need to explain or quantify why Pearson-correlation metabolite networks are denser than GLASSO-based partial correlation networks built from the same peak-intensity table, e.g. reproducing the DNEA paper's MetaBox2 vs DNEA edge-count comparison (576 vs 172 edges). When the analysis goal is a biologically interpretable network of direct interactions — the article notes marginal networks are dense 'due to the inclusion of edges representing both direct and indirect correlations. The latter can confound the results' When the dataset has far fewer samples than metabolites and no regularization is desired — partial correlation estimation requires regularization (GLASSO) to avoid unstable edges in the p >> n regime http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 A comparison workflow that builds a marginal (Pearson) correlation network with MetaBox2 and a regularized partial correlation network with DNEA on the same metabolomics data, then quantifies the density difference at a shared |r| >= 0.2 cutoff to demonstrate that marginal networks retain indirect associations. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-024-05994-1
skills.summary: A comparison workflow that builds a marginal (Pearson) correlation network with MetaBox2 and a regularized partial correlation network with DNEA on the same metabolomics data, then quantifies the density difference at a shared |r| >= 0.2 cutoff to demonstrate that marginal networks retain indirect associations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the analysis goal is a biologically interpretable network of direct interactions — the article notes marginal networks are dense 'due to the inclusion of edges representing both direct and indirect correlations. The latter can confound the results' When the dataset has far fewer samples than metabolites and no regularization is desired — partial correlation estimation requires regularization (GLASSO) to avoid unstable edges in the p >> n regime

skills.description: Use when a roughly-fractionated marine cyanobacterial (or other natural product) extract has per-fraction cancer cell cytotoxicity measurements (e.g., IC50-type values) and you must rank fractions to steer downstream isolation work.
skills.name: marine-cyanobacterial-extract-fractionation-context
skills.search_text: marine-cyanobacterial-extract-fractionation-context Use when a roughly-fractionated marine cyanobacterial (or other natural product) extract has per-fraction cancer cell cytotoxicity measurements (e.g., IC50-type values) and you must rank fractions to steer downstream isolation work. Input is a single crude (unfractionated) extract with one bulk cytotoxicity value — there are no per-fraction measurements to rank. The target bioactivity is not cancer-cell cytotoxicity (e.g., antimicrobial or enzyme-inhibition screens) — ranking by cancer cell cytotoxicity would misdirect isolation. No bioactivity data exist and prioritization must rest on chemistry alone (e.g., MS2-based molecular networking or SMART 2.0 annotation only). http://edamontology.org/topic_3473 http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 Ranks roughly-fractionated fractions of an environmental marine cyanobacterial (Symploca) extract by measured cancer cell cytotoxicity so the most potent fractions advance to isolation, replicating the study's bioactivity-guided prioritization. In the source work this cytotoxicity filter was applied alongside NMR-based SMART 2.0 and MS2-based molecular networking, which together surfaced symplocolide A, a chimeric swinholide-like macrolide. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jacs.9b13786

skills.description: Use when multiple LC-MS/MS datasets have been processed with the IIMN workflow (MZmine feature lists + GNPS FBMN-IIN) and you need to compare relative adduct-formation percentages between sample-type groups such as marine vs non-marine samples.
skills.name: marine-vs-non-marine-sample-group-contrast
skills.search_text: marine-vs-non-marine-sample-group-contrast Use when multiple LC-MS/MS datasets have been processed with the IIMN workflow (MZmine feature lists + GNPS FBMN-IIN) and you need to compare relative adduct-formation percentages between sample-type groups such as marine vs non-marine samples. The input is raw LC-MS/MS spectra or unprocessed feature lists — ion species assignments must already exist from MZmine feature grouping plus GNPS FBMN-IIN before group contrast is meaningful. Only one dataset is available with no sample-type grouping — group mean ± standard deviation contrasts require multiple datasets per group. Dataset metadata lacks sample-type labels (marine/non-marine), so the grouping step of the contrast cannot be defined. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Aggregates per-molecule ion species (adduct) assignments from IIMN-processed datasets into relative ion-formation percentages, then contrasts marine vs non-marine sample groups (e.g., [M+NH4]+ at 24±5% vs 10±8%). Provides a validated group-level comparison of MS1-based ion identity networking results across multiple public datasets. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-021-23953-9
skills.summary: Aggregates per-molecule ion species (adduct) assignments from IIMN-processed datasets into relative ion-formation percentages, then contrasts marine vs non-marine sample groups (e.g., [M+NH4]+ at 24±5% vs 10±8%). Provides a validated group-level comparison of MS1-based ion identity networking results across multiple public datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw LC-MS/MS spectra or unprocessed feature lists — ion species assignments must already exist from MZmine feature grouping plus GNPS FBMN-IIN before group contrast is meaningful. skills.description: Use when quantifying overlapped 1D NMR metabolomics spectra (e.g. ~100 peaks in a 1.50 ppm region) from time-domain FID data and peak tables must be derived automatically without manual deconvolution.
skills.name: markov-chain-monte-carlo-optimization
skills.search_text: markov-chain-monte-carlo-optimization Use when quantifying overlapped 1D NMR metabolomics spectra (e.g. ~100 peaks in a 1.50 ppm region) from time-domain FID data and peak tables must be derived automatically without manual deconvolution. Input spectra are nonexponential in signal shape — SAND is tuned for high-resolution metabolomics spectra and does not yet handle nonexponential signals natively. Data are multidimensional or nonuniformly sampled in a way that exceeds current 1D scope — SAND's ultimate goal is to adapt to multidimensional applications, but that is not yet realized. skills.search_text: mass-chromatogram-noise-similarity-indexing Use when filtering raw EIC intensity profiles from LC/MS-based metabolomics data for spike/background noise prior to chromatographic peak detection, or when benchmarking the MCQ index against alternative EIC quality metrics such as the EIC-related global zigzag index. The EICs being evaluated have high background signals or contain only a single peak — the paper explicitly states the MCQ index cannot fairly evaluate these cases; use the EIC-related global zigzag index instead The task is evaluating detected chromatographic peaks (not raw EICs) — the paper's peak-level metrics (sharpness, Gaussian similarity, SNR, peak significance level, TPASR, local peak-related zigzag index) apply at that downstream stage You need a reproducible end-to-end pipeline out of the box — the LC/MS profile dataset and Matlab scripts are available only upon request and no license is specified Computes the mass chromatographic quality (MCQ) index for extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) by measuring the similarity of each original mass chromatogram to its smoothed version (spike detection) and its mean-subtracted version (background detection), as described by Zhang & Zhao (2014), to flag noisy EICs before downstream peak detection. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/1471-2105-15-s11-s5
skills.summary: Computes the mass chromatographic quality (MCQ) index for extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) by measuring the similarity of each original mass chromatogram to its smoothed version (spike detection) and its mean-subtracted version (background detection), as described by Zhang & Zhao (2014), to flag noisy EICs before downstream peak detection.

skills.name: mass-defect-based-metabolite-bridging
skills.search_text: mass-defect-based-metabolite-bridging Use when you have LC-MS feature lists for in vivo metabolites plus a prototype (in vitro parent component) list from PATBS non-targeted identification, and need to bridge metabolites to prototypes and characterize metabolites across biological matrices. No in vitro prototype list is available, since the bridging approach fundamentally requires prototype-metabolite pairs to score mass defect variations You need only single-metabolite-to-prototype-database matching based on secondary mass spectrometry map similarity — the MTSF-style approach the article critiques as limited, distinct from MDRB's multi-dimensional scoring Compounds without a shared parent nucleus structure, where the mass-defect-based bridging rationale (metabolite MS2 fragment mass defects within a certain range of the prototype's) does not hold http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 A mass dataset relevance bridging (MDRB) data post-processing technique that characterizes in vivo TCM metabolites by bridging them to in vitro prototypes using a scoring approach integrating m/z, MS1/MS2 mass defect, and MS2 fragment similarity. It replaces manual characterization (110 metabolites, 31%) with an automated pipeline that raised CKXR metabolite characterization to 227 metabolites (65%). metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13020-024-01031-8
skills.summary: A mass dataset relevance bridging (MDRB) data post-processing technique that characterizes in vivo TCM metabolites by bridging them to in vitro prototypes using a scoring approach integrating m/z, MS1/MS2 mass defect, and MS2 fragment similarity. It replaces manual characterization (110 metabolites, 31%) with an automated pipeline that raised CKXR metabolite characterization to 227 metabolites (65%).
skills.when_to_use_negative: No in vitro prototype list is available, since the bridging approach fundamentally requires prototype-metabolite pairs to score mass defect variations You need only single-metabolite-to-prototype-database matching based on secondary mass spectrometry map similarity — the MTSF-style approach the article critiques as limited, distinct from MDRB's multi-dimensional scoring Compounds without a shared parent nucleus structure, where the mass-defect-based bridging rationale (metabolite MS2 fragment mass defects within a certain range of the prototype's) does not hold

skills.description: Use when a blank-filtered LC-HRMS feature table from a fluorine-rich sample (e.g. AFFF) must be narrowed to probable PFAS using exact mass matching, mass defect windows, and CF2 homologous-series evidence.
skills.name: mass-defect-filtering
skills.search_text: mass-defect-filtering Use when a blank-filtered LC-HRMS feature table from a fluorine-rich sample (e.g. AFFF) must be narrowed to probable PFAS using exact mass matching, mass defect windows, and CF2 homologous-series evidence. Input is already a curated suspect list of known PFAS where exact mass matching alone suffices — mass defect filtering adds little beyond catalog matching Analyzing lipidomics data — set Lipid <- TRUE instead, since the PFAS mass-defect window does not apply to lipids (README toggles Lipid/TWeen_pos for application type) Features lack fluorine-typical mass defects (e.g. purely hydrocarbon matrices) — the PFAS mass-defect window will not separate classes meaningfully http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 A FluoroMatch 2.0 pipeline stage that applies mass defect filtering alongside exact mass matching to the EPA PFAS structure list and CF2-based homologous series detection to strip features that are unlikely PFAS from LC-HRMS feature tables. In the AFFF demonstration it reduced 3740 blank-filtered features to 2290 potential and 1238 probable PFAS, a 96% overall reduction. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s00216-021-03392-7
skills.summary: A FluoroMatch 2.0 pipeline stage that applies mass defect filtering alongside exact mass matching to the EPA PFAS structure list and CF2-based homologous series detection to strip features that are unlikely PFAS from LC-HRMS feature tables. In the AFFF demonstration it reduced 3740 blank-filtered features to 2290 potential and 1238 probable PFAS, a 96% overall reduction.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a curated suspect list of known PFAS where exact mass matching alone suffices — mass defect filtering adds little beyond catalog matching Analyzing lipidomics data — set Lipid <- TRUE instead, since the PFAS mass-defect window does not apply to lipids (README toggles Lipid/TWeen_pos for application type) Features lack fluorine-typical mass defects (e.g. purely hydrocarbon matrices) — the PFAS mass-defect window will not separate classes meaningfully

skills.description: Use when a preprocessed spatial metabolomics peak table (X, Y coordinates plus m/z ion columns) needs isotope annotation to assess ion-detection reliability, e.g. when computing the isotopic peak ratio quality metric.
skills.name: mass-defect-isotope-annotation
skills.search_text: mass-defect-isotope-annotation Use when a preprocessed spatial metabolomics peak table (X, Y coordinates plus m/z ion columns) needs isotope annotation to assess ion-detection reliability, e.g. when computing the isotopic peak ratio quality metric. Input is raw instrument data rather than a preprocessed peak table matrix (X, Y coordinates plus m/z columns) — SMQVP expects the peak table format Data has not been denoised first: background pixels should be removed and noise ions filtered (noise score threshold 90) before isotope scanning, or spurious pairs will inflate the ratio The goal is adduct ion identification rather than isotopologue detection — SMQVP provides a separate adduct ion ratio module http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Identify isotopic peak pairs in spatial metabolomics peak tables by scanning for mass differences near the theoretical ~1.0035 Da M+1 offset (MetaboCoreUtils isotopologues approach) and confirming spatial co-localization via Pearson correlation. In the SMQVP workflow this flags the isotopic peak ratio (14.44% of AFADESI mouse brain ions) as a quality visualization point. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo15060354
skills.summary: Identify isotopic peak pairs in spatial metabolomics peak tables by scanning for mass differences near the theoretical ~1.0035 Da M+1 offset (MetaboCoreUtils isotopologues approach) and confirming spatial co-localization via Pearson correlation. In the SMQVP workflow this flags the isotopic peak ratio (14.44% of AFADESI mouse brain ions) as a quality visualization point.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw instrument data rather than a preprocessed peak table matrix (X, Y coordinates plus m/z columns) — SMQVP expects the peak table format Data has not been denoised first: background pixels should be removed and noise ions filtered (noise score threshold 90) before isotope scanning, or spurious pairs will inflate the ratio The goal is adduct ion identification rather than isotopologue detection — SMQVP provides a separate adduct ion ratio module

skills.description: Use when annotating features from AIF LC-MS metabolomics data and you must score/rank candidate metabolites per feature against a fragment library, combining m/z accuracy with pseudo-MS/MS fragment-match specificity.
skills.name: mass-defect-mz-error-weighting
skills.search_text: mass-defect-mz-error-weighting Use when annotating features from AIF LC-MS metabolomics data and you must score/rank candidate metabolites per feature against a fragment library, combining m/z accuracy with pseudo-MS/MS fragment-match specificity. Data were acquired with DIA schemes other than AIF (e.g., SWATH) — MetaboAnnotatoR only supports AIF. Features already have true targeted MS/MS spectra — direct spectral matching to METLIN/MassBank/GNPS libraries is more specific than pseudo-MS/MS-based scoring. The aim is fragment-library construction or pseudo-MS/MS reconstruction rather than candidate ranking — this skill only covers the scoring/ranking step. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Composite candidate-scoring scheme from MetaboAnnotatoR that ranks fragment-library matches per feature by combining a bounded reciprocal m/z error term (S_mz = min(1/E,1)) with a fragmentation match score (S_ma), weighting subscores (default w_mz = w_ma = 0.5) and downweighting fragments matched only in the AIF scan by a factor of two. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c03032
skills.summary: Composite candidate-scoring scheme from MetaboAnnotatoR that ranks fragment-library matches per feature by combining a bounded reciprocal m/z error term (S_mz = min(1/E,1)) with a fragmentation match score (S_ma), weighting subscores (default w_mz = w_ma = 0.5) and downweighting fragments matched only in the AIF scan by a factor of two.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data were acquired with DIA schemes other than AIF (e.g., SWATH) — MetaboAnnotatoR only supports AIF. Features already have true targeted MS/MS spectra — direct spectral matching to METLIN/MassBank/GNPS libraries is more specific than pseudo-MS/MS-based scoring. The aim is fragment-library construction or pseudo-MS/MS reconstruction rather than candidate ranking — this skill only covers the scoring/ranking step.

skills.description: Use when a post-FeatureFinding feature list (e.g., external_feature_list.xlsx from mzML data) must be reduced from thousands of matrix components to a small set of potential PFAS candidates in non-target screening.
skills.name: mass-defect-per-carbon-prioritization
skills.search_text: mass-defect-per-carbon-prioritization Use when a post-FeatureFinding feature list (e.g., external_feature_list.xlsx from mzML data) must be reduced from thousands of matrix components to a small set of potential PFAS candidates in non-target screening. Input is a single suspect list of known PFAS (e.g., PFASMASTER/PFASOECDNA hits) — suspect screening, not MD/C-m/C reduction, is the right step Data are not LC- or GC-HRMS features (no m/z, RT, isotopic traces) — the CH2-scaled Kendrick framework does not apply Raw spectra have not been converted to mzML or passed feature finding/blank correction — the skill requires a per-feature carbon-number calculation, not raw profile data http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Data-reduction skill that prioritizes potential PFAS features in HRMS feature lists using the CH2-scaled Kendrick-based MD/C-m/C approach (mass defect and mass per carbon), applied via PFΔScreen on mzML-derived features from LC/GC-HRMS data. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s00216-023-05070-2
skills.summary: Data-reduction skill that prioritizes potential PFAS features in HRMS feature lists using the CH2-scaled Kendrick-based MD/C-m/C approach (mass defect and mass per carbon), applied via PFΔScreen on mzML-derived features from LC/GC-HRMS data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a single suspect list of known PFAS (e.g., PFASMASTER/PFASOECDNA hits) — suspect screening, not MD/C-m/C reduction, is the right step Data are not LC- or GC-HRMS features (no m/z, RT, isotopic traces) — the CH2-scaled Kendrick framework does not apply Raw spectra have not been converted to mzML or passed feature finding/blank correction — the skill requires a per-feature carbon-number calculation, not raw profile data

skills.description: Use when raw scan-level mass-spectral data (m/z, intensity, retention time per scan) and detected TIC peak boundaries are available and a dataset-specific centWave ppm parameter must be estimated for XCMS/MZmine2 peak picking, without iterative parameter sweeping.
skills.name: mass-defect-ppm-estimation-via-gaussian-kde
skills.search_text: mass-defect-ppm-estimation-via-gaussian-kde Use when raw scan-level mass-spectral data (m/z, intensity, retention time per scan) and detected TIC peak boundaries are available and a dataset-specific centWave ppm parameter must be estimated for XCMS/MZmine2 peak picking, without iterative parameter sweeping. Input is already a feature table (post peak-picking) rather than raw scan-level data — the EIC-within-TIC-peak statistics require raw scans The target parameter is mzDiff or a non-continuous centWave parameter — AutoTuner optimizes seven continuous parameters plus one grouping parameter and does not estimate mzDiff (only a sensitivity analysis showed distinct mzDiff values had minimal effect on the returned feature table) Fewer than 3 raw samples are available (AutoTuner README input requirement) http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 AutoTuner's single-step statistical-inference method for estimating the centWave ppm (m/z tolerance) parameter: it fits a Gaussian kernel-density empirical distribution to per-bin ppm deviations computed from EICs within each detected TIC peak, then separates true-feature ppm values from noise-derived ppm values via k-means clustering with an outlier score, returning the sd of the retained values as the ppm estimate. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/812370
skills.summary: AutoTuner's single-step statistical-inference method for estimating the centWave ppm (m/z tolerance) parameter: it fits a Gaussian kernel-density empirical distribution to per-bin ppm deviations computed from EICs within each detected TIC peak, then separates true-feature ppm values from noise-derived ppm values via k-means clustering with an outlier score, returning the sd of the retained values as the ppm estimate.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a feature table (post peak-picking) rather than raw scan-level data — the EIC-within-TIC-peak statistics require raw scans The target parameter is mzDiff or a non-continuous centWave parameter — AutoTuner optimizes seven continuous parameters plus one grouping parameter and does not estimate mzDiff (only a sensitivity analysis showed distinct mzDiff values had minimal effect on the returned feature table) Fewer than 3 raw samples are available (AutoTuner README input requirement)

skills.description: Decision support for tuning the mass-defect tolerance in MDRB prototype-metabolite bridging when matching unpredictable metabolites and needing to trade off pathway coverage against false positives.
skills.name: mass-defect-range-optimization
skills.search_text: mass-defect-range-optimization Decision support for tuning the mass-defect tolerance in MDRB prototype-metabolite bridging when matching unpredictable metabolites and needing to trade off pathway coverage against false positives. The matching already uses a validated mass-defect range and the goal is routine metabolite bridging rather than parameter calibration. Metabolites are handled as predictable metabolic reactions (e.g., via Metworks 1.3.0.200 transformation rules) rather than unpredictable metabolites requiring mass-defect bridging. The dataset lacks MS1/MS2 mass-defect information or MS2 fragment similarity data, so the three-dimensional MDRB scoring cannot be evaluated per range. http://edamontology.org/topic_3382 An optimization procedure within the MDRB strategy that empirically selects the MS1/MS2 mass-defect tolerance window (±25 mmu in the paper) for bridging unpredictable metabolites to prototypes, balancing pathway coverage, positivity rate, and false-positive bridged pairs. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13020-024-01031-8
skills.summary: An optimization procedure within the MDRB strategy that empirically selects the MS1/MS2 mass-defect tolerance window (±25 mmu in the paper) for bridging unpredictable metabolites to prototypes, balancing pathway coverage, positivity rate, and false-positive bridged pairs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The matching already uses a validated mass-defect range and the goal is routine metabolite bridging rather than parameter calibration. Metabolites are handled as predictable metabolic reactions (e.g., via Metworks 1.3.0.200 transformation rules) rather than unpredictable metabolites requiring mass-defect bridging. The dataset lacks MS1/MS2 mass-defect information or MS2 fragment similarity data, so the three-dimensional MDRB scoring cannot be evaluated per range.

skills.description: Use when a pre-processed MALDI-MSI peak table (plain-text CSV exported from SCiLS or MSiReader, or a binned Cardinal MSProcessedImagingExperiment) needs putative adduct annotation, and you want to recover abundant Δmass peaks such as 21.985 and 37.955 Da from pairwise peak differences.
skills.name: mass-difference-adduct-annotation
skills.search_text: mass-difference-adduct-annotation Use when a pre-processed MALDI-MSI peak table (plain-text CSV exported from SCiLS or MSiReader, or a binned Cardinal MSProcessedImagingExperiment) needs putative adduct annotation, and you want to recover abundant Δmass peaks such as 21.985 and 37.955 Da from pairwise peak differences. The input spectrum still contains matrix-cluster peaks — template subtraction (subtractPeaks) should be run before re-running adduct identification, not this annotation step on raw peaks You only need peak picking or matrix subtraction rather than adduct assignment — this skill assumes an already pre-processed, peak-binned table, not raw imzML spectra A very large CSV will not fit in memory and no triplet-format conversion has been done — use the msimunging.pl pre-step or corrPairsMSIchunks instead of plain corrPairsMSI http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 A MALDI-MSI skill that tabulates all pairwise mass differences between detected peaks, bins them into a Δmass histogram, and matches abundant bins against a reference adduct table (e.g. the built-in `adducts` list in mass2adduct) to annotate metabolite–matrix and salt adducts such as [M + Na]+ and [M + (DHB-H2O) + H]+. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c04720
skills.summary: A MALDI-MSI skill that tabulates all pairwise mass differences between detected peaks, bins them into a Δmass histogram, and matches abundant bins against a reference adduct table (e.g. the built-in `adducts` list in mass2adduct) to annotate metabolite–matrix and salt adducts such as [M + Na]+ and [M + (DHB-H2O) + H]+.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input spectrum still contains matrix-cluster peaks — template subtraction (subtractPeaks) should be run before re-running adduct identification, not this annotation step on raw peaks You only need peak picking or matrix subtraction rather than adduct assignment — this skill assumes an already pre-processed, peak-binned table, not raw imzML spectra A very large CSV will not fit in memory and no triplet-format conversion has been done — use the msimunging.pl pre-step or corrPairsMSIchunks instead of plain corrPairsMSI

skills.description: Use when a positive-ion-mode spatial metabolomics peak table (pixels × m/z ions) needs adduct annotation, e.g., quantifying what proportion of filtered ions are M+H, M+K, or M+Na adducts of the same metabolite.
skills.name: mass-difference-matching-against-adduct-list
skills.search_text: mass-difference-matching-against-adduct-list Use when a positive-ion-mode spatial metabolomics peak table (pixels × m/z ions) needs adduct annotation, e.g., quantifying what proportion of filtered ions are M+H, M+K, or M+Na adducts of the same metabolite. The peak table is negative-ion-mode data — the predefined adduct list (M+H, M+K, M+Na) covers common positive-ion-mode adducts only The input is raw imaging data rather than a peak table matrix; SMQVP requires a peak table with X/Y coordinates and m/z intensity columns Only a single peak must be annotated (no partner ion present in the matrix), since the method relies on detecting mass-difference pairs between ions http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Identifies adduct ions in positive-ion-mode spatial metabolomics peak tables by computing pairwise m/z mass differences, matching them against a predefined adduct list (M+H, M+K, M+Na, etc.), and confirming candidates via spatial Pearson correlation, as implemented in SMQVP's adduct ion ratio module (QVP8). metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo15060354
skills.summary: Identifies adduct ions in positive-ion-mode spatial metabolomics peak tables by computing pairwise m/z mass differences, matching them against a predefined adduct list (M+H, M+K, M+Na, etc.), and confirming candidates via spatial Pearson correlation, as implemented in SMQVP's adduct ion ratio module (QVP8).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The peak table is negative-ion-mode data — the predefined adduct list (M+H, M+K, M+Na) covers common positive-ion-mode adducts only The input is raw imaging data rather than a peak table matrix; SMQVP requires a peak table with X/Y coordinates and m/z intensity columns Only a single peak must be annotated (no partner ion present in the matrix), since the method relies on detecting mass-difference pairs between ions

skills.description: Use when two MS/MS spectra (query and reference, e.g. MGF/h5py) must be encoded as Transformer input for TransExION spectral similarity scoring or post-hoc explanation, requiring aligned mass-difference and neutral-loss matrices.
skills.name: mass-difference-matrix-construction
skills.search_text: mass-difference-matrix-construction Use when two MS/MS spectra (query and reference, e.g. MGF/h5py) must be encoded as Transformer input for TransExION spectral similarity scoring or post-hoc explanation, requiring aligned mass-difference and neutral-loss matrices. Only a single spectrum is available with no reference spectrum — the MDM is inherently a pairwise query–reference construction You need a simple baseline similarity (Cosine or Modified Cosine) that does not use query–reference fragment mass differences Spectra lack precursor m/z information, so the neutral-loss variant (precursor minus fragment) cannot be computed http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 Constructs the TransExION input representation for an MS/MS spectrum pair: a mass difference matrix (MDM) of absolute query–reference fragment differences, aligned by nominal mass (columns 0–299 Da) with rounded mass-defect values (0–99) and pad fills, plus a CLS entry. A parallel neutral-loss MDM (precursor minus fragment) is built the same way. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00858-5
skills.summary: Constructs the TransExION input representation for an MS/MS spectrum pair: a mass difference matrix (MDM) of absolute query–reference fragment differences, aligned by nominal mass (columns 0–299 Da) with rounded mass-defect values (0–99) and pad fills, plus a CLS entry. A parallel neutral-loss MDM (precursor minus fragment) is built the same way.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only a single spectrum is available with no reference spectrum — the MDM is inherently a pairwise query–reference construction You need a simple baseline similarity (Cosine or Modified Cosine) that does not use query–reference fragment mass differences Spectra lack precursor m/z information, so the neutral-loss variant (precursor minus fragment) cannot be computed

skills.description: Use when a direct-injection (no chromatographic separation) DBDI-MS dataset contains multiple ion species from one analyte and adduct calls from identify_adducts() need independent confirmation via correlated XIC traces plus exact mass differences.
skills.name: mass-difference-network-annotation
skills.search_text: mass-difference-network-annotation Use when a direct-injection (no chromatographic separation) DBDI-MS dataset contains multiple ion species from one analyte and adduct calls from identify_adducts() need independent confirmation via correlated XIC traces plus exact mass differences. Input data already is a curated feature table — align_spectra() and matchms.importing are only needed for raw m/z-intensity spectra The dataset has chromatographic separation; this in-silico approach is tailored to time-resolved direct-injection plasma ionization data where coelution-based annotation is unavailable Only a single ion species per analyte exists (no rivaling adducts/in-source fragments), so correlation + mass-difference refinement has nothing to pair http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Validates adduct/in-source-fragment annotations from direct-injection DBDI-MS data by clustering features that share matching temporal intensity profiles (pointwise correlation) with systematic exact mass differences, e.g. an [M+nO+H]+ oxygenation series such as the C15H17O2N cluster confirmed by features 55 and 99 with r > 0.9. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad088
skills.summary: Validates adduct/in-source-fragment annotations from direct-injection DBDI-MS data by clustering features that share matching temporal intensity profiles (pointwise correlation) with systematic exact mass differences, e.g. an [M+nO+H]+ oxygenation series such as the C15H17O2N cluster confirmed by features 55 and 99 with r > 0.9.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data already is a curated feature table — align_spectra() and matchms.importing are only needed for raw m/z-intensity spectra The dataset has chromatographic separation; this in-silico approach is tailored to time-resolved direct-injection plasma ionization data where coelution-based annotation is unavailable Only a single ion species per analyte exists (no rivaling adducts/in-source fragments), so correlation + mass-difference refinement has nothing to pair

skills.description: Use when you have a feature table from untargeted metabolomics or isotope-tracing LC-MS (feature ID, m/z, rtime, intensities) and need to group degenerate ions into empirical compounds before formula/identity assignment.
skills.name: mass-difference-network-construction
skills.search_text: mass-difference-network-construction Use when you have a feature table from untargeted metabolomics or isotope-tracing LC-MS (feature ID, m/z, rtime, intensities) and need to group degenerate ions into empirical compounds before formula/identity assignment. Data are raw vendor files (mzML/Thermo raw) rather than a preprocessed feature table — run a peak-picking tool like asari 1.9.2 first A prior chemical formula or assumed base ion is already known for the features — direct formula assignment tools are then more appropriate Complete, high-confidence metabolite identification requiring authentic libraries or tandem MS data is the goal — this skill only performs generalized preannotation http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0157 Builds an untargeted mass-distance network over LC-MS feature m/z values by searching isotope mass differences (1.0034 Da for 13C/12C) and adduct mass differences (e.g. 22.9893 Da for Na+) to connect ion pairs as the first step of khipu preannotation. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.2c05810
skills.summary: Builds an untargeted mass-distance network over LC-MS feature m/z values by searching isotope mass differences (1.0034 Da for 13C/12C) and adduct mass differences (e.g. 22.9893 Da for Na+) to connect ion pairs as the first step of khipu preannotation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are raw vendor files (mzML/Thermo raw) rather than a preprocessed feature table — run a peak-picking tool like asari 1.9.2 first A prior chemical formula or assumed base ion is already known for the features — direct formula assignment tools are then more appropriate Complete, high-confidence metabolite identification requiring authentic libraries or tandem MS data is the goal — this skill only performs generalized preannotation

skills.description: Use when you have a preprocessed peak table exported as plain-text CSV from SCiLS or MSiReader (or an imzML/Cardinal peak-binned object) and want to screen for abundant adduct transformations among peaks in MALDI-mass spectrometry imaging data.
skills.name: mass-difference-pairwise-computation-msi-peaks
skills.search_text: mass-difference-pairwise-computation-msi-peaks Use when you have a preprocessed peak table exported as plain-text CSV from SCiLS or MSiReader (or an imzML/Cardinal peak-binned object) and want to screen for abundant adduct transformations among peaks in MALDI-mass spectrometry imaging data. If you only have raw continuous spectra without a preprocessed peak list — peaks must already be detected/binned (e.g. Cardinal peakBin()) before massdiff() can be applied If you need statistically validated adduct assignments rather than a screening histogram — use downstream spatial correlation (corrPairsMSI) instead of mass-difference counts alone If your CSV export is several Gb and cannot fit in memory — the README recommends reformatting with msimunging.pl to triplet format (and optionally filtering peaks by nonzero-pixel frequency) before importing http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Compute all pairwise mass differences between detected MALDI-MSI peaks and bin them into a frequency histogram so that abundant metabolite–matrix adducts (e.g. Na+, K+, DHB-derived species) stand out above the integer-spaced background, as implemented in the R package mass2adduct. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c04720
skills.summary: Compute all pairwise mass differences between detected MALDI-MSI peaks and bin them into a frequency histogram so that abundant metabolite–matrix adducts (e.g. Na+, K+, DHB-derived species) stand out above the integer-spaced background, as implemented in the R package mass2adduct.
skills.when_to_use_negative: If you only have raw continuous spectra without a preprocessed peak list — peaks must already be detected/binned (e.g. Cardinal peakBin()) before massdiff() can be applied If you need statistically validated adduct assignments rather than a screening histogram — use downstream spatial correlation (corrPairsMSI) instead of mass-difference counts alone If your CSV export is several Gb and cannot fit in memory — the README recommends reformatting with msimunging.pl to triplet format (and optionally filtering peaks by nonzero-pixel frequency) before importing

skills.description: Use when ranking precursor chemical formula candidates from LC-MS/MS spectra without training data or MS/MS database matching, i.e., when spectra must be scored via mass-difference relationships among fragment formulas.
skills.name: mass-difference-relationship-analysis
skills.search_text: mass-difference-relationship-analysis Use when ranking precursor chemical formula candidates from LC-MS/MS spectra without training data or MS/MS database matching, i.e., when spectra must be scored via mass-difference relationships among fragment formulas. The molecules of interest are outside the validated element set (C, H, O, N, S, P) or form adduct types not yet handled — FSA 'has so far been validated on datasets containing compounds composed of C, H, O, N, S, and P' Maximum identification accuracy is required over speed — the paper notes rank #1 accuracy 'was not yet comparable to that of state-of-the-art tools such as Buddy and SIRIUS' because FSA does not use structural information http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Reconstructs the FSA (formula subset analysis) ranking pipeline: convert MS/MS fragment m/z to monoisotopic masses, search candidate formulas within a mass tolerance against a PubChem-derived reference list, enumerate mass-difference relationships (MDRs), and rank precursor formulas with the Eq. (4) score. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-025-02379-0
skills.summary: Reconstructs the FSA (formula subset analysis) ranking pipeline: convert MS/MS fragment m/z to monoisotopic masses, search candidate formulas within a mass tolerance against a PubChem-derived reference list, enumerate mass-difference relationships (MDRs), and rank precursor formulas with the Eq. (4) score.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The molecules of interest are outside the validated element set (C, H, O, N, S, P) or form adduct types not yet handled — FSA 'has so far been validated on datasets containing compounds composed of C, H, O, N, S, and P' Maximum identification accuracy is required over speed — the paper notes rank #1 accuracy 'was not yet comparable to that of state-of-the-art tools such as Buddy and SIRIUS' because FSA does not use structural information

skills.description: Use when you have paired known-anchor and unknown-suspect molecules with precursor m/z values and a rule database of reaction mass shifts, and need to select only rules consistent with the observed mass difference before generating derivatives.
skills.name: mass-difference-rule-filtering
skills.search_text: mass-difference-rule-filtering Use when you have paired known-anchor and unknown-suspect molecules with precursor m/z values and a rule database of reaction mass shifts, and need to select only rules consistent with the observed mass difference before generating derivatives. No anchor molecule with known structure and precursor mass is available, so no anchor–suspect mass difference can be computed The observed precursor mass difference is unknown or unreliable (e.g., uncalibrated m/z), since rule selection is made at unit resolution You need structure candidates unrelated to biotransformations (e.g., formula-level annotation with SIRIUS), which is handled separately in the BAM workflow http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Filters a large biotransformation rule database (e.g., RetroRules) down to only those rules whose reaction mass shifts match the observed precursor mass difference between each anchor–suspect pair, so that downstream derivative generation only applies chemically plausible transformations. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c01565
skills.summary: Filters a large biotransformation rule database (e.g., RetroRules) down to only those rules whose reaction mass shifts match the observed precursor mass difference between each anchor–suspect pair, so that downstream derivative generation only applies chemically plausible transformations.

skills.search_text: mass-spectra-inference-latency-benchmarking Use when comparing end-to-end inference cost of a mass-spectra-to-structure generative model against diffusion/iterative baselines, or when an acceptance criterion specifies a per-spectrum latency and speed-up factor to reproduce. You only need accuracy metrics (Top-1/Top-10) on MassSpecGym or NPLIB1 and have no requirement to measure wall-clock inference cost or compare against diffusion baselines. You are evaluating a retrieval-based or rule-based structure-identification pipeline rather than a generative model with beam-search or diffusion sampling, where beam-width sweeps are inapplicable. You only have a small CPU-only environment; latency numbers would not be comparable to the GPU-timed A800/RTX-4090 measurements. http://edamontology.org/topic_3418 Benchmarks the wall-clock inference latency of MS-BART structure elucidation against diffusion-based competitors (DiffMS, FRIGID), sweeping beam-search widths 10–100 to show MS-BART is roughly one order of magnitude faster (~3 s vs ~160 s per spectrum). metabolomics/v3 10.48550/arxiv.2510.20615

skills.description: Use when preparing held-out EI-MS test sets from spectral libraries and you must prevent train/test compound overlap, remove deuterium-labeled compounds, or enforce the inference model's input limits (peak count, m/z range, SMILES length).
skills.name: mass-spectra-manifest-curation
skills.search_text: mass-spectra-manifest-curation Use when preparing held-out EI-MS test sets from spectral libraries and you must prevent train/test compound overlap, remove deuterium-labeled compounds, or enforce the inference model's input limits (peak count, m/z range, SMILES length). The spectra are training or validation data, not a held-out test set — overlap removal against the training split is only needed for evaluation sets. The downstream model accepts arbitrary peak counts, m/z ranges, or SMILES lengths — applying SpecTUS-specific thresholds (300 peaks, m/z 500, 100-char SMILES) would unnecessarily exclude valid spectra (≈3% of NIST was dropped by these thresholds alone). You are evaluating on the CASMI 2017 MS/MS competition set, which was filtered with its own model-specific filters (243 → 93 spectra) and follows a different protocol. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Filter held-out mass-spectral test libraries (NIST 20, SWGDRUG, Cayman, MONA) by canonical-SMILES de-leaking against training splits, deuterium removal, and model-specific thresholds (max 300 peaks, m/z ≤ 500, SMILES ≤ 100 chars) to produce leak-free evaluation manifests. metabolomics/v3 10.48550/arxiv.2502.05114
skills.summary: Filter held-out mass-spectral test libraries (NIST 20, SWGDRUG, Cayman, MONA) by canonical-SMILES de-leaking against training splits, deuterium removal, and model-specific thresholds (max 300 peaks, m/z ≤ 500, SMILES ≤ 100 chars) to produce leak-free evaluation manifests.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The spectra are training or validation data, not a held-out test set — overlap removal against the training split is only needed for evaluation sets. The downstream model accepts arbitrary peak counts, m/z ranges, or SMILES lengths — applying SpecTUS-specific thresholds (300 peaks, m/z 500, 100-char SMILES) would unnecessarily exclude valid spectra (≈3% of NIST was dropped by these thresholds alone). You are evaluating on the CASMI 2017 MS/MS competition set, which was filtered with its own model-specific filters (243 → 93 spectra) and follows a different protocol.

skills.description: Use when importing a GNPS or similar MS/MS spectral library whose metadata and peaks must be cleaned, corrected, and filtered (e.g., ALL_GNPS.json) before building training/query subsets.
skills.name: mass-spectra-metadata-cleaning
skills.search_text: mass-spectra-metadata-cleaning Use when importing a GNPS or similar MS/MS spectral library whose metadata and peaks must be cleaned, corrected, and filtered (e.g., ALL_GNPS.json) before building training/query subsets. The input is already a cleaned, filtered dataset that meets the ≥10-peak and m/z [0, 1000] constraints — re-filtering adds no value. The spectra lack any metadata/annotations and no external lookup (e.g., PubChem via pubchempy) is possible, so InChIKey-based subsetting cannot be performed. The analysis goal requires keeping spectra with fewer than 10 peaks, which this pipeline deliberately discards. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 A matchms-based procedure to clean and correct MS/MS spectra metadata (e.g., InChIKey annotations) and apply peak filters (m/z range [0, 1000], minimum 10 peaks) to a large GNPS spectral library before downstream similarity modeling or dataset construction. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008724
skills.summary: A matchms-based procedure to clean and correct MS/MS spectra metadata (e.g., InChIKey annotations) and apply peak filters (m/z range [0, 1000], minimum 10 peaks) to a large GNPS spectral library before downstream similarity modeling or dataset construction.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a cleaned, filtered dataset that meets the ≥10-peak and m/z [0, 1000] constraints — re-filtering adds no value. The spectra lack any metadata/annotations and no external lookup (e.g., PubChem via pubchempy) is possible, so InChIKey-based subsetting cannot be performed. The analysis goal requires keeping spectra with fewer than 10 peaks, which this pipeline deliberately discards.

skills.description: Use when concatenating OMSLs from GNPS (.MGF), MoNA (.MSP/.SDF/.JSON), MassBank, or MS-Dial-VS17 into a single library and you need to harmonize metadata fields (SMILES, InChI, precursor m/z, adduct, ion mode, instrument type) so the output is usable with MS-Dial, MZmine, and Flash Entropy Search.
skills.name: mass-spectra-metadata-harmonization
skills.search_text: mass-spectra-metadata-harmonization Use when concatenating OMSLs from GNPS (.MGF), MoNA (.MSP/.SDF/.JSON), MassBank, or MS-Dial-VS17 into a single library and you need to harmonize metadata fields (SMILES, InChI, precursor m/z, adduct, ion mode, instrument type) so the output is usable with MS-Dial, MZmine, and Flash Entropy Search. Spectra already in a single, harmonized library format — running harmonization again risks stripping valid metadata through the 'UNKNOWN' fallback mapping and re-dropping spectra. Collision energy harmonization is required: the article explicitly did not address it because ~70 different nonstandardized energy formats exist across OMSLs. Input contains only peak lists without any compound identifier (SMILES or InChI) and without adduct or precursor m/z — these spectra are removed during processing. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Harmonizes heterogeneous open mass spectral library (OMSL) metadata — field names, chemical identifiers, ionization modes, retention times, instrument descriptors — into a unified GNPS-compatible format, as implemented in the FragHub workflow (Analytical Chemistry 2024). metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c02219
skills.summary: Harmonizes heterogeneous open mass spectral library (OMSL) metadata — field names, chemical identifiers, ionization modes, retention times, instrument descriptors — into a unified GNPS-compatible format, as implemented in the FragHub workflow (Analytical Chemistry 2024).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Spectra already in a single, harmonized library format — running harmonization again risks stripping valid metadata through the 'UNKNOWN' fallback mapping and re-dropping spectra. Collision energy harmonization is required: the article explicitly did not address it because ~70 different nonstandardized energy formats exist across OMSLs. Input contains only peak lists without any compound identifier (SMILES or InChI) and without adduct or precursor m/z — these spectra are removed during processing.

skills.description: Use when raw profile-mode spectra or transients from MALDI FT-ICR MS (or reconstructed high-resolution equivalents) must be reduced to peak lists before m/z binning, TIC normalization, feature counting, or SNR comparison.
skills.name: mass-spectra-peak-centroiding
skills.search_text: mass-spectra-peak-centroiding Use when raw profile-mode spectra or transients from MALDI FT-ICR MS (or reconstructed high-resolution equivalents) must be reduced to peak lists before m/z binning, TIC normalization, feature counting, or SNR comparison. When the input is already a centroided peak/imzML feature table (e.g., peak_data_sc_regional_decode.imzML) — binning and normalization, not centroiding, is the next step When spectra come from ion-trap or orbitrap instruments where MEISTER's transient-reconstruction model was not trained and peak positions/patterns differ substantially When the goal is spectral visualization rather than feature extraction, since centroiding discards isotopic fine structure in profile data http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Converts continuous FT-ICR transient-based mass spectra into discrete peak lists by detecting local maxima above noise and reporting centroid m/z positions, which is a prerequisite for downstream feature alignment, SNR quantification, and cross-annotation in the MEISTER multiscale MSI/SCMS pipeline. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-024-02171-3
skills.summary: Converts continuous FT-ICR transient-based mass spectra into discrete peak lists by detecting local maxima above noise and reporting centroid m/z positions, which is a prerequisite for downstream feature alignment, SNR quantification, and cross-annotation in the MEISTER multiscale MSI/SCMS pipeline.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is already a centroided peak/imzML feature table (e.g., peak_data_sc_regional_decode.imzML) — binning and normalization, not centroiding, is the next step When spectra come from ion-trap or orbitrap instruments where MEISTER's transient-reconstruction model was not trained and peak positions/patterns differ substantially When the goal is spectral visualization rather than feature extraction, since centroiding discards isotopic fine structure in profile data

skills.search_text: mass-spectra-peak-filtering Use when raw MGF MS/MS spectra must be cleaned before clustering or spectral-library building and peak information dominates runtime (>95% of raw-file data volume). Input spectra are already preprocessed/clustered — re-filtering would apply the 1% base-peak and 5-peak/250-Da cutoffs redundantly Spectra lack precursor ion metadata, since the precursor-related peak removal step depends on precursor information The downstream workflow requires spectra with very low signal content preserved (the <5 valid peaks and <250 Da range filters intentionally discard them) http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3365 Fine-grained peak- and spectrum-level filtering of MS/MS spectra during preprocessing for spectral clustering, as implemented in HyperSpec's parallelized preprocessor: precursor/low-intensity peak removal, minimum-peak-count and mass-range spectrum filters, top-50 peak retention, and L2 intensity normalization. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.2c00612
skills.summary: Fine-grained peak- and spectrum-level filtering of MS/MS spectra during preprocessing for spectral clustering, as implemented in HyperSpec's parallelized preprocessor: precursor/low-intensity peak removal, minimum-peak-count and mass-range spectrum filters, top-50 peak retention, and L2 intensity normalization.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra are already preprocessed/clustered — re-filtering would apply the 1% base-peak and 5-peak/250-Da cutoffs redundantly Spectra lack precursor ion metadata, since the precursor-related peak removal step depends on precursor information The downstream workflow requires spectra with very low signal content preserved (the <5 valid peaks and <250 Da range filters intentionally discard them)

skills.search_text: mass-spectra-peak-filtering Use when raw GNPS MS/MS library spectra in MGF/mzML format must be cleaned and intensity-normalized before spectral similarity model training or inference, and peak count/intensity distributions are noisy. Input spectra are already processed/cleaned (e.g., a pipeline-processed file like the pesticides_processed.mgf test resource) — re-filtering could distort intensities The downstream task requires the original absolute intensities (e.g., quantitative comparisons rather than spectral similarity modeling) Working in negative ionisation mode or with spectra whose relevant features lie in the very-low-intensity (<0.1% of base peak) region the filter discards Curate raw MS/MS library spectra (e.g., 210,407 GNPS entries) by removing low-intensity peaks (<0.1% of the max peak intensity), capping spectra at their 1000 highest-intensity peaks, and square-root transforming intensities so they are ready for embedding-based models like MS2DeepScore. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-021-00558-4

skills.description: Use when comparing a query tandem mass spectrum against reference spectra (e.g., ESI-MS2 peak lists of authentic compounds) to produce a similarity score for compound identification, as in MassBank's Spectral Search.
skills.name: mass-spectra-peak-matching
skills.search_text: mass-spectra-peak-matching Use when comparing a query tandem mass spectrum against reference spectra (e.g., ESI-MS2 peak lists of authentic compounds) to produce a similarity score for compound identification, as in MassBank's Spectral Search. Comparing EI-MS spectra, where Stein and Scott's exponents (m = 0.6, n = 3) rather than the ESI-MS2-optimized m = 0.5, n = 2 are appropriate Input is raw instrument data (e.g., mzML/profile spectra) rather than peak lists — centroiding and peak picking must happen first Need for identity-level confirmation rather than similarity-based ranking; a score above 0.6 alone does not guarantee correct identification http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Compute the MassBank spectral search similarity score: a weighted cosine correlation between query and reference peak lists in which each peak is weighted by W_i = [Intensity_i]^m [m/z_i]^n, with exponents optimized for ESI-MS2 data as m = 0.5 and n = 2. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/jms.1777
skills.summary: Compute the MassBank spectral search similarity score: a weighted cosine correlation between query and reference peak lists in which each peak is weighted by W_i = [Intensity_i]^m [m/z_i]^n, with exponents optimized for ESI-MS2 data as m = 0.5 and n = 2.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Comparing EI-MS spectra, where Stein and Scott's exponents (m = 0.6, n = 3) rather than the ESI-MS2-optimized m = 0.5, n = 2 are appropriate Input is raw instrument data (e.g., mzML/profile spectra) rather than peak lists — centroiding and peak picking must happen first Need for identity-level confirmation rather than similarity-based ranking; a score above 0.6 alone does not guarantee correct identification

skills.search_text: mass-spectra-peak-parsing Use when a mass spectrum's peaks must be converted from a tabular or database record form (e.g. a MassBank record like PR100026) into the single-line 'ion:intensity' string format that SPLASH tools expect. The input is already a single-line 'ion:intensity' spectrum string — feed it directly to SplashUtil.splash() instead of re-parsing The input is a chemical structure (InChI/SMILES) or raw instrument data (mzML) for which SPLASH only defines identifier generation after spectrum extraction, not structure hashing http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Parses a mass spectrum's peak list into the single-line 'ion:intensity' representation required by the SPLASH (SPectraL hASH) algorithm, e.g. '138.0641:71.59 195.0815:261.7' for the caffeine spectrum MassBank PR100026. This canonical textual form is the input that all SPLASH reference implementations consume before block construction and SHA-256 hashing. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/nbt.3689
skills.summary: Parses a mass spectrum's peak list into the single-line 'ion:intensity' representation required by the SPLASH (SPectraL hASH) algorithm, e.g. '138.0641:71.59 195.0815:261.7' for the caffeine spectrum MassBank PR100026. This canonical textual form is the input that all SPLASH reference implementations consume before block construction and SHA-256 hashing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a single-line 'ion:intensity' spectrum string — feed it directly to SplashUtil.splash() instead of re-parsing The input is a chemical structure (InChI/SMILES) or raw instrument data (mzML) for which SPLASH only defines identifier generation after spectrum extraction, not structure hashing

skills.description: Use when an in-silico EI-MS library of predicted spectra (e.g. NEIMS predictions over f-NIST and f-ChEMBL) must be transformed into fixed-length spectral embeddings to enable approximate nearest-neighbor matching with HNSW.
skills.name: mass-spectra-peak-tokenization
skills.search_text: mass-spectra-peak-tokenization Use when an in-silico EI-MS library of predicted spectra (e.g. NEIMS predictions over f-NIST and f-ChEMBL) must be transformed into fixed-length spectral embeddings to enable approximate nearest-neighbor matching with HNSW. Input is raw GC-MS instrument data (e.g. Shimadzu QP2010Ultra acquisitions) rather than preprocessed peak-list spectra — tokenization presumes peak tokens are already derivable The matching task needs exact nearest-neighbor search on the full library (e.g. faiss.IndexFlatL2 weighted cosine similarity baseline) rather than the FastEI approximate HNSW pipeline Spectra come from a non-EI ionization method or a library not built from the NEIMS predicted-spectra pipeline; the embedding was trained on in-silico EI-MS from f-NIST/f-ChEMBL only http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Reconstructs the FastEI Word2vec spectral embedding step from Yang et al. 2023 (Nature Communications), in which each predicted EI-MS spectrum is formatted as a 'sentence' of peak tokens and a gensim CBOW model (dim 500, window 1000, negative 5, lr 0.025 with linear decay, 60 epochs) is trained on 2,123,695 predicted spectra so spectra can be converted into dense embeddings for library matching. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-023-39279-7
skills.summary: Reconstructs the FastEI Word2vec spectral embedding step from Yang et al. 2023 (Nature Communications), in which each predicted EI-MS spectrum is formatted as a 'sentence' of peak tokens and a gensim CBOW model (dim 500, window 1000, negative 5, lr 0.025 with linear decay, 60 epochs) is trained on 2,123,695 predicted spectra so spectra can be converted into dense embeddings for library matching.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw GC-MS instrument data (e.g. Shimadzu QP2010Ultra acquisitions) rather than preprocessed peak-list spectra — tokenization presumes peak tokens are already derivable The matching task needs exact nearest-neighbor search on the full library (e.g. faiss.IndexFlatL2 weighted cosine similarity baseline) rather than the FastEI approximate HNSW pipeline Spectra come from a non-EI ionization method or a library not built from the NEIMS predicted-spectra pipeline; the embedding was trained on in-silico EI-MS from f-NIST/f-ChEMBL only

skills.name: mass-spectra-reduced-spectrum-extraction
skills.search_text: mass-spectra-reduced-spectrum-extraction Use when a peak list (ion:intensity pairs) must be converted into the SPLASH second summary block, or when a 4-digit base-36 histogram block must be reproduced or verified against a known SPLASH identifier. Input is an unprocessed vendor raw file (mzML/raw) rather than a peak list in 'ion:intensity' string representation — peak picking/deconvolution must happen first You need the third or fourth SPLASH blocks (full histogram summary or SHA256-derived unique hash), not the reduced second block The spectrum should be compared structurally to other compounds — SPLASH is a hashed identifier, not a similarity score http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Computes the SPLASH second summary block by reducing a mass spectrum to its top-10 ions above 10% of the base peak, binning intensities into 5 Da m/z bins, scaling each bin to a base-3 digit (0–2), and encoding the resulting histogram as a 4-digit base-36 block. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/nbt.3689
skills.summary: Computes the SPLASH second summary block by reducing a mass spectrum to its top-10 ions above 10% of the base peak, binning intensities into 5 Da m/z bins, scaling each bin to a base-3 digit (0–2), and encoding the resulting histogram as a 4-digit base-36 block.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is an unprocessed vendor raw file (mzML/raw) rather than a peak list in 'ion:intensity' string representation — peak picking/deconvolution must happen first You need the third or fourth SPLASH blocks (full histogram summary or SHA256-derived unique hash), not the reduced second block The spectrum should be compared structurally to other compounds — SPLASH is a hashed identifier, not a similarity score

skills.search_text: mass-spectra-to-smiles-translation Use when you have a preprocessed low-resolution GC-EI-MS spectrum (intensity-binned, threshold-filtered) and need de novo molecular structure candidates as SMILES strings without a reference spectral library match. skills.summary: De novo translation of GC-EI-MS spectra into ranked SMILES candidate structures using the SpecTUS encoder-decoder transformer (354M parameters), pretrained on 17.2M synthetic NEIMS/RASSP spectra and finetuned on NIST 20 experimental spectra, bypassing spectral library database search.

skills.description: Use when annotated MS/MS spectra (e.g. from GNPS or MoNA libraries) carry an adduct or parent mass inconsistent with their SMILES annotation and precursor m/z, and the annotation needs repair before library matching or ML training.
skills.name: mass-spectral-adduct-repair
skills.search_text: mass-spectral-adduct-repair Use when annotated MS/MS spectra (e.g. from GNPS or MoNA libraries) carry an adduct or parent mass inconsistent with their SMILES annotation and precursor m/z, and the annotation needs repair before library matching or ML training. Spectra lack any SMILES (or other structure annotation) — the filter cannot test candidate adducts against a structure, so Derive Annotation From Compound Name via PubChem should run first or the spectrum should be discarded by Require Valid Annotation. Wrong chemical annotations that happen to be consistent with the measured precursor mass — the article notes such annotations go unnoticed because plausibility checks considering measured fragments are not yet implemented. Fragment-level validation is required (checking whether measured fragments match the annotation) — that is only a proposed future expansion in matchms, not part of this filter. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Corrects a spectrum's adduct annotation and precursor parent mass by testing which adduct explains the observed precursor m/z given the spectrum's SMILES structure, as implemented in the matchms library-cleaning pipeline for GNPS and other public MS/MS libraries. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00878-1
skills.summary: Corrects a spectrum's adduct annotation and precursor parent mass by testing which adduct explains the observed precursor m/z given the spectrum's SMILES structure, as implemented in the matchms library-cleaning pipeline for GNPS and other public MS/MS libraries.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Spectra lack any SMILES (or other structure annotation) — the filter cannot test candidate adducts against a structure, so Derive Annotation From Compound Name via PubChem should run first or the spectrum should be discarded by Require Valid Annotation. Wrong chemical annotations that happen to be consistent with the measured precursor mass — the article notes such annotations go unnoticed because plausibility checks considering measured fragments are not yet implemented. Fragment-level validation is required (checking whether measured fragments match the annotation) — that is only a proposed future expansion in matchms, not part of this filter.

skills.description: Use when you have MS/MS reference spectra (MGF from MZmine, or a USI list in CSV/TSV) and want to find matching or analog spectra in thousands of indexed public datasets (GNPS/MassIVE, Metabolomics Workbench, MetaboLights, NORMAN).
skills.name: mass-spectral-analog-search
skills.search_text: mass-spectral-analog-search Use when you have MS/MS reference spectra (MGF from MZmine, or a USI list in CSV/TSV) and want to find matching or analog spectra in thousands of indexed public datasets (GNPS/MassIVE, Metabolomics Workbench, MetaboLights, NORMAN). When only a single spectrum needs searching and an interactive web app (e.g., microbeMASST or plantMASST) suffices instead of a batch job When the input is already a feature table or quantified peak matrix rather than raw MS/MS spectra or USI lists — this skill searches spectra, not feature intensities When the goal is targeted quantification of known metabolites rather than analog discovery across public datasets http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Searches a reference MS/MS spectrum (or an MGF/USI list) against all publicly indexed untargeted metabolomics datasets via the GNPS Fast Search API to retrieve analog spectra passing a modified-cosine threshold, enabling domain-specific and drug-analog propagation across public repositories. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-025-65993-5
skills.summary: Searches a reference MS/MS spectrum (or an MGF/USI list) against all publicly indexed untargeted metabolomics datasets via the GNPS Fast Search API to retrieve analog spectra passing a modified-cosine threshold, enabling domain-specific and drug-analog propagation across public repositories.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When only a single spectrum needs searching and an interactive web app (e.g., microbeMASST or plantMASST) suffices instead of a batch job When the input is already a feature table or quantified peak matrix rather than raw MS/MS spectra or USI lists — this skill searches spectra, not feature intensities When the goal is targeted quantification of known metabolites rather than analog discovery across public datasets

skills.description: Use when raw MALDI-MS or ESI-MS intensity traces show an irregular, drifting baseline that must be removed before peak detection or normalization, and m/z/intensity data are held as plain data frames.
skills.name: mass-spectral-baseline-estimation
skills.search_text: mass-spectral-baseline-estimation Use when raw MALDI-MS or ESI-MS intensity traces show an irregular, drifting baseline that must be removed before peak detection or normalization, and m/z/intensity data are held as plain data frames. The input is already baseline-corrected and only needs smoothing, peak detection, or normalization Spectra are stored in S3/S4 class objects from other packages (e.g., MALDIquant, MSnbase) and cannot be provided as plain m/z/intensity data frames The analysis goal is alignment of spectra to an m/z grid rather than baseline removal Estimates and subtracts the underlying baseline of MALDI mass spectra using the subMALDI package's baselineCorr() with one of three methods — monotone_min, linear, or loess — producing baseline-corrected spectra whose baseline runs along the x-axis while peak intensities are retained. metabolomics/v3 10.21105/joss.02694
skills.summary: Estimates and subtracts the underlying baseline of MALDI mass spectra using the subMALDI package's baselineCorr() with one of three methods — monotone_min, linear, or loess — producing baseline-corrected spectra whose baseline runs along the x-axis while peak intensities are retained.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already baseline-corrected and only needs smoothing, peak detection, or normalization Spectra are stored in S3/S4 class objects from other packages (e.g., MALDIquant, MSnbase) and cannot be provided as plain m/z/intensity data frames The analysis goal is alignment of spectra to an m/z grid rather than baseline removal
