skills.name: matrix-peak-removal-workflow
skills.search_text: matrix-peak-removal-workflow Use when an MSI peak matrix (rMSIproc .zip format) contains redundant, non-biologically-relevant matrix-related signals (e.g. Agn+ clusters in silver-assisted LDI) that should be annotated and removed before downstream analysis such as PCA or spatial metabolomics. Input is raw profile-mode spectra (imzML) rather than an rMSIproc peak matrix — first run rMSIproc::ProcessWizard to generate the peak matrix The goal is simple blank/off-sample subtraction — rMSIcleanup was designed because such approaches ignore ion suppression and matrix adducts with endogenous compounds (best blank-subtraction metric only reached AUC 0.61 vs 0.97) http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Annotates and removes matrix-related peaks (e.g. silver cluster ions in AgLDI MSI) from an rMSIproc peak matrix using rMSIcleanup, which combines the LDI material's chemical formula, theoretical isotope patterns (enviPat), and spatial ion-image distributions, then generates a transparent PDF report justifying each annotation. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-020-00449-0
skills.summary: Annotates and removes matrix-related peaks (e.g. silver cluster ions in AgLDI MSI) from an rMSIproc peak matrix using rMSIcleanup, which combines the LDI material's chemical formula, theoretical isotope patterns (enviPat), and spatial ion-image distributions, then generates a transparent PDF report justifying each annotation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw profile-mode spectra (imzML) rather than an rMSIproc peak matrix — first run rMSIproc::ProcessWizard to generate the peak matrix The goal is simple blank/off-sample subtraction — rMSIcleanup was designed because such approaches ignore ion suppression and matrix adducts with endogenous compounds (best blank-subtraction metric only reached AUC 0.61 vs 0.97)

skills.description: Use when pre-processing raw multi-vendor MALDI MSI data (vendor formats converted to imzML) where matrix/spray pixels would contaminate peak lists, and the sample must be segmented into tissue vs. matrix regions automatically without manual ROI drawing.
skills.name: matrix-pixel-removal
skills.search_text: matrix-pixel-removal Use when pre-processing raw multi-vendor MALDI MSI data (vendor formats converted to imzML) where matrix/spray pixels would contaminate peak lists, and the sample must be segmented into tissue vs. matrix regions automatically without manual ROI drawing. The task is segmentation or IFM registration rather than MALDI MSI pre-processing — use msi_segmentation_flow, if_segmentation_flow or msi_if_registration_flow instead The input is already a peak list or processed imzML peak matrix, not raw vendor MALDI MSI data http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 An automated step of the msiFlow msi_preprocessing_flow that detects and removes matrix (MALDI matrix spray) pixels from raw MALDI MSI data using UMAP and HDBSCAN based on tissue architecture and borders, so that downstream peak picking, alignment, normalisation and de-isotoping operate only on true tissue pixels. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-55306-7
skills.summary: An automated step of the msiFlow msi_preprocessing_flow that detects and removes matrix (MALDI matrix spray) pixels from raw MALDI MSI data using UMAP and HDBSCAN based on tissue architecture and borders, so that downstream peak picking, alignment, normalisation and de-isotoping operate only on true tissue pixels.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is segmentation or IFM registration rather than MALDI MSI pre-processing — use msi_segmentation_flow, if_segmentation_flow or msi_if_registration_flow instead The input is already a peak list or processed imzML peak matrix, not raw vendor MALDI MSI data

skills.description: Use when pre-processing MALDI MSI (e.g. t-MALDI-2) imzML data and a binary mask separating matrix/off-tissue pixels from tissue-covered pixels must be generated automatically, without manually defined matrix peak lists.
skills.name: matrix-region-detection-in-maldi-msi
skills.search_text: matrix-region-detection-in-maldi-msi Use when pre-processing MALDI MSI (e.g. t-MALDI-2) imzML data and a binary mask separating matrix/off-tissue pixels from tissue-covered pixels must be generated automatically, without manually defined matrix peak lists. Input is already a peak-picked or feature table rather than raw pixel-level spectra, since the method depends on spectral similarity of full pixel spectra The sample covers the entire measured area with no matrix at the borders, so no border-connected matrix cluster exists The goal is lipid annotation or interpretation — msiFlow explicitly does not include an annotation or interpretation step http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Unsupervised detection of matrix/off-tissue pixels in MALDI MSI samples by embedding pixel spectra with UMAP, clustering with HDBSCAN, and selecting the border-connected cluster with the most pixels as the matrix cluster — no prior definition of known matrix peaks is required. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-55306-7
skills.summary: Unsupervised detection of matrix/off-tissue pixels in MALDI MSI samples by embedding pixel spectra with UMAP, clustering with HDBSCAN, and selecting the border-connected cluster with the most pixels as the matrix cluster — no prior definition of known matrix peaks is required.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a peak-picked or feature table rather than raw pixel-level spectra, since the method depends on spectral similarity of full pixel spectra The sample covers the entire measured area with no matrix at the borders, so no border-connected matrix cluster exists The goal is lipid annotation or interpretation — msiFlow explicitly does not include an annotation or interpretation step

skills.description: Use when an MSI peak matrix contains matrix-related signals (e.g. Agn+ cluster peaks in Ag-sputtered AgLDI data) that must be annotated and removed, and simple blank subtraction is insufficient because of ion suppression, adducts, or isobaric peaks.
skills.name: matrix-related-peak-annotation
skills.search_text: matrix-related-peak-annotation Use when an MSI peak matrix contains matrix-related signals (e.g. Agn+ cluster peaks in Ag-sputtered AgLDI data) that must be annotated and removed, and simple blank subtraction is insufficient because of ion suppression, adducts, or isobaric peaks. Input is raw profile-mode imzML that has not been processed into a centroided peak matrix with rMSIproc — the algorithm requires the rMSIproc peak-matrix format The chemical formula of the LDI-promoting material is unknown, so theoretical isotope patterns cannot be computed with enviPat and matched to experimental peaks The analysis is on non-imaging bulk MS data, since classification depends on ion images and spatial-distribution correlations http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Annotates matrix-related m/z signals in mass spectrometry imaging peak matrices by combining the chemical formula of the LDI-promoting material (e.g. 'Ag1') with the spatial distribution of its ions, and prevents misclassification of overlapped or isobaric ions via a bisecting k-means overlapping-peak detection routine. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-020-00449-0
skills.summary: Annotates matrix-related m/z signals in mass spectrometry imaging peak matrices by combining the chemical formula of the LDI-promoting material (e.g. 'Ag1') with the spatial distribution of its ions, and prevents misclassification of overlapped or isobaric ions via a bisecting k-means overlapping-peak detection routine.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw profile-mode imzML that has not been processed into a centroided peak matrix with rMSIproc — the algorithm requires the rMSIproc peak-matrix format The chemical formula of the LDI-promoting material is unknown, so theoretical isotope patterns cannot be computed with enviPat and matched to experimental peaks The analysis is on non-imaging bulk MS data, since classification depends on ion images and spatial-distribution correlations

skills.description: Use when the input is a molecular-species (LMS) intensity matrix whose row identifiers are LIPID MAPS shorthand names (e.g. 'PC 16:0_18:1') and a chain-level (LBB) matrix is required for downstream statistics or pathway analysis.
skills.name: matrix-row-expansion-and-aggregation
skills.search_text: matrix-row-expansion-and-aggregation Use when the input is a molecular-species (LMS) intensity matrix whose row identifiers are LIPID MAPS shorthand names (e.g. 'PC 16:0_18:1') and a chain-level (LBB) matrix is required for downstream statistics or pathway analysis. The matrix is already at the lipid class (LCL) or building-block (LBB) level and only needs direct statistical analysis — no expansion/aggregation is required. Row identifiers do not encode chain composition in LIPID MAPS shorthand notation, so chains cannot be parsed from the row names. You need to preserve molecular-species-level statistics unchanged; this skill intentionally redistributes each species' signal across its chains. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Reconstructs the lipid building block (LBB) sub-matrix from an LMS-level molecular-species intensity matrix by splitting each species row into its constituent chain rows, dividing intensities by the chain count, and summing duplicate pseudo-lipid rows. It automates the otherwise time- and labor-intensive submatrix calculations needed for chain-level lipidomics analysis in LipidOne 2.0. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/cpz1.70009
skills.summary: Reconstructs the lipid building block (LBB) sub-matrix from an LMS-level molecular-species intensity matrix by splitting each species row into its constituent chain rows, dividing intensities by the chain count, and summing duplicate pseudo-lipid rows. It automates the otherwise time- and labor-intensive submatrix calculations needed for chain-level lipidomics analysis in LipidOne 2.0.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The matrix is already at the lipid class (LCL) or building-block (LBB) level and only needs direct statistical analysis — no expansion/aggregation is required. Row identifiers do not encode chain composition in LIPID MAPS shorthand notation, so chains cannot be parsed from the row names. You need to preserve molecular-species-level statistics unchanged; this skill intentionally redistributes each species' signal across its chains.

skills.description: Use when you have paired pre-dosing (blank) and post-dosing LC-MS/MS acquisitions for multiple mouse biological matrices (e.g., plasma, lung, urine, feces) and need to count and classify dosage-related exogenous components per matrix.
skills.name: matrix-specific-component-profiling
skills.search_text: matrix-specific-component-profiling Use when you have paired pre-dosing (blank) and post-dosing LC-MS/MS acquisitions for multiple mouse biological matrices (e.g., plasma, lung, urine, feces) and need to count and classify dosage-related exogenous components per matrix. No corresponding pre-dosing (blank) matrix exists for a sample, so PATBS background subtraction cannot separate endogenous from exogenous peaks. Input is already an annotated component/feature table requiring prototype-metabolite bridging or pathway mapping rather than blank-subtracted exogenous profiling per matrix. Data are in vitro component lists rather than in vivo biological matrices, where the goal is exposure/metabolism bridging via MDRB rather than matrix-level disposition profiling. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Profiles exogenous (dose-related) components per biological matrix by running PATBS non-targeted background subtraction of post-dosing LC-MS/MS data against matched pre-dosing blanks, then annotating retained features as prototypes vs metabolites. Applied to CKXR (Semen Armeniacae Amarum) in mice, it yielded 351 exogenous components (41 prototypes, 310 metabolites) distributed across plasma, lung, urine, and feces. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13020-024-01031-8
skills.summary: Profiles exogenous (dose-related) components per biological matrix by running PATBS non-targeted background subtraction of post-dosing LC-MS/MS data against matched pre-dosing blanks, then annotating retained features as prototypes vs metabolites. Applied to CKXR (Semen Armeniacae Amarum) in mice, it yielded 351 exogenous components (41 prototypes, 310 metabolites) distributed across plasma, lung, urine, and feces.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No corresponding pre-dosing (blank) matrix exists for a sample, so PATBS background subtraction cannot separate endogenous from exogenous peaks. Input is already an annotated component/feature table requiring prototype-metabolite bridging or pathway mapping rather than blank-subtracted exogenous profiling per matrix. Data are in vitro component lists rather than in vivo biological matrices, where the goal is exposure/metabolism bridging via MDRB rather than matrix-level disposition profiling.

skills.description: Use when a metabolite-bridging or characterization pipeline reports an overall characterization rate and you must confirm per-matrix counts (e.g., 66/222/30/40) reconcile with the claimed total and percent improvement.
skills.name: matrix-wise-metabolite-count-verification
skills.search_text: matrix-wise-metabolite-count-verification Use when a metabolite-bridging or characterization pipeline reports an overall characterization rate and you must confirm per-matrix counts (e.g., 66/222/30/40) reconcile with the claimed total and percent improvement. The raw MS feature list or MDRB component relationship network has not yet been generated — counts cannot be verified upstream of characterization The study involves a single matrix or a herb whose reported per-matrix breakdown differs from plasma/urine/feces/lung; the tally structure must be adapted, not copied http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0607 Verifies a metabolite characterization campaign by tallying characterized metabolites per biological matrix (plasma, urine, feces, lung) and comparing the totals against reported baseline and improved counts (e.g., 110 at 31% manual vs 227 at 65% MDRB for CKXR). metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13020-024-01031-8
skills.summary: Verifies a metabolite characterization campaign by tallying characterized metabolites per biological matrix (plasma, urine, feces, lung) and comparing the totals against reported baseline and improved counts (e.g., 110 at 31% manual vs 227 at 65% MDRB for CKXR).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The raw MS feature list or MDRB component relationship network has not yet been generated — counts cannot be verified upstream of characterization The study involves a single matrix or a herb whose reported per-matrix breakdown differs from plasma/urine/feces/lung; the tally structure must be adapted, not copied

skills.description: Use when raw mzML LC-MS/MS metabolomics or lipidomics samples need peak detection and grouping into peak groups with associated MS/MS scans, rather than a precomputed feature table.
skills.name: maven-peak-group-detection
skills.search_text: maven-peak-group-detection Use when raw mzML LC-MS/MS metabolomics or lipidomics samples need peak detection and grouping into peak groups with associated MS/MS scans, rather than a precomputed feature table. Input is already a feature/peak table rather than raw mzML scan data Data lack MS/MS scans and only MS1 peak detection in prior-MAVEN style is needed without slice formation Analysis goal is in-silico lipid spectra library generation rather than peak grouping from measured data http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Detect and group chromatographic peak groups from LC-MS metabolomics data using MAVEN2's peak-grouping logic, optionally extended with MS/MS-based slice formation and merging in (m/z, retention time) space so fragmentation scans are attached to finalized peak groups. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo12080684
skills.summary: Detect and group chromatographic peak groups from LC-MS metabolomics data using MAVEN2's peak-grouping logic, optionally extended with MS/MS-based slice formation and merging in (m/z, retention time) space so fragmentation scans are attached to finalized peak groups.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a feature/peak table rather than raw mzML scan data Data lack MS/MS scans and only MS1 peak detection in prior-MAVEN style is needed without slice formation Analysis goal is in-silico lipid spectra library generation rather than peak grouping from measured data

skills.description: Use when tokenised BGCs (each gene as a (sub)Pfam domain combination, original gene order retained) must be grouped into sub-clusters via gene co-localisation and adjacency statistics.
skills.name: maximal-clique-subcluster-extraction
skills.search_text: maximal-clique-subcluster-extraction Use when tokenised BGCs (each gene as a (sub)Pfam domain combination, original gene order retained) must be grouped into sub-clusters via gene co-localisation and adjacency statistics. When gene order is unavailable or a bag-of-words representation is preferred — iPRESTO's PRESTO-TOP LDA approach, which does not consider original gene order, is the intended alternative When the input BGCs have not been tokenised into (sub)Pfam domain combinations with non-biosynthetic Pfams removed When singletons are of interest: putative sub-clusters with fewer than three genes or occurring in only one BGC are deliberately filtered out as noise http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3473 PRESTO-STAT procedure from iPRESTO that turns statistical co-occurrence of tokenised BGC genes into undirected graphs and extracts maximal cliques as biosynthetic sub-clusters. It is the statistical (co-localisation/adjacency) branch of iPRESTO's unsupervised sub-cluster detection. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1010462
skills.summary: PRESTO-STAT procedure from iPRESTO that turns statistical co-occurrence of tokenised BGC genes into undirected graphs and extracts maximal cliques as biosynthetic sub-clusters. It is the statistical (co-localisation/adjacency) branch of iPRESTO's unsupervised sub-cluster detection.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When gene order is unavailable or a bag-of-words representation is preferred — iPRESTO's PRESTO-TOP LDA approach, which does not consider original gene order, is the intended alternative When the input BGCs have not been tokenised into (sub)Pfam domain combinations with non-biosynthetic Pfams removed When singletons are of interest: putative sub-clusters with fewer than three genes or occurring in only one BGC are deliberately filtered out as noise

skills.description: Use when a study needs compound-level structural similarity ground truth to benchmark spectral alignment or spectral similarity scores (e.g., modified cosine, SIMILE p-values) against chemical structure.
skills.name: maximum-common-substructure-computation
skills.search_text: maximum-common-substructure-computation Use when a study needs compound-level structural similarity ground truth to benchmark spectral alignment or spectral similarity scores (e.g., modified cosine, SIMILE p-values) against chemical structure. When the input is mass spectra rather than structures — use spectral similarity/alignment scores (cosine, modified cosine, SIMILE) instead, since MCS requires parsed molecular structures When a faster fingerprint-based structural similarity (e.g., Tanimoto on Morgan fingerprints) is sufficient, since exhaustive MCS with a 1800 s per-pair timeout is computationally expensive When pairs contain stereochemical or salt-form nuances that RDKit's default MCS matching with ringMatchesRingOnly=False would mis-handle http://edamontology.org/topic_0081 http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 Computes an all-vs-all maximum common substructure (MCS) Jaccard similarity matrix between compounds using RDKit, serving as ground-truth structural similarity when benchmarking spectral alignment algorithms such as SIMILE against cosine-based scores. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-022-30118-9
skills.summary: Computes an all-vs-all maximum common substructure (MCS) Jaccard similarity matrix between compounds using RDKit, serving as ground-truth structural similarity when benchmarking spectral alignment algorithms such as SIMILE against cosine-based scores.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is mass spectra rather than structures — use spectral similarity/alignment scores (cosine, modified cosine, SIMILE) instead, since MCS requires parsed molecular structures When a faster fingerprint-based structural similarity (e.g., Tanimoto on Morgan fingerprints) is sufficient, since exhaustive MCS with a 1800 s per-pair timeout is computationally expensive When pairs contain stereochemical or salt-form nuances that RDKit's default MCS matching with ringMatchesRingOnly=False would mis-handle

skills.description: Use when enumerating candidate molecular formulas from LC-MS/MS fragment peaks with FSA and fragment formulas resolve to multiple maximum-difference-redundancy (MDR) combinations, and you must set MaxComb to control which fragments are dropped before scoring precursor candidates with Eq. 4.
skills.name: maximum-difference-redundancy-fragment-filtering
skills.search_text: maximum-difference-redundancy-fragment-filtering Use when enumerating candidate molecular formulas from LC-MS/MS fragment peaks with FSA and fragment formulas resolve to multiple maximum-difference-redundancy (MDR) combinations, and you must set MaxComb to control which fragments are dropped before scoring precursor candidates with Eq. 4. Do not rely on this as the sole ranking step when structural information matters — the paper notes FSA 'has not utilized structural information yet and therefore its accuracy may not be competitive with some of the state-of-the-art identification tools' such as Buddy and SIRIUS. Do not apply to compounds containing elements beyond C, H, O, N, S, P or to compounds forming various adduct types, since FSA has not been validated in those regimes. Do not use when chemical species/adduct-specific feasibility filtering is required — the paper reports that few chemical rules have been implemented to rank formulas and filter out unfeasible ones. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Applies the MaxComb parameter of FSA (Formula Subset Analysis) to limit how many maximum-difference-redundancy (MDR) combinations a fragment formula may carry; setting MaxComb=1 drops any fragment with multiple MDR combinations and, per the paper's Supplementary Fig S1 sweep, yields the highest rank#1 formula accuracy. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-025-02379-0
skills.summary: Applies the MaxComb parameter of FSA (Formula Subset Analysis) to limit how many maximum-difference-redundancy (MDR) combinations a fragment formula may carry; setting MaxComb=1 drops any fragment with multiple MDR combinations and, per the paper's Supplementary Fig S1 sweep, yields the highest rank#1 formula accuracy.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Do not rely on this as the sole ranking step when structural information matters — the paper notes FSA 'has not utilized structural information yet and therefore its accuracy may not be competitive with some of the state-of-the-art identification tools' such as Buddy and SIRIUS. Do not apply to compounds containing elements beyond C, H, O, N, S, P or to compounds forming various adduct types, since FSA has not been validated in those regimes. Do not use when chemical species/adduct-specific feasibility filtering is required — the paper reports that few chemical rules have been implemented to rank formulas and filter out unfeasible ones.

skills.description: Use when XCMS-corrected retention times remain misaligned for specific detected feature groups (e.g., flagged by ncGTW misalignment detection) and compound-specific, per-feature warping functions are needed instead of one global per-sample warp.
skills.name: maximum-flow-warping-estimation
skills.search_text: maximum-flow-warping-estimation Use when XCMS-corrected retention times remain misaligned for specific detected feature groups (e.g., flagged by ncGTW misalignment detection) and compound-specific, per-feature warping functions are needed instead of one global per-sample warp. The input is already an aligned feature table with no raw extracted-ion profiles available — ncGTW warping estimation operates on profile-level data, not peak tables. All features are well aligned by the standard XCMS single per-sample warping function and misalignment detection flagged no groups, so there is nothing to realign. A single global time-warping function per sample is sufficient (no compound-specific, m/z-bin-dependent RT drift to correct). http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Reference-free LC-MS retention-time warping estimation from ncGTW: solve combinatorial pairwise profile warpings via maximum-flow problems with neighboring-sample structural constraints, then aggregate all samples onto a virtual pseudo-reference to yield per-feature, sample-specific RT warping functions. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btaa037
skills.summary: Reference-free LC-MS retention-time warping estimation from ncGTW: solve combinatorial pairwise profile warpings via maximum-flow problems with neighboring-sample structural constraints, then aggregate all samples onto a virtual pseudo-reference to yield per-feature, sample-specific RT warping functions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already an aligned feature table with no raw extracted-ion profiles available — ncGTW warping estimation operates on profile-level data, not peak tables. All features are well aligned by the standard XCMS single per-sample warping function and misalignment detection flagged no groups, so there is nothing to realign. A single global time-warping function per sample is sufficient (no compound-specific, m/z-bin-dependent RT drift to correct).

skills.description: Use when a ready-to-identify dataset contains candidate structures with MS/MS scores and ROASMI retention-order probabilities P_ij, and you need top-k ranked annotations per peak, especially for isomers with similar fragmentation or peaks lacking informative spectra.
skills.name: maximum-marginal-topk-ranking-of-molecular-annotations
skills.search_text: maximum-marginal-topk-ranking-of-molecular-annotations Use when a ready-to-identify dataset contains candidate structures with MS/MS scores and ROASMI retention-order probabilities P_ij, and you need top-k ranked annotations per peak, especially for isomers with similar fragmentation or peaks lacking informative spectra. Input dataset lacks ROASMI-predicted retention-order probabilities P_ij (e.g. no trained ROASMI model or no ready-to-identify set) — the integration graph cannot be built. The chromatographic system is not reversed-phase LC at eluent pH ≈ 2.7 — ROASMI only applies to RPLC, and HILIC generalizability is future work. A candidate pair is marked indistinguishable by ROASMI (close retention with high variance) — such pairs must be excluded rather than ranked. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Integrates ROASMI-predicted retention-order probabilities with MS/MS spectral scores to rank candidate molecular structures for each detected peak, using a probabilistic framework over fully connected graphs of candidates with random spanning-tree ensembles. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-025-00968-8
skills.summary: Integrates ROASMI-predicted retention-order probabilities with MS/MS spectral scores to rank candidate molecular structures for each detected peak, using a probabilistic framework over fully connected graphs of candidates with random spanning-tree ensembles.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input dataset lacks ROASMI-predicted retention-order probabilities P_ij (e.g. no trained ROASMI model or no ready-to-identify set) — the integration graph cannot be built. The chromatographic system is not reversed-phase LC at eluent pH ≈ 2.7 — ROASMI only applies to RPLC, and HILIC generalizability is future work. A candidate pair is marked indistinguishable by ROASMI (close retention with high variance) — such pairs must be excluded rather than ranked.

skills.description: Use when you have ranked lists from replicate RNA-seq (or other high-throughput) experiments and need to identify reproducible signals with controlled false discovery rate, without parametric assumptions on dependence structures.
skills.name: maximum-rank-reproducibility-fdr-procedure
skills.search_text: maximum-rank-reproducibility-fdr-procedure Use when you have ranked lists from replicate RNA-seq (or other high-throughput) experiments and need to identify reproducible signals with controlled false discovery rate, without parametric assumptions on dependence structures. When the input data are unranked raw measurements and no meaningful ranking of genes by effect size is possible — MaRR operates on rank lists. When a parametric dependence model is preferred and the copula mixture model's assumptions hold (e.g., when you need per-gene class posterior probabilities rather than rank-based FDR control). When the analysis goal is differential expression within a single experiment rather than reproducibility across replicate experiments. http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 The MaRR procedure is a non-parametric method for assessing reproducibility of ranked gene lists from replicate high-throughput experiments. It uses a maximum rank statistic to detect the reproducible/irreproducible change point and computes marginal FDRs without parametric assumptions or tuning parameters. metabolomics/v3 10.1080/01621459.2017.1397521
skills.summary: The MaRR procedure is a non-parametric method for assessing reproducibility of ranked gene lists from replicate high-throughput experiments. It uses a maximum rank statistic to detect the reproducible/irreproducible change point and computes marginal FDRs without parametric assumptions or tuning parameters.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input data are unranked raw measurements and no meaningful ranking of genes by effect size is possible — MaRR operates on rank lists. When a parametric dependence model is preferred and the copula mixture model's assumptions hold (e.g., when you need per-gene class posterior probabilities rather than rank-based FDR control). When the analysis goal is differential expression within a single experiment rather than reproducibility across replicate experiments.

skills.description: Use when two gene rank lists from replicate high-throughput experiments (e.g., SEQC RNA-seq comparisons of 43,919 transcripts) must be converted to per-gene maximum rank statistics M_g = max(R_gx, R_gy) as input to MaRR thresholding and mFDR estimation.
skills.name: maximum-rank-statistic-computation
skills.search_text: maximum-rank-statistic-computation Use when two gene rank lists from replicate high-throughput experiments (e.g., SEQC RNA-seq comparisons of 43,919 transcripts) must be converted to per-gene maximum rank statistics M_g = max(R_gx, R_gy) as input to MaRR thresholding and mFDR estimation. When the data plausibly satisfy the copula mixture model's parametric assumptions and a full model-based fit is preferred — in Simulation A, MaRR was anti-conservative (inflated FDR) for weak, infrequent signals (muA=1, pi1=0.1) and systematically underestimated pi1 for a large weakly correlated group (muA in {1,2}, rho=0.4, pi1=0.8) When the two experiments cannot be ranked on a common gene universe (e.g., transcripts absent from one platform's mapping), since M_g requires paired ranks for every gene When continuous effect-size estimates or per-gene dependence strength (rho-hat) from a generative model are required rather than rank-based reproducibility calls http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Computes the maximum rank statistic M_g = max(R_gx, R_gy) for every gene from paired rank lists of replicate experiments, the core statistic of the nonparametric MaRR reproducibility procedure. It quantifies how extreme a gene is in both experiments simultaneously without parametric assumptions on dependence or distribution. metabolomics/v3 10.1080/01621459.2017.1397521
skills.summary: Computes the maximum rank statistic M_g = max(R_gx, R_gy) for every gene from paired rank lists of replicate experiments, the core statistic of the nonparametric MaRR reproducibility procedure. It quantifies how extreme a gene is in both experiments simultaneously without parametric assumptions on dependence or distribution.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the data plausibly satisfy the copula mixture model's parametric assumptions and a full model-based fit is preferred — in Simulation A, MaRR was anti-conservative (inflated FDR) for weak, infrequent signals (muA=1, pi1=0.1) and systematically underestimated pi1 for a large weakly correlated group (muA in {1,2}, rho=0.4, pi1=0.8) When the two experiments cannot be ranked on a common gene universe (e.g., transcripts absent from one platform's mapping), since M_g requires paired ranks for every gene When continuous effect-size estimates or per-gene dependence strength (rho-hat) from a generative model are required rather than rank-based reproducibility calls

skills.description: Use when a replicate-pair metabolomics (or other high-dimensional biological) dataset needs a nonparametric estimate of the proportion of reproducible metabolites (pi_1) plus a data-driven rejection threshold controlling mFDR at level alpha.
skills.name: maximum-rank-statistic-implementation
skills.search_text: maximum-rank-statistic-implementation Use when a replicate-pair metabolomics (or other high-dimensional biological) dataset needs a nonparametric estimate of the proportion of reproducible metabolites (pi_1) plus a data-driven rejection threshold controlling mFDR at level alpha. When a ready-made package call suffices — use the Marr() function from the Bioconductor marr package with thresholds pSamplepairs/pFeatures (default 0.75) instead of reconstructing the estimator When the data lack a replicate-pair structure (no technical or biological replicates), since the maximal rank statistic is defined per sample pair When the goal is a comprehensive evaluation of pre-processing steps (missing value imputation, normalization); the MaRR approach was designed only to benchmark comparisons between pipelines http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Reimplementation of the MaRR (Maximum Rank Reproducibility) core estimator as reusable R functions: the maximal rank statistic per replicate sample pair, the MSE(lambda)-based estimator of the reproducible metabolite proportion, and the mFDR thresholding step at a nominal FDR level alpha. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-021-04336-9
skills.summary: Reimplementation of the MaRR (Maximum Rank Reproducibility) core estimator as reusable R functions: the maximal rank statistic per replicate sample pair, the MSE(lambda)-based estimator of the reproducible metabolite proportion, and the mFDR thresholding step at a nominal FDR level alpha.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When a ready-made package call suffices — use the Marr() function from the Bioconductor marr package with thresholds pSamplepairs/pFeatures (default 0.75) instead of reconstructing the estimator When the data lack a replicate-pair structure (no technical or biological replicates), since the maximal rank statistic is defined per sample pair When the goal is a comprehensive evaluation of pre-processing steps (missing value imputation, normalization); the MaRR approach was designed only to benchmark comparisons between pipelines

skills.description: Use when you have two replicate rank lists (e.g., RNA-seq gene rankings from technical or biological replicates such as SEQC platform data) and need to detect the reproducible-to-irreproducible change point with FDR control, without parametric copula assumptions.
skills.name: maximum-rank-statistic-threshold-estimation
skills.search_text: maximum-rank-statistic-threshold-estimation Use when you have two replicate rank lists (e.g., RNA-seq gene rankings from technical or biological replicates such as SEQC platform data) and need to detect the reproducible-to-irreproducible change point with FDR control, without parametric copula assumptions. When parametric copula mixture modeling (Li et al. 2011) is specifically required and parametric dependence assumptions on reproducible genes are acceptable When the data are not replicate rank lists (e.g., unranked feature intensities that have not been converted to gene rank lists) When the goal requires rejection regions off the diagonal y=x under near-perfect signal correlation and a model-based boundary shape is expected rather than the square MaRR boundary http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Nonparametric MaRR (Maximum Rank Reproducibility) procedure that estimates where reproducible signals end in replicate rank lists by minimizing the mean squared error between observed and theoretical survival functions of maximum rank statistics, then derives gene-level marginal FDR calls with no tuning parameters. metabolomics/v3 10.1080/01621459.2017.1397521
skills.summary: Nonparametric MaRR (Maximum Rank Reproducibility) procedure that estimates where reproducible signals end in replicate rank lists by minimizing the mean squared error between observed and theoretical survival functions of maximum rank statistics, then derives gene-level marginal FDR calls with no tuning parameters.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When parametric copula mixture modeling (Li et al. 2011) is specifically required and parametric dependence assumptions on reproducible genes are acceptable When the data are not replicate rank lists (e.g., unranked feature intensities that have not been converted to gene rank lists) When the goal requires rejection regions off the diagonal y=x under near-perfect signal correlation and a model-based boundary shape is expected rather than the square MaRR boundary

skills.description: Use when a weighted molecular network has been partitioned into Louvain communities and each cluster must be reduced to an interpretable, fully connected subnetwork without dropping any member nodes.
skills.name: maximum-spanning-tree-extraction
skills.search_text: maximum-spanning-tree-extraction Use when a weighted molecular network has been partitioned into Louvain communities and each cluster must be reduced to an interpretable, fully connected subnetwork without dropping any member nodes. The goal is to threshold the full molecular network globally by a similarity cutoff rather than preserve all nodes per community — the article states arbitrary similarity thresholds can fracture natural metabolite families Input is an unweighted graph, since the spanning tree must be maximized on the spectral-similarity edge weight Community partitions have not yet been computed, as this skill operates on per-community subgraphs http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Prunes each Louvain-detected molecular community into a cycle-free maximum-weight spanning tree, retaining the strongest spectral-similarity edges while keeping all community nodes connected. This replaces arbitrary similarity-threshold cutoffs that fracture natural metabolite families. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.08.02.606356
skills.summary: Prunes each Louvain-detected molecular community into a cycle-free maximum-weight spanning tree, retaining the strongest spectral-similarity edges while keeping all community nodes connected. This replaces arbitrary similarity-threshold cutoffs that fracture natural metabolite families.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to threshold the full molecular network globally by a similarity cutoff rather than preserve all nodes per community — the article states arbitrary similarity thresholds can fracture natural metabolite families Input is an unweighted graph, since the spanning tree must be maximized on the spectral-similarity edge weight Community partitions have not yet been computed, as this skill operates on per-community subgraphs

skills.description: Use when a weighted molecular similarity graph built from tandem MS spectra edges must be re-connected so that every metabolite keeps its relationship instead of being fractured by a fixed cosine-0.7 cutoff.
skills.name: maximum-weight-spanning-tree-reconstruction
skills.search_text: maximum-weight-spanning-tree-reconstruction Use when a weighted molecular similarity graph built from tandem MS spectra edges must be re-connected so that every metabolite keeps its relationship instead of being fractured by a fixed cosine-0.7 cutoff. The goal is to reproduce the conventional molecular network defined by a fixed cosine similarity threshold (e.g. 0.7) rather than per-community optimized connectivity. The input lacks edge weights (cosine similarity scores) or tandem MS spectral nodes, since the maximum-weight spanning tree construction depends on weighted cosine edges. Only pairwise spectral similarity clustering is needed without any graph-wide re-ordering of molecular families. Reconstructs a molecular community network (MCN) by partitioning a cosine-similarity molecular graph with Louvain community detection and then computing a maximum-weight spanning tree within each community, replacing arbitrary cosine thresholds with per-community optimal connectivity that preserves natural metabolite families. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.08.02.606356
skills.summary: Reconstructs a molecular community network (MCN) by partitioning a cosine-similarity molecular graph with Louvain community detection and then computing a maximum-weight spanning tree within each community, replacing arbitrary cosine thresholds with per-community optimal connectivity that preserves natural metabolite families.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to reproduce the conventional molecular network defined by a fixed cosine similarity threshold (e.g. 0.7) rather than per-community optimized connectivity. The input lacks edge weights (cosine similarity scores) or tandem MS spectral nodes, since the maximum-weight spanning tree construction depends on weighted cosine edges. Only pairwise spectral similarity clustering is needed without any graph-wide re-ordering of molecular families.

skills.description: Use when comparing pairs or sets of MS/MS tandem spectra — e.g. from MassBank or molecular networking datasets — where compounds have multiple delocalized structural differences and cosine-based scores fail, and significance estimation (p-values) is needed.
skills.name: maximum-weight-spectral-matching
skills.search_text: maximum-weight-spectral-matching Use when comparing pairs or sets of MS/MS tandem spectra — e.g. from MassBank or molecular networking datasets — where compounds have multiple delocalized structural differences and cosine-based scores fail, and significance estimation (p-values) is needed. When the goal is straightforward compound identification via cosine or modified-cosine similarity and no significance testing is needed — the article recommends complementing SIMILE with cosine-based scoring rather than replacing it When fragment spectra come from adduct types outside protonation/deprotonation (e.g. [M+Na]+) — the article explicitly notes 'SIMILE is currently limited to analysis of protonation/deprotonation, which is certainly a limitation.' http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 SIMILE's maximum-weight matching step aligns fragment ions between tandem mass spectra using a pair-specific similarity matrix, then scores each alignment's significance via a permuted intra/inter-spectral null distribution (z-test), enabling statistically grounded spectral comparisons beyond cosine similarity. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-022-30118-9
skills.summary: SIMILE's maximum-weight matching step aligns fragment ions between tandem mass spectra using a pair-specific similarity matrix, then scores each alignment's significance via a permuted intra/inter-spectral null distribution (z-test), enabling statistically grounded spectral comparisons beyond cosine similarity.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is straightforward compound identification via cosine or modified-cosine similarity and no significance testing is needed — the article recommends complementing SIMILE with cosine-based scoring rather than replacing it When fragment spectra come from adduct types outside protonation/deprotonation (e.g. [M+Na]+) — the article explicitly notes 'SIMILE is currently limited to analysis of protonation/deprotonation, which is certainly a limitation.'

skills.description: Use when two or more omics datasets (e.g. metabolomics and proteomics) measured on the same samples have been transformed to pathway-level scores and you need a predictive, integrative multi-view model that ranks pathways and omics-layer contributions.
skills.name: mb-pls-multiview-model-fitting
skills.search_text: mb-pls-multiview-model-fitting Use when two or more omics datasets (e.g. metabolomics and proteomics) measured on the same samples have been transformed to pathway-level scores and you need a predictive, integrative multi-view model that ranks pathways and omics-layer contributions. You want to benchmark a molecular-level model — DIABLO at the molecular level is the appropriate non-pathway baseline, not MB-PLS on pathway scores Samples are not measured across all omics views — PathIntegrate requires all input omics on the same individuals and discards incomplete samples A purely exploratory pathway analysis without outcome prediction is needed — conventional ORA/GSEA-style tools are out of scope for this skill http://edamontology.org/topic_3941 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Fit a PathIntegrate Multi-View model that integrates multiple pathway-transformed omics datasets with a multi-block partial least squares (MB-PLS) regression using a shared pathway-based latent space, for supervised outcome prediction and pathway interpretation. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011814
skills.summary: Fit a PathIntegrate Multi-View model that integrates multiple pathway-transformed omics datasets with a multi-block partial least squares (MB-PLS) regression using a shared pathway-based latent space, for supervised outcome prediction and pathway interpretation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You want to benchmark a molecular-level model — DIABLO at the molecular level is the appropriate non-pathway baseline, not MB-PLS on pathway scores Samples are not measured across all omics views — PathIntegrate requires all input omics on the same individuals and discards incomplete samples A purely exploratory pathway analysis without outcome prediction is needed — conventional ORA/GSEA-style tools are out of scope for this skill

skills.description: Use when you have fitted a multi-block PLS model over concatenated HPOS/LPOS/LNEG feature tables, obtained per-feature empirical p-values from an MB-VIP permutation test, and need to count significant predictors per block and quantify reduction vs univariate models.
skills.name: mb-pls-significant-feature-counting
skills.search_text: mb-pls-significant-feature-counting Use when you have fitted a multi-block PLS model over concatenated HPOS/LPOS/LNEG feature tables, obtained per-feature empirical p-values from an MB-VIP permutation test, and need to count significant predictors per block and quantify reduction vs univariate models. Input is raw mass-spectrometry spectra rather than a processed, sample-by-feature table — MAMSI's MB-PLS/MB-VIP operates on feature tables, not peak-picking. The goal is structural clustering, adduct/isotopologue linking, or annotation of the selected features — that is MamsiStructSearch territory (rt_win=5, ppm tolerance 15 ppm), not feature counting. Only a single assay is available — the reduction comparison is specific to multi-assay MB-PLS integration vs univariate per-assay models. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Counts statistically significant LC-MS features per assay block after MB-VIP permutation testing on an MamsiPls MB-PLS model, and compares these multivariate counts against univariate-analysis counts to compute the per-experiment predictor-reduction percentages (83%, >92%, >92%, 94%) reported in the MAMSI Alzheimer's/AddNeuroMed case study. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c01327
skills.summary: Counts statistically significant LC-MS features per assay block after MB-VIP permutation testing on an MamsiPls MB-PLS model, and compares these multivariate counts against univariate-analysis counts to compute the per-experiment predictor-reduction percentages (83%, >92%, >92%, 94%) reported in the MAMSI Alzheimer's/AddNeuroMed case study.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw mass-spectrometry spectra rather than a processed, sample-by-feature table — MAMSI's MB-PLS/MB-VIP operates on feature tables, not peak-picking. The goal is structural clustering, adduct/isotopologue linking, or annotation of the selected features — that is MamsiStructSearch territory (rt_win=5, ppm tolerance 15 ppm), not feature counting. Only a single assay is available — the reduction comparison is specific to multi-assay MB-PLS integration vs univariate per-assay models.

skills.description: Use when a fitted MamsiPls MB-PLS model (e.g., on HPOS/LPOS/LNEG LC-MS feature tables) needs per-feature importance scores and empirical p-values to identify which predictors drive the predicted outcome.
skills.name: mb-vip-feature-importance-scoring
skills.search_text: mb-vip-feature-importance-scoring Use when a fitted MamsiPls MB-PLS model (e.g., on HPOS/LPOS/LNEG LC-MS feature tables) needs per-feature importance scores and empirical p-values to identify which predictors drive the predicted outcome. You need per-block (not per-feature) contribution estimates — use MamsiPls.block_importance instead of mb_vip You only need model performance assessment on a held-out test set — use evaluate_class_model/evaluate_regression_model rather than VIP-based feature scoring The fitted model is a single-block PLS where multiblock VIP is unnecessary; standard VIP suffices http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Scores predictor importance in a fitted multiblock PLS (MB-PLS) model using the multiblock variable importance in projection (MB-VIP) metric, then attaches empirical per-feature p-values via a permutation test on the outcome variable. This is the MAMSI framework's mechanism for selecting statistically significant features from multi-assay LC-MS metabolomics data. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c01327
skills.summary: Scores predictor importance in a fitted multiblock PLS (MB-PLS) model using the multiblock variable importance in projection (MB-VIP) metric, then attaches empirical per-feature p-values via a permutation test on the outcome variable. This is the MAMSI framework's mechanism for selecting statistically significant features from multi-assay LC-MS metabolomics data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need per-block (not per-feature) contribution estimates — use MamsiPls.block_importance instead of mb_vip You only need model performance assessment on a held-out test set — use evaluate_class_model/evaluate_regression_model rather than VIP-based feature scoring The fitted model is a single-block PLS where multiblock VIP is unnecessary; standard VIP suffices

skills.description: Use when an MB-PLS model (e.g. MamsiPls on multi-assay serum LC-MS intensity tables) has been fitted and you need per-feature statistical significance for feature selection before structural/correlation clustering, rather than relying on raw VIP scores alone.
skills.name: mb-vip-permutation-significance-testing
skills.search_text: mb-vip-permutation-significance-testing Use when an MB-PLS model (e.g. MamsiPls on multi-assay serum LC-MS intensity tables) has been fitted and you need per-feature statistical significance for feature selection before structural/correlation clustering, rather than relying on raw VIP scores alone. The goal is model prediction performance evaluation (use evaluate_regression_model / evaluate_class_model on the held-out test set instead of feature significance testing) Data are single-assay or non-LC-MS where a multi-block VIP formulation and structural-cluster interpretation (rt_win, ppm adduct/isotopologue grouping) is not applicable The model's number of latent variables has not yet been validated (run estimate_lv with k-fold cross-validation first, otherwise permuted VIPs reflect an ill-sized model) http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Assigns empirical p-values to every feature in a multi-block PLS (MB-PLS) model by permuting the outcome variable and recomputing Multi-Block Variable Importance in Projection (MB-VIP) scores, so that statistically significant cross-assay LC-MS features can be selected at a controlled p-value threshold (e.g. p < 0.01). metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c01327
skills.summary: Assigns empirical p-values to every feature in a multi-block PLS (MB-PLS) model by permuting the outcome variable and recomputing Multi-Block Variable Importance in Projection (MB-VIP) scores, so that statistically significant cross-assay LC-MS features can be selected at a controlled p-value threshold (e.g. p < 0.01).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is model prediction performance evaluation (use evaluate_regression_model / evaluate_class_model on the held-out test set instead of feature significance testing) Data are single-assay or non-LC-MS where a multi-block VIP formulation and structural-cluster interpretation (rt_win, ppm adduct/isotopologue grouping) is not applicable The model's number of latent variables has not yet been validated (run estimate_lv with k-fold cross-validation first, otherwise permuted VIPs reflect an ill-sized model)

skills.description: Use when you have latent factors from multi-omics data (e.g. MOFA factors), sample cluster memberships (e.g. SNF clusters), and behavioral dimension scores from MCA, and need cohort-aware association testing with multiple-testing correction.
skills.name: mca-behavioral-factor-association-analysis
skills.search_text: mca-behavioral-factor-association-analysis Use when you have latent factors from multi-omics data (e.g. MOFA factors), sample cluster memberships (e.g. SNF clusters), and behavioral dimension scores from MCA, and need cohort-aware association testing with multiple-testing correction. Samples are unrelated individuals only in a single cohort — plain regression or correlation without a GEE family-correlation structure is sufficient and simpler Factors have not yet been computed (no MOFA factors, SNF clusters, or MCA dimensions available) — run the factor extraction and clustering workflow steps first The association of interest involves raw omics features rather than latent factors — this skill tests precomputed MOFA factors and cluster memberships, not individual probes or metabolites http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 Tests whether MOFA omics factors (from buccal DNA methylation and urine metabolomics) and SNF cluster memberships are associated with MCA behavioral dimension scores, using GEE models in the NTR twin cohort (to adjust for family relatedness) and non-parametric tests plus Spearman correlations in the LUMC-Curium cohort, with FDR correction across all tested factor–dimension pairs. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/gigascience/giad115
skills.summary: Tests whether MOFA omics factors (from buccal DNA methylation and urine metabolomics) and SNF cluster memberships are associated with MCA behavioral dimension scores, using GEE models in the NTR twin cohort (to adjust for family relatedness) and non-parametric tests plus Spearman correlations in the LUMC-Curium cohort, with FDR correction across all tested factor–dimension pairs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Samples are unrelated individuals only in a single cohort — plain regression or correlation without a GEE family-correlation structure is sufficient and simpler Factors have not yet been computed (no MOFA factors, SNF clusters, or MCA dimensions available) — run the factor extraction and clustering workflow steps first The association of interest involves raw omics features rather than latent factors — this skill tests precomputed MOFA factors and cluster memberships, not individual probes or metabolites

skills.description: Use when a metabolomics concentration table (CSV/XLSX) has missing entries whose per-group, per-metabolite missingness percentage classifies them as MCAR, and statistically rigorous imputation (missForest, KNN, mean, or median) is required before normalization or PCA.
skills.name: mcar-missforest-imputation
skills.search_text: mcar-missforest-imputation Use when a metabolomics concentration table (CSV/XLSX) has missing entries whose per-group, per-metabolite missingness percentage classifies them as MCAR, and statistically rigorous imputation (missForest, KNN, mean, or median) is required before normalization or PCA. Missing values were classified as MNAR (missing not at random) — use zero or half-minimum imputation instead of missForest/KNN The table is not a metabolomics concentration table (e.g. already-normalized or fused multi-platform data) — Viime's intent is to pick up the workflow after preprocessing and annotation Data exceeds Viime's error thresholds (e.g. missing data exceeding the default threshold within a group or across all samples, non-numeric concentration data, missing or non-unique primary ID) — correct errors first, since imputation is only automatically performed once errors are corrected http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Imputes metabolite concentration values classified as Missing Completely At Random (MCAR) using Random Forest (missForest) or K-Nearest Neighbor (impute) R packages, or simple mean/median, as part of Viime's Armitage et al. (2015) MCAR/MNAR missingness strategy. metabolomics/v3 10.21105/joss.02410
skills.summary: Imputes metabolite concentration values classified as Missing Completely At Random (MCAR) using Random Forest (missForest) or K-Nearest Neighbor (impute) R packages, or simple mean/median, as part of Viime's Armitage et al. (2015) MCAR/MNAR missingness strategy.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Missing values were classified as MNAR (missing not at random) — use zero or half-minimum imputation instead of missForest/KNN The table is not a metabolomics concentration table (e.g. already-normalized or fused multi-platform data) — Viime's intent is to pick up the workflow after preprocessing and annotation Data exceeds Viime's error thresholds (e.g. missing data exceeding the default threshold within a group or across all samples, non-numeric concentration data, missing or non-unique primary ID) — correct errors first, since imputation is only automatically performed once errors are corrected

skills.description: Use when comparing spectral similarity measures (embedding cosine similarity, MS2DeepScore, spectral entropy, dot-product variants) on molecular analog retrieval, needing AUROC curves stratified by MCES distance thresholds on paired MS/MS spectra.
skills.name: mces-analog-retrieval-auc-evaluation
skills.search_text: mces-analog-retrieval-auc-evaluation Use when comparing spectral similarity measures (embedding cosine similarity, MS2DeepScore, spectral entropy, dot-product variants) on molecular analog retrieval, needing AUROC curves stratified by MCES distance thresholds on paired MS/MS spectra. When the input spectra are outside the paper's scope (e.g., negative ionization mode or multiply charged precursor ions), since DreaMS was trained only on positive-mode singly charged data When the goal is molecular fingerprint prediction or de novo structure annotation (MIST/CANOPUS benchmark) rather than similarity-based retrieval ranking When MS1 isotopic patterns or adduct distributions should drive the analysis — the method focuses solely on tandem mass spectra http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 A benchmark protocol that scores spectral similarity measures by how well they retrieve structural analogs, using AUROC computed at maximum common edge substructure (MCES) distance thresholds k = 0..7 on NIST20 spectra. It was used in the DreaMS paper to show fine-tuned embeddings outperform MS2DeepScore and 44 standard similarity measures. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41587-025-02663-3
skills.summary: A benchmark protocol that scores spectral similarity measures by how well they retrieve structural analogs, using AUROC computed at maximum common edge substructure (MCES) distance thresholds k = 0..7 on NIST20 spectra. It was used in the DreaMS paper to show fine-tuned embeddings outperform MS2DeepScore and 44 standard similarity measures.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input spectra are outside the paper's scope (e.g., negative ionization mode or multiply charged precursor ions), since DreaMS was trained only on positive-mode singly charged data When the goal is molecular fingerprint prediction or de novo structure annotation (MIST/CANOPUS benchmark) rather than similarity-based retrieval ranking When MS1 isotopic patterns or adduct distributions should drive the analysis — the method focuses solely on tandem mass spectra

skills.description: Use when scoring de novo structure-elucidation outputs (SELFIES/SMILES candidates from spectra) against reference molecules and you need a structural-graph distance in addition to exact-match and fingerprint-similarity metrics, e.g. filling MCES columns of benchmark comparison tables.
skills.name: mces-graph-distance-evaluation
skills.search_text: mces-graph-distance-evaluation Use when scoring de novo structure-elucidation outputs (SELFIES/SMILES candidates from spectra) against reference molecules and you need a structural-graph distance in addition to exact-match and fingerprint-similarity metrics, e.g. filling MCES columns of benchmark comparison tables. You only need exact structural identity — full InChIKey comparison is sufficient and MCES adds graph-distance computation overhead. You need a similarity score where higher is better and rewards bit overlap — maximum Tanimoto similarity (Morgan radius 2, 2048 bits) is the complementary metric. The candidate list has not been reduced/ranked (e.g. by formula distance), so 'minimum MCES over Top-k' is ill-defined. http://edamontology.org/topic_3332 Evaluate predicted molecular structures against ground-truth structures using the minimum common edge substructure (MCES) graph distance, reporting the minimum MCES over Top-1 and Top-10 candidate sets alongside InChIKey accuracy and Tanimoto similarity. This is one of the six key metrics MS-Bart reports on MassSpecGym and NPLIB1. metabolomics/v3 10.48550/arxiv.2510.20615
skills.summary: Evaluate predicted molecular structures against ground-truth structures using the minimum common edge substructure (MCES) graph distance, reporting the minimum MCES over Top-1 and Top-10 candidate sets alongside InChIKey accuracy and Tanimoto similarity. This is one of the six key metrics MS-Bart reports on MassSpecGym and NPLIB1.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need exact structural identity — full InChIKey comparison is sufficient and MCES adds graph-distance computation overhead. You need a similarity score where higher is better and rewards bit overlap — maximum Tanimoto similarity (Morgan radius 2, 2048 bits) is the complementary metric. The candidate list has not been reduced/ranked (e.g. by formula distance), so 'minimum MCES over Top-k' is ill-defined.

skills.search_text: mces-leakage-filtering-against-test-fold Use when building an auxiliary pretraining corpus (e.g. fingerprint-molecule pairs from unlabeled PubChem molecules) that must not leak structures from held-out benchmark test sets such as MassSpecGym test folds or NPLIB1. The corpus is already the MassSpecGym training fold itself (internal split leakage is handled by the benchmark, not this filter) Input molecules are intended for evaluation on NPLIB1 or MassSpecGym rather than for pretraining http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3316 Removes molecules from an auxiliary pretraining corpus that are too chemically similar to benchmark evaluation molecules, by excluding pairs with MCES distance < 2 against the MassSpecGym test fold and Tanimoto similarity > 0.5 against NPLIB1, preventing cross-split leakage. metabolomics/v3 10.48550/arxiv.2510.20615
skills.summary: Removes molecules from an auxiliary pretraining corpus that are too chemically similar to benchmark evaluation molecules, by excluding pairs with MCES distance < 2 against the MassSpecGym test fold and Tanimoto similarity > 0.5 against NPLIB1, preventing cross-split leakage.

skills.description: Use when evaluating FBMN or library-matching annotation quality: you have compound pairs (e.g., top-10 matches per query with SMILES) and need structural similarity scores to judge whether matches are identical, structural isomers, or dissimilar.
skills.name: mces-structural-similarity-scoring
skills.search_text: mces-structural-similarity-scoring Use when evaluating FBMN or library-matching annotation quality: you have compound pairs (e.g., top-10 matches per query with SMILES) and need structural similarity scores to judge whether matches are identical, structural isomers, or dissimilar. Input is raw MS/MS spectra or feature tables rather than resolved compound pairs with SMILES structures — spectrum-level metrics like cosine similarity are the appropriate choice instead You need a single scalar spectral similarity measure; MCES is a graph-based structural distance on molecular graphs, not a fragmentation-similarity metric Only identical-match confirmation is needed without structural comparison, since MCES computation carries nontrivial runtime cost for large pair sets Quantifies how similar matched compounds are by combining Tanimoto similarity (Morgan fingerprints, radius 2, 2048 bits) with myopic MCES distances, using the MSnLib criterion that MCES < 4 marks identical or structurally similar compounds. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-025-02813-0
skills.summary: Quantifies how similar matched compounds are by combining Tanimoto similarity (Morgan fingerprints, radius 2, 2048 bits) with myopic MCES distances, using the MSnLib criterion that MCES < 4 marks identical or structurally similar compounds.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw MS/MS spectra or feature tables rather than resolved compound pairs with SMILES structures — spectrum-level metrics like cosine similarity are the appropriate choice instead You need a single scalar spectral similarity measure; MCES is a graph-based structural distance on molecular graphs, not a fragmentation-similarity metric Only identical-match confirmation is needed without structural comparison, since MCES computation carries nontrivial runtime cost for large pair sets

skills.description: Use when a target 2D 1H,13C HSQC spectrum (grid or peak-list csv.gz) must be mapped against a compound library (e.g. 501-compound MetaboMiner/Wishart HMDB library) with mcfNMR, and values for assignment_radius, detection_threshold, and fit mode must be configured.
skills.name: mcf-configuration-parameter-selection
skills.search_text: mcf-configuration-parameter-selection Use when a target 2D 1H,13C HSQC spectrum (grid or peak-list csv.gz) must be mapped against a compound library (e.g. 501-compound MetaboMiner/Wishart HMDB library) with mcfNMR, and values for assignment_radius, detection_threshold, and fit mode must be configured. The library compound spectra are unknown or incomplete — a complete reconstruction requires knowledge of every constituent's peak pattern, and MCF cannot detect compounds absent from the library Precise quantification is the goal — the article lists limited quantification accuracy as a current limitation; results are at best semiquantitative The spectrum has strong temperature- or pH-induced peak shifts — the method is sensitive toward peak shifts, and the article offers no definitive protocol for choosing assignment_radius r, absorption cost cø, or detection threshold ϑ http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 Writes TOML configuration files for mcfNMR runs by selecting method variant (isolated_fit / incremental_fit), assignment_radius, and detection_threshold, then executing mcfNMR to produce pickled mcf-results and CSV result tables. This skill operationalizes the paper's four MCF setups (A–D) so library compounds are optimally fitted to a target spectrum via minimum cost flow. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c01652
skills.summary: Writes TOML configuration files for mcfNMR runs by selecting method variant (isolated_fit / incremental_fit), assignment_radius, and detection_threshold, then executing mcfNMR to produce pickled mcf-results and CSV result tables. This skill operationalizes the paper's four MCF setups (A–D) so library compounds are optimally fitted to a target spectrum via minimum cost flow.

skills.description: Use when two or more omics feature matrices (e.g. genes, proteins, lipids/metabolomics) share a sample set with a phenotype of interest and the goal is data-driven cross-omics integration to differentiate samples by phenotype.
skills.name: mcia-multi-omics-integration
skills.search_text: mcia-multi-omics-integration Use when two or more omics feature matrices (e.g. genes, proteins, lipids/metabolomics) share a sample set with a phenotype of interest and the goal is data-driven cross-omics integration to differentiate samples by phenotype. The datasets have no shared samples or phenotype, so the matrices cannot be co-inertia-aligned on a common sample space Only a single omics layer is available — MOI's individual omics modules (e.g. DE with edgeR/DESeq2/RankProduct) are the appropriate path, not MCIA integration A hypothesis-driven supervised classifier is required rather than the unsupervised, data-driven projection MCIA provides http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Apply Multiple Co-Inertia Analysis (MCIA) within the MultiOmicsIntegrator (MOI) Nextflow pipeline to project several omics layers (genes, miRNAs, isoforms, proteins, lipids) onto a common sample space, then feed the integrated features into correlation filtering and pathway enrichment. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioadv/vbae175
skills.summary: Apply Multiple Co-Inertia Analysis (MCIA) within the MultiOmicsIntegrator (MOI) Nextflow pipeline to project several omics layers (genes, miRNAs, isoforms, proteins, lipids) onto a common sample space, then feed the integrated features into correlation filtering and pathway enrichment.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The datasets have no shared samples or phenotype, so the matrices cannot be co-inertia-aligned on a common sample space Only a single omics layer is available — MOI's individual omics modules (e.g. DE with edgeR/DESeq2/RankProduct) are the appropriate path, not MCIA integration A hypothesis-driven supervised classifier is required rather than the unsupervised, data-driven projection MCIA provides

When you only need a single train/test partition for model development rather than a multi-tool benchmark with median aggregation over 101 splits When the molecules of interest are dimers ([2M+H]+, [2M-H]-), less common adducts, or in-source fragments, since the compendium training sets used here do not support them Generates 101 random 70:30 calibration/test splits of the cleaned McLean Unified CCS Compendium adduct data sets (567 [M-H]-, 518 [M+H]+, 461 [M+Na]+ ions) so that identical test sets can be shared across CCS prediction tools for fair benchmarking. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2022.08.09.503345

skills.search_text: mcmc-based-peak-parameter-estimation Use when 1D NMR spectra (especially highly overlapped metabolomics spectra) must be deconvoluted into peak tables with accurate peak parameters rather than fitted in the frequency domain. Input spectra are low-resolution or non-metabolomics: SAND's current version is tuned for high-resolution metabolomics spectra Signals are nonexponential: SAND does not yet handle nonexponential signals natively (exponential + Gaussian model only) Data are multidimensional or nonuniformly sampled: adaptation to multidimensional applications is a future goal, not implemented http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Estimate NMR peak parameters by fitting time-domain FID data with SAND's hybrid Markov chain Monte Carlo optimization, which subsamples both time-domain and frequency-domain points and randomly splits the time-domain data into training and validation sets to avoid overfitting. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c03078

skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra are low-resolution or non-metabolomics: SAND's current version is tuned for high-resolution metabolomics spectra Signals are nonexponential: SAND does not yet handle nonexponential signals natively (exponential + Gaussian model only) Data are multidimensional or nonuniformly sampled: adaptation to multidimensional applications is a future goal, not implemented

skills.search_text: mcmc-convergence-diagnostics Use when fitting Stan hierarchical/binomial multilevel models (e.g., PrediXcan-DEG enrichment or proportion-positive direction-of-effect models) and you must verify chain convergence before extracting marginal posterior means or 95% posterior-mass flags.
