skills.when_to_use_negative: When the model is fit by optimization only (e.g., the nlm/optimx bivariate-probit correlation estimation step) — no chains or MCMC diagnostics exist to check When the goal is frequentist inference (fgsea GSEA with Bonferroni/harmonic-mean p-values) rather than posterior-based enrichment calls When you intend to report posterior probabilities from a fit that has already failed the r-hat/ESS/divergence gates — refit instead

skills.description: Use when running a Gibbs sampler over a candidate-assignment network (e.g., ZODIAC reranking SIRIUS formula candidates) and you must set chain count, burn-in, sampling epochs, and verify the chains have stabilized before trusting posterior marginals.
skills.name: mcmc-convergence-diagnostics
skills.search_text: mcmc-convergence-diagnostics Use when running a Gibbs sampler over a candidate-assignment network (e.g., ZODIAC reranking SIRIUS formula candidates) and you must set chain count, burn-in, sampling epochs, and verify the chains have stabilized before trusting posterior marginals. The inference problem is not a Gibbs-samplable Markov network over discrete candidate assignments (e.g., no pairwise potentials between compound candidates), since the conditional-update and multi-chain design assume that structure You need a formally validated convergence measure or an empirically benchmarked sampler speedup — the paper only estimates the ~25-fold speedup theoretically and uses trajectory inspection, not formal diagnostics You need deterministic, reproducible reranking of SIRIUS candidates without stochastic sampling — a single-pass scoring approach avoids chain/burn-in configuration entirely Diagnose convergence and stability of Gibbs-sampler-based inference (as instantiated in ZODIAC for molecular formula reranking) by monitoring parallel chains, burn-in vs. sampling epochs, and per-epoch trajectory statistics such as total score and identification rate. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s42256-020-00234-6
skills.summary: Diagnose convergence and stability of Gibbs-sampler-based inference (as instantiated in ZODIAC for molecular formula reranking) by monitoring parallel chains, burn-in vs. sampling epochs, and per-epoch trajectory statistics such as total score and identification rate.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The inference problem is not a Gibbs-samplable Markov network over discrete candidate assignments (e.g., no pairwise potentials between compound candidates), since the conditional-update and multi-chain design assume that structure You need a formally validated convergence measure or an empirically benchmarked sampler speedup — the paper only estimates the ~25-fold speedup theoretically and uses trajectory inspection, not formal diagnostics You need deterministic, reproducible reranking of SIRIUS candidates without stochastic sampling — a single-pass scoring approach avoids chain/burn-in configuration entirely

skills.description: Use when a fractional-abundance vector (FAM) from an LC-MS isotope labeling experiment must be converted to a corrected, non-negative MDV and isotopic enrichment via an already-built total correction matrix (MDT and/or ULS).
skills.name: mdv-nonnegative-regression-solving
skills.search_text: mdv-nonnegative-regression-solving Use when a fractional-abundance vector (FAM) from an LC-MS isotope labeling experiment must be converted to a corrected, non-negative MDV and isotopic enrichment via an already-built total correction matrix (MDT and/or ULS). When the tracer element is not actually present in the compound's formula (e.g. C or S selected for a 15N-only compound) — the algorithm reports an error When the input is raw, uncorrected isotopologue intensities and no correction matrix has been built — this skill solves the correction equation, it does not construct the MDT/ULS matrix When instrument resolution is extremely high, ElemCor performs essentially no correction, so regression-based correction adds little http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Solves the correction-matrix equation C x' = z by non-negative linear regression (NNLS), then normalizes x' to sum to 1 to obtain the mass distribution vector (MDV), from which isotopic enrichment is computed as the tracer-count-weighted sum, exactly as ElemCor does for stable isotope labeling LC-MS data. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-019-2669-9
skills.summary: Solves the correction-matrix equation C x' = z by non-negative linear regression (NNLS), then normalizes x' to sum to 1 to obtain the mass distribution vector (MDV), from which isotopic enrichment is computed as the tracer-count-weighted sum, exactly as ElemCor does for stable isotope labeling LC-MS data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the tracer element is not actually present in the compound's formula (e.g. C or S selected for a 15N-only compound) — the algorithm reports an error When the input is raw, uncorrected isotopologue intensities and no correction matrix has been built — this skill solves the correction equation, it does not construct the MDT/ULS matrix When instrument resolution is extremely high, ElemCor performs essentially no correction, so regression-based correction adds little

skills.description: Use when a DatasetExperiment object from the struct framework needs per-column (feature) mean centring before downstream steps like PCA, or when implementing a custom centring model via set_obj_method.
skills.name: mean-centring-of-omics-feature-data
skills.search_text: mean-centring-of-omics-feature-data Use when a DatasetExperiment object from the struct framework needs per-column (feature) mean centring before downstream steps like PCA, or when implementing a custom centring model via set_obj_method. If a full struct model sequence is already available from structToolbox (e.g. mean_centre() composed with other models) and no custom method overloading is needed, using the companion toolbox object is simpler than hand-implementing the class. If centring is not required — e.g. the analysis operates on raw or already-normalised intensities and the downstream method is scale-invariant or does not assume zero-mean features — applying this skill adds an unnecessary preprocessing step. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Implements a mean-centring preprocessing model as a struct class-based template (model_train stores per-column means via colMeans; model_predict subtracts them), so the centred data can be chained into struct model sequences such as mean_centre() + PCA(). metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btaa1031
skills.summary: Implements a mean-centring preprocessing model as a struct class-based template (model_train stores per-column means via colMeans; model_predict subtracts them), so the centred data can be chained into struct model sequences such as mean_centre() + PCA().
skills.when_to_use_negative: If a full struct model sequence is already available from structToolbox (e.g. mean_centre() composed with other models) and no custom method overloading is needed, using the companion toolbox object is simpler than hand-implementing the class. skills.description: Use when validating delay-prediction models for NMR metabolomics data: you have fitted linear mixed models of metabolite change over pre-/post-centrifugation delays and need to score prediction accuracy against measured time-point values.
skills.name: mean-percentage-error-calculation-across-time-points
skills.search_text: mean-percentage-error-calculation-across-time-points Use when validating delay-prediction models for NMR metabolomics data: you have fitted linear mixed models of metabolite change over pre-/post-centrifugation delays and need to score prediction accuracy against measured time-point values. The metabolite's concentration does not follow a linear response over the delay range (e.g., glucose at 6 and 8 h), where MPE will misleadingly spike — consider a non-linear or stratified approach instead. You have only the discovery cohort (no independent validation cohort); MPE computed on the training data would overstate model robustness. http://edamontology.org/topic_3336 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Computes mean percentage error (MPE) between linear mixed-model predictions and measured NMR concentrations of blood-derived metabolites at each processing-delay time point, to quantify how robustly time-0 measurements predict later metabolite states. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c04938
skills.summary: Computes mean percentage error (MPE) between linear mixed-model predictions and measured NMR concentrations of blood-derived metabolites at each processing-delay time point, to quantify how robustly time-0 measurements predict later metabolite states.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The metabolite's concentration does not follow a linear response over the delay range (e.g., glucose at 6 and 8 h), where MPE will misleadingly spike — consider a non-linear or stratified approach instead. You have only the discovery cohort (no independent validation cohort); MPE computed on the training data would overstate model robustness.

skills.search_text: media-blank-background-component-removal Use when a Progenesis-format peak table contains blank groups (solvent or media blanks) and features overrepresented in those blanks must be identified and removed to correct between-sample carryover and contamination. The dataset has no blank/control group — filter_group requires a specified group whose overrepresented features define background components. skills.summary: Removes background components from LC-MS/MS peak tables by flagging features whose abundance exceeds a user-defined threshold in a specified group of samples (e.g. media blanks or solvent blanks) using mpactr's filter_group().

Input is raw MS/MS data rather than a pre-processed peak table; mpactr operates on pre-processed tandem MS/MS output such as Progenesis exports.

skills.summary: Aggregates per-spectrum Tanimoto similarities and modified Platt scores across candidate sets (MSNovelist de novo, naive generation, database search, training-set picks) into per-set median statistics, enabling a like-for-like comparison of de novo versus database candidate quality on GNPS spectra.

skills.name: median-rank-statistic-computation
skills.search_text: median-rank-statistic-computation Use when you have IDSL.IPA-generated individual peak lists plus an aligned peak table and need to summarize which molecular formula hits from IDSL.UFA are reproducibly ranked near the top across samples before downstream reporting or MS/MS cross-checking. You only have a single MS2 spectrum or DDA/DIA fragment spectrum to annotate — use IDSL.CSA or a spectral-library search instead; this skill summarizes MS1-derived formula ranks across samples. The input is already a curated feature table with structural identifications and no IDSL.IPA/UFA pipeline output — re-deriving median ranks adds no information. You need exhaustive elemental-composition enumeration rather than ranking of candidate formulas against an IPDB — use IDSL.UFAx. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Computes the median rank of a candidate molecular formula across individual peak lists from an IDSL.IPA workflow on untargeted LC/HRMS data, then aggregates ranks into an aligned annotated peak table so annotation quality (e.g. median rank ≤ 2 or ≤ 5) can be reported sample-wise. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.2c00563
skills.summary: Computes the median rank of a candidate molecular formula across individual peak lists from an IDSL.IPA workflow on untargeted LC/HRMS data, then aggregates ranks into an aligned annotated peak table so annotation quality (e.g. median rank ≤ 2 or ≤ 5) can be reported sample-wise.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only have a single MS2 spectrum or DDA/DIA fragment spectrum to annotate — use IDSL.CSA or a spectral-library search instead; this skill summarizes MS1-derived formula ranks across samples. The input is already a curated feature table with structural identifications and no IDSL.IPA/UFA pipeline output — re-deriving median ranks adds no information. You need exhaustive elemental-composition enumeration rather than ranking of candidate formulas against an IPDB — use IDSL.UFAx.

skills.description: Use when a collection of corrected/predicted CCS measurements with reference values needs its central accuracy quantified as a median relative error (MDRE), or when validating a calibration by reproducing a reported MDRE.
skills.name: median-relative-error-computation
skills.search_text: median-relative-error-computation Use when a collection of corrected/predicted CCS measurements with reference values needs its central accuracy quantified as a median relative error (MDRE), or when validating a calibration by reproducing a reported MDRE. The CCS values are already calibrated toward DT reference values and no linear correction from Figure S2 needs to be applied — a plain relative-error summary suffices without the calibration step The measurements are positive-mode or drift-gas conditions other than TIMS with the negative-mode linear corrections; the Figure S2 equations would not be applicable The goal is CCS prediction itself (e.g., training ML prediction models for the 22/23 lipid classes) rather than validating corrected measurements against DT references http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3954 Computes the median relative error (MDRE) of collision cross section (CCS) values against reference values after applying linear corrections — here, negative-mode TIMS CCS values from Vasilopoulou et al. and Tsugawa et al. calibrated toward DT reference values, reproducing the reported MDRE of −0.36%. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c02560
skills.summary: Computes the median relative error (MDRE) of collision cross section (CCS) values against reference values after applying linear corrections — here, negative-mode TIMS CCS values from Vasilopoulou et al. and Tsugawa et al. calibrated toward DT reference values, reproducing the reported MDRE of −0.36%.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The CCS values are already calibrated toward DT reference values and no linear correction from Figure S2 needs to be applied — a plain relative-error summary suffices without the calibration step The measurements are positive-mode or drift-gas conditions other than TIMS with the negative-mode linear corrections; the Figure S2 equations would not be applicable The goal is CCS prediction itself (e.g., training ML prediction models for the 22/23 lipid classes) rather than validating corrected measurements against DT references

skills.description: Use when you must simulate lower-quality fragmentation spectra from biological samples on clean reference MS/MS spectra and need an objective, similarity-based calibration of the noise level instead of arbitrary noise parameters.
skills.name: median-similarity-threshold-calibration
skills.search_text: median-similarity-threshold-calibration Use when you must simulate lower-quality fragmentation spectra from biological samples on clean reference MS/MS spectra and need an objective, similarity-based calibration of the noise level instead of arbitrary noise parameters. Input spectra are already low-quality biological-sample spectra — no synthetic distortion is needed; evaluate directly instead. The analysis goal is FDR estimation on real metabolomics runs rather than simulating degraded spectra for benchmarking. You need to assign confidence to structure annotations; use the confidence-score pipeline rather than spectrum-distortion calibration. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Calibrates a spectrum-distortion procedure so that injected noise reproduces a target median cosine similarity to the original reference MS/MS spectra (e.g. 0.880 for medium and 0.714 for high distortion in the COSMIC evaluation). metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41587-021-01045-9
skills.summary: Calibrates a spectrum-distortion procedure so that injected noise reproduces a target median cosine similarity to the original reference MS/MS spectra (e.g. 0.880 for medium and 0.714 for high distortion in the COSMIC evaluation).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra are already low-quality biological-sample spectra — no synthetic distortion is needed; evaluate directly instead. The analysis goal is FDR estimation on real metabolomics runs rather than simulating degraded spectra for benchmarking. You need to assign confidence to structure annotations; use the confidence-score pipeline rather than spectrum-distortion calibration.

skills.description: Use when you have a spatial metabolomics peak table (pixels × m/z ions) with manually or lasso-delineated regions and need one representative spectrum per region before computing region-pair metrics like Pearson correlation.
skills.name: median-spectrum-computation-per-region
skills.search_text: median-spectrum-computation-per-region Use when you have a spatial metabolomics peak table (pixels × m/z ions) with manually or lasso-delineated regions and need one representative spectrum per region before computing region-pair metrics like Pearson correlation. Input is already aggregated at region or sample level with no per-pixel peak table, so no per-pixel median can be computed The goal is pixel-level analysis (e.g., clustering or spatial pattern recognition), where collapsing pixels to a single median spectrum would destroy spatial resolution Regions have not been delineated and no pixel-coordinate or intensity criteria exist to define which pixels belong to background vs. tissue http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Computes a single representative spectrum for each delineated spatial region (background or tissue) by taking the per-ion median intensity across all pixels in the region, enabling region-level comparisons such as background-consistency Pearson correlations in the SMQVP workflow. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo15060354
skills.summary: Computes a single representative spectrum for each delineated spatial region (background or tissue) by taking the per-ion median intensity across all pixels in the region, enabling region-level comparisons such as background-consistency Pearson correlations in the SMQVP workflow.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already aggregated at region or sample level with no per-pixel peak table, so no per-pixel median can be computed The goal is pixel-level analysis (e.g., clustering or spatial pattern recognition), where collapsing pixels to a single median spectrum would destroy spatial resolution Regions have not been delineated and no pixel-coordinate or intensity criteria exist to define which pixels belong to background vs. tissue

skills.description: Use when you need an outlier-sensitivity benchmark for normalization methods on simulated single-feature drift data where the true drift is known, e.g. comparing QC-RLSC, QC-RSC, rLOESS, rGAM, and tGAM across 0, 1, 2, or 4 injected outliers.
skills.name: median-squared-prediction-error-computation
skills.search_text: median-squared-prediction-error-computation Use when you need an outlier-sensitivity benchmark for normalization methods on simulated single-feature drift data where the true drift is known, e.g. comparing QC-RLSC, QC-RSC, rLOESS, rGAM, and tGAM across 0, 1, 2, or 4 injected outliers. Input is experimental data without a known ground-truth drift curve — MSPE against an expected pattern requires simulated data where the true drift is defined; use replicate concordance or drift/batch-effect inspection instead. The goal is to assess downstream differential abundance impact or QC-RSD filtering — those are separate tasks, not drift-prediction error benchmarks. Outlier positions or magnitudes cannot be randomized per run (e.g. single fixed scenario) — the median-over-200-runs design is defined for the 0/1/2/4-outlier grid with feature-specific outlier parameters. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Benchmark normalization methods on simulated data with known ground-truth drift by computing, at each QC index, the squared difference between a method's predicted and the expected drift pattern, then taking the median of these squared errors across 200 simulation runs (MSPE) per method, QC density, and outlier count. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c06841
skills.summary: Benchmark normalization methods on simulated data with known ground-truth drift by computing, at each QC index, the squared difference between a method's predicted and the expected drift pattern, then taking the median of these squared errors across 200 simulation runs (MSPE) per method, QC density, and outlier count.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is experimental data without a known ground-truth drift curve — MSPE against an expected pattern requires simulated data where the true drift is defined; use replicate concordance or drift/batch-effect inspection instead. The goal is to assess downstream differential abundance impact or QC-RSD filtering — those are separate tasks, not drift-prediction error benchmarks. Outlier positions or magnitudes cannot be randomized per run (e.g. single fixed scenario) — the median-over-200-runs design is defined for the 0/1/2/4-outlier grid with feature-specific outlier parameters.

skills.description: Use when two annotation methods (e.g. METASPACE-ML vs MSM) have been run on many imaging MS datasets and you need per-group median annotation-count gains and log2 fold-changes at fixed FDR cutoffs (5% and 10%).
skills.name: median-statistics-summarization-across-datasets
skills.search_text: median-statistics-summarization-across-datasets Use when two annotation methods (e.g. METASPACE-ML vs MSM) have been run on many imaging MS datasets and you need per-group median annotation-count gains and log2 fold-changes at fixed FDR cutoffs (5% and 10%). You need per-annotation identity changes (which specific metabolites were gained/lost) rather than aggregate count statistics — MSM-vs-ML per-ion comparisons need a different skill. Only a single dataset is available, so per-dataset medians and group-level fold-changes are undefined or meaningless. The annotation tables lack FDR estimates, so confident-annotation filtering at 5%/10% FDR cannot be applied. Summarize per-dataset benchmarking deltas between METASPACE-ML and rule-based MSM annotation counts into median differences, median log2-fold-changes, and a consolidated CSV summary table, mirroring the METASPACE-ML (Nature Communications, 2024) evaluation. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-52213-9
skills.summary: Summarize per-dataset benchmarking deltas between METASPACE-ML and rule-based MSM annotation counts into median differences, median log2-fold-changes, and a consolidated CSV summary table, mirroring the METASPACE-ML (Nature Communications, 2024) evaluation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need per-annotation identity changes (which specific metabolites were gained/lost) rather than aggregate count statistics — MSM-vs-ML per-ion comparisons need a different skill. Only a single dataset is available, so per-dataset medians and group-level fold-changes are undefined or meaningless. The annotation tables lack FDR estimates, so confident-annotation filtering at 5%/10% FDR cannot be applied.

skills.description: Use when a CWT peak-detection step has produced ROI feature regions with intensity profiles from LC-MS/CE-MS metabolomics runs and noise features must be removed before feature integration and data augmentation.
skills.name: median-threshold-outlier-filtering
skills.search_text: median-threshold-outlier-filtering Use when a CWT peak-detection step has produced ROI feature regions with intensity profiles from LC-MS/CE-MS metabolomics runs and noise features must be removed before feature integration and data augmentation. Input is raw vendor MS data that has not yet been ROI-searched and CWT peak-detected — the filter operates on detected peaks, not raw traces The analysis goal is filtering outliers across biological samples (e.g., removing bad injections) — this filter discriminates noise peaks from true peaks within a run, not sample-level outliers Single-platform analysis without downstream augmentation, where an existing single-platform tool (XCMS Online, MZmine, MetaboAnalyst) already provides adequate false-positive handling http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 An information-entropy false-positive peak filter (H = -p*log2(p) - q*log2(q)) that discards CWT-detected ROI peaks whose entropy exceeds the median entropy across all detected features, treating high-entropy (disordered) profiles as noise in AriumMS. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s00216-023-04715-6
skills.summary: An information-entropy false-positive peak filter (H = -p*log2(p) - q*log2(q)) that discards CWT-detected ROI peaks whose entropy exceeds the median entropy across all detected features, treating high-entropy (disordered) profiles as noise in AriumMS.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw vendor MS data that has not yet been ROI-searched and CWT peak-detected — the filter operates on detected peaks, not raw traces The analysis goal is filtering outliers across biological samples (e.g., removing bad injections) — this filter discriminates noise peaks from true peaks within a run, not sample-level outliers Single-platform analysis without downstream augmentation, where an existing single-platform tool (XCMS Online, MZmine, MetaboAnalyst) already provides adequate false-positive handling

skills.description: Use when building a multi-species community metabolic model in PyCoMo and you must define which substrates the community can take up, or link exchange metabolites across member models to enable cross-feeding.
skills.name: medium-exchange-metabolite-matching
skills.search_text: medium-exchange-metabolite-matching Use when building a multi-species community metabolic model in PyCoMo and you must define which substrates the community can take up, or link exchange metabolites across member models to enable cross-feeding. You only need to analyse an existing community model (exchange feasibility, cross-feeding, growth rate prediction) rather than construct one with a defined medium Member models use non-identical metabolite identifiers for the same compounds, so ID-based matching would silently miss exchange links without prior identifier harmonization The task is visualization of an already-built community model — use ScyNet on the SBML file instead http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 http://edamontology.org/topic_2259 Configuring the community medium and matching exchange metabolites when building a compartmentalized community metabolic model with PyCoMo, so that shared exchange metabolites in the medium compartment are linked across member models. In the biogas case study this meant matching medium-compartment exchange metabolites by identical identifiers and supplying ethanol and CO2 as the available substrates per Koch et al. (2019). metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae153
skills.summary: Configuring the community medium and matching exchange metabolites when building a compartmentalized community metabolic model with PyCoMo, so that shared exchange metabolites in the medium compartment are linked across member models. In the biogas case study this meant matching medium-compartment exchange metabolites by identical identifiers and supplying ethanol and CO2 as the available substrates per Koch et al. (2019).
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need to analyse an existing community model (exchange feasibility, cross-feeding, growth rate prediction) rather than construct one with a defined medium Member models use non-identical metabolite identifiers for the same compounds, so ID-based matching would silently miss exchange links without prior identifier harmonization The task is visualization of an already-built community model — use ScyNet on the SBML file instead

skills.search_text: medoid-representative-selection Use when a redundant set of antiSMASH/gutSMASH gene-cluster GenBank outputs must be deduplicated before metagenomic read mapping, to avoid ambiguous mapping of reads to near-identical clusters. The gene-cluster collection is already nonredundant (e.g. one cluster per genome), so medoid selection would discard genuine diversity The input is raw sequencing reads or abundance tables rather than antiSMASH/gutSMASH GenBank outputs — this skill operates upstream of bigmap-map The goal is metagenome assembly or taxonomy profiling rather than profiling metabolic gene-cluster (MGC) abundance and expression http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Collapses redundant antiSMASH/gutSMASH-predicted gene clusters into a nonredundant representative collection by MASH MinHash sketching of protein sequences, selecting the medoid (minimal cumulative distance) per similarity cluster, with optional BiG-SCAPE-based GCF grouping. metabolomics/v3 10.1128/msystems.00937-21

skills.description: Use when reproducing reported TOP-3::HA (or related recombination-marker) focus counts per nucleus across C. elegans germline zones 2–4 from published Results text, e.g. for the rtel-1 sensitized background.
skills.name: meiotic-recombination-focus-count-extraction
skills.search_text: meiotic-recombination-focus-count-extraction Use when reproducing reported TOP-3::HA (or related recombination-marker) focus counts per nucleus across C. elegans germline zones 2–4 from published Results text, e.g. for the rtel-1 sensitized background. You need raw per-nucleus focus counts or new image-based counting from microscopy — this skill only transcribes reported zone-level means and SDs. The analysis concerns replication defects, crossover counts, or GFP::MSH-5 localization rather than TOP-3::HA focus numbers per germline zone. Reported values are given as figures without accompanying zone-wise mean/SD text, since the workflow depends on verbatim numeric extraction. Extracts published TOP-3::HA recombination-focus counts (mean ± SD foci per nucleus) for germline zones 2–4 across top-3::ha, top-3-ZnF::ha, rtel-1 and rmh-2 backgrounds from the article's Results text, and compiles them into a single pandas CSV. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkac408
skills.summary: Extracts published TOP-3::HA recombination-focus counts (mean ± SD foci per nucleus) for germline zones 2–4 across top-3::ha, top-3-ZnF::ha, rtel-1 and rmh-2 backgrounds from the article's Results text, and compiles them into a single pandas CSV.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need raw per-nucleus focus counts or new image-based counting from microscopy — this skill only transcribes reported zone-level means and SDs. The analysis concerns replication defects, crossover counts, or GFP::MSH-5 localization rather than TOP-3::HA focus numbers per germline zone. Reported values are given as figures without accompanying zone-wise mean/SD text, since the workflow depends on verbatim numeric extraction.

skills.description: Use when a paper reports heterologous recombination event counts or percentages across meiotic genotypes and you need a genotype-indexed table to compare mutant rates or test synergy of BTR-complex alleles.
skills.name: meiotic-recombination-genotype-annotation
skills.search_text: meiotic-recombination-genotype-annotation Use when a paper reports heterologous recombination event counts or percentages across meiotic genotypes and you need a genotype-indexed table to compare mutant rates or test synergy of BTR-complex alleles. The analysis targets crossover number or D-loop discouragement phenotypes (e.g. top-3-ZnF; rtel-1 double mutant CO counts), not heterologous recombination rate quantification. Input data are recombination foci immunofluorescence measurements (e.g. GFP::MSH-5 localization timing) rather than event counts/frequencies per genotype. http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Curates meiotic heterologous recombination rates per genotype (top-3-ZnF, rmh-2, rmh-1, him-6, and double mutants) from a C. elegans germline paper into a structured genotype-annotated table, enabling tests of whether TOP-3-ZnF and RMH-2 synergize to suppress recombination between heterologous DNA. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkac408
skills.summary: Curates meiotic heterologous recombination rates per genotype (top-3-ZnF, rmh-2, rmh-1, him-6, and double mutants) from a C. elegans germline paper into a structured genotype-annotated table, enabling tests of whether TOP-3-ZnF and RMH-2 synergize to suppress recombination between heterologous DNA.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis targets crossover number or D-loop discouragement phenotypes (e.g. top-3-ZnF; rtel-1 double mutant CO counts), not heterologous recombination rate quantification. Input data are recombination foci immunofluorescence measurements (e.g. GFP::MSH-5 localization timing) rather than event counts/frequencies per genotype.

skills.description: Use when you have few-shot labeled single-cell mass spectrometry (SCMS) metabolomic feature vectors from melanoma cell pairs (untreated or drug-treated) and need rapid phenotype classification plus selection of essential m/z species.
skills.name: melanoma-phenotype-classification
skills.search_text: melanoma-phenotype-classification Use when you have few-shot labeled single-cell mass spectrometry (SCMS) metabolomic feature vectors from melanoma cell pairs (untreated or drug-treated) and need rapid phenotype classification plus selection of essential m/z species. Input is bulk metabolomics or flow-cytometry data rather than single-cell SCMS feature vectors — the model is trained and evaluated on Single-probe SCMS cell-level metabolomic profiles. A large labeled SCMS training set is already available and PCA or conventional deep learning suffices — the article motivates MetaPhenotype only when limited data and rapid transfer to new cell groups are required. The cell pair to classify has very similar metabolomic profiles such that no meaningful classification is expected (e.g. PCA cannot discriminate IGR39/IGR37 without the meta-learning adaptation). http://edamontology.org/topic_3382 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Classifies single-cell SCMS metabolomics data of melanoma cells into primary (IGR39) vs metastatic (IGR37) phenotypes using the MAML-based 1D-CNN MetaPhenotype model, which trains and adapts with as few as 1–5 labeled cells per class. It exists because standard transfer learning and PCA fail when SCMS training data are limited. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c02038
skills.summary: Classifies single-cell SCMS metabolomics data of melanoma cells into primary (IGR39) vs metastatic (IGR37) phenotypes using the MAML-based 1D-CNN MetaPhenotype model, which trains and adapts with as few as 1–5 labeled cells per class. It exists because standard transfer learning and PCA fail when SCMS training data are limited.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is bulk metabolomics or flow-cytometry data rather than single-cell SCMS feature vectors — the model is trained and evaluated on Single-probe SCMS cell-level metabolomic profiles. A large labeled SCMS training set is already available and PCA or conventional deep learning suffices — the article motivates MetaPhenotype only when limited data and rapid transfer to new cell groups are required. The cell pair to classify has very similar metabolomic profiles such that no meaningful classification is expected (e.g. PCA cannot discriminate IGR39/IGR37 without the meta-learning adaptation).

skills.description: Use when you have pretreated SCMS metabolomics feature data (e.g., dataset.csv) from a primary/metastatic melanoma cell pair, PCA fails to discriminate the phenotypes, and only limited cells are available for training a classifier.
skills.name: melanoma-primary-vs-metastatic-classification
skills.search_text: melanoma-primary-vs-metastatic-classification Use when you have pretreated SCMS metabolomics feature data (e.g., dataset.csv) from a primary/metastatic melanoma cell pair, PCA fails to discriminate the phenotypes, and only limited cells are available for training a classifier. Input is raw, unprocessed single-cell spectra — the model expects pretreated data (noise/background subtraction, TIC normalization, 10 ppm peak alignment, missing-value removal) Cell populations whose metabolomic profiles are well separated by simpler methods such as PCA, where a deep meta-learning model is unnecessary Tasks with abundant training cells where standard supervised or transfer-learning models do not suffer from limited-sample overfitting — note MAML is memory/computationally intensive and sensitive to hyperparameters http://edamontology.org/topic_3473 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Classifies single melanoma cells (e.g., IGR39 primary vs IGR37 metastatic) into primary or metastatic phenotypes from Single-probe SCMS metabolomics data using the MAML-based MetaPhenotype meta-learning model with a 1D-CNN (LeNet) backbone, achieving >90% accuracy from limited training samples. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c02038
skills.summary: Classifies single melanoma cells (e.g., IGR39 primary vs IGR37 metastatic) into primary or metastatic phenotypes from Single-probe SCMS metabolomics data using the MAML-based MetaPhenotype meta-learning model with a 1D-CNN (LeNet) backbone, achieving >90% accuracy from limited training samples.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw, unprocessed single-cell spectra — the model expects pretreated data (noise/background subtraction, TIC normalization, 10 ppm peak alignment, missing-value removal) Cell populations whose metabolomic profiles are well separated by simpler methods such as PCA, where a deep meta-learning model is unnecessary Tasks with abundant training cells where standard supervised or transfer-learning models do not suffer from limited-sample overfitting — note MAML is memory/computationally intensive and sensitive to hyperparameters

skills.description: Use when samples were acquired on different LC-MS/MS platforms or LC methods, or with strong RT shift/poor feature overlap, and you need sample-level clustering without prior feature alignment.
skills.name: memo-matrix-alignment-across-instrument-platforms
skills.search_text: memo-matrix-alignment-across-instrument-platforms Use when samples were acquired on different LC-MS/MS platforms or LC methods, or with strong RT shift/poor feature overlap, and you need sample-level clustering without prior feature alignment. Input is already a fully aligned feature table from a single platform with good feature overlap — feature-table metrics (e.g., Bray-Curtis, or CSCS via q2-cscs) are more appropriate there The analysis requires retention-time-resolved information — MEMO is explicitly a retention time agnostic alignment and discards RT structure Only a handful of samples or a single instrument is involved — the cross-platform alignment machinery and platform-effect PERMANOVA add no value http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Vectorize metabolomics samples as MS2 peak/neutral-loss count fingerprints (MS2 fingerprints) with memo-ms, align the resulting MemoMatrix objects across acquisitions made on different instruments (e.g., Q-Exactive Orbitrap vs Maxis II Q-TOF), and validate cross-platform comparability via PCoA and PERMANOVA on the MEMO distance matrix. metabolomics/v3 10.3389/fbinf.2022.842964
skills.summary: Vectorize metabolomics samples as MS2 peak/neutral-loss count fingerprints (MS2 fingerprints) with memo-ms, align the resulting MemoMatrix objects across acquisitions made on different instruments (e.g., Q-Exactive Orbitrap vs Maxis II Q-TOF), and validate cross-platform comparability via PCoA and PERMANOVA on the MEMO distance matrix.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a fully aligned feature table from a single platform with good feature overlap — feature-table metrics (e.g., Bray-Curtis, or CSCS via q2-cscs) are more appropriate there The analysis requires retention-time-resolved information — MEMO is explicitly a retention time agnostic alignment and discards RT structure Only a handful of samples or a single instrument is involved — the cross-platform alignment machinery and platform-effect PERMANOVA add no value

skills.search_text: memo-matrix-alignment-across-samples Use when LC-MS/MS samples lack a prior RT-based feature alignment — e.g. chemodiverse datasets, strong RT shifts, or different LC/MS platforms — and you need comparable sample-by-word vectors from raw MS2 spectra (.mgf). skills.summary: Build an MS2-based sample fingerprint matrix (MEMO) directly from unaligned MGF MS2 spectra by counting peak@mz and loss@mz word tokens per sample and aligning the per-sample vectors into a sample-by-word matrix, bypassing retention-time-based feature alignment.

skills.search_text: memo-matrix-samplewise-normalization Use when MEMO MS2 fingerprints have been aligned into a matrix of chemodiverse samples (e.g. the 1,600-plant-extract T. cruzi dataset) and you need comparable sample vectors prior to UMAP/TMAP embedding or cluster membership verification. skills.summary: Normalizes the rows of a MEMO matrix — an aligned table of MS2-fingerprint counts (MS2 peaks and neutral losses to precursor) — sample-wise so that each metabolomics sample vector is comparable before ordination (UMAP, TMAP, MDS/PCoA) or clustering.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis depends on retention-time structure — MEMO is explicitly RT-agnostic, so RT-shift or chromatographic-alignment questions need other approaches The input is raw MS1 feature abundances without MS2 fragmentation spectra — the fingerprint counts require MS2 peaks and neutral losses to the precursor Samples are not chemodiverse and share good feature overlap with no RT shift, where standard feature-alignment-based metrics suffice

skills.description: Use when you have just applied a metabolite-merging strategy (e.g. MMS) to a combined multi-study dataset and need to report the merge's efficacy — counts of name-consistency and of compounds that would not have merged by name alone.
skills.name: merge-efficacy-quantification
skills.search_text: merge-efficacy-quantification Use when you have just applied a metabolite-merging strategy (e.g. MMS) to a combined multi-study dataset and need to report the merge's efficacy — counts of name-consistency and of compounds that would not have merged by name alone. You have not yet run the merge step (e.g. MMS step 1) — quantifying merge efficacy before the merged dataset exists is meaningless. Your dataset has no independent canonical identifier (e.g. PubChem 'title' name or InChIKey) to compare reported names against — exact string matching alone cannot distinguish synonyms from genuinely different metabolites. You need pathway-level or biological-signature results, not merge-quality statistics — MMS efficacy quantification does not test pathway enrichment outcomes. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Quantifies how much value a metabolite-merging strategy adds by measuring how many metabolites share their reported name versus the canonical (PubChem title) name after merging, and how many compounds would have been missed without the merge (e.g. 179 vs 212 of 391 metabolites; 213 of 372 unmerged without MMS). metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo13121167

skills.description: Use when processing LC-MS/MS runs (mzML/mzXML) where a feature (precursor ion) was fragmented at multiple collision energies and you need a single consolidated MS/MS spectrum per feature before formula and structure annotation.
skills.name: merged-fragmentation-spectrum-construction
skills.search_text: merged-fragmentation-spectrum-construction Use when processing LC-MS/MS runs (mzML/mzXML) where a feature (precursor ion) was fragmented at multiple collision energies and you need a single consolidated MS/MS spectrum per feature before formula and structure annotation. Input LC-MS runs contain profiled-mode spectra — these are discarded in the COSMIC pipeline, so centroid conversion is needed first The analysis requires separate per-collision-energy spectra (e.g. evaluating a 20-eV-only condition) rather than consolidated per-feature spectra Fragmentation spectra contain at most one peak (or the compound yields such a spectrum at any collision energy/noise level) — the compound is removed from all libraries http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Construct per-feature merged fragmentation spectra by grouping all fragmentation spectra assigned to the same precursor-ion feature via agglomerative clustering on cosine distance, as implemented in SIRIUS 4 during COSMIC processing. Merging improves both annotation rates and confidence-score separation compared with individual collision-energy spectra. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41587-021-01045-9
skills.summary: Construct per-feature merged fragmentation spectra by grouping all fragmentation spectra assigned to the same precursor-ion feature via agglomerative clustering on cosine distance, as implemented in SIRIUS 4 during COSMIC processing. Merging improves both annotation rates and confidence-score separation compared with individual collision-energy spectra.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input LC-MS runs contain profiled-mode spectra — these are discarded in the COSMIC pipeline, so centroid conversion is needed first The analysis requires separate per-collision-energy spectra (e.g. evaluating a 20-eV-only condition) rather than consolidated per-feature spectra Fragmentation spectra contain at most one peak (or the compound yields such a spectrum at any collision energy/noise level) — the compound is removed from all libraries

skills.description: Use when you hold two versions of a metabolite list — one harmonized/merged (e.g., via MMS InChIKey merging) and one unmerged — and need to quantify how harmonization changes which pathways reach significance (FDR < 0.05).
skills.name: merged-vs-unmerged-enrichment-comparison
skills.search_text: merged-vs-unmerged-enrichment-comparison Use when you hold two versions of a metabolite list — one harmonized/merged (e.g., via MMS InChIKey merging) and one unmerged — and need to quantify how harmonization changes which pathways reach significance (FDR < 0.05). You have only a single metabolite list with no merged/unmerged counterpart — there is no contrast to draw; run a single over-representation enrichment instead. The task is performing the MMS merging itself (InChIKey translation, attribute retrieval, three-step curation) rather than measuring its downstream effect on enrichment. The enrichment uses a method or pathway library other than over-representation against SMPDB in MetaboAnalyst 5.0 — the 2-vs-0 significance benchmark does not transfer. http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Benchmarks how metabolite identifier harmonization changes pathway enrichment results by rerunning the identical MetaboAnalyst 5.0 over-representation analysis (SMPDB pathways) on an MMS-merged urinary asthma metabolite list (391 metabolites) versus the unmerged 547-entry list, and comparing per-pathway p-values and FDR side by side. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo13121167
skills.summary: Benchmarks how metabolite identifier harmonization changes pathway enrichment results by rerunning the identical MetaboAnalyst 5.0 over-representation analysis (SMPDB pathways) on an MMS-merged urinary asthma metabolite list (391 metabolites) versus the unmerged 547-entry list, and comparing per-pathway p-values and FDR side by side.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have only a single metabolite list with no merged/unmerged counterpart — there is no contrast to draw; run a single over-representation enrichment instead. The task is performing the MMS merging itself (InChIKey translation, attribute retrieval, three-step curation) rather than measuring its downstream effect on enrichment. The enrichment uses a method or pathway library other than over-representation against SMPDB in MetaboAnalyst 5.0 — the 2-vs-0 significance benchmark does not transfer.

skills.search_text: mesh-taxonomy-mapping-analysis Decision support for benchmarking a manual chemical classification system's coverage (e.g. MeSH over PubChem) against an automated, structure-based classifier such as ClassyFire before choosing an annotation pipeline. skills.search_text: metaboanalyst-differential-abundance-analysis Use when comparing a MetaboAnalyst-based NMR peak-grouping and differential analysis pipeline against an alternative peak-based workflow (e.g. speaq 2.0) on the same peak list, or when a lower-resolution grouped feature table is acceptable for between-group testing. skills.summary: Applies MetaboAnalyst's moving-window peak grouping (0.03 ppm window, 0.015 ppm steps) to NMR peak lists and runs Benjamini-Hochberg FDR-corrected differential abundance analysis, producing a lower-resolution feature matrix that can be cross-validated against speaq 2.0 grouping results.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a processed feature table with metabolite-level annotations, since grouping would only further reduce resolution Multiplet information must be preserved, since MetaboAnalyst's grouping sums close peaks together and removes multiplet structure A high-resolution feature matrix (e.g. speaq 2.0's 677 features rather than 245) is required for the downstream statistical analysis

skills.summary: A statistical-analysis skill in which CloMet-converted metabolomics repository data (e.g., MetaboLights study MTBLS563 as a ready-to-use csv) is loaded into MetaboAnalyst's Statistical Analysis module and evaluated with class-discrimination ROC/AUC, reproducing published AUCs such as 0.82 (bacterial vs control) and 0.84 (viral vs control).

skills.description: Use when NMR metabolomics biomarker measurements (e.g., Nightingale platform) plus survival data are available and you must build a weighted mortality risk score and test whether it outperforms conventional risk factors in a held-out validation cohort.
skills.name: metabolic-biomarker-risk-scoring
skills.search_text: metabolic-biomarker-risk-scoring Use when NMR metabolomics biomarker measurements (e.g., Nightingale platform) plus survival data are available and you must build a weighted mortality risk score and test whether it outperforms conventional risk factors in a held-out validation cohort. Goal is clinical patient classification — the score is based on scaled biomarker values created separately per cohort and is not yet suitable for clinical use in concentration units The platform or measurement set is not the Nightingale NMR panel — the 14 selected biomarkers and the exclusion of lipids/creatinine from conventional factors depend on what the NMR platform captures The analysis target is a phenotype other than prospective all-cause mortality — whether similar multivariate direction-of-effect changes occur for other phenotypes was not investigated http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Constructs and validates a weighted metabolic biomarker risk score for all-cause mortality by multiplying Nightingale NMR-derived, log-transformed, SD-scaled biomarkers by ln(hazard ratio) weights and comparing predictive accuracy (C-statistic, IDI) against conventional risk factor models in an independent cohort. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-019-11311-9
skills.summary: Constructs and validates a weighted metabolic biomarker risk score for all-cause mortality by multiplying Nightingale NMR-derived, log-transformed, SD-scaled biomarkers by ln(hazard ratio) weights and comparing predictive accuracy (C-statistic, IDI) against conventional risk factor models in an independent cohort.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Goal is clinical patient classification — the score is based on scaled biomarker values created separately per cohort and is not yet suitable for clinical use in concentration units The platform or measurement set is not the Nightingale NMR panel — the 14 selected biomarkers and the exclusion of lipids/creatinine from conventional factors depend on what the NMR platform captures The analysis target is a phenotype other than prospective all-cause mortality — whether similar multivariate direction-of-effect changes occur for other phenotypes was not investigated

skills.description: Use when mortality-associated metabolic biomarkers and their meta-analysis hazard ratios are available and you need to reproduce a weighted, per-unit risk score plus age/sex stratified consistency checks.
skills.name: metabolic-biomarker-score-construction
skills.search_text: metabolic-biomarker-score-construction Use when mortality-associated metabolic biomarkers and their meta-analysis hazard ratios are available and you need to reproduce a weighted, per-unit risk score plus age/sex stratified consistency checks. If the goal is clinical patient classification — the paper explicitly states the score 'is not yet suitable for classification of patients in the clinic, since it is based on scaled biomarker values created separately for each cohort'. If the analysis is prediction (C-statistic/IDI evaluation in FINRISK 1997) rather than score construction — use the prediction-skill workflow instead. If biomarker values are already on concentration units — the score here is defined on per-cohort SD-scaled values, so applying it to raw concentrations changes its meaning. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 http://edamontology.org/topic_3053 Constructs a weighted metabolic biomarker score for all-cause mortality by multiplying per-cohort log-transformed, standard-deviation-scaled NMR biomarker values by ln(hazard ratio) weights (from Table 2 fixed-effect meta-analysis) and summing them, yielding the reported per-unit score HR = 2.73 (95% CI: 2.60–2.86). metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-019-11311-9
skills.summary: Constructs a weighted metabolic biomarker score for all-cause mortality by multiplying per-cohort log-transformed, standard-deviation-scaled NMR biomarker values by ln(hazard ratio) weights (from Table 2 fixed-effect meta-analysis) and summing them, yielding the reported per-unit score HR = 2.73 (95% CI: 2.60–2.86).
skills.when_to_use_negative: If the goal is clinical patient classification — the paper explicitly states the score 'is not yet suitable for classification of patients in the clinic, since it is based on scaled biomarker values created separately for each cohort'. If the analysis is prediction (C-statistic/IDI evaluation in FINRISK 1997) rather than score construction — use the prediction-skill workflow instead. If biomarker values are already on concentration units — the score here is defined on per-cohort SD-scaled values, so applying it to raw concentrations changes its meaning.

skills.description: Use when building the structural (graph-based) level of a KEGG organism's metabolic network from pathway KGML files, where pathways must be connected via shared non-ubiquitous compounds rather than reactions.
skills.name: metabolic-compound-overlap-graph-construction
skills.search_text: metabolic-compound-overlap-graph-construction Use when building the structural (graph-based) level of a KEGG organism's metabolic network from pathway KGML files, where pathways must be connected via shared non-ubiquitous compounds rather than reactions. The goal is reaction-level (functional-level) comparison — this skill only builds the structural compound-overlap graph, not the reactions-content representation. KEGG maplinks are the desired connection basis — the article explicitly treats maplinks as visual-only and unreliable, so maplink-based graphs are out of scope. Ubiquitous compounds should connect pathways — the method deliberately discards H2O, phosphate, ATP and ADP before edge construction. http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Reconstructs a structural-level metabolic network by treating KEGG reference pathways as nodes and drawing edges between pathways that share at least one non-ubiquitous compound, then serialises the result as an adjacency matrix for cross-organism comparison. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pone.0246962
skills.summary: Reconstructs a structural-level metabolic network by treating KEGG reference pathways as nodes and drawing edges between pathways that share at least one non-ubiquitous compound, then serialises the result as an adjacency matrix for cross-organism comparison.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is reaction-level (functional-level) comparison — this skill only builds the structural compound-overlap graph, not the reactions-content representation. KEGG maplinks are the desired connection basis — the article explicitly treats maplinks as visual-only and unreliable, so maplink-based graphs are out of scope. Ubiquitous compounds should connect pathways — the method deliberately discards H2O, phosphate, ATP and ADP before edge construction.

skills.description: Use when you have a table of metabolite measurements plus sample trait metadata and want to group metabolites into correlation modules (accounting for interaction topology) and test whether modules associate with traits like tumor_normal or gender.
skills.name: metabolic-correlation-network-analysis
skills.search_text: metabolic-correlation-network-analysis Use when you have a table of metabolite measurements plus sample trait metadata and want to group metabolites into correlation modules (accounting for interaction topology) and test whether modules associate with traits like tumor_normal or gender. Input is raw mass-spectrometry spectra rather than a table of metabolite measurements — MetaboDiff starts off from the measurement table The goal is only a two-group differential test (Student's T-Test) or multi-group ANOVA on individual metabolites without network/module analysis You have predefined, curated metabolite sets (e.g. SMPDB pathway enrichment as the primary analysis) rather than wanting data-derived, topology-aware module detection http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Builds a data-derived metabolic correlation network with MetaboDiff/WGCNA to identify metabolic correlation modules without a priori metabolite sets, then relates module significance and module of interest (MOI) measures to sample traits such as tumor vs normal status. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/bty344
skills.summary: Builds a data-derived metabolic correlation network with MetaboDiff/WGCNA to identify metabolic correlation modules without a priori metabolite sets, then relates module significance and module of interest (MOI) measures to sample traits such as tumor vs normal status.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw mass-spectrometry spectra rather than a table of metabolite measurements — MetaboDiff starts off from the measurement table The goal is only a two-group differential test (Student's T-Test) or multi-group ANOVA on individual metabolites without network/module analysis You have predefined, curated metabolite sets (e.g. SMPDB pathway enrichment as the primary analysis) rather than wanting data-derived, topology-aware module detection

skills.description: Use when you have draft GEMs of related isolates from multiple reconstruction pipelines and need to know whether structural differences between the models track organism phylogeny rather than pipeline artifacts.
skills.name: metabolic-distance-phylogenetic-correlation
skills.search_text: metabolic-distance-phylogenetic-correlation Use when you have draft GEMs of related isolates from multiple reconstruction pipelines and need to know whether structural differences between the models track organism phylogeny rather than pipeline artifacts. Your goal is functional community simulation or cross-feeding analysis of gap-filled models — use SMETANA/COMMIT downstream analysis instead of structural distance comparison Models come from a single reconstruction pipeline only — the substantial structural differences this skill measures arise across the four pipelines, so within-pipeline comparisons are not informative Identifier translation to a common namespace is impossible or largely fails — without MNXref normalization the distance measures reflect ID-space differences, not biology http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Quantifies structural differences among draft genome-scale metabolic reconstructions (e.g., from KBase, CarveMe, RAVEN 2.0, AuReMe/Pathway Tools) using eight pairwise distance measures combined into STATIS compromise matrices, then tests biological relevance by correlating them with 16S rRNA sequence (phylogenetic) distance. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009906
skills.summary: Quantifies structural differences among draft genome-scale metabolic reconstructions (e.g., from KBase, CarveMe, RAVEN 2.0, AuReMe/Pathway Tools) using eight pairwise distance measures combined into STATIS compromise matrices, then tests biological relevance by correlating them with 16S rRNA sequence (phylogenetic) distance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your goal is functional community simulation or cross-feeding analysis of gap-filled models — use SMETANA/COMMIT downstream analysis instead of structural distance comparison Models come from a single reconstruction pipeline only — the substantial structural differences this skill measures arise across the four pipelines, so within-pipeline comparisons are not informative Identifier translation to a common namespace is impossible or largely fails — without MNXref normalization the distance measures reflect ID-space differences, not biology

skills.description: Use when gap-filled community GEMs (e.g., Matlab workspaces from run_iterative_gap_filling.m) are available and the goal is to map which metabolites members secrete/uptake and derive helper/beneficiary dependency calls.
skills.name: metabolic-exchange-reaction-analysis
skills.search_text: metabolic-exchange-reaction-analysis Use when gap-filled community GEMs (e.g., Matlab workspaces from run_iterative_gap_filling.m) are available and the goal is to map which metabolites members secrete/uptake and derive helper/beneficiary dependency calls. Input models are still draft (pre-gap-filled) reconstructions without a complete exchange-reaction structure, so uptake-blocking FBA would produce artifacts rather than real dependencies The goal is to predict which metabolites are likely permeable/secreted for gap filling (COMMIT's leakage model) rather than to quantify community-wide uptake dependencies The analysis is single-isolate (no community composition), so there is no cross-feeding pool to attribute dependencies to http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Enumerates extracellular exchange/uptake reactions in gap-filled community genome-scale metabolic models and quantifies cross-feeding dependencies by sink-reaction maximization and uptake-blocking FBA, as applied to the Bulgarelli and Schlaeppi Arabidopsis soil communities. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009906
skills.summary: Enumerates extracellular exchange/uptake reactions in gap-filled community genome-scale metabolic models and quantifies cross-feeding dependencies by sink-reaction maximization and uptake-blocking FBA, as applied to the Bulgarelli and Schlaeppi Arabidopsis soil communities.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input models are still draft (pre-gap-filled) reconstructions without a complete exchange-reaction structure, so uptake-blocking FBA would produce artifacts rather than real dependencies The goal is to predict which metabolites are likely permeable/secreted for gap filling (COMMIT's leakage model) rather than to quantify community-wide uptake dependencies The analysis is single-isolate (no community composition), so there is no cross-feeding pool to attribute dependencies to

skills.description: Use when a metabolome-wide association (partial correlation or GLM) between a metabolic feature and a phenotype such as BMI needs confidence intervals or robustness validation by resampling, with confounders like Age, Gender, T2D adjusted.

skills.search_text: metabolic-feature-association-testing Use when a metabolome-wide association (partial correlation or GLM) between a metabolic feature and a phenotype such as BMI needs confidence intervals or robustness validation by resampling, with confounders like Age, Gender, T2D adjusted. The goal is a metabolome-wide screening p-value set rather than stability assessment of an already-selected feature's association — use the package's MWAS association models (partial correlations, generalized linear models) instead The data container is not a SummarizedExperiment/MultiAssayExperiment object with phenotype metadata for metabolite_id, disease_id and confounder_ids Quality control, STOCSY metabolite assignment, or network/visualization tasks are the goal — these are separate MWASTools functionalities http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Validates metabolite–phenotype association models (e.g. BMI vs metabolic features) by non-parametric bootstrapping with MWASTools' MWAS_bootstrapping(), which resamples study subjects with replacement and recomputes a confounder-adjusted association estimate per iteration. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btx477

skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is a metabolome-wide screening p-value set rather than stability assessment of an already-selected feature's association — use the package's MWAS association models (partial correlations, generalized linear models) instead The data container is not a SummarizedExperiment/MultiAssayExperiment object with phenotype metadata for metabolite_id, disease_id and confounder_ids Quality control, STOCSY metabolite assignment, or network/visualization tasks are the goal — these are separate MWASTools functionalities

skills.description: Use when single-cell (or bulk) RNA-seq count matrices are available and the goal is cell-type-resolved metabolic flux, metabolite concentration changes, or comparing flux landscapes (e.g., cancer vs stromal, AD vs control).
skills.name: metabolic-flux-estimation-from-transcriptomics
skills.search_text: metabolic-flux-estimation-from-transcriptomics Use when single-cell (or bulk) RNA-seq count matrices are available and the goal is cell-type-resolved metabolic flux, metabolite concentration changes, or comparing flux landscapes (e.g., cancer vs stromal, AD vs control). Input is proteomics or metabolomics data — flux estimation currently extends only to transcriptomics; other omics support is listed as future work The question requires reversible-reaction directionality or inter-cell metabolic exchange/competition — these are not yet implemented by scFEA/FLUXestimator Strict biochemical constraints (redox, pH, energy balance) must be enforced — the current loss function only supports flux balance and non-negative constraints http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_3407 Predict cell-wise metabolic flux and metabolite balance/stress from scRNA-seq or bulk transcriptomics using scFEA/FLUXestimator, a graph neural network solver that maps curated metabolic module networks (e.g., m168 human, M171, Glucose-Glutamine) onto gene expression after MAGIC imputation. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkad444
skills.summary: Predict cell-wise metabolic flux and metabolite balance/stress from scRNA-seq or bulk transcriptomics using scFEA/FLUXestimator, a graph neural network solver that maps curated metabolic module networks (e.g., m168 human, M171, Glucose-Glutamine) onto gene expression after MAGIC imputation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is proteomics or metabolomics data — flux estimation currently extends only to transcriptomics; other omics support is listed as future work The question requires reversible-reaction directionality or inter-cell metabolic exchange/competition — these are not yet implemented by scFEA/FLUXestimator Strict biochemical constraints (redox, pH, energy balance) must be enforced — the current loss function only supports flux balance and non-negative constraints

skills.description: Use when you have a human GEM paired with microbiota-derived aggregated in-/out-fluxes (fi, fo) and need to characterize how the α mixing weight scales the resulting exchange-reaction lower bounds across [0, 1].
skills.name: metabolic-flux-scaling-interpretation
skills.search_text: metabolic-flux-scaling-interpretation Use when you have a human GEM paired with microbiota-derived aggregated in-/out-fluxes (fi, fo) and need to characterize how the α mixing weight scales the resulting exchange-reaction lower bounds across [0, 1]. No microbiota-derived aggregated fluxes (fi, fo) are available for the selected microbes, so the update rule cannot be evaluated at any α The goal is to modify model upper bounds or reaction stoichiometry rather than exchange-reaction lower bounds — M2R's rule only updates lower bounds The target model is not a human GEM compatible with cobrapy (e.g. constraint-based microbiota-only model), where the host-bound term αLB_r has no meaning Sweeps the mixing weight α in M2R's lower-bound update rule (LB_r := αLB_r + (1−α)fi − (1−α)fo) to quantify how exchange-reaction lower bounds in a human GEM such as RECON3D interpolate between the host-model bound (α=1) and the aggregated microbiota in-/out-flux value (α=0). metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btab060
skills.summary: Sweeps the mixing weight α in M2R's lower-bound update rule (LB_r := αLB_r + (1−α)fi − (1−α)fo) to quantify how exchange-reaction lower bounds in a human GEM such as RECON3D interpolate between the host-model bound (α=1) and the aggregated microbiota in-/out-flux value (α=0).
skills.when_to_use_negative: No microbiota-derived aggregated fluxes (fi, fo) are available for the selected microbes, so the update rule cannot be evaluated at any α The goal is to modify model upper bounds or reaction stoichiometry rather than exchange-reaction lower bounds — M2R's rule only updates lower bounds The target model is not a human GEM compatible with cobrapy (e.g. constraint-based microbiota-only model), where the host-bound term αLB_r has no meaning

skills.search_text: metabolic-model-response-factor-inference Use when you have time-course relative-abundance GC-MS metabolomics data (concMatrix + timeVec), a stoichiometric matrix with concentration/flux bounds, and need standard-free inference of absolute concentrations or response factors. Metabolomics data from multiple intracellular compartments or eukaryotic systems needing transport reactions between compartments — MetaboPAC only applies to intracellular samples in a single compartment and does not model compartmental transport. Datasets where relative abundances cannot be tied to a metabolic network with mass balances, or where no penalty functions can be defined for the system of interest. Datasets with substantial missing values not addressable by imputation — 10% missingness with imputation measurably reduces accuracy of inferred concentrations. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Run MetaboPAC to infer response factors and absolute metabolite concentrations from relative-abundance time-course GC-MS data by leveraging metabolic mass balances, kinetic equations, and a penalty-function optimization, including robustness testing under noise and reduced sampling frequency. metabolomics/v3 10.1039/d2mo00168c

Datasets where relative abundances cannot be tied to a metabolic network with mass balances, or where no penalty functions can be defined for the system of interest. Datasets with substantial missing values not addressable by imputation — 10% missingness with imputation measurably reduces accuracy of inferred concentrations.
