skills.description: Use when evaluating the robustness of over-representation analysis results to the composition of the background/reference compound set, e.g. when the assay-specific background may be incomplete or when reporting how SEP proportions change as the background shrinks.
skills.name: metabolite-background-set-reduction-simulation
skills.search_text: metabolite-background-set-reduction-simulation Use when evaluating the robustness of over-representation analysis results to the composition of the background/reference compound set, e.g. when the assay-specific background may be incomplete or when reporting how SEP proportions change as the background shrinks. The goal is to test metabolite misidentification, pathway database choice, or organism-specific pathway sets — those are separate ORA parameter perturbations, not background-set size reduction. You need a definitive 'ideal' background set: the article states defining the ideal assay-specific background set remains an open problem, so this simulation quantifies sensitivity rather than prescribing a correct background. The input is not a metabolomics abundance matrix with an accompanying assay-specific compound background list (e.g. it is already a list of significant pathways). http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 In-silico simulation that iteratively shrinks an ORA background compound set (by random removal or non-DA-only removal) and recomputes right-tailed Fisher's exact tests to quantify how background size affects the proportion of significantly enriched pathways (SEPs). Grounded in Wieder et al. 2021's background-set sensitivity analysis of metabolomics ORA. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009105
skills.summary: In-silico simulation that iteratively shrinks an ORA background compound set (by random removal or non-DA-only removal) and recomputes right-tailed Fisher's exact tests to quantify how background size affects the proportion of significantly enriched pathways (SEPs). Grounded in Wieder et al. 2021's background-set sensitivity analysis of metabolomics ORA.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to test metabolite misidentification, pathway database choice, or organism-specific pathway sets — those are separate ORA parameter perturbations, not background-set size reduction. skills.description: Use when you have a metabolite-by-sample abundance matrix (e.g. example_data.csv with control and mutant lung cancer group labels) and need a statistically filtered significant-metabolite query set to drive Fisher's Exact Test pathway enrichment.
skills.name: metabolite-differential-abundance-analysis
skills.search_text: metabolite-differential-abundance-analysis Use when you have a metabolite-by-sample abundance matrix (e.g. example_data.csv with control and mutant lung cancer group labels) and need a statistically filtered significant-metabolite query set to drive Fisher's Exact Test pathway enrichment. You already have a defined metabolite query set as KEGG IDs/names — in that case supply inputMetabolites directly to enrichmet() instead of running run_de(). Your goal is MetSEA on the full ranked metabolite list (log2 fold change and p-values) rather than over-representation of a filtered significant set — MetSEA uses summary statistics, not the thresholded query set. The experiment has more than two conditions or paired/repeated-measure designs — the documented workflow is a two-group control vs mutant comparison. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Two-group differential analysis of a metabolomics abundance matrix using EnrichMet's run_de() in R, computing per-metabolite fold change, group-comparison p-values with Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment, and filtering to significant metabolites (|fold change| >= 1, adjusted p < 0.05) that feed downstream Fisher's Exact Test pathway enrichment. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.08.28.672951
skills.summary: Two-group differential analysis of a metabolomics abundance matrix using EnrichMet's run_de() in R, computing per-metabolite fold change, group-comparison p-values with Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment, and filtering to significant metabolites (|fold change| >= 1, adjusted p < 0.05) that feed downstream Fisher's Exact Test pathway enrichment.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You already have a defined metabolite query set as KEGG IDs/names — in that case supply inputMetabolites directly to enrichmet() instead of running run_de(). Your goal is MetSEA on the full ranked metabolite list (log2 fold change and p-values) rather than over-representation of a filtered significant set — MetSEA uses summary statistics, not the thresholded query set. The experiment has more than two conditions or paired/repeated-measure designs — the documented workflow is a two-group control vs mutant comparison.

skills.description: Use when a metabolomics abundance matrix (imputed, log2-transformed, auto-scaled) must be reduced to a list of DA metabolites via statistical testing before over-representation analysis.
skills.name: metabolite-differential-abundance-testing
skills.search_text: metabolite-differential-abundance-testing Use when a metabolomics abundance matrix (imputed, log2-transformed, auto-scaled) must be reduced to a list of DA metabolites via statistical testing before over-representation analysis. The analysis goal is pathway-level enrichment rather than compound-level DA testing — feed the DA list into ORA (right-tailed Fisher's exact test, scipy.stats.fisher_exact) after selection, not instead of it The dataset lacks a two-group contrast structure; this skill was validated on datasets such as MTBLS135 (12 Hi-Myc vs 12 wild-type Mus musculus tissue samples) and Yachida et al. 2019 (149 healthy control vs 148 colorectal cancer stool samples) with clear binary groupings Raw, un-normalized abundance data is supplied without prior imputation, log2 transformation, and auto-scaling — the t-test results depend on these preprocessing steps http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Runs two-tailed Student's t-tests on log2-transformed, auto-scaled metabolite abundance matrices to define the list of differentially abundant (DA) metabolites that serves as input to ORA; a key sensitivity parameter for pathway analysis outcomes. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009105
skills.summary: Runs two-tailed Student's t-tests on log2-transformed, auto-scaled metabolite abundance matrices to define the list of differentially abundant (DA) metabolites that serves as input to ORA; a key sensitivity parameter for pathway analysis outcomes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is pathway-level enrichment rather than compound-level DA testing — feed the DA list into ORA (right-tailed Fisher's exact test, scipy.stats.fisher_exact) after selection, not instead of it The dataset lacks a two-group contrast structure; this skill was validated on datasets such as MTBLS135 (12 Hi-Myc vs 12 wild-type Mus musculus tissue samples) and Yachida et al. 2019 (149 healthy control vs 148 colorectal cancer stool samples) with clear binary groupings Raw, un-normalized abundance data is supplied without prior imputation, log2 transformation, and auto-scaling — the t-test results depend on these preprocessing steps

skills.description: Use when you have a metabolite abundance matrix with disease/wild-type versus control groups and need to flag each metabolite as differentially abundant (increased/decreased) using p < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 1 thresholds before pathway enrichment.

skills.search_text: metabolite-direction-classification Use when you have a metabolite abundance matrix with disease/wild-type versus control groups and need to flag each metabolite as differentially abundant (increased/decreased) using p < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 1 thresholds before pathway enrichment. Input is already a pathway enrichment result table (no raw abundance matrix to compute log2FC from) The study has more than two groups (e.g. multi-factor designs) — pairwise log2FC/p-value direction-calling does not capture the experimental structure Metabolites lack replicate-level abundance values, so p-values cannot be computed and direction calling would be based on fold-change alone http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Classify metabolites as significantly increased or decreased between case and control groups using log2 fold-change direction and p-value significance, then verify named metabolites match their reported directions. This is the differential-abundance direction-calling step that underpins pathway enrichment in plant metabolomics workflows. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/plants12152880

skills.description: Use when two DESI-MSI developmental-gradient datasets have already been clustered (e.g., via DIMPLE) and the goal is to classify which clustered mass signatures keep the same enrichment pattern across varieties and which have shifted localization.
skills.name: metabolite-divergence-tabulation
skills.search_text: metabolite-divergence-tabulation Use when two DESI-MSI developmental-gradient datasets have already been clustered (e.g., via DIMPLE) and the goal is to classify which clustered mass signatures keep the same enrichment pattern across varieties and which have shifted localization. The MSI datasets have not yet been processed by DIMPLE — without cluster assignments and clustered linescans there is no enrichment pattern to compare across varieties. The analysis goal is metabolite identification/annotation of unknown m/z values (e.g., via METASPACE, Metlin Classic, or LOTUS) rather than cross-variety localization comparison. The samples are not comparable developmental gradients — this skill assumes a linear root developmental axis so clusters map between varieties. Cross-variety comparison workflow that maps DIMPLE cluster assignments of mass signatures from one maize variety (e.g., B73) onto another (e.g., Oaxacan Green) and tabulates each signature as conserved or divergent in developmental localization, exemplified by the B73 meristem-localized Cluster 1 set. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.09.22.677919

skills.search_text: metabolite-edge-table-export Use when FT-ICR MS peak tables with assigned molecular formulas are available and ab initio biochemical transformation networks based on mass differences must be built and exported per sample. Input is raw FT-ICR MS spectra: molecular formula assignment must be performed before MetaboDirect, so this skill cannot start from unprocessed spectra The peak table has not been filtered by m/z values, 13C isotopic peaks, formula-assignment error (0.5 ppm), and minimum sample presence — unfiltered tables will propagate spurious isotopic masses (~200 removed in the bacterium-phage dataset) into edges The goal is formula-level pathway annotation (KEGG Pathway/Module/Brite via KEGGREST) rather than mass-difference transformation networks Reconstructs MetaboDirect's mass-difference transformation phase: compute all pairwise m/z differences between peaks within each FT-ICR MS sample, match them to predefined biochemical transformation keys at a maximum error of 1 ppm, label each edge biotic or abiotic, and export per-sample edge .csv files plus a transformation_counts.csv. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s40168-023-01476-3

skills.description: Use when INADEQUATE-annotated metabolites from 13C-labeled amino acid feeding need to be assigned to tissue-enrichment categories across multiple organs (e.g. liver, spleen, pancreas, muscle, lung) to reproduce PyINETA tissue-distribution output.
skills.name: metabolite-enrichment-categorization
skills.search_text: metabolite-enrichment-categorization Use when INADEQUATE-annotated metabolites from 13C-labeled amino acid feeding need to be assigned to tissue-enrichment categories across multiple organs (e.g. liver, spleen, pancreas, muscle, lung) to reproduce PyINETA tissue-distribution output. When the goal is de novo compound annotation from raw INADEQUATE spectra — use the PyINETA peak-picking/clustering/matching pipeline instead, not the enrichment categorization step. When tissue samples are from unlabeled (natural abundance) feeding experiments, since tissue-specific enrichment of labeled metabolites is the basis of this categorization. When only a single tissue (e.g. liver-only spectra) is available, since Type-B and Type-C calls require relative abundance across multiple tissues. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Classify metabolites traced from a 13C-labeled diet into tissue-distribution categories (liver-enriched, liver-depleted, co-enriched) by quantifying their representative 13C-JRES peak intensities across mouse tissues, reproducing the PyINETA tissue-distribution analysis. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c03966
skills.summary: Classify metabolites traced from a 13C-labeled diet into tissue-distribution categories (liver-enriched, liver-depleted, co-enriched) by quantifying their representative 13C-JRES peak intensities across mouse tissues, reproducing the PyINETA tissue-distribution analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is de novo compound annotation from raw INADEQUATE spectra — use the PyINETA peak-picking/clustering/matching pipeline instead, not the enrichment categorization step. When tissue samples are from unlabeled (natural abundance) feeding experiments, since tissue-specific enrichment of labeled metabolites is the basis of this categorization. When only a single tissue (e.g. liver-only spectra) is available, since Type-B and Type-C calls require relative abundance across multiple tissues.

skills.description: Use when a human genome-scale metabolic model (e.g. RECON3D loaded in cobrapy as SBML) must be modified using gut microbiota metabolism: first aggregate and normalize the microbe's external-reaction fluxes before setting exchange-reaction lower bounds.
skills.name: metabolite-exchange-flux-aggregation
skills.search_text: metabolite-exchange-flux-aggregation Use when a human genome-scale metabolic model (e.g. RECON3D loaded in cobrapy as SBML) must be modified using gut microbiota metabolism: first aggregate and normalize the microbe's external-reaction fluxes before setting exchange-reaction lower bounds. The aim is to study a metabolic interaction without incorporating microbiota fluxes into the human GEM — this skill only supplies the aggregated/normalized fluxes M2R needs to modify exchange reaction lower bounds. A single overall omnibus hypothesis is needed rather than a battery of per-feature tests — the FDR adjustment assumes many independent per-feature tests, so this skill is inappropriate when only a few pre-specified features are of interest. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Run univariate statistical tests (parametric and non-parametric) across metabolite features in a preprocessed feature table and correct the resulting p-values for multiple testing. skills.search_text: metabolite-fold-change-classification Use when AriumMS mid-level fused feature intensity tables for growth-inhibitor-treated vs. control Saccharomyces cerevisiae extracts are available and per-metabolite regulation calls must be reported per ESI augmentation group. Input is a single-platform (one HILIC or one CE method only) feature table rather than the augmented mid-level fused output from the ESI negative or ESI positive platform groups Samples are not paired treated-vs-reference yeast extracts (no growth-inhibitor treatment contrast), so fold-change calls are not meaningful The metabolite of interest is not among the 40 target metabolites; targets absent from an augmentation group must be recorded as n.a., not inferred from other platforms http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Classifies each target metabolite in AriumMS-processed augmented multi-platform (HILIC-MS + CE-MS) yeast data into fold-change regulation calls (down/stable/up/knock out/induced, or n.a. if undetected), computed per augmentation group (ESI negative vs ESI positive). metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s00216-023-04715-6
skills.summary: Classifies each target metabolite in AriumMS-processed augmented multi-platform (HILIC-MS + CE-MS) yeast data into fold-change regulation calls (down/stable/up/knock out/induced, or n.a. if undetected), computed per augmentation group (ESI negative vs ESI positive).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a single-platform (one HILIC or one CE method only) feature table rather than the augmented mid-level fused output from the ESI negative or ESI positive platform groups Samples are not paired treated-vs-reference yeast extracts (no growth-inhibitor treatment contrast), so fold-change calls are not meaningful The metabolite of interest is not among the 40 target metabolites; targets absent from an augmentation group must be recorded as n.a., not inferred from other platforms

skills.description: Use when MetaPro Target Search quantification results (.xlsx report from Export Report) are available and you need SB-vs-SA log fold-change distributions to benchmark automatic semi-targeted quantification accuracy.
skills.name: metabolite-fold-change-computation
skills.search_text: metabolite-fold-change-computation Use when MetaPro Target Search quantification results (.xlsx report from Export Report) are available and you need SB-vs-SA log fold-change distributions to benchmark automatic semi-targeted quantification accuracy. Input is still raw vendor data (Thermo .raw, SCIEX .wiff) or .aird files rather than an exported MetaPro quantification report — Target Search and Export Report must run first The goal is manual QC inspection or library curation (Reset integration params, Reset TargetRT, Manual Integration) rather than quantifying automatic results The report contains manually reintegrated peaks, which would break comparison with the no-manual-inspection first-run benchmark http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Computes per-compound log-transformed fold changes of signal in blank (SB) relative to analyte sample (SA) from MetaPro-exported quantification peak areas to assess quantification accuracy and stability, mirroring the Fig. 4B/4F benchmark comparison in the MetaPro paper. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-023-02018-6
skills.summary: Computes per-compound log-transformed fold changes of signal in blank (SB) relative to analyte sample (SA) from MetaPro-exported quantification peak areas to assess quantification accuracy and stability, mirroring the Fig. 4B/4F benchmark comparison in the MetaPro paper.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is still raw vendor data (Thermo .raw, SCIEX .wiff) or .aird files rather than an exported MetaPro quantification report — Target Search and Export Report must run first The goal is manual QC inspection or library curation (Reset integration params, Reset TargetRT, Manual Integration) rather than quantifying automatic results The report contains manually reintegrated peaks, which would break comparison with the no-manual-inspection first-run benchmark

skills.description: Use when building synthetic chemical inputs for ViMMS 2.0 simulations and you need formulae sampled from a database like HMDB (e.g. m/z 100–1000) or drawn from a uniform m/z range rather than extracted from mzML.
skills.name: metabolite-formula-database-sampling
skills.search_text: metabolite-formula-database-sampling Use when building synthetic chemical inputs for ViMMS 2.0 simulations and you need formulae sampled from a database like HMDB (e.g. m/z 100–1000) or drawn from a uniform m/z range rather than extracted from mzML. You want chemicals derived from real experimental data — ViMMS 2.0 can alternatively extract chemical objects from existing mzML files (e.g. Beer_multibeers_1_T10_POS.mzML) instead of sampling synthetically. You need the full ViMMS simulation output (mzML scans) — this skill only covers the chemical-generation stage, not running controllers in an Environment or writing mzML. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Generate simulated metabolite lists in ViMMS 2.0 by plugging database-backed or uniform samplers (formulae, RT, intensity, chromatograms) into ChemicalMixtureCreator, producing KnownChemical objects with m/z, RT, intensity and formula fields. metabolomics/v3 10.21105/joss.03990
skills.summary: Generate simulated metabolite lists in ViMMS 2.0 by plugging database-backed or uniform samplers (formulae, RT, intensity, chromatograms) into ChemicalMixtureCreator, producing KnownChemical objects with m/z, RT, intensity and formula fields.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You want chemicals derived from real experimental data — ViMMS 2.0 can alternatively extract chemical objects from existing mzML files (e.g. Beer_multibeers_1_T10_POS.mzML) instead of sampling synthetically. You need the full ViMMS simulation output (mzML scans) — this skill only covers the chemical-generation stage, not running controllers in an Environment or writing mzML.

skills.description: Use when a centroided LC/MS/MS feature table contains structurally related features (e.g. molecular subnetworks) and a known diagnostic product ion can define a compound class across those features.
skills.name: metabolite-fragment-ion-annotation
skills.search_text: metabolite-fragment-ion-annotation Use when a centroided LC/MS/MS feature table contains structurally related features (e.g. molecular subnetworks) and a known diagnostic product ion can define a compound class across those features. Raw data has not yet been feature-detected — run xcms-based feature detection and alignment first to obtain the 'mz'/'rt' feature table No diagnostic fragment ion or pattern is known for the compound class of interest — pattern matching requires predefined m/z patterns MS2 scans are not associated with feature-table entries (e.g. no DDA data or parent-ion tolerance mismatch) http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Annotate molecular features in LC/MS/MS data by searching MS2 spectra for diagnostic fragment ions using Metaboseek's Find Patterns module — demonstrated by identifying >100 GLEA-like metabolites via the GLEA product ion at m/z 333.0592 plus phosphoglycerol- and glucose-derived fragments. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-022-28391-9
skills.summary: Annotate molecular features in LC/MS/MS data by searching MS2 spectra for diagnostic fragment ions using Metaboseek's Find Patterns module — demonstrated by identifying >100 GLEA-like metabolites via the GLEA product ion at m/z 333.0592 plus phosphoglycerol- and glucose-derived fragments.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Raw data has not yet been feature-detected — run xcms-based feature detection and alignment first to obtain the 'mz'/'rt' feature table No diagnostic fragment ion or pattern is known for the compound class of interest — pattern matching requires predefined m/z patterns MS2 scans are not associated with feature-table entries (e.g. no DDA data or parent-ion tolerance mismatch)

skills.description: Use when you have a RaMP MySQL dump loaded locally and need to quantify what fraction of metabolites or genes are annotated by each source database and what fraction is shared across all four.
skills.name: metabolite-gene-annotation-counting
skills.search_text: metabolite-gene-annotation-counting Use when you have a RaMP MySQL dump loaded locally and need to quantify what fraction of metabolites or genes are annotated by each source database and what fraction is shared across all four. The goal is pathway enrichment or Fisher overrepresentation testing on an analyte list, rather than characterizing annotation coverage of the database itself (use runFisherTest/runCombinedFisherTest instead). The backend database being queried is RaMP-DB 3.0 (ncats/RaMP-DB), which integrates additional sources (Lipid-MAPS, ChEBI, PFOCR, RefMet, Rhea) beyond the four original databases, so the 4-database overlap logic no longer applies. Input is not a RaMP MySQL dump but raw source-database files (HMDB, KEGG, Reactome, WikiPathways downloads); those must first be built into RaMP via RaMP-BackEnd main.py before counting. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 Quantifies per-database annotation coverage and cross-database overlap of metabolites and genes integrated in the RaMP relational database (KEGG, Reactome, HMDB, WikiPathways), reproducing the coverage/uniqueness statistics reported in the RaMP paper's Figure 2. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo8010016
skills.summary: Quantifies per-database annotation coverage and cross-database overlap of metabolites and genes integrated in the RaMP relational database (KEGG, Reactome, HMDB, WikiPathways), reproducing the coverage/uniqueness statistics reported in the RaMP paper's Figure 2.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is pathway enrichment or Fisher overrepresentation testing on an analyte list, rather than characterizing annotation coverage of the database itself (use runFisherTest/runCombinedFisherTest instead). The backend database being queried is RaMP-DB 3.0 (ncats/RaMP-DB), which integrates additional sources (Lipid-MAPS, ChEBI, PFOCR, RefMet, Rhea) beyond the four original databases, so the 4-database overlap logic no longer applies. Input is not a RaMP MySQL dump but raw source-database files (HMDB, KEGG, Reactome, WikiPathways downloads); those must first be built into RaMP via RaMP-BackEnd main.py before counting.

skills.description: Use when metabolite statistics data frames with KEGG compound identifiers (e.g. metabolites with adjusted p values <= 0.05) need functional orthology and gene metadata for hypothesis generation.
skills.name: metabolite-gene-functional-linkage
skills.search_text: metabolite-gene-functional-linkage Use when metabolite statistics data frames with KEGG compound identifiers (e.g. metabolites with adjusted p values <= 0.05) need functional orthology and gene metadata for hypothesis generation. When the input data frame lacks KEGG compound identifiers or was not loaded with read.metabo, since the KEGG column class must be proper for KEGG_gather to query the KEGG API. When you only need hierarchical compound classification without enzyme/gene linkage — plain assign_hierarchy on compound identifiers is sufficient. When no subset to metabolites of interest has been made — running KEGG_gather on every compound is inappropriate because compounds can have multiple functional orthologies and KEGGREST calls would be excessive. http://edamontology.org/topic_3391 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Links metabolomics compounds to their known enzyme orthologies and genes via KEGG_gather, which queries the KEGG API through KEGGREST, and annotates organisms and enzymes onto the resulting table with assign_hierarchy — supporting hypothesis generation about which organisms could metabolize compounds of interest. metabolomics/v3 10.1128/mra.00129-19
skills.summary: Links metabolomics compounds to their known enzyme orthologies and genes via KEGG_gather, which queries the KEGG API through KEGGREST, and annotates organisms and enzymes onto the resulting table with assign_hierarchy — supporting hypothesis generation about which organisms could metabolize compounds of interest.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input data frame lacks KEGG compound identifiers or was not loaded with read.metabo, since the KEGG column class must be proper for KEGG_gather to query the KEGG API. When you only need hierarchical compound classification without enzyme/gene linkage — plain assign_hierarchy on compound identifiers is sufficient. When no subset to metabolites of interest has been made — running KEGG_gather on every compound is inappropriate because compounds can have multiple functional orthologies and KEGGREST calls would be excessive.

skills.description: Use when a user supplies a list of metabolite and/or gene identifiers of mixed origin (hmdb, kegg, ensembl, uniprot, CAS, pubchem, chebi...) that must be translated to RaMP pathway IDs before Fisher enrichment.
skills.name: metabolite-gene-identifier-mapping
skills.search_text: metabolite-gene-identifier-mapping Use when a user supplies a list of metabolite and/or gene identifiers of mixed origin (hmdb, kegg, ensembl, uniprot, CAS, pubchem, chebi...) that must be translated to RaMP pathway IDs before Fisher enrichment. The input is already a set of RaMP pathway IDs or an enriched pathway table — mapping is only needed for raw analyte lists Only chemical-class or ontology annotations (not pathway membership) are needed from RaMP-DB 3.0; use the dedicated query functions instead The MySQL server/connection parameters (dbname, username, conpass, host) are unavailable and no cached SQLite version exists — RaMP cannot be queried offline without one of these http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3345 Maps user-supplied gene and metabolite analyte lists (e.g. hmdb:HMDB04824, kegg:C02712, ensembl:ENSG...) onto RaMP's integrated KEGG/Reactome/WikiPathways/HMDB pathway identifiers, with optional synonym resolution, as the prerequisite step for pathway overrepresentation analysis. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo8010016
skills.summary: Maps user-supplied gene and metabolite analyte lists (e.g. hmdb:HMDB04824, kegg:C02712, ensembl:ENSG...) onto RaMP's integrated KEGG/Reactome/WikiPathways/HMDB pathway identifiers, with optional synonym resolution, as the prerequisite step for pathway overrepresentation analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a set of RaMP pathway IDs or an enriched pathway table — mapping is only needed for raw analyte lists Only chemical-class or ontology annotations (not pathway membership) are needed from RaMP-DB 3.0; use the dedicated query functions instead The MySQL server/connection parameters (dbname, username, conpass, host) are unavailable and no cached SQLite version exists — RaMP cannot be queried offline without one of these

skills.description: Use when you have a standalone list of disease-associated metabolites (e.g. 39 plasma lipids or 56 urine metabolites) and need to convert them into gene sets for over-representation analysis against GWAS subnetworks.
skills.name: metabolite-gene-interaction-mapping
skills.search_text: metabolite-gene-interaction-mapping Use when you have a standalone list of disease-associated metabolites (e.g. 39 plasma lipids or 56 urine metabolites) and need to convert them into gene sets for over-representation analysis against GWAS subnetworks. When you have paired metabolomics-GWAS data with matched SNP-metabolite associations — this skill addresses the unpaired, standalone setting and is 'limited to genes with known metabolite interactions' When metabolites have no known interactions recorded in HMDB, since discovered associations are restricted to genes with known metabolite interactions http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Maps disease-associated metabolites to their interacting proteins/genes via online databases (HMDB), building the metabolic gene sets that metGWAS 1.0 compares against GWAS Catalog-derived genomic gene sets with a hypergeometric test. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad523
skills.summary: Maps disease-associated metabolites to their interacting proteins/genes via online databases (HMDB), building the metabolic gene sets that metGWAS 1.0 compares against GWAS Catalog-derived genomic gene sets with a hypergeometric test.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When you have paired metabolomics-GWAS data with matched SNP-metabolite associations — this skill addresses the unpaired, standalone setting and is 'limited to genes with known metabolite interactions' When metabolites have no known interactions recorded in HMDB, since discovered associations are restricted to genes with known metabolite interactions

skills.description: Use when you have an intersection gene set from a metabolic-vs-genomic hypergeometric comparison and need to determine, gene by gene, whether each gene sits at a primary keyword node or a first-neighbour node in the GWAS subnetwork.
skills.name: metabolite-gene-intersection-analysis
skills.search_text: metabolite-gene-intersection-analysis Use when you have an intersection gene set from a metabolic-vs-genomic hypergeometric comparison and need to determine, gene by gene, whether each gene sits at a primary keyword node or a first-neighbour node in the GWAS subnetwork. When the goal is to generate or statistically test the metabolic vs genomic gene sets themselves — that upstream step is metGWAS 1.0's hypergeometric test, not this provenance classification. When the metabolite-gene associations are paired (matched from the same metabolomics-GWAS study); the analysis is limited to genes with known metabolite interactions due to the unpaired nature of the datasets. When a gene of interest is not a discoverable gene in the HMDB/GWAS Catalog network objects (e.g. absent from discoverableGenes_akaAllGenesInHMDB_2021_10_14.RData), since its node type cannot be traced. A metGWAS 1.0-based R procedure that classifies each gene in a metabolic/GWAS intersection set by its provenance in the GWAS Catalog network — either a primary keyword node or a first-neighbour node — to establish where the intersecting genes originate. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad523
skills.summary: A metGWAS 1.0-based R procedure that classifies each gene in a metabolic/GWAS intersection set by its provenance in the GWAS Catalog network — either a primary keyword node or a first-neighbour node — to establish where the intersecting genes originate.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is to generate or statistically test the metabolic vs genomic gene sets themselves — that upstream step is metGWAS 1.0's hypergeometric test, not this provenance classification. When the metabolite-gene associations are paired (matched from the same metabolomics-GWAS study); the analysis is limited to genes with known metabolite interactions due to the unpaired nature of the datasets. When a gene of interest is not a discoverable gene in the HMDB/GWAS Catalog network objects (e.g. absent from discoverableGenes_akaAllGenesInHMDB_2021_10_14.RData), since its node type cannot be traced.

skills.description: Use when you have cluster-level differentially expressed metabolites and/or genes from an integrated spatial multi-omics object and need regional pathway enrichment plus an Enrichment Map network linking pathway feature sets.
skills.name: metabolite-gene-network-enrichment-visualisation
skills.search_text: metabolite-gene-network-enrichment-visualisation Use when you have cluster-level differentially expressed metabolites and/or genes from an integrated spatial multi-omics object and need regional pathway enrichment plus an Enrichment Map network linking pathway feature sets. Input is raw m/z imaging data that has not yet been metabolite-annotated — run the SpaMTP annotation pipeline first, since enrichment operates on named metabolites and genes Differential expression has not been performed per cluster — Fisher's exact test and rank-based enrichment both require FindAllDEMs-style differential metabolite/gene results as input The target pathways lie outside the RaMP-DB-derived annotation sources (KEGG, SMPdb, Reactome, WikiPathways) used by this implementation http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Regional pathway enrichment and Enrichment-Map-style network construction over metabolite and gene feature sets, as implemented in SpaMTP for paired spatial metabolomics (MALDI) and transcriptomics (Visium) data. It converts cluster-level differential analytes into Fisher over-representation and GSEA-like rank-based pathway results, then renders topology-weighted pathway networks. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.10.31.621429
skills.summary: Regional pathway enrichment and Enrichment-Map-style network construction over metabolite and gene feature sets, as implemented in SpaMTP for paired spatial metabolomics (MALDI) and transcriptomics (Visium) data. It converts cluster-level differential analytes into Fisher over-representation and GSEA-like rank-based pathway results, then renders topology-weighted pathway networks.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw m/z imaging data that has not yet been metabolite-annotated — run the SpaMTP annotation pipeline first, since enrichment operates on named metabolites and genes Differential expression has not been performed per cluster — Fisher's exact test and rank-based enrichment both require FindAllDEMs-style differential metabolite/gene results as input The target pathways lie outside the RaMP-DB-derived annotation sources (KEGG, SMPdb, Reactome, WikiPathways) used by this implementation

skills.description: Use when building or reimplementing a transformer model whose inputs are tabular metabolite (or similar numeric feature) vectors and you need feature-to-token embeddings plus interaction-aware attention biasing for pre-training or fine-tuning.
skills.name: metabolite-hadamard-embedding-layer-design
skills.search_text: metabolite-hadamard-embedding-layer-design Use when building or reimplementing a transformer model whose inputs are tabular metabolite (or similar numeric feature) vectors and you need feature-to-token embeddings plus interaction-aware attention biasing for pre-training or fine-tuning. Input is raw spectral or mass-spec data (e.g. mzML peaks) rather than a table of already quantified NMR metabolite values per sample The task is purely missing-value imputation or plain tabular prediction where a correlation-biased transformer's inductive bias is unnecessary (e.g. hundreds of weakly interacting features with simple linear relationships) Only a handful of metabolites are available, making a 768-dimensional 12-layer BERT-scale architecture over-parameterized relative to the data Designs the MetaboLM input pipeline that converts a table of 249 quantified NMR plasma metabolite values into 768-dimensional token embeddings via a Hadamard (element-wise) product, prepends a learnable [CLS] token, and feeds the sequence to a 12-layer BERT encoder whose attention incorporates a metabolite-metabolite correlation matrix as an additive bias. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-025-66163-3
skills.summary: Designs the MetaboLM input pipeline that converts a table of 249 quantified NMR plasma metabolite values into 768-dimensional token embeddings via a Hadamard (element-wise) product, prepends a learnable [CLS] token, and feeds the sequence to a 12-layer BERT encoder whose attention incorporates a metabolite-metabolite correlation matrix as an additive bias.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw spectral or mass-spec data (e.g. mzML peaks) rather than a table of already quantified NMR metabolite values per sample The task is purely missing-value imputation or plain tabular prediction where a correlation-biased transformer's inductive bias is unnecessary (e.g. hundreds of weakly interacting features with simple linear relationships) Only a handful of metabolites are available, making a 768-dimensional 12-layer BERT-scale architecture over-parameterized relative to the data

skills.description: Use when you have searched query spectra (e.g., CSA_MSP .msp composite spectra) against an MS/MS library (e.g., NIST 2020) with IDSL.FSA and need to extract and tabulate each spectrum's -scoring annotation into a CSV hit table.
skills.name: metabolite-hit-table-compilation
skills.search_text: metabolite-hit-table-compilation Use when you have searched query spectra (e.g., CSA_MSP .msp composite spectra) against an MS/MS library (e.g., NIST 2020) with IDSL.FSA and need to extract and tabulate each spectrum's -scoring annotation into a CSV hit table. The raw mzML/mzXML data have not yet been processed through IDSL.IPA peak detection and IDSL.CSA composite spectra export — no .msp query spectra exist to search or tabulate hits for You need de novo structural elucidation without any reference MS/MS library — this skill only compiles top hits from similarity searches against an existing library such as NIST 2020 Input is already an aligned, annotated peak table — this skill produces that annotation table rather than consuming it http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Compile a per-spectrum table of top-scoring library hits (compound name, InChIKey, similarity score) after mass spectral similarity searching of composite spectra (.msp) against a reference MS/MS library such as NIST 2020, using the IDSL.FSA R package. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c00376
skills.summary: Compile a per-spectrum table of top-scoring library hits (compound name, InChIKey, similarity score) after mass spectral similarity searching of composite spectra (.msp) against a reference MS/MS library such as NIST 2020, using the IDSL.FSA R package.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The raw mzML/mzXML data have not yet been processed through IDSL.IPA peak detection and IDSL.CSA composite spectra export — no .msp query spectra exist to search or tabulate hits for You need de novo structural elucidation without any reference MS/MS library — this skill only compiles top hits from similarity searches against an existing library such as NIST 2020 Input is already an aligned, annotated peak table — this skill produces that annotation table rather than consuming it

skills.description: Use when a metabolomics differential analysis has produced significant metabolites (|fold change| ≥ 1, adjusted p < 0.05) and you need to rank them as network hubs by relative betweenness centrality on a KEGG pathway–metabolite network.
skills.name: metabolite-hub-identification
skills.search_text: metabolite-hub-identification Use when a metabolomics differential analysis has produced significant metabolites (|fold change| ≥ 1, adjusted p < 0.05) and you need to rank them as network hubs by relative betweenness centrality on a KEGG pathway–metabolite network. No differential statistics exist, so there is no principled way to select significant metabolites (|FC| ≥ 1, adj p < 0.05) as query nodes for the centrality calculation The organism's metabolite–pathway associations are absent from KEGG and no user-supplied Pathway/Metabolites table is available (EnrichMet fetches annotations at runtime from KEGG REST and does not ship database dumps) The goal is pathway-level enrichment significance only (Fisher's exact test / MetSEA), not topological hub ranking of individual metabolites http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Identifies hub metabolites by computing relative betweenness centrality (RBC) on a bipartite pathway–metabolite network built from KEGG annotations and the significant metabolites from a differential analysis, as demonstrated in the EnrichMet lung cancer case study. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.08.28.672951
skills.summary: Identifies hub metabolites by computing relative betweenness centrality (RBC) on a bipartite pathway–metabolite network built from KEGG annotations and the significant metabolites from a differential analysis, as demonstrated in the EnrichMet lung cancer case study.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No differential statistics exist, so there is no principled way to select significant metabolites (|FC| ≥ 1, adj p < 0.05) as query nodes for the centrality calculation The organism's metabolite–pathway associations are absent from KEGG and no user-supplied Pathway/Metabolites table is available (EnrichMet fetches annotations at runtime from KEGG REST and does not ship database dumps) The goal is pathway-level enrichment significance only (Fisher's exact test / MetSEA), not topological hub ranking of individual metabolites

skills.description: Use when comparing two MS/MS spectral matching strategies (e.g., longitudinal fragment profiles vs cross-sectional entropy) on annotation accuracy and FDR per mode, using ROC-derived thresholds and a labeled cohort like CKD plasma.
skills.name: metabolite-identification-accuracy-benchmarking
skills.search_text: metabolite-identification-accuracy-benchmarking Use when comparing two MS/MS spectral matching strategies (e.g., longitudinal fragment profiles vs cross-sectional entropy) on annotation accuracy and FDR per mode, using ROC-derived thresholds and a labeled cohort like CKD plasma. You have only raw MS/MS spectra and no per-mode annotation results or ground-truth labels — preprocess via 001-007.ipynb first (spectrum filtering, invalid fragment removal, CQMU database construction) before benchmarking. Your comparison is between database search engines (Progenesis QI, Compound Discoverer, MS-DIAL) rather than between spectral-matching scoring algorithms (Jaccard longitudinal vs optimal-entropy cross-sectional). You need to establish the identification thresholds themselves — this skill consumes the ROC-derived 0.5/0.75 thresholds, it does not derive them. Benchmarks metabolite annotation accuracy and false discovery rate of spectral matching methods — here longitudinal Jaccard-similarity profiling of multi-CE MS/MS fragments (0.5 threshold) versus cross-sectional optimal-entropy matching (0.75 threshold) — across ionization modes using a real plasma cohort. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c01414
skills.summary: Benchmarks metabolite annotation accuracy and false discovery rate of spectral matching methods — here longitudinal Jaccard-similarity profiling of multi-CE MS/MS fragments (0.5 threshold) versus cross-sectional optimal-entropy matching (0.75 threshold) — across ionization modes using a real plasma cohort.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have only raw MS/MS spectra and no per-mode annotation results or ground-truth labels — preprocess via 001-007.ipynb first (spectrum filtering, invalid fragment removal, CQMU database construction) before benchmarking. Your comparison is between database search engines (Progenesis QI, Compound Discoverer, MS-DIAL) rather than between spectral-matching scoring algorithms (Jaccard longitudinal vs optimal-entropy cross-sectional). You need to establish the identification thresholds themselves — this skill consumes the ROC-derived 0.5/0.75 thresholds, it does not derive them.

skills.description: Use when MS/MS spectra (MSP/MGF) remain unmatched to spectral libraries (e.g. ARUS spectra) and candidate compound annotations are needed, with formulas assigned (e.g. BUDDY) and a precursor m/z available for filtering.
skills.name: metabolite-identification-annotation
skills.search_text: metabolite-identification-annotation Use when MS/MS spectra (MSP/MGF) remain unmatched to spectral libraries (e.g. ARUS spectra) and candidate compound annotations are needed, with formulas assigned (e.g. BUDDY) and a precursor m/z available for filtering. The target compound is not in the 520,083-compound reference database — candidate matching can only return molecules in the database, regardless of spectral quality Only individual collision-energy spectra are available without the ability to merge scans per feature — training/prediction with individual CE spectra underperforms merged spectra and inflates sparsity You need de novo formula/structure inference rather than library-style candidate ranking against a fixed reference (e.g. use SIRIUS instead) http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Annotate previously unidentified MS/MS spectra by predicting 300-dimensional Mol2vec embeddings from merged, binarized spectra with pre-trained CNN models, then matching embeddings against a 520,083-compound reference database by cosine similarity with precursor-mass pre-filtering. This is the ChemEmbed pipeline demonstrated on the ARUS plasma/urine validation set, where expert review of top-5 candidates confirmed 24 compounds. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.02.07.637102
skills.summary: Annotate previously unidentified MS/MS spectra by predicting 300-dimensional Mol2vec embeddings from merged, binarized spectra with pre-trained CNN models, then matching embeddings against a 520,083-compound reference database by cosine similarity with precursor-mass pre-filtering. This is the ChemEmbed pipeline demonstrated on the ARUS plasma/urine validation set, where expert review of top-5 candidates confirmed 24 compounds.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The target compound is not in the 520,083-compound reference database — candidate matching can only return molecules in the database, regardless of spectral quality Only individual collision-energy spectra are available without the ability to merge scans per feature — training/prediction with individual CE spectra underperforms merged spectra and inflates sparsity You need de novo formula/structure inference rather than library-style candidate ranking against a fixed reference (e.g. use SIRIUS instead)

skills.description: Use when evaluating a spectral-to-structure ranking model on labeled test spectra (MSP) against a fixed reference compound library, to reproduce or compare top-k annotation accuracy metrics.
skills.name: metabolite-identification-benchmarking
skills.search_text: metabolite-identification-benchmarking Use when evaluating a spectral-to-structure ranking model on labeled test spectra (MSP) against a fixed reference compound library, to reproduce or compare top-k annotation accuracy metrics. Input is raw IMC/SIMS images rather than per-cell intensity tables — run the registration, segmentation, and intensity extraction notebooks (01–04) first. Protein and metabolite modalities are not registered to shared single cells — cross-modality registration (Histone 3/Intercalator in IMC, Phosphate 79 m/z in TOF-SIMS) is a prerequisite for per-cell metabolite projection. The goal is static cell-type metabolite comparison or spatial metabolite competition between neighboring cells rather than differentiation dynamics — use the metabolite region analysis (notebook 06) instead. Projects co-registered SIMS metabolite intensities onto diffusion pseudotime trajectories built from single-cell IMC protein phenotypes (scSpaMet notebook 08), revealing metabolic patterns along cell differentiation paths such as tonsil germinal-center B-cell maturation. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-023-43917-5

skills.name: metabolite-leakage-medium-enlargement
skills.search_text: metabolite-leakage-medium-enlargement Use when gap-filling multiple draft genome-scale metabolic models of a microbial community (e.g. consensus reconstructions from KBase, CarveMe, RAVEN 2.0, AuReMe/Pathway Tools) and you want the solution to respect community composition and metabolite leakage. Gap-filling a single organism's reconstruction with no community context — leak-mediated medium enlargement has no meaning and standard individual gap filling is appropriate. When the goal is whole-community optimization via joint FBA-style methods (e.g. SteadyCom, MICOM) rather than per-member gap-filling: COMMIT is designed for gap-filling draft reconstructions, not community simulation. When the draft models were not first normalized to MNXref identifiers and a common format — identifier mismatch across KBase/CarveMe/RAVEN/AuReMe outputs invalidates the shared medium and database. http://edamontology.org/topic_2259 http://edamontology.org/topic_3954 COMMIT's gap-filling strategy that enlarges the shared community medium with metabolites secreted by already gap-filled member reconstructions, so subsequent members can take up leaked metabolites instead of receiving extra gap-filling reactions. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009906
skills.summary: COMMIT's gap-filling strategy that enlarges the shared community medium with metabolites secreted by already gap-filled member reconstructions, so subsequent members can take up leaked metabolites instead of receiving extra gap-filling reactions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Gap-filling a single organism's reconstruction with no community context — leak-mediated medium enlargement has no meaning and standard individual gap filling is appropriate. When the goal is whole-community optimization via joint FBA-style methods (e.g. SteadyCom, MICOM) rather than per-member gap-filling: COMMIT is designed for gap-filling draft reconstructions, not community simulation. When the draft models were not first normalized to MNXref identifiers and a common format — identifier mismatch across KBase/CarveMe/RAVEN/AuReMe outputs invalidates the shared medium and database.

skills.description: Use when you need to evaluate whether an imputation method (e.g., KNN-TN, KNN-CR, KNN-EU, zero, minimum, mean) preserves the downstream significant-metabolite list from t-tests, by comparing it against the complete-data metabolite list via the MLCI.
skills.name: metabolite-list-concordance-index-calculation
skills.search_text: metabolite-list-concordance-index-calculation Use when you need to evaluate whether an imputation method (e.g., KNN-TN, KNN-CR, KNN-EU, zero, minimum, mean) preserves the downstream significant-metabolite list from t-tests, by comparing it against the complete-data metabolite list via the MLCI. Downstream analysis is not a two-group significance test on metabolite lists — the MLCI as defined here measures concordance of statistically significant metabolite lists, not prediction accuracy (use RMSE instead for imputation accuracy). Missing data exceed 75% per metabolite: the paper's cleaning process removes metabolites with >75% missing values before imputation, so such entries would not be part of the evaluated list in the first place. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0219 Computes the metabolite list concordance index (MLCI), a similarity metric comparing the list of statistically significant metabolites identified after imputation to the gold-standard list from the complete data, to quantify how well an imputation method preserves downstream testing conclusions. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-017-1547-6
skills.summary: Computes the metabolite list concordance index (MLCI), a similarity metric comparing the list of statistically significant metabolites identified after imputation to the gold-standard list from the complete data, to quantify how well an imputation method preserves downstream testing conclusions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Downstream analysis is not a two-group significance test on metabolite lists — the MLCI as defined here measures concordance of statistically significant metabolite lists, not prediction accuracy (use RMSE instead for imputation accuracy). Missing data exceed 75% per metabolite: the paper's cleaning process removes metabolites with >75% missing values before imputation, so such entries would not be part of the evaluated list in the first place.

skills.description: Use when pre-processing targeted full-scan MSI-CE-MS data in PeakMeister and you need to distinguish true analyte peaks from near-noise signals, particularly for low-abundance serum metabolites whose signal sits near the method detection limit.
skills.name: metabolite-lod-flagging
skills.search_text: metabolite-lod-flagging Use when pre-processing targeted full-scan MSI-CE-MS data in PeakMeister and you need to distinguish true analyte peaks from near-noise signals, particularly for low-abundance serum metabolites whose signal sits near the method detection limit. The analyte peaks are strong, well-resolved reference-standard signals — snr.threshold is meant for borderline analyte signals, not landmark peaks used for migration-index calculation, which require reliable and always-the-most-intense peak areas. Input is not targeted full-scan MSI-CE-MS data (e.g. HILIC LC-MS or non-multiplexed CE-MS runs); PeakMeister's peak-space and migration-index logic does not apply. The mzML files have not yet been peak-picked and annotated — <LOD flagging operates on identified analyte peaks, not raw extracted-ion traces. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Flag metabolite signals as below the limit of detection ("<LOD") within PeakMeister by computing the signal-to-noise ratio of each annotated analyte peak and applying the snr.threshold parameter, ensuring low-abundance MSI-CE-MS serum metabolites are not spuriously integrated or quantified. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c03513
skills.summary: Flag metabolite signals as below the limit of detection ("<LOD") within PeakMeister by computing the signal-to-noise ratio of each annotated analyte peak and applying the snr.threshold parameter, ensuring low-abundance MSI-CE-MS serum metabolites are not spuriously integrated or quantified.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analyte peaks are strong, well-resolved reference-standard signals — snr.threshold is meant for borderline analyte signals, not landmark peaks used for migration-index calculation, which require reliable and always-the-most-intense peak areas. Input is not targeted full-scan MSI-CE-MS data (e.g. HILIC LC-MS or non-multiplexed CE-MS runs); PeakMeister's peak-space and migration-index logic does not apply. The mzML files have not yet been peak-picked and annotated — <LOD flagging operates on identified analyte peaks, not raw extracted-ion traces.

skills.search_text: metabolite-mass-balance-penalty-minimization Use when time-course GC-MS metabolomics data (relative abundance concMatrix plus timeVec) are available for a single-compartment intracellular metabolic network, and absolute concentrations or response factors must be inferred without chemical standards. The sample is not intracellular single-compartment metabolomics — MetaboPAC assumes all metabolites are directly connected via reactions and does not consider transport reactions across intracellular compartments in eukaryotic systems Response factors are known to vary with concentration (nonlinear dynamic range or ion suppression), since MetaboPAC assumes response factors are constant with concentration The dataset has very high noise or substantial missing values that violate mass balances and complicate assessment of biological feasibility of response factors http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 A MetaboPAC-based optimization approach that infers metabolite response factors (and hence absolute concentrations) from relative abundance time-course GC-MS data by penalizing solutions that violate metabolic mass balances and other biological characteristics of the system, avoiding the need for chemical standards. metabolomics/v3 10.1039/d2mo00168c
skills.summary: A MetaboPAC-based optimization approach that infers metabolite response factors (and hence absolute concentrations) from relative abundance time-course GC-MS data by penalizing solutions that violate metabolic mass balances and other biological characteristics of the system, avoiding the need for chemical standards.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The sample is not intracellular single-compartment metabolomics — MetaboPAC assumes all metabolites are directly connected via reactions and does not consider transport reactions across intracellular compartments in eukaryotic systems Response factors are known to vary with concentration (nonlinear dynamic range or ion suppression), since MetaboPAC assumes response factors are constant with concentration The dataset has very high noise or substantial missing values that violate mass balances and complicate assessment of biological feasibility of response factors

skills.description: Use when you have only an unknown metabolite's exact mass (no MS/MS spectrum) and need to prioritize which DeepMet-sampled candidate structure most likely accounts for the observed mass spectrometric signal.
skills.name: metabolite-mass-filtering-by-exact-mass-tolerance
skills.search_text: metabolite-mass-filtering-by-exact-mass-tolerance Use when you have only an unknown metabolite's exact mass (no MS/MS spectrum) and need to prioritize which DeepMet-sampled candidate structure most likely accounts for the observed mass spectrometric signal. You already have MS/MS spectral data — the paper states that in that regime spectral matching and meta-learning integration should be used instead, and mass-only filtering alone is less informative. The unknown's mass was measured at accuracy far worse than ~10 ppm — the ±10 ppm window is the paper's operating point and a looser window will flood the candidate set. You are annotating metabolites from evolutionarily distant organisms (plants, bacteria) — the model generating the candidate database was trained only on human metabolite structures, so the candidate pool itself is out of domain. The candidate structure is not in the sampled database at all — DeepMet has inherent limits anticipating metabolites from divergent, undiscovered biosynthetic routes, and mass filtering cannot recover an unsampled structure. http://edamontology.org/topic_3292 http://edamontology.org/topic_0219 Filters a chemical language model's generated-structure database by exact monoisotopic mass within a narrow ppm tolerance of an unidentified metabolite's mass, then ranks surviving candidates by sampling frequency so that the most frequently sampled structure becomes the top-1 annotation prior. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.11.13.623458
skills.summary: Filters a chemical language model's generated-structure database by exact monoisotopic mass within a narrow ppm tolerance of an unidentified metabolite's mass, then ranks surviving candidates by sampling frequency so that the most frequently sampled structure becomes the top-1 annotation prior.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You already have MS/MS spectral data — the paper states that in that regime spectral matching and meta-learning integration should be used instead, and mass-only filtering alone is less informative. The unknown's mass was measured at accuracy far worse than ~10 ppm — the ±10 ppm window is the paper's operating point and a looser window will flood the candidate set. You are annotating metabolites from evolutionarily distant organisms (plants, bacteria) — the model generating the candidate database was trained only on human metabolite structures, so the candidate pool itself is out of domain. The candidate structure is not in the sampled database at all — DeepMet has inherent limits anticipating metabolites from divergent, undiscovered biosynthetic routes, and mass filtering cannot recover an unsampled structure.

skills.name: metabolite-mass-shift-calculation
skills.search_text: metabolite-mass-shift-calculation Use when you need theoretical derivative m/z values for metabolites reacted with a derivatizing matrix (AMPP, FMP-10, or a custom reagent) and the reagent's mass shift per reactive site, e.g., for dopamine, GABA, spermidine panels. The input is already measured MALDI-MSI m/z features needing annotation against a database — use Met-ID's identify() workflow with recalibration and MS2 comparison instead of computing theoretical shifts The metabolites are underivatized and expected to ionize as standard [M+H]+ / [M-H]- adducts with no derivatizing matrix involved The reagent's reactive functional group or per-site mass shift is unknown and cannot be defined — substructure matching and shift addition cannot proceed Computes theoretical derivative m/z values by enumerating derivatization-reactive functional groups (e.g., amines) on a metabolite's SMILES and applying one reagent mass shift (e.g., AMPP, FMP-10) per reactive site, extending Met-ID beyond its preconfigured FMP-10 setup. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c00633
skills.summary: Computes theoretical derivative m/z values by enumerating derivatization-reactive functional groups (e.g., amines) on a metabolite's SMILES and applying one reagent mass shift (e.g., AMPP, FMP-10) per reactive site, extending Met-ID beyond its preconfigured FMP-10 setup.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already measured MALDI-MSI m/z features needing annotation against a database — use Met-ID's identify() workflow with recalibration and MS2 comparison instead of computing theoretical shifts The metabolites are underivatized and expected to ionize as standard [M+H]+ / [M-H]- adducts with no derivatizing matrix involved The reagent's reactive functional group or per-site mass shift is unknown and cannot be defined — substructure matching and shift addition cannot proceed

skills.search_text: metabolite-molecular-state-bookkeeping Use when starting CCS prediction from SMILES inputs of metabolites and you must enumerate all relevant ionization states (protonated, deprotonated, neutral) before conformation generation, ensuring agreement tables and consensus errors are attributed to the correct molecular state. Input is already a processed CCS table where the molecular state has been assigned — re-running state enumeration would duplicate or overwrite prior assignments. You need TWIMS drift-time calibration or arrival-time conversion rather than state enumeration; that belongs to the TWIMS validation steps (Tables S1 and S2), not this bookkeeping step. Your target molecules are outside the CHNO scope handled by the ANI potentials used for conformation filtering (ASE-ANI covers CHNO elements), since state enumeration would produce species the downstream filtering cannot process. http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 http://edamontology.org/topic_3335 Enumerate the possible protonated/deprotonated/neutral molecular states of each metabolite (e.g. [M + H]+ or [M − H]−) so that downstream CCS calculations are performed per state and can be matched to the correct ion species during benchmarking against TWIMS and literature values. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jasms.1c00315

skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a processed CCS table where the molecular state has been assigned — re-running state enumeration would duplicate or overwrite prior assignments.
