It serves as the unfiltered baseline that chemical-class methods such as NPClassScore are designed to prune.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is already class-matched, prioritised links — apply NPClassScore filtering (cut-off 0.25) on top of the Metcalf results instead of stopping at co-occurrence When no strain-level mapping between genomes and metabolomics samples is available, since co-occurrence scoring requires paired occurrence profiles When validated links are known to have low standardised Metcalf scores (e.g. the Nocardia dataset, where the threshold had to be lowered from 2.5 to 2)

skills.description: Use when linking AntiSMASH/BigScape-derived GCFs to GNPS molecular families by strain co-occurrence, or when raw Metcalf scores must be standardised against a null to compare links across GCFs and MFs of different sizes.
skills.name: metcalf-strain-correlation-scoring
skills.search_text: metcalf-strain-correlation-scoring Use when linking AntiSMASH/BigScape-derived GCFs to GNPS molecular families by strain co-occurrence, or when raw Metcalf scores must be standardised against a null to compare links across GCFs and MFs of different sizes. The spectra or genomes cannot be assigned to shared strains — strain co-occurrence vectors cannot be built and Metcalf scoring is undefined The analysis needs sequence-homology-based prioritisation against known BGCs (e.g. MIBiG homology plus IOKR) rather than strain co-occurrence — use the combined/IOKR scoring route instead of raw Metcalf alone Molecular networking input is not GNPS molecular networking data or the GCF clustering has not been produced from AntiSMASH BGC regions http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_3398 Computes strain co-occurrence correlation (Metcalf-style) scores between gene cluster families (GCFs) and molecular families (MFs) in NPLinker, then standardises each raw score against its hypergeometric null expectation to remove dependence on GCF and MF sizes, enabling fair comparison and prioritisation of GCF–MF links. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008920
skills.summary: Computes strain co-occurrence correlation (Metcalf-style) scores between gene cluster families (GCFs) and molecular families (MFs) in NPLinker, then standardises each raw score against its hypergeometric null expectation to remove dependence on GCF and MF sizes, enabling fair comparison and prioritisation of GCF–MF links.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The spectra or genomes cannot be assigned to shared strains — strain co-occurrence vectors cannot be built and Metcalf scoring is undefined The analysis needs sequence-homology-based prioritisation against known BGCs (e.g. MIBiG homology plus IOKR) rather than strain co-occurrence — use the combined/IOKR scoring route instead of raw Metcalf alone Molecular networking input is not GNPS molecular networking data or the GCF clustering has not been produced from AntiSMASH BGC regions

skills.description: Use when you have MetFrag candidate scores for each node in a spectral molecular network plus spectral cosine similarity between connected nodes, and you need to build a weighted graph for ChemWalker random-walk propagation.
skills.name: metfrag-annotation-score-averaging
skills.search_text: metfrag-annotation-score-averaging Use when you have MetFrag candidate scores for each node in a spectral molecular network plus spectral cosine similarity between connected nodes, and you need to build a weighted graph for ChemWalker random-walk propagation. You only have a single node's MetFrag candidates and no molecular network edges — MetFusion edge weighting requires pairs of connected nodes Spectral library has already confidently annotated the nodes and no in silico candidate expansion is needed — direct annotation needs no edge weighting Your graph edges are negative or zero-weighted — pyrwr's RWR only accepts positively weighted networks, so MetFusion-style weights must be rescaled first http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 Aggregate per-candidate MetFrag in silico fragmentation scores across connected molecular-network nodes into edge weights using the MetFusion-style alpha-weighted fusion of averaged MetFrag scores, spectral cosine similarity, and structural (chemical) similarity, producing a weighted graph for downstream random-walk annotation propagation. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad078
skills.summary: Aggregate per-candidate MetFrag in silico fragmentation scores across connected molecular-network nodes into edge weights using the MetFusion-style alpha-weighted fusion of averaged MetFrag scores, spectral cosine similarity, and structural (chemical) similarity, producing a weighted graph for downstream random-walk annotation propagation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only have a single node's MetFrag candidates and no molecular network edges — MetFusion edge weighting requires pairs of connected nodes Spectral library has already confidently annotated the nodes and no in silico candidate expansion is needed — direct annotation needs no edge weighting Your graph edges are negative or zero-weighted — pyrwr's RWR only accepts positively weighted networks, so MetFusion-style weights must be rescaled first

skills.description: Use when building the weighted molecular-network graph for ChemWalker propagation: you have MetFrag in silico fragmentation results for candidates of each network node, pairwise spectral cosine scores from library matching or network edges, and structural (chemical) similarity between candidate.
skills.name: metfusion-fusion-weight-function-implementation
skills.search_text: metfusion-fusion-weight-function-implementation Use when building the weighted molecular-network graph for ChemWalker propagation: you have MetFrag in silico fragmentation results for candidates of each network node, pairwise spectral cosine scores from library matching or network edges, and structural (chemical) similarity between candidate. The graph edges are already weighted by a different scheme and you only need to run the random walk; this skill is specifically the MetFusion-based weight construction step. You lack MetFrag candidate scores or structural similarity between candidate pairs — the weight function requires all three signal sources (MetFrag score, spectral cosine, chemical similarity) to combine. The goal is NAP-style local propagation only to first neighbors of spectral matches; ChemWalker's weighted-graph random walk is intended to expand propagation beyond directly connected nodes. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 Implementation of the MetFusion-derived Fusion weight function that combines MetFrag candidate scores, spectral cosine similarity, and chemical similarity of candidate structures into edge weights for the ChemWalker weighted graph. This weighted graphml is the substrate the ChemWalker random walk operates on, so correct edge weighting determines which annotations propagate. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad078
skills.summary: Implementation of the MetFusion-derived Fusion weight function that combines MetFrag candidate scores, spectral cosine similarity, and chemical similarity of candidate structures into edge weights for the ChemWalker weighted graph. This weighted graphml is the substrate the ChemWalker random walk operates on, so correct edge weighting determines which annotations propagate.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The graph edges are already weighted by a different scheme and you only need to run the random walk; this skill is specifically the MetFusion-based weight construction step. You lack MetFrag candidate scores or structural similarity between candidate pairs — the weight function requires all three signal sources (MetFrag score, spectral cosine, chemical similarity) to combine. The goal is NAP-style local propagation only to first neighbors of spectral matches; ChemWalker's weighted-graph random walk is intended to expand propagation beyond directly connected nodes.

skills.description: Decision support for building a ChemWalker-style weighted graph when you have a spectral network plus in silico fragmentation candidate lists (MetFrag results) and need edge weights that fuse spectral and structural similarity before random-walk propagation.
skills.name: metfusion-weighted-graph-construction
skills.search_text: metfusion-weighted-graph-construction Decision support for building a ChemWalker-style weighted graph when you have a spectral network plus in silico fragmentation candidate lists (MetFrag results) and need edge weights that fuse spectral and structural similarity before random-walk propagation. The goal is NAP-style local propagation only to first neighbors of spectral matches — ChemWalker's MetFusion-weighted graph plus random walk targets propagation to nodes not directly connected to spectral matches. No in silico fragmentation candidate lists are available, so structural similarity among candidates cannot be fused with the spectral network via the MetFusion scoring function. The graph contains zero or negative weights — pyrwr's RWR is defined only on positively weighted networks. Construct a weighted graph for annotation propagation by combining a spectral (molecular) network with structural similarity among candidate structures using the MetFusion scoring function as the weight function, as implemented in ChemWalker. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad078
skills.summary: Construct a weighted graph for annotation propagation by combining a spectral (molecular) network with structural similarity among candidate structures using the MetFusion scoring function as the weight function, as implemented in ChemWalker.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is NAP-style local propagation only to first neighbors of spectral matches — ChemWalker's MetFusion-weighted graph plus random walk targets propagation to nodes not directly connected to spectral matches. No in silico fragmentation candidate lists are available, so structural similarity among candidates cannot be fused with the spectral network via the MetFusion scoring function. The graph contains zero or negative weights — pyrwr's RWR is defined only on positively weighted networks.

skills.description: Use when a multi-platform metabolomics study reports a standards table with per-method detection flags (checkmark/cross plus RT/MT ± sd) and you must quantify how many metabolites each method or method combination covers.
skills.name: method-coverage-count-computation
skills.search_text: method-coverage-count-computation Use when a multi-platform metabolomics study reports a standards table with per-method detection flags (checkmark/cross plus RT/MT ± sd) and you must quantify how many metabolites each method or method combination covers. Input is already a processed feature table or abundance matrix rather than a per-method detection/standards table — coverage counting from flags does not apply Single-platform datasets where no combination coverage (HILIC vs CE vs all five) can be computed Yeast sample feature augmentation or chemometric evaluation tasks — use the AriumMS ROI/augmentation pipeline instead of coverage counting http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Computes per-method and per-method-combination detection coverage of a metabolite standard mixture across multi-platform LC-MS/CE-MS methods (e.g., HILIC-MS ESI+/ESI− plus three CE-MS methods), yielding counts such as 30/36 (HILIC combined), 32/36 (CE combined), and 36/36 (all five methods). metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s00216-023-04715-6
skills.summary: Computes per-method and per-method-combination detection coverage of a metabolite standard mixture across multi-platform LC-MS/CE-MS methods (e.g., HILIC-MS ESI+/ESI− plus three CE-MS methods), yielding counts such as 30/36 (HILIC combined), 32/36 (CE combined), and 36/36 (all five methods).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a processed feature table or abundance matrix rather than a per-method detection/standards table — coverage counting from flags does not apply Single-platform datasets where no combination coverage (HILIC vs CE vs all five) can be computed Yeast sample feature augmentation or chemometric evaluation tasks — use the AriumMS ROI/augmentation pipeline instead of coverage counting

skills.search_text: method-parameterized-spectra-transformation Use when a 1H-NMR spectra DataFrame (columns = chemical shifts in ppm, rows = samples) shows baseline distortions from incomplete relaxation, pulse sequence imperfections, magnetic field inhomogeneities, solvent effects, phase errors, or macromolecules. Input is still raw FID or pre-phase-correction data — baseline_correction is positioned after phase_correction and internal_referencing in the Protomix pipeline (ph_df -> ir_df -> bc_df) The spectra DataFrame is already baseline-corrected and the goal is peak alignment (px.Icoshift) or binning (px.binning) — those are separate downstream Protomix steps Input is not 1H-NMR spectra but a binned/statistical feature table — this skill operates on spectra matrices with ppm chemical-shift columns Apply Protomix's baseline_correction function to 1H-NMR spectra using a method-string parameter that selects between asymmetric least squares (ALS), adaptive reweighted penalized least squares (ARPLS), and automatic iterative reweighted penalized least squares (AIRPLS), all adapted from the pyBaselines package. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioadv/vbae192
skills.summary: Apply Protomix's baseline_correction function to 1H-NMR spectra using a method-string parameter that selects between asymmetric least squares (ALS), adaptive reweighted penalized least squares (ARPLS), and automatic iterative reweighted penalized least squares (AIRPLS), all adapted from the pyBaselines package.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is still raw FID or pre-phase-correction data — baseline_correction is positioned after phase_correction and internal_referencing in the Protomix pipeline (ph_df -> ir_df -> bc_df) The spectra DataFrame is already baseline-corrected and the goal is peak alignment (px.Icoshift) or binning (px.binning) — those are separate downstream Protomix steps Input is not 1H-NMR spectra but a binned/statistical feature table — this skill operates on spectra matrices with ppm chemical-shift columns

skills.description: Use when a buccal DNA methylation matrix (Infinium MethylationEPIC betas) must be reduced to its most variable autosomal probes as a preprocessing view for unsupervised multi-omics integration.
skills.name: methylation-probe-variability-filtering
skills.search_text: methylation-probe-variability-filtering Use when a buccal DNA methylation matrix (Infinium MethylationEPIC betas) must be reduced to its most variable autosomal probes as a preprocessing view for unsupervised multi-omics integration. The methylation matrix is the input for probe-level QC or annotation (e.g. retrieving the Infinium MethylationEPIC product file) rather than feature selection prior to factor analysis. The downstream method requires all probes or a fixed CpG panel rather than a variability-ranked subset (e.g. replication on preselected DMRs). Data are not methylation betas (e.g. the urine metabolomics view, which is instead filtered by 15% missing-value thresholds and creatinine normalization). http://edamontology.org/topic_3295 http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 Reduces a DNA methylation beta-value matrix to the top 10% most variable autosomal probes before multi-omics factor analysis, so that MOFA2 runs on a tractable, information-rich probe set rather than the full 787,711-probe QC-surviving EPIC array. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/gigascience/giad115
skills.summary: Reduces a DNA methylation beta-value matrix to the top 10% most variable autosomal probes before multi-omics factor analysis, so that MOFA2 runs on a tractable, information-rich probe set rather than the full 787,711-probe QC-surviving EPIC array.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The methylation matrix is the input for probe-level QC or annotation (e.g. retrieving the Infinium MethylationEPIC product file) rather than feature selection prior to factor analysis. Data are not methylation betas (e.g. the urine metabolomics view, which is instead filtered by 15% missing-value thresholds and creatinine normalization).

skills.name: metid-databaseclass-object-construction

skills.description: Use when two or more untargeted LC-HRMS batches must be combined into one data matrix and the target peaks show m/z and/or retention time shifts relative to a reference feature list, or when reference and target represent different ion adducts of the same metabolites.
skills.name: metmatch-alignment-configuration
skills.search_text: metmatch-alignment-configuration Use when two or more untargeted LC-HRMS batches must be combined into one data matrix and the target peaks show m/z and/or retention time shifts relative to a reference feature list, or when reference and target represent different ion adducts of the same metabolites. Data is still raw LC-HRMS signal — MetMatch aligns processed feature lists (m/z + retention time), not unprocessed chromatograms Only a very small number of common feature groups between reference and target is available (reliability degrades; F-measure >0.9 requires >=89 groups in the reported experiments) The task is peak picking or feature deconvolution rather than aligning/comparing already-processed feature lists across experiments http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Configure and run MetMatch to align LC-HRMS chromatographic peak lists from untargeted metabolomics experiments against a reference feature list, correcting both m/z and retention time shifts and accounting for differently formed ion species of detected metabolites. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo6040039
skills.summary: Configure and run MetMatch to align LC-HRMS chromatographic peak lists from untargeted metabolomics experiments against a reference feature list, correcting both m/z and retention time shifts and accounting for differently formed ion species of detected metabolites.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data is still raw LC-HRMS signal — MetMatch aligns processed feature lists (m/z + retention time), not unprocessed chromatograms Only a very small number of common feature groups between reference and target is available (reliability degrades; F-measure >0.9 requires >=89 groups in the reported experiments) The task is peak picking or feature deconvolution rather than aligning/comparing already-processed feature lists across experiments

skills.description: Use when multiple peak quality metrics computed on curated good/bad LC/MS peaks must be brought to a common scale, clustered across representative peaks, and ranked by maximum F-Score to identify which metrics are most discriminative.
skills.name: metric-clustering-normalization
skills.search_text: metric-clustering-normalization Use when multiple peak quality metrics computed on curated good/bad LC/MS peaks must be brought to a common scale, clustered across representative peaks, and ranked by maximum F-Score to identify which metrics are most discriminative. Evaluating whole extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) rather than individual detected peaks — the paper handles that with the MCQ index and the EIC-related global zigzag index, not these six peak metrics EICs with high background signals or containing only a single peak — the MCQ index cannot fairly evaluate these scenarios, so peak-metric normalization on such inputs is not meaningful Input is already a normalized feature matrix or clustering result; re-normalizing to [-1, 1] by mean-subtraction/max-division would distort existing scales http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Normalizes chromatographic peak quality metrics (sharpness, Gaussian similarity, SNR, peak significance level, TPASR, local zigzag index) to a common [-1, 1] range and clusters/ranks them to determine which metrics best discriminate good from bad LC/MS peaks. Grounded in the BMC Bioinformatics 2014 evaluation showing sharpness, peak significance level, and the zigzag index outperform the others. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/1471-2105-15-s11-s5
skills.summary: Normalizes chromatographic peak quality metrics (sharpness, Gaussian similarity, SNR, peak significance level, TPASR, local zigzag index) to a common [-1, 1] range and clusters/ranks them to determine which metrics best discriminate good from bad LC/MS peaks. Grounded in the BMC Bioinformatics 2014 evaluation showing sharpness, peak significance level, and the zigzag index outperform the others.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Evaluating whole extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) rather than individual detected peaks — the paper handles that with the MCQ index and the EIC-related global zigzag index, not these six peak metrics EICs with high background signals or containing only a single peak — the MCQ index cannot fairly evaluate these scenarios, so peak-metric normalization on such inputs is not meaningful Input is already a normalized feature matrix or clustering result; re-normalizing to [-1, 1] by mean-subtraction/max-division would distort existing scales

skills.description: Use when evaluating whether a chromatogram quality metric (e.g. MCQ, zigzag index, sharpness, SNR) is fair across EICs with high background signals, single-peak EICs, or zigzag-contaminated profiles, and you need an evidence-based robustness verdict per scenario.
skills.name: metric-robustness-comparison-across-chromatogram-scenarios
skills.search_text: metric-robustness-comparison-across-chromatogram-scenarios Use when evaluating whether a chromatogram quality metric (e.g. MCQ, zigzag index, sharpness, SNR) is fair across EICs with high background signals, single-peak EICs, or zigzag-contaminated profiles, and you need an evidence-based robustness verdict per scenario. When the input is raw centroided profile data not yet reduced to extracted ion chromatograms — EIC extraction and peak detection are prerequisites handled by a different module When you only need an absolute quality cutoff for filtering a large peak list (e.g. cutoff threshold tuning for Recall/Precision/F-Score) rather than a cross-scenario robustness comparison of metric definitions http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Compare candidate chromatogram/peak quality metrics side-by-side on representative EICs spanning easy and hard scenarios (high background, single peak, zigzag noise) to establish which metric is robust across all of them. Grounded in the MCQ vs. global zigzag index contrast from Zhang & Zhao's LC/MS metabolomics quality-evaluation study. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/1471-2105-15-s11-s5
skills.summary: Compare candidate chromatogram/peak quality metrics side-by-side on representative EICs spanning easy and hard scenarios (high background, single peak, zigzag noise) to establish which metric is robust across all of them. Grounded in the MCQ vs. global zigzag index contrast from Zhang & Zhao's LC/MS metabolomics quality-evaluation study.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is raw centroided profile data not yet reduced to extracted ion chromatograms — EIC extraction and peak detection are prerequisites handled by a different module When you only need an absolute quality cutoff for filtering a large peak list (e.g. cutoff threshold tuning for Recall/Precision/F-Score) rather than a cross-scenario robustness comparison of metric definitions

skills.search_text: mgf-ms2-spectra-loading-and-filtering Use when input is .mgf MS2 spectra per sample (e.g. a GNPS/FBMN job export) and you need retention-time-agnostic sample fingerprints from counted peaks and losses instead of RT-aligned feature tables. skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already an RT-aligned feature table from FBMN/MZmine — MEMO's benefit is bypassing feature alignment, so re-vectorizing an aligned table adds nothing Samples share strong feature overlap and were acquired on the same LC-MS platform with no RT shift — standard feature-based metrics may suffice and MEMO's word-count fingerprint loses intensity information Spectra have fewer than 10 peaks (min_peaks_required=10) or lack precursor mass needed to compute losses_from=10 to losses_to=200 — documents will be degenerate or empty

skills.description: Use when starting from Thermo RAW (or mzML/mzXML) LC-HRMS2 DDA files that must be converted into a feature quantification table plus per-feature MS2 .mgf spectra for each sample individually, before annotation or molecular networking.
skills.name: mgf-spectra-export
skills.search_text: mgf-spectra-export Use when starting from Thermo RAW (or mzML/mzXML) LC-HRMS2 DDA files that must be converted into a feature quantification table plus per-feature MS2 .mgf spectra for each sample individually, before annotation or molecular networking. Input is already a feature quantification table or .mgf spectra file (feature detection and export have already been done). The analysis goal requires a classical data set-centric RT/m/z feature alignment across all samples rather than per-sample processing — ENPKG deliberately processes each sample individually. Data were not acquired as LC-HRMS2 DDA (e.g. DIA or direct infusion), since the noise thresholds (1.0E4 MS1, 0 MS2) and MS2-scan filter assume DDA spectra. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Per-sample MZmine feature detection and export of deconvoluted LC-HRMS2 features plus their MS2 spectra as .mgf files (via the 'Export to GNPS' module), so downstream spectral matching (matchms-based ISDB) and molecular networking steps can consume them. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acscentsci.3c00800
skills.summary: Per-sample MZmine feature detection and export of deconvoluted LC-HRMS2 features plus their MS2 spectra as .mgf files (via the 'Export to GNPS' module), so downstream spectral matching (matchms-based ISDB) and molecular networking steps can consume them.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a feature quantification table or .mgf spectra file (feature detection and export have already been done). The analysis goal requires a classical data set-centric RT/m/z feature alignment across all samples rather than per-sample processing — ENPKG deliberately processes each sample individually. skills.search_text: mgf-spectra-file-handling Use when LC-MS/MS acquisitions (e.g. serum or food/feed samples) are exported as MGF files and the goal is direct tandem-spectrum comparison — phylogenetics, species identification, or dataset QC — before any database search. When sequence databases or spectral libraries are available and the goal is peptide/protein identification — that is the database-search or spectral-library-search branch of the tool taxonomy, not direct spectral comparison. When only a single MGF file is available and no reference set exists for spectra2species or phylogenetic comparison. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Prepare and supply MGF-format tandem mass spectrometry datasets as direct input to compareMS2 2.0, where pairwise spectral similarity is computed without prior peptide identification. Correct MGF handling is a prerequisite for reconstructing phylogenetic trees and QC/heatmap visualizations from LC-MS/MS data. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.2c00457
skills.summary: Prepare and supply MGF-format tandem mass spectrometry datasets as direct input to compareMS2 2.0, where pairwise spectral similarity is computed without prior peptide identification. Correct MGF handling is a prerequisite for reconstructing phylogenetic trees and QC/heatmap visualizations from LC-MS/MS data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When sequence databases or spectral libraries are available and the goal is peptide/protein identification — that is the database-search or spectral-library-search branch of the tool taxonomy, not direct spectral comparison. When the input is already processed (e.g. a feature table or identified-peptide list) rather than raw MGF tandem spectra — compareMS2 operates on the spectral content itself. When only a single MGF file is available and no reference set exists for spectra2species or phylogenetic comparison.

skills.description: Use when an NPLinker-based integrative omics workflow needs MS/MS spectra read from a GNPS molecular networking MGF file, e.g. as the input for CANOPUS class prediction on spectra below 850 Da.
skills.name: mgf-spectra-file-parsing
skills.search_text: mgf-spectra-file-parsing Use when an NPLinker-based integrative omics workflow needs MS/MS spectra read from a GNPS molecular networking MGF file, e.g. as the input for CANOPUS class prediction on spectra below 850 Da. When the spectra of interest are above 850 Da: the 850 Da mass cut-off is applied because CANOPUS fragmentation-tree calculation is time-consuming, and other methods like Spec2Vec or MS2DeepScore may be better suited for larger metabolites When MolNetEnhancer-based class propagation is required instead: MolNetEnhancer has to be run externally (e.g. on the GNPS platform) rather than within NPLinker When the MGF is not GNPS molecular networking output: NPLinker integrates molecular networking through GNPS specifically http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Loads and parses the spectra.mgf file produced by GNPS molecular networking (from the gnps directory of the NPLinker working directory) so downstream tools such as SIRIUS/CANOPUS can consume the MS/MS spectra for structure-based ClassyFire and NPClassifier class prediction. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s40168-022-01444-3
skills.summary: Loads and parses the spectra.mgf file produced by GNPS molecular networking (from the gnps directory of the NPLinker working directory) so downstream tools such as SIRIUS/CANOPUS can consume the MS/MS spectra for structure-based ClassyFire and NPClassifier class prediction.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the spectra of interest are above 850 Da: the 850 Da mass cut-off is applied because CANOPUS fragmentation-tree calculation is time-consuming, and other methods like Spec2Vec or MS2DeepScore may be better suited for larger metabolites When MolNetEnhancer-based class propagation is required instead: MolNetEnhancer has to be run externally (e.g. on the GNPS platform) rather than within NPLinker When the MGF is not GNPS molecular networking output: NPLinker integrates molecular networking through GNPS specifically

skills.search_text: mgf-spectra-fragment-filtering Use when assembling experimental MS/MS benchmarking sets from GNPS or third-party .mgf spectral libraries, and noisy, oversized, or adduct-mixed spectra must be normalized before annotation-tool evaluation. Input spectra are query features from sample profiling (e.g., MZmine feature MS2 scans) rather than reference library entries — the ≥6-fragment/500-peak and [M+H]+ criteria were designed for benchmarking set construction, not feature tables The analysis requires mixed adducts ([M+Na]+, [M-H]-) or spectra below 100 Da / above 1,500 Da parent mass — these entries are deliberately excluded by this filtering Spectral libraries have already been peak-count-filtered and deduplicated by first-layer InChIKey; re-applying risks redundant processing without changing results http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Filters concatenated GNPS spectral library .mgf files for metabolite-annotation benchmarking by retaining spectra with at least 6 fragments, keeping only the 500 most intense peaks in larger spectra, and retaining [M+H]+ entries with parent masses between 100 and 1,500 Da. metabolomics/v3 10.3389/fpls.2019.01329
skills.summary: Filters concatenated GNPS spectral library .mgf files for metabolite-annotation benchmarking by retaining spectra with at least 6 fragments, keeping only the 500 most intense peaks in larger spectra, and retaining [M+H]+ entries with parent masses between 100 and 1,500 Da.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra are query features from sample profiling (e.g., MZmine feature MS2 scans) rather than reference library entries — the ≥6-fragment/500-peak and [M+H]+ criteria were designed for benchmarking set construction, not feature tables The analysis requires mixed adducts ([M+Na]+, [M-H]-) or spectra below 100 Da / above 1,500 Da parent mass — these entries are deliberately excluded by this filtering Spectral libraries have already been peak-count-filtered and deduplicated by first-layer InChIKey; re-applying risks redundant processing without changing results

skills.description: Use when MS2 peak data lives as a Python object (e.g., a matchms.Spectrum loaded from MGF) but the analysis runs in R with Spectra, and you need lazy, on-demand access to peaks without duplicating data across languages.

skills.search_text: mgf-spectra-handling Use when MS2 peak data lives as a Python object (e.g., a matchms.Spectrum loaded from MGF) but the analysis runs in R with Spectra, and you need lazy, on-demand access to peaks without duplicating data across languages. The spectra are already fully available as an R Spectra object in memory (e.g., MsBackendDataFrame/MsBackendMemory) — lazy Python bridging adds reticulate overhead with no benefit The workflow is purely Python-side; matchms can access the MGF Spectrum directly without any R/SpectriPy involvement Custom RETICULATE_PYTHON or RETICULATE_PYTHON_ENV is set but the required Python libraries (matchms 0.31, spectrum_utils 0.3.2, numpy 2.2.0) are not installed — reticulate will not auto-install them and loading will fail http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Handles MGF-derived MS2 spectra across R and Python without copying peak data, using SpectriPy's MsBackendPy backend so an R Spectra::Spectra object references a Python-side matchms.Spectrum object and translates m/z and intensity values on-the-fly only when subsets are requested. metabolomics/v3 10.21105/joss.08070
skills.summary: Handles MGF-derived MS2 spectra across R and Python without copying peak data, using SpectriPy's MsBackendPy backend so an R Spectra::Spectra object references a Python-side matchms.Spectrum object and translates m/z and intensity values on-the-fly only when subsets are requested.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The spectra are already fully available as an R Spectra object in memory (e.g., MsBackendDataFrame/MsBackendMemory) — lazy Python bridging adds reticulate overhead with no benefit The workflow is purely Python-side; matchms can access the MGF Spectrum directly without any R/SpectriPy involvement Custom RETICULATE_PYTHON or RETICULATE_PYTHON_ENV is set but the required Python libraries (matchms 0.31, spectrum_utils 0.3.2, numpy 2.2.0) are not installed — reticulate will not auto-install them and loading will fail

Input is already a feature table (CSV) without fragment spectra — use MS1 m/z-based matching (matchMz) instead Data are raw vendor/mzML files requiring peak detection first — the MGF import path assumes spectra already processed by an external tool such as MZmine The reference library provides precursor m/z and requirePrecursor = TRUE filtering is intended — this skill's example disables precursor filtering because HMDB lacks precursor m/z http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Imports externally exported MS2 spectra files (e.g. MZmine or MS-DIAL GNPS-exported MGF) into R as a Spectra object using MsBackendMgf, so they can serve as query spectra for matchSpectra()-based MS2 annotation. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo12020173
skills.summary: Imports externally exported MS2 spectra files (e.g. MZmine or MS-DIAL GNPS-exported MGF) into R as a Spectra object using MsBackendMgf, so they can serve as query spectra for matchSpectra()-based MS2 annotation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a feature table (CSV) without fragment spectra — use MS1 m/z-based matching (matchMz) instead Data are raw vendor/mzML files requiring peak detection first — the MGF import path assumes spectra already processed by an external tool such as MZmine The reference library provides precursor m/z and requirePrecursor = TRUE filtering is intended — this skill's example disables precursor filtering because HMDB lacks precursor m/z

Data come from LC-separated (chromatographic) runs rather than direct-injection, time-resolved plasma ionization datasets for which DBDIpy is tailored. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Imports raw MS1 spectra from open file formats (.mgf, .mzML, .mzXML) via matchms.importing and aligns them into a 2D pandas feature DataFrame with DBDIpy.align_spectra(), the entry point of the DBDIpy plasma-ionization (DBDI-MS) processing workflow. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad088

skills.description: Use when you have ms1-id-derived pseudo MS/MS spectra from full-scan LC-MS (e.g. HILIC-positive mzML from Metabolomics Workbench PR000639) that must be reformatted into a cleaned MGF for GNPS2 molecular networking.
skills.name: mgf-spectral-file-preparation
skills.search_text: mgf-spectral-file-preparation Use when you have ms1-id-derived pseudo MS/MS spectra from full-scan LC-MS (e.g. HILIC-positive mzML from Metabolomics Workbench PR000639) that must be reformatted into a cleaned MGF for GNPS2 molecular networking. Input is already MS/MS data (real tandem spectra collected by the instrument) — no precursor-m/z cleaning of pseudo spectra is needed. The downstream tool expects raw mzML/mzXML/imzML for ms1-id annotation (ms1_id lcms/msi modes) rather than an MGF for networking. The pseudo spectra will not be used for modified-cosine networking — e.g. when only doing reverse spectral matching, where fragment peaks above the precursor are handled by the precursor-tolerant search. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Prepare pseudo MS/MS spectra (generated by ms1-id from MS1-only full-scan data) for GNPS2 classical molecular networking by cleaning each feature's spectrum to peaks at or below its precursor m/z and writing all spectra into a single MGF file. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.10.14.618269
skills.summary: Prepare pseudo MS/MS spectra (generated by ms1-id from MS1-only full-scan data) for GNPS2 classical molecular networking by cleaning each feature's spectrum to peaks at or below its precursor m/z and writing all spectra into a single MGF file.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already MS/MS data (real tandem spectra collected by the instrument) — no precursor-m/z cleaning of pseudo spectra is needed. The downstream tool expects raw mzML/mzXML/imzML for ms1-id annotation (ms1_id lcms/msi modes) rather than an MGF for networking. The pseudo spectra will not be used for modified-cosine networking — e.g. when only doing reverse spectral matching, where fragment peaks above the precursor are handled by the precursor-tolerant search.

skills.search_text: mgf-spectrum-file-formatting Use when pseudo MS/MS spectra have been generated from MS1-only LC-MS or MS imaging data and need to be written as MGF entries containing precursor feature m/z, peaks, and retention time/pixel metadata for annotation. skills.description: Use when raw vendor MS/MS files (e.g. from PRIDE or MassIVE antibody data sets) must be reformatted into an open, text-based spectral format as input for de novo peptide sequencing or database-search tools.
skills.name: mgf-spectrum-format-generation
skills.search_text: mgf-spectrum-format-generation Use when raw vendor MS/MS files (e.g. from PRIDE or MassIVE antibody data sets) must be reformatted into an open, text-based spectral format as input for de novo peptide sequencing or database-search tools. The spectra are already in an open format (mzML or MGF) that the downstream de novo sequencing tool accepts directly — re-conversion would only risk loss or corruption The analysis requires peak picking, deconvolution, or recalibration of the raw data — msConvert formatting alone does not perform those processing steps The downstream tool natively reads vendor raw formats and conversion would discard vendor-specific metadata needed later http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Converts vendor-specific raw MS/MS files of antibody proteomics data sets into Mascot Generic Format (MGF) text files using ProteoWizard msConvert, so that de novo peptide sequencing tools (e.g. Novor, Casanovo) can ingest the spectra. MGF stores the m/z and intensity pairs of multiple mass spectra in a single parseable text format. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bib/bbac542
skills.summary: Converts vendor-specific raw MS/MS files of antibody proteomics data sets into Mascot Generic Format (MGF) text files using ProteoWizard msConvert, so that de novo peptide sequencing tools (e.g. Novor, Casanovo) can ingest the spectra. MGF stores the m/z and intensity pairs of multiple mass spectra in a single parseable text format.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The spectra are already in an open format (mzML or MGF) that the downstream de novo sequencing tool accepts directly — re-conversion would only risk loss or corruption The analysis requires peak picking, deconvolution, or recalibration of the raw data — msConvert formatting alone does not perform those processing steps The downstream tool natively reads vendor raw formats and conversion would discard vendor-specific metadata needed later

skills.name: mgf-spectrum-import
skills.search_text: mgf-spectrum-import Use when a workflow starts from an MGF-formatted MS/MS file (e.g. all_your_spectrums.mgf or tests/testdata/pesticides.mgf) and spectra must be loaded into matchms Spectrum objects before applying default_filters or process_peaks pipelines. Input spectra are already parsed matchms Spectrum objects or already serialized to JSON — the import step is redundant and the workflow should begin at the filter/score stage. The task is similarity scoring on spectra already in memory; importing from MGF again adds no information and is not part of the score computation. Only a single spectrum's peak table is needed outside a matchms workflow — using pyteomics or pymzml directly may suffice rather than routing through matchms. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Import tandem mass spectra from MGF files into matchms Spectrum objects, built on pyteomics, as the entry point for matchms metadata-cleaning, peak-filtering, and similarity-scoring workflows. metabolomics/v3 10.21105/joss.02411
skills.summary: Import tandem mass spectra from MGF files into matchms Spectrum objects, built on pyteomics, as the entry point for matchms metadata-cleaning, peak-filtering, and similarity-scoring workflows.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra are already parsed matchms Spectrum objects or already serialized to JSON — the import step is redundant and the workflow should begin at the filter/score stage. The task is similarity scoring on spectra already in memory; importing from MGF again adds no information and is not part of the score computation. Only a single spectrum's peak table is needed outside a matchms workflow — using pyteomics or pymzml directly may suffice rather than routing through matchms.

skills.name: mgf-spectrum-parsing
skills.search_text: mgf-spectrum-parsing Use when tandem MS/MS data are provided as MGF peak lists (e.g. from a ProteomeXchange/PRIDE deposit such as PXD034932) and spectra must be read with precursor m/z for direct spectral comparison or parameter estimation. Input is raw instrument data (e.g. vendor RAW or mzML) rather than MGF peak lists — convert to peak lists first, since compareMS2 operates on MGF spectra The goal is peptide/protein identification via database search; compareMS2 works before and independently of database search and does not assign spectra to peptide sequences Only a similarity label between two datasets is needed with no spectral detail — use compareMS2's phylogenetic tree or spectra2species modes directly instead of custom parsing http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Parse MGF (Mascot Generic Format) peak list files so that each tandem mass spectrum is read together with its precursor m/z, enabling direct spectrum-to-spectrum comparison in compareMS2-style analyses before any database search. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.2c00457
skills.summary: Parse MGF (Mascot Generic Format) peak list files so that each tandem mass spectrum is read together with its precursor m/z, enabling direct spectrum-to-spectrum comparison in compareMS2-style analyses before any database search.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw instrument data (e.g. vendor RAW or mzML) rather than MGF peak lists — convert to peak lists first, since compareMS2 operates on MGF spectra The goal is peptide/protein identification via database search; compareMS2 works before and independently of database search and does not assign spectra to peptide sequences Only a similarity label between two datasets is needed with no spectral detail — use compareMS2's phylogenetic tree or spectra2species modes directly instead of custom parsing

skills.description: Use when deconvoluted GC-MS compound spectra are supplied as .mgf (from MSHub auto-deconvolution or another tool) and need to be parsed and annotated against GNPS GC-MS library standards.
skills.name: mgf-spectrum-parsing
skills.search_text: mgf-spectrum-parsing Use when deconvoluted GC-MS compound spectra are supplied as .mgf (from MSHub auto-deconvolution or another tool) and need to be parsed and annotated against GNPS GC-MS library standards. Input is raw (non-deconvoluted) GC-MS chromatographic data that first needs MSHub's unsupervised non-negative matrix factorization auto-deconvolution step. Input is LC-MS/MS feature-based molecular networking data for pyMolNetEnhancer-style chemical class annotation — a different GNPS workflow domain. Input is already an annotated feature or quantification table rather than fragment spectra in .mgf form. Load deconvoluted GC-MS spectra from an .mgf file (e.g., produced by MSHub/GNPS auto-deconvolution) so each compound fragmentation pattern can be matched against the GNPS GC-MS reference library via cosine similarity on fragment ions. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41587-020-0700-3
skills.summary: Load deconvoluted GC-MS spectra from an .mgf file (e.g., produced by MSHub/GNPS auto-deconvolution) so each compound fragmentation pattern can be matched against the GNPS GC-MS reference library via cosine similarity on fragment ions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw (non-deconvoluted) GC-MS chromatographic data that first needs MSHub's unsupervised non-negative matrix factorization auto-deconvolution step. Input is LC-MS/MS feature-based molecular networking data for pyMolNetEnhancer-style chemical class annotation — a different GNPS workflow domain. Input is already an annotated feature or quantification table rather than fragment spectra in .mgf form.

Input is already a Spectrum object or an in-memory list of spectra — import/parsing is not needed again File is mzML, mzXML, msp, JSON, or a metabolomics-USI rather than MGF; use the corresponding matchms importer for that format instead Metadata fields need cleaning/correction (e.g. harmonizing ionmode or checking InChI/SMILES) — that belongs to the matchms filtering pipeline, not to load_from_mgf http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Parse NIST-formatted MGF files into matchms Spectrum objects using matchms.importing.load_from_mgf, converting raw MGF peak/metadata blocks into iterable, typed in-memory spectra ready for filtering or scoring. metabolomics/v3 10.21105/joss.02411
skills.summary: Parse NIST-formatted MGF files into matchms Spectrum objects using matchms.importing.load_from_mgf, converting raw MGF peak/metadata blocks into iterable, typed in-memory spectra ready for filtering or scoring.

skills.description: Use when clustering large-scale MS/MS data where raw MGF files must be converted into numeric peak arrays and preprocessed, since peak information occupies over 95% of raw-file data volume and preprocessing is a critical bottleneck contributing 20-90% of overall runtime.
skills.name: mgf-spectrum-parsing
skills.search_text: mgf-spectrum-parsing Use when clustering large-scale MS/MS data where raw MGF files must be converted into numeric peak arrays and preprocessed, since peak information occupies over 95% of raw-file data volume and preprocessing is a critical bottleneck contributing 20-90% of overall runtime. Input spectra are already preprocessed numeric peak arrays rather than raw MGF files - the parser targets MGF text formats Running on CPU-only environments without GPU-backed clustering downstream, since HyperSpec requires Python 3.8+ with CUDA and a properly installed NVIDIA GPU Storage is slow (e.g. non-SSD), since the README recommends high-performance SSD for best performance and preprocessing I/O dominates for large data sets http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Optimized parallel parsing of MGF peak files followed by vectorized spectrum preprocessing (precursor/low-intensity peak removal, min-peaks and m/z-range filtering, top-50 peak retention, L2 normalization) to prepare MS/MS spectra for hyperdimensional clustering. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.2c00612
skills.summary: Optimized parallel parsing of MGF peak files followed by vectorized spectrum preprocessing (precursor/low-intensity peak removal, min-peaks and m/z-range filtering, top-50 peak retention, L2 normalization) to prepare MS/MS spectra for hyperdimensional clustering.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra are already preprocessed numeric peak arrays rather than raw MGF files - the parser targets MGF text formats Running on CPU-only environments without GPU-backed clustering downstream, since HyperSpec requires Python 3.8+ with CUDA and a properly installed NVIDIA GPU Storage is slow (e.g. non-SSD), since the README recommends high-performance SSD for best performance and preprocessing I/O dominates for large data sets

skills.description: Use when analyzing non-enzymatic MHC class I immunopeptidomics MS/MS runs where peptides may lie outside a known protein database, or when comparing de novo predictions against a no-enzyme database search at fixed FDR.
skills.name: mhc-class-i-immunopeptidomics-dataset-analysis
skills.search_text: mhc-class-i-immunopeptidomics-dataset-analysis Use when analyzing non-enzymatic MHC class I immunopeptidomics MS/MS runs where peptides may lie outside a known protein database, or when comparing de novo predictions against a no-enzyme database search at fixed FDR. The sample is a standard enzymatic (tryptic) digest whose peptides are fully representable in a known protein database — a conventional database search such as Tide/Percolator alone is the appropriate baseline. The data were acquired in DIA mode — Casanovo targets DDA bottom-up tandem MS datasets; use a DIA-specific de novo framework instead. You need calibrated per-spectrum PEP/q-values for de novo predictions — the field lacks a rigorous confidence-estimation method for de novo sequencing, so treat de novo peptide counts as uncalibrated. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 End-to-end analysis of MHC class I immunopeptidomics DDA runs by de novo sequencing with Casanovo's non-enzymatic fine-tuned model, benchmarked against a no-enzyme Tide database search post-processed with Percolator at 1% FDR, with NetMHCpan-4.1 binder scoring. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-49731-x
skills.summary: End-to-end analysis of MHC class I immunopeptidomics DDA runs by de novo sequencing with Casanovo's non-enzymatic fine-tuned model, benchmarked against a no-enzyme Tide database search post-processed with Percolator at 1% FDR, with NetMHCpan-4.1 binder scoring.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The sample is a standard enzymatic (tryptic) digest whose peptides are fully representable in a known protein database — a conventional database search such as Tide/Percolator alone is the appropriate baseline. The data were acquired in DIA mode — Casanovo targets DDA bottom-up tandem MS datasets; use a DIA-specific de novo framework instead. You need calibrated per-spectrum PEP/q-values for de novo predictions — the field lacks a rigorous confidence-estimation method for de novo sequencing, so treat de novo peptide counts as uncalibrated.

skills.description: Use when a processed, filtered and imputed LC-MS or DIMS feature table (post XCMS-Basic-Birmingham-Pipe, Replicate/Blank/Sample Filtering and missing value imputation) needs putative metabolite annotations attached to its peaks.
skills.name: mi-pack-metabolite-peak-annotation
skills.search_text: mi-pack-metabolite-peak-annotation Use when a processed, filtered and imputed LC-MS or DIMS feature table (post XCMS-Basic-Birmingham-Pipe, Replicate/Blank/Sample Filtering and missing value imputation) needs putative metabolite annotations attached to its peaks. Input is raw vendor LC-MS/DIMS spectra rather than a processed, filtered peak list — MI-Pack runs downstream of XCMS feature detection/alignment and the filtering/imputation tools The goal is statistical separation testing between sample groups rather than metabolite identification — use the Galaxy-M PLS-Toolbox PCA with Scores Test instead Only preliminary feature-group annotation (e.g. adduct/isotope grouping) is needed and MI-Pack's formula+pathway identification is out of scope — the paper also lists Camera and PUTMEDID as identification software Assign putative metabolite identifications to processed mass-spectral peaks using MI-Pack, which integrates accurate masses with metabolic pathways and empirical formula search against compound reference databases (KEGG, HMDB, LIPID MAPS). It is the annotation step of the Galaxy-M LC-MS and DIMS workflows. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13742-016-0115-8
skills.summary: Assign putative metabolite identifications to processed mass-spectral peaks using MI-Pack, which integrates accurate masses with metabolic pathways and empirical formula search against compound reference databases (KEGG, HMDB, LIPID MAPS). It is the annotation step of the Galaxy-M LC-MS and DIMS workflows.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw vendor LC-MS/DIMS spectra rather than a processed, filtered peak list — MI-Pack runs downstream of XCMS feature detection/alignment and the filtering/imputation tools The goal is statistical separation testing between sample groups rather than metabolite identification — use the Galaxy-M PLS-Toolbox PCA with Scores Test instead Only preliminary feature-group annotation (e.g. adduct/isotope grouping) is needed and MI-Pack's formula+pathway identification is out of scope — the paper also lists Camera and PUTMEDID as identification software

skills.description: Use when depositing a BGC of known function into the MIBiG repository, or when reconstructing/simulating its submission pipeline: an accession-request stage followed by an extended annotation form after staff approval.
skills.name: mibig-annotation-form-completion
skills.search_text: mibig-annotation-form-completion Use when depositing a BGC of known function into the MIBiG repository, or when reconstructing/simulating its submission pipeline: an accession-request stage followed by an extended annotation form after staff approval. The BGC is of unknown function — MIBiG is a repository for BGCs of known function, so such entries do not qualify for submission. The goal is to query or extract existing MIBiG entries programmatically rather than deposit a new one — use the MIBiG REST-like web API instead of the submission workflow. Only predicted/candidate BGCs from genome mining (e.g. antiSMASH or ClusterFinder output) are available without linked products of known chemical structure — these belong in databases like IMG-ABC or antiSMASH-DB, not the MIBiG annotation pipeline. http://edamontology.org/topic_0219 Captures the documented two-stage MIBiG crowdsourcing submission workflow: first requesting a MIBiG accession number with product name(s) and BGC sequence information, then, after MIBiG staff approval, completing the extended entry form with detailed annotation data. It exists so future agents can model or replicate deposition of a biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) of known function into MIBiG. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkz882
skills.summary: Captures the documented two-stage MIBiG crowdsourcing submission workflow: first requesting a MIBiG accession number with product name(s) and BGC sequence information, then, after MIBiG staff approval, completing the extended entry form with detailed annotation data. It exists so future agents can model or replicate deposition of a biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) of known function into MIBiG.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The BGC is of unknown function — MIBiG is a repository for BGCs of known function, so such entries do not qualify for submission. The goal is to query or extract existing MIBiG entries programmatically rather than deposit a new one — use the MIBiG REST-like web API instead of the submission workflow. Only predicted/candidate BGCs from genome mining (e.g. antiSMASH or ClusterFinder output) are available without linked products of known chemical structure — these belong in databases like IMG-ABC or antiSMASH-DB, not the MIBiG annotation pipeline.

skills.description: Use when a validated or known MIBiG BGC (e.g. BGC0001228, BGC0000241) must be mapped to its homologous GCF in an antiSMASH/BigScape-annotated genome set, and the corresponding metabolomic links in GNPS molecular families must be ranked.
skills.name: mibig-bgc-homology-mapping
skills.search_text: mibig-bgc-homology-mapping Use when a validated or known MIBiG BGC (e.g. BGC0001228, BGC0000241) must be mapped to its homologous GCF in an antiSMASH/BigScape-annotated genome set, and the corresponding metabolomic links in GNPS molecular families must be ranked. The dataset has no GNPS molecular networking data as input — NPLinker requires it and the metcalf/IOKR scoring cannot be computed No BigScape output exists and antiSMASH BGC data are absent, so no GCFs can be clustered or mapped to MIBiG homologues The goal is scoring links for molecular families not tied to any strain-mapped BGC, since strain_mapping.json is required to connect BGCs and spectra to strains http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_3361 Identify, within a strain-mapped NPLinker dataset, the BigScape-clustered gene cluster families (GCFs) homologous to known MIBiG BGCs (e.g. BGC0001228 retimycin A, BGC0000241 lomaiviticin A), then score and rank their links to all GNPS molecular families using standardised metcalf correlation, IOKR, and combined ℓ1/ℓ2/ℓ1.5 scores. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008920
skills.summary: Identify, within a strain-mapped NPLinker dataset, the BigScape-clustered gene cluster families (GCFs) homologous to known MIBiG BGCs (e.g. BGC0001228 retimycin A, BGC0000241 lomaiviticin A), then score and rank their links to all GNPS molecular families using standardised metcalf correlation, IOKR, and combined ℓ1/ℓ2/ℓ1.5 scores.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset has no GNPS molecular networking data as input — NPLinker requires it and the metcalf/IOKR scoring cannot be computed No BigScape output exists and antiSMASH BGC data are absent, so no GCFs can be clustered or mapped to MIBiG homologues The goal is scoring links for molecular families not tied to any strain-mapped BGC, since strain_mapping.json is required to connect BGCs and spectra to strains

skills.description: Use when you have antiSMASH annotations of curated MIBiG clusters plus a characterised natural-product structure, and need to diagnose why RAIChU-predicted scaffolds diverge from biosynthetic reality.
skills.name: mibig-cluster-annotation-curation
skills.search_text: mibig-cluster-annotation-curation Use when you have antiSMASH annotations of curated MIBiG clusters plus a characterised natural-product structure, and need to diagnose why RAIChU-predicted scaffolds diverge from biosynthetic reality. The input BGCs are RiPP, terpene, or trans-AT PKS clusters outside the cis-AT PKS/NRPS/NRPS-PKS hybrid scope of the curated MIBiG subset The goal is de novo scaffold generation from raw antiSMASH output without a characterised reference structure to curate against Clusters lack any experimentally characterised product structure, so no predicted-vs-characterised comparison is possible http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Curates MIBiG BGC annotations by running RAIChU on antiSMASH predictions of a manually curated MIBiG subset (cis-AT PKS, NRPS, NRPS/PKS hybrid clusters) and classifying every mismatch between RAIChU-rendered and experimentally characterised products into one of three cause categories. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00898-x
skills.summary: Curates MIBiG BGC annotations by running RAIChU on antiSMASH predictions of a manually curated MIBiG subset (cis-AT PKS, NRPS, NRPS/PKS hybrid clusters) and classifying every mismatch between RAIChU-rendered and experimentally characterised products into one of three cause categories.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input BGCs are RiPP, terpene, or trans-AT PKS clusters outside the cis-AT PKS/NRPS/NRPS-PKS hybrid scope of the curated MIBiG subset The goal is de novo scaffold generation from raw antiSMASH output without a characterised reference structure to curate against Clusters lack any experimentally characterised product structure, so no predicted-vs-characterised comparison is possible

skills.description: Use when a workflow needs real-world PKS/NRPS or hybrid BGC cluster definitions with known products — e.g. drawing MIBiG entries with RAIChU, validating predicted structures, or collecting SMILES for natural product visualisation.
skills.name: mibig-cluster-data-retrieval
skills.search_text: mibig-cluster-data-retrieval Use when a workflow needs real-world PKS/NRPS or hybrid BGC cluster definitions with known products — e.g. drawing MIBiG entries with RAIChU, validating predicted structures, or collecting SMILES for natural product visualisation. The task is to draw randomly generated or hypothetical PKS/NRPS systems rather than experimentally characterised MIBiG clusters A mature natural product must be generated directly from raw antiSMASH output without user specification — RAIChU generates scaffolds, not mature products, and predicted structures may not fingerprint-match the real product Tailoring regio- and stereochemistry must be predicted automatically; users must specify their reaction targets, so unannotated MIBiG entries alone are insufficient http://edamontology.org/topic_3361 Retrieve experimentally verified biosynthetic gene cluster definitions (DNA sequence and associated natural product) from the MIBiG database, with SMILES fallbacks to PubChem then NP Atlas, as grounded inputs for RAIChU spaghetti-diagram generation. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00898-x
skills.summary: Retrieve experimentally verified biosynthetic gene cluster definitions (DNA sequence and associated natural product) from the MIBiG database, with SMILES fallbacks to PubChem then NP Atlas, as grounded inputs for RAIChU spaghetti-diagram generation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is to draw randomly generated or hypothetical PKS/NRPS systems rather than experimentally characterised MIBiG clusters A mature natural product must be generated directly from raw antiSMASH output without user specification — RAIChU generates scaffolds, not mature products, and predicted structures may not fingerprint-match the real product Tailoring regio- and stereochemistry must be predicted automatically; users must specify their reaction targets, so unannotated MIBiG entries alone are insufficient

skills.description: Use when a new or existing BGC clustering method must be validated against the manually curated MIBiG reference groups, or when reporting a clustering-quality baseline (V-score, NMI, ARI) for a BGC-GCF grouping algorithm.
skills.name: mibig-curated-group-clustering-benchmarking
skills.search_text: mibig-curated-group-clustering-benchmarking Use when a new or existing BGC clustering method must be validated against the manually curated MIBiG reference groups, or when reporting a clustering-quality baseline (V-score, NMI, ARI) for a BGC-GCF grouping algorithm. The input is not an antiSMASH/BiG-SLiCE-prepared BGC dataset but an arbitrary feature table or an already-clustered result file — the skill expects raw BGC GenBank input and a clustering run. The goal is to cluster a large exploratory dataset (e.g. 1.2M BGCs) rather than to measure clustering quality against curated labels — use BiG-SLiCE's full clustering workflow instead. Expression data are high-throughput sequencing counts rather than microarray intensities; the method was demonstrated on microarray expression data and no count-model guidance is given here.

skills.description: Use when you have a cross-validated interaction-score matrix (microbes x metabolites) from MiMeNet and need to group features into modules and build a module-level interaction network.
skills.name: microbe-metabolite-interaction-biclustering
skills.search_text: microbe-metabolite-interaction-biclustering Use when you have a cross-validated interaction-score matrix (microbes x metabolites) from MiMeNet and need to group features into modules and build a module-level interaction network. You have raw abundance tables only (microbial taxa/metabolite abundances) and no interaction-score matrix — run MiMeNet's cross-validated prediction first; this skill operates on the score matrix, not on raw counts. You need per-metabolite well-predicted lists (SCC above the 95th-percentile threshold) — that is a separate MiMeNet output step, not module construction. You are using NED as the underlying model — NED models metabolites via a microbiome latent space, so its interactions do not reveal shared interaction-pattern modules in the way MiMeNet's biclustering does. http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 http://edamontology.org/topic_3391 Biclusters the MiMeNet microbe-metabolite interaction-score matrix into module sets via consensus clustering, then collapses scores into a weighted bipartite module-module network. Provides organism-level structure from per-pair attribution scores. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009021
skills.summary: Biclusters the MiMeNet microbe-metabolite interaction-score matrix into module sets via consensus clustering, then collapses scores into a weighted bipartite module-module network. Provides organism-level structure from per-pair attribution scores.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have raw abundance tables only (microbial taxa/metabolite abundances) and no interaction-score matrix — run MiMeNet's cross-validated prediction first; this skill operates on the score matrix, not on raw counts. You need per-metabolite well-predicted lists (SCC above the 95th-percentile threshold) — that is a separate MiMeNet output step, not module construction. skills.description: Use when paired microbiome–metabolome feature tables (samples in rows) have been modeled with a multi-layer neural network and you need a weighted microbe–metabolite interaction matrix for module construction or feature attribution.
skills.name: microbe-metabolite-interaction-matrix-construction
skills.search_text: microbe-metabolite-interaction-matrix-construction Use when paired microbiome–metabolome feature tables (samples in rows) have been modeled with a multi-layer neural network and you need a weighted microbe–metabolite interaction matrix for module construction or feature attribution. The input is a raw unnormalized abundance table — MiMeNet requires prior compositional transformation to RA or CLR and filtering of low-abundant features before training. You only need per-metabolite predictions without interaction attribution — the cross-validated evaluation step alone (Spearman correlations per metabolite) suffices; the interaction matrix requires the trained network weights. The model is a linear method like MelonnPan's Elastic Net, which produces coefficient weights per compound rather than multiplicative hidden-layer attribution scores. http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 Constructs a microbe-by-metabolite interaction score matrix from the weights of trained MiMeNet cross-validated MLPNN models, then thresholds it against a shuffled-data background to retain only statistically significant interactions and well-predicted metabolites. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009021
skills.summary: Constructs a microbe-by-metabolite interaction score matrix from the weights of trained MiMeNet cross-validated MLPNN models, then thresholds it against a shuffled-data background to retain only statistically significant interactions and well-predicted metabolites.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a raw unnormalized abundance table — MiMeNet requires prior compositional transformation to RA or CLR and filtering of low-abundant features before training. You only need per-metabolite predictions without interaction attribution — the cross-validated evaluation step alone (Spearman correlations per metabolite) suffices; the interaction matrix requires the trained network weights. The model is a linear method like MelonnPan's Elastic Net, which produces coefficient weights per compound rather than multiplicative hidden-layer attribution scores.

skills.description: Use when you have paired microbiome-metabolite data and want to replace thousands of original abundance features with a smaller set of module feature values (mean normalized abundance per biclustered or WGCNA-derived module) for a classification task such as IBD status prediction.
skills.name: microbiome-module-feature-engineering
skills.search_text: microbiome-module-feature-engineering Use when you have paired microbiome-metabolite data and want to replace thousands of original abundance features with a smaller set of module feature values (mean normalized abundance per biclustered or WGCNA-derived module) for a classification task such as IBD status prediction. You only need the predicted metabolomic profile itself — use MiMeNet's prediction workflow rather than extracting module features for classification. Your input feature table is already a low-dimensional set of module scores, so compressing further adds no value. The goal is mechanistic discovery of microbe-metabolite interaction modules rather than building a classification feature set. http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Engineering compact module-level features (mean normalized abundance per microbe/metabolite module) for downstream classification, as used in MiMeNet's comparison of its biclustered modules against WGCNA module features and original abundance features for IBD prediction. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009021
skills.summary: Engineering compact module-level features (mean normalized abundance per microbe/metabolite module) for downstream classification, as used in MiMeNet's comparison of its biclustered modules against WGCNA module features and original abundance features for IBD prediction.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need the predicted metabolomic profile itself — use MiMeNet's prediction workflow rather than extracting module features for classification. Your input feature table is already a low-dimensional set of module scores, so compressing further adds no value. The goal is mechanistic discovery of microbe-metabolite interaction modules rather than building a classification feature set.

skills.description: Decision support for taxon-level association testing on microbiome abundance tables (e.g. species-level ANCOM-BC2 output) where multiple hypotheses are tested and raw p-values must be adjusted before reporting differentially abundant taxa.
skills.name: microbiome-multiple-testing-correction
skills.search_text: microbiome-multiple-testing-correction Decision support for taxon-level association testing on microbiome abundance tables (e.g. species-level ANCOM-BC2 output) where multiple hypotheses are tested and raw p-values must be adjusted before reporting differentially abundant taxa. The input is already an adjusted result table (e.g. a published ANCOM-BC2 output with q-values) — re-correcting would double-penalize. The analysis is a single pre-registered hypothesis on one taxon, where no multiplicity correction is needed. The abundance table is a compositional mock community where only a handful of taxa are tested and the correction would obscure real signals without changing conclusions. http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Applies family-wise error rate or false-discovery-rate correction to taxon-level association tests (e.g. ANCOM-BC2, MaAsLin2) so that differentially abundant microbial species between conditions are reported with adjusted p-values, as done for the 3xTg vs WT fecal shotgun metagenomics comparison. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.04.28.651123
skills.summary: Applies family-wise error rate or false-discovery-rate correction to taxon-level association tests (e.g. ANCOM-BC2, MaAsLin2) so that differentially abundant microbial species between conditions are reported with adjusted p-values, as done for the 3xTg vs WT fecal shotgun metagenomics comparison.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already an adjusted result table (e.g. a published ANCOM-BC2 output with q-values) — re-correcting would double-penalize. The analysis is a single pre-registered hypothesis on one taxon, where no multiplicity correction is needed. The abundance table is a compositional mock community where only a handful of taxa are tested and the correction would obscure real signals without changing conclusions.

skills.description: Use when you have MetaPhlAn or LEfSe biomarker results (e.g., 16S rRNA profiles from hmp_aerobiosis) and need a compact, publication-quality circular phylogeny with clade-level biomarker highlighting and shaded backgrounds.
skills.name: microbiome-taxonomic-cladogram-annotation
skills.search_text: microbiome-taxonomic-cladogram-annotation Use when you have MetaPhlAn or LEfSe biomarker results (e.g., 16S rRNA profiles from hmp_aerobiosis) and need a compact, publication-quality circular phylogeny with clade-level biomarker highlighting and shaded backgrounds. When the tree and annotations already exist in GraPhlAn input format — export2graphlan is a converter, not a plotter; use GraPhlAn directly When interactive exploration of large-scale phylogenies is the goal — iTOL targets interactive analyses and Krona emphasizes hierarchical quantitative information, whereas GraPhlAn is command-driven for pipeline reproducibility For functional (HUMAnN/KEGG) heatmaps rather than taxonomic cladograms — hclust2 is the matching tool for heat-maps of abundance profiles http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Generates annotated circular taxonomic cladograms (e.g., the HMP aerobiosis cladogram, Fig. S1) by converting MetaPhlAn/LEfSe outputs into GraPhlAn tree and annotation files with export2graphlan, then rendering them with GraPhlAn/matplotlib. LEfSe biomarker LDA scores map to clade sizes and class assignments to shaded backgrounds. metabolomics/v3 10.7717/peerj.1029
skills.summary: Generates annotated circular taxonomic cladograms (e.g., the HMP aerobiosis cladogram, Fig. S1) by converting MetaPhlAn/LEfSe outputs into GraPhlAn tree and annotation files with export2graphlan, then rendering them with GraPhlAn/matplotlib. LEfSe biomarker LDA scores map to clade sizes and class assignments to shaded backgrounds.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the tree and annotations already exist in GraPhlAn input format — export2graphlan is a converter, not a plotter; use GraPhlAn directly When interactive exploration of large-scale phylogenies is the goal — iTOL targets interactive analyses and Krona emphasizes hierarchical quantitative information, whereas GraPhlAn is command-driven for pipeline reproducibility For functional (HUMAnN/KEGG) heatmaps rather than taxonomic cladograms — hclust2 is the matching tool for heat-maps of abundance profiles
