skills.description: Use when you need to determine which node attributes of a trained GNN (e.g. SigmaCCS CCS predictions) most affect prediction accuracy by perturbing each input feature and measuring the resulting performance drop.
skills.name: node-attribute-masking-perturbation-analysis
skills.search_text: node-attribute-masking-perturbation-analysis Use when you need to determine which node attributes of a trained GNN (e.g. SigmaCCS CCS predictions) most affect prediction accuracy by perturbing each input feature and measuring the resulting performance drop. You only have descriptor-based (e.g. AllCCS) or SMILES-encoding (e.g. DeepCCS) models with no per-node attribute graph representation to mask. The goal is CCS prediction or filtering of candidate molecules (use the Prediction/Filtering workflow), not model interpretability. The model input is not a molecular graph with distinct node attributes — masking one node attribute is only meaningful when attributes are separable in the feature matrix. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 A model-agnostic interpretation method that quantifies node-attribute importance in a graph neural network (SigmaCCS) by masking one node attribute at a time in the graph dataset and measuring the increase in CCS prediction error relative to the unmasked model. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s42004-023-00939-w
skills.summary: A model-agnostic interpretation method that quantifies node-attribute importance in a graph neural network (SigmaCCS) by masking one node attribute at a time in the graph dataset and measuring the increase in CCS prediction error relative to the unmasked model.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only have descriptor-based (e.g. AllCCS) or SMILES-encoding (e.g. DeepCCS) models with no per-node attribute graph representation to mask. The goal is CCS prediction or filtering of candidate molecules (use the Prediction/Filtering workflow), not model interpretability. The model input is not a molecular graph with distinct node attributes — masking one node attribute is only meaningful when attributes are separable in the feature matrix.

skills.description: Use when you have two processed abundance matrices (e.g., metabolite and protein feature tables across the same samples) and need to build a correlation-based network and identify hub nodes via centrality metrics.
skills.name: node-centrality-network-analysis
skills.search_text: node-centrality-network-analysis Use when you have two processed abundance matrices (e.g., metabolite and protein feature tables across the same samples) and need to build a correlation-based network and identify hub nodes via centrality metrics. The two omics datasets do not share samples — the correlation requires the retained intersection of samples (202 shared of 308 in the reference), and unmatched samples must be dropped first Input matrices are raw, unfiltered data — samples with >90% zeros and variables with >40% zeros must be removed and data CPM-normalized before correlation, or spurious edges will result The goal is raw-data preprocessing, peak picking, or metabolite annotation — iMAP explicitly did not implement these modules http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Constructs a metabolite-protein correlation network from processed multi-omics abundance matrices (Spearman correlation, FDR < 0.05, |r| > 0.3) and ranks nodes by graph-theory centralities (degree, betweenness, closeness, eigenvector) to identify hub metabolites and hub proteins. This reproduces the iMAP network module workflow demonstrated on IBD stool-sample metabolomics and proteomics data. metabolomics/v3 10.3389/fchem.2021.659656
skills.summary: Constructs a metabolite-protein correlation network from processed multi-omics abundance matrices (Spearman correlation, FDR < 0.05, |r| > 0.3) and ranks nodes by graph-theory centralities (degree, betweenness, closeness, eigenvector) to identify hub metabolites and hub proteins. This reproduces the iMAP network module workflow demonstrated on IBD stool-sample metabolomics and proteomics data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The two omics datasets do not share samples — the correlation requires the retained intersection of samples (202 shared of 308 in the reference), and unmatched samples must be dropped first Input matrices are raw, unfiltered data — samples with >90% zeros and variables with >40% zeros must be removed and data CPM-normalized before correlation, or spurious edges will result The goal is raw-data preprocessing, peak picking, or metabolite annotation — iMAP explicitly did not implement these modules

skills.description: Use when evaluating how noisy spectra and missing fragmentation ions affect de novo peptide sequencing, by annotating MGF spectra against validated PSMs and computing per-dataset noise factors.
skills.name: noise-factor-computation-across-datasets
skills.search_text: noise-factor-computation-across-datasets Use when evaluating how noisy spectra and missing fragmentation ions affect de novo peptide sequencing, by annotating MGF spectra against validated PSMs and computing per-dataset noise factors. Spectra have no validated PSMs (pseudo ground truth) from a 1% FDR database search, so theoretical fragment ions cannot be matched to observed peaks to call missing cleavage sites. The goal is de novo sequencing prediction itself (e.g. running Novor, pNovo 3, DeepNovo, SMSNet, PointNovo or Casanovo) rather than characterizing the spectral input quality fed to those tools. The input is already quality-annotated (peak labels and missing-cleavage-site counts exist) and only the downstream noise-factor ratios need recombination. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Annotates antibody MS/MS spectra by labeling every peak as peptide or noise peak and by flagging missing fragment-ion cleavage sites, then computes a per-dataset noise factor (ratio of high-intensity noise peaks to fragment ion peaks) to quantify spectral quality for de novo sequencing evaluation. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bib/bbac542
skills.summary: Annotates antibody MS/MS spectra by labeling every peak as peptide or noise peak and by flagging missing fragment-ion cleavage sites, then computes a per-dataset noise factor (ratio of high-intensity noise peaks to fragment ion peaks) to quantify spectral quality for de novo sequencing evaluation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Spectra have no validated PSMs (pseudo ground truth) from a 1% FDR database search, so theoretical fragment ions cannot be matched to observed peaks to call missing cleavage sites. The goal is de novo sequencing prediction itself (e.g. running Novor, pNovo 3, DeepNovo, SMSNet, PointNovo or Casanovo) rather than characterizing the spectral input quality fed to those tools. The input is already quality-annotated (peak labels and missing-cleavage-site counts exist) and only the downstream noise-factor ratios need recombination.

skills.description: Use when preprocessing a pixel × m/z feature matrix (X/Y coordinate columns plus ion intensity columns) to remove spatially random, likely non-biological ions before metabolite annotation, UMAP-kmeans/Seurat pixel clustering, SpaGene co-expression analysis, or differential analysis.
skills.name: noise-ion-filtering
skills.search_text: noise-ion-filtering Use when preprocessing a pixel × m/z feature matrix (X/Y coordinate columns plus ion intensity columns) to remove spatially random, likely non-biological ions before metabolite annotation, UMAP-kmeans/Seurat pixel clustering, SpaGene co-expression analysis, or differential analysis. The input is already a filtered or annotated ion list rather than a raw pixel × m/z feature matrix with X/Y coordinates — QC2 operates on the full spatial feature matrix. The goal is background consistency evaluation (QC1), intensity distribution analysis (QC3), or missing value assessment (QC4) — these are separate SMAnalyst QC modules, not noise-ion filtering. The dataset has no meaningful spatial structure or coordinates, since the score is derived from the spatstat quadrat test on spatial point patterns. http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 SMAnalyst's noise-ion filtering (QC2) scores every ion in a spatial metabolomics feature matrix by spatial randomness — the noise score is the negative log10 of the spatstat quadrat-test p-value against Complete Spatial Randomness — and removes ions below the default threshold (score ≥ 30 retained), so only spatially structured ions proceed to annotation, clustering, and differential analysis. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/biom15111562
skills.summary: SMAnalyst's noise-ion filtering (QC2) scores every ion in a spatial metabolomics feature matrix by spatial randomness — the noise score is the negative log10 of the spatstat quadrat-test p-value against Complete Spatial Randomness — and removes ions below the default threshold (score ≥ 30 retained), so only spatially structured ions proceed to annotation, clustering, and differential analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a filtered or annotated ion list rather than a raw pixel × m/z feature matrix with X/Y coordinates — QC2 operates on the full spatial feature matrix. The goal is background consistency evaluation (QC1), intensity distribution analysis (QC3), or missing value assessment (QC4) — these are separate SMAnalyst QC modules, not noise-ion filtering. The dataset has no meaningful spatial structure or coordinates, since the score is derived from the spatstat quadrat test on spatial point patterns.

skills.name: noise-ion-score-filtering
skills.search_text: noise-ion-score-filtering Use when preprocessing a spatial metabolomics peak table matrix (pixels x ions with X/Y coordinates) to remove randomly distributed noise ions that would interfere with spatial pattern recognition or downstream clustering. The input is already a filtered or feature-selected table where noise ions have been removed by another QC step The goal is to remove background pixels or evaluate background consistency rather than filter spatially random ions — SMQVP provides separate background-consistency and background-noise-removal modules The data are not spatially resolved (no per-pixel X/Y coordinates), so a quadrat test on spatial intensity patterns is undefined http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Score each spatial metabolomics ion by how strongly it deviates from Complete Spatial Randomness (noise score = -log10 of the spatstat quadrat test p-value) and filter ions with scores below a chosen threshold (e.g. 90), as implemented in SMQVP for AFADESI mouse brain data. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo15060354
skills.summary: Score each spatial metabolomics ion by how strongly it deviates from Complete Spatial Randomness (noise score = -log10 of the spatstat quadrat test p-value) and filter ions with scores below a chosen threshold (e.g. 90), as implemented in SMQVP for AFADESI mouse brain data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a filtered or feature-selected table where noise ions have been removed by another QC step The goal is to remove background pixels or evaluate background consistency rather than filter spatially random ions — SMQVP provides separate background-consistency and background-noise-removal modules The data are not spatially resolved (no per-pixel X/Y coordinates), so a quadrat test on spatial intensity patterns is undefined

skills.search_text: noise-model-function-implementation Use when implementing, reproducing, or validating SMITER's intensity-specific chromatographic peak-noise model — i.e., when you need sigma as a function of signal intensity for synthetic mzML generation or noise-model comparison. You need uniform, intensity-independent noise — use the default smiter.noise_functions.UniformNoiseInjector instead of the intensity-specific model. You only need to run an end-to-end SMITER simulation with existing noise generators rather than implement or validate a new noise model. skills.name: noise-perturbation-robustness-testing
skills.search_text: noise-perturbation-robustness-testing Use when you need to test whether a structure-annotation or scoring method degrades gracefully under degraded spectral quality — e.g. added noise levels, differing collision energies, or merged-versus-single spectra — and want ROC/hop-plot metrics as evidence. Input spectra are single-peak or the compound lacks all three collision energies — the article discards such compounds entirely, so robustness curves would be incomparable You need true FDR guarantees for biological annotations — the article states accurate FDR estimation from small-molecule fragmentation spectra is expected to remain highly challenging and the 0.64 threshold is practical guidance only Input is profiled-mode or negative-ion-mode LC-MS data — such runs were discarded in the article's processing (leaving 17,414 LC-MS/MS runs) http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Evaluate the robustness of an annotation pipeline (here, SIRIUS 4 → CSI:FingerID → COSMIC confidence score) by re-running it under synthetic noise levels and multiple collision energies (10/20/40 eV plus cosine-distance-merged spectra), then comparing correct-hit totals and annotation rates via hop plots. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41587-021-01045-9
skills.summary: Evaluate the robustness of an annotation pipeline (here, SIRIUS 4 → CSI:FingerID → COSMIC confidence score) by re-running it under synthetic noise levels and multiple collision energies (10/20/40 eV plus cosine-distance-merged spectra), then comparing correct-hit totals and annotation rates via hop plots.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra are single-peak or the compound lacks all three collision energies — the article discards such compounds entirely, so robustness curves would be incomparable You need true FDR guarantees for biological annotations — the article states accurate FDR estimation from small-molecule fragmentation spectra is expected to remain highly challenging and the 0.64 threshold is practical guidance only Input is profiled-mode or negative-ion-mode LC-MS data — such runs were discarded in the article's processing (leaving 17,414 LC-MS/MS runs)

skills.description: Use when LC/MS metabolomics extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) must be scored or filtered for quality — especially EICs with high background signals or only a single peak, where the MCQ index cannot fairly evaluate them.
skills.name: noise-robustness-evaluation-of-eics
skills.search_text: noise-robustness-evaluation-of-eics Use when LC/MS metabolomics extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) must be scored or filtered for quality — especially EICs with high background signals or only a single peak, where the MCQ index cannot fairly evaluate them. Input is a set of already-detected chromatographic peaks rather than full EIC traces — the paper's six peak quality metrics (sharpness, Gaussian similarity, SNR, peak significance level, TPASR, local peak-related zigzag index) apply to peaks instead. The goal is selecting and aligning analyte components for which the MCQ index is adequate — this skill targets the high-background and single-peak EICs that the MCQ index cannot fairly evaluate. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Implements the paper's EIC-related global zigzag index — a normalized first-order-derivative score with dynamic range 0–4.0 — to evaluate the quality of extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) in LC/MS-based metabolomics data, remaining robust for EICs with high background signals or only a single peak, where the mass chromatographic quality (MCQ) index fails. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/1471-2105-15-s11-s5
skills.summary: Implements the paper's EIC-related global zigzag index — a normalized first-order-derivative score with dynamic range 0–4.0 — to evaluate the quality of extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) in LC/MS-based metabolomics data, remaining robust for EICs with high background signals or only a single peak, where the mass chromatographic quality (MCQ) index fails.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a set of already-detected chromatographic peaks rather than full EIC traces — the paper's six peak quality metrics (sharpness, Gaussian similarity, SNR, peak significance level, TPASR, local peak-related zigzag index) apply to peaks instead. The goal is selecting and aligning analyte components for which the MCQ index is adequate — this skill targets the high-background and single-peak EICs that the MCQ index cannot fairly evaluate.

skills.description: Use when establishing an upper-bound accuracy baseline for methods that infer absolute concentrations from relative abundance time-course data, before testing noisy or sparse regimes.
skills.name: noiseless-time-course-simulation-for-model-benchmarking
skills.search_text: noiseless-time-course-simulation-for-model-benchmarking Use when establishing an upper-bound accuracy baseline for methods that infer absolute concentrations from relative abundance time-course data, before testing noisy or sparse regimes. When the goal is to assess robustness to measurement noise or sparse sampling — use MetaboPAC_*_noisy.m with timepoints [50 15] and CoV [5 15] instead When the dataset contains real experimental metabolomics measurements with missing values or instrument noise rather than simulated noiseless profiles http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Generate noiseless in silico time-course metabolomics data for benchmarking response-factor/concentration inference by running the first cell of GenData/driver_genDatasets*.m in MATLAB across the paper's two synthetic and two biological models, then evaluating inferred absolute concentrations against log2 error tolerances. metabolomics/v3 10.1039/d2mo00168c
skills.summary: Generate noiseless in silico time-course metabolomics data for benchmarking response-factor/concentration inference by running the first cell of GenData/driver_genDatasets*.m in MATLAB across the paper's two synthetic and two biological models, then evaluating inferred absolute concentrations against log2 error tolerances.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is to assess robustness to measurement noise or sparse sampling — use MetaboPAC_*_noisy.m with timepoints [50 15] and CoV [5 15] instead When the dataset contains real experimental metabolomics measurements with missing values or instrument noise rather than simulated noiseless profiles

skills.description: Use when building a curated MS2 training set from reference-standard or raw lipid spectra and noisy profiles must be excluded before model training or spectral storage.
skills.name: noisy-spectra-filtering
skills.search_text: noisy-spectra-filtering Use when building a curated MS2 training set from reference-standard or raw lipid spectra and noisy profiles must be excluded before model training or spectral storage. Input spectra are already centroided and base peak normalized with a known-good quality flag — re-filtering would discard valid low-intensity spectra. The task concerns model training or prediction itself (transformer configuration, mzML prediction) rather than training-data curation. The noise characterization of the target data differs from lipid standard measurements, where the 0.01 threshold was calibrated; the threshold should not be applied blindly to other data types. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Filters particularly noisy MS2 spectra by computing a base-peak normalized median intensity noise score and excluding spectra above a 0.01 threshold, as used to curate LipiDetective's lipid standard training data. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.10.07.617094
skills.summary: Filters particularly noisy MS2 spectra by computing a base-peak normalized median intensity noise score and excluding spectra above a 0.01 threshold, as used to curate LipiDetective's lipid standard training data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra are already centroided and base peak normalized with a known-good quality flag — re-filtering would discard valid low-intensity spectra. The task concerns model training or prediction itself (transformer configuration, mzML prediction) rather than training-data curation. The noise characterization of the target data differs from lipid standard measurements, where the 0.01 threshold was calibrated; the threshold should not be applied blindly to other data types.

skills.description: Use when fine-tuning or benchmarking a de novo sequencing model on non-tryptic/non-enzymatic spectra, and you need annotated MGF training/validation/test splits rather than tryptic MassIVE-KB data.
skills.name: non-enzymatic-psm-dataset-splitting
skills.search_text: non-enzymatic-psm-dataset-splitting Use when fine-tuning or benchmarking a de novo sequencing model on non-tryptic/non-enzymatic spectra, and you need annotated MGF training/validation/test splits rather than tryptic MassIVE-KB data. The task is standard tryptic DDA database searching or sequencing where MassIVE-KB-derived tryptic training data are appropriate — fine-tuning on non-enzymatic data is unnecessary and may reduce tryptic performance. Only a pretrained Casanovo model is needed for inference and no model retraining or non-tryptic benchmarking is planned — no split files need to be involved. The input spectra are DIA rather than DDA bottom-up tandem MS data. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Split non-enzymatic PSM data into training, validation, and test sets (delivered as annotated MGF files on MassIVE, MSV000094014) so that a pretrained Casanovo model can be fine-tuned and fairly evaluated on non-tryptic peptides. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-49731-x
skills.summary: Split non-enzymatic PSM data into training, validation, and test sets (delivered as annotated MGF files on MassIVE, MSV000094014) so that a pretrained Casanovo model can be fine-tuned and fairly evaluated on non-tryptic peptides.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is standard tryptic DDA database searching or sequencing where MassIVE-KB-derived tryptic training data are appropriate — fine-tuning on non-enzymatic data is unnecessary and may reduce tryptic performance. Only a pretrained Casanovo model is needed for inference and no model retraining or non-tryptic benchmarking is planned — no split files need to be involved. The input spectra are DIA rather than DDA bottom-up tandem MS data.

skills.description: Use when downloading Metabolomics Workbench REST responses (csv, json, or text) that cannot be parsed into mwTab format and need to be captured as raw payload via MWRESTFile.
skills.name: non-mwtab-response-handling-csv-json-text
skills.search_text: non-mwtab-response-handling-csv-json-text Use when downloading Metabolomics Workbench REST responses (csv, json, or text) that cannot be parsed into mwTab format and need to be captured as raw payload via MWRESTFile. The REST response is representable in mwTab format — use the MWTabFile parsing path via read_mwrest() instead of retaining raw content. The input is a local mwTab-format file rather than a downloaded REST response — use the standard mwtab file reading/conversion machinery. You need schema validation of mwTab data (validate/validate_file with ms/nmr required schemas) rather than raw non-mwTab payload retrieval. http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Handles MW REST interface responses that are not representable in mwTab format by retaining csv/json/text payloads as MWRESTFile instances, complementing mwTab-format parsing. Introduced in mwtab 1.0.1 alongside GenericMWURL for constructing validated REST request URLs. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo11030163
skills.summary: Handles MW REST interface responses that are not representable in mwTab format by retaining csv/json/text payloads as MWRESTFile instances, complementing mwTab-format parsing. Introduced in mwtab 1.0.1 alongside GenericMWURL for constructing validated REST request URLs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The REST response is representable in mwTab format — use the MWTabFile parsing path via read_mwrest() instead of retaining raw content. The input is a local mwTab-format file rather than a downloaded REST response — use the standard mwtab file reading/conversion machinery. You need schema validation of mwTab data (validate/validate_file with ms/nmr required schemas) rather than raw non-mwTab payload retrieval.

skills.description: Use when analyzing MHC class I immunopeptidomics (non-enzymatic) DDA spectra and you need a database-search reference peptide set at 1% FDR to compare against de novo sequencing predictions.
skills.name: non-specific-digest-database-search
skills.search_text: non-specific-digest-database-search Use when analyzing MHC class I immunopeptidomics (non-enzymatic) DDA spectra and you need a database-search reference peptide set at 1% FDR to compare against de novo sequencing predictions. The sample contains an enzymatic (e.g., tryptic) digest, where a standard enzyme-constrained database search is the appropriate baseline rather than a no-enzyme digest The set of proteins possibly present in the sample is unknown, since database searching cannot detect unexpected peptides (contaminants, sequence variants, unexpected PTMs, foreign peptides) The analysis goal is identifying peptides absent from any reference proteome, which requires de novo sequencing instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Establishes a non-enzymatic sequence-database-search baseline for MHC class I immunopeptidomics by running Tide with no-enzyme digest settings against the human proteome, then rescoring PSMs with Percolator at 1% FDR. It is used to benchmark de novo sequencing (Casanovo) peptide yield and overlap on the same spectra. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-49731-x
skills.summary: Establishes a non-enzymatic sequence-database-search baseline for MHC class I immunopeptidomics by running Tide with no-enzyme digest settings against the human proteome, then rescoring PSMs with Percolator at 1% FDR. It is used to benchmark de novo sequencing (Casanovo) peptide yield and overlap on the same spectra.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The sample contains an enzymatic (e.g., tryptic) digest, where a standard enzyme-constrained database search is the appropriate baseline rather than a no-enzyme digest The set of proteins possibly present in the sample is unknown, since database searching cannot detect unexpected peptides (contaminants, sequence variants, unexpected PTMs, foreign peptides) The analysis goal is identifying peptides absent from any reference proteome, which requires de novo sequencing instead

skills.description: Use when metabolite entries from merged studies carry non-systematic identifiers (CAS, HMDB, KEGG, etc.) instead of InChIKeys and a systematic, structure-based key is needed for dataset merging.
skills.name: non-systematic-identifier-mapping
skills.search_text: non-systematic-identifier-mapping Use when metabolite entries from merged studies carry non-systematic identifiers (CAS, HMDB, KEGG, etc.) instead of InChIKeys and a systematic, structure-based key is needed for dataset merging. Entries already carry an InChIKey — no translation is needed and the row should be routed directly to merging. The only available input is a metabolite *name* with no identifier; in that case the name-to-InChIKey retrieval branch of MMS Step 1 applies instead, not CTS identifier translation. You need chemical attributes (MW, formula, ontology) rather than a merge key; that belongs to MMS Step 2 attribute retrieval, not this translation step. Converts non-systematic metabolite identifiers (CAS, HMDB, KEGG, PubChem, ChEBI, LipidMaps, DrugBank, Bin ID) into InChIKeys via the Chemical Translation Service (CTS) so heterogeneous study datasets can be merged in MMS Step 1. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo13121167
skills.summary: Converts non-systematic metabolite identifiers (CAS, HMDB, KEGG, PubChem, ChEBI, LipidMaps, DrugBank, Bin ID) into InChIKeys via the Chemical Translation Service (CTS) so heterogeneous study datasets can be merged in MMS Step 1.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Entries already carry an InChIKey — no translation is needed and the row should be routed directly to merging. The only available input is a metabolite *name* with no identifier; in that case the name-to-InChIKey retrieval branch of MMS Step 1 applies instead, not CTS identifier translation. You need chemical attributes (MW, formula, ontology) rather than a merge key; that belongs to MMS Step 2 attribute retrieval, not this translation step.

skills.description: Use when a two-dataset LC-MS metabolomics feature correspondence already contains unique matches (post Step 2) but the plain box thresholds in RT, m/z, and FI are too tight for features under large local shift trends, so candidate matches need to be re-scored and poor matches deleted.
skills.name: nonlinear-threshold-definition
skills.search_text: nonlinear-threshold-definition Use when a two-dataset LC-MS metabolomics feature correspondence already contains unique matches (post Step 2) but the plain box thresholds in RT, m/z, and FI are too tight for features under large local shift trends, so candidate matches need to be re-scored and poor matches deleted. Unique matching has not yet been performed (only the initial candidate matching exists) — run Steps 1 and 2 first, since this skill tightens thresholds on already-matched pairs The analyst wants to keep borderline matches that may be biologically valid — the article notes this optional step 'may inadvertently delete some correct matches', so use it only when deletion is acceptable The task is the initial candidate matching with plain RT/m/z/FI box thresholds rather than re-defining thresholds from residual trends http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Redefines RT, MZ, and log10FI match thresholds as nonlinear functions of the reference/target feature positions by normalizing per-dimension residuals with median + F·MAD and flagging matches far from the modeled inter-dataset shift trends in the M2S toolbox (Step 3 of the feature-correspondence workflow). metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c03592
skills.summary: Redefines RT, MZ, and log10FI match thresholds as nonlinear functions of the reference/target feature positions by normalizing per-dimension residuals with median + F·MAD and flagging matches far from the modeled inter-dataset shift trends in the M2S toolbox (Step 3 of the feature-correspondence workflow).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Unique matching has not yet been performed (only the initial candidate matching exists) — run Steps 1 and 2 first, since this skill tightens thresholds on already-matched pairs The analyst wants to keep borderline matches that may be biologically valid — the article notes this optional step 'may inadvertently delete some correct matches', so use it only when deletion is acceptable The task is the initial candidate matching with plain RT/m/z/FI box thresholds rather than re-defining thresholds from residual trends

skills.description: Use when replicating or benchmarking individual parameter estimation in NONMEM for simulated PK profiles, especially to cross-check mapbayr or another open-source MAP-BE tool on the same model-profile pairs.
skills.name: nonmem-map-estimation-execution
skills.search_text: nonmem-map-estimation-execution Use when replicating or benchmarking individual parameter estimation in NONMEM for simulated PK profiles, especially to cross-check mapbayr or another open-source MAP-BE tool on the same model-profile pairs. The goal is population-level PK/PD model building or parameter estimation with mixed effects, not individual MAP-BE (use population tools like nlmixr or saemix). No NONMEM license is available — mapbayr alone performs the equivalent MAP-BE in R without external nonlinear mixed effect modeling software. Estimating dose-related parameters (lag time, infusion duration) or models with large IIV variances (ωk2 > 1), where NONMEM-mapbayr discordances are expected and OFVi exploration suggests mapbayr may be more likely. http://edamontology.org/topic_3307 http://edamontology.org/topic_3379 Perform maximum a posteriori Bayesian estimation (MAP-BE) of individual PK parameters in NONMEM using deposited control streams, as the reference implementation against which mapbayr's mapbayest() estimates are validated across 35 test models and 4000 simulated profiles each. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/psp4.12689
skills.summary: Perform maximum a posteriori Bayesian estimation (MAP-BE) of individual PK parameters in NONMEM using deposited control streams, as the reference implementation against which mapbayr's mapbayest() estimates are validated across 35 test models and 4000 simulated profiles each.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is population-level PK/PD model building or parameter estimation with mixed effects, not individual MAP-BE (use population tools like nlmixr or saemix). No NONMEM license is available — mapbayr alone performs the equivalent MAP-BE in R without external nonlinear mixed effect modeling software. Estimating dose-related parameters (lag time, infusion duration) or models with large IIV variances (ωk2 > 1), where NONMEM-mapbayr discordances are expected and OFVi exploration suggests mapbayr may be more likely.

skills.description: Use when validating an open-source MAP-BE implementation (e.g. mapbayr) against NONMEM on simulated PK profiles, especially when discrepancies arise from estimated lag time, infusion duration, or models with large IIV (omega^2 > 1).
skills.name: nonmem-mapbayr-concordance-analysis
skills.search_text: nonmem-mapbayr-concordance-analysis Use when validating an open-source MAP-BE implementation (e.g. mapbayr) against NONMEM on simulated PK profiles, especially when discrepancies arise from estimated lag time, infusion duration, or models with large IIV (omega^2 > 1). Input is a clinical dataset needing individualized dosing rather than a software-validation comparison against NONMEM The goal is assessing whether MAP-BE recovers the true individual eta values (eta_i) — MAP estimation cannot inform this A runtime benchmark is required — no proper mapbayr vs NONMEM runtime comparison was performed and mapbayr is acknowledged to be slower http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 A validation workflow that performs MAP-Bayesian estimation of individual PK parameters with both mapbayr (R/mrgsolve) and NONMEM on the same simulated profiles, classifies each estimation as concordant or discordant, and, for discordant cases, recomputes OFVi from NONMEM's eta estimates to determine which tool found the more likely etas. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/psp4.12689
skills.summary: A validation workflow that performs MAP-Bayesian estimation of individual PK parameters with both mapbayr (R/mrgsolve) and NONMEM on the same simulated profiles, classifies each estimation as concordant or discordant, and, for discordant cases, recomputes OFVi from NONMEM's eta estimates to determine which tool found the more likely etas.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a clinical dataset needing individualized dosing rather than a software-validation comparison against NONMEM The goal is assessing whether MAP-BE recovers the true individual eta values (eta_i) — MAP estimation cannot inform this A runtime benchmark is required — no proper mapbayr vs NONMEM runtime comparison was performed and mapbayr is acknowledged to be slower

skills.description: Decision support for mapping single-cell-derived chemical dictionaries onto tissue MSI pixels — use when you have cross-annotated SCMS clusters and a shared lipid feature matrix with a tissue pixel matrix and want per-cluster spatial contribution maps.
skills.name: nonnegative-least-squares-tissue-fitting
skills.search_text: nonnegative-least-squares-tissue-fitting Decision support for mapping single-cell-derived chemical dictionaries onto tissue MSI pixels — use when you have cross-annotated SCMS clusters and a shared lipid feature matrix with a tissue pixel matrix and want per-cluster spatial contribution maps. Do not apply when SCMS and tissue MSI feature lists have not been cross-annotated within a shared m/z window — modeling errors arise from falsely cross-annotated features caused by mass shifts or an inappropriate ppm window. Do not use for unclustered single-cell data; the union dictionary U requires per-cluster NMF dictionaries built from labeled cell clusters. Do not use on raw transient data — inputs must be the reconstructed and processed tissue MSI matrix (coronal3D_propagated_decoded.h5). http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Constrained linear least-squares fitting of a union of NMF cell-cluster chemical dictionaries (U) onto the tissue MSI pixel matrix (Y) under non-negative model weights (Y = UC, C ≥ 0), mapping per-cluster weight sub-vector norms back to pixel coordinates to resolve the spatial organization of hippocampal cell subpopulations. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-024-02171-3
skills.summary: Constrained linear least-squares fitting of a union of NMF cell-cluster chemical dictionaries (U) onto the tissue MSI pixel matrix (Y) under non-negative model weights (Y = UC, C ≥ 0), mapping per-cluster weight sub-vector norms back to pixel coordinates to resolve the spatial organization of hippocampal cell subpopulations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Do not apply when SCMS and tissue MSI feature lists have not been cross-annotated within a shared m/z window — modeling errors arise from falsely cross-annotated features caused by mass shifts or an inappropriate ppm window. Do not use for unclustered single-cell data; the union dictionary U requires per-cluster NMF dictionaries built from labeled cell clusters. Do not use on raw transient data — inputs must be the reconstructed and processed tissue MSI matrix (coronal3D_propagated_decoded.h5).

skills.description: Use when two independent score distributions (e.g., Known vs Random enzyme-substrate pairs scored via MEANtools createGnnSom) must be compared nonparametrically, with reported statistics available for validation.
skills.name: nonparametric-hypothesis-testing
skills.search_text: nonparametric-hypothesis-testing Use when two independent score distributions (e.g., Known vs Random enzyme-substrate pairs scored via MEANtools createGnnSom) must be compared nonparametrically, with reported statistics available for validation. When the two score sets are paired or matched observations rather than independent samples (the Mann-Whitney U test used here assumes independence between Known and Random pairs). When per-pair reaction-likelihood scores cannot be computed because the pretrained GNN-SOM state or the deposited Known/Random pair files are unavailable. When the goal is pathway reconstruction from transcriptomic-metabolomic data rather than validating that a scoring mechanism separates true reactions from random pairs. Applies the two-sided Mann-Whitney U test (scipy.stats.mannwhitneyu) to compare distributions of GNN-SOM + ReactionDecoder reaction-likelihood scores between experimentally characterized (Known) and randomly assembled (Random) enzyme-substrate pairs, establishing that the scoring mechanism prioritizes true reactions without distributional assumptions. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pbio.3003307
skills.summary: Applies the two-sided Mann-Whitney U test (scipy.stats.mannwhitneyu) to compare distributions of GNN-SOM + ReactionDecoder reaction-likelihood scores between experimentally characterized (Known) and randomly assembled (Random) enzyme-substrate pairs, establishing that the scoring mechanism prioritizes true reactions without distributional assumptions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the two score sets are paired or matched observations rather than independent samples (the Mann-Whitney U test used here assumes independence between Known and Random pairs). When per-pair reaction-likelihood scores cannot be computed because the pretrained GNN-SOM state or the deposited Known/Random pair files are unavailable. When the goal is pathway reconstruction from transcriptomic-metabolomic data rather than validating that a scoring mechanism separates true reactions from random pairs.

skills.description: Use when the target (metadata) design is a two- or three-group metabolomics/proteomics comparison whose features fail parametric assumptions, and per-feature p-values plus FDR adjustment are needed.
skills.name: nonparametric-rank-based-testing
skills.search_text: nonparametric-rank-based-testing Use when the target (metadata) design is a two- or three-group metabolomics/proteomics comparison whose features fail parametric assumptions, and per-feature p-values plus FDR adjustment are needed. The comparison is a two-group design where parametric t-test assumptions hold and you want POMAShiny's T-test/ANOVA panel instead — the article offers both, so pick the parametric panel when normality is defensible. Input is raw spectra needing spectral processing — the article directs such work to the RforMassSpectrometry packages first, and POMA is meant to be reached only after a feature matrix exists. Input data has not yet been through POMAShiny's imputation/normalization/outlier-removal pre-processing panels (e.g. features with >20% missing values per group are still present). http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Apply POMAShiny/POMA's rank-based univariate tests — Mann-Whitney U for two-group metabolomics/proteomics contrasts and Kruskal-Wallis for three-group designs — on the preprocessed feature matrix, with FDR-adjusted p-values computed for every tested feature. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009148
skills.summary: Apply POMAShiny/POMA's rank-based univariate tests — Mann-Whitney U for two-group metabolomics/proteomics contrasts and Kruskal-Wallis for three-group designs — on the preprocessed feature matrix, with FDR-adjusted p-values computed for every tested feature.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The comparison is a two-group design where parametric t-test assumptions hold and you want POMAShiny's T-test/ANOVA panel instead — the article offers both, so pick the parametric panel when normality is defensible. Input is raw spectra needing spectral processing — the article directs such work to the RforMassSpectrometry packages first, and POMA is meant to be reached only after a feature matrix exists. Input data has not yet been through POMAShiny's imputation/normalization/outlier-removal pre-processing panels (e.g. features with >20% missing values per group are still present).

skills.description: Use when two MS/MS prediction models yield per-compound cosine-similarity scores against the same experimental Q-TOF test set and you must claim one significantly outperforms the other per ion mode ([M+H]+, [M-H]-).
skills.name: nonparametric-significance-testing
skills.search_text: nonparametric-significance-testing Use when two MS/MS prediction models yield per-compound cosine-similarity scores against the same experimental Q-TOF test set and you must claim one significantly outperforms the other per ion mode ([M+H]+, [M-H]-). Only a single model's mean cosine similarity is needed and no baseline superiority claim is being made — simple aggregation of eval_results.csv suffices The compared models were evaluated on different test compounds or splits — the two similarity distributions are then not comparable samples and the U test is meaningless Only aggregated summary statistics (means/std) are available rather than per-compound scores — the rank-based test requires the full distribution http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Run Mann-Whitney U (Whitney U) tests on per-compound cosine-similarity distributions, separately per ion mode, to establish whether 3DMolMS significantly outperforms MS/MS prediction baselines; appropriate because the similarity distributions are broad/skewed, so means alone are not decisive evidence. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad354
skills.summary: Run Mann-Whitney U (Whitney U) tests on per-compound cosine-similarity distributions, separately per ion mode, to establish whether 3DMolMS significantly outperforms MS/MS prediction baselines; appropriate because the similarity distributions are broad/skewed, so means alone are not decisive evidence.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only a single model's mean cosine similarity is needed and no baseline superiority claim is being made — simple aggregation of eval_results.csv suffices The compared models were evaluated on different test compounds or splits — the two similarity distributions are then not comparable samples and the U test is meaningless Only aggregated summary statistics (means/std) are available rather than per-compound scores — the rank-based test requires the full distribution

skills.description: Use when comparing a gene's expression distributions between two independent, unpaired sample groups (e.g. LIHC tumor vs non-tumor) from an expression matrix and metadata, without assuming normality of expression values.
skills.name: nonparametric-significance-testing-mann-whitney
skills.search_text: nonparametric-significance-testing-mann-whitney Use when comparing a gene's expression distributions between two independent, unpaired sample groups (e.g. LIHC tumor vs non-tumor) from an expression matrix and metadata, without assuming normality of expression values. The query molecule already has an authentic HSQC reference spectrum in libraries such as NMRShiftDB, BioMagResBank, HMDB, CH-NMR-NP, NP-MRD, or CSEARCH — direct library search will be more reliable. skills.summary: Predicts NPClassifier chemical superclasses from a 1H-13C HSQC spectrum via DeepSAT's multi-task CNN softmax classification head, assigning each query spectrum a probability vector over structure classes used to find chemically similar molecules in structure databases.

skills.search_text: nrmse-pfc-imputation-error-assessment Use when missForest has imputed a matrix with known ground truth (or held-out complete data) and you need to quantify true imputation error via NRMSE/PFC, or to judge whether the built-in OOB error estimate is an adequate test-set-free error proxy. The complete (uncorrupted) dataset is unavailable, so true NRMSE/PFC cannot be computed against ground truth — only the OOB estimate can be reported, and its adequacy cannot be validated here. Missingness is not completely at random in the 10-30% range evaluated; the paper's OOB-adequacy finding is grounded solely on artificially introduced MCAR values of 10% to 30%. You need a formal statistical error assessment per variable rather than an informal one — the discussion explicitly frames the OOB estimates as a mean of informal reliability check for each variable. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Quantifies missForest imputation error with NRMSE (continuous variables) and PFC (categorical variables) against known complete data, and validates the random forest's built-in out-of-bag (OOB) error estimates as a test-set-free proxy for the true error. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btr597

skills.search_text: nrps-adenylation-domain-substrate-inventory Use when you need to quantify how comprehensively a biosynthesis-visualisation tool (RAIChU) covers tailoring reactions, NRPS A-domain substrates/starter units, KS subtypes, or extender units before relying on it to depict fully maturated natural product pathways. skills.description: Use when validating a new HRMS feature-extraction pipeline against established open-source tools (MSDIAL, XCMS) on mixed chemical standards of known composition, such as EPA ENTACT mixtures, where expected true peaks are enumerated.
skills.name: nta-benchmark-dataset-processing
skills.search_text: nta-benchmark-dataset-processing Use when validating a new HRMS feature-extraction pipeline against established open-source tools (MSDIAL, XCMS) on mixed chemical standards of known composition, such as EPA ENTACT mixtures, where expected true peaks are enumerated. The goal is quantitative annotation or MS/MS fragment identification rather than extraction-performance benchmarking — use fragment searching against the MoNA MassBank database instead. The sample mixture has no known chemical composition, so there is no ground-truth peak count to interpret overlap fractions against. The input is already a single curated feature table from one platform with no second tool's output to compare against. A cross-platform feature-overlap benchmark for HRMS non-targeted analysis: quantify what fraction of MSS-extracted features (m/z–RT pairs) are recovered by MSDIAL and XCMS on EPA ENTACT mixtures of known composition, yielding ~52% overlap figures that validate a new extraction pipeline. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-023-00741-9

skills.description: Use when processing multiplexed IMC (or similar multiplexed protein imaging) tissue stacks where individual cells must be segmented to extract per-cell protein/metabolite intensities and spatial locations, e.g., lung cancer, tonsil, or endometrium tissues.

skills.search_text: nuclei-segmentation-with-deep-learning Use when processing multiplexed IMC (or similar multiplexed protein imaging) tissue stacks where individual cells must be segmented to extract per-cell protein/metabolite intensities and spatial locations, e.g., lung cancer, tonsil, or endometrium tissues. skills.summary: Deep-learning-based single-cell segmentation of multiplexed IMC tissue images, using Cellpose on nuclear channels (DNA-intercalator/Histone 3) followed by Mesmer whole-cell mask expansion, as implemented in the scSpaMet framework to recover per-cell protein and metabolite measurements.

skills.summary: Simulates synthetic LC-MS/MS runs of (modified) nucleoside standards with SMITER by converting a standard-mix csv into a peak-properties dict, applying a nucleoside MS2 fragmentor and a noise injector (e.g. UniformNoiseInjector with 1000 counts of white noise), and writing the result as an mzML file via smiter.synthetic_mzml.write_mzml.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need fragmentation modelling for molecule classes outside SMITER's default scope — while SMITER can in principle simulate any biomolecule via chemical formulas, default fragmentors cover peptides, modified nucleosides, and lipids only You need realistic noise levels matching a real instrument run — the simulated run exhibits lower noise than the corresponding real measurement and only contains the deliberately injected white noise Your input is raw vendor data (e.g. raw Thermo/Agilent files) rather than chemical formulas/retention-time annotations — SMITER builds everything from chemical formulas

skills.search_text: nucleotide-metabolism-reaction-classification Use when MINNO (or equivalent KEGG-vs-metabolomics comparison) has surfaced candidate missing reactions in nucleotide or nicotinate pathways and they must be assigned to a pathway class and a support tier before writing a gap table or report. skills.when_to_use_negative: When the organism's metabolic network has no empirical metabolomics / boundary-flux layer and the goal is pure in-silico gap-filling from genome annotation alone (MINNO's key value is metabolite-derived evidence, not purely genomic prediction). When fragment-ion similarities would be invalid to exchange under the permutation null (e.g. spectra generated under different adduct assumptions). http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Generates an empirical null distribution of SIMILE spectral-alignment scores by permuting intra- and inter-spectral fragment-ion similarity scores under the exchangeability null, so that max-weight matching scores can be converted into z-scores and p-values for pairwise tandem-MS spectra comparisons. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-022-30118-9
skills.summary: Generates an empirical null distribution of SIMILE spectral-alignment scores by permuting intra- and inter-spectral fragment-ion similarity scores under the exchangeability null, so that max-weight matching scores can be converted into z-scores and p-values for pairwise tandem-MS spectra comparisons.

skills.name: null-peak-concentration-thresholding
skills.search_text: null-peak-concentration-thresholding Use when analyzing LDI/MSI peak matrices where many ions are undetected in a high percentage of pixels, which undermines the reliability of statistical tests comparing two ROIs. Input is already a filtered feature table with no undetected (null) pixels — the null-segregation step adds no value and parameter (a) is uninformative The goal is general clustering or ion-image visualization rather than statistical comparison of ions between two ROIs (use rMSIproc::plotClusterImage/plotPeakImage instead) Data are not in an rMSIproc peak_matrix structure and converting them would require reprocessing from raw LDI-MS images http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Handles undetected MS ions (null peaks) in metabolomic MSI images by thresholding concentrations at a zero-concentration cutoff (zeroThreshold = 2.5e-4 in the rMSIKeyIon demo), segregating null from detected pixels per ion before statistical testing. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo9080162
skills.summary: Handles undetected MS ions (null peaks) in metabolomic MSI images by thresholding concentrations at a zero-concentration cutoff (zeroThreshold = 2.5e-4 in the rMSIKeyIon demo), segregating null from detected pixels per ion before statistical testing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a filtered feature table with no undetected (null) pixels — the null-segregation step adds no value and parameter (a) is uninformative The goal is general clustering or ion-image visualization rather than statistical comparison of ions between two ROIs (use rMSIproc::plotClusterImage/plotPeakImage instead) Data are not in an rMSIproc peak_matrix structure and converting them would require reprocessing from raw LDI-MS images

skills.description: Use when an MSI peak matrix contains ions undetected in a high percentage of pixels and you must select up/down-regulated ions between ROIs or clusters (e.g., cluster-vs-rest or pairwise cluster comparisons) without null peaks biasing the tests.

skills.search_text: null-peak-exclusion-filtering Use when an MSI peak matrix contains ions undetected in a high percentage of pixels and you must select up/down-regulated ions between ROIs or clusters (e.g., cluster-vs-rest or pairwise cluster comparisons) without null peaks biasing the tests. Input is not an MSI peak matrix with per-pixel ion intensities and spatial clustering/ROIs (e.g., bulk metabolomics feature tables lack the null-peak pixel structure this filter addresses) You only need to visualize demo results without reproducing the filtering — just load results.Rdata instead No null/undetected peaks are present (all ions detected in every pixel), so the zeroThreshold exclusion is unnecessary http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Discards undetected MS signals (null peaks) from ion concentration histograms before computing Mann-Whitney U and fold-change statistics in mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) workflows, improving reliability of up/down-regulated ion selection with rMSIKeyIon. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo9080162
skills.summary: Discards undetected MS signals (null peaks) from ion concentration histograms before computing Mann-Whitney U and fold-change statistics in mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) workflows, improving reliability of up/down-regulated ion selection with rMSIKeyIon.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is not an MSI peak matrix with per-pixel ion intensities and spatial clustering/ROIs (e.g., bulk metabolomics feature tables lack the null-peak pixel structure this filter addresses) You only need to visualize demo results without reproducing the filtering — just load results.Rdata instead No null/undetected peaks are present (all ions detected in every pixel), so the zeroThreshold exclusion is unnecessary

skills.description: Use when validating or illustrating how undetected MS peaks (nulls) corrupt the Mann-Whitney U p-value in ion filtering between two MSI ROIs, and why rMSIKeyIon discards nulls before testing.
skills.name: null-peak-injection-in-msi-intensities
skills.search_text: null-peak-injection-in-msi-intensities Use when validating or illustrating how undetected MS peaks (nulls) corrupt the Mann-Whitney U p-value in ion filtering between two MSI ROIs, and why rMSIKeyIon discards nulls before testing. Input is real rMSIproc peak-matrix data rather than a controlled simulation designed to isolate the null-value effect The goal is ion discovery on a real LDI-MS image with more than two clusters, where the three-parameter filter (null percentage, Mann-Whitney U test, fold-change) must be applied in full The statistical test is not the Mann-Whitney U test and fold-change on histograms, since the null-segregation rationale is specific to those parameters http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Simulates ion intensity histograms for two MSI regions with injected null (undetected) values below the zeroThreshold = 2.5e-4 convention, then demonstrates that segregating nulls out of the distributions before the Mann-Whitney U test (via rMSIKeyIon::TestIonSelect) reverses a non-significant result (p ≈ 0.38) into an extremely significant one (p ≈ 1e-43). metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo9080162
skills.summary: Simulates ion intensity histograms for two MSI regions with injected null (undetected) values below the zeroThreshold = 2.5e-4 convention, then demonstrates that segregating nulls out of the distributions before the Mann-Whitney U test (via rMSIKeyIon::TestIonSelect) reverses a non-significant result (p ≈ 0.38) into an extremely significant one (p ≈ 1e-43).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is real rMSIproc peak-matrix data rather than a controlled simulation designed to isolate the null-value effect The goal is ion discovery on a real LDI-MS image with more than two clusters, where the three-parameter filter (null percentage, Mann-Whitney U test, fold-change) must be applied in full The statistical test is not the Mann-Whitney U test and fold-change on histograms, since the null-segregation rationale is specific to those parameters

skills.description: Use when comparing ion intensities between MSI regions-of-interest (e.g., k-means clusters of LDI-MS liver or brain images) and the peak matrix contains many ions undetected in a high percentage of pixels, which otherwise undermines the Mann-Whitney U test and fold-change reliability.
skills.name: null-peak-zero-threshold-filtering
skills.search_text: null-peak-zero-threshold-filtering Use when comparing ion intensities between MSI regions-of-interest (e.g., k-means clusters of LDI-MS liver or brain images) and the peak matrix contains many ions undetected in a high percentage of pixels, which otherwise undermines the Mann-Whitney U test and fold-change reliability. The peak matrix is already a dense feature table with essentially no undetected peaks, so the null-peak percentage filter adds no discriminating power. You only want to inspect precomputed demo results, in which case loading results.Rdata directly is sufficient and re-running TestIonSelect is unnecessary. The analysis goal is image segmentation itself (k-means clustering) rather than statistical ion selection between already-defined regions. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 A statistical ion-filtering refinement from the rMSIKeyIon R package that treats undetected MS signals ('null peaks') explicitly, using a zeroThreshold (default 2.5e-4) so ions missing in a high percentage of pixels do not corrupt p-value/fold-change comparisons between image regions. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo9080162
skills.summary: A statistical ion-filtering refinement from the rMSIKeyIon R package that treats undetected MS signals ('null peaks') explicitly, using a zeroThreshold (default 2.5e-4) so ions missing in a high percentage of pixels do not corrupt p-value/fold-change comparisons between image regions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The peak matrix is already a dense feature table with essentially no undetected peaks, so the null-peak percentage filter adds no discriminating power. You only want to inspect precomputed demo results, in which case loading results.Rdata directly is sufficient and re-running TestIonSelect is unnecessary. The analysis goal is image segmentation itself (k-means clustering) rather than statistical ion selection between already-defined regions.

skills.description: Use when spectrum preprocessing of large MGF-backed MS/MS datasets is CPU-bound in Python loops and peak-filtering rules (precursor removal, min-intensity cutoffs, top-N peak retention, L2 normalization) can be rewritten as vectorized Numba JIT kernels.
skills.name: numba-jit-vectorization
skills.search_text: numba-jit-vectorization Use when spectrum preprocessing of large MGF-backed MS/MS datasets is CPU-bound in Python loops and peak-filtering rules (precursor removal, min-intensity cutoffs, top-N peak retention, L2 normalization) can be rewritten as vectorized Numba JIT kernels. The workload is not numeric peak-array filtering/normalization (e.g., vendor raw files still needing conversion, or the GPU-side HD encoding and clustering stages). skills.search_text: numerical-boundary-condition-testing Use when a normalized score (e.g., a separation efficiency encoded from retention-time intervals) must be proven bounded before it is fed into downstream modeling such as Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization. Input is raw LC-MS data (mzML/mzXML) rather than an already-encoded numeric score — signal extraction and top-signal finding happen upstream via findTopSignals You need to optimize the gradient itself (acquisition function / gpModel step) rather than verify that the encoding of a given gradient is bounded The metric's boundary conditions cannot be stated analytically (no known worst/best case), since the derivation of GSI=0 and GSI=1 anchors is the core of the method A verification skill for composite numerical encodings: derive analytic extreme-case values (co-elution and perfect separation) of a metric such as BAGO's global separation index (GSI), then computationally confirm the encoded output stays within its declared [0,1] bounds. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2023.09.08.556930

skills.description: Use when porting or verifying a published statistical estimator (e.g. B-spline MI as in MOG) and you need ground-truth comparison, invariants, and a validation report before trusting the implementation.
skills.name: numerical-implementation-validation
skills.search_text: numerical-implementation-validation Use when porting or verifying a published statistical estimator (e.g. B-spline MI as in MOG) and you need ground-truth comparison, invariants, and a validation report before trusting the implementation. The goal is to compute MI for exploratory analysis directly rather than to validate a re-implementation — use an existing trusted MI library instead. The features under comparison are known to be dependent, so the I(X;Y)=0-for-independence invariant cannot serve as a sanity check. The estimator being validated is not a published, citable numerical method with an available reference implementation. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 http://edamontology.org/topic_3577 Re-implements a published numerical estimator — here the Daub et al. B-spline mutual information estimator used in MetaOmGraph's Mutual Information module — from scratch, then validates it against an independent reference implementation using sanity invariants (non-negativity, near-zero MI for independent features) and pairwise value agreement. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkz1209
skills.summary: Re-implements a published numerical estimator — here the Daub et al. B-spline mutual information estimator used in MetaOmGraph's Mutual Information module — from scratch, then validates it against an independent reference implementation using sanity invariants (non-negativity, near-zero MI for independent features) and pairwise value agreement.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to compute MI for exploratory analysis directly rather than to validate a re-implementation — use an existing trusted MI library instead. skills.description: Use when a protonated molecular ion (e.g. a metabolite <205 Da with a prepared protonation site) must be collided with an argon collider atom and bond breakages simulated from first principles to generate in silico CID-MS/MS spectra.
skills.name: nve-ensemble-dft-md-simulation-execution
skills.search_text: nve-ensemble-dft-md-simulation-execution Use when a protonated molecular ion (e.g. a metabolite <205 Da with a prepared protonation site) must be collided with an argon collider atom and bond breakages simulated from first principles to generate in silico CID-MS/MS spectra. When only fragment structures or spectra of stable molecules are needed without simulating the collision itself — a thermodynamic or rule-based predictor is far cheaper and CIDMD's ab initio MD is computationally heavy. When the molecule is too large or has many protomers/tautomers — the article reports average CIDMD prediction accuracy decreases as the number of protomers and tautomers increases. When a ground-state optimization or single-point energy is sufficient — this skill is specifically for reactive collision dynamics in the NVE (microcanonical) ensemble, not for geometry optimization. When simulating multiple successive collisions inside one trajectory — the article states 'an automatic multiple collision method has not yet been implemented yet', so one trajectory = one collision. http://edamontology.org/topic_3332 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Run collision-induced-dissociation dynamics of protonated metabolites as NVE-ensemble ab initio MD with TeraChem at unrestricted B3LYP/6-31G*, a 1.0 fs time step, and Mayer bond order tracking over at least 1,000 fs, so that bond breakages driving CID-MS/MS fragmentation can be extracted. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jcim.4c00760
skills.summary: Run collision-induced-dissociation dynamics of protonated metabolites as NVE-ensemble ab initio MD with TeraChem at unrestricted B3LYP/6-31G*, a 1.0 fs time step, and Mayer bond order tracking over at least 1,000 fs, so that bond breakages driving CID-MS/MS fragmentation can be extracted.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When only fragment structures or spectra of stable molecules are needed without simulating the collision itself — a thermodynamic or rule-based predictor is far cheaper and CIDMD's ab initio MD is computationally heavy. When the molecule is too large or has many protomers/tautomers — the article reports average CIDMD prediction accuracy decreases as the number of protomers and tautomers increases. When a ground-state optimization or single-point energy is sufficient — this skill is specifically for reactive collision dynamics in the NVE (microcanonical) ensemble, not for geometry optimization. When simulating multiple successive collisions inside one trajectory — the article states 'an automatic multiple collision method has not yet been implemented yet', so one trajectory = one collision.

skills.description: Use when LC-MS metabolomics data contain occasional outlier runs (disproportionately high/low metabolite intensities) that would bias mean-based or standard QC-based drift correction; normalization must stay robust without discarding samples outright.
skills.name: observation-weighted-robust-normalization
skills.search_text: observation-weighted-robust-normalization Use when LC-MS metabolomics data contain occasional outlier runs (disproportionately high/low metabolite intensities) that would bias mean-based or standard QC-based drift correction; normalization must stay robust without discarding samples outright. Data are already filtered or pre-cleaned with outlier runs removed, making robust weighting unnecessary — simple QC-RLSC or QC-RSC suffices. The analysis goal is batch-integration or feature-level filtering rather than per-compound signal-drift correction; the skill addresses intensity normalization, not RSD/CV filtering on QC samples. Downstream evaluation metrics are RSD-of-QC reduction or count of differentially abundant metabolites; the article flags these as common benchmarking pitfalls rather than evidence the skill was applied correctly. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Fit the metanorm tGAM/rGAM/rLOESS robust normalization models with per-observation weights derived from residuals (calcWeights), so runs with disproportionately high or low metabolite intensities are downweighted rather than excluded, preserving statistical power for downstream differential abundance testing. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.09.30.679445
skills.summary: Fit the metanorm tGAM/rGAM/rLOESS robust normalization models with per-observation weights derived from residuals (calcWeights), so runs with disproportionately high or low metabolite intensities are downweighted rather than excluded, preserving statistical power for downstream differential abundance testing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are already filtered or pre-cleaned with outlier runs removed, making robust weighting unnecessary — simple QC-RLSC or QC-RSC suffices. The comparison is a single, well-defined pairwise contrast between two concrete sample groups with no need for ontology-based term expansion Metadata combinations have few samples or few studies — the article notes quantitative comparisons are less robust for such combinations The dataset is not the curated BinBase snapshot (December 2021, 156,174 samples) or lacks ontology-mapped metadata; BinDiscover cannot incorporate later-added compounds http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Ontologically grouped differential analysis (OGDA) as implemented in BinDiscover: a broad biological question (e.g., Human Digestive Tract vs. Bacteria) is expanded via metadata ontologies (MeSH, NCBI taxonomy) into sets of concrete metadata triads, pairwise Welch t-tests are run per compound, and results are conservatively aggregated into a single p-value and fold-change per metabolite. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-023-00734-8

skills.description: Use when a biological question names a broad ontology category (e.g. 'Digestive Tract', 'rodents', 'Bacteria') and must be expanded into the concrete organ/species/disease metadata combinations it covers before statistical comparison.
skills.name: ontology-hierarchy-traversal
skills.search_text: ontology-hierarchy-traversal Use when a biological question names a broad ontology category (e.g. 'Digestive Tract', 'rodents', 'Bacteria') and must be expanded into the concrete organ/species/disease metadata combinations it covers before statistical comparison. The query is already a simple pairwise metadata contrast between two specific combinations, with no need for ontological broadening. Candidate expansion terms would cross ontology branches (e.g. merging stool, which maps to 'fluids and secretions', into a digestive-system expansion) — the expansion must not pool across branches. The sample metadata cannot be mapped to an established ontology (e.g. cryptic domain-specific acronyms), so no 'belongs to' relations can be built. http://edamontology.org/topic_0219 http://edamontology.org/topic_0089 Traverses an ontology hierarchy (MeSH for organs/diseases, NCBI taxonomy for species) with a NetworkX 'belongs to' graph so that broad biological query terms like 'Digestive Tract' or 'Bacteria' resolve into their constituent metadata combinations for downstream differential analysis. This is the expansion step that lets BinDiscover's OGDA compare broad biological categories rather than single metadata pairs. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-023-00734-8
skills.summary: Traverses an ontology hierarchy (MeSH for organs/diseases, NCBI taxonomy for species) with a NetworkX 'belongs to' graph so that broad biological query terms like 'Digestive Tract' or 'Bacteria' resolve into their constituent metadata combinations for downstream differential analysis. This is the expansion step that lets BinDiscover's OGDA compare broad biological categories rather than single metadata pairs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The query is already a simple pairwise metadata contrast between two specific combinations, with no need for ontological broadening. Candidate expansion terms would cross ontology branches (e.g. merging stool, which maps to 'fluids and secretions', into a digestive-system expansion) — the expansion must not pool across branches. The sample metadata cannot be mapped to an established ontology (e.g. cryptic domain-specific acronyms), so no 'belongs to' relations can be built.

skills.description: Use when you have downloaded released .h5 model files for an ontology-based classifier and need to confirm each network's output size matches the number of categories at its classification level before reuse or retraining.
skills.name: ontology-output-size-verification
skills.search_text: ontology-output-size-verification Use when you have downloaded released .h5 model files for an ontology-based classifier and need to confirm each network's output size matches the number of categories at its classification level before reuse or retraining. Your input is raw chemical structures or SMILES strings to be classified via the /classify?smiles=<> API rather than model files whose architecture must be audited. The target is a genuine multitask model with three simultaneous output heads on a single network — NPClassifier instead uses three separate single-task networks, so one-output-head-per-file checks would misfire. No reference ontology category counts are available, so there is no ground truth to compare output layer sizes against. Verifies that each released deep learning classifier's output layer dimension exactly matches its ontology level's category count (for NPClassifier: 7 Pathways, 70 Superclasses, 672 Classes), by enumerating layers of the downloaded HDF5 models with the TensorFlow 2.3.0/Keras API. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jnatprod.1c00399

When the task is annotating ISA-Tab experimental metadata itself rather than packaging an executable workflow as an RO-Crate — the ISA term 'sample collection' has no ontology match in EBI's OLS, so this skill cannot supply one. When the workflow will not be shared or registered (e.g., WorkflowHub) and human-readable documentation suffices; the article notes that manual semantic annotation is effortful. When EDAM or the recommended ontologies do contain suitable terms but the goal is free-text description — do not invent custom terms outside the chosen ontologies. http://edamontology.org/topic_0089 Annotates RO-Crate entities (workflow, input data, CreateAction analysis steps) with machine-readable ontology terms drawn from EDAM, NCIT, OBI, and SIO via EBI's Ontology Lookup Service, falling back to the eNanoMapper Ontology where EDAM lacks suitable terms. This is what turns a packaged computational workflow into a findable, interoperable FAIR Digital Object. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/gigascience/giad115

This is what turns a packaged computational workflow into a findable, interoperable FAIR Digital Object.

skills.description: Use when a literature-mining step has produced candidate keyword n-grams from abstracts and you need to reduce them to biologically interpretable terms by mapping against GO biological process and HPO vocabularies.
skills.name: ontology-vocabulary-keyword-filtering
skills.search_text: ontology-vocabulary-keyword-filtering Use when a literature-mining step has produced candidate keyword n-grams from abstracts and you need to reduce them to biologically interpretable terms by mapping against GO biological process and HPO vocabularies. The goal is pathway over-representation testing on a feature list rather than filtering text-mined abstract keywords — use EnrichR/GSEA instead, which BiomiX uses for biological process exploration. The input is already a curated gene/phenotype list mapped to ontologies; re-filtering n-grams adds nothing in that case. No ontology (GO-BP or HPO) coverage exists for the domain of the extracted keywords, so mapping-based filtering would discard everything. Filters text-mined, non-redundant keyword combinations extracted from PubMed abstracts (via litsearchr) so that only terms mappable to Gene Ontology biological process (GO-BP) or Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) vocabulary are kept, yielding biologically interpretable annotations of discriminant MOFA factor contributors in BiomiX. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-024-06022-y

skills.search_text: oob-error-rate-extraction Use when a trained randomForest object built on metabolomics feature data (e.g. the four selected metabolites Adenylosuccinate, Histidine, Hydroxyproline, Linolenic Acid) is available and you need OOB error rates to report or compare predictive performance per group pair. skills.name: oob-vs-true-error-calibration-analysis
skills.search_text: oob-vs-true-error-calibration-analysis Use when imputing missing values with missForest and you need to assess imputation accuracy per simulation run but have no complete reference matrix available at prediction time. skills.description: Use when assigning FDR to SSMs from an open modification spectral library search, where modified matches must be evaluated separately from unmodified ones because decoy mass differences are randomly distributed while true modified matches cluster at shared modification masses.
skills.name: open-modification-search-result-filtering
skills.search_text: open-modification-search-result-filtering Use when assigning FDR to SSMs from an open modification spectral library search, where modified matches must be evaluated separately from unmodified ones because decoy mass differences are randomly distributed while true modified matches cluster at shared modification masses. Standard (closed) search results or the unmodified peptide identifications from the first cascade-search level — these use the conventional target–decoy FDR calculation without subgrouping Subgroups containing fewer than 20 SSMs — these must be merged into the pooled residual group rather than filtered individually, or the FDR will be underestimated http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Estimates FDR for open-modification spectral library search results by partitioning spectrum–spectrum matches (SSMs) into subgroups based on their charge-normalized precursor mass difference and applying target–decoy FDR filtering per subgroup, as implemented in ANN-SoLo. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.8b00359
skills.summary: Estimates FDR for open-modification spectral library search results by partitioning spectrum–spectrum matches (SSMs) into subgroups based on their charge-normalized precursor mass difference and applying target–decoy FDR filtering per subgroup, as implemented in ANN-SoLo.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Standard (closed) search results or the unmodified peptide identifications from the first cascade-search level — these use the conventional target–decoy FDR calculation without subgrouping Subgroups containing fewer than 20 SSMs — these must be merged into the pooled residual group rather than filtered individually, or the FDR will be underestimated

skills.search_text: open-modification-spectral-library-search Use when large sets of unidentified spectra have been grouped into clusters (e.g. GLEAMS clusters) and you want to annotate them by open modification searching of cluster medoids against a spectral library such as MassIVE-KB, accepting unknown precursor mass shifts. When spectra are already identified by a standard (closed-mass) database or spectral library search — open modification searching is intended for previously unidentified spectra with unanticipated mass shifts.
