When strict identification of a known, narrow set of modifications is required and unanticipated mass shifts are unacceptable as evidence. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Annotates previously unidentified MS/MS spectra by searching them against a spectral library with tolerance for unanticipated precursor mass shifts (open modification search), then propagates hits to related spectra. Applied here to GLEAMS cluster medoids with ANN-SoLo to lift 45 million medoid identifications to ~49 million total PSMs. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-022-01496-1
skills.summary: Annotates previously unidentified MS/MS spectra by searching them against a spectral library with tolerance for unanticipated precursor mass shifts (open modification search), then propagates hits to related spectra. skills.description: Use when you need to identify modified peptides in high-resolution MS/MS spectra via spectral library search, especially for open searches with large precursor mass windows such as 500 Da.
skills.name: open-modification-spectrum-matching
skills.search_text: open-modification-spectrum-matching Use when you need to identify modified peptides in high-resolution MS/MS spectra via spectral library search, especially for open searches with large precursor mass windows such as 500 Da. When the analysis goal is a standard unmodified-peptide search — use ANN-SoLo's level-1 plain dot product (5 ppm precursor window) instead of the shifted dot product open-search mode. When only sequence-database searching is required and no spectral library is available; the shifted dot product specifically depends on curated (or predicted) library spectra with known modifications. When the spectral library is very small — approximate nearest neighbor indexing may not be necessary for candidate selection. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Sensitively match modified query MS/MS spectra to their unmodified spectral-library counterparts using ANN-SoLo's shifted dot product, which compensates for the peak shifts a modification induces in the fragment spectrum. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.8b00359
skills.summary: Sensitively match modified query MS/MS spectra to their unmodified spectral-library counterparts using ANN-SoLo's shifted dot product, which compensates for the peak shifts a modification induces in the fragment spectrum.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the analysis goal is a standard unmodified-peptide search — use ANN-SoLo's level-1 plain dot product (5 ppm precursor window) instead of the shifted dot product open-search mode. When the spectral library is very small — approximate nearest neighbor indexing may not be necessary for candidate selection.

skills.description: Use when multiple LC-MS runs (proteomic or metabolomic feature lists with m/z, RT, charge, intensity) must have corresponding analytes mapped across samples despite monotonic or non-monotonic RT shifts, or when benchmarking OpenMS feature grouping against a deep learning-based aligner.
skills.name: openms-feature-correspondence
skills.search_text: openms-feature-correspondence Use when multiple LC-MS runs (proteomic or metabolomic feature lists with m/z, RT, charge, intensity) must have corresponding analytes mapped across samples despite monotonic or non-monotonic RT shifts, or when benchmarking OpenMS feature grouping against a deep learning-based aligner. Input is a single LC-MS run or already-aligned feature table with one row per analyte — no correspondence across runs is needed. The task is identification-based peptide/protein matching (e.g. MaxQuant match-between-runs on MS/MS-identified peptides) rather than ID-free feature correspondence. Samples are extremely heterogeneous or dominated by features with nearly identical m/z such that the default QC yields very few results — here the recommendation is to set FDR to 1 and filter on score > 0.5 rather than rely on default correspondence QC. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3383 Feature correspondence (retention-time alignment / feature grouping) for large-cohort LC-MS data, using OpenMS-based feature grouping as the comparator and DeepRTAlign (deep learning-based direct matching over coarse alignment, binning, filtering, FDR quality control) as the primary alignment engine for proteomic and metabolomic feature lists. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-023-43909-5
skills.summary: Feature correspondence (retention-time alignment / feature grouping) for large-cohort LC-MS data, using OpenMS-based feature grouping as the comparator and DeepRTAlign (deep learning-based direct matching over coarse alignment, binning, filtering, FDR quality control) as the primary alignment engine for proteomic and metabolomic feature lists.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a single LC-MS run or already-aligned feature table with one row per analyte — no correspondence across runs is needed. The task is identification-based peptide/protein matching (e.g. MaxQuant match-between-runs on MS/MS-identified peptides) rather than ID-free feature correspondence. Samples are extremely heterogeneous or dominated by features with nearly identical m/z such that the default QC yields very few results — here the recommendation is to set FDR to 1 and filter on score > 0.5 rather than rely on default correspondence QC.

skills.search_text: operon-benchmarking-against-reference Use when a whole-genome or metagenomic operon prediction run has produced a predicted-operon file (e.g. Operon_File.tab) and reference operon annotations exist, and you need sensitivity, specificity and accuracy to validate the pipeline. No reference operon annotation exists for the organism, so no TP/FP/FN ground truth can be constructed The goal is de novo operon discovery on novel metagenomic samples rather than validation against known operons Input is a gene-prediction .tab file with no predicted-operon file and you are still upstream of the operon-calling step http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Benchmark predicted operons from a genome or metagenome run (e.g., MetaRon's Operon_File.tab) against curated reference operon annotations such as DOOR/RegulonDB by computing gene-pair-level sensitivity, specificity and accuracy, as done for E. coli K-12 MG1655 (97.8/94.1/92.4%), the simulated three-genome mixture (93.7/75.5/88.1%) and the E. coli c20 draft genome (87/91/88%). metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12864-020-07357-5
skills.summary: Benchmark predicted operons from a genome or metagenome run (e.g., MetaRon's Operon_File.tab) against curated reference operon annotations such as DOOR/RegulonDB by computing gene-pair-level sensitivity, specificity and accuracy, as done for E. coli K-12 MG1655 (97.8/94.1/92.4%), the simulated three-genome mixture (93.7/75.5/88.1%) and the E. coli c20 draft genome (87/91/88%).
skills.when_to_use_negative: No reference operon annotation exists for the organism, so no TP/FP/FN ground truth can be constructed The goal is de novo operon discovery on novel metagenomic samples rather than validation against known operons Input is a gene-prediction .tab file with no predicted-operon file and you are still upstream of the operon-calling step

skills.search_text: operon-co-directionality-proximity-clustering Use when you need to predict operons from raw shotgun FASTQ reads or from pre-assembled scaftigs with gene predictions, and no functional/experimental operon information is available. You already have curated, experimentally supported operon annotations for the organism — use those instead of de novo proximon calling Input data is functional/annotation tables rather than shotgun reads or scaftigs + gene predictions — MetaRon cannot operate without sequence data Read lengths exceed 128 bases and you pass the wrong --read_length flag ('l' vs 'r'), or reads are paired in one file but 'merge' is set — the pipeline parameters would be invalid http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Predict bacterial operons from shotgun sequencing data using MetaRon, which clusters co-directional gene pairs (proximons) by intergenic distance (IGD < 601 bp) and promoter presence/absence, without requiring functional or experimental annotations. The skill reproduces the MetaRon benchmark of 97.8% sensitivity, 94.1% specificity and 92.4% accuracy on E. coli K-12 MG1655 HiSeq reads. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12864-020-07357-5
skills.summary: Predict bacterial operons from shotgun sequencing data using MetaRon, which clusters co-directional gene pairs (proximons) by intergenic distance (IGD < 601 bp) and promoter presence/absence, without requiring functional or experimental annotations. The skill reproduces the MetaRon benchmark of 97.8% sensitivity, 94.1% specificity and 92.4% accuracy on E. coli K-12 MG1655 HiSeq reads.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You already have curated, experimentally supported operon annotations for the organism — use those instead of de novo proximon calling Input data is functional/annotation tables rather than shotgun reads or scaftigs + gene predictions — MetaRon cannot operate without sequence data Read lengths exceed 128 bases and you pass the wrong --read_length flag ('l' vs 'r'), or reads are paired in one file but 'merge' is set — the pipeline parameters would be invalid

skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already encoded as 2D grayscale molecular-fingerprint images destined for the MS2toImg CNN — the paper's image-based route bypasses the feature table entirely and was shown to outperform conventional baselines. skills.description: Use when annotating imaging MS datasets with METASPACE or METASPACE-ML and you must decide which default FDR threshold (e.g. 5%) gives the most reliable target-decoy-controlled annotations for a specific dataset or sample-type group.
skills.name: optimal-fdr-threshold-selection-per-dataset
skills.search_text: optimal-fdr-threshold-selection-per-dataset Use when annotating imaging MS datasets with METASPACE or METASPACE-ML and you must decide which default FDR threshold (e.g. 5%) gives the most reliable target-decoy-controlled annotations for a specific dataset or sample-type group. Input is already a per-dataset table of reliability scores or a pre-selected optimal FDR threshold — recomputation via target-decoy F-beta is redundant. You need a new FDR model or rescoring of raw spectra rather than threshold selection among the existing default FDR thresholds; use METASPACE-ML annotation itself instead. The dataset lacks decoy annotation results, since precision/recall of confident annotations cannot be estimated from target-decoy separation without decoys. Quantifies the reliability of METASPACE-ML metabolite annotations in imaging mass spectrometry by computing a precision-weighted F-beta score (beta = 0.5) of target-decoy FDR estimates at the four default FDR thresholds, then selecting the per-dataset FDR threshold that maximizes this reliability score. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-52213-9

skills.description: Use when 1H NMR mixture spectra have strongly overlapping peaks, distorted lineshapes (bad shimming), temperature- or solvent-induced peak shifts, or low-resolution benchtop acquisition where peak-picking quantification fails.

skills.search_text: optimal-transport-spectral-deconvolution Use when 1H NMR mixture spectra have strongly overlapping peaks, distorted lineshapes (bad shimming), temperature- or solvent-induced peak shifts, or low-resolution benchtop acquisition where peak-picking quantification fails. The mixture contains unknown components absent from the spectral library, since optimal transport deconvolution assigns signal only to supplied library spectra. Absolute quantification is required without a quantitative external-standard spectrum algebraically added to the mixture spectrum. Peaks are well resolved and peak-picking tools suffice; note MANIQ outperformed Magnetstein in Experiment 2 (AvRE 1.0% vs 3.0%). http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Quantify mixture components in 1H NMR spectra by treating mixture and library spectra as probability distributions of signal intensity and solving an optimal transport (Wasserstein) deconvolution with Magnetstein, using tunable sharpness parameters kappa_mixture and kappa_components. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c03594
skills.summary: Quantify mixture components in 1H NMR spectra by treating mixture and library spectra as probability distributions of signal intensity and solving an optimal transport (Wasserstein) deconvolution with Magnetstein, using tunable sharpness parameters kappa_mixture and kappa_components.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The mixture contains unknown components absent from the spectral library, since optimal transport deconvolution assigns signal only to supplied library spectra. Absolute quantification is required without a quantitative external-standard spectrum algebraically added to the mixture spectrum. Peaks are well resolved and peak-picking tools suffice; note MANIQ outperformed Magnetstein in Experiment 2 (AvRE 1.0% vs 3.0%).

skills.description: Use when quantifying components of a 1H NMR mixture spectrum against a spectral library whose peaks overlap, are shifted (e.g. by solvent or temperature, as in the 36.7 °C vs 22.27 °C Experiment 5), or have distorted lineshapes from an inhomogeneous field.
skills.name: optimal-transport-wasserstein-distance-computation
skills.search_text: optimal-transport-wasserstein-distance-computation Use when quantifying components of a 1H NMR mixture spectrum against a spectral library whose peaks overlap, are shifted (e.g. by solvent or temperature, as in the 36.7 °C vs 22.27 °C Experiment 5), or have distorted lineshapes from an inhomogeneous field. When the goal is absolute concentration against no spectral library — the optimal-transport formulation yields relative proportions πi; absolute quantification instead requires algebraically adding a quantitative external-standard spectrum to the mixture. When spectra are clean, well-resolved peak lists where peak-integration or peak-based tools already suffice — simpler peak-based methods (MANIQ, ACD/TP) can outperform in cases like Experiment 2 (MANIQ AvRE 1.0% vs Magnetstein 3.0%). When κmixture is set very small for a heavily imbalanced mixture (e.g. ~1:10 in Experiment 1) without checking that the minor component has not been absorbed into the vortex ω. http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Casts quantitative NMR mixture deconvolution as an optimal-transport problem: mixture and library spectra are normalized into discrete probability measures over the chemical-shift axis, and component proportions πi are recovered by solving a Wasserstein-distance transportation LP with denoising penalties κmixture and κcomponents. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c03594
skills.summary: Casts quantitative NMR mixture deconvolution as an optimal-transport problem: mixture and library spectra are normalized into discrete probability measures over the chemical-shift axis, and component proportions πi are recovered by solving a Wasserstein-distance transportation LP with denoising penalties κmixture and κcomponents.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is absolute concentration against no spectral library — the optimal-transport formulation yields relative proportions πi; absolute quantification instead requires algebraically adding a quantitative external-standard spectrum to the mixture. When spectra are clean, well-resolved peak lists where peak-integration or peak-based tools already suffice — simpler peak-based methods (MANIQ, ACD/TP) can outperform in cases like Experiment 2 (MANIQ AvRE 1.0% vs Magnetstein 3.0%). When κmixture is set very small for a heavily imbalanced mixture (e.g. ~1:10 in Experiment 1) without checking that the minor component has not been absorbed into the vortex ω.

skills.description: Decision support for choosing and reporting the background/reference compound set before running ORA on a list of differentially abundant metabolites.
skills.name: ora-background-set-parameterization
skills.search_text: ora-background-set-parameterization Decision support for choosing and reporting the background/reference compound set before running ORA on a list of differentially abundant metabolites. The analysis goal is pathway database comparison rather than background-set selection; the paper states an extensive comparison of pathway databases is beyond its scope. A ground-truth enriched-pathway dataset is available that can be used to evaluate ORA outputs directly, since the study explicitly lacked such a benchmark. Inputs are raw abundance matrices; post-processing (imputation with minimum/2, log2 transformation, auto-scaling) and metabolite-identifier harmonisation must precede background-set construction. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Parameterize over-representation analysis (ORA) in metabolomics with an explicit, assay- and pathway-database-matched background compound set, since using a non-assay-specific background inflates false-positive pathways. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009105
skills.summary: Parameterize over-representation analysis (ORA) in metabolomics with an explicit, assay- and pathway-database-matched background compound set, since using a non-assay-specific background inflates false-positive pathways.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is pathway database comparison rather than background-set selection; the paper states an extensive comparison of pathway databases is beyond its scope. A ground-truth enriched-pathway dataset is available that can be used to evaluate ORA outputs directly, since the study explicitly lacked such a benchmark. Inputs are raw abundance matrices; post-processing (imputation with minimum/2, log2 transformation, auto-scaling) and metabolite-identifier harmonisation must precede background-set construction.

skills.description: Use when you want to show how the composition of the differential metabolite list (thresholded at BH FDR or Bonferroni q<=0.005/0.05/0.1) affects ORA SEP counts across metabolomics datasets.
skills.name: ora-sensitivity-curve-visualization
skills.search_text: ora-sensitivity-curve-visualization Use when you want to show how the composition of the differential metabolite list (thresholded at BH FDR or Bonferroni q<=0.005/0.05/0.1) affects ORA SEP counts across metabolomics datasets. When you only have a single fixed DA metabolite list (e.g. one q <= 0.05 selection) and do not intend to sweep threshold or composition variants — ORA should be run directly instead of sweeping the list. When the goal is to compare pathway databases (KEGG, Reactome, BioCyc) or simulate metabolite misidentification; those are separate parameter-effect analyses in the same study and are not this sensitivity-curve workflow. When the background set itself is under investigation (defining the ideal assay-specific background remains an open problem in the source study, so sweeping the DA list will not resolve it). http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 A sensitivity analysis and visualization skill that plots how the number of significantly enriched pathways (SEPs) changes as the list of differentially abundant metabolites used as ORA input is varied, revealing rise-then-fall behaviour and single-compound-driven extrema. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009105
skills.summary: A sensitivity analysis and visualization skill that plots how the number of significantly enriched pathways (SEPs) changes as the list of differentially abundant metabolites used as ORA input is varied, revealing rise-then-fall behaviour and single-compound-driven extrema.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When you only have a single fixed DA metabolite list (e.g. one q <= 0.05 selection) and do not intend to sweep threshold or composition variants — ORA should be run directly instead of sweeping the list. When the goal is to compare pathway databases (KEGG, Reactome, BioCyc) or simulate metabolite misidentification; those are separate parameter-effect analyses in the same study and are not this sensitivity-curve workflow. When the background set itself is under investigation (defining the ideal assay-specific background remains an open problem in the source study, so sweeping the DA list will not resolve it).

skills.description: Use when benchmarking modification-site localization variants on the ModiFinder GNPS-library benchmark and you need to reproduce or compare MF-N, MF-R, and MF-O mean Average-distance scores.
skills.name: oracle-baseline-benchmark-evaluation
skills.search_text: oracle-baseline-benchmark-evaluation Use when benchmarking modification-site localization variants on the ModiFinder GNPS-library benchmark and you need to reproduce or compare MF-N, MF-R, and MF-O mean Average-distance scores. The goal is de novo structural elucidation rather than evaluating modification-site localization against known true sites — the oracle variant MF-O uses the true modification site and cannot be used for real predictions. Spectra are not from structurally related known/unknown analog pairs with an identical M+H adduct and exactly one modification site (RDKit GetSubstructMatch edge count), since benchmark eligibility checks would filter them out. Precursor masses exceed 2000 Da or the precursor mass difference is ≥ 50% of the smaller compound, violating the benchmark eligibility criteria. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Reproduce the ModiFinder benchmark evaluation of the three variants MF-N, MF-R, and MF-O by scoring per-atom modification-site likelihoods with the Average-distance evaluation function and matching the reported mean scores of 0.603 / 0.625 / 0.652 (Fig. 3-A). metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jasms.4c00061
skills.summary: Reproduce the ModiFinder benchmark evaluation of the three variants MF-N, MF-R, and MF-O by scoring per-atom modification-site likelihoods with the Average-distance evaluation function and matching the reported mean scores of 0.603 / 0.625 / 0.652 (Fig. 3-A).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is de novo structural elucidation rather than evaluating modification-site localization against known true sites — the oracle variant MF-O uses the true modification site and cannot be used for real predictions. Spectra are not from structurally related known/unknown analog pairs with an identical M+H adduct and exactly one modification site (RDKit GetSubstructMatch edge count), since benchmark eligibility checks would filter them out. Precursor masses exceed 2000 Da or the precursor mass difference is ≥ 50% of the smaller compound, violating the benchmark eligibility criteria.

skills.search_text: oracle-substructure-filtering Use when benchmarking ModiFinder on MS/MS compound pairs whose true modification site is known, and shifted-peak substructure assignments must be restricted to those containing that site before scoring. The modification site of the unknown compound is genuinely unknown — oracle filtering requires ground truth and would leak the answer The goal is de novo fragment annotation rather than restricting shifted-peak assignments to a known modification site Pairs fail benchmark eligibility checks (e.g., precursor mass >= 2000 Da or precursor mass difference >= 50%), since the oracle sweep is defined on the eligible 12,909-pair benchmark http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 An evaluation-mode filtering step in ModiFinder that removes any substructure assigned to a shifted MS/MS peak when that substructure does not contain the true modification site, enabling upper-bound (oracle) assessment of modification-site localization on benchmark compound pairs. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jasms.4c00061
skills.summary: An evaluation-mode filtering step in ModiFinder that removes any substructure assigned to a shifted MS/MS peak when that substructure does not contain the true modification site, enabling upper-bound (oracle) assessment of modification-site localization on benchmark compound pairs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The modification site of the unknown compound is genuinely unknown — oracle filtering requires ground truth and would leak the answer The goal is de novo fragment annotation rather than restricting shifted-peak assignments to a known modification site Pairs fail benchmark eligibility checks (e.g., precursor mass >= 2000 Da or precursor mass difference >= 50%), since the oracle sweep is defined on the eligible 12,909-pair benchmark

skills.description: Use when processing centroided high-resolution GC-CI-MS (GC-Orbitrap) mzML files for 13C stable-isotope labeling, where derivatized-metabolite formulas are known but the isotopologue peak series must be predicted and matched before quantification.
skills.name: orbitrap-formula-based-isotopologue-mz-prediction
skills.search_text: orbitrap-formula-based-isotopologue-mz-prediction Use when processing centroided high-resolution GC-CI-MS (GC-Orbitrap) mzML files for 13C stable-isotope labeling, where derivatized-metabolite formulas are known but the isotopologue peak series must be predicted and matched before quantification. Input is low-resolution GC-CI-MS data acquired in SIM or narrow-window scan (NS) mode; the skill's enviPat-based merging is specific to high-resolution spectra where Si/N/O isotopic satellites are resolved The derivatized formula table is unknown or unavailable, since the theoretical envelope cannot be computed without a formula Labeling is performed with an atom other than 13C, unless labelatom is changed accordingly and the theory still holds http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Predicts theoretical isotopologue m/z clusters for derivatized metabolite formulas in high-resolution GC-CI-MS (Orbitrap) tracing data by merging enviPat-predicted isotopic envelopes at an instrument resolution (e.g. 200,000), so that individual 13C-labeled isotopologue peaks from Si, N or O can be located and quantified. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c02998

skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is low-resolution GC-CI-MS data acquired in SIM or narrow-window scan (NS) mode; the skill's enviPat-based merging is specific to high-resolution spectra where Si/N/O isotopic satellites are resolved The derivatized formula table is unknown or unavailable, since the theoretical envelope cannot be computed without a formula Labeling is performed with an atom other than 13C, unless labelatom is changed accordingly and the theory still holds

skills.search_text: orbitrap-resolution-criterion-implementation Use when correcting isotope-labeling LC-MS data (e.g. 13C, 15N, 2H, 18O, 34S tracers) on a high-resolving-power Orbitrap, where same-nominal-mass isotopologs are partially resolvable and the correction matrix must be resolution-dependently zeroed instead of including all isotopologs as IsoCor does. When the instrument resolution is extremely low such that same-nominal-mass isotopologs cannot be resolved — there ElemCor/MDT is identical to IsoCor's combinatorial correction and the resolution criterion is moot When unlabeled-sample measurements are available and the compound is high-mass with relatively large spectral inaccuracy — use the ULS-based correction instead (MDT is recommended for low-mass compounds) When the selected tracer element is not present in a compound's formula — the README warns the algorithm will report an error (e.g. selecting C or S as tracer for 15N-labeled data) http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Implements the Orbitrap mass-difference-theory (MDT) criterion that decides which same-nominal-mass isotopologs are resolvable and thus excluded (zeroed) from the isotope correction matrix, including ElemCor's improved sum-of-mass-differences enumeration over isotope combinations. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-019-2669-9
skills.summary: Implements the Orbitrap mass-difference-theory (MDT) criterion that decides which same-nominal-mass isotopologs are resolvable and thus excluded (zeroed) from the isotope correction matrix, including ElemCor's improved sum-of-mass-differences enumeration over isotope combinations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the instrument resolution is extremely low such that same-nominal-mass isotopologs cannot be resolved — there ElemCor/MDT is identical to IsoCor's combinatorial correction and the resolution criterion is moot When unlabeled-sample measurements are available and the compound is high-mass with relatively large spectral inaccuracy — use the ULS-based correction instead (MDT is recommended for low-mass compounds) When the selected tracer element is not present in a compound's formula — the README warns the algorithm will report an error (e.g. selecting C or S as tracer for 15N-labeled data)

skills.description: Reference for building or validating an organ-partitioned metabolite database for ambient mass spectrometry imaging when adduct forms in MSI differ from LC-MS and annotation coverage must be expanded.
skills.name: organ-specific-metabolite-database-curation
skills.search_text: organ-specific-metabolite-database-curation Reference for building or validating an organ-partitioned metabolite database for ambient mass spectrometry imaging when adduct forms in MSI differ from LC-MS and annotation coverage must be expanded. The analysis is LC-MS/MS feature annotation in solution metabolomics, where LC-MS adduct forms are already correct and the MSI-specific adduct-form re-evaluation is unnecessary. The metabolite list has not yet been partitioned into organ-specific sheets (brain, liver, kidney, heart, spleen, lung, muscle, pancreas, serum); adduct expansion requires the organ partition as a starting point. The task is annotating an already processed MSI dataset against an existing database; use the MSIannotator.m workflow instead of rebuilding the database. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Curation of an organ-specific metabolite database for AFADESI-MSI by evaluating adduct-form differences between LC-MS/MS and MSI measurements, expanding 1298 positive-mode and 515 negative-mode organ metabolites into 27,407 adduct ions with theoretical m/z. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.2c00557
skills.summary: Curation of an organ-specific metabolite database for AFADESI-MSI by evaluating adduct-form differences between LC-MS/MS and MSI measurements, expanding 1298 positive-mode and 515 negative-mode organ metabolites into 27,407 adduct ions with theoretical m/z.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis is LC-MS/MS feature annotation in solution metabolomics, where LC-MS adduct forms are already correct and the MSI-specific adduct-form re-evaluation is unnecessary. The metabolite list has not yet been partitioned into organ-specific sheets (brain, liver, kidney, heart, spleen, lung, muscle, pancreas, serum); adduct expansion requires the organ partition as a starting point. The task is annotating an already processed MSI dataset against an existing database; use the MSIannotator.m workflow instead of rebuilding the database.

skills.description: Use when preparing to annotate a preprocessed ambient MSI dataset (e.g. AFADESI-MSI mouse tissue data) and you must choose which database sheet — organ and positive/negative mode — to supply as the 'Database' input before running MSIannotator.m.
skills.name: organ-specific-metabolite-database-selection
skills.search_text: organ-specific-metabolite-database-selection Use when preparing to annotate a preprocessed ambient MSI dataset (e.g. AFADESI-MSI mouse tissue data) and you must choose which database sheet — organ and positive/negative mode — to supply as the 'Database' input before running MSIannotator.m. The MSI dataset comes from an organ or tissue type not covered by the organ-specific database sheets (brain, liver, kidney, heart, spleen, lung, muscle, pancreas, serum) or from a species other than mouse, where a user-supplied database must be built instead. The detection mode of the available database sheet (positive or negative) does not match the ionization mode of the MSI data to be annotated — supplying the wrong mode would compare measured m/z against theoretical adduct ions that were not formed. The input is raw, unprocessed mass spectrometry imaging data rather than a preprocessed MSI dataset with measured m/z in the first column; database selection is a pre-annotation step, not a preprocessing step. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Selects and validates an organ- and ionization-mode-specific metabolite database (e.g. the MSIannotator 'Organ specific metabolite database.xlsx' sheets, 1298 metabolites in positive mode and 515 in negative mode, split by brain, liver, kidney, heart, spleen, lung, muscle, pancreas, and serum) so that downstream m/z annotation is matched against the correct theoretical adduct ions for the tissue being imaged. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.2c00557
skills.summary: Selects and validates an organ- and ionization-mode-specific metabolite database (e.g. the MSIannotator 'Organ specific metabolite database.xlsx' sheets, 1298 metabolites in positive mode and 515 in negative mode, split by brain, liver, kidney, heart, spleen, lung, muscle, pancreas, and serum) so that downstream m/z annotation is matched against the correct theoretical adduct ions for the tissue being imaged.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The MSI dataset comes from an organ or tissue type not covered by the organ-specific database sheets (brain, liver, kidney, heart, spleen, lung, muscle, pancreas, serum) or from a species other than mouse, where a user-supplied database must be built instead. The detection mode of the available database sheet (positive or negative) does not match the ionization mode of the MSI data to be annotated — supplying the wrong mode would compare measured m/z against theoretical adduct ions that were not formed. The input is raw, unprocessed mass spectrometry imaging data rather than a preprocessed MSI dataset with measured m/z in the first column; database selection is a pre-annotation step, not a preprocessing step.

skills.description: Use when a natural-products occurrence table contains free-text organism names — vernacular names, TCM names, or misspelled binomials — that must be mapped to standardized taxa before aggregation.
skills.name: organism-common-name-translation
skills.search_text: organism-common-name-translation Use when a natural-products occurrence table contains free-text organism names — vernacular names, TCM names, or misspelled binomials — that must be mapped to standardized taxa before aggregation. Organism strings are already canonical scientific binomials with no vernacular or TCM names present — skip translation and go directly to taxonomy resolution Names shorter than four characters (e.g. 'Aye') — these common names are removed by the pipeline and cannot be reliably translated You need a mapping to a specific lineage database like NCBI taxonomy rather than the Open Tree of Life Translates heterogeneous vernacular/common organism names into canonical scientific names using approximate string matching (stringdist), then resolves them to a unified taxonomy via rotl/Open Tree of Life, storing the mappings as an SQLite dictionary. This is the organism-harmonization step of the LOTUS curation pipeline. metabolomics/v3 10.7554/elife.70780
skills.summary: Translates heterogeneous vernacular/common organism names into canonical scientific names using approximate string matching (stringdist), then resolves them to a unified taxonomy via rotl/Open Tree of Life, storing the mappings as an SQLite dictionary. This is the organism-harmonization step of the LOTUS curation pipeline.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Organism strings are already canonical scientific binomials with no vernacular or TCM names present — skip translation and go directly to taxonomy resolution Names shorter than four characters (e.g. 'Aye') — these common names are removed by the pipeline and cannot be reliably translated You need a mapping to a specific lineage database like NCBI taxonomy rather than the Open Tree of Life

skills.description: Use when you have SMILES-tagged natural-product structures grouped by organism origin and want to identify which chemical pathway or superclass distributions differ between those groups.
skills.name: organism-level-metabolite-distribution-comparison
skills.search_text: organism-level-metabolite-distribution-comparison Use when you have SMILES-tagged natural-product structures grouped by organism origin and want to identify which chemical pathway or superclass distributions differ between those groups. When the input structures are not natural products or lack organism-origin labels — classification alone will not give a group comparison. When you need fine-grained Class-level rather than Pathway/Superclass-level comparison without prior aggregation, since the article's comparison was done at pathway/superclass level. When the server is not running or models are not downloaded (HDF5 TF2 models require tensorflow 2.3.0) — the /classify endpoint will not respond. http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Compares the structural-classification distribution of natural products across organism groups (e.g. bacterial vs fungal metabolites) by classifying each structure with NPClassifier and aggregating per-pathway/superclass counts per organism. Reveals biosynthetic-level patterns such as the terpenoid dominance in fungi. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jnatprod.1c00399
skills.summary: Compares the structural-classification distribution of natural products across organism groups (e.g. bacterial vs fungal metabolites) by classifying each structure with NPClassifier and aggregating per-pathway/superclass counts per organism. Reveals biosynthetic-level patterns such as the terpenoid dominance in fungi.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input structures are not natural products or lack organism-origin labels — classification alone will not give a group comparison. When you need fine-grained Class-level rather than Pathway/Superclass-level comparison without prior aggregation, since the article's comparison was done at pathway/superclass level. When the server is not running or models are not downloaded (HDF5 TF2 models require tensorflow 2.3.0) — the /classify endpoint will not respond.

skills.description: Use when a COCONUT subset must be attributed to source organisms and their geographic locations — e.g. to compute provenance overlap statistics or continent-level distributions from the molecule-organism-location records.
skills.name: organism-location-mapping
skills.search_text: organism-location-mapping Use when a COCONUT subset must be attributed to source organisms and their geographic locations — e.g. to compute provenance overlap statistics or continent-level distributions from the molecule-organism-location records. The input is a generic chemical structure file (SMILES/SDF) with no organism or provenance annotations — structure-level QC or descriptor computation is needed instead. The analysis goal is chemical classification (ClassyFire/NPclassifier) or annotation-level star scoring rather than geographic attribution. Only structure-centric properties (Murcko frameworks, Ertl functional groups, deepSMILES) are of interest and provenance/location is irrelevant. http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 http://edamontology.org/topic_3335 Maps COCONUT natural products to the organisms that synthesize them and, in turn, to the geographic location where those organisms were collected, enabling continent-level provenance analysis across the 695,133-molecule database. This skill bridges the COCONUT PostgreSQL provenance pivot tables (molecule–organism–location) to geographic aggregation statistics. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-020-00478-9
skills.summary: Maps COCONUT natural products to the organisms that synthesize them and, in turn, to the geographic location where those organisms were collected, enabling continent-level provenance analysis across the 695,133-molecule database. This skill bridges the COCONUT PostgreSQL provenance pivot tables (molecule–organism–location) to geographic aggregation statistics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a generic chemical structure file (SMILES/SDF) with no organism or provenance annotations — structure-level QC or descriptor computation is needed instead. The analysis goal is chemical classification (ClassyFire/NPclassifier) or annotation-level star scoring rather than geographic attribution. Only structure-centric properties (Murcko frameworks, Ertl functional groups, deepSMILES) are of interest and provenance/location is irrelevant.

skills.description: Use when natural product or metabolomics records contain unstructured free-text biological source fields that must be converted into scientific organism names before taxonomic resolution.
skills.name: organism-name-detection-from-free-text
skills.search_text: organism-name-detection-from-free-text Use when natural product or metabolomics records contain unstructured free-text biological source fields that must be converted into scientific organism names before taxonomic resolution. The biological source field already contains resolved, accepted scientific names with complete taxonomy — no name detection is needed. The target taxonomy backbone is not Catalogue of Life, since this workflow retains only entries resolved against Catalogue of Life down to species level. Text is short controlled vocabulary or organism codes rather than free prose where name detection adds no value. http://edamontology.org/topic_0659 http://edamontology.org/topic_3050 Detects scientific organism names in free-text biological-source strings (e.g. the DNP source field) using gnfinder, then matches detected names against the Global Names index to attach synonyms and prepare them for taxonomic resolution. metabolomics/v3 10.3389/fpls.2019.01329
skills.summary: Detects scientific organism names in free-text biological-source strings (e.g. the DNP source field) using gnfinder, then matches detected names against the Global Names index to attach synonyms and prepare them for taxonomic resolution.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The biological source field already contains resolved, accepted scientific names with complete taxonomy — no name detection is needed. The target taxonomy backbone is not Catalogue of Life, since this workflow retains only entries resolved against Catalogue of Life down to species level. Text is short controlled vocabulary or organism codes rather than free prose where name detection adds no value.

skills.description: Use when a natural-product dataset records a producing organism per molecule and you need to assign each NP to a taxonomic category (e.g. plants, bacteria, fungi, animals, marine) before computing provenance-level distributions or overlaps.
skills.name: organism-taxonomy-source-classification
skills.search_text: organism-taxonomy-source-classification Use when a natural-product dataset records a producing organism per molecule and you need to assign each NP to a taxonomic category (e.g. plants, bacteria, fungi, animals, marine) before computing provenance-level distributions or overlaps. The dataset lacks a populated organism field for the records of interest — COCONUT itself notes that provenance annotation is still an outstanding aim and some fields (organism_parts, locations) are left null. The goal is chemical-structure classification (e.g. ClassyFire chemical classes) rather than taxonomic source classification — these are distinct annotation layers. Only stereochemistry/unified-structure information is required and no organism-level provenance is needed. http://edamontology.org/topic_3316 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Classify COCONUT natural products by the taxonomic category of their provenance organism — mapping the organism field on each NP record to the taxonomic ranks used in COCONUT's organism annotation so NPs can be counted and compared across taxonomic sources. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-020-00478-9
skills.summary: Classify COCONUT natural products by the taxonomic category of their provenance organism — mapping the organism field on each NP record to the taxonomic ranks used in COCONUT's organism annotation so NPs can be counted and compared across taxonomic sources.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset lacks a populated organism field for the records of interest — COCONUT itself notes that provenance annotation is still an outstanding aim and some fields (organism_parts, locations) are left null. The goal is chemical-structure classification (e.g. ClassyFire chemical classes) rather than taxonomic source classification — these are distinct annotation layers. Only stereochemistry/unified-structure information is required and no organism-level provenance is needed.

skills.description: Use when deconvolving chimeric DDA MS2 spectra and the isolation window contains ions lacking their own measured MS2 spectrum — their component spectra must be predicted from MS1 scan peaks before elastic-net unmixing.
skills.name: orphan-isotopologue-spectrum-prediction
skills.search_text: orphan-isotopologue-spectrum-prediction Use when deconvolving chimeric DDA MS2 spectra and the isolation window contains ions lacking their own measured MS2 spectrum — their component spectra must be predicted from MS1 scan peaks before elastic-net unmixing. The isolation-window ion already has a clean (non-chimeric) MS2 scan — use Candidate Spectrum II from the nearest MS2 scans instead of predicting from MS1 Processing DIA/SWATH data, where deconvolution relinks precursors to fragment ions via PerformDIADeconvolution/reconstructChromPeakSpectra rather than MS1-based isotopologue prediction The MS2 spectrum is not chimeric (single centroid in the isolation window), so no component spectra are needed http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Predicts MS2 fragment spectra for orphan ions (MS1 features with no acquired MS2 spectrum) from the precursor's MS1 scan using DecoID-style isotopologue prediction, serving as Candidate Spectrum I in MetaboAnalystR 4.0's PerformDDADeconvolution chimeric-spectra deconvolution workflow. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-48009-6
skills.summary: Predicts MS2 fragment spectra for orphan ions (MS1 features with no acquired MS2 spectrum) from the precursor's MS1 scan using DecoID-style isotopologue prediction, serving as Candidate Spectrum I in MetaboAnalystR 4.0's PerformDDADeconvolution chimeric-spectra deconvolution workflow.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The isolation-window ion already has a clean (non-chimeric) MS2 scan — use Candidate Spectrum II from the nearest MS2 scans instead of predicting from MS1 Processing DIA/SWATH data, where deconvolution relinks precursors to fragment ions via PerformDIADeconvolution/reconstructChromPeakSpectra rather than MS1-based isotopologue prediction The MS2 spectrum is not chimeric (single centroid in the isolation window), so no component spectra are needed

skills.name: orphan-metabolite-bgc-linkage
skills.search_text: orphan-metabolite-bgc-linkage Use when an orphan metabolite's known substructures (e.g. sugars, methylaminosugars, halogenated aromatics) must be matched to a candidate BGC region in a genome assembly that antiSMASH annotates but BGC databases lack. The target BGC is already experimentally characterised and present in MIBiG, so sub-cluster-based linkage adds nothing over direct reference lookup The goal is full BGC product class prediction rather than linking a specific metabolite substructure to a region via sub-cluster motifs The metabolite has no known substructures and no sub-cluster motifs can be defined for it, leaving no motifs to query against http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Links orphan (or database-missing) metabolites to candidate biosynthetic gene clusters by tokenising antiSMASH-predicted BGCs into (sub)Pfam domains and querying them against PRESTO-TOP sub-cluster motifs, as demonstrated by proposing the akashin BGC QZWF01000007.1.region003 in Streptomyces sp. F001. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1010462

F001.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The target BGC is already experimentally characterised and present in MIBiG, so sub-cluster-based linkage adds nothing over direct reference lookup The goal is full BGC product class prediction rather than linking a specific metabolite substructure to a region via sub-cluster motifs The metabolite has no known substructures and no sub-cluster motifs can be defined for it, leaving no motifs to query against

skills.description: Use when building a draft GSMN for a species with a genome annotation but no dedicated metabolic model, using curated reference algal/plant networks as orthology donors (e.g., A. thaliana, G. sulphuraria, E. siliculosus → C. crispus).
skills.name: orthology-based-reaction-annotation-transfer
skills.search_text: orthology-based-reaction-annotation-transfer Use when building a draft GSMN for a species with a genome annotation but no dedicated metabolic model, using curated reference algal/plant networks as orthology donors (e.g., A. thaliana, G. sulphuraria, E. siliculosus → C. crispus). The target organism already has a manually curated GSMN — refinement of that model is preferable to orthology-based draft transfer. No genome annotation for the target organism is available, so gene-to-gene orthology mapping cannot be performed. The goal is de novo inference of novel reactions/pathway variants rather than transferring known reactions — in that case PathModel-style inference is the relevant approach. Reconstruct a draft genome-scale metabolic network (GSMN) for an organism lacking a curated model by mapping genes from reference GSMNs (A. thaliana, G. sulphuraria, E. siliculosus) onto the target organism's genes via orthology, importing the associated reactions into a draft network built with AuReMe. metabolomics/v3 10.1016/j.isci.2020.100849
skills.summary: Reconstruct a draft genome-scale metabolic network (GSMN) for an organism lacking a curated model by mapping genes from reference GSMNs (A. thaliana, G. sulphuraria, E. siliculosus) onto the target organism's genes via orthology, importing the associated reactions into a draft network built with AuReMe.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The target organism already has a manually curated GSMN — refinement of that model is preferable to orthology-based draft transfer. No genome annotation for the target organism is available, so gene-to-gene orthology mapping cannot be performed. The goal is de novo inference of novel reactions/pathway variants rather than transferring known reactions — in that case PathModel-style inference is the relevant approach.

skills.description: Use when a published paper states that its 'input and output data are available on OSF' and downstream reproduction or benchmarking requires those exact files (e.g. annotation outputs, benchmarking datasets) before any local computation can start.
skills.name: osf-deposit-data-retrieval
skills.search_text: osf-deposit-data-retrieval Use when a published paper states that its 'input and output data are available on OSF' and downstream reproduction or benchmarking requires those exact files (e.g. annotation outputs, benchmarking datasets) before any local computation can start. The analysis needs freshly acquired MS/MS data or a re-run of annotation tools (MS-Finder, SIRIUS) rather than the paper's deposited annotation outputs The target database is not the one behind the deposit — e.g. ISDB-UNPD is hosted separately at oolonek.github.io/ISDB and KNApSAcK is accessible online but not downloadable The deposit files lack taxonomic information resolved against Catalogue of Life down to species level, which the taxo_scorer workflow requires http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 http://edamontology.org/topic_0157 Retrieves the published input and output data of a study from its Open Science Framework (OSF) deposit so that reported analyses can be reproduced. skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis needs freshly acquired MS/MS data or a re-run of annotation tools (MS-Finder, SIRIUS) rather than the paper's deposited annotation outputs The target database is not the one behind the deposit — e.g. ISDB-UNPD is hosted separately at oolonek.github.io/ISDB and KNApSAcK is accessible online but not downloadable The deposit files lack taxonomic information resolved against Catalogue of Life down to species level, which the taxo_scorer workflow requires

skills.description: Use when an LA-ICP-MS elemental image (2D delimited text / NumPy export) needs tissue/background segmentation via automatic image thresholding, e.g. Otsu, median binary filter, or multi-level k-means.
skills.name: otsu-threshold-image-segmentation
skills.search_text: otsu-threshold-image-segmentation Use when an LA-ICP-MS elemental image (2D delimited text / NumPy export) needs tissue/background segmentation via automatic image thresholding, e.g. Otsu, median binary filter, or multi-level k-means. The image is spot-wise or imzML-format data without a contiguous 2D pixel grid — Pew2's Otsu selection assumes a standard line-by-line image after laser-log or CSV import. A fully supervised/manual segmentation is required; Pew2's dialog offers manual ROI tracing, and Otsu is an unsupervised method that will fail on images with only faint or gradient-like tissue contrast. The data has not yet been drift-corrected and spike-filtered in Pew2; raw instrument noise can distort the between-class variance Otsu relies on. http://edamontology.org/topic_0003 Automatic image segmentation of an LA-ICP-MS elemental image (e.g. 56Fe in a human pancreatic adenocarcinoma tissue microarray) using Otsu's thresholding method to separate tissue regions of interest from background, as implemented in Pew2's selection dialog and reproducible with NumPy array programming. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c02138
skills.summary: Automatic image segmentation of an LA-ICP-MS elemental image (e.g. 56Fe in a human pancreatic adenocarcinoma tissue microarray) using Otsu's thresholding method to separate tissue regions of interest from background, as implemented in Pew2's selection dialog and reproducible with NumPy array programming.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The image is spot-wise or imzML-format data without a contiguous 2D pixel grid — Pew2's Otsu selection assumes a standard line-by-line image after laser-log or CSV import. A fully supervised/manual segmentation is required; Pew2's dialog offers manual ROI tracing, and Otsu is an unsupervised method that will fail on images with only faint or gradient-like tissue contrast. The data has not yet been drift-corrected and spike-filtered in Pew2; raw instrument noise can distort the between-class variance Otsu relies on.
