skills.name: out-of-memory-spectral-data-processing
skills.search_text: out-of-memory-spectral-data-processing Use when raw MSI spectra (e.g. imzML or Analyze 7.5 files) are too large to fit in memory, and pre-processing (normalize, smooth, reduceBaseline, peakPick) or PCA must be run on the full dataset. Input is already a small peak-picked or feature table that fits comfortably in memory — streaming overhead offers no benefit Data is not MS imaging spectra (e.g. general genomic tables); matter/Cardinal is specialized for MSI experiments Using the unstable GitHub devel or Bioconductor devel version for critical work — README explicitly warns these should not be used for critical work http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Process MS imaging datasets larger than available RAM using Cardinal's matter backend, which streams spectral data from disk so raw imzML/Analyze 7.5 spectra need not be fully loaded into memory during pre-processing or statistical analysis. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btv146
skills.summary: Process MS imaging datasets larger than available RAM using Cardinal's matter backend, which streams spectral data from disk so raw imzML/Analyze 7.5 spectra need not be fully loaded into memory during pre-processing or statistical analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a small peak-picked or feature table that fits comfortably in memory — streaming overhead offers no benefit Data is not MS imaging spectra (e.g. general genomic tables); matter/Cardinal is specialized for MSI experiments Using the unstable GitHub devel or Bioconductor devel version for critical work — README explicitly warns these should not be used for critical work

skills.description: Use when sample-level outliers distort the metabolite measurement table — e.g. the outlier heatmap shows samples grouping into a distinct k-means cluster that should be removed prior to normalization or differential testing.
skills.name: outlier-cluster-filtering-of-metabolite-measurements
skills.search_text: outlier-cluster-filtering-of-metabolite-measurements Use when sample-level outliers distort the metabolite measurement table — e.g. the outlier heatmap shows samples grouping into a distinct k-means cluster that should be removed prior to normalization or differential testing. The measurement table is a raw vendor file that still needs create_mae assembly or missing-value imputation — imputation (knn_impute, cutoff 0.4) must precede cluster assessment The goal is differential testing or network analysis on an already quality-filtered sample set No sample-level outlier structure is visible — removing an arbitrary cluster would discard valid cohort samples http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Filters outlier sample clusters from a metabolomics MultiAssayExperiment by k-means clustering of the measurement data and removing an identified cluster (e.g. cluster 1) via MetaboDiff's remove_cluster function before downstream differential analysis. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/bty344
skills.summary: Filters outlier sample clusters from a metabolomics MultiAssayExperiment by k-means clustering of the measurement data and removing an identified cluster (e.g. cluster 1) via MetaboDiff's remove_cluster function before downstream differential analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The measurement table is a raw vendor file that still needs create_mae assembly or missing-value imputation — imputation (knn_impute, cutoff 0.4) must precede cluster assessment The goal is differential testing or network analysis on an already quality-filtered sample set No sample-level outlier structure is visible — removing an arbitrary cluster would discard valid cohort samples

skills.description: Use when QC-based drift correction (e.g. QC-RLSC) leaves suspicious non-monotonic intensity excursions in biological (non-QC) samples, and you need to locate and remove outlier features before normalization.
skills.name: outlier-identification-from-drift-plots
skills.search_text: outlier-identification-from-drift-plots Use when QC-based drift correction (e.g. QC-RLSC) leaves suspicious non-monotonic intensity excursions in biological (non-QC) samples, and you need to locate and remove outlier features before normalization. When the normalization method used is already outlier-robust (tGAM, rGAM, rLOESS) — the article shows these methods accommodate or downweight outliers without needing manual removal. When a large automated multivariate outlier-detection pipeline is available and preferred; the article notes manual outlier identification is subjective and labor-intensive for large feature counts. When the goal is QC-sample RSD filtering rather than drift-plot outlier diagnosis; QC-sample RSD filtering is invalidated when QC and biological samples differ. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Identifies outlier-contaminated metabolite features in LC-MS metabolomics data by inspecting per-compound pre- vs. post-normalization intensity-vs-run-order drift plots, using QC-RLSC failure patterns in biological samples as the diagnostic signal, and manually removing those outliers so that robust methods like tGAM can be compared on clean data. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.09.30.679445
skills.summary: Identifies outlier-contaminated metabolite features in LC-MS metabolomics data by inspecting per-compound pre- vs. post-normalization intensity-vs-run-order drift plots, using QC-RLSC failure patterns in biological samples as the diagnostic signal, and manually removing those outliers so that robust methods like tGAM can be compared on clean data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the normalization method used is already outlier-robust (tGAM, rGAM, rLOESS) — the article shows these methods accommodate or downweight outliers without needing manual removal. When a large automated multivariate outlier-detection pipeline is available and preferred; the article notes manual outlier identification is subjective and labor-intensive for large feature counts. When the goal is QC-sample RSD filtering rather than drift-plot outlier diagnosis; QC-sample RSD filtering is invalidated when QC and biological samples differ.

skills.description: Use when you must quantify whether outlier counts or magnitudes degrade QC-based normalization methods (e.g., QC-RLSC, QC-RSC) relative to robust alternatives (rLOESS, rGAM, tGAM) on data with a known drift pattern.
skills.name: outlier-injection-benchmarking
skills.search_text: outlier-injection-benchmarking Use when you must quantify whether outlier counts or magnitudes degrade QC-based normalization methods (e.g., QC-RLSC, QC-RSC) relative to robust alternatives (rLOESS, rGAM, tGAM) on data with a known drift pattern. You only need to normalize real experimental data and suspect outliers — use the robust methods directly (e.g., tGAM via metanorm()) rather than running the full injection benchmark Your normalization evaluation uses QC-sample RSD reduction or differential-abundance counts as proxies — the article flags these as common benchmarking pitfalls to avoid You lack a known ground-truth drift pattern; MSPE against expected drift is meaningless on data without simulated ground truth http://edamontology.org/topic_3336 Benchmark metabolomics normalization methods under controlled outlier contamination by simulating drift with known ground truth, injecting 0/1/2/4 outliers at random positions, and comparing methods via median squared prediction error (MSPE) at QC indices using the Metanorm R package. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c06841
skills.summary: Benchmark metabolomics normalization methods under controlled outlier contamination by simulating drift with known ground truth, injecting 0/1/2/4 outliers at random positions, and comparing methods via median squared prediction error (MSPE) at QC indices using the Metanorm R package.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need to normalize real experimental data and suspect outliers — use the robust methods directly (e.g., tGAM via metanorm()) rather than running the full injection benchmark Your normalization evaluation uses QC-sample RSD reduction or differential-abundance counts as proxies — the article flags these as common benchmarking pitfalls to avoid You lack a known ground-truth drift pattern; MSPE against expected drift is meaningless on data without simulated ground truth

skills.description: Use when benchmarking outlier robustness of QC-based LC-MS metabolomics normalization methods on simulated data where ground-truth drift is known and outliers can be injected at controlled counts and magnitudes.
skills.name: outlier-injection-robustness-assessment
skills.search_text: outlier-injection-robustness-assessment Use when benchmarking outlier robustness of QC-based LC-MS metabolomics normalization methods on simulated data where ground-truth drift is known and outliers can be injected at controlled counts and magnitudes. Input is real experimental data without known ground truth - drift-corrected output cannot be scored by squared prediction error and requires experimental (replicate/batch-effect based) evaluation instead Benchmarking where you would use proxies like reduction of the relative standard deviation of QC samples or increased numbers of differentially abundant metabolites - the paper flags these as common benchmarking pitfalls Simulating from a fitted model of one of the benchmarked methods - this breaks neutrality and can favor that method An in-silico benchmarking protocol that generates simulated metabolomics runs with known ground-truth signal drift, injects controlled numbers of feature-specific outliers, and scores QC-based normalization methods (QC-RLSC, QC-RSC, rLOESS, rGAM, tGAM) by median squared prediction error against the drift-free truth. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.09.30.679445
skills.summary: An in-silico benchmarking protocol that generates simulated metabolomics runs with known ground-truth signal drift, injects controlled numbers of feature-specific outliers, and scores QC-based normalization methods (QC-RLSC, QC-RSC, rLOESS, rGAM, tGAM) by median squared prediction error against the drift-free truth.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is real experimental data without known ground truth - drift-corrected output cannot be scored by squared prediction error and requires experimental (replicate/batch-effect based) evaluation instead Benchmarking where you would use proxies like reduction of the relative standard deviation of QC samples or increased numbers of differentially abundant metabolites - the paper flags these as common benchmarking pitfalls Simulating from a fitted model of one of the benchmarked methods - this breaks neutrality and can favor that method

skills.description: Use when a lipidomics experiment (e.g. Metabolomics Workbench study imported into R) must be quality-controlled before differential or multivariate analysis, and suspect samples must be identified and dropped.
skills.name: outlier-sample-removal-from-experiment
skills.search_text: outlier-sample-removal-from-experiment Use when a lipidomics experiment (e.g. Metabolomics Workbench study imported into R) must be quality-controlled before differential or multivariate analysis, and suspect samples must be identified and dropped. Input is a raw numerical matrix or Skyline CSV that has not yet been converted to a LipidomicsExperiment via as_lipidomics_experiment()/read_skyline() — import and annotation must precede QC The goal is filtering measured lipids rather than samples — lipidr filters lipids by %CV, which is a separate operation Only a handful of samples exist where a PCA score plot cannot meaningfully reveal dispersion outliers http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Identifies samples with abnormally large dispersion in a lipidomics dataset by inspecting a PCA score plot generated with lipidr's mva() function, then removes the flagged outliers from the LipidomicsExperiment before downstream analysis. This guards univariate and multivariate results against contamination by anomalous samples. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.0c00082
skills.summary: Identifies samples with abnormally large dispersion in a lipidomics dataset by inspecting a PCA score plot generated with lipidr's mva() function, then removes the flagged outliers from the LipidomicsExperiment before downstream analysis. This guards univariate and multivariate results against contamination by anomalous samples.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a raw numerical matrix or Skyline CSV that has not yet been converted to a LipidomicsExperiment via as_lipidomics_experiment()/read_skyline() — import and annotation must precede QC The goal is filtering measured lipids rather than samples — lipidr filters lipids by %CV, which is a separate operation Only a handful of samples exist where a PCA score plot cannot meaningfully reveal dispersion outliers

skills.description: Use when matched peak-area tables from two peak-detection tools on the same LC-HRMS dataset (e.g. PeakBot profile-mode vs XCMS centroid-mode on the PHM dataset) need an agreement metric, and a small fraction of features with too dissimilar areas must be excluded before reporting correlation.
skills.name: outlier-trimming-quantile-statistics
skills.search_text: outlier-trimming-quantile-statistics Use when matched peak-area tables from two peak-detection tools on the same LC-HRMS dataset (e.g. PeakBot profile-mode vs XCMS centroid-mode on the PHM dataset) need an agreement metric, and a small fraction of features with too dissimilar areas must be excluded before reporting correlation. The input is already a cleaned/trimmed correlation table — re-trimming would double-remove features and inflate R² Features are not matched one-to-one across the two tools, so relative area differences cannot be ranked per feature The analysis goal is peak detection or CNN model training itself rather than post-hoc agreement statistics on peak areas http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_3316 A reproducible statistical procedure for comparing LC-HRMS peak areas from two feature-detection tools: regress PeakBot peak areas against XCMS peak areas, trim the 5% tails of features ranked by relative area difference, and report R² plus the median XCMS-to-PeakBot area factor with its interquartile range. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btac344
skills.summary: A reproducible statistical procedure for comparing LC-HRMS peak areas from two feature-detection tools: regress PeakBot peak areas against XCMS peak areas, trim the 5% tails of features ranked by relative area difference, and report R² plus the median XCMS-to-PeakBot area factor with its interquartile range.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a cleaned/trimmed correlation table — re-trimming would double-remove features and inflate R² Features are not matched one-to-one across the two tools, so relative area differences cannot be ranked per feature The analysis goal is peak detection or CNN model training itself rather than post-hoc agreement statistics on peak areas

skills.description: Use when two alternative tools visualize or transform the same large dataset and you must quantify scalability by timing load performance and comparing output file sizes, e.g. EMPeror (26 MB) versus KiNG (1.85 GB) for PCoA plots.
skills.name: output-file-size-comparison-analysis
skills.search_text: output-file-size-comparison-analysis Use when two alternative tools visualize or transform the same large dataset and you must quantify scalability by timing load performance and comparing output file sizes, e.g. EMPeror (26 MB) versus KiNG (1.85 GB) for PCoA plots. The tools under comparison consume different input files or datasets, so any file-size or load-time difference would confound input size with tool efficiency The goal is rendering quality or statistical fidelity of visualizations rather than load-time scalability and output size on a large sample/metadata-rich dataset http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 A benchmarking method that compares competing visualization pipelines by measuring output file size and browser load time on the same dataset, as done for EMPeror versus KiNG on a 5,740-sample PCoA dataset with 120 metadata columns. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/2047-217x-2-16
skills.summary: A benchmarking method that compares competing visualization pipelines by measuring output file size and browser load time on the same dataset, as done for EMPeror versus KiNG on a 5,740-sample PCoA dataset with 120 metadata columns.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The tools under comparison consume different input files or datasets, so any file-size or load-time difference would confound input size with tool efficiency The goal is rendering quality or statistical fidelity of visualizations rather than load-time scalability and output size on a large sample/metadata-rich dataset

skills.description: Use when per-ion peak metrics for auto-tracked and user-specified ions have already been extracted and must be reported as CSV summaries plus JPG/PDF figures organized per ion and per metric for operator inspection.
skills.name: output-folder-organization-for-qc-reports
skills.search_text: output-folder-organization-for-qc-reports Use when per-ion peak metrics for auto-tracked and user-specified ions have already been extracted and must be reported as CSV summaries plus JPG/PDF figures organized per ion and per metric for operator inspection. The goal is global batch quality assessment rather than per-ion reporting — PeakQC's PCA on time-versus-m/z MS1 images covers that and does not require per-ion report folders Peak metrics have not yet been extracted (raw MS data still needs conversion/processing); reporting is a downstream packaging step Only fragmentation-spectra diagnostic plots or ion-mobility mobiligrams are needed, not per-ion peak-metric reports http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Package PeakQC's extracted precursor-ion peak metrics (mass error, retention time error, arrival time error) into per-ion and per-metric CSV summary reports and JPG/PDF figures arranged in navigable output folders so an instrument operator can inspect and track QC across an MS batch. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jasms.4c00146
skills.summary: Package PeakQC's extracted precursor-ion peak metrics (mass error, retention time error, arrival time error) into per-ion and per-metric CSV summary reports and JPG/PDF figures arranged in navigable output folders so an instrument operator can inspect and track QC across an MS batch.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is global batch quality assessment rather than per-ion reporting — PeakQC's PCA on time-versus-m/z MS1 images covers that and does not require per-ion report folders Peak metrics have not yet been extracted (raw MS data still needs conversion/processing); reporting is a downstream packaging step Only fragmentation-spectra diagnostic plots or ion-mobility mobiligrams are needed, not per-ion peak-metric reports

skills.description: Use when you have a query set of metabolite/lipid identifiers and a pathway-to-feature mapping table, and need to identify which pathways are over-represented at adjusted p-value < 0.05.
skills.name: over-representation-analysis-fishers-exact-test
skills.search_text: over-representation-analysis-fishers-exact-test Use when you have a query set of metabolite/lipid identifiers and a pathway-to-feature mapping table, and need to identify which pathways are over-represented at adjusted p-value < 0.05. When you have ranked feature lists with log2 fold change and p-values for GSEA-style testing — use EnrichMet's MetSEA/fgsea module instead of Fisher's Exact Test ORA When the question is network/topology impact (betweenness centrality, pathway impact scores) rather than set over-representation When no pathway-to-feature mapping table (KEGG or user-supplied Pathway/Metabolites table) is available for the feature type in question http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Performs pathway over-representation analysis (ORA) by applying Fisher's Exact Test to a 2x2 contingency table of query features (metabolites or lipids) mapped to pathways, with Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment; in EnrichMet this generic test is made applicable to lipidomics by swapping KEGG pathway maps for LION lipid-ontology associations. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.08.28.672951
skills.summary: Performs pathway over-representation analysis (ORA) by applying Fisher's Exact Test to a 2x2 contingency table of query features (metabolites or lipids) mapped to pathways, with Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment; in EnrichMet this generic test is made applicable to lipidomics by swapping KEGG pathway maps for LION lipid-ontology associations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When you have ranked feature lists with log2 fold change and p-values for GSEA-style testing — use EnrichMet's MetSEA/fgsea module instead of Fisher's Exact Test ORA When the question is network/topology impact (betweenness centrality, pathway impact scores) rather than set over-representation When no pathway-to-feature mapping table (KEGG or user-supplied Pathway/Metabolites table) is available for the feature type in question

skills.description: Use when you have a precomputed list of significant gene-expression or metabolite identifiers (e.g., KEGG IDs) and want to test whether KEGG pathways are over-represented, optionally feeding p-values into eSPIA or Pbine.
skills.name: over-representation-analysis-kegg
skills.search_text: over-representation-analysis-kegg Use when you have a precomputed list of significant gene-expression or metabolite identifiers (e.g., KEGG IDs) and want to test whether KEGG pathways are over-represented, optionally feeding p-values into eSPIA or Pbine. Input is raw spectral data (e.g., .raw, .d, mzXML) rather than a list of significant gene/metabolite identifiers — preprocessing and peak analysis modules should run first. You need topology-aware pathway impact scores rather than simple over-representation counts — eSPIA over KEGG pathway topology is the appropriate follow-up. Pathway database of interest is Reactome or WikiPathways rather than KEGG — ORA mapping here is specific to KEGG pathways. http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 Over-representation analysis (ORA) of significantly altered genes/metabolites against KEGG pathways, as implemented in the SMART 2.0 IOPA module, to identify enriched pathways (e.g., 51 significant pathways in the breast cancer multiomics demonstration, pFDR < 0.05). metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c03225
skills.summary: Over-representation analysis (ORA) of significantly altered genes/metabolites against KEGG pathways, as implemented in the SMART 2.0 IOPA module, to identify enriched pathways (e.g., 51 significant pathways in the breast cancer multiomics demonstration, pFDR < 0.05).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw spectral data (e.g., .raw, .d, mzXML) rather than a list of significant gene/metabolite identifiers — preprocessing and peak analysis modules should run first. You need topology-aware pathway impact scores rather than simple over-representation counts — eSPIA over KEGG pathway topology is the appropriate follow-up. Pathway database of interest is Reactome or WikiPathways rather than KEGG — ORA mapping here is specific to KEGG pathways.

skills.description: Use when you have a gene list associated with an exposure or network module (e.g. chemical-exposome-linked gene nodes from a MetaNet co_net object) and need enriched GO biological functions.
skills.name: over-representation-analysis-of-go-terms
skills.search_text: over-representation-analysis-of-go-terms Use when you have a gene list associated with an exposure or network module (e.g. chemical-exposome-linked gene nodes from a MetaNet co_net object) and need enriched GO biological functions. The goal is network construction or visualization itself (use MetaNet's c_net_calculate/c_net_build/c_net_plot workflow) rather than functional enrichment of an already-derived gene list The input is a full feature table (e.g. raw transcript abundance matrix) rather than a filtered, exposure-associated gene list — ORA needs the associated-gene background Gene identifiers cannot be mapped to GO terms, making the enrichment test undefined http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Performs ReporterScore-style Gene Ontology over-representation analysis in R on exposure-associated gene lists extracted from a MetaNet multi-omics network, to identify enriched biological functions (e.g. DNA damage response and cellular stress for the chemical exposome). metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.06.26.661636
skills.summary: Performs ReporterScore-style Gene Ontology over-representation analysis in R on exposure-associated gene lists extracted from a MetaNet multi-omics network, to identify enriched biological functions (e.g. DNA damage response and cellular stress for the chemical exposome).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is network construction or visualization itself (use MetaNet's c_net_calculate/c_net_build/c_net_plot workflow) rather than functional enrichment of an already-derived gene list The input is a full feature table (e.g. raw transcript abundance matrix) rather than a filtered, exposure-associated gene list — ORA needs the associated-gene background Gene identifiers cannot be mapped to GO terms, making the enrichment test undefined

skills.description: Use when a list of genes significantly associated with an exposure layer (e.g., microbial or chemical exposome nodes in a MetaNet multi-omics network) needs pathway-level functional interpretation via KEGG or GO over-representation testing.
skills.name: over-representation-analysis-of-kegg-pathways
skills.search_text: over-representation-analysis-of-kegg-pathways Use when a list of genes significantly associated with an exposure layer (e.g., microbial or chemical exposome nodes in a MetaNet multi-omics network) needs pathway-level functional interpretation via KEGG or GO over-representation testing. The input is a raw feature abundance table or network edges rather than a gene list derived from exposure-associated network nodes — no over-representation target exists The goal is network construction or visualization itself (MetaNet's c_net_build / c_net_plot workflow) rather than functional interpretation of selected genes The reference knowledge base needed is not KEGG or GO (e.g., taxonomic or metabolite-level pathway analysis on the non-transcriptome omics layers) http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Runs KEGG (and GO) over-representation analysis with ReporterScore on gene nodes drawn from the MetaNet exposome–transcriptome network, testing which functional pathways are enriched among genes associated with the microbial versus the chemical exposome. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.06.26.661636
skills.summary: Runs KEGG (and GO) over-representation analysis with ReporterScore on gene nodes drawn from the MetaNet exposome–transcriptome network, testing which functional pathways are enriched among genes associated with the microbial versus the chemical exposome.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a raw feature abundance table or network edges rather than a gene list derived from exposure-associated network nodes — no over-representation target exists The goal is network construction or visualization itself (MetaNet's c_net_build / c_net_plot workflow) rather than functional interpretation of selected genes The reference knowledge base needed is not KEGG or GO (e.g., taxonomic or metabolite-level pathway analysis on the non-transcriptome omics layers)

skills.description: Use when a SpaMTP-integrated Seurat object has per-cluster differentially expressed metabolites (FindAllDEMs) and genes, and you need region-level pathway enrichment (e.g. lesioned vs intact striatum).
skills.name: over-representation-pathway-analysis
skills.search_text: over-representation-pathway-analysis Use when a SpaMTP-integrated Seurat object has per-cluster differentially expressed metabolites (FindAllDEMs) and genes, and you need region-level pathway enrichment (e.g. lesioned vs intact striatum). Input is raw m/z data not yet annotated to metabolites or mapped onto a Seurat object - run the SpaMTP annotation and integration pipeline first. You need annotation-level metabolite prioritisation rather than pathway-level enrichment - use CalculateAnnotationStatistics / CalculateSingleAnnotationStatistics instead. No differential metabolite or gene contrast exists (e.g. only a single spatial region without cluster labels) - over-representation and regional enrichment both require defined analyte sets or ranked lists. http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 http://edamontology.org/topic_3391 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Regional pathway enrichment for spatial metabolomics/transcriptomics using Fisher's exact over-representation (FishersPathwayAnalysis) and GSEA-like ranked enrichment (FindRegionalPathways) on differentially expressed metabolites and genes, with Enrichment Map network visualisation via PathwayNetworkPlots. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.10.31.621429
skills.summary: Regional pathway enrichment for spatial metabolomics/transcriptomics using Fisher's exact over-representation (FishersPathwayAnalysis) and GSEA-like ranked enrichment (FindRegionalPathways) on differentially expressed metabolites and genes, with Enrichment Map network visualisation via PathwayNetworkPlots.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw m/z data not yet annotated to metabolites or mapped onto a Seurat object - run the SpaMTP annotation and integration pipeline first. You need annotation-level metabolite prioritisation rather than pathway-level enrichment - use CalculateAnnotationStatistics / CalculateSingleAnnotationStatistics instead. No differential metabolite or gene contrast exists (e.g. only a single spatial region without cluster labels) - over-representation and regional enrichment both require defined analyte sets or ranked lists.

skills.description: Use when several regression models (e.g. RF, BRNN, XGBoost, LightGBM, Keras) have been fit on the same training data with 80:20 splits and you must decide which model generalizes by comparing [test-training] and [validation-training] MAE gaps rather than raw test-set metrics alone.
skills.name: overfitting-assessment-via-error-differences
skills.search_text: overfitting-assessment-via-error-differences Use when several regression models (e.g. RF, BRNN, XGBoost, LightGBM, Keras) have been fit on the same training data with 80:20 splits and you must decide which model generalizes by comparing [test-training] and [validation-training] MAE gaps rather than raw test-set metrics alone. You only have a single train/test split with no external validation set — the [validation-training] gap, which is the core signal here, cannot be computed The task is model selection by lowest absolute error only, not generalization robustness — overfitting differences can invert the ranking (LightGBM's 0.51 min gap matters only if robustness is the criterion) Predictions are requested for compounds outside the chemical landscape of the training set (e.g. complex high-molecular-weight lipids such as triacylglycerols or phosphatidylcholines, which were excluded from the Retip training data) http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Assesses overfitting of regression models by comparing MAE differences between training vs test and training vs external validation sets, selecting the model with the smallest error differences. In the Retip retention-time study this identified Keras as the most robust of five ML models (average error difference 0.14 min vs 0.22–0.51 min for RF, BRNN, XGBoost, LightGBM). metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.9b05765
skills.summary: Assesses overfitting of regression models by comparing MAE differences between training vs test and training vs external validation sets, selecting the model with the smallest error differences. In the Retip retention-time study this identified Keras as the most robust of five ML models (average error difference 0.14 min vs 0.22–0.51 min for RF, BRNN, XGBoost, LightGBM).
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only have a single train/test split with no external validation set — the [validation-training] gap, which is the core signal here, cannot be computed The task is model selection by lowest absolute error only, not generalization robustness — overfitting differences can invert the ranking (LightGBM's 0.51 min gap matters only if robustness is the criterion) Predictions are requested for compounds outside the chemical landscape of the training set (e.g. complex high-molecular-weight lipids such as triacylglycerols or phosphatidylcholines, which were excluded from the Retip training data)

skills.description: Use when fitting time-domain 1D NMR FID data (e.g., 16,384 complex points) with an MCMC or iterative peak-decomposition model and you need to infer a reasonable number of peaks without overfitting.
skills.name: overfitting-control-in-mcmc-spectral-modeling
skills.search_text: overfitting-control-in-mcmc-spectral-modeling Use when fitting time-domain 1D NMR FID data (e.g., 16,384 complex points) with an MCMC or iterative peak-decomposition model and you need to infer a reasonable number of peaks without overfitting. The goal is rigorous k-fold cross-validation or generalization-error estimation — the article states this partitioning is intended to infer a reasonable number of peaks, not to serve as strict cross-validation. Input is already a processed/feature table or frequency-domain peak list rather than raw time-domain FID points requiring subsampling. http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_3420 Randomly partitions binned time-domain FID points (optionally after truncating trailing-noise points) into 70/20/10 training/validation/testing sets so that SAND's Markov chain Monte Carlo decomposition of 1D NMR spectra is optimized, stopped, and evaluated on disjoint data, avoiding overfitting of the peak model. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c03078
skills.summary: Randomly partitions binned time-domain FID points (optionally after truncating trailing-noise points) into 70/20/10 training/validation/testing sets so that SAND's Markov chain Monte Carlo decomposition of 1D NMR spectra is optimized, stopped, and evaluated on disjoint data, avoiding overfitting of the peak model.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is rigorous k-fold cross-validation or generalization-error estimation — the article states this partitioning is intended to infer a reasonable number of peaks, not to serve as strict cross-validation. skills.search_text: p-value-verification-against-publication-text Use when extracting reported model significance values (e.g. OPLS-DA p-values) from a metabolomics paper's text/figures and validating each against its verbatim source span before writing to a results table. Source text is a data file or figure image with no accompanying reported statistics — nothing to verify against Values are being computed from raw GCxGC-TOFMS data rather than extracted from published text The goal is reproducing the OPLS-DA models themselves (sample classification / ROC analysis), not verifying reported statistics http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0219 Verifies extracted OPLS-DA model significance p-values (e.g. 2.8*10−6, 0.0031, 0.07) from the typhoid carriage metabolomics study by cross-checking each number against its verbatim text span in the article, Fig 1/S1 Fig, and Table 1, and normalizing asterisk scientific notation to floats. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pntd.0006215
skills.summary: Verifies extracted OPLS-DA model significance p-values (e.g. 2.8*10−6, 0.0031, 0.07) from the typhoid carriage metabolomics study by cross-checking each number against its verbatim text span in the article, Fig 1/S1 Fig, and Table 1, and normalizing asterisk scientific notation to floats.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Source text is a data file or figure image with no accompanying reported statistics — nothing to verify against Values are being computed from raw GCxGC-TOFMS data rather than extracted from published text The goal is reproducing the OPLS-DA models themselves (sample classification / ROC analysis), not verifying reported statistics

skills.description: Use when a clean Ubuntu 18.04 environment needs a metabolomics software stack installed and manually resolving each tool's dependencies would be error-prone or time-consuming.
skills.name: package-manager-automation
skills.search_text: package-manager-automation Use when a clean Ubuntu 18.04 environment needs a metabolomics software stack installed and manually resolving each tool's dependencies would be error-prone or time-consuming. The target OS is not Ubuntu-based — MetumpX is explicitly a Ubuntu-based package (Windows is only supported via virtualization per the User Guide) Only a single tool with known, trivial dependencies is needed — direct installation is simpler than running a 103-tool catalogue installer The environment is not clean (pre-existing package versions may conflict with the automated dependency resolution) http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Automates installation of metabolomics software workstations by resolving each tool's individual dependencies (native packages and R/Bioconductor libraries) from a curated catalogue, as implemented by MetumpX covering 103 untargeted mass spectrometry tools on Ubuntu. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btz765
skills.summary: Automates installation of metabolomics software workstations by resolving each tool's individual dependencies (native packages and R/Bioconductor libraries) from a curated catalogue, as implemented by MetumpX covering 103 untargeted mass spectrometry tools on Ubuntu.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The target OS is not Ubuntu-based — MetumpX is explicitly a Ubuntu-based package (Windows is only supported via virtualization per the User Guide) Only a single tool with known, trivial dependencies is needed — direct installation is simpler than running a 103-tool catalogue installer The environment is not clean (pre-existing package versions may conflict with the automated dependency resolution)

skills.description: Use when you have clustered single-cell metabolic profiles (e.g. a Leiden-partitioned AnnData built from a SpaceM spatio-molecular matrix like MORPHnMOL.csv) and need to infer connectivity/relationships between metabolic states and embed them coherently with UMAP.
skills.name: paga-trajectory-inference
skills.search_text: paga-trajectory-inference Use when you have clustered single-cell metabolic profiles (e.g. a Leiden-partitioned AnnData built from a SpaceM spatio-molecular matrix like MORPHnMOL.csv) and need to infer connectivity/relationships between metabolic states and embed them coherently with UMAP. Input is still raw MALDI-imaging data (.RAW/.UDP/.imzML/.ibd) or unprocessed microscopy tiles — run the SpaceM pipeline (runAnalysis.py) first to obtain MORPHnMOL.csv No categorical cell grouping exists yet — PAGA requires pre-defined cluster labels (e.g. Leiden groups); it does not perform the state assignment itself The goal is marker-metabolite identification rather than state-relationship inference — METASPACE-based analysis is the appropriate step http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Apply Partition-based Graph Abstraction (PAGA) in Scanpy to infer and visualize relationships between single-cell metabolic states — e.g. homeostatic, intermediate, and steatotic hepatocyte states — after Leiden clustering of SpaceM spatio-molecular profiles, using the PAGA graph to initialize a UMAP embedding. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-021-01198-0
skills.summary: Apply Partition-based Graph Abstraction (PAGA) in Scanpy to infer and visualize relationships between single-cell metabolic states — e.g. homeostatic, intermediate, and steatotic hepatocyte states — after Leiden clustering of SpaceM spatio-molecular profiles, using the PAGA graph to initialize a UMAP embedding.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is still raw MALDI-imaging data (.RAW/.UDP/.imzML/.ibd) or unprocessed microscopy tiles — run the SpaceM pipeline (runAnalysis.py) first to obtain MORPHnMOL.csv No categorical cell grouping exists yet — PAGA requires pre-defined cluster labels (e.g. Leiden groups); it does not perform the state assignment itself The goal is marker-metabolite identification rather than state-relationship inference — METASPACE-based analysis is the appropriate step

skills.description: Use when clean consensus spectra from an LC–MS/MS untargeted metabolomics run contain multiple ionization variants (in-source fragments, adducts, dimers) of one precursor that must be deconvoluted to a single protonated [M+H]+ entity per variant group.
skills.name: pagerank-representative-ion-selection
skills.search_text: pagerank-representative-ion-selection Use when clean consensus spectra from an LC–MS/MS untargeted metabolomics run contain multiple ionization variants (in-source fragments, adducts, dimers) of one precursor that must be deconvoluted to a single protonated [M+H]+ entity per variant group. When the precursor ions are already deconvoluted (automatic [M + H]+ ion deconvolution was already applied) and no adduct/in-source-fragment variants remain to be grouped When the analysis is library identification (step 6, Tremolo/GNPS search) rather than ion deconvolution — the IVAMN does not assign chemical identities When the data is negative-mode and the ionization rules table was built only for positive-mode shifts (in-source fragments, adducts, dimers) without the corresponding negative-mode rules http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Selects the [M + H]+ representative ion for each group of in-source/adduct ionization variants of the same precursor by running the PageRank algorithm on the ionization variant annotation molecular network (IVAMN) built by NP3 MS Workflow, and writes the selection as node/edge attributes in a GraphML network. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c05829
skills.summary: Selects the [M + H]+ representative ion for each group of in-source/adduct ionization variants of the same precursor by running the PageRank algorithm on the ionization variant annotation molecular network (IVAMN) built by NP3 MS Workflow, and writes the selection as node/edge attributes in a GraphML network.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the precursor ions are already deconvoluted (automatic [M + H]+ ion deconvolution was already applied) and no adduct/in-source-fragment variants remain to be grouped When the analysis is library identification (step 6, Tremolo/GNPS search) rather than ion deconvolution — the IVAMN does not assign chemical identities When the data is negative-mode and the ionization rules table was built only for positive-mode shifts (in-source fragments, adducts, dimers) without the corresponding negative-mode rules

skills.description: Use when two feature-selection lists (e.g. VIP > 1 metabolites from PLS-DA under two processing strategies such as LMM vs M0) must be compared to quantify shared and uniquely identified discriminative metabolites.
skills.name: paired-adipose-tissue-lipidomics-context
skills.search_text: paired-adipose-tissue-lipidomics-context Use when two feature-selection lists (e.g. VIP > 1 metabolites from PLS-DA under two processing strategies such as LMM vs M0) must be compared to quantify shared and uniquely identified discriminative metabolites. The input is a raw metabolomics feature table rather than already-selected significant (VIP > 1) metabolite lists from fitted models Only one processing strategy was applied, so no paired LMM-vs-M0 comparison of feature lists can be made Samples are unpaired or lack a matched-patient design such as paired VAT/SAT tissue from the same subjects http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Compares discriminative-metabolite lists (VIP > 1) obtained from PLS-DA of LMM-processed versus M0-processed paired adipose tissue lipidomics data (158 annotated lipids, VAT and SAT of 59 CRC patients), computing intersection, set differences, and union counts as in Figure S-2. metabolomics/v3 10.1016/j.csbj.2019.04.009
skills.summary: Compares discriminative-metabolite lists (VIP > 1) obtained from PLS-DA of LMM-processed versus M0-processed paired adipose tissue lipidomics data (158 annotated lipids, VAT and SAT of 59 CRC patients), computing intersection, set differences, and union counts as in Figure S-2.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a raw metabolomics feature table rather than already-selected significant (VIP > 1) metabolite lists from fitted models Only one processing strategy was applied, so no paired LMM-vs-M0 comparison of feature lists can be made Samples are unpaired or lack a matched-patient design such as paired VAT/SAT tissue from the same subjects

skills.description: Use when two peak-integration approaches must be quantitatively compared on log2 peak areas per target, and replicate QC data are available to compute per-target CVs for a paired significance test.
skills.name: paired-coefficient-of-variation-comparison
skills.search_text: paired-coefficient-of-variation-comparison Use when two peak-integration approaches must be quantitatively compared on log2 peak areas per target, and replicate QC data are available to compute per-target CVs for a paired significance test. Data are untargeted peak tables from xcms, MZmine, or OpenMS rather than targeted integrated peak areas from TARDIS and a vendor tool No QC replicate structure exists, so per-target coefficients of variation cannot be computed for a paired comparison Peak areas are on the linear scale and the log2 transformation used by the article has not been applied, making results incomparable to the published benchmarks http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Benchmarks automated peak integration (TARDIS) against vendor software (Xcalibur) by comparing per-target coefficients of variation across QC replicates with a paired statistical test, alongside Spearman rho, regression R2, and slope of log2 peak areas. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c00567
skills.summary: Benchmarks automated peak integration (TARDIS) against vendor software (Xcalibur) by comparing per-target coefficients of variation across QC replicates with a paired statistical test, alongside Spearman rho, regression R2, and slope of log2 peak areas.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are untargeted peak tables from xcms, MZmine, or OpenMS rather than targeted integrated peak areas from TARDIS and a vendor tool No QC replicate structure exists, so per-target coefficients of variation cannot be computed for a paired comparison Peak areas are on the linear scale and the log2 transformation used by the article has not been applied, making results incomparable to the published benchmarks

skills.description: Use when two or more metabolomics normalization methods must be compared on identical GC-MS feature-intensity data with paired per-metabolite precision (RSD) values, to decide which method yields the highest coverage of compounds passing a <30% RSD threshold.
skills.name: paired-nonparametric-method-comparison
skills.search_text: paired-nonparametric-method-comparison Use when two or more metabolomics normalization methods must be compared on identical GC-MS feature-intensity data with paired per-metabolite precision (RSD) values, to decide which method yields the highest coverage of compounds passing a <30% RSD threshold. Data are unpaired or come from different metabolite sets under each method — the Wilcoxon signed-rank test requires matched per-metabolite RSDs from the identical QC samples. The goal is per-sample normalization rather than benchmarking normalization methods against each other; use the individual method workflow (e.g. run SERDA runner.R or Shiny-SERRF) instead of a paired-comparison harness. Input is not a GC-MS feature-intensity matrix with pooled QC and validation blocks (e.g. it is already a statistical summary or has no QC structure) — the RSD/coverage metrics depend on repeated QC measurements. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 A statistical benchmarking skill for comparing metabolite normalization methods (e.g. SERDA, SERRF, batchwise-LOESS) by computing per-metabolite RSDs under five-fold cross-validation on training pooled QCs and external validation QC pools, then testing per-metabolite differences with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test and reporting the fraction of compounds meeting the <30% RSD precision threshold. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo13080944
skills.summary: A statistical benchmarking skill for comparing metabolite normalization methods (e.g. SERDA, SERRF, batchwise-LOESS) by computing per-metabolite RSDs under five-fold cross-validation on training pooled QCs and external validation QC pools, then testing per-metabolite differences with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test and reporting the fraction of compounds meeting the <30% RSD precision threshold.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are unpaired or come from different metabolite sets under each method — the Wilcoxon signed-rank test requires matched per-metabolite RSDs from the identical QC samples. The goal is per-sample normalization rather than benchmarking normalization methods against each other; use the individual method workflow (e.g. run SERDA runner.R or Shiny-SERRF) instead of a paired-comparison harness. Input is not a GC-MS feature-intensity matrix with pooled QC and validation blocks (e.g. it is already a statistical summary or has no QC structure) — the RSD/coverage metrics depend on repeated QC measurements.

skills.description: Use when a paired omics (genome + metabolomics) dataset contains curated validated genome-metabolome links and you must quantify how many survive Metcalf and NPClassScore filtering, or verify prioritisation/rank improvements of known links.
skills.name: paired-omics-bgc-spectrum-link-validation
skills.search_text: paired-omics-bgc-spectrum-link-validation Use when a paired omics (genome + metabolomics) dataset contains curated validated genome-metabolome links and you must quantify how many survive Metcalf and NPClassScore filtering, or verify prioritisation/rank improvements of known links. Datasets with no curated/validated genome-metabolome links — the skill measures retention of known links, not discovery of new ones Metabolites >850 Da or spectra lacking CANOPUS/MolNetEnhancer predictions, where NPClassScore classes are unavailable and links are discarded by design Analyses needing structure-similarity scoring (e.g. MS2DeepScore/Spec2Vec) rather than chemical-class matching http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Reproduce and validate experimentally verified BGC–MS/MS spectrum links from PoDP datasets by running NPLinker's standardised Metcalf co-occurrence scoring followed by NPClassScore chemical-class filtering, recording retention fractions and rank changes of validated links. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s40168-022-01444-3
skills.summary: Reproduce and validate experimentally verified BGC–MS/MS spectrum links from PoDP datasets by running NPLinker's standardised Metcalf co-occurrence scoring followed by NPClassScore chemical-class filtering, recording retention fractions and rank changes of validated links.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Datasets with no curated/validated genome-metabolome links — the skill measures retention of known links, not discovery of new ones Metabolites >850 Da or spectra lacking CANOPUS/MolNetEnhancer predictions, where NPClassScore classes are unavailable and links are discarded by design Analyses needing structure-similarity scoring (e.g. MS2DeepScore/Spec2Vec) rather than chemical-class matching

skills.description: Use when a linking or benchmarking analysis needs paired genome+LC-MS/MS samples with validated BGC–metabolite links, e.g. from the PoDP or a GNPS job task, to build fingerprints or evaluate precision/recall.
skills.name: paired-omics-data-retrieval
skills.search_text: paired-omics-data-retrieval Use when a linking or benchmarking analysis needs paired genome+LC-MS/MS samples with validated BGC–metabolite links, e.g. from the PoDP or a GNPS job task, to build fingerprints or evaluate precision/recall. The analysis needs only single-omics data (genomes alone or spectra alone) with no pairing requirement — plain genome mining or GNPS library search suffices The target organism group lacks paired data in PoDP (e.g. plants, or RiPP-class validated metabolites), so no usable paired validation set can be assembled The goal is MS/MS library dereplication rather than linking spectra to biosynthetic gene clusters http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3365 Retrieves paired genome–metabolome sample sets (genomes/metagenomes plus matching untargeted LC-MS/MS data) from the Paired Omics Data Platform and GNPS, the prerequisite input layer for NPOmix-style BGC–MS/MS linking and benchmarking. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/pnasnexus/pgac257
skills.summary: Retrieves paired genome–metabolome sample sets (genomes/metagenomes plus matching untargeted LC-MS/MS data) from the Paired Omics Data Platform and GNPS, the prerequisite input layer for NPOmix-style BGC–MS/MS linking and benchmarking.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis needs only single-omics data (genomes alone or spectra alone) with no pairing requirement — plain genome mining or GNPS library search suffices The target organism group lacks paired data in PoDP (e.g. plants, or RiPP-class validated metabolites), so no usable paired validation set can be assembled The goal is MS/MS library dereplication rather than linking spectra to biosynthetic gene clusters

skills.description: Use when a paired genome–metabolome dataset with a Paired Omics Data Platform (PoDP) accession (e.g. MSV000078836, MSV000084950, MSV000084771) must be assembled in NPLinker for BGC–MS/MS spectrum linking.
skills.name: paired-omics-dataset-configuration
skills.search_text: paired-omics-dataset-configuration Use when a paired genome–metabolome dataset with a Paired Omics Data Platform (PoDP) accession (e.g. MSV000078836, MSV000084950, MSV000084771) must be assembled in NPLinker for BGC–MS/MS spectrum linking. The dataset has no Paired Omics Data Platform (PoDP) accession or paired genome–metabolome strain mapping You only need raw MS/MS processing (e.g. feature detection/mzML conversion) without linking to BGCs The genomes lack RefSeq or GenBank identifiers and cannot be retrieved from NCBI for antiSMASH/BiG-SCAPE http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Configure and load the three PoDP paired omics datasets (154 Streptomyces/Salinispora, 24 cyanobacterial, and 11 Nocardia strains) in NPLinker's podp mode via a nplinker.toml file, assembling GNPS molecular networking, antiSMASH/BiG-SCAPE GCFs, and strain mappings for BGC–MS/MS linking. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s40168-022-01444-3
skills.summary: Configure and load the three PoDP paired omics datasets (154 Streptomyces/Salinispora, 24 cyanobacterial, and 11 Nocardia strains) in NPLinker's podp mode via a nplinker.toml file, assembling GNPS molecular networking, antiSMASH/BiG-SCAPE GCFs, and strain mappings for BGC–MS/MS linking.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset has no Paired Omics Data Platform (PoDP) accession or paired genome–metabolome strain mapping You only need raw MS/MS processing (e.g. feature detection/mzML conversion) without linking to BGCs The genomes lack RefSeq or GenBank identifiers and cannot be retrieved from NCBI for antiSMASH/BiG-SCAPE

skills.description: Use when building a genome-mining workflow that needs matched genome (or metagenome) and metabolome data for the same samples, e.g., to train or query NPOmix against PoDP paired datasets.
skills.name: paired-omics-dataset-curation
skills.search_text: paired-omics-dataset-curation Use when building a genome-mining workflow that needs matched genome (or metagenome) and metabolome data for the same samples, e.g., to train or query NPOmix against PoDP paired datasets. The samples lack a genome (or metagenome) paired with MS/MS spectra of the same organism — NPOmix needs both sides of each pair The query organism has no BGC similar to any training-set BGC (e.g., a fungal species with no similar BGCs), which yields no answer You need experimentally confirmed metabolite structures rather than computational links — new NPOmix predictions still require proper elucidation of planar (2D) and absolute (3D) structure http://edamontology.org/topic_3407 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Curation and assembly of paired genome–MS/MS samples (each containing a genome or metagenome plus untargeted LC-MS/MS spectra of the same organism), retrieved from the Paired Omics Data Platform (PoDP), to serve as the labeled training matrix for NPOmix's k-nearest neighbor classifier linking metabolites to biosynthetic gene clusters. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/pnasnexus/pgac257
skills.summary: Curation and assembly of paired genome–MS/MS samples (each containing a genome or metagenome plus untargeted LC-MS/MS spectra of the same organism), retrieved from the Paired Omics Data Platform (PoDP), to serve as the labeled training matrix for NPOmix's k-nearest neighbor classifier linking metabolites to biosynthetic gene clusters.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The samples lack a genome (or metagenome) paired with MS/MS spectra of the same organism — NPOmix needs both sides of each pair The query organism has no BGC similar to any training-set BGC (e.g., a fungal species with no similar BGCs), which yields no answer You need experimentally confirmed metabolite structures rather than computational links — new NPOmix predictions still require proper elucidation of planar (2D) and absolute (3D) structure

skills.description: Use when you have paired genome/metagenome + LC-MS/MS samples and need to link MS/MS spectra (GNPS reference or cryptic) to biosynthetic gene clusters with confidence scores.
skills.name: paired-omics-fingerprint-vector-analysis
skills.search_text: paired-omics-fingerprint-vector-analysis Use when you have paired genome/metagenome + LC-MS/MS samples and need to link MS/MS spectra (GNPS reference or cryptic) to biosynthetic gene clusters with confidence scores. The query genome has no BGC similar to any BGC in the NPOmix training dataset (e.g., a fungal species distant from PoDP bacteria) — the output will contain no answer. You need to distinguish isomers or regioselectivity of homologs — the correlation-based approach lacks this resolution. Your dataset differs substantially from the PoDP training set — the reported precision may not be reproducible. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Build paired BGC and MS/MS fingerprint vectors from paired genome–metabolome samples and classify MS/MS spectra to gene cluster families with a k-nearest neighbor classifier (NPOmix), then apply a Jaccard co-occurrence threshold of 0.7 as a confidence filter on candidate BGC–metabolite links. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/pnasnexus/pgac257
skills.summary: Build paired BGC and MS/MS fingerprint vectors from paired genome–metabolome samples and classify MS/MS spectra to gene cluster families with a k-nearest neighbor classifier (NPOmix), then apply a Jaccard co-occurrence threshold of 0.7 as a confidence filter on candidate BGC–metabolite links.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The query genome has no BGC similar to any BGC in the NPOmix training dataset (e.g., a fungal species distant from PoDP bacteria) — the output will contain no answer. You need to distinguish isomers or regioselectivity of homologs — the correlation-based approach lacks this resolution. Your dataset differs substantially from the PoDP training set — the reported precision may not be reproducible.

skills.description: Use when an analysis needs systematically curated BGC–metabolite linkages: e.g. assembling validated paired datasets for NPLinker scoring, benchmarking link-ranking algorithms, or finding projects by genus, extraction method, or metadata ontology terms.
skills.name: paired-omics-metadata-retrieval
skills.search_text: paired-omics-metadata-retrieval Use when an analysis needs systematically curated BGC–metabolite linkages: e.g. assembling validated paired datasets for NPLinker scoring, benchmarking link-ranking algorithms, or finding projects by genus, extraction method, or metadata ontology terms. You need raw MS/MS spectra or genome sequence data themselves — the PoDP stores no metabolomics or genomics datasets, only metadata linking records in existing public databases. You need machine-readable values for fields entered as free text in 'Other' boxes — these are inherently not machine-readable. You expect high-throughput automated pairing of new datasets — the manual burden of paired data creation is likely too significant for high-throughput needs. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Retrieve community-curated paired genomic–metabolomic project metadata from the Paired Omics Data Platform (PoDP), via the per-project download button or the regularly archived Zenodo JSON dumps, and resolve the linked public records (GNPS-MassIVE/MetaboLights MS/MS accessions, NCBI GenBank or JGI Genome IDs, MIBiG identifiers) so downstream tools such as NPLinker can score BGC–metabolite links. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41589-020-00724-z
skills.summary: Retrieve community-curated paired genomic–metabolomic project metadata from the Paired Omics Data Platform (PoDP), via the per-project download button or the regularly archived Zenodo JSON dumps, and resolve the linked public records (GNPS-MassIVE/MetaboLights MS/MS accessions, NCBI GenBank or JGI Genome IDs, MIBiG identifiers) so downstream tools such as NPLinker can score BGC–metabolite links.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need raw MS/MS spectra or genome sequence data themselves — the PoDP stores no metabolomics or genomics datasets, only metadata linking records in existing public databases. You need machine-readable values for fields entered as free text in 'Other' boxes — these are inherently not machine-readable. You expect high-throughput automated pairing of new datasets — the manual burden of paired data creation is likely too significant for high-throughput needs.

skills.description: Use when NPOmix KNN predictions (GCF labels assigned to query MS/MS spectra) must be scored against validated BGC-metabolite links from MIBiG/PoDP to report top-1 and top-10 precision.
skills.name: paired-omics-precision-benchmark-evaluation
skills.search_text: paired-omics-precision-benchmark-evaluation Use when NPOmix KNN predictions (GCF labels assigned to query MS/MS spectra) must be scored against validated BGC-metabolite links from MIBiG/PoDP to report top-1 and top-10 precision. New links that are not experimentally validated in MIBiG/PoDP — these require proper structure elucidation and cannot serve as ground truth for precision scoring Datasets dissimilar to the PoDP training set (e.g. fungal species with no similar BGCs in the training data) — precision is not reproducible there and output may be empty http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Benchmark NPOmix KNN BGC-metabolite link predictions against curated MIBiG/PoDP validated links by computing top-1 and top-10 precision (expected 81.8% and 92.9% with similarity + biosynthetic class features and the Jaccard co-occurrence threshold of 0.7). metabolomics/v3 10.1093/pnasnexus/pgac257
skills.summary: Benchmark NPOmix KNN BGC-metabolite link predictions against curated MIBiG/PoDP validated links by computing top-1 and top-10 precision (expected 81.8% and 92.9% with similarity + biosynthetic class features and the Jaccard co-occurrence threshold of 0.7).
skills.when_to_use_negative: New links that are not experimentally validated in MIBiG/PoDP — these require proper structure elucidation and cannot serve as ground truth for precision scoring Datasets dissimilar to the PoDP training set (e.g. fungal species with no similar BGCs in the training data) — precision is not reproducible there and output may be empty

skills.description: Use when the analysis goal is to find PoDP projects by extraction or sample-preparation metadata (e.g. projects that used methanol to extract cell pellets) via keyword search over project documents.
skills.name: paired-omics-project-filtering
skills.search_text: paired-omics-project-filtering Use when the analysis goal is to find PoDP projects by extraction or sample-preparation metadata (e.g. projects that used methanol to extract cell pellets) via keyword search over project documents. The target metadata was entered as free text in the platform's 'Other' boxes — it is inherently not machine-readable, so keyword matching over structured fields will be unreliable. The goal is reliably selecting datasets by a controlled metadata criterion (e.g. only metagenomic datasets from aquatic invertebrates or only positive ionization mode) — use the platform's ontology-based selection rather than free-text keyword search. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 A keyword-search filtering skill for the Paired Omics Data Platform (PoDP): retrieve projects whose modular extraction-method and sample-preparation metadata match a query such as "methanol + cells", by searching the platform's List-tab index over the Zenodo-archived JSON project documents. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41589-020-00724-z
skills.summary: A keyword-search filtering skill for the Paired Omics Data Platform (PoDP): retrieve projects whose modular extraction-method and sample-preparation metadata match a query such as "methanol + cells", by searching the platform's List-tab index over the Zenodo-archived JSON project documents.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The target metadata was entered as free text in the platform's 'Other' boxes — it is inherently not machine-readable, so keyword matching over structured fields will be unreliable. The goal is reliably selecting datasets by a controlled metadata criterion (e.g. only metagenomic datasets from aquatic invertebrates or only positive ionization mode) — use the platform's ontology-based selection rather than free-text keyword search.

skills.description: Use when comparing replicate metabolite intensities measured on the same cultures at two time points (e.g. 0 h vs 72 h extracellular samples) and you must flag which metabolites show significant change before computing boundary fluxes.
skills.name: paired-t-test-metabolite-screening
skills.search_text: paired-t-test-metabolite-screening Use when comparing replicate metabolite intensities measured on the same cultures at two time points (e.g. 0 h vs 72 h extracellular samples) and you must flag which metabolites show significant change before computing boundary fluxes. Data are unpaired or the two time points come from different culture batches — a paired t-test is then inappropriate. The goal is reaction-gap annotation rather than significance screening; skip straight to the boundary-flux inference step. Only a single time-point measurement exists (no paired 0 h reference) — use a one-sample or single-factor test instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Screen temporal metabolomics measurements for statistically significant change by applying a paired t-test at α = 0.05 to 0 h vs 72 h intensities, then attaching z-scores to each metabolite's boundary flux. This is the significance-testing layer of the MINNO boundary-flux workflow that separates real consumption/production from noise. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c04501
skills.summary: Screen temporal metabolomics measurements for statistically significant change by applying a paired t-test at α = 0.05 to 0 h vs 72 h intensities, then attaching z-scores to each metabolite's boundary flux. This is the significance-testing layer of the MINNO boundary-flux workflow that separates real consumption/production from noise.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are unpaired or the two time points come from different culture batches — a paired t-test is then inappropriate.
