skills.name: pairwise-interaction-agreement-statistics
skills.search_text: pairwise-interaction-agreement-statistics Use when two independent methods (e.g., SMETANA and COMMIT) have predicted metabolite exchanges over the same gap-filled community member models and you need to quantify how much their pairwise interaction predictions agree, including shared metabolites. Only one interaction-prediction method is available, so no cross-method agreement can be computed The community member models are raw draft reconstructions rather than COMMIT gap-filled models, since agreement statistics depend on the gap-filling solution The goal requires donor-to-receiver directionality of exchanges rather than symmetrized undirected pairwise overlaps Cross-validates metabolic interaction predictions by comparing directed donor-to-receiver metabolite exchanges from SMETANA with exchanges predicted by COMMIT over the same gap-filled community models, symmetrizing directed interactions into undirected pairwise overlaps and computing agreement statistics such as member interaction potential (MIP), fraction of co-predicted pairs, total agreement, and the shared-metabolite intersection. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009906
skills.summary: Cross-validates metabolic interaction predictions by comparing directed donor-to-receiver metabolite exchanges from SMETANA with exchanges predicted by COMMIT over the same gap-filled community models, symmetrizing directed interactions into undirected pairwise overlaps and computing agreement statistics such as member interaction potential (MIP), fraction of co-predicted pairs, total agreement, and the shared-metabolite intersection.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only one interaction-prediction method is available, so no cross-method agreement can be computed The community member models are raw draft reconstructions rather than COMMIT gap-filled models, since agreement statistics depend on the gap-filling solution The goal requires donor-to-receiver directionality of exchanges rather than symmetrized undirected pairwise overlaps

skills.description: Use when you have peak-mass lists from MALDI-MSI datasets (e.g. SCiLS/MSiReader CSV exports or peakBinned Cardinal imzML) and need to find which peaks are matrix- or salt-adduct partners of parent ions.
skills.name: pairwise-mass-difference-histogram-analysis
skills.search_text: pairwise-mass-difference-histogram-analysis Use when you have peak-mass lists from MALDI-MSI datasets (e.g. SCiLS/MSiReader CSV exports or peakBinned Cardinal imzML) and need to find which peaks are matrix- or salt-adduct partners of parent ions. Peaks have not been peak-binned/processed — mass2adduct requires Cardinal data to be preprocessed with peakBin() before cardinal2msimat() The CSV is too large for available RAM and has not been converted to triplet format with the msimunging.pl script (e.g. 40 Gb file on a 32 Gb system) You only have raw spectra without peak lists — the skill operates on discrete peak masses, not raw profiles http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Annotate putative molecular adducts in MS/MSI data by computing all pairwise peak mass differences, binning them into a histogram, and matching bins against known adduct masses (e.g. Na+, K+, 13C, DHB-H2O). metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c04720
skills.summary: Annotate putative molecular adducts in MS/MSI data by computing all pairwise peak mass differences, binning them into a histogram, and matching bins against known adduct masses (e.g. Na+, K+, 13C, DHB-H2O).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Peaks have not been peak-binned/processed — mass2adduct requires Cardinal data to be preprocessed with peakBin() before cardinal2msimat() The CSV is too large for available RAM and has not been converted to triplet format with the msimunging.pl script (e.g. 40 Gb file on a 32 Gb system) You only have raw spectra without peak lists — the skill operates on discrete peak masses, not raw profiles

skills.description: Use when you have a QC-filtered, per-cell anndata object of normalized isotopologue-derived relative uptake fractions and need to test whether uptake of individual fatty acids co-varies across single cells (e.g. control/normoxic liver cancer cells).
skills.name: pairwise-metabolite-correlation-analysis
skills.search_text: pairwise-metabolite-correlation-analysis Use when you have a QC-filtered, per-cell anndata object of normalized isotopologue-derived relative uptake fractions and need to test whether uptake of individual fatty acids co-varies across single cells (e.g. control/normoxic liver cancer cells). Input is bulk (well-level or pixel-level) isotopologue data rather than per-cell anndata — the correlation structure reported here is a single-cell property hidden in bulk analyses Cells have not passed the published QC filtering (size, ion number, total detected ion intensity) — unfiltered cells distort the correlation structure The goal is to estimate absolute de novo synthesis vs uptake fractions — use the binomial model instead, which per the article was only applied to ACLYkd data because fitting is unreliable when overall substrate usage is very low http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 Computes the pairwise Pearson correlation matrix of per-cell relative uptake fractions for the five measured fatty acids (myristate, palmitate, palmitoleate, stearate, oleate) from the 13C-SpaceM single-cell anndata object, revealing which fatty acids co-vary in uptake across single control cells. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s42255-024-01118-4
skills.summary: Computes the pairwise Pearson correlation matrix of per-cell relative uptake fractions for the five measured fatty acids (myristate, palmitate, palmitoleate, stearate, oleate) from the 13C-SpaceM single-cell anndata object, revealing which fatty acids co-vary in uptake across single control cells.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is bulk (well-level or pixel-level) isotopologue data rather than per-cell anndata — the correlation structure reported here is a single-cell property hidden in bulk analyses Cells have not passed the published QC filtering (size, ion number, total detected ion intensity) — unfiltered cells distort the correlation structure The goal is to estimate absolute de novo synthesis vs uptake fractions — use the binomial model instead, which per the article was only applied to ACLYkd data because fitting is unreliable when overall substrate usage is very low

skills.description: Use when you have a filtered FT-ICR MS peak/formula table with assigned molecular formulas and sample-grouping metadata, and you need to quantify and visualize which molecular formulas are shared or unique between user-defined sample groups.
skills.name: pairwise-metabolite-overlap-venn-upset-visualization
skills.search_text: pairwise-metabolite-overlap-venn-upset-visualization Use when you have a filtered FT-ICR MS peak/formula table with assigned molecular formulas and sample-grouping metadata, and you need to quantify and visualize which molecular formulas are shared or unique between user-defined sample groups. Input is raw FT-ICR MS spectra or unfiltered masses — molecular formulas must be assigned and peaks pre-filtered (m/z, 13C isotopes, 0.5 ppm error, minimum samples) before MetaboDirect can be run The analysis goal is quantitative abundance comparison or differential statistics rather than set membership of detected formulas — use the MetaboDirect statistical analysis or chemodiversity steps instead Only one sample group is defined — pairwise overlap and Venn/UpSet visualization require at least two groups http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Part of the MetaboDirect data exploration step (step iii of the 6-step pipeline): compute pairwise overlaps of detected molecular formulas between user-defined sample groups and render them as Venn and UpSet plots. This reveals which metabolites are shared or unique across conditions, e.g., phage-infected vs. control exometabolomes. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s40168-023-01476-3
skills.summary: Part of the MetaboDirect data exploration step (step iii of the 6-step pipeline): compute pairwise overlaps of detected molecular formulas between user-defined sample groups and render them as Venn and UpSet plots. This reveals which metabolites are shared or unique across conditions, e.g., phage-infected vs. control exometabolomes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw FT-ICR MS spectra or unfiltered masses — molecular formulas must be assigned and peaks pre-filtered (m/z, 13C isotopes, 0.5 ppm error, minimum samples) before MetaboDirect can be run The analysis goal is quantitative abundance comparison or differential statistics rather than set membership of detected formulas — use the MetaboDirect statistical analysis or chemodiversity steps instead Only one sample group is defined — pairwise overlap and Venn/UpSet visualization require at least two groups

skills.description: Use when annotating isotope peaks and charge states within grouped LC/MS compound spectra (pseudospectra) from an xsAnnotate/CAMERA peak table, e.g. features from faahKO or MM39-style mixtures where spacing near 1.0033/z must be identified.
skills.name: pairwise-mz-distance-matrix-construction
skills.search_text: pairwise-mz-distance-matrix-construction Use when annotating isotope peaks and charge states within grouped LC/MS compound spectra (pseudospectra) from an xsAnnotate/CAMERA peak table, e.g. features from faahKO or MM39-style mixtures where spacing near 1.0033/z must be identified. You need adduct, fragment, or quasi-molecular-ion annotation from the CAMERA rule table — this skill covers only the isotope/charge-spacing step, not the full dynamic rule-table annotation. Features have not been grouped into compound spectra yet; a pairwise m/z distance matrix over ungrouped features across the whole run is not the CAMERA procedure. The compound spectrum contains only the molecular ion and fragment ions with no further adducts/isotopes — CAMERA reports such spectra cannot be annotated directly unless the neutral loss is added to the rule set. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Reconstructs CAMERA's in-pseudospectrum isotope detection by building a pairwise m/z distance matrix over all features in each compound spectrum, flagging pairs whose difference matches 1.0033/z within ppm and mzabs tolerances, checking intensity ratios, and deducing charge states from the observed 1/z spacing. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/ac202450g
skills.summary: Reconstructs CAMERA's in-pseudospectrum isotope detection by building a pairwise m/z distance matrix over all features in each compound spectrum, flagging pairs whose difference matches 1.0033/z within ppm and mzabs tolerances, checking intensity ratios, and deducing charge states from the observed 1/z spacing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need adduct, fragment, or quasi-molecular-ion annotation from the CAMERA rule table — this skill covers only the isotope/charge-spacing step, not the full dynamic rule-table annotation. Features have not been grouped into compound spectra yet; a pairwise m/z distance matrix over ungrouped features across the whole run is not the CAMERA procedure. The compound spectrum contains only the molecular ion and fragment ions with no further adducts/isotopes — CAMERA reports such spectra cannot be annotated directly unless the neutral loss is added to the rule set.

skills.description: Use when you have an unretrained pairwise ranking model (e.g., ROASMI ensemble) and one or more independent datasets with experimental elution orders, and need to quantify cross-dataset generalizability via rank score, accuracy, and Spearman correlation.
skills.name: pairwise-ranking-model-evaluation
skills.search_text: pairwise-ranking-model-evaluation Use when you have an unretrained pairwise ranking model (e.g., ROASMI ensemble) and one or more independent datasets with experimental elution orders, and need to quantify cross-dataset generalizability via rank score, accuracy, and Spearman correlation. The evaluation requires retraining the model — this skill evaluates only the initial, unretrained ensemble for generalizability; use a separate retraining workflow instead. The datasets are HILIC rather than RPLC — the article states ROASMI currently applies only to RPLC systems. The compounds fall outside the elemental restrictions of C, H, N, O, P, and S or are outside the application domain of the ROASMI model. The comparison is intended as a mechanistic study of retention outliers rather than a cross-dataset generalizability benchmark. http://edamontology.org/topic_3399 Evaluates a pairwise ranking model (e.g., a RankNet retention-order predictor) by computing per-dataset accuracy, Spearman correlation, and rank score against experimental elution orders, without retraining, to quantify generalizability. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-025-00968-8
skills.summary: Evaluates a pairwise ranking model (e.g., a RankNet retention-order predictor) by computing per-dataset accuracy, Spearman correlation, and rank score against experimental elution orders, without retraining, to quantify generalizability.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The evaluation requires retraining the model — this skill evaluates only the initial, unretrained ensemble for generalizability; use a separate retraining workflow instead. The datasets are HILIC rather than RPLC — the article states ROASMI currently applies only to RPLC systems. The compounds fall outside the elemental restrictions of C, H, N, O, P, and S or are outside the application domain of the ROASMI model. The comparison is intended as a mechanistic study of retention outliers rather than a cross-dataset generalizability benchmark.

skills.description: Use when you have top-hit annotation lists from multiple scorer/filter configurations (e.g. fingerprint, fragprint, totalscore scorers with element, formula, or InChI filters) and need to quantify whether they retrieve the same or distinct candidate subsets per spectrum.
skills.name: pairwise-result-set-comparison
skills.search_text: pairwise-result-set-comparison Use when you have top-hit annotation lists from multiple scorer/filter configurations (e.g. fingerprint, fragprint, totalscore scorers with element, formula, or InChI filters) and need to quantify whether they retrieve the same or distinct candidate subsets per spectrum. Input is raw MS/MS spectra or single unannotated candidate lists — run ChemDistiller annotation first (python annotate.py) before comparing result sets The goal is accuracy/retrieval-rate assessment against known ground-truth compounds rather than overlap between methods — overlap says nothing about which method is correct Comparing results from only one scorer/filter combination — pairwise overlap requires at least two configurations http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Computes pairwise percentage overlap between top-hit candidate sets returned by different annotation methods and filter combinations in ChemDistiller, quantifying how complementary each scorer/filter configuration is. This is the analysis behind Supplementary Table S5, where small-database overlaps (74–93%) are contrasted with large-database overlaps (27–78%). metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/bty080
skills.summary: Computes pairwise percentage overlap between top-hit candidate sets returned by different annotation methods and filter combinations in ChemDistiller, quantifying how complementary each scorer/filter configuration is. This is the analysis behind Supplementary Table S5, where small-database overlaps (74–93%) are contrasted with large-database overlaps (27–78%).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw MS/MS spectra or single unannotated candidate lists — run ChemDistiller annotation first (python annotate.py) before comparing result sets The goal is accuracy/retrieval-rate assessment against known ground-truth compounds rather than overlap between methods — overlap says nothing about which method is correct Comparing results from only one scorer/filter combination — pairwise overlap requires at least two configurations

skills.description: Use when several normalization outputs (e.g. tGAM, rGAM, rLOESS, QC-RLSC, SERFF, TIGER) of the same LC-MS metabolomics matrix must be compared, to visualize cross-method agreement via pairwise Spearman correlation heatmaps alongside DAM overlap percentages.
skills.name: pairwise-similarity-heatmap-visualization
skills.search_text: pairwise-similarity-heatmap-visualization Use when several normalization outputs (e.g. tGAM, rGAM, rLOESS, QC-RLSC, SERFF, TIGER) of the same LC-MS metabolomics matrix must be compared, to visualize cross-method agreement via pairwise Spearman correlation heatmaps alongside DAM overlap percentages. When the goal is to judge normalization quality of a single strategy on its own (use the individual pre-/post-normalization intensity-vs-order and PCA plots instead) rather than to compare several strategies head-to-head When datasets contain no common QC annotations or when strategies are applied on differently aligned/detected metabolite sets, making Spearman correlation across the full feature space meaningless As a substitute for the RSD/CV-based QC filtering or tGAM model selection steps — this is a downstream visualization/comparison step, not a normalization or filtering step http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Renders a heatmap of pairwise similarities (Spearman correlations) between normalized metabolomics data matrices across normalization strategies, as used in the Metanorm paper's Figure 5 to visually compare tGAM/rGAM/rLOESS, QC-RLSC, SERFF and TIGER agreement on the ENVIRONAGE dataset. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.09.30.679445
skills.summary: Renders a heatmap of pairwise similarities (Spearman correlations) between normalized metabolomics data matrices across normalization strategies, as used in the Metanorm paper's Figure 5 to visually compare tGAM/rGAM/rLOESS, QC-RLSC, SERFF and TIGER agreement on the ENVIRONAGE dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is to judge normalization quality of a single strategy on its own (use the individual pre-/post-normalization intensity-vs-order and PCA plots instead) rather than to compare several strategies head-to-head When datasets contain no common QC annotations or when strategies are applied on differently aligned/detected metabolite sets, making Spearman correlation across the full feature space meaningless As a substitute for the RSD/CV-based QC filtering or tGAM model selection steps — this is a downstream visualization/comparison step, not a normalization or filtering step

skills.description: Use when you need to score every pair of MS/MS peak lists (m/z and intensity values with precursor metadata) against each other with entropy similarity instead of dot-product similarity, e.g. to build a library-search similarity matrix.
skills.name: pairwise-similarity-matrix-computation
skills.search_text: pairwise-similarity-matrix-computation Use when you need to score every pair of MS/MS peak lists (m/z and intensity values with precursor metadata) against each other with entropy similarity instead of dot-product similarity, e.g. to build a library-search similarity matrix. The analysis goal is real-time querying of billion-entry spectral libraries rather than explicit pairwise scoring — flash entropy search is the article's accelerated alternative, since full pairwise entropy/dot-product comparisons of a single spectrum take more than 8 hours against such libraries. Input spectra are already a precomputed similarity matrix or a feature table rather than raw peak lists needing entropy-based scoring. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Compute a symmetric matrix of pairwise spectral-entropy similarity scores between MS/MS spectra, replacing dot-product similarity per Li et al.'s spectral-entropy formulation (Nat Methods 2021), as used by the EntropySearch library-search tool. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-023-02012-9
skills.summary: Compute a symmetric matrix of pairwise spectral-entropy similarity scores between MS/MS spectra, replacing dot-product similarity per Li et al.'s spectral-entropy formulation (Nat Methods 2021), as used by the EntropySearch library-search tool.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is real-time querying of billion-entry spectral libraries rather than explicit pairwise scoring — flash entropy search is the article's accelerated alternative, since full pairwise entropy/dot-product comparisons of a single spectrum take more than 8 hours against such libraries. Input spectra are already a precomputed similarity matrix or a feature table rather than raw peak lists needing entropy-based scoring.

skills.description: Use when you need to cluster a moderate-sized set of annotated BGCs (e.g. 92 MIBiG v1.3 curated groups) into GCFs by exhaustive pairwise comparison, and need non-convex clusters that partitional Euclidean-space methods may miss.
skills.name: pairwise-similarity-network-construction
skills.search_text: pairwise-similarity-network-construction Use when you need to cluster a moderate-sized set of annotated BGCs (e.g. 92 MIBiG v1.3 curated groups) into GCFs by exhaustive pairwise comparison, and need non-convex clusters that partitional Euclidean-space methods may miss. Input exceeds ~100k BGCs (e.g. genome-wide 1.2M BGC surveys): the O(n^2) pairwise comparison is intractable — the article estimates 37,000 hours of runtime on a 36-core CPU for BiG-SCAPE; use a near-linear Euclidean-space partitional approach like BiG-SLiCE instead. BGCs are already projected into Euclidean feature space and convex (spherical) clusters suffice — partitional clustering on centroid features is cheaper and scales better. BGCs are unannotated or fragmented raw contigs: the network requires reliable Pfam domain architectures from processed GenBank files, not raw nucleotide input. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Constructs a weighted BGC similarity network by computing all pairwise distances between biosynthetic gene clusters based on their Pfam domain architectures and sequences, enabling clustering algorithms like Affinity Propagation that can find non-convex gene cluster families (GCFs). metabolomics/v3 10.1093/gigascience/giaa154
skills.summary: Constructs a weighted BGC similarity network by computing all pairwise distances between biosynthetic gene clusters based on their Pfam domain architectures and sequences, enabling clustering algorithms like Affinity Propagation that can find non-convex gene cluster families (GCFs).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input exceeds ~100k BGCs (e.g. genome-wide 1.2M BGC surveys): the O(n^2) pairwise comparison is intractable — the article estimates 37,000 hours of runtime on a 36-core CPU for BiG-SCAPE; use a near-linear Euclidean-space partitional approach like BiG-SLiCE instead. BGCs are already projected into Euclidean feature space and convex (spherical) clusters suffice — partitional clustering on centroid features is cheaper and scales better. BGCs are unannotated or fragmented raw contigs: the network requires reliable Pfam domain architectures from processed GenBank files, not raw nucleotide input.

skills.description: Use when you need pairwise similarity/distance between complete MS/MS datasets (e.g. for phylogenetics, QC, or species identification) without peptide identification or spectral libraries.
skills.name: pairwise-spectral-overlap-quantification
skills.search_text: pairwise-spectral-overlap-quantification Use when you need pairwise similarity/distance between complete MS/MS datasets (e.g. for phylogenetics, QC, or species identification) without peptide identification or spectral libraries. You have identified peptides and want standard protein quantitation or database-search results — compareMS2 compares sets of tandem mass spectra directly rather than to predicted spectra of specific peptides You only have a single dataset (no comparison target) — D(A,A) is always zero, so pairwise spectral overlap cannot be quantified You need a distance metric that tolerates loose definitions of spectrum identity — the Jaccard similarity is very sensitive to the precise definition of when two spectra are considered identical http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Computes the distance between sets of tandem mass spectra (e.g. LC-MS/MS serum datasets) using compareMS2 2.0's fully symmetric spectral-similarity metric, assembling unique pairwise comparisons into a distance matrix without redundant recalculation. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.2c00457
skills.summary: Computes the distance between sets of tandem mass spectra (e.g. LC-MS/MS serum datasets) using compareMS2 2.0's fully symmetric spectral-similarity metric, assembling unique pairwise comparisons into a distance matrix without redundant recalculation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have identified peptides and want standard protein quantitation or database-search results — compareMS2 compares sets of tandem mass spectra directly rather than to predicted spectra of specific peptides You only have a single dataset (no comparison target) — D(A,A) is always zero, so pairwise spectral overlap cannot be quantified You need a distance metric that tolerates loose definitions of spectrum identity — the Jaccard similarity is very sensitive to the precise definition of when two spectra are considered identical

skills.description: Use when exploring an MS/MS feature set via its pairwise spectral similarity matrix — e.g. you have a .mgf-derived specXplore session object and want threshold-tunable local network views, heatmaps, and clustering overlays rather than fixed molecular networking output.
skills.name: pairwise-spectral-similarity-matrix-analysis
skills.search_text: pairwise-spectral-similarity-matrix-analysis Use when exploring an MS/MS feature set via its pairwise spectral similarity matrix — e.g. you have a .mgf-derived specXplore session object and want threshold-tunable local network views, heatmaps, and clustering overlays rather than fixed molecular networking output. You need a fixed, standard molecular networking output (e.g. classical GNPS molecular networking) rather than adjustable, exploratory local views — the paper positions specXplore as a complement, not a replacement. Your data set exceeds roughly 5000 features — the authors only anticipate good scaling to 5000 features and expect difficulties for larger data sets and liberal settings. Your metabolites/spectra lie outside or are poorly related to ms2deepscore's training data — the pretrained ML score cannot be expected to work well there. You are running on Windows — the current specXplore version fails on Windows; workflows rely on macOS/Linux (and Anaconda PowerShell workarounds). http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Analyze the raw pairwise spectral similarity matrix (ms2deepscore as primary score) directly within the specXplore dashboard, using the t-SNE embedding as an overview, k-medoid clustering overlays for grouping, and adjustable similarity thresholds plus top-K connectivity limits for localized partial network and heatmap exploration of LC-MS/MS features. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c04444
skills.summary: Analyze the raw pairwise spectral similarity matrix (ms2deepscore as primary score) directly within the specXplore dashboard, using the t-SNE embedding as an overview, k-medoid clustering overlays for grouping, and adjustable similarity thresholds plus top-K connectivity limits for localized partial network and heatmap exploration of LC-MS/MS features.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need a fixed, standard molecular networking output (e.g. classical GNPS molecular networking) rather than adjustable, exploratory local views — the paper positions specXplore as a complement, not a replacement. Your data set exceeds roughly 5000 features — the authors only anticipate good scaling to 5000 features and expect difficulties for larger data sets and liberal settings. Your metabolites/spectra lie outside or are poorly related to ms2deepscore's training data — the pretrained ML score cannot be expected to work well there. You are running on Windows — the current specXplore version fails on Windows; workflows rely on macOS/Linux (and Anaconda PowerShell workarounds).

skills.description: Use when a set of MS/MS feature spectra (e.g. .mgf with feature_id, precursor m/z, m/z-intensity tuples) must be converted into pairwise similarity matrices to drive downstream embedding, network, or heatmap visualizations.
skills.name: pairwise-spectral-similarity-scoring
skills.search_text: pairwise-spectral-similarity-scoring Use when a set of MS/MS feature spectra (e.g. .mgf with feature_id, precursor m/z, m/z-intensity tuples) must be converted into pairwise similarity matrices to drive downstream embedding, network, or heatmap visualizations. The input is already a processed similarity matrix or a specXplore session data object — rerunning the importing pipeline would redundantly recompute MS2Query and pairwise scores The spectra/metabolite classes are poorly covered by or unrelated to ms2deepscore's training data, since the pretrained model can only be expected to work well for spectra well covered by or related to its training data The dataset far exceeds ~5000 features after processing, where the article anticipates the dashboard and settings will face difficulties http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Compute the full pairwise spectral similarity matrices (ms2deepscore as primary, plus modified cosine and spec2vec) for LC-MS/MS feature spectra in .mgf format via the specXplore importing pipeline; these matrices are the quantitative backbone for t-SNE overviews, network views, and similarity heatmaps. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c04444
skills.summary: Compute the full pairwise spectral similarity matrices (ms2deepscore as primary, plus modified cosine and spec2vec) for LC-MS/MS feature spectra in .mgf format via the specXplore importing pipeline; these matrices are the quantitative backbone for t-SNE overviews, network views, and similarity heatmaps.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a processed similarity matrix or a specXplore session data object — rerunning the importing pipeline would redundantly recompute MS2Query and pairwise scores The spectra/metabolite classes are poorly covered by or unrelated to ms2deepscore's training data, since the pretrained model can only be expected to work well for spectra well covered by or related to its training data The dataset far exceeds ~5000 features after processing, where the article anticipates the dashboard and settings will face difficulties

skills.description: Use when a COCONUT snapshot contains organism annotations and the goal is to quantify NP production per taxonomic category and the pairwise sharing of NPs between superkingdoms.
skills.name: pairwise-superkingdom-overlap-computation
skills.search_text: pairwise-superkingdom-overlap-computation Use when a COCONUT snapshot contains organism annotations and the goal is to quantify NP production per taxonomic category and the pairwise sharing of NPs between superkingdoms. The input dataset lacks organism/provenance annotations (COCONUT's own provenance fields such as organism_parts and locations were nullified in pivot tables), so no producer taxonomy can be mapped The analysis concerns molecular property distributions (descriptors, ClassyFire chemical classes) rather than producer-organism taxonomy Data comes from a source-specific collection (e.g., SuperNatural II subset) that fails COCONUT quality control and has not been unified into the uniqueNaturalProduct table Computes the five-way taxonomic provenance breakdown of COCONUT natural products (plants, bacteria, fungi, animals, marine) and a pairwise superkingdom overlap matrix showing which NPs are attributed to more than one producer group, mirroring the COCONUT provenance analysis (Fig. 3). metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-020-00478-9
skills.summary: Computes the five-way taxonomic provenance breakdown of COCONUT natural products (plants, bacteria, fungi, animals, marine) and a pairwise superkingdom overlap matrix showing which NPs are attributed to more than one producer group, mirroring the COCONUT provenance analysis (Fig. 3).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input dataset lacks organism/provenance annotations (COCONUT's own provenance fields such as organism_parts and locations were nullified in pivot tables), so no producer taxonomy can be mapped The analysis concerns molecular property distributions (descriptors, ClassyFire chemical classes) rather than producer-organism taxonomy Data comes from a source-specific collection (e.g., SuperNatural II subset) that fails COCONUT quality control and has not been unified into the uniqueNaturalProduct table

skills.description: Use when an imputed MetaboSet from LC–MS metabolomics has two or more sample groups in the Group annotation and you need per-feature univariate statistics — e.g. ANOVA_P_FDR-selected features for post-hoc pairwise testing, or direct two-group comparisons.
skills.name: pairwise-welch-t-test-group-comparison
skills.search_text: pairwise-welch-t-test-group-comparison Use when an imputed MetaboSet from LC–MS metabolomics has two or more sample groups in the Group annotation and you need per-feature univariate statistics — e.g. ANOVA_P_FDR-selected features for post-hoc pairwise testing, or direct two-group comparisons. Input is still a raw instrument file or an unimputed MS-DIAL peak table — preprocessing (mark_nas, correct_drift, flag_quality, imputation) must come first. The analysis goal is multivariate (e.g. PCA/OPLS) rather than feature-wise univariate testing. Features are flagged low-quality by flag_quality/flag_detection — testing flagged features is not the intended use. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Feature-wise pairwise group comparison in the notame LC–MS metabolomics workflow: for each molecular feature, run Welch's two-sample t-test (Mann–Whitney U as the non-parametric alternative) between groups, producing feature-level p-values that are subsequently Benjamini–Hochberg FDR-corrected. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo10040135
skills.summary: Feature-wise pairwise group comparison in the notame LC–MS metabolomics workflow: for each molecular feature, run Welch's two-sample t-test (Mann–Whitney U as the non-parametric alternative) between groups, producing feature-level p-values that are subsequently Benjamini–Hochberg FDR-corrected.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is still a raw instrument file or an unimputed MS-DIAL peak table — preprocessing (mark_nas, correct_drift, flag_quality, imputation) must come first. The analysis goal is multivariate (e.g. PCA/OPLS) rather than feature-wise univariate testing. Features are flagged low-quality by flag_quality/flag_detection — testing flagged features is not the intended use.

skills.description: Use when reproducing the Hoadley et al. (2014) multiplatform cancer subtyping with klic/coca, or when integrative clustering of five omic layers (copy number, methylation, miRNA, mRNA, protein) with per-dataset kernel weights is needed.
skills.name: pan-cancer-subtyping-replication
skills.search_text: pan-cancer-subtyping-replication Use when reproducing the Hoadley et al. The input is already a deconvoluted peak/feature table rather than raw multi-way chromatographic data The analysis goal is targeted quantification with known reference spectra — annotation via duoID (cosine similarity > 0.7 against an msp library) is more appropriate Data are 1D GC–MS or non-chromatographic; the tri-linear PARAFAC tensor structure (m/z × RT2 × RT1) is required http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Blind PARAFAC deconvolution of GC × GC–MS peaks as implemented in GcDUO's Module III: iteratively fitting PARAFAC on m/z × RT2 × RT1 sub-tensors, increasing the component count until explained variance (R²) stops improving and all components are Gaussian with Tucker congruence > 0.9, followed by duplicate-feature removal and cross-sample consensus grouping. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bib/bbaf080

skills.description: Use when an untargeted LC/HRMS study has hundreds or thousands of sample files (e.g. 499–1,649 mzML/mzXML runs) and sequential peak-picking would be too slow; you need to parallelize peak detection and m/z-slice alignment across threads.
skills.name: parallel-batch-processing-of-large-metabolomics-studies
skills.search_text: parallel-batch-processing-of-large-metabolomics-studies Use when an untargeted LC/HRMS study has hundreds or thousands of sample files (e.g. 499–1,649 mzML/mzXML runs) and sequential peak-picking would be too slow; you need to parallelize peak detection and m/z-slice alignment across threads. The study contains only a handful of samples and sequential peak picking with MZmine 2, xcms, or MS-DIAL is fast enough — parallelization overhead is unnecessary. The goal is MS2/DDA or DIA fragmentation processing rather than MS1 peak detection and alignment; use a fragmentation-focused workflow instead. Input is already an aligned feature table that only needs downstream steps like adduct/fragment identification or molecular formula annotation (e.g. by IDSL.UFA). http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 A method for accelerating untargeted LC/HRMS peak processing of population-scale studies (hundreds to thousands of samples) by distributing peak detection and alignment across multiple computing threads, as implemented in the IDSL.IPA R package. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.2c00120
skills.summary: A method for accelerating untargeted LC/HRMS peak processing of population-scale studies (hundreds to thousands of samples) by distributing peak detection and alignment across multiple computing threads, as implemented in the IDSL.IPA R package.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The study contains only a handful of samples and sequential peak picking with MZmine 2, xcms, or MS-DIAL is fast enough — parallelization overhead is unnecessary. The goal is MS2/DDA or DIA fragmentation processing rather than MS1 peak detection and alignment; use a fragmentation-focused workflow instead. Input is already an aligned feature table that only needs downstream steps like adduct/fragment identification or molecular formula annotation (e.g. by IDSL.UFA).

skills.description: Use when comparing computational cost or parallel-scaling behavior of competing normalization/analysis methods (e.g., Metanorm's QC-RLSC/QC-RSC/rLOESS/rGAM/tGAM vs TIGER or SERFF) on the same data sets.
skills.name: parallel-compute-scaling-profiling
skills.search_text: parallel-compute-scaling-profiling Use when comparing computational cost or parallel-scaling behavior of competing normalization/analysis methods (e.g., Metanorm's QC-RLSC/QC-RSC/rLOESS/rGAM/tGAM vs TIGER or SERFF) on the same data sets. The goal is assessing normalization quality (drift/batch-effect removal, replicate concordance) rather than computational performance — use accuracy-based benchmarking instead Methods expose no core-count control (e.g., SERFF is only reachable through its Shiny web interface, so core scaling cannot be profiled) The data set is too small to amortize parallelization overhead, which the reference shows produces tapering/declining scaling curves on BioHEART http://edamontology.org/topic_3360 Benchmark the computational runtime and parallel-scaling behavior of metabolomics normalization methods by timing each method on fixed targeted and untargeted data sets while varying CPU core count (1–6), and expressing throughput as normalized compounds per minute to expose which methods scale and which saturate. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c06841
skills.summary: Benchmark the computational runtime and parallel-scaling behavior of metabolomics normalization methods by timing each method on fixed targeted and untargeted data sets while varying CPU core count (1–6), and expressing throughput as normalized compounds per minute to expose which methods scale and which saturate.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is assessing normalization quality (drift/batch-effect removal, replicate concordance) rather than computational performance — use accuracy-based benchmarking instead Methods expose no core-count control (e.g., SERFF is only reachable through its Shiny web interface, so core scaling cannot be profiled) The data set is too small to amortize parallelization overhead, which the reference shows produces tapering/declining scaling curves on BioHEART

skills.search_text: parallel-extraction-performance-measurement Use when you must quantify whether Shinyscreen's mzML extraction and prescreening steps are accelerated by parallel backends — i.e. you have multiple vendor-neutral mzML files, a compound list, and need a reproducible serial vs parallel timing comparison with a speedup ratio. This substantiates the paper's claim that Shinyscreen handles the thousands of HRMS peaks from high-throughput QC workloads efficiently. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-025-01044-x

skills.description: Reference for normalizing large-scale LC-MS metabolomics datasets (e.g. ~8913 untargeted features or ~53 targeted compounds across hundreds of samples) where single-threaded QC-based normalization would be too slow.
skills.name: parallel-high-throughput-normalization
skills.search_text: parallel-high-throughput-normalization Reference for normalizing large-scale LC-MS metabolomics datasets (e.g. ~8913 untargeted features or ~53 targeted compounds across hundreds of samples) where single-threaded QC-based normalization would be too slow. The dataset is tiny (e.g. only a handful of features) and single-threaded runtime is already negligible — the overhead of parallel setup offers no benefit. QCs are not representative of biological samples (metanorm's QCcheck flag returns a discrepancy); robust QC-based normalization may mis-correct biological samples and a different strategy is warranted. The data have already been normalized or are a derived feature table rather than raw intensities; re-running normalization would double-correct the signal. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Perform metabolomics normalization of large LC-MS data matrices (thousands of features, hundreds of samples) using the Metanorm R package's efficient parallel implementation of robust methods (tGAM, rGAM, rLOESS, QC-RLSC, QC-RSC), keeping runtime feasible for high-throughput datasets. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.09.30.679445
skills.summary: Perform metabolomics normalization of large LC-MS data matrices (thousands of features, hundreds of samples) using the Metanorm R package's efficient parallel implementation of robust methods (tGAM, rGAM, rLOESS, QC-RLSC, QC-RSC), keeping runtime feasible for high-throughput datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset is tiny (e.g. only a handful of features) and single-threaded runtime is already negligible — the overhead of parallel setup offers no benefit. QCs are not representative of biological samples (metanorm's QCcheck flag returns a discrepancy); robust QC-based normalization may mis-correct biological samples and a different strategy is warranted. The data have already been normalized or are a derived feature table rather than raw intensities; re-running normalization would double-correct the signal.

skills.description: Use when a multicore-capable implementation must be benchmarked for thread scalability — e.g. you need to know whether wall-clock time keeps decreasing or saturates as threads increase from 1 to 32 on real raw-data subsets.
skills.name: parallel-scaling-behavior-visualization
skills.search_text: parallel-scaling-behavior-visualization Use when a multicore-capable implementation must be benchmarked for thread scalability — e.g. you need to know whether wall-clock time keeps decreasing or saturates as threads increase from 1 to 32 on real raw-data subsets. When the goal is GPU-acceleration benchmarking — the article's scaling study is a CPU thread sweep and explicitly does not require the TensorFlow 2 GPU path When you need classification accuracy metrics (ROC, true/false-positive rates) rather than performance timing — use the roc pipeline instead of the scalability study When data access itself is the bottleneck to benchmark — this skill isolates compute scaling on a fixed 100-frame subset, not I/O throughput http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Sweeps the thread count of a CPU-parallel implementation (here the LSH signal-classification pipeline in pyproteolizard-algorithm/mzBucket) over TimsTOF raw-data frames, records wall-clock execution time per thread count, and plots/exports the scaling curve to reveal where parallelization gains saturate. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-022-04833-5
skills.summary: Sweeps the thread count of a CPU-parallel implementation (here the LSH signal-classification pipeline in pyproteolizard-algorithm/mzBucket) over TimsTOF raw-data frames, records wall-clock execution time per thread count, and plots/exports the scaling curve to reveal where parallelization gains saturate.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is GPU-acceleration benchmarking — the article's scaling study is a CPU thread sweep and explicitly does not require the TensorFlow 2 GPU path When you need classification accuracy metrics (ROC, true/false-positive rates) rather than performance timing — use the roc pipeline instead of the scalability study When data access itself is the bottleneck to benchmark — this skill isolates compute scaling on a fixed 100-frame subset, not I/O throughput

skills.description: Use when you have a set of recognized (e.g., off-sample-flagged) matrix cluster ion formulas and a predicted formula-to-parameter lookup table, and need to visualize which combinatorial parameter values dominate the clusters.
skills.name: parameter-distribution-histogram-visualization
skills.search_text: parameter-distribution-histogram-visualization Use when you have a set of recognized (e.g., off-sample-flagged) matrix cluster ion formulas and a predicted formula-to-parameter lookup table, and need to visualize which combinatorial parameter values dominate the clusters. You are analyzing on-sample (tissue-relevant) metabolite annotations rather than off-sample matrix cluster ions — the parameter interpretation only applies to matrix clusters. You lack a formula-to-parameter mapping (e.g., the Keller and Li 2000 combinatorial model predictions) for the matrix of interest, so formulas cannot be decomposed into n, p, x, z. Your goal is pixel-level segmentation of off-sample regions, which the paper explicitly states this approach does not solve. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Characterize recognized DHB matrix cluster ions by mapping each annotated molecular formula to its combinatorial cluster-generating model parameters (n = DHB molecule count, p, x = potassium count, z = sodium count), then tally parameter occurrences and plot per-parameter histograms in the layout of Fig. 3 of Ovchinnikova et al. (2020). metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-020-3425-x
skills.summary: Characterize recognized DHB matrix cluster ions by mapping each annotated molecular formula to its combinatorial cluster-generating model parameters (n = DHB molecule count, p, x = potassium count, z = sodium count), then tally parameter occurrences and plot per-parameter histograms in the layout of Fig. 3 of Ovchinnikova et al. (2020).
skills.when_to_use_negative: You are analyzing on-sample (tissue-relevant) metabolite annotations rather than off-sample matrix cluster ions — the parameter interpretation only applies to matrix clusters. skills.description: Use when a published pipeline result (e.g., DIMPLE peak counts per B73 root) must be stress-tested by re-running preprocessing at altered thresholds to report percent changes relative to the default-parameter baseline.
skills.name: parameter-sensitivity-analysis
skills.search_text: parameter-sensitivity-analysis Use when a published pipeline result (e.g., DIMPLE peak counts per B73 root) must be stress-tested by re-running preprocessing at altered thresholds to report percent changes relative to the default-parameter baseline. The goal is de novo annotation or identification of mass signatures (use Metlin Classic, LOTUS, or METASPACE instead of re-tuning DIMPLE thresholds). The data are not from a linear developmental gradient (e.g., MALDI or SIMS imaging of non-linear tissue), since DIMPLE is designed to leverage the linear root developmental axis. Quantifies how relaxing analysis thresholds in the DIMPLE DESI-MSI pipeline changes output metrics, by re-running preprocessing of B73 maize root data at relaxed ppm mass tolerance (2.5 → 5 ppm) and lowered background-enrichment thresholds (1.5 → 1.1) and comparing per-root peak counts against the ~196 peaks/root default baseline. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.09.22.677919
skills.summary: Quantifies how relaxing analysis thresholds in the DIMPLE DESI-MSI pipeline changes output metrics, by re-running preprocessing of B73 maize root data at relaxed ppm mass tolerance (2.5 → 5 ppm) and lowered background-enrichment thresholds (1.5 → 1.1) and comparing per-root peak counts against the ~196 peaks/root default baseline.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is de novo annotation or identification of mass signatures (use Metlin Classic, LOTUS, or METASPACE instead of re-tuning DIMPLE thresholds). The data are not from a linear developmental gradient (e.g., MALDI or SIMS imaging of non-linear tissue), since DIMPLE is designed to leverage the linear root developmental axis.

skills.description: Use when multiple apLCMS parameter settings (or apLCMS/XCMS vs a two-stage batch-aware pipeline) have produced feature tables for a two-group design, and you need to count features significant at FDR <= 0.2 per setting.

skills.search_text: parameter-setting-comparison-of-feature-tables Use when multiple apLCMS parameter settings (or apLCMS/XCMS vs a two-stage batch-aware pipeline) have produced feature tables for a two-group design, and you need to count features significant at FDR <= 0.2 per setting. skills.summary: Generates and statistically compares uncorrected LC/MS feature tables across multiple apLCMS parameter settings to test whether the two-stage batch-aware preprocessing detects more significant features (two-sample t-test, Benjamini-Hochberg FDR <= 0.2) than traditional preprocessing, e.g. on the ST000868 oak vs wine yeast metabolomics dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input feature tables have already been batch-effect corrected — post hoc correction changes intensity structure and defeats the purpose of comparing uncorrected preprocessing outputs There is only a single feature table with no parameter-setting variation to compare across The design is not a two-group comparison suitable for a two-sample t-test (e.g. multi-class or time-course labels)

skills.search_text: parameter-spreadsheet-workflow-configuration Use when processing raw untargeted LC/HRMS files (mzXML, mzML, netCDF) with IDSL.IPA and you must set data/output locations, peak-detection and recursive mass correction options (PARAM0019-PARAM0020) before calling IPA_workflow. skills.search_text: parameter-stability-visualization Use when you must decide how many samples are sufficient for stable parameter estimation, by tabulating CV across random subsets and plotting CV vs. sample size against an acceptance threshold (e.g. CV <= 0.1). The parameter cannot be recomputed automatically per subsample — e.g. AutoTuner's Group difference parameter is estimated through a non-automatable cross-sample comparison, so its robustness cannot be checked this way. Input is already a processed feature table rather than raw data — AutoTuner requires raw converted instrument files (.mzML, .mzXML, .CDF). Fewer than 3 samples are available, since AutoTuner requires at least 3 samples of raw data as input. Quantifies the stability of automatically estimated data-processing parameters by running repeated estimation on random subsamples and plotting coefficient of variation (CV) against subsample size to find the minimum number of samples needed for stable estimates. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/812370
skills.summary: Quantifies the stability of automatically estimated data-processing parameters by running repeated estimation on random subsamples and plotting coefficient of variation (CV) against subsample size to find the minimum number of samples needed for stable estimates.
