skills.when_to_use_negative: PeakForest does not include data clean-up or extraction tools, so do not use this mapping to clean or normalize dirty spectra/metadata — users must supply completely-cleaned data following the PeakForest team's SOPs The goal is storing raw spectral data rather than metabolite annotation report data and compound metadata; PeakForest is designed for the latter, not raw spectral data storage Only a handful of ad hoc compounds need manual entry — the manual 'Import compounds and spectral data' workflow via the Web interface is simpler than building a template-based batch import

skills.description: Use when per-sample IDSL.IPA peaklists (m/z–RT pairs from mzXML/mzML/netCDF HRMS files) must be RT-corrected and cross-referenced into one aligned table for a population-scale untargeted LC/HRMS study.
skills.name: peaklist-alignment-across-samples
skills.search_text: peaklist-alignment-across-samples Use when per-sample IDSL.IPA peaklists (m/z–RT pairs from mzXML/mzML/netCDF HRMS files) must be RT-corrected and cross-referenced into one aligned table for a population-scale untargeted LC/HRMS study. A single HRMS file is being processed with no cross-sample alignment needed (RT correction across batches has no reference pool to draw from). The aligned data matrix already exists and the goal is adduct/fragment identification, statistics filtering, or molecular formula annotation — those are handled by IDSL.UFA/IDSL.UFAx downstream. The dataset lacks recurring indigenous reference peaks, so the dynamic retention index marker pool and its median-drift fallback cannot be reliably constructed. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Cross-reference and align per-sample IDSL.IPA peaklists (m/z–RT pairs) into a single study-level matrix by correcting retention time drift with a dynamic pool of indigenous retention index reference markers. This removes systematic RT drift so that the same chemical signal is matched across hundreds to thousands of LC/HRMS samples. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.2c00120
skills.summary: Cross-reference and align per-sample IDSL.IPA peaklists (m/z–RT pairs) into a single study-level matrix by correcting retention time drift with a dynamic pool of indigenous retention index reference markers. This removes systematic RT drift so that the same chemical signal is matched across hundreds to thousands of LC/HRMS samples.
skills.when_to_use_negative: A single HRMS file is being processed with no cross-sample alignment needed (RT correction across batches has no reference pool to draw from). The aligned data matrix already exists and the goal is adduct/fragment identification, statistics filtering, or molecular formula annotation — those are handled by IDSL.UFA/IDSL.UFAx downstream. The dataset lacks recurring indigenous reference peaks, so the dynamic retention index marker pool and its median-drift fallback cannot be reliably constructed.

skills.description: Use when a peak-picked LC-MS peak list contains multiple co-eluting peaks differing by ~1 Da isotopic spacing that should be grouped into single deisotoped features before alignment across samples.
skills.name: peaklist-deisotoping
skills.search_text: peaklist-deisotoping Use when a peak-picked LC-MS peak list contains multiple co-eluting peaks differing by ~1 Da isotopic spacing that should be grouped into single deisotoped features before alignment across samples. Input is already a deisotoped or aligned feature table — re-running grouping on collapsed rows can strip genuine isotope information The analysis requires retaining individual isotopic peaks (e.g., isotopic labeling experiments) rather than collapsing them into grouped features The data are still raw profiles that have not been peak-picked; deisotoping operates on peak lists, not on raw mass spectra http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Group detected chromatographic peaks into isotope patterns and collapse each group to a single representative peak (adduct/monoisotopic row), as implemented in the MZmine 2 peak list deisotoping module using isotope distributions calculated with the Chemistry Development Kit (CDK). metabolomics/v3 10.1186/1471-2105-11-395
skills.summary: Group detected chromatographic peaks into isotope patterns and collapse each group to a single representative peak (adduct/monoisotopic row), as implemented in the MZmine 2 peak list deisotoping module using isotope distributions calculated with the Chemistry Development Kit (CDK).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a deisotoped or aligned feature table — re-running grouping on collapsed rows can strip genuine isotope information The analysis requires retaining individual isotopic peaks (e.g., isotopic labeling experiments) rather than collapsing them into grouped features The data are still raw profiles that have not been peak-picked; deisotoping operates on peak lists, not on raw mass spectra

skills.description: Use when a peak list has been deisotoped and aligned across multiple raw LC-MS data files, but individual samples are missing detections for peaks found in other samples, blocking normalization and export.
skills.name: peaklist-gap-filling
skills.search_text: peaklist-gap-filling Use when a peak list has been deisotoped and aligned across multiple raw LC-MS data files, but individual samples are missing detections for peaks found in other samples, blocking normalization and export. The input is already a normalized feature table — gap filling operates on aligned, non-normalized peak lists and must precede the normalization module Only a single raw data file is being processed with no cross-sample alignment, since there is no aligned peak list whose missing features can be recovered The data are not LC-MS — the paper's modules were tested mainly on LC-MS data, with GC-MS and MASCOT interoperability described only as possible future expansion http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Fills missing values in an aligned MZmine 2 peak list by detecting peaks that are expected but absent in individual samples, so that every LC-MS sample carries a complete feature table before normalization and export. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/1471-2105-11-395
skills.summary: Fills missing values in an aligned MZmine 2 peak list by detecting peaks that are expected but absent in individual samples, so that every LC-MS sample carries a complete feature table before normalization and export.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a normalized feature table — gap filling operates on aligned, non-normalized peak lists and must precede the normalization module Only a single raw data file is being processed with no cross-sample alignment, since there is no aligned peak list whose missing features can be recovered The data are not LC-MS — the paper's modules were tested mainly on LC-MS data, with GC-MS and MASCOT interoperability described only as possible future expansion

skills.description: Use when evaluating a spectral similarity metric against structural (Tanimoto) ground truth on MS/MS library testing pairs — e.g. mergedGNPS — to reproduce or compare correlation coefficients across multiple scoring methods.
skills.name: pearson-correlation-analysis
skills.search_text: pearson-correlation-analysis Use when evaluating a spectral similarity metric against structural (Tanimoto) ground truth on MS/MS library testing pairs — e.g. mergedGNPS — to reproduce or compare correlation coefficients across multiple scoring methods. When compound structures/fingerprints are unavailable for the spectrum pairs, so no Tanimoto ground truth can be computed to correlate against. When the goal is molecular networking or structure elucidation explanation rather than quantitative benchmarking of similarity-vs-structure correlation. http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Benchmark how well a predicted MS/MS spectral similarity (e.g. TransExION) tracks Tanimoto structural similarity on a fixed set of query-reference spectrum pairs, by computing the Pearson correlation coefficient r against the Tanimoto ground truth and comparing to baseline metrics (Cosine, Modified Cosine, Spec2Vec, MS2DeepScore). metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00858-5
skills.summary: Benchmark how well a predicted MS/MS spectral similarity (e.g. TransExION) tracks Tanimoto structural similarity on a fixed set of query-reference spectrum pairs, by computing the Pearson correlation coefficient r against the Tanimoto ground truth and comparing to baseline metrics (Cosine, Modified Cosine, Spec2Vec, MS2DeepScore).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When compound structures/fingerprints are unavailable for the spectrum pairs, so no Tanimoto ground truth can be computed to correlate against. When the goal is molecular networking or structure elucidation explanation rather than quantitative benchmarking of similarity-vs-structure correlation.

skills.description: Use when blinded biological replicate (duplicate) samples are embedded in a large metabolomics cohort and you need to quantify sample-level reproducibility via per-pair Pearson r across all metabolite features, e.g. 102 duplicate pairs in a 4104-sample T2D GC-MS plasma study.
skills.name: pearson-correlation-analysis-of-biological-duplicate-pairs
skills.search_text: pearson-correlation-analysis-of-biological-duplicate-pairs Use when blinded biological replicate (duplicate) samples are embedded in a large metabolomics cohort and you need to quantify sample-level reproducibility via per-pair Pearson r across all metabolite features, e.g. 102 duplicate pairs in a 4104-sample T2D GC-MS plasma study. The input is raw, unnormalized metabolite intensities — correlations on unnormalized data will not reflect the reported r_xy ≈ 0.98 because SERDA normalization is what brings replicate agreement to the reported range The replicate structure is technical (pooled QC) rather than biological duplicates pooled QC samples are handled by the separate SERDA/SERRF precision assessment (median 16% training RSD, 19% independent BioIVT RSD) http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Quantifies reproducibility of blinded biological duplicate pairs in large-scale GC-MS metabolomics by computing Pearson correlation coefficients (r_xy) across all metabolite features for each duplicate pair. Applied to the 4104-sample type 2 diabetes cohort's 102 duplicate pairs to validate SERDA-normalized intensities, distinguishing adjacent from nonadjacent replicates. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo13080944
skills.summary: Quantifies reproducibility of blinded biological duplicate pairs in large-scale GC-MS metabolomics by computing Pearson correlation coefficients (r_xy) across all metabolite features for each duplicate pair. Applied to the 4104-sample type 2 diabetes cohort's 102 duplicate pairs to validate SERDA-normalized intensities, distinguishing adjacent from nonadjacent replicates.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw, unnormalized metabolite intensities — correlations on unnormalized data will not reflect the reported r_xy ≈ 0.98 because SERDA normalization is what brings replicate agreement to the reported range The replicate structure is technical (pooled QC) rather than biological duplicates pooled QC samples are handled by the separate SERDA/SERRF precision assessment (median 16% training RSD, 19% independent BioIVT RSD)

skills.search_text: pearson-correlation-analysis-of-ion-intensities Use when you need to verify background-region signal stability in a spatial metabolomics peak table, e.g. before background noise removal, by checking that pairwise Pearson correlations of region spectra exceed 0.9. The input is not a pixel-coordinate-indexed peak table but already aggregated spectra or a feature table without X/Y coordinates The goal is quality visualization of tissue regions (e.g. intensity distribution, isotopic/adduct identification) rather than background consistency evaluation http://edamontology.org/topic_3292 Quantifies the consistency of spatial-metabolomics background regions by computing pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients between representative spectra (median ion intensities per region), applying the SMQVP QVP2 criterion that coefficients above 0.9 indicate stable signal acquisition. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo15060354
skills.summary: Quantifies the consistency of spatial-metabolomics background regions by computing pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients between representative spectra (median ion intensities per region), applying the SMQVP QVP2 criterion that coefficients above 0.9 indicate stable signal acquisition.

skills.description: Use when validating that automated RT assignments match manual RT assignments, e.g. comparing metScribeR-derived RTs against manually assigned MassHunter RTs on authentic metabolite standards.
skills.name: pearson-correlation-and-rmsd-analysis
skills.search_text: pearson-correlation-and-rmsd-analysis Use when validating that automated RT assignments match manual RT assignments, e.g. comparing metScribeR-derived RTs against manually assigned MassHunter RTs on authentic metabolite standards. The input is already a peak-quality label (Good/Bad/Multimodal) — use peak-review validation instead of RT correlation. The reference RTs are not from a single LC-MS method — RT is not consistently transferable across different LC-MS conditions, so cross-method comparison would not be meaningful. The goal is MS/MS library building rather than RT benchmarking — metScribeR does not require MS/MS data and MoNA MS/MS collection is slow and optional. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Benchmark the accuracy of automated retention-time assignments (e.g. metScribeR-derived RTs) against a manual reference set by computing the Pearson correlation coefficient and the root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of paired RT values. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.5c00548
skills.summary: Benchmark the accuracy of automated retention-time assignments (e.g. metScribeR-derived RTs) against a manual reference set by computing the Pearson correlation coefficient and the root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of paired RT values.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a peak-quality label (Good/Bad/Multimodal) — use peak-review validation instead of RT correlation. The reference RTs are not from a single LC-MS method — RT is not consistently transferable across different LC-MS conditions, so cross-method comparison would not be meaningful. The goal is MS/MS library building rather than RT benchmarking — metScribeR does not require MS/MS data and MoNA MS/MS collection is slow and optional.

skills.description: Use when you have a bioassay-annotated feature quantification table (e.g. features_quantification_matrix_edited_bioactivity.
skills.name: pearson-correlation-bioactivity-scoring
skills.search_text: pearson-correlation-bioactivity-scoring Use when you have a bioassay-annotated feature quantification table (e.g. features_quantification_matrix_edited_bioactivity. The input is already a bioactivity-scored table (features_quantification_matrix_transposed_with_significant_correlation_pvalue_corrected.csv); re-running the correlation would be redundant. The LC-MS/MS-analyzed fractions are not paired with a bioassay result, so there is no bioactivity vector to correlate against. The data are not LC-MS/MS feature intensities (e.g. direct-infusion spectra without fraction-level quantification), which the Pearson correlation scoring is not designed for. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Computes, for every detected feature, a Pearson correlation coefficient and its p-value between the feature's relative abundance profile across LC-MS/MS-analyzed fractions and the corresponding bioassay result vector, producing a bioactivity-score attribute table that is later overlaid onto a GNPS molecular network in Cytoscape. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jnatprod.7b00737
skills.summary: Computes, for every detected feature, a Pearson correlation coefficient and its p-value between the feature's relative abundance profile across LC-MS/MS-analyzed fractions and the corresponding bioassay result vector, producing a bioactivity-score attribute table that is later overlaid onto a GNPS molecular network in Cytoscape.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a bioactivity-scored table (features_quantification_matrix_transposed_with_significant_correlation_pvalue_corrected.csv); re-running the correlation would be redundant. The LC-MS/MS-analyzed fractions are not paired with a bioassay result, so there is no bioactivity vector to correlate against. The data are not LC-MS/MS feature intensities (e.g. direct-infusion spectra without fraction-level quantification), which the Pearson correlation scoring is not designed for.

skills.search_text: pearson-correlation-feature-collapsing Use when a two-condition metabolomics feature table contains redundant or highly correlated metabolites (e.g. |Pearson r| > 0.7) or co-classed compounds (e.g. BCAAs, fatty acids) that should be collapsed into single nodes before joint network estimation. The feature table has already been collapsed or contains few redundant features — the step is explicitly optional in the DNEA workflow (Step 1.2) and skipping it is valid. The goal is to collapse features across more than two experimental groups, since DNEA performs joint estimation across exactly two groups. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 The optional aggregateFeatures() step (DNEA Step 1.2) collapses metabolomics features that are highly correlated and/or belong to the same chemical class into singular features, producing a collapsed_DNEAobj with 134 TEDDY metabolites reduced to 130 aggregated features. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-024-05994-1

The data are not two-condition metabolomics/lipidomics peak intensities amenable to createDNEAobject(); DNEA requires raw peak intensity/concentration values for two experimental conditions. The goal is to collapse features across more than two experimental groups, since DNEA performs joint estimation across exactly two groups.

skills.description: Use when you have a trained VAE/latent-space MSI classifier (e.g. massNet Code layer output) plus decoded per-m/z spatial images and a pixel-level class-probability map, and need to identify which m/z peaks drive tumor delineation.

skills.search_text: pearson-correlation-feature-ranking Use when you have a trained VAE/latent-space MSI classifier (e.g. massNet Code layer output) plus decoded per-m/z spatial images and a pixel-level class-probability map, and need to identify which m/z peaks drive tumor delineation. skills.summary: Ranks m/z peaks by the Pearson correlation between each peak's reconstructed spatial ion image and the tumor-class prediction map from the massNet VAE, retaining co-localized (correlation ≥ 0.7) tumor-associated features for molecular annotation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need de novo peak picking or spectral preprocessing — massNet applies Pearson correlation on peaks identified by the VAE decoder without prior peak picking, so a classical peak-picking pipeline would duplicate/conflict with that step Your classification map comes from a multi-class model or a different tissue/tumor type — the demonstrated ground truth is binary (tumor vs. normal) histology annotation, and the paper notes multi-class classification and ground-truth establishment for other tissues are future work You lack spatially resolved pixel-level data (e.g. only bulk spectra or a precomputed feature table) — the correlation is computed between spatial patterns, not summary intensities

skills.description: Use when the same feature/gene pairs have Pearson correlation coefficients measured across multiple independent studies (each with its own sample size) and they must be combined into a single estimate with fixed or random effects weighting.
skills.name: pearson-correlation-meta-analysis
skills.search_text: pearson-correlation-meta-analysis Use when the same feature/gene pairs have Pearson correlation coefficients measured across multiple independent studies (each with its own sample size) and they must be combined into a single estimate with fixed or random effects weighting. Each gene pair is measured in only a single study — there is nothing to combine and the meta-analysis weights are undefined The per-study effect sizes are not Pearson correlation coefficients (e.g. they are fold changes or mutual information values); combining them with correlation-specific weights is invalid The input is raw expression data rather than already-computed per-study correlation coefficients and sample sizes — first run MOG's pairwise Pearson correlation analysis to produce per-study estimates http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Combines per-study Pearson correlation coefficients for the same gene pairs into sample-size-weighted fixed and random effects estimates (with between-study heterogeneity) using MetaOmGraph (MOG) and R. This lets large, well-powered studies dominate the combined correlation estimate rather than treating every study equally. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkz1209
skills.summary: Combines per-study Pearson correlation coefficients for the same gene pairs into sample-size-weighted fixed and random effects estimates (with between-study heterogeneity) using MetaOmGraph (MOG) and R. This lets large, well-powered studies dominate the combined correlation estimate rather than treating every study equally.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Each gene pair is measured in only a single study — there is nothing to combine and the meta-analysis weights are undefined The per-study effect sizes are not Pearson correlation coefficients (e.g. they are fold changes or mutual information values); combining them with correlation-specific weights is invalid The input is raw expression data rather than already-computed per-study correlation coefficients and sample sizes — first run MOG's pairwise Pearson correlation analysis to produce per-study estimates

skills.description: Use when comparing or validating the retention-time shift correction produced by MetMatch against an independent alignment (e.g., XCMS) on LC-HRMS feature lists, to confirm both tools recovered consistent non-linear Rt shifts.
skills.name: pearson-correlation-of-alignment-functions
skills.search_text: pearson-correlation-of-alignment-functions Use when comparing or validating the retention-time shift correction produced by MetMatch against an independent alignment (e.g., XCMS) on LC-HRMS feature lists, to confirm both tools recovered consistent non-linear Rt shifts. Only a single datafile or batch is involved and no independent alignment (e.g., XCMS) exists to compare the Rt shift functions against — the correlation step has no second function to correlate. The m/z and retention-time shifts between experiments are already negligible, so no shift correction or its validation is needed. The analysis goal is peak matching/adduct-aware feature alignment itself (e.g., reproducing 92/151 Phe-derived matches) rather than validating the alignment's Rt correction. Validates that MetMatch's retention-time shift correction of LC-HRMS datafiles agrees with an independent alignment tool (XCMS) by computing Pearson correlations between the two tools' Rt shift functions over defined chromatographic windows, as done for the wheat phenylalanine-derived metabolite benchmark. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo6040039
skills.summary: Validates that MetMatch's retention-time shift correction of LC-HRMS datafiles agrees with an independent alignment tool (XCMS) by computing Pearson correlations between the two tools' Rt shift functions over defined chromatographic windows, as done for the wheat phenylalanine-derived metabolite benchmark.

skills.search_text: pearson-correlation-of-pathway-activity-with-clinical-phenotype Use when you have a gene expression matrix paired with a continuous clinical variable (e.g. 1-hour OGTT blood glucose) and need to test which of ~400 predefined KEGG/Biocarta pathways' activity levels correlate with the phenotype. The analysis goal is comparing mean pathway activity between two sample groups (e.g. diabetic vs non-diabetic) rather than correlating with a continuous phenotype — PLAGE's pairwise t-statistic comparison is the appropriate variant. No predefined pathway gene sets (KEGG/Biocarta) are available and de novo pathway discovery is required. The phenotype is a binary label rather than a continuous variable — Pearson correlation of activity levels is not the right test. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Compute PLAGE pathway activity levels via SVD of standardized pathway gene-expression matrices, then Pearson-correlate each pathway's activity levels with a continuous clinical phenotype (e.g. 1-hour OGTT blood glucose in the Mootha et al. type 2 diabetes dataset), with permutation-based p-value estimation. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/1471-2105-6-225
skills.summary: Compute PLAGE pathway activity levels via SVD of standardized pathway gene-expression matrices, then Pearson-correlate each pathway's activity levels with a continuous clinical phenotype (e.g. 1-hour OGTT blood glucose in the Mootha et al. type 2 diabetes dataset), with permutation-based p-value estimation.

skills.description: Use when two co-registered LA-ICP-MS elemental images (identical pixel dimensions) require quantification of spatial colocalisation, and a significance probability for the observed Pearson R is needed beyond the raw correlation coefficient.
skills.name: pearson-correlation-significance-testing-by-random-shuffling
skills.search_text: pearson-correlation-significance-testing-by-random-shuffling Use when two co-registered LA-ICP-MS elemental images (identical pixel dimensions) require quantification of spatial colocalisation, and a significance probability for the observed Pearson R is needed beyond the raw correlation coefficient. The two channels have different pixel dimensions or are not spatially co-registered (e.g. spot-wise data without a shared grid) — Pearson R and shuffling-based ρ are undefined on misaligned arrays. Only a qualitative visual check of RGB overlay magenta overlap is required and no statistical significance is needed — a simple RGB overlay of 55Mn/56Fe/66Zn suffices. Data are time-series or spectra rather than 2D spatial images; the shuffling-based null assumes pixel-permutation exchangeability within an image. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Computes Pearson's R between two co-registered LA-ICP-MS elemental images (e.g. 55Mn and 66Zn) and derives an empirical significance probability ρ by comparing the observed R against R values from randomly shuffled pixel permutations of the two channels, as implemented in Pew2's colocalisation dialog. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c02138
skills.summary: Computes Pearson's R between two co-registered LA-ICP-MS elemental images (e.g. 55Mn and 66Zn) and derives an empirical significance probability ρ by comparing the observed R against R values from randomly shuffled pixel permutations of the two channels, as implemented in Pew2's colocalisation dialog.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The two channels have different pixel dimensions or are not spatially co-registered (e.g. spot-wise data without a shared grid) — Pearson R and shuffling-based ρ are undefined on misaligned arrays. Only a qualitative visual check of RGB overlay magenta overlap is required and no statistical significance is needed — a simple RGB overlay of 55Mn/56Fe/66Zn suffices. Data are time-series or spectra rather than 2D spatial images; the shuffling-based null assumes pixel-permutation exchangeability within an image.

skills.description: Use when an annotated massdiff object of matched adduct ion pairs has been generated from MSI peak data and the candidate parent–adduct pairs must be tested for spatial co-localization before being accepted as true adducts.
skills.name: pearson-correlation-testing-of-ion-pairs
skills.search_text: pearson-correlation-testing-of-ion-pairs Use when an annotated massdiff object of matched adduct ion pairs has been generated from MSI peak data and the candidate parent–adduct pairs must be tested for spatial co-localization before being accepted as true adducts. The data are not MS imaging data with pixel-level intensity co-ordinates — spatial correlation is meaningless without spatial context (e.g. a plain list of masses imported via scan() lacks the intensity matrix needed by corrPairsMSI). You are still at the histogram/annotation stage: if the mass differences have not been binned and matched to known adducts (adductMatch), there is no set of candidate pairs to test. skills.summary: Statistical validation of putative metabolite–matrix adduct pairs in MALDI-MSI data by running two-tailed Pearson correlation tests on the pixel intensities of each parent–adduct ion pair, using mass2adduct's corrPairsMSI/corrPairsMSIchunks with Bonferroni-corrected significance at p=0.05.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are not MS imaging data with pixel-level intensity co-ordinates — spatial correlation is meaningless without spatial context (e.g. a plain list of masses imported via scan() lacks the intensity matrix needed by corrPairsMSI). You are still at the histogram/annotation stage: if the mass differences have not been binned and matched to known adducts (adductMatch), there is no set of candidate pairs to test. The MSI intensity table exceeds available memory and has not been prepared for chunked processing — running plain corrPairsMSI will fail; use corrPairsMSIchunks or pre-filter/convert the CSV with msimunging.pl.

skills.description: Use when many metabolite hypotheses are tested simultaneously and raw p-value FDR is inflated: you have observed t statistics (z1), log standard errors (z2), and np permutations of null statistics, and need a calibrated local fdr2d threshold for biomarker discovery.
skills.name: penalized-likelihood-density-ratio-fitting
skills.search_text: penalized-likelihood-density-ratio-fitting Use when many metabolite hypotheses are tested simultaneously and raw p-value FDR is inflated: you have observed t statistics (z1), log standard errors (z2), and np permutations of null statistics, and need a calibrated local fdr2d threshold for biomarker discovery. Input is already a curated biomarker list or a feature table without test statistics and permutations — the density-ratio model needs z1, z2, and np permutation nulls. The analysis is a single-hypothesis or few-hypothesis test where two-dimensional FDR control over simultaneous metabolite tests is unnecessary. No permutations can be generated (too few replicates), since r(z) is estimated against the permutation-based null density f0. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Fits a smooth two-component density-ratio model r(z) between observed and permutation-based null test statistics via penalized log-likelihood, then plugs the fit into the two-dimensional local false discovery rate fdr2d(z) = pi0*r(z)/(np*(1-r(z))) to control FDR in simultaneous metabolite hypothesis testing. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo9050103
skills.summary: Fits a smooth two-component density-ratio model r(z) between observed and permutation-based null test statistics via penalized log-likelihood, then plugs the fit into the two-dimensional local false discovery rate fdr2d(z) = pi0*r(z)/(np*(1-r(z))) to control FDR in simultaneous metabolite hypothesis testing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a curated biomarker list or a feature table without test statistics and permutations — the density-ratio model needs z1, z2, and np permutation nulls. The analysis is a single-hypothesis or few-hypothesis test where two-dimensional FDR control over simultaneous metabolite tests is unnecessary. No permutations can be generated (too few replicates), since r(z) is estimated against the permutation-based null density f0.

skills.search_text: peptide-database-search-execution Use when MGF-converted MS/MS spectra (e.g. enzymatic antibody digests) need reference peptide identifications from a known protein database, to serve as pseudo-ground truth or benchmark labels for downstream tool evaluation. skills.name: peptide-fragment-ion-annotation
skills.search_text: peptide-fragment-ion-annotation Use when a molecular family of tandem mass spectra contains a shared core scaffold with variable modifications — e. The spectra are not from a molecular family with a shared, sequenceable scaffold — e.g. small-molecule families without predictable b/y fragment series, where consensus peaks cannot be assigned to N- or C-terminal fragment types. You need fully automatic, exhaustive fragment annotation — the greedy multiple alignment misses smaller alignments such as the y2 peaks in the albicidin family, so annotation is incomplete without manual inspection. Only two spectra are available — MMSA is designed for multiple-spectrum alignment across a molecular family; pairwise tools like Metabolomics Spectrum Resolver or ModiFinder may be more appropriate for single comparisons. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0157 Annotate aligned consensus peaks across an MS/MS molecular family as shared b- and y-type fragment ions and use their alignment boundaries to localize chemical modification sites, as demonstrated for the albicidin family where b4/b5 and y2/y3 align across all derivatives and y5 localizes central-residue modifications. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jasms.5c00237
skills.summary: Annotate aligned consensus peaks across an MS/MS molecular family as shared b- and y-type fragment ions and use their alignment boundaries to localize chemical modification sites, as demonstrated for the albicidin family where b4/b5 and y2/y3 align across all derivatives and y5 localizes central-residue modifications.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The spectra are not from a molecular family with a shared, sequenceable scaffold — e.g. small-molecule families without predictable b/y fragment series, where consensus peaks cannot be assigned to N- or C-terminal fragment types. You need fully automatic, exhaustive fragment annotation — the greedy multiple alignment misses smaller alignments such as the y2 peaks in the albicidin family, so annotation is incomplete without manual inspection. Only two spectra are available — MMSA is designed for multiple-spectrum alignment across a molecular family; pairwise tools like Metabolomics Spectrum Resolver or ModiFinder may be more appropriate for single comparisons.

skills.name: peptide-fragmentation-simulation
skills.search_text: peptide-fragmentation-simulation Use when you need a gold-standard synthetic proteomics mzML — e.g. to benchmark search/scoring algorithms, predict co-elution/co-fragmentation, or compare simulated vs. real TIC behavior for a peptide list on a defined gradient length. Input spectra lack reliable precursor m/z annotations, since the ppm tolerance comparison requires an observed precursor to compare against The task is database searching (Casanovo-DB mode) rather than de novo mode, where the precursor mass filter is applied differently — note the precursor mass filter is no longer applied in de novo mode http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Evaluates de novo peptide sequencing predictions by computing the fraction of predicted peptides whose theoretical precursor mass falls within 30 ppm of the observed precursor m/z, serving as a mass-accuracy quality check alongside peptide-level average precision. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-49731-x
skills.summary: Evaluates de novo peptide sequencing predictions by computing the fraction of predicted peptides whose theoretical precursor mass falls within 30 ppm of the observed precursor m/z, serving as a mass-accuracy quality check alongside peptide-level average precision.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra lack reliable precursor m/z annotations, since the ppm tolerance comparison requires an observed precursor to compare against The task is database searching (Casanovo-DB mode) rather than de novo mode, where the precursor mass filter is applied differently — note the precursor mass filter is no longer applied in de novo mode

skills.description: Use when MSFragger/FragPipe PSM tables (searched at 1% protein FDR) must be filtered to confident peptide/protein sets before generating MALDI-MS peptide images in MSIght.
skills.name: peptide-psm-filtering-from-fragpipe-output
skills.search_text: peptide-psm-filtering-from-fragpipe-output Use when MSFragger/FragPipe PSM tables (searched at 1% protein FDR) must be filtered to confident peptide/protein sets before generating MALDI-MS peptide images in MSIght. Input is already a filtered, protein-level feature table rather than raw PSM-level FragPipe output The goal is MSI dataset pre-processing, histology co-registration, or segmentation (use MSIght's cluster_msi / registration workflows instead) Peptide FDR or PSM-level FDR below 1% protein FDR has not been established upstream, since the cascade presumes 1% protein FDR identifications http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Applies MSIght's successive LC-MS/MS PSM filtering cascade (unique peptides, unique monoisotopic mass within 0.02 Da, and >=5 peptides per protein at 1% protein FDR) to MSFragger/FragPipe PSM output so that only confidently identified peptides are used for MALDI-MS image annotation. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.4c01140
skills.summary: Applies MSIght's successive LC-MS/MS PSM filtering cascade (unique peptides, unique monoisotopic mass within 0.02 Da, and >=5 peptides per protein at 1% protein FDR) to MSFragger/FragPipe PSM output so that only confidently identified peptides are used for MALDI-MS image annotation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a filtered, protein-level feature table rather than raw PSM-level FragPipe output The goal is MSI dataset pre-processing, histology co-registration, or segmentation (use MSIght's cluster_msi / registration workflows instead) Peptide FDR or PSM-level FDR below 1% protein FDR has not been established upstream, since the cascade presumes 1% protein FDR identifications

skills.description: Use when the input is a Thermo Fisher Orbitrap .raw file (e.g., 20181113_010_autoQC01.raw) containing iRT peptide runs and the goal is calibration-grade retention times for iRT regression, i.e., fitting rt = a + b * iRT-score.
skills.name: peptide-retention-time-peak-picking
skills.search_text: peptide-retention-time-peak-picking Use when the input is a Thermo Fisher Orbitrap .raw file (e.g., 20181113_010_autoQC01.raw) containing iRT peptide runs and the goal is calibration-grade retention times for iRT regression, i.e., fitting rt = a + b * iRT-score. Input data has already been converted to mzML or another open exchange format and the raw file itself is unavailable — this skill relies on direct readChromatogram access to Thermo .raw files via RawFileReader. The goal is MS2-level fragment analysis (e.g., spectrum interpretation of scan 9594 / LGGNEQVTR) rather than MS1-based retention-time extraction for iRT calibration. The peptides of interest lack assigned iRT scale scores, so no rt = a + b * score regression can be fit. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Extracts retention times for iRT (or indexed retention-time) peptides by computing extracted ion chromatograms (XICs) directly from Thermo Fisher .raw files via rawrr::readChromatogram, picking the RT at the maximum of each intensity trace, and fitting a linear iRT regression model rt = a + b * score with R's lm(). metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2020.10.30.362533
skills.summary: Extracts retention times for iRT (or indexed retention-time) peptides by computing extracted ion chromatograms (XICs) directly from Thermo Fisher .raw files via rawrr::readChromatogram, picking the RT at the maximum of each intensity trace, and fitting a linear iRT regression model rt = a + b * score with R's lm().
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data has already been converted to mzML or another open exchange format and the raw file itself is unavailable — this skill relies on direct readChromatogram access to Thermo .raw files via RawFileReader. The goal is MS2-level fragment analysis (e.g., spectrum interpretation of scan 9594 / LGGNEQVTR) rather than MS1-based retention-time extraction for iRT calibration. The peptides of interest lack assigned iRT scale scores, so no rt = a + b * score regression can be fit.

skills.description: Use when rescoring peptide-spectrum matches with predicted-fragment-intensity features and you need a stability feature that distinguishes a peptide from its adjacent-residue-swap neighbours.
skills.name: peptide-sequence-adjacent-swap-perturbation
skills.search_text: peptide-sequence-adjacent-swap-perturbation Use when rescoring peptide-spectrum matches with predicted-fragment-intensity features and you need a stability feature that distinguishes a peptide from its adjacent-residue-swap neighbours. No Prosit (or other) predicted fragment-ion intensities are available for the original or swapped peptide sequences — the contrast angle cannot be computed Input is already a rescoring feature table being consumed by a semi-supervised model (e.g. ristretto/Percolator) — this skill generates a feature, it does not rescore The PSM set is not being re-ranked and only final FDR-filtered identifications are needed http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Computes the Prosit-delta score used by inSPIRE: the stability of the normalized spectral contrast angle (SA) between observed and Prosit-predicted fragment-ion intensities after swapping adjacent amino acid positions in a candidate peptide. Low Prosit-delta flags PSMs likely misassigned to similar but incorrect peptide sequences, in the same spirit as Percolator's original ΔXCorr feature. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/pmic.202300336
skills.summary: Computes the Prosit-delta score used by inSPIRE: the stability of the normalized spectral contrast angle (SA) between observed and Prosit-predicted fragment-ion intensities after swapping adjacent amino acid positions in a candidate peptide. Low Prosit-delta flags PSMs likely misassigned to similar but incorrect peptide sequences, in the same spirit as Percolator's original ΔXCorr feature.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No Prosit (or other) predicted fragment-ion intensities are available for the original or swapped peptide sequences — the contrast angle cannot be computed Input is already a rescoring feature table being consumed by a semi-supervised model (e.g. ristretto/Percolator) — this skill generates a feature, it does not rescore The PSM set is not being re-ranked and only final FDR-filtered identifications are needed

skills.description: Use when you have a peptide FASTA file (e.g. 'Peptide sequence.fasta.txt' from the HORDB figshare deposit) and need to quantify or validate the sequence-length distribution of peptide hormones against the ~10 aa mode reported in Fig. 10.
skills.name: peptide-sequence-length-distribution-analysis
skills.search_text: peptide-sequence-length-distribution-analysis Use when you have a peptide FASTA file (e.g. 'Peptide sequence.fasta.txt' from the HORDB figshare deposit) and need to quantify or validate the sequence-length distribution of peptide hormones against the ~10 aa mode reported in Fig. 10. Your goal is classifying or annotating peptide sequences (activity, targets, IC50/EC50) rather than characterizing their length distribution The input is not peptide hormone sequences in FASTA form — e.g. nucleotide sequences or pharmaceutical preparation records from HORDB's 6024 entries You need peptide drugs or marketed pharmaceutical preparations statistics instead of the peptide hormone sequence-length profile http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Reproduces the HORDB peptide hormone length distribution by computing amino-acid lengths of sequences in 'Peptide sequence.fasta.txt' from the figshare deposit and plotting a histogram (mirroring Fig. 10), verifying that short ~10 aa peptides dominate. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41597-022-01287-5
skills.summary: Reproduces the HORDB peptide hormone length distribution by computing amino-acid lengths of sequences in 'Peptide sequence.fasta.txt' from the figshare deposit and plotting a histogram (mirroring Fig. 10), verifying that short ~10 aa peptides dominate.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your goal is classifying or annotating peptide sequences (activity, targets, IC50/EC50) rather than characterizing their length distribution The input is not peptide hormone sequences in FASTA form — e.g. nucleotide sequences or pharmaceutical preparation records from HORDB's 6024 entries You need peptide drugs or marketed pharmaceutical preparations statistics instead of the peptide hormone sequence-length profile

skills.description: Use when evaluating de novo sequencing output against pseudo-ground-truth PSMs (e.g. MS-GF+/X!Tandem at 1% FDR) and you need the relative frequency of mismatch categories such as >6 wrongly assigned amino acids or last-3-AA inversions.
skills.name: peptide-sequence-mismatch-alignment-msms
skills.search_text: peptide-sequence-mismatch-alignment-msms Use when evaluating de novo sequencing output against pseudo-ground-truth PSMs (e.g. MS-GF+/X!Tandem at 1% FDR) and you need the relative frequency of mismatch categories such as >6 wrongly assigned amino acids or last-3-AA inversions. When the goal is peptide identification itself rather than characterization of de novo prediction errors — use the database-search PSMs (MS-GF+/X!Tandem at 1% FDR) directly instead. When distinguishing isoleucine from leucine is required — MS/MS cannot discriminate these isomeric residues, so mismatch categories involving I/L cannot be resolved. When predictions come from tools not among the evaluated set (Novor, pNovo 3, DeepNovo, SMSNet, PointNovo, Casanovo) without re-deriving the 11 error categories for their output format. http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Aligns de novo peptide predictions (pNovo 3, SMSNet, PointNovo, Casanovo) against pseudo-ground-truth PSMs to classify every incorrect prediction into one of 11 error-type categories, revealing tool-specific mismatch signatures on antibody MS/MS data. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bib/bbac542
skills.summary: Aligns de novo peptide predictions (pNovo 3, SMSNet, PointNovo, Casanovo) against pseudo-ground-truth PSMs to classify every incorrect prediction into one of 11 error-type categories, revealing tool-specific mismatch signatures on antibody MS/MS data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is peptide identification itself rather than characterization of de novo prediction errors — use the database-search PSMs (MS-GF+/X!Tandem at 1% FDR) directly instead. When distinguishing isoleucine from leucine is required — MS/MS cannot discriminate these isomeric residues, so mismatch categories involving I/L cannot be resolved. When predictions come from tools not among the evaluated set (Novor, pNovo 3, DeepNovo, SMSNet, PointNovo, Casanovo) without re-deriving the 11 error categories for their output format.

skills.description: Use when you have two peptide identification result sets — e.g. de novo mzTab predictions and a database-search PSM list at a stated FDR — and must quantify their overlap and per-set properties.
skills.name: peptide-set-overlap-analysis
skills.search_text: peptide-set-overlap-analysis Use when you have two peptide identification result sets — e.g. de novo mzTab predictions and a database-search PSM list at a stated FDR — and must quantify their overlap and per-set properties. Input spectra come from DIA acquisition — Casanovo and this comparison target data-dependent acquisition, bottom-up tandem MS datasets The sample's protein set is fully known and the goal is standard identification — a plain database search suffices, and the overlap analysis adds no information about unexpected peptides Spectra have fewer peaks than the configured minimum (min_peaks) or predictions fail the minimum peptide length filter — these low-quality entries would distort set counts http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Compares de novo peptide predictions (Casanovo, exported as mzTab) against a non-enzymatic database-search peptide set (Tide + Percolator at 1% FDR) to quantify set overlap and binding-predicted fractions in MHC class I immunopeptidomics data. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-49731-x
skills.summary: Compares de novo peptide predictions (Casanovo, exported as mzTab) against a non-enzymatic database-search peptide set (Tide + Percolator at 1% FDR) to quantify set overlap and binding-predicted fractions in MHC class I immunopeptidomics data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra come from DIA acquisition — Casanovo and this comparison target data-dependent acquisition, bottom-up tandem MS datasets The sample's protein set is fully known and the goal is standard identification — a plain database search suffices, and the overlap analysis adds no information about unexpected peptides Spectra have fewer peaks than the configured minimum (min_peaks) or predictions fail the minimum peptide length filter — these low-quality entries would distort set counts

skills.description: Use when raw LC-MS files have been searched by a peptide/protein identification engine (e.g., FragPipe/MSFragger or DIA-NN) and you need per-file identification counts at a chosen FDR threshold for QC, throughput reporting, or result aggregation.
skills.name: peptide-spectrum-match-fdr-summarization
skills.search_text: peptide-spectrum-match-fdr-summarization Use when raw LC-MS files have been searched by a peptide/protein identification engine (e.g., FragPipe/MSFragger or DIA-NN) and you need per-file identification counts at a chosen FDR threshold for QC, throughput reporting, or result aggregation. MSConnect is not a standalone analysis tool — if the search engine has not yet produced identification results (no FragPipe/DIA-NN output), this skill cannot create them and only provides the wrapper/interface Input is already a quantified feature or protein table — this skill tabulates identifications passing an FDR filter, not downstream steps such as imputing missing values, normalization and batch correction, or differential expression Analyzing a single small dataset interactively where manual inspection of search-engine output is feasible and no automated, traceable per-file reporting is needed http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Tabulates per-file spectrum identification statistics — PSMs, peptides, and protein groups passing a given FDR filter — produced by search engines such as FragPipe (DDA/WWA) and DIA-NN (DIA), and aggregates them into a single summary table with one row per raw LC-MS file. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.4c00854
skills.summary: Tabulates per-file spectrum identification statistics — PSMs, peptides, and protein groups passing a given FDR filter — produced by search engines such as FragPipe (DDA/WWA) and DIA-NN (DIA), and aggregates them into a single summary table with one row per raw LC-MS file.
skills.when_to_use_negative: MSConnect is not a standalone analysis tool — if the search engine has not yet produced identification results (no FragPipe/DIA-NN output), this skill cannot create them and only provides the wrapper/interface Input is already a quantified feature or protein table — this skill tabulates identifications passing an FDR filter, not downstream steps such as imputing missing values, normalization and batch correction, or differential expression Analyzing a single small dataset interactively where manual inspection of search-engine output is feasible and no automated, traceable per-file reporting is needed

skills.description: Use when you need to select a defined subset of identified spectra (e.g. one peptide/charge, such as VATVSIPR charge 2 from P00761) from MassIVE/PRIDE identifications before joining them to spectrum clustering results.
skills.name: peptide-spectrum-match-filtering
skills.search_text: peptide-spectrum-match-filtering Use when you need to select a defined subset of identified spectra (e.g. one peptide/charge, such as VATVSIPR charge 2 from P00761) from MassIVE/PRIDE identifications before joining them to spectrum clustering results. Input is raw spectra (mzML/MGF) rather than already-searched peptide-spectrum matches — search and FDR filtering must precede this skill. The goal is clustering itself or tuning clustering thresholds (e.g. falcon's eps, precursor/fragment tolerances) rather than selecting identified spectra from existing identifications. Downstream evaluation of consensus spectra or cluster representatives rather than per-peptide cluster fragmentation analysis. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Filters peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) at a 1% FDR threshold and subsets them to a specific peptide (e.g. VATVSIPR/2) so that individual spectra can be mapped to per-tool cluster labels and clustered fragmentation can be quantified. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/rcm.9153
skills.summary: Filters peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) at a 1% FDR threshold and subsets them to a specific peptide (e.g. VATVSIPR/2) so that individual spectra can be mapped to per-tool cluster labels and clustered fragmentation can be quantified.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw spectra (mzML/MGF) rather than already-searched peptide-spectrum matches — search and FDR filtering must precede this skill. The goal is clustering itself or tuning clustering thresholds (e.g. falcon's eps, precursor/fragment tolerances) rather than selecting identified spectra from existing identifications. Downstream evaluation of consensus spectra or cluster representatives rather than per-peptide cluster fragmentation analysis.

skills.description: Use when building a ground-truth identification table (per-scan peptide assignments) to evaluate MS/MS clustering quality via DB-search-based purity, e.g. for PXD021518 or PXD023047 proteomics data.
skills.name: peptide-spectrum-match-table-preparation
skills.search_text: peptide-spectrum-match-table-preparation Use when building a ground-truth identification table (per-scan peptide assignments) to evaluate MS/MS clustering quality via DB-search-based purity, e.g. for PXD021518 or PXD023047 proteomics data. The input is metabolomics MS/MS data where FDR-controlled identifications are not currently practical — use the MS-RT retention-time-based evaluation instead Clustering tool outputs are already available and only need post-processing into consistent column formats (use the msCluster/Falcon/MaRaCluster post-processing scripts instead) http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Prepares the identified-PSM reference table used to evaluate MS/MS clustering on proteomics datasets: raw Thermo .raw files are converted to mzML, searched with MS-GF+ against a target-decoy database, and PSMs are filtered to 1% FDR, yielding per-spectrum peptide identifications that serve as the ground-truth purity labels. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.4c00881
skills.summary: Prepares the identified-PSM reference table used to evaluate MS/MS clustering on proteomics datasets: raw Thermo .raw files are converted to mzML, searched with MS-GF+ against a target-decoy database, and PSMs are filtered to 1% FDR, yielding per-spectrum peptide identifications that serve as the ground-truth purity labels.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is metabolomics MS/MS data where FDR-controlled identifications are not currently practical — use the MS-RT retention-time-based evaluation instead Clustering tool outputs are already available and only need post-processing into consistent column formats (use the msCluster/Falcon/MaRaCluster post-processing scripts instead)

skills.description: Use when a neural spectral-embedding model (e.g. GLEAMS) needs a labeled peptide-spectrum-match training corpus and no pre-packaged training set exists, requiring assembly from MassIVE-KB library metadata and raw spectra retrieval.
skills.name: peptide-spectrum-match-training-data-compilation
skills.search_text: peptide-spectrum-match-training-data-compilation Use when a neural spectral-embedding model (e.g. GLEAMS) needs a labeled peptide-spectrum-match training corpus and no pre-packaged training set exists, requiring assembly from MassIVE-KB library metadata and raw spectra retrieval. You only need embeddings or clustering of existing spectra — use `gleams embed`/`gleams cluster` instead; no training-data compilation is required Your spectra are not Human HCD data from MassIVE-KB; the compiled library is organism- and acquisition-specific, so a different labeled corpus is needed You lack the storage/bandwidth to fetch spectra from the MassIVE FTP server; the 30M PSM corpus is very large and not available as a single download http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Compile a large-scale PSM training corpus by downloading the MassIVE-KB (v1) Human HCD candidate library spectra metadata TSV (30 million PSMs, max top 100 PSMs per unique precursor) and retrieving the corresponding peak files from the MassIVE FTP server, extracting spectra by scan number. This provides the supervised training data required to train the GLEAMS Siamese encoder. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-022-01496-1
skills.summary: Compile a large-scale PSM training corpus by downloading the MassIVE-KB (v1) Human HCD candidate library spectra metadata TSV (30 million PSMs, max top 100 PSMs per unique precursor) and retrieving the corresponding peak files from the MassIVE FTP server, extracting spectra by scan number. This provides the supervised training data required to train the GLEAMS Siamese encoder.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need embeddings or clustering of existing spectra — use `gleams embed`/`gleams cluster` instead; no training-data compilation is required Your spectra are not Human HCD data from MassIVE-KB; the compiled library is organism- and acquisition-specific, so a different labeled corpus is needed You lack the storage/bandwidth to fetch spectra from the MassIVE FTP server; the 30M PSM corpus is very large and not available as a single download

skills.description: Use when raw centroided MS/MS spectra need to be assigned peptide identities by searching them against a protein reference database, e.g. after converting public tandem MS data into a standardized open format.
skills.name: peptide-spectrum-matching
skills.search_text: peptide-spectrum-matching Use when raw centroided MS/MS spectra need to be assigned peptide identities by searching them against a protein reference database, e.g. after converting public tandem MS data into a standardized open format. Input is already a list of identified peptides or a feature table — downstream feature detection and linking steps apply instead. The task is targeted quantitation or SWATH/DIA extraction rather than discovery-style database searching. Spectra are profile-mode and uncentroided — centroiding must precede database searching. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Matches experimental tandem MS/MS spectra against theoretical fragment spectra from a protein sequence database using OpenMS database searching, producing peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) that feed protein inference and downstream proteogenomics annotation. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/nmeth.3959
skills.summary: Matches experimental tandem MS/MS spectra against theoretical fragment spectra from a protein sequence database using OpenMS database searching, producing peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) that feed protein inference and downstream proteogenomics annotation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a list of identified peptides or a feature table — downstream feature detection and linking steps apply instead. The task is targeted quantitation or SWATH/DIA extraction rather than discovery-style database searching. Spectra are profile-mode and uncentroided — centroiding must precede database searching.

skills.description: Use when a synthetic (SMITER-generated) mzML must be quality-checked by searching it against the source proteome and reporting a 1% q-value PSM identification rate per peptide-set size.
skills.name: peptide-spectrum-search-fdr-filtering
skills.search_text: peptide-spectrum-search-fdr-filtering Use when a synthetic (SMITER-generated) mzML must be quality-checked by searching it against the source proteome and reporting a 1% q-value PSM identification rate per peptide-set size. When the input spectra are real experimental acquisitions rather than SMITER-simulated mzML with known ground truth — the identification-rate benchmark requires knowing which peptides were simulated. When the goal is simulating or writing synthetic mzML itself rather than downstream search/validation of existing simulated files. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Validate SMITER-simulated LC-MS/MS runs by searching the synthetic mzML files with X!Tandem, rescoring PSMs with Percolator, and computing peptide identification rates at 1% q-value to benchmark how recovery changes with peptide-set size. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/genes12030396
skills.summary: Validate SMITER-simulated LC-MS/MS runs by searching the synthetic mzML files with X!Tandem, rescoring PSMs with Percolator, and computing peptide identification rates at 1% q-value to benchmark how recovery changes with peptide-set size.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input spectra are real experimental acquisitions rather than SMITER-simulated mzML with known ground truth — the identification-rate benchmark requires knowing which peptides were simulated. When the goal is simulating or writing synthetic mzML itself rather than downstream search/validation of existing simulated files.

skills.description: Use when MS/MS spectra suspected of sharing a structural motif (e.g. a residue-specific neutral loss) are NOT linked in a GNPS molecular network and you need exact m/z-difference patterns to annotate them.
skills.name: peptide-structural-annotation-from-fragmentation
skills.search_text: peptide-structural-annotation-from-fragmentation Use when MS/MS spectra suspected of sharing a structural motif (e.g. a residue-specific neutral loss) are NOT linked in a GNPS molecular network and you need exact m/z-difference patterns to annotate them. The spectra of interest are already connected in the GNPS molecular network by modified cosine edges — pairwise network similarity suffices and pattern mining adds no linking information You need to mine patterns de novo from raw MGF/MZML spectra rather than query an existing mined pattern set — use the full mineMS2 pattern-mining workflow (discretizeMzDifferences, graph building, frequent-subgraph mining) instead Only a single spectrum is available — mineMS2 patterns require the m/z differences to be frequent, i.e. detected in at least two spectra http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 This skill uses exact mineMS2 fragmentation patterns queried by a residue-specific m/z loss (e.g. 186.079, putative tryptophan loss) to structurally annotate MS/MS spectra and recover spectral similarities that GNPS molecular networking (modified cosine edges) misses, e.g. grouping tryptophan-containing tetrapeptides. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-025-01051-y
skills.summary: This skill uses exact mineMS2 fragmentation patterns queried by a residue-specific m/z loss (e.g. 186.079, putative tryptophan loss) to structurally annotate MS/MS spectra and recover spectral similarities that GNPS molecular networking (modified cosine edges) misses, e.g. grouping tryptophan-containing tetrapeptides.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The spectra of interest are already connected in the GNPS molecular network by modified cosine edges — pairwise network similarity suffices and pattern mining adds no linking information You need to mine patterns de novo from raw MGF/MZML spectra rather than query an existing mined pattern set — use the full mineMS2 pattern-mining workflow (discretizeMzDifferences, graph building, frequent-subgraph mining) instead Only a single spectrum is available — mineMS2 patterns require the m/z differences to be frequent, i.e. detected in at least two spectra

skills.description: Use when raw search-engine PSM identifications (e.g. mzIdentML from X!Tandem, MaxQuant, or PEAKS) must be enriched with predicted-peptidoform features before semi-supervised rescoring, especially for non-tryptic immunopeptidomics data.
skills.name: peptidoform-prediction-feature-annotation
skills.search_text: peptidoform-prediction-feature-annotation Use when raw search-engine PSM identifications (e.g. mzIdentML from X!Tandem, MaxQuant, or PEAKS) must be enriched with predicted-peptidoform features before semi-supervised rescoring, especially for non-tryptic immunopeptidomics data. skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a post-rescoring feature table or scored PSM output — no further peptidoform prediction features are needed Data lacks LC-MS context (e.g. no retention time or fragment spectra available) so MS2PIP/DeepLC features cannot be computed The goal is tool comparison/availability review (e.g. reproducing Table 1 of the rescoring-pipeline comparison) rather than actual feature annotation

skills.description: Use when you have SigmaCCS-predicted CCS values for [M+H]+, [M+Na]+, or [M-H]- adducts and an independently calculated CCS database (e.g., ISiCLE/PNNL) and need to quantify per-adduct agreement.
skills.name: per-adduct-correlation-analysis
skills.search_text: per-adduct-correlation-analysis Use when you have SigmaCCS-predicted CCS values for [M+H]+, [M+Na]+, or [M-H]- adducts and an independently calculated CCS database (e.g., ISiCLE/PNNL) and need to quantify per-adduct agreement. The input is raw data (.mzML or .raw) rather than an already-preprocessed feature table; filtering operates after Asari preprocessing. The analysis legitimately requires rare features (e.g., xenobiotic-focused workflows like the Bowen et al 2023 sunitinib study) where dropping low-prevalence features would discard the signal of interest. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Restricts a pcpfm/Asari feature table to features present in at least a user-specified percentile of samples (e.g., TIC_normalization_percentile = 0.90) so that only common features contribute to downstream operations such as TIC-based normalization factor calculation. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011912
skills.summary: Restricts a pcpfm/Asari feature table to features present in at least a user-specified percentile of samples (e.g., TIC_normalization_percentile = 0.90) so that only common features contribute to downstream operations such as TIC-based normalization factor calculation.

skills.search_text: permanova-group-comparison-testing Use when FT-ICR MS peak-intensity data with assigned molecular formulas have been normalized and grouped by treatment metadata, and you need a significance test of between-group differences in metabolite composition that complements ordination. Raw spectra whose molecular formula assignment and peak filtering (m/z, 13C isotopes, 0.5 ppm error, minimum sample count) have not yet been done — MetaboDirect requires pre-processed formula-assigned data Situations where a single significant PERMANOVA result will be over-interpreted as visible group separation — the paper shows significant p-values can occur when NMDS/PCA ordination fails to discriminate groups Data lacking sample grouping metadata, since PERMANOVA tests dissimilarity against a grouping factor http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Non-parametric PERMANOVA testing of whether sample groups (e.g., different infecting phages in a bacterium-phage FT-ICR MS metabolomics experiment) differ significantly in metabolite content, applied within MetaboDirect's statistical analysis step on normalized peak-intensity tables and dissimilarity matrices. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s40168-023-01476-3
