skills.search_text: quality-control-run-selection Use when raw targeted LC-MS runs (e.g. mzML) need a pre-check that each target peak is present within its expected m/z and retention time window before committing to full peak detection and integration. The goal is full peak detection and integration with quality metrics, not a pre-run visual screening of target visibility — run TARDIS in normal (non-screening) mode instead Input is already preprocessed/peak-picked data or a feature table rather than raw LC-MS runs, since EIC extraction requires raw chromatographic data Untargeted preprocessing is needed — TARDIS is designed for targeted integration, and tools like xcms, MZmine or OpenMS are the appropriate alternative http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 A TARDIS (TArgeted Raw Data Integration In Spectrometry) R-package workflow in which QC runs of targeted LC-MS metabolomics/lipidomics data are automatically selected for screening, and extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) are rendered as diagnostic plots (five EICs per image) so target peak visibility can be verified before full peak integration. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c00567
skills.summary: A TARDIS (TArgeted Raw Data Integration In Spectrometry) R-package workflow in which QC runs of targeted LC-MS metabolomics/lipidomics data are automatically selected for screening, and extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) are rendered as diagnostic plots (five EICs per image) so target peak visibility can be verified before full peak integration.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is full peak detection and integration with quality metrics, not a pre-run visual screening of target visibility — run TARDIS in normal (non-screening) mode instead Input is already preprocessed/peak-picked data or a feature table rather than raw LC-MS runs, since EIC extraction requires raw chromatographic data Untargeted preprocessing is needed — TARDIS is designed for targeted integration, and tools like xcms, MZmine or OpenMS are the appropriate alternative

skills.description: Use when comparing batch-effect or run-order effect removal methods on metabolomics peak matrices that include pooled/quality control samples, and you need a quantitative, reference-free similarity metric to rank corrected datasets.
skills.name: quality-control-sample-correlation-analysis
skills.search_text: quality-control-sample-correlation-analysis Use when comparing batch-effect or run-order effect removal methods on metabolomics peak matrices that include pooled/quality control samples, and you need a quantitative, reference-free similarity metric to rank corrected datasets. The dataset contains no pooled quality control samples, so there are no replicate pairs to correlate. You want to assess between-batch effects on multi-batch data where batch labels are available — use PCA score plots, cumulative RSD curves, or batch-label-aware methods instead of QCS-pair PCC alone. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Quantifies batch/run-order effect removal in untargeted metabolomics by computing Pearson correlation coefficients (PCCs) between all pairs of quality control samples (QCSs), where PCCs approaching 1 indicate effective drift removal. Used in WaveICA 2.0 to show that only WaveICA 2.0 increased QCS similarity on single-batch data (PCC 0.973) versus QC-RLSC (0.941) and QC-SVRC (0.934). metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-021-01839-7
skills.summary: Quantifies batch/run-order effect removal in untargeted metabolomics by computing Pearson correlation coefficients (PCCs) between all pairs of quality control samples (QCSs), where PCCs approaching 1 indicate effective drift removal. Used in WaveICA 2.0 to show that only WaveICA 2.0 increased QCS similarity on single-batch data (PCC 0.973) versus QC-RLSC (0.941) and QC-SVRC (0.934).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset contains no pooled quality control samples, so there are no replicate pairs to correlate. You want to assess between-batch effects on multi-batch data where batch labels are available — use PCA score plots, cumulative RSD curves, or batch-label-aware methods instead of QCS-pair PCC alone.

skills.search_text: quality-control-signal-drift-correction Use when a metabolomic peak table (rows = samples, columns = metabolites) contains quality control samples and signal drift from instrumental variation must be corrected (stage S2) prior to S3 transformation and S4 normalization. skills.summary: Applies NOREVA's stage S2 quality control sample (QCS) correction to remove systematic signal drift from metabolomic peak tables before transformation and normalization, as one stage of the S1–S5 processing workflow.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The peak table contains no quality control samples — use the NOREVA variants designed for data without QCS (or with internal standards only) instead of QCS-based drift correction Input is still raw instrument data (proprietary format); it must first be converted (e.g., via Proteowizard/nmrML) and processed into a peak table before S2 can be applied The goal is to change the processing order — QCS correction is fixed as stage S2 in the S1→S2→S3→S4 sequence and cannot be reordered within the NOREVA workflow

skills.description: Use when MRM raw data (mzML) must be scored per peak candidate on quantifier/qualifier transition agreement and RT deviation — e.g., to rank peak candidates or feed an ML peak-reporting model.
skills.name: quantifier-qualifier-transition-agreement-characterization
skills.search_text: quantifier-qualifier-transition-agreement-characterization Use when MRM raw data (mzML) must be scored per peak candidate on quantifier/qualifier transition agreement and RT deviation — e.g., to rank peak candidates or feed an ML peak-reporting model. The acquisition method contains only quantifier transitions with no qualifier — automRm requires at least one qualifier in addition to the quantifier for optimal performance, so transition-agreement scores are not meaningful. Data are full-scan/DDA LC-MS rather than MRM-mode QQQ chromatograms; the skill is built around quantifier/qualifier MRM traces. Peak candidates already carry curated quality scores and only manual peak review is intended — the article notes manual review remains the fallback for excessively dirty samples, very-low-input samples, or new LC methods. http://edamontology.org/topic_3678 Computes per-candidate MRM peak quality scores that quantify agreement between the quantifier transition and its qualifier transitions (QS_To2, QS_T.h, QS_T.l, QS_cor123), together with peak-shape (QS_gauss) and retention-time deviation (QS_dRT, QS_dRTs) scores, as implemented in the automRm peak-picking module for LC-QQQ-MS data. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c05224
skills.summary: Computes per-candidate MRM peak quality scores that quantify agreement between the quantifier transition and its qualifier transitions (QS_To2, QS_T.h, QS_T.l, QS_cor123), together with peak-shape (QS_gauss) and retention-time deviation (QS_dRT, QS_dRTs) scores, as implemented in the automRm peak-picking module for LC-QQQ-MS data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The acquisition method contains only quantifier transitions with no qualifier — automRm requires at least one qualifier in addition to the quantifier for optimal performance, so transition-agreement scores are not meaningful. Data are full-scan/DDA LC-MS rather than MRM-mode QQQ chromatograms; the skill is built around quantifier/qualifier MRM traces. Peak candidates already carry curated quality scores and only manual peak review is intended — the article notes manual review remains the fallback for excessively dirty samples, very-low-input samples, or new LC methods.

skills.description: Reference for producing concentration-calibrated LA-ICP-MS images (e.g. 55Mn, 56Fe, 63Cu, 66Zn in tissue sections) when gelatin standards with known concentrations are available and raw vendor batch data must be turned into quantified images.
skills.name: quantitative-elemental-image-production
skills.search_text: quantitative-elemental-image-production Reference for producing concentration-calibrated LA-ICP-MS images (e.g. 55Mn, 56Fe, 63Cu, 66Zn in tissue sections) when gelatin standards with known concentrations are available and raw vendor batch data must be turned into quantified images. If the input data are already fully quantified elemental images or a calibration_coefficients_table.csv is already available — this skill is for producing them from raw signal. skills.search_text: r-package-data-handling Use when a metabolite count data frame (e.g., c57_nos2KO_mouse_countDF) has KEGG compound numbers and you need per-metabolite compound class and subclass metadata attached before statistics or plotting. The metabolite identifiers are not KEGG compound numbers — assign_hierarchy maps hierarchy via KEGG identifiers, so other ID systems will not resolve to class metadata. You need statistical testing or fold-change output rather than metadata annotation — those are separate omu functions (omu_summary, omu_anova, count_fold_changes). You need gene/enzyme-level annotation for each metabolite — that is the role of KEGG_gather, not assign_hierarchy. http://edamontology.org/topic_3489 Annotate a metabolomics count data frame with KEGG compound hierarchy metadata (Class, Subclass_1–4) using the omu R package's assign_hierarchy function, which maps each KEGG compound number to hierarchical class metadata. metabolomics/v3 10.1128/mra.00129-19
skills.summary: Annotate a metabolomics count data frame with KEGG compound hierarchy metadata (Class, Subclass_1–4) using the omu R package's assign_hierarchy function, which maps each KEGG compound number to hierarchical class metadata.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The metabolite identifiers are not KEGG compound numbers — assign_hierarchy maps hierarchy via KEGG identifiers, so other ID systems will not resolve to class metadata. You need statistical testing or fold-change output rather than metadata annotation — those are separate omu functions (omu_summary, omu_anova, count_fold_changes). You need gene/enzyme-level annotation for each metabolite — that is the role of KEGG_gather, not assign_hierarchy.

skills.description: Use when a metabolomics feature matrix (.csv, samples in rows, features in columns, batch levels in first column) shows samples clustering by batch (e.g. PCA groups by run order) and across-batch signal drift must be corrected and compared across statistical models.
skills.name: r-package-data-normalization
skills.search_text: r-package-data-normalization Use when a metabolomics feature matrix (.csv, samples in rows, features in columns, batch levels in first column) shows samples clustering by batch (e.g. PCA groups by run order) and across-batch signal drift must be corrected and compared across statistical models. The dataset has fewer features than the models need to estimate batch parameters reliably, or the input is not batch-annotated (no batch levels in the first column) — ComBat/ber cannot estimate L/S batch parameters without batch labels The goal is differential-analysis statistics (volcano plots, Log2FC > 1.5, adj-p < 0.05) or pathway enrichment (MSEA) rather than batch-effect correction — those are downstream analyses of the corrected matrices Missing-value handling is the bottleneck — use the dbnorm preprocessing functions emvd/emvf (imputation by lowest detected value) instead of the correction models http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Batch-effect correction of batch-annotated metabolomics matrices in R via the dbnorm package, which applies parametric ComBat, nonparametric ComBat, ber, and bagging-ber (n=150 partial bagging) models to remove across-batch signal drift and score model fit with adjusted-R2. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41598-021-84824-3
skills.summary: Batch-effect correction of batch-annotated metabolomics matrices in R via the dbnorm package, which applies parametric ComBat, nonparametric ComBat, ber, and bagging-ber (n=150 partial bagging) models to remove across-batch signal drift and score model fit with adjusted-R2.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset has fewer features than the models need to estimate batch parameters reliably, or the input is not batch-annotated (no batch levels in the first column) — ComBat/ber cannot estimate L/S batch parameters without batch labels The goal is differential-analysis statistics (volcano plots, Log2FC > 1.5, adj-p < 0.05) or pathway enrichment (MSEA) rather than batch-effect correction — those are downstream analyses of the corrected matrices Missing-value handling is the bottleneck — use the dbnorm preprocessing functions emvd/emvf (imputation by lowest detected value) instead of the correction models

skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw, un-integrated LC-MS vendor data — mzQuality works only on peak-integrated output (e.g. from SCIEX OS) and does not perform peak integration itself Data lacks one or more mandatory columns (aliquot, compound, area, type, injection_time, batch) — readData will fail column validation, so reformat the table first Goal is interactive compound/sample inspection rather than programmatic IS-selection reproduction — the mzQualityDashboard Shiny app is recommended for that use

Benchmarking core scaling for SERFF, which is only accessible through its Shiny web interface and does not support core-count scaling Small datasets where the fastest methods (e.g. QC-RSC, QC-RLSC) show tapering or declining scaling curves with additional cores — extra cores yield little throughput gain there Use cases where automated multivariate outlier detection or multiple testing correction for downstream inference is required — these are explicitly out of the package's scope http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Leverages the pleasingly parallel, compound-wise structure of metabolomics normalization in the Metanorm R package (R >= 4.4.0) to normalize large feature matrices efficiently across compute cores, and to benchmark throughput (normalized compounds per minute) of Metanorm methods against TIGER and SERFF. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c06841
skills.summary: Leverages the pleasingly parallel, compound-wise structure of metabolomics normalization in the Metanorm R package (R >= 4.4.0) to normalize large feature matrices efficiently across compute cores, and to benchmark throughput (normalized compounds per minute) of Metanorm methods against TIGER and SERFF.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Benchmarking core scaling for SERFF, which is only accessible through its Shiny web interface and does not support core-count scaling Small datasets where the fastest methods (e.g. QC-RSC, QC-RLSC) show tapering or declining scaling curves with additional cores — extra cores yield little throughput gain there Use cases where automated multivariate outlier detection or multiple testing correction for downstream inference is required — these are explicitly out of the package's scope

skills.description: Use when raw LC-MS mzXML files (e.g., serial-diluted urine MTBLS2631) must be processed with JPA in R to count PP vs. MR features and compute a per-sample MS2-based feature rescue percentage.
skills.name: r-package-metabolomics-workflow-execution
skills.search_text: r-package-metabolomics-workflow-execution Use when raw LC-MS mzXML files (e.g., serial-diluted urine MTBLS2631) must be processed with JPA in R to count PP vs. MR features and compute a per-sample MS2-based feature rescue percentage. Processing full-scan or DIA data — the README warns 'Please do not use this function when processing full-scan or DIA data set!' for MS2 recognition A single aligned multi-sample feature table is the input — JPA's custom.featureTable requires per-file CSV tables and 'Aligned feature table is not acceptable' The goal is multi-sample consolidated analysis — then peak.alignment (bw=5, minfrac=0.5, mzwid=0.015) is appropriate, not the per-dilution-level single-sample rescue computation http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Executes the JPA R package workflow (XCMS.featureTable -> find.level3features) on raw mzXML LC-MS data to quantify how many metabolic features missed by conventional peak picking (PP) can be rescued by MS2-recognition (MR), benchmarked against the ~25% rescue reported for the MTBLS2631 serial-diluted urine dataset. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo12030212
skills.summary: Executes the JPA R package workflow (XCMS.featureTable -> find.level3features) on raw mzXML LC-MS data to quantify how many metabolic features missed by conventional peak picking (PP) can be rescued by MS2-recognition (MR), benchmarked against the ~25% rescue reported for the MTBLS2631 serial-diluted urine dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Processing full-scan or DIA data — the README warns 'Please do not use this function when processing full-scan or DIA data set!' for MS2 recognition A single aligned multi-sample feature table is the input — JPA's custom.featureTable requires per-file CSV tables and 'Aligned feature table is not acceptable' The goal is multi-sample consolidated analysis — then peak.alignment (bw=5, minfrac=0.5, mzwid=0.015) is appropriate, not the per-dilution-level single-sample rescue computation

skills.summary: Executes the Metanorm R package (R >= 4.4.0) normalization pipeline for LC-MS metabolomics drift/batch correction, calling the metanorm function with a chosen model (tGAM, rGAM, rLOESS, QC-RLSC) plus diagnostic visualization (plotPCA, per-compound pre/post plots).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data has already been drift/batch-normalized or the task is downstream differential abundance testing with multiple testing correction — this skill only performs normalization QC samples are not representative of biological samples (metanorm's QCcheck flags discrepancies) — QC-based normalization is then inappropriate No QC samples exist in the run order — all methods here are QC sample-based normalization strategies

skills.when_to_use_negative: Input metabolite names are already standard HMDB IDs and no pathway re-mapping is needed — skip the feature mapping call The goal is group-level pathway enrichment (MetPA, IMPaLA, MPEA) rather than individual patient-level pathway matrices — Lilikoi was built precisely because those tools cannot generate per-sample PDS matrices The task is batch processing outside R or in another language — this skill specifically covers scripting the R package's exported functions

skills.description: Use when you need to assign elemental-composition (molecular formula) candidates to MS1 peaks from untargeted LC/HRMS files (mzXML/mzML/netCDF) at population scale using reproducible R scripts rather than GUI peak-picking tools.
skills.name: r-package-scripting-for-formula-annotation
skills.search_text: r-package-scripting-for-formula-annotation Use when you need to assign elemental-composition (molecular formula) candidates to MS1 peaks from untargeted LC/HRMS files (mzXML/mzML/netCDF) at population scale using reproducible R scripts rather than GUI peak-picking tools. Input is MS2-only data or you need structural identification requiring tandem spectra — IDSL.UFA only requires MS1 for formula annotation but cannot assign structures without additional MS2 workflows (use IDSL.CSA or database search instead). Data are peak tables already produced by other tools (e.g. MZmine 2, xcms-CAMERA, MS-DIAL) whose isotopologue grouping and RT correction were not generated via the IDSL.IPA pipeline — the UFA scoring assumes IDSL.IPA-derived per-sample peak properties. Study contains fewer than a handful of samples and the aligned-table statistics (detection frequency, median rank) are not meaningful — the ranking thresholds were calibrated for population-scale (n > 500) untargeted studies. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Drive molecular formula annotation of untargeted LC/HRMS peaks through R-based packages (IDSL.IPA → IDSL.UFA) by scripting parameter spreadsheets, IPDB theoretical isotope libraries, and per-sample/aligned peak-list processing in the R environment. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.2c00563
skills.summary: Drive molecular formula annotation of untargeted LC/HRMS peaks through R-based packages (IDSL.IPA → IDSL.UFA) by scripting parameter spreadsheets, IPDB theoretical isotope libraries, and per-sample/aligned peak-list processing in the R environment.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is MS2-only data or you need structural identification requiring tandem spectra — IDSL.UFA only requires MS1 for formula annotation but cannot assign structures without additional MS2 workflows (use IDSL.CSA or database search instead). Data are peak tables already produced by other tools (e.g. MZmine 2, xcms-CAMERA, MS-DIAL) whose isotopologue grouping and RT correction were not generated via the IDSL.IPA pipeline — the UFA scoring assumes IDSL.IPA-derived per-sample peak properties. Study contains fewer than a handful of samples and the aligned-table statistics (detection frequency, median rank) are not meaningful — the ranking thresholds were calibrated for population-scale (n > 500) untargeted studies.

skills.description: Use when benchmarking the run time of R-based metabolomics normalization methods across feature-count and sample-count scales, and you need wall-clock timings per method under fixed core allocations.
skills.name: r-package-timing-profiling
skills.search_text: r-package-timing-profiling Use when benchmarking the run time of R-based metabolomics normalization methods across feature-count and sample-count scales, and you need wall-clock timings per method under fixed core allocations. Your goal is to assess normalization quality (drift, batch-effect removal, replicate concordance) rather than run-time cost — use Metanorm's plotPCA and pre-/post-normalization intensity-vs-order plots instead. Your input is a single small matrix (< tens of features) where timing differences between methods are negligible and profiling would not be informative. You need statistical or biological validation of the normalized output, not a computational benchmark. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Wall-clock timing profiling of the Metanorm R package's normalization methods (rLOESS, rGAM, tGAM, QC-RLSC, QC-RSC) across targeted (53 compounds) and untargeted (8913 features) LC-MS metabolomics datasets, to characterize computational cost and parallelization behaviour. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.09.30.679445
skills.summary: Wall-clock timing profiling of the Metanorm R package's normalization methods (rLOESS, rGAM, tGAM, QC-RLSC, QC-RSC) across targeted (53 compounds) and untargeted (8913 features) LC-MS metabolomics datasets, to characterize computational cost and parallelization behaviour.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your goal is to assess normalization quality (drift, batch-effect removal, replicate concordance) rather than run-time cost — use Metanorm's plotPCA and pre-/post-normalization intensity-vs-order plots instead. Your input is a single small matrix (< tens of features) where timing differences between methods are negligible and profiling would not be informative. You need statistical or biological validation of the normalized output, not a computational benchmark.

skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to simulate isotopic fine structures of metabolites at natural abundance only — IsoSpec2-style Monte Carlo fine-structure simulation or Aerith's FFT envelope path on chemical formulas may be the more direct route than re-running the vignette The input is already raw MS data (Thermo .raw) needing conversion — use Raxport or ThermoRawFileParser instead of vignette execution The package vignette requires data or dependencies not shipped/installable in the environment, so chunk execution would fail regardless of method

Input is raw, un-integrated LC-MS vendor data — mzQuality processes peak-integrated data and expects peak areas already integrated (e.g. by SCIEX OS), not raw signal traces. skills.search_text: r-pipeline-end-to-end-execution Use when processing DDA mzXML files from pooled QC samples together with DIA mzXML files from individual biological samples and you need a single R script to extract features, rescue DDA-unique features, and annotate metabolites end-to-end. If your data are from a conventional DDA-only workflow with no DIA mzXML files to rescue against — the DaDIA.R pipeline is built specifically for hybrid DDA/DIA datasets. If the number of DIA mzXML files does not match the sample count set on line 38 of the script, the run will be mis-specified; fix the sample count first rather than forcing execution. If you need quantification of metabolites in DDA mode only (e.g., full-scan DDA on individual samples), the rescue step has no DIA counterpart and adds no value. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Executes DaDIA.R, an R-based program that automatically extracts metabolic features and performs metabolite annotation from hybrid DDA/DIA metabolomic data, running end-to-end on mzXML files with XCMS and metaMS as dependencies. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c05022
skills.summary: Executes DaDIA.R, an R-based program that automatically extracts metabolic features and performs metabolite annotation from hybrid DDA/DIA metabolomic data, running end-to-end on mzXML files with XCMS and metaMS as dependencies.
skills.when_to_use_negative: If your data are from a conventional DDA-only workflow with no DIA mzXML files to rescue against — the DaDIA.R pipeline is built specifically for hybrid DDA/DIA datasets. If you need quantification of metabolites in DDA mode only (e.g., full-scan DDA on individual samples), the rescue step has no DIA counterpart and adds no value.

skills.description: Use when categorical behavioral item data (e.g., parent-rated CBCL externalizing items) or paired omics matrices need unsupervised factor extraction and variance reporting inside a Nextflow-pipeline R environment.
skills.name: r-statistical-programming
skills.search_text: r-statistical-programming Use when categorical behavioral item data (e.g., parent-rated CBCL externalizing items) or paired omics matrices need unsupervised factor extraction and variance reporting inside a Nextflow-pipeline R environment. The data are continuous omics measurements (methylation betas, metabolite intensities) rather than categorical behavioral items — MOFA2, not MCA, is the paper's method for those. The raw cohort data have not yet been converted to standardized formats — run the Xomics/ACTIONdemonstrator_preprocessing workflow first. R statistical programming underpins the factor-analysis and group-comparison steps of the ACTION multi-omics workflow: MCA of categorical ASEBA CBCL behavior items with FactoMineR (v2.4), MOFA2 factor extraction from methylation/metabolomics data, and Mann–Whitney U, Kruskal–Wallis, GEE, and Spearman correlation testing. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/gigascience/giad115
skills.summary: R statistical programming underpins the factor-analysis and group-comparison steps of the ACTION multi-omics workflow: MCA of categorical ASEBA CBCL behavior items with FactoMineR (v2.4), MOFA2 factor extraction from methylation/metabolomics data, and Mann–Whitney U, Kruskal–Wallis, GEE, and Spearman correlation testing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are continuous omics measurements (methylation betas, metabolite intensities) rather than categorical behavioral items — MOFA2, not MCA, is the paper's method for those. skills.name: r-summarizedexperiment-container-introspection
skills.search_text: r-summarizedexperiment-container-introspection Use when you have a saved maplet pipeline container (.rds, read via readRDS) and need to recover what the pipeline did — function order, arguments, and per-step outputs — e.g. to auto-generate a report or audit reproducibility. You only have raw metabolomics data files and no completed maplet container — introspection requires the recorded annotations inside the SE-derived object, not raw spectra or feature tables. The pipeline was run outside maplet (e.g. a plain magrittr chain of non-maplet functions) — the container will not carry the recorded function entries and arguments this skill depends on. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Traverse a maplet pipeline container (a SummarizedExperiment-derived R object) to recover the ordered list of executed functions, their arguments, and the plots/statistics tables each step produced, enabling faithful reconstruction and reporting of a completed metabolomics pipeline. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btab741
skills.summary: Traverse a maplet pipeline container (a SummarizedExperiment-derived R object) to recover the ordered list of executed functions, their arguments, and the plots/statistics tables each step produced, enabling faithful reconstruction and reporting of a completed metabolomics pipeline.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only have raw metabolomics data files and no completed maplet container — introspection requires the recorded annotations inside the SE-derived object, not raw spectra or feature tables. The pipeline was run outside maplet (e.g. a plain magrittr chain of non-maplet functions) — the container will not carry the recorded function entries and arguments this skill depends on.

skills.description: Use when replicate mzML-derived feature lists must be aligned across analytical runs where RT and m/z vary — or extended to 3D ion-mobility data where features must remain distinct if separated only by drift time/CCS.
skills.name: r-tree-multidimensional-feature-basketing
skills.search_text: r-tree-multidimensional-feature-basketing Use when replicate mzML-derived feature lists must be aligned across analytical runs where RT and m/z vary — or extended to 3D ion-mobility data where features must remain distinct if separated only by drift time/CCS. Input is already a single processed feature table with no replicate structure to basket Data lacks replicate runs — replicate comparison is only possible 'where possible' and adds no value with unreplicated samples Feature separation depends on dimensions the basketing tolerances do not cover (e.g. scoring adduct/fragment stripes — NP Analyst scores each MS feature independently) http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0153 Uses an R-tree to build connected-component graphs of m/z features with overlapping error ranges across multiple dimensions (retention time, m/z, and optionally ion-mobility drift time/CCS), then combines them by averaging into replicated 'basketed' features for NP Analyst replicate comparison. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acscentsci.1c01108
skills.summary: Uses an R-tree to build connected-component graphs of m/z features with overlapping error ranges across multiple dimensions (retention time, m/z, and optionally ion-mobility drift time/CCS), then combines them by averaging into replicated 'basketed' features for NP Analyst replicate comparison.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a single processed feature table with no replicate structure to basket Data lacks replicate runs — replicate comparison is only possible 'where possible' and adds no value with unreplicated samples Feature separation depends on dimensions the basketing tolerances do not cover (e.g. scoring adduct/fragment stripes — NP Analyst scores each MS feature independently)

skills.search_text: r-web-tool-interactive-execution Use when a published R/Shiny web tool must be run interactively (via its web URL or locally from GitHub) to generate simulated pooled-QC sample data from a feature/sample intensity matrix for correction and normalization. The dataset already contains real, measured pooled-QC samples and only needs drift correction — pseudoQC is for simulating QC data when actual QC samples are absent The goal is regression modeling or normalization on the raw data directly rather than generating simulated QC sample data as intermediate inputs The input is not a metabolomics or proteomics feature/sample intensity matrix (pseudoQC targets these two data types) http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Execute an R-developed, interactive web-based tool (pseudoQC) through its web interface or locally from its GitHub repository to simulate QC sample data for metabolomics and proteomics datasets using four machine learning-based regression methods. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/pmic.201900264
skills.summary: Execute an R-developed, interactive web-based tool (pseudoQC) through its web interface or locally from its GitHub repository to simulate QC sample data for metabolomics and proteomics datasets using four machine learning-based regression methods.

skills.search_text: r6-object-data-access Use when an mpactR R6 object exists (after import_data) and you need to retrieve the raw or filtered Progenesis-format peak table, verify sample metadata columns, extract CV values from filter_cv, or compute group means. The input is still a raw Progenesis CSV or MS-DIAL/GNPS export that has not yet been passed through mpactR::import_data() — no R6 object exists to access. The goal is to apply or change filtering behavior (mispicked ions, blanks, CV, insource ions) — accessors only retrieve results, they do not run filters. Working in the original Python MPACT (BalunasLab/mpact) workflow rather than the R package, which does not expose R6 accessor methods. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Extracts peak tables, sample metadata, CV values, and group means from the mpactR R6 object using its accessor methods (get_peak_table, get_metadata, get_raw_data, get_cv_data, get_group_averages), which return data.table objects ready for downstream inspection or export. metabolomics/v3 10.1128/mra.00997-24
skills.summary: Extracts peak tables, sample metadata, CV values, and group means from the mpactR R6 object using its accessor methods (get_peak_table, get_metadata, get_raw_data, get_cv_data, get_group_averages), which return data.table objects ready for downstream inspection or export.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is still a raw Progenesis CSV or MS-DIAL/GNPS export that has not yet been passed through mpactR::import_data() — no R6 object exists to access. skills.search_text: r6-reference-semantics-data-updating Use when chaining multiple mpactr filters (mispicked, group, cv, insource) on one imported Progenesis peak table and you must decide whether each filter mutates the mpactR object in place or leaves the original intact via copy_object. When you need to branch a pipeline and run alternative filters from the same intermediate state — in-place reference updating (copy_object = FALSE) would mutate the shared object When the input is raw tandem MS/MS data rather than an already-imported mpactR object from a pre-processed Progenesis peak table — import_data() must run first http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 An R6/.reference-semantics skill for mpactr workflows: controlling whether each filter (e.g. filter_mispicked_ions with copy_object=FALSE) updates the mpactr object in place or operates on an independent copy, which determines how intermediate peak-table state is preserved across a multi-filter pipeline. metabolomics/v3 10.1128/mra.00997-24

skills.description: Use when building or reviewing an mpactr pipeline where successive filters (filter_mispicked_ions, filter_cv, filter_insource_ions, filter_group) must either mutate the shared R6 mpactr object in place or leave the original peak table untouched for downstream QC and comparison.
skills.name: r6-reference-semantics-feature-table-filtering
skills.search_text: r6-reference-semantics-feature-table-filtering Use when building or reviewing an mpactr pipeline where successive filters (filter_mispicked_ions, filter_cv, filter_insource_ions, filter_group) must either mutate the shared R6 mpactr object in place or leave the original peak table untouched for downstream QC and comparison. Input is already a deconvoluted feature table with no mpactr R6 object — this skill is about managing object-reference semantics during mpactr filter chains, not about importing generic CSVs. You are running a single one-off filter where you intend in-place mutation; reasoning about copy semantics adds no value there. The pipeline is written in Python using BalunasLab/mpact (the predecessor MPACT tool); the R6 copy_object semantics are specific to the R mpactr package. mpactR stores the LC-MS/MS peak table, metadata, and filter status in an mpactr R6 object whose copy semantics are controlled per-filter by copy_object; understanding these reference semantics is required to keep pre-filter and post-filter feature tables distinct. Misusing them silently overwrites the original peak table. metabolomics/v3 10.1128/mra.00997-24
skills.summary: mpactR stores the LC-MS/MS peak table, metadata, and filter status in an mpactr R6 object whose copy semantics are controlled per-filter by copy_object; understanding these reference semantics is required to keep pre-filter and post-filter feature tables distinct. Misusing them silently overwrites the original peak table.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a deconvoluted feature table with no mpactr R6 object — this skill is about managing object-reference semantics during mpactr filter chains, not about importing generic CSVs. You are running a single one-off filter where you intend in-place mutation; reasoning about copy semantics adds no value there. The pipeline is written in Python using BalunasLab/mpact (the predecessor MPACT tool); the R6 copy_object semantics are specific to the R mpactr package.

skills.description: Use when you have antiSMASH annotations for a PKS, NRPS, or hybrid PKS/NRPS BGC and need a module-resolution depiction of the biosynthetic pathway or the predicted end-product structure.
skills.name: raichu-pathway-visualisation
skills.search_text: raichu-pathway-visualisation Use when you have antiSMASH annotations for a PKS, NRPS, or hybrid PKS/NRPS BGC and need a module-resolution depiction of the biosynthetic pathway or the predicted end-product structure. You need mature natural products directly from raw antiSMASH output — RAIChU generates natural product scaffolds but not mature natural products without user-specified tailoring targets You need automated scaffold prediction for non-PKS/NRPS/non-hybrid classes without user-provided enzymatic steps The task is automated large-scale fingerprint-based validation of all MIBiG BGCs — this was considered but not implemented, and predicted vs. real-world structures may not show high fingerprinting similarity http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Run RAIChU on antiSMASH annotations of PKS, NRPS, or hybrid PKS/NRPS clusters to render automated 'spaghetti diagram' visualisations of biosynthetic transformations, and diagnose mismatches between predicted scaffolds and experimentally characterised natural products. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00898-x
skills.summary: Run RAIChU on antiSMASH annotations of PKS, NRPS, or hybrid PKS/NRPS clusters to render automated 'spaghetti diagram' visualisations of biosynthetic transformations, and diagnose mismatches between predicted scaffolds and experimentally characterised natural products.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need mature natural products directly from raw antiSMASH output — RAIChU generates natural product scaffolds but not mature natural products without user-specified tailoring targets You need automated scaffold prediction for non-PKS/NRPS/non-hybrid classes without user-provided enzymatic steps The task is automated large-scale fingerprint-based validation of all MIBiG BGCs — this was considered but not implemented, and predicted vs. real-world structures may not show high fingerprinting similarity

skills.description: Use when partitioning a 1D frequency-domain metabolomics NMR spectrum (ppm axis) into frequency bins inside SAND's adaptive binning stage, where each bin must be windowed at its edges to suppress spectral leakage prior to conversion to per-bin time-domain FIDs.
skills.name: raised-cosine-apodization-filtering
skills.search_text: raised-cosine-apodization-filtering Use when partitioning a 1D frequency-domain metabolomics NMR spectrum (ppm axis) into frequency bins inside SAND's adaptive binning stage, where each bin must be windowed at its edges to suppress spectral leakage prior to conversion to per-bin time-domain FIDs. Input is not a 1D frequency-domain metabolomics spectrum — SAND's current version is tuned for high-resolution metabolomics spectra and does not yet accommodate other cases Data is already in the time domain (FID) — this filter is part of the frequency-to-time conversion pipeline and would not apply A quantitative figure of merit is needed for the binning/filter stage alone — no quantitative metric is reported for this stage in isolation; validation is pass/fail against SAND test examples Applies a raised-cosine band with a 0.02 ppm roll-off at the edges of each adaptively defined frequency bin (nominal bin size 0.002 ppm) of a 1D metabolomics NMR spectrum, suppressing spectral leakage before Hilbert-transform and inverse-Fourier conversion of each bin into a time-domain FID for SAND's time-domain modeling. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c03078
skills.summary: Applies a raised-cosine band with a 0.02 ppm roll-off at the edges of each adaptively defined frequency bin (nominal bin size 0.002 ppm) of a 1D metabolomics NMR spectrum, suppressing spectral leakage before Hilbert-transform and inverse-Fourier conversion of each bin into a time-domain FID for SAND's time-domain modeling.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is not a 1D frequency-domain metabolomics spectrum — SAND's current version is tuned for high-resolution metabolomics spectra and does not yet accommodate other cases Data is already in the time domain (FID) — this filter is part of the frequency-to-time conversion pipeline and would not apply A quantitative figure of merit is needed for the binning/filter stage alone — no quantitative metric is reported for this stage in isolation; validation is pass/fail against SAND test examples

skills.description: Use when reconstructing an in-source fragment pseudo-MS/MS spectrum from centroided AIF LC–MS chromatograms processed with xcms/RAMClustR — e.g. when annotating isotopologues, adducts, or in-source fragments from AIF datasets where no targeted MS/MS acquisition exists.
skills.name: ramclustr-correlation-spectrum-assembly
skills.search_text: ramclustr-correlation-spectrum-assembly Use when reconstructing an in-source fragment pseudo-MS/MS spectrum from centroided AIF LC–MS chromatograms processed with xcms/RAMClustR — e.g. when annotating isotopologues, adducts, or in-source fragments from AIF datasets where no targeted MS/MS acquisition exists. The input is already a feature table (m/z, RT, intensity) without raw chromatographic profiles — the correlation method requires EIC peak-shape profiles, not summary intensities The data were acquired with a non-AIF DIA scheme (e.g. SWATH) or on instruments where AIF support has not been validated (e.g. Orbitraps) A targeted MS/MS spectrum already exists for the feature — direct spectral matching is preferable to reconstructing an in-source pseudo-MS/MS http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0153 Assembles a pseudo-MS/MS spectrum for a target LC–MS feature from all-ion-fragmentation (AIF) data by correlating the parent's MS1 extracted-ion chromatogram (EIC) against every AIF-scan EIC with RAMClustR/RSpec, retaining fragment peaks whose Pearson r exceeds a user-set threshold (default 0.8), and falling back to the full AIF spectrum at the feature's retention time when no fragment qualifies. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c03032
skills.summary: Assembles a pseudo-MS/MS spectrum for a target LC–MS feature from all-ion-fragmentation (AIF) data by correlating the parent's MS1 extracted-ion chromatogram (EIC) against every AIF-scan EIC with RAMClustR/RSpec, retaining fragment peaks whose Pearson r exceeds a user-set threshold (default 0.8), and falling back to the full AIF spectrum at the feature's retention time when no fragment qualifies.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a feature table (m/z, RT, intensity) without raw chromatographic profiles — the correlation method requires EIC peak-shape profiles, not summary intensities The data were acquired with a non-AIF DIA scheme (e.g. SWATH) or on instruments where AIF support has not been validated (e.g. Orbitraps) A targeted MS/MS spectrum already exists for the feature — direct spectral matching is preferable to reconstructing an in-source pseudo-MS/MS

skills.description: Decision support for benchmarking modification site-localization methods on MS/MS analog pairs, when top-1 accuracy would be mis and a proximity+ambiguity-balanced null baseline is needed.
skills.name: random-baseline-simulation-for-site-localization
skills.search_text: random-baseline-simulation-for-site-localization Decision support for benchmarking modification site-localization methods on MS/MS analog pairs, when top-1 accuracy would be mis and a proximity+ambiguity-balanced null baseline is needed. The analysis goal is plain top-1 hit accuracy on spectra-structure matches — this skill addresses site localization on analog pairs, where a constant-score algorithm would tie for first place under top-1 accuracy Benchmark pairs violate the eligibility checks (precursor ≥ 2000 Da, mass difference ≥ 50% of the smaller compound, different adducts, or structures differing at more than one modification site) The MS/MS peak alignment requires unshifted peak intensity comparison as the primary signal rather than likelihood distributions over atoms http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Reproduces the ModiFinder paper's null baselines for modification site localization: Random Choice (uniform atom pick) and Random Distribution (Normal(0,1) atom scores), plus the CFM-ID permutation alternative, all scored with the Average-distance (proximity/ambiguity cover) metric on the GNPS-derived analog benchmark. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jasms.4c00061
skills.summary: Reproduces the ModiFinder paper's null baselines for modification site localization: Random Choice (uniform atom pick) and Random Distribution (Normal(0,1) atom scores), plus the CFM-ID permutation alternative, all scored with the Average-distance (proximity/ambiguity cover) metric on the GNPS-derived analog benchmark.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is plain top-1 hit accuracy on spectra-structure matches — this skill addresses site localization on analog pairs, where a constant-score algorithm would tie for first place under top-1 accuracy Benchmark pairs violate the eligibility checks (precursor ≥ 2000 Da, mass difference ≥ 50% of the smaller compound, different adducts, or structures differing at more than one modification site) The MS/MS peak alignment requires unshifted peak intensity comparison as the primary signal rather than likelihood distributions over atoms

skills.description: Use when a trained Pass/Fail or other binary classifier's test-set performance must be shown to exceed chance before it is trusted for real filtering decisions.
skills.name: random-chance-baseline-performance-evaluation
skills.search_text: random-chance-baseline-performance-evaluation Use when a trained Pass/Fail or other binary classifier's test-set performance must be shown to exceed chance before it is trusted for real filtering decisions. The classifier's performance has already been benchmarked against an established null (e.g. published random-permutation results for the same metric set and datasets) and no re-run is needed. The datasets lack labeled examples or the label space has more than two classes, making random label permutation ill-defined for this Pass/Fail setup. Only a single train/test split exists with no labeled development set to permute, so a randomized counterpart cannot be trained. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Establishes a random-chance baseline by training the best-performing classifier (e.g. AdaBoost with the M11 metric set in MetaClean) on 100 randomly permuted label versions of the development dataset, then compares its real test-set performance against the averaged randomized counterparts to rule out chance. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-020-01738-3
skills.summary: Establishes a random-chance baseline by training the best-performing classifier (e.g. AdaBoost with the M11 metric set in MetaClean) on 100 randomly permuted label versions of the development dataset, then compares its real test-set performance against the averaged randomized counterparts to rule out chance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The classifier's performance has already been benchmarked against an established null (e.g. published random-permutation results for the same metric set and datasets) and no re-run is needed. The datasets lack labeled examples or the label space has more than two classes, making random label permutation ill-defined for this Pass/Fail setup. Only a single train/test split exists with no labeled development set to permute, so a randomized counterpart cannot be trained.

skills.description: Use when the same gene pairs have Pearson correlation coefficients measured in multiple studies, each with its own sample size, and you need pooled fixed and random effects estimates with a heterogeneity statistic.
skills.name: random-effects-heterogeneity-estimation
skills.search_text: random-effects-heterogeneity-estimation Use when the same gene pairs have Pearson correlation coefficients measured in multiple studies, each with its own sample size, and you need pooled fixed and random effects estimates with a heterogeneity statistic. Each gene pair is measured in only a single study — there is nothing to pool and no heterogeneity to estimate The effect sizes are differential expression fold-changes or other non-correlation statistics rather than per-study Pearson correlation coefficients The analysis goal is within-study co-expression (e.g. the Spearman >= 0.60 gene-pair screen in MOG) rather than combining estimates across studies http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Combines per-study Pearson correlation coefficients for the same gene pair via sample-size-weighted meta-analysis, estimating between-study heterogeneity (e.g. DerSimonian-Laird) to yield both fixed effects and random effects combined estimates. In MetaOmGraph (MOG) workflows this is how replicated gene-pair correlation evidence across multiple studies is consolidated. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkz1209
skills.summary: Combines per-study Pearson correlation coefficients for the same gene pair via sample-size-weighted meta-analysis, estimating between-study heterogeneity (e.g. DerSimonian-Laird) to yield both fixed effects and random effects combined estimates. In MetaOmGraph (MOG) workflows this is how replicated gene-pair correlation evidence across multiple studies is consolidated.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Each gene pair is measured in only a single study — there is nothing to pool and no heterogeneity to estimate The effect sizes are differential expression fold-changes or other non-correlation statistics rather than per-study Pearson correlation coefficients The analysis goal is within-study co-expression (e.g. the Spearman >= 0.60 gene-pair screen in MOG) rather than combining estimates across studies
