skills.description: Use when you have experimental EI-MS or ESI-MS/MS spectra of labeled bitter/non-bitter compounds and need to train, select, and evaluate a Random Forest against XGBoost and a naive baseline.
skills.name: random-forest-classifier-training
skills.search_text: random-forest-classifier-training Use when you have experimental EI-MS or ESI-MS/MS spectra of labeled bitter/non-bitter compounds and need to train, select, and evaluate a Random Forest against XGBoost and a naive baseline. The chemical structures of the query compounds are known — use the structure-based BitterPredict classifier instead of spectrum-based prediction. Compounds have no experimental mass spectrum available (only ~30% of training compounds had at least one MassBank spectrum, so coverage is a prerequisite). You only need to evaluate an already-trained model on precomputed descriptors rather than train from binned spectra. http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Trains a Random Forest classifier (BitterMasS) to predict bitterness directly from experimental mass spectra, using fixed-length 0.1 m/z binned spectral descriptors of EI-MS and ESI-MS/MS data and compound-level cross-validated splitting. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jafc.3c09767
skills.summary: Trains a Random Forest classifier (BitterMasS) to predict bitterness directly from experimental mass spectra, using fixed-length 0.1 m/z binned spectral descriptors of EI-MS and ESI-MS/MS data and compound-level cross-validated splitting.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The chemical structures of the query compounds are known — use the structure-based BitterPredict classifier instead of spectrum-based prediction. Compounds have no experimental mass spectrum available (only ~30% of training compounds had at least one MassBank spectrum, so coverage is a prerequisite). You only need to evaluate an already-trained model on precomputed descriptors rather than train from binned spectra.

skills.description: Use when a quality-controlled LC-MS feature table with sample metadata (e.g. age group, sex, brain region) is available and the goal is metabolome-informed phenotype prediction via a random forest with feature selection and ROC-AUC / cross-validation evaluation.
skills.name: random-forest-classifier-training
skills.search_text: random-forest-classifier-training Use when a quality-controlled LC-MS feature table with sample metadata (e.g. age group, sex, brain region) is available and the goal is metabolome-informed phenotype prediction via a random forest with feature selection and ROC-AUC / cross-validation evaluation. Input is raw LC-MS data (mzML or Bruker .d) that has not yet been processed to an aligned, quality-controlled feature table — run MassCube's peak detection and alignment pipeline first The goal is metabolite identification rather than phenotype prediction — MassCube does not directly perform metabolite identification, it only enhances annotation accuracy Labels for the phenotype of interest are absent from the sample metadata, since feature selection is driven by metadata and importance strength http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Train a random forest phenotype classifier on quality-controlled metabolomic feature tables using MassCube's build_classifier (Python), selecting features by metadata association and importance strength. This is how MassCube closes the loop from raw LC-MS processing to phenotype prediction, e.g. distinguishing adolescent from middle-age mouse brain metabolomes. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-025-60640-5
skills.summary: Train a random forest phenotype classifier on quality-controlled metabolomic feature tables using MassCube's build_classifier (Python), selecting features by metadata association and importance strength. This is how MassCube closes the loop from raw LC-MS processing to phenotype prediction, e.g. distinguishing adolescent from middle-age mouse brain metabolomes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw LC-MS data (mzML or Bruker .d) that has not yet been processed to an aligned, quality-controlled feature table — run MassCube's peak detection and alignment pipeline first The goal is metabolite identification rather than phenotype prediction — MassCube does not directly perform metabolite identification, it only enhances annotation accuracy Labels for the phenotype of interest are absent from the sample metadata, since feature selection is driven by metadata and importance strength

skills.description: Use when a labeled, high-dimensional lipid feature table (e.g., annotated by LipidIN, such as Supplementary Data 9 breast cancer cohorts) needs feature ranking and biomarker panel selection for patient-vs-healthy classification.
skills.name: random-forest-classifier-training
skills.search_text: random-forest-classifier-training Use when a labeled, high-dimensional lipid feature table (e.g., annotated by LipidIN, such as Supplementary Data 9 breast cancer cohorts) needs feature ranking and biomarker panel selection for patient-vs-healthy classification. Input is already a small, pre-selected lipid panel and the goal is only model fitting — no Gini-importance ranking step is needed. The task is spectral annotation or library search (e.g., LipidIN MS2 library search, Flash Entropy Search) rather than supervised classification of a feature table. Samples lack disease/healthy class labels, so no supervised random-forest training is possible. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Trains a random-forest classifier on an annotated lipid feature table to rank lipids by Gini importance, selecting a small biomarker panel (top 10 featured lipids) that downstream classifiers such as LightGBM use for disease-vs-control prediction across independent clinical cohorts. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-025-59683-5
skills.summary: Trains a random-forest classifier on an annotated lipid feature table to rank lipids by Gini importance, selecting a small biomarker panel (top 10 featured lipids) that downstream classifiers such as LightGBM use for disease-vs-control prediction across independent clinical cohorts.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a small, pre-selected lipid panel and the goal is only model fitting — no Gini-importance ranking step is needed. The task is spectral annotation or library search (e.g., LipidIN MS2 library search, Flash Entropy Search) rather than supervised classification of a feature table. Samples lack disease/healthy class labels, so no supervised random-forest training is possible.

skills.description: Use when a metabolomics intensity matrix (e.g., 234 samples, 113 metabolites, 3 phenotype groups) must be split into train/test sets, modeled with random forest, and validated via ROC AUC against a held-out test set.
skills.name: random-forest-classifier-training
skills.search_text: random-forest-classifier-training Use when a metabolomics intensity matrix (e.g., 234 samples, 113 metabolites, 3 phenotype groups) must be split into train/test sets, modeled with random forest, and validated via ROC AUC against a held-out test set. When raw spectra must first be peak-picked and annotated — iMAP does not implement raw data preprocessing or peak picking and annotation modules When the goal is unsupervised metabolite selection without a phenotype label; feature selection here requires group pairs and Kruskal-Wallis/Tukey comparisons When only a single train-set AUC (the paper's own pipeline) suffices and no held-out validation is needed http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Train and validate random forest classifiers on selected metabolite features using iMAP's predictive-modeling module, which automates train-test separation, feature selection, model construction, and ROC AUC validation (demonstrated on the Zhu et al. 2014 colorectal cancer metabolite dataset). metabolomics/v3 10.3389/fchem.2021.659656
skills.summary: Train and validate random forest classifiers on selected metabolite features using iMAP's predictive-modeling module, which automates train-test separation, feature selection, model construction, and ROC AUC validation (demonstrated on the Zhu et al. 2014 colorectal cancer metabolite dataset).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When raw spectra must first be peak-picked and annotated — iMAP does not implement raw data preprocessing or peak picking and annotation modules When the goal is unsupervised metabolite selection without a phenotype label; feature selection here requires group pairs and Kruskal-Wallis/Tukey comparisons When only a single train-set AUC (the paper's own pipeline) suffices and no held-out validation is needed

skills.description: Use when a binary-classification outcome is being predicted from pathway-transformed multi-omics abundance data (e.g. Su et al. COVID-19 mild vs moderate/severe metabolomics/proteomics scores) and an interpretable pathway-level model with feature selection is required.
skills.name: random-forest-classifier-tuning
skills.search_text: random-forest-classifier-tuning Use when a binary-classification outcome is being predicted from pathway-transformed multi-omics abundance data (e.g. Su et al. COVID-19 mild vs moderate/severe metabolomics/proteomics scores) and an interpretable pathway-level model with feature selection is required. When the goal is pathway-level integration of omics with latent-variable modelling of interactions between omics blocks — use PathIntegrate Multi-View (MB-PLS) instead of a single-view random forest. When the input is already a molecular-level feature table and no pathway transformation is desired — applying a random forest directly to concatenated molecular data yields the higher-dimensional baseline (AUC ≈0.98) rather than an interpretable pathway-level model. When samples from individuals lack data on all omics views — PathIntegrate requires all input omics measured on the same individuals, so such samples must be discarded before model fitting. http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Train and hyperparameter-tune a RandomForestClassifier on multi-omics pathway score matrices produced by PathIntegrate Single-View, then use recursive feature elimination with cross-validation (RFECV) to select the predictive pathways for a binary outcome such as COVID-19 severity (mild vs moderate/severe). metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011814
skills.summary: Train and hyperparameter-tune a RandomForestClassifier on multi-omics pathway score matrices produced by PathIntegrate Single-View, then use recursive feature elimination with cross-validation (RFECV) to select the predictive pathways for a binary outcome such as COVID-19 severity (mild vs moderate/severe).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is pathway-level integration of omics with latent-variable modelling of interactions between omics blocks — use PathIntegrate Multi-View (MB-PLS) instead of a single-view random forest. When the input is already a molecular-level feature table and no pathway transformation is desired — applying a random forest directly to concatenated molecular data yields the higher-dimensional baseline (AUC ≈0.98) rather than an interpretable pathway-level model. When samples from individuals lack data on all omics views — PathIntegrate requires all input omics measured on the same individuals, so such samples must be discarded before model fitting.

skills.description: Use when you need a supervised classification baseline on peak-aligned metabolomics feature tables (e.g., cosine-similarity or spectral-entropy similarity tables) with labeled bioactivity groups, reported as accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and ROC AUC.
skills.name: random-forest-cross-validated-classification
skills.search_text: random-forest-cross-validated-classification Use when you need a supervised classification baseline on peak-aligned metabolomics feature tables (e.g., cosine-similarity or spectral-entropy similarity tables) with labeled bioactivity groups, reported as accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and ROC AUC. When the goal is the paper's proposed method itself — direct CNN prediction from raw LC-MS/MS encoded as 2D grayscale molecular fingerprint images — this baseline skill bypasses that image-encoding pipeline entirely When features require chemical identification or annotation before modeling; this skill deliberately uses raw feature/similarity tables without compound identification When the sample labels are continuous rather than the paper's discretized classes (normalized DPPH values <0.4 vs >0.6), since intermediate values (0.4–0.6) are excluded http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Trains Random Forest classifiers (scikit-learn 1.3.0, default hyperparameters, 5-fold cross-validation) on LC-MS/MS-derived feature tables to predict DPPH bioactivity class for 545 wild soybean accessions, establishing the conventional-ML baseline that the MS2toImg-CNN framework is benchmarked against. metabolomics/v3 10.48550/arxiv.2510.09716
skills.summary: Trains Random Forest classifiers (scikit-learn 1.3.0, default hyperparameters, 5-fold cross-validation) on LC-MS/MS-derived feature tables to predict DPPH bioactivity class for 545 wild soybean accessions, establishing the conventional-ML baseline that the MS2toImg-CNN framework is benchmarked against.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is the paper's proposed method itself — direct CNN prediction from raw LC-MS/MS encoded as 2D grayscale molecular fingerprint images — this baseline skill bypasses that image-encoding pipeline entirely When features require chemical identification or annotation before modeling; this skill deliberately uses raw feature/similarity tables without compound identification When the sample labels are continuous rather than the paper's discretized classes (normalized DPPH values <0.4 vs >0.6), since intermediate values (0.4–0.6) are excluded

skills.description: Use when a trained random forest (e.g. scikit-learn) combines multiple candidate-scoring features and you must determine which feature contributes most to ranking performance.
skills.name: random-forest-feature-importance-analysis
skills.search_text: random-forest-feature-importance-analysis Use when a trained random forest (e.g. scikit-learn) combines multiple candidate-scoring features and you must determine which feature contributes most to ranking performance. You need feature importance for a model other than a tree-ensemble (e.g. linear models or neural networks like MS2Deepscore itself) — impurity-based feature_importances_ is specific to random forests. You want model performance benchmarking (e.g. recall@1 vs cosine/modified cosine score) rather than attributing performance to individual input features. The candidate features have not yet been computed for the query spectra — extract importances only from a trained model over existing feature columns. http://edamontology.org/topic_0153 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Quantify which input features drive a trained random forest's re-ranking performance by extracting scikit-learn's impurity-based feature_importances_ for each feature and ranking them. Applied to MS2Query's five analogue-search features to confirm the average MS2Deepscore over 10 similar library molecules is the dominant contributor. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-023-37446-4
skills.summary: Quantify which input features drive a trained random forest's re-ranking performance by extracting scikit-learn's impurity-based feature_importances_ for each feature and ranking them. Applied to MS2Query's five analogue-search features to confirm the average MS2Deepscore over 10 similar library molecules is the dominant contributor.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need feature importance for a model other than a tree-ensemble (e.g. linear models or neural networks like MS2Deepscore itself) — impurity-based feature_importances_ is specific to random forests. You want model performance benchmarking (e.g. recall@1 vs cosine/modified cosine score) rather than attributing performance to individual input features. The candidate features have not yet been computed for the query spectra — extract importances only from a trained model over existing feature columns.

skills.description: Use when trained random forest regression models (e.g. per-metabolite models over CCLE multiomics features) need their feature importances ranked, top-k features extracted, and robustness-confidence scores computed.
skills.name: random-forest-feature-importance-extraction
skills.search_text: random-forest-feature-importance-extraction Use when trained random forest regression models (e.g. per-metabolite models over CCLE multiomics features) need their feature importances ranked, top-k features extracted, and robustness-confidence scores computed. Extracting features from genomic mutation models — mutations were excluded from random forest results due to their binary structure Transferring the trained models or extracted features to predict metabolomics from other (e.g. in vivo) sources — the article states models are not directly transferable due to in vitro/in vivo differences and limited feature overlap Input omics data with too few samples/cell lines — differences in sample quantities influence accuracy and such omics may not perform well http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Extracts the top-20 most important predictor features from scikit-learn Random Forest Regressor models trained per metabolite across nine feature sets of CCLE omics data, and assigns each feature a 0–8 confidence score based on how many of 8 control experiments it reappears in. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.08.17.608400
skills.summary: Extracts the top-20 most important predictor features from scikit-learn Random Forest Regressor models trained per metabolite across nine feature sets of CCLE omics data, and assigns each feature a 0–8 confidence score based on how many of 8 control experiments it reappears in.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Extracting features from genomic mutation models — mutations were excluded from random forest results due to their binary structure Transferring the trained models or extracted features to predict metabolomics from other (e.g. in vivo) sources — the article states models are not directly transferable due to in vitro/in vivo differences and limited feature overlap Input omics data with too few samples/cell lines — differences in sample quantities influence accuracy and such omics may not perform well

skills.description: Use when an n x p matrix with 10–30% of values removed completely at random contains mixed variable types (continuous + categorical) and a non-parametric imputation is needed, or when nonlinear relations/complex interactions are suspected.
skills.name: random-forest-iterative-imputation
skills.search_text: random-forest-iterative-imputation Use when an n x p matrix with 10–30% of values removed completely at random contains mixed variable types (continuous + categorical) and a non-parametric imputation is needed, or when nonlinear relations/complex interactions are suspected. Data where MissPALasso-style lasso imputation is preferred and dimensionality is low — MissPALasso performed slightly better than missForest on the gene expression data Datasets with ill-distributed and nearly dependent variables intended for MICE-style regression imputation (required ad-hoc removal of nearly dependent variables on the Children's Hospital data) Data with missingness mechanisms other than completely at random — evaluation covered only artificially introduced MCAR values of 10% to 30% http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Imputes missing values in an n x p data matrix by iteratively training random forests on observed entries to predict missing entries, handling mixed continuous/categorical data with no structural assumptions. Includes OOB-based error estimation without a test set. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btr597
skills.summary: Imputes missing values in an n x p data matrix by iteratively training random forests on observed entries to predict missing entries, handling mixed continuous/categorical data with no structural assumptions. Includes OOB-based error estimation without a test set.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data where MissPALasso-style lasso imputation is preferred and dimensionality is low — MissPALasso performed slightly better than missForest on the gene expression data Datasets with ill-distributed and nearly dependent variables intended for MICE-style regression imputation (required ad-hoc removal of nearly dependent variables on the Children's Hospital data) Data with missingness mechanisms other than completely at random — evaluation covered only artificially introduced MCAR values of 10% to 30%

skills.description: Use when you must show how a spectral classifier's precision and recall change as the training set is grown from small to full size, e.g. to justify a data-collection effort or reproduce a published learning curve.
skills.name: random-forest-learning-curve-analysis
skills.search_text: random-forest-learning-curve-analysis Use when you must show how a spectral classifier's precision and recall change as the training set is grown from small to full size, e.g. to justify a data-collection effort or reproduce a published learning curve. The input is a chemical structure rather than a spectrum — BitterPredict (structure-based classifier) is the appropriate tool, not spectrum-based retraining. Only individual EI-MS or individual ESI-MS/MS sets are available: the article reports that prediction on the individual sets showed poor results compared with the combined set. You need a final production predictor rather than an assessment of training-data sufficiency — use the fully trained BitterMasS model directly. http://edamontology.org/topic_3473 Retrains a Random Forest classifier (BitterMasS configuration) on progressively larger subsets of a combined spectral training corpus and plots precision/recall against training-set size to characterize the data-efficiency of the model. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jafc.3c09767
skills.summary: Retrains a Random Forest classifier (BitterMasS configuration) on progressively larger subsets of a combined spectral training corpus and plots precision/recall against training-set size to characterize the data-efficiency of the model.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a chemical structure rather than a spectrum — BitterPredict (structure-based classifier) is the appropriate tool, not spectrum-based retraining. Only individual EI-MS or individual ESI-MS/MS sets are available: the article reports that prediction on the individual sets showed poor results compared with the combined set. You need a final production predictor rather than an assessment of training-data sufficiency — use the fully trained BitterMasS model directly.

skills.description: Use when a preprocessed LC-MS MetaboSet object still contains NA values in exprs and a statistically sound fill-in (random forest, per Kokla et al.) is needed before feature-wise tests or multivariate models.
skills.name: random-forest-matrix-completion
skills.search_text: random-forest-matrix-completion Use when a preprocessed LC-MS MetaboSet object still contains NA values in exprs and a statistically sound fill-in (random forest, per Kokla et al.) is needed before feature-wise tests or multivariate models. When the missingness pattern should drive feature filtering instead of imputation — notame first flags low-quality features with flag_detection/flag_quality and only imputes what remains; do not impute instead of flagging. When QC samples must remain in the object (e.g. ongoing batch correction such as normalize_batches/ruvs_qc, which rely on QC signal) — impute_rf is applied only after QCs are dropped. When a deterministic simple strategy is preferred or random forest is too slow for the feature count — impute_simple offers simpler alternatives. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Fills missing values in a MetaboSet feature-abundance matrix using random-forest imputation (missForest), following the notame workflow, after quality-flagged features and QC samples have been set aside. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo10040135
skills.summary: Fills missing values in a MetaboSet feature-abundance matrix using random-forest imputation (missForest), following the notame workflow, after quality-flagged features and QC samples have been set aside.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the missingness pattern should drive feature filtering instead of imputation — notame first flags low-quality features with flag_detection/flag_quality and only imputes what remains; do not impute instead of flagging. When QC samples must remain in the object (e.g. ongoing batch correction such as normalize_batches/ruvs_qc, which rely on QC signal) — impute_rf is applied only after QCs are dropped. When a deterministic simple strategy is preferred or random forest is too slow for the feature count — impute_simple offers simpler alternatives.

skills.description: Use when the analysis goal is supervised classification of metabolomics samples into class labels (e.g., treatment groups from a design file) and identification of which features differentiate those classes.
skills.name: random-forest-metabolomics-classification
skills.search_text: random-forest-metabolomics-classification Use when the analysis goal is supervised classification of metabolomics samples into class labels (e.g., treatment groups from a design file) and identification of which features differentiate those classes. The task is unsupervised or exploratory visualization (e.g., PCA, hierarchical cluster heatmap, modularity clustering) rather than classification against known class labels Only basic statistical testing is needed — SECIMTools' basic methods (PLS-DA, ANOVA, t-test, Kruskal-Wallis) are a better fit than random forest The input is raw spectra requiring peak picking / feature identification rather than a processed feature table http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Trains a random forest ensemble to classify metabolomics samples (e.g., treatment groups) from a wide-format feature table using SECIMTools' advanced classification tool, and ranks features by variable importance to identify the most differentiating metabolite features. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-018-2134-1
skills.summary: Trains a random forest ensemble to classify metabolomics samples (e.g., treatment groups) from a wide-format feature table using SECIMTools' advanced classification tool, and ranks features by variable importance to identify the most differentiating metabolite features.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is unsupervised or exploratory visualization (e.g., PCA, hierarchical cluster heatmap, modularity clustering) rather than classification against known class labels Only basic statistical testing is needed — SECIMTools' basic methods (PLS-DA, ANOVA, t-test, Kruskal-Wallis) are a better fit than random forest The input is raw spectra requiring peak picking / feature identification rather than a processed feature table

skills.description: Use when a behavioral item matrix (e.g. ASEBA CBCL parent-rated externalizing items) contains missing item responses and a completed matrix is required before factor extraction such as multiple correspondence analysis.
skills.name: random-forest-missing-value-imputation
skills.search_text: random-forest-missing-value-imputation Use when a behavioral item matrix (e.g. ASEBA CBCL parent-rated externalizing items) contains missing item responses and a completed matrix is required before factor extraction such as multiple correspondence analysis. The omics data blocks (urine metabolomics, DNA methylation) — those use MOFA2 and their own QC/filters (e.g. discarding samples/metabolites with ≥15% missing values), not missForest The input matrix has no missing values — imputation is unnecessary and would only add noise A parametric imputation is required that depends on distributional assumptions; missForest is explicitly non-parametric for mixed-type data http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Impute missing values in mixed-type behavioral data (ASEBA CBCL externalizing behavior items) using the non-parametric missForest random-forest imputation (R library missForest v1.4), so the completed item matrix can feed the downstream MCA step of the Nextflow multi-omics workflow. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/gigascience/giad115
skills.summary: Impute missing values in mixed-type behavioral data (ASEBA CBCL externalizing behavior items) using the non-parametric missForest random-forest imputation (R library missForest v1.4), so the completed item matrix can feed the downstream MCA step of the Nextflow multi-omics workflow.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The omics data blocks (urine metabolomics, DNA methylation) — those use MOFA2 and their own QC/filters (e.g. discarding samples/metabolites with ≥15% missing values), not missForest The input matrix has no missing values — imputation is unnecessary and would only add noise A parametric imputation is required that depends on distributional assumptions; missForest is explicitly non-parametric for mixed-type data

skills.description: Use when running missForest on data with artificially or naturally missing values and you need an imputation error estimate without holding out a test set, e.g. to report NRMSE/PFC reliability per simulation run.
skills.name: random-forest-oob-error-estimation
skills.search_text: random-forest-oob-error-estimation Use when running missForest on data with artificially or naturally missing values and you need an imputation error estimate without holding out a test set, e.g. to report NRMSE/PFC reliability per simulation run. You need a formal, per-variable error assessment — the paper states OOB estimates represent 'an informal reliability check for each variable', not a formal evaluation Missingness does not fall within the evaluated 10-30% MCAR range — reliability of OOB estimates was only established for artificially introduced missing values from 10% to 30% The imputation method is not random-forest-based (e.g. KNNimpute, MissPALasso, MICE) — those methods lack built-in OOB error estimates http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Assess the true imputation error of missForest using its built-in random forest out-of-bag (OOB) error estimates, avoiding a separate test set; the OOB estimates approximate the true error within ~10-15% proportional deviation. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btr597
skills.summary: Assess the true imputation error of missForest using its built-in random forest out-of-bag (OOB) error estimates, avoiding a separate test set; the OOB estimates approximate the true error within ~10-15% proportional deviation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need a formal, per-variable error assessment — the paper states OOB estimates represent 'an informal reliability check for each variable', not a formal evaluation Missingness does not fall within the evaluated 10-30% MCAR range — reliability of OOB estimates was only established for artificially introduced missing values from 10% to 30% The imputation method is not random-forest-based (e.g. KNNimpute, MissPALasso, MICE) — those methods lack built-in OOB error estimates

skills.description: Use when TARDIS-integrated targeted LC–MS peaks across biofluid matrices (stool, saliva, urine) have labeled quality classes and you need to reproduce or evaluate the RF 'Bad'-peak classifier and its variable-importance ranking.
skills.name: random-forest-peak-quality-classification
skills.search_text: random-forest-peak-quality-classification Use when TARDIS-integrated targeted LC–MS peaks across biofluid matrices (stool, saliva, urine) have labeled quality classes and you need to reproduce or evaluate the RF 'Bad'-peak classifier and its variable-importance ranking. Peaks have not been integrated and quality metrics computed yet — run TARDIS peak integration and quality-metric extraction first The task is generic supervised classification on arbitrary features rather than chromatographic peak quality filtering in targeted LC–MS data Unlabeled peak data without Good/Bad/Ambiguous quality annotations is all that is available, so the RF model cannot be trained or its accuracy evaluated Trains single-matrix and multimatrix random-forest classifiers on TARDIS peak quality metrics (AUC, maximum intensity, points over the peak, custom signal-to-noise ratio, bell-curve similarity) to identify 'Bad' chromatographic peaks in targeted LC–MS metabolomics, evaluating against the reported FGFP accuracy targets. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c00567
skills.summary: Trains single-matrix and multimatrix random-forest classifiers on TARDIS peak quality metrics (AUC, maximum intensity, points over the peak, custom signal-to-noise ratio, bell-curve similarity) to identify 'Bad' chromatographic peaks in targeted LC–MS metabolomics, evaluating against the reported FGFP accuracy targets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Peaks have not been integrated and quality metrics computed yet — run TARDIS peak integration and quality-metric extraction first The task is generic supervised classification on arbitrary features rather than chromatographic peak quality filtering in targeted LC–MS data Unlabeled peak data without Good/Bad/Ambiguous quality annotations is all that is available, so the RF model cannot be trained or its accuracy evaluated

skills.description: Use when peaks have already been detected from .mzML HRMS scans with mssmain.peak_pick and you need to filter out poor-quality features (peak splitting, insufficient scan numbers, high baseline noise) using a pre-trained ML model.
skills.name: random-forest-peak-quality-scoring
skills.search_text: random-forest-peak-quality-scoring Use when peaks have already been detected from .mzML HRMS scans with mssmain.peak_pick and you need to filter out poor-quality features (peak splitting, insufficient scan numbers, high baseline noise) using a pre-trained ML model. Input is already a curated feature table (e.g., a CSV of m/z–RT pairs) — scoring operates on raw peak candidates from peak_pick, not on aligned features. You need feature grouping/merging of isotopes, adducts, or in-source fragments — the article lists this as not yet implemented (future work), so the RF scorer cannot substitute for it. Your peaks come from non-mzML vendor formats — the pipeline's import stage only supports .mzML in this workflow. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Optional peak quality assessment step in the Mass-Suite (MSS) feature extraction pipeline that scores detected chromatographic peaks with a packaged pre-trained random forest model to exclude noisy, split, or poor-quality features before exporting the m/z–RT feature table. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-023-00741-9
skills.summary: Optional peak quality assessment step in the Mass-Suite (MSS) feature extraction pipeline that scores detected chromatographic peaks with a packaged pre-trained random forest model to exclude noisy, split, or poor-quality features before exporting the m/z–RT feature table.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a curated feature table (e.g., a CSV of m/z–RT pairs) — scoring operates on raw peak candidates from peak_pick, not on aligned features. You need feature grouping/merging of isotopes, adducts, or in-source fragments — the article lists this as not yet implemented (future work), so the RF scorer cannot substitute for it. Your peaks come from non-mzML vendor formats — the pipeline's import stage only supports .mzML in this workflow.

skills.description: Use when a large-scale LC-MS metabolomics or proteomics feature table contains repeatedly injected pooled QC samples interleaved with biological samples (e.g. QC after every 5–8 injections) and per-feature intensities drift with injection order or vary across batches.
skills.name: random-forest-regression-model-fitting
skills.search_text: random-forest-regression-model-fitting Use when a large-scale LC-MS metabolomics or proteomics feature table contains repeatedly injected pooled QC samples interleaved with biological samples (e.g. QC after every 5–8 injections) and per-feature intensities drift with injection order or vary across batches. The dataset has no repeated pooled QC injections interleaved with real samples (use the QC-free shiftCor_dQC Combat route instead, as statTarget notes 'Combat is also provided for QC free datasets'). Input is already corrected or aggregated per-batch and per-feature drift has already been modeled. A feature has more than 20 percent missing values or fails the 80-percent non-zero rule, so there is insufficient QC signal to fit a stable RF regression. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Fit an ensemble of 500 random forest regression trees on QC-sample intensities versus injection order to learn unwanted signal drift and batch variation, then use the fitted model to predict per-feature correction factors that are applied to every real sample in LC-MS or SRM proteomics data. metabolomics/v3 10.1016/j.aca.2018.08.002
skills.summary: Fit an ensemble of 500 random forest regression trees on QC-sample intensities versus injection order to learn unwanted signal drift and batch variation, then use the fitted model to predict per-feature correction factors that are applied to every real sample in LC-MS or SRM proteomics data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset has no repeated pooled QC injections interleaved with real samples (use the QC-free shiftCor_dQC Combat route instead, as statTarget notes 'Combat is also provided for QC free datasets'). Input is already corrected or aggregated per-batch and per-feature drift has already been modeled. A feature has more than 20 percent missing values or fails the 80-percent non-zero rule, so there is insufficient QC signal to fit a stable RF regression.

skills.description: Use when you have matched multi-omics and metabolite abundance matrices across samples (e.g. CCLE cancer cell lines) and need cross-validated, per-target regression to identify which feature set most accurately predicts each metabolite.
skills.name: random-forest-regression-model-training
skills.search_text: random-forest-regression-model-training Use when you have matched multi-omics and metabolite abundance matrices across samples (e.g. CCLE cancer cell lines) and need cross-validated, per-target regression to identify which feature set most accurately predicts each metabolite. The candidate input features are genomic mutations — these are excluded from random forest model results due to their binary structure The goal is causal mechanism identification — this 'guilt by association' regression approach yields descriptive associations that are not necessarily mechanistic The omics modality has too few matched samples, since differences in sample quantities can influence accuracies http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Trains a separate scikit-learn RandomForestRegressor for each metabolite (225 metabolites) from each omics feature set (9 classes from the CCLE), then scores predictions by Pearson's correlation to rank which omics classes best predict metabolomic variation. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.08.17.608400
skills.summary: Trains a separate scikit-learn RandomForestRegressor for each metabolite (225 metabolites) from each omics feature set (9 classes from the CCLE), then scores predictions by Pearson's correlation to rank which omics classes best predict metabolomic variation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The candidate input features are genomic mutations — these are excluded from random forest model results due to their binary structure The goal is causal mechanism identification — this 'guilt by association' regression approach yields descriptive associations that are not necessarily mechanistic The omics modality has too few matched samples, since differences in sample quantities can influence accuracies

skills.description: Use when experimental MS1 features must be matched to MRN metabolites with a relative RT tolerance (30%) in addition to m/z, and only a subset of metabolites (seed annotations) have observed retention times to learn from.
skills.name: random-forest-retention-time-prediction
skills.search_text: random-forest-retention-time-prediction Use when experimental MS1 features must be matched to MRN metabolites with a relative RT tolerance (30%) in addition to m/z, and only a subset of metabolites (seed annotations) have observed retention times to learn from. Seed annotations lack reliable observed retention times (e.g., no RT recalibration table available), leaving the random-forest model nothing to learn from CCS values are available and CCS-based matching (ccs_tol_rel in getErrorAndScore) is preferred, or m/z-only matching without RT filtering is the goal The task is downstream annotation propagation on the already-constrained network rather than building the MS1-constrained MRN Trains a column-type-specific random-forest model on seed metabolite annotations to predict retention times for every metabolite in the knowledge-based metabolic reaction network (MRN), enabling RT-based filtering of experimental features during MetDNA3 MS1 pre-mapping. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-025-63536-6
skills.summary: Trains a column-type-specific random-forest model on seed metabolite annotations to predict retention times for every metabolite in the knowledge-based metabolic reaction network (MRN), enabling RT-based filtering of experimental features during MetDNA3 MS1 pre-mapping.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Seed annotations lack reliable observed retention times (e.g., no RT recalibration table available), leaving the random-forest model nothing to learn from CCS values are available and CCS-based matching (ccs_tol_rel in getErrorAndScore) is preferred, or m/z-only matching without RT filtering is the goal The task is downstream annotation propagation on the already-constrained network rather than building the MS1-constrained MRN

skills.description: Use when building or reproducing an MS2Query-style analogue search pipeline where MS2Deepscore preselection must be re-ranked to place the analogue or exact match at the top.
skills.name: random-forest-spectrum-pair-reranking
skills.search_text: random-forest-spectrum-pair-reranking Use when building or reproducing an MS2Query-style analogue search pipeline where MS2Deepscore preselection must be re-ranked to place the analogue or exact match at the top. When only an exact spectral library match is needed — plain cosine or modified cosine score matching (matchms, 0.05 Da fragment tolerance) is sufficient and the re-ranker adds unneeded complexity When the query set has not been reduced to representative MS2 spectra — MS2Query performs no peak picking or clustering, so running the re-ranker on many near-duplicate MS2 spectra per feature wastes computation; cluster or preprocess with MZMine/FBMN first When evaluating raw spectral similarity rather than analogue-search ranking — MS2Deepscore or Spec2Vec scores alone are the right outputs, not the re-ranked 0–1 match score http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Train and apply a random forest re-ranker that combines 5 spectrum-pair features to rank the top 2000 MS2Deepscore-preselected library spectra, outputting a calibrated 0–1 match score for analogue and exact-match search in MS2Query. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-023-37446-4
skills.summary: Train and apply a random forest re-ranker that combines 5 spectrum-pair features to rank the top 2000 MS2Deepscore-preselected library spectra, outputting a calibrated 0–1 match score for analogue and exact-match search in MS2Query.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When only an exact spectral library match is needed — plain cosine or modified cosine score matching (matchms, 0.05 Da fragment tolerance) is sufficient and the re-ranker adds unneeded complexity When the query set has not been reduced to representative MS2 spectra — MS2Query performs no peak picking or clustering, so running the re-ranker on many near-duplicate MS2 spectra per feature wastes computation; cluster or preprocess with MZMine/FBMN first When evaluating raw spectral similarity rather than analogue-search ranking — MS2Deepscore or Spec2Vec scores alone are the right outputs, not the re-ranked 0–1 match score

skills.description: Use when a preprocessed, imputed LC-MS MetaboSet feature table with a class label (e.g. group column) is available and you need supervised, model-based identification of the most interesting molecular features rather than univariate feature-wise tests.
skills.name: random-forest-variable-importance-ranking
skills.search_text: random-forest-variable-importance-ranking Use when a preprocessed, imputed LC-MS MetaboSet feature table with a class label (e.g. group column) is available and you need supervised, model-based identification of the most interesting molecular features rather than univariate feature-wise tests. The data are raw LC-MS files that have not yet been peak-picked and preprocessed into a MetaboSet feature table — notame expects preprocessed LC-MS data. The dataset still contains flagged low-quality features or missing values that have not been imputed — the ranking must run on the unflagged, imputed features. The goal is an unsupervised exploratory overview (e.g. PCA/visual QC) rather than supervised feature selection against a class label. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0153 Applies the MUVR package's repeated double cross-validated random-forest (and PLS) models to rank molecular features by importance, producing minimal-optimal ('min'), 'mid' and all-relevant ('max') variable-selection sets for non-targeted LC-MS metabolomics data. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo10040135
skills.summary: Applies the MUVR package's repeated double cross-validated random-forest (and PLS) models to rank molecular features by importance, producing minimal-optimal ('min'), 'mid' and all-relevant ('max') variable-selection sets for non-targeted LC-MS metabolomics data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are raw LC-MS files that have not yet been peak-picked and preprocessed into a MetaboSet feature table — notame expects preprocessed LC-MS data. The dataset still contains flagged low-quality features or missing values that have not been imputed — the ranking must run on the unflagged, imputed features. The goal is an unsupervised exploratory overview (e.g. PCA/visual QC) rather than supervised feature selection against a class label.

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify how reliably MetaFetcheR resolves identifiers for a given compound database — e.g. to reproduce the Supplementary Tables S2-S6 quality test before trusting mapping output.
skills.name: random-identifier-sampling
skills.search_text: random-identifier-sampling Use when you need to quantify how reliably MetaFetcheR resolves identifiers for a given compound database — e.g. to reproduce the Supplementary Tables S2-S6 quality test before trusting mapping output. You want to map an actual study's metabolite identifier list — this skill is a randomized quality benchmark of the cache database, not a data-fetching workflow The local PostgreSQL cache has not been populated via install_databases / bulk_insert_hmdb, bulk_insert_chebi, bulk_insert_lipidmaps and on-the-fly KEGG/PubChem caching The identifiers of interest belong to databases outside the five supported ones (HMDB, ChEBI, PubChem, KEGG, LIPID MAPS) http://edamontology.org/topic_3366 A quality-test procedure for MetaFetcheR in which random identifiers drawn from the five supported small compound databases (HMDB, ChEBI, PubChem, KEGG, LIPID MAPS) are repeatedly resolved via the queue-based mapping routine to measure per-database consistency, ambiguity, and unresolved rates. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2021.02.28.433248
skills.summary: A quality-test procedure for MetaFetcheR in which random identifiers drawn from the five supported small compound databases (HMDB, ChEBI, PubChem, KEGG, LIPID MAPS) are repeatedly resolved via the queue-based mapping routine to measure per-database consistency, ambiguity, and unresolved rates.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You want to map an actual study's metabolite identifier list — this skill is a randomized quality benchmark of the cache database, not a data-fetching workflow The local PostgreSQL cache has not been populated via install_databases / bulk_insert_hmdb, bulk_insert_chebi, bulk_insert_lipidmaps and on-the-fly KEGG/PubChem caching The identifiers of interest belong to databases outside the five supported ones (HMDB, ChEBI, PubChem, KEGG, LIPID MAPS)

skills.description: Use when metabolomics data contain paired/repeated samples per subject (e.g. VAT and SAT lipid profiles from the same 59 CRC patients) and per-metabolite variance or outliers must be reduced using subject metadata.
skills.name: random-intercept-paired-data-modeling
skills.search_text: random-intercept-paired-data-modeling Use when metabolomics data contain paired/repeated samples per subject (e.g. VAT and SAT lipid profiles from the same 59 CRC patients) and per-metabolite variance or outliers must be reduced using subject metadata. Data are unpaired single-sample-per-subject profiles with no repeated measurements or subject Id, so a random intercept '(1|Id)' cannot be defined No patient metadata are available to serve as fixed effects, leaving nothing for the LMM to adjust beyond the random intercept The input is already a normalized/processed feature table intended directly for classification, and you only need feature selection (e.g. VIP > 1) rather than signal readjustment http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Fit a per-metabolite linear mixed-effects model (LMM) with patient metadata as fixed effects and a subject-specific random intercept '(1|Id)', using the lmm2met R package built on lme4's lmer procedure, to systematically minimize subject-specific variation in each metabolite prior to multivariate analyses. metabolomics/v3 10.1016/j.csbj.2019.04.009
skills.summary: Fit a per-metabolite linear mixed-effects model (LMM) with patient metadata as fixed effects and a subject-specific random intercept '(1|Id)', using the lmm2met R package built on lme4's lmer procedure, to systematically minimize subject-specific variation in each metabolite prior to multivariate analyses.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are unpaired single-sample-per-subject profiles with no repeated measurements or subject Id, so a random intercept '(1|Id)' cannot be defined No patient metadata are available to serve as fixed effects, leaving nothing for the LMM to adjust beyond the random intercept The input is already a normalized/processed feature table intended directly for classification, and you only need feature selection (e.g. VIP > 1) rather than signal readjustment

skills.description: Use when you have a computed correlation matrix (e.g. occor.r from omics features) and must pick a defensible r_threshold for building a co-occurrence network instead of choosing a cutoff arbitrarily.
skills.name: random-matrix-theory-threshold-estimation
skills.search_text: random-matrix-theory-threshold-estimation Use when you have a computed correlation matrix (e.g. occor.r from omics features) and must pick a defensible r_threshold for building a co-occurrence network instead of choosing a cutoff arbitrarily. The correlation threshold is already prescribed by the study design or prior protocol — RMT re-derivation is unnecessary and may conflict with the fixed cutoff. The similarity structure is not a linear correlation matrix — the article notes correlation-based network optimization may overlook complex, non-linear, or indirect associations. You need full multi-omics cross-layer network construction rather than threshold determination — use multi_net_build / c_net_set workflows instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 Determines an objective correlation cutoff (r_threshold) for co-occurrence network edges by sweeping candidate cutoffs in MetaNet and selecting the one whose thresholded correlation matrix best matches the random matrix theory (RMT) eigenvalue-spacing expectation, replacing subjective manual threshold choice. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.06.26.661636
skills.summary: Determines an objective correlation cutoff (r_threshold) for co-occurrence network edges by sweeping candidate cutoffs in MetaNet and selecting the one whose thresholded correlation matrix best matches the random matrix theory (RMT) eigenvalue-spacing expectation, replacing subjective manual threshold choice.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The correlation threshold is already prescribed by the study design or prior protocol — RMT re-derivation is unnecessary and may conflict with the fixed cutoff. The similarity structure is not a linear correlation matrix — the article notes correlation-based network optimization may overlook complex, non-linear, or indirect associations. You need full multi-omics cross-layer network construction rather than threshold determination — use multi_net_build / c_net_set workflows instead.

skills.description: Use when you need to tune or characterize the collision probability P(m,n)([x_i,x_j]) of an LSH scheme as a function of pair similarity, e.g. to pick (m,n) settings like (32,16), (64,32) or (32,32) for signal/noise classification.
skills.name: random-projection-locality-sensitive-hashing-implementation
skills.search_text: random-projection-locality-sensitive-hashing-implementation Use when you need to tune or characterize the collision probability P(m,n)([x_i,x_j]) of an LSH scheme as a function of pair similarity, e.g. to pick (m,n) settings like (32,16), (64,32) or (32,32) for signal/noise classification. The goal is explicit candidate scoring rather than probabilistic retrieval: the article's pipeline selects candidates via LSH and then computes cosine similarity explicitly for each candidate isotope pattern, so LSH alone does not replace explicit similarity scoring The signal of interest is self-similar chemical noise (repeated contaminants), which the LSH approach would misclassify as true signal Signals with low relative intensity to noise peaks are the target, since the similarity measure on which the LSH is based drops and such signals can be lost http://edamontology.org/topic_3524 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Implements a random-projection locality-sensitive hash h(x) = sign(<x,r>) for random unit vectors r and composes it into the paper's augmented LSH scheme with n AND-connectives and m OR-connectives, so that the (m,n) pair sets the effective similarity threshold for window-pair collisions. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-022-04833-5
skills.summary: Implements a random-projection locality-sensitive hash h(x) = sign(<x,r>) for random unit vectors r and composes it into the paper's augmented LSH scheme with n AND-connectives and m OR-connectives, so that the (m,n) pair sets the effective similarity threshold for window-pair collisions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is explicit candidate scoring rather than probabilistic retrieval: the article's pipeline selects candidates via LSH and then computes cosine similarity explicitly for each candidate isotope pattern, so LSH alone does not replace explicit similarity scoring The signal of interest is self-similar chemical noise (repeated contaminants), which the LSH approach would misclassify as true signal Signals with low relative intensity to noise peaks are the target, since the similarity measure on which the LSH is based drops and such signals can be lost

skills.description: Use when performing open modification spectral library searching against large libraries (e.g. NIST human HCD or MassIVE-KB), where exhaustive shifted-dot-product comparison of every query against all library spectra is too slow and a limited candidate set suffices.
skills.name: random-projection-tree-index-construction
skills.search_text: random-projection-tree-index-construction Use when performing open modification spectral library searching against large libraries (e.g. NIST human HCD or MassIVE-KB), where exhaustive shifted-dot-product comparison of every query against all library spectra is too slow and a limited candidate set suffices. When an exact search is required — the index is deliberately approximate; the paper tolerates this only because a large number of candidates is returned, so do not use it when guaranteed retrieval of all nearest neighbors is mandatory For small libraries where exhaustive brute-force comparison is already fast enough — the ANN index overhead is not justified When searching for unmodified peptides in the first cascade level — the paper uses a cascade search where unmodified peptides are identified before the open search that needs ANN candidate selection http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Constructs an ensemble of random projection trees over sparse 1-Da-binned spectral library vectors (ANN-SoLo) so that a limited, high-recall candidate set of library spectra can be retrieved per query during open modification searching instead of brute-force comparison. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.8b00359
skills.summary: Constructs an ensemble of random projection trees over sparse 1-Da-binned spectral library vectors (ANN-SoLo) so that a limited, high-recall candidate set of library spectra can be retrieved per query during open modification searching instead of brute-force comparison.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When an exact search is required — the index is deliberately approximate; the paper tolerates this only because a large number of candidates is returned, so do not use it when guaranteed retrieval of all nearest neighbors is mandatory For small libraries where exhaustive brute-force comparison is already fast enough — the ANN index overhead is not justified When searching for unmodified peptides in the first cascade level — the paper uses a cascade search where unmodified peptides are identified before the open search that needs ANN candidate selection

skills.description: Use when you need to benchmark a gap-filling approach (e.g., COMMIT vs. individual gap filling) by injecting controlled corruption—randomly removed reactions—into published species models and scoring recovery by precision and recall.
skills.name: random-reaction-removal-perturbation
skills.search_text: random-reaction-removal-perturbation Use when you need to benchmark a gap-filling approach (e.g., COMMIT vs. individual gap filling) by injecting controlled corruption—randomly removed reactions—into published species models and scoring recovery by precision and recall. The models are already complete and you only need to compare their reaction sets directly—no perturbation or gap-filling benchmark is needed. The question is whether a model can grow on a defined medium rather than how well gap filling recovers removed reactions—use growth/feasibility simulations instead. You only have a single-species draft model with no community composition available—COMMIT's community-aware advantage cannot be exercised, so individual gap filling is the appropriate target. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 A validation protocol that randomly deletes a known fraction of reactions (1%, 2%, 5%, 10%, repeated 50 times per fraction) from published species models, then measures how well a gap-filling method recovers the removed reactions using precision and recall. Used here to show that COMMIT's community-aware gap filling slightly outperforms individual gap filling on the D. vulgaris / M. maripaludis two-species community. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009906
skills.summary: A validation protocol that randomly deletes a known fraction of reactions (1%, 2%, 5%, 10%, repeated 50 times per fraction) from published species models, then measures how well a gap-filling method recovers the removed reactions using precision and recall. Used here to show that COMMIT's community-aware gap filling slightly outperforms individual gap filling on the D. vulgaris / M. maripaludis two-species community.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The models are already complete and you only need to compare their reaction sets directly—no perturbation or gap-filling benchmark is needed. The question is whether a model can grow on a defined medium rather than how well gap filling recovers removed reactions—use growth/feasibility simulations instead. You only have a single-species draft model with no community composition available—COMMIT's community-aware advantage cannot be exercised, so individual gap filling is the appropriate target.

skills.description: Use when an MS-DIAL-derived feature abundance table in an untargeted LC-MS/MS metabolomics workflow contains NA values that must be filled before normalization or statistical testing, and low-abundance-proportional imputation is desired.
skills.name: random-value-imputation-with-minimum-scaling
skills.search_text: random-value-imputation-with-minimum-scaling Use when an MS-DIAL-derived feature abundance table in an untargeted LC-MS/MS metabolomics workflow contains NA values that must be filled before normalization or statistical testing, and low-abundance-proportional imputation is desired. The feature abundance table contains no NA values — margheRita skips imputation and reports 'No NAs: imputation not performed.' Missingness is extensive or non-random and a model-based strategy is preferred (e.g. notame recommends random forest imputation for missing values) The input is raw instrument data or an already-normalized matrix rather than a preprocessed MS-DIAL feature abundance table feeding the margheRita filtering() chain http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Imputes missing (NA) metabolite abundances in an LC-MS/MS feature table by drawing a seeded random number between 10% (a) and 25% (b) of the minimum observed value of the corresponding feature, as implemented in the margheRita filtering() pre-processing chain. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.06.20.599545
skills.summary: Imputes missing (NA) metabolite abundances in an LC-MS/MS feature table by drawing a seeded random number between 10% (a) and 25% (b) of the minimum observed value of the corresponding feature, as implemented in the margheRita filtering() pre-processing chain.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The feature abundance table contains no NA values — margheRita skips imputation and reports 'No NAs: imputation not performed.' Missingness is extensive or non-random and a model-based strategy is preferred (e.g. notame recommends random forest imputation for missing values) The input is raw instrument data or an already-normalized matrix rather than a preprocessed MS-DIAL feature abundance table feeding the margheRita filtering() chain

skills.description: Use when molecular networking (e.g. GNPS) leaves most nodes unannotated because NAP only propagates library matches to first neighbors, and you need walking probabilities for candidate structures not directly connected to any spectral match.
skills.name: random-walk-annotation-propagation
skills.search_text: random-walk-annotation-propagation Use when molecular networking (e.g. GNPS) leaves most nodes unannotated because NAP only propagates library matches to first neighbors, and you need walking probabilities for candidate structures not directly connected to any spectral match. Nodes of interest are direct first neighbors of spectral library matches — NAP's local propagation is sufficient and the random-walk machinery is unnecessary. The graph contains non-positive edge weights — RWR in pyrwr is defined only on positively weighted networks. Seed nodes exceed 10% of all nodes — propagation from such a large seed fraction is outside ChemWalker's tested regime. http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Propagate spectral library match annotations across molecular networks beyond first neighbors using ChemWalker: a MetFusion-weighted graph of the spectral network plus structural similarity among MetFrag candidate structures is submitted to random walk with restart (pyrwr) from seed nodes. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad078
skills.summary: Propagate spectral library match annotations across molecular networks beyond first neighbors using ChemWalker: a MetFusion-weighted graph of the spectral network plus structural similarity among MetFrag candidate structures is submitted to random walk with restart (pyrwr) from seed nodes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Nodes of interest are direct first neighbors of spectral library matches — NAP's local propagation is sufficient and the random-walk machinery is unnecessary. The graph contains non-positive edge weights — RWR in pyrwr is defined only on positively weighted networks. Seed nodes exceed 10% of all nodes — propagation from such a large seed fraction is outside ChemWalker's tested regime.

skills.description: Use when you need to benchmark runtime, memory and scalability of random-walk annotation propagation (e.g. ChemWalker vs NAP) on a molecular network benchmark, or validate performance claims about a propagation tool.
skills.name: random-walk-runtime-profiling
skills.search_text: random-walk-runtime-profiling Use when you need to benchmark runtime, memory and scalability of random-walk annotation propagation (e.g. ChemWalker vs NAP) on a molecular network benchmark, or validate performance claims about a propagation tool. Your goal is to compare annotation accuracy (top-10 candidate classification) rather than runtime — ChemWalker's top-10 classification cannot be statistically differentiated from NAP on this benchmark. The molecular network has not been preprocessed into the weighted graph format (MetFrag candidates plus MetFusion weights) required by the pyrwr-based propagation. You are profiling a propagation method other than a random-walk implementation (e.g. NAP itself) whose execution path differs from the pyrwr power-iteration pipeline. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Profile ChemWalker's random-walk propagation (pyrwr implementation) over the NIST 555-spectra weighted molecular network to measure wall-clock running time, memory usage and scalability, and compare against the NAP webserver baseline to validate the paper's qualitative improvement claims. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad078
skills.summary: Profile ChemWalker's random-walk propagation (pyrwr implementation) over the NIST 555-spectra weighted molecular network to measure wall-clock running time, memory usage and scalability, and compare against the NAP webserver baseline to validate the paper's qualitative improvement claims.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your goal is to compare annotation accuracy (top-10 candidate classification) rather than runtime — ChemWalker's top-10 classification cannot be statistically differentiated from NAP on this benchmark. The molecular network has not been preprocessed into the weighted graph format (MetFrag candidates plus MetFusion weights) required by the pyrwr-based propagation. You are profiling a propagation method other than a random-walk implementation (e.g. NAP itself) whose execution path differs from the pyrwr power-iteration pipeline.

skills.description: Use when annotating GNPS molecular networks where only ~10% of nodes have spectral library matches and you need annotations on nodes lacking a direct edge to any matched seed node.
skills.name: random-walk-seed-node-analysis
skills.search_text: random-walk-seed-node-analysis Use when annotating GNPS molecular networks where only ~10% of nodes have spectral library matches and you need annotations on nodes lacking a direct edge to any matched seed node. Every target node already has a direct neighbour with a spectral library match, so NAP-style local first-neighbour propagation suffices No candidate structures are available from in silico fragmentation (ChemWalker relies on MetFrag combinatorial fragmentation results) The graph contains non-positive edge weights — pyrwr's RWR is defined only on positively weighted networks http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Propagate spectral library match identities across a molecular network using random walk with restart (pyrwr) on a MetFusion-weighted graph, so that nodes with no direct neighbour matching a spectral library still receive candidate annotations. This extends annotation propagation beyond NAP's local first-neighbour limitation. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad078
skills.summary: Propagate spectral library match identities across a molecular network using random walk with restart (pyrwr) on a MetFusion-weighted graph, so that nodes with no direct neighbour matching a spectral library still receive candidate annotations. This extends annotation propagation beyond NAP's local first-neighbour limitation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Every target node already has a direct neighbour with a spectral library match, so NAP-style local first-neighbour propagation suffices No candidate structures are available from in silico fragmentation (ChemWalker relies on MetFrag combinatorial fragmentation results) The graph contains non-positive edge weights — pyrwr's RWR is defined only on positively weighted networks

skills.description: Use when a newly trained link-scoring function (e.g. IOKR on paired MIBiG/GNPS BGC-spectrum data) must be compared to a randomised baseline to quantify whether it ranks true links above chance, especially at low top-n.
skills.name: randomised-baseline-auc-evaluation
skills.search_text: randomised-baseline-auc-evaluation Use when a newly trained link-scoring function (e.g. IOKR on paired MIBiG/GNPS BGC-spectrum data) must be compared to a randomised baseline to quantify whether it ranks true links above chance, especially at low top-n. skills.search_text: rank-aggregation-evaluation Use when a molecule has multiple query spectra (e.g. three collision-energy levels) and you must choose between consensus-spectrum annotation versus aggregating per-spectrum candidate rankings, with rank@1 as the decision metric. Test molecules with fewer or more than exactly three spectra — the article limits this comparison to 'a subset of the test set for which a test molecule has exactly three spectra', so applying it to molecules with 1–2 or 4+ spectra extrapolates beyond the evidence. Single-spectrum annotation tasks where no aggregation decision exists — there is nothing to aggregate and the consensus-vs-ranking comparison is moot. Spectrum simulation or de novo generation challenges in MassSpecGym — this skill only addresses the molecule retrieval task's ranking aggregation choice. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Benchmarks whether annotating a molecule with multiple MS/MS spectra via an aggregate-then-rank consensus spectrum outperforms rank-then-aggregate strategies (average rank / reciprocal rank) on the MassSpecGym test set, using MVP's candidate-ranking views and rank@1 metrics. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.11.12.688047
skills.summary: Benchmarks whether annotating a molecule with multiple MS/MS spectra via an aggregate-then-rank consensus spectrum outperforms rank-then-aggregate strategies (average rank / reciprocal rank) on the MassSpecGym test set, using MVP's candidate-ranking views and rank@1 metrics.

Single-spectrum annotation tasks where no aggregation decision exists — there is nothing to aggregate and the consensus-vs-ranking comparison is moot. skills.description: Decision support for comparing candidate-ranking tools (e.g. JESTR vs SIRIUS vs CFM-ID) when each tool outputs a ranked candidate list per query spectrum and you need a single, interpretable top-1 accuracy figure plus a percent-improvement delta on matched test subsets.
skills.name: rank-at-1-metric-comparison
skills.search_text: rank-at-1-metric-comparison Decision support for comparing candidate-ranking tools (e.g. JESTR vs SIRIUS vs CFM-ID) when each tool outputs a ranked candidate list per query spectrum and you need a single, interpretable top-1 accuracy figure plus a percent-improvement delta on matched test subsets. The task is to evaluate ranking quality beyond the top hit — use the full rank@[1-20] sweep instead, since rank@1 ignores deeper positions where the paper reports 55.5%–302.6% gains. Tools are evaluated on different query subsets or candidate pools — percent improvement is only meaningful on matched subsets, e.g. filtered MassSpecGym subsets excluding molecules seen in SIRIUS/CFM-ID pre-training. A stochastic tool's output varies across runs and only a single run is available — medians over repeated runs are needed for stable percent-improvement figures. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Compute and compare rank@1 (top-1 candidate ranking accuracy) across annotation tools on the same query spectra subsets, then express tool differences as percent improvement. This is the core metric used by JESTR to demonstrate gains over SIRIUS and CFM-ID on MassSpecGym subsets. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btaf354
skills.summary: Compute and compare rank@1 (top-1 candidate ranking accuracy) across annotation tools on the same query spectra subsets, then express tool differences as percent improvement. This is the core metric used by JESTR to demonstrate gains over SIRIUS and CFM-ID on MassSpecGym subsets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is to evaluate ranking quality beyond the top hit — use the full rank@[1-20] sweep instead, since rank@1 ignores deeper positions where the paper reports 55.5%–302.6% gains. Tools are evaluated on different query subsets or candidate pools — percent improvement is only meaningful on matched subsets, e.g. filtered MassSpecGym subsets excluding molecules seen in SIRIUS/CFM-ID pre-training. A stochastic tool's output varies across runs and only a single run is available — medians over repeated runs are needed for stable percent-improvement figures.

skills.description: Reference for evaluating molecular retrieval models on MassSpecGym when you have per-query ranked candidate lists and need rank@1 scores under the by-mass and by-formula candidate conditions.
skills.name: rank-at-k-metric-computation
skills.search_text: rank-at-k-metric-computation Reference for evaluating molecular retrieval models on MassSpecGym when you have per-query ranked candidate lists and need rank@1 scores under the by-mass and by-formula candidate conditions. When the task is de novo molecule generation or spectrum simulation rather than retrieval/ranking of candidate structures — MassSpecGym defines these as separate challenges with different metrics. When aggregating rankings from constituent spectra for molecules that do not have exactly three spectra (the rank-aggregation comparison is limited to the 1,531 test molecules with exactly three spectra, one per collision energy level). When evaluating on custom candidate pools not derived from MassSpecGym's by-mass/by-formula retrieval conditions, since the published rank@1 baselines (35.99%/13.96% consensus, 26.37%/11.10% individual) assume those conditions. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_0219 Computes rank@1 retrieval metrics for molecular candidate ranking on the MassSpecGym benchmark, where a model scores a ranked list of candidate structures for each query MS/MS spectrum and the metric measures whether the ground-truth molecule is ranked first. It is the primary evaluation metric used to compare MVP against MIST, ESP, and JESTR for both candidates-by-mass and candidates-by-formula conditions. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.11.12.688047
skills.summary: Computes rank@1 retrieval metrics for molecular candidate ranking on the MassSpecGym benchmark, where a model scores a ranked list of candidate structures for each query MS/MS spectrum and the metric measures whether the ground-truth molecule is ranked first. It is the primary evaluation metric used to compare MVP against MIST, ESP, and JESTR for both candidates-by-mass and candidates-by-formula conditions.

skills.description: Use when a metabolite abundance table (e.g., SMART narcotics or breast cancer demonstrative data) shows high variance and non-normally distributed metabolite abundances that would compromise downstream association or classification analysis.
skills.name: rank-based-inverse-normal-transformation
skills.search_text: rank-based-inverse-normal-transformation Use when a metabolite abundance table (e.g., SMART narcotics or breast cancer demonstrative data) shows high variance and non-normally distributed metabolite abundances that would compromise downstream association or classification analysis. skills.summary: Apply RINT, a new data normalization module in SMART 2.0, to metabolite abundance tables so each metabolite's distribution is mapped to a standard normal scale, stabilizing variance and facilitating downstream statistical analysis alongside Pareto scaling (PS).

skills.search_text: rank-correlation-statistics Use when two chemical prioritization/ranking schemes (e.g., risk index vs. PrHQ) cover overlapping substances and you need to quantify whether their rank orders agree via a Pearson correlation coefficient. The two rankings do not share overlapping chemicals, so paired rank statistics cannot be computed You need concordance of ordinal/tied ranks rather than linear correlation — a rank-based coefficient (e.g., Spearman/Kendall) should be considered instead of assuming Pearson on ranks is adequate The goal is toxicity-only prioritization without an exposure term; the PrHQ or ToxPi-only pathway applies, not the RI-vs-PrHQ comparison http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 Computes and interprets a Pearson correlation between two chemical prioritization schemes — here the risk index (RI = rescaled log-normalized SEEM exposure × ToxPi score) ranks and the probabilistic hazard quotient (PrHQ) ranks — to quantify agreement between risk- and hazard-driven rankings over overlapping chemicals. metabolomics/v3 10.1289/ehp7722
skills.summary: Computes and interprets a Pearson correlation between two chemical prioritization schemes — here the risk index (RI = rescaled log-normalized SEEM exposure × ToxPi score) ranks and the probabilistic hazard quotient (PrHQ) ranks — to quantify agreement between risk- and hazard-driven rankings over overlapping chemicals.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The two rankings do not share overlapping chemicals, so paired rank statistics cannot be computed You need concordance of ordinal/tied ranks rather than linear correlation — a rank-based coefficient (e.g., Spearman/Kendall) should be considered instead of assuming Pearson on ranks is adequate The goal is toxicity-only prioritization without an exposure term; the PrHQ or ToxPi-only pathway applies, not the RI-vs-PrHQ comparison
