skills.description: Use when a reimplementation or rerun of an aggregation/prioritization pipeline (GNPS + Sirius + ISDB-LOTUS indicators) must be validated by reproducing specific per-feature ranks reported in a publication.
skills.name: rank-reproducibility-verification-against-published-values
skills.search_text: rank-reproducibility-verification-against-published-values Use when a reimplementation or rerun of an aggregation/prioritization pipeline (GNPS + Sirius + ISDB-LOTUS indicators) must be validated by reproducing specific per-feature ranks reported in a publication. The dataset lacks the required FBMN export pair (quantitative .csv + .mgf) or the Sirius structure_identifications.tsv, so the three-tool aggregation cannot be run as published No published/reference rank values exist for the dataset, in which case a direct k-ranking run is appropriate rather than a reproducibility verification Only raw MS/MS spectra are available without GNPS, Sirius, and ISDB-LOTUS annotation outputs — the k pipeline aggregates these three, not raw spectra http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Reproduce a published feature-prioritization ranking (here the MS2DECIDE k-pipeline over 754 LC-MS/MS ion features of the Pleiocarpa mutica alkaloid extract) and verify that node-level ranks match the values reported in the article, e.g. pleiomutine (m/z 631.3986) at rank 525/754. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/cmtd.202400088
skills.summary: Reproduce a published feature-prioritization ranking (here the MS2DECIDE k-pipeline over 754 LC-MS/MS ion features of the Pleiocarpa mutica alkaloid extract) and verify that node-level ranks match the values reported in the article, e.g. pleiomutine (m/z 631.3986) at rank 525/754.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset lacks the required FBMN export pair (quantitative .csv + .mgf) or the Sirius structure_identifications.tsv, so the three-tool aggregation cannot be run as published No published/reference rank values exist for the dataset, in which case a direct k-ranking run is appropriate rather than a reproducibility verification Only raw MS/MS spectra are available without GNPS, Sirius, and ISDB-LOTUS annotation outputs — the k pipeline aggregates these three, not raw spectra

skills.description: Use when you need to benchmark a retention-order predictor's generalizability across many independent RPLC datasets and present the rank-score distribution against a fingerprint baseline.
skills.name: rank-score-distribution-visualization
skills.search_text: rank-score-distribution-visualization Use when you need to benchmark a retention-order predictor's generalizability across many independent RPLC datasets and present the rank-score distribution against a fingerprint baseline. The candidate molecules are outside the conventional elemental restrictions of C, H, N, O, P, and S, or the chromatographic system is HILIC rather than RPLC at eluent pH around 2.7 — ROASMI does not generalize to these spaces. The two compounds' chromatographic peaks are too close (indistinguishable pairs, e.g. 4-hydroxybenzoic acid vs 2,5-dihydroxybenzoic acid) — their retention order is not reproducible and rank-score visualization would overstate distinguishability. You already have per-dataset retention-order metrics and only need to compare top-k or MS/MS score integration results rather than assess rank-score generalizability. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Aggregates per-dataset retention-order rank scores from the ROASMI ensemble (D-MPNN embeddings plus RankNet) and the Morgan_count fingerprint baseline across 71 independent RPLC datasets, and visualizes the resulting rank-score distributions and average comparisons (0.696 vs 0.795) as Fig. 5 panels. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-025-00968-8
skills.summary: Aggregates per-dataset retention-order rank scores from the ROASMI ensemble (D-MPNN embeddings plus RankNet) and the Morgan_count fingerprint baseline across 71 independent RPLC datasets, and visualizes the resulting rank-score distributions and average comparisons (0.696 vs 0.795) as Fig. 5 panels.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The candidate molecules are outside the conventional elemental restrictions of C, H, N, O, P, and S, or the chromatographic system is HILIC rather than RPLC at eluent pH around 2.7 — ROASMI does not generalize to these spaces. The two compounds' chromatographic peaks are too close (indistinguishable pairs, e.g. 4-hydroxybenzoic acid vs 2,5-dihydroxybenzoic acid) — their retention order is not reproducible and rank-score visualization would overstate distinguishability. You already have per-dataset retention-order metrics and only need to compare top-k or MS/MS score integration results rather than assess rank-score generalizability.

skills.description: Use when ranks of features (e.g. genes) are available from two or more independent replicate experiments and you need the theoretical null CDF of the maximum rank statistic to estimate pi1 or assign marginal FDRs to reproducible features.
skills.name: rank-statistic-null-distribution-derivation
skills.search_text: rank-statistic-null-distribution-derivation Use when ranks of features (e.g. genes) are available from two or more independent replicate experiments and you need the theoretical null CDF of the maximum rank statistic to estimate pi1 or assign marginal FDRs to reproducible features. Input is raw expression/counts data rather than feature rank lists — MaRR's derivations operate on ranks and require per-replicate rankings first The dependence structure of reproducible features cannot satisfy the nonnegative rank-correlation assumption (assumption I2) or irreproducible features lack independent ranks (assumption I3), since the null CDF derivation relies on these assumptions A parametric, model-based joint distribution of reproducible features is preferred and its assumptions are justified — MaRR is explicitly nonparametric and makes no parametric assumptions on reproducible-gene dependence or distributions http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Derives the marginal null distribution of maximum-rank statistics (fn,0, the pi1-weighted CDF F_n,pi1, and its k-replicate generalization such as Mg(3)=max{Rgx,Rgy,Rgz}) that underpins the MaRR reproducibility procedure. These closed-form distributions enable nonparametric estimation of the reproducible signal proportion pi1 and marginal FDR control without tuning parameters. metabolomics/v3 10.1080/01621459.2017.1397521
skills.summary: Derives the marginal null distribution of maximum-rank statistics (fn,0, the pi1-weighted CDF F_n,pi1, and its k-replicate generalization such as Mg(3)=max{Rgx,Rgy,Rgz}) that underpins the MaRR reproducibility procedure. These closed-form distributions enable nonparametric estimation of the reproducible signal proportion pi1 and marginal FDR control without tuning parameters.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw expression/counts data rather than feature rank lists — MaRR's derivations operate on ranks and require per-replicate rankings first The dependence structure of reproducible features cannot satisfy the nonnegative rank-correlation assumption (assumption I2) or irreproducible features lack independent ranks (assumption I3), since the null CDF derivation relies on these assumptions A parametric, model-based joint distribution of reproducible features is preferred and its assumptions are justified — MaRR is explicitly nonparametric and makes no parametric assumptions on reproducible-gene dependence or distributions

skills.description: Use when benchmarking a rank-based reproducibility method under realistic correlation decay — e.g., testing whether MaRR maintains FDR, power, and low bias when correlation between replicate pairs decreases with rank.
skills.name: rank-statistic-simulation-generation
skills.search_text: rank-statistic-simulation-generation Use when benchmarking a rank-based reproducibility method under realistic correlation decay — e.g., testing whether MaRR maintains FDR, power, and low bias when correlation between replicate pairs decreases with rank. The goal is not simulation-based benchmarking but reproducibility assessment on real MS-Metabolomics replicate data (Tech, BioTech, Bio datasets), which uses the Real_Data folder workflows instead A comprehensive evaluation of pre-processing steps (imputation: BPCA/kNN; normalization: quantile/median/RUV) is the goal — the paper states the aim was only to benchmark comparisons, not evaluate pipelines http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Generate simulated replicate datasets in which the correlation between replicate pairs decreases linearly with rank, then apply the nonparametric MaRR maximal rank statistic to assess FDR control, power (1-NDR), and bias in estimating the proportion of reproducible signals. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-021-04336-9
skills.summary: Generate simulated replicate datasets in which the correlation between replicate pairs decreases linearly with rank, then apply the nonparametric MaRR maximal rank statistic to assess FDR control, power (1-NDR), and bias in estimating the proportion of reproducible signals.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is not simulation-based benchmarking but reproducibility assessment on real MS-Metabolomics replicate data (Tech, BioTech, Bio datasets), which uses the Real_Data folder workflows instead A comprehensive evaluation of pre-processing steps (imputation: BPCA/kNN; normalization: quantile/median/RUV) is the goal — the paper states the aim was only to benchmark comparisons, not evaluate pipelines

skills.description: Use when you have both feature-wise test results with FDR-adjusted p-values and multivariate model (e.g., RF 'mid' model) importance ranks, and you need one ordered shortlist of robust features for metabolite identification.
skills.name: rank-sum-selection-scoring
skills.search_text: rank-sum-selection-scoring Use when you have both feature-wise test results with FDR-adjusted p-values and multivariate model (e.g., RF 'mid' model) importance ranks, and you need one ordered shortlist of robust features for metabolite identification. Only one line of evidence exists (e.g., feature-wise FDR results but no multivariate importance ranks) — a single-rank sort, not rank-sum scoring, is appropriate Input is raw LC-MS vendor data or a peak table not yet preprocessed and statistically analyzed; notame expects preprocessed LC-MS data before statistical selection http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 Combines per-feature statistical significance (FDR q-value rank) with multivariate model importance rank (e.g., MUVR random forest) by summing the two ranks into a single 'Final Ranks' column, so the most robust LC-MS metabolic features can be prioritized for identification. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo10040135
skills.summary: Combines per-feature statistical significance (FDR q-value rank) with multivariate model importance rank (e.g., MUVR random forest) by summing the two ranks into a single 'Final Ranks' column, so the most robust LC-MS metabolic features can be prioritized for identification.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only one line of evidence exists (e.g., feature-wise FDR results but no multivariate importance ranks) — a single-rank sort, not rank-sum scoring, is appropriate Input is raw LC-MS vendor data or a peak table not yet preprocessed and statistically analyzed; notame expects preprocessed LC-MS data before statistical selection

skills.description: Use when two reproducibility-assessment methods have each declared top-k reproducible transcripts from replicate rank lists and an external gold-standard subset (e.g., 1129 Taqman PCR transcripts) is available to judge which method's method-specific genes are more biologically relevant.
skills.name: ranked-gene-list-overlap-analysis
skills.search_text: ranked-gene-list-overlap-analysis Use when two reproducibility-assessment methods have each declared top-k reproducible transcripts from replicate rank lists and an external gold-standard subset (e.g., 1129 Taqman PCR transcripts) is available to judge which method's method-specific genes are more biologically relevant. The experiment lacks an external gold-standard subset (e.g., Taqman PCR measurements) for only a fraction of transcripts — without it, method-specific genes cannot be ranked by PCR rank and the t-test comparison is undefined Only one method's reproducible set is available — this skill is designed for pairwise comparison at matched k, so a single top-k set cannot be validated relatively The goal is the reproducibility discovery itself (ranked-list reproducibility assessment with FDR control) rather than post-hoc external validation of already-declared top-k sets http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 External validation of reproducibility methods (MaRR vs a copula mixture model) by intersecting each method's top-k reproducible transcript sets with a Taqman PCR gold-standard subset and comparing PCR-measurement ranks of method-specific genes via two-sample t-tests. metabolomics/v3 10.1080/01621459.2017.1397521
skills.summary: External validation of reproducibility methods (MaRR vs a copula mixture model) by intersecting each method's top-k reproducible transcript sets with a Taqman PCR gold-standard subset and comparing PCR-measurement ranks of method-specific genes via two-sample t-tests.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The experiment lacks an external gold-standard subset (e.g., Taqman PCR measurements) for only a fraction of transcripts — without it, method-specific genes cannot be ranked by PCR rank and the t-test comparison is undefined Only one method's reproducible set is available — this skill is designed for pairwise comparison at matched k, so a single top-k set cannot be validated relatively The goal is the reproducibility discovery itself (ranked-list reproducibility assessment with FDR control) rather than post-hoc external validation of already-declared top-k sets

skills.description: Use when training a retention-order model from pairwise elution comparisons of molecular pairs rather than absolute RT regression, e.g. when chromatographic RTs are non-replicable across methods but relative elution orders are consistent.
skills.name: ranknet-pairwise-loss-implementation
skills.search_text: ranknet-pairwise-loss-implementation Use when training a retention-order model from pairwise elution comparisons of molecular pairs rather than absolute RT regression, e.g. when chromatographic RTs are non-replicable across methods but relative elution orders are consistent. The chromatographic system is HILIC rather than RPLC — ROASMI currently applies only to RPLC systems and HILIC generalizable models are future work. Compounds lie outside the elemental restrictions of C, H, N, O, P, and S — model applicability is limited to conventional compounds within these elements. Absolute retention times are the target; RankNet learns pairwise elution order, not RT values. http://edamontology.org/topic_3336 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Implementation of the RankNet (Ranking Neural Network) pairwise loss used in ROASMI to learn elution order: the loss is binary cross-entropy between the sigmoid of predicted retention scores — the pairwise probability P_ij that compound Ci elutes before Cj — and the observed pairwise elution-order label. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-025-00968-8
skills.summary: Implementation of the RankNet (Ranking Neural Network) pairwise loss used in ROASMI to learn elution order: the loss is binary cross-entropy between the sigmoid of predicted retention scores — the pairwise probability P_ij that compound Ci elutes before Cj — and the observed pairwise elution-order label.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The chromatographic system is HILIC rather than RPLC — ROASMI currently applies only to RPLC systems and HILIC generalizable models are future work. Compounds lie outside the elemental restrictions of C, H, N, O, P, and S — model applicability is limited to conventional compounds within these elements. Absolute retention times are the target; RankNet learns pairwise elution order, not RT values.

skills.description: Use when you need to retrain ROASMI on a user-defined RPLC reference set (e.g. dataset_83/dataset_84) and predict pair-wise retention scores to rank candidate molecules for small-molecule identification.
skills.name: ranknet-retention-prediction
skills.search_text: ranknet-retention-prediction Use when you need to retrain ROASMI on a user-defined RPLC reference set (e.g. dataset_83/dataset_84) and predict pair-wise retention scores to rank candidate molecules for small-molecule identification. Retention data were measured under HILIC or other non-RPLC chromatographic systems — ROASMI applies only to RPLC at eluent pH ~2.7 and HILIC generalizability is still future work Compounds contain elements outside C, H, N, O, P, and S — the model is restricted to this elemental chemical space Two candidate molecules' chromatographic peaks are close enough that retention order is not consistent across experiments — these indistinguishable pairs should be excluded from identification http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3345 Use a Ranking Neural Network (RankNet), coupled to a D-MPNN molecular embedding module (chemprop), to learn compound elution orders from RPLC reference sets and predict retention scores for candidate molecules in ROASMI. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-025-00968-8
skills.summary: Use a Ranking Neural Network (RankNet), coupled to a D-MPNN molecular embedding module (chemprop), to learn compound elution orders from RPLC reference sets and predict retention scores for candidate molecules in ROASMI.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Retention data were measured under HILIC or other non-RPLC chromatographic systems — ROASMI applies only to RPLC at eluent pH ~2.7 and HILIC generalizability is still future work Compounds contain elements outside C, H, N, O, P, and S — the model is restricted to this elemental chemical space Two candidate molecules' chromatographic peaks are close enough that retention order is not consistent across experiments — these indistinguishable pairs should be excluded from identification

skills.description: Use when quantifying how much labeled retention time data from the target chromatographic system is needed, or when comparing single-system training against training on all heterogeneous LC systems at varying target-data fractions.
skills.name: ranksvm-learning-curve-experiment
skills.search_text: ranksvm-learning-curve-experiment Use when quantifying how much labeled retention time data from the target chromatographic system is needed, or when comparing single-system training against training on all heterogeneous LC systems at varying target-data fractions. When the target question is absolute retention time accuracy on a single system without varying training-set size — use the baseline_single scenario (Tables 3/4) instead When the goal is to evaluate multi-system benefit at full training size with the target system left single-out — the all_on_one scenario (LTSO=False columns of Table 4) is the appropriate fixed-size variant When the analysis concerns metabolite identification performance combined with MS/MS scores (met_ident_perf_GS_BS scenario / IOKR integration), not learning curves http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Runs retention-order learning-curve experiments in which the percentage of target-system retention time measurements used for training is varied, comparing RankSVM (and SVR) pairwise accuracy under single-system (baseline_single_perc) versus all-systems (all_on_one_perc) training to reproduce Figure 4 trends. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/bty590
skills.summary: Runs retention-order learning-curve experiments in which the percentage of target-system retention time measurements used for training is varied, comparing RankSVM (and SVR) pairwise accuracy under single-system (baseline_single_perc) versus all-systems (all_on_one_perc) training to reproduce Figure 4 trends.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the target question is absolute retention time accuracy on a single system without varying training-set size — use the baseline_single scenario (Tables 3/4) instead When the goal is to evaluate multi-system benefit at full training size with the target system left single-out — the all_on_one scenario (LTSO=False columns of Table 4) is the appropriate fixed-size variant When the analysis concerns metabolite identification performance combined with MS/MS scores (met_ident_perf_GS_BS scenario / IOKR integration), not learning curves

skills.description: Use when you have retention time measurements from one or more LC systems and need to predict elution order from molecular structure, especially when retention times are on incomparable scales across systems so pairwise preferences within a system are the only consistent supervision.
skills.name: ranksvm-pairwise-order-training
skills.search_text: ranksvm-pairwise-order-training Use when you have retention time measurements from one or more LC systems and need to predict elution order from molecular structure, especially when retention times are on incomparable scales across systems so pairwise preferences within a system are the only consistent supervision. The task is predicting absolute retention times on a common scale — use the SVR baseline instead; the paper notes SVR was 'limited in this capacity' to exploit data from other chromatographic systems, which is exactly the setting where RankSVM on pairwise order should be preferred. The training and target molecules come from different chromatographic systems but you intend to train on cross-system time comparisons — preferences must be built only within a system (s_i = s_j); cross-system pairs are not valid supervision. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Trains a ranking support vector machine (RankSVM) to predict the pairwise order in which molecules elute from an LC column, using molecular fingerprint kernels (MinMax on counting MACCS, Tanimoto on binary MACCS) and the dual Q = A K_m A^T decomposition so the full pairwise kernel matrix never has to be materialized. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/bty590
skills.summary: Trains a ranking support vector machine (RankSVM) to predict the pairwise order in which molecules elute from an LC column, using molecular fingerprint kernels (MinMax on counting MACCS, Tanimoto on binary MACCS) and the dual Q = A K_m A^T decomposition so the full pairwise kernel matrix never has to be materialized.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is predicting absolute retention times on a common scale — use the SVR baseline instead; the paper notes SVR was 'limited in this capacity' to exploit data from other chromatographic systems, which is exactly the setting where RankSVM on pairwise order should be preferred. The training and target molecules come from different chromatographic systems but you intend to train on cross-system time comparisons — preferences must be built only within a system (s_i = s_j); cross-system pairs are not valid supervision.

skills.description: Decision support for choosing between RANSAC and Join aligners in MZmine when aligning peak lists across LC-MS fractions, especially when feature counts exceed thousands of rows and alignment quality must be quantified.
skills.name: ransac-alignment-performance-comparison
skills.search_text: ransac-alignment-performance-comparison Decision support for choosing between RANSAC and Join aligners in MZmine when aligning peak lists across LC-MS fractions, especially when feature counts exceed thousands of rows and alignment quality must be quantified. Input is raw MS data not yet peak-picked — alignment comparison requires already-detected peak lists Only synthetic datasets with a single correct alignment are needed — for those, RANSAC already achieved 100% precision and recall, so a comparative Join benchmark adds little No ground-truth alignment table exists, making precision/recall computation impossible http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Benchmarks the MZmine 2 RANSAC peak list aligner against the Join aligner by computing precision and recall against ground-truth alignment tables, and attributes performance degradation to high feature counts (e.g. the P2 fraction 00 case with over 6800 rows). metabolomics/v3 10.1186/1471-2105-11-395
skills.summary: Benchmarks the MZmine 2 RANSAC peak list aligner against the Join aligner by computing precision and recall against ground-truth alignment tables, and attributes performance degradation to high feature counts (e.g. the P2 fraction 00 case with over 6800 rows).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw MS data not yet peak-picked — alignment comparison requires already-detected peak lists Only synthetic datasets with a single correct alignment are needed — for those, RANSAC already achieved 100% precision and recall, so a comparative Join benchmark adds little No ground-truth alignment table exists, making precision/recall computation impossible

skills.description: Use when annotating MS2 fragment peaks with chemical subformulae for a candidate molecular formula (e.g., MIST-CF pipeline) and you need a fast, tree-free peak-to-formula assignment instead of SIRIUS fragmentation tree computation.
skills.name: rdbe-constrained-fragment-formula-filtering
skills.search_text: rdbe-constrained-fragment-formula-filtering Use when annotating MS2 fragment peaks with chemical subformulae for a candidate molecular formula (e.g., MIST-CF pipeline) and you need a fast, tree-free peak-to-formula assignment instead of SIRIUS fragmentation tree computation. Negative-mode MS/MS data — MIST-CF models (and the subformula assignment step they consume) were trained only for positive-mode data Analyses that require explicit fragmentation-event relationships (arcs/losses between fragment formulae) rather than independent per-peak subformula labels — this routine deliberately avoids fragmentation tree construction Cases where the fragment subformulae may come from a different adduct than the precursor — the article notes 'we do not consider adduct switching in MS2 subformula assignment' http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 MIST-CF's internal subformula assignment step: after subtracting the precursor adduct mass from MS2 peak masses, candidate subformulae are enumerated via SIRIUS-style decomposition, filtered with an RDBE >= 0 heuristic, and each peak is matched to its nearest subformula within an instrument-specific ppm tolerance — replacing fragmentation tree construction. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jcim.3c01082
skills.summary: MIST-CF's internal subformula assignment step: after subtracting the precursor adduct mass from MS2 peak masses, candidate subformulae are enumerated via SIRIUS-style decomposition, filtered with an RDBE >= 0 heuristic, and each peak is matched to its nearest subformula within an instrument-specific ppm tolerance — replacing fragmentation tree construction.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Negative-mode MS/MS data — MIST-CF models (and the subformula assignment step they consume) were trained only for positive-mode data Analyses that require explicit fragmentation-event relationships (arcs/losses between fragment formulae) rather than independent per-peak subformula labels — this routine deliberately avoids fragmentation tree construction Cases where the fragment subformulae may come from a different adduct than the precursor — the article notes 'we do not consider adduct switching in MS2 subformula assignment'

skills.summary: Builds an RDF knowledge graph (ENPKG) from individually processed LC-HRMS2 metabolomics samples, integrating MZmine features, ISDB-LOTUS/SIRIUS annotations, and Open Tree of Life taxonomy as .ttl triples loadable in GraphDB. Replaces classical RT-based feature alignment with sample-centric, semantically queryable integration.

skills.search_text: rdkit-molecule-preprocessing Use when a metabolite or chemical structure dataset arrives as raw SMILES strings that need cleanup (salt stripping, charge neutralization, element/token filtering) before training or evaluating a chemical language model. Input is already a curated, canonical SMILES set that has previously passed charge-neutralization and token filtering — rerunning would risk unnecessary molecule loss. Downstream model does not operate on SMILES tokens (e.g., it consumes molecular descriptors or graphs directly) and rare-token elimination is irrelevant. The goal is not to train/evaluate a chemical language model but rather to generate in silico MS/MS libraries from already-generated structures that need no further canonicalization. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Standardize raw metabolite SMILES into canonical, model-ready strings using RDKit: parse molecules, strip light fragments/salts, neutralize charges, filter for valid elements and rare SMILES vocabulary tokens, then canonicalize for chemical language model training or evaluation. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.11.13.623458
skills.summary: Standardize raw metabolite SMILES into canonical, model-ready strings using RDKit: parse molecules, strip light fragments/salts, neutralize charges, filter for valid elements and rare SMILES vocabulary tokens, then canonicalize for chemical language model training or evaluation.

skills.description: Use when assembling structurally related compound pairs (e.g., from MS/MS libraries) where the heavier compound must contain the lighter compound as a substructure and exactly one bond links the matched and unmatched atoms.
skills.name: rdkit-substructure-matching
skills.search_text: rdkit-substructure-matching Use when assembling structurally related compound pairs (e.g., from MS/MS libraries) where the heavier compound must contain the lighter compound as a substructure and exactly one bond links the matched and unmatched atoms. The two compounds differ by more than one structural modification (edge count > 1), so the pair is not a valid single-modification analog. No substructure match exists between the compounds, meaning they are not analogs sharing a common substructure. The pair fails upstream eligibility filters (e.g., precursor mass ≥ 2000 Da or mass difference ≥ 50%), making substructure verification moot. http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 Use RDKit's GetSubstructMatch to confirm that a candidate analog pair shares a substructure relationship, enabling identification of the single structural modification linking a known compound to an unknown analog. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jasms.4c00061
skills.summary: Use RDKit's GetSubstructMatch to confirm that a candidate analog pair shares a substructure relationship, enabling identification of the single structural modification linking a known compound to an unknown analog.

No substructure match exists between the compounds, meaning they are not analogs sharing a common substructure. skills.search_text: reactant-product-classification Use when a pathway-metabolite association table (met_path) exists with KEGG reaction IDs and you must determine each metabolite's role (reactant vs product) in its reaction for mechanistic annotation. skills.description: Use when transcriptomics data (e.g. an FPKM table per cell line) must be converted into per-reaction scores via the GPR rules of a specific metabolic model (ENGRO2, Recon3D subset) to feed downstream RAS integration, t-tests or concordance analysis.
skills.name: reaction-activity-score-computation-from-gpr-rules
skills.search_text: reaction-activity-score-computation-from-gpr-rules Use when transcriptomics data (e.g. an FPKM table per cell line) must be converted into per-reaction scores via the GPR rules of a specific metabolic model (ENGRO2, Recon3D subset) to feed downstream RAS integration, t-tests or concordance analysis. Transcriptomics is already a per-reaction score table (e.g. a precomputed RAS file) — re-running getGPRsFromModel/getRASscore would duplicate work The analysis goal is flux-level or metabolomics-level prediction (randomSampling, createMetabolicDataset) rather than transcriptional reaction expression The metabolic model and the transcriptomics gene identifiers cannot be matched by any regex — the score would be undefined for most rules http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 Computes per-reaction activity scores for each cell line by propagating gene expression values through the gene-protein-reaction (GPR) rules extracted from a constraint-based metabolic model, as done in the INTEGRATE pipeline using ENGRO2 or Recon3D-derived models and FPKM breast transcriptomics data. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009337
skills.summary: Computes per-reaction activity scores for each cell line by propagating gene expression values through the gene-protein-reaction (GPR) rules extracted from a constraint-based metabolic model, as done in the INTEGRATE pipeline using ENGRO2 or Recon3D-derived models and FPKM breast transcriptomics data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Transcriptomics is already a per-reaction score table (e.g. a precomputed RAS file) — re-running getGPRsFromModel/getRASscore would duplicate work The analysis goal is flux-level or metabolomics-level prediction (randomSampling, createMetabolicDataset) rather than transcriptional reaction expression The metabolic model and the transcriptomics gene identifiers cannot be matched by any regex — the score would be undefined for most rules

skills.description: Use when you have a SBML metabolic model with GPR rules and a gene-level transcriptomics table (e.g. FPKM values for breast cancer cell lines) and need reaction-level expression scores for constraint-based flux analysis or multi-omics flux-regulation classification.
skills.name: reaction-activity-score-computation-from-transcriptomics
skills.search_text: reaction-activity-score-computation-from-transcriptomics Use when you have a SBML metabolic model with GPR rules and a gene-level transcriptomics table (e.g. FPKM values for breast cancer cell lines) and need reaction-level expression scores for constraint-based flux analysis or multi-omics flux-regulation classification. Input is a pre-computed reaction-level score file (e.g. already-computed RAS floats without GPR rules to resolve) — use the normalization step directly instead of re-running GPR extraction and score resolution Transcriptomics data are not gene-level measurements matched to the model's gene identifiers, or the model has no GPR rules to extract The goal is metabolomics-derived flux prediction (e.g. mass-action substrate-availability scoring) rather than transcriptomics-derived reaction expression scoring http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_2259 http://edamontology.org/topic_3922 Computes per-cell-line Reaction Activity Scores (RAS) by resolving the GPR logical rules of a constraint-based metabolic model (e.g. ENGRO2) over transcriptomics data: taking the minimum transcript value across AND-linked genes (enzyme subunits) and the sum across OR-linked genes (isoforms). These RAS values are the transcriptomics-derived input for INTEGRATE's cell-relative model integration and downstream regulation-classification steps. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009337
skills.summary: Computes per-cell-line Reaction Activity Scores (RAS) by resolving the GPR logical rules of a constraint-based metabolic model (e.g. ENGRO2) over transcriptomics data: taking the minimum transcript value across AND-linked genes (enzyme subunits) and the sum across OR-linked genes (isoforms). These RAS values are the transcriptomics-derived input for INTEGRATE's cell-relative model integration and downstream regulation-classification steps.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a pre-computed reaction-level score file (e.g. already-computed RAS floats without GPR rules to resolve) — use the normalization step directly instead of re-running GPR extraction and score resolution Transcriptomics data are not gene-level measurements matched to the model's gene identifiers, or the model has no GPR rules to extract The goal is metabolomics-derived flux prediction (e.g. mass-action substrate-availability scoring) rather than transcriptomics-derived reaction expression scoring

skills.description: Use when comparing transcriptomics-derived RAS scores and sampled-flux FFD significance across sample pairs to identify reactions whose flux variation is concordant with substrate-availability (metabolic) versus enzyme-expression (transcriptional) regulation in a constraint-based model such as.
skills.name: reaction-activity-score-statistical-testing
skills.search_text: reaction-activity-score-statistical-testing Use when comparing transcriptomics-derived RAS scores and sampled-flux FFD significance across sample pairs to identify reactions whose flux variation is concordant with substrate-availability (metabolic) versus enzyme-expression (transcriptional) regulation in a constraint-based model such as. When only transcriptomics data are available and no intracellular metabolomics / sampled flux solutions exist to compute FFD concordance. When the goal is to test metabolomics differences directly (e.g. raw metabolite abundance tests) rather than to classify reaction-level flux regulation; use the metabolomics t-test outputs alone. When the input model is fully reversible with no irreversible-split model available, since RAS t-tests are computed on the irreversible-split reaction set. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Statistical testing of Reaction Activity Scores (RAS) and flux fold-differences (FFD) from INTEGRATE: pairwise t-tests on RAS across cell-line pairs, Mann-Whitney U tests on randomly sampled steady-state flux solutions, and concordance analysis with Cohen's kappa to classify flux regulation as metabolic, transcriptional, or combined. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009337
skills.summary: Statistical testing of Reaction Activity Scores (RAS) and flux fold-differences (FFD) from INTEGRATE: pairwise t-tests on RAS across cell-line pairs, Mann-Whitney U tests on randomly sampled steady-state flux solutions, and concordance analysis with Cohen's kappa to classify flux regulation as metabolic, transcriptional, or combined.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When only transcriptomics data are available and no intracellular metabolomics / sampled flux solutions exist to compute FFD concordance. When the goal is to test metabolomics differences directly (e.g. raw metabolite abundance tests) rather than to classify reaction-level flux regulation; use the metabolomics t-test outputs alone. When the input model is fully reversible with no irreversible-split model available, since RAS t-tests are computed on the irreversible-split reaction set.

skills.description: Use when a concordance table of Cohen's kappa and Pearson correlation scores (RPS vs RAS, RPS vs FFD) exists and reactions with statistically significant RPS–FFD concordance must be identified after multiple-comparison correction.
skills.name: reaction-activity-score-statistics
skills.search_text: reaction-activity-score-statistics Use when a concordance table of Cohen's kappa and Pearson correlation scores (RPS vs RAS, RPS vs FFD) exists and reactions with statistically significant RPS–FFD concordance must be identified after multiple-comparison correction. The goal is to compute the raw concordance scores themselves rather than test their significance — use the upstream concordanceAnalysis step instead Only a small number of reactions are tested and no multiple-comparison correction is needed, since the Benjamini-Hochberg step at 5% FDR is specific to family-wise multiplicity No replicated pairwise-variation distribution is available to bootstrap an empirical null, so empirical p-values cannot be formed http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 A downstream statistical procedure of the INTEGRATE pipeline that assigns empirical p-values to Cohen's kappa concordance scores (RPS vs RAS / RPS vs FFD) via 1000-fold bootstrap resampling, then applies Benjamini-Hochberg correction at 5% FDR to call significantly concordant reactions. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009337
skills.summary: A downstream statistical procedure of the INTEGRATE pipeline that assigns empirical p-values to Cohen's kappa concordance scores (RPS vs RAS / RPS vs FFD) via 1000-fold bootstrap resampling, then applies Benjamini-Hochberg correction at 5% FDR to call significantly concordant reactions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to compute the raw concordance scores themselves rather than test their significance — use the upstream concordanceAnalysis step instead Only a small number of reactions are tested and no multiple-comparison correction is needed, since the Benjamini-Hochberg step at 5% FDR is specific to family-wise multiplicity No replicated pairwise-variation distribution is available to bootstrap an empirical null, so empirical p-values cannot be formed

skills.description: Use when you need to annotate untargeted LC-HRMS MS1 features from biotransformation assays (e.g., human liver S9 incubations of xenobiotics) using reaction rules and a curated metabolite database, rather than spectral-library 'bottom-up' matching.
skills.name: reaction-based-pseudo-ms1-annotation
skills.search_text: reaction-based-pseudo-ms1-annotation Use when you need to annotate untargeted LC-HRMS MS1 features from biotransformation assays (e.g., human liver S9 incubations of xenobiotics) using reaction rules and a curated metabolite database, rather than spectral-library 'bottom-up' matching. Input MS2 spectra already match reference spectral libraries with high confidence — bottom-up library matching is the appropriate route and RCS adds reaction-rule assumptions unnecessarily The xenobiotic parent set has no reaction-rule or database coverage (no analog in the curated PMDB), so theoretical matching cannot generate candidates The analysis goal is intact-compound profiling rather than discovery of biotransformation-derived metabolites http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Reaction-based pseudo-MS1 candidature space (RCS) annotation from the CMDN framework: applies 290 curated biotransformation reaction rules against a curated pesticide metabolite database (PMDB, N = 492) to theoretically match and deduplicate MS1 features from untargeted LC-HRMS data of enzymatic assays, enabling high-throughput annotation of xenobiotic metabolites without spectral libraries. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.est.5c08558
skills.summary: Reaction-based pseudo-MS1 candidature space (RCS) annotation from the CMDN framework: applies 290 curated biotransformation reaction rules against a curated pesticide metabolite database (PMDB, N = 492) to theoretically match and deduplicate MS1 features from untargeted LC-HRMS data of enzymatic assays, enabling high-throughput annotation of xenobiotic metabolites without spectral libraries.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input MS2 spectra already match reference spectral libraries with high confidence — bottom-up library matching is the appropriate route and RCS adds reaction-rule assumptions unnecessarily The xenobiotic parent set has no reaction-rule or database coverage (no analog in the curated PMDB), so theoretical matching cannot generate candidates The analysis goal is intact-compound profiling rather than discovery of biotransformation-derived metabolites

skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is bottom-up discovery against spectral reference libraries for intact (non-biotransformed) chemicals — RCS requires a known parent to seed mass-shift candidates Input lacks accurate-mass feature data (e.g., low-resolution MS only), since pseudo-MS1 candidature depends on m/z matching of reaction-rule mass deltas Authentic analytical or stable-isotopic-labeled standards are already available and direct standard verification is planned instead of candidate enumeration

skills.description: Use when you need a library of reaction-center-based biotransformation rules derived from a curated reaction dataset (e.g. RetroRules or KEGG reactions with SMILES-annotated metabolites) to drive rule-based derivative generation.
skills.name: reaction-center-extraction
skills.search_text: reaction-center-extraction Use when you need a library of reaction-center-based biotransformation rules derived from a curated reaction dataset (e.g. RetroRules or KEGG reactions with SMILES-annotated metabolites) to drive rule-based derivative generation. skills.summary: Extract biotransformation rules—each encoding a reaction-center substructure plus the structural change around it—from reaction databases (RetroRules, KEGG, MetaCyc) using PROXIMAL2, so they can later be applied to anchor molecules to enumerate biotransformed derivatives in BAM.

skills.search_text: reaction-center-substructure-matching Use when you have an anchor molecule SMILES, a precursor mass difference to a suspect molecule, and a reaction dataset (RetroRules/KEGG/MetaCyc) from which biotransformation operators should be extracted and matched. skills.summary: Match biotransformation operators to observed anchor–suspect mass differences and apply them as SMARTS-like substructure transformations at candidate reaction centers using PROXIMAL2's operator extraction (extract reaction pairs, generate operators, check applicability to the query, and generate predicted products), producing candidate derivative SMILES ranked by GNN-SOM.

skills.description: Use when you have Pickaxe-generated novel reactions in a MongoDB database and need to exclude reactions with unfavorable physiology or unlikely catalytic transformation before downstream pathway design or metabolomics annotation.
skills.name: reaction-feasibility-prediction
skills.search_text: reaction-feasibility-prediction Use when you have Pickaxe-generated novel reactions in a MongoDB database and need to exclude reactions with unfavorable physiology or unlikely catalytic transformation before downstream pathway design or metabolomics annotation. When ΔG values fall outside the scope of eQuilibrator predictions — the filter cannot comment on their feasibility, so reactions must be retained rather than pruned. When reactions are already experimentally validated rather than novel generated reactions; DeepRFC's substrate-product pair predictions target KEGG-derived transformations and may not generalize to curated pathways. When the analysis goal is compound-level filtering (e.g. molecular weight or m/z matching) rather than reaction-level feasibility. Predict whether reactions generated during Pickaxe network expansion are thermodynamically and mechanistically feasible, using eQuilibrator physiological Gibbs free energies (ΔG > 50 kJ/mol cutoff) and the DeepRFC substrate–product feasibility neural net, and prune infeasible reactions from the expanding network. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-023-05149-8
skills.summary: Predict whether reactions generated during Pickaxe network expansion are thermodynamically and mechanistically feasible, using eQuilibrator physiological Gibbs free energies (ΔG > 50 kJ/mol cutoff) and the DeepRFC substrate–product feasibility neural net, and prune infeasible reactions from the expanding network.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When ΔG values fall outside the scope of eQuilibrator predictions — the filter cannot comment on their feasibility, so reactions must be retained rather than pruned. When reactions are already experimentally validated rather than novel generated reactions; DeepRFC's substrate-product pair predictions target KEGG-derived transformations and may not generalize to curated pathways. When the analysis goal is compound-level filtering (e.g. molecular weight or m/z matching) rather than reaction-level feasibility.

skills.description: Use when a Pickaxe-generated network expansion (e.g. EcoCyc <600 Da compounds, top 50 JN1224min rules, two generations) yields too many candidate compounds for unannotated metabolomics peaks and you need to prune reactions by enzymatic feasibility with DeepRFC.
skills.name: reaction-feasibility-scoring
skills.search_text: reaction-feasibility-scoring Use when a Pickaxe-generated network expansion (e.g. EcoCyc <600 Da compounds, top 50 JN1224min rules, two generations) yields too many candidate compounds for unannotated metabolomics peaks and you need to prune reactions by enzymatic feasibility with DeepRFC. The question is purely thermodynamic plausibility (ΔG cutoffs) — use the eQuilibrator thermodynamics filter instead, which removes reactions with physiological Gibbs free energy greater than 50 kJ/mol but retains reactions with no computable Gibbs energy. The network has not yet been generated by Pickaxe — feasibility scoring operates on Pickaxe-generated reactions/compounds (e.g. stored in MongoDB), not on raw peak lists or starting databases. You only need m/z matching of compounds to peaks (metabolomics filter alone), e.g. when network size is not a limiting factor. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3345 Applies DeepRFC-based reaction feasibility scoring as an on-the-fly filter in Pickaxe/MINE network expansions, pruning generated compounds and compound–peak pairs before metabolomics peak annotation (as demonstrated for the EcoCyc Figure 6 E. coli case). metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-023-05149-8
skills.summary: Applies DeepRFC-based reaction feasibility scoring as an on-the-fly filter in Pickaxe/MINE network expansions, pruning generated compounds and compound–peak pairs before metabolomics peak annotation (as demonstrated for the EcoCyc Figure 6 E. coli case).

skills.description: Use when merging automatically generated draft GEMs from heterogeneous pipelines (KBase, CarveMe, RAVEN 2.0, AuReMe/Pathway Tools) whose metabolite/reaction/gene identifiers differ, to build a consensus reconstruction via MNXref translation and cosine-similarity reaction matching.
skills.name: reaction-matching-across-draft-reconstructions
skills.search_text: reaction-matching-across-draft-reconstructions Use when merging automatically generated draft GEMs from heterogeneous pipelines (KBase, CarveMe, RAVEN 2.0, AuReMe/Pathway Tools) whose metabolite/reaction/gene identifiers differ, to build a consensus reconstruction via MNXref translation and cosine-similarity reaction matching. The draft models already share a common identifier namespace and comparable GPRs, so direct content comparison is possible without MNXref translation and matching. The goal is gap filling or community interaction prediction rather than merging drafts — use COMMIT gap filling or SMETANA instead. The models to compare are curated reference models (e.g. iMZ1055, iRP911) lacking cross-references to other namespaces, which the paper notes hampers translation and comparison. http://edamontology.org/topic_2259 http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Merging metabolically redundant draft genome-scale reconstructions (e.g. from KBase, CarveMe, RAVEN 2.0, and AuReMe/Pathway Tools) into a single consensus model by translating all identifiers to the MNXref namespace and matching reactions via identifier equality plus cosine-similarity reaction matching, with gene IDs harmonized by one-to-one BLAST. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009906
skills.summary: Merging metabolically redundant draft genome-scale reconstructions (e.g. from KBase, CarveMe, RAVEN 2.0, and AuReMe/Pathway Tools) into a single consensus model by translating all identifiers to the MNXref namespace and matching reactions via identifier equality plus cosine-similarity reaction matching, with gene IDs harmonized by one-to-one BLAST.

skills.description: Use when a Pickaxe network expansion explodes (e.g. 13.7 M reactions from KEGG) and you must constrain compounds/reactions before the next generation, for metabolomics peak annotation, thermodynamic feasibility screening, or targeted compound discovery.
skills.name: reaction-network-filtering
skills.search_text: reaction-network-filtering Use when a Pickaxe network expansion explodes (e.g. 13.7 M reactions from KEGG) and you must constrain compounds/reactions before the next generation, for metabolomics peak annotation, thermodynamic feasibility screening, or targeted compound discovery. You need a full, unpruned network expansion — filters remove compounds/reactions before the next generation, so the final network is incomplete by design (e.g. EcoCyc expansion pruned from 906,086 compounds to 2000 sampled ones). Your starting reaction rules or targets fall outside eQuilibrator's scope: no ΔG is returned and the thermodynamics filter cannot judge those reactions, so pruning decisions are unsupported. The goal is database-wide rule coverage assessment (e.g. JN1224min mapping percentages on KEGG/BRENDA) rather than constrained generation — no filter inputs (targets, peaks, ΔG) exist to drive pruning. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 On-the-fly pruning of Pickaxe-generated reaction networks using four composable filters — chemical similarity (cutoff or weighted sampling), metabolomics m/z matching, thermodynamics via eQuilibrator (ΔG > 50 kJ/mol removal), and DeepRFC reaction-feasibility scoring — so expansions stay small enough to interpret. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-023-05149-8
skills.summary: On-the-fly pruning of Pickaxe-generated reaction networks using four composable filters — chemical similarity (cutoff or weighted sampling), metabolomics m/z matching, thermodynamics via eQuilibrator (ΔG > 50 kJ/mol removal), and DeepRFC reaction-feasibility scoring — so expansions stay small enough to interpret.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need a full, unpruned network expansion — filters remove compounds/reactions before the next generation, so the final network is incomplete by design (e.g. EcoCyc expansion pruned from 906,086 compounds to 2000 sampled ones). Your starting reaction rules or targets fall outside eQuilibrator's scope: no ΔG is returned and the thermodynamics filter cannot judge those reactions, so pruning decisions are unsupported. The goal is database-wide rule coverage assessment (e.g. JN1224min mapping percentages on KEGG/BRENDA) rather than constrained generation — no filter inputs (targets, peaks, ΔG) exist to drive pruning.

skills.search_text: reaction-network-generation-benchmarking Use when running multi-generation network expansions (e.g., 100-rule ruleset on YMDB) and you need to measure exponential compound/reaction growth and per-generation runtime to identify tractability limits. You only need a single-application network for a downstream purpose (e.g., metabolomics peak annotation or similarity-sampling analysis) rather than scaling/benchmark measurements. The target question is filtering quality (thermodynamics, metabolomics, similarity filters) rather than raw expansion size and runtime behavior. An expansion is already known to be tractable and pre-computed; benchmarking adds compute cost without new information. http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Quantify how a rule-based metabolic reaction network (Pickaxe/minedatabase) scales across expansion generations by recording per-generation compound and reaction counts and benchmarking runtime, exposing when promiscuous-enzyme expansion becomes computationally intractable. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-023-05149-8

skills.name: reaction-propensity-score-computation
skills.search_text: reaction-propensity-score-computation Use when you need to predict how differences in substrate availability translate into differences in metabolic fluxes from intracellular metabolomics data and an irreversible stoichiometric model, to discriminate metabolically regulated reactions in INTEGRATE. When substrates of a reaction are not all quantified in the intracellular metabolomics dataset — such reactions must be omitted, and the RPS cannot be computed for them. When the goal is to characterize transcriptional regulation rather than metabolic regulation — RPS isolates the metabolic layer and neglects enzymatic activity; use getGPRsFromModel/getRASscore instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Computes the Reaction Propensity Score (RPS) dataset from intracellular metabolomics data for each model reaction and sample by applying the mass action law: the product of quantified substrate concentrations each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient, neglecting enzymatic activity. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009337
skills.summary: Computes the Reaction Propensity Score (RPS) dataset from intracellular metabolomics data for each model reaction and sample by applying the mass action law: the product of quantified substrate concentrations each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient, neglecting enzymatic activity.

skills.description: Use when integrating unlabeled metabolome mass features with reaction-rule-based pathway prediction: you need neutral-mass candidates per m/z feature and mass shifts attached to RetroRules reaction rules before filtering by correlated enzymes.
skills.name: reaction-rule-mass-shift-annotation
skills.search_text: reaction-rule-mass-shift-annotation Use when integrating unlabeled metabolome mass features with reaction-rule-based pathway prediction: you need neutral-mass candidates per m/z feature and mass shifts attached to RetroRules reaction rules before filtering by correlated enzymes. Annotating mass features from MS/MS spectra — MEANtools currently supports no MS/MS data loading or spectral library/networking-based annotation; use a spectral library tool instead. Reactions involving stereoisomers or multiple substrates — RetroRules-based rules are designed for single-substrate reactions only, and MEANtools filters stereomeric conversion rules to avoid complexity. Generating all product molecules for every RetroRules reaction exhaustively — with the substantial number of cataloged rules this is time-consuming and computationally intensive; the adduct/mass-shift lookup strategy exists precisely to avoid it. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Builds a mass-shift-annotated reaction-rule database by cross-referencing RetroRules reactions against MetaNetX identifier mappings, then assigns putative molecular structures to metabolome mass features by enumerating adducts and querying the LOTUS SQLite database within a 20 ppm mass accuracy tolerance. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pbio.3003307
skills.summary: Builds a mass-shift-annotated reaction-rule database by cross-referencing RetroRules reactions against MetaNetX identifier mappings, then assigns putative molecular structures to metabolome mass features by enumerating adducts and querying the LOTUS SQLite database within a 20 ppm mass accuracy tolerance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Annotating mass features from MS/MS spectra — MEANtools currently supports no MS/MS data loading or spectral library/networking-based annotation; use a spectral library tool instead. Reactions involving stereoisomers or multiple substrates — RetroRules-based rules are designed for single-substrate reactions only, and MEANtools filters stereomeric conversion rules to avoid complexity. Generating all product molecules for every RetroRules reaction exhaustively — with the substantial number of cataloged rules this is time-consuming and computationally intensive; the adduct/mass-shift lookup strategy exists precisely to avoid it.

skills.description: Use when validating that MEANtools' reaction-rule prediction (strict RetroRules dataset) anticipates known experimentally characterized biochemical reactions, or when reproducing reported coverage percentages and chi-square significance for reaction-rule databases.

skills.search_text: reaction-rule-matching-validation Use when validating that MEANtools' reaction-rule prediction (strict RetroRules dataset) anticipates known experimentally characterized biochemical reactions, or when reproducing reported coverage percentages and chi-square significance for reaction-rule databases. The reference reactions rely on stereomeric or multi-substrate conversions that RetroRules-based rules in MEANtools cannot represent (single-substrate rules only, stereomeric rules filtered). http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Benchmarks the coverage of RetroRules-derived reaction rules in MEANtools against a reference set of experimentally characterized biosynthetic reactions, tabulating found/missing reaction IDs and testing significance with a chi-square statistic. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pbio.3003307
skills.summary: Benchmarks the coverage of RetroRules-derived reaction rules in MEANtools against a reference set of experimentally characterized biosynthetic reactions, tabulating found/missing reaction IDs and testing significance with a chi-square statistic.

The reference reactions rely on stereomeric or multi-substrate conversions that RetroRules-based rules in MEANtools cannot represent (single-substrate rules only, stereomeric rules filtered).

skills.search_text: reaction-type-classification Use when counting or categorizing BoM records by ReactionType in an annotated SDF dataset (e.g., EBoMD.sdf), or when verifying reported reaction-category frequencies such as η+η-forming Cyclization counts. The input is raw structures without BoM annotations and no bond-pair predictions exist — ReactionType rules operate on 〈X, Y〉 pairs, not unannotated molecules The goal is SoM localization (which atom reacts) rather than reaction-type assignment — use the CypBoM / FAME comparison workflow instead Analyzing non-CYP450 metabolism where the η-η / η-H / η-SPN BoM taxonomy and SMIRKS rule set do not apply http://edamontology.org/topic_3370 Classifies CYP450 bond-of-metabolism (BoM) records into ReactionType categories (e.g., Cyclization, EpOxidation, Reduction, Dealkylation, Deamination, RingRearrangement) by applying structural rules to predicted η-η / η-H bond pairs, enabling rarity and distribution analyses like the '4 of 828 η+η-forming reactions' finding in EBoMD. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jcim.1c00144
skills.summary: Classifies CYP450 bond-of-metabolism (BoM) records into ReactionType categories (e.g., Cyclization, EpOxidation, Reduction, Dealkylation, Deamination, RingRearrangement) by applying structural rules to predicted η-η / η-H bond pairs, enabling rarity and distribution analyses like the '4 of 828 η+η-forming reactions' finding in EBoMD.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw structures without BoM annotations and no bond-pair predictions exist — ReactionType rules operate on 〈X, Y〉 pairs, not unannotated molecules The goal is SoM localization (which atom reacts) rather than reaction-type assignment — use the CypBoM / FAME comparison workflow instead Analyzing non-CYP450 metabolism where the η-η / η-H / η-SPN BoM taxonomy and SMIRKS rule set do not apply

skills.description: Use when metabolite annotation tables carry BioTransformer reaction-type tags (oxidation, glucuronidation, hydrolysis, etc.) and you need detected-vs-predicted counts and detection fractions per biotransformation reaction, as for PharmMet DB Study ST003991.
skills.name: reaction-type-count-aggregation
skills.search_text: reaction-type-count-aggregation Use when metabolite annotation tables carry BioTransformer reaction-type tags (oxidation, glucuronidation, hydrolysis, etc.) and you need detected-vs-predicted counts and detection fractions per biotransformation reaction, as for PharmMet DB Study ST003991. Upstream curation is not done: raw MZmine 2.53 feature tables or 0-hour vs 24-hour MS1/RT differential features lack reaction-type tags, so counts cannot be attributed to a biotransformation reaction. The goal is identifying which specific novel (unpredicted) metabolites a drug produced rather than aggregate per-reaction totals — 89% of drugs had such products and they require feature-level triage. The metabolism of interest is extrahepatic or driven by enzymes not abundant/active in liver S9 (e.g. intestine, kidney), since ST003991 counts reflect only human liver S9 biotransformation. http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Aggregates experimentally detected human liver S9 drug metabolites by biotransformation reaction type and compares each detected count against the corresponding BioTransformer 3.0 prediction set, quantifying which phase I/II pathways were observed (e.g. 30,752 of 59,296 predicted oxidations detected; glucuronidation dominant in phase II with 6311). metabolomics/v3 10.1016/j.dmd.2025.100183
skills.summary: Aggregates experimentally detected human liver S9 drug metabolites by biotransformation reaction type and compares each detected count against the corresponding BioTransformer 3.0 prediction set, quantifying which phase I/II pathways were observed (e.g. 30,752 of 59,296 predicted oxidations detected; glucuronidation dominant in phase II with 6311).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Upstream curation is not done: raw MZmine 2.53 feature tables or 0-hour vs 24-hour MS1/RT differential features lack reaction-type tags, so counts cannot be attributed to a biotransformation reaction. The goal is identifying which specific novel (unpredicted) metabolites a drug produced rather than aggregate per-reaction totals — 89% of drugs had such products and they require feature-level triage. The metabolism of interest is extrahepatic or driven by enzymes not abundant/active in liver S9 (e.g. intestine, kidney), since ST003991 counts reflect only human liver S9 biotransformation.

skills.description: Use when annotating MALDI-MSI or LC-MS features acquired with a derivatizing matrix (e.g. FMP-10), where the candidate target list must be restricted to metabolites containing moieties the matrix reacts with (e.g. phenolic hydroxyls, primary/secondary amines).
skills.name: reactive-moiety-target-filtering
skills.search_text: reactive-moiety-target-filtering Use when annotating MALDI-MSI or LC-MS features acquired with a derivatizing matrix (e.g. FMP-10), where the candidate target list must be restricted to metabolites containing moieties the matrix reacts with (e.g. phenolic hydroxyls, primary/secondary amines). Input is already a filtered target list or feature table — the filtering step has already been applied Data were acquired with a conventional (non-derivatizing) matrix producing standard [M+H]+/[M-H]- ions — no reactive-moiety restriction is warranted Structures lack machine-readable SMILES/SDF records, since the filter requires RDKit-parseable structures http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Filters metabolite database candidates (e.g. HMDB, LIPID MAPS) down to those bearing functional groups reactive toward a specific derivatizing matrix, by substructure-matching SMARTS patterns against parsed SMILES structures with RDKit. This mirrors how Met-ID 'utilizes structural information for derivatizing matrices to generate a subset of targets that contain only functional groups specific to the derivatization agent'. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c00633
skills.summary: Filters metabolite database candidates (e.g. HMDB, LIPID MAPS) down to those bearing functional groups reactive toward a specific derivatizing matrix, by substructure-matching SMARTS patterns against parsed SMILES structures with RDKit. This mirrors how Met-ID 'utilizes structural information for derivatizing matrices to generate a subset of targets that contain only functional groups specific to the derivatization agent'.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a filtered target list or feature table — the filtering step has already been applied Data were acquired with a conventional (non-derivatizing) matrix producing standard [M+H]+/[M-H]- ions — no reactive-moiety restriction is warranted Structures lack machine-readable SMILES/SDF records, since the filter requires RDKit-parseable structures

skills.description: Use when annotated peak features carry ChEBI (or KEGG COMPOUND) IDs and metabolite sets must be drawn from Reactome pathways for Homo sapiens or other supported species, rather than KEGG.
skills.name: reactome-neo4j-pathway-query
skills.search_text: reactome-neo4j-pathway-query Use when annotated peak features carry ChEBI (or KEGG COMPOUND) IDs and metabolite sets must be drawn from Reactome pathways for Homo sapiens or other supported species, rather than KEGG. Compound annotations are KEGG IDs and KEGG pathway sets suffice — use the PiMP_KEGG offline database instead of standing up a Neo4j Reactome instance The metabolite sets of interest are GNPS Molecular Families or MS2LDA Mass2Motifs rather than curated pathways — retrieve those from GNPS/MS2LDA outputs instead Peaks lack ChEBI/KEGG annotations entirely — unannotated peaks are excluded from pathway analysis, so Reactome querying cannot help http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Retrieves Reactome pathway membership for annotated MS peaks by querying a local Neo4j-hosted Reactome database (online mode) or pre-downloaded Reactome pathway files (offline mode), building the feature-to-pathway mapping tables that PALS uses for mPLAGE/ORA/GSEA scoring. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo11020103
skills.summary: Retrieves Reactome pathway membership for annotated MS peaks by querying a local Neo4j-hosted Reactome database (online mode) or pre-downloaded Reactome pathway files (offline mode), building the feature-to-pathway mapping tables that PALS uses for mPLAGE/ORA/GSEA scoring.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Compound annotations are KEGG IDs and KEGG pathway sets suffice — use the PiMP_KEGG offline database instead of standing up a Neo4j Reactome instance The metabolite sets of interest are GNPS Molecular Families or MS2LDA Mass2Motifs rather than curated pathways — retrieve those from GNPS/MS2LDA outputs instead Peaks lack ChEBI/KEGG annotations entirely — unannotated peaks are excluded from pathway analysis, so Reactome querying cannot help

skills.when_to_use_negative: There is no reference/ground-truth lipid list — recall is undefined without a set of reported lipids to recover; use coverage or FDR metrics instead The goal is de novo discovery of lipids not present in any reference atlas, where recall against a fixed lipid list would trivially cap at the reference content Input is already a processed feature/annotation table where only one library was ever used — there is no cross-library comparison to visualize

skills.description: Use when reproducing or verifying reported per-nucleus recombination foci counts (GFP::RMH-1, GFP::MSH-5) across germline zones (2–4) for BTR-complex genotypes such as gfp::rmh-1, top-3-ZnF, and rmh-2; top-3-ZnF::ha from a Results text.
skills.name: recombination-foci-quantification
skills.search_text: recombination-foci-quantification Use when reproducing or verifying reported per-nucleus recombination foci counts (GFP::RMH-1, GFP::MSH-5) across germline zones (2–4) for BTR-complex genotypes such as gfp::rmh-1, top-3-ZnF, and rmh-2; top-3-ZnF::ha from a Results text. The task requires re-counting foci from raw immunofluorescence images — this skill only transcribes and structures values already reported in the article text. The input text reports only qualitative descriptions (e.g. 'delayed and reduced in number') without explicit numeric means and SDs per zone. Statistics beyond transcription are needed (e.g. p-values, ANOVA) — these were performed separately in Prism 6/GraphPad, not by this extraction step. Extracts and tabulates the reported mean numbers and SDs of recombination foci per nucleus (e.g. GFP::RMH-1 and GFP::MSH-5) across C. elegans germline zones, where zone 2 = early, zone 3 = mid, and zone 4 = late pachynema. It turns prose numbers from the Results text into a structured 16-row CSV for verification and downstream statistics. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkac408
skills.summary: Extracts and tabulates the reported mean numbers and SDs of recombination foci per nucleus (e.g. GFP::RMH-1 and GFP::MSH-5) across C. elegans germline zones, where zone 2 = early, zone 3 = mid, and zone 4 = late pachynema. It turns prose numbers from the Results text into a structured 16-row CSV for verification and downstream statistics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task requires re-counting foci from raw immunofluorescence images — this skill only transcribes and structures values already reported in the article text. skills.description: Use when you have a table of matched public spectra (e.g. MASST hits for synthesized conjugated bile acids) with ReDU metadata attached and need to test whether detections are enriched in specific tissues (fecal vs blood/liver) or health phenotypes (IBD vs healthy).
skills.name: redu-metadata-stratification
skills.search_text: redu-metadata-stratification Use when you have a table of matched public spectra (e.g. MASST hits for synthesized conjugated bile acids) with ReDU metadata attached and need to test whether detections are enriched in specific tissues (fecal vs blood/liver) or health phenotypes (IBD vs healthy).
