skills.description: Use when you have small-molecule structures with measured LC retention times (e.g. a METLIN SMRT-style dataset) and need an accurate data-driven retention time regression model for structural identification support.
skills.name: retention-time-regression-model-training
skills.search_text: retention-time-regression-model-training Use when you have small-molecule structures with measured LC retention times (e.g. a METLIN SMRT-style dataset) and need an accurate data-driven retention time regression model for structural identification support. When you only have MS/MS spectra or mass spectral features and no molecular structures with retention time labels — the GNN-RT model requires molecular graph inputs from structures, not spectral features. When you need retention time prediction for a chromatographic system fundamentally different from the SMRT training system without doing transfer learning — the article notes the SMRT-trained model transfers easily only to 'the same type of chromatographic systems'. When your molecules are outside the small-molecule scope (e.g. large biomolecules), since the method is designed for small molecule LC retention time. http://edamontology.org/topic_3336 Train a graph neural network (GNN-RT) that predicts liquid chromatographic retention time directly from molecular graph representations of small molecules, avoiding handcrafted molecular descriptors, and benchmark it against regression baselines (random forest, Bayesian ridge regression, CNN, DLM) on the METLIN SMRT dataset. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c04071
skills.summary: Train a graph neural network (GNN-RT) that predicts liquid chromatographic retention time directly from molecular graph representations of small molecules, avoiding handcrafted molecular descriptors, and benchmark it against regression baselines (random forest, Bayesian ridge regression, CNN, DLM) on the METLIN SMRT dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When you only have MS/MS spectra or mass spectral features and no molecular structures with retention time labels — the GNN-RT model requires molecular graph inputs from structures, not spectral features. When you need retention time prediction for a chromatographic system fundamentally different from the SMRT training system without doing transfer learning — the article notes the SMRT-trained model transfers easily only to 'the same type of chromatographic systems'. When your molecules are outside the small-molecule scope (e.g. large biomolecules), since the method is designed for small molecule LC retention time.

skills.description: Use when authentic standards are unavailable and LC-HRMS annotations (e.g. CMDN-annotated metabolites with accurate m/z and RT) need chromatographic plausibility checks by predicting RT from SMILES/InChIKey structures.
skills.name: retention-time-regression-modeling
skills.search_text: retention-time-regression-modeling Use when authentic standards are unavailable and LC-HRMS annotations (e.g. CMDN-annotated metabolites with accurate m/z and RT) need chromatographic plausibility checks by predicting RT from SMILES/InChIKey structures. No compounds with experimentally measured LC-HRMS retention times are available to train or benchmark the regression models The validation goal is structural confirmation (MS2 spectral matching or authentic standard verification) rather than chromatographic plausibility of an annotation The chemical space of candidate metabolites falls far outside the pesticide library used for training, where RT regression would extrapolate unreliably http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 Trains and benchmarked machine-learning regressors (XGBoost, Random Forest, BRNN) on molecular descriptors to predict LC-HRMS retention times, enabling chromatographic validation of CMDN-annotated pesticide metabolites when authentic standards are unavailable. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.est.5c08558
skills.summary: Trains and benchmarked machine-learning regressors (XGBoost, Random Forest, BRNN) on molecular descriptors to predict LC-HRMS retention times, enabling chromatographic validation of CMDN-annotated pesticide metabolites when authentic standards are unavailable.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No compounds with experimentally measured LC-HRMS retention times are available to train or benchmark the regression models The validation goal is structural confirmation (MS2 spectral matching or authentic standard verification) rather than chromatographic plausibility of an annotation The chemical space of candidate metabolites falls far outside the pesticide library used for training, where RT regression would extrapolate unreliably

skills.description: Use when you have a large set of molecules with experimental retention times (e.g., SMRT reversed-phase LC-MS data) plus alvaDesc fingerprints/descriptors and need to train or compare RT prediction regressors.
skills.name: retention-time-regression-training
skills.search_text: retention-time-regression-training Use when you have a large set of molecules with experimental retention times (e.g., SMRT reversed-phase LC-MS data) plus alvaDesc fingerprints/descriptors and need to train or compare RT prediction regressors. Your molecules lack a way to generate alvaDesc features (no license); the README suggests RDKit fingerprints via train_with_rdkit.ipynb instead, with possibly different performance. Your goal is projecting predicted RTs to a specific chromatographic method or annotating metabolites from m/z and RT — use the meta-learned GP projection workflow, not RT regressor training. Your dataset is small (e.g., a handful of identified molecules); the meta-learning projection approach was designed to learn from as few as 10 molecules, whereas this skill requires tens of thousands of RTs. http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Train and benchmark machine learning regressors (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, DKL, and heavily regularized DNNs) to predict chromatographic retention times from molecular fingerprints and descriptors on the 80,038-molecule METLIN SMRT dataset, using nested cross-validation with Bayesian hyperparameter search. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-022-00613-8
skills.summary: Train and benchmark machine learning regressors (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, DKL, and heavily regularized DNNs) to predict chromatographic retention times from molecular fingerprints and descriptors on the 80,038-molecule METLIN SMRT dataset, using nested cross-validation with Bayesian hyperparameter search.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your molecules lack a way to generate alvaDesc features (no license); the README suggests RDKit fingerprints via train_with_rdkit.ipynb instead, with possibly different performance. Your goal is projecting predicted RTs to a specific chromatographic method or annotating metabolites from m/z and RT — use the meta-learned GP projection workflow, not RT regressor training. Your dataset is small (e.g., a handful of identified molecules); the meta-learning projection approach was designed to learn from as few as 10 molecules, whereas this skill requires tens of thousands of RTs.

skills.description: Use when validating LC-MS reference analytes from >=3 replicate runs (e.g. HILIC standard mixtures in mzML/mzXML) and you must quantify retention-time reproducibility per analyte against a user-specified threshold c (default 15%).
skills.name: retention-time-rsd-computation-across-replicates
skills.search_text: retention-time-rsd-computation-across-replicates Use when validating LC-MS reference analytes from >=3 replicate runs (e.g. HILIC standard mixtures in mzML/mzXML) and you must quantify retention-time reproducibility per analyte against a user-specified threshold c (default 15%). Data consist of a single LC-MS injection per analyte — RSD across replicates is undefined without repeated runs Goal is mobile-phase optimization scoring (peak quality score Sp + Saf comparison across candidate mobile phases) rather than replicate-based analyte validation Retention times are already curated from a trusted reference library and only peak-shape metrics (MCQ, asymmetry factor) need computing Computes the relative standard deviation (RSD) of chromatographic peak retention times across replicate LC-MS injections, used in the MetaMOPE three-threshold validation criterion (with Std/Blk ratio r=6 and intensity I=1000) to decide which standard analytes enter a reference library. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioadv/vbad061
skills.summary: Computes the relative standard deviation (RSD) of chromatographic peak retention times across replicate LC-MS injections, used in the MetaMOPE three-threshold validation criterion (with Std/Blk ratio r=6 and intensity I=1000) to decide which standard analytes enter a reference library.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data consist of a single LC-MS injection per analyte — RSD across replicates is undefined without repeated runs Goal is mobile-phase optimization scoring (peak quality score Sp + Saf comparison across candidate mobile phases) rather than replicate-based analyte validation Retention times are already curated from a trusted reference library and only peak-shape metrics (MCQ, asymmetry factor) need computing

skills.description: Use when scoring metabolite annotations from MS/MS spectra in negative mode where retention time is available, e.g. verifying that a candidate like 1-O-beta-D-glucopyranosyl sinapate at RT 1.27 min receives the expected RT score of 1.
skills.name: retention-time-score-evaluation
skills.search_text: retention-time-score-evaluation Use when scoring metabolite annotations from MS/MS spectra in negative mode where retention time is available, e.g. verifying that a candidate like 1-O-beta-D-glucopyranosyl sinapate at RT 1.27 min receives the expected RT score of 1. When retention time is unavailable or unreliable for the query peak — the RT component cannot be scored and the integrated score reduces to other components When the goal is database-wide candidate retrieval rather than scoring a candidate annotation against a known RT (candidate retrieval is handled by the 25 ppm MS1 cutoff step, not the RT score) http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 Computes the retention-time component score within PlantMetSuite's metabolite annotation scoring, where an RT score of 1 denotes a perfect retention-time match, and combines it with the MS/MS score and additional criteria via the integrated score formula (Equation (3)) to produce a final annotation score. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/plants12152880
skills.summary: Computes the retention-time component score within PlantMetSuite's metabolite annotation scoring, where an RT score of 1 denotes a perfect retention-time match, and combines it with the MS/MS score and additional criteria via the integrated score formula (Equation (3)) to produce a final annotation score.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When retention time is unavailable or unreliable for the query peak — the RT component cannot be scored and the integrated score reduces to other components When the goal is database-wide candidate retrieval rather than scoring a candidate annotation against a known RT (candidate retrieval is handled by the 25 ppm MS1 cutoff step, not the RT score)

skills.description: Use when re-detecting peaks from LC-HRMS mzXML chromatograms for a known reference feature list, and narrowed m/z + retention-time search windows are available or can be derived per feature.
skills.name: retention-time-search-frame-restriction
skills.search_text: retention-time-search-frame-restriction Use when re-detecting peaks from LC-HRMS mzXML chromatograms for a known reference feature list, and narrowed m/z + retention-time search windows are available or can be derived per feature. Input is already a processed feature table (m/z, retention time, peak area) and no raw chromatographic peak re-detection is needed Runtime budget is strict and the dataset is large — MassSpecWavelet is very reliable but has significantly longer runtimes than the Gaussian correlation or Savitzky-Golay alternatives Data is not LC-HRMS chromatographic data with m/z and retention time dimensions, since MetMatch's correction and alignment operate on LC-HRMS shifts relative to a reference chromatogram http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Restrict MetMatch's chromatographic peak-picking search to narrowed m/z and retention-time frames around expected features in an LC-HRMS reference chromatogram, choosing between the MassSpecWavelet, Gaussian peak-correlation, and Savitzky-Golay filter algorithms while benchmarking their runtimes. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo6040039
skills.summary: Restrict MetMatch's chromatographic peak-picking search to narrowed m/z and retention-time frames around expected features in an LC-HRMS reference chromatogram, choosing between the MassSpecWavelet, Gaussian peak-correlation, and Savitzky-Golay filter algorithms while benchmarking their runtimes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a processed feature table (m/z, retention time, peak area) and no raw chromatographic peak re-detection is needed Runtime budget is strict and the dataset is large — MassSpecWavelet is very reliable but has significantly longer runtimes than the Gaussian correlation or Savitzky-Golay alternatives Data is not LC-HRMS chromatographic data with m/z and retention time dimensions, since MetMatch's correction and alignment operate on LC-HRMS shifts relative to a reference chromatogram

skills.description: Use when a targeted or suspect HRMS prescreening run has produced EICs and MS2 scans per compound and you must pass/fail each parent point against experimental m/z error, RT error, and MS1/MS2 intensity thresholds before further identification.
skills.name: retention-time-shift-and-noise-thresholding
skills.search_text: retention-time-shift-and-noise-thresholding Use when a targeted or suspect HRMS prescreening run has produced EICs and MS2 scans per compound and you must pass/fail each parent point against experimental m/z error, RT error, and MS1/MS2 intensity thresholds before further identification. When the task is de novo feature detection or peak picking across the full sample (e.g. untargeted discovery without a compound or mass list) — Shinyscreen's focus is exclusively on a preselected list of compounds or masses of interest, not general peak detection. When the goal is database-independent compound identification itself — this skill only prescreens and flags peaks; identification is delegated to tools such as MetFrag. When input data are already vendor-curated and quality-assessed (e.g. Xcalibur-processed results) — this skill targets raw vendor-independent HRMS data requiring automated QC. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 A QC filtering stage from Shinyscreen in which each extracted MS1 parent data point is judged by the existence of MS1 and MS2 data, the noise level, and the retention time shift, with failures flagged via MS1/MS2 intensity thresholds and retention-time-shift tolerance rather than silently dropped. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-025-01044-x
skills.summary: A QC filtering stage from Shinyscreen in which each extracted MS1 parent data point is judged by the existence of MS1 and MS2 data, the noise level, and the retention time shift, with failures flagged via MS1/MS2 intensity thresholds and retention-time-shift tolerance rather than silently dropped.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the task is de novo feature detection or peak picking across the full sample (e.g. untargeted discovery without a compound or mass list) — Shinyscreen's focus is exclusively on a preselected list of compounds or masses of interest, not general peak detection. When the goal is database-independent compound identification itself — this skill only prescreens and flags peaks; identification is delegated to tools such as MetFrag. When input data are already vendor-curated and quality-assessed (e.g. Xcalibur-processed results) — this skill targets raw vendor-independent HRMS data requiring automated QC.

skills.description: Use when aligning XCMS-derived feature lists or target chromatograms from different LC-HRMS batches where retention times are shifted (e.g. 7–52 s or -9 to -24 s ranges) and m/z deviates slightly (e.g. -3.4 ppm) relative to a reference.
skills.name: retention-time-shift-correction
skills.search_text: retention-time-shift-correction Use when aligning XCMS-derived feature lists or target chromatograms from different LC-HRMS batches where retention times are shifted (e.g. 7–52 s or -9 to -24 s ranges) and m/z deviates slightly (e.g. -3.4 ppm) relative to a reference. Input is already an aligned, combined feature matrix with corrected retention times — re-alignment would not apply Data were measured in a single batch against its own reference, so no cross-experiment m/z or retention-time shift exists Target files contain no reference-metabolite-derived features in the expected windows (e.g. peaks eluting early with too few neighboring peaks for shift-function fitting) http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Semi-automated correction and alignment of LC-HRMS datasets that exhibit m/z and non-linear retention-time shifts relative to a reference feature list, performed with MetMatch (Java JRE 1.8+), including accounting for differently formed ion adducts. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo6040039
skills.summary: Semi-automated correction and alignment of LC-HRMS datasets that exhibit m/z and non-linear retention-time shifts relative to a reference feature list, performed with MetMatch (Java JRE 1.8+), including accounting for differently formed ion adducts.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already an aligned, combined feature matrix with corrected retention times — re-alignment would not apply Data were measured in a single batch against its own reference, so no cross-experiment m/z or retention-time shift exists Target files contain no reference-metabolite-derived features in the expected windows (e.g. peaks eluting early with too few neighboring peaks for shift-function fitting)

skills.description: Use when isotope-labelling experiments (deuterium- or 13C-labelled substrates) shift chromatographic retention times, and m/z-difference-based substrate-metabolite discovery would otherwise miss the labelled peak pair.
skills.name: retention-time-shift-correction-isotope-labelling
skills.search_text: retention-time-shift-correction-isotope-labelling Use when isotope-labelling experiments (deuterium- or 13C-labelled substrates) shift chromatographic retention times, and m/z-difference-based substrate-metabolite discovery would otherwise miss the labelled peak pair. Data are already deisotoped compound spectra with no isotope-labelled substrate fed — there is no label mass difference to search for The chromatographic method induces retention-time shifts far larger than the 8 s sliding window assumed here Only a single ionization mode was acquired and CAMERA's cross-polarity combinexsAnnos verification cannot be run http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Screens XCMS/CAMERA-annotated LC/MS feature pairs for a stable isotope mass shift (e.g. 5.031 Da for a D5-labelled tryptophan feeding) using a sliding retention-time window that absorbs deuterium-induced chromatographic drift. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/ac202450g
skills.summary: Screens XCMS/CAMERA-annotated LC/MS feature pairs for a stable isotope mass shift (e.g. 5.031 Da for a D5-labelled tryptophan feeding) using a sliding retention-time window that absorbs deuterium-induced chromatographic drift.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are already deisotoped compound spectra with no isotope-labelled substrate fed — there is no label mass difference to search for The chromatographic method induces retention-time shifts far larger than the 8 s sliding window assumed here Only a single ionization mode was acquired and CAMERA's cross-polarity combinexsAnnos verification cannot be run

skills.description: Use when you need to stress-test an LC-MS RT alignment tool against ground-truth correspondences, or to determine at what RT-shift variability an aligner's precision and recall degrade.
skills.name: retention-time-shift-simulation
skills.search_text: retention-time-shift-simulation Use when you need to stress-test an LC-MS RT alignment tool against ground-truth correspondences, or to determine at what RT-shift variability an aligner's precision and recall degrade. The goal is quantification accuracy assessment — the article notes alignment has less influence on quantification than feature extraction, and this simulation alters only RT Input is raw LC-MS profile data rather than post-feature-extraction feature lists; DeepRTAlign expects processed feature lists, not centroided spectra Only a single RT shift level is needed as a quick sanity check — this skill targets a systematic sigma sweep to map degradation boundaries Simulates controlled retention time (RT) shifts on LC-MS feature lists to benchmark RT alignment tools such as DeepRTAlign against OpenMS feature grouping. It exposes generalizability boundaries — where alignment precision/recall collapse as RT shift variability grows — for proteomic and metabolomic data. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-023-43909-5
skills.summary: Simulates controlled retention time (RT) shifts on LC-MS feature lists to benchmark RT alignment tools such as DeepRTAlign against OpenMS feature grouping. skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is quantification accuracy assessment — the article notes alignment has less influence on quantification than feature extraction, and this simulation alters only RT Input is raw LC-MS profile data rather than post-feature-extraction feature lists; DeepRTAlign expects processed feature lists, not centroided spectra Only a single RT shift level is needed as a quick sanity check — this skill targets a systematic sigma sweep to map degradation boundaries

skills.description: Use when a pair of untargeted LC-MS metabolomics data sets acquired under different gradient elution methods must be combined and RT drift must be corrected before ranking feature pair alignments by mapped retention time.
skills.name: retention-time-spline-fitting
skills.search_text: retention-time-spline-fitting Use when a pair of untargeted LC-MS metabolomics data sets acquired under different gradient elution methods must be combined and RT drift must be corrected before ranking feature pair alignments by mapped retention time. The two data sets were acquired with excessively disparate chromatographic techniques (e.g. RPLC vs HILIC) where elution order of metabolites is not mostly preserved — metabCombiner states these are not suitable The feature pair alignments have already been scored and the combined table reduced; spline fitting is only used for RT mapping before scoring The data sets are from different ionization modes or the samples are not biologically similar — prerequisites for the metabCombiner workflow that the spline serves http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Fits a retention-time mapping spline (GAM via fit_gam, scaled-t family, or loess via fit_loess) through a set of selected retention time ordered pairs to map RTs between two disparately acquired untargeted LC-MS metabolomics data sets, correcting for retention time drift before feature alignment scoring. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c03693
skills.summary: Fits a retention-time mapping spline (GAM via fit_gam, scaled-t family, or loess via fit_loess) through a set of selected retention time ordered pairs to map RTs between two disparately acquired untargeted LC-MS metabolomics data sets, correcting for retention time drift before feature alignment scoring.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The two data sets were acquired with excessively disparate chromatographic techniques (e.g. RPLC vs HILIC) where elution order of metabolites is not mostly preserved — metabCombiner states these are not suitable The feature pair alignments have already been scored and the combined table reduced; spline fitting is only used for RT mapping before scoring The data sets are from different ionization modes or the samples are not biologically similar — prerequisites for the metabCombiner workflow that the spline serves

Compounds are not yet standardized — salts or metal-containing structures present will fail or distort CDK descriptor calculation and must be removed first The goal is quantitative prediction-error benchmarking (MAE, cross-validation) rather than exploratory structural-overlap assessment — use Retip's model-building workflow instead The compound set lacks SMILES structures or the descriptor matrix cannot be computed (e.g., non-small-molecule entries like high molecular weight lipids excluded in the original training) http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Visualizes chemical-space overlap between training, test, and validation compound libraries by running PCA on 286 2D CDK descriptors with Retip's chem.space() function, to judge whether an RT prediction model can generalize beyond its training set. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.9b05765
skills.summary: Visualizes chemical-space overlap between training, test, and validation compound libraries by running PCA on 286 2D CDK descriptors with Retip's chem.space() function, to judge whether an RT prediction model can generalize beyond its training set.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Compounds are not yet standardized — salts or metal-containing structures present will fail or distort CDK descriptor calculation and must be removed first The goal is quantitative prediction-error benchmarking (MAE, cross-validation) rather than exploratory structural-overlap assessment — use Retip's model-building workflow instead The compound set lacks SMILES structures or the descriptor matrix cannot be computed (e.g., non-small-molecule entries like high molecular weight lipids excluded in the original training)

skills.description: Use when benchmarking a metabolite annotation engine against MetFrag, CFM-ID or CSI:FingerID: you have tandem MS/MS test spectra with known structures and ranked candidate lists per tool, and need top-1/top-k retrieval rates for side-by-side comparison.
skills.name: retrieval-rate-benchmark-computation
skills.search_text: retrieval-rate-benchmark-computation Use when benchmarking a metabolite annotation engine against MetFrag, CFM-ID or CSI:FingerID: you have tandem MS/MS test spectra with known structures and ranked candidate lists per tool, and need top-1/top-k retrieval rates for side-by-side comparison. skills.summary: Computes top-k (top-1) retrieval rates for tandem MS metabolite annotation engines and baseline tools (MetFrag, CFM-ID, SIRIUS/CSI:FingerID) on identical train/test spectra splits, to support claims like ChemDistiller's rates being comparable to or exceeding state-of-the-art solutions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Test spectra compounds lack known chemical structures — correct hits cannot be scored and retrieval statistics cannot be computed (ChemDistiller's built-in test set is chosen precisely because structures are known) Tools are run on different datasets, splits, or precursor mass tolerances — the comparison is then not 'under the same conditions' and top-k rates are not comparable The task is a single metabolite annotation run rather than an engine-vs-engine performance benchmark

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify how well a spectrum-identifier or bucketing key reduces a mass spectral search space while preserving similarity-based recall, using the SPLASH second-block scheme and NIST cosine scoring.
skills.name: retrieval-recall-evaluation
skills.search_text: retrieval-recall-evaluation Use when you need to quantify how well a spectrum-identifier or bucketing key reduces a mass spectral search space while preserving similarity-based recall, using the SPLASH second-block scheme and NIST cosine scoring. Input spectra cannot be assigned SPLASH identifiers (e.g. no peak-intensity representation compatible with the ion:intensity string format) The evaluation target is exact-match deduplication via the fourth hash block rather than prefilter recall — hash-block collisions were assessed separately on 53.25 million spectra The query task requires full-library exhaustive search where no search-space reduction is acceptable; the second block trades ~13% missed true matches (87% recall) for a 94%+ reduction http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 Evaluates a spectral identifier block (the SPLASH second summary block) as a search prefilter by measuring search-space reduction against the 563,902-spectrum MoNA-deposited dataset and the recall of true matches under NIST cosine similarity at a score cutoff of 700. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/nbt.3689
skills.summary: Evaluates a spectral identifier block (the SPLASH second summary block) as a search prefilter by measuring search-space reduction against the 563,902-spectrum MoNA-deposited dataset and the recall of true matches under NIST cosine similarity at a score cutoff of 700.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra cannot be assigned SPLASH identifiers (e.g. no peak-intensity representation compatible with the ion:intensity string format) The evaluation target is exact-match deduplication via the fourth hash block rather than prefilter recall — hash-block collisions were assessed separately on 53.25 million spectra The query task requires full-library exhaustive search where no search-space reduction is acceptable; the second block trades ~13% missed true matches (87% recall) for a 94%+ reduction

skills.description: Use when you have a reference set of characterized biochemical reaction IDs and want to quantify how many are anticipated by RetroRules reaction-rule predictions in MEANtools, with a statistical significance test.
skills.name: retrometabolic-reaction-presence-quantification
skills.search_text: retrometabolic-reaction-presence-quantification Use when you have a reference set of characterized biochemical reaction IDs and want to quantify how many are anticipated by RetroRules reaction-rule predictions in MEANtools, with a statistical significance test. Your goal is de novo biosynthetic pathway reconstruction from paired transcriptomic-metabolomic data (e.g. mutual-rank clustering of mass features), not benchmarking rule-database coverage. You want to evaluate the loose or medium rule sets, which include ECDomainMiner predictions and spurious reaction–Pfam links rather than only experimentally validated entries. Your reactions lack identifiers mappable to the RetroRules/Rhea/KEGG cross-referenced rule-enzyme associations, so found/missing tagging cannot be assigned. Benchmark the coverage of a curated set of experimentally characterized biosynthetic reactions against MEANtools' RetroRules reaction-rule predictions, quantifying reaction presence as a percentage and testing its significance with a chi-square test on found/missing counts. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pbio.3003307
skills.summary: Benchmark the coverage of a curated set of experimentally characterized biosynthetic reactions against MEANtools' RetroRules reaction-rule predictions, quantifying reaction presence as a percentage and testing its significance with a chi-square test on found/missing counts.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your goal is de novo biosynthetic pathway reconstruction from paired transcriptomic-metabolomic data (e.g. mutual-rank clustering of mass features), not benchmarking rule-database coverage. You want to evaluate the loose or medium rule sets, which include ECDomainMiner predictions and spurious reaction–Pfam links rather than only experimentally validated entries. Your reactions lack identifiers mappable to the RetroRules/Rhea/KEGG cross-referenced rule-enzyme associations, so found/missing tagging cannot be assigned.

skills.description: Use when initial MAGMa annotation rankings leave specific MS/MS peaks unexplained or correct candidates rank poorly, and you need to retrospectively test whether a more permissive fragmentation depth or mass tolerance resolves the miss.
skills.name: retrospective-annotation-evaluation
skills.search_text: retrospective-annotation-evaluation Use when initial MAGMa annotation rankings leave specific MS/MS peaks unexplained or correct candidates rank poorly, and you need to retrospectively test whether a more permissive fragmentation depth or mass tolerance resolves the miss. When the goal is a fresh de novo annotation for a new sample rather than diagnosing why an existing MAGMa run ranked a known candidate poorly — use a standard MAGMa run instead When the candidate of interest is absent from the PubChem snapshot used for retrieval, since the retrospective rerun can only reshuffle molecules already in the candidate list When the input is MSn multistage fragmentation data with n>2 rather than simple MS/MS peak lists, as the hierarchical nesting described here targets MS/MS spectral trees http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Rerun MAGMa's in silico fragmentation with relaxed or extended parameters (e.g. up to 5 bond dissociations instead of 3, or looser mass tolerance) after a contest or benchmark round, to explain previously unmatched MS/MS peaks and diagnose ranking failures across challenges. metabolomics/v3 10.5702/massspectrometry.s0033
skills.summary: Rerun MAGMa's in silico fragmentation with relaxed or extended parameters (e.g. up to 5 bond dissociations instead of 3, or looser mass tolerance) after a contest or benchmark round, to explain previously unmatched MS/MS peaks and diagnose ranking failures across challenges.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is a fresh de novo annotation for a new sample rather than diagnosing why an existing MAGMa run ranked a known candidate poorly — use a standard MAGMa run instead When the candidate of interest is absent from the PubChem snapshot used for retrieval, since the retrospective rerun can only reshuffle molecules already in the candidate list When the input is MSn multistage fragmentation data with n>2 rather than simple MS/MS peak lists, as the hierarchical nesting described here targets MS/MS spectral trees

skills.description: Use when a benchmark-contest solution set (e.g. CASMI challenges with known ground-truth molecules) must be re-analyzed after the fact to isolate the effect of a ranking or filtering parameter on correct-candidate rank.
skills.name: retrospective-challenge-benchmark-analysis
skills.search_text: retrospective-challenge-benchmark-analysis Use when a benchmark-contest solution set (e.g. CASMI challenges with known ground-truth molecules) must be re-analyzed after the fact to isolate the effect of a ranking or filtering parameter on correct-candidate rank. The input is a fresh prospective analysis with no known ground-truth structures — rank-improvement trends of the correct molecule cannot be evaluated. The candidate lists were not scored by MAGMa's substructure penalty score with refscore tie-breaking; refscore thresholds have no defined effect on other scoring schemes. The goal is de novo structure elucidation rather than benchmarking of an existing annotation workflow against challenge answers. A retrospective benchmarking procedure in which MAGMa's submitted CASMI 2013 results (candidate rankings based on substructure penalty scores and PubChem refscore) are re-analyzed offline to quantify how processing parameters, especially refscore candidate-list filtering, affect the rank of the correct chemical structure. metabolomics/v3 10.5702/massspectrometry.s0033
skills.summary: A retrospective benchmarking procedure in which MAGMa's submitted CASMI 2013 results (candidate rankings based on substructure penalty scores and PubChem refscore) are re-analyzed offline to quantify how processing parameters, especially refscore candidate-list filtering, affect the rank of the correct chemical structure.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a fresh prospective analysis with no known ground-truth structures — rank-improvement trends of the correct molecule cannot be evaluated. The candidate lists were not scored by MAGMa's substructure penalty score with refscore tie-breaking; refscore thresholds have no defined effect on other scoring schemes. The goal is de novo structure elucidation rather than benchmarking of an existing annotation workflow against challenge answers.

skills.description: Use when pseudo MS/MS spectra reconstructed from MS1-only data must be annotated against a reference MS/MS library but contain fragment peaks not present in the reference spectra (in-source fragments of adducts, multimers, co-eluting species).
skills.name: reverse-cosine-spectrum-search
skills.search_text: reverse-cosine-spectrum-search Use when pseudo MS/MS spectra reconstructed from MS1-only data must be annotated against a reference MS/MS library but contain fragment peaks not present in the reference spectra (in-source fragments of adducts, multimers, co-eluting species). When you have true MS/MS spectra with a single predefined precursor — the reverse search discards unmatched query peaks and is designed for composite/pseudo MS/MS spectra containing multiple ion forms; for MS2 data the modified cosine in forward mode is the appropriate comparator When reference spectra were collected at medium-to-high collision energies without applying the k=10 peak intensity scaling — the article reports that without peak scaling, ground-truth matches scoring >0.7 are substantially fewer For molecular-network edge construction, which instead requires modified cosine >= 0.8 and matched peaks >= 6 and removes all ions larger than the feature m/z from the pseudo MS/MS http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Asymmetric precursor-tolerant reverse spectral search that treats a reference MS/MS spectrum as a template, discarding unmatched query peaks so pseudo MS/MS spectra containing extra ion forms (adducts, multimers, co-eluting contaminants) can be matched against indexed MS/MS libraries. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.10.14.618269
skills.summary: Asymmetric precursor-tolerant reverse spectral search that treats a reference MS/MS spectrum as a template, discarding unmatched query peaks so pseudo MS/MS spectra containing extra ion forms (adducts, multimers, co-eluting contaminants) can be matched against indexed MS/MS libraries.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When you have true MS/MS spectra with a single predefined precursor — the reverse search discards unmatched query peaks and is designed for composite/pseudo MS/MS spectra containing multiple ion forms; for MS2 data the modified cosine in forward mode is the appropriate comparator When reference spectra were collected at medium-to-high collision energies without applying the k=10 peak intensity scaling — the article reports that without peak scaling, ground-truth matches scoring >0.7 are substantially fewer For molecular-network edge construction, which instead requires modified cosine >= 0.8 and matched peaks >= 6 and removes all ions larger than the feature m/z from the pseudo MS/MS

skills.description: Use when you have a dependency-network edge list of R packages annotated by hosting repository (CRAN, Bioconductor, GitHub) and need reverse-dependency connectivity metrics per repository.
skills.name: reverse-dependency-degree-computation
skills.search_text: reverse-dependency-degree-computation Use when you have a dependency-network edge list of R packages annotated by hosting repository (CRAN, Bioconductor, GitHub) and need reverse-dependency connectivity metrics per repository. The input is not a dependency network (e.g. it is a feature table, spectra file, or unstructured package list without dependency edges). Packages cannot be reliably annotated with a hosting repository, making per-repository in-degree aggregation meaningless. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3366 Computes per-repository reverse-dependency (in-degree) statistics for the metabolomics R package network catalogued in the metaRbolomics review, quantifying whether Bioconductor-hosted packages exhibit higher connectivity than CRAN-hosted ones due to Bioconductor's interoperability policy. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo9100200
skills.summary: Computes per-repository reverse-dependency (in-degree) statistics for the metabolomics R package network catalogued in the metaRbolomics review, quantifying whether Bioconductor-hosted packages exhibit higher connectivity than CRAN-hosted ones due to Bioconductor's interoperability policy.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is not a dependency network (e.g. it is a feature table, spectra file, or unstructured package list without dependency edges). Packages cannot be reliably annotated with a hosting repository, making per-repository in-degree aggregation meaningless.

skills.description: Use when a catalogued list of R packages (e.g. metabolomics packages from CRAN, Bioconductor and GitHub) is available and you need to know which other packages depend on them, to compare connectivity across repositories.
skills.name: reverse-dependency-network-construction
skills.search_text: reverse-dependency-network-construction Use when a catalogued list of R packages (e.g. metabolomics packages from CRAN, Bioconductor and GitHub) is available and you need to know which other packages depend on them, to compare connectivity across repositories. The package catalogue has not yet been built (this skill consumes the task_001 catalogue of metabolomics R packages, it does not produce it) You need forward dependencies of a single package rather than the reverse-dependency network over a whole package catalogue You are interested in GitHub-only packages with no CRAN or Bioconductor metadata, since edge extraction relies on CRAN available.packages() and Bioconductor metadata dumps http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 Builds the reverse-dependency network of the metabolomics R packages catalogued in the metaRbolomics review, by parsing Depends/Imports/LinkingTo fields from CRAN and Bioconductor metadata and keeping edges that point at catalogued packages. It quantifies the relative connectivity of CRAN versus Bioconductor packages, which the review attributes to Bioconductor's reuse-friendly policy. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo9100200
skills.summary: Builds the reverse-dependency network of the metabolomics R packages catalogued in the metaRbolomics review, by parsing Depends/Imports/LinkingTo fields from CRAN and Bioconductor metadata and keeping edges that point at catalogued packages. It quantifies the relative connectivity of CRAN versus Bioconductor packages, which the review attributes to Bioconductor's reuse-friendly policy.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The package catalogue has not yet been built (this skill consumes the task_001 catalogue of metabolomics R packages, it does not produce it) You need forward dependencies of a single package rather than the reverse-dependency network over a whole package catalogue You are interested in GitHub-only packages with no CRAN or Bioconductor metadata, since edge extraction relies on CRAN available.packages() and Bioconductor metadata dumps

skills.description: Use when you have MS1-only LC-MS or imaging MS data (mzML/mzXML or imzML) that lack DDA MS/MS files, and you want level 2/3 structural metabolite annotations by leveraging in/post-source fragment ions against an indexed MS/MS library.
skills.name: reverse-spectral-library-search
skills.search_text: reverse-spectral-library-search Use when you have MS1-only LC-MS or imaging MS data (mzML/mzXML or imzML) that lack DDA MS/MS files, and you want level 2/3 structural metabolite annotations by leveraging in/post-source fragment ions against an indexed MS/MS library. The input is already a feature table without chromatographic or spatial correlation information to build pseudo MS/MS spectra The goal is molecular formula assignment (MSI level 4) only, as METASPACE-style target-decoy FDR approaches address that rather than library-based reverse search The query spectra are true DDA MS/MS at matching collision energies — for those, conventional forward MS/MS search (e.g., the gnps.pkl library via ms1_id's MS/MS annotation) applies instead of peak-scaled reverse search of in-source fragments http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Annotate full-scan MS1 data by searching pseudo MS/MS spectra (built from correlated in-source fragments) against reference MS/MS libraries using precursor-tolerant reverse spectral matching with mass-dependent peak-intensity scaling, as implemented in the ms1-id package. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.10.14.618269
skills.summary: Annotate full-scan MS1 data by searching pseudo MS/MS spectra (built from correlated in-source fragments) against reference MS/MS libraries using precursor-tolerant reverse spectral matching with mass-dependent peak-intensity scaling, as implemented in the ms1-id package.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a feature table without chromatographic or spatial correlation information to build pseudo MS/MS spectra The goal is molecular formula assignment (MSI level 4) only, as METASPACE-style target-decoy FDR approaches address that rather than library-based reverse search The query spectra are true DDA MS/MS at matching collision energies — for those, conventional forward MS/MS search (e.g., the gnps.pkl library via ms1_id's MS/MS annotation) applies instead of peak-scaled reverse search of in-source fragments

skills.description: Use when you have paired RPLC datasets (two analytical runs or configurations sharing detected compounds) with retention order data and configuration metadata (eluent pH, organic-phase modifier/percentage, temperature), and need to identify which chromatographic factor drives retention-order.
skills.name: reversed-phase-liquid-chromatography-data-comparison
skills.search_text: reversed-phase-liquid-chromatography-data-comparison Use when you have paired RPLC datasets (two analytical runs or configurations sharing detected compounds) with retention order data and configuration metadata (eluent pH, organic-phase modifier/percentage, temperature), and need to identify which chromatographic factor drives retention-order. The datasets are HILIC rather than RPLC — the paired retention-order replicability analysis here applies to the reversed-phase system (HILIC generalizability is stated as future work in the article) The goal is predicting retention scores or ranking candidate structures for identification (use ROASMI itself) rather than assessing cross-method replicability of existing experimental retention orders The input is a single dataset with no chromatographically paired configuration to compare against — no CCRS can be computed http://edamontology.org/topic_0219 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 A paired-dataset comparison workflow that quantifies how well retention orders replicate across RPLC configurations using the CCRS (correlation coefficient of retention sequences), then attributes differences to chromatographic factors — chiefly eluent pH (ΔpH), organic-phase percentage (ΔF), modifier type, and column temperature. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-025-00968-8
skills.summary: A paired-dataset comparison workflow that quantifies how well retention orders replicate across RPLC configurations using the CCRS (correlation coefficient of retention sequences), then attributes differences to chromatographic factors — chiefly eluent pH (ΔpH), organic-phase percentage (ΔF), modifier type, and column temperature.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The datasets are HILIC rather than RPLC — the paired retention-order replicability analysis here applies to the reversed-phase system (HILIC generalizability is stated as future work in the article) The goal is predicting retention scores or ranking candidate structures for identification (use ROASMI itself) rather than assessing cross-method replicability of existing experimental retention orders The input is a single dataset with no chromatographically paired configuration to compare against — no CCRS can be computed

skills.description: Use when simulating MRS metabolite basis sets with repeated shaped pulses (e.g. PRESS/MEGA-PRESS/HERMES/HERCULES with editTp 14 ms or 20 ms) and per-sample propagator recalculation is the dominant runtime cost.
skills.name: rf-pulse-time-evolution-operator-computation
skills.search_text: rf-pulse-time-evolution-operator-computation Use when simulating MRS metabolite basis sets with repeated shaped pulses (e.g. PRESS/MEGA-PRESS/HERMES/HERCULES with editTp 14 ms or 20 ms) and per-sample propagator recalculation is the dominant runtime cost. The target experiment is STEAM or SPECIAL localization — MRSCloud does not implement these and this propagator workflow is built around PRESS/sLASER An exact vendor-specific parameter set is required — MRSCloud simulates the most commonly used parameter set and cannot capture all Philips experiments or all disseminated MEGA-PRESS versions within a vendor The pulse shapes/timings differ from the stored product-sequence RF waveforms, which are not shared in the GitHub repo Computes the density-matrix time-evolution propagator for each shaped RF refocusing/editing pulse exactly once and reuses it, instead of recalculating and applying an individual propagator per sampled spatial point (the elementwise FID-A approach), accelerating density-matrix basis set simulation in MRSCloud. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/mrm.29370
skills.summary: Computes the density-matrix time-evolution propagator for each shaped RF refocusing/editing pulse exactly once and reuses it, instead of recalculating and applying an individual propagator per sampled spatial point (the elementwise FID-A approach), accelerating density-matrix basis set simulation in MRSCloud.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The target experiment is STEAM or SPECIAL localization — MRSCloud does not implement these and this propagator workflow is built around PRESS/sLASER An exact vendor-specific parameter set is required — MRSCloud simulates the most commonly used parameter set and cannot capture all Philips experiments or all disseminated MEGA-PRESS versions within a vendor The pulse shapes/timings differ from the stored product-sequence RF waveforms, which are not shared in the GitHub repo

skills.description: Use when you have a centroided MSI peak matrix (e.g. rMSIproc .zip) and need an exploratory, per-pixel spatial visualization of dominant variance sources — e.g. to compare data quality before vs after peak filtering or cleaning.
skills.name: rgb-principal-component-image-compositing
skills.search_text: rgb-principal-component-image-compositing Use when you have a centroided MSI peak matrix (e.g. rMSIproc .zip) and need an exploratory, per-pixel spatial visualization of dominant variance sources — e.g. to compare data quality before vs after peak filtering or cleaning. The input is raw profile-mode spectra or an imzML file rather than a processed centroided peak matrix — preprocess with rMSIproc::ProcessWizard first. The goal is quantitative biomarker discovery or statistical testing rather than qualitative visual exploration of morphological contrast. The peak matrix has already been cleaned of matrix-related peaks and no before/after comparison is intended. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Compute PCA on an MSI peak matrix and encode the first three principal component scores per pixel as the red, green and blue channels of a spatial RGB composite image, as used in the rMSIcleanup paper's Figure 3 to visually demonstrate that removing matrix-related Ag peaks enhances morphological contrast. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-020-00449-0
skills.summary: Compute PCA on an MSI peak matrix and encode the first three principal component scores per pixel as the red, green and blue channels of a spatial RGB composite image, as used in the rMSIcleanup paper's Figure 3 to visually demonstrate that removing matrix-related Ag peaks enhances morphological contrast.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw profile-mode spectra or an imzML file rather than a processed centroided peak matrix — preprocess with rMSIproc::ProcessWizard first. The goal is quantitative biomarker discovery or statistical testing rather than qualitative visual exploration of morphological contrast. The peak matrix has already been cleaned of matrix-related peaks and no before/after comparison is intended.

skills.description: Use when a molecular-networking component of rhamnolipid or homologous lipid MS/MS spectra (positive mode, [M+Na]+ fragments) must be interpreted by annotating diagnostic fragment peaks and checking which shifted homolog peaks the MMSA multiple alignment failed to capture.
skills.name: rhamnolipid-fragment-mz-annotation
skills.search_text: rhamnolipid-fragment-mz-annotation Use when a molecular-networking component of rhamnolipid or homologous lipid MS/MS spectra (positive mode, [M+Na]+ fragments) must be interpreted by annotating diagnostic fragment peaks and checking which shifted homolog peaks the MMSA multiple alignment failed to capture. The spectra are not rhamnolipid (or closely homologous lipid) MS/MS with sodium-adduct fragments — the diagnostic m/z values 135.017, 211.130, 357.189, 239.162, 385.219 will not apply. The goal is a single pairwise spectrum comparison (e.g. Metabolomics Spectrum Resolver or ModiFinder for one pair) rather than a multiple-spectrum alignment across a whole molecular family. The data is already processed into a feature table (FBMN feature intensity matrix) without the underlying MS/MS peaks needed for fragment-level annotation. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Annotates diagnostic rhamnolipid fragment m/z values (e.g. rhamnose m/z 135.017, C10 HAA m/z 211.130, C10+rhamnose m/z 357.189) in MS/MS spectra of a Pseudomonas aeruginosa rhamnolipid molecular family, and checks whether MMSA alignment captures the shifted C12 analogues (m/z 239.162, 385.219). metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jasms.5c00237
skills.summary: Annotates diagnostic rhamnolipid fragment m/z values (e.g. rhamnose m/z 135.017, C10 HAA m/z 211.130, C10+rhamnose m/z 357.189) in MS/MS spectra of a Pseudomonas aeruginosa rhamnolipid molecular family, and checks whether MMSA alignment captures the shifted C12 analogues (m/z 239.162, 385.219).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The spectra are not rhamnolipid (or closely homologous lipid) MS/MS with sodium-adduct fragments — the diagnostic m/z values 135.017, 211.130, 357.189, 239.162, 385.219 will not apply. The goal is a single pairwise spectrum comparison (e.g. Metabolomics Spectrum Resolver or ModiFinder for one pair) rather than a multiple-spectrum alignment across a whole molecular family. The data is already processed into a feature table (FBMN feature intensity matrix) without the underlying MS/MS peaks needed for fragment-level annotation.

skills.description: Use when metabolomics samples have patient survival times and event indicators and the goal is prognosis prediction from pathway-level features (e.g., 67 NCI breast tumor samples × 536 metabolites reduced to PDS features).
skills.name: ridge-penalized-cox-proportional-hazards-modeling
skills.search_text: ridge-penalized-cox-proportional-hazards-modeling Use when metabolomics samples have patient survival times and event indicators and the goal is prognosis prediction from pathway-level features (e.g., 67 NCI breast tumor samples × 536 metabolites reduced to PDS features). The analysis goal is disease classification (case/control labeling) rather than survival prediction — use Lilikoi's machine-learning/DL classification module instead (lilikoi.machine_learning). Input features are raw metabolite abundances that have not yet been transformed to pathway deregulation scores; run MetaTOpathway/PDSfun first. No survival times or event indicators are available for the samples — the Cox framework is inapplicable. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Fits a penalized Cox proportional hazards survival model on pathway deregulation score (PDS) features derived from metabolomics data, as implemented in Lilikoi v2.0's prognosis module, and evaluates risk stratification by concordance index and log-rank test with Kaplan-Meier curves. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/gigascience/giaa162
skills.summary: Fits a penalized Cox proportional hazards survival model on pathway deregulation score (PDS) features derived from metabolomics data, as implemented in Lilikoi v2.0's prognosis module, and evaluates risk stratification by concordance index and log-rank test with Kaplan-Meier curves.

skills.search_text: risk-index-computation Use when prioritizing chemicals that have both exposure estimates (e.g., SEEM) and predicted toxicity data (e.g., ToxPi scores from ToxCast), and you need a combined risk-based ranking. When only one dimension (exposure alone or toxicity alone) is available for prioritization — the RI requires both a normalized exposure term and a ToxPi score. When the goal is hazard-only prioritization — use the PrHQ approach for the 13,441-chemical hazard-based ranking instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_3407 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Computes a risk index (RI) for each chemical as the product of normalized log-transformed SEEM exposure estimates and ToxCast-derived ToxPi toxicity scores, then ranks chemicals and compares RI ranks to probabilistic hazard quotient (PrHQ) ranks via Pearson correlation. metabolomics/v3 10.1289/ehp7722

skills.search_text: rna-seq-replicate-reproducibility-analysis Use when you have read counts or rank lists for the same transcript/gene set from two replicate RNA-seq experiments (within-lab or between-lab, e.g. SEQC comparisons) and need to quantify reproducibility with error control at a target mFDR such as alpha = 0.01. skills.name: roc-auc-metabolite-retrieval-assessment
skills.search_text: roc-auc-metabolite-retrieval-assessment Use when you have a set of generated structures with sampling frequencies and need to quantify how well that frequency signal retrieves withheld or newly-discovered metabolites (ROC AUC, enrichment, hypergeometric p-value). The evaluation set is drawn from the same time period / release as the model's training data, so 'novel' structures may already be in the training corpus (e.g. metabolites absent from or misannotated within the HMDB due to curation errors require explicit curation-error handling, not just frequency ranking) You need prioritization for metabolites from evolutionarily distant organisms (plant or bacterial metabolism) — the article notes the language model was trained and evaluated only on human metabolites and such applications will likely require a bespoke model You have no sampling-frequency or other model-intrinsic signal available and only possess an experimental mass-to-charge ratio to filter on http://edamontology.org/topic_0153 Evaluates whether a generative chemical language model's sampling frequency prioritizes genuinely novel metabolites by ranking generated SMILES, matching withheld cross-validation and prospective (e.g. HMDB v5.0) additions against the ranked table, and reporting ROC AUCs plus enrichment statistics. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.11.13.623458
skills.summary: Evaluates whether a generative chemical language model's sampling frequency prioritizes genuinely novel metabolites by ranking generated SMILES, matching withheld cross-validation and prospective (e.g. HMDB v5.0) additions against the ranked table, and reporting ROC AUCs plus enrichment statistics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The evaluation set is drawn from the same time period / release as the model's training data, so 'novel' structures may already be in the training corpus (e.g. metabolites absent from or misannotated within the HMDB due to curation errors require explicit curation-error handling, not just frequency ranking) You need prioritization for metabolites from evolutionarily distant organisms (plant or bacterial metabolism) — the article notes the language model was trained and evaluated only on human metabolites and such applications will likely require a bespoke model You have no sampling-frequency or other model-intrinsic signal available and only possess an experimental mass-to-charge ratio to filter on

skills.description: Use when a trained classifier (e.g. massNet's sigmoid output layer) emits per-spectrum class probabilities for labeled normal/tumor MSI spectra and you must report ROC AUC, confusion matrix, accuracy, and runtime.
skills.name: roc-auc-metric-computation
skills.search_text: roc-auc-metric-computation Use when a trained classifier (e.g. massNet's sigmoid output layer) emits per-spectrum class probabilities for labeled normal/tumor MSI spectra and you must report ROC AUC, confusion matrix, accuracy, and runtime. Input is a small feature-engineered peak table rather than raw high-dimensional mass spectral data — the SVM comparison context and paper's scope are end-to-end classification from 85,062 m/z variables The classification task is multi-class rather than binary normal/tumor — the paper only demonstrates binary class classification and defers multi-class extension to future work http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Computes ROC AUC, confusion matrix, accuracy, and per-class precision/recall/F1 over massNet's probabilistic pixel-based classifications of MALDI FT-ICR MSI spectra, to quantify tumor-vs-normal delineation performance on a withheld test set. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btac032
skills.summary: Computes ROC AUC, confusion matrix, accuracy, and per-class precision/recall/F1 over massNet's probabilistic pixel-based classifications of MALDI FT-ICR MSI spectra, to quantify tumor-vs-normal delineation performance on a withheld test set.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a small feature-engineered peak table rather than raw high-dimensional mass spectral data — the SVM comparison context and paper's scope are end-to-end classification from 85,062 m/z variables The classification task is multi-class rather than binary normal/tumor — the paper only demonstrates binary class classification and defers multi-class extension to future work

skills.description: Use when a longitudinal metabolomics dataset has a two-class outcome label (e.g. COVID-19 recovered vs. deceased) and the goal is classifier performance quantified by ROC/AUC plus feature-importance ranking.
skills.name: roc-auc-model-evaluation
skills.search_text: roc-auc-model-evaluation Use when a longitudinal metabolomics dataset has a two-class outcome label (e.g. COVID-19 recovered vs. deceased) and the goal is classifier performance quantified by ROC/AUC plus feature-importance ranking. The outcome is multi-class, continuous, or has no reliable binary labels — MeTEor's Prediction module is explicitly restricted to binary classification (LR, RF, XGB) Data still contains missing values, duplicate cases, or non-numeric metabolite columns — MeTEor requires imputation, duplicate removal, and numeric data types before modeling The analysis goal is unsupervised exploration or dimensionality reduction (PCA, TCAM) rather than supervised performance benchmarking Evaluate binary classifiers (logistic regression, random forest, or XGBoost) in MeTEor's Prediction module by computing ROC curves and AUC on held-out, stratified cross-validated predictions, benchmarked against the COVID-19 recovered-vs-deceased severity classification that reproduces More et al. (2022) at ~78.3% AUC. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioadv/vbae178
skills.summary: Evaluate binary classifiers (logistic regression, random forest, or XGBoost) in MeTEor's Prediction module by computing ROC curves and AUC on held-out, stratified cross-validated predictions, benchmarked against the COVID-19 recovered-vs-deceased severity classification that reproduces More et al. (2022) at ~78.3% AUC.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The outcome is multi-class, continuous, or has no reliable binary labels — MeTEor's Prediction module is explicitly restricted to binary classification (LR, RF, XGB) Data still contains missing values, duplicate cases, or non-numeric metabolite columns — MeTEor requires imputation, duplicate removal, and numeric data types before modeling The analysis goal is unsupervised exploration or dimensionality reduction (PCA, TCAM) rather than supervised performance benchmarking

skills.description: Use when a labeled metabolomics feature table (e.g. 234 CRC/PolyP/HC serum samples) must be split into train/test sets, modeled with RF and elastic net, and its discriminative power reported as ROC AUC values.
skills.name: roc-auc-model-validation
skills.search_text: roc-auc-model-validation Use when a labeled metabolomics feature table (e.g. 234 CRC/PolyP/HC serum samples) must be split into train/test sets, modeled with RF and elastic net, and its discriminative power reported as ROC AUC values. Raw mass-spectrometry pre-processing is needed — iMAP does not implement raw data preprocessing or peak picking and annotation modules Only differential metabolite screening is required (Kruskal-Wallis/Tukey/log2FC) with no predictive modeling or AUC estimation The dataset has unlabeled samples, so stratified train-test separation and supervised classification cannot be performed http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Build and validate predictive classifiers (random forest and elastic net) on selected metabolites using iMAP's automatic pipeline, then quantify discriminative performance with ROC AUC (pROC) on both train and held-out test sets. metabolomics/v3 10.3389/fchem.2021.659656
skills.summary: Build and validate predictive classifiers (random forest and elastic net) on selected metabolites using iMAP's automatic pipeline, then quantify discriminative performance with ROC AUC (pROC) on both train and held-out test sets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Raw mass-spectrometry pre-processing is needed — iMAP does not implement raw data preprocessing or peak picking and annotation modules Only differential metabolite screening is required (Kruskal-Wallis/Tukey/log2FC) with no predictive modeling or AUC estimation The dataset has unlabeled samples, so stratified train-test separation and supervised classification cannot be performed

skills.description: Use when you have a list of candidate structures filtered by predicted-vs-experimental ΔCCS and a known set of true annotations, and need to quantify threshold-dependent discrimination via ROC AUC.
skills.name: roc-auc-performance-evaluation
skills.search_text: roc-auc-performance-evaluation Use when you have a list of candidate structures filtered by predicted-vs-experimental ΔCCS and a known set of true annotations, and need to quantify threshold-dependent discrimination via ROC AUC. Input already contains ROC AUC values from the CCSP 2.0 paper; no need to recompute. The user only wants a single ΔCCS threshold applied without any ROC/AUC evaluation. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Evaluate CCS-based metabolite annotation filtering by sweeping ΔCCS thresholds and computing ROC curves plus AUC, e.g. reproducing the reported AUC drop from 0.657 to 0.589 when mass windows shrink. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.2c03491
skills.summary: Evaluate CCS-based metabolite annotation filtering by sweeping ΔCCS thresholds and computing ROC curves plus AUC, e.g. reproducing the reported AUC drop from 0.657 to 0.589 when mass windows shrink.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input already contains ROC AUC values from the CCSP 2.0 paper; no need to recompute. The user only wants a single ΔCCS threshold applied without any ROC/AUC evaluation.

skills.description: Use when evaluating a binary LC-MS peak classifier that emits true/false peak probability scores, by computing ROC/AUC on held-out calibration and test sets or by tracing performance versus training-set size.
skills.name: roc-auc-performance-evaluation
skills.search_text: roc-auc-performance-evaluation Use when evaluating a binary LC-MS peak classifier that emits true/false peak probability scores, by computing ROC/AUC on held-out calibration and test sets or by tracing performance versus training-set size. Peak groups have not yet been extracted (e.g., via MZmine 2) and converted to raster images with probability scores — there is nothing to evaluate with ROC/AUC yet The prediction task is multi-class or a continuous regression rather than binary true/false peak classification — the threshold-based ROC/AUC framing does not apply No manually reviewed ground-truth peak labels (true vs false) are available to compute true positive and true negative rates http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Evaluates the binary LC-MS peak-classification deep neural network (true vs false spectral peak) using ROC curves, AUC, and score-threshold selection, including learning-curve analysis of model performance versus training-set size. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.9b02983
skills.summary: Evaluates the binary LC-MS peak-classification deep neural network (true vs false spectral peak) using ROC curves, AUC, and score-threshold selection, including learning-curve analysis of model performance versus training-set size.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Peak groups have not yet been extracted (e.g., via MZmine 2) and converted to raster images with probability scores — there is nothing to evaluate with ROC/AUC yet The prediction task is multi-class or a continuous regression rather than binary true/false peak classification — the threshold-based ROC/AUC framing does not apply No manually reviewed ground-truth peak labels (true vs false) are available to compute true positive and true negative rates

skills.description: Use when you have per-feature ROC AUC values (e.g. one AUC per metabolite with 95% CIs from an OPLS-DA model) and need to verify that a multivariate pattern or panel outperforms every individual feature.
skills.name: roc-auc-ranking-analysis
skills.search_text: roc-auc-ranking-analysis Use when you have per-feature ROC AUC values (e.g. one AUC per metabolite with 95% CIs from an OPLS-DA model) and need to verify that a multivariate pattern or panel outperforms every individual feature. Input is raw GCxGC-TOFMS spectra or peak tables rather than precomputed per-metabolite AUC values — classification modeling (OPLS-DA, ROC curves) must come first. The goal is separating S. Typhi from S. Paratyphi A carriers rather than combined Salmonella carriage vs non-carriage controls; the 0.935 and >= 0.95 benchmarks apply to the combined-carriage comparison. No multivariate benchmark (pattern or panel AUC) exists to compare against, so the ranking cannot test the outperformance claim. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 A benchmarking procedure that ranks per-feature ROC AUC values against a multivariate-pattern AUC to verify that a combined metabolite pattern outperforms any single metabolite. In this paper, it tests whether any of 195 GCxGC-TOFMS metabolites matches the OPLS-DA carriage-pattern AUC. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pntd.0006215
skills.summary: A benchmarking procedure that ranks per-feature ROC AUC values against a multivariate-pattern AUC to verify that a combined metabolite pattern outperforms any single metabolite. In this paper, it tests whether any of 195 GCxGC-TOFMS metabolites matches the OPLS-DA carriage-pattern AUC.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw GCxGC-TOFMS spectra or peak tables rather than precomputed per-metabolite AUC values — classification modeling (OPLS-DA, ROC curves) must come first. The goal is separating S. Typhi from S. Paratyphi A carriers rather than combined Salmonella carriage vs non-carriage controls; the 0.935 and >= 0.95 benchmarks apply to the combined-carriage comparison. No multivariate benchmark (pattern or panel AUC) exists to compare against, so the ranking cannot test the outperformance claim.

skills.description: Use when an annotation-filtering step (e.g., ΔCCS 2.8% threshold at varying ppm mass tolerances) must be quantified as retained-correct-annotation vs. filtered-candidate trade-offs across mass windows.
skills.name: roc-based-filtering-evaluation
skills.search_text: roc-based-filtering-evaluation Use when an annotation-filtering step (e.g., ΔCCS 2.8% threshold at varying ppm mass tolerances) must be quantified as retained-correct-annotation vs. filtered-candidate trade-offs across mass windows. Candidate structures include dimers such as [2M+H]+ or [2M-H]-, other less common adducts, or in-source fragments — the CCSP 2.0 training sets do not support these Filtering is based on non-CCS evidence (retention-time matching to standards, MS/MS spectra, isotope clusters) rather than predicted-vs-observed ΔCCS CCS predictions are needed across different IM-MS instrument types (drift tube vs. travelling wave) — the effect of such experimental variance on the CCS threshold is not yet investigated http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Evaluates how well a candidate-annotation filter (e.g., ΔCCS-based filtering from CCSP 2.0) discriminates correct annotations from false positives by generating receiver operating characteristic curves and area-under-curve scores across multiple precursor mass windows (10, 7, 5, 3, 1, and 0 ppm). metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2022.08.09.503345
skills.summary: Evaluates how well a candidate-annotation filter (e.g., ΔCCS-based filtering from CCSP 2.0) discriminates correct annotations from false positives by generating receiver operating characteristic curves and area-under-curve scores across multiple precursor mass windows (10, 7, 5, 3, 1, and 0 ppm).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Candidate structures include dimers such as [2M+H]+ or [2M-H]-, other less common adducts, or in-source fragments — the CCSP 2.0 training sets do not support these Filtering is based on non-CCS evidence (retention-time matching to standards, MS/MS spectra, isotope clusters) rather than predicted-vs-observed ΔCCS CCS predictions are needed across different IM-MS instrument types (drift tube vs. travelling wave) — the effect of such experimental variance on the CCS threshold is not yet investigated

skills.description: Use when similarity scores from longitudinal fragment profiling (multi-collision-energy MS/MS matched against an in-house spectral library) must be converted into identification calls via ROC-derived thresholds, or when verifying match rates under a loosened criterion.
skills.name: roc-criterion-threshold-application
skills.search_text: roc-criterion-threshold-application Use when similarity scores from longitudinal fragment profiling (multi-collision-energy MS/MS matched against an in-house spectral library) must be converted into identification calls via ROC-derived thresholds, or when verifying match rates under a loosened criterion. Spectra are cross-sectional (single collision energy), so no longitudinal fragment profile can be built for Jaccard-based scoring against the multi-CE library. The goal is de novo annotation of unknowns with no reference MS/MS library — the ROC criteria only threshold similarity scores against the in-house ~180,000-spectrum library. Input is already a curated, identified feature/annotation table rather than raw QC MS/MS spectra needing match-rate evaluation. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Applies ROC-derived identification criteria (and a 0.7-fold loosened variant) to similarity scores produced by the optimized Jaccard longitudinal fragment profiling method, converting spectral-match scores into per-metabolite accept/reject calls and per-class correct-match rates for spiked plasma QC samples. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c01414
skills.summary: Applies ROC-derived identification criteria (and a 0.7-fold loosened variant) to similarity scores produced by the optimized Jaccard longitudinal fragment profiling method, converting spectral-match scores into per-metabolite accept/reject calls and per-class correct-match rates for spiked plasma QC samples.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Spectra are cross-sectional (single collision energy), so no longitudinal fragment profile can be built for Jaccard-based scoring against the multi-CE library. The goal is de novo annotation of unknowns with no reference MS/MS library — the ROC criteria only threshold similarity scores against the in-house ~180,000-spectrum library. Input is already a curated, identified feature/annotation table rather than raw QC MS/MS spectra needing match-rate evaluation.

skills.description: Use when a binary filter (e.g. RT-error agreement) must be tuned to a threshold that maximizes true-positive retention while quantifying false-identity removal, with ROC curves built via scikit-learn.
skills.name: roc-curve-analysis
skills.search_text: roc-curve-analysis Use when a binary filter (e.g. RT-error agreement) must be tuned to a threshold that maximizes true-positive retention while quantifying false-identity removal, with ROC curves built via scikit-learn. The task is pure RT prediction (e.g. fine-tuning RT-Transformer on a new chromatographic method via transfer.py) rather than threshold calibration for identity filtering — then ROC analysis is premature. Candidate compounds have no observed retention time to compare against, so relative RT error cannot be computed and a ROC sweep is not defined. The filter criterion is not a continuous score threshold (e.g. a hard MS/MS spectral-match rule), for which a ROC curve over that score is not meaningful. http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Construct receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves by sweeping a molecular-feature threshold (here, relative retention-time error between RT-Transformer-predicted and observed RT) to select an optimal operating point and quantify how many false-identity candidates the filter eliminates on held-out test sets such as SMRT and SMRT_Retained. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae084
skills.summary: Construct receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves by sweeping a molecular-feature threshold (here, relative retention-time error between RT-Transformer-predicted and observed RT) to select an optimal operating point and quantify how many false-identity candidates the filter eliminates on held-out test sets such as SMRT and SMRT_Retained.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is pure RT prediction (e.g. fine-tuning RT-Transformer on a new chromatographic method via transfer.py) rather than threshold calibration for identity filtering — then ROC analysis is premature. Candidate compounds have no observed retention time to compare against, so relative RT error cannot be computed and a ROC sweep is not defined. The filter criterion is not a continuous score threshold (e.g. a hard MS/MS spectral-match rule), for which a ROC curve over that score is not meaningful.

skills.description: Use when you have per-compound ranked candidate structure lists with a known correct structure and want to quantify whether a score (e.g. COSMIC confidence score or tool hit score) separates correct from incorrect annotations.
skills.name: roc-curve-auc-analysis
skills.search_text: roc-curve-auc-analysis Use when you have per-compound ranked candidate structure lists with a known correct structure and want to quantify whether a score (e.g. COSMIC confidence score or tool hit score) separates correct from incorrect annotations. Input is raw LC-MS/MS data (mzML/mzXML) rather than per-compound ranked hit scores with known correct structures — process spectra first with SIRIUS 4/CSI:FingerID.
