You need to estimate a score threshold for a new biological dataset — the article warns that accurate FDR estimation from small-molecule fragmentation spectra remains highly challenging and thresholds are practical guidance only. You want to interpret the confidence score as the probability that an annotation is correct — the article states this is impossible by design of the score. http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Evaluates how well a ranking score (e.g. COSMIC confidence scores versus in silico tool hit scores from MetFrag, MAGMa+, CFM-ID, CSI:FingerID) separates correct from incorrect structure annotations on CASMI 2016, using ROC curves, AUC, hop plots, and correct-hit counts at fixed FDR levels. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41587-021-01045-9
skills.summary: Evaluates how well a ranking score (e.g. COSMIC confidence scores versus in silico tool hit scores from MetFrag, MAGMa+, CFM-ID, CSI:FingerID) separates correct from incorrect structure annotations on CASMI 2016, using ROC curves, AUC, hop plots, and correct-hit counts at fixed FDR levels.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw LC-MS/MS data (mzML/mzXML) rather than per-compound ranked hit scores with known correct structures — process spectra first with SIRIUS 4/CSI:FingerID. You need to estimate a score threshold for a new biological dataset — the article warns that accurate FDR estimation from small-molecule fragmentation spectra remains highly challenging and thresholds are practical guidance only. You want to interpret the confidence score as the probability that an annotation is correct — the article states this is impossible by design of the score.

skills.description: Use when a supervised classification model (e.g. OPLS-DA in SIMCA) produces cross-validated scores that must be converted into ROC curves and AUC values with bootstrap confidence intervals to report diagnostic performance.
skills.name: roc-curve-auc-evaluation
skills.search_text: roc-curve-auc-evaluation Use when a supervised classification model (e.g. OPLS-DA in SIMCA) produces cross-validated scores that must be converted into ROC curves and AUC values with bootstrap confidence intervals to report diagnostic performance. The model outputs are unsupervised PCA scores with no class labels — ROC/AUC requires labeled pairwise comparisons The task is comparing acute enteric fever profiles rather than classifying carriage vs non-carriage samples The goal is to report chemometric separation significance (e.g. CV-ANOVA p = 0.0031) rather than classifier diagnostic performance http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0219 Builds and evaluates ROC curves from cross-validated OPLS-DA model scores of GCxGC-TOFMS plasma metabolite data to quantify diagnostic performance (AUC) for distinguishing Salmonella carriage from non-carriage controls, with 95% confidence intervals from 1,000-percentile bootstraps. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pntd.0006215
skills.summary: Builds and evaluates ROC curves from cross-validated OPLS-DA model scores of GCxGC-TOFMS plasma metabolite data to quantify diagnostic performance (AUC) for distinguishing Salmonella carriage from non-carriage controls, with 95% confidence intervals from 1,000-percentile bootstraps.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The model outputs are unsupervised PCA scores with no class labels — ROC/AUC requires labeled pairwise comparisons The task is comparing acute enteric fever profiles rather than classifying carriage vs non-carriage samples The goal is to report chemometric separation significance (e.g. CV-ANOVA p = 0.0031) rather than classifier diagnostic performance

skills.description: Use when two binary signal/noise classifiers on labeled synthetic mass-spectrometry windows (e.g., LSH vs. intensity thresholding) must be compared by receiver operating characteristic performance.
skills.name: roc-curve-computation
skills.search_text: roc-curve-computation Use when two binary signal/noise classifiers on labeled synthetic mass-spectrometry windows (e.g., LSH vs. intensity thresholding) must be compared by receiver operating characteristic performance. Input is real (non-synthetic) timsTOF data without gold-standard peak-level ground-truth labels — the article notes no such annotation was available, so ROC evaluation is not well-defined there. The task is data reduction (e.g., applying the strong (32,32) filter to shrink large datasets) rather than classifier performance comparison. Peak labels are absent, so noise_2 peaks cannot be excluded and classification rates would be biased. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Computes and plots ROC curves comparing the LSH-based signal classifier against the intensity (SNR) thresholding baseline on labeled synthetic timsTOF windows, with per-threshold true-positive and false-positive rates excluding noise_2 peaks. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-022-04833-5
skills.summary: Computes and plots ROC curves comparing the LSH-based signal classifier against the intensity (SNR) thresholding baseline on labeled synthetic timsTOF windows, with per-threshold true-positive and false-positive rates excluding noise_2 peaks.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is real (non-synthetic) timsTOF data without gold-standard peak-level ground-truth labels — the article notes no such annotation was available, so ROC evaluation is not well-defined there. The task is data reduction (e.g., applying the strong (32,32) filter to shrink large datasets) rather than classifier performance comparison. Peak labels are absent, so noise_2 peaks cannot be excluded and classification rates would be biased.

skills.description: Use when a trained binary classifier on metabolite reaction-pair (RP vs. non-RP) predictions needs held-out performance evaluation via ROC analysis, threshold selection, and AUC reporting.
skills.name: roc-curve-evaluation
skills.search_text: roc-curve-evaluation Use when a trained binary classifier on metabolite reaction-pair (RP vs. non-RP) predictions needs held-out performance evaluation via ROC analysis, threshold selection, and AUC reporting. Evaluating the filtered candidate set of the curated MRN — no clearly defined non-RPs exist under the screening conditions, and GNN-based performance metrics are inapplicable, so no FDR can be reported Tasks needing calibration or precision-recall analysis rather than ROC/threshold-Youden evaluation of an RP-vs-non-RP classifier http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Evaluates a binary reaction-pair classifier (the GNN used to curate MetDNA3's metabolic reaction network) by sweeping decision thresholds on a held-out test set, selecting the cutoff via the weighted Youden index, and reporting the ROC curve/AUC. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-025-63536-6
skills.summary: Evaluates a binary reaction-pair classifier (the GNN used to curate MetDNA3's metabolic reaction network) by sweeping decision thresholds on a held-out test set, selecting the cutoff via the weighted Youden index, and reporting the ROC curve/AUC.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Evaluating the filtered candidate set of the curated MRN — no clearly defined non-RPs exist under the screening conditions, and GNN-based performance metrics are inapplicable, so no FDR can be reported Tasks needing calibration or precision-recall analysis rather than ROC/threshold-Youden evaluation of an RP-vs-non-RP classifier

skills.description: Use when multiple peak-curation strategies (e.g., active-learning scores, CV-of-QC-peak-area filters, NeatMS) must be ranked by how well their scores separate manually annotated true peaks from artifacts.
skills.name: roc-curve-performance-evaluation
skills.search_text: roc-curve-performance-evaluation Use when multiple peak-curation strategies (e.g., active-learning scores, CV-of-QC-peak-area filters, NeatMS) must be ranked by how well their scores separate manually annotated true peaks from artifacts. No manual annotations of true peaks versus artifacts exist, so there is no ground truth to compute a ROC curve against The goal is unsupervised peak filtering with a fixed cutoff rather than comparative benchmarking of curation methods Input is a single method's binary pass/fail filter output with no continuous score, since ROC requires score variation across thresholds http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Compute ROC curves and AUROC values to benchmark peak-curation methods against manual annotations of true peaks versus artifacts, as done in PeakDetective's evaluation of active learning against CV filtering, peak-area filtering, NeatMS, and supervised training on Dataset 1 (negative-mode human plasma HILIC/TOF LC/MS). metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c00764
skills.summary: Compute ROC curves and AUROC values to benchmark peak-curation methods against manual annotations of true peaks versus artifacts, as done in PeakDetective's evaluation of active learning against CV filtering, peak-area filtering, NeatMS, and supervised training on Dataset 1 (negative-mode human plasma HILIC/TOF LC/MS).
skills.when_to_use_negative: No manual annotations of true peaks versus artifacts exist, so there is no ground truth to compute a ROC curve against The goal is unsupervised peak filtering with a fixed cutoff rather than comparative benchmarking of curation methods Input is a single method's binary pass/fail filter output with no continuous score, since ROC requires score variation across thresholds

skills.description: Use when two weighted risk scores must be compared for predictive accuracy of a time-to-event outcome with right censoring — e.g. biomarker vs conventional scores for 5-/10-year all-cause mortality in a cohort like FINRISK 1997.
skills.name: roc-curve-visualization
skills.search_text: roc-curve-visualization Use when two weighted risk scores must be compared for predictive accuracy of a time-to-event outcome with right censoring — e.g. biomarker vs conventional scores for 5-/10-year all-cause mortality in a cohort like FINRISK 1997. The risk scores were trained in the same cohort used for evaluation — weights must come from an independent cohort (here the Estonian Biobank) to avoid overestimation of predictive ability The outcome is a binary, uncensored endpoint — a standard ROC/AUC on case-control labels is then appropriate instead of a censoring-aware C-statistic from a Cox model The goal is clinical patient classification — the article explicitly states the biomarker score 'is not yet suitable for classification of patients in the clinic, since it is based on scaled biomarker values created separately for each cohort' http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Compares the discrimination of competing mortality risk scores in a censored cohort by computing Harrell's C-statistics and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI) from Cox proportional hazards models fitted with age at blood sampling as the time scale, producing a Table 4-style contrast (ΔC with SE/P, IDI with SE/P) for 5- and 10-year follow-up windows. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-019-11311-9
skills.summary: Compares the discrimination of competing mortality risk scores in a censored cohort by computing Harrell's C-statistics and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI) from Cox proportional hazards models fitted with age at blood sampling as the time scale, producing a Table 4-style contrast (ΔC with SE/P, IDI with SE/P) for 5- and 10-year follow-up windows.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The risk scores were trained in the same cohort used for evaluation — weights must come from an independent cohort (here the Estonian Biobank) to avoid overestimation of predictive ability The outcome is a binary, uncensored endpoint — a standard ROC/AUC on case-control labels is then appropriate instead of a censoring-aware C-statistic from a Cox model The goal is clinical patient classification — the article explicitly states the biomarker score 'is not yet suitable for classification of patients in the clinic, since it is based on scaled biomarker values created separately for each cohort'

skills.description: Use when a binary lipid-biomarker classifier (e.g., LightGBM on RF-selected featured lipids) has produced predicted probabilities for case/control cohorts and you must quantify and visualize discrimination per cohort, as in reproducing Fig. 5c.
skills.name: roc-curve-visualization
skills.search_text: roc-curve-visualization Use when a binary lipid-biomarker classifier (e.g., LightGBM on RF-selected featured lipids) has produced predicted probabilities for case/control cohorts and you must quantify and visualize discrimination per cohort, as in reproducing Fig. 5c. Input is raw LC-MS/MS spectra or unannotated features — run LipidIN annotation (MS2 library search against the theoretical library) first; ROC visualization operates on a labeled feature table The classification task is multiclass without a defined case/control binarization — roc_curve and roc_auc_score require binary labels or one-vs-rest probabilities No class labels or predicted probabilities exist (e.g., only unsupervised PCA/PLS-DA QC output) — ROC curves cannot be computed http://edamontology.org/topic_3524 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Computes and plots ROC curves with AUC for lipid-biomarker classifiers (e.g., LightGBM on random-forest-selected lipids) across two breast cancer cohorts, mirroring Fig. 5c of the LipidIN paper to demonstrate panel discrimination between patients and healthy subjects. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-025-59683-5
skills.summary: Computes and plots ROC curves with AUC for lipid-biomarker classifiers (e.g., LightGBM on random-forest-selected lipids) across two breast cancer cohorts, mirroring Fig. 5c of the LipidIN paper to demonstrate panel discrimination between patients and healthy subjects.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw LC-MS/MS spectra or unannotated features — run LipidIN annotation (MS2 library search against the theoretical library) first; ROC visualization operates on a labeled feature table The classification task is multiclass without a defined case/control binarization — roc_curve and roc_auc_score require binary labels or one-vs-rest probabilities No class labels or predicted probabilities exist (e.g., only unsupervised PCA/PLS-DA QC output) — ROC curves cannot be computed

skills.description: Use when query MS/MS spectra (e.g. Exploris 480, 150 CP and 134 CN modes) must be scored against a multi-collision-energy reference library and a binary match/no-match decision is needed using validated Figure 2 cutoff thresholds.
skills.name: roc-cutoff-based-match-calling
skills.search_text: roc-cutoff-based-match-calling Use when query MS/MS spectra (e.g. Exploris 480, 150 CP and 134 CN modes) must be scored against a multi-collision-energy reference library and a binary match/no-match decision is needed using validated Figure 2 cutoff thresholds. Query spectra were acquired on the same instrument as the reference library under identical collision energies — cross-sectional (single-CE) similarity methods such as dot product or optimal entropy may suffice No ROC-derived cutoff criteria exist for the reference library in use; thresholds would have to be re-derived before calling matches The goal is candidate ranking rather than binary match calling — similarity scores alone, without cutoff application, are the appropriate output http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Calls MS/MS query-to-reference metabolite matches by applying cutoff criteria derived from ROC analysis of thousands of isomers in the in-house CQMD database, optionally with 0.8-fold relaxed cutoffs for sensitivity-oriented re-scoring. Used here to quantify inter-instrument transferability (Exploris 480 queries vs Exploris 120 CQMD references). metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c01414
skills.summary: Calls MS/MS query-to-reference metabolite matches by applying cutoff criteria derived from ROC analysis of thousands of isomers in the in-house CQMD database, optionally with 0.8-fold relaxed cutoffs for sensitivity-oriented re-scoring. Used here to quantify inter-instrument transferability (Exploris 480 queries vs Exploris 120 CQMD references).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Query spectra were acquired on the same instrument as the reference library under identical collision energies — cross-sectional (single-CE) similarity methods such as dot product or optimal entropy may suffice No ROC-derived cutoff criteria exist for the reference library in use; thresholds would have to be re-derived before calling matches The goal is candidate ranking rather than binary match calling — similarity scores alone, without cutoff application, are the appropriate output

skills.description: Use when you have confidence-scored structure candidates from multiple spectral conditions (e.g. 10/20/40 eV, merged) and need to benchmark how many correct hits each condition recovers at a given annotation rate threshold.
skills.name: roc-endpoint-annotation-rate-analysis
skills.search_text: roc-endpoint-annotation-rate-analysis Use when you have confidence-scored structure candidates from multiple spectral conditions (e.g. 10/20/40 eV, merged) and need to benchmark how many correct hits each condition recovers at a given annotation rate threshold. When input is a feature-abundance table or an already-validated list of compound identities rather than candidate rankings with confidence scores. When the goal is quantification of abundances rather than benchmarking the correctness/annotation-rate trade-off of structure annotation. When spectra are in profiled mode or negative ion mode only — the underlying workflow discards these (only positive centroided .mzML/.mzXML are processed). http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Evaluates a confidence-scored in-silico structure annotation workflow (COSMIC/CSI:FingerID) by plotting correct-hit count versus annotation rate across collision energies, noise levels, and datasets, reading each curve's endpoint (ROC end) to recover expected correct-hit totals such as 1,829–1,948 on NIST Orbitrap (n=3,721) and QTOF (n=3,013) sets. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41587-021-01045-9
skills.summary: Evaluates a confidence-scored in-silico structure annotation workflow (COSMIC/CSI:FingerID) by plotting correct-hit count versus annotation rate across collision energies, noise levels, and datasets, reading each curve's endpoint (ROC end) to recover expected correct-hit totals such as 1,829–1,948 on NIST Orbitrap (n=3,721) and QTOF (n=3,013) sets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When input is a feature-abundance table or an already-validated list of compound identities rather than candidate rankings with confidence scores. When the goal is quantification of abundances rather than benchmarking the correctness/annotation-rate trade-off of structure annotation. When spectra are in profiled mode or negative ion mode only — the underlying workflow discards these (only positive centroided .mzML/.mzXML are processed).

skills.description: Use when comparing NMR preprocessing/summarization methods (peak-picking-then-grouping vs binning vs alignment+binning) on case-vs-control spectra and you need ROC and Precision-Recall curves as the performance metric.
skills.name: roc-precision-recall-curve-analysis
skills.search_text: roc-precision-recall-curve-analysis Use when comparing NMR preprocessing/summarization methods (peak-picking-then-grouping vs binning vs alignment+binning) on case-vs-control spectra and you need ROC and Precision-Recall curves as the performance metric. Input is already a feature table or the analysis goal is a single method's performance rather than comparing spectral preprocessing/summarization alternatives The spectra are not labeled into case vs control groups, since ROC/PRC curves require known class membership http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Benchmarking method that evaluates 1D NMR spectral summarization workflows (speaq 2.0 peak-based processing vs binning and alignment-plus-binning) by computing ROC and Precision-Recall curves from case-vs-control classification of the resulting feature matrices, as used in the speaq 2.0 simulated-data comparison. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1006018
skills.summary: Benchmarking method that evaluates 1D NMR spectral summarization workflows (speaq 2.0 peak-based processing vs binning and alignment-plus-binning) by computing ROC and Precision-Recall curves from case-vs-control classification of the resulting feature matrices, as used in the speaq 2.0 simulated-data comparison.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a feature table or the analysis goal is a single method's performance rather than comparing spectral preprocessing/summarization alternatives The spectra are not labeled into case vs control groups, since ROC/PRC curves require known class membership

skills.description: Use when a lipidomics table with lipid abundances and attached study variables contains a binary nominal variable (e.g., condition/treatment group) and you need to quantify which selected lipid subset separates the two classes.
skills.name: roc-separation-evaluation-binary-variables
skills.search_text: roc-separation-evaluation-binary-variables Use when a lipidomics table with lipid abundances and attached study variables contains a binary nominal variable (e.g., condition/treatment group) and you need to quantify which selected lipid subset separates the two classes. The study variable is continuous/numerical rather than a binary nominal variable — rank models by AIC only, ROC accuracy does not apply The imported data contains fewer than two study variables, so a 'Complete feature analysis' relating variables to each other cannot be computed The goal is lipidome structural comparison (MCS + Jaccard distances, PCA lipid space model, Hausdorff distances) rather than identifying lipids that distinguish study variables http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 LipidSpace's feature analysis evaluates how well the lipid subsets selected by sequential forward selection (SFS) separate binary nominal study variables by additionally computing ROC accuracy alongside the AIC-ranked regression models, writing the per-variable results to feature_analysis_results.csv. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c02449
skills.summary: LipidSpace's feature analysis evaluates how well the lipid subsets selected by sequential forward selection (SFS) separate binary nominal study variables by additionally computing ROC accuracy alongside the AIC-ranked regression models, writing the per-variable results to feature_analysis_results.csv.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The study variable is continuous/numerical rather than a binary nominal variable — rank models by AIC only, ROC accuracy does not apply The imported data contains fewer than two study variables, so a 'Complete feature analysis' relating variables to each other cannot be computed The goal is lipidome structural comparison (MCS + Jaccard distances, PCA lipid space model, Hausdorff distances) rather than identifying lipids that distinguish study variables

skills.description: Use when a trained binary classifier outputs probability scores for LC-MS peak groups and you need to characterize discriminative performance and pick an operating point.
skills.name: roc-threshold-optimization
skills.search_text: roc-threshold-optimization Use when a trained binary classifier outputs probability scores for LC-MS peak groups and you need to characterize discriminative performance and pick an operating point. The classifier has not yet produced probability scores for each peak group Peak group labels are not manually reviewed so no ground-truth true/false peaks exist to compute rates A single fixed threshold has already been chosen and no threshold sweep is needed http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Computes receiver operating characteristic curves from the trained LC-MS peak-classification model's probability scores and selects the optimum score threshold, reporting sensitivity (true positive rate) and specificity (false positive rate) at each cutoff. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.9b02983
skills.summary: Computes receiver operating characteristic curves from the trained LC-MS peak-classification model's probability scores and selects the optimum score threshold, reporting sensitivity (true positive rate) and specificity (false positive rate) at each cutoff.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The classifier has not yet produced probability scores for each peak group Peak group labels are not manually reviewed so no ground-truth true/false peaks exist to compute rates A single fixed threshold has already been chosen and no threshold sweep is needed

skills.description: Use when candidate identities from accurate mass search (e.g. 10 ppm HMDB search) must be filtered or ranked by predicted-vs-experimental RT error, and you need an objective error-threshold choice.
skills.name: roc-threshold-optimization
skills.search_text: roc-threshold-optimization Use when candidate identities from accurate mass search (e.g. 10 ppm HMDB search) must be filtered or ranked by predicted-vs-experimental RT error, and you need an objective error-threshold choice. When candidate filtering is by m/z accuracy alone rather than predicted-vs-experimental RT error (e.g. no experimental RT data exist for the chromatographic method) When a single fixed RT tolerance window is already established and no threshold optimization against TP/TN/FP/FN trade-offs is required When evaluating a classifier on continuous scores unrelated to RT error — the 2.5% relative-RT-error discretization is specific to RT-based candidate filtering Discretizes the relative retention-time (RT) error between projected predicted RTs and experimental RTs into 2.5% bins, computes TP/TN/FP/FN per bin to build ROC curves, and selects the filtering threshold that maximizes TPR while minimizing FPR for candidate identity ranking. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-019-13680-7
skills.summary: Discretizes the relative retention-time (RT) error between projected predicted RTs and experimental RTs into 2.5% bins, computes TP/TN/FP/FN per bin to build ROC curves, and selects the filtering threshold that maximizes TPR while minimizing FPR for candidate identity ranking.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When candidate filtering is by m/z accuracy alone rather than predicted-vs-experimental RT error (e.g. no experimental RT data exist for the chromatographic method) When a single fixed RT tolerance window is already established and no threshold optimization against TP/TN/FP/FN trade-offs is required When evaluating a classifier on continuous scores unrelated to RT error — the 2.5% relative-RT-error discretization is specific to RT-based candidate filtering

skills.description: Use when establishing identification criteria (similarity-score thresholds) for MS/MS spectral matching of isomer pairs, e.g., computing I/N-ratio ROC cutoffs and sensitivity/specificity across CP, CN, AP, AN ionization modes in a spectral database like CQMD.
skills.name: roc-threshold-optimization-for-spectral-matching
skills.search_text: roc-threshold-optimization-for-spectral-matching Use when establishing identification criteria (similarity-score thresholds) for MS/MS spectral matching of isomer pairs, e.g., computing I/N-ratio ROC cutoffs and sensitivity/specificity across CP, CN, AP, AN ionization modes in a spectral database like CQMD. The goal is cross-sectional spectral matching with a single collision-energy spectrum — the cutoffs here are derived from multi-CE longitudinal fragment profiles (I/N ratio), not single-spectrum similarity scores Comparing metabolites against public libraries (MoNA, GNPS, METLIN) without isomer-pair labels — ROC analysis requires known identical vs constitutional isomer pairs to define positives and negatives Quantifying metabolite abundance rather than establishing identification criteria — this skill only optimizes similarity-score thresholds, it does not perform identification itself http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Derives isomer-identification similarity-score cutoffs for the longitudinal fragment profiling (LFP) method by running ROC analysis on I/N (intensity-based over number-based Jaccard) similarity ratios within LFP-number bins, then reports per-bin AUCs and per-ionization-mode sensitivity/specificity. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c01414
skills.summary: Derives isomer-identification similarity-score cutoffs for the longitudinal fragment profiling (LFP) method by running ROC analysis on I/N (intensity-based over number-based Jaccard) similarity ratios within LFP-number bins, then reports per-bin AUCs and per-ionization-mode sensitivity/specificity.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is cross-sectional spectral matching with a single collision-energy spectrum — the cutoffs here are derived from multi-CE longitudinal fragment profiles (I/N ratio), not single-spectrum similarity scores Comparing metabolites against public libraries (MoNA, GNPS, METLIN) without isomer-pair labels — ROC analysis requires known identical vs constitutional isomer pairs to define positives and negatives Quantifying metabolite abundance rather than establishing identification criteria — this skill only optimizes similarity-score thresholds, it does not perform identification itself

skills.description: Use when benchmarking spectral similarity algorithms on isomer vs non-isomer pairs across multiple collision energies (13 individual NCEs or stepped NCE 20/40/60%) and you need threshold-based sensitivity/specificity figures to set identification criteria.
skills.name: roc-threshold-sensitivity-specificity-evaluation
skills.search_text: roc-threshold-sensitivity-specificity-evaluation Use when benchmarking spectral similarity algorithms on isomer vs non-isomer pairs across multiple collision energies (13 individual NCEs or stepped NCE 20/40/60%) and you need threshold-based sensitivity/specificity figures to set identification criteria. The spectra were acquired at only a single collision energy, so neither the 13-individual-NCE sweep nor stepped NCE 20/40/60% comparison can be reproduced There is no isomer/non-isomer ground-truth labeling of pairs, making sensitivity/specificity and ROC analysis undefined The results are intended for clinical decision-making — the README states the data 'are intended for experimental reference only and should not be directly interpreted or used to guide human medicine' http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Establishes MS/MS spectral-matching identification criteria via ROC analysis over thousands of isomer pairs in the CQMD database, then evaluates each similarity algorithm (dot product, modified dot product, entropy, optimized Jaccard) x collision-energy condition as binary sensitivity/specificity at a 0.95 score threshold. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c01414
skills.summary: Establishes MS/MS spectral-matching identification criteria via ROC analysis over thousands of isomer pairs in the CQMD database, then evaluates each similarity algorithm (dot product, modified dot product, entropy, optimized Jaccard) x collision-energy condition as binary sensitivity/specificity at a 0.95 score threshold.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The spectra were acquired at only a single collision energy, so neither the 13-individual-NCE sweep nor stepped NCE 20/40/60% comparison can be reproduced There is no isomer/non-isomer ground-truth labeling of pairs, making sensitivity/specificity and ROC analysis undefined The results are intended for clinical decision-making — the README states the data 'are intended for experimental reference only and should not be directly interpreted or used to guide human medicine'

skills.description: Use when you have 1H NMR spectra of plasma (or other biofluid) samples plus a curated metabolite reference library, and need per-metabolite concentration estimates to benchmark against a new quantification method.
skills.name: roi-based-targeted-metabolite-fitting
skills.search_text: roi-based-targeted-metabolite-fitting Use when you have 1H NMR spectra of plasma (or other biofluid) samples plus a curated metabolite reference library, and need per-metabolite concentration estimates to benchmark against a new quantification method. When the goal is automatic quantification without a manually curated ROI library or prior metabolite selection — the article notes rDolphin requires manual library adjustment and Batman requires customized libraries built from specialized knowledge, whereas NMRQNet automates candidate selection. When you need to quantify metabolites absent from the predefined ROI/reference library — targeted fitting cannot recover signal outside the curated metabolite set. http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_3336 Targeted profiling of 1H NMR plasma spectra by fitting predefined regions-of-interest (ROIs) from a curated metabolite library to each sample spectrum, as used for rDolphin and Batman baselines in the NMRQNet comparison on 40 MDS-family plasma samples. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2023.03.01.530642
skills.summary: Targeted profiling of 1H NMR plasma spectra by fitting predefined regions-of-interest (ROIs) from a curated metabolite library to each sample spectrum, as used for rDolphin and Batman baselines in the NMRQNet comparison on 40 MDS-family plasma samples.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is automatic quantification without a manually curated ROI library or prior metabolite selection — the article notes rDolphin requires manual library adjustment and Batman requires customized libraries built from specialized knowledge, whereas NMRQNet automates candidate selection. When you need to quantify metabolites absent from the predefined ROI/reference library — targeted fitting cannot recover signal outside the curated metabolite set.

skills.description: Use when you have already detected ROIs on each GC-IMS sample in a dataset and need one consolidated list of peaks, with per-sample intensity values, to feed peak integration and peakTable().
skills.name: roi-clustering-across-samples
skills.search_text: roi-clustering-across-samples Use when you have already detected ROIs on each GC-IMS sample in a dataset and need one consolidated list of peaks, with per-sample intensity values, to feed peak integration and peakTable(). Before per-sample peak detection has been run — there are no ROIs to cluster yet When samples have not been aligned in drift and retention time, so ROI coordinates are not comparable across samples http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Groups regions of interest (ROIs) detected independently in each GC-IMS sample into a shared, sample-consistent peak list so that peaks can be integrated and tabulated across samples. It is the step that turns per-sample peak detections into a single cross-sample peak inventory in the GCIMS R package. metabolomics/v3 10.1016/j.chemolab.2023.104938
skills.summary: Groups regions of interest (ROIs) detected independently in each GC-IMS sample into a shared, sample-consistent peak list so that peaks can be integrated and tabulated across samples. It is the step that turns per-sample peak detections into a single cross-sample peak inventory in the GCIMS R package.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Before per-sample peak detection has been run — there are no ROIs to cluster yet When samples have not been aligned in drift and retention time, so ROI coordinates are not comparable across samples

skills.description: Decision support for setting per-method AriumMS ROI search and false-positive filter parameters before processing multi-platform CE-MS/HILIC-MS datasets, e.g. when peaks differ in width between separation methods and DOE-significant parameters must be carried forward.
skills.name: roi-detection-parameter-curation
skills.search_text: roi-detection-parameter-curation Decision support for setting per-method AriumMS ROI search and false-positive filter parameters before processing multi-platform CE-MS/HILIC-MS datasets, e.g. when peaks differ in width between separation methods and DOE-significant parameters must be carried forward. Input is already a processed feature table or peak-integrated matrix — ROI search parameters no longer apply at that stage. Single-platform analysis where existing single-platform tools (XCMS Online, MetaboAnalyst, MetaboAnalystR, MZmine) are sufficient, since those are not designed for augmentation of different separation techniques but work fine per platform. Tasks requiring MS/MS spectral networking between features of different methods — AriumMS does not implement this; it is listed as future development. http://edamontology.org/topic_3337 Curate and record the AriumMS non-target ROI-detection parameters for each of the five CE-MS and HILIC-MS analytical methods, prioritizing the four parameters the D-optimal DOE flagged as significant (ROI intensity threshold, mass spectra alignment, m/z error, feature occurrence filter) into method-keyed structured records. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s00216-023-04715-6
skills.summary: Curate and record the AriumMS non-target ROI-detection parameters for each of the five CE-MS and HILIC-MS analytical methods, prioritizing the four parameters the D-optimal DOE flagged as significant (ROI intensity threshold, mass spectra alignment, m/z error, feature occurrence filter) into method-keyed structured records.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a processed feature table or peak-integrated matrix — ROI search parameters no longer apply at that stage. Single-platform analysis where existing single-platform tools (XCMS Online, MetaboAnalyst, MetaboAnalystR, MZmine) are sufficient, since those are not designed for augmentation of different separation techniques but work fine per platform. Tasks requiring MS/MS spectral networking between features of different methods — AriumMS does not implement this; it is listed as future development.

skills.description: Use when starting nontargeted LC-MS feature detection from raw MS1 scans and every detected m/z signal must be assigned to a feature before peak-shape or intensity filtering.
skills.name: roi-extension-mass-trace-building
skills.search_text: roi-extension-mass-trace-building Use when starting nontargeted LC-MS feature detection from raw MS1 scans and every detected m/z signal must be assigned to a feature before peak-shape or intensity filtering. Input is already an aligned feature table or gap-filled data matrix — ROI extension applies to raw MS1 scans only You need isotope/adduct grouping or MS/MS annotation — those are downstream steps that consume the ROI feature table You require a graphical interface for peak detection — MassCube has no GUI in the current version http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Cluster m/z signals across continuous MS1 scans into open regions of interest (ROIs) without imposing peak-shape or fluctuation requirements, achieving 100% signal coverage for feature detection in MassCube. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-025-60640-5
skills.summary: Cluster m/z signals across continuous MS1 scans into open regions of interest (ROIs) without imposing peak-shape or fluctuation requirements, achieving 100% signal coverage for feature detection in MassCube.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already an aligned feature table or gap-filled data matrix — ROI extension applies to raw MS1 scans only You need isotope/adduct grouping or MS/MS annotation — those are downstream steps that consume the ROI feature table You require a graphical interface for peak detection — MassCube has no GUI in the current version

skills.description: Use when raw CE-MS or LC-MS (mzXML/mzML) MS1 data must be reduced to candidate ROIs (m/z, scan-based region, intensity) prior to feature detection, especially for multi-platform metabolomics augmentation.
skills.name: roi-extraction-from-ms1-scans
skills.search_text: roi-extraction-from-ms1-scans Use when raw CE-MS or LC-MS (mzXML/mzML) MS1 data must be reduced to candidate ROIs (m/z, scan-based region, intensity) prior to feature detection, especially for multi-platform metabolomics augmentation. Input is already a preprocessed feature table rather than raw mzXML/mzML MS1 data — ROI search would be redundant Data are MS/MS-level spectra or targeted MS2 acquisitions; AriumMS ROI search operates on MS1 scans and MS/MS spectral networking is not implemented Single-platform analysis where existing tools like XCMS Online, MetaboAnalyst, MetaboAnalystR, or MZmine already suffice http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0153 Extracts regions of interest (ROIs) from consecutive MS1 scans in mzXML/mzML metabolomics data as implemented in AriumMS, reducing computation time and false-positive features before peak detection in multi-platform CE-MS and HILIC-MS workflows. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s00216-023-04715-6
skills.summary: Extracts regions of interest (ROIs) from consecutive MS1 scans in mzXML/mzML metabolomics data as implemented in AriumMS, reducing computation time and false-positive features before peak detection in multi-platform CE-MS and HILIC-MS workflows.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a preprocessed feature table rather than raw mzXML/mzML MS1 data — ROI search would be redundant Data are MS/MS-level spectra or targeted MS2 acquisitions; AriumMS ROI search operates on MS1 scans and MS/MS spectral networking is not implemented Single-platform analysis where existing tools like XCMS Online, MetaboAnalyst, MetaboAnalystR, or MZmine already suffice

skills.description: Use when after running TestIonSelect on an MSI peak matrix, you need the up/down-regulated ions in each per-ROI comparison output table ordered by descending contrast rather than in their raw 'ions' list order.
skills.name: roi-ion-contrast-ranking
skills.search_text: roi-ion-contrast-ranking Use when after running TestIonSelect on an MSI peak matrix, you need the up/down-regulated ions in each per-ROI comparison output table ordered by descending contrast rather than in their raw 'ions' list order. The goal is to filter/select significant ions between ROIs — that is TestIonSelect's role; this skill only orders already-selected ions. The required ranking is by Mann-Whitney U p-value or fold-change alone rather than the one-ROI-vs-all-others contrast defined in Appendix B. Input is not an MSI peak matrix with ROI/cluster labels (e.g. already-aggregated feature tables without spatial or ROI structure). http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Ranks the ions selected by the rMSIKeyIon TestIonSelect filtering algorithm within each ROI comparison by the Appendix B contrast parameter, which measures how strongly an ion's concentration in one ROI differs from the set of all other ROIs jointly. This produces the ordered per-comparison up/down-regulated ion tables of the rMSIKeyIon workflow. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo9080162
skills.summary: Ranks the ions selected by the rMSIKeyIon TestIonSelect filtering algorithm within each ROI comparison by the Appendix B contrast parameter, which measures how strongly an ion's concentration in one ROI differs from the set of all other ROIs jointly. This produces the ordered per-comparison up/down-regulated ion tables of the rMSIKeyIon workflow.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to filter/select significant ions between ROIs — that is TestIonSelect's role; this skill only orders already-selected ions. The required ranking is by Mann-Whitney U p-value or fold-change alone rather than the one-ROI-vs-all-others contrast defined in Appendix B. Input is not an MSI peak matrix with ROI/cluster labels (e.g. already-aggregated feature tables without spatial or ROI structure).

skills.description: Use when raw CE-MS or LC-MS ROI chromatographic profiles (intensity-vs-retention-time traces) must have a per-ROI noise level estimated from smoothed-minus-original residuals before peak criteria (e.g., CWT peak picking) are applied.
skills.name: roi-noise-estimation-from-smoothed-residuals
skills.search_text: roi-noise-estimation-from-smoothed-residuals Use when raw CE-MS or LC-MS ROI chromatographic profiles (intensity-vs-retention-time traces) must have a per-ROI noise level estimated from smoothed-minus-original residuals before peak criteria (e.g., CWT peak picking) are applied. The data are already a processed feature/peak table (e.g., post feature detection and integration) — noise estimation applies to raw chromatographic ROI profiles before peak calling A single-platform tool (XCMS Online, MetaboAnalyst, MZmine) is already configured with its own noise/centWave thresholds and ROI augmentation is not the goal The traces are not chromatographic profiles (e.g., MS/MS spectra or spectroscopic data), where smoothed-minus-residual noise scaling is not the described criterion http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Estimates the local noise floor of each chromatographic region of interest (ROI) by taking the difference between a smoothed signal and the original raw trace, so that downstream peak-detection criteria in the AriumMS/AriumMSEval pipeline are scaled to the actual noise of CE-MS/LC-MS intensity-vs-retention-time profiles. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s00216-023-04715-6
skills.summary: Estimates the local noise floor of each chromatographic region of interest (ROI) by taking the difference between a smoothed signal and the original raw trace, so that downstream peak-detection criteria in the AriumMS/AriumMSEval pipeline are scaled to the actual noise of CE-MS/LC-MS intensity-vs-retention-time profiles.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are already a processed feature/peak table (e.g., post feature detection and integration) — noise estimation applies to raw chromatographic ROI profiles before peak calling A single-platform tool (XCMS Online, MetaboAnalyst, MZmine) is already configured with its own noise/centWave thresholds and ROI augmentation is not the goal The traces are not chromatographic profiles (e.g., MS/MS spectra or spectroscopic data), where smoothed-minus-residual noise scaling is not the described criterion

skills.description: Use when an imported LA-ICP-MS elemental image in Pew2 contains discrete high- or low-intensity spikes from instrument noise and you need to selectively replace those outliers without distorting surrounding valid pixels.
skills.name: rolling-median-filter-application
skills.search_text: rolling-median-filter-application Use when an imported LA-ICP-MS elemental image in Pew2 contains discrete high- or low-intensity spikes from instrument noise and you need to selectively replace those outliers without distorting surrounding valid pixels. The data requires uniform smoothing across the entire image rather than selective removal of discrete spikes — a blanket mean/median convolution would alter valid pixels, whereas this skill's threshold logic is designed to leave them untouched The image already contains calibration or segmentation results that would be invalidated by re-filtering the underlying raw intensities Noise is broad-band or baseline-level rather than discrete spikes; the Pew2 drift-correction or standardization tools, not the spike filter, are the appropriate choice http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Applies a local (rolling) median filter within Pew2 to remove instrument-noise spikes from LA-ICP-MS elemental images: each pixel is compared against a user-defined threshold relative to the local median, and only outlying values are replaced by the local median, leaving valid pixels untouched. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c02138
skills.summary: Applies a local (rolling) median filter within Pew2 to remove instrument-noise spikes from LA-ICP-MS elemental images: each pixel is compared against a user-defined threshold relative to the local median, and only outlying values are replaced by the local median, leaving valid pixels untouched.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data requires uniform smoothing across the entire image rather than selective removal of discrete spikes — a blanket mean/median convolution would alter valid pixels, whereas this skill's threshold logic is designed to leave them untouched The image already contains calibration or segmentation results that would be invalidated by re-filtering the underlying raw intensities Noise is broad-band or baseline-level rather than discrete spikes; the Pew2 drift-correction or standardization tools, not the spike filter, are the appropriate choice

skills.description: Use when starting from raw GC×GC–MS CDF files (4D intensities array with two retention-time dimensions and m/z fragments) and you need untargeted ROI selection and blob extraction before peak deconvolution, with user-set S/N thresholds and win_size in modulations.
skills.name: rolling-window-modulation-segmentation
skills.search_text: rolling-window-modulation-segmentation Use when starting from raw GC×GC–MS CDF files (4D intensities array with two retention-time dimensions and m/z fragments) and you need untargeted ROI selection and blob extraction before peak deconvolution, with user-set S/N thresholds and win_size in modulations. Input is already a peak table or feature matrix from commercial software (e.g. ChromaTOF peak tables) rather than raw CFD/CDF data — no ROI segmentation is needed Data are 1D GC–MS without a second chromatographic dimension or modulation time — the rolling-window two-dimensional segmentation does not apply The goal is library-based annotation or PARAFAC/PARAFAC2 deconvolution of already-segmented ROIs — use downstream GcDUO modules (duoID, ConsProcessing) instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3361 Segment GC×GC–MS chromatographic data into rolling windows of modulations and delineate regions of interest (ROIs) with the inverse watershed algorithm, extracting candidate blobs (3D peaks with 2D coordinates) filtered by signal-to-noise ratio and Gaussian peak form. This is Module II of GcDUO's raw-data processing pipeline, preceding PARAFAC/PARAFAC2 deconvolution. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bib/bbaf080
skills.summary: Segment GC×GC–MS chromatographic data into rolling windows of modulations and delineate regions of interest (ROIs) with the inverse watershed algorithm, extracting candidate blobs (3D peaks with 2D coordinates) filtered by signal-to-noise ratio and Gaussian peak form. This is Module II of GcDUO's raw-data processing pipeline, preceding PARAFAC/PARAFAC2 deconvolution.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a peak table or feature matrix from commercial software (e.g. ChromaTOF peak tables) rather than raw CFD/CDF data — no ROI segmentation is needed Data are 1D GC–MS without a second chromatographic dimension or modulation time — the rolling-window two-dimensional segmentation does not apply The goal is library-based annotation or PARAFAC/PARAFAC2 deconvolution of already-segmented ROIs — use downstream GcDUO modules (duoID, ConsProcessing) instead

skills.description: Use when DESI-MSI data along a linear root developmental gradient have been clustered by DIMPLE and you need to identify which mass signatures are enriched in specific cell layers or in bimodal developmental zones.
skills.name: root-histological-region-metabolite-mapping
skills.search_text: root-histological-region-metabolite-mapping Use when DESI-MSI data along a linear root developmental gradient have been clustered by DIMPLE and you need to identify which mass signatures are enriched in specific cell layers or in bimodal developmental zones. Input is raw, unclustered DESI-MSI spectra — DIMPLE must first process mass signatures along the linear gradient into clusters before histological inspection is meaningful Data are bulk metabolomics measurements with no spatial pixel information, so cell-layer localization cannot be assessed The tissue geometry is not a linear developmental axis (the DIMPLE design leverages 'the linear developmental axis' of the root) http://edamontology.org/topic_3382 Assigns DESI-MSI mass signatures to root histological regions (cortex vs. vasculature) and developmental zones (meristem vs. mature tissue) by inspecting DIMPLE hyperspectral channel clusters along the linear root axis, then annotating enriched m/z values with METASPACE, Metlin Classic, and LOTUS. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.09.22.677919
skills.summary: Assigns DESI-MSI mass signatures to root histological regions (cortex vs. vasculature) and developmental zones (meristem vs. mature tissue) by inspecting DIMPLE hyperspectral channel clusters along the linear root axis, then annotating enriched m/z values with METASPACE, Metlin Classic, and LOTUS.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw, unclustered DESI-MSI spectra — DIMPLE must first process mass signatures along the linear gradient into clusters before histological inspection is meaningful Data are bulk metabolomics measurements with no spatial pixel information, so cell-layer localization cannot be assessed The tissue geometry is not a linear developmental axis (the DIMPLE design leverages 'the linear developmental axis' of the root)

skills.description: Use when implementing or auditing the adjacency-matrix connectivity feature representation of rooted fragment graphs (root = atom adjacent to a cleaved bond), where the flattened feature vector must be invariant to arbitrary vertex ordering.
skills.name: rooted-graph-invariance-testing
skills.search_text: rooted-graph-invariance-testing Use when implementing or auditing the adjacency-matrix connectivity feature representation of rooted fragment graphs (root = atom adjacent to a cleaved bond), where the flattened feature vector must be invariant to arbitrary vertex ordering. The input is already a flat feature table or numeric descriptor matrix — this skill operates on rooted fragment graphs prior to flattening, not on downstream ML features You need an unrooted whole-molecule representation or features independent of a cleavage site — the canonical indexing is defined relative to the root atom (adjacent to the cleaved bond) You are predicting spectra purely via hand-written fragmentation rules (e.g. MSRB class rules) without the machine-learned C2MS component that consumes these topology features http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 A validation technique for CFM-ID 4.0's connectivity-matrix feature extractor, verifying that the flattened bond-tensor/vertex-tensor vector for a rooted fragment graph is canonical — i.e., identical for two graphs with the same underlying structure and root atom regardless of their original vertex indexing. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.1c01465
skills.summary: A validation technique for CFM-ID 4.0's connectivity-matrix feature extractor, verifying that the flattened bond-tensor/vertex-tensor vector for a rooted fragment graph is canonical — i.e., identical for two graphs with the same underlying structure and root atom regardless of their original vertex indexing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a flat feature table or numeric descriptor matrix — this skill operates on rooted fragment graphs prior to flattening, not on downstream ML features You need an unrooted whole-molecule representation or features independent of a cleavage site — the canonical indexing is defined relative to the root atom (adjacent to the cleaved bond) You are predicting spectra purely via hand-written fragmentation rules (e.g. MSRB class rules) without the machine-learned C2MS component that consumes these topology features

skills.description: Use when a MZmine (MZmine2/MZmine3) or GNPS-FBMN feature quantification table must be converted to row-wise relative abundances per extract before flagging features as specific (min_specificity = 90) for Inventa FC scoring.
skills.name: row-wise-intensity-normalization
skills.search_text: row-wise-intensity-normalization Use when a MZmine (MZmine2/MZmine3) or GNPS-FBMN feature quantification table must be converted to row-wise relative abundances per extract before flagging features as specific (min_specificity = 90) for Inventa FC scoring. The feature table is already normalized to relative abundances — re-normalizing would distort the ≥90% specificity proportions used by the FC calculation. The goal is a component that does not depend on feature-intensity normalization: the Literature Component (LC) is independent of spectral data, and the Similarity Component (SC) uses the MEMO MS2 peak/neutral-loss matrix instead of the aligned feature table. Only one intensity column can be used at a time — 'Peak height' and 'Peak area' must not be combined in a single normalization pass. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Row-wise normalization of an MZmine feature quantification table converts raw peak areas into relative feature abundances per extract, which is the prerequisite step inside Inventa for computing feature specificity and the Feature Component (FC) score. metabolomics/v3 10.3389/fmolb.2022.1028334
skills.summary: Row-wise normalization of an MZmine feature quantification table converts raw peak areas into relative feature abundances per extract, which is the prerequisite step inside Inventa for computing feature specificity and the Feature Component (FC) score.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The feature table is already normalized to relative abundances — re-normalizing would distort the ≥90% specificity proportions used by the FC calculation. The goal is a component that does not depend on feature-intensity normalization: the Literature Component (LC) is independent of spectral data, and the Similarity Component (SC) uses the MEMO MS2 peak/neutral-loss matrix instead of the aligned feature table. Only one intensity column can be used at a time — 'Peak height' and 'Peak area' must not be combined in a single normalization pass.

skills.description: Use when a lipidomic intensity matrix at the molecular-species (LMS) level contains absent cells or zeros that must be filled before downstream statistics, and row-relative low-value imputation is acceptable.
skills.name: row-wise-missing-value-imputation
skills.search_text: row-wise-missing-value-imputation Use when a lipidomic intensity matrix at the molecular-species (LMS) level contains absent cells or zeros that must be filled before downstream statistics, and row-relative low-value imputation is acceptable. The input matrix is at the lipid class (LCL) or building block (LBB) structural level rather than the molecular-species (LMS) level The matrix already contains no missing or zero values, so imputation would only add artificial noise A deterministic, seed-controlled missing-value method is required and the non-deterministic random draw is unacceptable Reconstructs a complete lipid molecular species (LMS) sub-matrix from an uploaded lipidomic data matrix by imputing every missing or '0' entry with a random number drawn between one-twentieth and one-tenth of the row's minimum valid value, as done by LipidOne 2.0. metabolomics/v3 10.1002/cpz1.70009
skills.summary: Reconstructs a complete lipid molecular species (LMS) sub-matrix from an uploaded lipidomic data matrix by imputing every missing or '0' entry with a random number drawn between one-twentieth and one-tenth of the row's minimum valid value, as done by LipidOne 2.0.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input matrix is at the lipid class (LCL) or building block (LBB) structural level rather than the molecular-species (LMS) level The matrix already contains no missing or zero values, so imputation would only add artificial noise A deterministic, seed-controlled missing-value method is required and the non-deterministic random draw is unacceptable

skills.description: Use when WGS/metatranscriptomic reads have been mapped to MGC/GCF reference sequences (BiG-MAP.GCF.fna) and per-sample cluster abundance must be normalized as RPKM before phenotype-level differential analysis.
skills.name: rpkm-normalization
skills.search_text: rpkm-normalization Use when WGS/metatranscriptomic reads have been mapped to MGC/GCF reference sequences (BiG-MAP.GCF.fna) and per-sample cluster abundance must be normalized as RPKM before phenotype-level differential analysis. Input is still raw FASTQ that has not been mapped to gene cluster reference sequences — mapping (bigmap-map) must precede RPKM computation The goal is taxonomic/species-level profiling rather than MGC/GCF metabolic gene cluster abundance No gene cluster predictions exist yet — antiSMASH/gutSMASH must first be run and clusters deduplicated via bigmap-family before abundance can be profiled http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Computes RPKM (Reads Per Kilobase per Million mapped reads) abundance profiles of metabolic gene clusters (MGCs) and gene cluster families (GCFs) from mapped metagenomic/metatranscriptomic reads using BiG-MAP, enabling cross-sample comparison and differential abundance testing (e.g. Kruskal-Wallis between healthy and caries-associated oral samples). metabolomics/v3 10.1128/msystems.00937-21
skills.summary: Computes RPKM (Reads Per Kilobase per Million mapped reads) abundance profiles of metabolic gene clusters (MGCs) and gene cluster families (GCFs) from mapped metagenomic/metatranscriptomic reads using BiG-MAP, enabling cross-sample comparison and differential abundance testing (e.g. Kruskal-Wallis between healthy and caries-associated oral samples).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is still raw FASTQ that has not been mapped to gene cluster reference sequences — mapping (bigmap-map) must precede RPKM computation The goal is taxonomic/species-level profiling rather than MGC/GCF metabolic gene cluster abundance No gene cluster predictions exist yet — antiSMASH/gutSMASH must first be run and clusters deduplicated via bigmap-family before abundance can be profiled

skills.description: Use when raw read counts per gene cluster family must be converted to comparable abundance units (TPM/RPKM) and coverage from shotgun metagenomic or metatranscriptomic FASTQ data.
skills.name: rpkm-tpm-abundance-normalization
skills.search_text: rpkm-tpm-abundance-normalization Use when raw read counts per gene cluster family must be converted to comparable abundance units (TPM/RPKM) and coverage from shotgun metagenomic or metatranscriptomic FASTQ data. The input is already a normalized abundance or feature table rather than raw reads/counts The data are amplicon reads rather than shotgun metagenomic/metatranscriptomic FASTQ, since mapping to full cluster references is not meaningful The goal is differential abundance/expression testing or visualization — that belongs to the bigmap-analyse module http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 Normalizes read counts mapping to representative metabolic gene clusters (MGCs/GCFs) into TPM and RPKM abundance tables, and derives per-cluster read coverage, as implemented in the BiG-MAP.map module for metagenomic/metatranscriptomic profiling. metabolomics/v3 10.1128/msystems.00937-21
skills.summary: Normalizes read counts mapping to representative metabolic gene clusters (MGCs/GCFs) into TPM and RPKM abundance tables, and derives per-cluster read coverage, as implemented in the BiG-MAP.map module for metagenomic/metatranscriptomic profiling.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a normalized abundance or feature table rather than raw reads/counts The data are amplicon reads rather than shotgun metagenomic/metatranscriptomic FASTQ, since mapping to full cluster references is not meaningful The goal is differential abundance/expression testing or visualization — that belongs to the bigmap-analyse module

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify how well an unretrained retention-prediction model generalizes to new reversed-phase liquid chromatography (RPLC) datasets versus a fingerprint baseline, e.g. computing average rank scores, accuracy, and Spearman correlation.
skills.name: rplc-dataset-benchmark-evaluation
skills.search_text: rplc-dataset-benchmark-evaluation Use when you need to quantify how well an unretrained retention-prediction model generalizes to new reversed-phase liquid chromatography (RPLC) datasets versus a fingerprint baseline, e.g. computing average rank scores, accuracy, and Spearman correlation. Input chromatography is HILIC rather than RPLC — ROASMI only applies to RPLC systems with an eluent pH around 2.7; HILIC generalizability is explicitly left as future work. The model has already been retrained on a user-defined reference set — this skill specifically benchmarks the initial, unretrained ensemble for out-of-the-box generalizability. Target compounds fall outside the elemental restrictions of C, H, N, O, P, and S — the model's applicability domain does not cover the broader chemical space. Evaluates the out-of-the-box generalizability of a retention-order model (ROASMI) against an Morgan_count fingerprint baseline across 71 independent RPLC datasets, reporting rank scores (e.g. 0.696 vs the initial-set 0.795) without any retraining. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-025-00968-8
skills.summary: Evaluates the out-of-the-box generalizability of a retention-order model (ROASMI) against an Morgan_count fingerprint baseline across 71 independent RPLC datasets, reporting rank scores (e.g. 0.696 vs the initial-set 0.795) without any retraining.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input chromatography is HILIC rather than RPLC — ROASMI only applies to RPLC systems with an eluent pH around 2.7; HILIC generalizability is explicitly left as future work. The model has already been retrained on a user-defined reference set — this skill specifically benchmarks the initial, unretrained ensemble for out-of-the-box generalizability. Target compounds fall outside the elemental restrictions of C, H, N, O, P, and S — the model's applicability domain does not cover the broader chemical space.

skills.description: Use when a concordance table of Cohen's kappa and Pearson correlation scores (RPS vs RAS and RPS vs FFD) exists and you need to determine which reactions' RPS-FFD concordance survives multiple-testing correction.
skills.name: rps-flux-concordance-significance-filtering
skills.search_text: rps-flux-concordance-significance-filtering Use when a concordance table of Cohen's kappa and Pearson correlation scores (RPS vs RAS and RPS vs FFD) exists and you need to determine which reactions' RPS-FFD concordance survives multiple-testing correction. The concordance table has not yet been computed — this skill presupposes output of the concordanceAnalysis step, not raw metabolomics or sampling data The goal is to classify flux regulation by intersecting transcriptomics-based (RAS) and metabolomics-based (FFD) predictions, rather than to statistically test kappa concordance significance The analysis concerns RPS vs RAS (transcriptional-layer) concordance without a multiple-comparison correction requirement http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Assigns empirical p-values to Cohen's kappa concordance scores between Reaction Propensity Scores (RPSs) and FFD-derived flux variations via bootstrap resampling, then applies Benjamini-Hochberg correction at 5% FDR to identify reactions with statistically significant RPS-vs-FFD concordance. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009337
skills.summary: Assigns empirical p-values to Cohen's kappa concordance scores between Reaction Propensity Scores (RPSs) and FFD-derived flux variations via bootstrap resampling, then applies Benjamini-Hochberg correction at 5% FDR to identify reactions with statistically significant RPS-vs-FFD concordance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The concordance table has not yet been computed — this skill presupposes output of the concordanceAnalysis step, not raw metabolomics or sampling data The goal is to classify flux regulation by intersecting transcriptomics-based (RAS) and metabolomics-based (FFD) predictions, rather than to statistically test kappa concordance significance The analysis concerns RPS vs RAS (transcriptional-layer) concordance without a multiple-comparison correction requirement

skills.description: Use when Rapid QC-MS has processed an ongoing LC-MS/MS run and you need to compare the RS annotations from the current analysis against historical RS annotations stored in a user-supplied .msp library file to detect drift in mass accuracy or retention time.
skills.name: rs-annotation-library-alignment
skills.search_text: rs-annotation-library-alignment Use when Rapid QC-MS has processed an ongoing LC-MS/MS run and you need to compare the RS annotations from the current analysis against historical RS annotations stored in a user-supplied .msp library file to detect drift in mass accuracy or retention time. The biological matrix has changed or no previously annotated reference specimens exist, so no gold-standard .msp library can be constructed from prior analyses. Only internal standard (IS) or evaluation specimen (ES) data need QC — the RS annotation alignment step is specific to reference standard annotations, not general IS RT/m/z/intensity monitoring. The input is already an aligned feature table rather than raw vendor files or mzML; MSConvert/MS-DIAL-based RS extraction and alignment would be redundant. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0218 Benchmark current LC-MS/MS instrument performance by aligning reference standard (RS) annotations from the ongoing Rapid QC-MS run against a previously curated gold-standard .msp library, computing mass accuracy drift and retention time shifts. This enables comparison of today's RS annotations with those from earlier analyses in the same well-defined biological matrix. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c00786
skills.summary: Benchmark current LC-MS/MS instrument performance by aligning reference standard (RS) annotations from the ongoing Rapid QC-MS run against a previously curated gold-standard .msp library, computing mass accuracy drift and retention time shifts. This enables comparison of today's RS annotations with those from earlier analyses in the same well-defined biological matrix.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The biological matrix has changed or no previously annotated reference specimens exist, so no gold-standard .msp library can be constructed from prior analyses. Only internal standard (IS) or evaluation specimen (ES) data need QC — the RS annotation alignment step is specific to reference standard annotations, not general IS RT/m/z/intensity monitoring. The input is already an aligned feature table rather than raw vendor files or mzML; MSConvert/MS-DIAL-based RS extraction and alignment would be redundant.

skills.description: Use when MS2 peak data and metadata (msLevel, precursorMz, retention times, compound name/id) live in an R Spectra::Spectra object but the next processing step is a Python matchms or spectrum_utils routine.
skills.name: rs-python-spectra-object-conversion
skills.search_text: rs-python-spectra-object-conversion Use when MS2 peak data and metadata (msLevel, precursorMz, retention times, compound name/id) live in an R Spectra::Spectra object but the next processing step is a Python matchms or spectrum_utils routine. Data already exists as Python matchms.Spectrum objects and only needs to move back to R — use pyspec_to_rspec() instead The task is similarity scoring or filtering rather than data exchange — compareSpectriPy() and filterSpectriPy() perform the conversion internally, so a manual conversion step is redundant No Python environment is available or reticulate < 1.41 is installed, since SpectriPy's Python library management relies on py_require() from reticulate 1.41 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Converts R Spectra::Spectra objects into Python matchms.Spectrum (or spectrum_utils MsmsSpectrum) objects via SpectriPy's rspec_to_pyspec(), translating peak arrays and metadata across the reticulate bridge. metabolomics/v3 10.21105/joss.08070
skills.summary: Converts R Spectra::Spectra objects into Python matchms.Spectrum (or spectrum_utils MsmsSpectrum) objects via SpectriPy's rspec_to_pyspec(), translating peak arrays and metadata across the reticulate bridge.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data already exists as Python matchms.Spectrum objects and only needs to move back to R — use pyspec_to_rspec() instead The task is similarity scoring or filtering rather than data exchange — compareSpectriPy() and filterSpectriPy() perform the conversion internally, so a manual conversion step is redundant No Python environment is available or reticulate < 1.41 is installed, since SpectriPy's Python library management relies on py_require() from reticulate 1.41

skills.description: Use when a replicate-structure metabolomics dataset needs a per-metabolite variability score (RSD/CV) across biological or technical replicates, or when evaluating whether an RSD filter removes irreproducible features.
skills.name: rsd-computation-replicate-metabolomics
skills.search_text: rsd-computation-replicate-metabolomics Use when a replicate-structure metabolomics dataset needs a per-metabolite variability score (RSD/CV) across biological or technical replicates, or when evaluating whether an RSD filter removes irreproducible features. The goal is not to benchmark a variability filter but to fully compare pre-processing pipelines — the paper's stated goal 'was not to do a comprehensive evaluation of pre-processing steps, but instead to show how this measure can be used as a benchmark for comparison' Only a single sample per condition is available, so no replicate-based variability (RSD/CV) can be computed A reproducibility assessment is needed that does not rely on parametric or fixed-threshold assumptions — prefer the MaRR maximal rank statistic itself http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Computes the relative standard deviation (RSD, %) of metabolite abundances across biological and technical replicates and benchmarks this conventional variability measure against MaRR-based reproducibility labels, showing whether a fixed RSD cutoff (e.g. 25%) can separate reproducible from irreproducible metabolites. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-021-04336-9
skills.summary: Computes the relative standard deviation (RSD, %) of metabolite abundances across biological and technical replicates and benchmarks this conventional variability measure against MaRR-based reproducibility labels, showing whether a fixed RSD cutoff (e.g. 25%) can separate reproducible from irreproducible metabolites.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is not to benchmark a variability filter but to fully compare pre-processing pipelines — the paper's stated goal 'was not to do a comprehensive evaluation of pre-processing steps, but instead to show how this measure can be used as a benchmark for comparison' Only a single sample per condition is available, so no replicate-based variability (RSD/CV) can be computed A reproducibility assessment is needed that does not rely on parametric or fixed-threshold assumptions — prefer the MaRR maximal rank statistic itself

skills.description: Use when a metabolomics or lipidomics study has QCpool samples injected at regular intervals during one or more sequences and you need tabulated per-feature RSD precision estimates to judge and report overall data quality.
skills.name: rsd-precision-estimation-from-qc-pools
skills.search_text: rsd-precision-estimation-from-qc-pools Use when a metabolomics or lipidomics study has QCpool samples injected at regular intervals during one or more sequences and you need tabulated per-feature RSD precision estimates to judge and report overall data quality. No pooled QC samples were measured at regular intervals during the sequence — RSD estimation from QC pools is not possible Input is non-MS omics or non-MS metabolomics data without a pooled-QC injection structure You only need a single-step QC fix (e.g. only drift correction) rather than the sequential protocol whose final step is precision assessment Final assessment step of the QComics multistep QC protocol: estimate per-feature relative standard deviation (RSD) across pooled QC samples (measured at regular intervals in Sciex MultiQuant-exported txt data) and export tabulated RSD estimations alongside QC report figures as the package's reproducible quality report. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c03660
skills.summary: Final assessment step of the QComics multistep QC protocol: estimate per-feature relative standard deviation (RSD) across pooled QC samples (measured at regular intervals in Sciex MultiQuant-exported txt data) and export tabulated RSD estimations alongside QC report figures as the package's reproducible quality report.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No pooled QC samples were measured at regular intervals during the sequence — RSD estimation from QC pools is not possible Input is non-MS omics or non-MS metabolomics data without a pooled-QC injection structure You only need a single-step QC fix (e.g. only drift correction) rather than the sequential protocol whose final step is precision assessment

skills.description: Use when you have an XCMS peak table plus pooled QC injections and want a threshold-based reproducibility filter (RSD < 30%) on features before statistical analysis, or as a baseline to compare against classifier-driven Pass/Fail flagging.
skills.name: rsd-qc-filtering
skills.search_text: rsd-qc-filtering Use when you have an XCMS peak table plus pooled QC injections and want a threshold-based reproducibility filter (RSD < 30%) on features before statistical analysis, or as a baseline to compare against classifier-driven Pass/Fail flagging. When peaks are already labeled Pass/Fail by a trained peak-quality classifier such as MetaClean — RSD filtering cannot assess integration quality, only reproducibility. When the dataset contains no pooled QC injections (RSD must be computed on a repeatedly injected QC sample). When vendor-processed outputs are the only available input — the MetaClean paper notes this scope limitation, so convert to an XCMS object or feature table first. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Filter untargeted LC–MS metabolomics features by relative standard deviation (RSD) computed on peaks in a routinely injected pooled QC sample, retaining peaks with RSD < 30% as a lightweight, label-free alternative to classifier-based peak quality flagging. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-020-01738-3
skills.summary: Filter untargeted LC–MS metabolomics features by relative standard deviation (RSD) computed on peaks in a routinely injected pooled QC sample, retaining peaks with RSD < 30% as a lightweight, label-free alternative to classifier-based peak quality flagging.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When peaks are already labeled Pass/Fail by a trained peak-quality classifier such as MetaClean — RSD filtering cannot assess integration quality, only reproducibility. When the dataset contains no pooled QC injections (RSD must be computed on a repeatedly injected QC sample). When vendor-processed outputs are the only available input — the MetaClean paper notes this scope limitation, so convert to an XCMS object or feature table first.

skills.description: Use when curating an untargeted LC–MS feature table where pooled/intrastudy QC injections are available and features with poor analytical repeatability (RSD > 20%) must be removed before statistical analysis.
skills.name: rsd-repeatability-assessment-in-qc-samples
