skills.search_text: spectral-embedding-model-training Use when you have a large curated MS/MS library (e.g. GNPS-derived AllPositive: 95,320 positive-mode spectra, 77,092 InChIKey-annotated) and need a learned spectral similarity model for library matching or molecular networking beyond plain cosine scoring. When no suitable training data exist and a training-free score is needed — Spec2Vec, unlike cosine scores, requires training data to learn fragment peak relationships When the query data contain many fragment/loss features absent from the training set (missing-word issue), e.g. models trained on smaller datasets or with more m/z decimals included in words For GC-MS data — performance was only demonstrated on LC-MS data and GC-MS utility was not assessed http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Trains a Word2Vec (gensim) model on mass spectra converted to documents of peak and neutral-loss words, producing learned spectral embeddings whose cosine similarity serves as the Spec2Vec spectral similarity score. It exists because learnt embeddings correlate better with structural (Tanimoto) similarity than cosine-based scores and scale to large library searches. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008724
skills.summary: Trains a Word2Vec (gensim) model on mass spectra converted to documents of peak and neutral-loss words, producing learned spectral embeddings whose cosine similarity serves as the Spec2Vec spectral similarity score. It exists because learnt embeddings correlate better with structural (Tanimoto) similarity than cosine-based scores and scale to large library searches.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When no suitable training data exist and a training-free score is needed — Spec2Vec, unlike cosine scores, requires training data to learn fragment peak relationships When the query data contain many fragment/loss features absent from the training set (missing-word issue), e.g. models trained on smaller datasets or with more m/z decimals included in words For GC-MS data — performance was only demonstrated on LC-MS data and GC-MS utility was not assessed

skills.description: Use when retraining or reproducing the GLEAMS Siamese spectral embedder — e.g. ablating precursor/fragment/reference-spectrum feature blocks — from MassIVE-KB PSMs rather than running the pretrained model.
skills.name: spectral-embedding-neural-network-training
skills.search_text: spectral-embedding-neural-network-training Use when retraining or reproducing the GLEAMS Siamese spectral embedder — e.g. ablating precursor/fragment/reference-spectrum feature blocks — from MassIVE-KB PSMs rather than running the pretrained model. You only need 32-dimensional embeddings or cluster labels from new spectra — use the released pretrained weights with 'gleams embed' and 'gleams cluster' instead of retraining. The goal is clustering already-computed embeddings — that is the 'gleams cluster --distance_threshold 0.3' workflow, not network training. No CUDA-enabled GPU or Linux environment is available — GLEAMS requires Python 3.8, Linux, and a CUDA GPU for training. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Trains the GLEAMS Siamese neural network that embeds MS/MS spectra into a 32-dimensional L2-regularized space using a contrastive loss on positive/negative spectra pairs drawn from 30 million MassIVE-KB PSMs. This is the training/reproduction skill (including feature-ablation retraining), distinct from applying the released pretrained weights. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-022-01496-1
skills.summary: Trains the GLEAMS Siamese neural network that embeds MS/MS spectra into a 32-dimensional L2-regularized space using a contrastive loss on positive/negative spectra pairs drawn from 30 million MassIVE-KB PSMs. This is the training/reproduction skill (including feature-ablation retraining), distinct from applying the released pretrained weights.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need 32-dimensional embeddings or cluster labels from new spectra — use the released pretrained weights with 'gleams embed' and 'gleams cluster' instead of retraining. The goal is clustering already-computed embeddings — that is the 'gleams cluster --distance_threshold 0.3' workflow, not network training. No CUDA-enabled GPU or Linux environment is available — GLEAMS requires Python 3.8, Linux, and a CUDA GPU for training.

skills.description: Use when you have held-out MS/MS spectra (e.g., GeMS HDF5) and want to verify that pre-trained spectral embeddings organize linearly by molecular structure, or to quantify structural clustering of spectra across differing ionization/fragmentation conditions.
skills.name: spectral-embedding-pca-clustering
skills.search_text: spectral-embedding-pca-clustering Use when you have held-out MS/MS spectra (e.g., GeMS HDF5) and want to verify that pre-trained spectral embeddings organize linearly by molecular structure, or to quantify structural clustering of spectra across differing ionization/fragmentation conditions. The goal is direct structure annotation or library retrieval from spectra — use fine-tuned DreaMS annotation heads or library search (e.g., against MoNA/NIST20/PubChem) instead of unsupervised clustering of pre-trained embeddings Spectra are outside the pre-training distribution described by the authors (e.g., negative ionization mode, multiply charged precursor ions), where representation quality is not established The input is already a molecular structure table or fingerprint matrix — clustering spectra embeddings is redundant when structures, not spectra, are the objects of analysis http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Extracts 1,024-dimensional real-valued DreaMS embeddings from tandem MS/MS spectra and tests whether the representation space linearly clusters spectra by molecular structure (via PCA to 1,023 dims and k=3 clustering on 2D InChI-key groups), the core validation that self-supervised pre-training learns structure-aware representations. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41587-025-02663-3
skills.summary: Extracts 1,024-dimensional real-valued DreaMS embeddings from tandem MS/MS spectra and tests whether the representation space linearly clusters spectra by molecular structure (via PCA to 1,023 dims and k=3 clustering on 2D InChI-key groups), the core validation that self-supervised pre-training learns structure-aware representations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is direct structure annotation or library retrieval from spectra — use fine-tuned DreaMS annotation heads or library search (e.g., against MoNA/NIST20/PubChem) instead of unsupervised clustering of pre-trained embeddings Spectra are outside the pre-training distribution described by the authors (e.g., negative ionization mode, multiply charged precursor ions), where representation quality is not established The input is already a molecular structure table or fingerprint matrix — clustering spectra embeddings is redundant when structures, not spectra, are the objects of analysis

skills.description: Use when you need to organize repository-scale collections of unannotated tandem mass spectra (e.g. the 201 million positive-mode MS/MS spectra in MassIVE GNPS) into a similarity network that enables propagation of annotations from spectral-library nodes to unknowns.
skills.name: spectral-embedding-similarity-networking
skills.search_text: spectral-embedding-similarity-networking Use when you need to organize repository-scale collections of unannotated tandem mass spectra (e.g. the 201 million positive-mode MS/MS spectra in MassIVE GNPS) into a similarity network that enables propagation of annotations from spectral-library nodes to unknowns. When spectra are outside the positive-ionization, singly-charged precursor regime (e.g. negative ionization mode or multiply charged precursors), which DreaMS does not model. When spectra already have reference library matches, direct spectral-library retrieval outperforms network-based annotation and the network adds no benefit. When the goal is MS1 isotopic-pattern or adduct-distribution analysis; this skill ignores those features entirely. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Constructs a molecular network by embedding MS/MS spectra into a 1,024-dimensional DreaMS representation space and building an approximate 3-NN graph over 34 million spectra that represent 201 million GeMS-C spectra, then annotating nodes with predicted properties and library metadata. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41587-025-02663-3
skills.summary: Constructs a molecular network by embedding MS/MS spectra into a 1,024-dimensional DreaMS representation space and building an approximate 3-NN graph over 34 million spectra that represent 201 million GeMS-C spectra, then annotating nodes with predicted properties and library metadata.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When spectra are outside the positive-ionization, singly-charged precursor regime (e.g. negative ionization mode or multiply charged precursors), which DreaMS does not model. When spectra already have reference library matches, direct spectral-library retrieval outperforms network-based annotation and the network adds no benefit. When the goal is MS1 isotopic-pattern or adduct-distribution analysis; this skill ignores those features entirely.

skills.description: Use when MS2DeepScore Tanimoto predictions must be accompanied by a reliability measure, or when only the most confident subset of spectrum-pair scores is acceptable and a precision/retention trade-off is needed.
skills.name: spectral-embedding-uncertainty-estimation
skills.search_text: spectral-embedding-uncertainty-estimation Use when MS2DeepScore Tanimoto predictions must be accompanied by a reliability measure, or when only the most confident subset of spectrum-pair scores is acceptable and a precision/retention trade-off is needed. You only need a single deterministic similarity matrix without per-prediction confidence (plain MS2DeepScore scoring suffices) You want to train a new Siamese model rather than estimate uncertainty of an existing trained model Predictions must be deterministic and reproducible across re-trained models — the paper notes scores 'might change when a new model is trained' http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Quantify per-prediction uncertainty of MS2DeepScore Tanimoto-score predictions via Monte-Carlo dropout, then filter predictions by interquartile range (IQR) to trade retrieval rate for lower RMSE. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-021-00558-4
skills.summary: Quantify per-prediction uncertainty of MS2DeepScore Tanimoto-score predictions via Monte-Carlo dropout, then filter predictions by interquartile range (IQR) to trade retrieval rate for lower RMSE.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need a single deterministic similarity matrix without per-prediction confidence (plain MS2DeepScore scoring suffices) You want to train a new Siamese model rather than estimate uncertainty of an existing trained model Predictions must be deterministic and reproducible across re-trained models — the paper notes scores 'might change when a new model is trained'

skills.description: Use when MS/MS peak arrays ([m/z, intensity] pairs, intensities summing to 1) need a complexity measure or when scoring query-vs-library spectral matches for small-molecule identification, e.g. against NIST20 or MassBank of North America.
skills.name: spectral-entropy-calculation
skills.search_text: spectral-entropy-calculation Use when MS/MS peak arrays ([m/z, intensity] pairs, intensities summing to 1) need a complexity measure or when scoring query-vs-library spectral matches for small-molecule identification, e.g. against NIST20 or MassBank of North America. Input spectra are ion-rich with high entropy (S >= 3): do not apply power weighting with w < 1, as the paper shows this decreases similarity scoring performance The analysis goal is to guarantee zero false positives: the paper states no single similarity threshold can prevent false-positive discoveries, even with entropy similarity scores Spectra are profile (uncentroided) raw data and the workflow assumes clean_spectrum=False; you must preprocess with ms_entropy.clean_spectrum first http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Compute Shannon-inspired spectral entropy from centroided, intensity-normalized MS/MS peak lists and use it as the basis for entropy similarity scoring of small-molecule spectra via the ms_entropy package, outperforming dot-product similarity for compound identification. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-021-01331-z
skills.summary: Compute Shannon-inspired spectral entropy from centroided, intensity-normalized MS/MS peak lists and use it as the basis for entropy similarity scoring of small-molecule spectra via the ms_entropy package, outperforming dot-product similarity for compound identification.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra are ion-rich with high entropy (S >= 3): do not apply power weighting with w < 1, as the paper shows this decreases similarity scoring performance The analysis goal is to guarantee zero false positives: the paper states no single similarity threshold can prevent false-positive discoveries, even with entropy similarity scores Spectra are profile (uncentroided) raw data and the workflow assumes clean_spectrum=False; you must preprocess with ms_entropy.clean_spectrum first

skills.description: Use when matching experimental MS/MS spectra against spectral libraries (NIST20, MassBank/MoNA, GNPS), when comparing similarity scoring algorithms for compound identification, or when quantifying noise robustness of spectral similarity scores.
skills.name: spectral-entropy-similarity-scoring
skills.search_text: spectral-entropy-similarity-scoring Use when matching experimental MS/MS spectra against spectral libraries (NIST20, MassBank/MoNA, GNPS), when comparing similarity scoring algorithms for compound identification, or when quantifying noise robustness of spectral similarity scores. Input spectra have not been centroided/cleaned — applying similarity directly to raw profile peaks without clean_spectrum degrades matching (ions above precursor_mz - 1.6 must be removed first) The goal is isomer-level discrimination requiring structure-aware scoring — the plain entropy similarity score cannot separate highly similar structures; the one-bond-difference variant is needed instead Spectra are ion-rich with high entropy values and power transformations at w < 1 are being applied — the paper reports such transformations decrease similarity scoring performance http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Computes entropy similarity between MS/MS spectra using the ms_entropy package (after clean_spectrum preprocessing), outperforming dot-product/cosine similarity for library matching on NIST20 and MassBank of North America spectra, with FDR < 10% at score 0.75. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41592-021-01331-z
skills.summary: Computes entropy similarity between MS/MS spectra using the ms_entropy package (after clean_spectrum preprocessing), outperforming dot-product/cosine similarity for library matching on NIST20 and MassBank of North America spectra, with FDR < 10% at score 0.75.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra have not been centroided/cleaned — applying similarity directly to raw profile peaks without clean_spectrum degrades matching (ions above precursor_mz - 1.6 must be removed first) The goal is isomer-level discrimination requiring structure-aware scoring — the plain entropy similarity score cannot separate highly similar structures; the one-bond-difference variant is needed instead Spectra are ion-rich with high entropy values and power transformations at w < 1 are being applied — the paper reports such transformations decrease similarity scoring performance

skills.description: Use when comparing MS/MS spectra (query peaks + precursor m/z against a spectral library) to rank matches with entropy similarity instead of dot-product/cosine, or when benchmarking search speed against LipidIN's EQ module.
skills.name: spectral-entropy-similarity-scoring
skills.search_text: spectral-entropy-similarity-scoring Use when comparing MS/MS spectra (query peaks + precursor m/z against a spectral library) to rank matches with entropy similarity instead of dot-product/cosine, or when benchmarking search speed against LipidIN's EQ module. Searching very large libraries (e.g. LipidIN's 168.6-million-entry theoretical library or 10M-spectrum MassBank variants) where LipidIN's EQ module, with its linear-time hash-table/bisection data structure (~2.3 µs per query), is faster than Flash Entropy Search's squared time complexity Feature annotation workflows where similarity-based algorithms introduce redundancy — the LipidIN discussion notes similarity algorithms such as MS-DIAL, LipidSearch, and MS entropy might cause feature redundancy When the query peaks and precursor m/z are not available (only MS1 features), since both `precursor_mz` and `peaks` keys are required inputs http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Scores MS/MS spectral similarity using spectral entropy (entropy similarity) via the Flash Entropy Search algorithm (YuanyueLi/MSEntropy, `ms_entropy` package), used in the LipidIN context both as a baseline similarity method and to validate regenerated lipid fingerprint spectra against reference libraries. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-025-59683-5
skills.summary: Scores MS/MS spectral similarity using spectral entropy (entropy similarity) via the Flash Entropy Search algorithm (YuanyueLi/MSEntropy, `ms_entropy` package), used in the LipidIN context both as a baseline similarity method and to validate regenerated lipid fingerprint spectra against reference libraries.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Searching very large libraries (e.g. LipidIN's 168.6-million-entry theoretical library or 10M-spectrum MassBank variants) where LipidIN's EQ module, with its linear-time hash-table/bisection data structure (~2.3 µs per query), is faster than Flash Entropy Search's squared time complexity Feature annotation workflows where similarity-based algorithms introduce redundancy — the LipidIN discussion notes similarity algorithms such as MS-DIAL, LipidSearch, and MS entropy might cause feature redundancy When the query peaks and precursor m/z are not available (only MS1 features), since both `precursor_mz` and `peaks` keys are required inputs

skills.description: Use when scoring PSMs in a proteomic SIP workflow and you need an intensity-distribution-sensitive similarity metric (spectral entropy) alongside MVH/Xcorr/WDP to compare observed vs. theoretical spectra.
skills.name: spectral-entropy-similarity-scoring
skills.search_text: spectral-entropy-similarity-scoring Use when scoring PSMs in a proteomic SIP workflow and you need an intensity-distribution-sensitive similarity metric (spectral entropy) alongside MVH/Xcorr/WDP to compare observed vs. theoretical spectra. Input is an MS1 isotopic-envelope comparison rather than an MS2 PSM — Aerith's envelope simulation and fine-structure tools, not PSM scoring, apply there You only need the single best discriminator for SIP-labeled PSMs — the article reports the weighted dot product (WDP) outperforms the other functions (including spectral entropy) for SIP-labeled PSMs The peptide has not been matched to a theoretical spectrum — spectral entropy requires both observed and theoretical intensity distributions on matched peaks http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Computes a spectral-entropy similarity score between an observed MS/MS spectrum and a matched theoretical b/y-ion spectrum, as one of Aerith's four PSM scoring functions (MVH, Xcorr, WDP, spectral entropy) used to quantitatively evaluate peptide-spectrum matches in SIP proteomics. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c03207
skills.summary: Computes a spectral-entropy similarity score between an observed MS/MS spectrum and a matched theoretical b/y-ion spectrum, as one of Aerith's four PSM scoring functions (MVH, Xcorr, WDP, spectral entropy) used to quantitatively evaluate peptide-spectrum matches in SIP proteomics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is an MS1 isotopic-envelope comparison rather than an MS2 PSM — Aerith's envelope simulation and fine-structure tools, not PSM scoring, apply there You only need the single best discriminator for SIP-labeled PSMs — the article reports the weighted dot product (WDP) outperforms the other functions (including spectral entropy) for SIP-labeled PSMs The peptide has not been matched to a theoretical spectrum — spectral entropy requires both observed and theoretical intensity distributions on matched peaks

skills.description: Use when a SMART 2.0 (or comparable NMR-based CNN) class probability assignment must be verified against the underlying 1D/2D NMR and LC-MS/MS spectra before the compound annotation is accepted.
skills.name: spectral-evidence-cross-validation
skills.search_text: spectral-evidence-cross-validation Use when a SMART 2.0 (or comparable NMR-based CNN) class probability assignment must be verified against the underlying 1D/2D NMR and LC-MS/MS spectra before the compound annotation is accepted. When the compound structure is already confirmed — e.g., the planar structure has already been confirmed by 1D/2D NMR and LC-MS2 analysis — no cross-validation of a predicted class is needed. When only SMILES strings (not spectra) are available and the goal is programmatic structural classification; use the NP Classifier /classify?smiles= API instead of spectral evidence checking. http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Validates machine-learning natural-product class assignments (e.g., SMART 2.0 NMR-based CNN predictions) by cross-checking each predicted class against the raw supporting spectral evidence — 1D/2D NMR and LC-MS/MS data — before committing the annotation. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/jacs.9b13786
skills.summary: Validates machine-learning natural-product class assignments (e.g., SMART 2.0 NMR-based CNN predictions) by cross-checking each predicted class against the raw supporting spectral evidence — 1D/2D NMR and LC-MS/MS data — before committing the annotation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the compound structure is already confirmed — e.g., the planar structure has already been confirmed by 1D/2D NMR and LC-MS2 analysis — no cross-validation of a predicted class is needed. When only SMILES strings (not spectra) are available and the goal is programmatic structural classification; use the NP Classifier /classify?smiles= API instead of spectral evidence checking.

skills.description: Use when a specXplore-style .mgf MS/MS feature set needs a tabular, multi-k grouping overlay derived from the ms2deepscore similarity matrix rather than network edge thresholds.
skills.name: spectral-feature-cluster-assignment-table-generation
skills.search_text: spectral-feature-cluster-assignment-table-generation Use when a specXplore-style .mgf MS/MS feature set needs a tabular, multi-k grouping overlay derived from the ms2deepscore similarity matrix rather than network edge thresholds. You need hierarchically constrained medoid clusters — the authors avoided hierarchical clustering with medoid linkage because of lacking Python implementation and suboptimality at any level of k. You need guaranteed consistency of cluster assignments across different k settings — k-medoid assignments may vary across k since no cross-k agreement is enforced. Your feature set contains spectra/metabolites poorly covered by ms2deepscore training data — similarity scores may be unreliable (also beware ms2deepscore issue 199 on macOS arm64). http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Generate a per-feature table of k-medoid cluster labels across multiple values of k, computed from the ms2deepscore pairwise similarity matrix that backs the specXplore dashboard, so that clustering overlays can complement the t-SNE overview. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c04444
skills.summary: Generate a per-feature table of k-medoid cluster labels across multiple values of k, computed from the ms2deepscore pairwise similarity matrix that backs the specXplore dashboard, so that clustering overlays can complement the t-SNE overview.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need hierarchically constrained medoid clusters — the authors avoided hierarchical clustering with medoid linkage because of lacking Python implementation and suboptimality at any level of k. You need guaranteed consistency of cluster assignments across different k settings — k-medoid assignments may vary across k since no cross-k agreement is enforced. Your feature set contains spectra/metabolites poorly covered by ms2deepscore training data — similarity scores may be unreliable (also beware ms2deepscore issue 199 on macOS arm64).

skills.description: Use when FSA (or similar formula-ranking) result files contain per-spectrum rank outcomes plus spectral features, and you need to identify which features statistically separate R1 from R2+ assignments.
skills.name: spectral-feature-discrimination-analysis
skills.search_text: spectral-feature-discrimination-analysis Use when FSA (or similar formula-ranking) result files contain per-spectrum rank outcomes plus spectral features, and you need to identify which features statistically separate R1 from R2+ assignments. Spectra lack rank outcomes or the four per-spectrum features (fragment count, inter-peak-distance SD, CF ratio, top-two-score gap), so no R1/R2+ grouping is possible You need absolute ranking accuracy of FSA (rank #1/top-5 rates) rather than feature-level discrimination between correct and incorrect assignments Features are normally distributed and a parametric comparison (t-test/ANOVA) is the appropriate test — the article applies Wilcoxon because fragment numbers are not normally distributed Statistically discriminates correctly-ranked (rank #1) from incorrectly-ranked (R2+) MS/MS formula assignments by comparing per-spectrum spectral features — fragment count, inter-peak-distance SD, CF ratio, and top-two-score gap — with two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests and annotated boxplots. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-025-02379-0
skills.summary: Statistically discriminates correctly-ranked (rank #1) from incorrectly-ranked (R2+) MS/MS formula assignments by comparing per-spectrum spectral features — fragment count, inter-peak-distance SD, CF ratio, and top-two-score gap — with two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests and annotated boxplots.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Spectra lack rank outcomes or the four per-spectrum features (fragment count, inter-peak-distance SD, CF ratio, top-two-score gap), so no R1/R2+ grouping is possible You need absolute ranking accuracy of FSA (rank #1/top-5 rates) rather than feature-level discrimination between correct and incorrect assignments Features are normally distributed and a parametric comparison (t-test/ANOVA) is the appropriate test — the article applies Wilcoxon because fragment numbers are not normally distributed

skills.description: Use when ranking top-k candidate molecular formulas per MS/MS spectrum (Orbitrap or Q-TOF) by predicted confidence, after FIDDLE's refinement step has generated candidates.
skills.name: spectral-feature-vector-concatenation
skills.search_text: spectral-feature-vector-concatenation Use when ranking top-k candidate molecular formulas per MS/MS spectrum (Orbitrap or Q-TOF) by predicted confidence, after FIDDLE's refinement step has generated candidates. You only need the FIDDLE formula prediction itself, not re-ranking of the refinement step's candidates You are using FIDDLE v2.0.0+, where the rescore model has been redesigned as a Siamese architecture and the five-layer concatenation design no longer matches the released code Spectra are chimeric (co-eluting), where FIDDLE's performance decreases as spectral mixing increases FIDDLE's secondary rescoring approach: build training pairs by concatenating condition-independent MS/MS spectral features with each candidate formula vector, then train a five-layer fully connected rescore network to predict confidence scores used to rank candidate formulas. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-025-66060-9
skills.summary: FIDDLE's secondary rescoring approach: build training pairs by concatenating condition-independent MS/MS spectral features with each candidate formula vector, then train a five-layer fully connected rescore network to predict confidence scores used to rank candidate formulas.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need the FIDDLE formula prediction itself, not re-ranking of the refinement step's candidates You are using FIDDLE v2.0.0+, where the rescore model has been redesigned as a Siamese architecture and the five-layer concatenation design no longer matches the released code Spectra are chimeric (co-eluting), where FIDDLE's performance decreases as spectral mixing increases

skills.description: Use when LC-MS/MS spectra intended for NPDtools (Dereplicator, VarQuest, Dereplicator+) are not centroided or not in MGF, mzXML, mzML, or mzData format and must be prepared for database search.
skills.name: spectral-file-format-conversion
skills.search_text: spectral-file-format-conversion Use when LC-MS/MS spectra intended for NPDtools (Dereplicator, VarQuest, Dereplicator+) are not centroided or not in MGF, mzXML, mzML, or mzData format and must be prepared for database search. The spectra are already centroided and in MGF, mzXML, mzML, or mzData format and can be parsed natively by NPDtools. The downstream analysis is not an NPDtools database-search pipeline and requires a different conversion target (e.g., proteomics search engines expecting mzML with vendor peak picking). The spectra are profile-mode and you have no centroiding step available; converting without centroiding will not satisfy NPDtools' centroided-data requirement. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Convert vendor or non-MGF tandem mass spectrometry files into MGF (or read MGF/mzXML/mzML/mzData directly) with ProteoWizard's msconvert so centroided spectra can be fed into NPDtools database-search pipelines such as DEREPLICATOR+. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-018-06082-8
skills.summary: Convert vendor or non-MGF tandem mass spectrometry files into MGF (or read MGF/mzXML/mzML/mzData directly) with ProteoWizard's msconvert so centroided spectra can be fed into NPDtools database-search pipelines such as DEREPLICATOR+.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The spectra are already centroided and in MGF, mzXML, mzML, or mzData format and can be parsed natively by NPDtools. The downstream analysis is not an NPDtools database-search pipeline and requires a different conversion target (e.g., proteomics search engines expecting mzML with vendor peak picking). The spectra are profile-mode and you have no centroiding step available; converting without centroiding will not satisfy NPDtools' centroided-data requirement.

skills.description: Use when input data are MS/MS spectra in .mgf format (e.g., from MZmine feature-based molecular networking) and you need to read scan records, attach or filter metadata, subset spectra by condition, and write a new .mgf for a batch search.
skills.name: spectral-file-parsing-mgf
skills.search_text: spectral-file-parsing-mgf Use when input data are MS/MS spectra in .mgf format (e.g., from MZmine feature-based molecular networking) and you need to read scan records, attach or filter metadata, subset spectra by condition, and write a new .mgf for a batch search. Input is already a processed feature table or a list of USIs in a .csv/.tsv file — the microbeMASST batch script accepts USIs directly and does not need .mgf re-parsing. The spectra are in a vendor raw format or mzML; convert through MZmine first rather than attempting .mgf-style parsing. You only need to view or search a single spectrum; the standalone web apps (e.g., microbeMASST) accept one spectrum at a time without file parsing. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Parse and manipulate MS/MS spectra stored in .mgf ( Mascot Generic Format) files—such as those exported from MZmine or the GNPS molecular networking workflow—so they can be filtered, subset, and re-serialized for downstream batch tools like the microbeMASST Fast Search API. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41564-023-01575-9
skills.summary: Parse and manipulate MS/MS spectra stored in .mgf ( Mascot Generic Format) files—such as those exported from MZmine or the GNPS molecular networking workflow—so they can be filtered, subset, and re-serialized for downstream batch tools like the microbeMASST Fast Search API.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a processed feature table or a list of USIs in a .csv/.tsv file — the microbeMASST batch script accepts USIs directly and does not need .mgf re-parsing. The spectra are in a vendor raw format or mzML; convert through MZmine first rather than attempting .mgf-style parsing. You only need to view or search a single spectrum; the standalone web apps (e.g., microbeMASST) accept one spectrum at a time without file parsing.

skills.description: Use when you have processed tandem MS test spectra (peak lists, precursor m/z) whose true formula may be unknown and you need ranked formula candidates to feed downstream de novo structure generation.
skills.name: spectral-formula-prediction-inference

skills.description: Use when a mass spectrum must be assigned a database-independent identifier, cross-referenced across MassBank/MoNA/GNPS/HMDB, or checked for consistent SPLASH generation across tools and implementations.
skills.name: spectral-hash-reference-validation
skills.search_text: spectral-hash-reference-validation Use when a mass spectrum must be assigned a database-independent identifier, cross-referenced across MassBank/MoNA/GNPS/HMDB, or checked for consistent SPLASH generation across tools and implementations. The input is not a mass spectrum but a chemical structure — use an InChIKey-based approach instead, since SPLASH is explicitly a spectral counterpart to the InChIKey and not a general chemical identifier. The spectrum representation cannot be normalized to the 'ion:intensity ion:intensity …' single-line format — the canonicalization and SHA-256 hash block depend on this exact representation, and other encodings will yield a different identifier. You need to reverse the SPLASH back into the original peak list — the fourth block is a SHA-256 hash and does not encode the peaks recoverably. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0157 A method for generating and validating SPLASH identifiers (SPectraL hASH) for mass spectra, by building a four-block identifier (SPLASH10 prefix, two summary blocks, and a SHA-256 hash block) and verifying it against the reference Java implementation so that identical spectra from MassBank, MoNA, GNPS, HMDB, MetaboLights, and mzCloud converge on the same database-independent identifier. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/nbt.3689
skills.summary: A method for generating and validating SPLASH identifiers (SPectraL hASH) for mass spectra, by building a four-block identifier (SPLASH10 prefix, two summary blocks, and a SHA-256 hash block) and verifying it against the reference Java implementation so that identical spectra from MassBank, MoNA, GNPS, HMDB, MetaboLights, and mzCloud converge on the same database-independent identifier.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is not a mass spectrum but a chemical structure — use an InChIKey-based approach instead, since SPLASH is explicitly a spectral counterpart to the InChIKey and not a general chemical identifier. The spectrum representation cannot be normalized to the 'ion:intensity ion:intensity …' single-line format — the canonicalization and SHA-256 hash block depend on this exact representation, and other encodings will yield a different identifier. You need to reverse the SPLASH back into the original peak list — the fourth block is a SHA-256 hash and does not encode the peaks recoverably.

skills.description: Use when generating or verifying the third block of a SPLASH (SPectraL hASH) identifier from a mass spectrum given as ion:intensity pairs, e.g. to compare spectra across MassBank, MoNA, GNPS or HMDB entries.
skills.name: spectral-histogram-digit-scaling
skills.search_text: spectral-histogram-digit-scaling Use when generating or verifying the third block of a SPLASH (SPectraL hASH) identifier from a mass spectrum given as ion:intensity pairs, e.g. to compare spectra across MassBank, MoNA, GNPS or HMDB entries. You need the second SPLASH summary block (chosen from 136 candidate block formats for search-space reduction), not the 100 Da binned histogram block You need the fourth block, which is the SHA256-derived unique hash, not a spectral histogram The spectrum is not an MS spectrum (the validation tool defaults to spectrum type MS) http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Computes the third summary block of a SPLASH identifier by summing ion intensities into ten 100 Da m/z bins and scaling each bin's summed intensity to a single base-10 digit (0–9). This yields a length-10 digit string such as caffeine's '0900000000' in splash10-0002-0900000000-b112e4e059e1ecf98c5f. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/nbt.3689
skills.summary: Computes the third summary block of a SPLASH identifier by summing ion intensities into ten 100 Da m/z bins and scaling each bin's summed intensity to a single base-10 digit (0–9). This yields a length-10 digit string such as caffeine's '0900000000' in splash10-0002-0900000000-b112e4e059e1ecf98c5f.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need the second SPLASH summary block (chosen from 136 candidate block formats for search-space reduction), not the 100 Da binned histogram block You need the fourth block, which is the SHA256-derived unique hash, not a spectral histogram The spectrum is not an MS spectrum (the validation tool defaults to spectrum type MS)

skills.search_text: spectral-identification-rank-accuracy-evaluation Use when a tandem mass spectrum database-search tool (e.g. CycloBranch) returns ranked structure identifications and you must quantify how often the known compound appears at rank 1 or within the top 10. Input is not tandem mass spectral data (e.g. MS1-only feature tables or chromatographic profiles), so no b/a-ion fragment matching or ranked identification report can be produced. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Benchmarking workflow that runs a tandem-MS dereplication (database) search with CycloBranch against a custom NRP/PK sequence database and computes top-1 and top-10 accuracy of correct structure retrieval from the ranked identification report. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-021-00530-2
skills.summary: Benchmarking workflow that runs a tandem-MS dereplication (database) search with CycloBranch against a custom NRP/PK sequence database and computes top-1 and top-10 accuracy of correct structure retrieval from the ranked identification report.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is de novo spectrum annotation/sequencing rather than database-search dereplication against a known sequence database. The analytes are non-peptidic natural products or arbitrary small molecules outside the NRP/PK/siderophore sequence space supported by the MassSpecBlocks-exported database. Input is not tandem mass spectral data (e.g. MS1-only feature tables or chromatographic profiles), so no b/a-ion fragment matching or ranked identification report can be produced.

skills.summary: Generates the SPLASH (SPectraL hASH) — an unambiguous, database-independent identifier for mass spectra composed of a splash10 identifier block, two summary blocks, and a SHA-256 hash block — from a single-line 'ion:intensity' peak-list string, enabling cross-database identity checks (e.g. the same caffeine spectrum in MassBank, HMDB, and GNPS).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is not a mass spectrum peak list but a chemical structure identifier — SPLASH is deliberately scoped to spectra, with InChIKey serving the analogous role for structures Only the second block is needed for high-precision database subsetting and a full hash is overkill; the paper positions block 2 as the search-space reducer (94% or above) rather than a unique ID Spectra contain a single ion only — collision testing showed identical SPLASHes arise exactly from mass spectra containing a single ion of the same mass, so hash uniqueness is not guaranteed in that edge case

skills.summary: Applies the matchms normalize_intensities filter to MS2 spectra held in an R Spectra::Spectra object via SpectriPy's filterSpectriPy(), scaling each spectrum's peak intensities so the maximum equals 1 by translating data to Python, running the filter, and converting results back to R.

skills.name: spectral-intensity-scaling-and-binning
skills.search_text: spectral-intensity-scaling-and-binning Use when raw MS/MS spectra (m/z–intensity peak lists from MoNA/NIST libraries or in-house data) must be converted into fixed-length feature vectors for training or inference with a neural-network fingerprint predictor such as MetFID. When spectra are already in a fixed-length feature representation (e.g. binned intensity vectors) — applying scaling/filtering again would corrupt the data. When the downstream task is clustering or library comparison rather than neural-network fingerprint prediction, and raw peak lists are preferred for interpretability. When spectra have fewer than five peaks with relative intensity above 2% — they will be removed anyway and no useful vector can be produced. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Pre-processing of MS/MS spectra for ML-based fingerprint prediction: scale peak intensities to a 0–100 range, filter out spectra with fewer than five peaks above 2% relative intensity, denoise by removing peaks below 10 intensity, then bin the m/z range into prespecified bins, using 0.1 m/z merging and loss-feature calculation as input steps. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-020-01726-7

skills.name: spectral-library-cleaning-pipeline-configuration
skills.search_text: spectral-library-cleaning-pipeline-configuration Use when a public MS/MS spectral library (e.g. GNPS msp, MassBank, MoNA) has inconsistent or missing metadata, missing/broken SMILES-InChI-InChIKey annotations, or parent mass/adduct mismatches that must be repaired or used to remove spectra before library searching or ML training. The goal is spectral similarity scoring or library searching itself, not cleaning the library beforehand — this skill only harmonizes/repairs/validates metadata and discards spectra. Wrong chemical annotations consistent with the measured parent mass are the target of the cleaning: the pipeline lacks plausibility checks that consider both metadata and measured fragments, so such errors go unnoticed and another validation approach is needed. Standardization of fields like instrument type or collision energies is required — current matchms filters do not clean or standardize these metadata fields. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Configure and run the matchms 0.26.4 library-cleaning pipeline (SpectrumProcessor/Pipeline) that harmonizes metadata, repairs structure annotations (SMILES/InChI/InChIKey via RDKit and PubChem), and discards spectra with invalid annotations from public MS/MS libraries such as GNPS, MassBank, and MoNA, with reproducibility captured in an auto-generated YAML file and processing report. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00878-1
skills.summary: Configure and run the matchms 0.26.4 library-cleaning pipeline (SpectrumProcessor/Pipeline) that harmonizes metadata, repairs structure annotations (SMILES/InChI/InChIKey via RDKit and PubChem), and discards spectra with invalid annotations from public MS/MS libraries such as GNPS, MassBank, and MoNA, with reproducibility captured in an auto-generated YAML file and processing report.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is spectral similarity scoring or library searching itself, not cleaning the library beforehand — this skill only harmonizes/repairs/validates metadata and discards spectra. Wrong chemical annotations consistent with the measured parent mass are the target of the cleaning: the pipeline lacks plausibility checks that consider both metadata and measured fragments, so such errors go unnoticed and another validation approach is needed. Standardization of fields like instrument type or collision energies is required — current matchms filters do not clean or standardize these metadata fields.

skills.search_text: spectral-library-curation Use when preparing a training-ready spectral feature table from multiple MS/MS spectra per compound (e.g. MoNA Vaniya/Fiehn, GNPS, RIKEN PlaSMA, MassBank, Fiehn HILIC, or NIST 17) and raw spectra differ in collision energy, ion mode, or adduct. Input is already a curated, single-spectrum-per-compound feature table — the merge and denoise steps would be redundant or harmful. Analyzing experimental analyte spectra for candidate ranking (post-training) rather than building the training set — use the MetFID prediction workflow instead. Spectra are negative mode, H- or Na+ adducts, or outside 100–1010 Da range — these fail the homogeneity criteria and must not be included in the training table. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Curate and merge MS/MS spectra from MoNA and NIST 17 libraries into a unified, denoised, binned spectral feature table ready for training a fingerprint predictor. Rationale: raw library spectra vary in collision energy, instrument type, and adduct, so merging same-compound spectra and removing bins of all zeros produces a consistent feature vector. This is why MetFID merges multiple MS/MS spectra per compound before feature extraction. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-020-01726-7

skills.search_text: spectral-library-matching Use when a GC/EI-MS (70 eV) analyte spectrum fails to match any known reference spectra (NIST, Wiley, or SWGDRUG libraries) and you need to rank potential NPS identities by combined spectral and fingerprint similarity against a synthetic derivative database. skills.when_to_use_negative: When the analyte's mass spectrum already matches a known reference spectrum — conventional library matching against NIST/Wiley/SWGDRUG is sufficient and cheaper.
