skills.search_text: spectral-word-embedding-vector-aggregation Use when you have a trained Spec2Vec Word2Vec model and processed spectra as peak/loss word documents, and need pairwise spectral similarity scores for library matching or molecular networking. No trained model is available and the training set does not include a large fraction of the fragment ions and losses present in the query data — Spec2Vec needs training data, unlike cosine scores The task is plain peak-by-peak cosine matching of already-aligned peaks — use the cosine score instead Query spectra are far outside the model's learned peaks/losses (missing fraction > 0.05), e.g. spectra from an instrument or chemistry domain absent from training http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Converts processed MS/MS spectra into fixed-length spectrum vectors by summing each peak/loss word's Word2Vec embedding weighted by peak intensity, then scores spectral similarity as the cosine between two spectrum vectors (the Spec2Vec score). metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008724
skills.summary: Converts processed MS/MS spectra into fixed-length spectrum vectors by summing each peak/loss word's Word2Vec embedding weighted by peak intensity, then scores spectral similarity as the cosine between two spectrum vectors (the Spec2Vec score).

skills.name: spectrogram-deconvolution-error-correction
skills.search_text: spectrogram-deconvolution-error-correction Use when low-resolution MSn spectra from a miniaturized mass spectrometer feed de novo fragment-tree or formula prediction and raw mass errors would corrupt constraints such as the <500 Da cutoff or ten-element formula search. High-resolution, high-accuracy spectra where the instrument's mass accuracy already satisfies formula-annotation constraints without deconvolution correction Spectra recorded in negative ion mode — TeFT was trained only on positive ion mode (H+) spectra, so corrected peaks would leave the model's applicability domain Peak lists already deconvoluted and error-corrected upstream; re-applying averaging/deconvolution could distort intensities http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 An error-correction preprocessing step from the TeFT workflow that compensates for mass inaccuracies of low-resolution miniaturized-MS spectra by averaging multiple measurements and applying deconvolution integration on the spectrogram data before fragment-tree construction. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s42004-024-01189-0

skills.description: Use when UK Biobank NMR biomarker concentrations still show within-spectrometer drift over time after correction for sample degradation time, plate row (A-H), and plate column (1-12), and must be adjusted via date-binned robust regression.
skills.name: spectrometer-drift-time-binning
skills.search_text: spectrometer-drift-time-binning Use when UK Biobank NMR biomarker concentrations still show within-spectrometer drift over time after correction for sample degradation time, plate row (A-H), and plate column (1-12), and must be adjusted via date-binned robust regression. skills.search_text: spectrum-preprocessing-denoising Use when raw GNPS-derived MGF MS/MS spectra must be normalized and denoised before feeding a spectral-similarity model such as TransExION, Cosine, Spec2Vec, or MS2DeepScore. Input is already a preprocessed h5py spectrum database produced by ms_convert_mgf2h5py.py — re-filtering would double-apply the thresholds. The downstream task needs low-mass reporter ions or diagnostic peaks below 10 Da or above 1000 Da, which this filter discards. The analysis targets raw profile-mode data or peak picking, rather than peak-list-level cleaning of centroided library spectra. Cleans raw MS/MS spectra before similarity modeling by rounding m/z values to two decimals, converting peak intensities to relative abundance percentages, and removing low-intensity and out-of-range peaks (<0.1% intensity, outside 10–1000 Da), with optional MGF-to-h5py conversion for large-scale processing. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-024-00858-5
skills.summary: Cleans raw MS/MS spectra before similarity modeling by rounding m/z values to two decimals, converting peak intensities to relative abundance percentages, and removing low-intensity and out-of-range peaks (<0.1% intensity, outside 10–1000 Da), with optional MGF-to-h5py conversion for large-scale processing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a preprocessed h5py spectrum database produced by ms_convert_mgf2h5py.py — re-filtering would double-apply the thresholds. skills.description: Use when an MGF/mzML/msp MS/MS collection contains sparse or noisy spectra — e.g. fewer than ~10 peaks above a relative-intensity threshold — and you must flag or drop low-quality spectra before library cleaning or spectral similarity comparison.
skills.name: spectrum-quality-assessment
skills.search_text: spectrum-quality-assessment Use when an MGF/mzML/msp MS/MS collection contains sparse or noisy spectra — e.g. fewer than ~10 peaks above a relative-intensity threshold — and you must flag or drop low-quality spectra before library cleaning or spectral similarity comparison. The input is already a cleaned, filtered feature/spectral library — stacking require_minimum_number_of_peaks again would only remove legitimately sparse spectra without adding information. The goal is metadata-only harmonization (ionmode, adduct, InChIKey correction) with no need to assess peak count/intensity quality — a metadata-cleaning pipeline without peak filters is the right fit. Spectra are raw profile-mode or centroided precursor-only data where peak-count thresholds are not meaningful — quality assessment by peak counts presupposes processed MS2 peak lists. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Assess and enforce per-spectrum quality in MS/MS libraries using matchms filter steps — stacking peak-count and intensity/mz selection filters such as require_minimum_number_of_peaks (n_required=10), select_by_mz (mz_from=0, mz_to=1000), and select_by_relative_intensity (intensity_from=0.001) to classify spectra as pass/fail and remove low-quality or sparse spectra before similarity scoring. metabolomics/v3 10.21105/joss.02411
skills.summary: Assess and enforce per-spectrum quality in MS/MS libraries using matchms filter steps — stacking peak-count and intensity/mz selection filters such as require_minimum_number_of_peaks (n_required=10), select_by_mz (mz_from=0, mz_to=1000), and select_by_relative_intensity (intensity_from=0.001) to classify spectra as pass/fail and remove low-quality or sparse spectra before similarity scoring.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a cleaned, filtered feature/spectral library — stacking require_minimum_number_of_peaks again would only remove legitimately sparse spectra without adding information. The goal is metadata-only harmonization (ionmode, adduct, InChIKey correction) with no need to assess peak count/intensity quality — a metadata-cleaning pipeline without peak filters is the right fit. Spectra are raw profile-mode or centroided precursor-only data where peak-count thresholds are not meaningful — quality assessment by peak counts presupposes processed MS2 peak lists.

skills.description: Use when an integrated OMSL (e.g. .MSP or .MGF files from GNPS, MoNA, MassBank) must be cleaned before export, and spectra with too few peaks or weak high-intensity peaks should be removed.
skills.name: spectrum-quality-filtering
skills.search_text: spectrum-quality-filtering Use when an integrated OMSL (e.g. .MSP or .MGF files from GNPS, MoNA, MassBank) must be cleaned before export, and spectra with too few peaks or weak high-intensity peaks should be removed. Input is already a curated spectral library where every spectrum is known to satisfy the minimum peak-count and high-intensity criteria — reapplying the filters would only add overhead Peak lists are required in full, unfiltered form (e.g. for raw reprocessing or fragmentation-detail mining) rather than for spectral matching, since these filters permanently drop low-peak spectra Spectra lack SMILES, InChI, precursor m/z, or adduct metadata; FragHub removes these inconsistent spectra during processing anyway, so quality filtering alone will not salvage them Applies FragHub's generic spectral-quality filters to mass spectra in an integrated Open Mass Spectra Library (OMSL), dropping spectra that lack a minimum number of MS/MS peaks or sufficient high-intensity peaks so the resulting library contains only usable reference spectra. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c02219
skills.summary: Applies FragHub's generic spectral-quality filters to mass spectra in an integrated Open Mass Spectra Library (OMSL), dropping spectra that lack a minimum number of MS/MS peaks or sufficient high-intensity peaks so the resulting library contains only usable reference spectra.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a curated spectral library where every spectrum is known to satisfy the minimum peak-count and high-intensity criteria — reapplying the filters would only add overhead Peak lists are required in full, unfiltered form (e.g. for raw reprocessing or fragmentation-detail mining) rather than for spectral matching, since these filters permanently drop low-peak spectra Spectra lack SMILES, InChI, precursor m/z, or adduct metadata; FragHub removes these inconsistent spectra during processing anyway, so quality filtering alone will not salvage them

skills.summary: Quantifies spectral quality of validated antibody MS/MS spectra — missing cleavage sites, noise-peak fraction, and noise factor — and relates these quality metrics to peptide recall of de novo sequencing tools (Novor, pNovo 3, DeepNovo, SMSNet, PointNovo, Casanovo). skills.summary: Prunes MADByTE chemical similarity networks by removing spin-system nodes with only a single connection and dropping non-reciprocal edges, so that only mutually supported feature matches survive before the full association, similarity, and hybrid networks are serialized as graphML for Gephi visualization.

skills.description: Use when you have spin system feature tables (1H/13C shifts with spin system IDs) for multiple samples and need a pairwise sample-similarity matrix for network/dereplication analysis.

skills.search_text: spin-system-feature-matching Use when you have spin system feature tables (1H/13C shifts with spin system IDs) for multiple samples and need a pairwise sample-similarity matrix for network/dereplication analysis. Input is still raw or peak-picked TOCSY/HSQC spectra rather than spin system feature tables — run spin system construction first. Only a single sample is available — pairwise feature matching requires at least two samples. http://edamontology.org/topic_0749 Scores pairwise overlap of (1H, 13C) spin system features between samples in a MADByTE analysis set to build the asymmetric correlation matrix that seeds chemical similarity network generation. It operationalizes MADByTE's sample-comparison step, where the higher of two directional scores (A vs B or B vs A) defines each edge. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jnatprod.0c01076
skills.summary: Scores pairwise overlap of (1H, 13C) spin system features between samples in a MADByTE analysis set to build the asymmetric correlation matrix that seeds chemical similarity network generation. It operationalizes MADByTE's sample-comparison step, where the higher of two directional scores (A vs B or B vs A) defines each edge.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is still raw or peak-picked TOCSY/HSQC spectra rather than spin system feature tables — run spin system construction first. Only a single sample is available — pairwise feature matching requires at least two samples.

skills.description: Use when analyzing picked peaks from an INADEQUATE NMR spectrum and you need to reconstruct the 13C spin-system networks of a metabolite before compound matching.
skills.name: spin-system-network-construction
skills.search_text: spin-system-network-construction Use when analyzing picked peaks from an INADEQUATE NMR spectrum and you need to reconstruct the 13C spin-system networks of a metabolite before compound matching. Input spectra are not INADEQUATE (e.g. single-dimension 13C or 1H spectra) - the network logic relies on double-quantum transition structure and is not meaningful for non-INADEQUATE peak lists Peak picking has not yet been performed - the network step requires the picked peak list as input, not raw spectra You already have a curated connectivity table and only need compound identification - then the downstream matching step is the right entry point, not network construction http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 PyINETA method for grouping picked INADEQUATE peaks into horizontal carbon networks (via DQT, SumXY, SDT thresholds) and then chaining those networks vertically by shared-carbon CST similarity, reconstructing spin systems from 13C INADEQUATE NMR data. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c03966
skills.summary: PyINETA method for grouping picked INADEQUATE peaks into horizontal carbon networks (via DQT, SumXY, SDT thresholds) and then chaining those networks vertically by shared-carbon CST similarity, reconstructing spin systems from 13C INADEQUATE NMR data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra are not INADEQUATE (e.g. single-dimension 13C or 1H spectra) - the network logic relies on double-quantum transition structure and is not meaningful for non-INADEQUATE peak lists Peak picking has not yet been performed - the network step requires the picked peak list as input, not raw spectra You already have a curated connectivity table and only need compound identification - then the downstream matching step is the right entry point, not network construction

skills.search_text: splash-block-format-verification Use when a mass spectrum in single-line 'ion:intensity' format has an associated SPLASH identifier and you must confirm a specific block (e.g., the 100 Da-binned third block) matches what the reference implementation would emit. The goal is to generate a new SPLASH identifier rather than verify an existing one against a reference block The spectrum is not representable in the single-line 'ion:intensity' format and cannot be converted to ion-intensity pairs The task is chemical structure identification or spectral similarity scoring — SPLASH blocks are summaries, not similarity measures Verifies that individual blocks of a SPLASH identifier (e.g., the third 100 Da-binned summary block such as '0900000000' for caffeine) are correctly computed from a mass spectrum, using the reference implementations and validation tool from the spectra-hash project. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/nbt.3689
skills.summary: Verifies that individual blocks of a SPLASH identifier (e.g., the third 100 Da-binned summary block such as '0900000000' for caffeine) are correctly computed from a mass spectrum, using the reference implementations and validation tool from the spectra-hash project.

skills.description: Use when an MS/MS spectrum has been retrieved via a metabolomics USI (e.g. mzspec:GNPS:GNPS-LIBRARY:accession:...) and it must be compared across public resources, but no standardized spectrum identifier is available.
skills.name: splash-identifier-computation
skills.search_text: splash-identifier-computation Use when an MS/MS spectrum has been retrieved via a metabolomics USI (e.g. mzspec:GNPS:GNPS-LIBRARY:accession:...) and it must be compared across public resources, but no standardized spectrum identifier is available. The goal is only to retrieve or visualize a spectrum (PNG/SVG/mirror plots), not to obtain a database-independent cross-resource identifier The spectrum's peak list is unavailable or cannot be fetched via the /json/ endpoint, since SPLASH computation requires the peak list A plain proteomics USI lookup via ProteomeXchange is sufficient — USIs are easy to construct for proteomics data deposited via ProteomeXchange without needing SPLASH hashing Computes SPLASH (SPectraL hASH) identifiers from the peak lists of MS/MS spectra retrieved via the Metabolomics Spectrum Resolver's /json/ endpoint, yielding an unambiguous, database-independent spectrum identifier that can be paired with the input metabolomics-extended USI for cross-resource comparison. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2020.05.09.086066
skills.summary: Computes SPLASH (SPectraL hASH) identifiers from the peak lists of MS/MS spectra retrieved via the Metabolomics Spectrum Resolver's /json/ endpoint, yielding an unambiguous, database-independent spectrum identifier that can be paired with the input metabolomics-extended USI for cross-resource comparison.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is only to retrieve or visualize a spectrum (PNG/SVG/mirror plots), not to obtain a database-independent cross-resource identifier The spectrum's peak list is unavailable or cannot be fetched via the /json/ endpoint, since SPLASH computation requires the peak list A plain proteomics USI lookup via ProteomeXchange is sufficient — USIs are easy to construct for proteomics data deposited via ProteomeXchange without needing SPLASH hashing

skills.description: Use when a mass spectrum (ion-intensity pairs, e.g. m/z 138.0641:71.59 195.0815:261.7) must be assigned a canonical, database-independent identifier, or when spectra from different libraries must be matched or deduplicated by identifier.
skills.name: splash-identifier-generation
skills.search_text: splash-identifier-generation Use when a mass spectrum (ion-intensity pairs, e.g. m/z 138.0641:71.59 195.0815:261.7) must be assigned a canonical, database-independent identifier, or when spectra from different libraries must be matched or deduplicated by identifier. The input is not a mass spectrum (e.g. chemical structures — use InChIKey instead, which SPLASH is modeled after for structures) You need a human-readable or database-native record identifier (MassBank PR100026, HMDB 5464, GNPS CCMSLIB00000222858) rather than a content-derived spectral hash NIST library entries must be included in an openly redistributable output — only all-but-NIST spectra are publicly available on MoNA http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Generates SPLASH (SPectraL hASH) identifiers — unambiguous, database-independent identifiers for mass spectra — from ion-intensity pairs using the reference Java implementation, so identical spectra across MassBank, MoNA, GNPS, HMDB and other libraries can be recognized as the same spectrum. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/nbt.3689
skills.summary: Generates SPLASH (SPectraL hASH) identifiers — unambiguous, database-independent identifiers for mass spectra — from ion-intensity pairs using the reference Java implementation, so identical spectra across MassBank, MoNA, GNPS, HMDB and other libraries can be recognized as the same spectrum.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is not a mass spectrum (e.g. chemical structures — use InChIKey instead, which SPLASH is modeled after for structures) You need a human-readable or database-native record identifier (MassBank PR100026, HMDB 5464, GNPS CCMSLIB00000222858) rather than a content-derived spectral hash NIST library entries must be included in an openly redistributable output — only all-but-NIST spectra are publicly available on MoNA

skills.description: Use when a mass spectrum in single-line 'ion:intensity' representation (e.g. MassBank PR100026 caffeine) has a published SPLASH and you need to verify the identifier's blocks are reproducible from the spectrum.
skills.name: splash-identifier-structure-verification
skills.search_text: splash-identifier-structure-verification Use when a mass spectrum in single-line 'ion:intensity' representation (e.g. MassBank PR100026 caffeine) has a published SPLASH and you need to verify the identifier's blocks are reproducible from the spectrum. Input is a processed feature table or peak list in another format rather than the single-line 'ion:intensity' spectrum string The goal is spectral similarity search or library matching rather than verifying identifier structure — use the SPLASH second block only as a search-space reducer, not as a similarity score The spectrum is not a mass spectrum of type MS (the validation tool defaults to '-t ms') http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Recomputes the summary blocks of a SPLASH (SPectraL hASH) identifier from a raw mass spectrum and checks them against the published identifier, verifying that block generation (top-10 ion filtering, 5 Da binning, base-3 scaling, base-36 encoding, SHA256 hash block) is reproduced correctly. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/nbt.3689
skills.summary: Recomputes the summary blocks of a SPLASH (SPectraL hASH) identifier from a raw mass spectrum and checks them against the published identifier, verifying that block generation (top-10 ion filtering, 5 Da binning, base-3 scaling, base-36 encoding, SHA256 hash block) is reproduced correctly.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a processed feature table or peak list in another format rather than the single-line 'ion:intensity' spectrum string The goal is spectral similarity search or library matching rather than verifying identifier structure — use the SPLASH second block only as a search-space reducer, not as a similarity score The spectrum is not a mass spectrum of type MS (the validation tool defaults to '-t ms')

skills.description: Use when integrating or repeatedly re-processing spectra from heterogeneous mass spectral libraries (.MSP, .MGF, .JSON, .CSV) and you need database-independent spectral identifiers plus skip-if-seen incremental updates.
skills.name: splash-key-deduplication
skills.search_text: splash-key-deduplication Use when integrating or repeatedly re-processing spectra from heterogeneous mass spectral libraries (.MSP, .MGF, .JSON, .CSV) and you need database-independent spectral identifiers plus skip-if-seen incremental updates. When the task is to deduplicate compounds by chemical structure only (identical InChIKeys) rather than spectra — FragHub handles structure dedup as a separate downstream step in the partitioning stage. When spectra lack peak lists or have been so heavily pre-filtered that the peak array is empty — SPLASH keys are computed from m/z:intensity pairs and would be meaningless or colliding. When you need cross-run identity of collision-energy-aware spectra: FragHub explicitly does not harmonize collision energies (around 70 different formats), so SPLASH keys may not discriminate spectra differing only in collision energy encoding. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Generates a SPLASH (SPectraL hASH) identifier for every mass spectrum in an OMSL integration workflow (FragHub) and persists all keys in an 'update.json' repository so that, on re-runs or library updates, only spectra whose SPLASH key is absent are processed — enabling incremental, database-independent spectral deduplication. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c02219
skills.summary: Generates a SPLASH (SPectraL hASH) identifier for every mass spectrum in an OMSL integration workflow (FragHub) and persists all keys in an 'update.json' repository so that, on re-runs or library updates, only spectra whose SPLASH key is absent are processed — enabling incremental, database-independent spectral deduplication.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the task is to deduplicate compounds by chemical structure only (identical InChIKeys) rather than spectra — FragHub handles structure dedup as a separate downstream step in the partitioning stage. When spectra lack peak lists or have been so heavily pre-filtered that the peak array is empty — SPLASH keys are computed from m/z:intensity pairs and would be meaningless or colliding. When you need cross-run identity of collision-energy-aware spectra: FragHub explicitly does not harmonize collision energies (around 70 different formats), so SPLASH keys may not discriminate spectra differing only in collision energy encoding.

skills.description: Decision support for assigning the PP3 evidence rule during ACMG 2015 classification when SpliceAI and/or CADD scores are available for variants, and for handling its suppression by PVS1.
skills.name: splice-priority-scoring-thresholds
skills.search_text: splice-priority-scoring-thresholds Decision support for assigning the PP3 evidence rule during ACMG 2015 classification when SpliceAI and/or CADD scores are available for variants, and for handling its suppression by PVS1. The variant already qualifies for PVS1 via LoF coding impact — PP3 must be disabled rather than scored. No CADD or SpliceAI scores are available for the variants, so the >25.3 / >0.5 thresholds cannot be evaluated. The analysis targets ACMG rules other than splice-priority evidence (e.g., PS4, PM3, PP4, BP2, BP5, which the GDK engine excludes). http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 http://edamontology.org/topic_3574 Implements the ACMG PP3 (splice-priority) rule with concrete scoring thresholds—CADD > 25.3 or SpliceAI > 0.5—as used by the in-house GDK platform's ACMG rule engine, including the interplay rule that PP3 is disabled whenever PVS1 is triggered by a loss-of-function coding impact. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2024.10.11.617756
skills.summary: Implements the ACMG PP3 (splice-priority) rule with concrete scoring thresholds—CADD > 25.3 or SpliceAI > 0.5—as used by the in-house GDK platform's ACMG rule engine, including the interplay rule that PP3 is disabled whenever PVS1 is triggered by a loss-of-function coding impact.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The variant already qualifies for PVS1 via LoF coding impact — PP3 must be disabled rather than scored. No CADD or SpliceAI scores are available for the variants, so the >25.3 / >0.5 thresholds cannot be evaluated. The analysis targets ACMG rules other than splice-priority evidence (e.g., PS4, PM3, PP4, BP2, BP5, which the GDK engine excludes).

skills.description: Use when a machine-learning model on spectral pairs (e.g. MS2DeepScore Tanimoto prediction) is trained and evaluated on spectra derived from shared molecules, and you must confirm the split is molecule-disjoint before trusting test-set metrics.
skills.name: split-integrity-verification
skills.search_text: split-integrity-verification Use when a machine-learning model on spectral pairs (e.g. MS2DeepScore Tanimoto prediction) is trained and evaluated on spectra derived from shared molecules, and you must confirm the split is molecule-disjoint before trusting test-set metrics. Input spectra lack InChIKey (or other molecule-level) annotations, so molecule identity cannot be collapsed and disjointness cannot be checked The downstream task is spectrum-level (not molecule-level) prediction, where molecule-disjoint splitting is not required The split is already certified molecule-disjoint by an upstream tool and only needs re-use, not re-verification http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Verifies that a train/validation/test split of mass spectral data is molecule-disjoint: all spectra of a given InChIKey must map to exactly one split, and per-set unique-InChIKey counts (14,062/500/500 in the MS2DeepScore GNPS dataset) must match the declared design. This prevents structural-similarity leakage between model training and held-out evaluation. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-021-00558-4
skills.summary: Verifies that a train/validation/test split of mass spectral data is molecule-disjoint: all spectra of a given InChIKey must map to exactly one split, and per-set unique-InChIKey counts (14,062/500/500 in the MS2DeepScore GNPS dataset) must match the declared design. This prevents structural-similarity leakage between model training and held-out evaluation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input spectra lack InChIKey (or other molecule-level) annotations, so molecule identity cannot be collapsed and disjointness cannot be checked The downstream task is spectrum-level (not molecule-level) prediction, where molecule-disjoint splitting is not required The split is already certified molecule-disjoint by an upstream tool and only needs re-use, not re-verification

skills.search_text: split-peak-quantification Use when you have a validated mzRAPP benchmark of target-molecule peaks and a tool-specific NPP output table (XCMS, MZmine 2, MS-DIAL, etc.) and need the proportion of benchmark peaks split into multiple detected peaks. You have only a raw feature table and no benchmark of target molecules with known retention-time boundaries — mzRAPP cannot classify split peaks without the benchmark The question concerns alignment errors across files rather than peak-picking quality within files (use the alignment error counting metrics instead) Data are not LC-HRMS peak tables in a supported NPP tool's export format (mzRAPP supports XCMS, XCMS3, MZmine 2/3, MS-DIAL, OpenMS, El-MAVEN, SLAW, etc.) http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Quantifies the split-peaks metric of peak-picking performance by matching a mzRAPP-generated benchmark (e.g. Benchmark.csv built from MTBLS267 LC-HRMS mzML files) against non-targeted pre-processing (NPP) output tables such as XCMS run 2 unaligned/aligned CSVs, using mzRAPP's non-equivalent joins. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btab231
skills.summary: Quantifies the split-peaks metric of peak-picking performance by matching a mzRAPP-generated benchmark (e.g. Benchmark.csv built from MTBLS267 LC-HRMS mzML files) against non-targeted pre-processing (NPP) output tables such as XCMS run 2 unaligned/aligned CSVs, using mzRAPP's non-equivalent joins.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have only a raw feature table and no benchmark of target molecules with known retention-time boundaries — mzRAPP cannot classify split peaks without the benchmark The question concerns alignment errors across files rather than peak-picking quality within files (use the alignment error counting metrics instead) Data are not LC-HRMS peak tables in a supported NPP tool's export format (mzRAPP supports XCMS, XCMS3, MZmine 2/3, MS-DIAL, OpenMS, El-MAVEN, SLAW, etc.)

skills.search_text: spreadsheet-data-ingestion Use when a targeted LC–MS metabolomics/lipidomics workflow starts from a tabular target list (e.g., targets.xlsx in the TARDIS vignette) that must be loaded and standardized into the TARDIS data frame schema before peak integration. The input is raw LC–MS data (.raw/.mzML) needing targeted peak extraction — use TARDIS' integration/quality-assessment steps instead, which come after this ingestion step. The input is already a TARDIS-parsed data frame in the canonical schema (target ID, name, m/z, expected RT, polarity) — no spreadsheet parsing is needed. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Ingest a user-supplied target compound spreadsheet (.xlsx or .csv) into R as a structured data frame via TARDIS' createTargetList() parsing mechanism, yielding the canonical target schema (target ID, name, m/z, expected RT, ion polarity) that feeds TARDIS' targeted peak integration and quality assessment. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c00567
skills.summary: Ingest a user-supplied target compound spreadsheet (.xlsx or .csv) into R as a structured data frame via TARDIS' createTargetList() parsing mechanism, yielding the canonical target schema (target ID, name, m/z, expected RT, ion polarity) that feeds TARDIS' targeted peak integration and quality assessment.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw LC–MS data (.raw/.mzML) needing targeted peak extraction — use TARDIS' integration/quality-assessment steps instead, which come after this ingestion step. skills.description: Use when the starting material is a spreadsheet or delimited text file (e.g. .xlsx from the Instant Clue tutorial bundle) that must be ingested as a DataFrame before filtering, visualization, or row-wise fitting can begin.

skills.search_text: spreadsheet-data-loading Use when the starting material is a spreadsheet or delimited text file (e.g. .xlsx from the Instant Clue tutorial bundle) that must be ingested as a DataFrame before filtering, visualization, or row-wise fitting can begin. The data are not tabular spreadsheet/delimited text — e.g. optical recordings such as the Example Data 03 POMC neuron activity traces, which need their own handling The data are already loaded as a DataFrame and the goal is modeling (linear/polynomial/Michaelis-Menten fitting, correlation) rather than ingestion The data need batch-effect correction rather than loading — that is the role of the pyComBat/combat package, which must be installed separately http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Load tabular experimental data (e.g. the bundled Tutorial_Data_01.xlsx spreadsheet) into an analysis-ready form, either through Instant Clue's upload path (Excel, txt, csv, xml, gz, zip) or by reading the .xlsx into a pandas DataFrame for scripted activities such as curve fitting. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41598-018-31154-6
skills.summary: Load tabular experimental data (e.g. the bundled Tutorial_Data_01.xlsx spreadsheet) into an analysis-ready form, either through Instant Clue's upload path (Excel, txt, csv, xml, gz, zip) or by reading the .xlsx into a pandas DataFrame for scripted activities such as curve fitting.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are not tabular spreadsheet/delimited text — e.g. optical recordings such as the Example Data 03 POMC neuron activity traces, which need their own handling The data are already loaded as a DataFrame and the goal is modeling (linear/polynomial/Michaelis-Menten fitting, correlation) rather than ingestion The data need batch-effect correction rather than loading — that is the role of the pyComBat/combat package, which must be installed separately

skills.description: Use when raw adduct-level CCS spreadsheets ([M-H]-, [M+H]+, [M+Na]+) from the McLean Unified CCS Compendium must be cleaned into training sets for linear support vector regression CCS prediction.

skills.search_text: spreadsheet-data-scrubbing Use when raw adduct-level CCS spreadsheets ([M-H]-, [M+H]+, [M+Na]+) from the McLean Unified CCS Compendium must be cleaned into training sets for linear support vector regression CCS prediction. The input is already a cleaned, model-ready training CSV with post-scrubbing counts (567/518/461) matching the published tables The target adducts are dimers ([2M+H]+, [2M-H]-), less common adducts, or in-source fragments, which the CCSP 2.0 training sets do not support The goal is CCS-based filtering of annotation candidates (ΔCCS threshold of 2.8%, 10 ppm mass error) rather than training-set curation http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Curation procedure that scrubs McLean Unified CCS Compendium spreadsheets before CCS model training: averaging duplicate CCS entries and excluding entries with m/z deviations >1 mDa, rare chemical elements, or incompatibility with DeepCCS/AllCCS/CCSbase mass ranges. metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2022.08.09.503345
skills.summary: Curation procedure that scrubs McLean Unified CCS Compendium spreadsheets before CCS model training: averaging duplicate CCS entries and excluding entries with m/z deviations >1 mDa, rare chemical elements, or incompatibility with DeepCCS/AllCCS/CCSbase mass ranges.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a cleaned, model-ready training CSV with post-scrubbing counts (567/518/461) matching the published tables The target adducts are dimers ([2M+H]+, [2M-H]-), less common adducts, or in-source fragments, which the CCSP 2.0 training sets do not support The goal is CCS-based filtering of annotation candidates (ΔCCS threshold of 2.8%, 10 ppm mass error) rather than training-set curation

skills.search_text: spreadsheet-tabular-data-extraction Use when a multi-sheet .xlsx workbook organizes entities per condition (e.g. organ/serum sheets and ion-mode sheets) and per-sheet counts must be verified against reported totals and pooled/deduplicated. skills.summary: Extract, count, and reconcile tabular metabolite records stored across multiple sheets of an .xlsx workbook (here 'Organ specific metabolite database.xlsx' with 11 sheets) using MATLAB, verifying sheet-level counts against reported totals (1298 positive, 515 negative) and deduplicating pooled names to reach the reported union (1620 unique metabolites).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The workbook contains mass-spectrometry feature intensities to be annotated (e.g. MSIdata.xlsx) rather than a metabolite name database — use MSIannotator.m annotation instead The data are raw spectra or imaging data rather than tabular spreadsheet records; spreadsheet extraction does not apply to m/z feature lists or IMS imaging files

skills.summary: Implements MESSES's tagging-based extraction mechanism: a layer of tags (#export, #automate, #modify directives) added to messy Excel/CSV spreadsheets drives transformation of data tables into key-based JSON records suitable for Metabolomics Workbench depositions.

skills.summary: Maps rows of a tabular template file (XLSX) onto a target database entity — here, the chemical compound entity of the PeakForest data model — validating mandatory fields per row and serializing each valid row into a structured record ready for database ingestion.

skills.description: Use when a paper's supplementary data ships as a multi-worksheet Excel file (e.g. Additional file 3, Table S4) and a published figure (e.g. 210 lipid ions, 159 features, 15 lipid types) must be recounted from a single software's annotation columns.
skills.name: spreadsheet-worksheet-subsetting
skills.search_text: spreadsheet-worksheet-subsetting Use when a paper's supplementary data ships as a multi-worksheet Excel file (e.g. Additional file 3, Table S4) and a published figure (e.g. 210 lipid ions, 159 features, 15 lipid types) must be recounted from a single software's annotation columns. skills.summary: Selects the correct worksheet from a multi-sheet Excel supplementary workbook and subsets rows/columns to one software's annotations (here, LipidMatch columns in Additional file 3 Table S4) so counts can be independently recomputed with pandas.

skills.description: Use when a metabolomics dataset contains peripheral-blood samples with variable pre- and post-centrifugation delays and you need sample-type-aware stability annotation (EDTA plasma, serum, LiHep plasma) sorted by SPREC classification.
skills.name: sprec-classified-biobank-sample-annotation
skills.search_text: sprec-classified-biobank-sample-annotation Use when a metabolomics dataset contains peripheral-blood samples with variable pre- and post-centrifugation delays and you need sample-type-aware stability annotation (EDTA plasma, serum, LiHep plasma) sorted by SPREC classification. Samples are not peripheral blood plasma/serum (e.g., urine or tissue homogenates) — the panel's models and stability time points were derived for blood-derived matrices only. You only need Bruker BiobankQC's pass/fail output and do not need per-parameter stability annotation or preanalytical delay exploration. Sample cohorts lack date/time stamps or preanalytical metadata, so pre- and post-centrifugation times cannot be computed or verified. http://edamontology.org/topic_0736 Annotate biobank-derived metabolomics samples with SPREC-classified pre- and post-centrifugation delay times so stability time points can be attached per sample type (EDTA plasma, serum, LiHep plasma) and delay type before downstream thresholding. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c04938
skills.summary: Annotate biobank-derived metabolomics samples with SPREC-classified pre- and post-centrifugation delay times so stability time points can be attached per sample type (EDTA plasma, serum, LiHep plasma) and delay type before downstream thresholding.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Samples are not peripheral blood plasma/serum (e.g., urine or tissue homogenates) — the panel's models and stability time points were derived for blood-derived matrices only. You only need Bruker BiobankQC's pass/fail output and do not need per-parameter stability annotation or preanalytical delay exploration. Sample cohorts lack date/time stamps or preanalytical metadata, so pre- and post-centrifugation times cannot be computed or verified.

skills.description: Use when a biobank cohort dataset carries date/time stamps and SPREC classifications for pre- and postcentrifugation delays, and you need to stratify samples by delay category for NMR metabolomics QC.
skills.name: sprec-delay-classification
skills.search_text: sprec-delay-classification Use when a biobank cohort dataset carries date/time stamps and SPREC classifications for pre- and postcentrifugation delays, and you need to stratify samples by delay category for NMR metabolomics QC. The input already contains the SPREC-classified delay tables and you only need a pass/fail quality verdict — Bruker's BiobankQC or the PRIMA 'Single' tab report is the more direct tool. The samples are urine or tissue rather than peripheral blood plasma/serum — the PRIMA Panel models processing delays for plasma/serum NMR metabolomics, and delay-stratum behaviour may not transfer. No date+time stamps or SPREC codes are available, so delays cannot be computed or classified. http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 Use the PRIMA Panel's Data tab to split pre- and postcentrifugation delay measurements into SPREC-classified delay distributions, visualized as stability time-point highlights or lollipop plots, before further metabolomics quality assessment. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c04938
skills.summary: Use the PRIMA Panel's Data tab to split pre- and postcentrifugation delay measurements into SPREC-classified delay distributions, visualized as stability time-point highlights or lollipop plots, before further metabolomics quality assessment.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input already contains the SPREC-classified delay tables and you only need a pass/fail quality verdict — Bruker's BiobankQC or the PRIMA 'Single' tab report is the more direct tool. The samples are urine or tissue rather than peripheral blood plasma/serum — the PRIMA Panel models processing delays for plasma/serum NMR metabolomics, and delay-stratum behaviour may not transfer. No date+time stamps or SPREC codes are available, so delays cannot be computed or classified.

skills.description: Use when a sample cohort table contains collection, centrifugation, and freezing date-time stamps and each sample must receive a SPREC classification (letters 2 and 6) reflecting its pre- and postcentrifugation processing delays.
skills.name: sprec-sample-classification
skills.search_text: sprec-sample-classification Use when a sample cohort table contains collection, centrifugation, and freezing date-time stamps and each sample must receive a SPREC classification (letters 2 and 6) reflecting its pre- and postcentrifugation processing delays. The cohort lacks collection, centrifugation, or freezing timestamps — the Tools tab requires date+time stamps to compute the delay differences Samples are not peripheral blood plasma/serum — the PRIMA Panel explicitly targets 'samples of peripheral blood (plasma / serum)' and its SPREC codes and stability models are NMR-metabolomics specific The goal is a pass/fail QC verdict only (e.g., Bruker BiobankQC-style output) rather than SPREC-coded delay classification and concentration-change prediction http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 Assigns SPREC codes to each plasma/serum sample in a cohort by computing pre- and postcentrifugation delays from collection, centrifugation, and freezing date-time stamps, enabling standardized sorting of NMR-metabolomics stability time-points in the PRIMA Panel. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.4c04938
skills.summary: Assigns SPREC codes to each plasma/serum sample in a cohort by computing pre- and postcentrifugation delays from collection, centrifugation, and freezing date-time stamps, enabling standardized sorting of NMR-metabolomics stability time-points in the PRIMA Panel.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The cohort lacks collection, centrifugation, or freezing timestamps — the Tools tab requires date+time stamps to compute the delay differences Samples are not peripheral blood plasma/serum — the PRIMA Panel explicitly targets 'samples of peripheral blood (plasma / serum)' and its SPREC codes and stability models are NMR-metabolomics specific The goal is a pass/fail QC verdict only (e.g., Bruker BiobankQC-style output) rather than SPREC-coded delay classification and concentration-change prediction

skills.search_text: sql-transaction-management Use when building a local PostgreSQL cache database from HMDB/ChEBI/LIPID MAPS dump files via bulk insertion, or when storing fetched KEGG/PubChem records for later reuse without re-querying APIs. skills.description: Use when a BiG-SLiCE run (full or --query) must persist processed BGCs, GCF models, and cluster assignments into the SQLite3 database in the output folder for later SQL retrieval, visualization, or GCF query mode.
skills.name: sqlite-biosynthetic-datastore-population

skills.search_text: sqlite-compound-database-construction Use when a metabolomics annotation workflow needs a self-contained compound/spectral reference database: you have a raw public release (e.g. HMDB 5.0 XML records and experimental MS2 spectra) and must convert it into a CompDb SQLite file. A ready-made CompDb database (e.g. CompDb.Hsapiens.HMDB.5.0.sqlite) already exists — just load it with CompDb() instead of rebuilding The task is matching experimental spectra against an existing reference library — that is the matchSpectra/matchMz functionality of MetaboAnnotation, not database construction The target compounds are outside the coverage of the source resource (e.g. non-human-metabolite or lipid-only references), since the build content is defined by the downloaded HMDB release Builds a portable CompDb SQLite database of compound annotations and experimental MS2 spectra from a public resource release (here HMDB 5.0, 2 November 2021), excluding predicted spectra, so it can be used as the reference backend for MS1/MS2-based annotation in the R Metabolomics ecosystem. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo12020173

skills.description: Use when the analysis input is a BiG-SLiCE output SQLite3 database (e.g., from full_run_result.zip covering ~1.2M BGCs) and you need to aggregate BGC counts, GCF memberships, or class proportions per taxon.
skills.name: sqlite-relational-querying
skills.search_text: sqlite-relational-querying Use when the analysis input is a BiG-SLiCE output SQLite3 database (e.g., from full_run_result.zip covering ~1.2M BGCs) and you need to aggregate BGC counts, GCF memberships, or class proportions per taxon. The data are already aggregated into a flat table/TSV — BiG-SLiCE v2 supports --export-csv to export pre-calculated BGCs and GCFs tables into TSVs, avoiding manual SQL joins. Only the web-based visualization is needed — run the bundled flask mini web-app rather than querying the database programmatically. http://edamontology.org/topic_0769 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Load BiG-SLiCE's output SQLite3 database and run SQL joins between the BGC/class tables and genome taxonomy tables (GTDB-derived) to aggregate BGC counts and GCF assignments per taxonomic group for downstream visualization. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/gigascience/giaa154
skills.summary: Load BiG-SLiCE's output SQLite3 database and run SQL joins between the BGC/class tables and genome taxonomy tables (GTDB-derived) to aggregate BGC counts and GCF assignments per taxonomic group for downstream visualization.

skills.description: Use when an MS/MS spectrum's peak intensities are dominated by a few very intense peaks (e.g. after precursor and noise-peak removal) and downstream analysis or visualization needs a compressed dynamic range.
skills.name: square-root-intensity-scaling
skills.search_text: square-root-intensity-scaling Use when an MS/MS spectrum's peak intensities are dominated by a few very intense peaks (e.g. after precursor and noise-peak removal) and downstream analysis or visualization needs a compressed dynamic range. spectrum_utils does not provide functionality to read spectral data files — use pymzML or another reader first; this skill is not for raw file import. The spectrum's peaks have not yet had the precursor peak removed and noise filtered — scaling the unfiltered peak list would still leave the base peak and noise dominating the transformed intensities. A downstream tool requires linear (untransformed) intensities, e.g. absolute quantification-style comparisons rather than spectral pattern matching or visualization. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Scale MS/MS peak intensities by their square root using spectrum_utils' scale_intensity('root') to de-emphasize overly intense base peaks while preserving relative peak ordering. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.9b04884

The spectrum's peaks have not yet had the precursor peak removed and noise filtered — scaling the unfiltered peak list would still leave the base peak and noise dominating the transformed intensities. skills.description: Use when SRM or vendor HRMS raw LC-MS files must be processed for a known target list of small molecules — importing precursor/fragment transitions, extracting ion chromatograms, integrating peaks, and quantifying via isotope dilution or external calibration.
skills.name: srm-hrms-targeted-chromatogram-extraction
skills.search_text: srm-hrms-targeted-chromatogram-extraction Use when SRM or vendor HRMS raw LC-MS files must be processed for a known target list of small molecules — importing precursor/fragment transitions, extracting ion chromatograms, integrating peaks, and quantifying via isotope dilution or external calibration. The goal is nontargeted feature-finding in MS1 spectra followed by run alignment and identification — that workflow belongs to XCMS, MZmine, or MS-DIAL, not Skyline's extract-known-targets paradigm. The task requires importing and scoring against external small-molecule fragmentation libraries (METLIN, MassBank, HMDB, NIST) — these workflows are stated as future work and are not yet implemented in Skyline. The input is GC-MS or ion-mobility small-molecule data, for which Skyline support is explicitly described as still ongoing. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Targeted extraction of small-molecule fragment-ion chromatograms from SRM and HRMS raw data using Skyline's molecule-centric mode, covering scheduled transition lists, peak integration, and calibrated quantification across six major instrument vendors. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.9b00640
skills.summary: Targeted extraction of small-molecule fragment-ion chromatograms from SRM and HRMS raw data using Skyline's molecule-centric mode, covering scheduled transition lists, peak integration, and calibrated quantification across six major instrument vendors.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is nontargeted feature-finding in MS1 spectra followed by run alignment and identification — that workflow belongs to XCMS, MZmine, or MS-DIAL, not Skyline's extract-known-targets paradigm. The task requires importing and scoring against external small-molecule fragmentation libraries (METLIN, MassBank, HMDB, NIST) — these workflows are stated as future work and are not yet implemented in Skyline. The input is GC-MS or ion-mobility small-molecule data, for which Skyline support is explicitly described as still ongoing.

skills.description: Use when targeted LC-MS/MS peak areas (e.g., Skyline-exported, from PRM/SRM runs) must be benchmarked against the NIST SRM 1950 plasma reference material to demonstrate quantitative agreement across cohorts or labs.
skills.name: srm-reference-material-correlation-analysis
skills.search_text: srm-reference-material-correlation-analysis Use when targeted LC-MS/MS peak areas (e.g., Skyline-exported, from PRM/SRM runs) must be benchmarked against the NIST SRM 1950 plasma reference material to demonstrate quantitative agreement across cohorts or labs. The input is untargeted lipidomics data without Skyline peak areas or a LipidCreator transition list — the QC filtering depends on targeted PRM/SRM triplicate measurements No reference material (e.g., NIST SRM 1950) values are available to join against, so a correlation benchmark cannot be computed The goal is FDR estimation or isobaric/coeluting lipid resolution — LipidCreator explicitly does not provide a dedicated scoring algorithm or address coeluting/isobaric lipids and peak area integration http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Quantitative cross-lab agreement assessment that correlates lipid abundances measured in a study cohort (here, plasma from 21 healthy Asian subjects quantified via a LipidCreator/Skyline PRM/SRM assay) against the NIST SRM 1950 standard reference material values, verifying inter-population/inter-lab agreement by Pearson R². metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-020-15960-z
skills.summary: Quantitative cross-lab agreement assessment that correlates lipid abundances measured in a study cohort (here, plasma from 21 healthy Asian subjects quantified via a LipidCreator/Skyline PRM/SRM assay) against the NIST SRM 1950 standard reference material values, verifying inter-population/inter-lab agreement by Pearson R².
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is untargeted lipidomics data without Skyline peak areas or a LipidCreator transition list — the QC filtering depends on targeted PRM/SRM triplicate measurements No reference material (e.g., NIST SRM 1950) values are available to join against, so a correlation benchmark cannot be computed The goal is FDR estimation or isobaric/coeluting lipid resolution — LipidCreator explicitly does not provide a dedicated scoring algorithm or address coeluting/isobaric lipids and peak area integration

skills.name: srm-targeted-quantification
skills.search_text: srm-targeted-quantification Use when raw SRM/MRM acquisition files (e.g. Waters Xevo TQ-S) must be independently quantified against a vendor result such as TargetLynx, or when a targeted amino-acid/metabolite panel (e.g. the 19 amino acids from a Biocrates p180 kit) needs calibrated concentrations outside vendor software. skills.summary: Reprocess SRM (triple-quadrupole MRM) small-molecule data in Skyline by importing raw vendor files, integrating scheduled transitions, and computing absolute concentrations from an external calibration curve — demonstrated here by reanalyzing 76 ADNI serum Xevo TQ-S files from a Biocrates AbsoluteIDQ p180 plate against TargetLynx results.

skills.description: Use when an SRM or label-free LC-MS proteomics/omics feature table (e.g. Skyline transition intensities with pooled QC injections) shows inter-batch signal drift that must be corrected before downstream statistical analysis.
skills.name: srn-proteomics-signal-drift-correction
skills.search_text: srn-proteomics-signal-drift-correction Use when an SRM or label-free LC-MS proteomics/omics feature table (e.g. Skyline transition intensities with pooled QC injections) shows inter-batch signal drift that must be corrected before downstream statistical analysis. When the dataset lacks pooled quality-control samples injected at regular intervals — QC-RFSC requires QC-anchored regression and statTarget instead offers Combat via shiftCor_dQC for QC-free datasets. When the input is already a drift-corrected or post-integration matrix; re-running correction on corrected data is not covered by the method. When the goal is only statistical analysis (grouping, univariate testing) without signal correction; statAnalysis handles those steps independently. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Apply quality control-based random forest signal correction (QC-RFSC) to SRM proteomics feature tables to remove inter- and intra-batch signal drift, evaluated via RSD cumulative distributions and pre/post-correction PCA. metabolomics/v3 10.1016/j.aca.2018.08.002
skills.summary: Apply quality control-based random forest signal correction (QC-RFSC) to SRM proteomics feature tables to remove inter- and intra-batch signal drift, evaluated via RSD cumulative distributions and pre/post-correction PCA.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the dataset lacks pooled quality-control samples injected at regular intervals — QC-RFSC requires QC-anchored regression and statTarget instead offers Combat via shiftCor_dQC for QC-free datasets. skills.description: Use when you need to compile biosample-specific NMR reference databases (chemical shift peaks and SRRM multiplet regions) from HMDB records to power ROI-based metabolite identification in ROIAL-NMR.
skills.name: srrm-multiplicity-extraction
skills.search_text: srrm-multiplicity-extraction Use when you need to compile biosample-specific NMR reference databases (chemical shift peaks and SRRM multiplet regions) from HMDB records to power ROI-based metabolite identification in ROIAL-NMR. When the target metabolite database is not HMDB-based — the paper notes ROIAL-NMR can also use BMRB or any database containing NMR assignments, so re-deriving SRRMs from HMDB is unnecessary if another curated database is already loaded When the task is ROI identification or filtering (match ratio, significance ratio) rather than reference-database construction — those are downstream ROIAL-NMR steps, not database building When automated ROI identification is the goal — that is beyond the current scope of the program http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Builds the program-specific metabolic lookup databases used by ROIAL-NMR by parsing HMDB metabolite records to extract per-metabolite 1H NMR chemical shift values and spectral region resonance multiplets (SRRMs), organized by biosample type. skills.summary: Builds the program-specific metabolic lookup databases used by ROIAL-NMR by parsing HMDB metabolite records to extract per-metabolite 1H NMR chemical shift values and spectral region resonance multiplets (SRRMs), organized by biosample type. skills.when_to_use_negative: When the target metabolite database is not HMDB-based — the paper notes ROIAL-NMR can also use BMRB or any database containing NMR assignments, so re-deriving SRRMs from HMDB is unnecessary if another curated database is already loaded When the task is ROI identification or filtering (match ratio, significance ratio) rather than reference-database construction — those are downstream ROIAL-NMR steps, not database building When automated ROI identification is the goal — that is beyond the current scope of the program

skills.description: Use when a matched scRNA-seq/metabolomics dataset has ssGSEA module scores and metabolite abundances for knockdown vs control conditions, and the goal is to test whether substrate-level metabolic module activity tracks metabolite abundance changes.
skills.name: ssgsea-module-score-analysis
skills.search_text: ssgsea-module-score-analysis Use when a matched scRNA-seq/metabolomics dataset has ssGSEA module scores and metabolite abundances for knockdown vs control conditions, and the goal is to test whether substrate-level metabolic module activity tracks metabolite abundance changes. Input is raw scRNA-seq expression without precomputed ssGSEA module scores or module clusters — run ssGSEA/scFEA module scoring first The question is flux prediction itself rather than validating predicted variation against matched metabolomics — use the scFEA/FLUXestimator flux estimation pipeline instead Metabolomics data lack matched knockdown/control conditions, making fold-change computation and the correlation undefined Reproduces the Figure S2 analysis from the scFEA/Pa03c APEX1-knockdown study: correlating observed metabolomic fold changes of eight metabolites against knockdown-minus-control differences of averaged ssGSEA module scores for modules consuming those metabolites, linking predicted flux behavior to measured metabolite variation. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/nar/gkad444
skills.summary: Reproduces the Figure S2 analysis from the scFEA/Pa03c APEX1-knockdown study: correlating observed metabolomic fold changes of eight metabolites against knockdown-minus-control differences of averaged ssGSEA module scores for modules consuming those metabolites, linking predicted flux behavior to measured metabolite variation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw scRNA-seq expression without precomputed ssGSEA module scores or module clusters — run ssGSEA/scFEA module scoring first The question is flux prediction itself rather than validating predicted variation against matched metabolomics — use the scFEA/FLUXestimator flux estimation pipeline instead Metabolomics data lack matched knockdown/control conditions, making fold-change computation and the correlation undefined

skills.description: Use when FDR must be estimated for open modification search SSMs whose mass shifts span many values: group matches by charge-normalized mass difference, estimate decoy/target FDR per group, and merge groups with fewer than 20 SSMs.
skills.name: ssm-subgrouping-by-charge-normalized-mass-difference
skills.search_text: ssm-subgrouping-by-charge-normalized-mass-difference Use when FDR must be estimated for open modification search SSMs whose mass shifts span many values: group matches by charge-normalized mass difference, estimate decoy/target FDR per group, and merge groups with fewer than 20 SSMs. Standard (closed) searches with a single or small predefined set of mass shifts — FDR can be estimated directly on the full SSM set without subgrouping Subgroups are needed with fewer than 20 SSMs and cannot be pooled — the paper warns the actual FDR may be underestimated when too-small groups are used Percolator-style semisupervised rescoring is the goal rather than target–decoy per-subgroup FDR estimation Partitions open-search spectrum–spectrum matches (SSMs) into subgroups by charge-normalized precursor mass difference between query and library spectra so that target–decoy FDR can be estimated per subgroup, exploiting the fact that true modified matches cluster at shared modification masses while decoy mass differences are randomly distributed. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.8b00359
skills.summary: Partitions open-search spectrum–spectrum matches (SSMs) into subgroups by charge-normalized precursor mass difference between query and library spectra so that target–decoy FDR can be estimated per subgroup, exploiting the fact that true modified matches cluster at shared modification masses while decoy mass differences are randomly distributed.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Standard (closed) searches with a single or small predefined set of mass shifts — FDR can be estimated directly on the full SSM set without subgrouping Subgroups are needed with fewer than 20 SSMs and cannot be pooled — the paper warns the actual FDR may be underestimated when too-small groups are used Percolator-style semisupervised rescoring is the goal rather than target–decoy per-subgroup FDR estimation

skills.search_text: sssr-ring-perception-analysis Use when a rule-based drug-like filter must be applied to an enumerated derivative SMILES set and per-ring-count screening (messy rings, >7 smallest sets of smallest rings) is one of the filtering criteria. The goal is spectrum or fingerprint prediction (NEIMS/DeepEI) or analyte ranking rather than structure filtering of the enumerated database Input structures are not enumerated derivatives of a drug core (e.g., raw experimental spectra or already-curated reference libraries such as NIST/SWGDRUG) The filtering task only involves ΔSCScore synthetic-difficulty screening or mass-weight (M+ peak tolerance) filtering and no ring-count criterion is required http://edamontology.org/topic_3332 Computes smallest sets of smallest rings (SSSR) for enumerated derivative SMILES in the PS²MS pipeline and applies the 'messy rings' rule (>7 SSSR) — the single most effective drug-like filter — to prune the cathinone-derivative set down to the ~422-million-compound synthetic NPS database. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c05019
skills.summary: Computes smallest sets of smallest rings (SSSR) for enumerated derivative SMILES in the PS²MS pipeline and applies the 'messy rings' rule (>7 SSSR) — the single most effective drug-like filter — to prune the cathinone-derivative set down to the ~422-million-compound synthetic NPS database.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is spectrum or fingerprint prediction (NEIMS/DeepEI) or analyte ranking rather than structure filtering of the enumerated database Input structures are not enumerated derivatives of a drug core (e.g., raw experimental spectra or already-curated reference libraries such as NIST/SWGDRUG) The filtering task only involves ΔSCScore synthetic-difficulty screening or mass-weight (M+ peak tolerance) filtering and no ring-count criterion is required

skills.description: Use when applying ICA (e.g. FastICA) to a transcriptomic expression matrix and you must decide the decomposition order (number of components) from component reproducibility across restarts rather than an arbitrary choice.
skills.name: stability-plateau-detection
skills.search_text: stability-plateau-detection Use when applying ICA (e.g. FastICA) to a transcriptomic expression matrix and you must decide the decomposition order (number of components) from component reproducibility across restarts rather than an arbitrary choice. The decomposition order is already fixed by prior knowledge or a previous MSTD analysis — recomputing the stability plateau is unnecessary. The data are not omics expression data suitable for ICA source separation (e.g. already a feature table or metadata). Only a single ICA run is planned — stability indices require multiple restarts per component order to quantify reproducibility. http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Determines the optimal number of independent components (MSTD — most stable transcriptomic dimension) for ICA on transcriptomic data by running repeated decompositions over a range of component orders, computing per-component stability indices, and selecting the smallest order at which average stability reaches a plateau. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/ijms20184414
skills.summary: Determines the optimal number of independent components (MSTD — most stable transcriptomic dimension) for ICA on transcriptomic data by running repeated decompositions over a range of component orders, computing per-component stability indices, and selecting the smallest order at which average stability reaches a plateau.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The decomposition order is already fixed by prior knowledge or a previous MSTD analysis — recomputing the stability plateau is unnecessary. The data are not omics expression data suitable for ICA source separation (e.g. already a feature table or metadata). Only a single ICA run is planned — stability indices require multiple restarts per component order to quantify reproducibility.
