skills.search_text: violin-plot-peak-quality-assessment Use when you have manually reviewed LC-MS peak examples labeled true/false and need to identify which of the 59 peak group parameters separates true from false peaks before building a classifier. You need a full multivariate classifier — this skill only assesses individual parameters; use the forward-selected multiple logistic regression model (15 variables) or the image-based deep neural network for classification instead Peak examples are not manually reviewed/labeled true vs. false — distributional separation cannot be evaluated without ground-truth labels Your features are raw raster peak images rather than computed scalar shape parameters — the image-based deep neural network workflow applies in that case http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Assesses the predictive value of individual LC-MS peak group shape parameters (e.g., medRelFWHM, derived from duration, height, area, FWHM, tailing factor, asymmetry) by plotting violin plots of each parameter's distribution for manually labeled true vs. false peaks and complementing them with single-variable logistic regression models. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.9b02983
skills.summary: Assesses the predictive value of individual LC-MS peak group shape parameters (e.g., medRelFWHM, derived from duration, height, area, FWHM, tailing factor, asymmetry) by plotting violin plots of each parameter's distribution for manually labeled true vs. false peaks and complementing them with single-variable logistic regression models.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need a full multivariate classifier — this skill only assesses individual parameters; use the forward-selected multiple logistic regression model (15 variables) or the image-based deep neural network for classification instead Peak examples are not manually reviewed/labeled true vs. false — distributional separation cannot be evaluated without ground-truth labels Your features are raw raster peak images rather than computed scalar shape parameters — the image-based deep neural network workflow applies in that case

skills.description: Use when Retip RT predictions (predicted minus experimental retention time) are available for HILIC or RPLC test/validation compounds and you need to visualize per-model error distributions and quantify true-positive coverage within ±1 min windows, as in Figure 2 of the Retip paper.
skills.name: violoin-plot-error-distribution-visualization
skills.search_text: violoin-plot-error-distribution-visualization Use when Retip RT predictions (predicted minus experimental retention time) are available for HILIC or RPLC test/validation compounds and you need to visualize per-model error distributions and quantify true-positive coverage within ±1 min windows, as in Figure 2 of the Retip paper. When the goal is model training or hyperparameter tuning rather than post-hoc evaluation of already-trained Retip models. When chromatographic data fall outside the training chemical landscape (e.g., triacylglycerols or phosphatidylcholines that were largely excluded) — error distributions and coverage percentages will be unreliable. When you need to discriminate closely eluting isomers in short UPLC runs; the paper notes 1 min prediction errors preclude discriminating closely eluting compounds in typical 12 min UPLC methods. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3391 Generates ggplot2 violin plots of retention time prediction error distributions for Retip machine learning models, annotating the fraction of true positives falling within the ±1 min RT window (HILIC test 65%, RPLC test 87%, validation 76%) to judge model coverage and error skew. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.9b05765
skills.summary: Generates ggplot2 violin plots of retention time prediction error distributions for Retip machine learning models, annotating the fraction of true positives falling within the ±1 min RT window (HILIC test 65%, RPLC test 87%, validation 76%) to judge model coverage and error skew.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is model training or hyperparameter tuning rather than post-hoc evaluation of already-trained Retip models. When chromatographic data fall outside the training chemical landscape (e.g., triacylglycerols or phosphatidylcholines that were largely excluded) — error distributions and coverage percentages will be unreliable. When you need to discriminate closely eluting isomers in short UPLC runs; the paper notes 1 min prediction errors preclude discriminating closely eluting compounds in typical 12 min UPLC methods.

skills.description: Use when a PLS/PLS-DA classifier on metabolomics or integrated gene-expression + metabolomics data is overfit or underperforming, and a compact, statistically filtered feature set is needed to raise cross-validated Q2Y.
skills.name: vip-feature-filtering-for-pls-models
skills.search_text: vip-feature-filtering-for-pls-models Use when a PLS/PLS-DA classifier on metabolomics or integrated gene-expression + metabolomics data is overfit or underperforming, and a compact, statistically filtered feature set is needed to raise cross-validated Q2Y. The analysis goal is univariate association testing (e.g., ANCOVA association analysis or IntLIM interaction modeling) rather than PLS-based classification — VIP filtering is defined only for projection models The feature table is already a small, curated marker panel where additional filtering would discard informative variables The data lack a phenotype/class response, so supervised PLS-DA and its Q2Y metric are not applicable http://edamontology.org/topic_3577 A dual-filter variable selection strategy for SMART 2.0 PLS/PLS-DA models: first restrict features to those passing pFDR < 0.05, then keep the top-10 VIP-scored variables, to boost cross-validated predictive accuracy (Q2Y) on integrated omics data. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c03225
skills.summary: A dual-filter variable selection strategy for SMART 2.0 PLS/PLS-DA models: first restrict features to those passing pFDR < 0.05, then keep the top-10 VIP-scored variables, to boost cross-validated predictive accuracy (Q2Y) on integrated omics data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is univariate association testing (e.g., ANCOVA association analysis or IntLIM interaction modeling) rather than PLS-based classification — VIP filtering is defined only for projection models The feature table is already a small, curated marker panel where additional filtering would discard informative variables The data lack a phenotype/class response, so supervised PLS-DA and its Q2Y metric are not applicable

skills.description: Use when a supervised PLS-DA genotype/colonization classifier (e.g. 3xTg_SPF vs WT_SPF or 5xFAD vs WT per tissue) has been fit on metabolomics feature tables and discriminatory molecular features must be extracted via VIP scores.
skills.name: vip-feature-selection
skills.search_text: vip-feature-selection Use when a supervised PLS-DA genotype/colonization classifier (e.g. 3xTg_SPF vs WT_SPF or 5xFAD vs WT per tissue) has been fit on metabolomics feature tables and discriminatory molecular features must be extracted via VIP scores. The goal is MS/MS structural annotation rather than supervised feature discrimination — use GNPS library spectral matching (Level 2/3 MSI annotations) instead. No class labels exist (e.g. exploratory QC or cohort-structure checks) — the paper uses unsupervised PCA on RCLR-transformed data for that purpose. Input is raw MS/MS spectra rather than a preprocessed peak-area feature table; feature extraction must occur before PLS-DA/VIP fitting. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Extracts genotype-affected molecular features from PLS-DA classification models by ranking variables on Variable Importance in Projection (VIP) scores and retaining those with VIP > 1, as done for the 3xTg and 5xFAD multi-organ mouse metabolomics datasets (Tables S1–S12). metabolomics/v3 10.1101/2025.04.28.651123
skills.summary: Extracts genotype-affected molecular features from PLS-DA classification models by ranking variables on Variable Importance in Projection (VIP) scores and retaining those with VIP > 1, as done for the 3xTg and 5xFAD multi-organ mouse metabolomics datasets (Tables S1–S12).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is MS/MS structural annotation rather than supervised feature discrimination — use GNPS library spectral matching (Level 2/3 MSI annotations) instead. No class labels exist (e.g. exploratory QC or cohort-structure checks) — the paper uses unsupervised PCA on RCLR-transformed data for that purpose. Input is raw MS/MS spectra rather than a preprocessed peak-area feature table; feature extraction must occur before PLS-DA/VIP fitting.

skills.description: Use when a fitted PLS-DA or OPLS-DA model on metabolomics data (e.g. 158 annotated lipids from VAT/SAT of 59 CRC patients) must be reduced to significant/discriminative features for downstream comparison of feature sets.
skills.name: vip-score-feature-selection
skills.search_text: vip-score-feature-selection Use when a fitted PLS-DA or OPLS-DA model on metabolomics data (e.g. 158 annotated lipids from VAT/SAT of 59 CRC patients) must be reduced to significant/discriminative features for downstream comparison of feature sets. skills.summary: Selects discriminative metabolites from PLS-DA (or OPLS-DA) models by extracting variable importance in projection (VIP) scores and applying a VIP > 1 threshold on the first component, as used to compare LMM- vs M0-processed CRC adipose tissue lipidomics data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw MS data that has not yet been pre-processed (noise reduction, peak matching, retention time correction) or log2-transformed and modeled — VIP selection requires a fitted PLS-DA/OPLS-DA model The analysis goal is unsupervised exploration (e.g. PCA of SAT vs VAT separation); VIP scores are defined only for supervised PLS-based classification Selecting features from held-out test data; the article selects significant features from training-set models and evaluates prediction on the corresponding test set

skills.description: Use when you have an SBML integrated host-virus genome-scale metabolic model and need to compute maximal host biomass or viral biomass growth rates via FBA, or verify that forcing maximal viral flux abolishes host biomass.
skills.name: viral-biomass-objective-optimization
skills.search_text: viral-biomass-objective-optimization Use when you have an SBML integrated host-virus genome-scale metabolic model and need to compute maximal host biomass or viral biomass growth rates via FBA, or verify that forcing maximal viral flux abolishes host biomass. skills.search_text: volcano-plot-visualization-of-regulated-lipids Use when a segmented, group-annotated MALDI MSI pixel-intensity table exists and you need to visualize which lipid species are significantly up- or down-regulated between two groups (e.g. UPEC-infected vs. control) within specific tissue ROIs. Input is raw imzML/Bruker/Waters data that has not been pre-processed and segmented (run msi_preprocessing_flow and msi_segmentation_flow first) The analysis goal is lipid annotation/identification rather than differential regulation visualization — msiFlow explicitly does not include an annotation or interpretation step Comparing more than two groups: region_group_analysis_flow performs statistical analysis of molecular changes in ROIs between exactly two groups http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Generates volcano plots (log2 fold change vs. -log10 p-value) of lipids regulated between groups within mass spectrometry imaging ROIs, using msiFlow's region_group_analysis_flow statistical output to highlight significant lipid classes such as TG, DG, PC, PE and ST in infected vs. control tissue. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-024-55306-7
skills.summary: Generates volcano plots (log2 fold change vs. -log10 p-value) of lipids regulated between groups within mass spectrometry imaging ROIs, using msiFlow's region_group_analysis_flow statistical output to highlight significant lipid classes such as TG, DG, PC, PE and ST in infected vs. control tissue.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw imzML/Bruker/Waters data that has not been pre-processed and segmented (run msi_preprocessing_flow and msi_segmentation_flow first) The analysis goal is lipid annotation/identification rather than differential regulation visualization — msiFlow explicitly does not include an annotation or interpretation step Comparing more than two groups: region_group_analysis_flow performs statistical analysis of molecular changes in ROIs between exactly two groups

skills.description: Use when a metabolomics meta-analysis dataset (csv/xls/xlsx/txt of compound name, trend/behaviour, and reference) needs qualitative vote-counting and visual verification that reports agree on up/down regulation.
skills.name: vote-counting-compound-trend-analysis
skills.search_text: vote-counting-compound-trend-analysis Use when a metabolomics meta-analysis dataset (csv/xls/xlsx/txt of compound name, trend/behaviour, and reference) needs qualitative vote-counting and visual verification that reports agree on up/down regulation. You have P-values and fold-changes and need quantitative combined significance/effect size — use amanida's quantitative mode (compute_amanida) or volcano_plot instead of vote-counting. The dataset lacks trend/behaviour labels (only raw intensities or spectral data) — vote-counting requires identifier and trend labels per report. You need error/variance-based meta-analysis of raw or integral data with standard deviations; amanida explicitly targets non-integral data where SD is not disclosed. http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Qualitative meta-analysis skill that performs compound vote-counting (+1 up, −1 down, 0 no trend, divided by number of reports) and renders a mixed-type explore plot to check whether metabolomics reports agree on trend direction, e.g. Hippuric acid and Phenol in the CRC urinary sample_data. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/bioinformatics/btab591
skills.summary: Qualitative meta-analysis skill that performs compound vote-counting (+1 up, −1 down, 0 no trend, divided by number of reports) and renders a mixed-type explore plot to check whether metabolomics reports agree on trend direction, e.g. Hippuric acid and Phenol in the CRC urinary sample_data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have P-values and fold-changes and need quantitative combined significance/effect size — use amanida's quantitative mode (compute_amanida) or volcano_plot instead of vote-counting. The dataset lacks trend/behaviour labels (only raw intensities or spectral data) — vote-counting requires identifier and trend labels per report. You need error/variance-based meta-analysis of raw or integral data with standard deviations; amanida explicitly targets non-integral data where SD is not disclosed.

skills.description: Use when benchmarking BiG-SLiCE GCF clustering against curated MIBiG compound-group reference groupings, e.g., to pick a clustering threshold T by maximizing the V-score across a sweep.
skills.name: vscore-clustering-quality-evaluation
skills.search_text: vscore-clustering-quality-evaluation Use when benchmarking BiG-SLiCE GCF clustering against curated MIBiG compound-group reference groupings, e.g., to pick a clustering threshold T by maximizing the V-score across a sweep. Your dataset has no trusted reference labels (e.g., 1.2M predicted BGCs from NCBI RefSeq genomes) — there is no ground truth to compute a V-score against; use the clustering skill itself instead You are using BiG-SLiCE v2.0, which switched to cosine-like (l2-normalized) distances and PFAM 35.0 — published V-scores from the v1 Euclidean-space paper will not directly transfer Your input is fragmented BGCs only, or you need pairwise BGC network analysis (BiG-SCAPE territory) rather than Euclidean-space partitional clustering evaluation http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Evaluates BiG-SLiCE GCF clustering quality against a curated reference set by sweeping distance thresholds T = 300–1,500, querying the output SQLite3 database, and computing the V-score (harmonic mean of homogeneity and completeness) against MIBiG compound-group labels to select an optimal threshold. metabolomics/v3 10.1093/gigascience/giaa154
skills.summary: Evaluates BiG-SLiCE GCF clustering quality against a curated reference set by sweeping distance thresholds T = 300–1,500, querying the output SQLite3 database, and computing the V-score (harmonic mean of homogeneity and completeness) against MIBiG compound-group labels to select an optimal threshold.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your dataset has no trusted reference labels (e.g., 1.2M predicted BGCs from NCBI RefSeq genomes) — there is no ground truth to compute a V-score against; use the clustering skill itself instead You are using BiG-SLiCE v2.0, which switched to cosine-like (l2-normalized) distances and PFAM 35.0 — published V-scores from the v1 Euclidean-space paper will not directly transfer Your input is fragmented BGCs only, or you need pairwise BGC network analysis (BiG-SCAPE territory) rather than Euclidean-space partitional clustering evaluation

skills.description: Use when reproducing or verifying rtmsEcho's reported processing-speed benchmark on acoustic ejection mass spectrometry (AEMS) data — specifically, timing a complete 384-well MRM plate (<5 transitions) against the reported <2 s threshold.
skills.name: wall-clock-runtime-benchmarking
skills.search_text: wall-clock-runtime-benchmarking Use when reproducing or verifying rtmsEcho's reported processing-speed benchmark on acoustic ejection mass spectrometry (AEMS) data — specifically, timing a complete 384-well MRM plate (<5 transitions) against the reported <2 s threshold. The acquisition is full-scan mode (precursor ion / neutral loss, up to a 60 Da window) rather than MRM — the applicable benchmark is then <30 s per 384-well plate, not <2 s The goal is a speedup comparison against conventional AEMS processing methods — the article names no benchmark datasets or baseline details to support its reported 10- to 100-fold efficiency-gain claim The input is a partial run or sub-plate rather than a complete 384-well plate, so the reported full-plate timing threshold does not directly apply http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Measures end-to-end wall-clock runtime of rtmsEcho's automated AEMS processing pipeline over a full 384-well plate to verify the paper's benchmark: <2 s for MRM runs with <5 transitions (vs. <30 s for full-scan runs up to a 60 Da window). metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.5c03730
skills.summary: Measures end-to-end wall-clock runtime of rtmsEcho's automated AEMS processing pipeline over a full 384-well plate to verify the paper's benchmark: <2 s for MRM runs with <5 transitions (vs. <30 s for full-scan runs up to a 60 Da window).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The acquisition is full-scan mode (precursor ion / neutral loss, up to a 60 Da window) rather than MRM — the applicable benchmark is then <30 s per 384-well plate, not <2 s The goal is a speedup comparison against conventional AEMS processing methods — the article names no benchmark datasets or baseline details to support its reported 10- to 100-fold efficiency-gain claim The input is a partial run or sub-plate rather than a complete 384-well plate, so the reported full-plate timing threshold does not directly apply

skills.name: wall-clock-runtime-measurement
skills.search_text: wall-clock-runtime-measurement Use when benchmarking spectral clustering tools (HyperSpec, MS-Cluster, spectra-cluster, MaRaCluster) on MS/MS data such as PXD000561 and you need runtime shares per stage or end-to-end wall-clock times. The goal is clustering quality (incorrect clustering ratio, completeness, peptide identification from consensus spectra) rather than runtime — quality comparisons need different evaluation metrics The input is not a large-scale MS/MS clustering workload; profiling 20–90% preprocessing shares was established specifically for state-of-the-art spectral clustering tools on large datasets GPU memory is insufficient: the README notes that clustering the PXD000561 dataset requires a GTX 3090 with larger memory, so a GTX 1080Ti cannot reproduce the runtime numbers on that dataset http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Stage-wise and end-to-end wall-clock profiling of MS/MS spectral clustering pipelines: measuring spectrum preprocessing time versus total clustering runtime with the Linux wall clock to locate bottlenecks and validate speedup claims. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.2c00612
skills.summary: Stage-wise and end-to-end wall-clock profiling of MS/MS spectral clustering pipelines: measuring spectrum preprocessing time versus total clustering runtime with the Linux wall clock to locate bottlenecks and validate speedup claims.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is clustering quality (incorrect clustering ratio, completeness, peptide identification from consensus spectra) rather than runtime — quality comparisons need different evaluation metrics The input is not a large-scale MS/MS clustering workload; profiling 20–90% preprocessing shares was established specifically for state-of-the-art spectral clustering tools on large datasets GPU memory is insufficient: the README notes that clustering the PXD000561 dataset requires a GTX 3090 with larger memory, so a GTX 1080Ti cannot reproduce the runtime numbers on that dataset

skills.description: Use when benchmarking the speed of open modification spectral library searches across engines, or when verifying that an ANN-indexed search engine reproduces the reported ~10x runtime speedup over SpectraST.
skills.name: wall-clock-runtime-profiling
skills.search_text: wall-clock-runtime-profiling Use when benchmarking the speed of open modification spectral library searches across engines, or when verifying that an ANN-indexed search engine reproduces the reported ~10x runtime speedup over SpectraST. When the goal is to compare identification sensitivity (number of confident SSMs at a given FDR) rather than search speed When benchmarking a sequence database search engine (e.g. MSFragger) rather than spectral library search engines, since indexing strategies and candidate sets are not comparable When the two engines are run on different hardware or with materially different preprocessing (e.g. peak count or fragment tolerance), making the wall-clock ratio meaningless http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Measures and compares total wall-clock search time of spectral library search engines performing open modification searches (e.g. ANN-SoLo vs SpectraST on the HEK293 data set), to quantify the order-of-magnitude speedup from approximate nearest neighbor indexing. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.jproteome.8b00359
skills.summary: Measures and compares total wall-clock search time of spectral library search engines performing open modification searches (e.g. ANN-SoLo vs SpectraST on the HEK293 data set), to quantify the order-of-magnitude speedup from approximate nearest neighbor indexing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is to compare identification sensitivity (number of confident SSMs at a given FDR) rather than search speed When benchmarking a sequence database search engine (e.g. MSFragger) rather than spectral library search engines, since indexing strategies and candidate sets are not comparable When the two engines are run on different hardware or with materially different preprocessing (e.g. peak count or fragment tolerance), making the wall-clock ratio meaningless

skills.description: Use when profiling the runtime of an R mass-spectrometry pipeline (e.g. Shinyscreen's mzML extraction and prescreening) to quantify how much parallelisation reduces processing time.
skills.name: wall-clock-timing-comparison-analysis
skills.search_text: wall-clock-timing-comparison-analysis Use when profiling the runtime of an R mass-spectrometry pipeline (e.g. Shinyscreen's mzML extraction and prescreening) to quantify how much parallelisation reduces processing time. The goal is compound identification or spectrum annotation rather than quantifying wall-clock speedup of the extraction step. The workflow is a single-file, interactive exploratory run where parallel overhead would dwarf any gain. Input is not vendor-independent mzML data amenable to Shinyscreen's list-based (compound or mass) screening. http://edamontology.org/topic_0003 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Benchmarks Shinyscreen's high-resolution MS prescreening/extraction pipeline by running the identical workload twice — once serially and once with a future-parallel backend — and reporting elapsed wall-clock times and speedup ratios. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-025-01044-x
skills.summary: Benchmarks Shinyscreen's high-resolution MS prescreening/extraction pipeline by running the identical workload twice — once serially and once with a future-parallel backend — and reporting elapsed wall-clock times and speedup ratios.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is compound identification or spectrum annotation rather than quantifying wall-clock speedup of the extraction step. The workflow is a single-file, interactive exploratory run where parallel overhead would dwarf any gain. Input is not vendor-independent mzML data amenable to Shinyscreen's list-based (compound or mass) screening.

skills.description: Use when LC/MS feature peak boundaries are inconsistent across samples (artifacts flagged by PeakDetective) and you want to improve boundary definition and reduce peak-area CV.
skills.name: warpgroup-style-mean-boundary-peak-reintegration
skills.search_text: warpgroup-style-mean-boundary-peak-reintegration Use when LC/MS feature peak boundaries are inconsistent across samples (artifacts flagged by PeakDetective) and you want to improve boundary definition and reduce peak-area CV. If the classifier scores all peaks of a feature as true peaks in every sample, there are no artifact boundaries to fix and reintegration is unnecessary. If you only need peak classification/filtering rather than improved boundary definition and reduced CV, curatePeaks alone suffices without reintegration. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Reintegrates peaks labeled as artifacts using mean peak boundaries derived from non-artifact samples of the same feature, analogous to Warpgroup, to better define peak boundaries and reduce coefficient of variation of peak areas in LC/MS metabolomics. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c00764
skills.summary: Reintegrates peaks labeled as artifacts using mean peak boundaries derived from non-artifact samples of the same feature, analogous to Warpgroup, to better define peak boundaries and reduce coefficient of variation of peak areas in LC/MS metabolomics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: If the classifier scores all peaks of a feature as true peaks in every sample, there are no artifact boundaries to fix and reintegration is unnecessary. If you only need peak classification/filtering rather than improved boundary definition and reduced CV, curatePeaks alone suffices without reintegration.

skills.description: Use when converting per-node energy-propagation traces (e.g. from Algorithm 1 of NetAurHPD) into waveforms for downstream averaging/aggregation, and the stabilized steady-state energy needs to be stripped from each vector.
skills.name: waveform-dc-component-removal
skills.search_text: waveform-dc-component-removal Use when converting per-node energy-propagation traces (e.g. from Algorithm 1 of NetAurHPD) into waveforms for downstream averaging/aggregation, and the stabilized steady-state energy needs to be stripped from each vector. The input is already a finalized waveform tensor (e.g. waveforms.npy) rather than raw propagation traces — re-running DC removal would corrupt the signal. The task is centrality learning from auralized nodes (e.g. centrality_from_auralized_nodes in the cnai-lab repo) where the stabilized component itself may carry positional information and is not meant to be stripped. The analysis goal is the propagation dynamics itself (e.g. studying how energy is evenly distributed), where removing the DC component discards the quantity of interest. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3315 During network auralization of a Metabolite CN, each node's propagated energy over iterations forms a waveform; this skill removes the stabilized (DC) component from each node's vector so downstream aggregation compares only the transient signal that encodes the node's position. metabolomics/v3 10.48550/arxiv.2410.22030
skills.summary: During network auralization of a Metabolite CN, each node's propagated energy over iterations forms a waveform; this skill removes the stabilized (DC) component from each node's vector so downstream aggregation compares only the transient signal that encodes the node's position.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a finalized waveform tensor (e.g. waveforms.npy) rather than raw propagation traces — re-running DC removal would corrupt the signal. The task is centrality learning from auralized nodes (e.g. centrality_from_auralized_nodes in the cnai-lab repo) where the stabilized component itself may carry positional information and is not meant to be stripped. The analysis goal is the propagation dynamics itself (e.g. studying how energy is evenly distributed), where removing the DC component discards the quantity of interest.

skills.name: wavelet-based-peak-detection
skills.search_text: wavelet-based-peak-detection Use when raw 1D NMR spectra plus a ppm vector need to be converted into peak lists before grouping into a feature/sample/value matrix, especially when binning would lose multiplet information. Input is already a binned/bucketed feature table or a processed peak list — wavelet peak detection operates on raw spectra Only raw-spectra alignment and quantitation are needed; the older speaq (<= 1.2.3) CluPA alignment / BW-ratio workflow is the appropriate path The goal is concentration estimation of known metabolites, which BATMAN targets rather than peak-based profiling http://edamontology.org/topic_0593 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 speaq 2.0's wavelet (Mexican hat) peak detection summarizes raw 1D NMR spectra into picked-peak lists with minimal information loss and no user interaction, replacing binning/bucketing and avoiding baseline correction and smoothing. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1006018
skills.summary: speaq 2.0's wavelet (Mexican hat) peak detection summarizes raw 1D NMR spectra into picked-peak lists with minimal information loss and no user interaction, replacing binning/bucketing and avoiding baseline correction and smoothing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a binned/bucketed feature table or a processed peak list — wavelet peak detection operates on raw spectra Only raw-spectra alignment and quantitation are needed; the older speaq (<= 1.2.3) CluPA alignment / BW-ratio workflow is the appropriate path The goal is concentration estimation of known metabolites, which BATMAN targets rather than peak-based profiling

skills.name: wavelet-based-peak-detection-mexican-hat
skills.search_text: wavelet-based-peak-detection-mexican-hat Use when you have ROI chromatographic profiles (intensity vs. retention time) extracted from CE-MS or LC-MS data by the AriumMS ROI search, and need automatic peak detection with integration of apex RT, area, and height — especially for the narrow peaks typical of CE-MS separations. The full mzML/mzXML runs have not yet been reduced to regions of interest by the AriumMS ROI search — this skill operates on ROI traces, not raw files Input is already a detected-peak/feature table needing augmentation, false-positive filtering, or chemometric evaluation rather than peak detection You need MS/MS spectral networking to connect features across methods — explicitly listed as future development, not part of this workflow http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 Automatic peak detection and integration for CE-MS/LC-MS regions of interest in the AriumMSEval workflow: candidate peaks are found by continuous wavelet transform (CWT) of the second derivative of the smoothed ROI using the Mexican hat mother wavelet, then boundary-corrected and integrated into an RT/area/height peak table. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s00216-023-04715-6
skills.summary: Automatic peak detection and integration for CE-MS/LC-MS regions of interest in the AriumMSEval workflow: candidate peaks are found by continuous wavelet transform (CWT) of the second derivative of the smoothed ROI using the Mexican hat mother wavelet, then boundary-corrected and integrated into an RT/area/height peak table.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The full mzML/mzXML runs have not yet been reduced to regions of interest by the AriumMS ROI search — this skill operates on ROI traces, not raw files Input is already a detected-peak/feature table needing augmentation, false-positive filtering, or chemometric evaluation rather than peak detection You need MS/MS spectral networking to connect features across methods — explicitly listed as future development, not part of this workflow

skills.description: Use when starting from centroid-mode mzML raw LC–MS files (e.g., Waters RAW converted with ProteoWizard msconvert) and you need chromatographic/spectrum peak picking to build an (Rt, m/z) feature table.
skills.name: wavelet-based-signal-peak-picking
skills.search_text: wavelet-based-signal-peak-picking Use when starting from centroid-mode mzML raw LC–MS files (e.g., Waters RAW converted with ProteoWizard msconvert) and you need chromatographic/spectrum peak picking to build an (Rt, m/z) feature table. Input is already a preprocessed feature/data matrix rather than raw mzML files — peak picking on raw scans is unnecessary and would duplicate earlier processing. Data are profile-mode or non-centroid spectra where the centroided mzML assumption of the MSData read path is violated. The goal is feature annotation or downstream statistical analysis rather than raw-data peak detection — TidyMS explicitly lacks feature annotation capability, so other tools should handle that step. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Applies a continuous wavelet transform (CWT)-based peak-picking algorithm (Du et al., Bioinformatics 2006) via TidyMS's MSData interface to detect chromatographic and spectral peaks in centroid-mode mzML LC–MS raw data, feeding feature detection in untargeted metabolomics. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo10100416
skills.summary: Applies a continuous wavelet transform (CWT)-based peak-picking algorithm (Du et al., Bioinformatics 2006) via TidyMS's MSData interface to detect chromatographic and spectral peaks in centroid-mode mzML LC–MS raw data, feeding feature detection in untargeted metabolomics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a preprocessed feature/data matrix rather than raw mzML files — peak picking on raw scans is unnecessary and would duplicate earlier processing. Data are profile-mode or non-centroid spectra where the centroided mzML assumption of the MSData read path is violated. The goal is feature annotation or downstream statistical analysis rather than raw-data peak detection — TidyMS explicitly lacks feature annotation capability, so other tools should handle that step.

skills.description: Use when an untargeted LC-MS metabolomics feature table shows batch effects or within-batch intensity drift, and batch labels are unavailable or there is only one batch — only injection order information is required.
skills.name: wavelet-ica-batch-effect-correction
skills.search_text: wavelet-ica-batch-effect-correction Use when an untargeted LC-MS metabolomics feature table shows batch effects or within-batch intensity drift, and batch labels are unavailable or there is only one batch — only injection order information is required. Input is raw MS data (.d, mzXML) or a retention-time/m/z list rather than an already-processed peak intensity matrix — preprocess with XCMS/CAMERA first You have reliable batch labels and multiple batches and want the original WaveICA (F-test, P < 0.05) approach instead — though WaveICA 2.0 gives similar performance on multi-batch data The data contain no QC samples and you need QC-based signal correction such as QC-RLSC/QC-SVRC fitted on QCSs http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 WaveICA 2.0 removes inter-batch and run-order (intra-batch) effects from untargeted metabolomics peak tables using injection order instead of batch labels, via MODWT wavelet decomposition, ICA, and GAM-based selection of batch-related independent components. metabolomics/v3 10.1007/s11306-021-01839-7
skills.summary: WaveICA 2.0 removes inter-batch and run-order (intra-batch) effects from untargeted metabolomics peak tables using injection order instead of batch labels, via MODWT wavelet decomposition, ICA, and GAM-based selection of batch-related independent components.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw MS data (.d, mzXML) or a retention-time/m/z list rather than an already-processed peak intensity matrix — preprocess with XCMS/CAMERA first You have reliable batch labels and multiple batches and want the original WaveICA (F-test, P < 0.05) approach instead — though WaveICA 2.0 gives similar performance on multi-batch data The data contain no QC samples and you need QC-based signal correction such as QC-RLSC/QC-SVRC fitted on QCSs

skills.description: Use when a samples x features LC/MS intensity matrix carries batch labels plus a two-group annotation (e.g., cell type), and you need post-hoc WaveICA batch correction followed by per-feature differential testing and FDR-binned significant-feature counts.
skills.name: wavelet-ica-intensity-normalization
skills.search_text: wavelet-ica-intensity-normalization Use when a samples x features LC/MS intensity matrix carries batch labels plus a two-group annotation (e.g., cell type), and you need post-hoc WaveICA batch correction followed by per-feature differential testing and FDR-binned significant-feature counts. The goal is to fix peak misalignment or incomplete weak signal recovery after preprocessing — post-hoc batch correction can only adjust signal intensity and cannot correct alignment errors The data are single-batch or lack batch labels, so no between-batch intensity correction is applicable A batch-aware two-stage preprocessing method is already applied in the preprocessing stage and no post-hoc correction comparison (e.g., vs ComBat) is needed http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Applies WaveICA batch-effect correction to LC/MS metabolomics feature intensity matrices (e.g., the ST000868 cell-type dataset), then evaluates detection of significant metabolic features via two-sample t-tests with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR ≤ 0.2, as in Fig. 3f of the apLCMS two-stage preprocessing paper. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41598-020-70850-0
skills.summary: Applies WaveICA batch-effect correction to LC/MS metabolomics feature intensity matrices (e.g., the ST000868 cell-type dataset), then evaluates detection of significant metabolic features via two-sample t-tests with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR ≤ 0.2, as in Fig. 3f of the apLCMS two-stage preprocessing paper.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to fix peak misalignment or incomplete weak signal recovery after preprocessing — post-hoc batch correction can only adjust signal intensity and cannot correct alignment errors The data are single-batch or lack batch labels, so no between-batch intensity correction is applicable A batch-aware two-stage preprocessing method is already applied in the preprocessing stage and no post-hoc correction comparison (e.g., vs ComBat) is needed

skills.description: Use when a task asks which kinds of repository data (e.g., computed properties, annotations, bulk synonyms, tabular data) are served by each of several programmatic interfaces, and which fall outside all of them.
skills.name: web-service-capability-comparison
skills.search_text: web-service-capability-comparison Use when a task asks which kinds of repository data (e.g., computed properties, annotations, bulk synonyms, tabular data) are served by each of several programmatic interfaces, and which fall outside all of them. The task only requires retrieving annotation data from one interface (e.g., a PUG-View request for a single record) rather than systematically comparing interface capabilities. The input text contains no explicit accessibility or limitation statements distinguishing the interfaces — classification rows would be invented rather than grounded in verbatim quotes. The goal is bulk structured data retrieval (e.g., computed properties, synonyms) where PUG-REST or the PubChem FTP site is the known correct route and no interface comparison is needed. http://edamontology.org/topic_3315 A method for systematically comparing which data categories are accessible through which programmatic web service interfaces of a data repository — here, PubChem's PUG-View (unstructured textual annotation reports) versus PUG-REST (structured data such as computed compound properties and cross-references) — and flagging data reachable through neither interface. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-019-0375-2
skills.summary: A method for systematically comparing which data categories are accessible through which programmatic web service interfaces of a data repository — here, PubChem's PUG-View (unstructured textual annotation reports) versus PUG-REST (structured data such as computed compound properties and cross-references) — and flagging data reachable through neither interface.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task only requires retrieving annotation data from one interface (e.g., a PUG-View request for a single record) rather than systematically comparing interface capabilities. The input text contains no explicit accessibility or limitation statements distinguishing the interfaces — classification rows would be invented rather than grounded in verbatim quotes. The goal is bulk structured data retrieval (e.g., computed properties, synonyms) where PUG-REST or the PubChem FTP site is the known correct route and no interface comparison is needed.

skills.summary: Fit both linear and quadratic calibration curves with weighting to a concentration standard series, apply Cook's-distance-based outlier removal with refitting, and select/apply the model via adjusted R² to estimate unknown sample concentrations with relative errors.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are untargeted feature tables without a serial concentration standard series — calibration requires known standard concentrations Analyte signal quality is inadequate (e.g., amphetamine's S/N ratio of 0.19 in the narcotics data set), making curve fitting and quantification unreliable LC-MS experimental conditions vary across standard and test injections — consistency is crucial for a reliable calibration curve

skills.description: Use when you have pre-derived hazard-ratio weights and cohort-level metabolite/risk-factor measurements and need to build, apply, and comparatively evaluate weighted risk scores for mortality prediction (C-statistic, IDI) in an independent cohort.
skills.name: weighted-risk-score-construction
skills.search_text: weighted-risk-score-construction Use when you have pre-derived hazard-ratio weights and cohort-level metabolite/risk-factor measurements and need to build, apply, and comparatively evaluate weighted risk scores for mortality prediction (C-statistic, IDI) in an independent cohort. You need a clinically deployable score: the constructed metabolic biomarker score is based on scaled biomarker values created separately for each cohort and 'is not yet suitable for classification of patients in the clinic' You are discovering which biomarkers associate with mortality (use the stepwise forward-backward meta-analysis selection procedure instead) rather than applying already-derived weights The biomarker weights come from the same cohort being scored, which would overestimate predictive ability http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Construct weighted metabolic biomarker and conventional risk factor scores by multiplying log-transformed, SD-scaled biomarkers by ln(HR) weights derived from an external cohort (Estonian Biobank), then evaluate predictive ability in an independent cohort (FINRISK 1997) using Cox-based C-statistics and IDI. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-019-11311-9
skills.summary: Construct weighted metabolic biomarker and conventional risk factor scores by multiplying log-transformed, SD-scaled biomarkers by ln(HR) weights derived from an external cohort (Estonian Biobank), then evaluate predictive ability in an independent cohort (FINRISK 1997) using Cox-based C-statistics and IDI.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need a clinically deployable score: the constructed metabolic biomarker score is based on scaled biomarker values created separately for each cohort and 'is not yet suitable for classification of patients in the clinic' You are discovering which biomarkers associate with mortality (use the stepwise forward-backward meta-analysis selection procedure instead) rather than applying already-derived weights The biomarker weights come from the same cohort being scored, which would overestimate predictive ability

skills.description: Use when expanding a compound database with Pickaxe rules and unfiltered or similarity-cutoff expansion grows exponentially (e.g. YMDB one-generation expansion gives 575,262 compounds), but you need a fixed-size, target-biased network.
skills.name: weighted-similarity-score-compound-sampling
skills.search_text: weighted-similarity-score-compound-sampling Use when expanding a compound database with Pickaxe rules and unfiltered or similarity-cutoff expansion grows exponentially (e.g. YMDB one-generation expansion gives 575,262 compounds), but you need a fixed-size, target-biased network. When the goal is an exhaustive network of all compounds above a similarity threshold — use the similarity cutoff filter (0.4, 0.5, 0.8) or no filter instead, accepting exponential growth When no target compound set exists, since the filter weights a distribution of similarity scores to targets When filtering is needed on other criteria (m/z peaks, thermodynamics >50 kJ/mol, carbon count <12) — those require the metabolomics, thermodynamics, or atomic composition filters A Pickaxe filter that bounds reaction-network growth by sampling a fixed number of compounds per expansion (e.g. 2000) from a similarity-score distribution raised to a power (zeroth, third, or sixth) against a target set, rather than keeping all compounds above a similarity cutoff. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-023-05149-8
skills.summary: A Pickaxe filter that bounds reaction-network growth by sampling a fixed number of compounds per expansion (e.g. 2000) from a similarity-score distribution raised to a power (zeroth, third, or sixth) against a target set, rather than keeping all compounds above a similarity cutoff.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is an exhaustive network of all compounds above a similarity threshold — use the similarity cutoff filter (0.4, 0.5, 0.8) or no filter instead, accepting exponential growth When no target compound set exists, since the filter weights a distribution of similarity scores to targets When filtering is needed on other criteria (m/z peaks, thermodynamics >50 kJ/mol, carbon count <12) — those require the metabolomics, thermodynamics, or atomic composition filters

skills.description: Use when you have a Qemistree chemical tree plus a feature table of MS1 peak areas and need tree-informed sample comparisons, e.g., to quantify how chemically similar foods or samples are.
skills.name: weighted-unifrac-computation
skills.search_text: weighted-unifrac-computation Use when you have a Qemistree chemical tree plus a feature table of MS1 peak areas and need tree-informed sample comparisons, e.g., to quantify how chemically similar foods or samples are. Input is raw LC-MS/MS spectra (.mzXML/.mzML) with no Qemistree hierarchy yet — build the tree first with q2-qemistree and MZmine2 preprocessing Only MS1 features without fingerprints are present in the feature table — these are filtered out and cannot be placed on the chemical hierarchy The analysis goal is molecular annotation (spectral library matching, ClassyFire taxonomy) rather than sample-to-sample comparison — use annotation workflows instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 Computes Weighted UniFrac sample-to-sample distances using the QIIME 2 diversity plugin on a Qemistree chemical hierarchy, adapting a phylogenetic beta-diversity metric designed for DNA sequence data to untargeted metabolomics feature tables. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41589-020-00677-3
skills.summary: Computes Weighted UniFrac sample-to-sample distances using the QIIME 2 diversity plugin on a Qemistree chemical hierarchy, adapting a phylogenetic beta-diversity metric designed for DNA sequence data to untargeted metabolomics feature tables.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw LC-MS/MS spectra (.mzXML/.mzML) with no Qemistree hierarchy yet — build the tree first with q2-qemistree and MZmine2 preprocessing Only MS1 features without fingerprints are present in the feature table — these are filtered out and cannot be placed on the chemical hierarchy The analysis goal is molecular annotation (spectral library matching, ClassyFire taxonomy) rather than sample-to-sample comparison — use annotation workflows instead

skills.description: Use when a metabolomics chemical-feature table (FeatureTable[Frequency]) is paired with a Qemistree hierarchy and you need tree-informed sample distances, PCoA ordination, or PERMANOVA that reduces chromatography-driven batch signal.
skills.name: weighted-unifrac-distance-estimation-on-chemical-tree
skills.search_text: weighted-unifrac-distance-estimation-on-chemical-tree Use when a metabolomics chemical-feature table (FeatureTable[Frequency]) is paired with a Qemistree hierarchy and you need tree-informed sample distances, PCoA ordination, or PERMANOVA that reduces chromatography-driven batch signal. Only MS1 features are available (no MS/MS fragmentation spectra), so no fingerprints can be predicted and no Qemistree hierarchy can be built to support UniFrac. The feature table has not been matched to the hierarchy (MS1 features without fingerprints still present) — filter those features first or the phylogenetic beta computation cannot run. The goal is per-molecule chemical taxonomy assignment (ClassyFire kingdom through direct parent) rather than between-sample beta diversity — use get-classyfire-taxonomy/prune-hierarchy instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_3293 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Computes weighted UniFrac between-sample distances for metabolomics data using a Qemistree chemical hierarchy — built from SIRIUS/CSI:FingerID-predicted fingerprints — as the tree, so beta diversity and PCoA reflect chemical relatedness instead of raw feature co-occurrence. This mitigates technical variation such as chromatographic batch shifts: on the 162-sample evaluation dataset the batch pseudo-F drops from 120.75 (Bray-Curtis) to 18.2239 (weighted UniFrac), both p=0.001. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41589-020-00677-3
skills.summary: Computes weighted UniFrac between-sample distances for metabolomics data using a Qemistree chemical hierarchy — built from SIRIUS/CSI:FingerID-predicted fingerprints — as the tree, so beta diversity and PCoA reflect chemical relatedness instead of raw feature co-occurrence. This mitigates technical variation such as chromatographic batch shifts: on the 162-sample evaluation dataset the batch pseudo-F drops from 120.75 (Bray-Curtis) to 18.2239 (weighted UniFrac), both p=0.001.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only MS1 features are available (no MS/MS fragmentation spectra), so no fingerprints can be predicted and no Qemistree hierarchy can be built to support UniFrac. The feature table has not been matched to the hierarchy (MS1 features without fingerprints still present) — filter those features first or the phylogenetic beta computation cannot run. The goal is per-molecule chemical taxonomy assignment (ClassyFire kingdom through direct parent) rather than between-sample beta diversity — use get-classyfire-taxonomy/prune-hierarchy instead.

skills.name: weisfeiler-lehman-fragment-deduplication
skills.search_text: weisfeiler-lehman-fragment-deduplication Use when enumerating MAGMa substructure-annotation fragments (up to breakage depth 3) from molecule–spectrum pairs and you must collapse isomorphic fragment graphs into canonical nodes before assigning spectral peaks and building the fragmentation DAG. When working at the chemical-formula level rather than fragment-graph level (e.g., SCARF-style subformula classification, where formula deduplication suffices) When only running inference with pretrained ICEBERG/GLACIER weights — deduplication happens once at training-data construction, not at prediction time When spectra come from instruments/protocols where the 20 ppm mass tolerance is inappropriate (e.g., low-resolution MS/MS) http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Canonicalizes the combinatorially enumerated MAGMa-style fragment substructures used to bootstrap ICEBERG training data by deduplicating isomorphic fragment graphs with Weisfeiler-Lehman hashes, while retaining per-fragment hydrogen rearrangement shifts so peak annotation stays chemically faithful. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c04654
skills.summary: Canonicalizes the combinatorially enumerated MAGMa-style fragment substructures used to bootstrap ICEBERG training data by deduplicating isomorphic fragment graphs with Weisfeiler-Lehman hashes, while retaining per-fragment hydrogen rearrangement shifts so peak annotation stays chemically faithful.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When working at the chemical-formula level rather than fragment-graph level (e.g., SCARF-style subformula classification, where formula deduplication suffices) When only running inference with pretrained ICEBERG/GLACIER weights — deduplication happens once at training-data construction, not at prediction time When spectra come from instruments/protocols where the 20 ppm mass tolerance is inappropriate (e.g., low-resolution MS/MS)

skills.description: Use when a preprocessed MetaboSet peak table from MS-DIAL via notame must be tested feature-wise across two or more study groups, and per-feature p-values need multiple-testing correction.
skills.name: welch-oneway-anova-metabolite-features
skills.search_text: welch-oneway-anova-metabolite-features Use when a preprocessed MetaboSet peak table from MS-DIAL via notame must be tested feature-wise across two or more study groups, and per-feature p-values need multiple-testing correction. The data has not yet been preprocessed — missing values not marked, drift not corrected with correct_drift, low-quality features not flagged with flag_quality, or missing values not imputed (random-forest imputation recommended) The research question calls for multivariate modelling or quality-control visualization rather than feature-wise hypothesis testing The input is still raw LC–MS instrument files — peak picking (e.g. with MS-DIAL) must precede any notame statistical testing http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Feature-wise univariate testing for non-targeted LC–MS metabolomics in the notame workflow: Welch's one-way ANOVA per molecular feature across study groups (Welch's t-test for two-group designs), followed by Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction producing per-feature q-values. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo10040135
skills.summary: Feature-wise univariate testing for non-targeted LC–MS metabolomics in the notame workflow: Welch's one-way ANOVA per molecular feature across study groups (Welch's t-test for two-group designs), followed by Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction producing per-feature q-values.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data has not yet been preprocessed — missing values not marked, drift not corrected with correct_drift, low-quality features not flagged with flag_quality, or missing values not imputed (random-forest imputation recommended) The research question calls for multivariate modelling or quality-control visualization rather than feature-wise hypothesis testing The input is still raw LC–MS instrument files — peak picking (e.g. with MS-DIAL) must precede any notame statistical testing

skills.description: Use when comparing log-transformed GC-TOF MS metabolite intensity distributions between two groups of biological metadata triads (organ/species/disease) and you need per-compound p-values with unequal-variance robustness.
skills.name: welch-t-test-log-transformed-intensities
skills.search_text: welch-t-test-log-transformed-intensities Use when comparing log-transformed GC-TOF MS metabolite intensity distributions between two groups of biological metadata triads (organ/species/disease) and you need per-compound p-values with unequal-variance robustness. Input is raw or unnormalized chromatographic intensities — BinBase intensities must first be normalized by the sum of FAME ion intensities, deconvoluted, and missing values imputed before testing The metadata combinations have very few samples or few studies — the paper states quantitative comparisons are less robust than differential analyses in that regime, and triads with <10 samples or >20% failed FAME samples were already removed The question is a single pairwise metadata contrast rather than an ontologically expanded broad comparison; OGDA's group-expansion and aggregation machinery is unnecessary there http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Computes Welch t-tests on log-transformed metabolite intensity distributions for each pair of metadata combinations across two query groups, as done in BinDiscover's ontologically grouped differential analysis (OGDA) to generate per-compound p-value and fold-change matrices. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-023-00734-8
skills.summary: Computes Welch t-tests on log-transformed metabolite intensity distributions for each pair of metadata combinations across two query groups, as done in BinDiscover's ontologically grouped differential analysis (OGDA) to generate per-compound p-value and fold-change matrices.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw or unnormalized chromatographic intensities — BinBase intensities must first be normalized by the sum of FAME ion intensities, deconvoluted, and missing values imputed before testing The metadata combinations have very few samples or few studies — the paper states quantitative comparisons are less robust than differential analyses in that regime, and triads with <10 samples or >20% failed FAME samples were already removed The question is a single pairwise metadata contrast rather than an ontologically expanded broad comparison; OGDA's group-expansion and aggregation machinery is unnecessary there

skills.description: Use when comparing metabolite intensities across two broad biological ontology categories (e.g. 'digestive tract' vs 'Bacteria') over many metadata-combination pairs, where unequal variances and log-normal intensity distributions require Welch's t-test on log-transformed values.
skills.name: welch-test-log-transformed-intensity-comparison
skills.search_text: welch-test-log-transformed-intensity-comparison Use when comparing metabolite intensities across two broad biological ontology categories (e.g. 'digestive tract' vs 'Bacteria') over many metadata-combination pairs, where unequal variances and log-normal intensity distributions require Welch's t-test on log-transformed values. Quantitative (not differential) comparisons for biological metadata combinations with few samples and few studies, where the article states such comparisons are less robust Cross-organ comparisons mixing biofluids versus tissues (different units of biomass), which the article flags as a bias in fold-change interpretation Bulk metabolite queries across heterogeneous external databases (HMDB, MetabolomicsWorkbench) lacking standardized metadata; this skill requires harmonized BinBase triad metadata http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Performs pairwise Welch t-tests on log-transformed GC/MS metabolite intensity distributions across ontology-defined metadata combinations, then conservatively aggregates per-compound p-values and fold changes into a single differential-analysis result per metabolite. This is the statistical core of BinDiscover's ontologically grouped differential analysis (OGDA). metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-023-00734-8
skills.summary: Performs pairwise Welch t-tests on log-transformed GC/MS metabolite intensity distributions across ontology-defined metadata combinations, then conservatively aggregates per-compound p-values and fold changes into a single differential-analysis result per metabolite. This is the statistical core of BinDiscover's ontologically grouped differential analysis (OGDA).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Quantitative (not differential) comparisons for biological metadata combinations with few samples and few studies, where the article states such comparisons are less robust Cross-organ comparisons mixing biofluids versus tissues (different units of biomass), which the article flags as a bias in fold-change interpretation Bulk metabolite queries across heterogeneous external databases (HMDB, MetabolomicsWorkbench) lacking standardized metadata; this skill requires harmonized BinBase triad metadata

skills.description: Use when raw per-metabolite p-values are needed from a two-group comparison (e.g., sex) of ungrouped log-transformed metabolite abundances via Welch's unequal-variance t-tests, prior to eigen-analysis-based FWER adjustment.
skills.name: welch-two-sample-t-test-metabolomics
skills.search_text: welch-two-sample-t-test-metabolomics Use when raw per-metabolite p-values are needed from a two-group comparison (e.g., sex) of ungrouped log-transformed metabolite abundances via Welch's unequal-variance t-tests, prior to eigen-analysis-based FWER adjustment. The comparison has more than two levels or requires covariate adjustment — Welch's two-sample t-test supports only a single binary grouping (sex in this application) P-values will be corrected with generic FDR/BH rather than the eigen-analysis-based FWER procedures (PrsCo, Gao, Galwey and their DisCo P-ad modifications) this pipeline is designed to feed Features are aggregated into metabolite groups or pathways rather than the 761 ungrouped metabolite abundance columns used in the real-data application http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Applies Welch's unequal-variance two-sample t-tests of a binary grouping (sex) against each of 761 ungrouped log-transformed metabolite abundances within COPDGene strata (GOLD 3/4 severe, n=183; GOLD 0 controls, n=448), producing raw per-metabolite p-values that feed eigen-analysis-based FWER adjustment (PrsCo, Gao, Galwey, and their DisCo P-ad modifications) at FWER alpha=0.05. metabolomics/v3 10.3390/metabo15010028
skills.summary: Applies Welch's unequal-variance two-sample t-tests of a binary grouping (sex) against each of 761 ungrouped log-transformed metabolite abundances within COPDGene strata (GOLD 3/4 severe, n=183; GOLD 0 controls, n=448), producing raw per-metabolite p-values that feed eigen-analysis-based FWER adjustment (PrsCo, Gao, Galwey, and their DisCo P-ad modifications) at FWER alpha=0.05.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The comparison has more than two levels or requires covariate adjustment — Welch's two-sample t-test supports only a single binary grouping (sex in this application) P-values will be corrected with generic FDR/BH rather than the eigen-analysis-based FWER procedures (PrsCo, Gao, Galwey and their DisCo P-ad modifications) this pipeline is designed to feed Features are aggregated into metabolite groups or pathways rather than the 761 ungrouped metabolite abundance columns used in the real-data application

skills.description: Use when validating ion-identity/adduct assignments from an aligned MS1 feature table across experimental conditions where a specific adduct class should change in abundance (e.g. post-column salt infusion of sodium acetate or ammonium acetate vs H2O control).
skills.name: welch-two-sample-ttest-adduct-abundance-comparison
skills.search_text: welch-two-sample-ttest-adduct-abundance-comparison Use when validating ion-identity/adduct assignments from an aligned MS1 feature table across experimental conditions where a specific adduct class should change in abundance (e.g. post-column salt infusion of sodium acetate or ammonium acetate vs H2O control). Input is raw spectral data or an unaligned feature list — grouping, ion-identity annotation and feature-height extraction must be completed first (e.g. via MZmine IIMN) before the t-test is meaningful. Comparing ion species whose abundance should NOT differ across conditions (e.g. isotopes of the same molecule within one sample group) — the test targets condition-induced adduct shifts, not within-run annotation. Datasets with heavily missing or imputed feature heights where the normality/variance assumptions of a t-test are indefensible; use non-parametric alternatives instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Statistical validation of Ion Identity Molecular Networking (IIMN) adduct annotations by comparing [M+Na]+ and [M+NH4]+ feature abundances across salt-infusion versus control conditions using Welch two-sample t-tests. metabolomics/v3 10.1038/s41467-021-23953-9
skills.summary: Statistical validation of Ion Identity Molecular Networking (IIMN) adduct annotations by comparing [M+Na]+ and [M+NH4]+ feature abundances across salt-infusion versus control conditions using Welch two-sample t-tests.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw spectral data or an unaligned feature list — grouping, ion-identity annotation and feature-height extraction must be completed first (e.g. via MZmine IIMN) before the t-test is meaningful. Comparing ion species whose abundance should NOT differ across conditions (e.g. isotopes of the same molecule within one sample group) — the test targets condition-induced adduct shifts, not within-run annotation. Datasets with heavily missing or imputed feature heights where the normality/variance assumptions of a t-test are indefensible; use non-parametric alternatives instead.

skills.description: Use when you have paired microbial feature tables (RA or CLR transformed) and metabolite tables and need to flag which metabolites a MiMeNet model predicts significantly better than chance, rather than reporting only mean SCC.
skills.name: well-predicted-metabolite-identification
skills.search_text: well-predicted-metabolite-identification Use when you have paired microbial feature tables (RA or CLR transformed) and metabolite tables and need to flag which metabolites a MiMeNet model predicts significantly better than chance, rather than reporting only mean SCC. You only need the mean prediction SCC across all metabolites — the mean is reported directly and does not require the shuffled background cutoff procedure. The metabolites' prediction correlations are already being thresholded by a user-supplied fixed value via -threshold; use that path instead of deriving a new background percentile. No paired (matched samples) microbial-metabolite data exist — the background shuffle-and-compare design requires paired samples per dataset. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Identify which metabolites a microbiome-metabolome prediction model (MiMeNet MLPNN) predicts significantly well by comparing each metabolite's cross-validated Spearman correlation coefficient (SCC) against a dataset-specific 95th-percentile cutoff derived from a shuffled-label background distribution. This converts raw per-metabolite SCCs into a principled count of well-predicted metabolites per dataset. metabolomics/v3 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009021
skills.summary: Identify which metabolites a microbiome-metabolome prediction model (MiMeNet MLPNN) predicts significantly well by comparing each metabolite's cross-validated Spearman correlation coefficient (SCC) against a dataset-specific 95th-percentile cutoff derived from a shuffled-label background distribution. This converts raw per-metabolite SCCs into a principled count of well-predicted metabolites per dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need the mean prediction SCC across all metabolites — the mean is reported directly and does not require the shuffled background cutoff procedure. The metabolites' prediction correlations are already being thresholded by a user-supplied fixed value via -threshold; use that path instead of deriving a new background percentile. skills.search_text: wes-candidate-list-integration Use when a patient has a DeepVariant/Exomiser candidate gene list and per-gene metabolomic enrichment scores, and you need to rank those candidates by network-propagated metabolomic evidence and benchmark against Exomiser's phenotype ranking. skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is not an Exomiser-filtered WES candidate list (e.g., no variant data, or variant calling/filtered candidate genes have not been produced by DeepVariant/Exomiser) The goal is metabolomic preprocessing itself (XCUS/median-scaling, 10%-of-samples feature filtering, HMDB annotation, DAM identification at |z| ≥ 2) — that upstream pipeline is a separate skill Feature-to-metabolite identity matters for the analysis: in the TIDEX setting the mapping was unavailable, so exact metabolite identities could not be determined and results rely on uncurated features

skills.name: wgcna-module-detection-metabolomics
skills.search_text: wgcna-module-detection-metabolomics Use when a normalized metabolite measurement table (e.g. Metabolon®-style data with SUB_PATHWAY annotations) should be partitioned into co-abundance modules and tested against sample traits such as tumor vs normal status or gender, without predefined metabolite sets.
