skills.name: z-score-feature-normalization
skills.search_text: z-score-feature-normalization Use when a multi-sample HRMS feature table (e.g., Agilent .csv export with 136 features from the dienogest/drospirenone time-course at 0, 4, 10, 29 h) is about to be clustered by dm.ms_cluster and per-feature abundance trends must be made comparable before DBSCAN eps/min_samples are set. The input is still raw .mzML data — feature extraction (mssmain.get_scans, mssmain.peak_pick with peak width, replicated peak, and baseline-noise filters) must occur first, before normalization/clustering. The analysis goal preserves absolute abundance or fold-change magnitudes (e.g., dilution prediction or background subtraction on peak area fold-change criteria), since Z-scoring removes the intensity scale and keeps only relative trend shape. There is only one sample per feature — the per-feature standard deviation σ is undefined, so z=(x-μ)/σ cannot be computed. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Standardizes per-feature abundances across samples with z=(x-μ)/σ, the default preprocessing inside the MSS dm.ms_cluster function, so that unsupervised clustering (DBSCAN/OPTICS) groups features by abundance-trend shape rather than absolute intensity scale, eliminating skewness and kurtosis in the feature table. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s13321-023-00741-9

skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is still raw .mzML data — feature extraction (mssmain.get_scans, mssmain.peak_pick with peak width, replicated peak, and baseline-noise filters) must occur first, before normalization/clustering. skills.search_text: z-score-standardization-of-fluxes Use when you have triplicate metabolite intensity measurements at 0 h and 72 h (culture and medium samples) and need to convert raw boundary flux estimates into standardized z-scores for cross-metabolite or cross-species comparison, e. When the data are absolute intracellular concentrations rather than 0 h vs 72 h extracellular (medium-corrected) changes — the flux estimator and its STD propagation assume the ΔCsp vs ΔCmed formulation of eq 1. When you need pathway-level reaction predictions rather than standardized flux magnitudes — use MINNO's boundary-flux-to-missing-reaction inference instead of z-score standardization. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Computes z-scores for metabolite boundary fluxes estimated from 0 h vs 72 h extracellular metabolomics data, using the medium-evaporation-corrected flux estimator (eq 1) with STD propagation of triplicate standard deviations, so that flux magnitudes can be compared across metabolites and species and flagged reactions validated. metabolomics/v3 10.1021/acs.analchem.3c04501
skills.summary: Computes z-scores for metabolite boundary fluxes estimated from 0 h vs 72 h extracellular metabolomics data, using the medium-evaporation-corrected flux estimator (eq 1) with STD propagation of triplicate standard deviations, so that flux magnitudes can be compared across metabolites and species and flagged reactions validated.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the data are absolute intracellular concentrations rather than 0 h vs 72 h extracellular (medium-corrected) changes — the flux estimator and its STD propagation assume the ΔCsp vs ΔCmed formulation of eq 1. skills.description: Decision support for imputing missing metabolite values where missingness is due to missing at random combined with a limit of detection (LOD); apply z-score standardization before computing neighbor distances and back-transform imputed values afterwards.
skills.name: z-score-standardization-with-back-transformation
skills.search_text: z-score-standardization-with-back-transformation Decision support for imputing missing metabolite values where missingness is due to missing at random combined with a limit of detection (LOD); apply z-score standardization before computing neighbor distances and back-transform imputed values afterwards. When there is no limit of detection involved — if missingness is due to a metabolite truly being absent or purely MAR with no threshold below which values are censored, the truncated-normal MLE has no truncation point to anchor and this skill's rationale does not apply. When metabolite data are strongly non-normal — the method relies on a normality assumption for estimating the truncated mean and SD, so heavy skew or multimodal distributions violate the model. When there are very small samples or excessive missing data per metabolite — estimation of the truncated normal mean and variance becomes unstable, giving higher RMSE variability. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Standardizes metabolites to mean zero and SD one using truncation-based maximum likelihood estimates of the mean and SD, imputes missing values on the standardized scale, then back-transforms imputed values to the original metabolite scale. metabolomics/v3 10.1186/s12859-017-1547-6
skills.summary: Standardizes metabolites to mean zero and SD one using truncation-based maximum likelihood estimates of the mean and SD, imputes missing values on the standardized scale, then back-transforms imputed values to the original metabolite scale.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When there is no limit of detection involved — if missingness is due to a metabolite truly being absent or purely MAR with no threshold below which values are censored, the truncated-normal MLE has no truncation point to anchor and this skill's rationale does not apply. When metabolite data are strongly non-normal — the method relies on a normality assumption for estimating the truncated mean and SD, so heavy skew or multimodal distributions violate the model. When there are very small samples or excessive missing data per metabolite — estimation of the truncated normal mean and variance becomes unstable, giving higher RMSE variability.

workflows.description: Use when you have paired genomic and metabolomic data from the same microbial strains and want to link biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) to the metabolite features they plausibly encode — mine BGCs from assembled genomes with antiSMASH, tokenize BGC domains with iPRESTO/Pfam and cluster them into gene cluster families (GCFs) with BiG-SCAPE, build an MS/MS molecular network from paired LC-MS/MS data with GNPS to obtain molecular families (MFs), then score GCF-MF co-occurrence across strains (NPLinker-style Metcalf/hypergeometric scoring) to produce a ranked table of candidate BGC-metabolite links for natural-product discovery.
